## Volume front matter

### Series title page

# THE COMPLETE COURSE OF PATROLOGY, OR UNIVERSAL, COMPLETE, UNIFORM, CONVENIENT, ECONOMICAL LIBRARY OF ALL THE HOLY FATHERS, DOCTORS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL WRITERS WHO FLOURISHED FROM THE APOSTOLIC AGE DOWN TO THE TIME OF INNOCENT III

A chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully corrected by comparison both with one another and with numerous manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters distributed throughout the text itself, together with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reissued, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; and above all, this collection, unified, systematic, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## FIRST SERIES

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF JEROME OF STRIDON]

[Col. 0009]

# PREFACE

I shall briefly explain what ought to be brought to the Reader’s attention—not so much to adorn my own work as to enable him to approach the reading better instructed. This fourth volume of Jerome’s works contains his Commentaries on Isaiah and Jeremiah. The books explaining the former prophet number eighteen. The fifth of these, which treats the ten Visions by historical exposition, was composed by the holy Doctor long before he undertook to write on the Prophet as a whole. A certain Amabilis, a bishop of some region of Pannonia, diligently requested this work, and the book is dedicated to him by name.

Later, when Jerome had undertaken to expound Isaiah in its entirety, he also incorporated that book into the Commentary, so that he would not unnecessarily repeat the history of those Visions which he had previously explained. Accordingly, in the next two books, the sixth and seventh, he investigates only the allegorical meaning, returning through the same divisions of the Visions while omitting the historical account.

In our Chronological Notes on Letter 68, according to our recension, we assigned that work to the year 397. If we wished to test that date here again by arguments, too much would have to be said and repeated about the illness into which Jerome fell the following year—a fact previously unnoticed by chronologists—and too much would have to be brought in from elsewhere concerning that matter. We have discussed these points more suitably in connection with the aforementioned Letter and with Letters 71 and 72.

What must now be sought is the date of the Commentary on the Prophet as a whole. Yet, since it is a lengthy work, I have not assigned its composition to a single year, especially because Jerome says in the prefaces to the books that he was then occupied with other concerns, suffering from a shortage of scribes, and finally worn down by age and bodily weakness.

Tillemont, however, with considerable learning, judged that the work begun in 408 was completed and finished in the ninth or tenth year thereafter. He had conjectured that the death of Stilicho, which took place in August of 408, was indicated in the Preface to the eleventh book by the words with which the holy Doctor clears himself of the accusation that he had mocked a barbarian commander of the Roman army:

> “Nor is this a general dispute arising from an injury done to one person. While the diligence of my friends was guarding against it, he was suddenly removed by the judgment of God.”

Yet, although this conjecture is very close to the truth, that passage indicates only that the book was written after Stilicho’s death, without indicating how much time had elapsed. For that reason, a much more certain calculation of the date is gathered from the sequence of Jerome’s other works. In particular, since we assign his Commentary on Ezekiel to the beginning of the year 411, we may also be certain—on the authority of the author himself, who testifies in its Preface—that it was begun immediately after the completion of the Commentary on Isaiah. He says:

> “When the eighteen volumes of explanations on Isaiah had been completed, I wished to pass on to Ezekiel … And behold, suddenly the death of Pammachius and Marcella, the siege of the city of Rome, and the falling asleep of many brothers and sisters were announced to me,”

and other matters follow in the same sequence, indicating the same period.

Conversely, lest anyone think that the beginning of the work occurred after 410, this is decisively excluded by a most explicit testimony in the third book of the Commentary on Isaiah itself:

> “About thirty years ago, when I was in Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures by the most eloquent man, Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that same city, I know that I dictated a brief and hastily composed treatise on this Vision, to test my little talent.”

These approximately thirty years must be counted from the eighty-first year and the middle of the year after 300—that is, from the period during which Gregory occupied the episcopal chair of the imperial city, from May, after the removal of Maximus the Cynic, until July, when he resigned at the Ecumenical Council. Thus, if one makes the shortest calculation and supposes that “thirtieth” is a round number for the twenty-ninth year, the total comes out so that one must admit that the exposition of that prophet was begun at least in the tenth year after 400.

The Commentaries on Jeremiah were dictated by the holy Doctor at intervals, interrupted from time to time by other labors as circumstances required. This is nearly the last memorial and labor of his intellect; death, or the illness that preceded death, together with the changing circumstances of the Church as its affairs deteriorated and required his assistance, interrupted the work when its completion was near. Only one or perhaps two books are lacking to complete it, in which the historical narrative would have been gathered in a more compressed style.

For in the General Preface we demonstrated that the opinion long prevalent among ancient and modern writers—that Jerome had composed twenty complete books, fourteen of which had later been lost through the ravages of time—is false. We also pointed out, almost as if with a finger, the cause of this error: in some exemplar, already before Cassiodorus, fourteen Homilies of Origen on Jeremiah, which the holy Doctor had translated into Latin, had been appended to Jerome’s six books and counted as the equivalent of fourteen additional books.

For more on this matter, see that Preface, section 30. I mention it here if it is worth recalling: for it is certain from the sequence of events that the holy Doctor, carried away from his undertaking by the great and sudden disturbances of the Pelagian heresy and by the factions of impious men who laid hands upon him while he was vigorously fighting for the true faith, could not complete the exposition through to the end, as he had wished.

As for the six books that he either composed alone or at least allowed to be published, we place them, with respect to their date, between the Letter to Ctesiphon in our recension 133 and the Dialogue against the Pelagians, in accordance with the commonly accepted view. The chief reason is that in the Prologues to several books he mentions the letter in which he fought against the Pelagian heresy, and in the same number of passages he threatens that, unless the heretics repent, he will respond to their madness in a proper volume.

Such is the passage in the Preface to the second book:

> “For a little while we turn our ears away, lest we hear a judgment of blood and lament the souls of those who have been slain—those who, under the reputation of virtues, fall daily into pride and consider themselves like God … We have answered their fury as best we could, and, if the Lord grants life, we shall answer more fully.”

And in the fourth book:

> “I remained silent for a long time in answering that heresy of the Pelagians, swallowing my grief in silence, but I was compelled by the repeated complaints of the brothers; nevertheless, I have not yet gone so far as to name the authors, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced.”

And at the end:

> “But we shall deal with these matters more fully in a work of their own, unless they keep silent.”

These words appear to be understood in this way: when Jerome says that he first answered the heretics briefly and in some fashion, he refers to the first disputation against the Pelagians, undertaken at the request of Ctesiphon. When he promises to deal with the matter more fully and in a work of its own, he refers to the three books of the Dialogues.

Indeed, Jerome himself indicates that this was his intention in the opening words of the earlier Prologue:

> “After the letter already written to Ctesiphon, in which I responded to his questions, there were repeated complaints from the brothers as to why I was delaying any longer the work I had promised, in which I undertook to answer all the little questions of those who preach *apatheia*—‘freedom from passion.’”

Since it is therefore clear, and since we have shown in the appropriate places, that nearly a year intervened between the two works, and that this was the fifteenth year after 400, or at least most of that year, there is no doubt that the Commentaries belong to that same year.

If the letter to Ctesiphon transcribed in the first book seems to leave no trace, one should nevertheless by no means agree with Garner, who for this reason, in Dissertation 6 on Marius Mercator, assigns the book back to the beginnings of the Pelagian heresy, or dates it to the thirteenth year after 400. For in the book itself, in the third chapter of Jeremiah, Jerome praises the letter to Dardanus concerning the Promised Land. We have shown in our Chronological Notes that this letter belongs to the fourteenth year after 400, when Dardanus had already again completed his term as prefect of the praetorium of Gaul.

Jerome’s words are:

> “I have recently published a little book on the Promised Land.”

I shall not resist assigning the last two books—the fifth and sixth—to the following year, if that is preferred, since by then the heretics seem to have grown so powerful that they were inflicting not only curses but even physical violence upon their opponents who held the correct view.

We shall even readily admit that what we observe the holy Doctor saying in the Preface to the fourth book—that he was compelled by the repeated complaints of the brothers to answer the heretics, but had not yet gone so far as to name the authors—may more correctly be referred to the books of the Dialogues than, as we did, to the letter to Ctesiphon.

But let these considerations not move others; nor are they so conclusive that they can dislodge the reader from the opinion commonly accepted beforehand.

A much greater difficulty concerns the material which we append. Since we undertook to omit nothing that properly belongs to the complete collection of Jerome’s works, we ordered that the nine surviving Homilies of Origen on Isaiah, once explained in Latin with the translator’s name suppressed, should be included here, because highly learned critics strongly attribute them to Jerome, although, as we are about to prove, the matter is otherwise. They are included as a servant offspring alongside the legitimate children.

Those who wish to regard them as having proceeded from Jerome’s pen—omitting many others—include the three principal men of letters Erasmus, Huet, and Tillemont.

Erasmus proves the attribution from the fact that the holy Doctor himself testifies in his Catalogue that he translated something of this kind from Origen’s Commentaries on Isaiah into Latin. After listing the eighteen Homilies on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, which he had translated from the Greek of Adamantius into Latin, Jerome adds another work, “On the Seraphim,” and “On Hosanna.” The first of the surviving Homilies concerns the Seraphim standing above the Lord’s throne in Isaiah 6:2.

Yet everyone can see how weak this argument is for proving that Jerome was also the translator of the remaining homilies, which recount other Visions. It is especially false to say that the work entitled “On the Seraphim” denotes anything other than the letter to Damasus bearing that title and numbered eighteenth in our recension. Far from having been taken from some treatise of Origen and rendered into Latin in that form, it repeatedly fights against Origen’s own opinion.

Huet’s conjecture is more plausible. It is based on the style and on the selection of certain words which, he says, Jerome commonly liked to use. The examples he gives are:

- *absconsus*, “hidden”;
- *Dominicus*, “of the Lord”;
- *nuncupativus*, “nominal”;
- *principale*, “the ruling principle,” for the Greek *to hegemonikon*;
- *principari*, “to exercise rule over someone”;
- *principalis*, “principal”;
- *Prophetes*, “Prophet”;
- *repromitto*, “I promise”;
- *repromissio*, “promise”;
- *speculatorius*, “watchful” or “of a watcher”;
- *turpiloquium*, “shameful speech”;
- *Zabulus*, “the Devil”;
- *cuncta Evangeliorum*, “all the things of the Gospels.”

But I entirely deny that some of these words of later Latin—such as *nuncupativus*, *principari*, *speculatorius*, *turpiloquium*, *cuncta Evangeliorum*, and similar expressions—are more frequent in Jerome’s writings, or indeed that they are found there at all. If the others happen to occur, I maintain that they are not peculiar to him but common to him and the whole chorus of writers of his age.

Huet then says that, since the ninth of these Homilies on Isaiah is truncated at its end in both the printed and manuscript books, and since its missing conclusion was once supplied from the final portion of the ninth Homily on Jeremiah—which no one doubts to be Jerome’s translation—it could easily have happened that an unwary copyist, when copying the conclusion of the former, accidentally came upon the conclusion of the latter. From this, he argues, a substantial proof may be obtained that the Homilies on Isaiah had Jerome as translator in the same way as the Homilies on Jeremiah.

He should instead have said that what may certainly be inferred is that the Homilies on both prophets were gathered into a single exemplar of Origen’s works, with no regard to the translator, as commonly happened in ancient books, but only to the author; and that this circumstance misled the old copyist, causing the ninth Homily in each work to occupy the same place.

But let us now examine Tillemont’s arguments.

Rufinus, he says, in order to clear Jerome of the suspicion that he favored Origen after Origen’s example, writes in the Preface to the book *On First Principles* that Jerome translated more than seventy of Origen’s little books, which he called homiletical. If one calculates from all the works, there are twenty-eight on Jeremiah and Ezekiel, thirty-nine on Luke, and two on the Song of Songs: in all, only sixty-nine. Thus there seems to be no doubt that the Homilies on Isaiah must also be counted among them. Tillemont points especially to the passage in the second book of the *Invectives*, section 26, where Rufinus says that they were adapted by Jerome to Catholic meaning, with certain changes, when they were rendered into Latin.

I shall speak of this second testimony shortly. As for the first argument, which is based on the total, I say that there is nothing surprising if Rufinus called the sixty-nine works we have counted “more than seventy,” using a round number, as is customary. He may also have exaggerated somewhat so that he would appear more excusable in translating Origen’s books into Latin, if he boasted that his adversary had been exercised in the same arena.

[Note: [Col. 0013] He may also have had before his eyes the ten Treatises on the Psalms, which are more probably believed to have been translated by Jerome from Origen’s Greek into Latin.]

He may also have deliberately brought forward the scattered fragments (*apospasmata*) of Adamantius intermingled with Jerome’s writings. In short, one may imagine anything else by which to fill out the number, so that the presbyter of Aquileia could truthfully say “more than seventy,” rather than suppose, as they wish, that he included Homilies on Isaiah that do not exist. For, in my opinion, if he had known of these—beyond the sixty-nine mentioned—he would have praised not seventy but more than eighty through that oblique diligence.

I do not conceal that the testimony from the second book of the *Invectives*, section 26, although it troubles others much more, must be considered. Rufinus charges Jerome with having removed entirely from his Latin translations, or explained in an acceptable sense, many passages from Origen’s books that offended Christian ears. After giving several examples, he says:

> “These and a thousand other things like them in your translations—whether in these very Homilies on Luke, or in those on Jeremiah or Isaiah, and especially in Ezekiel—you have removed.”

This is plainly a striking argument for attributing the Homilies on Isaiah to Jerome’s translation. For they are Homilies, as no one could doubt, and they were unquestionably rendered into Latin from Adamantius by Jerome—namely, the works immediately preceding and following them, on Jeremiah and Ezekiel.

Nevertheless, I am entirely certain that this was not Rufinus’s meaning, that he was not thinking of Homilies on Isaiah, but intended to mock another writing of Jerome concerning that Prophet; and I shall demonstrate this briefly.

The holy Doctor had written to Damasus a treatise, or letter numbered eighteenth in our recension, on the Seraphim, which is the Vision in the sixth chapter of Isaiah. In that passage, two Seraphim are described as standing around the throne and crying out. Origen had interpreted them as our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit, but Jerome interpreted them as the Old and New Testaments, an opinion which Greeks and Latins alike had commonly accepted, though many had rejected it.

Afterward, whenever Jerome was insultingly represented by his rivals as an accomplice of Origen, he repeatedly demonstrated how far he differed from Origen’s views by using this very example. This may be seen in several places, but especially in Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus, section 3, where he says:

> “In the reading of Isaiah, where two crying Seraphim are described, with Origen interpreting them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, did I not change the detestable interpretation into the two Testaments? The book has been in circulation for twenty years.”

This is the little book, or treatise on the Vision of Isaiah, which Rufinus is pointing to: the Origenian opinion which Jerome says he allowed himself to change from the sense it had previously received to a better one. There are no Homilies on Isaiah here. Nor is there any need, as Tillemont does, to labor to find in the first of those Homilies a passage that has been softened by a convenient interpretation or entirely concealed.

But, having rejected the arguments that supported their attribution, let us finally present certain reasons establishing that they must be wholly denied to Jerome. I would regard as especially important the best argument for distinguishing ancient writers: the argument drawn from style.

Anyone who takes a half-Latin translator, to say no more, for Jerome must be a complete stranger to Jerome’s manner of writing. Huet, I think, when he produced certain words of Middle Latin in support of his preconceived opinion—words which, as we have shown by comparison, actually overturn it—cleverly concealed expressions much more alien to Jerome. Such are *figuraliter*, “figuratively”; *invenibile*, “discoverable”; *illud negotiorum*, for *illud rei*, “that matter”; *magniloquax*, “grandiloquent”; and *sufficiens isto*, for *hac contentus re*, “content with this matter,” along with similar expressions.

The entire remaining discourse has this character: somewhat obscure, unpolished, and ill-formed—not to mention a syntax that is either rustic or childishly fashioned after the Greek. This style is, if I may state what I think, that of Rufinus. We know that Rufinus devoted himself especially to translating Origen’s writings into Latin, and that Jerome so often accused him of barbarous expression that he said he made good Greek into not-good Latin.

If I have touched the matter accurately, I am even more surprised that Rufinus himself is being used as a guarantor for passing off his own offspring as another’s.

There are also other considerations that remove these works from Jerome. In his Catalogue, the holy Father lists the other works he had translated from Origen, but he never mentions the Homilies on Isaiah. Nor is it reasonable to suppose that he undertook their translation after the Catalogue, for from that time onward Origen’s doctrine was sliding into heresy, and Jerome rejected it so thoroughly in his mind that thereafter he sought rather to refute it than to offer it to Latin ears.

Moreover, in the Commentaries on Isaiah themselves, when there was not merely an opportunity but a necessity to mention that translation, he never refers to it. In the Preface to the first book, while praising Origen’s twenty-five Homilies on this prophet, he does not even hint that he had translated these nine into Latin.

Finally, these Homilies lack a Prologue. Gelasius identifies this as one of the distinguishing marks by which Jerome’s translations may be separated from those of others. They also lack manuscript authority or the support of any ancient testimony. In short, they differ so radically from Jerome’s intellect that I shall never cease to wonder how the most learned men could have been able to regard them as Jerome’s.

[Col. 0017] The volume concludes with a brief Abridgment on Isaiah, consisting of a few chapters. We now publish it for the first time, so that its value for testing the identity of its author may be assessed. It is indeed attributed to Jerome in the most ancient manuscript book of the Veronese library, a manuscript of especially excellent quality, marked with the number 24 in black ink—there are others marked in red—which also contains certain genuinely Jeromean works.

Nevertheless, I do not think we should labor, by producing arguments, to prove falsely that this work is attributed to the great Jerome, since its spurious character is exposed by comparison with Jerome’s genuine Explanation of this prophet. It is enough for the learned Reader to have glanced over it with some care, so that he does not allow this memory of antiquity to deceive him, and so that he clearly understands that some diligent person extracted almost everything from Jerome’s genuine Commentary, joined it together without especially happy results, and adapted it to his own intellect, partly by adding and partly by removing words.

[Col. 0017]

# THE EIGHTEEN BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET ISAIAH BY ST. EUSEBIUS JEROME, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON (C)

## Prologue

[Col. 0017A] 1–2. Having completed, with scarcely any delay, twenty books of explanations on the Twelve Prophets and the Commentaries on Daniel, you compel me, virgin of Christ, Eustochium, to pass on to Isaiah, and to repay to you what I promised your holy mother Paula while she was alive.

I remember also having promised this to your brother Pammachius. Since you are equal in affection, you surpass him in your present opportunity. Therefore, through you, I repay both to you and to him what I owe, obeying the commandments of Christ, who says:

> “Search the Scriptures” (John 5:39);

and:

> “Seek, and you shall find” (Matthew 7:7).

Let me not hear from the Jews:

> “You are mistaken, not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God” (Matthew 22:29).

For if, according to the apostle Paul (2 Corinthians 1:24), Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, then whoever does not know the Scriptures does not know the power of God or his wisdom. Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.

Therefore, supported by the help of your prayers—for day and night you meditate upon the law of God, and you are a temple of the Holy Spirit—I shall imitate the head of a household who brings forth new things and old things from his treasure. I shall also imitate the bride who says in the Song of Songs:

> “My beloved, new things and old things, I have kept for you” (Song of Songs 7:13).

[Note: [Col. 0017B] We examined these books of Commentaries on Isaiah against the Palatine codex 172 and another Vatican codex, 322. We also consulted most of them in two Ambrosian manuscripts, one marked with the letter S and the number 45, the other with E and the number 98. Whenever we used other codices that contained only one or another book of this Jeromean exposition, we cite them in their respective places.]

[Note: [Col. 0017B] “Your brother,” etc. Jerome calls Eustochium’s brother Pammachius because Eustochium’s sister Paulina was married to Pammachius. MARTIAN.—It may be thought that the word “spirit” is intended, not “flesh”; although Eustochium truly was the sister of Paulina, who had married Pammachius.]

3–4. And so I shall explain Isaiah in such a way that I shall show him to be not only a Prophet but also an evangelist and an Apostle. For he himself says of himself and of the other evangelists:

> “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things, who evangelize peace” (Isaiah 52:7).

And God speaks to him as though to an Apostle:

> “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?”

And he replies:

> “Here am I; send me” (Isaiah 6:8).

Let no one suppose that I wish to encompass the subject of this volume in a brief discourse, since the present Scripture contains all the mysteries of the Lord: Emmanuel born of a Virgin, the performer of illustrious works and signs, dead and buried, rising from the underworld, and proclaimed as the Savior of all nations.

[Note: [Col. 0019C] Vatican 322 reads: “rising from the dead.”]

What shall I say about physics, ethics, and logic? Everything that belongs to the Holy Scriptures, everything that the human tongue can express and the understanding of mortals can receive, is contained in this volume.

[Note: [Col. 0017B] Palatine 172 reads *salvatus*, “saved,” instead of *fultus*, “supported.”]

Concerning its mysteries, the very author who wrote it testifies:

> “And the vision of all this shall be for you like the words of a sealed book. When they give it to one who knows letters, they will say, ‘Read this.’ And he will answer, ‘I cannot, for it is sealed.’ And the book will be given to one who does not know letters, and they will say to him, ‘Read,’ and he will answer, ‘I do not know letters’” (Isaiah 29:11–12).

Whether, therefore, you give this book to the unlettered People of the nations, they will answer, “I cannot read,” because I have not learned the letters of the Scriptures; or whether you give it to the scribes and Pharisees, who boast that they know the letters of the King, they will answer, “We cannot read,” because the book is sealed.

Why, then, is it sealed to them? Because they did not receive the one whom the Father sealed (John 6:27), who holds the key of David:

> “He opens, and no one shuts; he shuts, and no one opens” (Revelation 3:7).

[Col. 0019D]

Nor, indeed, does Montanus dream, together with his mad women, that the Prophets spoke in ecstasy, so that they did not know what they were saying; and that while they instructed others, they themselves were ignorant of what they said.

[Note: [Col. 0019D] “As Montanus,” etc. Jerome says the same below, in the first chapter of Isaiah: “Let the ravings of Montanus fall silent, who thinks that the Prophets spoke in ecstasy and madness of heart about things to come.” He therefore understands “ecstasy” as madness of heart, by which the holy Prophets were never seized, as Montanus, Prisca, Maximilla, and the other false prophets of the heretics were. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 15 or 16; Chrysostom, Homily 29 on 1 Corinthians, chapter 12; and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, concerning Melito, Apollonius, and Tertullian. MARTIAN.]

Concerning such people the Apostle says:

> “Understanding neither what they say nor concerning what they affirm” (1 Timothy 1:7).

But, according to Solomon, who speaks in Proverbs:

> “The wise man understands what he utters from his mouth, and upon his lips he will carry knowledge” (Proverbs 16:23),

they too knew what they were saying.

For if the Prophets were wise—and this we cannot deny; and Moses, instructed in all wisdom, spoke with the Lord, and the Lord answered him; and concerning Daniel it is said to the prince of Tyre, “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezekiel 28:3); and David was wise, since he exulted in the Psalm:

> “You have revealed to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom” (Psalm 50:8)—

how could wise Prophets, like brute animals, have been ignorant of what they were saying?

We also read in another passage of the Apostle:

> “The spirits of the Prophets are subject to the Prophets” (1 Corinthians 14:32),

so that they have it in their own power when they should be silent and when they should speak.

[Note: [Col. 0020C] The Palatine manuscript reads: “The spirit is subject, and is in his own power.”]

And if this seems weak to anyone, let him hear the same Apostle:

> “Let two or three Prophets speak, and let the others judge. But if something is revealed to another who is sitting, let the first be silent” (ibid., 29).

By what reason can they remain silent, if the spirit that speaks through the Prophets is under their control, whether to remain silent or to speak?

[Note: [Col. 0020C] “Since it is under control,” etc. Nearly all manuscript codices read: “since the Spirit is in the giving,” or “in the act of being given.” MARTIAN.]

Therefore, if they understood what they were saying, everything is full of wisdom and reason.

5–6. It was not merely air struck by a voice that reached their ears; rather, God spoke in the minds of the Prophets, in accordance with what another Prophet says:

> “The angel who was speaking in me” (Zechariah 1:9),

and:

> “Crying out in our hearts, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4:6);

and:

> “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Psalm 84:9).

Therefore, after the historical truth, everything is to be understood spiritually. Thus Judaea and Jerusalem, Babylon and Philistia, Moab and Damascus, Egypt and the desert sea, Idumaea and Arabia, [Note: [Col. 0020C] “And the Valley of Vision.” The printed editions add some words, namely, “and the Valley of Zion,” which are absent from all the manuscript codices and are not found in Jerome’s version. In that version, after this title, “Burden of Arabia,” there follows: “Burden of the Valley of Vision.” Consult volume I, that is, the Divine Library of Saint Jerome. MARTIAN.] and the Valley of Vision, and finally Tyre, and the Vision of the Four-Footed Creatures, are to be understood in this way: we should seek everything in the spiritual sense, and in all these matters the Apostle Paul, like a wise architect, lays the foundation, which is none other than Jesus Christ.

It is a task and undertaking of great labor to wish to expound the whole Book of Isaiah, in which the intellects of our predecessors—by “the Greeks” I mean—labored. Among the Latins, however, there is profound silence, apart from the martyr Victorinus of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0020D] “Martyr Victorinus.” In the *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*, Saint Jerome says of this same Victorinus: “He did not know Latin as well as Greek; hence his works are great in thought, but inferior in verbal composition.” In his Letter to Magnus likewise: “Although the martyr Victorinus lacks learning in his books, he nevertheless does not lack the desire for learning.” More will be said concerning this Victorinus’s homeland and episcopate in volume IV of our edition. Moreover, the recent author who supposed that Victorinus wrote Commentaries on Isaiah as far as the Vision of the Four-Footed Creatures in the desert is mistaken. These statements must be understood not of Victorinus but of Origen, as is clear to anyone reading this passage of Jerome attentively. MARTIAN.], who, together with the Apostle, could say: [Note: [Col. 0020D] “For although unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:6), says Jerome himself in the Catalogue; he has similar remarks in Letter 70, to Magnus. Victorinus’s Commentary, however, along with many others, has perished. MARTIAN.] “Though unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge” (2 Cor. 11:9).

[Col. 0021A] For Origen wrote thirty volumes on this Prophet, according to the four editions, up to the Vision of the Four-Footed Creatures in the desert; of these, the twenty-sixth book is not extant. There are also twenty-five [Note: [Col. 0021B] The Palatine manuscript reads, “and twenty-six Homilies,” etc. A different sense of σημειώσεων (*sēmeiōseōn*) seems, moreover, to be conveyed in the *Philocalia*, as the learned Huet observed—as though they were *sēmeiōseis* themselves. The volumes would thus consist of these and should by no means be regarded as Excerpts or Scholia, but as proper Commentaries. Properly, σημειοῦσθαι means “to annotate,” or “to write a commentary,” or “to append some written material to another”; hence “Annotations” is a suitable interpretation.] Homilies, and Σημειώσεις (*Sēmeiōseis*), which we may call Excerpts.

Eusebius Pamphili, too, produced fifteen volumes according to the historical interpretation [Note: [Col. 0021B] “As it seems, through a lapse of memory—unless the fault is to be blamed on the copyists—he here numbers fifteen books of Eusebius on Isaiah, although in the catalogue he had said only ten. Nor is it established by other evidence that more actually existed. Jerome often transferred much from them into his own Commentaries; we shall occasionally indicate these passages from the edition of the learned Montfaucon. MARTIAN.]”; and Didymus, whose friendship we have recently enjoyed, produced eighteen volumes, from the passage where it is written, “Comfort, comfort my people, priests; speak to the heart of Jerusalem” (Isa. 40:1), to the end of the book. [Note: [Col. 0021B] Approximately fifteen years, nevertheless, had elapsed since Didymus died, since he ended his life in the year 396, as is confirmed by reliable authorities: Palladius in chapter 4 of the *Lausiac History*, Sigebert, and above all Jerome himself in the Catalogue. The holy Doctor was composing these Commentaries around the year 410. MARTIAN.]

Apollinaris, following his customary manner, explains everything in such a way that he runs rapidly through the whole work and, with certain pauses and intervals—or rather, with abridgements—flies over the great distances of the road, so that we seem to be reading not Commentaries but indexes of chapters. From this you can perceive how difficult it is for our Latins, whose ears are fastidious, who grow nauseated at understanding the Holy Scriptures, and who delight only in the applause of eloquence, to forgive me if I speak at greater length, since Isaiah, according to the number of verses, is equal to or greater than the Twelve Prophets. [Note: [Col. 0022B] “Or equal.” In Prologue IV to the *Divine Library* of Saint Jerome, I composed a *tetrapla* of the ancient and the new division of the verses of Holy Scripture. From it one can know that Isaiah is, according to the number of verses, either equal to or greater than the Twelve Prophets. For according to the ancient division, before Jerome, Isaiah contains 3,600 verses, whereas the Book of the Twelve Prophets contains only 3,110. Then, in manuscripts of Jerome’s version, Isaiah has 3,580 verses, while the Book of the Twelve Prophets has 3,800. MARTIAN.] Whenever, however, leaving aside the Seventy, I have discussed the Hebrew, the reason is that most passages are identical or similar to those in the others and have been presented in a twofold edition. I did not wish to extend the books of interpretation, which even in a single explanation exceed the bounds of brevity.

But now let us carry out our purpose.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0021]

[Col. 0021C] 7

## Chapter 1, verse 1

“The vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”

In place of “Judah,” in which the two tribes are signified, the Septuagint and Theodotion wrote “Judaea,” which indicates the whole land of the twelve tribes. And for what we translated from the Hebrew as “concerning Judah and Jerusalem,” they translated “against Judaea and Jerusalem.” Symmachus, in his customary clearer manner, translated “of Judah and Jerusalem,” [Note: [Col. 0021D] In Eusebius’s *Demonstration of the Gospel*, page 66, Symmachus has ὑπὲρ τῆς Ἰουδαίας καὶ ὑπὲρ τῆς Ἱερουσαλήμ, “for Judaea and for Jerusalem.” Jerome more correctly reads περὶ Ἰούδα καὶ Ἱερουσαλήμ, “concerning Judah and Jerusalem.”] so that he does not wish either prosperity or adversity to be indicated by the title, but rather those things which the prophetic utterance foretold concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in either sense.

Isaiah therefore speaks principally about the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, excluding the ten that were in Samaria and were called Ephraim and Israel. Under Uzziah, king of Judah, these had already begun to be devastated by Pul, king of the Assyrians. Finally, in the fifty-second year of his reign, when Pekah son of Remaliah was reigning in Samaria, Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, came and captured Aijalon and Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee—the whole land of Naphtali—and carried them away into Assyria (2 Kings 15:18–19). From this it is shown that all these things are narrated as a warning to the two tribes, since the overthrow of Samaria was near.

Uzziah himself is also called Azariah, under two names. From the kings listed in the title, we learn that Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, and Amos prophesied at one and the same time. Yet the word of the Lord began with Hosea son of Beeri. Amos, however, the father of Isaiah, is not, as most maintain, the third of the Twelve Prophets, but another person; among the Hebrews they are written with different letters. 8

The former has as his first and last letters *aleph* and *tsade* (א…צ); the latter *ayin* and *samekh* (ע…ס). According to some, the former is interpreted as “strength” or “strong”; the latter as “a hard or burdensome people.” We have discussed him more fully in Amos.

Not only this prophet, but also others, although their titles contain “The vision which Isaiah saw,” or “which Obadiah saw,” do not state what they saw. For example: “I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and two Seraphim around him”; rather, they report what was said, namely: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (Isa. 6:1–2). And: “Thus says the Lord God to Edom: I have surely heard from the Lord, and he has sent a messenger to the nations” (Obad. 1:1).

For prophets [Note: [Col. 0023C] They were formerly called “seers.” We read in 1 Samuel 9:9: “Formerly in Israel, when anyone went to inquire of God, he would say, ‘Come, and let us go to the seer.’ For the one who is now called a prophet was formerly called a seer.” Thus, in the Books of Kings and Chronicles, prophets are very often called seers. Isaiah also says below, in chapter 30:10, “Say to the seers,” that is, to the prophets. Again, in chapter 32:3 and chapter 33:7, prophets are called by the same name, “seers.” MARTIAN.] were formerly called seers, who could say: “Our eyes are always toward the Lord” (Ps. 25:15); and: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 123:1). Hence the Savior also commands the Apostles: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4:35).

The bride in the Song of Songs also possessed these eyes of the heart, to whom the bridegroom says: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9). And in the Gospel we read: “The lamp of your body is your eye” (Matt. 6:22). In the Old Testament, too, it is said that the people saw the voice of God (Exod. 20:18).

Let the ravings of Montanus therefore fall silent: he thinks that prophets, in ecstasy and madness of heart, spoke of things to come; for they could not see what they did not know.

I know that some interpret Judaea and Jerusalem as heavenly realities, and Isaiah as speaking in the person of the Lord Savior: [Note: [Col. 0023C] “That he foretells the captivity…” Jerome here censures the millenarians, who reject the same tradition in his *Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the section on Papias, saying: “He is said to have published a Jewish *deuterosis*—δευτέρωσιν—of a thousand years. Irenaeus, Apollinaris, and the others followed him, saying that after the resurrection the Lord would reign bodily with the saints.” Tertullian, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, Victorinus of Pettau, and Lactantius are also led by this opinion. To these must be added Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Athenagoras, and several other ancient writers. MARTIAN.] that he foretells the captivity of that province in our land and afterward its return and ascent to the holy mountain in the last days. Since we judge these things contrary to the faith of Christians, we reject them all. Following the historical truth, we interpret them spiritually, referring whatever they dream about the heavenly Jerusalem to the Church of Christ and to those who either go out from it because of their sins or return through repentance to their former seat. Of this same matter, we think, it is said in this same Prophet:

“Shine, shine, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you”; and: “The Lord will appear in you, and his glory will be seen over you”; and: “Kings will walk in your light, and nations in your splendor”; when all his sons will come from afar, and his daughters will be carried upon shoulders; and the camels of Midian and Ephah will cover her, bringing gold and frankincense; the flocks of Kedar will be gathered in Jerusalem, and the rams of Nebaioth will hasten there, and acceptable sacrifices will be offered upon the altar of the Lord (Isa. 60:1ff.).

The fact that the title says that he prophesied under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, is not to be understood vaguely, as with other prophets, so that we do not know what was said specifically under which king. Rather, to the end of the book it is reported what was revealed to him by the Lord separately under Uzziah, what under Jotham, what under Ahaz, and what under Hezekiah.

Let us also know that Hezekiah began to reign in Jerusalem in the twelfth [Note: [Col. 0023D] “In Jerusalem in the twelfth year,” etc. Jerome took this from the later book of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, which he always cites as authority for his statements in historical narratives and chronological notices. Thus, in his Letter to Damasus concerning the vision of the Seraphim, he proves the date of Uzziah’s reign and of Romulus’s birth with these words: “After his death,” he says, “the prophet Isaiah saw this vision, which we are now attempting to explain—that is, in the year in which Romulus, founder of the Roman empire, was born—as will be clear to those who wish to read the *Book of Chronology*, which we translated from Greek into Latin.” The reader should also be warned that Joseph Scaliger was greatly mistaken when he called the Vision of the Seraphim Isaiah’s first vision. It should be sixth according to the division of the chapters and the order of the visions in the manuscript books, as Jerome often notes. For in the Cluniac manuscript, after the text of the first chapter and Jerome’s Commentaries, we read as follows: “The Second Vision of Isaiah.” Scaliger’s error may be found in his *Notes on the Chronology of Eusebius*, page 66, column 2, at the end. Consult below the Commentaries on the first chapter of Isaiah. MARTIAN.—Similar statements are found in Letter 18 to Damasus, section 1, which Martian also cites here: “Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years, during which Amulius ruled among the Latins and Agamestor, the eleventh king, among the Athenians. After his death, the prophet Isaiah saw this vision, which we are now attempting to explain—that is, in the year in which Romulus, founder of the Roman empire, was born—as will be clear to those who wish to read the *Book of Chronology*, which we translated from Greek into Latin. It is commonly accepted that Rome was founded in the year of the world 3256.”]

year of Romulus, who founded a city in Italy bearing his own name. Thus it clearly appears how much more ancient our histories are than those of the other nations.

Isaiah is interpreted as “saved of the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0024D] “Saved of the Lord.” In the ancient editions of Erasmus and Marianus, and in many manuscripts, we read “Savior of the Lord”; but other codices consistently retain “saved of the Lord,” and Jerome’s Commentary subsequently confirms this reading. MARTIAN.—In the books of names it is generally explained as “salvation of the Lord”; formerly it was “savior.”]

Judah means “confession”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace”; Uzziah, “strength of the Lord”; Jotham, “perfection of the Lord”; Ahaz, “holding” or “strong”; Hezekiah, “the rule of the Lord.” Therefore, whoever is saved while the Lord presides, and is the son of Amoz—that is, of one who is strong and robust—spiritually sees the vision of confession while he mourns his former sins, and of peace while, after repentance, he passes into the light and rests in eternal peace. All his times pass under the strength of the Lord, and under his perfection and might. 10 And when he has done everything, he will say the Gospel saying: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were bound to do” (Luke 17:10).

## Verse 2

“Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken.”

Above, the title showed which prophet saw the vision, whose son he was, what he saw against Judah and Jerusalem—or concerning Judah and Jerusalem—and at what time. Now he summons heaven and earth to hear.

By heaven he signifies the higher and angelic powers; by earth, the human race—metonymically, naming what contains for what is contained. Or because, through Moses, the Lord had called heaven and earth as witnesses when he gave his law to the people of Israel and had said: “Attend, O heaven, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. 31:1). After the people’s transgression, he again calls the same witnesses, so that all the elements may know that God has been justly provoked to anger in order to avenge the commandments he gave.

In place of “heaven,” the Hebrew word *shamayim* (שמים) means “heavens,” in the plural, especially since he says “hear,” *semu* (שמעו), which is expressed in the plural, not the singular. Some, however, wish “heavens” to be plural in form but singular in meaning, [Note: [Col. 0025D] “According to the saying…” The same point is made in the Letter to Marcella concerning the ten Names of God, under the name *Elohim*. MARTIAN.] as when we call individual cities Thebes and Athens by plural names.

It is also an idiom of the Hebrew language that [Note: [Col. 0025D] “That all things…” Some exceptions occur among words ending in *-im* that are feminine, such as *nashim*, “women,” and among those ending in *-oth* that are masculine, for example *avoth*, “fathers,” and *shemoth*, “names.” MARTIAN.—Some exceptions occur on both sides, as grammarians commonly note.] all words ending in the syllable *-im* (ים) are masculine and plural, such as *cherubim* and *seraphim*, while those ending in *-oth* (ות) are feminine and plural, such as *Sabaoth*.

It should also be noted that the heavens are told “hear,” while earth is told “give ear,” since higher things possess greater understanding, whereas lower things are enclosed in earthly senses. Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. 11:15). If, therefore, someone is heaven and has citizenship among heavenly things, let him hear mystically what is said. If someone is earthly, let him follow the simple historical sense.

It should also be observed that he did not say, “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, to what the Lord has spoken to you,” but “to what he has spoken to me” [Note: [Col. 0026D] Two manuscripts read “is about to speak” here instead of “has spoken.”], so that I may report to you what I heard in the spirit, since you do not deserve to hear him speaking himself. Some—Origenists—think that heaven and earth are summoned to hear as living beings [Note: [Col. 0026D] “As living beings…” He is referring to the Origenists. Consult the Letter to Avitus concerning the books *On First Principles*. MARTIAN.], according to what is said of the earth elsewhere: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. 104:32), whereas this is an exercise of God’s power, not of earthly understanding.

[Col. 0025D] “I have begotten sons and exalted them, but they have spurned me.”

For this, Symmachus and Theodotion translated: “I have nourished sons and exalted them” (Exod. 4:22). From this point the Prophet narrates what the Lord has spoken: that he changed the people of Israel, whom he had established as servants under the common law, into sons, and said: “Israel is my firstborn son.” Finally, in the Gospel the Lord also promises the Apostles that, if they do his will, he will no longer call them servants but friends (John 15:15).

If Israel grew proud upon hearing that it was the firstborn, let it understand that it is called firstborn because other sons are signified from the nations. For he is not called “only-begotten,” which would exclude the other brothers, but “firstborn,” to show that others would follow. Yet, according to the mysteries of Scripture, it is not the firstborn who receive the inheritance, but the second-born.

Cain was the firstborn, but Abel’s offerings pleased God. Ishmael was the firstborn, but Isaac received the inheritance. Esau was the firstborn, but Jacob the supplanter seized his father’s blessing. Reuben was the firstborn, but the blessing of the seed of Christ was transferred to Judah.

Thus they were first according to the order of calling and were called the head; we, who were called the tail, have been changed into the head and are called sons of God. “To all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God” (John 1:12). Nor did we receive the spirit of slavery in fear, but the spirit of adoption, in which we cry: “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15), because perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

It is better, however, to read according to the Hebrew, “I have nourished sons,” rather than “I have fathered them,” lest it seem contrary to what we read in the Letter of John: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9). If, therefore, these were born of God, how could they have sinned, 12 since everyone born of God cannot sin?

## Verse 3

“The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; Israel does not know, my people does not understand.”

For this, only the Septuagint translated: “But Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me,” so that, according to the others and the Hebrew, Israel did not know its owner, and the people did not understand the manger of its Lord.

The meaning is clear: “I adopted them as sons, made them a special people, my portion and the lot of my inheritance, and called them firstborn. Yet they did not even do what irrational animals do: they were not overcome by benefits and did not recognize their shepherd and nurse.”

He did not compare them with dogs, which are a very intelligent kind of animal and, for a small amount of food, defend their masters’ homes, but with the ox and the donkey, whose understanding is more dull. One of them, drawing carts, turns the hardest clods of earth with the plow; the other carries burdens and eases human labor while walking. Hence they are also called *jumenta*, from the fact that they assist human beings.

This passage can also be understood of God the Father, but it refers more properly to the Son: Israel did not know him or receive him, although Abraham saw his day and rejoiced, and in whose coming the hopes of all the Prophets were suspended. In the Gospel he also speaks to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. 23:37)!

We ask where else we read of an ox and a donkey together. In Deuteronomy it is written: “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” (Deut. 22:10). And in this same Isaiah: “Blessed is the one who sows beside every water, where the ox treads and the donkey” (Isa. 32:20).

Ebion plows together with an ox and a donkey, worthy of the poverty of his understanding, in accordance with his name. [Note: [Col. 0027D] The Hebrew *Ebion* is interpreted as “poor,” as though “desiring,” because the poor person is always characterized by desire. The heretic Ebion was therefore rightly called poor, since, while the Gospel of Christ was already shining, he embraced the shadows of the Law, empty and impoverished elements, and did not accept the divinity of our Lord, whom he regarded as a mere human being. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 3, chapter 21: “The name Ebionaeans indicates the smallness or poverty of their mind and understanding.” MARTIAN.—Most learned writers, however, deny that the Ebionites were named after a certain Ebion, the founder of their heresy. They seem rather to have adopted the name by an easy allusion to voluntary poverty, since in Hebrew it means “poor”; Christians named them from their deadly poverty and the destitution of their mind and understanding. Origen, in the *Philocalia*, calls them “namesakes of the poverty of their mind”—τῆς πτωχείας τῆς διανοίας ἐπώνυμους. And Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 1: “The name Ebion indicates the poverty of their mind”—τοῦ Ἐβίων ὀνόματος τὴν τῆς διανοίας πτωχείαν αὐτῶν ὑποφαίνοντος; for among the Hebrews a poor man is customarily called by this name. MARTIAN.]

He receives the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which preceded in shadow and image.

Blessed is the one who sows in the words of the Scriptures, both the Old and the New Testament, and treads upon the waters of the letter that brings death, so that he may reap the fruit of the Spirit that gives life. 13 Allegorically, the ox refers to Israel, which bore the yoke of the Law and is a clean animal. The donkey, weighed down by the burden of sins, is understood as the people of the nations, to whom the Lord said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28).

While the Pharisees and scribes, who did not believe, possessed the key and knowledge of the Law and were truly called Israel—that is, [Note: [Col. 0028D] “That is, a mind seeing God.” Here he follows the common Greek interpretation, which he corrects below in chapter 44 with these words: “A man seeing God lies not in the elements but in the sound of the voice.” See also the discussion of this name in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*. MARTIAN.—See what we have said about this etymology in the *Book of Names* and in the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*: Jerome himself notes below, in chapter 44, that it lies not in the elements but in the sound of the voice, as Martian also observes.] “a mind seeing God”—a portion of the Jewish people believed, so that on one day three thousand believed together, and on another day five thousand.

When the wise men of the world did not receive the cross of Christ, the uneducated multitude of the nations accepted it. Hence the Apostle said: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many are wise according to the flesh, not many are powerful, not many are noble; but God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:26–27).

But this interpretation is forced; the preceding one is the true interpretation.

## Verse 4

“Woe to the sinful nation, the people heavy with iniquity, wicked offspring, criminal children! They have forsaken the Lord; they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned away backward.”

The final phrase, “they have turned away backward,” which I included, is absent from the Septuagint. In place of “they have blasphemed,” their text reads “they have provoked to anger”; and in place of “wicked offspring,” “most evil offspring.” The others, following the Hebrew *mere‘im* (מרעים), translated “of the worst,” [Note: [Col. 0028D] “The Hebrew *Mereim,” etc. In very many manuscript codices it is written *merechim*, according to the custom of ancient scribes, who wrote *mehe* for *me*, and *michi* for *mi* or *mii*. MARTIAN.] so that it is not so much a defect of the seed—for otherwise the nature of good and evil might be thought different—as the wickedness of those who deliberately abandoned the Lord.

At the beginning of the book, the title mentions the person, the cause, and the time. In the second section, he makes the hearers attentive. In the third, he narrates what the Lord has spoken. In the fourth, as though in a denunciation, he rebukes the sinful nation and the people full of or weighed down by iniquity.

This does not mean that there is one nation and another people, as some think. Israel itself is called both a nation and a people, and “criminal children” or “unrighteous children.” Those who were first called the Lord’s sons as a benefit were afterward, through their own fault, called sons of iniquity; or, as the others said in agreement, “children who corrupt,” that is, [suppl. υἱοὶ] διαφθείροντες, “sons who corrupt,” who through their own fault lost the good of their nature.

The phrase “they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel” is properly said of the Jews who cried out: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15); and: “Is this not the carpenter’s son?” (Matt. 13:55); and: “He has a demon, and he is a Samaritan” (John 8:48).

Because they abandoned Christ and blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, therefore they turned away backward, so that those who were called God’s portion and sons were afterward called: “The sons of strangers have lied to me” (Ps. 18:45).

The Savior commanded that, after taking hold of the plow, we should not look behind us (Luke 9:62), lest we imitate Lot’s wife. Hence the Apostle, stretching forward toward what lies ahead, forgets what is behind (Phil. 3:13).

When, according to the Septuagint, he said “a people full of sins” (Zech. 5:7), he showed that there was no kind of sin absent from the people of Israel. [Note: [Col. 0028D] Two manuscripts read “no sin was absent from the people.”]

But if we read, as it is in the Hebrew, “a people heavy with iniquity,” let us remember that testimony which says that iniquity sits upon a leaden talent, and the statement spoken in the person of the sinner in Psalm 38: “My iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have become too heavy for me” (Ps. 38:4).

We pass rapidly over what is evident, so that we may linger over what is more obscure and over matters requiring explanation.

## Verse 5

“Where shall I strike you again, as you continue to add transgression?”

From this testimony we learn that the Lord strikes those who sin in order to correct those who have been struck, so that the blow is not so much punishment as amendment.

The meaning is: “I cannot find what medicine I can apply to your wounds. All your limbs are full of injuries; I find no part of the body that has not already been struck.” Or certainly it means this: “I find no blows with which I can break your hardness.” For the greater the torments, the more impiety and iniquity increase—or, as Theodotion translated, “declension,” so that you withdraw and turn away from the Lord.

Such is the saying of Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your sons; you did not accept correction” (Jer. 2:30). Hence he speaks in anger through Hosea: “I will not punish your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery” (Hos. 4:14). And through Ezekiel: “My jealousy will depart from you, and I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. 16:42).

Of these things we also read in the Psalms: “There is no firmness in their affliction; they are not in the labors of human beings, nor will they be scourged with human beings” (Ps. 73:4–5). 15

“Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving.”

Joy of mind sometimes lessens bodily pain. But if mental distress is added to bodily illness, the weakness is doubled. Among the senses themselves and all the members of the body, the head occupies the principal place, since sight, smell, hearing, and taste are located in it. Therefore, when the head hurts, all the limbs are weak.

By metaphor he teaches that from the rulers to the lowest common people, from the teachers to the uneducated crowd, there is health nowhere; rather, all agree with equal fervor in impiety.

[Col. 0029C] “From the sole of the foot to the crown, there is no soundness in it: wound, bruise, and swelling sore.”

He preserves the translation he began: from the feet to the crown, that is, from [Note: [Col. 0029D] “That is, from below…” Many manuscripts that I examined read as follows: “From top to top”; but the sense is the same in both places. MARTIAN.—The Palatine manuscript, as do others cited by Martian, reads “from top to top.”] the lowest to the highest, from the extremities to the foremost parts, they are pierced throughout the body.

“Wound,” he says, “and bruise and swelling sore”: either their bodies are bruised by blows, or they swell from wounds, or they gape with injuries.

We ask to what period these things should be applied. After the Babylonian captivity, under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, Israel returned to Judaea and recovered its former condition. Under various leaders and kings, a more splendid temple was also built, to such an extent that they even merited the friendship of foreign nations—the Lacedaemonians, Athenians, and Romans.

Therefore, when he says, “There is no soundness in it,” he refers to the final captivity. After Titus and Vespasian, and the final destruction of Jerusalem, under Aelius Hadrian and continuing to the present time, there has been no remedy. What is written has been fulfilled: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Rom. 3:12).

When it adds, “There is no soundness in it,” understand this either of the people, or of the body, or of the head.

## Verse 6

“It has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” [Col. 0030A]

For this the Septuagint translated: “There is no poultice to apply, neither oil nor bandages.” 16

To this day the wound, bruise, and swelling sore of the people of Israel have not been bound with strips of cloth nor treated with medicine. Aquila translated this as μώτωσιν (*mōtōsin*) [Note: [Col. 0030D] The Palatine manuscript has *motosin* in Latin letters. Martian notes that μότοσιν should be μότωσιν, a word that properly denotes the treatment of a wound.], namely, linen cloths applied to dry the discharge and draw out the pus from wounds.

“Nor softened with oil”: so that their hardness might be softened by tears of repentance. In place of the strips with which Israel’s wounds have by no means been bound, the Septuagint translated “poultice.”

Israel therefore lies pierced and butchered, because it killed the physician who had come to heal the house of Israel. Hence in Jeremiah, figuratively, the angels speak in the person of Babylon: “We treated Babylon, but she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9)—the city, namely, of confusion and vices.

In the Gospel (Luke 10), too, we read of the man descending from Jerusalem to Jericho, wounded by robbers and healed by a Samaritan, and of the soothing oil poured into his wounds after the harshness of wine.

From the passage where he said above, “Where shall I strike you?” and “Every head is sick,” up to the present statement, “It has not been treated with medicine, nor softened with oil,” the similarity of the metaphor is preserved, and the description of incurable wounds expresses the Jews’ eternal captivity.

## Verse 7

“Your land is desolate; your cities are burned with fire; foreigners devour your region in your presence, and it will be desolated as in an enemy’s devastation.”

These things were partly fulfilled under the Babylonians, when the temple was burned and Jerusalem overthrown, at the time when the Samaritans possessed the region of the ten tribes. The land of promise was reduced to such utter solitude that it was ravaged by lions.

More fully and perfectly, however, what would happen under Roman captivity is described: when the Roman army devastated all Judaea, the cities were burned, and foreigners are presently devouring their region. The devastation of the Jews will continue to the end of the world.

We can also understand these things tropologically of sinners who have fallen from their former holiness after being handed over to hostile powers: all their goods pass into desolation; God no longer remembers their former righteousness; everything is set ablaze by the fire of the devil; and they become food for beasts, concerning which it is written elsewhere: “Do not give the soul that confesses you to the beasts” (Ps. 74:19).

### (Verse 8)

“Zion’s daughter shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber field.” That all Israel was called a vineyard the same Prophet testifies in what follows, saying: “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is His beloved and newly planted vine” (below, chapter 5, verse 7); and in the Psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; You drove out the nations and planted it” (Psalm 79:9).

As long as this vineyard produced the richest fruits, it had God as its keeper, of whom it is written: “He shall neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Psalm 120:4). But after all passers-by had stripped it of its grapes, and the boar from the forest had ravaged it, the Lord abandoned His temple. Rising in anger, He said:

> “Rise; let us go away from here”; and: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38).

[Note: “Rise.” In the Gospel according to John, chapter 14, verse 31, we read: “Rise, let us go away from here.” How He rose in anger may easily be gathered from the context of that same chapter, since there He discoursed about the world and the prince of this world, who cannot receive Christ’s spirit. MARTIAN.]

[Note: He argues almost in the same way in Letter 68, to Paulinus: “The Savior, speaking to His disciples while He was in the temple, said, ‘Rise, let us go away from here’; and to the Jews: ‘Your house shall be left to you desolate.’ These two statements were made at different times: the first in the upper room to the disciples, the second in the temple to the Jews. But here they seem to have been quoted from Matthew’s Gospel according to the Hebrews.” In the Palatine manuscript, *to you* is missing. See what we observe concerning this in that letter, no. 3. MARTIAN.]

And through Jeremiah: “I have abandoned My house; I have dismissed My inheritance. My inheritance has become to Me like a lion in the forest; it has raised its voice against Me; therefore I have hated it” (Jeremiah 12:7).

The comparison of the devastation of the Temple and Jerusalem is taken from farmers, who, as long as a vineyard is full of grapes, place guards in shelters. In a cucumber field also—which the Septuagint calls “the guardianship of fruits”—little huts are made to ward off the heat and rays of the sun; from them they drive away either people or the small animals that are accustomed to lie in wait for newly sprouting crops.

[Note: This discussion of huts and the keeper of the vineyard has been taken from Eusebius’s Commentaries, from which many other things have also been extracted, though expressed only in shorter words.]

When such produce has been removed, the dry shelters and huts remain, once the keeper has withdrawn, because he no longer has anything to guard. Thus Almighty God also abandoned the Temple and caused the city to become desolate. There is no need to prove this with words—especially for us, who see Zion desolate, Jerusalem overthrown, and the Temple demolished down to its foundations.

By calling it “Zion’s daughter,” He shows the affection of a most merciful parent. Nor is it surprising that Zion is called a daughter, since Babylon too is very often called a daughter. By nature we are all children of God, but through our own fault we become estranged.

According to the allegorical sense, God’s vineyard and orchard of fruits may be called our soul. If the mind—that is, the *νοῦς*—presides over it, it has God as the keeper of the mind. But if vices, like wild beasts, have ravaged us, we are abandoned by God our keeper, and everything belonging to us is reduced to desolation.

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah.”

The Apostle Paul discusses this passage more fully in Romans, writing: “I ask, then, has God rejected His people? Certainly not. For I myself am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected His people whom He foreknew” (Romans 11:1–2). And shortly afterward: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (ibid., verse 5).

From this it is shown that the preceding threats pronounced by the prophetic word against Jerusalem and Judah should not be referred to the time of the Babylonian captivity, but to the final captivity under the Romans, when a remnant of the Jewish people was saved in the Apostles: three thousand believed in one day, five thousand on another, and the Gospel was sown throughout the whole world.

In place of “Lord of hosts,” which, following Aquila, we have rendered in Latin, the Hebrew reads *Dominus sabaoth*—“the Lord Sabaoth.” The Septuagint translators render it in two ways according to the circumstances of the passages: either “Lord of powers” or “Lord Almighty.” It must be asked whether this is said of the Father or of the Son.

There can be no doubt that the words found in Psalm 23—“Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, everlasting doors, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord Sabaoth” (Psalm 23:7–8)—that is, “the Lord of powers,” refer to Christ. He is the King of glory who, after the triumph of His Passion, ascended victoriously into heaven.

In another place also Christ is called the King of glory: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2:8). Therefore, not only according to the Apocalypse of John and the Apostle Paul, but also in the Old Testament, Christ is called *Dominus sabaoth*, that is, “the Almighty.”

For if everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son, and, as He Himself says in the Gospel, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (Matthew 28:18), and, “All that is Mine is Yours, and I am glorified in them”—

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “and I shall be glorified in them.”]

—why should the name “Almighty” not also be referred to Christ, so that, just as He is God of God and Lord of Lord, He may likewise be the Son of the Almighty?

### (Verse 10)

“Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah.”

After the remnant of the people of Israel had been saved through the Apostles, the prophetic word is turned against the scribes and Pharisees and the shouting crowd: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John 19:6). It calls them “rulers of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah,” in accordance with what we read later: “They proclaimed and displayed their sin like Sodom. Woe to their soul, because they devised an evil plan against themselves, saying: ‘Let us bind the righteous man, for he is useless to us’” (below, chapter 3).

Therefore they are called “rulers of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah” because they devised an evil plan, bound the righteous man, and said: “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15). And again: “We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know who he is” (John 9:29).

At the same time, boasting in the Gospel, “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone” (John 8:53), they hear from the Lord and Savior: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham”; and again: “You are born of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s works” (ibid., 8:39, 44).

Ezekiel also says something similar to Jerusalem: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezekiel 16:45).

The Hebrews say that Isaiah was killed for two reasons: because he had called them “rulers of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah,” and because, when the Lord said to Moses, “You cannot see My face” (Exodus 33:20), Isaiah had dared to say: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up” (below, chapter 6, verse 1).

[Note: The same manuscript reads: “I saw the Lord Sabaoth, sitting, etc.”]

They did not consider that the words “face” and “feet,” whether referring to God or to the Seraphim, are read ambiguously in Hebrew: “the Seraphim covered …” and that Isaiah wrote that he had seen only the middle part of Him.

[Note: “Because in Hebrew …” In Hebrew we read *phanau* and *reglau*, which may be interpreted either as “His” or “their”—that is, we may understand that the Seraphim covered God’s face and feet with their wings, or their own face and feet. There is therefore an ambiguity in the Hebrew suffix or pronoun, of which Jerome speaks here and below in chapter 6. See also the letter to Damasus concerning this same vision of Isaiah. MARTIAN.]

[Note: The suffix in these words may be translated either “His” or “their.” In the Palatine manuscript: “Isaiah saw only the middle part of Him,” etc. MARTIAN.]

A human being, therefore, cannot see the face of God.

[Note: Saint Augustine, in his *Commonitorium* to Fortunatianus, or Letter 148, explains and comments on this passage of Jerome—quoting it in full to the end of the section—as follows: “Many things must be considered in these words of the man of God. First, according to the Lord’s most explicit statement, he too believes that we shall see God’s face when we have advanced into the condition of angels—that is, when we have become equal to the angels, which will certainly take place in the resurrection of the dead. Furthermore, by apostolic testimony he made it sufficiently clear that the face intended is not that of the outward but of the inward man, when we shall see face to face; for the Apostle was speaking of the face of the heart when he said what Jerome has recalled here: ‘But we, with unveiled face …’ And after inserting certain other matters: ‘Finally, lest anyone, observing and distinguishing these things insufficiently, should believe that God is visible either to angels or to human beings, whether now or in the future, when we have become equal to the angels, he expressed with complete clarity what he thought, saying that no creature sees the face of God according to the proper nature of God, and that God is then perceived by the mind when He is believed to be invisible. Thus he sufficiently indicated that, when He was seen by human beings through bodily eyes, as though He were corporeal, He was not seen according to the proper nature in which He is then perceived by the mind when He is believed to be invisible.” If you wish, compare the remainder of his letter and the notes of learned men upon it.]

But the angels of even the least in the Church always see the face of God (Matthew 18:10). And: “Now we see in a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12), when we human beings have advanced into the condition of angels and can say with the Apostle: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as though by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

[Note: “Into the condition of angels …” This seems to reflect Origen’s error, which Jerome himself corrected in his letter to Avitus: “When we have progressed so far,” he says, “that we are no longer flesh and bodies—perhaps not even souls—but mind and sense brought to perfection, with no cloud of disturbances obscuring us, we shall behold rational and intelligible substances face to face.” Thus, in this passage, the advancement of human beings into angels must be understood as likeness: in the time of heavenly blessedness we shall be like the angels of God, seeing Him as He is. MARTIAN.]

Although no creature sees the face of God according to His proper nature, and He is then perceived by the mind when He is believed to be invisible.

### (Verse 11)

“What is the multitude of your sacrifices to Me?” says the Lord. “I am full. I do not desire the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats.”

For “I did not desire,” the Septuagint translated “I do not desire,” using the present tense for the past. According to the Hebrew, God shows that He never desired the sacrifices of the Jews. We read the same in Psalm 49:

> “I shall not accept calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks; for all the beasts of the forest are Mine, the cattle on the mountains and the oxen. I know all the birds of the sky, and the beauty of the field is with Me. If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are Mine. Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (Psalm 49 and following).

After rejecting the ceremonies of the old Law, He passes to evangelical purity and shows what He desires in their place:
