> “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God, and fulfill your vows to the Most High. Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I shall deliver you, and you shall honor Me.”

Thus the entire content of this chapter, up to the place where it says, “Judge the orphan, defend the widow, and come, let us reason together,” rejects sacrificial offerings and teaches that obedience to the Gospel is superior to sacrifice.

[Note: The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts add: “says the Lord.”]

As for the statement, “I am full,” it should be understood in this sense: “I lack nothing.” “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm 24:1). Hence we too have all received from His fullness.

This may also be understood of those who, without doing what God commands, believe that they can buy God off with gifts and offerings; or of those who offer on the altar and to the poor things acquired through robbery and greed.

[Note: “Do not do.” The manuscript codices read this way; the printed editions, however, read: “with various gifts and offerings.” MARTIAN.]

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, as in the earlier printed editions, reads: “with various gifts and offerings.”]

### (Verse 12)

“For who has required these things from your hands?”

Let the Ebionites hear this, those who think that after Christ’s Passion the abolished Law must still be observed. Let the associates of the Ebionites hear it, those who decree that these things must be observed only by Jews and by those descended from the Israelite race.

Sacrifices and the offering of victims were not originally required by God. Rather, they were given so that sacrifices might not be made to idols, and so that we might pass from carnal victims, as through a type and image, to spiritual sacrifices.

But by saying that He did not seek sacrifices, He shows that the Law is spiritual and that everything the Jews perform carnally is fulfilled by us spiritually.

[Note: “So that they might be made to idols.” This is also how the earlier printed books read in this passage: “so that they might be offered to idols”; but the manuscript codices consistently read: “so that they might be made to idols.” The sense is the same as “sacrificed,” for “to make,” or “to make for God,” means to offer a sacrifice, as is plainly evident among authors of purer Latin. MARTIAN. The Palatine manuscript, in a second hand, reads: “to offer they might be made”; formerly, as in the old printed editions, “might be offered.”]

### (Verse 13)

“You shall no longer tread my court.”

Observe that after the Babylonian devastation the Temple was rebuilt again by Zerubbabel, and sacrifices were offered in the Temple for many years (1 Esdras 5). Therefore He indicates the final destruction of the Temple under Vespasian and Titus, which will continue until the consummation of the world.

### (Verse 14)

“I shall not endure your new moons, Sabbaths, and other festivals; your assemblies are wicked.”

Every assembly that offers no spiritual sacrifices and does not heed what is sung in Psalm 50—“The sacrifice acceptable to God is a broken spirit; a broken and humbled heart God does not despise”—is abominable to God.

[Note: “God does not despise.” Many passages from the sacred context are found in Erasmus and Marianus Victor, but they do not occur in the manuscript copies and were not quoted by Jerome. We have therefore removed such clauses of sacred Scripture as additions to Jerome’s Commentaries. Those who wish may compare the old editions with this new one and will find countless interpolated passages, both Latin verses and Greek explanations—that is, words and clauses from Greek interpretations. MARTIAN. The Vatican manuscript likewise reads: “does not despise.”]

For this reason He adds: “Your new moons and your festivals,” so that He does not call them His own festivals, but festivals belonging to those who misuse them.

As for the Septuagint’s rendering, “fasting and idleness,” we may say that the fasting accepted by God is that which has no idleness in good works.

“My soul hates them.” This is *anthropopathically*—that is, not because God has a soul, but because He speaks according to our manner of feeling.

### (Verse 15)

“You have become a burden to Me; I shall by no means forgive your sins.”

For this Aquila translated: “I have labored, enduring.” Symmachus translated *ἐκοπώθην ἱλασκόμενος*—“I have been exhausted in showing mercy”—to indicate that He would no longer have mercy, since it is one thing to kill servants sent to Him and another to kill the Son.

We read the same sense in the Prophet Hosea: “Your destruction is from yourself, Israel; only in Me is your help” (Hosea 13:9). This means: “Perish, Israel, because you are saved not by your own merit but only by My help.”

“Your hands are full of blood.”

He reveals the reason why God turns His eyes away from them and does not hear their multiplied prayers: they have poured out the blood of the righteous and, as wicked husbandmen, have killed the heir sent to them.

Hence the Savior also says to them: “And you, fill up the measure of your fathers” (Matthew 23:31). They killed the Prophets sent to them; you slaughter the Son of the Master of the household.

This testimony may also be used against those who, although their hands are full of blood through their daily actions, join themselves to prayer day and night.

### (Verse 16)

“Wash yourselves; be clean.”

In place of the previous sacrifices, burnt offerings, fat of fattened animals, blood of bulls and goats, incense, new moons, Sabbaths, festival days and fasts, new moons and other solemnities, the religion of the Gospel pleases Me: that you should be baptized in My blood through the washing of regeneration, which alone can forgive sins.

“For unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:5). The Lord Himself, ascending to the Father, said: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

“Take away the evil of your thoughts from before My eyes.”

This is what John the Baptist said: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance” (Matthew 3:7; Luke 3:7). Thus the person who has received Christ’s baptism must remove evil from his heart, cease to act perversely, and afterward learn to do good, according to the command given elsewhere: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27).

“Learn to do good.”

Virtue must therefore be learned. Natural goodness alone is not sufficient for righteousness unless a person is educated by appropriate disciplines (1 Peter 2:11). Jesus son of Sirach also says something similar: “You have desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you.”

And later the same Isaiah recalls: “Everyone who has not learned righteousness upon the earth will not practice truth” (chapter 26:10, according to the Septuagint). Righteousness must therefore be learned, and the thresholds of teachers of wisdom must be worn down.

### (Verse 18)

“Seek judgment, help the oppressed, judge the orphan, defend the widow; and come, and reprove Me,” says the Lord.

The evangelical commandments take the place of the sacrifices of the Jews. Provision is therefore made for orphans and widows, so that, secure in the protection of their spouses and children, martyrs may go forth to battle.

“When you have done these things,” He says, “reprove Me, if I do not give you the rewards that I have promised.”

When He says, “Seek justice,” He shows that not everyone is able to judge rightly, but only those who are prudent. Indeed, Solomon asked this of the Lord in a dream-vision: that, having received wisdom, he might judge the people justly.

“If your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made white like snow. And if they are red like crimson, they shall become white like wool.”

The order is reversed—

[Note: The word “principal” here has no significance. From the entire context and Jerome’s intention, I would prefer *praeposterus*—“reversed.” This is a familiar expression in the speech of the holy Doctor. MARTIAN.]

—for it is not enough to have said, “Wash yourselves,” unless He adds, “Be clean,” so that after the washing of water the heart may possess purity. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Once they possess purity of heart, they must remove evil from their minds—not in the sight of human beings, but in the sight of God, whom nothing can conceal. The addition, “Cease to act perversely,” echoes the Gospel: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

Having therefore departed from vices, a person should learn to do good, seek justice, help the oppressed, and support the orphan and the widow. If he does this, then the sins that were previously blood-red, like scarlet, will be forgiven; and works of gore and blood will be changed into the garment of the Lord, which is made from the fleece of the Lamb. Those who shine with the whiteness of virginity follow Him in the Apocalypse (chapter 5).

### (Verses 19, 26)

“If you are willing and listen, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen”—or, as the Hebrew has it, “and provoke Me to anger”—

[Note: Martianus reads: “and provoke Me to anger.”]

—“the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

He preserves free choice, so that the outcome in either direction—punishment or reward—may depend not on God’s prejudice but on the merits of individuals.

[Note: It would seem that the word *ut* should be removed: “He preserves free choice in either direction, so that the outcome may not depend on a prior judgment,” etc.]

By “the good things of the land,” I think those things are meant of which we read in the Psalm: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13); and: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matthew 5:5).

Or, certainly, because He was speaking to Jews who were not yet able to grasp spiritual things, He promises them the good things of the present age, so that at least, attracted by present benefits, they might do what was commanded.

Because they refused to listen and, on the contrary, provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger, the sword therefore devoured them—that is, the Roman army destroyed them.

“And all these things,” He says, “shall happen because the mouth of the Lord has spoken.” His sentence cannot be changed while human sins continue.

### (Verse 21)

“How the faithful city, full of judgment, has become a prostitute! Righteousness once rested in her, but now there are murderers.”

[Note: “The Hebrew word *JALIN* …” Hebrew grammarians teach us this also, especially our Thomas Dufour, in chapter 10 on Syntax: “Generally speaking, and particularly in meters, the past and future are often used for one another in universal statements that are not precisely determined in time. When this expression is poorly understood, it produces a remarkable appearance of difference between the Text and the Vulgate edition, especially in the Psalms.” MARTIAN.]

The Hebrew word *JALIN* (יָלִין), which the Septuagint translated “it slept,” means “it rested” and “it will rest”—that is, it signifies both past and future time. Hence Aquila and Theodotion also speak as though of the future.

The Prophet wonders, in the prophetic spirit, that a city which once was faithful—or was a refuge for the faithful—should suddenly have become a prostitute. This may indeed be understood of Isaiah’s own times, but it refers more fully to the Passion of Christ, when “all turned aside and together became useless” (Psalm 13:3).

Although “Zion” is not found in the Hebrew, the Septuagint added it in order to make the sense clearer. Zion is the mountain on which the city of Jerusalem was founded. After David captured it, it was called the city of David.

I do not doubt that holy men were once in it, when it possessed God’s tabernacle and, later, the Temple was built; when Nathan and Gad prophesied; and when Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, and the sons of Korah were appointed over the choirs—which are described more fully in the Book of Chronicles—so that worship might gradually pass from sacrifices of victims to the praises of the Lord (1 Chronicles 25).

[Note: The Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read: “Nathan and Gad the prophets came.”]

Thus the city of the faithful, which formerly was full of judgment and in which righteousness rested, is now full of murderers, who killed the Prophets and the Lord Himself, the Savior.

Ezekiel develops Jerusalem’s fornication under the name Oholibah, describing how she spread her legs to every passer-by. Her name means “My tent is in her.” This is what is now expressed in other words by “righteousness rested in her.”

In place of “righteousness,” the Hebrew has *SEDEC* (צֶדֶק), which sounds more like “righteous” than “righteousness.” We are therefore to understand that the Lord formerly dwelt in her, of whom it is said elsewhere: “But the righteous man—what has he done? The Lord is in His holy temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (Psalm 10:5).

[Note: “Sedech.” Modern Hebrews and Hebraists will hardly concede Jerome’s interpretation: *tsedec* sounds more like “righteous” than “righteousness.” But if they remember that in the time of the holy Doctor the noun *sedech* may have been written with an unpronounced *yod* in this form, they cannot deny Jerome’s interpretation to be true. What is read today as *sadiq* Jerome may have read as *sedech*, especially since elsewhere he maintains that the word may indifferently be read *Salem* and *Salim*. MARTIAN.]

[Note: In support of Jerome’s interpretation, Martianaeus supposes that *sadiq* was formerly written with an unpronounced *yod*, so that it could be read *sedech*.]

All these things may, according to the allegorical sense, be referred to the soul of a once-holy man, in whom God’s righteousness formerly dwelt, but who later sinned, so that murderous demons dwelt in him in place of God as his guest.

### (Verse 22)

“Your silver has become dross.”

He addresses the city of Zion, in which righteousness formerly rested. Its silver—that is, the teaching of the Scriptures, concerning which we read in the Psalms, “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, tried in the earth, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7)—has become dross, which in Hebrew is called *SIGIM* (סִיגִים): the rust of metals, or the impurities and refuse that are removed by fire. Since He had mentioned silver, He preserves the metaphor.

It may also be said that the just and holy men who formerly lived in the city later became the refuse of sinners.

“Your tavern-keepers mix wine with water.”

For this Symmachus translated: “Your wine has been mixed with water.” The sense is that God’s Law, pure and unalloyed and—so to speak—supported by unmixed truth (Matthew 15), has been violated by the traditions of the Pharisees. The Lord teaches this more fully in the Gospel: they abandoned God’s law and followed human commandments.

Every teacher who turns the severity of the Scriptures—which can correct his hearers as severely as possible—toward mere indulgence, and speaks in such a way that he pleases rather than corrects his hearers, violates and corrupts the wine of the Holy Scriptures by his own interpretation.

Heretics also corrupt evangelical truth through perverse understanding. They are the worst tavern-keepers, making water from wine, whereas our Lord turned water into wine (John 2)—and into such wine that the master of the feast admired it, like the Queen of Sheba, who admired Solomon’s banquet and praised his cupbearers and wine-servants with her own voice (2 Chronicles 9).

Ecclesiastes too describes the services of wine and of his banquet in mystical language (Ecclesiastes 2).

Therefore Aquila translated “wine” as *συμπόσιον*, that is, “banquet,” which among the Greeks is more correctly named from *πότος*—“drinking”—and among us from fellowship at table.

[Note: In place of *συμπόσιον*, *πότον* should probably be read here. Drusius conjectured this, despite the manuscripts and Jerome himself, who interprets it as “banquet.”]

### (Verse 23)

“Your rulers are disobedient, companions of thieves.”

For “disobedient,” Aquila translated “those who withdraw”; Symmachus, “those who turn aside.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “for disobedient”: “those who withdraw,” and the Palatine: “Aquila, those who withdraw.”]

By “rulers” he means the scribes and Pharisees, who withdrew from the Lord—or rather, abandoned the path of truth—and walked along a perverse road. They were companions of the betrayer and of the thief Judas.

We too must beware of this, lest, receiving gifts from worldly people who accumulate wealth through robbery and the tears of the poor, we be called not thieves themselves but companions of thieves. Let it not be said to us: “You saw a thief and ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your portion” (Psalm 49:18).

“All love gifts and pursue rewards.”

Those who love gifts are also counted in the catalogue of vices. He did not say “those who receive them,” since this often happens through necessity, but “those who love them”: people who do not regard anyone as a friend unless they have received presents from him; who consider not the face of their friends but their hands; and who judge those to be holy whose purses they drain.

Ecclesiastes also speaks of such people: “He who loves money shall not be satisfied with money” (Ecclesiastes 5:9).

Such people pursue rewards, either praising those from whom they have received something, or giving nothing to anyone unless they think they will receive something in return.

In place of “rewards,” Symmachus translated “exchanges” or “acts of vengeance,” so that those too are guilty who return evil for evil, and tooth for tooth, eye for eye (Exodus 21), rather than imitating David’s words: “If I have repaid those who repaid me with evil” (Psalm 7:5), or Jeremiah’s words concerning the righteous man: “He gives his cheek to the one who strikes him; he is filled with reproaches” (Lamentations 3:30), fulfilling the Gospel command addressed to the righteous man: “If anyone strikes you on the cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

### (Verse 24)

“Therefore says the Lord of hosts, the Mighty One of Israel.”

In place of “the Mighty One of Israel,” which everyone translated in the same way, only the Septuagint, for reasons unknown to me, wrote:

> “Woe to the mighty ones of Israel.”

[Note: “Woe to the mighty ones of Israel.” We have removed many Greek words and clauses from Jerome’s Commentaries because he himself nowhere mentions them, as all the manuscript codices testify. They consistently preserve the Greek words quoted by Jerome, while adding the others, as in this passage: *οὐαὶ οἱ ἰσχύοντες Ἰσραήλ*. Having been warned by this observation, let the reader not look for our notes on the Greek additions that follow, which are extremely numerous. MARTIAN.]

We can explain this by saying that the rulers too are rebuked, as are the powerful, of whom it is written: “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7); and: “To whom more has been given, from him more will be required” (Luke 12:48).

We misuse this testimony whenever it is needed against rulers of the Church who destroy their dignity by their works.

“Alas, I shall be comforted over My enemies, and I shall be avenged upon My adversaries.”

Again, in this passage the Septuagint adds what is not found in the Hebrew: “For My anger against My enemies has not ceased.”

He rebukes the scribes and Pharisees, of whom He also speaks in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees” (Matthew 23:13 and following). And elsewhere: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39).

The most merciful Father mourns the rulers who have sinned, calls them His enemies and adversaries, and says that they perish because they refuse to repent and did not receive Him when He came.

As He approached Jerusalem, He wept and said: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the Prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wished to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matthew 23:37).

God’s consolation, therefore, is over His enemies and adversaries, so that those who did not perceive His benefits may be corrected by punishments.

### (Verse 25)

“And I shall turn My hand toward you; I shall smelt away your dross to purity, and I shall remove all your tin.”

For “dross,” Symmachus translated *σκωρίαν*, “dross”; Aquila, *στέμφυλα*, that is, “grape-pomace”; and Theodotion, *γιγαρτῶδες*, that is, “the grape-seed.” The Septuagint alone, translating the sense rather than the words, rendered it “the unbelieving” or “the disobedient.”

[Note: Martianaeus printed this corruptly, without adding any punctuation, as though “Symmachus and Aquila interpreted …” were all governed by “translated,” so that *σκορίαν*, which belongs to Symmachus, was not really attributed either to Symmachus or to Aquila. This was the cause of the learned men’s error. We have removed the conjunction in accordance with the Palatine manuscript and explained the sense according to Jerome’s intention.

Eusebius writes concerning this passage: “Therefore, according to Symmachus, it is said: ‘And I shall smelt your dross to purity’; but according to Aquila”—read Theodotion—“‘And I shall smelt your grape-seed to purity.’”]

Since He had said above, “Your silver has become dross,” He now preserves the metaphor, turning His hand against it—that is, extending His hand to punish and purify—and smelting away all the impurities and vices of sins, so that, once the tin has been separated, pure silver may remain. This cannot happen without fire, by which He signifies that they will suffer torments.

We also read in Malachi concerning the Lord: “He shall come forth like a refiner’s fire and like fuller’s soap, and He shall sit refining and purifying as silver and gold, and He shall purify the sons of Levi” (Malachi 3:2–3), so that after they have been cleansed it may be said of them: “And they shall offer sacrifices to the Lord in righteousness.”

Ezekiel too says that the whole house of Israel is mixed with bronze, iron, lead, and tin, and that afterward it must be purified, so that, once it has been cleansed, it may know that He is the Lord (Ezekiel 22:18).

The same meaning is also displayed in the Gospel under another metaphor: “His winnowing-fork is in His hand, and He will cleanse His threshing floor, gather the wheat into His barns, and burn the chaff with unquenchable fire” (Matthew 3:12).

[Alternative readings: “cleanse” for “purify,” and “purify” for “cleanse.”]

### (Verse 26)

“And I will restore your judges as they were formerly, and your counselors as at the beginning.”

In the faithful city, Zion, which afterward became a harlot, and in place of a righteous man—or of righteousness—murderers dwelt in it. Therefore the Lord turns his hand, to smelt it until it is pure, remove all its tin, and restore its judges as they were at the beginning, and its counselors as formerly.

The earlier judges were Moses, Joshua son of Nun, and the others from whom the book of Holy Scripture also received its name; afterward, David and the other righteous kings. He will therefore restore the likeness of the Judges: either after the Babylonian captivity, as the Jews hold—Zerubbabel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and the other leaders who ruled the people down to Hyrcanus, whom Herod succeeded in the kingship—or, more truly and correctly, the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles and were appointed leaders of the churches, as we said at the beginning of this vision. Both the threat and the promise pertain to the time of the Lord’s Passion and to the faith which, after his Passion, founded the Church.

**Note:** We said “of this vision.” Let the careful and diligent investigator of Scripture observe that Jerome calls the preceding vision the first chapter of Isaiah, and likewise the second a second vision. See below, the Commentary on verse 1 of chapter II. —MARTIAN.

“After this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city.”

The prophetic word plainly embraces here the Church, which would believe in the Lord both from the Jews and from the Gentiles. It will be called the city of the righteous—that is, of the Lord and Savior—or it will itself be called righteous, concerning which it is said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14).

**Note:** Two Vatican and Palatine manuscripts insert this here: “If this is so.”

Calling it faithful also, or “metropolis” according to the Septuagint, he shows that it is to be so called by those who will believe in the Lord.

### (Verses 27–29)

“Zion shall be redeemed in judgment, and they shall bring her back to righteousness, and he shall crush the wicked and sinners together; and those who abandoned the Lord shall be consumed.”

**Note:** “And he shall crush,” etc. The words of the sacred text, “And he shall crush the wicked” through “For they shall be,” are omitted in the manuscript codices. We nevertheless retain them from the printed editions because Jerome explains them in the present Commentary. —MARTIAN.

**Note:** What follows from “and he shall crush the wicked” to the end of the sacred text is found neither in our manuscripts nor in those used by Martian.**

They shall be ashamed because of the idols to which they sacrificed, and you shall be ashamed of the gardens that you chose.

Not everyone will be redeemed, nor will everyone be saved, but only the remnant, of whom it was said above. They will be brought back to righteousness when the wicked and sinners have been crushed and those who abandoned the Lord have been consumed. When they have been saved, those who formerly sacrificed to idols will be ashamed, and they will blush for the gardens that they had chosen. He signifies places of luxury, sacred groves, and woodland sanctuaries.

### (Verse 30)

“For they shall be like a terebinth with falling leaves, and like a garden—or paradise—without water.”

To this day, when reading the Holy Scriptures, the Jews are like a terebinth, or an oak, as Symmachus translated it. According to the Gospel (Matt. XXI), they are also like the fig tree that withered, when the Lord sought fruit on it and found none, and condemned it to eternal barrenness.

The leaves and fruits of words have also now ceased to exist among them. The well-watered garden—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures—or paradise of various trees, is without spiritual grace and produces not even the vegetables of which the Apostle speaks: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV, 2). With its roots dried up, all its verdure has been turned into aridity and desolation.

### (Verse 31)

“And your strength shall become like the ash of tow.”

Instead of “ash,” Symmachus translated ἀποτίναγμα, “that which is shaken off,” referring to what happens when tow is combed and whatever filth it contains is discarded.

Thus all the strength and pride of the sinful and wicked Israel, who abandoned the Lord and were therefore consumed, who sacrificed to idols and will blush for the gardens they chose, will be reduced to the refuse of tow, which is devoured by a light fire. For it follows:

“And his work”—that is, the work of your strength, or of the idolatry in which you had gone astray—“a tiny spark shall consume.”

“And both shall burn together, and there shall be no one to extinguish them.”

This means, namely, the knowledge of the Jews and all the works they perform; or the idol and Jerusalem, in which the idol was placed. When the Lord sets them ablaze, no one will be able to extinguish them.

We may also understand all these things of contrary doctrines: both teachers and disciples perish together, and all their work becomes fuel for the fire.

## Chapter II

### (Verse 1)

“The word that Isaiah, son of Amoz, saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.”

In the preceding Vision, which we have already explained, where the Septuagint translated “which he saw against Judea and against Jerusalem,” it is written in Hebrew, **AL JUDA UJERUSALEM** (על יהודה וירושלם); and in this, which is the second, the same wording is likewise contained.

**Note:** The Palatine manuscript reads somewhat more correctly: “Judah Uhirusalaim.”

**Note:** It is written thus. The manuscript copies that preserve the aspiration before *Ujerusalem* read *Hujerusalem*, according to the practice of ancient books. —MARTIAN.

I wonder why the Septuagint translators said in the former passage “against Judea and Jerusalem,” but in this one “concerning Judea and Jerusalem”—unless perhaps, because there the nation is called sinful, a people full of sins, an evil seed, sons of iniquity, rulers of Sodom, and a people of Gomorrah, a harlot city, and other things of this kind, they translated the sense rather than the word; whereas here, because prosperity is immediately promised—“It shall be in the last days: the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest, and the house of God on the summit of the mountains”—they understood the prophecy as concerning Judea and Jerusalem, not against Judea and Jerusalem.

Yet in the former passage also, after the threat, we read a promise of prosperity: “I will restore your judges as they were formerly, and your counselors as at the beginning; after this you shall be called the city of the righteous, the faithful city.” And in this passage, after the promises, there is a savage threat: “Behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, will remove from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong, all the strength of bread, and all the strength of water,” and what follows.

Therefore, according to the Hebrew, both in that vision and in this discourse—which Isaiah, son of Amoz, saw—we should understand the words as concerning Judah and Jerusalem, not against Judea and Jerusalem, nor “for Judah and Jerusalem,” as Symmachus translated, but simply concerning Judah and Jerusalem, so that both joyful and sorrowful things may be contained in it.

This too should be considered: there Isaiah sees a vision, whereas here he sees the Word that was in the beginning with God. In the former, while threatening the Jews, he proceeds to the salvation of the Gentiles; in this one, beginning with the salvation of the Gentiles and punishing Israel, he gathers believers from both callings into the Church of Christ.

### (Verse 2)

“And it shall be in the last days: the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains.”

We also read of the last days in Genesis. When Jacob called his sons and said, “Come, and I will announce to you what shall happen in the last days” (Gen. XLIX, 1), he afterward said to Judah, from whose seed Christ was born: “The ruler shall not depart from Judah, nor the leader from his loins, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he shall be the expectation of the nations.”

In these last days there will be a final hour, of which the Apostle John speaks: “My little children, it is the last hour” (I John II, 18). In that hour the stone cut from the mountain without hands grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth. From this mountain, according to the Septuagint, the prince of Tyre is said to have been wounded in Ezekiel (Ezek. XXVIII, 16).

This mountain is in the house of the Lord, for which the Prophet longs when he says:

**Note:** “One thing I asked,” etc. Jerome frequently reads it this way in his Commentaries, although in his translation of the Scriptures he used the feminine form: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.” Concerning this variation of readings he argues as follows in his Commentary on Ecclesiastes VII: “For whereas above, when interpreting the Hebrew text, we said, ‘one to one . . .,’ Symmachus translated it more plainly, ‘one to one . . .’ For what we customarily express absolutely and in the neuter gender—namely, ‘this I sought; this I wished to find’—the Hebrews pronounce in the feminine gender, as in the Psalm: ‘One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek,’ instead of ‘one thing.’” —MARTIAN.

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript reads, “One thing I asked,” and immediately afterward, “this I shall seek.” Martianus likewise retained “one thing” and “this,” and cites the testimony of the holy Doctor in Ecclesiastes VII: “What we customarily express absolutely and in the neuter gender—namely, ‘this I sought; this I wished to find’—the Hebrews pronounce in the feminine gender, as in the Psalm: ‘One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek,’ instead of ‘one thing.’”

“One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI, 4). Concerning this house Paul writes to Timothy: “But if I delay, so that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (I Tim. III, 15).

This house has been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, who themselves are also mountains, as imitators of Christ (Eph. II).

**Note:** The same manuscript reads, “Concerning this house and Jerusalem.”

Concerning this house the Psalmist cries out:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion; he shall not be moved forever, the one who dwells in Jerusalem. Mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. CXXIV, 1).

Therefore Christ also establishes his Church upon one of the mountains and says to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI, 18).

The holy man speaks similarly to the soul that longs and impatiently desires to see the house of God:

“Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. XLI, 6).

And again:

“These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me, for I shall pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, amid the voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of those who feast” (ibid., 5).

The Septuagint translated the passage, “The manifest mountain of the Lord, and the house of God above the summits of the mountains.” The prophet Micah also set down this testimony in the same words; I explained it in its proper place (Mic. IV).

“And it shall be exalted above the hills.”

The mountain that was shown and prepared on the summits of the mountains shall be exalted above the hills. Concerning these mountains and hills the bride also speaks in the Song of Songs:

“The voice of my beloved: behold, he comes, leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills. My beloved is like a gazelle or a fawn of deer upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song II, 8–9).

“And all nations shall flow toward it, and many peoples shall go.”

For all nations will serve him, to whom it was said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. II, 8), so that they may serve him, according to Zephaniah, under one yoke. The same prophet testifies concerning them: “From the borders of the rivers of Ethiopia they shall bring you offerings” (Zeph. III, 10).

And in the seventy-first Psalm we read: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall” (Ps. LXXI, 9). For in the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. II).

### (Verse 3)

“And they shall say: Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us his ways, and we shall walk in his paths.”

The nations and the peoples, not content with their own salvation, will exhort one another and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.” Above we explained which is the prepared mountain of the Lord and which is the house of the Lord upon the summit of the mountains.

The house of the Lord is called the house of the God of Jacob so that we may accept the Old Testament and, following Manichaeus, seek some other house outside the house of the God of Jacob.

When we have entered the house of the God of Jacob, then he will teach us his ways, by which we may walk toward him, and we shall walk in his paths, which others have also trodden.

**Note:** I would certainly wish that *tribuerunt* be rewritten as *triverunt*, “have trodden,” since the former makes no sense here, although it is read equally in the printed editions and the manuscripts.

Finally, when Jesus ascended the mountain, he taught his disciples the eight beatitudes and the other things contained in the Gospel discourse (Luke VI). Therefore the ways of the Lord must first be learned, and afterward we must walk in his paths.

“For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

All the nations and many peoples will therefore exhort one another and say: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord,” and the rest that follows: “For the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

It will be neither from Sinai, nor from the wilderness, nor from Mount Horeb, but from Mount Zion, upon which Jerusalem was built; and from Jerusalem, in which the Temple and the worship of God are found.

We read that the Lord often taught in the Temple (Matt. XIII), and that a prophet ought not to perish outside Jerusalem. Above, the word and the law were likewise mentioned together. The rulers are commanded to hear the word; the people are to receive the law with their ears. For whoever first practices the law afterward comes to the word of God.

Moreover, the Church was first founded in Jerusalem and spread churches throughout the whole world. We should also say that whoever is in the watchtower and in the vision of peace has both the law and the word of the Lord established in him.

Beautifully, he did not say, “In Zion and in Jerusalem the word and law of the Lord shall be and remain,” but “shall go forth,” signifying that all nations are to be watered with the teaching of God from that fountain.

“And he shall judge the nations and rebuke many peoples.”

Therefore there must also be judgment among the nations.

**Note:** The Vatican, together with the Palatine, reads: “There must be judgment between nations and nations.”

Nor are all unbelievers to be condemned with the same sentence; rather, according to the diversity of their merits, they will suffer different things. After he has judged the nations, then he will rebuke many peoples, or, as the Septuagint translated it, “a numerous people.”

Observe the order: the nations will be judged because they will believe. “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 18). But the numerous people, understood as Israel, will not be judged but rebuked, because it did not receive the Son of God who had been sent to it.

### (Verse 4)

“And they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into sickles.”

Every zeal for warfare will be turned toward peace, and throughout the whole world there will be concord instead of discord. Swords will be changed into plowshares and spears into sickles, so that, abandoning the fury of warfare, they may serve agriculture and cut down abundant harvests with sickles.

This may also be understood spiritually, when all the hardness of our heart is broken by Christ’s plow, and the thorns of vices are uprooted, so that the seed of God’s word may grow into fruit. Then we shall eat the labor of our hands, when “those who come shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV, 6).

“No nation shall lift up the sword against another nation, nor shall they train any longer for war.”

Let us review the ancient histories, and we shall find that down to the twenty-eighth year of Caesar Augustus—whose forty-first year was the year in which Christ was born in Judea—there was discord throughout the whole world, and that every nation burned with the zeal for waging war against its neighboring peoples, so that they killed and were killed.

**Note:** He appears to have taken this from Tertullian, who in chapter 8 of his book Against the Jews defines the time of the Savior’s birth as follows: “Cleopatra reigned jointly with Augustus for thirteen years; after Cleopatra, Augustus ruled for another forty-three years, for all the years of Augustus’ reign amounted to fifty-six. We see, then, that Christ was born in the forty-first year of Augustus’ reign, after Cleopatra’s death.” —MARTIAN.

**Note:** “In the forty-first year,” etc. At that time the human race enjoyed the deepest peace. Augustus had shortly before closed the temple of Janus, as Suetonius testifies in chapter 22 of his Life of Augustus: “The temple of Janus Quirinus, which had been closed only twice from the foundation of the city down to his time, he closed three times within a very short interval, peace having been secured by land and sea.” See also Eusebius, *Praeparatio Evangelica*, book I, chapter 4; Orosius, book VI, chapter 22, and book VII, chapter 3. Joseph Scaliger further indicates that this passage requires correction in his *Chronology of Eusebius*, p. 161. I do not, however, see Jerome’s error, since he says that discord existed throughout the whole world up to Augustus’ twenty-eighth year. Nor is he speaking there of the victory at Actium or of Augustus’ consulship; he merely indicates that not long before Christ’s birth all wars had ceased, and that the Lord Jesus was born in the forty-first year of Augustus’ reign. This was firmly maintained by the unanimous agreement of the ancient Church. —MARTIAN.

But when the Lord and Savior arose, when under Quirinius, governor of Syria, the first registration was made throughout the world, and peace was prepared for the teaching of the Gospel by the Roman Empire, then all wars ceased. They were no longer trained for battle throughout towns and villages; instead, the soldiers and Roman legions alone were assigned the task of waging war against barbarian nations, while the angelic hymn was fulfilled:

“Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace among people of good will” (Luke II, 14).

And in his days righteousness arose, together with an abundance of peace.

**Note:** The same manuscript reads: “and on earth peace among people,” etc. Compare the Eusebian-Jeromian *Chronicle* under Augustus’ forty-second year, which is the first year of Christ.

### (Verses 5–6)

“House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord; for you have rejected your people, the house of Jacob.”

After the calling of the Gentiles and the manifestation of the Lord’s mountain upon the summit of the mountains, the Prophet turns to his own people—that is, to the Jewish people, who are called the house of Jacob—and exhorts them to receive the light of truth and walk in the light of the Lord, since they are wandering in the darkness of error.

In a certain sense he sings that Davidic verse:

“Draw near to him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Ps. XXXIII, 6).

For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be exposed. But you, house of Jacob, house of my people, come with me, and let us walk together in the light of the Lord. Let us receive the Gospel of Christ and be enlightened by him who says: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12).

After speaking this to the Jewish people, seeing that their heart was impenitent and their soul hardened by the most stubborn unbelief, he turns his speech toward the Lord and says: “For this reason I exhort them to come to you and enjoy your light with me: because, according to the merit of their sins, you have abandoned your people, once the house of Jacob.”

### (Verse 7)

“For they were formerly filled, and they had diviners, like the Philistines.”

The Septuagint consistently translated *Philistines* as “foreigners.”

**Note:** “The Septuagint: ‘foreigners,’ etc.” Modern critics utter many absurdities concerning this passage. From it they wish to teach us that the letter *F* should be rejected from the book of Hebrew Names and that the Greek letter phi, φ, should be used in its place. They fail to observe that Jerome, in the book just mentioned, followed the order of the Latin alphabet and treated the letters *F* and *PH* interchangeably. —MARTIAN.

**Note:** See what we have said concerning the letter *P*, both elsewhere and in the book of Names.

The Septuagint translated the common noun instead of the proper name. It refers to the people now called Palestinians, as though they were Philistines, since the Hebrew language does not possess the letter *P* but uses the Greek phi in its place.

Thus the statement in the Psalms, in the enumeration of the other nations, “Foreigners have been subjected to me” (Ps. LIX, 10), does not signify all foreign nations but specifically the Palestinians.

He gives the reasons why God rejected his people, the house of Jacob: “For they were filled,” he says, as they had been at the beginning, “with diviners and omens,” and with every impurity of idolatry.

**Note:** “And with omens.” Earlier printed books read *dreams* instead of *omens*, contrary to the agreement of the manuscript codices. —MARTIAN.

We know from Moses’ writing that omens and auguries are not to be heeded. Such practices were found among the nations whom the Lord drove out from before Israel—the Canaanites, Amorites, and Hittites.

**Note:** The Vatican reads “dreams,” which the older printed books also prefer here and above instead of “omens.”

The interpreters of the Church explain this passage in different ways. Some wish it to signify that, once the Jewish people had been rejected, the Roman army entered the land that had formerly been promised; after the Jews were expelled, foreigners dwelt in Judea—settlers from various nations throughout the world, brought there by Titus, Vespasian, Hadrian, and the other rulers.

Others, however, think that this does not refer to Roman times but to an earlier period, before the land was devastated by the Babylonians, when, as is reported, they lived under wicked kings and were abandoned by the Lord.

**Note:** Two manuscripts read, “are reported to have done.”

“And they clung to foreign boys.”

For this the Septuagint translated: “And many sons of foreigners were born to them.” Symmachus: “And they applauded along with foreign boys.”

The Hebrew reads **JESPHICU** (יפיקו), which the Hebrews interpret as ἐσφηνώθησαν, “they were fastened together,” and which we translated as “they clung,” so that the shamefulness of the vices among the Jewish people might be displayed.

The Greeks and Romans once suffered from this vice to such an extent that even the most distinguished philosophers of Greece had public concubines.

**Note:** “They had publicly,” etc. Compare what Jerome himself says about Xenocrates and Socrates in his Commentary on Hosea I. Concerning Hadrian, the Eusebian Chronicle records: “Hadrian was highly educated in both languages, but insufficiently restrained in his love of boys.” And again: “Antinous, a royal boy of extraordinary beauty, died in Egypt. Hadrian, grieving for him intensely—for he had kept him among his favorites—enrolled him among the gods; a city was also named after him.” Whoever wishes may consult Isaac Casaubon’s notes on this catamite in the *Historia Augusta* of Spartianus. The city of Antinoopolis is also mentioned by the Roman Martyrology on September 22 and March 8. —MARTIAN.

See also *Against Jovinianus*, book II, p. 336, note h (here column 297, note a).

Hadrian, trained in the arts of philosophy, consecrated Antinous as a god and established a temple, sacrifices, and priests for him; from this the city and region of Egypt also received its name. Among prostitutes, boys also stood in the entrances of theaters, exposed to public lust, until, under the Emperor Constantine—

**Note:** “Until under Constantine,” etc. In the *Tripartite History*, book I, chapter 8, the following is drawn from Sozomen: “Moved by this consideration, Constantine restrained immoderate and lustful unions, which previously had not been prohibited at all, as can easily be understood by anyone who takes the trouble to examine the laws enacted concerning them.” —MARTIAN.

**Note:** Sozomen, book I, chapter 8, at the end, says that this was first done when Constantine issued a law against immoderate and dissolute unions: “He restrained immoderate and dissolute unions, which had previously not been prohibited at all, as may be learned from the laws enacted concerning them.” See also the law on the abduction of virgins and widows in the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 24, and Valesius’ commentary on the cited passage of Sozomen.**

—when the Gospel of Christ shone forth, both the unbelief of all the nations and this shamefulness were destroyed.

The Septuagint, however, indicates that their wives were violated, since they bore foreign sons to the Jews. Symmachus, by a circumlocution and in decent language, points to the same shamefulness of applauding boys.

### (Verse 8)

“And their land was filled with silver and gold, and there was no end to their treasures.”

Among the other vices of the land of the house of Jacob, the abundance of gold and silver is also enumerated. Alongside omens and diviners, horses and chariots—which God forbade the kings of Israel to multiply—and idols, which are the work of human hands, avarice is condemned.

Therefore the Lord commanded in the Gospel that we should not store up treasures for ourselves on earth, nor make treasures which a thief could steal, concluding with these words: “You cannot serve God and Mammon” (Matt. VI, 24).

Beautifully, the saying “The miser is always in need” is expressed by the Prophet in other words: “And there is no end to his treasures.” This does not mean that treasures have no end, but that the mind of those who possess them is never filled.

Both peoples, the Jews and the Romans, are reproached for avarice in these words. Greek and Latin histories alike report that no people was more avaricious than the Jewish and Roman peoples.

Therefore the law concerning the recovery of extorted money was established, and every day we see the Apostolic saying fulfilled: “You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal?” (Rom. II, 21).

**Note:** “The thief hears the judge,” etc. The manuscript copies read this way; in the printed editions *arguit*, “convicts,” is written instead of *audit*, “hears.” The variant readings seem not to differ greatly and are not significant. —MARTIAN.

The more thievish judge hears and condemns the thief, pronouncing in another person a sentence upon himself.

“And his land was filled with horses, and his chariots were innumerable.”

What is possessed against God’s command is not worthy of being counted. Hence it is said in the Psalms: “The horse is deceitful for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 17). And in Exodus: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV, 1). And in another Psalm: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. XIX, 8).

Both meanings may be understood: the Jewish people multiplied horses and chariots for itself against God’s command, and the land of Judea was filled with the horses and chariots of its conquerors.

### (Verse 9)

“And his land was filled with idols. They worshiped the work of their hands, which their fingers had made; and the human being bowed down, and the man was humbled.”

Where once the Temple and the worship of God stood, there the statue of Hadrian and the idol of Jupiter were placed. Many interpret this with reference to the testimony that we read in the Gospel: “When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place” (Mark XIII, 14).

They bowed down before the work of their hands: the human being, a rational animal, worshiped bronze and stone.

Some interpret these words of the Jews, saying that they did all these things before they were captured by the Babylonians, and that for this reason they were abandoned by God. Hence the conclusion of the chapter states: “Therefore do not forgive them.”

According to the allegorical sense, we can also say that every doctrine opposed to the truth worships the works of its hands, establishes idols in its land, and causes the human being to bow and the man to be humbled, unable to rise again, because he has been bound by the devil—unless the Lord raises him up, as in the case of the woman whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, so that she could look continually not toward heaven but toward the earth (Luke XIII).

“Therefore do not forgive them.”

For this the Septuagint translated: “And I will not forgive them.”

If God is speaking, it should be understood thus: “Because they have done such things, I will not spare them, nor forgive their innumerable sins.”

If the Prophet is speaking, the meaning is: “Therefore do not forgive those who have perpetrated such great crimes.”

If we understand the words of the Romans, the more accurate interpretation is that they overturned the Temple of God and did not worship the one who had granted them victory, but the idols made by their hands.

If, however, the words concern the Jews, the Prophet’s sentence is savage, as though he were praying against his own people, to whom he had said above: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.”

### (Verse 10)

“Enter into the rock; hide in a pit in the earth from the face of the fear of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty.”

I had indeed exhorted the people, saying: “House of Jacob, come, and let us walk in the light of the Lord.” But because the Lord rejected the people of Jacob—and he rejected them because they either did or suffered the things explained above—I therefore foretell the evils that are coming and urge you to enter the rocks and hide in caves from the face of the Babylonian or Roman army, when everything will be laid waste, according to what we read in the Gospel:

“Then they will say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the rocks, ‘Hide us’” (Luke XXIII, 30).

According to the allegorical sense, however, we are commanded to assume the strength of the rock before the face of the Lord’s majesty. Concerning this it is said: “The rock is a refuge for the rabbits” (Ps. CIII, 18), and, “You have exalted me upon a rock” (Ps. XXVI, 6).

Moses too is placed in a cleft of the rock so that he may see the back parts of God (Exod. XXXIII). And: “The people drank from the spiritual rock that followed them” (I Cor. X, 4).

The one who enters his room and, having shut the door, worships the Father is hidden in the rock, so that, established in an earthly body, he may not feel the storm of the passing world.

### (Verse 11)

“The lofty eyes of the human being shall be humbled, and the height of men shall be bowed down; but the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day.”

When the enemies have come, when the Babylonian or Roman sword has devastated the whole province, and armies of warriors have surrounded Jerusalem, neither wealth, nor nobility of birth, nor the power of rank will be able to defend anyone. There will be one captivity for all, and God alone will be exalted, whose anger no one will be able to escape.

Many understand these words of the day of judgment, when every creature will be humbled and bowed down in comparison with the divine glory and will recognize that it is nothing.

### (Verse 12)

“For the day of the Lord of hosts shall be against every proud and lofty person, and against every arrogant person.”

**Note:** Two manuscripts, the Vatican and Palatine, add: “and the rest.”

These words are joined to what precedes. “On that day,” he says, on which the Lord alone will be exalted—that is, on the day of the Lord’s vengeance—all the lofty, arrogant, and exalted will be subjected to captivity and the sword.

Μεταφορικῶς, “figuratively,” the statement concerns the great and the rulers: the more greatly they have exalted themselves, the more severely they will be brought low. For “the Lord resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V).

Those who understand the passage of the day of judgment think that “the proud,” “the lofty,” “the exalted,” and “the arrogant” signify the devil. In his pride he says:

“I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will sit upon the high mountain, above all the lofty mountains toward the north; I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV, 13–14).

Then the praise will be perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children, so that the enemy and avenger may be destroyed (Ps. VIII, 3).

### (Verse 13)

“And over all the lofty and upright cedars of Lebanon, and over all the oaks of Bashan.” And in the twenty-eighth Psalm it is sung: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars; the Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon and shatter them like a calf of Lebanon” (Ps. 28:5). And in the thirty-sixth Psalm: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 36:34).

[Note: Martian wrongly reads “in the thirtieth psalm only” [Col. 0049D] instead of “in the thirty-sixth” [Col. 0050D], as is in fact the case and as the manuscripts attest.]

The oaks of Bashan, which Aquila translated as δρῦας, Symmachus and Theodotion as βαλάνους, we know to be acorn-bearing trees. Although they produce fruit, it is food for pigs, not for human beings. Bashan is a region of Arabia, ruled by Og, who was called “king of Bashan”; the name is interpreted as αἰσχύνη, that is, “disgrace.”

[Note: Victorius’s wording is somewhat more polished than if we translate it as “confusion,” that is, σύγχυσιν, which signifies Babylon more than Bashan. In this matter he cites another passage of Jerome, in the commentary on Amos, chapter 4. Apart from the testimony of the manuscripts, we have thought that we may do nothing.]

If we choose to translate it as “confusion,” that is, σύγχυσιν, it signifies Babylon more than Bashan. Therefore the Lord’s vengeance will rise against all who lift themselves up in pride, perform works of disgrace, and roll about in the filth of lust.

But if a discerning reader asks why cedar wood has been placed in the temple of the Lord, and why in the 103rd Psalm we read, according to the Hebrew truth: “The trees of the Lord will be filled, the cedars of Lebanon which you planted; there the sparrows will make their nests” (Ps. 103:18); and why, among the other trees, the cedars are also summoned to the praises of the Lord; and why, at the coming of the Savior, when all the trees and woodland trees will applaud with their branches, it is written: “I will set in the thirsty land the cedar, the boxwood, the cypress, and the pine” (Isa. 41:19, according to the Septuagint); and why now the prophetic discourse threatens the day of the Lord against the cedars of Lebanon, this must be said: from the same class of human beings some are raised up to the kingdom, while others are dragged down to punishment. The cedars of Lebanon, which will be crushed because of their pride, are chosen when they have been of good fragrance and have said with the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:15).

### (Verse 14)

“And over all the lofty mountains, and over all the raised-up hills.” Just as mountains and hills are named in a positive sense according to the variety of virtues, so among the impious, according to the diversity of vices—and especially of pride—some are mountains and others hills. The day of the Lord will be over them. Concerning them it is written in Ezekiel: “Thus says Adonai the Lord to the mountains and hills: Behold, I will bring a sword upon you, and your high places will be laid waste, your altars will be broken down, and the rest” (Ezek. 6:3).

### (Verse 15)

“And over every lofty tower, and over every fortified wall.” Those who refer these words to the times of Vespasian and Hadrian say that what is written was fulfilled in a bodily sense: neither a lofty tower, nor the strongest wall, nor any multitude of ships or commercial enterprise could prevail against the force of the Roman army. The inhabitants of Judaea were seized by such terror that they themselves, together with their wives and children, sank into underground pits and sought out the deepest caves, along with the gold and silver which they thought would help them. For if the belly of gluttonous and luxurious people is their god, why should gold and silver not be called the god of the avaricious?

Others refer these things to the times of Babylon. Therefore, in accordance with the principles of allegorical interpretation, I shall examine each item individually.

A tower is built either for the fortification of a city or as a watchtower, so that an enemy approaching from far away may be seen. Each of us, therefore, ought to build a tower, first calculating the expense, lest, according to the Gospel parable (Luke 14), when he cannot complete the work, he be mocked. A well-constructed tower remains standing. But if, raised up in pride, it does not have firm foundations, it will fall upon the one by whom it was built, like the tower at Siloam, which killed eighteen people. Hence the Lord also says to those who hear: “If you do not repent, you will all likewise perish” (Luke 13:3).

In what follows we shall also read that the Lord built a tower in his vineyard, made a winepress, and surrounded it with a wall; but all these things were destroyed and laid waste because they had swollen with the empty arrogance of pride (Isa. 5).

Lofty walls are also built so that a city may not quickly be destroyed and may not lie open to enemies. Churches are surrounded by the wisest men and fortified by every kind of reasoning, lest any perverse doctrine prevail against the truth. Concerning such walls God speaks to Jerusalem: “Behold, I have painted your walls upon my hands, and they are always before my eyes” (below, 45:16, according to the Septuagint).

But if those who formerly attacked the Church, after learning the truth, pass over to the faith and fight for the Church which they had formerly attacked, then this will be fulfilled: “You will quickly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed” (ibid., 17).

In Leviticus also we read that if a house situated in a walled city is not redeemed within a year, it is secured to the purchaser as an everlasting possession; but if it is in villages and hamlets without walls, it can always be redeemed, and the purchaser’s price remains subject to change (Lev. 25).

### (Verse 16)

“And over all the ships of Tarshish, and over everything beautiful to look upon.”

For Tarshish, which all the translators rendered alike, only the Septuagint translated “sea.” The Hebrews think that in their own language the sea is properly called THARSIS; but when it is called IAM (), they say that this is not a Hebrew word but a Syriac one.

[Note: This is the opinion of the rabbis, to which the Greeks also agreed: the Paraphrast published by Corderius, Theodorus of Heraclea, and others. Yet I can scarcely believe that the Hebrews formerly thought this way; for, as Drusius also observed, it may even be questioned whether Tharsis signifies “sea” at all. It is even more remarkable that what follows is now said not in Hebrew but in Syriac. On the contrary, the Syrians say famma, which derives entirely from the Hebrew yam, just as the whole Syriac language does, although its form is so different.]

Jehoshaphat also had ships which he sent to Tarshish (1 Kings 22:49), but they were wrecked at Ezion-geber. Solomon too had ships which went to Tarshish (1 Kings 10:22); they returned after three years, bringing the king silver and gold, ivory and apes. But since both kings had sinned—one devoted to pleasure and loving foreign women, the other joining himself to the king of Samaria—both cases refer to pagans and heretics. In them there is nothing except the brilliance of eloquence, a meaning constructed by the devil’s art, dead speech—which is interpreted as being “in the teeth”—and the likeness of human reasoning, which is represented by the apes.

[Note: “And the meaning,” etc. In the earlier printed books we read: “And the meaning constructed by the art of dialectic.” MARTIAN. —Our manuscripts and Martian likewise prefer this reading. The older printed editions have “dialectic,” an art which Jerome regularly censures in heretics. See below, and also in the commentary on Hosea, chapter 5.]

Therefore we read in the Psalms: “With a violent spirit you will break the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. 47:8). And Isaiah speaks of these ships in the same way: “Woe to the wings of the ships which are beyond Ethiopia” (below, chapter 18:1, according to the Septuagint).

There are, on the other hand, good ships, concerning which it is said in the same Psalms: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters: they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 106:23–24). Those who are not idle amid the waves of this world, but work, carry the Lord’s merchandise, and hasten to reach the harbor of rest—these see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep when they have attained profound knowledge and, searching all things, have also beheld the deep things of God and his wonders.

Josephus thinks that Tarshish is Tarsus, a city of Cilicia. Others believe it to be a region of India, and say that by this name one of the twelve precious stones is also called—the stone which among us is called chrysolite—because of its resemblance to the color of the sea.

[Note: Chrysolite. The manuscript codices write this Greek name as κρυσόλιθος. Chrysolite is a golden or golden-colored gem which also contains a greenish or sea-colored hue; hence among the Hebrews it is called Tharsis, and among the Chaldeans Kerum jama, because of its sea color. Josephus, moreover, thinks that Tharsis is the Cilician city of Tarsus (Antiquities, book 1, chapter 6; likewise book 8, chapter 2). Concerning the stone called Tharsis or chrysolite, consult the Sacred Scriptures, Exodus 28:20 and Revelation 21:20. MARTIAN.]

It is better, however, to understand Tharsis simply as “sea” or “open sea.” For Jonah, sailing from Joppa, could not reach India, since it is not possible to sail to India by that sea; rather, he simply went out into the open sea and proceeded toward whatever islands he might reach.

[Note: “It is not possible to sail there.” I heard a modern geographer who strongly disagreed with Jerome; he maintains that it is possible to sail from Joppa to India. Yet I think it better to listen to a witness who has seen the Mediterranean Sea and the harbor of Joppa than to a recent conjecturer or one who relies upon hearsay. MARTIAN. —Compare Jerome on Jonah, chapter 1; also Pliny, book 5, chapters 13 and 31, and book 9, chapter 5; Solinus, chapter 38; Strabo, book 6; and finally Ovid, Metamorphoses, book 4, whose authority most clearly shows that Ethiopian India is meant, to which Jonah was sailing. On the strength of this testimony, Laurentius Valla frees Jerome from the charge of slander in his Elegances, book 5, chapter 6.]

And what follows—“and over everything beautiful to look upon,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “and over every beautiful appearance of ships”—is to be understood in the same sense: whatever appears beautiful in words and is constructed by human reasoning will be destroyed by the day of the Lord if it rises up against the knowledge of God.

### (Verse 18)

“And the sublimity of human beings will be bowed down, and the height of men will be humbled, and the Lord alone will be exalted on that day, and the idols will be utterly crushed.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts have: “and the strength of men will be lifted up,” etc.]

Human speech appears to possess reason only so long as it has not been compared with divine knowledge. But when falsehood approaches the truth like straw approaching fire, it is quickly consumed and perishes; and all doctrines of falsehood—which are now called idols because they are imitated and fabricated—will be utterly crushed.

### (Verse 19)

“On that day a man will cast away the idols of his silver and the images of his gold, which he made for himself in order to worship moles and bats; and he will enter into the clefts of the rocks and the caves of the stones, from the face of the terror of the Lord and from the glory of his majesty, when he rises to strike the earth.”

We have often said that silver and gold are understood as speech and thought. Although these have been given by God to human beings so that they may speak of God, or think of him, and praise their Creator, they abuse this gift in fashioning idols, according to what is written: “I gave them silver and gold, but they made Baal from my silver and gold” (Hos. 2:8).

When someone, terrified by the fear of the Lord, has first hidden idols in the cave of his own breast and concealed them in the hollows of the earth, not daring to bring forth what he had wickedly fashioned, he has made the first step. The second is that he casts away what he had previously carved and does not permit it to remain within him.

For “moles,” which we have translated, the Septuagint has “vain things”; Aquila has ὀρυκτά; Symmachus, “fruitless things”; and Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself, PHARPHAROTH ().

[Note: Montfaucon reports Aquila’s reading as follows. The Sangermanensis, the best and oldest of all the manuscripts, which usually renders the Greek words accurately, has ὀρυκτά, and so does Regius 3756. Colbertinus 2628 has oricta for ὀρυκτά; one Colbertinus alone has orictas. Another Sangermanensis of ours has ΟΡΥΚΣΑ. Guided by the authority of the manuscripts, we read ὀρυκτά. The old printed editions of Jerome have ὄρυγας. Drusius also read this and thought that it could signify moles, but I would scarcely believe this even if the reading were genuine. Martianaeus had read ὀρυκτάς.]

[Note: “He placed Pharpharoth.” This passage is entirely different in the Masoretic Hebrew text. For the Masoretes divide the name Pharpharoth into two words, laphyor peroth, which is interpreted as “for digging holes.” The Septuagint and Jerome make it a single word; Aben Ezra agrees with this: “They are written as two words,” he says, “but my opinion is that they are only one.” For pharpharoth, or phapharpharoth, Aquila wrote ὀρώκτας, not ὄρυγας, as the printed editions have. MARTIAN. —Our manuscripts differ from this one point in reading Farfaroth with f, as do two other Sangermanensis manuscripts, two Colbertini, and one Regius, according to Montfaucon. Nevertheless, it seems that the reading should be Hapharpharoth, or Hafarfaroth, with the initial radical letter of the verb. Bochart explains why moles would be called by this name in his Hierozoicon, part 1, book 3, chapter 35. The Hebrew has: [Hebrew text].]

It is an animal without eyes which is always digging the earth, turning up the soil, and eating the roots beneath; it is harmful to crops. The Greeks call it ἀσπάλαξ. The bat is a nocturnal bird, which received from them the appropriate name νυκτερίς, because it flies at night. It is a small animal, resembling a mouse, making itself heard not so much by voice or song as by a squeak. Although it appears to fly, it flees the light and cannot endure seeing the sun.

Idols are compared to such creatures: blind and dark things worshiped by the blind, and all doctrines opposed to the truth. When these have been abandoned on the day of the Lord, those who cast them away will enter into the clefts of the rocks and the caves of the stones, so that they may dwell not in the dust of the earth and worthless mud, but in firm reasoning, and may discover for themselves the various openings of the virtues through which they can reach the truth.

I have touched upon these matters briefly, as I was able, according to the allegorical sense. The Hebrews refer them to the times of Babylon and the overthrow of Jerusalem, when the Lord rose to strike the earth of the Jews.

### (Verse 20)

“Therefore cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is regarded as exalted.”

The Septuagint omitted this, and in the Greek manuscripts it was added by Origen under asterisks from Aquila’s edition. In Hebrew it reads as follows:

[Note: “Hedalu lachem,” etc. I dare not say how numerous and how great are the corruptions in Jerome’s text in the earlier printed books, lest some hostile critic accuse me of slander, as he did in his usual manner when he saw the published Prodromus of St. Jerome, in which I had spoken of the present corruption: “Let the fair-minded judge of these matters read this entire passage, and he will immediately perceive that nothing more corrupt could have been printed in Jerome’s works.” For what he himself censures in the Jews, semi-Jews, and Ebionites, they themselves inflict upon the holy Doctor through their corrupt reading of the Hebrew text, or of the word bama, which they read bamme with the blinded Jews who twisted the ambiguous expression toward an impious meaning so that they would not say anything glorious about Christ. I do not omit that several manuscripts have Eser for Aser and nesama for nasama. We read the Hebrew as: [Hebrew text]. MARTIAN. —Our manuscripts have Eser nesama baaffo, and I would prefer the text to be restored in this way. But the very learned Drusius thought that several further corrections should be made from the manuscripts: namely, Hedlu instead of Hedalu, since the manuscripts usually have Hedal; then Haadam instead of Hadam; finally, Bamma with a doubled m, although the manuscripts have a single one. For, he says, what follows demonstrates that the latter is correct: “If we wish to read ‘in which,’ we say Bamma; but if we say ‘lofty’ or ‘exalted,’ we say Bama.” Finally, in Nesab, according to ancient usage, the elision of the aspiration heth and its vowel is noted, although the complete word is Nehesab.]

HEDALU LACHEM MEN AADAM ASER NASAMA BAAPHPHO CHI BAMA NESAB HU.

Where we said, “he is regarded as exalted,” Aquila translated, “in whom this one is regarded.”

The Hebrew word BAMA (), or ὕψωμα, means “a high place” or “something lofty”; we read it in this sense both in the Books of Kings and in Ezekiel. Or else it means “in which,” and is written with the same letters—BETH, MEM, HE. According to the context, if we wish to read “in which,” we say BAMMA; but if we wish to read “lofty” or “exalted,” we say BAMA.

The Jews, therefore, understanding the prophecy to concern Christ, interpreted the ambiguous word in the worse sense, so that they might appear not to praise Christ but to regard him as worthless. For what consistency of words, what order of reasoning and meaning is there in saying: “Since these things are so, and the day of the Lord is coming, on which the entire condition of Judaea is to be overturned and all things crushed, I warn and command you to cease from the man who breathes and lives as we human beings do, because he is to be counted as nothing”? Would anyone praise a person in such a way as to say: “Take care not to offend him who is utterly worthless”?

Therefore the passage must be understood in the opposite way: “Since all these things are going to come upon you, and are proclaimed by the prophetic Spirit, I warn and command you to cease from him who, according to the flesh, is indeed a human being, possessing a soul, breathing and drawing breath through his nostrils as we human beings breathe and live; but according to the divine majesty, he is exalted, and is regarded and believed to be so.”

[Note: “Considering this silently within my own mind,” etc. Let the hostile-to-Jerome John Clericus, devoted to slandering the holy Fathers, now see whether the commentaries of the ascetic of Bethlehem defame the Septuagint interpreters by saying that those same translators did not wish to reveal clearly to the pagans the mysteries of their faith. Certainly anyone who reads this Socinian’s *Questions on Jerome* will find here the infamous stumbling-block of Clericus’s slander. Jerome further suspects, in his commentary on Jeremiah 17, that this prophecy was omitted by the Septuagint interpreters so that they might spare their own people. MARTIAN.]

Considering this silently within my own mind, I cannot find a reason why the Septuagint did not wish to translate into Greek so clear a prophecy concerning Christ. As for the others who did translate it but dragged the ambiguous wording toward an impious meaning, it is not surprising that they interpreted it badly and did not wish to say anything glorious about Christ, in whom they did not believe—namely, Jews or semi-Jews, that is, Ebionites.

[Note: Some copies have “cum ut,” that is, “as the Jews,” etc.]

But that Christ is exalted, or most high—who in another language among the Hebrews is called ELION ()—we read in the eighty-sixth Psalm: “Shall a man say to Zion, and a man was born in her? And he himself, the Most High, founded her” (Ps. 86:5). And in the Gospel: “And you, child, will be called the prophet of the Most High” (Luke 1:76).

And, not to draw out the discussion at excessive length—for in the exposition of the Holy Scriptures we must pursue truth, not contention—in this passage BAMA among the Hebrews does not mean “exalted,” but “the exalted thing,” that is, exaltation itself and sublimity. It is as though we were to say of someone: “He is not divine, but divination”; “he is not a stream, but the source”; “he is not a human being, but humanity itself.”

Origen interpreted this passage as follows: “Because it is said specifically of one man, it can also be referred to the Lord and Savior. The Prophet commands them to cease from him who is regarded as something great, although for the present he appears to be a human being and to have breath in his nostrils, as the other human beings breathe.”

## BOOK TWO

### 45–46

Having completed the first volume on Isaiah—which I dictated in a hurried discourse as I was able, not as I wished, seeking the meaning of the Scriptures rather than the words of polished speech—I shall now proceed to the second. Whatever strength I possess, and whatever willing devotion I have toward the Lord, I shall offer to him who spoke through the Prophet: “I multiplied visions, and I became like a likeness in the hands of the prophets” (Hos. 12:10).

Therefore I beg you, virgin of Christ, Eustochium, that while we struggle in the explanation of the Scriptures, you may raise your hands to the Lord with Moses, so that we who, coming out of Egypt, have crossed the Red Sea, may defeat Amalek, whose name is interpreted as “devouring” and “licking,” and may be able to say with you: “Blessed is the Lord my God, who trains my hands for battle and my fingers for war” (Ps. 143:1).

### (Chapter 3.—Verse 1)

“For behold, the Lord, the ruler of armies, will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the mighty and the strong: every support of bread and every support of water.”

Up to this point they think the passage concerns judgment. What follows, they say, concerns the captivity that was to come; some refer it to the Babylonians, others to the Romans. But it is better, as we said above, to refer everything to the Lord’s Passion.
