After his killing, all graces and gifts were taken away from the Jews, according to what is written in the Gospel: “The Law and the Prophets were until John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:13).

The sequence is this: “Because you did not cease from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, who was regarded as exalted, but instead shed the blood of the righteous and devised a most wicked plan, saying, ‘Let us bind the righteous, because he is useless to us’ (Wis. 2:12), therefore you will eat the fruit of your devices.”

Among the Jews after the Lord’s Passion nothing is strong, nothing is mighty; everything is weak and languid. No one among them can say: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13), Christ Jesus our Lord.

And because according to the Septuagint we read “the mighty” and “the mighty woman,” we can apply to “the mighty” the following: “Until we all attain to the perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:13).

As for “the mighty woman”: “I wish,” he says, “to present you all as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2).

The strength of bread and the strength of water are understood as every kind of food and drink. We read that Moses was on Mount Sinai and for forty days neither ate bread nor drank water (Exod. 34). Likewise, what is said to Adam must be understood in the same way: “In the sweat of your face you will eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Gen. 3:19). So too what the Savior says: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds through the mouth of God” (Matt. 4:4).

Therefore the strength of bread will be taken away from them—the one who says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). And the strength of water, concerning which the same Lord said: “Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst; rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

Concerning such bread we also read in Proverbs: “Open your eyes, and be filled with bread” (Prov. 20:13).

[Note: Supply “and he will take away,” or something similar.]

[Note: Since Jerome expressed this entire sense from the Commentaries of Eusebius, he translated these words almost literally:

Ἰουδαῖοί γε μὴν ἔχουσι μὲν τὸν ἄρτον καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ· ἔτι πολυπραγμονοῦσι γὰρ τὰ Μωσέως γράμματα, καὶ ἀναγινώσκουσι τὸν νόμον· ἐπειδὴ δὲ γινώσκουσιν οὐδέν, οὐκ ἔχουσι τὴν ἰσχὺν τοῦ ἄρτου, οὔτε μὴν τὴν ἰσχὺν τοῦ ὕδατος, etc.

“That is: The Jews indeed have bread and water, for they continue to examine the writings of Moses and read the Law; but since they understand nothing, they do not possess the strength of bread, nor indeed the strength of water,” etc.]

The Jews have bread, but without strength; they have waters, but without power. For they read the Scriptures but do not understand them. They hold the parchment, but they have lost Christ, who was written upon the parchment (1 Cor. 3). They are nourished with milk, like little children, and not with solid food. And because they have lost their strength and are weak, they eat vegetables. Solid food belongs to athletes; it both sustains human life and provides strength to those who live (Rom. 14).

Another Prophet also testifies that this kind of bread and water will be taken away from the Jews, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will send a famine upon the earth—not a famine of bread nor a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the Lord” (Amos 8:11).

### (Verse 2)

“The mighty man and the warrior, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder.”

For “the mighty man,” which stands alone in the Hebrew, the Septuagint translated two words together, “giant and mighty,” wishing the same person to be both giant and mighty. We have spoken above about the mighty man.

We read of “giant” in a positive sense, that is, of the Lord Savior, in the eighteenth Psalm: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the highest heaven, and his circuit reaches to its highest point” (Ps. 18:6).

But if we read of Nimrod the giant (Gen. 10), who was a hunter before the Lord, and of the giants (Gen. 6), because of whom the Flood came upon the earth, the word must be understood in the opposite sense.

We understand “warrior” historically in this way: they have been taken captive and remain servants to this day; they have not laid aside the yoke of servitude. They do not even have judges of their own, but are subjected to Roman judges, to such an extent that the Roman rulers judge those of their princes who appear to hold authority among the people.

It must also be said that among them there is no warrior learned in the Law and possessing the knowledge of judgment; everything is vain, transitory, and full of folly.

That the prophet has ceased to exist among them is beyond doubt. According to the Hebrew, we ask how we should interpret “diviner,” which all have translated as “divine,” except the Septuagint, who translated it as “one who makes conjectures.” It must be said that future events are often also announced by diviners, as we read concerning Balaam the diviner, and concerning the diviners of the five Palestinian cities—Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron, and Ashdod—who give counsel concerning how the ark of the Lord should be sent back (1 Sam. 6).

The meaning is: both true and false things will alike be taken away from the Jews.

The elder, whom the Septuagint translated as “presbyter,” is understood to have been taken away from the Jews—the one who knew that presbyters are chosen in the Holy Scriptures for merit and wisdom, not for age. For elders have not ceased to exist among the Jews; we often see them reach extreme old age. And in Daniel we read, according to Theodotion, of two elders who had grown old in days of evil (Dan. 13).

[Note: At the beginning of Daniel we read this. The churches of Christ read the book of Daniel according to Theodotion’s edition, in which the story of Susanna was placed at the beginning of the volume; Jerome moved it to the end because it is not found in the Hebrew text. This is now near the end of his book, where it is entitled “The Eleventh Vision.”]

Moses too is commanded to choose elders whom he knows to be elders (Exod. 18). And the Apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy concerning what kind of presbyter should be chosen (1 Tim. 5). Hence it is said in Proverbs: “The glory of the elders is their gray hair” (Prov. 20:29).

What is this gray hair? Without doubt, wisdom, concerning which it is written: “The gray hair of human beings is prudence” (Wis. 4:8).

Although we read that people lived nine hundred years and more, from Adam to Abraham (Gen. 24), no one was first called a presbyter, that is, an elder, except Abraham, who is shown to have lived many fewer years. Hence John, after addressing children and young men, also writes to the elders, saying: “I have written to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2:13).

Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, also lost the kingdom because he refused to listen to the elders (1 Kings 12).

### (Verse 3)

“A prince over fifty.”

Συνεκδοχικῶς: the whole is designated from a part. For just as those who command one hundred soldiers are called centurions, and those who command a thousand are called chiliarchs—which we call tribunes, from the fact that they preside over a tribe—so in the Israelite army those who were in command of fifty soldiers were called “fifties.”

Hence we also speak of decans, who command ten men. Nor is it surprising that among the Jews the entire dignity of warriors has perished, since they have no authority to serve under the sword or bear arms.

Because the number fifty is always associated with repentance, and because Christ is the prince of repentance and the head of those who are saved through repentance, let us briefly unfold the mysteries of this number.

In Genesis we read that Abraham said to the Lord that if fifty righteous people were found in a city, the city should be saved. And in Numbers there is the famous festival of seven weeks, that is, Pentecost.

The Jubilee, too—that is, the year of remission, which is formed by seven weeks of years, namely forty-nine years, in which the trumpets sound and the ancient possession returns to everyone—contains this mystery.

Hence David writes the Psalm of repentance under the number fifty.

We also read in the same book of Numbers that from the spoils and plunder the priests receive every fiftieth person, both human and animal, and the Levites receive every fiftieth, since they guard the doors of the tabernacle.

The Gospel parable in which two debtors are mentioned, one owing five hundred denarii and the other fifty, also refers to this interpretation (Luke 7 and 16).

Hence the Apostle, writing to the Ephesians, to whom he had unfolded all the mystical meanings, wishes to remain until Pentecost, until they are perfectly converted to the Lord, saying: “For a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries” (1 Cor. 16:9).

[Note: Victor restores the text as “in Leviticus,” since in Numbers only the bare name of the chapter—namely, chapter 28—is found, the matter having already been explained in Leviticus. Hence shortly afterward he substitutes the book of Leviticus for “we also read in the same book of Numbers.” Nothing in the manuscripts, however, supports him.]

The devil also imitates the Israelite army. Jethro had given Moses counsel through his kinsman to appoint over the people tribunes, centurions, and leaders of fifty (Exod. 18).

[Note: The scribe of the Vatican manuscript inserts this gloss here: “It should be noted that Jethro is called his father-in-law, although in Exodus we read that Raguel was Moses’ father-in-law.”]

Hence the wicked king (2 Kings 1) sends two leaders of fifty, with the soldiers subject to them, to bring Elijah before him; they were consumed by divine fire. But the third was saved because, having turned to prayer, he had learned the mystery of repentance.

Therefore the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge that the Lord is perfect or the leader of fifty, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (John 8:57). But he, knowing that he was not only the leader of penitents but also of the righteous, answered: “Before Abraham was, I am” (ibid., 58).

That the Lord is the leader of fifty we can understand from one festival, concerning which he says: “The Son of Man is Lord of the Sabbath” (Matt. 12:8). If he is Lord of the Sabbath, then also of the Kalends; if of the Kalends, then also of Passover, that is, of Unleavened Bread; if of Passover, then also of the Jubilee; if of the Jubilee, then also of Tabernacles; if of Tabernacles, then also of Pentecost, which is reckoned according to the number fifty.

### (Verse 4)

“And the honorable in appearance, and the counselor.”

For the two expressions—“honorable in appearance” and “counselor”—the Septuagint translated one expression: “an admirable counselor.”

Among the other graces, the Lord will also take this away from Judaea: that they will have no counselor, but will do everything without counsel.

And the Greek poets say:

[Note: “A commendable poet,” etc. A similar saying appears in Cicero, *Pro Cluentio*: “They say that he is wisest who himself thinks of what is needed; next to him is the one who obeys another’s good discoveries.” The Greek poet cited by Jerome is Hesiod of Ascra, who in his poem *Works and Days*, line 290, has the following:

Οὗτος μὲν πανάριστος ὃς αὐτῷ πάντα νοήσει·  
Ἐσθλὸς δ’ αὖ κακεῖνος ὃς εὖ εἰπόντι πείθηται.

“That one is best of all who understands everything for himself; but he too is good who obeys the one who speaks well.”]

Again, that man too is good who obeys one giving good advice. MARTIAN.]

That famous and admirable saying is worthy of praise: “The first is blessed who is wise by himself; the second, who listens to the wise.” But whoever lacks both is useless, both to himself and to everyone else. Hence we also read in our books: “Let your friends be many, but your counselor one in a thousand” (Eccl. VI, 6). And again: “Do everything with counsel” (Prov. XIII, 10); and he will give you a remarkable counselor. Senate decrees are also so called, and the Roman leaders were once called consuls, either from counseling the citizens or [Col. 0062D] from directing everything by counsel.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript agrees almost with the old editions: “or conducting all things with counsel.”] 51 We too have our senate in the Church: the assembly of presbyters. Since, then, among the other things Judah has also lost its elders, how can it have counsel, which properly belongs to the elders?

And a wise architect. In place of this Aquila translated “the wisest of craftsmen,” to show that they once had many craftsmen. Such was Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and skill, so that he was a most accomplished artisan in every work—not only in gold and silver, but also in bronze and the other materials Moses lists—when he built the Tabernacle of God (Exod. XXXI). Since they have therefore lost their architects, all the grace of building has been transferred to the Church. Hence the apostle Paul says: “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (I Cor. III, 10). Jeremiah too was an architect, for he not only uprooted, demolished, [Col. 0061C] and destroyed, but also built (Jerem. XVIII). Hence the same Apostle says: “We are God’s field, God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9). Our Lord too is called the builder of walls (Eph. II). And in the Gospel the son of the craftsman is taunted, though he established all things (Matt. XIII). In the Book of Kings we also read that King Solomon sent for and brought Hiram the Tyrian, the son of a widow, who was from the tribe of Naphtali and whose father was a Tyrian, a worker in bronze. He came to King Solomon and made all the works for him. In this there is a type of the Church that was to be built: he was born not only from the tribe of Judah, but also from Naphtali and from a Tyrian father, and his mother was a widow because she had lost her first husband (III Kings VII). “But the children of the deserted woman are many more” [Col. 0061D] “than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. XV). We also read in the Book of Chronicles of the Valley of Craftsmen: “Seraiah begot Joab, the father of the Valley of Craftsmen; for there were craftsmen there” (I Chron. IV, 14). They are said to dwell in a valley because knowledge did not inflate them; rather, they followed Jesus in humility and gentleness, and could say with the Apostle: “For I am the least of the Apostles, unworthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV, 9). And elsewhere: “We know in part and we prophesy in part, and now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 9).

And prudent in mystical speech. For this the Septuagint translated “a prudent hearer”; Theodotion, “a prudent enchanter”; Aquila, “a prudent whisperer”; Symmachus, “prudent in mystical speech”—and we have followed him here. First, according to the Septuagint, it must be said that, among the other spiritual gifts, a prudent hearer is also necessary in the Church. “To one is given prophecy; to another, the discernment of spirits” (I Cor. XII, 10). Hence among the Jewish people priestly ranks had been established to distinguish prophets from false prophets: that is, to understand who spoke from the Spirit of God and who from the opposing spirit. Let us read Jeremiah. But the prudent man of mystical speech (Jerem. XIV), or “whisperer,” and, as Theodotion wished, “enchanter,” seems to me to be an educated and practiced man, learned both in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel and the Apostles, who can heal each disturbance of the soul by his teaching and restore it to a sound state of mind: so that the fornicator receives chastity, the glutton moderation, and the former miser gives alms.

[Note: An old glossator in the Vatican manuscript adds that ganeo is to be understood as a spendthrift or a glutton.] Search through all the synagogues of the Jews, and you will not be able to find a teacher who commands holiness and teaches that poverty should be pursued after riches have been despised. David spoke in the Psalm about such enchanters against serpents and asps—that is, against sinners who have abandoned the justice of God: “Sinners are estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehoods. Their fury is like the fury of a serpent, like a deaf asp that stops its ears, which does not hear the voice of enchanters, or of the magician who practices his art wisely” (Ps. LXVII, 4 ff.). Every word of the Apostle is an enchantment against serpents and asps, but sinners and heretics do not hear it because they close their ears lest they hear the truth.

(Vers. 4.) And I will give boys as their princes. If this is said in the person of the Prophet—“For behold, the sovereign Lord of hosts will take away from Jerusalem and from Judah the strong man and the strong woman, all the strength of bread, all the strength of water,” and the rest—how does the same prophet now say: “I will give boys as their princes, and the effeminate will rule over them”? Therefore, while the Prophet is speaking according to prophetic custom, God suddenly speaks through the Prophet in his own person and says: “I will give boys as their princes.” For after removing those things that I had previously given and, as though in anger, had taken away as good things, I shall now instead give evil things. I have taken away the old man, the man of fifty years, the remarkable counselor, the wise architect, and the prudent hearer, and so forth. In their place I will give boys as princes. Those who have lost the presbyter, such as the preceding passage described—and Abraham was first called a presbyter—properly receive young men as princes (Gen. VII). Concerning them we also read in Ecclesiastes: “Woe to you, land whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning. Blessed are you, land whose king is the son of nobles” (Eccl. X, 16). Such was the youthful king Rehoboam, son of Solomon, who followed the counsels of young men (III Kings XII). He was not young in age, but in wisdom; otherwise, he is reported to have received the kingdom when he was more than forty years old. Conversely, Solomon was twelve years old when he assumed power, and because he possessed wisdom he was not called a boy. For there was in him breadth of heart and an extent of wisdom as great as the sand on the seashore. Hence the Apostle also writes to Timothy: “Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV, 12). Whoever is young in age is old in maturity. Daniel too, according to Theodotion, was called a boy before he judged (Dan. XIII). But after God stirred up the spirit within him and he judged the elders, he received the dignity of a presbyter.

To Jeremiah also, who had said to the Lord who was sending him, “You who are sovereign, Lord: Behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am young” (Jerem. I, 6), the Lord replied: “Do not say, ‘I am young’; for before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came out of your mother’s womb I sanctified you and appointed you as a prophet to the nations” [Col. 0063C]. For this reason, I think, the Apostle also commands young widows (II Tim. V) to take husbands, become heads of households, and raise their children, because many have turned back after Satan. And when they have grown wanton against Christ, they wish to marry, bearing condemnation because they have nullified their first faith. Nor is a widow supported by ecclesiastical provisions unless she is sixty years old and possesses maturity both of conduct and of age. Someone might also think that what the Apostle forbids (I Tim. III)—that a bishop should be a novice—pertains to this, because he is a child in faith, lest, puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil. The devil’s judgment is nothing other than pride, because of which he fell from the heavenly realms. Hence the Savior says: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke XX, 18).

And the effeminate will rule over them. In Hebrew it is written THALULIM (𐤕𐤋𐤋𐤉𐤌), which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as “mockers”; Aquila, ἐναλλάκτας, “those who change themselves and practice exchanges of disgrace.” Such men as these we read of in the Book of Judges in the account of the Levite’s concubine at Gibeah (Judg. XIX). Let us consider the patriarchs of the Jews, and the young men or boys, effeminate and overflowing with luxury, and we shall see that the prophecy has been fulfilled. We may call the teachers of the people of Israel “mockers,” since they devour God’s people as though they were bread and perversely interpret the holy Scriptures, mocking the foolishness of their disciples.

[Note: Eusebius is being imitated; these are his words: “Who, then, seeing those called patriarchs among the Jews—truly young men, not in the age of their bodies but in their souls, incomplete and lacking understanding—and their other teachers, would not say that they are mockers?” Understand “patriarchs” as referring to those after the destruction of Jerusalem, and see the Theodosian Code, Book XVI, title 8.]

(Vers. 5.) And the people will fall, man against man, each against his neighbor; the boy will be insolent toward the old man, and the ignoble toward the noble. When young men are princes and mockers of the Lord, such as the prophetic word describes, then no order of dignity, age, or learning will be preserved. Rather, boys will rebel against old men, the ignoble against the noble, and they will all fall against one another. And the Apostolic saying will be fulfilled: “By biting and devouring one another, you have been consumed by one another” (Gal. V, 15). Josephus writes that this happened to the Jewish people under Titus, son of Vespasian (Book V of The Jewish War), and that, when they were being attacked by the Romans, Jerusalem was divided by faction into three parts: some held the citadel and the Temple, others the lower part, and others the upper part of the city.

(Vers. 6.) For a man will seize his brother, a member of his father’s household: “You have clothing; be our prince. But this ruin is under your hand.” In place of “ruin,” Symmachus and Theodotion translated “weakness,” and the Septuagint “food.”

[Note: Clearly through an obvious error they substituted [an unreadable term] for [another unreadable term], and Monfaucon also notes this; they read “cooked” or “cooking.”]

This indicates the scarcity of people and, above all, the shortage of everything: whoever possesses food and clothing is considered powerful, rich, and renowned. But what he says according to the Hebrew—“This ruin is under your hand”—has this meaning: “Let our misery and calamity be sustained and protected by your help.” We must also consider that each person chooses a prince for himself, and that there is factional conflict in the choice of princes, since some consider one person and others another worthy of rule. They do not say to them, “Your possessions, wealth, and revenues will be able to sustain us,” but rather, “This weakness of mine—or this food of mine—will be healed by and depend upon your decision.”

(Vers. 7.) And on that day he will answer, saying: “I am not a physician, and there is no bread or clothing in my house; do not appoint me as prince of the people.” In place of “physician,” Symmachus and the Septuagint translated “prince”; Theodotion, ἐπιδεσμεύοντα, “one who binds wounds and provides for health.”

[Note: In the Palatine manuscript, in Latin letters, epidesmeunta. But when the holy Doctor says that “he will answer” is not found in the Hebrew, this seems false to Martianus and other learned men, since it is clearly written as “he will take” or “he will restore.” Yet in the more accurate books that word is written with a circellus. This Masoretic sign indicates that in the oldest volumes—whether written by the Prophets themselves or revised by Ezra—such words were either written differently or were entirely absent from other exemplars. Such may have been the form used by Jerome.]

“‘He will answer’”—[Note: “It is not found in the Hebrew. In Hebrew is jissa, that is, ‘he will take,’ which the Septuagint translates very well as ἀποκριθεὶς, ‘answering,’ according to the expression frequently used in the Gospel, ‘But answering, he said.’ The same word, ‘he will answer,’ is read by all the interpreters—Chaldean, Syriac, and Arabic. It therefore appears that Jerome was mistaken here, unless he used a defective Hebrew exemplar. MARTIAN.”]—is not found in the Hebrew, but has been added from the Septuagint. In the Hebrew, the words written above are followed by this: “On that day he will say, ‘I am not a physician,’” and the rest. The speaker will be the one who has been elected as prince.

And just as the people desire to have as prince the person whom they understand to be richer in comparison with themselves, so the man who is elected, considering his poverty and weakness, declares himself unworthy of the honor conferred and unable to heal their vices—that is, to tend the sick, give food to the hungry, and clothe the naked—since he himself can scarcely sustain himself. Therefore, let us not immediately submit to the judgment of the multitude; but those elected to leadership should recognize their measure and humble themselves beneath the mighty hand of God, because “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V).

How many who have neither bread nor clothing, while they themselves are hungry and naked, possessing neither spiritual food nor having preserved Christ’s unbroken tunic, promise others both nourishment and clothing; and, though full of wounds, boast that they are physicians. They do not observe the Mosaic command: “Provide another whom you may send,” nor the other instruction: “Do not seek to become a judge, lest you be unable to remove iniquities” (Eccl. VII, 6). Jesus alone heals all sicknesses and infirmities. Of him it is written: “He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds” (Ps. CXLVI, 3).

56 (Vers. 8, 9.) For Jerusalem has fallen, and Judah has collapsed, because their tongue and their inventions are against the Lord, provoking the eyes of his majesty. The recognition of their faces answered them, and they proclaimed their sin like Sodom; they did not conceal it. The Prophet is speaking here, not—as many suppose—the man who had been elected prince. He says that no one wishes to rule over the sinful people because both Judah and Jerusalem—both the city and the province of Judea, or the tribe of Judah—have fallen together. He gives the reasons for their impiety: they blasphemed against the Lord and said, “Take away, take away, crucify such a man; we have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 15–16). By the fury of their tongue they provoked the most merciful Lord to bitterness.

[Note: The Palatine manuscript reads: “And the recognition of their faces will answer them.”]

“The recognition of their faces will answer them”—that is, they received their own sins; or, as the Septuagint translated it, “The shame of their faces stood against them”—that is, they always kept their own offenses before their eyes.

[Note: “The shame of their faces,” and so forth. At this point the printed books published before our edition also add the Greek words of the Septuagint translators, which are not found in Jerome’s manuscript copies. We have tried to remove almost innumerable interpolated passages of this kind. MARTIAN.]

And just as the Sodomites, sinning with complete freedom and having no shame at all in their crime, said to Lot, “Bring the men out to us, so that we may have intercourse with them” (Gen. XIX, 5), so these men, publicly proclaiming their sin, advertised it and had no shame whatsoever in blaspheming. For the second plank after shipwreck, and the consolation of misery, is to conceal one’s impiety. Hence they are also called the princes of Sodom.

[Note: “Because they had Sodomite sins,” and so forth. Here too the books printed before ours add the word “repentance,” which is superfluous according to the evidence of the manuscript copies and according to Jerome’s judgment. MARTIAN. The Vatican manuscript reads: “who had Sodomite sins.”]

(Vers. 10, 11.) Woe to their soul, because evils have been repaid to them. “Say to the righteous that it is well, because they will eat the fruit of their inventions. Woe to the wicked, for evil will come upon him; the recompense of his hands will be done to him.” According to the Hebrew and the other interpreters, this has the following meaning: “Woe to them, because they have received their own crimes.” Therefore, you who hear, or who read the Prophet’s book, praise the justice of God, because he has done well, because the wicked have eaten the labor of their hands. And woe to the wicked people for evil: they have received what they deserved. The man who handed over his prince to Roman power is himself subject to Roman servitude.

According to the Septuagint interpreters, who said, “Woe to their soul, because they devised an evil plan against themselves,” 57 saying, “Let us bind the righteous, because he is useless to us,” it plainly refers to Christ’s Passion: they devised an evil plan not so much against the righteous as against themselves and their own soul, and now they eat the fruit of their works. For “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Gal. VI, 5–8), and each person will bear his own burden.

(Vers. 12.) My people—those who exact from them have plundered them, and women have ruled over them. In place of “women,” which only Symmachus translated, and which in Hebrew is NASIM (נשים), Aquila and the Septuagint translated ἀπαιτοῦντας, “those who exact”; Theodotion, δανειστὰς, that is, “moneylenders.” The prophetic word speaks against the scribes and Pharisees, who, for the sake of sordid gain and in order to receive tithes and firstfruits, denied the Son of God. It does not call them teachers, scribes, and doctors, but exactors (Luke XX), who consider piety a means of profit. They devour not merely widows’ houses, as the Apostle says, but the whole people. And, accusing their luxury and shameful conduct, it calls them not only exactors, so that they appear to extort money from the unwilling, but also women, because they do everything for lust and are devoted to pleasures.

Let us therefore take care that we too do not become exactors among the people; let us ensure that, in accordance with the impious Porphyry, matrons and women do not become our senate, ruling over the Churches, and that favor among the priestly order is not determined by women.

[Col. 0066D] (Vers. 13.) My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy—or confuse—the way of your steps. He had called the scribes and Pharisees exactors, not teachers; and above, mockers, who, for the sake of gifts that blind even the eyes of the wise, not only failed to rebuke the sinners among the people but, for the sake of wealth and profit, lifted them up with praise, calling them blessed, pillars of God’s house, and the other things flatterers usually say.

The true ecclesiastical teacher is therefore one who provokes tears, not laughter; who rebukes sinners; who says that no one is blessed, no one happy; and who does not anticipate the judgment of his Judge, since holy Scripture says: “Do not call anyone blessed before death” (Eccl. II, 30). We also read elsewhere (Prov. XXVII, 14): “He who blesses his friend in a loud voice in the morning is no different from one who curses.” Therefore, scorning human judgments, let us neither be lifted up by their praises nor saddened by their slanders. Let us walk on the straight way and along the paths worn by the holy Prophets. Let us hear the prophet Jeremiah saying: “Stand in the ways and see, and ask about the everlasting paths of the Lord, which is the good way, and walk in it” (Jer. VI, 16). But if at some time we go astray and, like human beings, proceed along a crooked road, let us await the Lord’s promises through Ezekiel, where he says: “I will give them another way and another heart” (Ezek. XXXVI).

The exactors, however, perverted and confused the way of the Lord, so that, having the key of knowledge, they neither entered themselves nor allowed the people to enter; instead, they made them lose the way of truth, which speaks in the Gospel: “I am the way, and the life, and the truth” (John XIV, 6).

(Vers. 13, 14.) The Lord stands to judge, and stands to judge the peoples. The Lord will come to judgment with the elders of his people and with its princes. The people, deceived through simplicity and ignorance, is still called God’s people; and for this reason it is judged, so that it may be saved. The Lord does not sit in the posture of one judging, as we read in Daniel: “Thrones were placed, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII, 9); rather, he stands to judge and stands in order to judge the people, wishing those to stand whose way had been destroyed.

[Col. 0067D] Against the princes [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “with the princes and also with the presbyters,” and shortly afterward, “he will come.”] and presbyters of his people he comes to judgment, not in order to judge but in order to be judged together with them, giving them an opportunity for defense if they are able to offer any reply, according to what is said in the fifty-first Psalm: “That you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (v. 6). We read something similar in the prophet Micah (chap. VI), which we have interpreted in its proper place. Therefore, the present passage is understood as referring to the Pharisees and the Deuteronomists (Δευτερωταί). I think that what existed among the elders and princes in the ancient people is now found among presbyters and bishops.

[Col. 0067D] For you have devoured my vineyard.

[Note: Two manuscripts, together with the common translator, do not add “my.”]

The plunder of the poor is in your houses. Why do you crush my people, and why do you grind down—or, as the Septuagint translated it, confuse—the faces of the poor? He preserves the prophetic custom of suddenly changing speakers. Above, the Lord himself had said: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you”; and afterward the Prophet had added: “The Lord stands to judge; the Lord will come to judgment.” Therefore, after the Prophet, the Lord himself, who had come to judgment with the elders of his people and its princes, speaks to them and rebukes the guilty: “Why do you devour my vineyard?” Concerning it is written: “You brought a vine out of Egypt” (Ps. LXXIX, 9). And in this same prophet: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V, 7). In the Gospel too the Lord leased this vineyard to the worst husbandmen, who killed the son of the master of the household when he was sent to them (Matt. XXVIII).

“The plunder of the poor,” he says, “is in your houses.” Understand “poor” either simply as the person who needs alms, or certainly as “poor in spirit,” of whom it is written: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Ps. XL, 1). And the Apostle Paul says: “Only that we should remember the poor” (Gal. II, 10). What follows—“Why do you crush my people, and why do you grind down, or confuse, the faces of the poor?”—is plainly addressed to the princes of the Jews.

It can also be applied to our own princes if they crush the people subject to them, publicly rebuke and shame the poor when they sin, yet do not dare even to utter a sound against the rich when they commit worse sins. And the plunder of the poor is in their houses when they fill their treasuries and abuse the resources of the Church for their pleasures; when they either keep for themselves or distribute among their relatives the public offerings given for the support of the poor; and when they make the poverty of others into wealth for themselves and their own people.

[Note: Up to this point the printed editions read “not even a single word”; in other manuscripts, “not even a sound,” and so forth. We have substituted the interjection “mu.” On this see Varro, Book VI. Elsewhere the holy Doctor writes, in Letter 12: “I have already sent ten letters . . . while you do not deign even to make a sound.” Lucilius:

“Never to praise a man, nor ever to utter a sound.”]

(Vers. 15.) And the Lord said: Because the daughters of Zion have become haughty, have walked with an outstretched neck, and have gone about with glances of their eyes, clapping and walking, and proceeding with measured steps.

Above, both the people and the princes had been rebuked by the Prophet and by the Lord. Now the prophetic word turns to the women, of whom he had previously said, “And women have ruled over them,” so that they do not consider themselves strangers to the crime. On account of their luxury and wantonness, the exactors have devoured the Lord’s vineyard; the plunder of the poor is in their houses; they have crushed his people and confused the faces of the poor.

Some think that these are literally the women of the Jews; others interpret them metaphorically as the cities of Judea, which are called the daughters of Zion—that is, the smaller cities, villages, and towns. Hence in the Book of Joshua the names of the cities are listed according to each tribe (Josh. XV), and afterward the villages and fortified settlements are described and called daughters.

Others, according to the tropological interpretation, consider the women to be souls. If these walk with an outstretched neck and raise themselves up in pride, and pursue not manly firmness but the dissolution of women, they are rebuked by the prophetic word and lose all the ornaments of the virtues, which are described under the figures of crescents, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, headdresses, hair ornaments, and other such things.

This testimony may also be used against the women of the Church who walk with an outstretched neck, speak with the gestures of their eyes, clap with both hands and feet, and, in order to walk with measured steps, do not follow nature as their guide but hire actors as their instructors.

(Vers. 16.) The Lord will make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion and will uncover their hair.

[Note: Victor, an unskilled editor, rashly judged that the words “and in place of ornament there will be disgrace” had been inserted into the text and deleted them, because they are found neither in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint nor in the common edition, and because Jerome does not acknowledge them in his Commentary. Nevertheless, all the manuscripts contain them. In Greek, instead of these words, some copies have: καὶ Κύριος ἀνακαλύψῃ τὸ σχῆμα αὐτῶν, “and the Lord will uncover their form”; in other copies, σχῆμα is replaced by αἰσχάνωμα, “disgrace.”]

And in place of ornament there will be disgrace. This will also happen to us, whose sins are concealed, when what is written is fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Luke VIII, 17). For as long as we are protected by hair and by the garment of ignorance, and people think us whitewashed tombs (Matt. XXIII), though inwardly we are full of the bones of the dead, we appear to possess some purity. But when what is hidden becomes manifest, all the hair will be removed, [Col. 0069B] and the shameful baldness will appear to everyone.

(Vers. 17.) On that day the Lord will take away the ornament of the footwear. On what day? The Jews think it means the Babylonian captivity. We prove more convincingly that it refers to the time when they were captured by the Romans and lost all the ornaments of their clothing, gems, gold, jewelry, and various furnishings. Or, by metaphor from women, it is said that all the adornment of the cities was destroyed. Understand the adornments of cities as their streets and colonnades, forums and gymnasia, and public walls.

If we refer this to the state of souls, let us remember that we read of the feet of the one who was to eat the lamb’s flesh and celebrate Passover, and of those passing through the wilderness, that neither their clothing nor their footwear wore out. What footwear is this? That of which the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: “With your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” (Eph. VI, 15). The soul will lose this footwear when it walks with an outstretched neck, drags its garments with its feet, and, instead of the cleanliness of a married woman, sweeps the filth of the earth.

(Vers. 18–21.) And the crescents, necklaces, pendants, bracelets, headdresses, hair ornaments, anklets, chains, perfume boxes, earrings, rings, and jewels hanging on the forehead. He describes women’s ornaments, and through them the insignia of cities—or, according to the anagogical interpretation, the various adornments of the virtues.

Women wear little pendants hanging like the moon, which we transfer to the adornments of the Church, which is illuminated by the Sun of justice. Necklaces, hanging down as far as the breast, signify understanding and the ruling faculty (ἡγεμονικόν) of the mind, which is shown in the heart. Pendants signify all ornaments by one general term. Bracelets signify good works, such as those Rebecca received at her betrothal (Gen. XXIV). Headdresses are ornaments of the head; hair ornaments signify discernment, so that one may judge each matter. Anklets adorn our walk, so that we may hear: “Your foot will not stumble” (Ps. XC); and: “He will rescue my feet from falling” (Ps. LV). Chains, woven from rods of gold and silver, signify the meaning and words of the Scriptures. Perfume boxes signify that we should be the good fragrance of Christ (II Cor. II, 15). Earrings signify that we should not hear the judgment of blood but the words of the Lord who says: “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear” (Luke VIII, 18). Rings signify that we are marked for the service of the Lord, whom God the Father sealed. Hence it is said to the prince of Tyre: “You are the seal of likeness” (Ezek. XXVIII, 12). The prodigal son also received a ring along with his robe (Luke XV), and footwear, and jewels hanging from the forehead, by which our face is adorned. Concerning this ornament of the head we also read in the Psalm: “Like ointment on the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” (Ps. CXXXII, 1).

[Col. 0070B] Although the Septuagint interpreters, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion interpret all these things in different ways, we have woven the exposition as best we could, either from the Hebrew or from their translations. Nor do we wish to linger longer over each item, lest the exposition become frivolous and weary the prudent reader.

(Vers. 22.) And changes of garments, cloaks, and linen garments. In place of “linen garments,” [Note: Martianus: “In place of ‘linen garment.’”] the Septuagint translated “transparent Laconian garments,” wishing to signify the thinnest clothing with which the bodies of the Lacedaemonians—who were extremely ready for war and led a more austere life—were covered. Yet “Laconian” is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any other interpreter.

“Changes of garments” and “cloaks,” which Symmachus translated more significantly as ἀναβολαῖα, are ornaments of women’s clothing by which the shoulders and breasts are covered. According to the anagogical interpretation, changes of garments are those of which it is said: “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII, 8). Linen garments signify that, washed in the Lord, we may enjoy delights, according to what is written in the Psalms: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV, 9).

But the daughters of Zion lost all these things because they walked with an outstretched neck and displayed pride through the gestures of their eyes, thinking that what they possessed belonged to their own power and not to the grace of the Lord.

(Vers. 23.) And pins, mirrors, fine linen, ribbons, and summer cloaks. Women have pins with which the structure of their adorned hair is held together, so that it does not flow too loosely or scatter into disordered locks. They also have mirrors in which they examine their face, and if they see anything lacking, add it to their adornment. They have fine linen garments, which are called coverings, and ribbons with which their hair is bound; these they call ταινίαι. They also have summer cloaks, which we may call mantles, in which Rebecca too was wrapped.

Even today the women of Arabia and Mesopotamia cover themselves with these garments. In Hebrew they are called ARDIDIM; in Greek, θέριστρα—so called because in summer (θέρει), that is, in the heat, they protect women’s bodies.

[Note: Aridim. The manuscript copies read this consistently with the Hebrew hardidim; the printed books, with no authority, removed the letter h, which Jerome reads as an a.]

Therefore the daughters of Zion lost the pins by which the rule of all the commandments was fastened together. They lost the mirrors that the women who remained at the doors of the Tabernacle offered in Exodus for making the Lord’s basin (Exod. XXXVIII). Concerning these the Apostle Paul also spoke: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (I Cor. XIII, 12). They lost the fine linen and ribbons with which they covered their shoulders and restrained the mind that flowed here and there; and the summer cloak, that safest shade in which they were protected from the heat.

We say these things so that we may not appear entirely to evade the tropological meaning of this passage. Otherwise, it is extremely laborious to linger over each detail and seek an extended explanation.

(Vers. 24.) And there will be, in place of sweet fragrance, stench; and in place of a belt, a cord. The penitent speaks of sins that stink: “My wounds have festered and become corrupt because of my foolishness” (Ps. XXXVII, 6). The Apostle commanded that the loins be girded with a belt, saying: “Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Eph. VI, 14). And concerning the sinner we read: “Each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22).

Thus, in place of the good fragrance of the virtues, the daughters of Zion will have the rottenness of sins; and in place of the belt of truth, they will be bound with cords of falsehood—the cords worn on their heads by those who, clad in rags and filth, begged the king of Syria for their life.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, with the opposite meaning, reads: “they begged the king of Syria for life.” The printed editions of Erasmus and Marianus add here: “And in place of curled hair, baldness,” and append the following exposition: “In place of continuous, lengthy, ascending prayers, which are signified by the hair, they had baldness—a mind blocked on every side and fixed in silence, away from prayers.” There is no trace of this gloss in the manuscript copies, nor does it sufficiently resemble Jerome’s style. MARTIAN.]

And instead of a breast-band, sackcloth. In place of the breast-band, which Symmachus translated, the Septuagint rendered it as a μεσοπορφύρα tunic, that is, a tunic ornamented with purple bands: [Note: Earlier printed editions, and even the manuscripts, incorrectly read *clavatam purpuram* (“purple ornamented with bands”) instead of *clavatam purpura* (“a garment ornamented with purple bands”), a reading which we have restored by conjecture, compelled by the correct sense. For the ancients called a garment ornamented with purple bands, and a garment interwoven with purple stripes, μεσοπορφύρα in Greek; they certainly did not call purple itself *clavata*.] Aquila expressed it as “a girdle of exultation.” [Col. 0071C] Theodotion retained the Hebrew word PHTHIGIL (), which is a kind of women’s ornament. The breast-band covers the chest and occupies among women the place that the *Rationale* occupies among the High Priests. Concerning this breast-band Jeremiah also spoke in mystical language: “Can a bride forget her adornment, or a virgin her breast-band? And I will forget you,” says the Lord (Jer. II, 32).

The virgin whom the Apostle wishes us to present to Christ (II Cor. II), so long as she is not corrupted in Egypt and her breasts are not broken—those breasts bound by the breast-band—is joined to her bridegroom. And although she gives birth daily to children of virtue, she does not cease to be a virgin. But if at some time she has spread her legs to every passer-by and followed her lovers; and if, in accordance with the prophecy of Hosea, the Lord has fenced in her ways and blocked her paths, she will return to her former husband and will hear: [Note: Two Vatican and Palatine manuscripts read: “Take off the garments of mourning,” etc.] “Take off the garments of your mourning and put on the garments of your glory” (Hos. II).

[Col. 0072A] (Verse 25.) “Your most handsome men also shall fall by the sword, and your strong men in battle.” Instead of “the most handsome men,” the Septuagint translated: “Your most handsome son, whom you love, shall fall by the sword.” If we understand this concerning the state of the soul, which has sinned after attaining virtue, let us take its most handsome son to mean its good works, which have fallen beneath the hostile sword; and let us understand that the strong men also have perished in battle, because “the righteousness of the righteous man shall not deliver him on whatever day he goes astray” (Ezek. XXXIII, 12).

But if we follow the historical sense, we shall learn from these words that the prophet is speaking not of women whose husbands fell in battle, but of the cities of Judaea, which he called the daughters of Zion and whose warriors fell in combat. Finally, the following verse speaks about this same Zion.

[Col. 0072B] (Verse 26.) “And her gates shall mourn and lament, and the city itself shall sit desolate upon the ground.” We see this with our own eyes even today. According to the tropological sense, the interpretation is easy: whoever gives place to the devil and does not guard his heart with complete vigilance will have his gates in mourning; and, in the absence of the bridegroom, he will remain perpetually in grief and, falling from exalted places, will sit in the dust of the earth.

(Cap. IV.—Verse 1.) “And seven women shall seize one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach.’”

When Jerusalem’s most handsome men have fallen by the sword, her strong men have perished in battle, her gates have mourned and lamented, and the city itself has been left desolate because of the great scarcity of inhabitants, after the warriors have been killed, seven women will seize one man, desiring to have offspring in Zion and members of their households in Jerusalem. They will say that they have food and clothing of their own; they ask only not to appear to be without a husband and to be subject to the curse [Note: Palatine manuscript: “which is written.” On this Scriptural text, see our annotations on the second Paschal epistle.] written in Scripture: “Cursed is the barren woman, and she who does not produce offspring in Israel” (Deut. VII).

Zechariah also agrees with this meaning: “In those days ten men from all the languages of the nations shall seize the fringe of a Jewish man’s garment, saying: ‘We shall go with you, for we have heard that God is with you’” (Zech. VIII, 23). The numbers seven and ten, on account of the Sabbath and the Ten Commandments of the Law, are familiar to the Jews; and therefore they frequently employ them figuratively. Nevertheless, in accordance with the ambiguity of the Hebrew word SABA (), which they interpret sometimes as “seven,” sometimes as “many,” and sometimes as “an oath,” it may be that here it signifies not seven but many. This is the literal interpretation.

Moreover, at the coming of the Lord and Savior, the seven women—that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, about which the same prophet will say later: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and he shall be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI, 1–2)—will seize Jesus, whom they had long desired, because they could find no other in whom they might rest in an eternal dwelling.

Hence John the Baptist also reports in the Gospel: “He who sent me himself said to me: ‘Upon whom you see the Holy Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one’” (John I, 33). In Zechariah too we read of seven eyes upon one stone, and in one golden lampstand seven lamps and seven pouring vessels, with two olive trees firmly rooted on either side of the lamp (Zech. III). That the grace of the Holy Spirit possesses all things requires no explanation. But because it was continually suffering reproach among human beings, since no one was living as the gifts of the Holy Spirit demanded, they therefore desire Jesus’ name to be invoked over them, so that what was imperfect in the Law might be completed in the Gospel.

(Verses 2, 3.) “On that day the Branch of the Lord shall be in magnificence and glory, and the fruit of the earth shall be exalted and a source of rejoicing for those of Israel who have been saved. And everyone who has been left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy—everyone who has been written among the living in Jerusalem.”

When the daughters of Zion, because of their pride, have lost all their adornment; when her gates have mourned and lamented, and the city itself, desolate, has fallen down [Note: Victorius says that both the text and the commentary require *has sat down* to be read at the end of the preceding chapter.]; and when all her warriors have perished in battle, so that many women can scarcely have one man among them, then the Branch of the Christian name will arise, and the earth will give its fruit. There will be rejoicing for those of Israel who have been saved, concerning whom it was said above: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. I, 9).

And note that not all Israel will be saved, but the remnant of the people of Zion and those remaining in Jerusalem: everyone who has been written among the living in Jerusalem. To them the Lord also spoke: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). [66] He signifies the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles.

(Verses 4.) “When the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.”

Then the remnant of Israel will be saved, when their sins have been forgiven in the Savior’s baptism and that blood has been washed away which the erring people called down upon themselves: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25). Hence above we read: “When you stretch out your hands, I will not hear you; for your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15–16). And afterward, calling them to repentance, he adds: “Wash yourselves; be clean.”

And note that he washes away the filth of the daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment, but the blood of Jerusalem by the spirit of burning. What is light is washed away; what is heavier is burned. John the Baptist spoke in the Gospel concerning this spirit of judgment and spirit of burning: “I baptize you with water, but he who comes after me will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. III, 11). From this we learn that a human being gives only water, but God gives the Holy Spirit, by whom both filth is washed away and the sins of blood are purified.

(Verses 5.) “And the Lord will create” (another reading: “created”) “over every place of Mount Zion and wherever he has been invoked, a cloud by day, and smoke and the brightness of flaming fire by night.”

For in Christ there is a new creation, concerning which we read elsewhere: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (II Cor. V, 17). Instead of this, the Septuagint translated: “And he will come, and every place of Mount Zion and all that is around it shall be protected by a cloud by day and by the light of flaming fire by night.” But who will come except the one of whom it is written: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers” (Isa. LIX, 20, according to the Septuagint), and of whom another prophet recalls: “Still a little while, and the one who is to come will come and will not delay” (Hab. II, 3)?

When he has come, the people will receive again the former happiness which they once possessed in the wilderness, with the Lord going before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire (Exod. XIII), so that they may never be disturbed either in prosperity or in adversity. The same is said in the Psalm: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX, 6). [Note: Martianus has less correctly: “that they may be disturbed for a while.”]

Smoke in this passage signifies not error and ignorance but glory, according to what we shall read in this same prophet, in the opinion of some, below (chapter 6): “And the house was filled with smoke.” And in Joel it is said concerning the grace of the Holy Spirit, which descended upon the Apostles: “I will pour out from my spirit, and they shall prophesy” (Joel II). And: “I will give wonders in heaven above and signs on earth below, blood and fire and vapor of smoke” (Acts II, 17). I think that the same thing is signified in the Psalms: “He touches the mountains, and they will smoke” (Ps. CIII, 32). [Note: Victor prefers: “At once they smoke,” according to the Septuagint, καπνίζονται.]

(Verses 6.) “And over all the glory there shall be protection. And there shall be a tabernacle for shade by day from the heat, and for security, and for concealment from storm and rain.”

The Jews refer this passage to the Antichrist, whom they think is signified by the storm and tempest, when they believe that the Lord will defend them from their most powerful adversary. We, however, should refer everything to the first coming of Christ, concerning which we also read in the Psalms: “He protected me in the secret place of his tabernacle; he exalted me upon a rock” (Ps. XXVI, 9–10). Upon this rock the Church has been founded and is shaken by no storm, overturned by no tempest or winds.

Very many Jews understand both this passage and all the passages associated with it as referring to the Babylonian captivity and the return to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah.

(Cap. V.—Verse 1.) “Now I will sing for my beloved the song of my kinsman, concerning his vineyard.”

The prophet sings a lamentable song for the people of Israel, composed by the one of whom it is written in the Gospel: “When he saw it”—there is no doubt that this means Jerusalem—“he wept over it and said: ‘If you too had known the things that are for your peace! For days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with fortifications, and they will enclose you, and they will overthrow you and your children’” (Luke XIX, 41 and following). And again: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings [Note: Victorius deletes *her*, on the authority of other manuscripts.], and you were unwilling? Behold, your house will be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII, 37–38). This resembles what is now said in the song: “I will abandon my vineyard.”

That Christ is called beloved and dearest, whom Aquila translated as πατράδελφος, “paternal uncle” or “cousin,” is shown by the superscription of Psalm 44: “A song concerning the beloved.” And the voice of God the Father in the Gospel says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III, 17). In Psalm 67 we read: “The Lord will give a word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power: the King of the beloved” (Ps. LXVII, 12–13).

This beloved, therefore, made a mournful song for his vineyard, which I shall sing for my beloved and pitiable people. Or certainly it should be understood in this way: I shall sing to Almighty God the Father the song of Christ, who is my cousin—that is, born from the same people as I.

That the people of Israel are called God’s vineyard we read at the end of this song: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is his beloved plant.” And in Psalm 79 (verse 9): “You brought a vineyard out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it.” In the Gospel also the Lord constructed a parable in almost the same words in which the Prophet now speaks: “There was a certain householder who planted a vineyard, placed a hedge around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, and leased it to farmers,” and so forth (Matt. XXI, 33).

And in Jeremiah we read: “I planted you as a fruitful vineyard, wholly true; how have you turned into bitterness, foreign vine?” (Jer. II, 21). Thus Jerusalem, as we have said, is mourned, and its ruin is sung in prophetic language.

For the Church and for the people formerly belonging to the nations, another song has been composed, concerning which we read in the Psalms: “Sing to the Lord, all the earth; announce his salvation from day to day. Announce his glory among the nations, his wonders among all peoples” (Ps. XCV, 2–3). And again: “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done marvelous things. The Lord has made his salvation known; before the nations he has revealed his righteousness” (Ps. XCVII, 1–2).

“A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, the son of oil.” [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, *meo* (“my”) is consistently absent here and below.] According to the Hebrew, Theodotion and Aquila translated this: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn.” Symmachus, however, following his usual practice, made the sense clearer: “A vineyard was made for my beloved on a horn, in the midst of olive trees.”

The Septuagint interpreted the sense rather than the word: “A vineyard was planted for my beloved on a horn, in a rich or fertile place,” for πίων signifies both. And indeed nothing is more fertile than the Promised Land, if one considers not merely its mountains and deserts but its entire extent, from the Brook of Egypt to the great River Euphrates toward the East, and northward to Mount Taurus and Zephyrium of Cilicia, which projects over the sea.

We often read that a horn signifies a kingdom and power, as in the Gospel: “He raised up the horn of our salvation in the house of David his servant” (Luke I, 69); and: “In you we shall toss our enemies with the horn” (Ps. XLIII, 6). In Zechariah also the four horns signify four most powerful kingdoms (Zech. I).

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: “A vineyard was planted for Christ on a horn,” that is, in a strong and exalted place, which is called “the son of oil,” either because it needs God’s mercy and is sustained by his help, or because it has supplied all the nations with the bright light of the knowledge of God.

(Verses 2.) “And he fenced it, cleared it of stones, planted a Sorec vine, built a tower in its midst, and constructed a winepress in it.”

By the metaphor of the vineyard, as we said earlier, he describes the Jewish people, whom he fenced in with the help of the angels. He cleared stones from it, either idols or everything that could impede the worship of God. He planted it as a Sorec vine, which Symmachus alone translated as “choice,” not, as it seems to me, expressing the word literally but the sense contained in it.

For the Hebrews say that Sorec is a kind of excellent vine which produces abundant and lasting fruit. Hence some translate Sorec as καλλίκαρπος, “fruitful,” which we may render as “producing very beautiful fruit.”

He also built a tower in its midst, namely, the temple in the middle of the city; and he constructed a winepress in it, which some think signifies the altar. For just as all grapes are carried to the winepress and trodden there so that wine may be pressed from them, so the altar receives the fruits of the whole people and consumes the sacrificed victims, in accordance with what we read concerning Benjamin, in whose tribe the temple and altar were located: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall eat, and in the evening he shall give food” (Gen. XLIX, 27).

Everything said concerning the vineyard may also be referred to the state of the human soul, which, planted by God for good, produced not grapes but wild grapes and afterward was handed over to be trampled by beasts; nor did it receive the divine rain of teachings, because it had despised the gifts previously bestowed.

“And I expected it to produce grapes, but it produced wild grapes.” For the wild grapes, which we have translated, the Hebrew has BUSIM (): Aquila translated this as σαπρίας, that is, “very bad fruits”; [Note: The manuscripts here transpose π and ρ, for the ancient scribes write σαρπίας. In Athenaeus, book I, σαπρίας is the name of a certain wine preserved with herbs rotting or decaying in it, and taking on their odor from that decay. MARTIANUS.] Symmachus as ἀτελῆ, that is, “imperfect”; the Septuagint and Theodotion as “thorns,” with which the Jews crowned the Lord.

For while he expected them, at the time of the vintage, to bring grapes to the winepresses—whose titles are found on Psalms 8 and 83—these people, drowning themselves in the cares and vices of the age, which are interpreted as thorns in the Gospel (Mark IV), offered the goads of blasphemy. I think, however, that Busim should better be understood as “wild grapes” than as “thorns,” so that the similarity of the translation already begun may be preserved. Hence the Savior also says in the Gospel: “Are grapes gathered from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (Matt. VII, 16).

(Verses 3, 4.) “Now therefore, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard: What more ought I to have done for my vineyard that I have not done for it? Or that I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes?” [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads: “Now therefore, inhabitants and men of Judah,” without the name “Jerusalem.”]

“I did,” he says, “everything that I ought to have done. I planted the vineyard in a fertile place, surrounded it with a hedge, cleared away the stones, and raised its branches upon poles and reeds. The vine itself was not one among many, but a choice and καλλίκαρπος vine. I built a very strong tower in which I might store the fruits and from which I might watch for beasts lying in wait for the fruits. I constructed a winepress so that the grapes might be pressed in that very place and pour forth their wine.

“Since, therefore, I did all that I ought to have done, let the inhabitants of Jerusalem and Judah answer me—or rather, let them judge between me and my vineyard. What ought I to have done that I have not done? And when they remain silent, he answers himself: ‘Unless perhaps I erred in this: I expected it to produce grapes for my labor, not wild grapes, which an uncultivated and deserted vineyard is accustomed to produce.’”

The prophet Nathan, sent to David, says something similar (II Kings XII). He questions him through a parable, so that while judging another he may pronounce sentence against himself. Here too the people are questioned as though concerning the vineyard, so that they themselves may answer against themselves.

The Savior develops this passage more fully in the Gospel (Matt. XXI), and asks the scribes and Pharisees what is omitted here. In Isaiah nothing is said about the farmers, nor is it indicated what they will suffer; there is only speech about the vineyard. In the Gospel, however, as though there were another vineyard and other farmers, he speaks of the people and its leaders, so that he may destroy the wicked wickedly and lease the vineyard to other farmers, signifying the Apostles and those who will succeed the Apostles.

Nor is there a ταυτολογία, as many think, in the words: “Or that I expected it to produce grapes, and it produced wild grapes?” Above, he speaks silently to himself; here he asks others what he had been considering. [Note: Vatican manuscript: *in recto*; another manuscript.]

(Verses 5, 6.) “And now I shall show you what I will do to my vineyard: I will remove its hedge, and it shall be plundered; I will tear down its wall, and it shall be trampled. I will leave it desolate; it shall not be pruned, and it shall not be dug; and thorns and briars shall rise up over it.” [Note: The word “over it” is absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

“I appealed earlier to you, inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of the tribe of Judah, to judge between me and my vineyard, and I asked you to say what I ought to have done that I had not done. And because, in accordance with the Gospel parable, you do not wish to answer what I ask, I shall answer for you myself, declaring what I am going to do:

“Because I did everything that I ought to have done for my vineyard, and it produced wild grapes instead of grapes, I shall remove everything I had given it. I shall take away the assistance of the angels, concerning which it is written in the Psalms: ‘The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him and will deliver them’ (Ps. XXXIII, 8), and it will be plundered by adversaries. I shall destroy its walls, and it will be subject to hostile nations. It will be left desolate; it will not be pruned forever, nor will it be dug; it will be reduced to briars, and thorns will rise up in it.”

These things are said under the metaphor of the vineyard concerning the desolation of Jerusalem and Judaea. Many Jews think that they happened under the Babylonians; nor can we deny that this occurred in part. But since what follows is: “And I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it,” this cannot be understood of that captivity. For after the city had already been captured, Jeremiah prophesied among the people; and Ezekiel, Daniel, and the three boys are reported either to have prophesied or even to have performed miraculous signs in captivity. Later Haggai and Zechariah spoke of future things for the consolation of the enslaved people.

God’s help is removed from those who are unworthy, so that, because they had not perceived God through benefits, they may perceive him through punishments. Or he threatens such savage and harsh things for this reason: so that, converted to repentance, they may avoid the torments that threaten them.

All have translated the Hebrew word SAITH () with the same word, “thorns.” If, therefore, Saith in the present passage means “thorns,” according to Aquila, Theodotion, and the Septuagint, let them explain why above they translated Busim not as “wild grapes” but as “thorns.”

“And I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” These are the clouds which the Lord brought out from the end of the earth, concerning which we also read in the Psalm: “Your truth reaches to the clouds” (Ps. XXXV, 6). Since under Elijah all were idolaters, these clouds did not rain upon the land of Israel for three years and six months (III Kings XVIII).

We may understand this not only of the prophets but also of the Apostles: after the Lord’s Passion, the Jews had neither prophets nor Apostles, so that instead of grapes they might bring forth thorns, but because of their barrenness and dryness they might pray to him who can provide the rains of virtues.

Hence in Leviticus he also says to them: “I will make your heaven like iron and your earth like bronze” (Lev. XXVI, 19). And in Deuteronomy: “The heaven over your head shall be bronze, and the earth beneath you shall be iron” (Deut. XXVIII, 23–24). And again: “The Lord will give the rain of your land” [Note: Victor adds “and dust,” from the Greek κονιορτόν and the Hebrew .]. And: “Ashes shall descend upon you from heaven until it uproots and destroys you,” because land which frequently receives the rain falling upon it and produces not grain but thorns and thistles is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning.

(Verses 7.) “For the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his delightful plant”—that is, God’s; or, as the Septuagint translated, “his most beloved new plantation.”

Israel and Judah differ in this respect: the whole people was first called Israel. Later, when David reigned over the tribe of Judah and Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, over two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, those who were in Samaria—that is, the ten tribes—were called Israel, while those over whom kings of David’s line reigned were called Judah.

And because Israel worshiped calves in Dan and Bethel, Samaria was first captured by the Assyrians; much later Judah was led away to Babylon by the Chaldaeans, because they had committed fewer sins. Hence in Ezekiel, for the purification of the sins of both peoples, Israel is placed on the left side for one hundred ninety days according to the Septuagint, or, more accurately, as the Hebrew contains it, three hundred ninety days; and Judah for forty days (Ezek. IV, according to the Septuagint and the Hebrew).

I say this in order to show Judah to be lovely and beloved in comparison with Israel—that is, the ten tribes—in which there were priests and Levites and the worship of God was practiced at the time when the prophet Isaiah was speaking to the people.

Israel, that is, the whole people, is beautifully called a house; but Judah, which later sprang forth after the tribes were separated, is called a beloved new plant. It should also be noted that, in accordance with prophetic practice, what was first said metaphorically or in a parable is later explained more clearly: the vineyard and the new plantation are Israel and Judah.

[Col. 0079C] “And I expected it to produce judgment, and behold, iniquity; and righteousness, and behold, a cry”—or, as the Septuagint translated: “I expected it to produce judgment, and it produced iniquity; not righteousness, but a cry.”

We wish to explain to Latin ears what we have learned from the Hebrews. “Judgment” is called MESPHAT (); “iniquity,” or “destruction,” as Aquila translated it, is MESPHAA (). Again, “righteousness” is called SADACA (); but “cry” is called SAACA (). Thus, by adding or changing a single letter, he adjusted the similarity of the words, putting MESPHAA in place of MESPHAT and SAACA in place of SADACA, and reproducing an elegant structure and sound of words in accordance with the Hebrew language. [Note: The same Vatican manuscript reads: “instead of *mesphat*, he would say *mestphan*,” etc.]

God expected the Jewish people to produce judgment—that is, grapes—and it produced iniquity—that is, wild grapes. He expected righteousness, so that it might receive the giver of such great gifts, sent by the Father; and it produced a cry, with which it shouted against the Lord and cried out, saying: “Take him away, take him away, crucify such a man!” (John XIX, 15).

Hence the Apostle Paul also writes: “Let all bitterness and anger and wrath and shouting and blasphemy be taken away from you, together with all malice” (Eph. IV, 31). Or certainly, because they had shed the blood of the righteous, the blood of the Lord’s Passion cried out to the Lord; therefore they returned a cry instead of righteousness, in accordance with what we read in Genesis: “The voice of your brother Abel’s blood cries out to me” (Gen. IV, 10).

(Verses 8.) “Woe to those who join house to house and connect field to field, even to the boundary of the place. Will you dwell alone upon the earth?”

For what we have translated as “even to the boundary of the place,” the Septuagint translated: “or you remove your neighbor”; Symmachus and Theodotion: “until the land fails,” or “until there is no place,” so that when the earth is exhausted greed may no longer be satisfied.

I think this was said generally against all those for whom nothing is enough, and specifically against the Lord’s vineyard, which produced wild grapes instead of grapes—that is, iniquity instead of judgment and a cry instead of righteousness.

What madness is it, when houses and fields ought to be possessed for warding off the rains and sowing crops [alternative reading: “sorting crops”], to desire to possess more than you can all inhabit or cultivate, and to make another person’s necessity your pleasure?

According to the tropological interpretation, some think this was said against heretics, who, after moving their feet from the East, came into the plain of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking of teeth,” and built a city of confusion and a tower of pride. They hear this in other words: “Hear these things, leaders of the house of Jacob and remnant of the house of Israel, who abhor judgment and pervert everything that is right, who build Zion with blood and Jerusalem with iniquity” (Mic. III, 9–10).

These people join houses to houses—that is, they join doctrines to doctrines. Through Micah they are told: “Do not build upon a house of derision” (Mic. III), lest upon the foundation of Christ, which the Apostle Paul laid (I Cor. III), and upon which they ought to build gold, silver, and precious stones, they instead build wood, hay, and stubble, whose end is burning.

Concerning such houses the Savior speaks in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears my words and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew and struck that house, and it fell; and its fall was great” (Matt. VII, 26–27).

Heretics continue seeking to join new things to old and to alter the same things through newer ones until both human understanding and speech fail.

(Verses 9.) “In my ears are these words of the Lord of hosts: Unless many houses are left desolate, great and beautiful, without an inhabitant.”

For what we have translated according to the Hebrew as “In my ears are these words of the Lord of hosts”—that is, “the words which the Lord spoke still resound in my ears”—the Septuagint translated: “These things have been heard in the ears of the Lord of hosts.” This does not mean that the Prophet heard the Lord’s words, but that what the Prophet is about to say was heard in the ears of the Lord, whereas it is more consistent to understand that the Prophet heard what the Lord spoke.

The Lord said that after the captivity great and beautiful houses would be left desolate, without an inhabitant.

(Verses 10.) “For ten [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “ten yokes of vineyards.”] yokes of vineyards shall produce one small jar, and thirty measures of seed shall produce three measures.”

For the small jar, which only the Septuagint translated, all the others rendered “bath,” called BETH () in Hebrew. And for the thirty measures, which we placed for the *cor*, called OMER () in Hebrew, the Septuagint translated “six artabas,” [Note: Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*: “Artaba: this measure was called thus among the Egyptians.” This is an Egyptian measure. So too the scholiast of Aristophanes, *Acharnians*, book I, act I, scene 2, p. 375.] which is an Egyptian measure and amounts to twenty measures.
