Thus, in the great barrenness that follows the captivity, ten yokes of vineyards will produce one bath, that is, three amphorae; and thirty measures of seed—that is, one cor—will produce one ephah, which the Septuagint translated as three measures, that is, three measures of grain. A bath is used for liquids, and an ephah or epha, the same measure, for dry substances.

Thus in Ezekiel, according to the Hebrew, we read: “You shall have a just ephah and a just bath. The ephah and the bath shall be equal and of one measure, so that the bath shall contain a tenth of a cor and the ephah a tenth of a cor; their measure shall be according to the cor” (Ezek. XLV, 10–11).

According to the allegorical sense, we ask how the houses of heretics can be great and beautiful if, when the time of judgment comes, they will have no inhabitant. For all the pomp and elaborate structure of words, and all dialectical arguments, will be reduced to nothing.

And because, according to the Apostle Paul (II Cor. III), we are not only God’s building but also his cultivation, which heretics imitate, and by Jeremiah are undermined and uprooted [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “which heretics destroy,” etc.]. Therefore, where ten yokes of vineyards—or where ten yokes of oxen—work, they will produce one bath, and thirty measures of seed will produce one ephah (Jer. XVIII), so that the number ten, which is mystical and perfect in the Holy Scriptures, and the number thirty, in which Ezekiel prophesied (Ezek. I) and the Lord was baptized (Luke III), may be reduced to an ephah, which, in comparison with a multiplied number, is confined to unity.

That building and cultivation refer to spiritual understanding the Apostle Paul also teaches elsewhere (Eph. IV), testifying that believers are founded and rooted in love. Hence Ecclesiastes (Eccl. II) not only built houses for himself but also planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, planted every kind of fruit tree, and constructed pools to irrigate the forest.

But heretics, possessing only the image and shadow of virtues and not the truth itself, promise leaves of words without the fruit of works. Concerning their trees the Lord says: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. XV, 13).

“For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah; their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is bitterness to them; their wine is the fury of dragons, and the incurable fury of asps” (Deut. XXXII, 32 and following).

(Verses 11–12.) “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine. Harp and lyre, tambourine and flute, wine at your banquets; yet you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.”

For “drunkenness,” which Aquila translated, Symmachus likewise, the Septuagint retained the Hebrew word *sikera* (σίκερα), which signifies every drink capable of causing intoxication and overturning the state of the mind. In accordance with the progression of the explanation begun above, he rebukes the farmers of the vineyard who, with barrenness impending and a nearby fire by which the briars and thorns are to be burned, have surrendered themselves to luxury and pleasures—not only in eating and drinking, but also in the delight of the ears and in various kinds of musical art. While they do these things, they do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider what is to come.

Let us use this testimony against the leaders of the Church who rise early to pursue *sikera* and drink until evening. Of them it is said elsewhere: “Woe to you, city, whose king is a boy, and whose princes eat in the morning” (Eccl. X, 16). Occupied with delicacies, they do not understand the Creator from the things he created, nor consider the works of his hands, concerning which we read: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII, 6).

According to a higher understanding, every disturbance of the soul may be called drunkenness. It is conceived from “the wine of the fury of dragons” and “the incurable poison of asps,” which some drink from youth to old age—that is, from morning until evening (Deut. XXXII). Others are roused from their banquet at the third, sixth, ninth, or eleventh hour, and it is said to them: “Awake, you who are drunk, from your wine.” Over this wine, and over such grapes and vineyards, the Lord rains sulfur and fire from the Lord; and whoever drinks from their wine burns and is consumed.

He seeks harp and psalter, whose inventor was Jubal, descended from the stock of Cain (Gen. IV), and does not hear the Lord saying to Aaron: “You and your sons shall not drink wine or *sikera* when you enter the tent of testimony or approach the altar” (Lev. X, 8). The Babylonian king possessed these harps, lyres, tambourines, and flutes; when they sounded together, the peoples of every nation fell to the ground and worshiped the golden statue (Dan. III).

That the first period of human wisdom—when we leave childhood and reach the rational age—is understood in Scripture as “morning,” many testimonies can teach us. A few may be given by way of example: “In the morning I sent the prophets”; and, “In the morning you will hear my prayer. In the morning I will stand before you, and I will see” (Ps. V, 4–5); and, “By night my spirit rises” (Ps. LXII, 1); and, “O God, my God, I keep watch for you from the light of dawn” (Ps. C, 8); and, “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who practice iniquity” (Ps. XXIX, 7); and elsewhere: “In the evening weeping will linger, but in the morning there will be joy,” and many similar passages.

We rise in the morning when we abandon vices in childhood and can say: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV, 7). When the sun of righteousness has risen for us, the darkness is driven away, and immediately we kill all the thoughts that provoke us to sin; from the city of our mind we drive out those sinners of whom the Savior speaks: “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies” (Matt. XV, 19), and the rest. Most miserable are those who, from morning until evening, are occupied with drunkenness, gluttony, and various pleasures, and do not understand the works of the Lord within themselves, nor consider why they were created.

(Verses 13.) “Therefore my people have been led captive, because they had no knowledge; and their nobles have died of hunger, and their multitude has dried up from thirst.”

[Note: Eusebius: “These things therefore came upon them literally, in accordance with history, under Vespasian and Hadrian, Roman emperors; but spiritually also, deprived of the rational bread of life, they still even now hunger in their souls for heavenly nourishment, according to the Scripture that speaks concerning them.” This has been rendered almost word for word in Latin by Jerome.]

That this happened literally to the Jewish people under Vespasian and Titus, Roman rulers, both Greek and Latin history relates. Spiritually also they suffer this today, enduring not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God, because they neither regarded the work of the Lord nor considered the works of his hands, nor possessed knowledge of him who always spoke through the prophets (Amos VIII). Hence it is said of them in the Psalms: “They will return at evening, and suffer hunger like dogs, and go around the city” (Ps. LVIII, 16).

That every word of teaching is called bread and water is shown by the Gospel passage: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Luke IV, 4); and, “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst” (John IV, 13). And in the psalm it is said: “He led me beside waters of refreshment” (Ps. XXII, 2). Hence the Lord does not wish to send away those who are hungry in the wilderness, lest they grow faint, fall, and perish from hunger (Matt. XV). And concerning the righteous man it is said: “I was young, and now I am old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. XXXVI, 25).

Some wish to interpret the words, “My people have been led captive, because they had no knowledge; and their nobles have died of hunger, and their multitude has dried up from thirst,” generally of the underworld and Gehenna, in which everyone who has not possessed knowledge of God will be punished.

(Verses 14–15.) “Therefore Sheol has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without limit, and its mighty ones, its people, and its high and glorious ones will descend to it. And a human being will be bowed down, and a man humbled, and the eyes of the lofty will be brought low.”

Those who rose early to pursue *sikera* and remained in drunkenness until evening, occupied with pleasure and delicacies, did not wish to regard the work of the Lord or contemplate the works of his hands. Therefore they were led into captivity, because they did not possess knowledge of the Son of God, who said to them: “You know neither me nor the one who sent me” (John VIII, 19). In that captivity they perished from hunger and dried up from thirst.

Therefore the underworld and death enlarged their soul and opened their mouth, and without number or satiety devoured those destined to be punished forever, so that the leaders and people, and the high and glorious of the land of Judah, descended to it; every pride was humbled, and the eyes of the lofty were brought low, when they understood that they were mortal. Thus everything was fulfilled that the Lord had announced through the prophets as future.

The underworld is said to have a soul—not because it is an animal, according to the error of some, but because in the language of human custom we express the disposition of insensible things, namely, that it is insatiable and is never filled by the multitude of the dead. Thus death is said to be “in the hand of the tongue” (Prov. XVIII), and almighty God is said to speak of hating in his soul the Sabbaths and new moons of the Jews (Isa. I).

Whatever we have said concerning the Jewish people may be referred tropologically to those who, occupied with the pleasures of the world and not regarding the works of God, are led captive into sin and do not possess knowledge of God. Therefore they perish from hunger and thirst for good works and virtues, and are dragged down into Gehenna; there, assigned to eternal torments, they will see power and pride changed into misery and humility.

(Verses 16.) “And the Lord of hosts will be exalted in judgment, and the holy God will be sanctified in righteousness.”

When the people have been led captive because they had no knowledge, have perished from hunger and dried up from thirst, and Sheol has enlarged its soul; when the mighty, the high, and the glorious have descended into the depths; when the human being has been bowed down, the man humbled, and all have received according to their merits—then the Lord will be exalted in judgment, whose judgment previously seemed unjust, and the holy God will be sanctified by all in righteousness, so that what is said in the Gospel may be fulfilled: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI, 9); and, “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John XVII, 25).

Therefore we must beware of anticipating the judgment of God, whose judgments are great and indescribable, and concerning whom the Apostle says: “His judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable” (Rom. XI, 33), until he brings to light the hidden things of darkness and reveals the counsels of hearts (I Cor. IV, 5). He says in the Gospel: “Do not judge, so that you may not be judged” (Matt. VII, 1). In agreement with this sentence, the Apostle Paul commanded: “Who are you to judge another’s servant? Before his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for God is able to make him stand” (Rom. XIV, 4).

(Verses 17.) “And lambs will feed according to their order; and the deserted places, turned into abundance, will be eaten by newcomers.”

For “lambs will feed according to their order,” which is understood in a favorable sense, I do not know what the Septuagint intended when they translated: “They will feed, having been plundered, like bulls,” understanding bulls instead of lambs, and again translating lambs instead of newcomers.

When the Lord has been exalted in judgment, and the holy one sanctified in his righteousness, so that the wicked husbandmen perish wickedly and the exalted cedar is cut down by the Lord’s axe, then those who belong to the number of lambs, not of goats, will feed in the meadows of the Church and say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. XXII, 1). What has been laid waste by the Jews, turned into abundance, the people of the nations will eat.

This is according to the tropological interpretation. But, to complete the historical sequence, the same thing is said in other words, concerning which we read above: “Foreigners devour your land in your presence, and it is laid waste and overturned by foreign peoples” (Isa. I, 7). For a multitude of nations gathered from the whole world inhabits Judaea; and after the former peoples were expelled, partial blindness has happened to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter (Rom. XI).

Beautifully, according to the Septuagint, they were plundered, devastated, and led into captivity like bulls, concerning whom the Lord had said: “Fat bulls surrounded me,” so that lambs might occupy the places of bulls.

(Verses 18–19.) “Woe to those who drag iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as though with a cart rope; who say: ‘Let his work hurry and come quickly, so that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come, and we shall know it.’”

For “cart rope,” the Septuagint translated “the leather strap of the yoke of a heifer or cow.” That sins are called bonds we read frequently. Among these is the passage: “Each one is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V, 22). And the Lord, rebuking the sinful people who had joined sin to sin, made a whip from cords, showing them how they had made the house of God a den of robbers (John II) and had turned the seat of prayer into a house of commerce (Matt. XXI). The guest at the Lord’s supper who does not have a wedding garment is cast out, bound hand and foot, into the outer darkness (Matt. XXII).

The Lord came to say to those who were in bonds: “Come out” (Isa. XLIX, 9); and to those who dwelt in darkness: “Be revealed” (Ps. CLXV, 8). For he himself releases those in fetters and gives light to the blind—those whom Jeremiah calls bound to the earth.

He does not lament those who have begun to sin and immediately ceased, for “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins” (Eccl. VII, 2), but those who have prolonged their sins with a long cord. Hence in Numbers we read (chapter XIX) that the red heifer, whose ashes are the purification of the people, may be sacrificed and offered on the Lord’s altar only if it has done no earthly work, has not drawn a yoke, and has not been bound with the bonds of Nebuchadnezzar’s yoke.

In this same prophet, instead of the belt of truth, the daughters of Zion are girded with a cord. Ahithophel and Judas also—one of whom betrayed David and the other the Lord—dragging their sins with a very long rope, perished by hanging, thinking that the evil of conscience could be ended by present death and that nothing existed after death.

That, according to the Hebrew and all the other translators, they are called “cords of vanity” signifies that for those committing sin a cord is easily woven; it is as insubstantial and easy as the threads of spiders. But when we wish to escape from it, we are entangled in the strongest bonds.

Those who remember that impiety sits upon a talent of lead understand more easily the cart that is full and burdened with sins, as it is written in Zechariah (Zech. V), and the Egyptians, who were weighed down by the heavy burden of their sins, being plunged into the Red Sea like lead (Exod. XV). Elsewhere the sinner says: “My iniquities have gone over my head; like a heavy burden they have become too heavy for me” (Ps. XXXVII, 5).

These words are addressed to the leaders of the Jews, who above were rebuked for avarice and luxury: when summoned to repentance by the Lord and afterward by his Apostles, they have persisted to this day in blasphemies and, three times each day in all the synagogues, anathematize the Christian name under the title “Nazarenes.”

The meaning is this: Woe to you who think that the day of judgment will not come, or that the captivity predicted by the prophetic word will not come—who say to the prophet: “How long will you threaten us with God’s anger? We wish to know it; let it come now.” They speak ironically, because they do not think it will come, but pretend that the prophet is merely making threats.

(Verses 20.) “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who make darkness light and light darkness, who make bitter sweet and sweet bitter.”

It is the same crime to call good, light, and sweet by contrary names as it is to call evil, darkness, and bitter by the names of virtues. This is directed against those who do not regard it as sin if they disparage the good, and do not consider it a transgression if they praise evil.

The Jews make good evil, light darkness, and sweet bitter when they accept Barabbas, the author of robbery and sedition, and crucify Jesus, who had come only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, to save what had perished. In Barabbas we may understand the devil, who, although he is night and darkness, transforms himself into an angel of light (Matt. XXVII).

Hence the Apostle says: “What partnership has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial?” (II Cor. VI, 14–15). Nor should a lamp be taken away and placed under a bushel or under a bed, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all. Nor should a tree producing bad fruit be called by the name of a good tree (Matt. V).

Hence in Genesis it is related in mystical language that God divided light from darkness, which in the beginning moved over the abyss (Gen. I). That the good Savior was called good, he himself says in the Gospel: “The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep” (John X, 11).

[Note: Victor, on the authority of his manuscript copies, prefixes: “I am the good shepherd.” A third time, from this verse onward, he again prefixes, from those same manuscripts, “and concerning his sweetness daily,” etc.; and from this passage argues that the sacred Eucharist is celebrated daily, adding another passage from the Commentary on Ezekiel XLVI.]

He also says that he is the light: “I am the light of the world” (John VIII, 12); and, daily filled with heavenly bread, we say: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. XXIII, 9). Conversely, when we say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. VI, 13), and, “The world is placed in the evil one” (I John V, 19), we desire to be freed from the devil’s snares.

That he is signified by the names of darkness and bitterness we read frequently. We can also say that all doctrines opposed to the truth are bitter, and that only the truth is sweet. Therefore we must beware of following falsehood in place of truth, and darkness in place of light.

For there are many ways that seem right to human beings, but their ends reach the depths of hell. There is also a righteous person who perishes in his righteousness, to whom it is said: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. VII, 17). For these reasons Israel promises that it will walk on the royal road and turn neither to the left nor to the right (Deut. V).

And to say what I think: who can easily escape this curse, when we frequently flatter the wicked because of their power and despise the good because of their poverty? Hence Aquila translated more pointedly: “Woe to him who says to the evil person, ‘You are good,’ and to the good person, ‘You are evil’” (Prov. XVII, 13).

To this meaning belongs what Solomon says in Proverbs: “He who declares the righteous unjust and the unjust righteous is an abomination to God.” The scribes and Pharisees also, refusing to receive the words of the Savior but accepting human traditions and old-wives’ tales, made good evil and evil good.

(Verses 21.) “Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent before themselves.”

He says: Woe to those who seem wise to themselves, who pursue not the wisdom of God but that of human beings; and because they do not receive the power of God and the wisdom of God, they think themselves wise (I Cor. I).

The Stoics say that wisdom and prudence differ in this respect: wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters, whereas prudence concerns only mortal affairs. Accordingly, these words are spoken against the scribes and Pharisees, who possess the key of knowledge but neither enter into Christ themselves nor permit others to enter (Luke XI).

[Col. 0087C] (Verses 22.) “Woe to those who are powerful at drinking wine and strong men at mixing *sikera*,” that is, drunkenness.

To those whom he had said above, “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine,” he now speaks of these same people: those who are powerful at drinking wine and strong men at mixing *sikera* (Deut. XXXII). Drunk with the wine of the dragon and the incurable poison of asps, they slandered by the power of the Lord. Drunk themselves, they intoxicated the peoples, so that, raging with the same fury, they shouted against the Lord.

According to the tropological interpretation, we have already said that priests entering the tabernacle of God ought not to drink wine or *sikera* (Lev. X). To this we now add that the same was commanded also to the Nazirite, who sanctifies himself to the Lord: he must not drink wine or *sikera*, nor anything made from grapes; he must not eat even a dried grape or vinegar made from wine (Num. VI).

Proverbs also commands: Those who are powerful and prone to anger must not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom.

According to the anagogical interpretation, I think the difference between wine and *sikera* is this: wine is one disturbance arising from several sources—for example, lust, avarice, gluttony, and envy. *Sikera*, that is, drunkenness, contains within itself all the passions of the vices, which we may more correctly call disturbances in Latin, because they overturn the state of the mind and make drunk people unaware of what they are doing.

Therefore those who preside ought above all to be free from vices, and especially from anger, which is close to madness, lest, the more power they possess, the more they harm those subject to them.

[Note: More correctly, it seems, the Vatican manuscript reads: “Therefore those who have great power ought,” etc.]

He mixes *sikera* who, although full of drunkenness, pretends to possess certain shadows and images of virtues in order to deceive people.

(Verses 23.) “Who justify the impious for gifts and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him.”

This too is a vice of the vineyard, which produced wild grapes instead of grapes and, while the Lord expected it to produce judgment, produced iniquity: justifying the impious for gifts and considering not cases but gifts, which blind even the eyes of the wise.

Therefore we must beware lest we become drunk with wine, in which there is wantonness (Deut. XVI, 19; Eph. V), and the thighs of our shame be exposed (Gen. IX), and lest we flatter the impious for gifts and despise the righteousness of the righteous because of poverty. The Epistle of James also commands this: we must not honor impious rich people and despise holy poor people, becoming judges of iniquity.

(Verses 24.) “Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours straw and the heat of flame consumes it, so their root will be like ashes, and their sprout will rise like dust. For they rejected the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel.”

Because of the preceding causes—pride, drunkenness, and avarice—because instead of grapes they produced thorns, hay, wood, and straw, and briars destined to burn, their root of wickedness will therefore be reduced to ashes, and all the flower and beauty of wealth and the body will be compared to dust (I Cor. III).

They not only did these things, but by these stages reached blasphemy, so that they would not receive the law of the Lord and would blaspheme the word of the Holy One of Israel. Concerning them we read above: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II, 3).

The root may be understood as evil thoughts, and the fruit and sprout as evil deeds and words, so that what lies hidden in the root may be displayed in the sprout. Both will be consumed by the Lord’s fire. Hence the Apostle speaks of “the root of bitterness” of the wicked, which grows upward into a sprout (Heb. XII, 15).

85 (Verses 25.) “Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand over them and struck them; and the mountains were shaken, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of the streets. In all these things his anger was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out.”

For they rejected the law of the Lord of hosts, which the Lord promises through Jeremiah to give, saying: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XXXI, 31–32).

And they blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel, saying: “He has a demon, and he is a Samaritan” (John VIII, 48); and, “Is this not the son of the carpenter?” (Matt. XIII, 55).

Therefore the anger of the Lord was kindled against his people. Previously it had been kindled against the leaders and powerful men who were wise in their own eyes, justified the impious for gifts, and whom the tongue of fire had devoured [another reading: devours] like straw, and the heat of flame had consumed, so that the powerful might suffer powerful torments.

He stretched out his hand against the one whom he calls his people, because it was a portion of his inheritance and the cord of his possession (Deut. XXXII). He stretched out his hand to strike, and his anger burned. Concerning this we read elsewhere: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. VI, 1). And Jeremiah says: “Correct us, Lord; nevertheless, in judgment and not in your fury” (Jer. X, 24).

The Lord is said to rage not because he is subject to human disturbances, but because we who sin will not fear him unless we hear him as angry. Hence the Apostle writes (Rom. II) that the goodness and patience of God urge us to repentance; but according to the hardness and impenitence of our heart, we store up anger for ourselves on the day of anger and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment.

What the hand is that is stretched out or raised over the sinful people, Job explains more clearly: “For the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job XIX, 21). Hence the devil, knowing the powerful hand of the Lord and the arm revealed to all the nations, says to the Lord: “Stretch out your hand and touch everything he has; surely he will bless you to your face” (Job II, 5).

That what is future is spoken of as though it were past follows prophetic custom, in which future events are so certain that they are thought to have already occurred. This is also sung in the Psalms: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. LXVIII, 22). And again: “They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots” (Ps. XXI, 19).

What follows, “And he struck him,” that is, his people, “and the mountains were shaken,” some think refers to hostile powers, or to those spirits who serve God and to whom sinners are handed over for punishment. We, however, think it is said hyperbolically: because of the magnitude of the impending evils, even the mountains are shaken, and all the streets of the cities are filled with the corpses of the dead.

No one doubts that this happened to the Jews after the Lord’s Passion, under Vespasian and Hadrian. When these things had occurred, his anger was not turned away, but his hand was still stretched out, or raised up, displaying the attitude of one who is angry and striking.

It should be noted in all these matters that he does not reproach them for idolatry or other sins by which they offended God, but because they rejected the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the word of the Lord.

(Verses 26 and following.) “And he will raise a sign among the nations from afar, and will whistle for him from the ends of the earth; and behold, he will come swiftly and quickly. He will not be feeble or weary; he will not slumber or sleep, nor will the belt of his loins be loosened, nor the strap of his sandal broken. His arrows are sharp, and all his bows are drawn; the hooves of his horses are like flint, and his wheels like the rush of a storm. His roar is like that of a lion; he will roar like young lions, growl, seize the prey, carry it away, and there will be no one to rescue it. In that day he will roar over it like the roaring of the sea. We will look toward the land, and behold, darkness of tribulation; the light has been darkened by its gloom.”

The Hebrews understand this passage as a prophecy concerning the Babylonians and Nebuchadnezzar: that he was brought into Judaea and Jerusalem by God’s will and overthrew the temple.

But, following the sequence and joining what follows to what precedes, we say that the sign raised among the nations from afar and the Lord’s whistling—or drawing them— from the ends of the earth occurred because they rejected the law of the Gospel and blasphemed the holy word.

[Note: Jerome learnedly compares “whistled” with “drew”; Philip the priest, his disciple, does the same in the interlinear exposition at the end of Job, chapter XXVII, where he explains “and he will whistle over him” as “and he will draw him.” Indeed, Greek *syrein* (σύρειν) signifies both.]

For if the subject were the Babylonians, according to prophetic custom he would have said: “I will summon the one who is from the north,” since, in relation to the location of Judaea, the Assyrians and Chaldaeans are in the northern region. Or certainly he would have described the Babylonians and Assyrians more explicitly.

But now, by saying, “He will raise a sign among the nations from afar, and will whistle for him from the ends of the earth,” he signifies nations situated far away and dwelling at the ends of the earth—clearly the Romans and all the peoples of Italy, Gaul, and Spain, who under Vespasian and Hadrian were subject to Roman rule. Hence Italy was formerly called Hesperia, because Hesperus sets there.

When this one came, he was struck down, and all the mountains of Judaea were shaken, as Theodotion and Symmachus translated; or “moved,” as Aquila rendered it; or “embittered,” as the Septuagint translated it, so that through the assault of the enemy all the streets were filled with the corpses of the dead.

The divine word therefore describes the speed of the approaching army, which came not by its own will but by the Lord’s—indeed, was drawn and summoned by his whistle. It did not fail or grow weary from so long a journey; in its desire for plunder it allowed no sleep to its eyes, and its footwear was not worn away. The passage describes the multitude of archers, the squadrons of horsemen, and the fervor of the chariots and four-horse teams. It came like a lion, not so much to fight as to plunder and devour, and the howling of the victorious army is compared with the waves of the sea.

From this we should note what “the sound of the sea” signifies wherever it is named in Scripture. When the Roman army came, seized the prey, and there was no one to rescue it, the prophet, in a compassionate attitude, joins himself to the people and says: “We will look toward the land, and behold, darkness of tribulation.” We will not dare to look toward heaven, whose inhabitant we have offended; and our light, which we always had in God, has been darkened by the gloom of tribulations.

I have read in the Commentary of someone—[Note: This is thought to be St. Basil’s work. In his exposition of this passage of Isaiah, he understands the raised standard among the nations as the banner of the Cross and the immediate acceptance of faith in Christ; the holy Doctor does not approve this interpretation.]—that the words, “He will raise a sign among the nations from afar, and will whistle for him from the ends of the earth,” should be understood of the calling of the nations: that, once the sign of the Cross had been raised and the burdens of sins laid down, they came swiftly and believed.

But I do not know how the things that follow can accord with this interpretation.

THE THIRD BOOK

[Col. 0091]

The magnitude of the volumes that is woven through the exposition of the prophet Isaiah is sufficient for me, since in this work to omit anything is a loss to understanding.

[Note: If the manuscript books supported it, we would prefer, with Victorius, to read “It is not sufficient,” with the negative particle prefixed, for a more coherent sense.] For this reason, in each book, which indicates only its number and order, I have placed brief prefaces.

And I beg you, virgin of Christ, Eustochium, to assist me with your prayers in the exposition of a most difficult vision. In it almighty God is seen in his majesty, and two Seraphim standing around him and crying out: “Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.” The threshold of the temple is shaken and trembles, and the Jewish house is filled with the darkness of error.

In comparison with the divine glory, the Prophet says that he has unclean lips and dwells among a blaspheming people, who cry out with a harmonious voice of impiety: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” and, “We have no king but Caesar” (John XIX, 6, 15). One of the Seraphim is sent to Isaiah, who purifies the prophet’s lips with a coal seized from the altar by tongs, while the people remain unclean.

The third book on Isaiah therefore begins as follows.

(Chapter VI—Verse 1.) “In the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and raised up.”

That Isaiah prophesied under four kings, concerning Judah and Jerusalem, was demonstrated by the title of the first vision: namely, under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. When Uzziah died, under whom all the matters explained above were spoken, his son Jotham succeeded him. He reigned for sixteen years, did what was right in the sight of the Lord, and built the high gate of the temple.

While he was ruling, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and raised up, so that he might display the bearing of one who reigns.

And the things beneath it filled the Temple; or, as Theodotion and Symmachus translated it: “And the things beneath his feet filled the Temple.” In place of this, the Seventy translated: “And the house was full of his glory.”

Concerning this vision, approximately thirty years ago, when I was in Constantinople and was being instructed in the study of the Holy Scriptures by the most eloquent man, Gregory of Nazianzus, then bishop of that city, I know that I dictated a brief and spontaneous treatise, both to test my little talent and to obey the requests of my friends.

[Note: When I was in Constantinople, etc. In the year of Christ 380 or 381, Jerome dictated a sudden treatise and dedicated it, at the command of Pope Damasus, to him; this work occupies the eighteenth place among the letters. MARTIAN.—Around the middle of the year 381, as has been established for us, when we printed the Treatise in volume I among Letter XVIII.]

I therefore refer the reader to that little book, and ask him to be satisfied with the brief exposition of that earlier period. Sacred history relates that Uzziah, because he claimed for himself an unlawful priesthood, was struck with leprosy; after his death, the Lord is seen in the Temple that he had polluted (II Chronicles 26). From this we understand that, while a leprous king reigns among us, we cannot see the Lord reigning in his majesty, nor know the mysteries of the Holy Trinity.

Thus also in Exodus, after Pharaoh died—the man who oppressed Israel with clay, straw, and bricks—the people cried out to the Lord, whereas while he lived they could not cry out. And Ezekiel, after the death of Pelatiah son of Benaiah, a most wicked ruler, fell upon his face and cried out to the Lord in a loud voice.

And, beautifully, according to the Hebrew, it was not the Lord himself who filled the Temple—he whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth, and of whom we read elsewhere, “The Lord is in his holy Temple; the Lord’s throne is in heaven” (Psalm 10:5)—but the things beneath his feet filled the Temple (Isaiah 66).

Who this Lord is who is seen, we learn more fully in the Gospel of John and in the Acts of the Apostles. John says: “Isaiah said this when he saw his glory and spoke about him” (John 12:41), plainly signifying Christ. Again, Paul, in the Acts of the Apostles, when speaking to the Jews at Rome, says:

“Beautifully did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; you will see with your eyes and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull; they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn, and I heal them” (Acts 28:26–27).

The Son was seen in the appearance of one who reigns, and the Holy Spirit spoke because of the sharing of majesty and the unity of substance.

Someone may ask how the Prophet now says that he saw the Lord—not simply “the Lord,” but “the Lord of hosts,” as he himself testifies below—when the evangelist John said, “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:20), and when God says to Moses, “You cannot see my face; for no human being shall see my face and live” (Exodus 33:20).

[Note: Augustine also quotes this passage from Jerome in the Commonitorium, or Letter 148, to Fortunatianus, and explains it according to his own understanding in these words: “What could be clearer than this manifestation? For if he had said only that neither the divinity of the Father, nor of the Son, nor of the Holy Spirit could be seen by the eyes of the flesh, and had not afterward added ‘but by the eyes of the mind,’ someone might perhaps say that flesh should no longer be called flesh once the body had become spiritual. By adding and saying ‘but by the eyes of the mind,’ he removed this kind of vision from every bodily category. And lest anyone think that he spoke only about the present time, he added the testimony of the Lord, wishing to show what he meant by ‘the eyes of the mind.’ That testimony declares a promise not of present but of future vision: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.’”]

To this we shall reply that not only the divinity of the Father, but also that of the Son and the Holy Spirit—for there is one nature in the Trinity—cannot be seen by the eyes of the flesh, but by the eyes of the mind, of which the Savior himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

We read that the Lord appeared to Abraham in the form of a man, and that Jacob wrestled as with a man—with one who was God. Hence that place was called Peniel, that is, “the face of God”: “For I have seen God face to face,” he says, “and my life has been preserved” (Genesis 32). Ezekiel also saw the Lord in human form, seated upon the Cherubim; from his waist downward there was something like fire, while above he had the appearance of electrum (Ezekiel 1).

Therefore God’s nature is not perceived, but he is seen by human beings in whatever manner he has willed.

### Verse 2

“Seraphim were standing above it; each had six wings, and the other had six wings. With two they covered his face, with two they covered his feet, and with two they flew. And they cried out, one to the other, and said: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

What we, following the other translators and the Hebrew truth—in which MEMMALLO is written, that is, ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ, which in Latin is said to mean “above it”—have translated as “above it,” the Seventy translated as “around him,” so that the Seraphim are described not as standing above the Temple but around the Lord.

Again, where we said that one of the Seraphim covered his face and his feet—by which “his” is understood to refer to God—the Hebrew has PHANAU and REGLAU (פניו ורגליו), which can be interpreted both as “his” and as “their own.” Thus, according to the ambiguity of the Hebrew language, the Seraphim may be said to cover both the face and feet of God and their own face and feet.

[Note: It was wrongly read as “only in the seventy-ninth Psalm.”]

In the seventy-ninth Psalm we read: “You who sit upon the Cherubim, manifest yourself” (Psalm 79:3). In our language, Cherubim is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge.” Hence the Lord is openly shown to sit above the Cherubim in the manner of a charioteer.

[Note: Seraphim. The name Seraphim is not found elsewhere in the canonical Scriptures as a designation of angels. But we read the Hebrew name Saraph and Seraphim, meaning “fiery,” “fiery beings,” or “burning beings,” in Numbers 21:6 and 8: “Make yourself a Saraph,” that is, a fiery serpent; and “God sent Seraphim,” fiery serpents. Kimchi calls the angels Seraphim Malache esch, “angels of fire,” as if one were to say “shining and flashing angels,” who are of a fiery nature. MARTIAN.]

Apart from this passage, I do not know that I have read of Seraphim elsewhere in the canonical Scriptures under this meaning: that they stand above the Temple or around the Lord.

Therefore those who customarily say in their prayers, “You who sit upon the Cherubim and Seraphim,” are in error, since Scripture has not taught this. Seraphim is interpreted as ἐμπρησταί, which we may render “those who set aflame” or “those who burn,” according to what we read elsewhere: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Psalm 103:5).

[Note: Martianus has ἐμπρησταί. See what we have noted on the Book of Names.]

Hence the Apostle Paul also says in the Epistle to the Hebrews, an epistle that Latin custom does not accept: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14).

Daniel too, after describing the Lord in the appearance of one who reigns, added: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Daniel 7:10).

In the Cherubim the Lord is shown; in the Seraphim he is shown in part and concealed in part. For they cover his face and feet, because we cannot know either the things that preceded the world or those that will come after the world; we contemplate only the intermediate things that were made in the six days.

Nor is it surprising that we should believe this about the Seraphim, since the apostles reveal the Savior to believers and conceal him from unbelievers; and there was also a veil before the Ark of the Covenant (Exodus 40).

They are also said to have wings because of their speed and their movement everywhere—or because they always dwell in higher places. For what is said about the winds, “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Psalm 103:4), does not truly testify that the winds have wings, according to the tales of poets and the license of painters; rather, it signifies rapid movement everywhere.

And each has six wings because we know only about the making of the world and of the present age.

As for their crying out, one to the other—or, according to the Hebrews, “this one to that one,” that is, one to one—they exhort one another in turn to praise the Lord and say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of hosts,” displaying the mystery of the Trinity in the one Divinity. They testify that it is no longer the Jewish Temple, as formerly, but the whole earth that is full of his glory—he who for our salvation deigned to assume a human body and descend to the earth.

Finally, when Moses was praying to the Lord for pardon for the sinful people because of the worshiped calf, the Lord answered him: “I will be gracious to them. Nevertheless, as I live, and as my name lives, the whole earth shall be filled with my glory” (Numbers 14:20–21).

And the seventy-first Psalm sings: “The whole earth shall be filled with his glory” (Psalm 71:19). Hence the angels also cried out to the shepherds: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

[Note: “Therefore some,” etc. These words are directed against Origen, as is clear from the letter to Pammachius and Oceanus: “In this reading of Isaiah,” he says, “in which two Seraphim are described as crying out, while he [Origen] interprets them as the Son and the Holy Spirit, have I not changed his detestable interpretation into two Testaments?” MARTIAN.—Origen, plainly, whose “detestable interpretation I changed into two Testaments,” as Jerome says in Letter 84 to Pammachius and Oceanus, section 3.]

Therefore it is impious for someone to understand the two Seraphim as the Son and the Holy Spirit, when, according to the evangelist John and the apostle Paul, we teach that the Son of God was seen in the majesty of one who reigns, and that the Holy Spirit spoke.

Some among the Latins understand the two Seraphim as the Old and New Testaments, which speak only about the present age. Hence they are also said to have six wings, to cover the face and feet of God, to bring forward the testimony of truth in rivalry with one another, and to display in everything the mysteries of the Trinity. They marvel at one another that the Lord of hosts, existing in the form of God the Father, took the form of a servant and humbled himself even to death, and death on a cross (Philippians 2), and that they now recognize him not only in heavenly things, as formerly, but also in earthly things.

### Verse 4

“And the lintels of the hinges were shaken by the voice of the one crying out, and the house was filled with smoke.”

When the Seraphim were crying out and proclaiming the mystery of the Trinity throughout the whole earth, at the time when the whole earth learned of the passion of the Lord and Savior, immediately the lintel of the Temple was shaken—or removed—and all its hinges collapsed, fulfilling the Savior’s threat when he said: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Matthew 23:38).

And how beautiful is the order of the words! After the earth was filled with the glory of the Lord of hosts, the Temple of the Jews was filled with the darkness of ignorance, with gloom, and with smoke, which is harmful to the eyes. Or certainly the burning of the Temple is indicated through the smoke. For first the Gospel of the Savior was preached throughout the whole world, and forty-two years after the Lord’s passion Jerusalem was captured and the Temple was burned.

The Jews think that the Temple being filled with smoke signifies incense, that is, burning incense, and through it the arrival of the divine majesty.

### Verse 5

“And I said: Woe is me, for I was silent; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips; and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.”

After Abraham saw the Lord and heard his voice, he said that he was earth and ashes (Genesis 18). Isaiah, according to the Seventy Translators, testifies that he was pierced with remorse—not on account of other crimes, but because he had unclean lips.

Blessed is the conscience that sinned only in speech, not through its own fault but through association with a people having unclean lips, with whom it was very often compelled to speak. From this it is shown to be harmful to live with sinners: “Whoever touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclesiasticus 13:1).

But because in the Hebrew we read, “Woe is me, for I was silent,” the Prophet laments that he was not worthy to praise the Lord of hosts together with the Seraphim, whom we understand as angelic powers. He did not dare to praise the Lord because he had unclean lips. And he had unclean lips for this reason: because he lived among a sinful people.

Or the passage may be understood in this way: “Because I was silent, and did not boldly rebuke Uzziah, the wicked king, therefore my lips are unclean, and I do not dare to sing the praises of the Lord with the angels, lest it be said to me: ‘Why do you recite my statutes and take my covenant upon your mouth?’” (Psalm 49:16). “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 15:9).

We say this not because we teach that Isaiah was such a man, but because he himself, in humility, confesses that he is unworthy of God’s praise on account merely of his unclean lips.

### Verse 6

“And one of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal that he had taken from the altar with tongs. He touched my mouth and said: Behold, I have touched your lips; your iniquity shall be taken away, and your sin shall be cleansed.”

[Note: From the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin translator himself, according to most manuscript codices, Victorius restored “he touched,” in place of the previous reading.]

“One of the Seraphim”—whose name means “the one who sets aflame”—flew, or was sent, in order to cleanse the Prophet’s unclean lips and to refine them with the ember or coal that he had taken from the altar.

Many think that there are two Seraphim because one cried out to the other, although individual beings among a plurality may cry out each to another; and the edition of the Seventy more clearly indicates a plurality, since they translated, “Seraphim stood around him.” If two were intended, they would have said not “around him” but “on either side.”

This also agrees with the multitude of angels prepared for God’s service. Seraphim is a plural form, and Seraph singular, just as Cherubim is plural and Cherub singular.

As for the altar beneath which the souls of the martyrs appear to be in heaven, John also speaks of it in the Apocalypse (Revelation 6). And this coal, which only the Seventy translated as ἄνθραξ, that is, “carbuncle”—or, in another reading, “is interpreted”—may signify not coal or an ember, as most think, but ἄνθρακα, that is, a carbuncle stone, which is called fiery because of its resemblance to a flame-colored fire.

From this we understand that God’s altar is full of carbuncles, that is, of fiery coals and embers that cleanse sins. Hence we read concerning God: “Coals were kindled by him” (Psalm 17:9). And it is said of the Lord himself that he is a consuming fire. The Savior likewise says in the Gospel: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), so that he might baptize with the Holy Spirit and with fire. “The work of each one will be tested by fire” (I Corinthians 3). And the one who is to be saved will be saved as though he had passed through fire.

This too should be noted: when Jeremiah was told, “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from your mother’s womb I sanctified you” (Jeremiah 1:5), because he did not have unclean lips but had merely said, “I do not know how to speak, for I am young,” the Lord himself stretched out his hand, touched his mouth, and said: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth.”

But to Isaiah, who had said, “I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people having unclean lips,” God does not stretch out his hand; rather, a Seraphim is sent by God, or flies of his own will, because he is devoted to this service. In his hand he holds a coal which, according to the Seventy and Theodotion, he grasped with tongs; according to Aquila and Symmachus, who followed the Hebrew, with pincers—that is, MALCAIM (מלקחים)—so that he might touch Isaiah’s mouth and cleanse his former sins.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the Vulgate, has “I dwell.” The material that follows in Jerome’s exposition is borrowed from Eusebius.]

The hand is sent both by God and by the Seraphim, so that the Prophet, seeing a bodily member of his own, might not be frightened by an external touch.

Some of our writers think that the tongs with which the coal is grasped signify the two Testaments, which are joined to each other through the unity of the Holy Spirit.

Since the Lord is introduced as seated, seated in the Temple, and the house is filled with smoke—which the Jews take to mean incense—the tongs are appropriately introduced as well, for we also read of them in the priestly ministry (Exodus 37).

### Verse 8

“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? And I said: Here am I; send me.”

In place of what we and all the other translators rendered “for us”—which in Hebrew is LANU (לנו)—the Seventy, for some reason of their own, inserted “to this people,” a phrase that is entirely absent from the Hebrew.

When “for us” is said from the person of God, it must be understood in the same sense in which we read in Genesis: “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness” (Genesis 1:26), so that it may indicate the mystery of the Trinity.

For just as we read in the Gospel, when the Lord says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), and refer “one” to nature but “are” to the distinction of persons, so, when the Lord commands, the Trinity gives the command.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “the Lord saying.”]

The Lord does not say whom he is ordering to go; rather, he offers those who hear a choice, so that willingness may receive its reward.

And the Prophet does not promise to go through the rashness and arrogance of his own conscience, but with confidence, because his lips have been cleansed, his iniquity taken away, and his sin purified.

Thus Moses too, to whom the Lord had said, “Come, I will send you to Pharaoh, king of Egypt” (Exodus 3:10), replied, “I beg you, Lord, I am not worthy; send someone else whom you will send”—or, as it is read in the Hebrew, “Send whomever you are going to send” (Exodus 4:13). He answered not from contempt but from humility, since he had heard nothing about his lips having been cleansed, although he had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

Isaiah, however, offers himself for service not through his own merit but through the grace of the Lord by which he has been cleansed.

Others think that Isaiah offered himself for this reason: he supposed that he would announce prosperity to the people. But when he heard, “Go and say to this people: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; you will see with your eyes and will not perceive” (Isaiah 6:9), for this reason later, when the voice of the Lord said to him, “Cry out,” he did not immediately cry out but asked, “What shall I cry?”

Jeremiah too, to whom it had been said, “Take the cup and give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you” (Jeremiah 25:15), willingly accepting the cup of punishments so that he might offer it to hostile nations, and so that they might drink, vomit, and fall, replied after hearing, “Go, and first give it to Jerusalem”: “You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived” (Jeremiah 20:7).

This is the Hebrew interpretation. For our part, we say that Isaiah’s offering himself to be sent was not an act of rashness but of obedience.

### Verses 9–following

“And he said: Go, and say to this people: Hear by hearing, and do not understand; see by seeing, and do not perceive. Make the heart of this people dull, burden its ears, and close its eyes, lest it perhaps see with its eyes, hear with its ears, understand with its heart, turn, and be healed.”

The Seventy translated this passage as the evangelist Luke placed it in the Acts of the Apostles:

“When they disagreed among themselves”—plainly, the Jews—“they were departing, while Paul said one word: The Holy Spirit spoke well through Isaiah the prophet to our fathers, saying: Go to this people and say: You will hear with your ears and will not understand; you will see with your eyes and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown dull; they have heard heavily with their ears and have closed their eyes, lest they perhaps see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and turn, and I heal them” (Acts 28:25–27).

At what time this prophecy was fulfilled, the Apostle Paul himself explains in what follows: “Therefore let it be known to you that this salvation of God has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will hear it” (Acts 28:28).

Hence we also read in the same Acts of the Apostles that Paul and Barnabas, when the Jews refused to believe, said: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken first to you; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46–47).

[Note: Victorius prefers “you reject” and “you judge.”]

For thus the Lord commanded us: “I have appointed you as a light to the Gentiles, that you may be for salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

According to the Seventy, therefore, the interpretation is easy: the prophet Isaiah, at the Lord’s command, announces what the people are going to do.

In the Hebrew there is a difficulty: how can God himself command the people to hear and not understand, to see and not perceive, and afterward introduce the Prophet speaking and praying to the Lord: “Make the heart of this people dull, burden its ears, and close its eyes, lest it perhaps see with its eyes, hear with its ears, understand with its heart, turn, and be healed” (Isaiah 6:10)?

First, the question that may be raised against us must be resolved: why did the apostle Paul, disputing with the Hebrews, speak not according to the Hebrew text, which he knew to be correct, but according to the Seventy?

The ancient commentators on the Church report that the evangelist Luke was highly skilled in the medical art and knew Greek letters better than Hebrew. Hence his language, both in the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles—that is, in both volumes—is more polished, has the flavor of secular eloquence, and uses Greek testimonies more often than Hebrew ones.

Matthew and John, however, one of whom composed his Gospel in Hebrew and the other in Greek, bring forward testimonies from the Hebrew, as in the following passages: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Hosea 2:1); “He shall be called a Nazarene” (Matthew 2:23); “From his belly shall flow rivers of living water” (John 7:38); “They shall look upon him whom they pierced” (Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37); and other passages like these.

Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews is likewise opposed for this reason: although he writes to Hebrews, he uses testimonies that are not found in the Hebrew volumes.

If someone says that the Hebrew books were afterward falsified by the Jews, let him hear what Origen replies to this little question in the eighth volume of his Expositions of Isaiah: the Lord and the apostles, who reproach the scribes and Pharisees for their other crimes, would never have kept silent about this crime, which was the greatest of all.

But if they say that the Hebrew books were falsified after the coming of the Lord and Savior and the preaching of the apostles, I shall not be able to restrain my laughter: as though the Savior, the evangelists, and the apostles had brought forward their testimonies in such a way that the Jews would later falsify them.

Concerning the present passage, this must be said: it is pointless for us to take refuge in the translation of the Seventy so that what is said according to the Hebrew may not appear blasphemous: “Hear by hearing, and do not understand; see the vision, and do not perceive.” For we find testimonies of this kind even among the Seventy Translators, such as the statement made to Pharaoh in Exodus: “For this reason I raised you up, that I might show my power in you” (Exodus 9:16).

If he himself raised him up and hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he would not believe; and if it is said of others, “God gave them a spirit of remorse, eyes so that they might not see, and ears so that they might not hear” (Romans 11:8); and in the Psalms: “Let their table become a snare and a trap and a stumbling-block and a retribution; let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and make their backs continually bent” (Psalm 68:23–24)—then those who do not see are not at fault, but the one who gave eyes for not seeing is.

Therefore, even without this testimony that we are now attempting to explain, the same question remains in the churches. Either this passage will be resolved together with the others, or, if the others are resolved, this one will remain insoluble.

The blessed apostle Paul explains this passage more fully in his Epistle to the Romans. What he pursued through nearly the whole epistle, we would make superfluous if we tried to encompass it in a brief statement.

After many other things he says: “God has shut up all things in unbelief, that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:32).

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “God shut up all things under sin, so that,” despite the Greek text and the Latin translator himself.]

And, marveling at the mysteries of the Lord, he adds: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable [variant: unsearchable] his ways!”

And again, disputing concerning the unbelief of the Jews, he says: “Did they stumble so that they might fall? Certainly not; but through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, in order to provoke them to jealousy” (Romans 11:11).

And shortly afterward: “For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?”

And again: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: a hardening in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and then all Israel will be saved.”

And a little later (Romans 11:25): “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers. For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.”

“For just as you,” he says, “once did not believe God but now have received mercy because of their unbelief, so they too have now not believed because of the mercy shown to you, so that they also may receive mercy. For God has shut up all things under sin, that he may have mercy on all.”

Therefore it is not God’s cruelty, but his mercy, that one nation should perish so that all may be saved: that part of the Jews should not see, so that the whole world might see.

Hence the Lord himself, in the Gospel, turned the mystery of the man blind from birth who had received his sight toward a spiritual interpretation and said: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

And elsewhere Simeon says: “Behold, this child is appointed for the fall and rising of many” (Luke 2:34).

While they do not see, therefore, we see; while they fall, we rise.

Understanding this, the Prophet in a sense says in other words:

“O Lord, you command me to speak to the Jewish people so that they may hear but not understand the Savior, and see him but not recognize him. If you wish your command to be fulfilled and the whole world to be saved—which I too desire to happen—then make the heart of this people dull, burden their ears, and close their eyes, lest they understand, hear, or see. For if they see, turn, understand, and are healed, the whole world will not receive healing.”

From this we perceive that, although the sin is grave, if someone turns, he can be healed.

At the same time, we must understand that, because of the magnitude of their crimes, they were judged unworthy even of repentance, as the Lord himself says to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

### Verses 11–13

“And I said: How long, Lord? And he said: Until the cities are laid waste, without an inhabitant, and the houses without human beings, and the land is left desolate. And the Lord will remove human beings far away, and what had been abandoned will be multiplied in the midst of the land. And there will still be a tenth in it, and again it will be for destruction, like a terebinth and like an oak that has cast off its fruit; the holy seed will be what remains standing in it.”

When the Lord said, “Go and say to this people that they should hear and not hear, see and not see,” they should neither hear nor see because they would not understand the Lord’s words or recognize his works, and because they had grown fat, swollen, and forgetful of their Creator (Deuteronomy 32).

[Note: Two manuscripts read, “therefore he answered.” The present material is from Eusebius, but is explained at greater length.]

The Prophet responds and anxiously asks about his people: “How long, Lord, will this sentence remain, so that one who hears does not hear and one who sees does not see?”

The Lord answers him: They will neither hear nor see, and their hearts will remain blinded, until the cities of Judea, while Vespasian and Titus wage war, are utterly overturned—to such an extent that not even their former name remains—and whatever houses survive are without inhabitants, and the land is reduced to desolation; and the Jewish people, whether through flight or captivity, are dispersed throughout the whole world. The Jewish people will no longer multiply in Judea as before, but among all the nations.

When I say that it will multiply, I mean that the remnant people will suffer such misfortune that, in comparison with their former multitude, scarcely a tenth part will remain.

And when there is desolation even in that land—for this passage can be understood in two ways, namely, that scarcely a tenth part will remain in the whole world and that in Judea itself only a small remnant of the people will be preserved—then those remnants themselves will again be given over to plunder, when, approximately fifty years later, Hadrian comes and utterly devastates the land of Judea, so that it may be compared with a terebinth and an oak that has lost its acorns.

[Note: This alludes to the edict of the emperor Hadrian, issued in the year of the Lord 137, during the consulship of Pompeianus and Acilianus. See Eusebius, Chronicle, and Book IV, chapter 6, of his History; also Tertullian, Apology, chapter 21, and again Against the Jews, chapter 13. Jerome himself likewise mentions this dispersion and law elsewhere, in his Commentary on Jeremiah 31 and on Daniel 9.]

Finally, after the final devastation, public laws were also imposed, and the Jews were forbidden to enter the land from which they had been expelled.

But if someone believes in Christ, and what we read above is fulfilled—“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:9)—when, according to the Apostle, the remnant is saved (Romans 9), this will be the holy seed, and from the stock of the apostles all the churches will spring forth.

What we have said—“the holy seed will be what remains standing in it”—or, according to Aquila, “the holy seed will be its offspring,” is not found in the Seventy Translators, but was added from the Hebrew and Theodotion’s edition by Origen. It is reported in copies of the Church, so that, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel may then be saved; and in this too the word of the Lord may be fulfilled, when he says: “I kill, and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39).

[Note: Nevertheless, countless codices have survived to our time that do not contain this addition. Procopius has likewise noted that ἐν τῷ γενέσθαι τὸ σπέρμα ἅγιον ἐν τῇ στάσει καὶ βεβαιότητι αὐτῶν, “when the holy seed shall be in their standing and steadfastness,” derives from Theodotion’s addition.]

## Chapter VII

### Verses 1–2

“And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah: Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to fight against it, but they could not conquer it. And they reported to the house of David, saying: ‘Syria has allied itself with Ephraim’; and his heart and the heart of his people were shaken, as the trees of the forests are shaken by the face of the wind.”

Uzziah, who is also called Azariah, king of Judah, reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years (2 Kings 15). At the end of his reign Isaiah saw what the preceding passage has described. After Uzziah’s death, when his son Jotham, a most righteous king, reigned in his place, the prophet immediately saw the Lord and Savior reigning in his majesty, announcing the blindness of the Jewish people, the overthrow of Jerusalem and the other cities under Vespasian and Hadrian, and how the remnant was to be saved among the Apostles.

The third king, Ahaz, the son of Jotham, succeeded him. He was exceedingly impious (2 Kings 16; 2 Chronicles 28). He closed the doors of the Temple, worshiped the Baals in the valley of Ben-hinnom,

[Note: [Col. 0102D] We have emended this with Victor to “Ben-hinnom,” where previously “Gehenna” stood.]

and consecrated his son to idols. He even removed the bronze altar that Solomon had made and placed in the Temple of God an altar of idols, the model of which he had received from Damascus.

Therefore he was justly abandoned by the Lord’s help. Rezin, king of Syria—that is, of Aram—and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel in Samaria, rose up against him and came to Jerusalem to attack it (ibid.). We read in the book of Chronicles that Rezin, king of Damascus, after defeating Ahaz, transferred many people from Judea to Damascus; and that Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of the ten tribes called Israel, who reigned in Samaria, struck down in one day one hundred and twenty thousand fighting men of Judah and led captive to Samaria two hundred thousand women, boys, and girls, together with immeasurable spoil.

The prophet is silent here about that battle, but now reports a second encounter: having experienced their own strength and victory, and enticed by the size of the spoil, they come again to Judea and wish to conquer Jerusalem, but they cannot, because the Lord helped it. By the occasion of the mercy through which he was rescuing the besieged people, he announced that his Son would be born of a Virgin.

When the house of David—that is, the royal house—heard that Syria and Ephraim, Rezin and Pekah, were coming with a united army, it was terrified and greatly afraid. Both king and people trembled so that one might think the leaves of trees were being tossed about by gusts of wind.

According to the allegorical interpretation, the meaning is readily apparent. While the impious king Ahaz was reigning, the king of Aram—which is interpreted as “lofty” and “exalted,” indicating the arrogance of worldly wisdom—and Pekah, son of Remaliah, who likewise, according to the prophet Hosea, belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, from which Jeroboam son of Nebat had established golden calves in Bethel and Dan (1 Kings 12:32), and had separated God’s people from David,

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Vaticanus has: “and from the house of David,” etc., more correctly.]

are referred to heretics who agree among themselves in order to attack the Church.

When the house of David hears this—the house of David whom we read in Ezekiel will be raised up as the good shepherd (Ezekiel 34)—and when its people, believing simply in the Lord, hear it, they will tremble. They will tremble because they are compared not with fruit-bearing trees but with a fruitless forest.

[Note: [Col. 0102D] Previously the reading was “the same,” namely, the heretics. But, with two manuscripts, “those same,” namely, swords, was preferred.]

No one doubts that these same heretics and gentiles fight against the house of David with the swords of arguments and dialectical skill,

[Col. 0102D]

so that, although they disagree among themselves, they agree in attacking the Church—according to the saying that Herod and Pilate, though at variance with each other, were united in friendship during the Lord’s Passion.

### Verses 3–4 and following

“And the Lord said to Isaiah: ‘Go out to meet Ahaz, you and your son Shear-jashub, who has been left, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field. And you shall say to him: See that you keep silent; do not fear, and do not let your heart be afraid because of the two tails of these smoking firebrands, in the anger of the fury of Rezin, and of Syria, and of the son of Remaliah, because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah have taken evil counsel against you, saying: Let us go up against Judah, stir it up, tear it away to ourselves, and set the son of Tabeel as king in its midst.’

“Thus says the Lord God: It shall not stand, and it shall not be so. But the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within another sixty-five years Ephraim shall cease to be a people. And the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is the son of Remaliah. If you do not believe, you shall not endure.”

Isaiah’s son Shear-jashub, whose name means “a remnant” or “one who converts,” represents the people of Judah, who were to be delivered from the hands of the two kings. He is commanded to go out with his father and meet Ahaz, king of Judah, at the place of the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field. In that place we shall later read that, under Hezekiah king of Judah, the Rabshakeh stood and, at the command of Sennacherib king of the Assyrians, blasphemed the people of God. The officials of the city whom we read about in the book of Kings were sent by Hezekiah to that place.

Ahaz is commanded (2 Kings 18), although he was an impious king, because of the Lord’s mercy, to keep silent and not be terrified; his heart is not to fear, thinking that he will suffer things like those he had endured before. He calls Rezin king of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Samaria “two tails of smoking firebrands,” that is, of smoking torches,

[Col. 0103C]

because the kingdom of Syria—that is, of Damascus—and the kingdom of Samaria—that is, of the ten tribes, which were otherwise called Ephraim—were coming to an end in them.

For it is written (2 Kings 16) that Tiglath-pileser, king of the Assyrians, went up against Damascus under King Ahaz, devastated it, transferred its inhabitants to Cyrene, and killed Rezin. It is also written that Hoshea son of Elah lay in wait for Pekah son of Remaliah, struck and killed him, and reigned in his place over Israel for nine years; that Shalmaneser, king of Assyria, came and besieged Samaria, now called Sebaste, for three years; and that in the ninth year of Hoshea’s reign he captured it, sent Hoshea bound into prison, transferred Israel to Assyria, and settled them in Halah and Habor beside the river Gozan, in the cities—or, as the Septuagint translated, in the mountains of the Medes (2 Kings 17).

Although the two wicked kings had taken counsel to go up against Judah, whose region lies in the mountains, to stir up the people who were resting and, in a sense, sleeping, and to subjugate them to their power, and although they intended to set over them a king, the son of Tabeel—whose name means “good God,” whether it indicated a man of that name or an idol—nevertheless, the Lord God says this:

“This plan shall not stand.” For the present, Damascus will be the chief city of Syria, and Rezin will rule in Damascus itself. In Ephraim, because of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was the first to reign from Ephraim, the head will be Samaria—that is, the royal house in the city of Samaria—and the head of Samaria will be the son of Remaliah, that is, Pekah. But the kingdom of the ten tribes, namely the people of Ephraim, will cease to exist after sixty-five years.

This cannot stand unless we examine the matter carefully.

[Note: [Col. 0103D] “In the twelfth year,” etc. Many very ancient manuscripts read, “in the fourteenth year.” Hence arose the error in Erasmus’s edition, which Marianus Victorius corrected. MARTIAN. Vaticanus and several other manuscripts in Martianus read “fourteenth,” the error having been removed by Victorius.]

In the twelfth year of Ahaz son of Jotham, in the tribe of Judah, Hoshea reigned over Samaria, and in the ninth year of his reign he was captured (2 Kings 17). Ahaz reigned over Judah for sixteen years (2 Kings 16), and after his death Hoshea was captured in the seventh year of his own reign,

[Note: [Col. 0103D] Victorius inserts “besieged,” and “in the ninth,” so that, since the siege lasted three years, Hoshea would not be said to have been besieged and captured in the same year.]

Samaria was destroyed, and the whole people were deported to the Medes. Thus, if we count the sixteen years of Ahaz and the seven years of Hoshea, they amount to twenty-three years, or at most twenty-four.

[Note: [Col. 0104D] Victorius again restored “twenty-five” from his own edition, since, if Hoshea’s nine years—the year in which he was captured—are added to Ahaz’s sixteen years, that is, if we consider not the year in which Hoshea was besieged but the year in which he was captured, the total must be twenty-five years.]

Where, then, are the sixty-five years in which the kingdom of Israel is said to be destined to end?

The Hebrews therefore explain this passage as follows. Amos, who began to prophesy under Uzziah, at the same time when Isaiah began his prophetic ministry, was the first to prophesy against Israel, saying: “Israel shall surely be led away captive out of his land” (Amos 7:11, 17). The title of his prophecy was also directed against Samaria. He began to prophesy in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, two years before the earthquake, which they believe occurred at the time when Uzziah entered the Temple of God and claimed the priesthood for himself; the earth was struck, the ashes of the altar were scattered, and the king himself was struck with leprosy (2 Chronicles 26).

They hold that this occurred in the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah, leaving him twenty-seven years thereafter. Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years (2 Kings 15); after him his son Jotham reigned for sixteen years, and Jotham’s son Ahaz for another sixteen years. After Ahaz, Hezekiah reigned, and in the sixth year of his reign Samaria was captured. Thus the total comes to sixty-five years (2 Kings 16).

Although the Lord proclaimed these things through the prophet, Ahaz and the people did not believe what was to come. Hence it follows:
