“If you do not believe, you shall not endure,” as Symmachus translated it; that is, “you shall not remain in your kingdom, but shall be led into captivity, suffering the punishments of those whose unbelief you imitated.”

Or, according to the Septuagint, “you shall not understand.” The sense is: because you do not believe what the Lord says will happen, you will have no understanding.

This is what we have said according to the historical interpretation. But according to the allegorical interpretation already begun, we must consider that Isaiah is commanded to meet the impious king, leaving his own place—not at the beginning of the conduit, but at the farthest end of the upper pool, which was in the fuller’s field, where dirt and stains were cleansed.

Although Ahaz reigned over Judah, because he was impious he remained at the farthest end of the upper pool. God therefore has compassion not so much on the king, whom he considered unworthy of salvation, as on his own people.

As we said earlier, the two tails of smoking torches signify worldly wisdom and heretical speech, whose end is burning. They took counsel in vain to go up against Judah, to seize it as though it were careless and asleep, to join it to their errors, and to set over it a king, the son of Tabeel,

[Col. 0105B]

that is, “good God.” For each adversary considers truth and the best doctrine to be with himself. Thus the heretic Marcion thinks that Christ is the son of the good God—that is, of another god—and not of the just God, whose prophets are the ones whom he calls bloodthirsty, cruel, and judges.

While they say these things, the Lord threatens that their plan shall not stand. Yet, for the present, so long as this world stands and the things of the world rule within their own boundaries and cities, they will have power. But when the time of consummation has come—that is, the sixty-five years—and both the things of the world made during the six

[Note: [Col. 0105D] I would prefer the Vatican reading, “which were made in six thousand years.” He appears to be discussing the end of all things made from the creation of the world up to that time, according to the calculations commonly accepted among the Greeks.]

days and everything pertaining to the five senses have reached their end, then everything will be dissolved—things which gentiles and heretics do not believe will come, and which, because of their unbelief, they do not understand when they are announced.

### Verses 10–11

“And the Lord continued to speak to Ahaz, saying: ‘Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depth of hell or in the height above.’”

The Lord had first spoken to Ahaz through the prophet: “See that you keep silent; do not fear,” and so forth. But because Ahaz did not believe and therefore did not understand, the Lord himself speaks to him, so that, terrified at least by the Lord’s authority, he may accept what is said.

“Because,” he says, “it seems difficult to you that the most powerful kingdoms should be brought to an end within a short time and that you, together with your people, should be rescued from great danger, ask for a sign—not from the idols whose error holds you captive, but from the Lord your God, who promises you help. And let the sign be from wherever you choose to request it, whether from the depths or from the heights.”

Since only the Septuagint translators said “from the depth,” the others, following the Hebrew, translated more expressively, “from the depth of hell.” Therefore, just as “the depth” signifies hell, so we should understand “the height above” as meaning above the heavens. When you receive a sign from hell or from the height, you will believe the future things I have declared.

“Do you wish,” he says, “that the earth be split open and the underworld, said to be in the heart of the earth, be laid open in a great chasm? Or that the heavens be opened?”

Both alternatives refer typologically to the Lord’s death and ascension: “He who descended is the one who also ascended” (Ephesians 4:10). And we read in the Apostle:

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”

[Note: [Col. 0105D] According to the Greek: “will ascend and will descend,” ἀναβήσεται καὶ καταβήσεται, “he will ascend and he will descend.”]

—that is, to bring Christ down. Or:

“Who will descend into the abyss?”

—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead (Romans 10:6–7).

And elsewhere, discussing Christ, he says:

“What is the breadth and length and height and depth of the surpassing knowledge and love of Christ?” (Ephesians 3:18).

This concerns the mystical interpretation.

But Moses also received signs from the earth, of which we read in the Psalms:

“He sent signs and wonders in your midst, O Egypt” (Psalm 134:9),

namely frogs, locusts, gnats, and dog-flies. From heaven there were hail, fire, and darkness lasting three days.

I think that Hezekiah also received a sign from heaven when the sun went back ten lines (2 Kings 20), and Joshua son of Nun received one at Gibeon and Ajalon when the sun and moon stood still (Joshua 10).

Many think that Saul received a sign from the earth and from the depth of hell when he seemed to raise Samuel through incantations and magical arts (1 Samuel 28). The prophet Jonah also, delivered from the abyss, the depths, and the jaws of death, gave and received a sign of hell (Jonah 2).

I have read in someone’s Commentaries that this passage was weakened allegorically, so that “the depth” and “the height” were understood as αἰσθητά and νοητά—that is, things perceptible and intelligible. We may call them sensible and intelligible: the one pertains to the senses, the other to the mind and reason.

He also interprets the Virgin as the soul, which has not been corrupted by any consciousness of sin and can generate from itself Emmanuel—“God with us,” that is, the present Word of God.

But we do not eat the lamb’s flesh boiled (Exodus 12), but roasted: that is, we eat what can dry up within us all the humors of pleasure, lest, while we understand more than we ought to understand, we neglect the sacrament of our faith.

### Verse 12

“And Ahaz said: ‘I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.’”

This was not humility but pride: he did not wish to ask the Lord for a sign. Although it is written in Deuteronomy, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:16), and although the Savior used this testimony against the devil (Matthew 4), nevertheless, when he was commanded to ask, he ought to have fulfilled the command through obedience, especially since Gideon and Manoah both asked for and received a sign (Judges 6 and 13).

[Note: [Col. 0105D] Epiphanius, in the Ancoratus, nevertheless considers this an act of humility; Basil thinks that Ahaz did it so as not to violate the command, “You shall not tempt the Lord your God.” Most others agree with Jerome, especially the teachers of the Hebrews.]

Yet, in view of the ambiguity of the Hebrew expression, where it is written ULO ENASSE ADONAI,

[Note: [Col. 0106D] As you can see, the Hebrew also adds the particle eth, which Jerome omits.]

and where all the translators rendered it similarly, “I will not tempt the Lord,” it could be read, “I will not exalt the Lord.”

For the impious king knew that if he asked for a sign, he would receive it, and the Lord would be glorified. Therefore, as a worshiper of idols—he had set up altars in every street corner, on the mountains, and in wooded groves, and regarded fanatics as Levites—he did not wish to ask for the sign that had been commanded.

### Verse 13

“And he said: ‘Hear, then, O house of David: Is it not enough for you to be troublesome to men, that you are troublesome also to my God?’”

Who is the one who said, “Hear, then, O house of David”? It was certainly not God, who had earlier said to Ahaz, “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God,” but the prophet, as is proved by what follows: “Because you are troublesome also to my God.”

The sense is: you not only persecute the prophets and despise their words, but also contradict the judgment of the present and commanding God, so that you make him labor who says elsewhere, “I have labored, enduring” (Isaiah 1:14). Therefore the Lord will do the things that follow.

For “labor” and “trouble,” which Aquila and Symmachus translated, the Septuagint and Theodotion interpreted ἀγών—that is, “struggle” and “contest”—because contentious people do not submit their necks to the Lord’s service. When he wishes to heal their wounds, they reject health.

It should also be noted that, when the most impious king Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, the prophetic word is directed to the house of David—that is, to the royal tribe—from which we earlier read:

“And they reported these things to the house of David, saying: ‘Syria and Ephraim have allied themselves.’”

### Verse 14

“Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a Virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel.”

God will no longer speak, according to the Apostle Paul, “in many parts and in many ways” (Hebrews 1), nor, according to another prophet, “be likened in the hands of the prophets” (Hosea 12). Rather, he who formerly spoke through others will himself say, “Here I am” (below, chapter 58).

Of him the Bride also asked in the Song of Songs:

“Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song of Songs 1:2).

For the Lord of hosts himself is the King of glory (Psalm 23:10). He himself will descend into the Virgin’s womb and enter and leave through the eastern gate, which is always closed (Ezekiel 44). Of this gate Gabriel says to the Virgin:

“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born in you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

And in Proverbs:

“Wisdom built herself a house” (Proverbs 9:1).

When it is said, “The Lord himself will give you a sign,” the sign must be new and marvelous. But if a young woman or girl, as the Jews maintain, and not a virgin, gives birth, what sort of sign can it be, since this word indicates age, not virginity?

Indeed, to argue with the Jews and not give them occasion to laugh at our ignorance through contentious wrangling, we should note that “virgin” in Hebrew is BETHULA,

[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text.]

a word not written in the present passage. Instead, the word ALMA is used,

[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text.]

which all the translators except the Septuagint rendered “young woman.”

ALMA among them is an ambiguous word: it means both “young woman” and “hidden,” that is, ἀπόκρυφος, “concealed.” [lacuna]

Thus, in the title of the ninth Psalm, where the Hebrew has ALAMOTH,

[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text.]

the other translators rendered it “for youth,” while the Septuagint translated it “for hidden things.”

[Note: [Col. 0107C] Vaticanus has Almaboth; but I prefer Almoth, as Vaticanus renders it in Greek letters, ἄλμωθ, according to Montfaucon’s testimony. Symmachus must also be excepted from the other interpreters, who, as the Greek books report, translated it “concerning youth,” since the Greek works say that he rendered it περὶ θανάτου, “concerning death.”]

In Genesis, when Rebecca is called ALMA (Genesis 24), Aquila translated the word not as “young woman” or “girl,” but as “hidden one.”

Likewise, when the Shunammite woman, after losing her son, had fallen at Elisha’s feet and Gehazi tried to prevent her, she heard from the prophet:

“Leave her, for she is in distress, and the Lord has hidden it from me” (2 Kings 4:27).

Where Latin says “he has hidden it from me,” the Hebrew has EELIM MEMMENNI.

[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text.]

Therefore ALMA means not only “girl” or “virgin,” but, with emphasis, “a hidden virgin.”

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “And secret.” In former times girls were brought up in such a way that they remained concealed at home with their mothers and did not appear in public unless necessity or the requirements of divine worship demanded it. Hesiod refers to this custom of the ancients in book II of the Works and Days, line 138:

Ἤτε δόμων ἔντοσθε φύλῃ παρὰ μητέρα μίμνει.

“That one who remains within the house beside her dear mother.”

Josephus also, in his account of the Maccabees, book XVIII, introduces their exceptionally courageous mother speaking to her sons:

Ὅτι ἐγενήθην παρθένος ἁγνή, οὐδ᾽ ὑπερέβην πατρικὸν οἶκον etc.

“Because I was born a pure virgin, and did not leave my father’s house.”

Finally, in the books of the Maccabees, virgins are called hidden or enclosed, κατάκλειστοι. See 1 Maccabees 3:19 and book III, chapter I:

Αἵτε κατάκλειστοι παρθένοι ἐν θαλάμοις σὺν τεκούσαις ἐξώρμησαν.

“The enclosed virgins in their chambers burst forth with their mothers.” MARTIAN.]

It means a virgin who has never been exposed to the gaze of men but has been guarded with great care by her parents.

The Punic language also, which is said to flow from the Hebrew sources,

[variant: “is said to be derived from”]

properly calls a virgin ALMA. And, to provoke laughter among the Jews, in our own language too ALMA means “holy.”

[Note: [Col. 0108D] Critics who are mere slanderers fault this observation. But let them first show that aphirion is not a Hebrew word and φορεῖον a Greek word; likewise, that nuge and misura are not the Latin words nugae and mensura. MARTIAN.]

The Hebrews use words from almost all languages. Thus, in the Song of Songs (3:9), Solomon made himself a φορεῖον, that is, a litter; and we read the same word in Hebrew.

[Col. 0108C]

[Note: [Col. 0108D] In Hebrew it is [Hebrew term omitted], which denotes a splendidly constructed litter. The fact that the Hebrews likewise use words corresponding to “nonsense” and “measure” is discussed below, at the end of this book.]

The Hebrews also use words for “nonsense” and “measure” in the same form and with the same meanings.

As far as I can recall, I do not think I have ever read ALMA of a married woman, but only of one who is a virgin: not merely a virgin, but a virgin of younger age, in the years of adolescence. A virgin may be an old woman, whereas this one was a virgin in the years of girlhood.

Or it may mean a virgin, not a little girl, who could not yet know a man, but one already marriageable.

Finally, in Deuteronomy (22:25 and following), “girl” and “young woman” refer to a virgin. It says:

“If a man finds a betrothed girl in the field, and, having overpowered her by force, lies with her, you shall put to death the man who lay with her alone. You shall do nothing to the girl; there is no sin of death in the girl. For as when a man rises against his neighbor in an ambush and kills his life, so this matter has occurred. He found her in the field; the betrothed girl cried out, and there was no one to help her.”

And in the book of Kings we read (1 Kings 1) that they sought a girl, a virgin named Abishag, and brought her to the king to sleep with him and warm him. She was an exceedingly beautiful girl, served him, and the king did not know her.

As for what follows, “And you shall call his name Emmanuel,” the Septuagint and the three other translators likewise rendered it “you shall call,” whereas in Matthew it is written “they shall call.” The latter wording is not found in the Hebrew.

Therefore, O house of David, let this child who will be born of the Virgin now be called by you “Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us.” You will prove by the facts themselves that, having been delivered from the two hostile kings, you have God present with you. He who later will be called Jesus—that is, “Savior,” because he will save the entire human race—should now be called by you by the name Emmanuel.

The word CARATHI,

[Hebrew term omitted in the supplied text.]

which all the translators rendered “you shall call,” can also be understood as “he shall call”: namely, that the Virgin herself who will conceive and bear will call Christ by this name.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] The word CARATHI. All the Latin manuscripts read CARATHI as we have printed it, in the first person. But this is either an error of ancient scribes or Jerome’s freedom, since, following Syriac usage, he read yod in the feminine singular second person of the perfect: carathi instead of carath. As Jerome himself observes, it can be understood as “he shall call,” not according to the grammatical sense of the verbs, but according to the prophetic sense, which looks to the Virgin who will give birth. MARTIAN.]

In many testimonies that the Evangelists or Apostles took from the ancient books, one must observe carefully that they did not follow the order of the words but the sense. Thus, in the present passage, instead of “she shall conceive in the womb,” Matthew wrote “she shall have in the womb” (Matthew 1:13); and instead of “you shall call,” he wrote “they shall call.”

[Note: [Col. 0109D] The common Greek manuscripts of the New Testament likewise have ἕξει, “will have,” although many manuscripts read λήψεται, “will receive.” Both the Vulgate and most Latin and Greek Fathers prefer “they shall call.” The Old Latin has “she shall call.” Cyprian has “you shall call.”]

The Hebrews believe that this was prophesied concerning Hezekiah, son of Ahaz, because Samaria was captured during his reign. This cannot be proved at all. Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned over Judah and Jerusalem for sixteen years (2 Kings 16). His son Hezekiah succeeded him, being twenty-five years old, and reigned over Judah and Jerusalem for twenty-nine years.

How, then—assuming that this prophecy was made to Ahaz in the first year of his reign—can it be said to concern Hezekiah’s conception and birth, when at the time Ahaz began to reign Hezekiah was already nine years old? Unless, perhaps, they call the sixth year of Hezekiah’s reign, when Samaria was captured, his infancy—not of his age but of his reign. Even fools can see that this is forced and absurd.

One of our own writers maintains that the prophet Isaiah had two sons, Shear-jashub and Emmanuel; that Emmanuel was begotten by his wife, the prophetess, as a type of the Lord and Savior. Thus the first son, Shear-jashub, whose name means “left” or “turning back,” signifies the Jewish people, who were left behind and would later return.

The second, Emmanuel—“God with us”—signifies the calling of the gentiles, after the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

### Verse 15

“He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know to reject evil and choose good.”

For this, the Septuagint translated “before he knows.” What follows, “to take up evil,” is not present in the Hebrew.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] Vaticanus has “and what follows, ‘to reject evil,’ etc.,” incorrectly. The Septuagint has προελέσθαι, “to choose beforehand,” which is the proper sense; Jerome notes that this is not found in the Hebrew, or that the meaning of the verb is not “to choose” but “to reject.”]

The sense is as follows:

“O house of David, to whom the word of God commands that you call upon—that is, invoke—the name of Emmanuel, ‘God with us,’ when you are in danger, do not be astonished at the novelty of the matter if a Virgin gives birth to God, who possesses such power that, although he is destined to be born much later, he now rescues you when invoked. For he is the one who appeared to Abraham and spoke with Moses.

“I shall say something still more marvelous, lest you think that he will be born merely in appearance.

[Note: [Col. 0110D] Eusebius says in Greek: “What happens will not be merely apparent, but he will truly undergo such a birth as to share the food of infants—namely, butter and honey—equally with other babies. This is human; but what would display his divinity is that, before he knows or chooses evil things, he will choose the good, and so forth.”]

He will use the food of infancy; he will eat butter and drink milk.”

Although many centuries later the Evangelist testifies concerning him:

“And the child advanced in wisdom and age and grace before God and men” (Luke 2:52),

and although this is said to establish the truth of his human body, nevertheless, while still wrapped in swaddling clothes and fed with butter and honey, he will possess judgment of good and evil, so that, rejecting evil, he may choose good.

This does not mean that he actually rejected or chose, but that he knew how to reject and choose. Through these words we understand that the infancy of his human body did not prejudice his divine wisdom.

Thus, while he lay in a manger, angels announced him to the shepherds. Magi came from the East and worshiped him; we must surely believe that they were chosen. Conversely, Herod, the scribes, and the Pharisees are rejected (Matthew 2), because on account of one infant they slaughtered many thousands of little children.

### Verse 16

“For before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good, the land that you detest shall be abandoned by the presence of its two kings.”

In the sixth year of Hezekiah’s reign, Samaria was captured by the Assyrians (2 Kings 18), that is, in the thirty-first year of Hezekiah’s age. Therefore, if this child who was to be born—whether of a Virgin, as we maintain, or of a young woman, as the Jews wish—will eat butter and honey, and will be so small that he cannot distinguish evil from good, and if, before he passes beyond the time of infancy, the land of Syria and Samaria is to be devastated by the Assyrians, let the Hebrews answer how Hezekiah is proclaimed to have been an infant at thirty-one years of age, so immature that, eating honey and butter like the children of Nineveh, he knew neither left nor right—that is, neither evil nor good.

But when the passage is referred to Emmanuel, whose name means “God with us,” its meaning is readily understood: through the mystery and invocation of his name, the land of Syria and Samaria is devastated by the Assyrian conqueror, and the house of David is delivered from the two kings whom it fears, namely Rezin and Pekah.

### Verse 17

“The Lord will bring upon you, upon your people, and upon your father’s house days such as have not come since the days when Ephraim was separated from Judah, together with the king of the Assyrians.”

This passage must be read with a hyperbaton. Accordingly, following the Hebrew truth, we have interpreted it thus:

“O house of David, listen to what I say. While the land of Syria and Samaria is abandoned before the faces of the two kings whom you fear exceedingly, the Lord will bring upon you and upon the house of your father David days such as you have never had since the time when the ten tribes were separated from the two tribes and began to have a kingdom in Samaria.

“He will bring these days—that is, these times—together with the king of the Assyrians, so that, when those kings have been overcome and overthrown, you may be delivered by the presence of Emmanuel.”

The Septuagint translated this passage as follows:

“The Lord will bring upon you, upon your people, and upon the house of your father days that have not yet come, from the day when Ephraim removed the king of the Assyrians from Judah”—

a wording whose meaning we cannot determine, unless perhaps it is to be explained by saying that, because of the magnitude of its sins, Ephraim—that is, Samaria—first caused the attack of the Assyrians to turn against itself.

Alternatively: the two kings, Rezin and Pekah, who now besiege you and hasten to devastate you, will soon be overthrown. But the time of your devastation will come when the Assyrian arrives—something that you had never hoped for,

[Note: [Col. 0111D] The words “you had hoped,” or rather “you had never,” were deleted by Victorius with the help of his manuscripts as superfluous, since the subject is fear of a future evil, not hope.]

indeed, something you had never feared.

Through these words he teaches the house of David that it is not Syria and Samaria but the Assyrians whom it must fear. He therefore frees it from its present terror and threatens it with a future time.

### (Verses 18, 19)

“And it shall come to pass in that day that the Lord will hiss for the fly which is at the extremity of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee which is in the land of Assyria. And they shall come and rest in all the torrents of the valleys, and in the caves of the rocks, and in all the thickets, and in every opening. When the land of the two kings, Damascus and Samaria—which you now detest and fear—has been laid waste, then the Lord will bring upon you, O house of Judah, and upon your people, days such as you have never seen before, and the king of the Assyrians.”

Therefore you fear the present in vain: these are half-burned brands, possessing no fire at all. For you must know that by his hiss the Lord will summon the flies of Egypt and of its rivers—without doubt meaning the seven *diōryches* [διώρυχαι], that is, the canals of the Nile—and the bee which is in the land of Assyria.

He calls the Egyptians “flies” because of the filth of idolatry and the unwarlike character of the people; and he calls the Assyrians “bees,” because at that time their kingdom was exceedingly powerful and very ready for war—or because nearly the whole region of Assyria and Persia made use of arrows.

[Note: The Vaticanus has: “From this point, therefore, they will all come.”]

These peoples, then, and all the others, will come and occupy your land—in the torrents of the valleys, in the caves of the rocks, in all the thickets, in the openings, and in the wooded places. These things are spoken metaphorically: because he had once named flies and bees, he preserves the metaphor in what follows.

Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find that the holy king Josiah was slain by the Egyptians and that the people of Israel were subjected to Egyptian power (IV Kings 23; II Chronicles 35), so that the Egyptians even appointed a king over them. And, after not much time had passed, Nebuchadnezzar came with an innumerable multitude of warriors; he captured Jerusalem, destroyed the other cities of Judea, burned the Temple, and settled Assyrians in Judea (IV Kings 24).

[Note: The editor has drawn the following from Eusebius: “Then, not long afterward, the king of the Babylonians, Nebuchadnezzar, came with a great army and force, utterly destroyed the city itself, having set the Temple on fire, enslaved the whole nation, laid waste the remaining cities, and established Assyrian inhabitants in the land of the Jews.” The preceding material, too, has been expressed from Eusebius, though with somewhat different meanings.]

### (Verse 20)

“In that day the Lord will shave with a hired razor—with those who are beyond the River, with the king of the Assyrians—the head, the hair of the feet, and the entire beard.”

Some think that this is prophesied concerning the Assyrians, who, thirteen hundred years before they overthrew Jerusalem, possessed the kingdoms of Asia, Egypt, and Libya, and that they would be conquered by the Medes and Persians and their empire destroyed. Others, however, believe that the Egyptians were slain beyond the river Euphrates.

We, for our part, understand the hired razor to be the Assyrian himself, whom in Jeremiah, because of the vengeance against the sinful people, he even calls his “dove” (Jeremiah 25). Finally, in the vision concerning Tyre (Ezekiel 28:29), because Nebuchadnezzar had labored greatly in constructing fortifications and carrying up the siege ramp, and because the Tyrians had escaped by ship and he had been deprived of his payment, Egypt was given to him as the reward for his labor.

Therefore, with this exceedingly sharp razor—that is, with those who dwell beyond the river Euphrates, namely, with the Assyrian king—the Lord will shave from Judea all the hair and body hair, from head to feet, as well as the adornment of the beard, which is a sign of manliness, so that nothing strong and nothing beautiful may remain in it, but that its inhabitants may be compared with effeminate men, or rather with dishonorable women.

### (Verses 21 and following)

“And it shall come to pass in that day that a man will nourish a heifer of the herd and two sheep; and because of the abundance of milk he will eat butter. For everyone who is left in the midst of the land will eat butter and honey. And it shall come to pass in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines worth a thousand pieces of silver shall become thorns and briars. With arrows and bow they shall enter there, for briars and thorns shall be throughout the whole land. And all the mountains that shall be cultivated with the hoe shall not come there the fear of thorns and briars; and it shall become pasture for cattle and a trampling-place for sheep.”

After the overthrow of Jerusalem, the captivity of the people, and the burning of the Temple, Nebuzaradan, the commander of the army—whom the Septuagint call *archimageiros* [ἀρχιμάγειρος], “chief cook”—left a few of the people in the land, and these were poor, so that they might cultivate the vineyards and fields. Indeed, Gedaliah, who had been appointed over them and had been left from the royal line, exhorts them and says: “Do not fear the Chaldeans; dwell in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you” (IV Kings 25:24).

“In that day,” therefore—that is, at that time, when all the wealth of the Jews had been transferred to Chaldea—there will be such desolation in the land of Judea and such unbelievable devastation that they will possess neither herds of cattle nor flocks of sheep, as they had formerly been accustomed to possess. Scarcely will a rare inhabitant be able to nourish one cow and two sheep—not for plowing, but for food and for clothing in milk and wool.

Because of the scarcity of grain and of everything that the earth produces for food, they will live on milk, butter, and wild honey. And what he says, “Because of the abundance of milk he will eat butter,” signifies that the land is more fertile because of the scarcity of cultivators and is more suitable for pasture.

At that time, because of the scarcity of people, there will be such a shortage of wine in the abandoned vineyards—which, through fear of the enemy, will certainly not be pruned—that individual vines will scarcely be bought for a single silver shekel each. For the whole land will be reduced to briars and thorns. Such fear will prevail, with swords raging everywhere, that no one will dare visit his own field without bow and arrows. Abandoning the level places, they will flee to the mountains; there, protected by the difficulty of the terrain, they will scarcely dig the rugged mountains with their hands, since they will have neither oxen, plows, nor plowshares.

If, therefore, a rare cultivator is found in the mountains, from that place they will sustain their miserable life. The rest of the land will lie open to pasture and, without any keeper, will be trampled by beasts.

Would that we did not know that such things customarily occur after captivity! But now a large part of the Roman world, once similar to Judea, has become the same. We do not think this has happened without the anger of God, who does not avenge contempt of himself through the Assyrians and Chaldeans, but through savage nations formerly unknown to us, whose faces and speech are terrifying and who display women’s faces, slashed and shaven—he means the Goths, who shaved the beard—who stab the fleeing backs of men, even of well-bearded men.

[Note: From the Vaticanus, partly, and partly by conjecture, we have restored “of the Roman world,” in place of “of the Roman city,” which formerly stood with an inconvenient meaning.]

I know that I have read in these passages an exceedingly broad and intricate allegory: that everything which we have explained according to the historical sense also happened spiritually to the Jews, who scarcely possessed one heifer and two sheep—that is, clean animals—so that they were nourished not by solid food but by the milk of infancy, and ate the honey of words dripping from the lips of a prostitute; and they had no wine that makes the heart of man glad. Rather, all their works were reduced to thorns, so that they might be wounded by adversaries who strike in darkness those upright in heart (Psalm 10).

And if at any time they wished to understand something higher and, sweating through excessive labor, to discover something mystical in the holy Scriptures, nevertheless they produced no fruits of teaching but were filled with briars and thorns, which spring up in the hands of the drunkard. Their land and their teaching were not trampled by men—rational animals—but by oxen, of whom God has no care, and by brute animals.

### (Chapter 8, verses 1–4)

“And the Lord said to me: ‘Take for yourself a large book and write in it with a human pen: Quickly seize the spoil; hasten to plunder.’ And I took as my witnesses faithful men: Uriah the priest, and Zechariah the son of Berechiah. And I approached the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. And the Lord said to me: ‘Call his name: Hurry, seize the spoil; hasten to plunder. For before the child knows how to call his father and his mother, the strength of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria will be taken away before the king of the Assyrians.’”

[Note: “Uriah the priest.” The Erasmian edition retains “Zechariah” in place of “Uriah.” In several very ancient manuscript codices, “Zechariah” was written in the first hand; but the correctors restored the name Uriah. —Martianus.]

Instead of “a large book,” the Septuagint translated “a new and large book.” And for what is found in the Hebrew, “I took as my witnesses faithful men,” they said: “For he is present, and make faithful men my witnesses.” Instead of “Uriah the priest,” they have simply “Uriah”; the rest is similar.

First the Prophet was sent to Ahaz (Isaiah 7), to foretell to him what Scripture records. When Ahaz refused to listen, the Lord himself speaks to Ahaz and commands him to ask for a sign, either in the depths or in the heights. When Ahaz replies, “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord,” the wicked king is dismissed, and God’s words are directed to the house of David. A Virgin is promised who will bear a son whose name will be Emmanuel—that is, “God with us.”

If he is frequently invoked, Samaria and Syria will be overthrown; they will be overthrown by the king of the Assyrians, who will afterward also take Judah itself, so that the whole land of Judea will be turned into a wilderness.

Again, therefore, the virginal birth is described under another figure. The Lord tells the Prophet not to make public among the peoples the mystery of the new birth, but to write it in this large volume, which we now read. And, to make it more wondrous, he is to contain God’s mysteries in human words and with the pen by which human beings customarily write.

What, then, is that which is written with a human pen? “Let the child who is born quickly seize the spoil and hasten to plunder.” That is: let him no longer permit the devil to reign; let him not send angels or prophets, but descend himself to save his creatures.

The Prophet therefore does what he has been commanded and takes two faithful witnesses: Uriah the priest, who is a teacher of the Law, as Malachi says, “For the priest’s lips shall guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Malachi 2:7); and Zechariah the son of Berechiah, who was certainly a prophet.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript, as also in certain other manuscripts, according to Martianus, and in Erasmus, “Zechariah” is written in place of “Uriah.”]

We read that, while Ahaz was reigning, Uriah was priest of the Temple of the Lord (IV Kings 4); Ahaz commanded him to make an altar like the altar of Damascus. And the book of Chronicles relates (II Chronicles 29) that Hezekiah, the son of Ahaz, sought the Lord in the days of Zechariah, who was instructed in the fear of God.

Isaiah showed himself worthy of the prophetic spirit and gave himself to the prophetess—that is, to the Holy Spirit, who in Hebrew is feminine in gender and is called *RUA* (), in accordance with what is written: “Draw near to the Lord, and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:6). Thus the Lord was conceived of the Holy Spirit.

Although human speech cannot explain the mysteries of his birth, Gabriel nevertheless speaks to the Virgin herself, who conceived: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Some interpret the prophetess as the holy Mary, whom there is no doubt to have been a prophetess. She herself speaks in the Gospel: “For behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed, because he who is mighty has done great things for me” (Luke 1:48–49), and the rest.

[Note: In this passage the manuscripts vary between *prophetess* and *prophet*. Erasmus reads “prophet” here and below; Marianus Victorius reads “prophetess” and “prophets.” The manuscripts first have *prophet* and *prophetess*, and afterward *prophets*. We have followed this reading because the Greek *prophētēs* is masculine and *prophētis* feminine; in the accusative the feminine form is *prophētin*, or *prophētida*. In manuscripts, however, *e* and *i* are written interchangeably, as are the consonants *m* and *n*; hence *prophetem* appears for *prophetin*. —Martianus. It is known that in Greek the accusative form is *prophētin* [προφῆτιν], “prophetess.”]

Isaiah is commanded to call the child himself—who previously was called Emmanuel—“Hurry, seize the spoil; hasten to plunder.” For, ascending on high, “he led captivity captive; he received gifts among men” (Psalm 67; Ephesians 4:8).

Before he assumed a human body and, in accordance with infancy, called God “Father” and Mary “Mother,” the strength of Damascus would be taken away, and the spoil of Samaria would be taken by the king of the Assyrians, so that, although not yet born, he might save his people, the house of David, by invocation alone.

Uriah means “light of the Lord”; Zechariah, “memory of the Lord”; and Berechiah, “blessing of the Lord.” By these witnesses Christ’s birth is confirmed. For in the Gospel, to the two men going to Emmaus (Luke 24), beginning with Moses and the Prophets, he explained that all things had been prophesied concerning him.

According to the allegorical sense, in a virginal soul, unstained by any impurity, the word of God is conceived through the Holy Spirit; it quickly strips the opposing powers of their spoil and makes all things serve itself. Since the soul now sees in part and prophesies in part (I Corinthians 13), before it can become perfect and rightly call God its Father and its mother the heavenly Jerusalem, while it is still in infancy and progressing, it will conquer the strength of Damascus—that is, the teaching of worldly wisdom—and take away the spoil of Samaria, with which heretics have stripped the Church, saying: “We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse” (III Kings 12:16), while the king of those Assyrians—the devil—is present but unable to help them.

Such children are begotten not only by Mary, the ever-virgin prophetess, but also by holy women for the patriarchs: Sarah, whose name means *archousa* [ἄρχουσα], that is, “ruler”; and Rebecca, whose name in our language signifies “patience.”

### (Verses 5 and following)

“And the Lord continued to speak to me, saying: ‘Because this people rejected the waters of Shiloah, which flow gently, and preferred Rezin and the son of Remaliah, therefore, behold, the Lord will bring upon them the mighty and abundant waters of the river: the king of the Assyrians and all his glory. He will rise over all his channels and flow over all his banks. He will pass through Judah, flooding it; and, passing through, he will reach up to the neck. And the spreading of his wings will fill the breadth of your land, O Emmanuel.’”

Above he had said that the strength of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria would be taken away in the sight of the king of the Assyrians, and that the two kings would be captured while the Assyrian fought. Now God speaks to the Prophet in the customary figurative language of Scripture, comparing the fountain of Shiloah with the extremely violent river of the Assyrians, which floods the entire land of Israel with its waters and rises beyond its banks. It advances with such force that, after occupying the land of the ten tribes, it reaches Judah and, passing through, comes up to the neck. By this he signifies the captivity that was near.

Judah was not captured at that time, however. Rather, after all the cities of the two tribes had been subjected, Jerusalem alone remained, and it was delivered by the incredible mercy of God.

Thus he had described the power of the Assyrians and their innumerable army under the image of a flooding river; now he displays it through another metaphor: with its wings—that is, its commanders and its immeasurable multitude—it covered the land of Emmanuel, that is, of the God who defended it. Yet it did not possess it, although the Septuagint joins “Emmanuel” to the following chapter—not as a proper name, as it is called among the Hebrews, but in its translated sense, “God with us.”

We cannot doubt that Shiloah is a fountain at the foot of Mount Zion, which does not well up in a continuous stream but at fixed hours and on fixed days, and which comes with a great sound through the hollows of the earth and the caves of the exceedingly hard rock—especially those of us who live in this province.

The meaning is this: because the people of the ten tribes preferred to be subject to Rezin and the son of Remaliah—that is, to the kings of Damascus and Samaria—rather than to the stock of David, which began to reign by my judgment, I will make them serve not the kings whom they chose but the Assyrian king. His power, as he occupies the land of Samaria, is compared with the flooding of a river.

An apostrophe is then addressed to Emmanuel—that is, to the God who is present—because the Assyrian rose so high that he even attempted to possess his own land, Judah.

According to the anagogical sense, every heretic who joins worldly wisdom to his aid and wishes to attack Jerusalem—that is, the Church—abandoning the waters of the fountain of Shiloah (John 9), which means “sent” and which leaps up into eternal life, will be handed over to the ruler of the Assyrians. We shall read this meaning at length later. Once delivered into his power, the sinner will descend into the depths of sins.

For such is his arrogance that he has dared to show the Savior all the kingdoms of the world and to say: “All these things have been delivered to me” (Matthew and Luke 4). He will also attempt to enter Judah—that is, the house of confession—and, frequently through those who are negligent in the Church, he will reach up to the neck, seeking to strangle believers in Christ. He will spread his wings and fill the entire region of Emmanuel, but he will not be able to possess it, because Judah has the God who is present.

We read in the Gospel according to John (John 9) that the Lord sent a man blind from birth, whose eyes he had anointed with mud made from his saliva, to the waters of Shiloah. When the blind man washed away the mud, his blindness was removed and he received clear sight. After the magnitude of this sign, it indicates that the blindness of the Jews and of every unbeliever can be healed in no other way than when the teaching of Christ’s waters—which flows gently, without the noise and clamor of words—drives away the darkness of former error.

What is read in the Septuagint—“And he will walk upon your entire wall and remove from Judea a man who can lift his head or perhaps do anything”—is not found in the Hebrew. In the Greek manuscripts it has been struck through by a sign of deletion, as though pierced by a sword.

### (Verses 9, 10)

“Gather yourselves, peoples, and be conquered; hear, all you distant lands: be strengthened and be conquered. Gird yourselves, and be conquered; take counsel, and it shall be scattered; speak a word, and it shall not be done, because God is with us.”

Instead of “gather yourselves,” or “be weakened and be broken,” as others translated it, the Septuagint placed “know.” For, because of the similarity between the Hebrew letters *resh* and *daleth*, they understood the Hebrew word *ROU* () as *DOU* ().

O peoples of Samaria and Syria, recognize that you are weak and powerless, and that, with Emmanuel present, you can do nothing against Jerusalem, the city of God. Let not only you, who are neighbors, know this, but let the whole distant earth know it.

Although you gather an army, gird yourselves for battle, and the number of those besieging is greater than that of those besieged, nevertheless I shall say it not once but again: be conquered.

Whatever counsel you take against Jerusalem will be scattered. And although you said above, “Let us go up against Judah, rouse him from his repose, and set over him the son of Tabeel as king” (Isaiah 7:6), you may indeed speak the word, but it will not happen, because God is with us—that is, Emmanuel.

We can also use this testimony against the nations in a time of persecution. Although they may seem strong and may overcome us in those who have fallen, nevertheless they will be conquered in those who have shed their blood for Christ. After the wars, peace will be restored to the Churches, and all their counsels against Emmanuel will be scattered, because God is with us.

Those who contradict the truth may also profitably hear this, so that at last they may be overcome by reason. Let them not wish to prevail in falsehood, because whatever they say, perversity can never overcome what is right.

### (Verses 11 and following)

“For thus the Lord said to me: As with a strong hand he instructed me not to go in the way of this people, saying: ‘Do not call it conspiracy,’ for everything that this people speaks is conspiracy; and do not fear their fear, nor be terrified. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself; let him be your fear, and let him be your terror. And he shall be for you as a sanctuary, but as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the two houses of Israel; as a snare and a ruin to the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And many of them shall stumble, and fall, and be broken, and be ensnared, and be taken.”

The Septuagint translated this passage as follows:

“Thus says the Lord: They have withdrawn with a strong hand from the way of this people, saying, ‘Perhaps they will say, It is hard.’ For everything that this people speaks is hard. But do not fear their fear, nor be troubled. Sanctify the Lord of hosts himself, and he will be your fear. And if you trust in him, he will be your sanctuary, and you will not meet him as a stone of stumbling or as a rock of ruin. But the house of Jacob will be in a snare and in a valley for those sitting in Jerusalem. Therefore many among them will be weak, and they will fall and be broken, and they will draw near and be taken.”

What follows—“men in protection”—should be marked with an obelus. Since the Hebrew differs greatly from the Vulgate edition, we have included both. First, the Hebrew must be discussed.

The Lord spoke these things to me.

[Note: The passage beginning “who because of” is exceedingly involved and obscure. The edition of Marianus Victorius altered it to read: “Who, because of the good works and grace which I have obtained through good works; or, he instructed and trained me with his strong hand, so that I should not walk…” I could not find this reading in any manuscript; all those I examined consistently retain, according to Erasmus’s edition, “and the grace which I have obtained because of good works,” with the single exception of a Cluniac manuscript, which we have followed because its meaning is clearer. Let the prudent reader choose whichever reading he wishes, provided that he does not introduce the meaning and error of the Pelagians, and acknowledges that grace is given by God so that good works may be performed, not on account of works already done by us. —Martianus. The words “and the grace which because of good works…”—which cause considerable difficulty—are absent from the Vatican manuscript. Victorius had read “the grace which I have obtained through good works,” and shortly afterward read “or” where the text has “either.”]

“Who, because of the good works and the grace which I have obtained because of good works; or whether he instructed and trained me with his strong hand, so that I should not walk in the way of this people and be held in the same error; or certainly, he made me withdraw from the exceedingly evil way of this people and said to me: ‘Do not fear the conspiracy of the two kings. Rather, consider this: everything that this people speaks against me is conspiracy.’ According to Symmachus, who translated the word as *antarsis* [ἄνταρσιν], it has become rebellion against me.

“But you, Prophet, and those who are with you, do not fear the people’s ambushes; fear the Lord, and let him himself be your fear. For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord (Proverbs 1:7; Psalm 110:9). To believers he will be sanctification, but to unbelievers a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense—namely, to the two houses of Judah and Israel. Above all, he will be a snare and a ruin to those dwelling in Jerusalem. Many will stumble over him, fall, and be broken; ensnared by the bonds of their sins, they will be led into captivity.”

The Nazarenes interpret the two houses—who receive Christ in such a way that they do not omit—or, according to another reading, do not abandon—the observances of the old Law—as the two families of Shammai and Hillel, from whom the scribes and Pharisees arose.

[Note: Up to this point and below, “Hillel” is written incorrectly, contrary to the manuscripts and to the usage of the ancients, who are known in six hundred examples to have substituted *e* for short *i*. Drusius observes this in such names as Emmanuel for Imanuel and Hinnom for Hennom; see his *On the Three Sects*, book 2, chapter 11. Hillel, or Ellel, was the head of the Jewish school around the year 3730 according to Jewish chronology, at the age of eighty, thirty years before Christ. His pupil was Shammai, whom Josephus calls *Sameas* [Σαμέας]. Shammai later became his colleague in directing the teaching to be transmitted to the Jews, and finally his opponent. Both teachers are frequently mentioned in Hebrew books, in the Talmud, by Zacuto, in the *Juchasin*, by Abraham Ben Dior, and by others. Jerome also sometimes cites their opinions, as in Letter 121 to Algasia, question 10, and elsewhere.]

[Note: “Scribes and Pharisees.” On these Jewish sects, consult Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities* 18.2 and *The Jewish War* 2.12. See also Jerome’s letter to Algasia, question 10, where he attacks the Jewish *deuterōseis* [δευτερώσεις], or secondary traditions. —Martianus. Certain distinguished critics unjustly become angry with the holy Doctor because he says that the Scribes, who are often mentioned in the Old Testament, arose from Shammai. Jerome does not use “Scribes” here in that sense. Rather, he specifically means those who accepted Scripture alone, rejecting the traditions of the rabbis, and who constituted a house and sect distinct from the Pharisees. They are called *Karaei*, or Karaites, from a Hebrew word. In contrast, the Pharisees are called Rabbanites, from Ellel, because they also give credence to the writings of the rabbis and Fathers. Origen gives very clear testimony on this matter in treatise 24 on Matthew: “Those who do not depart from the letter of the Law are called SCRIBES; but those who profess something greater and separate themselves as though better than the multitude are, for this reason, called PHARISEES.”]

From them arose the Scribes and Pharisees, whose school Akiba took up; Aquila the proselyte is thought to have had him as his teacher. After Akiba came Meir, who was succeeded by Johanan son of Zacchai; after him, Eliezer; and in succession, Telphon, Joseph the Galilean, and, down to the captivity of Jerusalem, Joshua.

[Note: In this passage “Delphon” is written, contrary to the manuscripts—including those used by Martianay—which consistently read “Telphon.” Moreover, no Delphon is found among Jewish writers. If, by changing one small letter of the same organ of speech, we may restore “Therphon,” the matter is resolved, for Tharphon, as the Jews pronounce it, is a native Hebrew name and is thought to be the same as the Greek name Tryphon [Τρύφων]. Learned men have therefore thought that this was the Jewish Tryphon against whom Justin Martyr argues in his *Dialogue*. I dare not decide the matter, but the chronology certainly offers no objection: the author of the *Juchasin* and Maimonides state that Tryphon was a colleague of Akiba. Akiba died in the revolt of Bar Kokhba around A.D. 120, and Saint Justin is known to have suffered martyrdom in A.D. 136. Joseph the Galilean, who follows, was also nearly contemporary with Rabbi Akiba, as is clear from *Bava Kamma*, chapter 8. Some learned men nevertheless think that “Joseph” should be read “Jose”; in Hebrew the name is also written [term not legible in the supplied text]. The last person, whom Jerome here simply calls Joshua, is called in Jewish books Joshua ben Hananiah, a disciple of Johanan ben Zacchai.]

Shammai and Hillel arose in Judea not long before the Lord’s birth.

[Note: That is, approximately thirty years, as we have said. Jerome interprets the name of the former master as though it derived from a word meaning “to lay waste,” and that of the latter, somewhat more boldly, as though it derived from a word meaning “profane.”]

The first is interpreted as “destroyer,” the second as “profane,” because through their traditions and *deuterōseis* they destroyed and defiled the precepts of the Law. These, then, are the two houses that did not receive the Savior, who became for them a ruin and a stumbling block.

According to the Septuagint, the people resisted the will of God with a strong hand and said that everything the Lord commanded was hard, in accordance with what we read in the Gospel: “This saying is hard; who can hear it?” (John 6:61). Therefore they are commanded to hear the Lord and fear him alone. If they trust in him, they will have him as their sanctuary and will not stumble as against a stone of offense or a rock of ruin.

From this passage the Apostle also takes his testimony that Christ became a stumbling block to the Jews, but foolishness to the Gentiles (I Corinthians 1:23). Again: “Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain to the law of righteousness” (Romans 9:31). Why? Because they stumbled, not from faith but as though from works of the Law, against the stone of offense, as it is written: “Behold, I place in Zion a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling; everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame” (ibid., 33).

Therefore those who did not receive Emmanuel, but for whom he became a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling, will be broken and led away captive.

What he says—“The house of Jacob will be in a snare and in a valley for those sitting in Jerusalem”—signifies that they do not dwell in the mountains or occupy the lofty places of Scripture, but always understand humble things, joining sins to sins and bound by the snares of transgressions.

### (Verses 16, 17)

“Bind up the testimony; seal the law among my disciples, and I will await the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob, and I will wait for him.”

This is the voice of the Lord speaking to the Prophet: Because, he says, the Lord has become a stone of offense and a rock of stumbling to the two houses of Israel, and they did not wish to receive Emmanuel who had been sent to them, bind up the testimonies of the Old Testament and deliver them to my disciples, who have received the Gospel—that is, to the Apostles or apostolic men.

Or certainly, let the Law and prophecy be bound up among them until John (Matthew 11), and let them be closed and sealed, so that they do not understand what they read. For, owing to an ambiguity in the Hebrew language, instead of “disciples” we may also interpret “teachings.”

Therefore the Prophet replied: Since, with the Gospel succeeding, the Law has been closed and sealed among the Jews, and you command that it be assigned not to the Jews but to the Gentiles, for this reason I will await Emmanuel, whom you promise is to come, of whom you said above that he himself is our fear and our terror and that he will be our sanctification. And I will wait for the Lord, who has hidden his face from the house of Jacob—that is, from the Jews—because they did not wish to receive him.

The Septuagint translated this passage as follows:

“Then those who are sealed will be manifest, so that they may not learn the Law.”

This has the following meaning: When many have fallen, have been broken, and have stumbled over the stone of offense and the rock of stumbling, then those who are sealed among the people will be revealed, so that they may no longer learn the Law of Moses but obey the evangelical commandments.

### (Verse 18)

“Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me as signs and portents for Israel, from the Lord of hosts who dwells on Mount Zion.” The Lord commanded me, he says, to bind up the testimony among the Jews and to deliver and seal the law to his disciples, because he had hidden his face from the house of Jacob. Therefore I will await him, and I will wait for my Lord—not I alone, but also the children whom the Lord has given me, namely, the other prophets and the sons of the prophets, who were born not from the will of flesh and blood but from God (John 1:13). Concerning them the Apostle also spoke: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

These children, that is, the prophets, were given as signs and portents to Israel, according to what we read in Ezekiel: “Ezekiel shall be a sign to you” (Ezek. 24:24). In Zechariah also, holy men and disciples of the prophets are called τερατοσκόποι, that is, “observers of portents and signs” [Note: The Vatican manuscript improperly calls them “makers of signs.”], because the prophets have always gone before as signs of things to come (Zech. 3:16). This is the interpretation according to the literal sense for the present.

Otherwise, blessed Paul teaches in the Epistle written to the Hebrews—although Latin usage does not receive it among the canonical Scriptures—that this testimony must be understood as spoken in the person of the Lord and Savior. For this reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: “I will proclaim your name to my brothers; in the midst of the church I will praise you” (Heb. 2:12); and again: “I will put my trust in him” (ibid., 13); and once more: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.” Since, therefore, the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise became a partaker of the same sufferings (Isa. 8:18).

But how these children were a sign and portent against the wisdom of the world and the pride of the Jews, the same Apostle explains. He says that the Lord Savior chose the foolish things of the world and the weak things, in order to confound the wise and the strong (1 Cor. 1). Hence the Savior also said to the Apostles: “Unless you are converted and become like one of these children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:3). A child is made a preacher of the new Gospel when he lays aside the old man, who is corrupted by deceitful desires, and puts on the new man, who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of the Creator (Col. 3:9–10).

That the Lord of hosts dwells on Mount Zion is likewise written by the Apostle: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. 12:22). I therefore marvel that one of our writers understands these two children as the two sons of Isaiah, whom he fathered through the conception of the prophetess: namely, Jasub and Emmanuel. The first, he says, went before as a figure of the rejection of the former people, and the second as a figure of the calling of the Gentiles. Whoever accepts this will consequently also affirm that the prophet Hosea truly had a prostitute for his wife.

### (Verses 19 ff.)

“And when they say to you, ‘Seek answers from the Python-spirits and from diviners, who chirp in their incantations,’ should not a people seek from its God, on behalf of the living, answers from the dead? To the law rather and to the testimony. But if they do not speak according to this word, there will be no morning light for them. And it will pass through it: it will fall and hunger; and when it has hungered, it will grow angry and curse its king and its God. It will look upward and gaze upon the earth, and behold: distress and darkness, dissolution, anguish, and pursuing gloom; and it will not be able to escape from its anguish.”

If this is the voice of the prophet Isaiah, as the Jews believe—“Behold, I and the children whom the Lord has given me as a sign and a portent for Israel”—then we must believe that what follows is spoken by Isaiah to his disciples. “When,” he says, “the Gentiles and peoples concerning whom we read above say to you, ‘Be weakened, peoples, and be defeated,’ why do you wish to hear prophets? Why are you deceived by Isaiah’s words and suppose that he knows what is going to happen? Seek rather from the Python-spirits and from the diviners, who chirp in their incantations.”

For “diviners” the Septuagint translated: “those who speak from the earth, who cry out from the belly.” Everyone who is from the earth speaks from the earth (John 3:31). And he whose god is his belly, and whose glory is in his shame (Phil. 3:19), must be understood to cry out from his belly.

You should answer them and say: “Should not a people seek from its God, on behalf of the living, answers from the dead?” If, he says, on account of the variety of your idols—for you do not have one god but many—you consult those whom you consider gods, and from the dead, or from images of dead men, you ask about the living, how much more ought we to hear our God through the prophets?

He therefore teaches the disciples and adds: “To the law rather and to the testimony.” If you are uncertain about something, he says, know what is written: “The nations whom the Lord your God is destroying before you listen to dreams [Note: Victorius contends that “all things” (*omnia*), rather than “dreams” (*somnia*), should be read, on the basis of the text of Deuteronomy.] and diviners; but the Lord your God has not given this to you. The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him” (Deut. 18:14–15). [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “a prophet from among you,” and so forth.]

Therefore, if you wish to know what is uncertain, devote yourselves rather to the law and to the testimonies of the Scriptures. But if your assembly is unwilling to seek the word of the Lord, it will not have the light of truth; it will wander in error and darkness. Light will pass through it—that is, through your assembly or through the land—and you will fall and hunger. When you hunger, you will grow angry, according to what is written: “When they were not satisfied, they murmured” (Ps. 58:16). You will curse God, your king, and in your necessities you will look upward to heaven and downward upon the earth. Behold: distress and darkness, dissolution of the knees, anguish of mind, and dimness of the eyes; and you will not be able to escape from your anguish.

This is according to the Hebrews. Otherwise, as we said above, if it is Christ who speaks in the person of the one saying, “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me,” then he himself also speaks these words to the Apostles and to the believers from the Gentiles who received his Gospel.

“If,” he says, “your fathers whom you abandoned say: ‘Seek ventriloquists’”—by whom we understand the Python-spirits, such as the slave girl whom we read about in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter 16), who brought profit to her masters—“and those who speak from the earth,” which magicians claim to do when they summon souls, along with the other kinds of magical arts: you must know that each nation consults its own gods and asks the dead about the welfare of the living.

But God has given you the law as a help, so that you can say: “The divination of the Gentiles is not like this. Their gods often deceive their worshipers, whereas our divination is given freely from the law, without any payment.” Hence the Septuagint translated: “Not according to this word,” for which there is no giving of gifts. “Freely,” he says, “you have received; freely give” (Matt. 10:8).

A very severe famine will come upon unbelievers—not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the word of God (Amos 8). When you hunger, you will be distressed, and you will curse your ruler and the traditions of your fathers, that is, the devil and ancient errors.

He speaks this to those who will suffer hunger for the truth and will look upward toward heaven and downward toward the earth. They will be in anguish, darkness, and distress, so that they will not see for a time, until they too turn to the Lord.

These passages require a lengthy explanation, but we spare the size of the books in order to remove the weariness of reading. We have touched briefly on these matters according to the Septuagint translation, which in many places differs from the Hebrew. But the Nazaraeans [Alternative reading: Nazarenes] explain this passage as follows:

“When the scribes and Pharisees say to you that you should listen to those who do everything for the sake of their belly, and who, after the manner of magicians, chirp in their incantations in order to deceive you, you ought to answer them: ‘It is no wonder that you follow your traditions, since every nation consults its own idols. Therefore we also ought not to consult you, the dead, about the living. Rather, God has given us the law and the testimonies of the Scriptures. If you are unwilling to follow them, you will have no light; instead, darkness will always oppress you. It will pass through your land and your doctrine, so that when those deceived by you perceive that they are in error and are suffering hunger for the truth, they will be distressed—or become angry—and will curse you, whom they had regarded as their gods and kings. And they will look in vain toward heaven and earth, since they will always be in darkness and will not be able to escape from your snares.’”

### Chapter 9

#### (Verses 1 ff.)

“At the first time the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were relieved, and at the last the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, was burdened. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; for those dwelling in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen.”

The Septuagint: “Drink this first; act swiftly, region of Zebulun, land of Naphtali, and the rest who dwell by the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; you who dwell in the region and shadow of death, light will shine upon you.”

We have set down both editions because the testimony is widely known and was employed by the Evangelist Matthew, so that either the difference of interpretation or the similarity may be recognized.

First, it must be noted that the Evangelist Matthew placed this testimony not according to the Septuagint but according to the Hebrews. For the Gospel narrative says:

“When Jesus heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth, he came and lived in Capernaum, which is by the sea in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled: ‘Land of Zebulun and land of Naphtali, way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations: the people who sat in darkness have seen a great light; and for those sitting in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen.’ From that time Jesus began to preach and to say: ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near’” (Matt. 4:13 ff.).

The Evangelist John also reports that Jesus, invited with his disciples to a wedding at Cana of Galilee, performed his first sign there by changing water into wine: “Jesus did this beginning of signs at Cana of Galilee, and manifested his glory; and his disciples believed in him” (John 2:11).

Hence the Septuagint says: “Drink this first; act swiftly,” because the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali were the first to see Christ’s miracles, so that the first to see the Lord performing signs might be the first to drink the draught of faith.

According to the Hebrew, it is said to have been relieved at the first time from the burden of sins, because the Savior first preached the Gospel in the regions of the two tribes. Hence also in the sixty-seventh Psalm it is said: “Bless the Lord from the fountains of Israel. There is Benjamin, the youngest” (Ps. 67:27–28; Acts 9), namely, the Apostle Paul, in an ecstasy of mind, who elsewhere also said: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5:13). “The princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali, their leaders,” because in these tribes there were villages from which our leaders, the Apostles, believed.

According to Symmachus, they believed quickly, as soon as they heard: “Come, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19); immediately they left both their father and their little boat.

At the last time, however, their faith was burdened by the many Jews who remained in error. Here “sea” means the lake called Gennesaret, which is formed by the Jordan flowing into it. Capernaum, Tiberias, Bethsaida, and Chorazin are situated on its shore. The Lord dwelt especially in this region, so that the people who either sat or walked in darkness might see light—not a small light, like that of the other prophets, but a great one, like that of him who speaks in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12).

“For those who dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light has arisen.” I think this is the difference between death and the shadow of death: death belongs to those who have gone down to the underworld with dead works. “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20). The shadow of death belongs to those who sin but have not yet departed from this life, since, if they wish, they are able to practice repentance.

In place of “Galilee of the nations,” Aquila translated “mounds of the nations” (θῖνες gentium), and Symmachus “boundaries of the nations.” By θῖνες we understand sand-mounds, whether on shores or riverbanks.

Hebrews who believe in Christ explain this passage as follows. At the first time, these two tribes, Zebulun and Naphtali, were captured by the Assyrians and led into a hostile land; and Galilee was deserted (2 Kings 15). The prophet now says that it was relieved because it bore the sins of the people. Afterwards, not only the two tribes but also the rest who lived beyond the Jordan and in Samaria were led into captivity (2 Kings 17–18). Scripture now says, they maintain, that the region whose people were first led into captivity and began to serve the Babylonians, and which had previously lived in the darkness of error, was itself the first to see the light of Christ preaching; and from it the Gospel was sown among all the nations.

The Nazaraeans, whose opinion I gave above, attempt to explain the passage in this way:

“When Christ came and his preaching shone forth, the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali was first freed from the errors of the scribes and Pharisees and shook the very heavy yoke of Jewish traditions from its neck. Afterwards, through the Gospel of the Apostle Paul, who was the last of all the Apostles, the preaching was burdened—that is, multiplied—and the Gospel of Christ shone to the boundaries of the nations and along the way of the whole sea. Finally, the whole world, which had previously walked or sat in darkness and was held by the bonds of idolatry and death, saw the clear light of the Gospel.”

#### (Verses 2–4)

“You have multiplied the nation, but you have not magnified the joy. They will rejoice before you as those rejoice at harvest, as conquerors exult when they divide captured spoil. For you have broken the yoke of its burden, the rod of its shoulder, and the scepter of its exactor, as on the day of Midian. For every violent plundering with tumult, and every garment mixed with blood, will be for burning and fuel for fire.”

The Septuagint: “You have led the greater part of the people into your joy, and they will rejoice before you as they are accustomed to rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide spoil rejoice; for the yoke that had been placed upon them has been removed, and the rod from their neck. For the rod of the exactors will be destroyed, as on the day of Midian. For every garment gathered by deceit and every garment of exchange they will return, and they will desire to be burned by fire.”

We place both editions in obscure passages so that the diligent reader may recognize how far the common translation differs from the other editions and from the Hebrew truth.

An apostrophe is now made to the light itself that appeared to the people situated in darkness, that is, to the Lord Savior. It is said to him: “You have multiplied the nation,” that is, you have filled all the nations with knowledge of yourself; “but you have not magnified the joy.” In accordance with this, the Apostle says that he has continual sorrow for his brothers who are Israelites (Rom. 10). Jonah too is saddened that the Ninevites were saved (Jonah 4), while the gourd, or *CICEION* (), withered. The Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “I did not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). And in his passion: “Father,” he says, “if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. 26:39).

This passage has the following sense: If it can happen that the multitude of the nations believes without the destruction of the Jews, I refuse the passion. But if they are to be blinded, so that all the nations may see, then, Father, let your will be done.

When Christ therefore comes, and the Christian people is gathered from all the nations, then the Apostles will rejoice as harvesters rejoice at harvest. Of them the Lord said: “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37). They will also rejoice as conquerors who divide captured spoil. For when the strong man has been captured and bound, his whole household is plundered and the spoils are divided (Matt. 12).

But you, Lord and Savior, have removed from their shoulders the yoke of his burden—that is, of the devil, who previously exulted in the world, ruled all the nations, and pressed the necks of all beneath the very heavy yoke of slavery—and the rod with which he struck everyone and compelled them to return their sins to him as a kind of tribute. You made those whom you freed serve you without any army and without the shedding of blood, by a hidden hand, just as once, under Gideon, you granted the people of Israel victory over the Midianites (Judg. 7). [Note: The reading *Israeli Madianitis* without the preposition *de* was faulty; the manuscripts correct it.]

Just as a garment stained [alternative reading: bloodied] with human blood cannot be washed but, infected with blood, is burned by fire so that the stains of foul gore may perish with the garment, so the devil’s violent plundering, and the tumult and disorders by which he had subjected the human race to himself, have been assigned to the fires of Gehenna.

The Septuagint indicates that not all but only a certain part of the people believed, although for what they said, “you have led into joy,” others translated, “you have magnified.” While they preserve the same sense in the rest, they add that he will return the garment gathered by deceit and the exchanged garment—that is, the devil will return all the souls whom he had stripped with God’s help, together with their former adornments. He will do this not alone but also with his attendant demons, who, if given the choice, would prefer to perish in flames rather than surrender their spoil.

#### (Verse 6)

“For a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us; and the principality has been placed upon his shoulder. And his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. His rule shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace upon the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish and strengthen it in judgment and righteousness, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.”

The Septuagint: “Because a child has been born to us, a son has been given to us, whose principality has been placed upon his shoulder; and his name is called Messenger of the Great Counsel. For I will bring peace upon the rulers and his health. His principality is great, and there is no boundary of his peace, upon the throne of David and his kingdom, to set it right and assist it in judgment and righteousness, from now and forever. The zeal of the Lord Sabaoth will do these things.”

Therefore the devil, and all his violent plundering by which he had oppressed the human race and mingled blood with blood, will be for burning and fuel for eternal fire, because a child has been born to us from a Virgin, of whom it was said above: “Before the child knows how to reject evil and choose good” (Isa. 7:16); and later, in the generation of the prophetess: “Before the child knows how to call his father and his mother” (Isa. 8:4).

This child, therefore, who was born of the Virgin, is called Emmanuel, that is, “God with us.” And from the prophetess—that is, generated from the Holy Spirit—he was named “Hasten, strip the spoil, hurry to plunder.” Now he is called by many names.

Although by saying above “Emmanuel,” that is, “God with us,” he showed that he is God, nevertheless he now says that his principality was placed upon his shoulder. This may mean that he himself carried his cross, or, through the shoulder, indicate the strength of his arm, as the same Isaiah says: “The Lord God has revealed his holy arm before all the nations” (Isa. 52:10). And again: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1). [Note: Victorius restores “will reveal” (*Revelabit*) from the Greek ἀποκαλύψει.]

After the two names, therefore, he will be called by six other names: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace. For we should not, as many think, join the names in pairs so as to read “Wonderful Counselor” and again “Mighty God.” Rather, “Wonderful” is to be read separately; in Hebrew it is *PHELE* (). “Counselor” is separate, called in their language *IDES* [the supplied text leaves the Hebrew form incomplete]. “God” is separate, called in Hebrew *EL* ().

Finally, in the passages where we read: “For you are God, and we did not know,” and again: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isa. 45:5), and many similar passages, what is written “God” in Latin is written *EL* in Hebrew.
