What follows, “Mighty,” is called *GIBBOR* () in Hebrew. Hence in the passage where the same prophet says: “They shall trust in the Holy God of Israel in truth; and what remains of Jacob shall trust in the Mighty God” (Isa. 8), the Hebrew has *EL GIBBOR* (), “Mighty God.”

As for “Father of the age to come and of the resurrection,” which is fulfilled in our calling, and “Prince of Peace,” who said to the Apostles, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27), no one who has read according to the Apostle Paul that our peace is the Savior will doubt this.

I think that, struck with terror by the majesty of these names, the Septuagint translators did not dare to say openly of the child that he should be called God, and the rest. Instead of these six names they placed what is not found in the Hebrew: “Angel of the Great Counsel,” “I will bring peace upon the rulers,” and “his health.”

This seems to me to have the following sense: He is the Angel of the Great Counsel who announced to us that Israel was to be rejected for a time and that the Gentiles were to be saved. He gave peace to his rulers, the Apostles and apostolic men, and left the health of his doctrines to believers.

As for what follows, “His rule shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace”—for which the Septuagint translated, “His principality is great”—we must know that the Hebrew word *MESRA* (), both here and above, was translated by the Septuagint as ἀρχή, that is, “principality.” Where the Hebrew occurs above, we translated it “principality”; here we have translated it “rule.”

Aquila, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated it as μέτρον, that is, “measure.” This is called by the same name in Hebrew [*mesura*] and in Latin, and, being almost identical with the Latin word “measure,” differs very little from the Hebrew form found in the text, which means “principality.” [Note: In the Vatican manuscript: “that is, beginning.” The Hebrew form *mesura* is noted as nearly identical with Latin *mensura*, “measure,” but as differing slightly from the form in the text, which means “principality.”]

No one who has read in the Psalms, “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8), and again, “An abundance of peace until the moon is removed” (Ps. 71:7)—that is, until the consummation of the age—can doubt the Savior’s manifold rule and his peace, which has no end.

His principality and rule will be over the throne and kingdom of David, which had been destroyed after the Babylonian captivity, so that he might establish and strengthen it and show it to be perpetual—for otherwise God’s promise would seem empty—from the time of the Incarnation and forever. [Note: The Vatican manuscript again reads “to show him to be a prophet,” lest God’s promise be judged empty.]

Therefore the zeal, that is, the emulation, of the Lord of hosts did this, because they provoked him to emulation through those who were not gods, and he provoked them to emulation through a nation that was not a nation (Deut. 32).

The prophecy of Emmanuel and of the child being born from the Virgin, beginning with the passage where it is said to Ahaz, “Ask a sign for yourself from the Lord your God,” ends with this verse, which adds: “The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this” (Isa. 7:11). Now let us pass to what follows.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0127]

We compose books of unequal length [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “we dictate explanatory books”; and, shortly below, “let us pass” for “we pass.”]: according to the diversity of the visions and meanings, one is compressed and another extended.

Since the third volume has now been completed, we pass to the fourth, which is one-third shorter in the measure of its verses than the preceding volume—especially since the fifth, which we have placed after this book, consists of historical exposition and is almost twice as long.

Because we do not wish to divide connected material or pass over what we interpreted long ago, we have steered our little boat between the two Symplegades of the Pontic Sea, and, with the Holy Spirit blowing and the Lord Savior directing our course, it is escaping into the open sea. You say, virgin of Christ, Eustochium: “Come from the four winds, O spirit, and make the dead bones live” (Ezek. 37:9), so that what lay in the dust of the earth may be raised up when the Lord breathes.

### Chapter 9

#### (Verses 8 ff.)

“The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. And all the people shall know—Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria—who say in pride and greatness of heart: ‘The bricks have fallen, but we will build with squared stones; the sycamores have been cut down, but we will replace them with cedars.’ And the Lord will raise up the enemies of Rezin against him and turn his enemies into tumult: Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west; and they shall devour Israel with their whole mouth. In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out. Yet the people have not returned to the one striking them, and they have not sought the Lord of hosts.”

We read above (2 Kings 16) that in the days of Ahaz, son of Jotham, son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah, son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up against Jerusalem to attack it. We also read (Isa. 7) that the prophet Isaiah was sent to meet Ahaz with his son Jasub, to tell him not to fear and not to let his heart be afraid because of the two tails of smoking firebrands, since the rule of Syria and Israel was destined to end in them.

When Ahaz did not believe this because of the magnitude of the matter and the present danger, he was commanded to ask for a sign. Since he was an idolater, he refused to do even this. Therefore the Lord gives the sign not to the king himself but to the house of David: his Son would be born of a virgin, and by calling upon him they would be delivered from the impending danger, together with the other matters that we have interpreted up to the present passage.

After inserting many mysteries in the intervening discussion, Isaiah now returns to what he had begun and prophesies the overthrow of Rezin and Ephraim—that is, of Syria and Samaria:

“The Lord sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel.” Among the Hebrews, *DABAR* (דבר), written with three consonants—DALETH, BETH, and RES—means “word” when read *DABAR*, but “death” and “pestilence” when read *DEBER*, according to the context. For this reason many, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, say that not a word but death was sent.

The Lord therefore sent a word into Jacob, and it fell upon Israel. He wished Judah to reign, as Jacob prophesies in Genesis (chapter 49); but Israel—that is, the ten tribes—claimed the rule for itself. Concerning them it was said: “They reigned, but not through me” (Hos. 8:4).

Thus the dignity of rule, which had begun in David with Samuel’s anointing after Saul had been rejected, was sent into Jacob—that is, into the twelve tribes formerly called Jacob—and fell upon Israel. It did not come, as the Septuagint translated, but fell; for it fell upon the impious, although what had been ordained was directed toward the saints.

The people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria, who on account of their multitude are lifted up in pride, will therefore know this. They say: “The kingdom of Judah is small and, in comparison with ours, utterly worthless. Therefore, while their kingdom falls like bricks, let us build ourselves a house with squared stones. When their sycamores—cheap timbers—have been cut down by the enemy’s attack, let us construct our rule with cedars, which do not decay, so that our kingdom may signify permanence.”

Let all the people of Ephraim and the inhabitants of Samaria know that the Syrian who is now their ally will turn into their enemy. Or certainly, sudden wars of adversaries may rise against Syria itself, and all may be thrown into tumult, so that Syria attacks Israel from the east and the Philistines—that is, the Palestinians—from the west, and together they devour Israel.

When they have done these things, nevertheless my hand is still stretched out, or raised high, over Israel, and does not cease to strike them. Though struck down by God, they will not return to the one who strikes them, nor will they seek the Lord of hosts, worshiping golden calves instead of God.

According to the allegorical interpretation, our writers explain this passage as follows: God sent his Son to Jacob—that is, to the Jews—and he came to Israel—that is, to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Apostle also says are called Israel (Rom. 9).

Others interpret it in this way: The Lord sent his Word to the Church, which supplanted the former people, and it fell upon Israel—that is, upon the heretics, who boast that they see God.

Let their leaders, then, and all who dwell in Samaria—that is, all who claim to keep God’s law and to abound in virtues and bear fruits of righteousness—for Ephraim is interpreted in this way, know that in the pride of their hearts they despise the Church. Considering its simplicity ignorance, they say: “In place of its bricks, we will build our churches with squared and exceedingly strong stones; and in place of its unfruitful and quickly perishing trees, we will erect the loftiest cedars.” The Lord will crush these cedars, and the righteous man, speaking in the person of the wicked, says that he saw them, but that their place was not found (Ps. 36).

The Lord therefore says that Rezin—whose name is interpreted as “worldly wisdom,” and whose aid Ephraim was using—will be turned against him, and that all his enemies will fight against him. He will be attacked from both east and west, and they will be about to devour Israel with their whole mouth. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “and all his friends”; it also has “they devour” for “they are about to devour.”]

For these words the Septuagint translated: “And let us build ourselves a tower; and God will strike those who rise up against Mount Zion, and he will scatter its enemies.” They wish, in imitation of God’s Temple, to build themselves a temple in Samaria. But although they may move their feet from the east and say, “Come, let us build a tower and make a name for ourselves before we are scattered” (Gen. 11:4), when the Lord attacks them their agreement will be dissolved and scattered [Note: The same manuscript reads “their understanding will be scattered”; hence it has “those who understand” instead of “those who agree.”], and their languages will be divided against one another, lest they become worse by agreeing, but rather destroy one another.

Although they have thus been struck and devoured by their enemies, they still will not return to the Lord. His hand will remain prepared to strike them, according to what we read in Jeremiah: “In vain I struck your children; you did not accept discipline” (Jer. 2:30).

(Verses 14 ff.) “And the Lord will destroy from Israel head and tail, the one bending and perverting, in a single day. The elder and honorable man is the head; and the prophet who teaches falsehood is the tail. Those who call this people blessed will be deceivers, and those who are called blessed will be cast down.

“Therefore the Lord will not rejoice over their young men, nor will he have mercy on their orphans and widows, because everyone is a hypocrite and wicked, and every mouth speaks folly. In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.

“For wickedness will be kindled like a fire: it will devour thornbush and briar, and it will burn in the dense thicket of the forest, while it is wrapped in the pride of smoke. At the anger of the Lord of hosts the earth trembled, and the people became like fuel for the fire. A man will not spare his brother; he will turn to the right and be hungry, and he will eat on the left and not be satisfied. Each will devour the flesh of his own arm. Manasseh will devour Ephraim, and Ephraim Manasseh; together they will be against Judah.

“In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.”

Not only will the Lord raise the enemies of Rezin against him and turn his enemies into tumult—Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west—so that they may devour Israel with their whole mouth; but because he has not returned to the one striking him, nor sought the Lord of hosts, he will stretch out his hand to strike, in order to destroy from Israel head and tail, the one bending and perverting—that is, the one who perverts what is straight (Jer. 2). He himself has explained who the head is: “the elder and honorable man.” And who the tail is: “the prophet,” he says, “who teaches falsehood,” that is, the false prophet.

He has spoken of the leaders; now he joins the nobles and the people, showing that teachers and disciples, the learned and the uneducated multitude, alike perish. Those who called the people blessed are deceivers; and those who were called blessed—not on account of virtue but on account of gifts—will be cast down into death. Hence we read above also: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and pervert the paths of your feet” (Isa. 3:12).

In such a people God will spare no one: neither orphan nor widow, because everyone is a hypocrite, pretending one thing and doing another—promising chastity while living luxuriously, professing poverty while filling his purse. Hence he adds: “And every mouth has spoken folly.” On account of all these things the Lord does not cease to be angry, but still raises his hand to strike. And because they have done these things, wickedness will be kindled like a fire, so that the flame may devour not cultivated land but thornbushes and briars, and consume not fruit-bearing trees but an unfruitful thicket, where wild beasts dwell. [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, a second hand has “raging”; previously it read “wise.”] The flame will seize it and consume it. Hence it is said that, once fire has been placed beneath it, the dense thicket will be wrapped in the pride and height of smoke. Everything that is lofty and rises on high can be called proud.

Instead of this, I do not know what the Septuagint intended when they translated: “And it will devour everything around the hills.” Hence, at the Lord’s anger, the earth trembled, and the people became fuel for the fire, because such cruelty prevailed among them that it spared not even the dearest name of kinship. Abandoning and despising the right hand, they filled themselves with what was on the left, while suffering hunger for pleasures and evils and always desiring to join worse things to bad.

Manasseh and Ephraim themselves, born from one womb and begotten by the same father, erupted into such madness that they quarreled with one another in hostile hatred. Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles, and we shall find the civil wars among the Samaritans, while some fought on behalf of one king and others on behalf of another, and how, after killing their own kings, they united in attacking Judah.

According to the tropological interpretation, the Lord will remove the head and the tail, the greater and the lesser alike. By calling them “tail,” he demonstrates that they are not human beings but beasts of burden, which use this limb to cover excrement and ward off small animals. After “head,” he joins “the one bending” and “the one perverting,” because they overturn the commandments of the Law and pervert the straight path.

[Note: Martianus and others wrongly and nonsensically read “who was captured” for “because he is the head”; we correct this from the manuscripts in accordance with Jerome’s meaning and the sequence of the argument.]

He will destroy the elder also, because he is the head, and the false prophet placed in the tail; he will destroy teachers and pupils alike: some who praise sinners for gifts, and others who, when praised, neither recognize their own evils nor repent. Therefore the Lord will not rejoice over their young men: “Woe to the city whose king is a boy” (Eccl. 10:16). And those who have lost God the Father, or the true Lord, will not obtain mercy.

For every heretic is a hypocrite, doing one thing and pretending another; and whatever he says, even if it appears to be wisdom, is nevertheless folly. On account of these things he stretches out his hand to punish, and consuming flame will devour all their wickedness like thorns. Words without deeds, compared to an unfruitful thicket, will be enveloped in the pride of smoke.

At their punishment every land will tremble, and deceived peoples will be handed over to eternal fires, because, for the sake of disgraceful gain, they do not spare even their own people but eagerly plunder those whom they have deceived, abandoning what is good and persisting in what is worst. Although they continually find what is on the left, they are never satisfied with their own errors, devouring the flesh of their own arm and fighting against the Church with equal zeal.

On account of luxury, pleasures, and profits from the peoples, they are divided among themselves, so that one heresy becomes two, and then these are themselves divided into factions, in order to lead away their own flocks, devour the houses of widows, and prey upon sinful women, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (2 Tim. 3). In all these things the Lord’s anger will not turn away—consuming vices and overthrowing them—but the more they advance in sinning, the more he stretches out his hand for punishment.

## Chapter 10

(Verses 1 ff.) “Woe to those who make unjust laws and, writing, have written injustice, in order to oppress the poor in judgment and do violence to the cause of the humble among my people, so that widows may be their prey and they may plunder orphans. What will you do on the day of visitation and in the calamity that comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? And where will you leave your glory? Do not bend beneath the fetter and fall with those who have been killed. In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.”

Most people still think that these words are spoken against the ten tribes that lived in Samaria, because they added these offenses to their earlier crimes [another reading: “would add them again”]. We, however, think that the prophetic speech cries out against the judges of the tribe of Judah and of Jerusalem—namely, the scribes and the deuterotai (δευτερωταί, “second-ranking officials”)”—because they wrote unjust laws against the Law of God and overturned the truth of judgment by their traditions.

For when God said, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12), they, on the contrary, instructed children to say to their parents: “Whatever gift is from me will benefit you,” so that they would not honor father and mother [another reading: “would not honor”] (Matt. 15:5–6; Mark 7:11), and other things similar to these. For this reason they wrote the worst laws: to oppress the poor and humble among the people, to plunder widows, and to rob orphans.

They are asked what they will do when either the day of captivity or the day of judgment arrives, and the calamity that was foretold long beforehand comes from afar. “To whom,” he says, “will you flee for help when you have offended God, who is the true helper? And where will you leave your glory?” Riches will not profit on the day of wrath, lest the Assyrian lead you bound into a hostile land, lest you fall in battle (Prov. 11:4).

Finally, just as above he repeatedly spoke against Samaria, “In all these things his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out,” so he also speaks against Judah: their final captivity will not be the end of their evil [Note: “of their wickedness” is found in another manuscript], but even in the hostile land the Lord’s sword will pursue them.

According to the anagogical interpretation, every heretic writes wickedness in order to deceive the poor and humble among the people, and to plunder widows and orphans. For the rich man, of whom we read, “A man’s riches are the ransom of his own life” (Prov. 13:8), does not endure the threat and is not quickly captured by them. [Note: Victorius conjectures that the negative particle should be removed, so that the text should read: “But the rich man endures the threat.”] But the poor man, and the one who is humble and little among the people, is quickly scandalized by them.

The widow, who has lost God as her husband, and the orphan, who has lost the Creator as his father—of whom it is written, “You abandoned God who begot you and forgot God who nourished you” (Deut. 32:18)—are easily overthrown.

What, then, will they do on the day of judgment, when they have deceived so many, and when the calamity that comes from afar arrives? For just as it is said to the righteous man, “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8), and elsewhere, “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke 17:2), so the calamity of the heretics will come from afar, prepared for them long beforehand.

To whom will they flee, when they have a fabricated god? To whom will they surrender their glory, when everything is pretended? Nor will they be able to escape the fetter with which they have bound so many. Hence, in the vision of the valley of Zion—which, abandoned by the height of God and deceived by heretical humility, is said of the teachers of falsely named knowledge: “All your princes have fled, and those who were captured have been bound with harsh bonds” (Isa. 22:3). They will fall with each of those who have been killed, perish in the death of others, and, though they suffer many things, when the day of visitation arrives, their destruction will not end; rather, they will continually tremble at the hand of the Lord hanging over them.

Up to this point the threat of God has been directed against the twelve tribes—that is, against Samaria and Jerusalem—which began among the people while Ahaz was still reigning. Of these tribes, two and a half were captured under him, and the rest under Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz in the kingdom (2 Kings 16:17). The following prophecy is written against the Assyrians.

(Verses 5 ff.) “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my wrath; he himself is the staff, and my indignation is in his hand. I will send him against a deceitful nation, and I will command him against the people of my wrath, to carry off spoils and plunder booty and to make him a trampling-place like the mud of the streets.

“But he did not so intend, nor did his heart so reckon; rather, his heart was set on crushing and destroying many nations. For he says: ‘Are not my princes all kings? Is not Charchemish like Chalanne, and Arphad like Hamath? Is not Damascus like Samaria? As my hand has seized the kingdoms of idols, so also their images from Jerusalem and from Samaria. Shall I not do to Jerusalem and its images as I did to Samaria and its idols?’”

Let us place here the translation of the Septuagint, which differs from the Hebrew in many respects.

**Septuagint:** “Woe to the Assyrians: he is the rod of my wrath in their hands. I will send my anger against an unrighteous nation, and I will command my people to take spoil and booty, to trample cities, and to reduce them to dust. But he did not think so, nor did he judge in that way; rather, his mind was set on crushing and destroying many nations.

“And if they say to him, ‘You alone are prince,’ he will answer: ‘I did not take the region beyond Babylon, nor Chalanne, where the tower was built. But I took Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria. As I took these, so I will seize all the kingdoms.’

“Wail, carved images, in Jerusalem and Samaria. For as I did to Samaria and its idols, so I will do to Jerusalem and its images.”

First, it should be known that the Hebrew does not have *Chalane*, but *Chalanno*. The final letter of this name is not *yod*, as they thought, but *waw*; the two letters differ from one another only in size. The tower was built in the plain of Shinar, where were Arec [another manuscript: Arce], Acad, Chalanne, and Babylon, which received its name from the confusion of languages (Gen. 11).

“Arabia” is not found in the Hebrew, but rather “Hamath,” which the Syrians still call Epiphaneia. “Wail, carved images, in Jerusalem” they added from their own text. And what is written above—“If they say to him, ‘You alone are prince,’ he will answer: ‘I did not take that region and that one, but I took Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria’”—suggests this meaning:

When, he says, those who have been captured tell the Assyrian, “You are prince of all,” he, still conscious of his weakness, will answer [another reading: “answered”]: “How do you call me prince, when I have captured only Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria, and have not yet subjected to my power the nations lying far away beyond Babylon? But just as I captured Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria, so I will lay all kingdoms beneath myself.”

Let us pass to the Hebrew and briefly record what seems to us correct.

“Woe to the Assyrian”—that is, Sennacherib—“because he is the rod and staff of my wrath; for my indignation is in his hand. Through him I will strike the utterly deceitful nation, which has always limped between me and idols, which lied that it would carry out my commandments. Against the people of my wrath I myself will command him to strip and plunder them, reduce them to dust, and trample them like the mud of the streets”—that is, to strike them but not kill them, to wound them but not take away their life.

But he went beyond the measure of my anger, and not only raged against Israel, against whom he had been directed, but also against many nations, crushing all the kingdoms around him, so that his sword raged even to the destruction of many nations.

Raised up in pride, he dared to say: “My commanders are kings of other nations; subject to me, they will rule all peoples. As I captured Charchemish, so I captured Chalanno [another reading: “Chalan and Arphad”]; as Arphad, so I conquered Hamath; as Damascus, so I subjected Samaria to myself. As I subjected the remaining kingdoms that served the worship of idols beneath my feet, so I will subject Jerusalem and Samaria, in which the same idols are found, to my power. As I captured Samaria with its idols, so I will capture Jerusalem, because it worships the same gods.”

Instead of “Charchemish,” the Septuagint, adding material of its own, interpreted “the region beyond Babylon”; it interpreted “Chalanne” as “where the tower was built,” and entirely omitted Arphad.

According to their translation, and granting the freedom of tropological interpretation—provided that it is pious—we may also say this: from the words, “I will command my people to take spoil and booty, to trample cities, and to reduce them to dust,” the Lord daily commands his people to reduce to dust the cities of their adversaries that rise up against the knowledge of God and that have been built by heretics through immense labor, and to demonstrate that they are nothing.

The one who recognizes the weakness of the human heart, and that, enclosed in mortal flesh, he cannot possess perfect victory over the virtues or capture all nations, although others admire him and say, “You alone are prince,” will answer them: “There are many things that I ought to destroy, and that I have not yet been able to destroy. I know that I do not know.” And although I have overcome many arguments of the adversaries, there are still very many that must be overcome. At the same time, from the things he has conquered he promises himself victory over the rest, trusting in future hope.

The images of Jerusalem and Samaria are commanded to wail—not the things that have been fashioned themselves, but those who fashioned them: by metonymy, those who made them are represented by the things that were made. Thus not only those who have fabricated idols in heresies, but also those who in the Church defend falsehood instead of truth through ignorance, are to testify by wailing and repentance that they have gone astray.

[Note: The words from “Let us place here” through “many nations” had been wrongly moved by Martianus to the end of the Septuagint translation; we have restored them here from the manuscript.]

(Verses 12–14.) “And it shall be, when the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, that I will visit the fruit of the magnificent heart of the king of Assyria and the glory of the loftiness of his eyes. For he said: ‘By the strength of my hand I have acted, and by my wisdom I have understood. I removed the boundaries of peoples, plundered their princes, and brought down, like a powerful man, those who dwelt in lofty places. My hand found the strength of the peoples as though it were a nest; and as eggs are gathered when they have been abandoned, so I gathered the whole earth, and there was no one who moved a wing, opened his mouth, or chirped.’”

Instead of “fruit,” the Septuagint translated “sense” or “great mind.”

After the captivity of Samaria, the victory of the Assyrians, and the threat against Jerusalem—since Samaria’s imitation of idols means that Jerusalem must be struck by a similar sentence—the Prophet now speaks against the Assyrian himself, who was lifted up in pride and thought that his victory was the result of his own strength.

For the Assyrian said, boasting in the swelling of his heart, that by the strength of his hand he had conquered all nations and by his extraordinary wisdom had taken possession of everyone’s boundaries. According to the Septuagint, his power was so great that he utterly overthrew the cities of armed men, seized the whole world as though it were a nest, and turned it into his booty as eggs abandoned by their mothers.

And because he had once taken his metaphor from birds, a nest, and eggs, he maintained it in what followed, saying: “There was no one who moved a wing, opened his mouth, or chirped.” Such, he says, was the terror produced by my strength and victory that the defeated could not freely utter even a cry or groan.

Some think that these words are spoken generally against the kingdom of the Assyrians: once the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem—that is, once Jerusalem has been overthrown—the empire of the Assyrians will be destroyed. To me, however, from what follows, the threat appears to be directed specifically against Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians.

When he says, “After the Lord has completed all his works on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem,” he does not mean the destruction of the city but its siege, when Rabshakeh, the commander of Sennacherib, came and did what the same Prophet recalls later (Isa. 37:17). [Note: Previously the text read, “and did in it.”]

According to the tropological interpretation, when Samaria and Jerusalem have endured the Lord’s anger and have recognized that they went astray in the making of idols, then the great mind of the Assyrian will be destroyed—the mind that was so puffed up against the Lord that it thought everything would yield to its wisdom, and that every lofty doctrine, fortified by dialectical skill, could be shaken and utterly destroyed. They will be so reduced that, like the young of birds, they will be unable to rise on high; like eggs, they will be shown to be lifeless, insensible, and numb, unable even to mutter or move their tongue against the reason and strength of their own speech.

(Verses 15.) “Will the axe boast against the one who cuts with it, or will the saw exalt itself against the one who draws it? As though a rod should be lifted against the one lifting it, and a staff should exalt itself, though it is merely wood.”

Against Sennacherib—or, as many think, Nebuchadnezzar—boasting and saying, “By the strength of my hand I have acted, by my wisdom I have understood,” and the rest, the holy Prophet replied: [Note: The Greek belongs to Eusebius: “O most foolish of all men, do you not see that an axe can never move itself to cut wood unless another acts?,” and so forth. Jerome transferred these words into his own work.]

“O most foolish of mortals, do you think God’s anger is your wisdom, and do you attribute his command to your own strength? What if an axe were to boast against the one holding the axe, or a saw against the one who draws it, and they were to say that all the works accomplished through the axe and saw had been perfected by their own skill? And if someone raised a rod and lifted a staff to strike whomever he wished, and the rod and staff themselves boasted and said that the person struck had been struck by them—so you, when you are an instrument of God’s will, are raised up in pride and boast that everything accomplished is the result of your own power.”

Whatever is said to the Assyrian can also be referred to the pride of heretics and to the devil, who in Scripture is called an axe, a saw, and a rod, because through him unfruitful trees are cut down and divided, the hardness of unbelievers is sawn through, and those who do not accept discipline are struck with the rod.

Heretics also—whose mouth is set against heaven and whose tongue traverses the earth—misuse for what is contrary and perverse the understanding they received from God for a good purpose, speaking against the one by whom they were created. They turn the ministry of the tongue, by which the Lord ought to be praised, into blasphemy (Ps. 72).

(Verses 16 ff.) “Therefore the Lord, the ruler of hosts, will send leanness upon his fat ones, and beneath his glory a burning fire will burn like the consuming of fire. And the light of Israel will be as fire, and his Holy One as a flame; and it will burn and devour his thornbush and briars in a single day. And the glory of his forest and his Carmel will be consumed from soul to flesh; and he will flee in terror, and the remnant of the trees of his forest will be counted because of their small number, and a child will write them down.”

Because you have done these things and spoken the words I have related above, the Lord will send his angel, and in one night 185,000 of your army will die, so that even the most powerful—whom he calls “fat”—will be reduced to leanness and nothingness. And, as the Hebrews transmit, while the clothing of the Assyrians remained unharmed, their bodies were secretly consumed by burning heat.

Then “the light of Israel and his Holy One”—that is, the angel—will be fire and flame, and all the thorns and briars of the Assyrians, that is, their wickedness, will be consumed, not over a long period but in a single day and moment. And just as a forest and Carmel—a mountain in Galilee thickly planted with woods—are quickly burned when fire is placed beneath them, so all the glory of the Assyrian, from soul to flesh, will be consumed.

Then the stripped army will flee, as the Prophet testifies in what follows. From that innumerable multitude, compared with Carmel and the forest, it will be reduced to so few that a small child could count and describe them. The Hebrews transmit that only ten men remained from his army.

Some of our writers hold that this king is a type of the hostile power. Just as in Daniel we read of the princes of the kingdom of the Persians, the kingdom of the Medes, and the kingdom of the Greeks (Dan. 10), so they think there is also a prince of the Assyrians, who, because of his pride, is called “the great mind” and is handed over to the fires of Gehenna on the day of judgment—the fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

Then the light of Israel and the Holy One, that is, the Lord himself, will set fire to the briars and thorns of the Assyrian, reducing all his power and his innumerable peoples to nothing. Terrified by fear, he will wish to escape the punishment hanging over him like a twisting, fleeing serpent.

Those who are able to escape from his forest, confusion, and perishing trees will prove worthy to be counted and described by the child whose rule is upon his shoulders.

This can also be referred to the heretics: after ecclesiastical teaching has shone forth and all their traps have been exposed, they will be reduced to such a wilderness that, from the forest of their unfruitful trees and their innumerable multitude—by which they had deceived people through heretical fraud—scarcely a few will remain to follow their error.

Where we translate, “The Lord will send leanness upon his fat ones,” the Septuagint translated, “The Lord will send disgrace upon your honor.” And where we said, “His Holy One will be in flame,” they translated, “He will sanctify him in fire.” Some wish this to mean that punishments and torments are imposed on sinners so that they may be purified by divine fire.

Where we said, “The glory of his forest and his Carmel,” they translated, “The mountains, hills, and forest will be extinguished,” by which all the Assyrians’ glory, pride, and multitude will be humbled through extinction.

(verses 20 ff.) “And it shall be in that day that the remnant of Israel and those who have been saved from the house of Jacob will no longer continue to rely upon the one who strikes [another reading: “will strike”] them, but will rely in truth upon the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. The remnant will return—the remnant, I say, of Jacob—to the mighty God. For though your people, Israel, be like the sand of the sea, a remnant of them will return. A consummation that is shortened will overflow with righteousness. For the Lord, the God of hosts, will make a consummation and a shortening in the midst of the whole earth.”

Where the Greek says, “The remnant of Jacob will return to the mighty God,” instead of “to the mighty God,” the Hebrew has *El Gibbor*, two of the six names by which above we read that the little child and son given to us would be called.

And where it is written, “The remnant will return,” the Hebrew uses the singular number: “what remains will return,” that is, τὸ ὑπόλειμμα ἐπιστρέψει. In Hebrew it is written *Sar-Yashub*. On this basis some think that Isaiah’s son, Jasub, went before as a sign of the people of Israel who would be saved.

Therefore, when the light of Israel and the Holy One have consumed the forest, briars, and thorns of Carmel, and the king of the Assyrians has fled with a few men, then the remnant of Israel—who, while Hezekiah was ruler, were besieged in Jerusalem after the other cities of Judea had been captured—will no longer put their confidence in the Assyrian, as they now do under King Ahaz. Ahaz sent messengers to the king of Assyria, saying, “I am your servant; come up and save me from the hand of the king of Syria and from the hand of the king of Israel, who have risen up against me” (2 Kings 16:7).

At that time he took the gold and silver found in the treasuries of the house of the Lord and in the royal house, sent gifts to the king of Assyria, and the king of Assyria listened to him, came to Damascus, captured and deported it, and killed Rezin. But, delivered from the Assyrian striker—who had first been a friend and afterward became an enemy—they will rely upon and trust in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, no longer falsely, as they had done under the earlier kings, but in truth.

We read that this happened under Hezekiah, when, abandoning the idols, they turned to the worship of God. [Note: The earlier reading was “they will turn.” Other such matters, which it is scarcely important to mention to the reader, we silently correct throughout on the authority of manuscripts.]

Because he had said that a remnant would be saved, he passes to later times and declares that complete salvation would come under Christ. The apostle Paul, understanding this, writes to the Romans: “Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved.’ For he is bringing his word to completion and shortening it in righteousness, because the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth” (Rom. 9:27).

And as Isaiah said: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9). Since the authority of so great a man precedes us here, every other interpretation should cease.

Indeed, if we read Josephus (Book 10, chapter 2) and consider how great the multitude of people in Jerusalem and Judea was when the Lord suffered, we understand that scarcely a few Jews were saved—or were to be saved—among the apostles and apostolic men.

The shortened and perfected word is the Gospel, which, in place of all the elaborate ceremonies of the Law, gave the brief commandment of love and faith: what we do not wish to be done to us, let us not do to another. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

Some refer this chapter to the time when, under Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Joshua son of Jehozadak, Ezra, and Nehemiah, a part of the people returned to Judea. We shall answer them that they do not preserve the order of the history, especially since what follows is spoken not against the Babylonians, whose king was Nebuchadnezzar, but against Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians.

(Verses 24 ff.) “Therefore thus says the Lord God of hosts: Do not fear, my people who dwell in Zion, because Assyria will strike you with the rod and lift his staff against you on the road to Egypt. For yet a little while, a very little, and my indignation will be completed, and my anger against their crime.

“And the Lord of hosts will raise a scourge against him, as in the plague of Midian at the rock of Oreb, and his rod over the sea, and he will lift it on the road to Egypt. And it shall be in that day: his burden will be taken away from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck, and the yoke will decay before the oil.”

For “rock,” which Aquila interpreted according to the Hebrew, Symmachus and Theodotion preserved the Hebrew word itself, *Sur Oreb*. The Septuagint translated it “a place of tribulation”; we shall discuss this in its proper place.

“It seems difficult to you,” he says, “O inhabitant of Zion, that, while all the surrounding nations have been subjected by the Assyrian, you alone should be delivered from his hands. Listen to what I say: do not fear, my people, that you will be captured when Assyria conquers. For although in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 18) Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, will come against all the fortified cities of Judah [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “the fortified cities of Judah, and he will capture them”], in order to capture them, and will send Rabshakeh to terrify the people besieged in Jerusalem, nevertheless you must know that he will strike you not with a sword but with a rod. As he proceeds against Taracham, king of Ethiopia, and against the Egyptians and the Red Sea by the road to Egypt, he will merely raise his staff against you and will not be able to strike you.

“For yet a little while, and, having returned from Egypt with an innumerable army and wishing to besiege you, he will immediately be struck by my indignation. That scourge which I once raised against the Midianites under Gideon (Judg. 7), who was also called Jerubbaal, will be raised against him: when Oreb and Zeeb, the princes of Midian, were killed upon the very hard rock—that is, flint—which in Hebrew is called *Sur*. Thus, from the rock and from the king who was killed upon it, the place received the name ‘the rock of Oreb.’

“He will therefore lift his rod over the Red Sea as he proceeds against the Ethiopians, and, returning to you by the road to Egypt, he will lift it again. But as soon as he comes from Egypt, the burden will be removed from your shoulders, along with the yoke of his rule, and you will cease to serve. That yoke—that is, the power of the Assyrian—will decay before the oil, that is, before God’s mercy.”

We may also understand the words, “He will strike you with the rod and lift his staff against you on the road to Egypt,” and again, “His rod over the sea, and he will lift it on the road to Egypt,” in this way: he struck many from the tribe of Judah and captured the cities surrounding the kingdom of Jerusalem because they had placed their confidence not in God but in the Egyptians.

Hence Rabshakeh reproaches them, saying: “Behold, you trust in the staff of a broken reed, Egypt. If a man leans upon it, it will enter his hand and pierce it” (2 Kings 18:21)—so Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is to all who trust in him.

The history of the Midianites is written in the Book of Judges (Judg. 7), and we also read it in the Psalm: “Set their princes like Oreb and Zeb, and Zebee and Salmana” (Ps. 82:12).

Therefore those are mistaken who think that the passage refers to the time when, in the Book of Numbers, the Midianites are reported to have been killed by Israel from the wilderness of Sur to Mount Oreb (Num. 25). The names are written with different letters among the Hebrews, and at that time they were not at Mount Oreb but in the wilderness of Shittim. [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “and the wilderness of Sur, and the mountain of God, Oreb.”]

According to the anagogical interpretation, the people dwelling in the Church are commanded not to fear adversaries who are always prepared for battle and who have overturned many souls through their extensive disputation. The reason they are allowed to exercise a little power against God’s people, and to strike them not so much with a sword as with a rod—that is, not to kill but to threaten—is that they have walked on the road to Egypt and have not trusted in the Lord.

But when they return to God and abandon the road to Egypt, then God’s scourge will be raised by judgment against the adversaries. For Midian is interpreted as “from judgment,” so that by the breath of his mouth and the oil of his mercy the yoke of the enemies may decay.

(Verses 28 ff.) He will come to Aiath; he will pass through Magron; at Michmash he will deposit his baggage. They have hurried past Geba; our lodging is there (or, as we find it written elsewhere: “they have remained at the lodging”). Rama was stunned; Gibeah of Saul has fled. Cry aloud with your voice, daughter of Gallim; pay attention, Laish, poor little Anathoth. Madmenah has migrated; inhabitants of Gebim, take courage. There is still a day for him to halt at Nob; he will shake his hand over the mountain of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.

**The Septuagint:** “For he will come to the city of Aggai and pass through Maggedo; at Michmash he will deposit his baggage. He will pass through the valley and come to Aggai. Fear will seize Rama, the city of Saul; the daughter of Gallim will flee. Pay attention, Laish; it will be heard in Anathoth. Madmenah was stunned, and the inhabitants of Gebim. Take comfort today on the road, so that he may remain; take comfort, mountain of the daughter of Zion and hill of Jerusalem.”

The Septuagint differs greatly from the Hebrew in this passage. For that reason we have set out both editions, so that, if Christ inspires us and we are worthy, we may state what seems to us appropriate in each.

The prophetic utterance describes the route and the pomp of the Assyrian returning from Egypt to Jerusalem, and with what tumult and speed he will come to attack it. “First,” he says, “he will come to Aiath” [or Aiath], where, because of his excessive haste, unwilling to remain, he will pass on to Magron. He will have such confidence in capturing the city that at Michmash he will entrust his baggage, as though he would soon return after the city had been overthrown. Once these things have been deposited, he will hurry past it and have an inn at Geba. When he pauses there briefly to refresh his exhausted army, the neighboring city of Rama will be terrified; Gibeah, once the city of Saul, will flee.

Then the daughter of Gallim, called in Hebrew **Beth-gallim** [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], will wail so loudly that you might think it the neighing of horses. Therefore, O Laish, and poor—or obedient, or humble—Anathoth (for the name can be interpreted in three ways), pay close attention and, if you can, avoid the assault of the one who is rushing forward. The city of Madmenah has already migrated from its dwellings. But you who live in the hills—which is what Gebim means—protected by the height of your places, take courage, that is, seize your weapons.

Only so much of the day remained that, standing at the little town of Nob and seeing Jerusalem from afar, he might shake his hand and brandish it over Mount Zion—either looking down upon and despising it, or insulting and threatening it, and wondering that, although the entire East was subject to him, so small a city dared resist his power.

These things, according to the Hebrews, as they have been handed down to us by them, we have touched upon briefly. Now let us add what ecclesiastical writers think about this passage according to the Septuagint edition.

When the Assyrian yoke—or, as some wrongly suppose, the Babylonian yoke—has been removed from your shoulders and broken, the fleeing Assyrian, Sennacherib, will come with a few survivors to Aggai, which is not found in the Hebrew text. Such will be the panic of the fugitive that he will not dare remain there, but will pass on to Maggedo, which likewise is not contained in Scripture. And because, hindered by his baggage, he will be unable to flee more quickly, he will deposit his vessels at Michmash and cross the valley at a rapid pace; the Hebrew text likewise does not mention this valley. Again he will come to Aggai, which is placed twice in this passage but is absent from the Hebrew.

At the sound of his flight Rama, the city of Saul, will tremble—something plainly false. For Gibeah is called the city of Saul, as the Hebrew text contains. Then he will come to Gallim; Laish will hear, Anathoth will hear, and Madmenah will tremble. But the inhabitants of Gebim and the hills, which are in Jerusalem—that is, all the men of exalted rank—are summoned to console Jerusalem, not after a long time but immediately, on that very day while the Assyrian is on the road, so that they may remain in their places and, disturbed by fear, not flee at all.

This is the literal meaning. But since one interpreter cannot find the etymologies of the false names according to the Septuagint, and admits that he was unable to discover them in the book of Hebrew Names, he sends us into uncertainty by saying that, at the end of the world and the consummation of this age, when punishments are imminent, the great meaning is that the prince of the Assyrians will flee, and that through various places and changing journeys he will desire to escape from the wrath of God.

When he has fled, the inhabitants of Gebim—that is, all the exalted virtues—are, in prophetic language, summoned to console the fugitive and teach him not to flee but to remain on the road and await the mercy of God. They are also summoned not merely to console the fugitive, but to recall the daughter of Zion from mourning through good works and summon her to the salvation of repentance. These, he says, are the hills in Jerusalem of which we read later in this prophet: “Comfort, comfort my people, priests”; [Note: Victor supplies “says God” from the sacred text itself, not from Jerome’s copies.] “speak to the heart of Jerusalem” (Isa. XL, 1).

He said this because, compelled by the truth of the matter, he had nothing else to say.

Behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, will break the flask in terror; the tall will be cut down, and the lofty will be humbled; the dense thickets of the forest will be overthrown by the iron, and Lebanon with its tall trees will fall.

Some think that this passage still concerns the Assyrian: once he has been crushed, all the surrounding nations subject to his rule will be cut down and humbled, and the very dense forest will be overthrown. By the forest they wish, metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*), to understand the people and their princes. They likewise understand Lebanon falling with its tall trees to mean that nothing at all of Assyria’s power will remain.

Others, however, think that the passage concerning Christ begins here, especially since both what follows and the Circumcision itself acknowledge in writing that they concern him. [Note: “And Circumcision,” etc. That is, the Jews, whom he calls “Circumcision” in accordance with the Apostle. Not understanding this, Marianus Victorius thought that “Circumcision” was a section or period of the prophetic discourse; but the interpretation is incongruous, not to say utterly inept. — MARTIAN.] [That is, the circumcised nation, or the Jews. Martianus also notes this against Victorius, who thought that the word signified a section of the prophetic text.]

Above he had spoken of the name of the child to be born from the Virgin, who would be called Emmanuel; and afterward, of the child conceived in the womb of the Prophetess, who would be called “Hasten, strip the spoil, hurry to plunder” (Isa. VIII, 3). He himself would be a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to the two houses of Israel; his principality would be upon his shoulder, and he would be called by six names: Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the Age to Come, and Prince of Peace. His dominion would be multiplied, and there would be no end of peace.

Now, in the prelude to his coming, before it is said that he will be born from the stock of Jesse and David, his passion is shown by the image of the broken flask: God willed that his flesh be handed over to death for this reason, so that the exalted position of the Jews might be destroyed, the formerly lofty might fall to the earth, and Lebanon with its cedars might be cut down. Concerning this we read in Zechariah: “Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars. Howl, cypress, because the cedar has fallen, because the magnificent have been laid waste” (Zech. XI, 1–2).

That he is said to have been crushed and struck by the Father is also indicated by the words: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. XIII, 7). Another testimony says: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck” (Ps. LXVIII, 2).

The Hebrew word **PHURA** [the Hebrew term is absent in the supplied text], which Aquila translated as **κεραμεῖον**, “a clay vessel” [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, in diminutive form, **κεραμίδιον**, “a little earthenware vessel.”], Theodotion and Symmachus rendered **ληνόν**, that is, “winepress.” This also, according to the superscription of three psalms, signifies the Lord’s passion, as he himself says in Isaiah: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and no man from the nations was with me” (Isa. LXIII, 3). The Septuagint, however, introducing a new meaning in place of “winepress,” translated it as “glorious.”

## Chapter XI

### Verses 1–2

“And a rod will come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety. And the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him.”

Up to the beginning of the Vision, or Burden, of Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw, this entire prophecy concerns Christ. We wish to explain it section by section, so that, when everything is proposed and discussed at once, the reader’s memory may not be confused.

The Jews interpret the rod and flower from the root of Jesse as the Lord himself: in the rod, they say, the power of the one who reigns is shown; in the flower, his beauty.

Let us understand the rod from the root of Jesse as the holy Virgin Mary, who had no adjoining branch of her own; concerning her we read above: “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isa. VII, 14). Let us understand the flower as the Lord and Savior, who says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II, 1).

In place of “root,” which only the Septuagint translated, the Hebrew has **GEZA** [the Hebrew term is absent], which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as **κορμός**, that is, “a trunk.” In place of “flower,” which in Hebrew is **NESER** [Note: See below, at chapter XVIII, verse 19.], they translated “shoot,” to show that, long after the Babylonian captivity, when no one from David’s stock possessed the glory of the ancient kingdom, Christ arose from Mary as from a trunk, and from Mary herself.

The point that all ecclesiastical writers seek in Matthew’s Gospel but do not find written there—“For he will be called a Nazarene” (Matt. II, 23)—learned Hebrews think was taken from this passage. But it must be known that **NESER** is written with the letter *ṣade*, whose character and sound Latin speech cannot express between *z* and *s*. It is a hissing sound, scarcely produced by pressing the tongue against closed teeth. The city of Zion is also written with this letter.

The Nazarenes, however, whom the Septuagint translated as “sanctified” and Symmachus as “separated,” are always written with **ZAIN** [Note: We have often said that *zai* is read for *zain* in manuscripts.] as their letter.

Upon this flower, therefore, which will suddenly rise from the trunk and root of Jesse through the Virgin Mary, the Spirit of the Lord will rest, because in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily—not in portions, as in the other saints, but, according to the Gospel that the Nazarenes read in Hebrew, “The whole fountain of the Holy Spirit will descend upon him.” “The Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III, 17).

In the same volume of Matthew we read the passage that follows: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased; I will put my Spirit upon him; he will proclaim judgment to the nations” (Matt. XII, 18). This refers to the Savior, upon whom the Spirit of the Lord rested—that is, remained in eternal habitation—not so that he might fly away and descend upon him again, but so that, according to the testimony of John the Baptist, he might remain continually. John says: “I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and remaining upon him, and I did not know him. But the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John I, 32–33). [Note: This account of the Savior’s baptism from the codex of the Ebionites—which Jerome reports to have been the same as this Gospel of the Nazarenes, in his commentary on Matthew, chapter XII—is related by Epiphanius, *Heresies* XXX, §13, though more briefly and in somewhat different terms. See what we say elsewhere, and at the cited passage of Matthew, concerning the Gospel of the Nazarenes.]

In the Gospel mentioned above we find the following written:

“It happened that, when the Lord had come up from the water, the whole fountain of the Holy Spirit descended and rested upon him, and said to him: ‘My Son, in all the prophets I was waiting for you, that you might come and that I might rest in you. For you are my rest; you are my firstborn Son, who reigns forever.’”

This Spirit is called the Spirit of the Lord and the Spirit of wisdom, for all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made (John I, 3). In the Psalms it is sung: “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord! You made all things in wisdom” (Ps. XCI, 24). The Apostle writes: “Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I). And in Proverbs we read: “God founded the earth in his wisdom and prepared the heavens in his prudence” (Prov. III, 19).

Just as the same Word of God is called light, life, and resurrection, so he is called the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord—not because he is different according to the differences of these names, but because he is one and the same fountain and source of all virtues.

Without Christ, therefore, no one can be wise, understanding, a counselor, strong, learned, pious, or full of the fear of God.

It should also be noted that the Spirit of the Lord—the spirits of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord, that is, the number seven, which are called the seven eyes in one stone in Zechariah (chapter III)—rests upon the rod and flower that arose from Jesse, and therefore from the stock of David.

More particularly, the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him for the sake of those who need the fear of the Lord, because they are infants, whom perfect love casts out. “The one who fears has punishment, and is not perfect” (I John IV, 18). Hence the Apostle also says to believers: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. VIII, 15). And in Malachi we read: “If I am a father, where is my glory? And if I am the Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. I, 6). Concerning this fear it is sung in the Psalm: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Ps. XXXIII, 12).

### Verses 3 ff.

“He will not judge according to the appearance of his eyes, nor reprove according to the hearing of his ears; but he will judge the poor in righteousness, and reprove the meek of the earth with equity. He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he will kill the wicked. Righteousness will be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his kidneys.”

We refer these words to the Savior’s first coming; the Jews contend that they will be fulfilled at the end of the world.

The Septuagint translated: “He will not judge according to glory, nor reprove according to speech, but he will judge with humble judgment and reprove the humble of the earth.” [Note: Eusebius wrote in Greek: “For he accepts no person’s face, but reproved with great frankness—at one time the scribes and Pharisees, at another the chief priests inside the temple, to whom he also said: ‘The kingdom will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.’ Yet he did not reprove according to their speech. For some approached him saying, ‘Teacher, we know that you are true,’ and what follows; but he did not reprove according to their speech. Therefore, knowing their wickedness, he said: ‘Why do you test me, hypocrites?’” Jerome renders this in Latin in almost the same words.]

For he accepts no one’s person in judgment, but speaks to the scribes, Pharisees, and rulers: “Woe to you, hypocrites!” and “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXIII, 13; XXI, 43).

Nor did he reprove according to speech or the hearing of ears. When they said, “Teacher, we know that you are truthful and teach the way of God in truth, and you do not concern yourself with anyone; for you do not look at the face of men” (Matt. XXII, 16), he knew their wickedness and answered: “Why are you testing me, hypocrites?” and other similar things.

He judged in righteousness the poor in spirit, whose is the kingdom of God; and he reproved in equity the meek and humble of the earth, saying to the Apostles: “Are you still without understanding?” And again: “Do you not yet know or understand?” And to Peter specifically: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Mark VIII, 17; Matt. XIV, 31). Or certainly, for the sake of the humble and meek, he reproved those who were trying to oppress them.

He also struck all earthly works with a rod—or, as the Septuagint translated, with the word of his mouth—when he said in the Gospel: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. X, 34; Luke XII, 51). Concerning this we read in the ninth Psalm: “You rebuked the nations, and the wicked perished; you blotted out their name forever and ever” (Ps. IX, 6). The Apostle Paul writes: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (II Thess. II, 8; Eph. VI).

After the wicked had been struck, the Lord was girded with righteousness, truth, and faith. For he was made for us by God wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (I Cor. I), and in the Gospel he says: “I am the light, and the life, and the truth” (John VIII, 6; XIV). In the Psalms it is said: “Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV, 2). Therefore the Apostle also exhorts the Ephesians: “Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth and clothed with the breastplate of righteousness” (Eph. VI, 14).

If “faith” is read in place of “truth,” this should be said: the Lord’s belt, with which Jeremiah was girded (Jer. XIII), is the faith of believers.

### Verses 6 ff.

“The wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the kid; the calf, the lion, and the sheep will remain together, and a little child will lead them. The calf and the bear will feed; their young will rest together, and the lion will eat straw like an ox. The infant at the breast will delight over the hole of the asp; and into the den of the basilisk the one who has been weaned will put his hand. They will neither harm nor kill throughout all my holy mountain, because the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as waters covering the sea.”

The Jews and our Judaizers likewise contend that these things are literally future: in the glory of Christ, whom they think will come at the end of the world, all beasts will be reduced to gentleness, and, having laid aside their former savagery, wolf and lamb will feed together, along with the other creatures that we now see to be mutually opposed.

We must ask them whether everything in this passage is to be understood exactly as it is written, with nothing referred to spiritual understanding, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Blessed be God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (II Cor. I, 3). If so, then the root, rod, and flower must not refer to any spiritual meaning; the earth struck by the word of God and the wicked killed by the breath of his lips must be understood exactly as written; and they must explain how righteousness and truth, which are incorporeal things, can surround the Lord’s loins.

Let us also ask them what is worthy of the Lord’s majesty in the wolf and lamb feeding together, the leopard lying down with the kid, the lion eating straw, and a little child putting his hand into the hole of asps—unless perhaps, according to the tales of the poets, they will restore for us the golden age of Saturn, in which wolves and lambs will feed together, rivers will flow full of honeyed wine, and the sweetest honey will drip from the leaves of trees, while everything will be filled with fountains of milk.

If they reply that these things will occur as a blessing of the times, so that human beings may enjoy every good without harming anyone, let them hear from us that nothing is good except virtue and nothing evil except vice, as the Psalmist says: “Who is the person who desires life and loves to see good days? Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXIII, 14; XXXI, 27). Wealth, bodily health, abundance of all things, and their opposites—poverty, sickness, and want—are not counted among goods or evils even by the philosophers of the world, but are called indifferent things. Hence the Stoics, who in many respects agree with our doctrine, call nothing good except moral nobility and virtue, and nothing evil except disgrace and vice.

We have said this briefly to prove that our Judaizers are snoring in the deepest sleep.

Otherwise, according to the life-giving Spirit, the meaning is easy. The wolf is Paul, who at first persecuted and tore apart the Church. Of him it is said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf” (Gen. XLIX, 27). He dwelt with the lamb—either with Ananias, by whom he was baptized (Acts VIII), or with the Apostle Peter, to whom it was said: “Feed my lambs” (John XXI).

The leopard, which formerly did not change its spots, washed in the Lord’s fountain lay down with the kid—not the kid placed on the left, but the one sacrificed at the Lord’s Passover.

It should be noted that it is not the lamb and kid who dwell and lie down with the wolf and leopard, but the wolf and leopard who imitate the innocence of the lambs and kids.

The formerly most savage lion, together with the sheep and calf, will also remain there. [Note: With a few changes, this passage too was reproduced by Eusebius, the holy Father. There is not time to indicate the shorter parallels that occur elsewhere.]

We see this daily in the Church: rich and poor, powerful and humble, kings and private persons dwelling together, and being governed by little children—by whom we understand the Apostles and apostolic men, unskilled in speech but not in knowledge. When they have been joined together among themselves by the discipline of the Lord, so that their households also are united, then the words will be fulfilled: “Their young will rest together.”

The lion will not eat meat but straw, meaning that it will feed on simple food. Here too it should be observed that it is not the ox that eats meat, but the lion that eats straw. I think that in the Holy Scriptures straw signifies simple words; wheat and the inner marrow signify the meaning found within the letter. It often happens that worldly people, who do not know the mysteries, are nourished by the simple reading of the Scriptures.

The infant, who is little in wickedness, also puts his hand into the hole of the asp and drives demons from the bodies of people possessed. But the one who has been weaned is no longer nourished with the milk of infancy but already eats solid food. He puts his hand into the basilisk’s den—that is, into Satan’s own dwelling—and draws him out from there. Hence power was given to the Apostles to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy (Luke X).

The formerly poisonous animals will not be able to harm or kill those who dwell on the holy mountain of God, which is interpreted as the Church. Of it the Gospel says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14).

But lest we think that this refers to Mount Zion according to the error of the Hebrews, the mysteries of evangelical preaching are shown in the following verse: “Because the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord.” This is what was said above in a more obscure manner: “The wolf will dwell with the lamb, and the leopard will lie down with the kid.” And, according to the prophetic custom, the final words disclose the meaning: “As waters,” he says, “covering the sea.” Just as the waters of the sea cover the depths of the sea—that is, the earth covered by the waves—so the whole earth will be filled with the knowledge of the Lord.

The joining together of people formerly diverse in character is also testified to by the blessed Apostle Peter in the linen vessel that was lowered from heaven (Acts X). It had four beginnings, which we understand as the four regions of the world, so that we may recognize the earth as filled with the knowledge of God. In that vessel were four-footed animals, serpents, beasts, and birds of heaven, so that what the ark accomplished in the flood, the Church might accomplish in the world.

“In that day the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples: the nations will entreat him, and his tomb will be glorious.”

**The Septuagint:** “And in that day there will be the root of Jesse, and the one who will arise to be ruler of the nations; in him the nations will hope, and his resting-place will be honor.”

In place of “his resting-place,” the Hebrew has **MNUATHO** [the Hebrew term is absent], which all have translated similarly. In place of “honor,” the Hebrew reads **CHABOD** [the Hebrew term is absent], which plainly means “glory.”

The meaning is that his death will be glorious, so that what the Savior asks in the Gospel may be fulfilled: “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII, 5).

His birth has been discussed, as have the other mysteries in the middle of the discourse; he comes to death, which is called not by the customary name used for mortal beings but “rest,” because life perpetual was in Christ. To make the meaning clear to the reader, we have translated “tomb” in place of “sleep” and “rest,” using a different word but retaining the same meaning.

At that time, therefore, when Christ’s Gospel has shone throughout the whole world and the entire earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as waters cover the sea, there will be the root of Jesse, and the one who rises from his stock will stand as a sign for all peoples, so that the peoples may see the sign of the Son of Man in heaven (Matt. XIV). He will have horns in his hands, in which his strength will be hidden, so that, once exalted, he may draw all things to himself (Hab. III).

Or, as the Septuagint translated, he will rise from the dead to be ruler of all nations, and all peoples will hope in him. Jacob also testifies to this in mystical speech concerning the tribe of Judah: “The ruler will not fail from Judah, nor the leader from his thighs, until he comes to whom it has been reserved; and he will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

“And in that day the Lord will again extend his hand to possess the remnant of his people, which will be left by the Assyrians and Egypt, Pathros and Ethiopia, Elam and Shinar, Hamath and the islands of the sea. And he will raise a sign among the nations, and gather the fugitives of Israel, and collect the dispersed of Judah from the four quarters of the earth. And the jealousy of Ephraim will be removed, and the enemies of Judah will perish. Ephraim will not be jealous of Judah, and Judah will not fight against Ephraim. And they will fly upon the shoulder of the Philistines by sea; together they will plunder the children of the East. And Edom and Moab will be subject to their hands, and the children of Ammon will be obedient.”

“In that day,” that is, at that time of which he also spoke above, when the root of Jesse rises as a sign for the peoples, or to rule the nations, the Lord will again extend his hand, so that—not, according to our Judaizers, at the end of the world, when the fullness of the nations has entered and then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XI)—we should understand all these things as occurring at the first coming.

For since one day is spoken of both here and above, we cannot refer the former to the first coming and the latter to the second. Otherwise, because of what follows and what preceded, those passages too would have to be referred to Christ, whom the Jews insist has not yet come but is still to come.

After the calling of the nations, which were formerly counted as the tail, Israel will be counted as the tail (above, chapter X), so that the Lord may again extend his hand and possess the remnant of his people. Concerning this remnant we also read above: not all Israel, but the remnants that will be saved, those left by the Assyrians, Egypt, and the various surrounding nations.

First, the twelve Apostles, the seventy, the one hundred and twenty souls, and the five hundred to whom the Lord appeared when they had gathered together, believed in the Lord; afterward, three thousand and five thousand Jews believed. James also speaks to the Apostle Paul, who himself was one of the remnant: “You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews there are who believe; they are all zealous for the Law” (Acts XXI, 20).

In the same volume we read: “Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. They were all amazed and said: ‘Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how do we each hear our own language in which we were born? Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and inhabitants of Mesopotamia and Syria, Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the regions of Libya around Cyrene, Roman visitors, Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs—we hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God’” (Acts II, 5 ff.).

From all these nations, therefore, the remnant of Israel will be saved through the Apostles.

Ecclesiastical histories report that the Apostles preached the Gospel throughout the whole world, so that some penetrated even to the Persians and Indians, Ethiopia gave its hands to God, and gifts were brought from beyond the rivers of Ethiopia to Christ.

And lest this seem to signify only the eastern peoples, he adds the rest: “and from the islands of the sea.” By the islands of the sea he signifies the western region, which is enclosed by the circuit of the Ocean.

He will therefore raise the sign of the Cross among all nations and gather the people of Israel first from the synagogues of the Jews, so that the Apostles might fulfill the Savior’s command: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. X, 6).

Finally, Paul speaks to unbelievers from among the Jews: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations, as the Lord commanded us” (Acts XIII, 46–47).

By the four quarters he signifies east, west, south, and north, so that through these the calling of the world may be shown.

“At that time,” says Isaiah, “Ephraim and Judah, who now, while I am prophesying, are divided from one another by hostile hatred, will no longer be enemies. Rather, according to Ezekiel’s prophecy, the two rods will be joined into one rod and united in the Church of Christ, although previously separated” (Ezek. XXXVII). Thus they will labor together among the nations and fly upon the shoulder of the Philistines by sea—that is, they will first preach to the maritime Palestinians [or Palestine] and, flying swiftly over the sea, proceed to the other nations.

Or, according to the Septuagint interpreters: “They will fly in the ships of foreigners; together they will plunder the sea.” Let us understand this from the example of the Apostle Paul, who was carried in the ships of foreigners through Pamphylia, Asia, Macedonia, Achaia, and various islands and provinces, even to Italy (Acts XXVIII), and, as he himself writes, to Spain (Rom. XV).

Thus Ephraim and Judah—that is, those from the twelve tribes who believed in Christ from among the Jews—will together plunder the East and extend their hands over Edom and Moab, in accordance with what Christ mystically says under the person of David: “Upon Edom I will extend my sandal; foreigners will serve me” (Ps. LIX, 10).

These nations were adversaries of the Jewish people at the time when Isaiah prophesied. Therefore he now says that after the root of Jesse has arisen to reign among the nations, and the banner of the Cross has been raised for the salvation of the whole world, Edom, Moab, and the children of Ammon—in short, the whole breadth of Arabia—will also give their hands to the Apostles, and churches of Christ will be established in places of idolatry.

And the Lord will lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea, and will raise his hand over the River with the power of his spirit, and will strike it into seven channels, so that they may cross it shod.
