And there will be a way for the remnant of my people who will be left by the Assyrians, just as there was for Israel on the day when he came up from the land of Egypt.

Just as Idumea and Moab and the sons of Ammon will give their hands to the Apostles so as to obey the evangelical preaching, so the Lord himself, who accomplished those things through his Apostles, will lay waste—not the sea, according to the Seventy, [Col. 0151C] but, according to the Hebrews, the tongue of the Egyptian sea, which formerly blasphemed against the Lord and presided over Egyptian superstition. Hence also we read in the Psalms: “This sea is great and wide; there are creeping things there without number” (Ps. X, 25, 26). To this is added: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him.”

Therefore he will lay waste, or “kill,” that is, [Note: [Col. 0151D] We read in the Vatican manuscript ἀναθεματίσει (“he will curse”). Thus Eusebius gives this passage: “The three translators, in agreement, rendered it thus: Καὶ ἀναθεματίσει Κύριος τὴν γλῶσσαν θαλάσσης Αἰγύπτου—‘And the Lord will lay waste the tongue of the Egyptian sea.’ Yet in the editions of Jerome previously published there was ἀναθεματίσεται (‘it will be cursed’).] ἀναθεματίσει, as Theodotion, Aquila, and Symmachus translated it, the tongue of the Egyptian sea; and he will raise his hand over the rivers of Egypt with the power of his spirit, or with a most violent spirit. By this we understand the kingdom of the Romans.

For when Caesar Augustus was reigning (Luke 2), when the flower had sprung up from the root of Jesse and the first census was made in the Roman world, the formerly most powerful kingdom of the Egyptians, which had lasted through many generations, was destroyed by the death of Cleopatra, [Col. 0151D] 165 and the Egyptian river was struck into seven channels, or into seven valleys. The Nile, a river of many waters, which had previously flowed in a single bed and was uncrossable, was divided and cut into seven very low valleys and channels, so that it could be crossed by people wearing shoes.

This, interpreted tropologically, signifies that he distributed the Egyptian people—so devoted to idolatry and the most futile superstition that they consecrated hawks, owls, dogs, goats, and asses in the divine name—from the infinite power of the kingdom among the individual magistrates of the Roman Empire, so that Thebes has one magistrate, Libya another, Pentapolis another, Egypt another, Alexandria another, and the various regions [Note: [Col. 0152D] Martianus reads quos (“which”), and thought—though not very skillfully—that νόμους meant not “regions” but “judges” among the Egyptians, an opinion he later retracted. See below, at the beginning of chapter 19.] which the Egyptians call νόμοι.

For this reason the Nile is metaphorically divided into parts and cut [Alternative: struck] into channels, so that the evangelical word may travel without any impediment and reach the remotest peoples of Egypt. And just as in the time of Moses the Red Sea was dried up so that the people might flee from Egypt, so conversely the rivers of Egypt will be dried up so that the remnants of God’s people, who will be saved from the Assyrians and various nations, may cross into Egypt—not at all fleeing from it, but capturing it [Col. 0152B] and trampling it under their feet.

Let the prudent and Christian reader hold to this rule concerning the prophetic promises: what the Jews and our own people—or rather, those who Judaize but are not truly ours—insist will take place carnally, let us teach as having already taken place spiritually, lest through the pretext of such fables and “endless questions,” as the Apostle says (2 Tim. 2), we be compelled to Judaize.

## CHAPTER XII

### Verses 1–2

“And you will say on that day: ‘I will confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me; your wrath has turned away, and you have comforted me. Behold, God is my Savior; I will act confidently and will not fear, because the Lord God is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.’” [Note: [Col. 0152D] He follows Eusebius closely, almost word for word.]

Previously, in the wilderness, when you came up from the land of Egypt and the Red Sea was dried up, you said: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted” [Col. 0152C] (Exod. 15:1), and what follows. Now, after the tongue of the Egyptian sea has been struck and its river dried up, cut into channels, and humbled, glorify the Lord and say: “I will confess to you, Lord”: for although I deserved your anger and wrath, I have obtained mercy. For you are my Savior—that is, Jesus—and I place no confidence in idols, nor will I fear what ought not to be feared; rather, you are my strength and my praise, you who have become my salvation. Let the most wicked heresy hear that the Lord has become such for those who are saved, and for those whose Lord he previously was not; so that in the Holy Scriptures we may understand “creation” and “making” not always as the bringing into existence of things that did not exist, but sometimes as grace bestowed upon those who have deserved that God become theirs.

[Col. 0152D] ### Verse 3

“You will draw water with joy from the fountains of the Savior.”

The one whom above he had called Emmanuel, then “strip off the spoil,” “hasten to plunder,” and by the remaining names—lest he seem to be someone other than the one whom Gabriel announced to the Virgin, saying, “You will call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people” (Matt. 1:21)—he now calls Savior, and proclaims that water is to be drawn from his fountains, certainly not from the waters of the Egyptian river, which were struck, nor from the waters of the river of Rasin, but from the fountains of Jesus; for in the language of the Hebrews this is what “Savior” means.

Hence he himself also cried out in the Gospel: “Let anyone who thirsts come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, ‘Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.’” But the Evangelist says that he spoke this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were going to receive. And elsewhere in the Gospel he himself says: “Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst; but the water that I will give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 7:8; 4:13–14). Let us understand the fountains of the Savior as evangelical teaching, concerning which we read in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “Bless God the Lord in the churches, from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. 67:27).

[Col. 0153B] ### Verses 4–5

“And you will say on that day: ‘Confess to the Lord and invoke his name; make his deeds known among the peoples; remember that his name is exalted. Sing to the Lord, for he has acted magnificently; proclaim this throughout the whole earth.’”

These things are commanded by the Apostles and by the remnant of Israel to those from the nations who have believed: that they alone should confess to the Lord and, abandoning idols, invoke his name; and that they should proclaim all his works to unbelievers, [167] so that they may know that he alone is exalted, to whom one must sing because of the magnificent things he has done, and whose mercy must be proclaimed throughout the whole world.

### Verse 6

“Exult and praise, habitation of Zion, because great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.”

First, according to the literal sense, it should be said: “O habitation of Zion, exult and praise your God, because the one who previously seemed to be your God, confined within the narrow limits of the small land of Judea, has now filled the whole earth with his knowledge; and, rising from the dead, he reigns among the nations, and the nations themselves beseech and worship him”—provided, that is, that he also stretches out his hand a second time to take possession of what remains of his people, to gather the exiles of Israel, and to collect the scattered of Judah from the four quarters of the earth. For the seed of the Gospel, through the Apostles [Col. 0154B] who were Jews, came forth from the fountains of Israel.

It is better, however, to interpret Zion—that is, “watchtower,” placed on high—as the Church, concerning which the fiftieth Psalm also sings: “Do good, Lord, in your good pleasure to Zion, and let the walls of Jerusalem be built” (Ps. L, 20); so that in it a sacrifice of righteousness, offerings, whole burnt offerings, and the calf whom the most merciful father sacrificed for his repentant son may become acceptable to God (Luke 15).

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0153]

[Col. 0153C] 167–168 It is almost thirteen years since, having been asked by Amabilis, a bishop of holy memory, to write on the ten Visions of Isaiah, I briefly indicated, in view of the difficulties of that time, what seemed to me about each one, explaining only the history he had requested. Now, most laborious Eustochium, I am compelled to write Commentaries on the entire prophet, and meanwhile, at your prayers, I have reached Babylon, which is the first of the ten visions about which I spoke earlier.

It seemed superfluous to me either to repeat the same things or to put forward different opinions in a single work. Therefore this will be the fifth book on Isaiah, which was once published on its own; and when it has been completed to the end, we will take up the beginning of the sixth volume according to the tropological sense, and, with you praying to the Lord for the same purpose, we will pursue the heights of spiritual understanding.

“Thus far, Pope Amabilis, [Note: [Col. 0153D] In the Vatican manuscript: ‘summit of charity,’ and so forth.] a pillar and very name of charity, and the one dearest to me of all whom the earth has produced, you repeatedly urged me by letter to explain to you, in a historical exposition, the ten visions that are most obscure in Isaiah; and, omitting the Commentaries of our own writers, who, following various opinions, composed many volumes, to disclose the Hebrew truth. You often reminded me of this, even as I kept reconsidering the matter and postponing this most troublesome kind of explanation to another time.

But this year you sent our son Heraclius the deacon, who summoned me before the court with hand joined to hand and demanded the promised work moment by moment. What, then, shall I do? Shall I undertake a work over which the most learned men have labored—I mean Origen and Eusebius Pamphili? One of them wanders freely through the open spaces of allegory and, by interpreting the names of individuals, turns his own ingenuity into the mysteries of the Church; the other, promising a historical exposition in his title, sometimes [169–170] forgets his purpose, [Note: [Col. 0153D] Erasmus reads “and yields to the opinions of Origen.” Others read “and Origen’s fortunes collapse.” I suspect that Erasmus altered the text; [Col. 0154C] for the manuscript codices distinctly read “and yields to the opinions of Origen.” He uses this phrase below in chapter 58: “Symmachus, yielding to Theodotion’s opinions, placed a chain,” and so forth. Livy, *The Macedonian War*, book 2, uses *concedere in sententiam alicuius* in the same sense. MARTIAN.] and yields to the opinions of Origen?

Or shall I remain silent and openly say that I do not know how to produce an exposition of this kind? And when will I be able to persuade you that I was unable rather than unwilling to do more—of which the one is a sign of weakness and the other of arrogance? Driven by these considerations, I preferred that you should seek my ability rather than my willingness. I will briefly note what I have learned, laying the foundations of the Scriptures. But if you wish, or if there is time, and if Christ grants consent to our desire, a spiritual building must be erected above it, so that, once the summit has been placed upon it, we may display the Church’s perfected ornaments.

You proposed the Vision of Babylon in Isaiah, and those of Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Idumea, Arabia, the Valley of Vision, and Tyre. If I try to expound them at greater length, many books will be required, and my demanding visitor’s voyage will be postponed for another year. Therefore, as you wish, I will attach brief statements to each testimony, so that I may leave you in a few words not so much an exposition of my opinion as something for you to consider. I dictate these things rather than write them; the speech runs along with the hand of the stenographers. For we do not wish our own work to be praised, but the Prophet’s words to be understood; nor do we boast of eloquence, but seek knowledge of the Scriptures. Let us therefore begin with Babylon.’”

[Col. 0155B] ## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah, son of Amoz, saw.”

The Hebrew word *Massa* (), or “burden” or “weight,” can be understood in either sense. Wherever it is placed as a heading, the things said are full of threats. Hence I am surprised that the translators of the Seventy, in a gloomy matter, wished to put “vision”; but we will discuss that elsewhere.

Now let us pursue what we have begun. Babylon was the capital of the Chaldeans. Its king Nebuchadnezzar, after conquering all the nations as far as Ethiopia, devastated Judea among the rest. After besieging Jerusalem for a long time, he captured it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah’s reign. He himself also captured Zedekiah and led him to Antioch, which was then called Riblah; there, after having his sons killed before their father, he ordered Zedekiah’s eyes to be removed, and, having blinded him, sent him into a cage and dragged him to Babylon like a wild beast. Thus Jeremiah’s prophecy was fulfilled, which said: [Note: [Col. 0155D] “You will enter Babylon.” There is no verse in Jeremiah corresponding to this statement; but in Ezekiel 12:13 these words concerning Zedekiah are found: “And I will bring him to Babylon, to the land of the Chaldeans; yet he will not see it, and there he will die.” Jerome himself should be heard on this point in his commentary on Ezekiel 17: “We read,” he says, “that Zedekiah was captured and taken to Riblah, where, after his sons had been killed, he was blinded and, like a wild beast shut in a cage, transferred to Babylon. Thus Scripture, although it may appear contradictory, is nevertheless completely true in both passages. For it had been said to Zedekiah: ‘You will enter Babylon, and you will not see it.’ He entered, because he was led to Babylon; and he did not see it, because he had been blinded.” From such statements it is sufficiently clear that Jerome recited Jeremiah’s meaning, not his exact words. MARTIAN.] “You will enter Babylon, and you will not see it” (Jer. 34; 39; 52).

Therefore, for the consolation of the Jewish people, the fall of Babylon is foretold: just as Nineveh, the capital of the Assyrians—whose kings Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, and Sennacherib had captured the ten tribes—was overthrown by the devastation of the Chaldean, so this city also, which had grown proud against God, would be overthrown by the assault of the Medes and Persians.

### Verse 2

“Raise a banner on a mountain of mist; lift up your voice; raise your hand.”

Understand the mountain of mist, or darkness, which in Hebrew is called *Nespe* (), as Babylon because of its pride. These are the dark mountains, bringing sadness and gloom, concerning which Jeremiah says: “Give glory to the Lord your God, before your feet stumble against the dark mountains” (Jer. 13:16). The command is given either to Angels or to whatever ministers there may be, so that, at God’s command and with the hand of the messengers raised, the captivity about to come upon Babylon may be proclaimed.

### Verses 3–4

“Let the commanders enter the gates: I have commanded my sanctified ones, and I have summoned my strong ones, rejoicing in my anger, exulting in my glory.”

Eusebius, following the translators of the Seventy, interprets the “princes” and “giants” as Angelic powers and the worst demons, who were sent for Babylon’s overthrow. We, however, following the order of the history, say that they are the Medes. Concerning them Scripture testifies more clearly in what follows, saying: “Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver, nor desire gold.”

Nor is it surprising that he calls the Medes sanctified for the overthrow of Babylon, since through Jeremiah he called Nebuchadnezzar himself, because he served God’s command in destroying apostate Jerusalem, his servant and his dove. Moreover, when he says “my strong ones” and “those exulting in my glory,” he shows that they overthrew the power of so lofty a kingdom not by their own strength but by God’s anger.

171 ### Verses 4–5

“The sound of a multitude in the mountains, like that of many peoples; the sound of the din of kingdoms, of nations gathered together. The Lord of hosts has commanded the army of war, coming from a distant land, from the end of heaven. The Lord and the vessels of his wrath, to destroy the whole land.”

The assault of the Medes and Persians is described: having gathered many auxiliary forces with them, and with the Lord preceding their army, they come to devastate Babylon and destroy the whole land—not because they devastated the entire world, but the whole land of Babylon and the Chaldeans. It is an idiom of Holy Scripture that “the whole land” signifies the whole land of the province about which the discourse is taking place. Some, not understanding this, apply it to the destruction of all lands.

[Col. 0156C] ### Verse 6

“Wail, because the day of the Lord is near; destruction will come from the Lord like a devastation.”

An apostrophe is addressed to the Chaldean people, so that they may make the evils about to come resound with weeping and not doubt the city’s destruction when the Lord the devastator arrives.

### Verses 7–8

“Therefore all hands will be slack, and every human heart will melt and be crushed. They will be seized by spasms and pains; they will suffer like a woman in labor. Each will be astonished at his neighbor; their faces will be faces of flame.”

This requires no exposition. It is indicated briefly that such a weight of evils will press upon them that the hands of Babylon’s warriors will be weakened, their hearts will languish with fear, and pain will torment their inward parts in the manner of women in labor. Each will seek help from the other, carrying a livid face surrounded by pallor. For it is natural that, when great evils threaten [Alternative: when overwhelming evils threaten], we think others wiser than ourselves.

### Verse 9

“Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel and full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the land a desert and to destroy its sinners from it.”

He calls it a cruel day, not because of its own character, [Note: [Col. 0157D] In the Vatican manuscript the words “but of the people” are not added.] but because of the people. For the one who slaughters the cruel is not cruel; rather, he appears cruel to those who suffer. A robber hanging on the gallows likewise considers the judge cruel. At the same time, the desolation and devastation of the Babylonian land are announced, and the reason for the devastation is explained [Alternative: stated]: all these things happen because of its inhabitants.

### Verse 10

“For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread their light; the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light.” 172

The Hebrew word *Chisile* [Note: [Col. 0157D] The Vatican manuscript has *Cksle*; an old manuscript of Drusius has *Chyile*. He himself would prefer to read *Chsile* or *Xyle*. See below, Jerome’s seventh book, where he expounds this same chapter and verse again.] (), the Seventy translated as Ὠρίων, “Orion.” The Hebrew teacher whom I used interpreted it as “Arcturus.” Following Symmachus generally, we have said “star” [Alternative: “stars.”]

The meaning is that, when the cruel day of the Lord arrives and his fury has devastated everything, through the magnitude of their fear mortals will find all things darkened; even the sun, moon, and shining stars will seem to deny their own brilliance. Hence heaven is also clothed in sackcloth: darkness covers everything, and, under the pressure of evils, people perceive nothing except what their minds are compelled to see.

### Verse 11

“And I will visit the evils of the inhabited world, and their iniquity upon the wicked; I will bring the pride of the faithless to rest, and I will humble the arrogance of the strong.”

From this passage and from the preceding one, where it is written that the sun is darkened at its rising, the moon is filled with darkness, the stars withdraw their radiance, and the iniquity of the whole inhabited world is visited, some think that the prophecy concerns not Babylon’s fall but the consummation of the world. Yet, in accordance with what precedes, the “inhabited world”—which in Hebrew is called *Thebel* () and in Greek οἰκουμένη—must be understood as Babylon.

For οἰκουμένη in our language means “inhabited,” and Babylon is called “inhabited” because of the immense multitude of its people: where previously there had been an innumerable crowd of peoples, there will be desolation and a dwelling place for beasts.

### Verse 12

“A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold.”

The reason why God visits the οἰκουμένη—that is, Babylon—with evils is evident: so that, once deprived of inhabitants, it may be reduced to desolation. Anything rare is called precious; thus above, according to the historical sense, we read that because of the scarcity of human beings seven women will seize one man, saying: “We will eat our own bread and wear our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us, and take away our reproach” (Isa. 4:1).

And in the Book of Samuel it is contained: “The word of the Lord was precious in those days” (1 Sam. 3:1), that is, rare. Note that in Hebrew *Paz* () is written for ordinary gold, and *Ophir* () for pure gold.

### Verse 13

“Because of this I will shake heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place, because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts and because of the day of his anger and fury.” 173

Either take this in the sense in which we explained above the stars, sun, moon, and inhabited world; or understand it ὑπερβολικῶς, “hyperbolically”: because of God’s indignation heaven becomes sorrowful, earth is moved, and all the elements acknowledge the anger of their Creator.

### Verse 14

“And it will be like a fleeing doe and like a sheep, and there will be no one to gather it.”

This signifies the Babylonian and Chaldean people: so fearful at the incursion of the Medes and Persians that they flee like a doe and a sheep before the roar of a lion and the howling of a wolf. Nor do they have a defender or prince whose command they may follow.

“Each will turn back to his own people, and each will flee to his own land.”

After Babylon has been captured and the hostile army has entered through its gates, all the auxiliaries and bands of different nations by whom the city had previously been defended will return to their own provinces.

[Col. 0158B] ### Verse 15

“Everyone who is found will be killed, and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword.”

Whoever does not flee will be struck by the sword. Whoever either wishes to resist or to return will be of no help to the captured city; rather, he himself will shed blood [Note: [Col. 0158D] The same Vatican manuscript reads “shed their blood.”]

### Verse 16

“Their infants will be dashed before their eyes; their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be violated.”

This is what David prophesies in the Spirit: “Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is he who repays you with the repayment you made to us. Blessed is he who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXIX, 8).

So great will be the city’s devastation and the victors’ savagery that not even innocent age will be spared; the wealth of all the houses will be plundered, and in the sight of their husbands the chastity of their wives will be violated.

[Col. 0158C] ### Verse 17

“Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver, nor desire gold.”

What was hidden has been made clear: the “strong ones” and “giants” are by no means to be understood as Angels and demons, but as the nation of the Medes. Their leader Darius the First destroyed the empire of the Babylonians after killing Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, who was the son of Evil-merodach [Alternative: Evilmarodach] (Dan. 5).

He describes the savagery of the Medes and Persians as so great that, in their eagerness to shed blood, they despise gold and silver [174] and regard offered riches as filth.

### Verse 18

“But with arrows they will kill the infants; they will not pity the fruit of the womb, and their eyes will not spare the children.”

The infants will be killed; their wounds will be no smaller than their bodies. The wombs of pregnant women will be cut open, the infants will be dashed out, and the cruel victor will kill the children pressed to their mothers’ breasts.

### Verse 19

“And that Babylon, glorious among kingdoms and renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them: it will not be inhabited forever, and it will not be rebuilt from generation to generation.”

We have heard of the Medes; we have heard of Babylon; we have heard of the city renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans. We do not wish to understand what actually was, and we seek to hear what was not. We say this not because we condemn the tropological understanding, but because spiritual interpretation ought to follow the order of history. Many, failing to understand this, wander through the Scriptures in a frenzied error.

Therefore, to the present day, the prophecy concerning Babylon is being fulfilled. Just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah, so this city, once overthrown, will not be inhabited forever. In its place the Persians made the famous cities of Seleucia and Ctesiphon.

### Verses 20–22

“Nor will the Arab pitch tents there; nor will shepherds rest there. But beasts will be there; their houses will be filled with dragons; ostriches will dwell there, and hairy creatures will dance there. And owls will answer in its buildings, and Sirens in its pleasure shrines.”

Babylon will be so devastated and deserted that it will not even be useful as pasture for herds and flocks. The Arab and the Saracen will not pitch tents there, [Col. 0159B] nor will shepherds, wearied by their labor, rest there after following their flocks. Rather, amid the walls and narrow spaces of the ancient ruins will dwell the *siim* (), which only the Seventy translated as “beasts”; others, wishing the names of kinds of demons or phantoms to be understood, retain the very name written among the Hebrews.

“And their houses will be filled,” as we have said, “with dragons”; Aquila translated this as “typhons,” while Symmachus [Note: [Col. 0159D] In Greek letters, ὠχείμ.] rendered *ohim* (), reproducing the Hebrew word itself. The Seventy and Theodotion, however, interpreted it as “cries” or “sounds.”

What follows, “The hairy creatures will dance there,” may mean incubi, satyrs, or certain wild men whom some call *Fatuos ficarios* [Note: [Col. 0159D] The printed books read *Faunos ficarios*, “fig Fauns”; but all our manuscripts retain *Fatuos ficarios*. Fauns and Fatuos are the same monsters, or wild men, who were thought to be gods of fields and forests. Among the Latins, Fauns are those whom the Greeks call satyrs, the sons of Saturn. See Pliny, book 12, chapter 1. They were called Fauns from *fari*, “to speak,” because tradition held that they were accustomed to speak in wild places. Incubi were also called Fauns and Satyrs, from *ineundo*, because they had intercourse indiscriminately with all animals. Consult Varro, book 6 of *On the Latin Language*. MARTIAN. [Col. 0160D] See what we have observed concerning the Life of Saint Paul, the first hermit, volume 2, page 7, note.] or understand as kinds of demons.

In place of “owls,” all manuscripts preserve the Hebrew word *Iim* (), which only the Seventy translated as “onocentaurs.” The Sirens are called *Thennim* (), which we will interpret either as demons, certain monsters, or, more precisely, large dragons [Note: [Col. 0160D] Previously it had been less correctly rendered “which we interpreted.”], which are crested and flying.

Through all these things signs of devastation and desolation are displayed: such will be the depopulation of the once most powerful city that, because of the multitude of demons and beasts, no shepherd—that is, no seeker of the desert—will dare to enter it.

We learned from a certain Elamite brother, who came out of those regions and now leads the monastic life at Jerusalem, that royal hunts take place in Babylon, and that beasts of every kind are confined by the circuit of its walls [Note: [Col. 0160D] We read only “so much,” instead of the previous *tamen*, “nevertheless.” On this matter, consult our Pliny, book 6, chapter 26; Strabo also, book 16, page 738; and finally Pausanias, in the *Arcadica*. Our Jerome has similar statements below, at the verse following in this chapter.]

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 1

“Its time is near to come, and its days will not be prolonged.”

He says that the time is imminent when it is to be captured by enemies. For after Jerusalem’s captivity, not much time intervened before it was devastated by the Medes and Persians.

“For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will make them rest upon their own soil.”

Zephaniah speaks more fully about this: “Praise, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, Israel; rejoice and exult with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem, because the Lord has removed your judgment and has turned away your enemies” (Zeph. 3:14–15).

He signifies the time when Cyrus, king of the Persians, permitted the captive people to return to Jerusalem. Read the Book of Ezra (Ezra 1), Haggai (Hag. 1), and Zechariah (Zech. 1), when, under Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, Ezra, and Nehemiah, the altar, the Temple, and the walls of the city were built.

### Verse 2

“And the foreigner will be joined to them and will cling to the house of Jacob; and the peoples will take them and bring them to their place. And the house of Israel will possess them on the land of the Lord as male and female servants; and they will take captive those who had captured them, and they will subject their exactors.”

We suppose that many people from different nations came to Jerusalem with the Jewish people, believing in the God of Israel and abandoning the idols of their errors. There is no doubt that they were brought back by letters from the king and received gifts and funds for the Temple.

Only this seems to constrain the interpretation: how Israel could possess its former conquerors in the land of the Lord and subject its exactors, having them as male and female slaves. Unless perhaps we understand the whole by synecdoche, from a part: they later enjoyed such great prosperity that they acquired households of male and female servants from the various surrounding nations as well.

It may also be understood of the time of Ahasuerus (Esth. 9; Judith 13), when, after Holofernes was killed, the hostile army was slaughtered by Israel [Col. 0160C]. That I cling to the letter and, like a serpent, eat dust is your choice, since you wished to hear only the historical interpretation.

### Verse 3

“And it will be on the day when the Lord gives you rest from your labor, your disturbance, and your hard servitude in which you formerly served [Alternative: which you formerly served]: you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say…”

The speech is directed to Israel: after returning to Jerusalem and shaking off the yoke of servitude, it will remember the former power of Nebuchadnezzar and the height of Babylon, and will lament him in a voice of pity, because he has come to such calamity that even his enemies regard him as worthy of compassion.

### Verses 4–7

“How the exactor has ceased! The tribute has come to rest! The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers who struck peoples in fury, subjecting nations to an incurable blow in anger, persecuting them cruelly. He has become quiet and has fallen silent; the whole earth has rejoiced and exulted.”

This is the voice of Israel mourning and expressing pity: how the one who was once the conqueror of the earth and who despoiled everything through tribute has been broken and reduced to nothing. He, I say, who was the staff of the wicked, whose royal scepter and rod furiously struck everyone, whose blow could not be endured, and who cruelly pursued even those who fled—how has he become quiet and been humbled, and how has the whole earth become still at his ruin, emitting only [Alternative: nevertheless emitting] the voice of jubilant joy?

### Verse 8

“The fir trees also rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon: ‘Since you have lain down, no one has come up to cut us down.’”

By the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon understand the rulers of the nations, who were cut down when Nebuchadnezzar struck. They too, bursting into a voice of joy, say: “Since you have been led down to the underworld, no one else has been found who could cut down the great and powerful.”

### Verse 9

“The underworld beneath you was disturbed to meet your arrival; it roused the giants for you. All the rulers of the earth rose from their thrones; all the rulers of the nations will answer and say to you…”

These words should be read emphatically and as a scene, not as something that actually happened, but as something that could have happened—unless perhaps we believe that the souls of the kings whom he had killed came to meet the Babylonian king and insult him. For it is a consolation in misfortunes when people see their enemies suffering the same things.

### Verses 10–11

“And you have been wounded as we were; you have become like us. Your pride has been brought down to the underworld. Your corpse has fallen [Alternative: will fall]; beneath you maggots will be spread, and worms will be your covering.”

The speech of the powerful and rulers of the earth, whom above he had called cedars and fir trees, is directed to the Babylonian king, established in the underworld. We no longer grieve that we were cut down, since you too have fallen beneath the same ax. All your power, and your pride raised to heaven, have been dragged down to earth. Will your corpse, then, also be sustained by maggots, and will a multitude of swarming worms cover it? Through human death you will feel the lowliness of the one who displayed God’s power in yourself.

### Verses 12–14

“How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, who used to rise at dawn! You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations. You who said in your heart: ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’”

For the sake of ease of understanding, we translated this as: “How you have fallen from heaven, morning star, who used to rise at dawn.” But in Hebrew, if we render the word literally, it reads: “How you have fallen from heaven, howl, son of dawn.” It is signified by other words as “morning star,” and he is told that he must weep and mourn who was once so glorious that he was compared with the splendor of the morning star.

“As,” he says, “the morning star, dispersing darkness, shines bright, ardent, and glowing, so your advance among the peoples and into public view seemed like that of a bright star. But you have fallen to the earth, wounded of the nations, you who spoke arrogantly: ‘I have attained such power that only heaven and the stars remain for me, so that the heights must lie beneath my feet.’”

Although the Jews wish heaven and the stars of God to be understood from what follows: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant,” that is, in the Temple where God’s laws have been established, “and on the sides of the north,” that is, in Jerusalem. For it is written: “The sides of the north are Mount Zion” (Ps. XLVII, 3).

Nor would it have been enough for his pride to desire heavenly things unless he had rushed into such madness as to claim for himself likeness to God.

### (Verse 15)

Nevertheless, you shall be brought down to the underworld, to the deepest part of the pit. He who had said in his pride, “I shall ascend into heaven; I shall be like the Most High,” is brought down not merely to the underworld but to the lowest underworld. This is what the depth of the pit signifies; for it we read in the Gospel “the outer darkness,” where there is “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Luke 13:28).

### (Verses 16–17)

Those who see you will bow toward you and gaze upon you—understand, saying: “Is this the man who disturbed the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities, who did not open the prison for his captives?” This is the voice of those who taunt and wonder at how the devastator of all has himself been devastated. But when he says, “He did not open the prison for his captives,” the magnitude of his cruelty and impiety is expressed: he even kept prisoners confined in prison. The wretched were not burdened by chains alone, unless the horror of darkness also enclosed them.

### (Verses 18–19)

All the kings of the nations, every one of them, slept in glory, each man in his own house. But you have been cast out of your tomb like a useless shoot, defiled and wrapped together with those who were slain by the sword and went down to the foundations of the pit. Like a rotting corpse, you shall have no fellowship, nor shall you share burial with them.

The Hebrews tell the following story:

[Note: And this story is indeed characteristic of that people, born to devise marvels. It is more plausible that, after Nebuchadnezzar had been restored to the kingdom, Evil-Merodach was his associate in the empire.]

Evil-Merodach, who had previously ruled for seven years while his father Nebuchadnezzar lived among the beasts, after his father had been restored to the kingdom, remained imprisoned with Jehoiachin, king of Judah, until his father’s death. When his father died and Evil-Merodach was again succeeding to the kingdom, he was not accepted by the nobles, who feared that the man said to be dead might still be alive. To establish the fact of his father’s death, he opened the tomb and dragged out his corpse with a hook and ropes.

The meaning is: “When all those whom you have killed have been buried, you alone shall lie unburied.”

Others interpret this passage in the following way: All souls in the underworld will receive some rest; you alone will be bound in the uttermost darkness. For you will be covered with the blood of all, and the blood of everyone will weigh upon you like a covering of the corruption of the dead.

Symmachus translated this passage as follows: “Even with those who are killed in war, you will not be deemed worthy to have a share in burial.”

For what we translated as “like a useless shoot,” the Hebrew reads **CHANESER NETHAB** (), and Aquila translated it “like defiled corruption.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “like corruption defiled.” See below, where Jerome discusses this same chapter again in the following book.]

**NESER** () properly denotes a shoot, which grows at the roots of trees and is cut away by farmers as useless. We can therefore understand it here as corruption and decay. At the same time, we learn that the underworld is beneath the earth, since Scripture says, “down to the foundations of the pit.”

### (Verse 20)

For you have destroyed your own land; you have slain your own people.

[Note: The nearby text was missing; we supply it from the manuscripts.]

According to the Seventy Translators, who read, “Because you have destroyed my land and slain my people,” there is no doubt about their meaning. Nebuchadnezzar destroyed and ruined the land of Judah and its people, Israel.

According to the Hebrew, however, the meaning is difficult: how did he destroy his own land and slay his own people? Unless perhaps it must be understood in this sense: those whom God had given you for correction, you utterly destroyed.

Or alternatively: the ancient kingdom of the Assyrians was completely destroyed because you became excessively proud and lifted your neck against God. If you had acted humbly and known your proper measure, the Assyrian and Babylonian kingdoms would have continued to rule to this day.

Or it may be understood in this way: you were so cruel toward foreigners that, in your madness, you also oppressed the peoples subject to you.

### (Verse 21)

It shall never again be called the seed of the wicked. Prepare his sons for slaughter because of the iniquity of their fathers. They shall not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities.

All histories agree that, after Belshazzar, Nebuchadnezzar’s grandson, was killed and Darius succeeded to the kingdom of the Chaldeans, no one thereafter from Nebuchadnezzar’s line ruled. Scripture therefore foretells that Babylon will come to such devastation that no one from the royal seed will remain, but that, because of the father’s impiety, the entire offspring will be destroyed.

For what we translated in the final part of the sentence as “nor fill the face of the world with cities,” the Hebrew has, instead of “cities,” **ARIM** (ערים), which we can also render “adversaries.” The meaning would then be: “No one from your seed who desires to restore the kingdom will be raised up as an adversary.”

According to the Seventy Translators, who read, “Evil seed, prepare your sons for slaughter because of your father’s sins,” I cannot determine what their meaning is.

### (Verses 22–23)

“And I will rise up against them,” says the Lord of hosts, “and I will destroy Babylon’s name, its remnant, its shoot, and its offspring,” says the Lord. “And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog and marshes of water; and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” says the Lord of hosts.

Herodotus and many others who wrote Greek histories report that Babylon was extremely powerful and lay on a square plain. From corner to corner of its walls it extended sixteen thousand paces; that is, altogether around its circumference, sixty-four thousand paces.

[Note: Victor reads “fifteen thousand”; that total gives sixty thousand around the whole circuit, or four hundred and eighty stadia.]

[Note: Herodotus reports this. I find this passage thoroughly corrupted in the editions of Erasmus and Marianus, who followed not Jerome’s manuscripts but Herodotus’ Greek words and their own conjectures. Relying on the authority of the manuscript codices, we have restored the true, Jeromean reading. The genuine reading is found when sixteen thousand paces from one corner of the wall to the other, together around the circuit of the square city, make sixty-four thousand paces. According to Herodotus, *Histories* 1.178, Babylon was square, “being square” (ἐούσης τετραγώνου). —Martianus.]

The citadel, that is, the Capitol of that city, was a tower built after the Flood. It is said to have been four thousand paces high, gradually narrowing from a broader base toward a tighter summit, so that the weight above might more easily be supported by the broader lower portions.

[Note: Against this, the Palatine codex reads not “in height” but “in width,” and not four thousand but only three thousand. The author of the book *Places from the Acts*, who records this entire passage, omits “in width or in height” altogether. Others cite a Jerome who is altogether inconsistent about the height, from the Eusebian *Chronicle*, where he says that the height was five thousand one hundred and seventy-four paces. Yet the truth cannot be established either from Herodotus in *Clio*, where he gives the length and breadth as a stadion, making the thickness and width of the stadion, or from Diodorus and Strabo, who disagree with one another.]

They describe there marble temples, golden statues, streets glittering with stones and gold, and many other things that seem almost unbelievable. We have recounted all this to show that, in the face of God’s anger, every power is dust and is compared with sparks and ashes.

If it were possible to enter the lands of the barbarians and see the final remains of so great a city, we would see a possession of the hedgehog and marshes of water, and would truly find fulfilled what is now sung in Isaiah’s words: “I will sweep it with the broom of destruction.” For, apart from the baked-brick walls, which are repeatedly restored after many years in order to enclose wild animals, the entire space within is desolate.

[Note: Recall what was noted above concerning the final verse of the preceding chapter.]

### (Verses 24–25)

The Lord of hosts swore, saying: “If it is not as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have planned in my mind, so shall it come to pass: I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and trample him on my mountains. His yoke shall be removed from them, and his burden shall be taken from their shoulders.”

He returns to the present—that is, to Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, who devastated Samaria and Judah and, except for Jerusalem, destroyed everything around it. He joins events far in the future to those that were near, so that the impending fear might be removed, since his hearers could say: “We are enduring a present siege, while he promises something that will come many ages later.”

The order of the prophecy is therefore this: although Babylon will be destroyed after many years and the entire stock of the Assyrian and Chaldean race will be utterly dispersed, yet, so that you will not fear the captivity that is near, the Lord swears—although he must be believed even without swearing—that his judgment will not be mistaken and that what he has conceived in his mind will not fail.

He speaks here according to human feeling, namely, that the one who cannot be deceived will not be deceived: “I will crush the Assyrian in my land,” he says, “and trample him on my mountains.” In a single night one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army were destroyed when the angel laid waste to them (2 Kings 19).

And from those who were besieged in Jerusalem his yoke shall be removed, as well as the harsh rule that threatened everyone and the burden beneath which they were crushed; it will instead be thrust back upon him. For when the king of the Assyrians fled to his own land, Hezekiah went out free with the remnant of his people.

### (Verses 26–27)

This is the plan that I have conceived concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed it, and who can weaken it? His hand is stretched out, and who can turn it back?

Some think that this passage contains a general prophecy against the whole world, and that the devastation of Babylon and the Assyrian city is a type of the consummation of the world. We do not at all contradict them, provided that we understand “the whole earth” here to mean specifically the land of the Assyrians, and that “all the nations” indicates the peoples allied with the Assyrian king.

Whatever the Lord has decreed cannot be prevented by anyone’s power. No one will be able to restrain his hand when it is stretched out and ready to strike.

### (Verse 28)

In the year when King Ahaz died, this oracle came to pass.

We read that four kings of Judah were set over the people under the title of the prophet: Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Each succeeded the preceding one in order and by descent. We have already read of the death of Uzziah, when Isaiah says: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne.”

From this we understand that both the vision of the Lord sitting and the matters commanded to the prophet, up to the place where it is written (chapter 6), “Like a terebinth and like an oak which spreads out its branches: its shoot will be a holy seed,” were prophesied under King Jotham (ibid., chapter 7).

Ahaz, the third king, succeeded: he was the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah. Under him Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, came up to Jerusalem to fight against it, along with the other events that Scripture records.

Thus, from the reign of Ahaz up to the present passage, which we are now attempting to explain, we recognize that everything placed between these sections was prophesied. After Ahaz died, the fourth—that is, the final—king, Hezekiah, succeeded him, and under Hezekiah the book is woven together all the way to its end.

### (Verse 29)

Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of your striker has been broken. For from the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth, and its offspring will devour the flying creature.

What we are saying is natural: when the king of an enemy nation dies, enemies always rejoice, awaiting civil wars, seditions, and ignorance of how to rule amid the new circumstances.

After the death of the sinful Ahaz, who had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and had been joined to them by kinship, we understand that the nearby Philistines rejoiced and mocked Israel, since, after losing a mature king, they were subject to the young Hezekiah.

As we said above, “Philistines” signifies Palestinians, whom the Vulgate edition calls “foreigners”; yet this is not the name of one nation alone, but of all foreign peoples.

“Do not rejoice,” he says, “Philistia; do not mock my people because the rod of your striker, Ahaz, has been broken; because the staff that was accustomed to strike you appears to have been shattered by death; because the serpent has been killed. For in his place a more harmful one will be born, Hezekiah, the basilisk”—which the Greeks call *basiliskos*—“who will destroy you by his gaze and kill you with the breath of his mouth.”

For just as no bird can pass unharmed before the gaze of a basilisk but, even if it is far away, is swallowed by its mouth, so you also will perish entirely at the sight of King Hezekiah.

He has fittingly preserved the metaphor: since he had named a serpent and a basilisk, he says that birds are devoured by its mouth and breath.

But that no king of Judah struck the Philistines as Hezekiah devastated them, hear the Book of Kings: “He himself struck the Philistines as far as Gaza and its territory, from the tower of the watchmen to the fortified cities” (2 Kings 18:8).

For what we translated as “devouring the flying creature,” the Hebrew reads **SARAPH MOPHETH** (), which can be translated “flying serpent.” The meaning would then be: “From the root of the serpent a basilisk will be born, and its offspring—that is, the basilisk’s offspring—will be a flying serpent,” so that you understand a flying dragon.

### (Verse 30)

The firstborn of the poor will be pastured, and the poor will rest in security.

When the basilisk has struck you and the flying dragon has devastated your borders, you will no longer lie in wait for Judah or terrify my poor people by your deceit. Rather, pressed by your own troubles, you will weep over your calamity.

But the humble and the poor, who trusted not in riches and power but in my name, will rest in secure peace and fear no attack from any enemy.

And I will cause your root to perish in famine, and I will kill your remnant.

He speaks entirely through figures. The meaning is that, while God’s people rest securely, the root of the Philistines will dry up and all their remnants will be consumed.

### (Verse 31)

Howl, O gate; cry out, O city; all Philistia has been laid low. For smoke will come from the north, and no one will escape its ranks.

[Note: The words “cry out, O city” are absent from the Vatican manuscript.]

He calls the gate by the name of those who are in the gate, and the city by the name of its inhabitants. He also addresses the cities of the Palestinians, telling them that they must wail and mourn when Sennacherib comes, devastating everything like a torrent.

Under King Hezekiah the Assyrian came and, among the other nations, devastated the Philistines.

To them Jeremiah speaks: “Behold, waters will rise from the north and will be like an inundating torrent; they will cover the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants” (Jeremiah 47:2).

The Assyrian came from the north, and those proceeding from his burning force subjugated Nineveh and the other nations.

At the time when these words were being sung, smoke was rising into the heights—that is, rumor was spreading among the peoples through all the nations in succession—that the Phoenicians and the Palestinians too were to be devastated.

### (Verse 32)

What will be answered to the messengers of the nation? Because the Lord founded Zion, and in it the poor of his people will hope.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the Vulgate, reads “What will be answered?”]

Since he had said, “There is no one who will escape its ranks,” it seemed that Judah too had been included in the general sentence.

[Note: We have restored from the same manuscript “Judah and included” in place of “the Jews and included.”]

“If,” he says, “the angels of the Assyrian nation ask why Judah alone escaped, answer them that the Lord founded Zion and that he protected the humble people by his power.”

For “angels” (), the Seventy translated “kings” (), having been misled by the error of a single letter, **aleph**.

## Chapter 15

### (Verse 1)

The oracle of Moab: Because Ar was devastated in the night, Moab fell silent; because the wall was devastated in the night, Moab fell silent.

It is enough to have spoken once about “oracle” and “burden.” I merely offer this brief reminder: a burden is always followed by gloomy events, whereas a vision is either immediately joyful or joyful at the end, after sorrows.

Moab is a province of the Arabs, in which Balak son of Beor lived (Numbers 22). He hired the diviner Balaam from Mesopotamia to curse Israel, and there the people were initiated into the worship of Beelphegor (ibid., 25).

Its capital is the city of **AR** (אר), which today, formed from Hebrew and Greek, is called Areopolis—not, as many think, because it is the city of **Ares** (Ἄρης), that is, Mars.

But **Ar** is interpreted as **ἀντίδικος**, “adversary.”

Jeremiah testifies to how powerful it was (Jeremiah 48:2, 7 and following), saying: “There is no longer rejoicing in Moab.” And again: “You trusted in your fortifications and in your treasures.” And again: “Moab was fertile from its youth and rested upon its dregs; it was not poured from vessel to vessel, and it did not go into exile. Therefore its taste remained in it, and its odor was not changed.”

And elsewhere: “How the strong rod, the glorious staff, has been broken!” And shortly afterward: “We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud. I know his loftiness, his arrogance, his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart,” says the Lord, “and his boasting.”

Therefore, just as the prophet foretold concerning Babylon and the Philistines, because they had oppressed the people of Judah, so now the devastation of the Moabites—that is, of Arabia—is foretold by the Assyrians and Babylonians.

They were devastated by both nations: when Sennacherib led Israel into captivity and when Nebuchadnezzar overthrew Jerusalem (2 Kings 17 and 25).

Moab had mocked Ephraim and Judah before each of the two enemies, as Jeremiah says: “Moab will clap his hand over his vomit, and he himself will become an object of derision. For Israel was an object of derision to you, as though you had found him among thieves” (Jeremiah 68:26–27). Therefore, because of your words, which you spoke against him, you will be led into captivity.

But when he says, “Ar was devastated in the night; Moab fell silent,” this is an appropriate beginning to the denunciation: he who was conceived from his father’s incest at night would be devastated in darkness.

Unless perhaps we understand “night” as the magnitude of terror. Since it trusted in its walls, we should believe that it was overcome by ambushes and underground passages.

I heard an inhabitant of Areopolis—and the whole city bears witness to it—that, during a great earthquake in my childhood, when the seas crossed the shores of the entire world, the walls of this city collapsed that same night.

[Note: “When the whole…” This seems to have occurred, according to Ammianus, under the consulship of Valentinian and Valens, in the year of the Lord 365. It has commonly been believed that the passage refers to the famous earthquake felt throughout the world, which Ammianus Marcellinus and other historians of that period report as occurring under the first consulship of Valentinian with his brother Valens, that is, in the year of the Lord 365. But since Jerome says that he was then a child, and since, according to the Pythagorean method of reckoning, that age would amount to at most fifteen years, it would be necessary to place Jerome’s birth after the year 350; this is entirely incompatible with the other evidence concerning his life. It is therefore more plausible that another earthquake is being indicated, one that Jerome himself records in his *Chronicle* under the year 344, when many cities of the East collapsed in a terrible earthquake.]

### (Verse 2)

The house has gone up, and Dibon has gone up to the high places in mourning. Moab will howl over Nebo and over Medeba.

Do not be annoyed that I proceed by way of history; you yourself wished me to do this.

The royal house and the city of Dibon are understood to have gone up to the idols placed in high places. Over Nebo and Medeba, noble cities, the whole province will howl.

In Nebo the idol Chemosh had been consecrated, which is also called Beelphegor by another name.

[Note: On the contrary, Nebo appears to be not the name of a city but the name of a Moabite idol. This is established by Isaiah 46:1 itself: “Bel is broken; Nebo is crushed; their images have become beasts and cattle.” Nor is the view acceptable that some hold, namely, that the god Nebo could have been named after the city. The Seventy call this god Dagon.]

Every head of his people will be bald; every beard will be shaved.

Among the ancients, shaving the beard and head was a sign of mourning. Through these actions, therefore, the magnitude of the grief is shown, as Jeremiah likewise cries out against Moab: “Every head is bald, and every beard is shaved; on all hands there is cutting, and sackcloth upon every back” (Jeremiah 48:37).

### (Verse 3)

In its crossroads they gird themselves with sackcloth. Upon its roofs and in its streets every wail will descend into weeping.

These will not be private tears; public lamentations will echo public mourning. Neither matrons nor virgins, neither the tender age of children nor the faltering steps of the old, will remain within their houses. Extreme captivity will recognize neither modesty nor weakness.

### (Verse 4)

Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out.

These are the names of cities in the Moabite province. Heshbon was once the city of the king of the Amorites. Concerning it Jeremiah says: “A fire has gone forth from Heshbon, and a flame from the midst of Sihon.”

Heshbon is interpreted as “thought”; therefore Jeremiah, alluding to the name, says concerning Heshbon, “They devised evil” (Jeremiah 45).

Their cry has been heard as far as Jahaz.

The city of Jahaz—or Jasa—stands over the Dead Sea, where the territory of the Moabites ends. This indicates that the wailing of the province will resound as far as its outermost boundaries.

Hence Jeremiah also says: “From the cry of Heshbon, as far as Elealeh and Jahaz, they have uttered their voice” (Jeremiah 48:34).

For this reason the armed men of Moab will howl; its soul will howl for itself.

The Hebrew word **ELUSE** (אלוס), for which Aquila translated **ἐξώμους**, “with bare shoulders,” and Symmachus “girded,” some think refers not to men but to the name of a city, which is today called Elusa and is situated in the regions of Moab.

We can also say that the entire strength of the warriors has fallen and that the whole land has resounded with mutual weeping.

But if **Eluse**, as Aquila wished, is understood to mean “with bare shoulders,” the following meaning is suggested to us: everyone uncovered his breast in order to mourn.

### (Verse 5)

My heart will cry out for Moab.

The prophet speaks with the affection of one who grieves, either because even enemies are creatures of God and so many evils have overtaken them, or because they are to be oppressed by such great calamities that they will become objects of pity even to their enemies.

Jeremiah says the same: “Therefore my heart will resound for Moab like a flute.”

His bars will reach as far as Zoar, a three-year-old heifer.

And Jeremiah says: “From Zoar,” he says, “as far as Horonaim, a three-year-old heifer.”

[Note: And in the books of the *Hebrew Questions*, etc. Consult the *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, column 306. —Martianus. See also the *Questions on Genesis*, vol. III, pp. 326 and 334, and our notes there, as well as the *Books of Hebrew Names*. In Paula’s epitaph Jerome says: “Zoar, a three-year-old heifer, which was formerly called Bela and in the Syriac language was translated Zoara, that is, little,” and so forth.]

We have spoken of this in the books of the *Hebrew Questions*, and we now briefly note that it is the fifth city after Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim, which was preserved as a small city at Lot’s prayers.

It is called Bela, that is, “swallowed up,” the Hebrews reporting that it was overthrown in a third earthquake. It is the city now called Zoara—or Zora—in Syriac, and Segor in Hebrew; in both languages the name means “little.”

We can understand the “three-year-old heifer” as referring to full maturity. For just as the thirtieth year is the strongest in human beings, so the third year is strongest in cattle and beasts of burden.

Understand “bars” as boundaries and strength, because Zoar is situated on the borders of the Moabites, separating their land from the land of the Philistines.

For by the ascent of Luhith he will ascend weeping.

And Jeremiah says: “By the ascent of Luhith, weeping, he will ascend in tears.”

We understand this to be a slope along the road that leads toward the Assyrians, and through it captivity is signified.

And on the road to Horonaim they will raise a cry of destruction.

Again Jeremiah says: “The voice of the cry of Horonaim: devastation and great destruction.”

It would be tedious to speak of each place individually, since it is clear that these are names either of cities in Moab or of places abandoned by those who are migrating.

### (Verse 6)

For the waters of Nimrim will be desolate.

This settlement is beside the Dead Sea, whose waters are salty and therefore barren. Whether the prophet alluded to the name, or whether this happened because what had not existed before came to pass after the devastation, the result was that even the waters were turned bitter.

For the grass has withered; the shoot has failed; all verdure has perished.

The whole grass did not wither, as some think, because the waters of Nimrim are naturally barren; Scripture speaks metaphorically.

The meaning is that throughout Moab the waters of Nimrim will be salty and bitter. Just as no grass sprouts there, so drought will overtake the whole province—from Zoar to Horonaim, from one boundary to the other.

Jeremiah says the same: “The waters of Nimrim will be very bad” (Jeremiah 48:34).

### (Verse 7)

According to the greatness of the work, and their visitation, they will lead them to the torrent of the willows.

For “willows,” the Hebrew reads **ARABIM** (), which can mean “Arabs”; it may also be read **ORBIM** (), that is, “a village situated in their borders.” Many think that its inhabitants were those said to have provided Elijah with food on Mount Horeb. Because of the ambiguity, the name is translated both as “ravens” and as “the West,” as well as for level and open places.

[Note: Learned men have recently attempted to revive the view that the inhabitants of Mount Horeb, rather than ravens, provided Elijah with food. But that interpretation is contrary not only to the most ancient tradition but also to the obvious and natural sense of Scripture, which consistently uses the word “ravens” for birds, not human beings. Moreover, Elijah was fed not on Mount Horeb but beside the torrent of Cherith; and the Arabs cannot in any way, as Jerome seems to suppose, be understood either as those ravens or as inhabitants of Horeb.]

The meaning is: the visitation will correspond to the magnitude of the sickness. Understand “visitation” here not as a remedy but as a plague. “I will visit their iniquities with a rod,” he says, “and their sins with scourges” (Psalm 88:33).

By “the torrent of the willows,” understand the rivers of Babylonia, concerning which David says, “Upon the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Psalm 136:2); or the valley of Arabia, through which one travels toward the Assyrians.

### (Verse 8)

For the cry will surround the territory of Moab; its wailing will reach as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim.

Jeremiah writes nearly all the same things. These are cities and places of the Moabites in which the cry and lamentation of the captive people are described.

### (Verse 9)

For the waters of Dibon are filled with blood.

Where previously there had been luxury because of irrigated fields and springs flowing continually, there streams of blood will flow because of the multitude of the slain.

For I will place further afflictions upon Dibon: a lion upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “Dimon,” a reading that Jerome discusses immediately below.]

Let no one think this is a fault of the writer and, in wishing to correct an error, create one. The same city is written with both the letter **M** and the letter **B**. From these forms, they interpret **Dimon** as “silence” and **Dibon** as “flowing.”

Because of the streams that flow silently, this little town is still indifferently called both Dimon and Dibon.

But when he says, “I will place additions upon Dibon,” and the question seems to arise what these additions might be, he explains it in the following verse, saying: “A lion upon those who have fled from Moab, and upon the remnant of the land,” so that even those who have escaped by flight may be consumed by wild beasts.

Although, metaphorically, we can understand the lion as the king of the enemy, so that no one can escape his power, like a roar.

## Chapter 16

### (Verse 1)

Send forth the lamb, the ruler of the land, from the rock of the desert to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.

What we interpret here is not history but prophecy.

Every prophecy is wrapped in riddles and expressed in broken statements. While speaking about one subject, it passes to another, lest, if Scripture preserved a continuous order, it be not prophecy but narrative.

The meaning is: O Moab, against whom the fiercest lion is about to rage, and from whom not even a remnant will be able to escape, receive this consolation: from you will go forth the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world and rules over the earth.

“From the rock of the desert” means from Ruth, who, widowed by her husband’s death, bore Obed to Boaz; Obed begot Jesse, Jesse David, and David Christ.

We may understand “the mountain of the daughter of Zion” either as the city of Jerusalem itself or, according to the sacred interpretation, as the Church, established upon the summit of the virtues.

### (Verse 2)

And it will be as a fleeing bird, and as young birds flying away from the nest; so will the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon.

He returns to the order with which he began.

“When I set,” he says, “against those who have fled from Moab and the remnant of the land the fiercest lion, which will break their limbs and bones, then they will fly away in terror. All the daughters—that is, the villages and cities—of the province of Moab will migrate at the crossing of the Arnon, which is the boundary of the Amorites and the Moabites.”

By using “crossing” here also, he signifies captivity.

### (Verses 3–4)

Form a plan; convene a council. Make your shadow like night at midday; hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers.

Let my refugees dwell with you. Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator, for the dust has come to an end; the miserable one has been consumed; he who trampled the earth has failed.

For “miserable one,” the Hebrew reads **SOD** (סד), which can also be understood as “devastator.”

He addresses Moab, urging it to find a plan of salvation and, after gathering the elders, to convene a saving council.

“Do you wish,” he says, “to be saved and to obtain God’s mercy? In broad daylight and in the open flight of my people, be like night and shadow: receive the fugitives and do not betray the wanderers.”

He immediately explains why he has said this: “Let my refugees dwell with you.”

When Jerusalem has been devastated, and all Judea bordering the Moabites has been laid waste, my people will migrate to you. Therefore be their hiding place. Do not fear the attack of the devastator, because he will pass quickly like dust; the plunderer of the whole earth, who trampled it and subjected it beneath his feet, will perish when the wind blows.

Some wrongly interpret this passage of the Antichrist, thinking that at that time the saints will cross over to the Arabs because of the city of Jerusalem’s proximity, and that they are now being instructed not to betray the fugitives who come to them.

### (Verse 5)

And a throne will be prepared in mercy, and he will sit upon it in truth, in the tent of David, judging and seeking judgment and swiftly rendering what is just.

[Note: Martianus read “he will sit upon him.”]

The Hebrews interpret this passage as follows: after the Assyrian has been put to flight, Hezekiah, a righteous man, will reign over Judah, retain the throne of David, and judge the people of God subject to him in truth.

Others understand it of Christ. When the dust of the Antichrist has come to an end and the devastator who trampled the whole earth has been removed, Christ the king will come. He will sit in the tent of David and, on the day of judgment, repay all according to their works.

There is no doubt that this chapter prophesies about Christ. Yet we can understand it also of his first coming and demonstrate it in the tent of the Church, since throughout the land of Moab the rising trophies of the Churches bear witness to Christ’s rule.

### (Verses 6–7)

We have heard of the pride of Moab; he is exceedingly proud—his pride, arrogance, and indignation exceed his strength.

Therefore Moab will howl to Moab; all of it will howl. Speak of his wounds to those who rejoice over walls of baked brick.

He again returns to the present and rebukes Moab for its pride: it had become much more exalted than its strength required. Because of this pride, Moab will howl to Moab—that is, the people to the city, or the capital to the province—and the whole land will resound with wailing over walls of baked brick.

Jeremiah likewise says: “Therefore I will howl over Moab, and I will cry out to all Moab, over the men lamenting at the wall of baked brick” (Jeremiah 48:31).

Through these words he shows both the power of its former prosperity and the wounds of its sudden overthrow.

### (Verse 8)

For the suburbs of Heshbon are desolate; the vineyard of Sibmah.

[Note: In his own version he prefers “and the vineyard of Sibmah.”]

There are scarcely five hundred paces between Heshbon and Sibmah. Through the metaphor of a vineyard, he signifies the devastation of the entire province.

The lords of the nations have cut down its branches.

He preserves the metaphor with which he began, showing that the kings of the nations who devastated Moab have ravaged all its villages and fortified settlements.

As far as Jazer they have reached; they have wandered in the desert; its branches have been left; they have crossed the sea.

Understand “branches” as its people and fugitives, and understand the crossing of the sea as captivity into Babylon, about which we shall read later: “The oracle of the desert of the sea.”

### (Verse 9)

“Because of this I shall weep in the weeping of Jazer, the vineyard of Sibmah; I shall drench you with my tears, Heshbon and Elealeh.” This is the voice of the lamenting Prophet, bearing witness to the magnitude of the devastation by the magnitude of his tears. He weeps for Jazer, Sibmah, Heshbon, and Elealeh, once exceedingly strong cities, cut down by the Assyrian.

“For upon your vintage and upon your harvest the voice of the treaders has broken in.” Understand by the treaders of grapes and those gathering the joy of the vintage the armies of the enemy, and understand that, at the very season of rejoicing, the time of captivity had arrived.

### (Verse 10)

“And joy and gladness shall be taken away from Carmel.” It is an idiom of Scripture always to compare Mount Carmel, a rich and wooded mountain overlooking Ptolemais, where Elijah prayed, with fertility and abundance. Accordingly, this signifies that all joy and fertility will be taken away from cities once exceedingly fruitful.

“And in the vineyards he shall not rejoice, nor shall he shout for joy.” The previous vintner is understood—that is, the cultivator of the province of Moab. Accordingly, he immediately adds:

“He who was accustomed to tread the winepress shall not tread wine in the winepress; I have taken away the cry of the treaders.” The vintner will by no means sing a joyful vintage song [Note: A song of sailors and vintners.], but everywhere there will arise the devastation of the enemy and the cry of the victorious.

### (Verse 11)

“Therefore my belly shall sound like a lyre for Moab, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick.” So that no one might think that the Prophet’s lament was uttered in exultation, by which he would rejoice that the enemies of the people of Israel had been taken captive, he says that, out of affection and from the innermost pain of his heart, he mourns the overthrow of a once most powerful city.

### (Verse 12)

“And it shall be, when it appears that Moab has labored upon his high places, that he will enter his sanctuaries to supplicate, but he will not prevail.” The ultimate misery is not to have assistance even in those whom one has always revered. “Abandoned,” he says, “by your strength and with all your defenders slain, you will go to the idols and revere the shrines, but you will find no help in them; devastation will come upon them together with you.”

### (Verse 13)

“This is the word which the Lord spoke concerning Moab from that time.” From what time, do you suppose? Clearly, from the time when Moab was created. And the Lord said: “The Moabites and Ammonites shall not enter the assembly of God” (Deut. 23:3). Or let us understand “from that time” as referring to ancient times, when long ago this decree was established by the divine judgment—not that God’s foreknowledge caused the devastation, but that the future devastation was already known to the majesty of God.

### (Verse 14)

“And now the Lord has spoken, saying: Within three years, like the years of a hired laborer, the glory of Moab shall be taken away, despite all its great population, and a small and insignificant remnant shall be left, by no means a multitude.” As we said above, this prophecy is directed against the Moabites after the death of Ahaz, during the reign of Hezekiah, under whom the ten tribes were led into captivity by Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians. Therefore, just as a hired laborer waits only for sunset and looks forward, through days and nights, to the end of his work so that he may receive his appointed wage, so after three years Moab too, when the Assyrian arrives, will be destroyed, and scarcely a few will be left in the land to inhabit the ruined cities and cultivate the deserted fields.

It may also be prophesied of the Babylonian captivity: after Jerusalem had been captured and three years had passed, Moab was to be devastated by the Chaldeans—or because no rest was to be granted to them during the period of three years.

## Chapter XVII

### (Verse 1)

“The burden of Damascus. Behold, Damascus shall cease to be a city, and it shall be like a heap of stones in a ruin. The cities of Aroer shall be abandoned to flocks; they shall lie down there, and there shall be no one to frighten them away. Help shall cease from Ephraim, and kingship from Damascus, and the remnant of Syria shall be like the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts.”

After Babylon, the Philistines, and Moab, the discourse turns to Damascus—that is, to Aram [Note: These are the words of Eusebius: “For at that time Damascus alone ruled over all Syria, before the famous cities of our own age had arisen in Syria—Antioch, that is, and the others.” Jerome acts almost as his translator.]. Damascus itself had once been a royal city and held supremacy throughout Syria. Antioch, Laodicea, and Apamea had not yet flourished; we know that these cities were enlarged after Alexander and the Macedonian empire.

Since Damascus had always furnished assistance to the ten tribes against Judah, as the history of Kings and Chronicles relates, Isaiah also indicates that devastation by the Assyrians was approaching for them. The Assyrian king says: “I have captured Arabia, Damascus, and Samaria. Just as I captured them and all the kingdoms, so I shall capture you also.” And in the Book of Kings we read: “The king of Assyria went up against Damascus, captured it, and transferred it to Cyrene” (4 Kings 16:9). He also killed Rezin, who was king of Damascus. All this occurred while Hezekiah was reigning in Jerusalem.

“Behold,” he says, “Damascus shall cease to be a city; captivity is already near; the Assyrian has already set his army in motion.” “And it shall be like a heap of stones in a ruin,” so that only walls and traces of its former power would be displayed amid the magnitude of the ruins.

“The cities of Aroer shall be abandoned to flocks.” Aroer is interpreted as *tamarisk*, a tree that grows especially in the wilderness and in salty soil; hence devastation is indicated. “They shall lie down there”—flocks are understood—“and there shall be no one to frighten them away.” Such will be the solitude that no ambusher need be feared.

“And help shall cease from Ephraim”: the ten tribes will no longer have assistance there against Judah. “And kingship from Damascus”—the verb “shall cease” is understood by *zeugma* [ἀπὸ κοινοῦ] (from the shared or common construction). When he says that kingship will cease and that it will rest, he does not signify perpetual devastation, but removes for the present the power by which Damascus had previously ruled throughout Syria.
