“And the remnant of Syria shall be like the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts.” “Just as,” he says, “the ten tribes were destroyed when the Assyrian ravaged them, and all their glory was led into captivity, so the few who remain in Damascus will be changed and will possess the glory of the allied nation.” Understand “glory” as spoken ironically, in place of disgrace. All this will happen because the Lord has spoken, and his words cannot be rendered void.

Some think that this prophecy is the same as the one we read in Jeremiah: “Damascus has been undone; it has turned to flight; trembling has seized her; anguish and pains have taken hold of her like a woman in labor” (Jer. 49:24, 27). And again: “I shall kindle a fire upon the wall of Damascus, and it shall devour the walls of Ben-hadad.”

But it must be understood that Jeremiah describes the Babylonian captivity of Damascus, that is, of the few whom the Assyrian king had left there. Isaiah, however, announces the captivity by the Assyrians, which was already near. Others believe that the Roman captivity is being foretold, since the people of the Jews too were captured, and Damascus, over which Aretas ruled, endured a similar servitude. Thus everything written above it may be transferred to the time of Christ and to the mysteries of the Apostles.

### (Verse 4)

“And it shall be on that day: the glory of Jacob shall be weakened, and his fat flesh shall wither.” “When,” he says, “Damascus has been captured and has ceased to be a city, and a glory such as crowned Israel—that is, the ten tribes—has crowned it, then all Jacob’s protection, richest flesh, and refuge will wither.” For he will no longer have allies with whom he may devastate Jerusalem.

Above we read that Rezin, king of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up against Jerusalem to fight against it, and that the house of David was told: “Syria has rested upon Ephraim.” Concerning them the Prophet speaks to Ahaz: “Do not fear, and let your heart not be afraid because of these two tails of smoking firebrands, in the anger of the fury of Rezin king of Syria and the son of Remaliah, because Syria has plotted evil against you, Ephraim and the son of Remaliah.”

### (Verses 5–6)

“And it shall be like one gathering what remains in the harvest, and his arm shall gather ears of grain; and it shall be like one seeking ears of grain in the valley of Rephaim. And what remains in it shall be like a cluster of grapes, and like the shaking of an olive tree: two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five fruits at its highest branches, says the Lord God of Israel.”

Those who understand the present devastation of Damascus as occurring under Roman rule insist that these things signify the Apostles: just as a few ears of grain and olives ordinarily remain in a field or on trees, so the remnant of Israel would be saved—especially because what follows says: “On that day a man shall incline toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel,” that is, toward Christ.

They interpret the two, three, four, and five olives as fourteen Apostles: the twelve who were chosen, together with James, who is called the brother of the Lord [Note: This is Eusebius’s view, which he himself derived from Origen. Jerome was so far from agreeing with it—as Montfaucon thought in his notes on this passage of Eusebius—that he reports it here under the name of others and had already rejected it long before in his book against Helvidius. Eusebius’s words are: “The others besides these three [namely Peter, James, and John, whom he mentioned above] are four and five; and if you make the four and the five, they will make fourteen in all. Of these, you may say that twelve are the first Apostles; and Paul, himself also a called Apostle, was no less virtuous than they, as was James, who became the brother of the Lord, etc.” Jerome wished to offer this material to Latin ears solely in his capacity as commentator.], and Paul the Apostle, the chosen vessel (Acts 7).

Those who think that these things were fulfilled in the time of the Assyrians want it understood that Damascus was not completely destroyed during the Assyrian captivity. Some inhabitants were transferred to Cyrene, while another portion of those cultivating the land was left behind; this portion too was later destroyed when the Babylonian ravaged the city. Then, under the Macedonians and the Ptolemies [Note: Drusius, on the basis of his old manuscript, wishes *Ptolemaeis* to be read instead of *Tholomaeis*, as has also been noted by us elsewhere in the customary spelling of the ancients. See the Book of Names, under the name Bartholomew.], it was rebuilt again. At the coming of Christ it was indeed a city, but it no longer possessed the power it had formerly enjoyed.

The meaning is therefore this: so few will remain in Damascus as the few ears of grain that usually remain after the reapers, which the poor commonly gather in the broad and powerful valley of Rephaim; or as the few olives on an olive tree that have escaped the diligence of the gatherer.

### (Verses 7–8)

“On that day a man shall incline toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel. He shall not incline toward the altars that his hands have made, nor toward what his fingers have fashioned; he shall not look to the sacred groves and shrines.”

They think that this was fulfilled in the time of Christ, when, after the destruction of the kingdom of Damascus, the everlasting reign of the Savior succeeded, and the error of idolatry was diminished. The intention of the interpreters is pious, but it does not preserve the order of the historical account.

We, however, say that when Damascus had been overthrown and the ten tribes had been led away among the Assyrians, the remnant of the tribes that belonged to Israel, responding to the letters of Hezekiah, turned to the worship of God and came to the temple of Jerusalem, as the history of Chronicles relates (2 Chron. 3). Therefore, when Damascus had been destroyed, people would turn to their Maker—that is, to the one who created them—and their eyes would look not toward the idols they had made in Bethel and Dan, but toward God, while despising the shrines and altars their fingers had fashioned.

### (Verse 9)

“On that day his fortified cities shall be abandoned like plowed fields and the crops that were abandoned before the children of Israel, and it shall be desolate.”

This is not spoken against Damascus, but against the ten tribes called Israel [Note: See Procopius, *On the Vandals*, book II, ch. 10.]. Just as, at the arrival of the people of God from Egypt, all the nations inhabiting the promised land, suddenly terrified, abandoned their plows, their heaps of grain, and their unfinished work, seeking safety with their feet, so the land of Israel would also remain desolate for a long time.

Hence I am astonished that Aquila wished to interpret “plows” and “heaps of grain” as “a potsherd” and “Emir”; Symmachus, as “forest” and “Amir”; and the Septuagint, as “Amorites” and “Hivites.” Only Theodotion retained the Hebrew word, *ARS ET EMIR*. Among them it is read more accurately as *HORES* () and *AMIR* (), that is, “plowshares” and “heaps of grain.”

### (Verse 10)

“Because you have forgotten the God of your salvation, and you have not remembered the mighty helper who supports you.” “You will suffer these things,” he says, “O Israel, because you abandoned the God your Savior, who delivered you from Egypt and subjected hostile nations to you; and you did not remember your helper.”

“Therefore you shall plant a faithful planting, and you shall sow a foreign shoot.” This should be read more precisely and ironically. “Because,” he says, “you have forgotten the God of your salvation, and you have not remembered your mighty helper, will you therefore plant a faithful planting, rather than sowing a foreign shoot that the enemy will seize?” Or certainly understand it this way: “You planted my sons, who were begotten from the stock of my people, in the land for this reason: that you might make them foreign and utterly wicked.”

### (Verse 11)

“On the day of your planting your vine shall become a wild grapevine, and in the morning your seed shall blossom. The harvest has been taken away on the day of inheritance, and he will grieve”—or, according to another reading, “you will grieve”—“bitterly.”

“You will receive,” he says, “such fruits from your works: your vine of Sorek will degenerate into a wild grape; your seed will promise hope in its young growth, but when maturity arrives, it will be harvested by another. Then you will grieve bitterly, when you have lost what you had hoped for and had almost already grasped.”

### (Verses 12–14)

“Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of a roaring sea; and the tumult of nations, like the sound of many waters. The peoples shall roar like the roaring of overflowing waters; he shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far away. He shall be carried off like dust from the mountains before the wind and like a whirlwind before a storm. At evening—behold, terror in the morning—and it shall not remain. This is the portion of those who devastated us, and the lot of those who plundered us.”

Those who believe that the preceding captivity of Damascus was inflicted by the Romans, and who refer the words “A man shall incline toward his Maker, and his eyes shall look toward the Holy One of Israel” to the time of Christ and the Apostles, also interpret what follows—“You shall plant a faithful planting, and you shall sow a foreign shoot; on the day of your planting you shall cause the wild grape to flourish,” and the rest—as referring to the unbelief of the Jews [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “they understand these things as referring to misfortune,” etc.].

They interpret this chapter, which we have now set forth, as concerning the Gentiles who persecute the Church. They also understand the following words, “He shall rebuke him, and he shall flee far away,” as referring to the devil, indicating allegorically the devastation of the persecutors and demons.

We, however, follow the order that we began and protect historical foundations with a historical conclusion. “Woe,” he says, “to all the nations that waged war against my people, whose assault was so great that it could be compared with the waves of the sea. But when they come raging and flood my land, then their prince, Sennacherib, rebuked by him, will flee; and just as dust is scattered when the wind carries it away and a whirlwind is rolled upward in a storm, so he will indeed approach Jerusalem and besiege it, but he will be struck by the Angel. Morning will come, and he will see the army of his power destroyed. This will be the portion of those who devastated us.”

The Prophet speaks either in the person of the people or joining himself to his nation (2 Kings 19:35–36). Later we read: “The Angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. They arose in the morning, and behold, all were corpses of the dead. Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, departed, went away, returned, and dwelt in Nineveh.”

## Chapter XVIII

### (Verse 1)

“Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia.”

The Hebrew word *SELSEL* (), which Symmachus translated as “sound,” and Theodotion as “birds,” we have rendered as “cymbal.” Aquila translated it twice as “shadow.”

But it should be understood that *SEL* () means “shadow,” while here the syllable itself is doubled. From this we may understand the saying as follows: “Woe to the land that promises assistance in the shadow of its wings.” And since Scripture says, “He who dwells in the help of the Most High shall abide in the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90:1)—for in Hebrew it is written, “He shall abide in the shadow of the Almighty”—the land boasts that it possesses God’s own likeness and promises to support others while it itself is exposed to dangers.

It signifies either No, a city of Egypt, which is now called Alexandria, or Egypt itself, upon which Jerusalem has always leaned as upon a shaken reed, which, when broken, pierces the hand of the one leaning upon it. The order here is exceptionally beautiful: just as in the preceding vision the prophetic word threatened Damascus, because the ten tribes had found assistance in it while seeking the mercy of God, so now devastation is also foretold for Egypt, because reliance upon its assistance had caused the invocation of God to be neglected.

This is the land that is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia—that is, beyond the channels of the Nile River, which, no one doubts, flows from Ethiopia into Egypt. Egypt may be called “the cymbal of wings” because of the speed of its crops; for the swift and rapid flight of birds produces the sound of a cymbal.

Some, on account of what follows—“Who sends ambassadors upon the sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters”—understand the Roman empire and refer the entire history to the time of Vespasian and Titus, by whom Jerusalem was overthrown. But this is incompatible with our faith: that the Lord should threaten the Roman empire because it overthrew an impious nation and should again say that gifts were to be brought to Mount Zion—unless perhaps these things too are understood spiritually in the Church.

### (Verse 2)

“Who sends ambassadors upon the sea, and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters.”

“Go, swift messengers, to a nation torn apart and mangled; to a terrible people, after whom there was no other; to a nation waiting and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land.”

Among the Hebrews, Egypt, an Egyptian man, and the Egyptians are all designated by one word, *MESRAIM* (). This should be mentioned so that no one may stumble over the word when he finds the masculine used for the feminine—that is, a man for a land. For here too it says, “Who sends ambassadors upon the sea,” meaning Mesraim itself, the Egyptian himself, because ambassadors were sent from Alexandria—which, as we said, was then called No—to Jerusalem in vessels of papyrus, that is, in letters or ships [Note: Recall what we observed in Epistle 51, no. 1.].

They promised them their assistance and said: “Go quickly to the nation of the Jews, torn apart and mangled by the assault of the Assyrians; to the once terrible people who exercised the authority of God, whose power no other can equal; to the nation that always awaited God’s help and yet is trampled by human beings; whose land the rivers—that is, various kings—have ravaged.”

Others think that the address is directed apostrophically to the Lord, with this meaning: “O God, who sends Prophets upon the sea of this age, sailing, as it were, by letters, and commands your messengers to admonish the people: Go quickly to my nation, wounded and torn apart; to the strongest people, once a terror to all the surrounding nations; to the people that always awaited God’s help but, because of the greatness of its sins, does not deserve to receive what it hopes for; whose land the kings of various nations have ravaged,” and so forth.

Eusebius of Caesarea, promising a historical interpretation in the title, wanders through various meanings. When I was reading his books, I found something quite different from what the title promised. Whenever history failed him, he passed over to allegory, and he joined separated things together in such a way that I marvel at his new construction of language, by which he welds stone and iron into a single body.

I have mentioned this briefly so that no one may think that we borrowed from his sources what we say [Note: I think he denies that he borrowed his exposition of this chapter from Eusebius—or, as Montfaucon prefers, he understands the remark to concern the whole Commentary. Certainly Jerome assembled here much material that Eusebius neither touched nor could have touched. Moreover, the passages we occasionally note themselves bear witness that the holy Doctor took from him not only certain historical interpretations but also some allegorical ones.].

For in the present chapter Eusebius says that the prophecy is directed against the Jews and Jerusalem: at the beginning of the Christian faith they sent letters to all the nations so that they would not accept the passion of Christ, and they sent them as far as Ethiopia and the western region, filling the whole world with the dissemination of this blasphemy.

### (Verse 3)

“All the inhabitants of the world, you who dwell upon the earth: when a sign has been raised upon the mountains, you shall see it, and you shall hear the sound of the trumpet.”

“All nations,” he says, “when you hear my command, raised like a sign upon the mountains, and my authority, resounding on high like the sound of a trumpet, you will then see what I have commanded.”

### (Verse 4)

“For thus the Lord said to me: I shall rest, and I shall look upon my place.”

What is it that the Lord spoke to the Prophet? The following: “Until the things that I have commanded come to pass, I shall rest in my seat”—according to the Jews, in the Temple; according to us, in the heavenly places. “And I shall look,” he says, “to see what end comes to these affairs.”

“As the clear light of midday and as a cloud of dew on the day of harvest.” Just as nothing during the whole day is brighter than midday, when the sun gleams from the middle of heaven and illuminates the entire world equally, and just as, in the heat and burning warmth, when the naked reaper is scorched and his breathing reveals the magnitude of his labor, the coolness of dew is most welcome [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “like withered stalks,” and then continues with “he does.”], if the morning moisture makes dry stalks easy to cut, so my word, which I shall contemplate in my place, will come pleasantly to all who believe in me.

### (Verses 5–6)

“For before the harvest it all blossomed, and premature ripeness put forth its shoot; and its branches shall be cut off with pruning hooks, and whatever is left shall be cut away and shaken off. And they shall all be left to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth; and the birds shall remain upon it throughout the summer, and all the beasts of the earth shall winter upon it.”

Because he had spoken of midday and had introduced the cloud of dew in summer and at harvest, and had drawn his metaphor from agriculture, he maintains it in what follows. He describes the pride of Egypt, the devastation of that people, and the corpses throughout the province that are to be devoured by birds.

For just as crops that burst forth before maturity quickly perish, and shoots that grow before the fullness of the season arrives are useless, so, he says, the Egyptian people, like useless branches, will be cut down with pruning hooks, and all their shoots will be stripped bare.

And so that you would not think that he is speaking about a vine rather than about human beings, he turns the metaphor into the truth of history: “And they shall all be left,” he says, “to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth.” Birds and beasts do not devour branches cut from trees, but corpses.

Let us read Ezekiel more fully, where he prophesies against Pharaoh and against Egypt; we shall find all these things written there most explicitly (Ezek. 29). And when he says, “The birds shall remain upon it throughout the summer, and all the beasts shall winter upon it,” this either signifies the great multitude of the slain or, through the same metaphor, demonstrates that Egypt will be ravaged by all nations.

### (Verse 7)

“At that time a gift shall be brought to the Lord of hosts by a people scattered and torn apart, by a terrible people, after whom there was no other; by a nation waiting, waiting and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion.”

After Egypt has been devastated and its empire destroyed, Israel will no longer trust in the emptiness of its shadow, but will return to the Lord and bring its gifts to Mount Zion—that is, to his temple—entreating him alone, whose protection is true and eternal. We understand this to have occurred under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and Ezra and Nehemiah.

The Septuagint, instead of what we have rendered “waiting, waiting”—which in Hebrew is written “hoping, hoping”—translated the expression conversely as ἀνέλπιστον, that is, “without hope.” For this reason they gave Eusebius an opportunity to think that the passage should be understood more of the nations, which have neither hope nor the Testament of God nor Prophets, than of the Jews. He thought that gifts would later be sent by them to the Church, which is established on a watchtower, and that spiritual sacrifices would be offered [Note: Eusebius actually recalls here the Lord’s command to his disciples, “Go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel,” and then, “Go and teach all nations in my name.” He adds: “For they were not sent to acquaintances, relatives, or brothers, but to people who were strangers, unknown men and foreigners among all the nations, among whom they were truly unsettled, standing firmly upon nothing, wandering and being carried about by every wind of polytheistic error.”].

## Chapter XIX

### (Verse 1)

“The burden of Egypt. Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud, and shall enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt shall be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt shall melt within it.”

It is customary for the Scriptures to append manifest things to obscure ones and to express openly what they first uttered through riddles. Accordingly, in the present passage, because he had threatened Egypt—“Woe to the land overshadowing with wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia,” and the rest woven together by the prophetic word—he now makes the meaning clearer and, threatening Egypt itself, says that the Lord will come not through angels but in person, upon a light cloud, that is, a swift one. He will enter Egypt, the idols of Egypt will tremble, and the heart of the strong will melt. Thus the prophecy of Ezekiel [or Jeremiah, according to another reading] will be fulfilled: “I shall destroy the images, and I shall cause the idols of Memphis to cease” (Ezek. 30:13).

Some refer this entire prophecy to the time of the Savior, when he entered upon a light cloud—that is, the human body which he had assumed from the Virgin, unburdened by any seed of human union—or because he was carried by a light cloud, namely, a virginal body. At his entrance all the demons trembled, and then the first collapse of the idols occurred, since they could not endure the presence of the Lord.

### (Verse 2)

“And I shall stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and a man shall fight against his brother, and a man against his neighbor, city against city, and kingdom against kingdom.”

When the Lord has entered Egypt and destroyed the most powerful nation by his presence, the first victory will be that the Egyptians will disagree among themselves and fight against one another with rebellious hatred. This happened in the times of the Assyrians and of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, with some sitting still and others resisting.

That he foretells these things concerning the Babylonian captivity is confirmed by Jeremiah, who says: “Egypt is a beautiful and graceful heifer; a goad from the north shall come upon her.” And again: “The daughter of Egypt is confounded and delivered into the hand of the northern people” (Jer. 46:20, 24).

Ezekiel too, agreeing with equal prophetic authority, says: “I shall cause the multitude of Egypt to cease in the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.” And again: “I shall strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and I shall place my sword in his hand, and I shall break the arms of Pharaoh. And they shall know that I am the Lord, when I have given my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he has stretched it out over the land of Egypt, and I have scattered Egypt among the nations” (Ezek. 30:10, 24, and following).

But if we refer these things to the time of the Savior, let us take the example from the Gospel: “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace, but a sword. For I have come to divide a man against his neighbor, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and a man’s enemies will be those of his household” (Matt. 10:34 and following). And again in another passage: “Two will be divided against three, and three against two: father against son, and mother against daughter, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law” (Luke 12:52–58).

### (Verse 3)

“And the spirit of Egypt shall be broken within it, and I shall bring its counsel to nothing. Then they shall inquire of their images and their diviners, their python-spirits and their augurs.”

When rebellion has arisen in Egypt—whether among those wishing to serve Babylon and those unwilling to submit their necks to its yoke, or among those believing in Christ and those resisting him—the spirit of Egypt will be broken and divided, since not everyone will desire the same things, and all their counsel will be reduced to nothing.

Then they will go to their images, diviners, augurs, and prophets instructed in magical arts, and ask why these things have happened.

### (Verse 4)

“And I shall deliver Egypt into the hand of cruel masters, and a strong king shall rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts.”

We follow a twofold interpretation: either that of the Chaldean period, when Egypt was conquered by Nebuchadnezzar, or that of the Roman empire, when Augustus Caesar subjugated Egypt after defeating Antony and Cleopatra.

That the Babylonians were cruel is attested by all Scripture: they spared neither children, whom they wounded with their arrows, nor pregnant women. The Roman empire, however, was exceedingly strong, as the Book of Daniel also testifies (chapter 7), describing the fourth beast as having iron teeth and claws.

### (Verses 5–7)

“And the water shall dry up from the sea, and the river shall be desolate and dry; the streams shall fail, they shall become shallow and dry, the channels of the banks. The reed and the rush shall wither; the riverbed shall be exposed from its spring, and every sown field watered by it shall dry up, wither, and cease to be.”

It is natural that, when captivity comes through the anger of God, pestilence should follow his indignation and that all the elements together should rage against those who have offended God. Hence it is written in another Prophet (Jer. 12) that birds of the air and fish in the waters will fail, so that all things will be withdrawn from human use.

We say this if we wish to understand the passage simply as referring to the drying up of the Nile River and its channels. But if we understand it metaphorically, let the river signify the kingdom and its channels its leaders, and let the greenery, rush, and papyrus signify all Egypt’s abundance, so that through these things Egypt’s wealth is described, for Egypt is exceedingly fertile.

Let us read Ezekiel, where Pharaoh the king is described as a great dragon dwelling in the rivers, and says: “The river is mine, and I made myself.” And he hears: “I shall put a bridle in your jaws, and I shall fasten the fish of your rivers to your scales, and I shall draw you out from the midst of your rivers, and all the fish of your rivers shall cling to your scales, and I shall cast you into the wilderness” (Ezek. 29:3–4).

At the coming of Christ all these things are to be understood tropologically, in accordance with what we read above: “The Lord will make the sea of Egypt a desert.” And again: “The Lord shall bring his hand upon the violent river of Egypt and strike it in seven valleys, so that someone may cross it with shod foot.” This evidently means that every error of the Egyptian waters, and the magical arts by which they deceived the peoples subject to them, would be dried up by the coming of Christ.

When he says, “The water shall dry up from the sea,” we may also understand it historically: the Great Sea is not signified, but Lake Mareotis, since Scripture calls all collections of waters “seas.” The words may also be understood hyperbolically.

And what follows—“The riverbed shall be exposed from its spring”—describes the river and its source drying up together.

### (Verses 8–10)

“And the fishermen shall mourn, and all who cast hooks into the river shall lament; and those who spread nets over the surface of the water shall languish. And those who work with flax, twisting and weaving fine materials, shall be confounded; and its irrigation channels shall become slack: all who made pools for catching fish.”

Understand this in two ways. First, when Egypt has been devastated and the whole province dried up through drought, the fishermen shall mourn, and those who cast hooks into the river shall lament, as shall those who worked with nets and seines and wove vessels of various kinds from reeds—that is, the princes, those of royal descent, and the rulers. Second, at Christ’s coming, all fishermen of a perverse kind, who, contrary to apostolic discipline, caught human beings for destruction and wove nets and seines with foolish wisdom, by which they might entangle the lost, were confounded; and there is no such fisherman, or scarcely one, left to be found in the land of Egypt.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscript: “in the land of Egypt no such fisherman shall any longer be caught.” This, etc.]

We see this work fulfilled: the trophies of the Churches rise up, and throughout all Egypt the idols have fallen.

### (Verses 11–13)

“The princes of Tanis are fools; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. How will you say to Pharaoh, ‘I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings’? Where are your wise men now? Let them announce it to you and declare what the Lord of hosts has purposed concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools; the princes of Memphis have withered away. They have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples.”

The Psalmist also declares that Tanis was the metropolis of Egypt and that Moses performed many signs there, which are described in Exodus: “He set his signs in Egypt, and his wonders in the plain of Tanis” (Psalm 77:11).

The fact that Memphis was devoted to magical arts is shown by the traces of its former error, which remain to the present time. This too is briefly indicated: when the devastation of Babylon comes, all the counsels of the magicians and of those who promised knowledge of future things are proved foolish; and at Christ’s coming all these things are reduced to nothing, since Egypt’s diviners cannot find counsel as to how they might suppress the Christian doctrine.

It is an idiom of Scripture to use “corner” for a kingdom, because it contains peoples and is, as it were, the strongest part of the whole house. Hence Christ, who holds together the walls of two peoples, is called the cornerstone (Ephesians 2).

When it adds, “How will you say to Pharaoh, ‘I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings?’” it signifies that the Egyptians pretend that heroes and gods—Horus, Isis, Osiris, and Typhon—were the founders of their nation.

[Note: The same writer has “Horus”; these passages too are excerpted from Eusebius.]

### (Verses 14–15)

“The Lord has mixed within her a spirit of dizziness; and they have caused Egypt to go astray in all her work, as a drunkard goes astray while vomiting. Egypt shall have no work that it can accomplish, whether head or tail, bending or restraining.”

Let us speak first about the translation, and afterward discuss what is written. Instead of “a spirit of dizziness,” one may translate “a spirit of error.” In the phrase which we translated “bending and restraining,” we may also say “bent and wanton,” so that we understand an old man and a child.

The Hebrew word is **AGMON** (אגמון). While quickly translating what was written, we were deceived by its ambiguity and rendered it “restraining”; Aquila translated it more precisely as **στρεβλοῦντα** (*streblounta*), that is, “one who does nothing rightly but makes everything crooked,” signifying a child.

[Note: Martianus read “Acmon,” and in Hebrew, [the reading is defective]. The manuscripts prefer “Egmon”; the text itself, as we have restored it, reads [the restored form]. See below, Book VII, where this same chapter and passage recur.]

The sense, therefore, is this: the princes of Tanis have become fools, the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel, the princes of Memphis have withered away, and they have deceived Egypt, the corner of its peoples, because the Lord has mixed within them a spirit of error and dizziness, so that they do not know what they are saying and cause Egypt to go astray.

As a drunkard vomits up what he has swallowed and does not know where he is, but lies there bereft of reason, so Egypt shall have no work or counsel that possesses either a head or an end, or that is suitable either for old men or for children. Some, through excessive age, become foolish and delirious; others, through wantonness and childishness, do not know what they are doing.

Whether you wish to receive this with reference to the devastation of Babylon, to Christ’s coming, or according to both the literal and the spiritual sense, it will have its proper coherence.

### (Verses 16–17)

“On that day Egypt shall be like women, and they shall be astonished and afraid before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he will shake over it. And the land of Judah shall be a cause of celebration—or fear—to Egypt; everyone who remembers it shall tremble before the purpose of the Lord of hosts, which he has purposed against it.”

I consider it better to correct my own error than, while ashamed to confess ignorance, to persist in error. In what I translated, “And the land of Judah shall be a cause of celebration to Egypt,” the Hebrew has **AGGA** (אגה) instead of “celebration.” This may be interpreted both as “celebration” (whence Haggai’s name is rendered as “festive”) and as “fear.” Aquila translated it more expressively as **γύρωσις** (*gyrosis*), when someone, frightened and trembling, casts his eyes about and fears an approaching enemy.

Therefore, if we wish to understand in a favorable sense that the remembrance of Judah is a source of joy to Egypt, “celebration” is rightly used. But if, as I think, it is translated as “fear” instead of “celebration,” let us understand dread or terror: when Nebuchadnezzar comes and the hands of all the valiant men have become like women’s hands, even the name of Judah will be a terror to Egypt, because, while Egypt wished to provide assistance to Judah, it suffered such great disasters.

No one doubts how this applies to our own times: in comparison with Christians, all the pagans are like women, possessing feeble opinions, and whatever they say is turned into folly, while they are astonished at so great a conversion of the nations, marvel at it, and recognize the hand of the Lord. Whoever among the Gentiles remembers the Christian name confesses, with fear, the weakness of idolatry.

### (Verse 18)

“On that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts; one shall be called the City of the Sun.”

Instead of “City of the Sun,” I do not know what the Septuagint translators intended when they rendered it **Asedec**.

[Note: **Asedec.** In Origen’s *Hebrew Names*, the name Asedec is interpreted as “the righteousness of the sun”; hence I infer that Origen is being noted here. I had considered the name Asedec insignificant when I published the Greek *Lexicon of Names*. It should not seem surprising that, together with Jerome, I failed to recognize a word that was not Hebrew but had been fabricated by the Septuagint translators. From what source, however, the Greeks derived the name Asedec is now entirely clear to me: namely, from Isaiah 19:18, which I had previously understood less accurately, setting against this word the term Asedemoth. —Martianus.]

[Note: In other manuscripts of the same version, **ἀχειρές** (*acheires*) is more correctly found, from the Hebrew [reading defective]. See what we have noted in Origen’s *Lexicon*.]

One of our writers interprets it as “the city of righteousness,” and, misled by the fact that the Hebrew **ARES** (ארץ) is written here, supposes it to mean “land,” although that word is written with different letters.

[Note: By calling him “one of ours,” the holy Doctor seems to imply that he was a Latin writer. I suppose that Victorinus of Petovium is meant, since, apart from him, Jerome had already said in the Preface to this work that there was a great silence among Latin commentators on Isaiah. Eusebius, however, held the same view and, I might almost say, used nearly the same words: “According to the accurate manner of his exposition, it is called the city of the land, which could be rendered in this way: ‘One city shall be called the city of the land,’” and so forth. A little earlier he says: “According to the Septuagint it is called Asedec, which means ‘of righteousness.’”]

Symmachus therefore translated it better: “One shall be called the City of the Sun.” **ARES** is an ambiguous word, meaning both “clay vessel” and “sun,” because both are dry and parched.

Not understanding this passage, Onias built a temple in Egypt, in the town of Heliopolis.

[Note: Josephus has “in the district of Heliopolis,” or “in the territory of Heliopolis.” Compare Jerome below, Book VII, on this same chapter, and the notes made there.]

Read the histories of Josephus (Josephus, Book XII, chapter 9).

Others wish **Ares**, that is, **ὄστρακον** (*ostrakon*), “a potsherd,” to signify the city of Ostracine, together with the other cities near Rhinocorura and Casium. It is clear that, even to the present day, these cities speak in Egypt the language of Canaan, that is, Syriac. They suppose that Syrians and Arabs from the neighboring region were transferred into that land by Nebuchadnezzar.

Those who interpret the prophecy with reference to Christ’s coming and the Roman Empire understand the five cities either as the law of the Lord, which was first interpreted in Alexandria,

[Note: He refers to catechetical schools and to the interpretation of Scripture, which were first established at Alexandria, where, as he himself says in the *Catalogue* concerning Pantaenus, ecclesiastical teachers had always been present since the time of Mark the Evangelist.]

or as the five orders of the Church: bishops, presbyters, deacons, the faithful, and catechumens.

[Note: “Bishops.” In this passage Jerome recognizes the episcopate as an order distinct from the presbyterate; nor does he mention the lower orders, namely subdeacons and the other minor orders. —Martianus.]

[Note: These words are Eusebius’s: “As there are five cities in the Church, so there may be different forms of life; and five orders divided, or rather three enumerations: first, the order of presidents; second, that of presbyters; third, that of deacons; fourth, that of those enlightened in Christ; and beyond these, that of those undergoing instruction.” As for what Martianus would have preferred—that the lower orders, the subdeacon and the others, should also be named, even if they had been established everywhere—it was beside the point. The lesser clergy were commonly included under the name “deacons,” and did not constitute another class distinct from them in the Church. Optatus, Book II, says: “Since there are four kinds of heads in the Church: bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the faithful.” Moreover, as we have said, Jerome is not speaking here from his own judgment but from Eusebius’s.]

Or else they understand it spiritually as the law, concerning which the Apostle also says: “I would rather speak five words in the Churches in my understanding than ten thousand words in a tongue” (1 Corinthians 14).

And that one of the five cities is called the City of the Sun means, namely, the city of righteousness, “in whose wings there is healing.”

### (Verses 19–21)

“On that day there shall be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar beside its boundary for the Lord. And it shall be for a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they shall cry to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and Defender who will deliver them. The Lord shall be known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know the Lord on that day; they shall worship him with sacrifices and offerings, make vows to the Lord, and fulfill them.”

From this point to the end of the Vision—or Burden—concerning Egypt, both the Jews and our own writers wish the passage to be understood of Christ’s coming. They, however, defer its fulfillment to the future, whereas we regard it as having already been accomplished.

Understand “day” as “time,” although Josephus maintains that these things happened under Onias. As a refugee in Egypt, Onias built a temple and an altar there with a great multitude of Jews, and attempted, with reckless presumption, to fulfill the prophecy concerning Christ.

It is said to be one altar in the same way that there is one faith, one baptism, and one Church.

[Note: Eusebius says: “Just as one faith, one baptism, and one Church are spoken of, so also there is one altar, erected throughout all Egypt, existing in the Churches of God.” He then adds: “The pillar joined to Christ’s altar would be the Gospel of the New Testament, distinguishing those Egyptians who have believed in Christ from the unbelievers.”]

“And a pillar beside its boundary for the Lord” undoubtedly signifies the Gospel and the writings of the Apostles. For just as, according to the tropological interpretation above, the land of Judah is understood as something fearful—or solemn—to Egypt, namely, the Old Testament, so also the pillar at the boundaries of Egypt signifies the history of the Gospels.

Finally, he joins the words: “And it shall be for a sign and a testimony,” namely, of the Lord’s Passion. Then those who have believed, when Egyptians rise against Egyptians, and man fights against his brother, and city battles against city, will implore the Lord’s mercy when the time of persecution comes; and immediately the Savior will arrive—that is, Jesus, for this is what the name means in our language.

[Note: Martianus reads “will break in” (*irruerit*), incorrectly.]

The Lord will be known by the Egyptians, and they will know him: either the persecutors, after they have been overcome, or the believers, delivered by his present assistance. “They shall worship him with sacrifices and offerings, make vows to the Lord, and fulfill them.”

Let the Jews answer: It is commanded by the Law that an altar may be made only in the one place which the Lord God has chosen, and that sacrifices may be offered only by priests of the Levitical line (Deuteronomy 26). Yet Isaiah plainly teaches that the Egyptians will know the Lord, worship him, offer sacrifices and gifts, make vows, and fulfill them. If the Egyptians have a priesthood, then Paul’s testimony is also fulfilled among them: “When the priesthood is transferred, there must also be a transfer of the law” (Hebrews 7:12).

### (Verse 22)

“And the Lord shall strike Egypt with a plague and heal it; they shall return to the Lord, and he shall be appeased toward them and heal them.”

“For whom the Lord loves, he chastises, and he scourges every son whom he receives.” Persecution concerns not the denial of believers but their testing and their crown.

### (Verse 23)

“On that day there shall be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians; the Assyrian shall enter Egypt, and the Egyptian the Assyrians; and the Egyptians shall serve Assur.”

Before Christ’s coming, each nation had its own king, and no one could pass from one nation to another. Under the Roman Empire, however, everything became one.

[Note: Jerome expressed this entire interpretation from Eusebius, though more briefly. At times he actually translates Eusebius’s words, as in the following: “Before Roman rule, both the Egyptians and the Assyrians had kings of their own.” Then: “Here I think Scripture calls Assyrians those who are now called Syrians; in ancient times, those who inhabited Syria and Mesopotamia were called Assyrians.” And below: “Who, seeing with his own eyes Roman armies encamped over the heads of Syrian men against the Egyptians, and Egyptians serving them, would not be struck with amazement at the fulfillment of the prophecy?” Finally: “But the present passage prophesies fellowship and intermingling between them,” which he repeats below.]

Let the learned reader consult the ancient histories and recognize that the whole region between the Euphrates and the Tigris belonged to the Assyrians. Thus those whom the ancients called Assyrians we now call Syrians, naming the whole from a part.

As for the statement, “The Egyptians shall serve the Syrians,” it may be understood either in this way: Roman legions supplied with Syrian soldiers [variant: “with a Syrian soldier”] guard Egypt; or, alternatively, the two peoples maintain commercial relations with one another, and the cities of Syria receive Egypt’s abundance, just as, conversely, Egypt is enriched by the goods of Palestine and Phoenicia.

Some of our writers wrongly refer these things to a thousand years in the future and, following Jewish custom, declare that they will occur at the end of the world, when Antichrist, coming from the Assyrians, will possess Egypt and Ethiopia.

### (Verses 24–25)

“On that day Israel shall be third with the Egyptian and the Assyrian, a blessing in the midst of the earth, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: ‘Blessed is my people Egypt, and the work of my hands Assyria; but Israel is my inheritance.’”

Israel will not be crushed between Egypt and Assyria, with Antiochus and Demetrius at one time drawing the kingdom of Judah to themselves,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “of Judea”; it also has “Tholomaeis” shortly afterward instead of “Ptolemaeis.” We discussed this reading somewhat earlier.]

and at another time the Ptolemies claiming its possession for themselves. Rather, once it too has been established under the Roman Empire—and therefore under the rule of Christ—it will share the condition of Egypt and Assyria and will be blessed throughout the whole earth. For “the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

Then the Lord will say: “Blessed is my people Egypt,” when countless thousands of human beings, no longer led by Moses but by Christ the Lord, have filled the deserts and, with Pharaoh drowned, have said in the wilderness: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified: horse and rider he has cast into the sea” (Exodus 15:1).

Then Assyria too will be the work of the Lord’s hands. These are among the greatest nations, flourishing with swarms of monks: Egypt and Mesopotamia vie with one another in equal devotion.

“But Israel is Christ’s inheritance”—that is, the places of his birth, crucifixion, resurrection, and ascension, toward which people come together from the whole world.

## Chapter 20

### (Verse 1)

“In the year when Thartan entered Azotus, sent by Sargon king of the Assyrians, and fought against Azotus and captured it, at that time the Lord spoke by Isaiah son of Amoz, saying: ‘Go and loosen the sackcloth from your loins, and take your sandals off your feet.’ And he did so, going naked and barefoot.

“And the Lord said: ‘Just as my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent for three years against Egypt and against Ethiopia. Thus the king of the Assyrians shall threaten Egypt with captivity and Ethiopia with exile, young and old, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks uncovered, to the shame of Egypt. And they shall be afraid and ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and because of Egypt, their glory.

“And the inhabitant of this island shall say on that day: ‘Behold, this was our hope, to whom we fled for help, that he might deliver us from the presence of the king of the Assyrians; and how shall we ourselves escape?’””

We have set out the whole content of this chapter so that we may discuss each part individually.

Azotus, called **ESDOD** (אשדוד) in Hebrew, was one of the five most powerful cities of Palestine. Sargon, king of the Assyrians, who is called by seven names, sent the commander of his army, whose name was Thartan, and he captured and held it.

At the time when this neighboring city was captured, Isaiah was commanded to remove his sackcloth—for this was the prophetic garment of one mourning the sins of the people—and to walk naked and barefoot, without sandals, which the Septuagint calls *caligae*, thereby presenting a type of the captivity of Egypt and the Ethiopians, who had come to the aid of the Egyptians.

Just as Isaiah would walk naked and display his naked buttocks as an object of shame to those who saw him, so all Egypt and Ethiopia, when the Assyrians ravaged them, would be made naked, with absolutely nothing remaining in the land.

No one should think that this contradicts the prosperity promised to the Egyptians above. There, future blessedness is proclaimed after the evils; here, a present captivity is narrated, through which, after Israel, Damascus, and the Philistines had been destroyed, the Assyrian proceeded by a direct route into Egypt and defeated the Ethiopians as well.

Lest this seem doubtful to anyone, let us set down Isaiah’s own testimony: “When Rabshakeh returned, he found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. And he heard them say concerning Tirhakah king of Ethiopia: ‘He has gone out to fight against you’” (2 Kings 19:8–9).

At the same time we learn the obedience of the prophets. Isaiah was a noble man—for the Hebrews report that he was the father-in-law of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, king of Judah—yet he was not ashamed to walk naked. Judging nothing more honorable than God’s commands, he removed the sackcloth and, once it had been cast aside, went naked, having only one garment, and that one of haircloth.

[Note: The word was *suffecimus*; we have restored it from two manuscripts. We have similarly restored other readings from manuscripts here and there.]

When it says, “It shall be a sign and portent for three years against Egypt and against Ethiopia,” this means that Egypt and Ethiopia were to be ravaged by the Assyrians for three years.

“Then,” he says, “the inhabitant of this island,” that is, Jerusalem, which is battered by the waves of the neighboring nations, will say: “Was this our hope? Did we flee to these people so that they might provide us assistance, though they themselves were unable to rescue themselves from the evil of captivity?”

Here, therefore, is the order of God’s providence, by which he governs the whole human race through an ineffable judgment. Israel hoped in Damascus against God’s anger: let the city that wickedly provides assistance against his will be destroyed. Judah hoped in the Egyptians: let Egypt be destroyed. The Egyptians trusted in the Ethiopians: let the Ethiopians too be defeated by the Assyrians. The Assyrians grew proud, attributing victory not to God but to their own strength: let them too be defeated by the Babylonians. Babylon lifted its head against God: let it itself be overcome by the Medes and Persians.

The Persians and Medes partly persecuted God’s people, and the fiercest ram scattered all the peoples to the east and west. Let Alexander, the he-goat, come and trample it under his feet. And let this man, who has been lifted up beyond measure, perish by poison, and let his kingdom be divided into parts. After those parts have long been at odds with one another, let the Roman prevail and lay them waste.

The Roman himself tore the flesh of the saints with iron teeth and claws and mangled it with his bloodstained mouth. Let a stone be cut from the mountain without hands and crush the exceedingly powerful first kingdom, the iron one, and then the fragile and weak one, in the form of pottery (Daniel 2).

## Chapter 21

### (Verse 1)

“The burden of the desert of the sea.”

If I did not read later in this chapter, “Babylon, the beloved, has become a marvel to me,” and again, “Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all the images of her gods have been crushed to the ground,” and above, “Go up, Elam; besiege Media,” I would wonder what this Burden might be that is imposed upon the desert sea.

It is therefore clear that Babylon is called the desert sea, as Jeremiah says in God’s person: “I will make her sea a desert, and dry up her land, and Babylon shall become heaps of sand” (Jeremiah 51:36–37).

It is called “sea” because of the multitude of its inhabitants. Hence above too the multitude of Egypt was compared with the sea: “The Lord will make the sea of Egypt a desert.”

That the Medes and Persians fought against Babylon and overthrew it we read in the aforementioned Jeremiah: “Sharpen the arrows, fill the quivers. The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes against Babylon, and his mind is directed against it, to destroy it, for it is the vengeance of the Lord, the vengeance of his Temple. Raise a banner over the walls of Babylon, increase the guard, set up watchmen, prepare ambushes, for the Lord has planned and done whatever he spoke against the inhabitants of Babylon.”

And again: “Raise a banner in the land, blow the trumpet among the nations, consecrate nations against her, announce against her to the kings of Ararat, Minni, and Ashkenaz; muster against her Tapsar; bring up the horse like a bristling locust. Consecrate nations against her, the kings of Media, her governors and all her magistrates, and the whole land of her dominion. And the earth shall be shaken and disturbed, because the Lord’s thought has kept watch against Babylon, to make the land of Babylon desolate and uninhabited” (Jeremiah 51:11 ff.).

### (Verses 1–2)

“As whirlwinds come from the south, so he comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A harsh vision has been announced to me.”

The voice of the Babylonian people, afraid, is introduced—or that of Babylon itself, hearing that the Medes and Elamites are preparing an army against it and coming from the desert. He gives an example by comparison:

“As,” he says, “a violent storm commonly comes from the south wind, so devastation comes to me from the desert, from a terrible land whose very name I cannot hear without fear. A harsh vision has been announced to me.” For what is harsher than the present captivity?

“He who is faithless acts faithlessly, and he who is a plunderer devastates.”

In Hebrew this may be read: “You who kill, kill; you who devastate, devastate,” so that the prophetic oracle is directed toward the Elamite and Mede themselves, urging them to complete what they have begun and to ascend fearlessly and besiege the most powerful city.

But if it is read as we have translated it, as referring to a third person—“He who is faithless acts faithlessly, and he who is a plunderer devastates”—it must be joined with the preceding words, in which Babylon declares that a harsh vision has been announced to it.

“Go up, Elam; besiege, Media. I have made all her groaning cease.”

“Do not fear,” he says, “O Persian and Mede, the multitude of Babylon, and do not dread her former power. I have caused all her groaning and burden, by which she was accustomed to oppress you, to cease.”

This may mean either that no one now groans or grieves under Babylon’s power, or that Babylon herself has been overwhelmed by such evils that she does not even have the freedom to groan.

### (Verses 3–4)

“Therefore my loins have been filled with pain; anguish has seized me like the anguish of a woman in labor. I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw. My heart languished; darkness overwhelmed me. Babylon, my beloved, has been made a marvel to me.”

The prophets are obscure because their persons frequently change within them. Thus here too the voice of Isaiah is introduced, mourning Babylon in the prophetic spirit, because such great evils will come upon her that he himself, overcome by fear, cannot break into words as he sees the blood of such a vast multitude poured out.

Moved by compassion—for a human being is speaking of human beings—he suffers no less than a woman accustomed to cry out in labor. Troubled and trembling, falling to the ground, with his eyes clouded, he does not know what to say.

Instead of what we translated as “Babylon, my beloved,” the Hebrew reads **NESEPH ESCI** (נשף עשי). This is the same word that we placed at the beginning of the Burden of Babylon, “upon the mountain of darkness.” For “dark” or “shadowy” it is written **Neseph**. Properly, this is what the city is called because of its height and the proud summit of its tower, raised up to heaven.

### (Verse 5)

“Set the table, look out from the watchtower at those eating and drinking; rise up, princes, seize the shield.”

This passage is understood in two ways.

First: “O Medes and Elamites, to whom I said above, ‘Go up, Elam; besiege, Media,’ take food and prepare yourselves for the coming battle, lest, when the time of combat arrives, weariness hold you back. When you have eaten and drunk, rise, seize your weapons, and wage war against Babylon.”

The statement, “Look out from the watchtower,” is read in this sense: “Look carefully and foresee what is about to happen.”

It may also be understood in this way: “O Babylon, prepare a table and banquet for Belshazzar, your king, the son of Evil-merodach and grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, and see what happens after the meal, at which he will drink with prostitutes and concubines from the vessels of the Lord. O princes who recline with the king”—by whom he means the Medes and Persians—“rise and seize weapons to kill the king.”

We learn this more fully in the Book of Daniel (chapter 5).

### (Verses 6 ff.)

“For thus the Lord said to me: ‘Go and set a watchman, and let him announce whatever he sees.’ And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on a donkey, and a rider on a camel. And he looked carefully, with much attention, and the lion cried out: ‘Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights. Behold, this one comes, the rider of a chariot of horsemen.’ And he answered and said: ‘Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all the images of her gods have been crushed to the ground. My threshing, and the son of my threshing-floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.’”

He explains the cause of the earlier terror: why anguish seized him like a woman in labor, why he collapsed when he heard, why he was terrified and surrounded by dark horror.

“This,” he says, “the Lord said to me: Go and appoint a watchman, so that by the prophetic spirit he may announce future things to you. When I had set him upon the watchtower, he saw a chariot approaching, with a driver above it, and a donkey and a camel drawing the chariot.”

This signifies Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, coming with a small and a great empire. Before Cyrus, the Persians were insignificant and held no position among the nations; the Medes had always been extremely powerful.

Thus this single rider, supported by the army of two nations, comes against Babylon. The watchman who had been appointed to foresee what was coming cried out like a lion—or perhaps the prophet himself is called the lion.

Since there was uncertainty about the identity of the watchman who saw Cyrus ascending, he explains it more clearly and says: “Upon the Lord’s watchtower I stand continually by day,” declaring himself to be the Lord’s watchman, always stationed in prophetic service and obeying the Lord’s command by day and night, speaking whatever he orders.

What, then, did the lion cry out? “Behold, this one comes, the rider of a chariot of horsemen”—there is no doubt that Cyrus is indicated.

And the same lion who had cried out above answered and said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all the images of her gods have been crushed to the ground.”

When the rider of the chariot devastates it, Babylon is destroyed forever, and the temple of Bel, together with all its idols, is thrown down to its foundations.

The words that follow, “My threshing, and the son of my threshing-floor,” address Jerusalem by apostrophe, and refer to the Temple situated on Ornan’s threshing-floor. He says to her:

“O Jerusalem, and people who are the son of my Temple, do not think what I have said unbelievable. These are not my words, but the Lord’s; his words have resounded through my mouth.”

Some think—but wrongly—that this is said not to Jerusalem but to Babylon, of which it was also said above: “Babylon, my beloved, has been made a marvel to me.” They understand the sense to be: “You who have crushed me will yourself be crushed—not by my word, but by the power of the Lord, which foretells these things that are to come upon you.”

I do not sufficiently understand what the Septuagint translators intended in this passage when, instead of “lion,” which is **ARIA** (אריה) in Hebrew, they rendered it **uria**, especially since the aforementioned priest Uriah, who is cited as a witness, is written with different letters.

### (Verses 11–12)

“The burden of Dumah. Someone calls to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ And the watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; return, come.’”

Instead of Dumah, the Septuagint gives Idumea.

Dumah, however, is not the whole province of Idumea but one of its regions, lying toward the south and twenty miles from the Palestinian city now called Eleutheropolis. Near it are the mountains of Seir, which take their name from their founder. For Seir means “rough” and “hairy,” which Esau was.

We have discussed this people more fully in our commentary on the prophet Obadiah. There it was necessary to review the ancient history and to bring forward, as witnesses, the corresponding Visions of Ezekiel and Jeremiah, especially the prophecy against Mount Seir (Ezekiel 25 and 35; Jeremiah 49). Also relevant is the passage from the Psalms: “Into Edom I will extend my sandal.” And elsewhere: “The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagrites, Gebal and Ammon and Amalek” (Psalms 59:10; 82:7–8).

Amos also says: “For three crimes of Edom, and for four, I will not revoke his punishment, because he pursued his brother with the sword and violated his mercy” (Amos 1:11); or, as Symmachus translated it, “his inward parts,” because Edom dared to fight against related peoples and to disagree with them in hostile hatred.

The region of Esau was in Dumah, that is, in the mountains of Seir.

[Variant: Some manuscripts read “royal region” instead of “region.”]

We believe that this region, as a metropolis and in accordance with the sequence of the preceding Visions, was conquered by the Assyrians or by Nebuchadnezzar. Remembering its former descent from Abraham and Isaac, it implored God’s assistance and, compelled by necessity, begged for his mercy.

The Lord now relates that the one who is besieged in Seir and surrounded by enemies implores my help and says:

“O guardian of Israel, who protect your people with everlasting watchfulness and, as though they were sleeping at night, keep watch so that the enemy may not break in—why do you not protect us also, who are descended from his seed, with similar mercy?”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “who are of his stock.”]

To them I, the guardian and watchman, answer—of whom it is written: “He shall neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Psalm 120:4):

“Morning has come for my people, and night for the nation of the Idumeans. I will provide light for them; I will leave you in darkness.”

Or certainly it may be understood this way: “The light has come after the night has passed. If you call upon my help, and if you are descended from Abraham, my servant, do not seek me only in times of necessity, but turn to me with your whole heart. Come, and I will receive those who repent.”

Let this be understood according to the historical sense. But because of the similarity of the letters, and because **RES** and **DALETH** differ little from one another, some Hebrews read “Rome” instead of “Dumah,” wishing the prophecy to be directed against the Roman Empire. They do so through the frivolous persuasion by which they always suppose that the Romans are signified under the name Idumea.

**Dumah**, however, means “silence.”

### (Verses 13 ff.) The oracle concerning Arabia

In the thicket you shall spend the night toward evening, on the paths of Dodanim. Meet the thirsty with water; you who inhabit the land of the South, meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of swords, from the face of the imminent sword, from the face of the drawn bow, from the face of grievous battle.

For thus the Lord says to me: “Still within one year, as within the year of a hired laborer, all the glory of Kedar shall be removed, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar shall be diminished; for the Lord God of Israel has spoken.”

When I was seeking, and for a long time carefully considering, what Arabia might be—the region to which the prophetic discourse is directed—whether the Moabites, Ammonites, and Edomites, or all the other regions that are now called Arabia, the following passage in this same Vision provided the answer: “All the glory of Kedar shall be removed, and the remnant of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar shall be diminished” (Isa. 21:16–17). The Ishmaelites, therefore, are to be understood.

The Book of Genesis teaches that Kedar and the Hagarenes—who, by a distorted name, are called Saracens—were descended from Ishmael. They inhabit the entire desert. I think the poet refers to them in the words: “The Barcaeans wandering far and wide” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 4); and the book mentioned above says: “He shall dwell over against all his brethren” (Gen. 16:12). For an exceedingly broad wilderness stretches from India all the way to Mauretania and the Atlantic Ocean—what I think the title of Jeremiah signifies: “Against Kedar and against the kingdoms of Hazor, which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon struck” (Jer. 49:28). Immediately afterward it continues:

> Thus says the Lord: Rise up and go up against Kedar, and lay waste the sons of the East. They shall seize their tents and their flocks; they shall take for themselves their skins and all their vessels, and they shall carry off their camels (ibid., 29).

And again:

> For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has taken counsel against you; he has devised plans against you. Rise up and go against a tranquil nation, dwelling in security, says the Lord; they have no doors or bars; they dwell alone. Their camels shall become plunder, and the multitude of their beasts prey. I shall scatter to every wind those who have their hair cropped, and from every side of them I shall bring destruction upon them, says the Lord. And Hazor shall become a dwelling place of dragons, desolate forever; no man shall dwell there, nor shall a son of man inhabit it (ibid., 30 ff.).

I have set out the whole testimony from Jeremiah so that you may understand without doubt what Kedar is. Consider also how precisely he has described the nation of the Ishmaelites—that is, the Saracens. They live in tents; wherever night has driven them, there they establish their dwellings. They possess herds, flocks, and camel herds; they have neither doors nor bars. For they do not live in cities but in the wilderness.

These people, then, were also destroyed by the Babylonians, because they overturned Hazor, the city that had been the capital of that nation in the desert, down to its foundations. Yet when their camel and sheep herds were captured, and their skins and tents divided by lot [*Al.* “are divided”], this did not signify the destruction of the entire nation, since as many as a hundred thousand or more dromedary camels customarily flee in a single day through the vast desert.

“All the glory of Kedar shall be removed,” he says; and when the number of the archers has been diminished, since they are especially powerful in the art of warfare, the others who have fled will remain.

Now that we understand what Kedar is, and what Arabia and Hazor are, let us see what the prophet Isaiah says: “In the thicket you shall spend the night toward evening, on the paths of Dodanim.”

The word *ARAB* (ערב), as we have often said, is used for “evening,” “Arabia,” “raven,” “plain,” and “West.” [Note: [Col. 0194D] See a little above, in chapter 15, col. 188.] Instead of what we have translated according to the Septuagint—“you shall spend the night”—it can be interpreted as “you shall remain” or “you shall dwell,” that is, αὐλισθήσεσθε, which in Hebrew is called *THALINU* (תלינו). *DODANIM* (דדנים) likewise is translated as “near ones” and “kinsmen.”

Thus it is now foretold to the Jews who might have escaped the Babylonian siege and crossed from the devastation of the entire province into the neighboring desert that they would dwell in the solitude of Arabia, on the road that leads to their brothers.

Then the discourse turns again to the Ishmaelites and exhorts them to mercy: “Run, and meet your weary brothers and those endangered by the heat of thirst with water. For the sun’s heat is so intense that, unless you come to their aid, they will perish in the desert. Bring not only water but also bread to the fugitives, so that those whom the siege has exhausted may be restored by your compassion.”

At the same time he gives the reason why he commands this, saying: “They have fled the Babylonian sword; they have fled the bows of the Elamites; they have fled the imminent battle. Do not despise the wretched: your own captivity will soon come.”

For just as the year of a hired laborer passes swiftly, and he considers all his labor brief while he hastens toward the wage he desires, so all the glory of the sons of Kedar shall be taken from you; your arrows shall be shattered, and only a small number of warriors shall remain.

Some wish to infer from the words “still within one year” and “all the glory of Kedar shall be removed” that the prophecy concerns not the Babylonian captivity, of which Jeremiah also speaks, but the Assyrians, who, after one year of Judah’s devastation, pursued the Saracens over a very wide area.

Moreover, concerning the passage that we have translated, “You who inhabit the land of the South, meet the fugitive with bread,” they assert that the Hebrew can be read as follows: “Those who inhabit the land of the South met the fugitive with bread.” Thus, when God had said to them, “Meet the thirsty with water,” they brought bread with hostile intent, without water, so that food might increase their thirst [*Al.* “so that they might increase their thirst”].

### (Chapter 22.—Verse 1.) The oracle concerning the Valley of Vision

The Septuagint, although the word is not found in the Hebrew, translated more explicitly “the word of the valley of Sion” [Note: [Col. 0195D] In the Vatican manuscript: “the word of the valley of the vision of Sion.”]

For this is the city that is the seedbed of the prophets, in which the Temple was built and the visions of the Lord were multiplied. Since, therefore, it is placed among the other nations and counted as one among the many, it is by no means called a mountain, in accordance with the prophetic statement: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Sion above all the tents of Jacob” (Ps. 86:1). Rather, it is called a valley because it has been humbled.

Jeremiah expresses the same thing in other words. When he received the cup full of wine, he gave it to all the nations and finally extended it to Jerusalem, so that she might drink, vomit, fall, and rage, signifying that she too was to be devastated by the Babylonians (Jer. 25). The historical account in Kings and Jeremiah relates this more fully.

From this we understand that the Creator of all is equally God and governs all things by the same judgment, in accordance with what he himself says through Amos: “Are you not like the sons of the Ethiopians to me, O sons of Israel? says the Lord. Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, and the Philistines from Cappadocia, and the Syrians from Cyrene? Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon the sinful kingdom” (Amos 9:7). So that the Jews would not think that they possessed a privilege of merit because they had been led out of Egypt, he also says that the other nations had been transferred by his authority to other lands.

What is the matter with you also, that you have gone up—all of you—to the rooftops, a city full of shouting, a populous city, an exultant city?

A Hebrew told me that the present Vision does not concern the time when Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem and carried Zedekiah, bound and deprived of his eyes, to Babylon, but rather the time of Sennacherib, when Shebna the high priest betrayed a large part of the city, and only Sion—that is, the citadel and the Temple—and the nobles remained. This was like the city of Rome, which, when the Gauls attacked, preserved its patricians and the flower of its youth in the citadel.

We, however, can also interpret it of the Babylonian captivity, although Eusebius refers everything to the coming of Christ and thinks that it was fulfilled in the time of Vespasian and Titus. Let us therefore take up each point, briefly touching upon a threefold interpretation.

“What is the matter with you also?” What do you have, he says, O Sion, that you too have gone up—all of you—to the rooftops? When he says “you too,” he shows that the others had gone up first. Have you also been counted among the nations, which are besieged by enemies and climb onto rooftops filled with the howling and lamentation of miserable women—once a royal city?

### (Verse 3.)

Your slain were not slain by the sword, nor did they die in battle. All your princes fled together; they were bound with harsh bonds. All who were found were bound together; they fled far away.

If you refer this to the time of Sennacherib, when the city was captured in part, they are rightly said not to have been defeated by the sword or killed in battle, but by treachery: some fled from the city, while others, whom the enemy overtook, were bound in chains.

But if it refers to the Babylonian captivity, which is also the more truthful interpretation, we shall say that they were overcome not in battle but by siege.

If, following Eusebius, you wish to understand it tropologically of the coming of Christ, you will say that they were killed not by the sword but by unbelief; that all their princes withdrew from God and were bound by the cords of their sins; and that there was no one among the Pharisees who was not bound in the nets of the devil.

### (Verse 4.)

Therefore I said, “Move away from me; I shall weep bitterly. Do not press upon me in order to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people.”

If the Prophet laments the devastation of Babylon with the emotion of one mourning and says, “Distress has seized me, like the distress of a woman in labor; I have collapsed when I heard it; I was troubled when I saw it; my heart withered; darkness stupefied me. Babylon, my beloved, has been made a terror to me,” how much more, now, amid the ruin of his own city, can he accept no consolation, surrendering himself wholly to lamentation?

### (Verse 5.)

For the Lord God of hosts has appointed a day of slaughter, trampling, and weeping in the Valley of Vision.

In accordance with the threefold understanding, he gives the reasons why he said, “Move away from me; I shall weep bitterly”: because Sion, once a mountain of visions, has been trampled down and has now become a valley of tears.

### (Verse 6.)

He examines the wall, and the magnificent one upon the mountain; Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of the mounted man, and the shield stripped the wall bare.

The army of Babylon is described as entering the city, occupying the Temple, and advancing proudly through the streets with chariots. The fact that the shield, which ordinarily covers other things, stripped bare the gilded doorposts and the walls clad in marble veneers is elegantly expressed in Hebrew. The sense is especially beautiful: the shield did not protect anyone but stripped everything bare, because all the wealth was torn away through the strength of the soldiers.

But if the Elamites are placed in the battle—and Elam is a city of the Assyrians—the passage cannot refer to the time of Rome’s destruction, unless perhaps we interpret everything allegorically.

### (Verses 7–9.)

And your chosen valleys shall be full of chariots, and the horsemen shall station themselves at the gate. The covering of Judah shall be removed, and on that day you shall see the armory of the House of the Forest; you shall see the breaches of the city of David, because they have multiplied.

He plainly describes the captivity that took place in the eleventh year of King Zedekiah. Jeremiah also speaks of it:

> Behold, I shall summon all the families of the kingdoms of the North, says the Lord, and they shall come, and each one shall set up his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and against all its surrounding walls (Jer. 1:15).

So that we would not think this was foretold in words but not fulfilled in deed, the same Jeremiah says:

> In the eleventh year of Zedekiah, in the fourth month, on the fifth day of the month, the city was opened, and all the princes of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the middle gate (Jer. 39:2).

At that time an innumerable army was poured out around the city of Jerusalem; the Holy of Holies was opened; the armory, which had been planted in a wooded place, was exposed to hostile plundering; and, when the walls had been breached throughout the city, the enemy entered.

### (Verses 10–11.)

And you gathered the waters of the lower pool; you counted the houses of Jerusalem; and you demolished houses to fortify the wall. You made a pool between the two walls [Note: [Col. 0197D] Another reading: “to the water,” preferred by Victor.] and the water of the old pool; but you did not look to him who made it, nor did you see from afar its creator.

He explains how they prepared the city for the siege: they transferred the waters of the lower pool, which could be captured, to the upper and more strongly fortified position [Note: [Col. 0197D] The Vatican manuscript: “they transferred them to the upper and more strongly fortified position”]; after demolishing the houses, they built walls; and they counted, by each family, how much water each house ought to receive. They made a cistern between the two walls and restored the old pool for preserving the water.

Yet they did not rather invoke the help of God, who was the city’s founder and the lord of the pool—as though he had said in other words: “You placed your trust in man, and not in God, who is the maker of man.”
