Some, according to mystical interpretations, understand the old pool as the shadow of the Law; and the pool built between the two walls—that is, between the New and Old Testaments—as the pool constructed by the traditions and commandments of the Pharisees, which cannot hold water. They say that these people did not look to the Son of God, nor believe in his presence, whom they had not seen in former times, because they had always been unbelieving toward God’s commandments.

### (Verses 12–14.)

And on that day the Lord God of hosts called for weeping, lamentation, baldness, and the wearing of sackcloth. But behold, joy and gladness: killing calves, slaughtering rams, eating meat, and drinking wine—“Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.” And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: “This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die,” says the Lord God of hosts.

While the captivity was present and Jerusalem was under siege, when the sword, famine, and thirst were pressing upon the city, Jeremiah summoned the people to repentance (Jer. 34). But, on the contrary, the kings, princes, and miserable common people surrendered themselves, in the desperation of those who were perishing, to feasting.

Nothing, however, so offends God as a neck lifted up after sins and contempt born of despair. Amos also says this: “For three and four transgressions I shall not turn him away”—that is, because he both conceived and committed the sin, did not repent, and moreover taught evil. Hence it is also said here: “This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die” (Amos 1:4).

Allegorical interpreters think that this was foretold concerning the Passion of Christ: that even after the crucifixion of the Lord and Savior, God called the wretched people to repentance, yet they nevertheless gave themselves over to despair and pleasure.

They refer the beginning of this Vision, where it says, “a city full of shouting, a populous city, an exultant city,” to the time when the people, stirred up by the Pharisees, cried out with a common voice against Jesus: “Crucify, crucify such a man; we have no king except Caesar” (John 19:6–7).

The Apostle also used the example of this testimony when writing to the Corinthians about the resurrection: “If the dead are not raised, let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. 15:32).

### (Verses 15 ff.)

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Go, enter to the one who dwells in the tent, to Shebna, the steward of the Temple, and say to him: “What are you doing here? Or who are you here, that you have hewn out a tomb for yourself here? You have hewn out a memorial for yourself on the height; you have carefully made yourself a dwelling in the rock.”

Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away; as a rooster is carried away, so he will lift you up like a garment. He will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will throw you into a broad and spacious land. There you shall die, and there shall be the chariots of your glory—the disgrace of your lord’s house.

And I shall drive you out from your station and remove you from your office.

And on that day I shall call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah. I shall clothe him in your tunic and strengthen him with your belt, and I shall place your authority in his hand. He shall be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah.

And I shall place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder. He shall open, and no one shall shut; he shall shut, and no one shall open.

I shall fix him like a peg in a secure place, and he shall become a throne of glory for the house of his father. They shall hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house, vessels of every kind: every small vessel, from the vessels of mixing bowls to every kind of musical vessel.

On that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in a secure place shall be removed; it shall be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it shall perish, for the Lord has spoken.

Above we said that Shebna was the high priest who betrayed the city to the Assyrians. [Note: [Col. 0198D] Eusebius says: “The Hebrew therefore said that Somnas had become high priest, a certain voluptuary and a man of immoral life, so as even to betray the people,” etc.] But since this belongs to Hebrew tradition and Scripture does not say so, let us understand him as proud, arrogant, and pleasure-loving, trampling peoples under his feet; and because he did everything that the Prophet describes, let us understand that his priesthood was transferred to Eliakim son of Hilkiah, so that, once Shebna had been expelled, a new high priest might be appointed.

From this we understand that pride must be avoided with every effort. It offends God and cannot be protected even by the privilege of the high priesthood.

This is the Shebna—and, as some think, the Eliakim—of whom the same Prophet later says:

> The king of Assyria sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to King Hezekiah with a great army. He stood by the conduit of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, went out to him, together with Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder (Isa. 36:2 ff.).

The Prophet is therefore commanded to enter to the high priest who, according to the Septuagint, lived in a *pastophorium*; according to Aquila, in a tent. Following the Hebrew truth, Theodotion says instead: “Enter to this Socen,” which can be interpreted as “equitable” and “upright”—so that, by irony (*κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν*), he may be understood as wicked and perverse—to the high priest of the Temple.

And you shall say to him: “You who dwell in the house of God, whose crimes are raging throughout the entire city, why are you secure in your deeds, as though you did not fear captivity? You have hewn out a tomb for yourself in the rock and built it so proudly that ambition would follow you even in death.

Hear what sentence the Lord has passed against you: just as a rooster is carried away on the shoulder of its bearer, and each person lifts his cloak upon his shoulder, so your transfer into captivity will be easy.

You shall have a crown not of a golden plate and the Lord’s sanctification, but of tribulation and distress. For just as a ball, when thrown down a slope, cannot remain still but rolls on with swift motion, so you shall be taken down to a very broad land. We may understand this as Egypt or the fields of Babylonia. There you shall die; and there shall be the chariots of your glory, all the powers and riches upon which you now rely as you walk.

There you shall experience the disgrace of the house of your lord, because you shall suffer these things on account of your evil deeds and the violation of the Temple of your God.

I shall draw you down from your rank and cast you out of the office of the high priesthood. In your place I shall clothe Eliakim my servant, son of Hilkiah, in your garments and adorn him with your belt, just as Eleazar was clothed in the garments of Aaron his father.

To him I shall give authority over the Temple. He will have a people subject to him not as slaves but loving him as a son. He will receive the key of my house and carry it upon his shoulder; he will possess authority over all the ceremonies.

And just as, when a peg is fixed in the wall of the Temple and placed in a most secure position, all the vessels of the priests and Levites—both those necessary for sacrifices and those of every kind of music—are hung upon it, so the entire people will depend upon the authority of Eliakim my servant.”

But when he says, “On that day the peg that had been fixed in a secure place shall be removed; it shall be broken and fall, and what had hung upon it shall perish,” many refer this to Shebna: once Eliakim has been fixed as a peg, the former peg that had been fixed falls.

But since it follows, “What had hung upon it shall perish,” and this did not happen when Shebna was deposed, we understand the statement to mean that, after Shebna was removed, Eliakim received the high priesthood, whose priestly dignity was overturned by the final captivity.

Those who understand everything according to *anagoge* wish to say that in Shebna’s priesthood the priesthood of the Jews fell, while in the succession of Eliakim—whose name means “God rising again”—the sacraments of evangelical worship are signified. Thus the following passage, “On that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fixed in a secure place shall be removed, and it shall be broken and fall,” pertains to the ruin of the former people.

No one doubts, whether according to the historical or the allegorical interpretation, that since he had spoken of a peg, the metaphor is preserved in the hanging of vessels of various kinds, and that when the former vessels are broken, others are hung in their place.

### (Chapter 23.—Verse 1.) The oracle concerning Tyre

Howl, ships of the sea, because the house from which they used to come has been devastated; the land of Cethim has revealed it to them. Be silent, you who inhabit the island; the merchants of Sidon have crossed the sea.

The prophet Ezekiel explains more clearly and fully both the overthrow of Tyre and the reasons for its overthrow, saying:

> Son of man, because Tyre said concerning Jerusalem, “Aha! The gates of the nations are broken; she has turned toward me; I shall be filled; she has been laid waste,” therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I am against you, Tyre, and I shall bring many nations up against you, as the sea brings up its waves; I shall destroy the walls of Tyre and demolish its towers, and I shall scrape away its dust from it (Ezek. 26:2 ff.).

Which nations these are—those that will flood Tyre like a surging sea—he names explicitly later:

> Behold, I shall bring against Tyre Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the North, the king of kings, with horses, chariots, horsemen, and a great assembly and people. Your daughters who are in the countryside he shall kill with the sword. He shall surround you with fortifications; he shall bring up a ramp around you; he shall raise a shield against you; he shall set up siegeworks and battering rams against your walls; he shall demolish your towers with his weapons—and the rest that follows to the end of the vision.

In another prophecy, also directed against the Egyptians, the same Scripture adds:

> Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon made his army perform great service against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder rubbed bare, yet no compensation was given to him or to his army from Tyre (Ezek. 29).

By this he signifies that the Babylonian army carried earth for a ramp over a long period, so that what Alexander later did by joining the island to the mainland, Nebuchadnezzar had earlier attempted to do (Quintus Curtius, book 4).

Just as above we read God’s threats against Babylon, the Philistines, Moab, Egypt, Edom, and the Ishmaelites because they had mocked the captivity of his people, so now a prophecy is composed against Tyre, which was hostile to Jerusalem and mocked its overthrow, declaring that Tyre too would be destroyed by the same enemy.

Let us read the histories of the Greeks, especially those who describe the wars of the Assyrian nation. There we find that after the captivity of Jerusalem, the Philistines, Arabs, Damascenes, and subsequently the Egyptians were overthrown.

That these nations, and especially Tyre, had always attacked Israel and rejoiced in its destruction is explained by the prophet Amos at the beginning of his book (Amos 1). The Psalmist briefly declares the same thing while singing praise to God:

> O God, who is like you? Do not be silent or restrained, O God. For behold, your enemies have sounded forth, and those who hate you have raised their heads. Against your people they have devised an evil plan and plotted against your saints. They said, “Come, let us destroy them from the nation, and let the name of Israel be remembered no more.” For they have conspired unanimously; together they have made a covenant against you: the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon and Amalek, foreigners together with the inhabitants of Tyre (Ps. 82:1 ff.).

From all this we learn that the weight of God’s anger came upon Tyre, the harlot, who here is described under the figure of a prostitute and in Ezekiel under the image of a ship (Ezek. 26).

“Howl, ships of the sea,” he says. Instead of this, the Septuagint reads “ships of Carthage,” while the Hebrew has *THARSIS* (תרשיש). I have discussed this in the prophet Jonah and in a certain letter [Note: [Col. 0201D] Letter 37 in our recension, to Marcella, section 2. The *Book of Hebrew Questions* on Genesis 10:4, note, should also be consulted. Finally, Procopius, on this passage of Isaiah, concerning the name that the ancient interpreters translated as Χετιείμ, says: “It is said that Cyprus is signified in this way, and that Citium is a city in it. They say that Cyprus is signified in this way, and that the city of Citium is located there.”]

Since Carthage is a colony of the Tyrians, we can understand *Tharsis* in the present passage not as the sea in general but also as Carthage. It is not, however, the case that ships come to Tyre from Africa, or from the land of Cethim, which some interpret as Cyprus. Even today there is among them the city of Citium, from which Zeno, the founder of the Stoic sect, came.

Nevertheless, most of our writers, and especially the beginning of the Book of Maccabees, think that Cethim refers to the islands of Italy and Macedonia. For Scripture records that Alexander, king of the Macedonians, came forth from the land of Cethim.

In calling it an island, the text also speaks truthfully: afterward, whether by Nebuchadnezzar or by Alexander, it was joined to the mainland, because, for the purpose of conquering it, many embankments were carried into the narrow strait within a short time.

He also calls it “the commerce of Sidon,” in accordance with the following verse, where he says: “Be ashamed, Sidon.” For history relates that Tyre was a colony of Sidon.

### (Verse 3.)

Those crossing the sea have filled you; the seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river, its produce.

That Tyre rejoices in commerce and is the marketplace of the whole world is demonstrated both by the present age and by Ezekiel, who describes it at length. No one doubts that merchants cross the seas while transporting their goods. Nor does the city itself possess as much wealth from the land of its own region—which is very narrow and hemmed in by the territories of Galilee and Damascus—as it obtains from the transport of ships.

All the produce of the Nile and the fertility of Egypt pour into Tyre from nearby.

Instead of “Nile,” the Hebrew reads *SIOR* (שיחור). The Septuagint and Theodotion interpreted the word as “merchants.” The word means “turbid,” and thus signifies the waters of the Nile, as Jeremiah testifies: “What have you and Egypt to do, that you drink the waters of Geon?” (Jer. 2:18). In the Hebrew, instead of Geon, it has *Sior*, that is, “turbid.”

### (Verse 4.)

Be ashamed, Sidon, for the sea has spoken—the strength of the sea has said: “I have not labored in childbirth, nor given birth; I have not nourished young men, nor raised virgins to maturity.”

I said above that Tyre is a colony of the Sidonians. Hear, therefore, mother, all the seas crying out together against your daughter, uttering, in a certain sense, a voice, although by nature they cannot speak: “In vain did I gather wealth; without purpose I brought riches from the whole world into Tyre. That city was rich, luxurious, and once rejoiced in the multitude of peoples. There crowds of mortals were born, throngs of children and companies of young people; its streets once resounded with the games of virgins, infants, youths, and girls. Now it has been reduced to solitude.”

It is customary for personification (*προσωποποιΐα*) to be made from things that are mute [Note: [Col. 0202D] I read “mute,” although the manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have hitherto preferred “many.” I am surprised that so obvious an error has lasted so long.]

### (Verse 5.)

When the report is heard in Egypt, they shall grieve when they hear about Tyre.

The meaning is clear: after the Egyptians hear that a most powerful neighboring nation has been destroyed by a long siege, they will know that destruction is also drawing near to them.

### (Verse 6.)

Cross over the seas; howl, you who inhabit the island.

Again, instead of “sea” and *Tharsis*, the Septuagint translated “Carthage.” We read in the histories of the Assyrians that, after the Tyrians under siege saw no hope of escape, they boarded ships and fled to Carthage, or to other islands of the Ionian and Aegean seas.

Hence Ezekiel also says: “No compensation was given to him or to his army from Tyre” (Ezek. 29), because all the wealth of the city had been transported away [*Al.* “has been transported away”], and the nobles and others had abandoned it empty [Note: [Col. 0202D] Previously: “and the nobles also,” which is less correct and contrary to the manuscript evidence.]

### (Verse 7.)

Is this not your city, which gloried from former days, in its antiquity?

He accuses Tyre of pride because it gloried in the antiquity of its origin and did not look to God. Recalling the names of its ancestors, it thought itself eternal.

Its own feet shall carry it far away to dwell as a stranger.

He refers to those who had remained in the city and were led captive to Babylon.

### (Verse 8.)

Who planned this against Tyre, once crowned?

Read Ezekiel again (Ezek. 27), and from the lamentation over its prince you will learn how great Tyre’s glory was. He calls it “crowned” because, just as a king among a great multitude of people raises his diadem-adorned head, so Tyre, shining and exalted in wealth and gleaming with gold, gems, silk, and purple, was regarded as queen among all the nations.

Its merchants were princes; its traders were renowned throughout the earth.

We are astonished that Pyrrhus’ envoy once said of the city of Rome, “I have seen a city of kings.” Behold, long before that time, the merchants and traders of Tyre are described as princes and renowned men, so that the greatness of its wealth may be shown by this: a merchant of Tyre could, in another’s words, be a king.

### (Verse 9.)

The Lord of hosts planned this, to bring down the pride of all glory and to reduce all the renowned men of the earth to disgrace.

Above, in the manner of one asking a question, he had said: “Who planned this against Tyre, once crowned?” Now he answers himself: “It was not that the threads of fate, as fools think, had been spun in this way; it was not that the wheel of fortune had run its course. It was accomplished by the judgment and will of God himself, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble” (James 4). He admonishes the arrogant concerning their condition, so that through misery they may learn his power, whose mercy they had been unwilling to recognize through benefits.

### (Verse 10.)

Cross through your land like a river, daughter of the sea; you no longer have a girdle.

“As a river,” he says—or, as the Hebrew expresses it more precisely, “a stream,” for this is called *IOR* (יאור)—“is easily crossed on foot, so you too, having been led into captivity, shall cross your land, O daughter of the sea,” either because you are an island or because it was said above concerning you: “The sea, the strength of the sea, said, ‘I have not labored in childbirth, nor given birth.’”

As for what follows, “You no longer have a girdle,” Symmachus makes the meaning clearer: “You will no longer be able to resist.” That is, you will have neither strength nor loins girded for battle, so that you can oppose your adversaries.

### (Verse 11.)

He stretched out his hand over the sea; he troubled kingdoms.

Who stretched out his hand? From the context of the discourse there can be no doubt that it was God, of whom he said above: “The Lord of hosts planned this, to bring down the pride of all glory.”

He therefore stretched out his hand over all the seas, signifying the world and the whole inhabited earth, and he troubled all the nations, among whom you too, Tyre, have been troubled—or over the sea on which you are situated in particular.

### (Verse 12.)

The Lord commanded against Canaan, to crush its strong ones.

He shows what sea it was over which the Lord stretched out his hand when he says, “He commanded against Canaan.” For Tyre was founded in the land of Canaan.

Read the Scriptures, and especially the Gospel (Mark 7), where the Syrophoenician woman, interceding for her daughter, comes from the land of Canaan and is called a Canaanite woman.

At the same time, because he had said, “He stretched out his hand,” lest you think that the Lord acted through bodily limbs and a physical function, he added, “He commanded,” so that God’s action might be understood as his command.

### (Verse 13.)

And he said: “You shall no longer continue to glory, enduring oppression, virgin daughter of Sidon. Rise up in Cethim and cross over; there too you shall have no rest.”

The God who planned to bring down the pride of all glory, who commanded against Canaan to crush its strong ones, himself says: “You shall by no means glory any longer or trust in your own power.”

O virgin daughter of Sidon—that is, colony of the Sidonians—you will indeed flee by ship to the islands of the West, or to Cyprus and the other lands of Macedonia and Greece; but there too, because God opposes you, you will not be able to find rest.

Otherwise, every wanderer and exile throughout the world, with uncertain dwelling places, is always in distress and continually in sorrow [Note: [Col. 0203] Previously: “always in distress, continually in sorrow.” We have often corrected similar errors from the manuscripts.]

### (Verses 13–14)

“Behold, the land of the Chaldeans: such a people did not exist. Assyria founded it for captivity; they led away its strong men, dug up its houses, and reduced it to ruin. Howl, ships of the sea, because your stronghold has been devastated.”

Since above he had said, “Her feet will lead her far away to wander,” and again, “Cross your land like a river,” and since the people of Tyre were divided into two groups—those who had fled and crossed over to Cyprus, and those who had remained in the city—he addresses both groups. Concerning those who had fled, he said above: “Rise up, cross over to Cyprus; there also you will have no rest.” Concerning those who had remained and were led into captivity, he says: “Behold, the inhabitants of the land of the Chaldeans, whose power no people previously possessed, and which was founded by the Assyrian: they have led away the strong men of Tyre. They dug up not only the walls but also all the dwellings of the city, and reduced it to ruin.”

Since, therefore, some fled and others were captured, “Howl, ships,” whether of the sea or of Carthage; for your commerce and colony have been destroyed. At the same time, consider how he praised the Chaldeans. He did not say, “Such a people will no longer exist,” for the Roman kingdom is more powerful and more formidable; rather, he said, “There was no such people before.” Whoever denied the former has conceded what follows.

### (Verse 15)

“And it will come to pass on that day that you, O Tyre, will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king.”

From this point to the end of this prophecy, favorable things are announced concerning Tyre: that it must do penance, that it is to be rebuilt, and that the destruction of Tyre will last only seventy years—the same period during which the temple of God was desolate—so that the time of its ruin may imitate the ruin that Tyre had mocked.

Many think that the seventy years of one king mean Nabuchodonosor, during which the rule of the Assyrian nation persisted in Jerusalem. Others understand it as a general statement: whoever has had a long period of reigning cannot exceed seventy years.

### (Verse 16)

“After seventy years Tyre will be like the song of a prostitute. Take up the lyre, go around the city, prostitute delivered over to oblivion; sing well, repeat your song, so that you may be remembered.”

Because you prostituted yourself with many nations, and because your former lovers despised you when you had been left desolate, naked, and filthy with the squalor of captivity, now take up the lyre, repeat your songs, go around the city, mourn your former brothel, and wash away the traces of your ancient error with tears, so that you may be able to call forth God’s mercy upon yourself.

### (Verse 17)

“And it will come to pass that, after seventy years, the Lord will visit Tyre and restore her to her commerce; and she will again prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the earth upon the face of the earth.”

That all these things were fulfilled according to the historical account is indicated by the concordant testimony of Greek and Phoenician writings: after being restored following seventy years, Tyre returned to her former power and became the commercial center of all nations. I think that these commercial dealings are called “prostitutions,” because, just as one who prostitutes herself enters a brothel and receives the price of her shame, so the trader, coming together from the whole world, filled the beauty of the city, as though she were a prostitute.

### (Verse 18)

“And her commerce and her wages will be consecrated to the Lord; they will not be stored up or laid away.”

[Note: Victorius thinks that this passage is corrupt and that, according to his five manuscripts, it should read *mercedes* (“wages”) instead of *merces* (“goods”), both here and in Jerome’s commentary.]

“For those who dwell before the Lord, her commerce will be that they may eat to satiety and be clothed even into old age.”

[Note: Martianus had read: “Her wages will be her commerce,” and so forth. We have removed the word *merces* from this place under the compulsion of the Vatican manuscript and of the very text of Scripture, which recognizes that word here neither in the Hebrew nor in the Greek or Latin versions.]

According to the historical sense, we do not yet find these things fulfilled—unless perhaps one should think that, after the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the restoration of Tyre, the two cities became friendly with one another and Tyre frequently sent gifts to the temple of God. Thus in Ezra we read (Ezra 13:16) that he drove away the Tyrians who sold fish on the Sabbath and did not allow them to enter the city; and from this single instance of commerce it may be judged that the same applied to other matters.

The Jews defer these empty hopes to the future, asserting that these things will be fulfilled during the thousand years after the Antichrist. It is not surprising that they fabricate such things, since, having rejected the truth of Christ, they are going to receive the Antichrist, the instrument of the devil; even Christians who Judaize maintain that these words refer to the blessedness of the thousand years.

But just as in the vision of Babylon I understand the time of the consummation under the figure of its overthrow; and in Egypt, where the idols have been destroyed and an altar of the Lord has been established, I refer the passage to the time of Christ; and in the vision of Moab I recognize the throne of the Savior set up in its land; and in all the other visions, including those concerning Damascus, I do not doubt that the mysteries belong to our own times—so also, in the vision of Tyre, which is the final one, I interpret the period of Christian blessedness. After Tyre has been rebuilt and has recovered its former condition, and every merchant has entered its harbor according to the old custom, their goods and their labor will be dedicated to the Lord.

[Note: Eusebius had written: “This is indeed also being fulfilled in our own time, for the church of God has been established in the city of the Tyrians. Just as among the other nations, much of what is obtained from the commerce conducted there is sanctified to the Lord when it is offered to his church, and those who bring these things offer them with reverence . . . namely, to the attendants of the altar.”]

Let us see the churches of Christ built in Tyre; let us consider the wealth of all, which is neither stored up nor hoarded, but is given to those who dwell before the Lord, who serve at the altar and share in the altar (1 Cor. 9). The Tyrians minister not for riches or to accumulate the wealth of priests, but to provide what is necessary for sustenance, so that, according to the Apostle, having food and clothing, we may be content with these things (1 Tim. 6).

And observe that he did not say that the commerce and goods of Tyre would be given to those who dwell in Jerusalem, as the Jews suppose, but to those who are before the Lord, who serve him. For the Lord also established that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel (1 Cor. 9). To serve the Lord and dwell before him is a matter not of place but of merit.

Up to this point we have discussed Isaiah’s visions, or the burdens that he imposed upon particular nations, as you requested and as we were able, explaining them historically and closely following the traces of the Hebrew truth. What follows concerns all nations and, in general, the consummation of the whole world. You did not ask me to write about these matters, nor was I so idle as to dictate, needlessly and in excess, things that had not been requested, when I scarcely managed to write what had been requested.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0205]

[Col. 0205C] 233–234

What I promised in the preceding volume—that upon the foundations of history, if Christ should grant our desire, I would construct a spiritual building and, when its summit had been placed, display the ornaments of the perfected Church—I shall endeavor to do in the following two books, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium, through your prayers and the Lord’s mercy. With the same labor by which the fifth book embraced the historical sense, the sixth and seventh will touch upon the spiritual interpretation (*anagoge*), not discussing everything lest the volumes become too numerous, but briefly indicating what ecclesiastical men before us have thought.

### (Chapter 13, verse 1)

“The burden, or vision, against Babylon, which Isaiah son of Amoz saw.”

He saw, not with the eyes of the flesh but with those of the mind, how great and weighty a burden was to be imposed upon Babylon. Since Babylon, which in Hebrew is called BABEL (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source), is interpreted as “confusion”—because there the language of those building the tower was confused—the present world is understood spiritually, for it is “set in the evil one” and confounds not only the languages but also the works and minds of individuals.

The true Nabuchodonosor is the king of this Babylon, boasting against the Lord. He says in his heart:

“I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne. I will sit upon the mountain of the Covenant, on the sides of the north. I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.”

This is the one who showed the Lord all the kingdoms of the world and said to him: “All these things have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

Accordingly, in what follows the threat is not at all against Babylon but against the whole world. The Lord of hosts commanded a most warlike nation to come from a distant land, from the summit of heaven, to destroy the whole world. And again: “Behold, the day comes, incurable in fury and wrath, to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it.” Then: “I will command evil against the entire world, and their sins against the impious.” From these statements it is proved that everything said against Babylon pertains to the confusion and destruction of this world.

### (Verse 2)

“Raise a signal upon the dark mountain, or upon the plain.”

The command is given to the Apostles, to apostolic men, and to teachers of the churches: when they are going to fight against Babylon, they must raise the sign of the Lord’s cross—not in a low place or in sunken valleys, but upon a dark mountain or upon a plain.

The first expression signifies the hidden mysteries of the Church. In order to see them and hear God’s voice, Moses entered darkness and thick gloom. “He made darkness his hiding place; and clouds and thick darkness were around him” (Ps. 17:12).

The second teaches that we must climb to the heights of ecclesiastical doctrines in such a way that, according to the Apostle Paul, we humble ourselves and say: “I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9). He himself also raised the signal upon a plain mountain when, with the humility inherent in him, he said: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

This is also the signal that he will raise above—the one who sprang from the root of Jesse among the nations, in order to gather the lost of Israel.

“Raise your voice; lift up your hand.”

For this the Septuagint translated: “Comfort the hand.”

[Note: “Comfort the hand.” From this point to “Lord of hosts,” the text of the Septuagint had lost its proper place in the previously printed books. We have restored it with the utmost care, in accordance with all the manuscript codices. Martianus.]

He raises his voice who speaks of heavenly things and despises present realities as brief and transitory. He hears from the same Isaiah: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem.”

He lifts up his hand who can say with David: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2); and who lifts up holy hands in every place, so that he not only raises his hands but also comforts with his hand—so that he does not say to the poor, “Come tomorrow and receive,” but consoles his poverty and need through present mercy.

“And let the leaders enter the gates.”

The Septuagint: “Open, rulers.”

The leaders of the Church enter the gates of God’s mysteries and learn the secrets of the Scriptures. They possess the key of knowledge so that they may open them to the peoples entrusted to them. Therefore the command is given that the teachers open and the disciples enter.

### (Verse 3)

“I have commanded my sanctified ones.”

For this the Septuagint reads: “I will command, and I will bring them.”

For he himself sanctifies his ministers, so that both the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified may all be from one source. In another place also he speaks to believers: “Be holy, because I too am holy”; he himself commands and will bring his leaders, so that they may do what has been commanded (Lev. 19:2).

“And I have called my strong men in my wrath, rejoicing in my glory.”

The Septuagint: “Giants are coming to fulfill my fury, rejoicing together and committing outrage.”

According to the Hebrew, these words are joined to what precedes: he himself has called his strong men, rejoicing in his glory, he who had commanded his sanctified ones.

According to the Septuagint, however, the giants who come to fulfill the Lord’s fury, rejoicing and exulting in another’s injury, must be understood as evil and opposing powers. Concerning them we also read in the Psalms: “He sent upon them the fury of his anger, wrath and indignation and distress, a sending through evil angels” (Ps. 77:49).

Among these is the destroyer in Egypt, who did not dare enter the houses whose doorposts had been smeared with the blood of the lamb (Exod. 12); and that spirit who went forth, stood before the Lord, and said: “I will deceive Ahab.” The Lord said to him: “You will deceive him and prevail; go out and do so” (1 Kings 22:21–22).

Therefore, in the same book of Kings, Micaiah said: “I saw the Lord of Israel sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven stood around him on his right and on his left” (ibid. 22:19).

The powers on the right are those angels who are sent for good purposes; those on the left are the ones to whom we are handed over for punishment. Hence the Apostle also says: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

The name “giants,” for which the Hebrew has GEBORIM (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source), that is, “strong ones,” the Septuagint and Theodotion translated in the manner of gentile fables, just as they name Sirens, Titans, Arcturus, the Hyades, and Orion—figures who among the Hebrews are called by other names.

[Note: Victor reads “the Pleiades” instead of “the Hyades,” following the Greek *pleikda*, in Job 9, according to the Septuagint.]

[Note: They are called by other names. Among the Hebrews, Arcturus is called *Asch*; Orion, *Kesil*; the Hyades are called *Chima*; and “the inner parts of the south,” *Hhadre theman*. Martianus.]

[Note: “Where they translate Σειρῆνες [Sirens], the Hebrew has [blank in source]; where they translate Τιτᾶνες [Titans], the Hebrew calls Arcturus [blank in source], and Orion [blank in source]. See also Martianus, if desired.]

If the giants are rebels against God, and all heresies opposing the truth rebel against God, then all heretics are giants: they rejoice in their error and glory especially when they have insulted the Church.

[Col. 0208C] ### (Verse 5)

“The voice of a multitude in the mountains, like that of many peoples; the voice of the sound of kings of nations gathered together.”

This passage is understood in three ways.

First, after the signal has been raised upon the plain mountain, a multitude of nations comes; and once established upon the mountains, it is divided into two groups—peoples and kings, disciples and teachers—concerning whom the Savior spoke in the Gospel: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11).

It is called one voice, and harmonious, so that the apostolic saying may be demonstrated: “All say the same thing, and let there be no divisions among you, but be perfect in the same mind and in the same judgment” (1 Cor. 1:10).

Second, the pride of heretics is described. They think that they are upon mountains, raise themselves against the knowledge of God, speak iniquity on high, and set their mouths in heaven. They too have peoples and kings, who devour the people they have deceived.

The third interpretation is this: since he had said above, “Giants are coming to fulfill my fury, rejoicing together and committing outrage,” he describes the arrogance of those giants and their agreement, in the evil sense, to punish those who have been handed over to them.

“The Lord of armies has commanded the army of war, those coming from a distant land, from the summit of heaven: the Lord and the vessels of his wrath, to destroy the whole earth.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord of hosts has commanded a most warlike nation to come from a distant land, from the summit—÷ foundation ** of heaven—the Lord and his warriors, to destroy the whole inhabited world.”

“Foundation” should be marked with an obelus.

In the books of Kings and Chronicles we read (2 Kings 24; 1 Chron. 21) that God’s anger was kindled against Israel when David numbered the people and offended the Lord. In the Psalms also it is written: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger,” and similar statements. Concerning this I read in the commentaries of a certain writer—he means Basil—that God’s anger can be understood as an opposing power to which we are handed over for punishment. Concerning this also it is sung in the eighth Psalm: “That you may destroy the enemy and the avenger” (Ps. 8:2).

The warriors who come from a distant land and from the summit of heaven may also be understood as ministering angels, who will be sent at the consummation of the world to make bundles of the weeds and prepare those separated from the wheat for the eternal fire (Matt. 13).

The whole earth is also destroyed when earthly works are overthrown. There are other warriors of the Lord equipped with the Apostle’s armor who daily destroy, in the Church—which is understood as *oikoumenē*, that is, “the inhabited world”—those who rise up against the knowledge of God, and put them to death.

### (Verses 6–7)

“Howl, because the day of the Lord is near; destruction will come like devastation from the Lord. Therefore all hands will be weakened, and every human heart will melt and be crushed.”

Since the Lord’s warriors are going to come to destroy the whole earth, howl and do penance, you upon whom punishment is coming. For the day of the Lord is near—whether the consummation and judgment of the whole world, or each person’s departure from life.

A plundering comes from the Lord, which we have called “devastation” in order to preserve the metaphor, since he had mentioned warriors beforehand. When the day of judgment or of death arrives, all hands will be weakened. To them it is said elsewhere: “Strengthen the weak hands.”

Hands will be weakened because no work worthy of God’s justice will be found: “No living person will be justified in his sight” (Ps. 142:2). Hence the Prophet says in the Psalms: “If you should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could endure?” (Ps. 129:3).

Every heart—or soul—of a human being will also melt, and conscience will tremble at its sin. This is the fearful and dreadful day of which Zephaniah also speaks: “Fear before the face of the Lord, because the day of the Lord is near” (Zeph. 1:14). And again: “The great day of the Lord is near; it is near and exceedingly swift.” Amos likewise says: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord! Why do you desire the day of the Lord? It is darkness and not light” (Amos 5:18).

As for what is added according to the Septuagint—“the envoys will be disturbed, and pains will seize them”—we may understand those envoys as the citizens who had sent them against the man who had gone into a distant land to obtain a kingdom for himself (Luke 19:27). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “But bring here my enemies who did not want me to reign over them, and kill them before me.”

### (Verse 8)

“Torsions and pains will seize them; they will suffer like a woman in labor. Each one will be astonished at his neighbor; their faces will be burned.”

When the Lord’s warriors come from a distant land, and all hands have been weakened, and the heart is fearful and crushed, then *strophomata*—which we have interpreted as abdominal torsions—and pains will seize them, like the pains of women in labor.

This shows that they are tormented by their own conscience and have faces burned by the fire they themselves had kindled, because they cannot say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us” (Ps. 4:6); nor: “We all, with unveiled face, contemplating the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image” (2 Cor. 3:18).

Each one will be astonished at his neighbor when he sees him suffering the same torments by which he himself is afflicted.

### (Verse 9)

“Behold, the day of the Lord comes, cruel, full of indignation, wrath, and fury, to make the earth desolate and destroy its sinners from it.”

Instead of “earth,” the Septuagint translated *tēn oikoumenēn*, that is, “the inhabited world”; instead of “cruel,” “incurable.”

When the day of judgment or death arrives, what is written in the sixth Psalm will be fulfilled: “But in the underworld, who will confess you?” (Ps. 6:5). For that is not the time of repentance but of punishments.

Elsewhere it is said: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!” Therefore God’s abundant mercy is hidden from those who are still placed in fear and do not possess perfect love of God, so that, when they hear that the day of the Lord is cruel, incurable, and full of indignation and fury, they may cease from sinning.

The inhabited world, or the earth, will also be made desolate, and sinners will be crushed from it—though previously it had been weighed down by the burden of sinners—so that, once crimes have been erased and destroyed, justice alone may dwell and reign upon the earth.

### (Verse 10)

“For the stars of heaven and their splendor will not spread their light; the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon will not shine with its light.”

The Septuagint: “For the stars of heaven, and Orion, and all the ornament of heaven will not give [or: possess] their light; they will be darkened when the sun rises, and the moon will not give its light.”

Instead of what we translated as “their splendor,” Aquila and Theodotion undoubtedly used the Hebrew word CHISILEEM (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source).

[Note: *Chisileem*. The editions of Erasmus and Marianus corrupt the Hebrew word by reading *Cesile* without the pronominal suffix, entirely corrupting Jerome’s ancient reading *CHISILEEM*. Martianus.]

[Note: More correctly, it seems, the Vatican manuscript has *Xileem*. Recall what we noted above concerning this word, col. 172.]

For this the Septuagint translated “Orion,” adding on its own words “and all the ornament of heaven,” which should be marked with an obelus.

The fables of the gentiles say that Orion has twenty-two stars, of which four are of the third magnitude, nine of the fourth, and another nine of the fifth; others call them Bootes.

[Note: “And others call them,” etc. In printed editions and in several manuscript codices we read the singular, “who is called by others Bootes,” namely Orion, which is the subject here. Marianus Victorius, moreover, changes the following reading to: “We also read in Job, the Hyades,” and holds that “the Pleiades” should be read according to the Septuagint. But this is futile, since all the manuscript codices retain “the Hyades,” and Saint Jerome also read this way in Job 9:9: “Who makes Arcturus, Orion, and the Hyades,” etc. Martianus.]

We also read in Job of the Hyades, the Evening Star, Arcturus, and the treasures—or inner chambers—of the south (Job 9:9), concerning which we shall speak in their proper place.

Nor should we think that among the Hebrews these stars are called by the names that Greek and Latin speech convey; rather, they have their own names. For just as God called the light “day,” the firmament “heaven,” the dry land “earth,” and the gatherings of waters “seas” (Gen. 1), so he also called each individual star by its own name, though our language does not express their particular designations.

It is written elsewhere concerning God: “He numbers the multitude of the stars,” and “he calls them all by name.”

[Note: The same reading is found in the Vatican manuscript: “and he calls them all by name.”]

When, therefore, the day of the Lord comes to make the inhabited world desolate and to remove sinners from it completely (Ps. 146:4), then, in comparison with the divine majesty, the stars of heaven and all their splendor will withdraw their light.

It is not surprising to say this of the lesser stars, since even the sun is darkened at its rising, and the moon does not retain its customary brightness. But what the Septuagint translated—that the stars, Orion, and all the ornament of heaven are darkened when the sun rises—contains no sign or miracle [variant: “no sign of a miracle”]. This happens all the time: once the sun has risen, the stars in heaven are not visible.

Nor is it surprising that this is said of the sun, since, even when the moon is full and shines throughout the night, many stars do not give light. That stars are also present in the sky during the day is proved by an eclipse of the sun: when, as the philosophers argue, it is obscured by the shadow of the earth and by the intervening disk of the moon, the brighter stars become visible in the sky.

### (Verse 11)

“And I will visit the evils of the world, and their iniquities upon the impious.”

When God visits and strikes, he strikes for the purpose of correction. But when he is exceedingly angry with those who do not do penance, he says: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery” (Hos. 4:14).

Conversely, concerning those who will believe in Christ, it is said: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. 88:33).

“And I will make the pride of the unbelieving cease, and I will humble the arrogance of the strong.”

The Septuagint: “I will destroy the outrage of the wicked, and I will humble the outrage of the proud.”

The Hebrew word GAON (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source), which plainly signifies arrogance and pride, Theodotion and the Septuagint always translated as “outrage,” expressing the sense rather than the word, because every proud person is ready to commit outrage.

Therefore the Lord visits the evils of the world and their iniquities upon the impious in order to restrain the arrogance of the proud and humble the pride of the strong. For “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5:5).

And in Proverbs we read: “Before destruction a man’s heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled” (Prov. 16:18). Pride is always followed by ruin, and humility by glory: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

We read elsewhere: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Cor. 1:19). This does not mean that true wisdom and true prudence are destroyed by the Lord, but knowledge falsely so called: those who store up a tongue of deceit, who weary themselves searching deeply and find nothing, speaking iniquity on high and setting their mouths in heaven.

Hence the pride of heretics is properly called an outrage against the truth.

### (Verse 12)

“A man will be more precious than gold, and a human being than pure gold.”

The Septuagint: “Those who are left will be honored more than refined gold, and a human being will be more precious than the stone of Sophir.”

At the consummation of the world, when the inhabited world has been reduced to desolation, the sun has been darkened at its rising, and the moon has not given its light, such signs and portents will be performed by the Antichrist that, as iniquity increases, the love of many will grow cold, so that even God’s elect, if possible, may be deceived (Matt. 24:24).

Then a man will be more precious than gold, which in Hebrew is called PHAZ (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source), and which Aquila translated as *kirrhon* (κιρρόν), a substance of excellent, bloodlike color.

[Note: We read—or correct to—κιρρόν according to the Vatican manuscript, with which several other manuscripts examined by Martianus agree, preferring *Cirron* in Latin letters. Drusius had previously advised reading it this way from his old book; Aquila in fact translated it thus elsewhere also, for example in Proverbs 8:19. Jerome himself, in the book on Names, says from Jeremiah: “Ophaz is *obrizum*.” It is a kind of gold that the Greeks call κιρρόν. The etymology also agrees, since κιρρόν signifies a tawny and reddish color, like red wine. Nevertheless, Martianus mistakenly retained πύρρον.]

And a human being will be more precious than pure gold, which in Hebrew is called OPHIR (the Hebrew term is left blank in the source), and which Aquila translated as *spēlōma Ophēr* (σπήλωμα Ὀφείρ). The Septuagint, though I do not know what they meant by it, translated it as “the stone of Sophir.”

Ophir is a place in India where the finest gold is produced, just as we read in Genesis concerning the river Pishon: “This is the one that surrounds the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold; and the gold of that land is excellent; there also are a carbuncle and a green stone” (Gen. 2:11).

He is said to be more precious because he is rarer. Everything rare is precious, as we also read in the book of Samuel: “The word of the Lord was precious in Israel” (1 Sam. 3:1).

### (Verse 13)

“Because of this I will shake heaven, and the earth will be moved from its place.”

The Septuagint: “For heaven will rage, and the earth will be shaken from its foundations.”

When a man has become more precious than gold and a human being than pure gold, and what is written has been fulfilled—“When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8)—then both heaven and earth will be moved.

Heaven and earth will pass away, not by their own will or independent choice, as many suppose, believing them to be living beings, but because of the indignation of the Lord of hosts and because of the day of his fury. He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.

Therefore what is said in the Septuagint—“For heaven will rage”—must be understood *metonymically* of those who dwell in heaven, just as if we were to say, “The whole city cried out,” and “the entire city came out to meet the judge.”

We also read of the foundations of the earth in Proverbs: “God founded the earth by wisdom” (Prov. 3:19). And the Lord says to Job: “Where were you when I founded the earth?” (Job 38:4).

This does not mean that the earth has foundations sunk down as a massive structure. Rather, God’s will and power, by which all things are held together, must be called its foundations. For he founded it upon the seas, set it upon the rivers, and suspended it upon nothing (Ps. 23:2; Job 26:7).

### (Verses 14–16)

“And it will be like a doe fleeing, and like a flock of sheep, with no one to gather it. Each one will turn back to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Everyone who is found will be killed, and everyone who comes upon them will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed before their eyes; their houses will be plundered, and their wives will be violated.”

When heaven and earth have been shaken, the devil—the crooked serpent—or every doctrine opposed to the truth will flee. It is divided into teachers and disciples. The former, because of their sharpness of sight, are called *Dorcades* in Greek, that is, “wild goats”; the latter are like brute animals. Wandering here and there, they have no one to guide them, for they have lost the one of whom it is written: “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord” (Prov. 20:24).

[Note: Origen, translated into Latin by Jerome, in the second treatise on the Song of Songs: “She was called *dorcas* because she sees more sharply, that is, ὀξυδερκέστερον. See what we have noted on that passage, vol. 3, col. 528.”]

Those who have been freed from evil teachers will return to their own people, and each will flee to his own land, from which he originated. Whoever is found will be killed, or slaughtered.

This does not happen only at the consummation of the world but continues to happen in the Church to this day: when the teachers have been overcome, the deceived flock returns to its own people and its own land; and in the very fact that someone is found, he is killed, so that he may cease to be a heretic. Whoever comes upon them will fall by the spiritual sword.

Then their infants and little ones, who have not yet reached the full maturity of error, will be dashed before the eyes of their teachers. They will plunder their houses and violate their wives—that is, their corrupt wisdom and perverse doctrine.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “They will plunder their churches, and their wives will be violated by evil wisdom and perverse doctrine.”]

Therefore, for such fathers, whose little ones are to be killed, we ought to pray and say: “Give them, O Lord.” What will you give them? “A barren womb and dry breasts” (Hos. 9:14). For they gave birth to iniquity, conceived pain, and gave birth to injustice.

### (Verses 17–18)

“Behold, I will raise up the Medes against them, who will not seek silver and will not desire gold; but they will kill the little ones with arrows, they will not pity the fruit of the womb, and their eye will not spare the children.”

We find in Genesis (Gen. 10) that Madai was the founder of the nation of the Medes. His name is interpreted as “measure,” or “from the powerful,” or “from the strong.”

Therefore, against the Babylonians, who are confused in mind, ministers of punishment are raised up by the powerful and strong God, so that they may repay each according to his works. For with the measure by which they measured, it will be measured back to them. They will return into their laps a measure shaken, pressed down, full, and overflowing (Matt. 7:2; Luke 6:38).

They will receive neither silver nor gold—that is, neither the beauty of eloquence nor the sharpness of intellect in which they formerly applauded themselves—but will afflict those handed over to them with punishments. They will not pity the little ones or the fruit of the womb, so that they may show greater mercy.

Would that we too might be raised up by the Lord and receive this power, so that we might desire neither silver nor gold—neither secular eloquence nor worldly wisdom—but might kill the children of heretics and of all who have been deceived with spiritual arrows, that is, with testimonies from the Scriptures. May those nourished on the milk of error be slaughtered without any pity, so that they may perish through merciful cruelty; may we spare no infancy of theirs and be worthy of that beatitude:

“Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock!”

### (Verses 18 ff.)

And that glorious Babylon among the kingdoms, renowned in the pride of the Chaldeans, shall be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. It shall not be inhabited forever, nor shall it be founded for generation after generation; nor shall an Arab pitch his tent there, nor shall shepherds rest there. Rather, wild beasts shall rest there, and their houses shall be filled with dragons; ostriches shall dwell there, and shaggy creatures shall dance there; owls shall answer one another in its houses, and sirens in its pleasure shrines.

### (Chapter 14, verse 1)

Its time is near to come, and its days shall not be prolonged.

The Septuagint has: “And Babylon, which is called glorious, renowned, and the king of the Chaldeans, shall be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. It shall not be inhabited forever, nor shall anyone enter it for many generations; Arabs shall not pass through it, nor shall shepherds rest in it. Rather, beasts shall rest there, and its houses shall be filled with sound; sirens shall lie there, demons shall dance there, onocentaurs shall dwell there, and hedgehogs shall make their beds in their houses. It shall come quickly and shall not delay.”

What follows—“and its days shall not be prolonged”—must be marked with asterisks, because it has been added from Theodotion.

When the Medes have been roused against the city of confusion—those who count neither gold nor silver among valuable things, who kill the little ones with arrows, show no pity to nursing infants, and do not spare their eyes for the children—the once-renowned city that was in the pride of the Chaldeans, who are interpreted as meaning “demons,” shall be overthrown just as Sodom and Gomorrah were overthrown, so that no trace of its former habitation may remain there. But after there has been a new heaven and a new earth, and the form of this world has passed away (1 Cor. 7), the city of confusion shall not be inhabited forever, nor shall it ever recover the same condition.

For after it has ceased to exist in its former glory, an Arab shall not pitch his tents there. “Arab” is interpreted as “western” and “evening-dwelling,” so that he would desire to live in a place he had seen to be deserted. In the present passage, however, “Arab” is understood in a good sense: as one who is always pressing toward the end and, forgetting what lies behind, stretches forward to what lies ahead.

Nor shall shepherds rest there—those who are accustomed to feed the Lord’s most gentle flock in Jerusalem. Rather, wild beasts shall rest there, which the Psalmist detests, saying: “Do not hand over the soul confessing you to the beasts” (Ps. 73:19). In their place Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion have retained the Hebrew word itself, *SIIM* ().

“And their houses shall be filled”—that is, the houses of the Babylonians. According to the Septuagint and Theodotion, they shall be filled with ἤχου, that is, with sound and shouting; according to Aquila, with “typhoons,” which we have translated as “dragons”; according to Symmachus, with *OIIM* (), a word that is also found in the Hebrew.

“And ostriches shall dwell there,” an animal that always seeks out desolate places. It is discussed more fully in Job: although it appears to have wings, it does not rise higher from the earth. In its place the Septuagint translated σειρῆνας, that is, “sirens.”

As for the shaggy creatures, called *SIRIM* () in Hebrew, Theodotion translated the word as “those with erect and standing hair.” Symmachus and the Septuagint rendered it “demons.”

In place of “onocentaurs,” which only the Septuagint translated—imitating the stories of the pagans, who say that there were hippocentaurs—the other three translators retained the Hebrew word itself, *IIM* (), which we have translated as “owls.”

Whereas the Septuagint says, “hedgehogs shall make their beds in their houses,” the Hebrew has *THANNIM* (). Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated this as “sirens,” indicating either that they are certain kinds of beasts or, according to the pagan error, demons who sing sweetly and deceive human beings—those who cannot pass through the shipwreck of this age with their ears closed.

Moreover, the name “onocentaur,” composed from “donkey” and “centaur,” seems to me to signify those who possess some human understanding in part, but who are again drawn away by pleasures and the mire of shame into vices.

According to the tropological interpretation, therefore, it is said that at the end of the world—or at the death of each individual—all the glory and pride of the Chaldeans, and the confusion of the world, will withdraw from us. Everything will thus be overthrown just as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah; nor will the present condition of this world exist any longer, but it will perish forever.

Nor shall an Arab pitch his tents there. Of him it is said in the sixty-seventh Psalm: “Make a way for him who rides upon the setting sun; the Lord is his name” (Ps. 67:5).

Nor shall shepherds rest there—that is, the angels who preside over the human race and daily see the face of the Father. Rather, beasts and dragons, ostriches, shaggy creatures, owls, and sirens shall rest there. We understand all these beasts figuratively as angels or demons, and as those to whose punishment we are handed over.

And in the houses that were once places of pleasure, where there had been happiness and joy, let there be the mourning of owls and the lamentable voice of sirens, which leads their hearers to death.

No one who has seen Babylon daily overthrown through holy men in those who believe in the Lord will be surprised that the time of judgment is near and that the day of Babylon’s consummation is not prolonged; for, when compared with eternity, every length of time is near.

We have spoken briefly of the kinds of beasts—or rather, monsters—because in the preceding book they were treated in part according to the historical sense.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] “Toward the end of this book.”]

This too must be considered: after ecclesiastical discourse and the teaching of the Savior have overthrown the city of confusion, so that it is compared with Sodom and Gomorrah, it is not inhabited by holy men, nor do shepherds rest in it—those who were accustomed to feed Christ’s flock. Rather, beasts and dragons rest there, and ostriches and shaggy creatures dance in it.

Whatever the heretics utter in the synagogues of Satan is not the Lord’s teaching but the howling of demons and shaggy creatures, whom Esau imitated. And sirens shall rest in the shrines of pleasure, drawing souls into the depths by their sweet and deadly song, so that, while the shipwreck rages, they may be devoured by wolves and dogs.

The time of the heretics’ ruin is therefore near and presses upon us daily, and their overthrow is not delayed.

For the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will again choose Israel, and will make them rest upon their own land. The sojourner will be joined to them and will cleave to the house of Jacob. Peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them upon the Lord’s land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who had taken them captive, and will subject those who had exacted tribute from them.

And it shall be on that day, when God gives you rest from your labor, your agitation, and the hard servitude in which you previously served, that you will take up this parable against the king of Babylon and say:

In place of “sojourner,” that is, “proselyte,” the Septuagint translated γηώραν, which is called *GER* () in Hebrew. Hence I think that Moses’ son, who was a sojourner in the land, was named by his father Gershom (Exod. 1).

“Georas,” then, is a Hebrew word declined according to Greek usage, although someone ignorant of the Hebrew language tries to express a Greek etymology in it, deriving it from the fact that he cares for earthly matters.

[Note: [Col. 0215D] “It does not seem to have been formed from the Hebrew word *Ger*, but from the Syriac word *Giora*, producing *Gioras* by the addition of *s*, just as *Judas* comes from *Juda*, and similarly in other cases. From *Ger*, according to Greek usage, the form ought rather to be declined *Gera* or *Geras*. Thus Jerome here takes the Hebrew in a broader sense for the Syriac.”]

[Note: [Col. 0216D] “For γῆ,” he says, “means ‘earth,’ and ὤρα, φροντὶς means ‘care’ or ‘concern.’”]

[Note: [Col. 0216D] “Manuscript copies read *ge* with Latin letters, and *ora* and *phrontis*. Above also they retain *georas* and *gioras* indiscriminately, because this name is written γειώρας, not γηώρας, in the Septuagint. The Greek ει is represented among Latins by either *i* or *e*. MARTIAN.”]

Again, for *MASAL* (), which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as “parable”—and whom we too have followed—the Septuagint translated “lamentation.”

The order is as follows: after Babylon has been deserted forever, so that it becomes a dwelling-place of beasts, the Lord will have mercy on Jacob—that is, on the one who has supplanted vices—and will choose Israel, the one who perceives God with the mind.

Observe the precision of the words: mercy is fitted to Jacob, who is still engaged in struggle; but to Israel, who received the name after victory, not mercy but election is appropriately assigned.

He will also make them rest upon their own land, concerning which the Savior says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the land” (Matt. 5:4), and: “I believe that I shall see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

To the house of Jacob—those who were chosen through the Apostles—there will also be joined a multitude of the nations. They will take the remnant of the house of Israel and bring them to their own place, so that they may dwell in their tents; and the house of Israel will possess them upon the Lord’s land as male and female slaves.

It benefits the wicked to serve the good. Hence it is said to Esau: “You shall serve your brother”; and to Jacob: “Your brother shall serve you” (Gen. 27).

They will take captive those who had previously deceived them with sophistries, and will reduce to servitude those who do everything for the sake of profit.

But after Jacob and Israel have rested from their labor—the great labor in which they had struggled against the world and the heretics—and from their agitation and servitude, in which they had previously served evil interpretation and false doctrines, they will then take up lamentation and a parable against the king of Babylon: namely, a discourse concerning heretical error and confusion. And they will say what follows.

The Jews interpret this passage in a carnal sense, but they cannot demonstrate that it was fulfilled after they returned from Babylon. For the Babylonians did not serve those who had previously captured them; nor, after the Babylonians were defeated, did their house possess them; nor did they have them as male and female slaves.

It remains, therefore, that according to their own fables they think this will happen concerning the Roman empire: after the Romans have been conquered at the end of time, the nations that formerly served them will serve them. But if, by following the letter, they deceive themselves with a false hope, who will grant them that Rome may be called Babylon and that Nebuchadnezzar may be the king of the Roman empire?

### (Verses 5–6)

“How the exactor has ceased, how the tribute has come to rest! The Lord has broken the staff of the wicked, the rod of rulers, which struck peoples in indignation, with an incurable blow, which in fury subjected nations and cruelly persecuted them.”

In Peter’s Epistle we read: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” (1 Pet. 4:17). And in Ezekiel it is said to the executioners: “Begin with my holy ones” (Ezek. 9:6).

The order of judgment is arranged according to the diversity of sin, so that those who have offended less may be purified first. But the last enemy to be destroyed is death.

Therefore, when Israel has been delivered from hard servitude, it will take up a parable against the king of Babylon, which we must understand as a parable. For if the discourse concerns Nebuchadnezzar and is a simple exposition of history, how can it be called a “parable,” which is not compared—*paraballetai*—with anything else?

Israel therefore marvels at how the exactor has ceased—the one who was accustomed to exact payment down to the last quarter.

The exactor is accustomed to exact payment from none but debtors, who say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). These debtors are handed over by the judge to the exactor, who sends them into prison and exacts payment down to the smallest sin.

Finally, the apostle Paul handed over the Corinthian fornicator, who had taken his father’s wife, as well as Phygelus and Hermogenes, to the exactor (1 Cor. 5; 2 Tim. 1).

[Note: [Col. 0217D] “Martian: ‘the fornicator in Corinth,’ etc.”]

The following is also said above concerning these exactors: “My people, your exactors plunder you, and those who demand payment from you rule over you.”

In place of “tribute,” Aquila translated “hunger.” For after the Bridegroom has been taken away from us, we suffer hunger for the word of God and continually fast from the body of the Lord.

Therefore the rod and staff of the wicked—in place of which the seventy translated “yoke”—strikes or oppresses us, because we were unwilling to bear the lightest yoke, the yoke of the Savior.

With this staff and this rod he struck the nations in incurable fury and cruelly pursued those who fled: he did not wish to correct those handed over to him but to kill them.

### (Verses 7 ff.)

“The whole earth has come to rest and has fallen silent. It has rejoiced and exulted. Even the fir trees have rejoiced over you, and the cedars of Lebanon. From the time you fell asleep, no one has come up to cut us down.

Sheol beneath was disturbed for you; at your coming it roused the giants to meet you. All the rulers of the earth rose from their thrones; all the rulers of the nations, every one of them, answered and said to you: ‘You too have been wounded as we were; you have become like us?’

Your pride has been brought down to the underworld; your corpse has fallen. Beneath you maggots will be spread, and worms will be your covering.”

[Note: [Col. 0217D] “The noun *putredo* (‘rottenness’), which could perhaps have been written by Jerome with a preposition or adverb as another interpretation of a Hebrew verb, is here set down simply and almost disturbs the sense. Nor is it found in Jerome’s own version from the Hebrew truth.”]

At the destruction of the wicked king who struck the nations with an incurable blow and cruelly persecuted them, the whole earth came to rest and fell silent—the earth that had previously been full of disturbances and sedition. So greatly did the fir trees and cedars of Lebanon rejoice, concerning which it is written in the Psalms: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you cast out the nations and planted it. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God” (Ps. 79:9).

Because these cedars of God once sinned, the Lord handed them over to be crushed by punishments. Hence it is said in another Psalm: “The Lord will crush the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 28:5).

The lofty fir trees, however, and all who are exalted in the Lord’s service, should be understood as those that said with one voice: “From the time you fell asleep.” Observe that even the death of death is called sleep.

“No one has come up to cut us down.” For when the strong one was conquered and his vessels plundered, all his other satellites also fell. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

How many of these cutters of wood and trees did they cut down with their axes and make fall?

Sheol too, whether disturbed or turned into bitterness, at the coming of the true Nebuchadnezzar, is the place of punishments and torments. There the rich man clothed in purple is seen.

[Note: [Col. 0219] “To which he descended, etc. This refers to the passage of the prophet Zechariah, chapter 9:11: ‘You too, by the blood of your covenant, have released your prisoners from the pit in which there is no water.’ He may also have had in mind the passage of the blessed Peter’s First Epistle, chapter 3:19: ‘In which he also went and preached to the spirits who were in prison,’ etc. MARTIAN.”]

The Lord also descended there to release the captives from prison.

We can understand “Sheol” as referring to the angel who presides over the punishments below and who roused all the giants. Some translators rendered the word as “Rephaim,” others as “Titans.”

The giants are called this according to pagan usage, since the pagans regard them as earth-born, begotten by the earth. We, however, following the etymology of the Greek word, can call giants those who have served earthly works.

Then it follows: “All the rulers of the earth rose from their thrones,” at the coming of the ruler who had once been theirs. Those who had previously honored him because of his power would afterward marvel at him in his punishments and say: “You too have been wounded as we were; you have become like us.”

These words have the following meaning: “We thought that, because of our weakness, we had been unable to resist God’s power, and that you alone would remain in your exalted position. But events show that you too have been wounded and captured and have become like us, so that those whom rank separated on earth may be joined together by punishment in the underworld.”

“Your pride,” or “your glory,” has been brought down to the underworld, and your corpse has fallen—or, as the Septuagint translated, “your great joy,” with which you previously rejoiced over the nations subjected to you.

“Beneath you rottenness will be spread, and worms will be your covering.”

This is the rest of the devil and the bed of the tempter, who was raised to such great pride that he even dared to tempt the Lord, saying: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

“Rottenness,” “maggots,” and the covering of worms may be understood either as the eternal punishments produced by one’s own conscience, or as the material of punishments that arises from one’s own sins. For just as, so long as there is the substance of a corpse and some moisture in the corpse, worms are born from rottenness, so punishments are generated from the very substance of sins.

Hence, after the apostle Paul had destroyed death—the death to which the prophetic word spoke through Hosea: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O Sheol” (Hos. 13:14)—he says to it: “Where is your contest, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

Once death has been destroyed, no one will cut us down; for there will be no sin that needs to be cut down, since sin is the sting of death.

### (Verse 12)

“How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise at dawn! You have fallen to the earth, you who wounded the nations?”

The Septuagint has: “How Lucifer fell from heaven, who was rising at dawn; he has been crushed upon the earth, who sent against all the nations.”

In place of “Lucifer,” who is called *ELIL* () in Hebrew, Aquila translated “the howling son of dawn.” Indeed, he ought to howl and lament, since on account of his pride he was hurled from heaven to earth and crushed.

Hence the Savior says to the disciples: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). He does not say merely, “I am watching,” but “I was watching,” referring to the time when he fell.

And if he fell from such greatness on account of pride, you too should not rejoice because the demons are subject to you, but because your names are written in heaven. Thus, from the place where he fell through pride, you may ascend through humility.

This is the ruler of the world who once rose at dawn among the other stars, but through his own fault was changed from Lucifer into Vesper, and became not rising but setting—the one who wounded the nations, or who sent his satellites against the nations in order to deceive them all by his fraud.

These are the false apostles, deceitful workers who transform themselves into apostles of Christ. They sow weeds over the good seed while the teachers of the churches sleep and are unwilling or unable to resist their wickedness.

Jacob and Israel, on whom the Lord has had mercy and whom he has chosen, continue to say this to the devil—or, as the Septuagint wishes, concerning the devil; that is, not to the second person but to the third.

### (Verses 13–14)

“You who said in your heart: ‘I shall ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I shall exalt my throne. I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north. I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds; I shall be like the Most High.’”

Either he said these things before he fell from heaven, or after he had fallen from heaven.

If he was still in heaven, how can he say, “I shall ascend into heaven” (Ps. 113:16)? But because we read, “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord,” while he was in heaven—that is, in the firmament—he desired to ascend into the heaven where the Lord’s throne is, not through humility but through pride.

But if he speaks these words after he fell from heaven, we should understand arrogance: even though he had been hurled down, he did not rest but still promised himself great things—not that he would be among the stars, but that he would be above the stars of God.
