When the Lord says to the Apostles, “It is enough for the disciple to be like his teacher, and for the servant to be like his lord” (Matt. 10:25), and says to the Father, “Holy Father, grant that, just as you and I are one, they too may be one in us” (John 17:11), this one arrogates so much to himself that he boasts that he will place his throne above the stars of heaven, which did not fall.

As for what follows—“I shall sit upon the mountain of the covenant, on the sides of the north”—for which the Septuagint translated “upon the high mountain, above the lofty mountains that are toward the north,” we should refer it to what is said in Jeremiah: “From the north evils shall blaze forth upon all the inhabitants of the earth” (Jer. 1:14), and to the fact that the boiling pot is kindled from the face of the north.

This is the exceedingly harsh north wind, from which the Lord wishes to free his captives and bring them back to the holy city, saying: “I shall say to the north, ‘Give them up,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder’; bring my sons from the far-off land” (Isa. 43:6).

What might seem contrary to this—that Zion is called “the mountains, the sides of the north, the city of the great king”—is easily resolved. Those who were once exceedingly harsh inhabitants of the sides of the north afterward began, through repentance, to be in the city of God.

This kind of Lucifer always seeks to ascend above those who bear the image of the heavenly, who shine in the Church like the stars of God; and he seeks to sit upon the mountain of the covenant or testament—that is, in the Church, which has been placed in high places and possesses inhabitants who once belonged to the sides of the north.

He has forgotten himself so completely that he wishes to ascend above the clouds, to which the Lord commanded that they should not rain upon Israel and to which the truth of the Lord reached. Obadiah too speaks to him, saying: “If you are exalted like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars of heaven, from there I shall bring you down, says the Lord” (Obad. 4).

Unhappy Judas! Like a cloud, he was sent with the other Apostles to rain upon Israel; and like a star among the other stars, he was among those to whom the Lord said: “Let your light shine before human beings” (Matt. 5:16). Yet through his own fault he received the devil as his rider. To fulfill his words of pride, the devil even dared to say: “I shall be like the Most High,” so that, just as Christ has his prophets and Apostles, he too might have false apostles.

All these things, however, must be referred to the heretics, who, although they are below, boast with their ruler that they are exalted.

### (Verse 15)

“Yet you shall be brought down to the underworld, to the depth of the pit.”

The Septuagint has: “But now you shall descend into the underworld and to the foundations of the earth.”

You shall not descend voluntarily into the underworld—for this belongs to the Lord and Savior, who frees the captives from the underworld—but you shall be dragged there unwillingly. You who could ascend to the heights through virtues will be dragged down to punishments through vices.

The saints have the wings of eagles and the wings of doves, and they can say: “I shall fly and rest” (Ps. 54). But the wicked, like the Egyptians, have been submerged like lead in exceedingly mighty waters, and have sunk into the depths like a stone (Exod. 15).

Hence iniquity—or, as it is more accurately found in the Hebrew, impiety—is seen sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. 5).

Thus what we read elsewhere—“Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 18:14)—was also suffered by the king of confusion: he was dragged down to the foundations of the earth, or, as the Hebrew more accurately has it, to the depth of the pit.

Concerning the foundations of the earth it is written in Deuteronomy: “A fire has been kindled in my anger; it shall burn to the lowest underworld. It shall devour the earth and its foundations” (Deut. 32:22)—that is, those who are earthly.

The following testimonies also show that the pit signifies the depths of the underworld: “I have become like those who descend into the pit”; and: “They placed me in the lowest pit” (Ps. 87:5, 7).

For just as a pit receives waters descending into it, so the underworld receives souls. To this pit Benaiah descended in the time of snow and cold and killed a lion there (2 Sam. 23; 1 Chron. 11).

Hence the heretics abandon the fountain of living water, the Lord, and dig for themselves broken pits that cannot hold water.

These are pits that have no fervor of the Holy Spirit. Nor are they like the prophet Jeremiah, who, according to the Septuagint translators, said: “I found hot water in the desert” (Jer. 2).

But as love grew cold, they lost the warmth of the Holy Spirit. This is the pit of which the same Jeremiah speaks: “As a pit cools water, so wickedness cools those who possess it” (Jer. 6:7).

Would that, according to the Apocalypse of John, they were either hot or cold (Rev. 3)—that is, that they either believed or did not believe at all—so that through lukewarmness and the pretense of faith they would not be rejected by the Lord!

### (Verses 16–17)

“Those who see you will bend toward you and gaze upon you. Is this the man who disturbed the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a desert and destroyed its cities, and did not open the prison for his captives?”

Or, as the Septuagint translated: “Did not release those who were being led away?”

Those who see Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, having fallen from heaven to the underworld—not with the eyes but with the vision of the heart—will bend down in humility, which is contrary to pride, and will look upon him, saying: “Is this the man, or human being, who disturbed or agitated the earth?”

The sense is this: the one who had said, “I shall be like the Most High,” and had boasted that he was God, is proved to be human. Concerning him it is said in the ninth Psalm, which is specifically directed against the devil: “Arise, O Lord; let not man prevail” (Ps. 9:1).

And in the Gospel: “An enemy, a man, sowed weeds over it” (Matt. 13:25).

Hence we read that it was said to him and his companions: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.’ But you shall die like human beings, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 81:6).

And to the same one, under the figure of the prince of Tyre, it is said: “Because your heart was exalted and you said, ‘I am God; I have dwelt in the dwelling-place of God, in the heart of the sea’—yet you are a man and not God, and you have made your heart like the heart of God” (Ezek. 28:2).

This man, this human being, disturbed the whole earth—that is, those who hear with Adam: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19)—and shook kingdoms, or kings, whose hearts are in the hand of the Lord (Prov. 21).

He shook them, it says, but did not overthrow them. Hence one of those who had been shaken but had not fallen said: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. 72:2).

And the Apostle speaks to believers so that they may take up the armor of God and stand against the devil’s schemes (Eph. 6). A house founded upon a rock is shaken by no storm (Matt. 7).

It follows: “Who made the inhabited world a desert,” or, according to the Hebrew—for all the others except the Septuagint translated it this way—“as a desert.”

By vices and sins he made the world, which is called *THEBEL* () in Hebrew, into a desert, so that it had no virtue or was subject to the same vices with which the wilderness of the nations is filled.

He also destroyed the cities of that same world, in order to make the churches of Christ into synagogues of the devil and to pollute the purity of the true faith with heretical filth.

But he did not open the prison for his captives—that is, for the world.

We were all captives and were held shut in prison. To these captives the Savior said: “Come out,” and to those who were in darkness: “Be revealed.” For the Lord releases those who are bound.

After being freed by him, they give thanks, saying: “You have loosed my bonds” (Ps. 115:17; Jer. 2; Prov. 5).

Each person is bound by the cords of his sins. The Apostles can loose these cords and bonds by imitating their teacher, who had said to them: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 18).

The Apostles loose them through the word of God, the testimonies of Scripture, and exhortation to virtue.

### (Verses 18–19)

“All the kings of the nations, every one of them, slept in glory, each in his own house. But you have been cast out of your tomb like filth: polluted, wrapped up with those slain and pierced by the sword, who descend to the stones of the pit.”

[Note: [Col. 0223D] “In the Vatican manuscript and in the Septuagint, the preposition *cum* is omitted here.”]

The Septuagint has: “All the kings of the nations slept in honor, each man in his own house. But you shall be cast out upon the mountains like an abortion, abominable, and wrapped up with those slain by the sword who descend to the foundations of the earth.”

[Note: [Col. 0223D] “From the Greek ὡς νεκρὸς ἐβδελυγμένος, not from Jerome’s Hebrew version. Victorius restores: ‘like an abominable dead man.’”]

The kings of the nations, whom God, according to the Song of Deuteronomy, had entrusted with governing the nations (Deut. 32), were shaken by Nebuchadnezzar but not overthrown. Sin did not at all reign in them, because their heart was in the hand of God; therefore they did not fall.

For just as the Savior is called God of gods, so he is Lord of lords and King of kings.

These kings, therefore, all rested in their glory, each in his own house. For there are many dwelling-places with the Father (John 14), and differences among habitations corresponding to differences in virtues.

Nebuchadnezzar, however, was cast out from his tomb and did not rest from torments even in death.

He was cast out like filth, which is called *NESER* () in Hebrew. Aquila translated it as ἰχώρα, that is, corruption and stench; Symmachus as ἔκτρωμα, “abortion”; the Septuagint as “dead”; and Theodotion as “shoot.”

Although this same word appears above (chapter 11:1), where we read concerning Christ, “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root,” the Septuagint translated it “flower,” Theodotion “shoot,” and Aquila ἀκρέμονα, that is, “branch.”

[Note: [Col. 0224D] “The Vatican manuscript has ‘that is, a little branch’; thus ἀκρέμων can suitably be rendered in this way.”]

Properly speaking, *Neser* means a shoot that grows at the roots of trees and is pulled up by farmers and thrown away as useless. Hence we translated it “useless stem.”

Nebuchadnezzar, therefore, like a useless stem prepared for burning, or like polluted filth, wrapped up with those whom he killed by the sword and who descended to the foundations of the pit, will be dragged down into the depths. He will not share even the burial of those whom he killed.

For the author of a crime receives one punishment, and the person compelled by the author receives another.

This is the sword by which many were wounded and killed, concerning which we read in the seventh Psalm: “Unless you repent, he will brandish his sword; he has bent his bow and prepared it. And in it he has prepared the instruments of death; he has made his arrows for those who burn” (Ps. 7:13–14)—namely, for those who have received the devil’s fiery darts into their own hearts.

According to the Septuagint, however, the corpse of Nebuchadnezzar, polluted and pierced along with many slain men, will lie upon the mountains of pride and will be led down to the underworld.

In place of “the stones of the pit,” Symmachus translated “the foundations of the pit,” signifying in other words the depth and Tartarus of the underworld.

### (Verse 20)

“You shall have no fellowship with them in burial, like a rotting corpse. For you have destroyed your land; you have slain your people.”

The Septuagint: “As a garment mixed with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean, because you have destroyed my land and slain my people.”

Because the Hebrew differs greatly from the Septuagint edition, let us discuss each separately.

“Like a rotting corpse”—or, as Aquila translated it, “trampled upon”—you shall have no fellowship in burial, not even with those whom you have slain. For you are the teacher, and they were the disciples; and from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more is required. For you destroyed your land and killed your people, namely those entrusted to you to govern.

Hence he dares to say to the Savior: “All these things have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if, falling down, you will worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

No one who has read that sin is exceedingly foul-smelling can doubt that the devil’s corpse is rotten, since the sinner himself says: “My wounds have become foul and festering because of my foolishness” (Ps. 37:6).

By contrast, virtue is the fragrance of goodness. Hence the love of spiritual brothers is compared with the ointment that descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, and upon the hem of his garment (Ps. 133). And the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your fragrance is sweet, and your face is beautiful” (Song 2:14).

The Apostle teaches us how the devil’s corpse is spiritually trampled: “God will crush Satan under your feet speedily” (Rom. 16:20). Likewise the words of the Lord: “I will wipe them away like the mud of the streets” (Ps. 18:43).

Because he destroyed the land entrusted to him and slaughtered the people committed to his care, never preserving them alive for God but preparing them as companions of his own burial, therefore he will not exist and will not be called forever “the offspring of the wicked.”

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is this: O Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning, when you possessed works of virtue and light, you were God’s garment, and it could be said of you: “You are clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 104:2). But because you killed many with the sword, who descended into hell, and because you were stained with their blood, you will no longer be called God’s garment, but a garment mixed with blood—not merely spotted and stained, as though you might still possess something clean, but entirely bloodied.

It must also be noted that this is said to the devil: “As a garment mixed with blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean.” Where, then, are those who grant the devil repentance and say that he can be cleansed? Let us not at once accept the heresy that asserts that there are different natures, one of which can never receive healing.

For this garment is not unclean in itself, nor was it created by God in such a state—the garment with which God was formerly clothed. Rather, because it has been mixed with blood and has wholly polluted itself through its own fault and through the evils that have been added to it, it will not be clean.

Therefore it will not be clean because it destroyed the Lord’s land and killed his people: the land of Judea—and [perhaps, that is] the land of confession—and all the saints, whom it destroyed and killed. For this reason it will not remain forever. Hence it is also said in the Gospel: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

Just as the saint is God’s garment, a new garment, and is clothed with the robe of salvation and joy, saying, “My soul shall rejoice in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and covered me with the robe of joy” (Isa. 61:10), so, conversely, the sinner who bears the image of the old and earthly man deserves to hear: “Behold, you will all grow old like a garment, and the moth will devour you” (Isa. 50:9).

But whoever advances in wickedness and refuses to cleanse his old age through renewal will be compared not merely to an old garment but to a menstruating woman’s cloth, saying: “We have gone astray, and we have all become unclean, and all our righteousness is like a menstruating woman’s cloth.”

### (Verses 21–22)

“Offspring of the wicked, prepare your sons for the slaughter of the iniquities of their fathers, so that they may not rise up, nor inherit the land, nor fill the face of the world with cities. And I will rise up against them, says the Lord of hosts, and I will destroy Babylon’s name and its remnants, its shoot and its offspring, says the Lord of hosts.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the Vulgate translator, has *in iniquitate* (“in iniquity”), while the Septuagint has *peccatis* (“sins”) instead of *peccati* (“sin”); the same preference is consistently maintained in the exposition that follows.]

The Septuagint: “O most wicked offspring, prepare your sons for the slaughter of your father’s sin, so that they may not rise up and possess the land and fill the land with cities. And I will rise against them, says the Lord Sabaoth, and I will destroy their name, their remnants, and their seed.”

For “most wicked offspring,” the Hebrew has **ZERA MRIM** [זֶרַע מְרֵעִים], which the other translators rendered “offspring of the wicked.” This does not mean that the offspring itself is evil in its own nature—for “God made all things good” (Gen. 1)—but that evil offspring has arisen from those who are wicked by their own will. Evil results from the will, not from nature.

Hence we read in Daniel: “Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah” (Dan. 13:56). And concerning good children the Apostle says: “In Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Cor. 4:15). The Gospel likewise says: “As many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1:12). For everyone who commits sin is from the devil.

This offspring is therefore commanded to prepare its sons—that is, all its most wicked thoughts and evil works—for slaughter. Since they are born from ungodly fathers, there is no doubt that they signify hostile powers. These most wicked sons are slaughtered in the iniquities of their fathers so that they may no longer rise up and possess the land destined to be possessed and filled by the saints, so that the Lord’s cities may be built in it.

And because human victory is not perfect—for “unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it watch in vain” (Ps. 127:2)—the Lord himself will rise against the sons of the wicked. He will destroy their name, their remnants, and every shoot and offspring in their confusion, so that they may not sprout again in the Lord’s cities.

We read in the Gospel (John 8) that the devil was a liar from the beginning, and that he is its father—that is, the father of lying. Many who do not understand this want the devil’s father to be the dragon who rules in the sea, whom the Hebrews call Leviathan.

They think that this interpretation suits the present passage according to the Septuagint translators, who said, “for the sins of your father,” whereas it is perfectly clear that the Hebrew **ABOTHAM** [אֲבֹתָם] [elsewhere **OBOTHUM**] means not “your father” but “their fathers.”

### (Verse 23)

“And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog and marshes of waters; I will sweep it with a sweeping broom,” says the Lord of hosts.

The Septuagint: “And I will make Babylon desolate,” says the Lord, “so that hedgehogs will dwell in it, and it will come to nothing. And I will make it a muddy pit, for destruction.”

When the Lord of hosts has destroyed Babylon’s name, its remnants, its shoot, and its entire offspring, he will not be content with its destruction unless he makes it a possession of the hedgehog and marshes of waters, and sweeps it—

[Note: The Vatican manuscript adds *scopa* (“with a broom”).]

—not lightly or casually, but by rubbing it down, so that none of its ancient filth remains in it.

In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 10 and 11), we read that in the linen vessel lowered from heaven by its four corners there were all kinds of four-footed animals, reptiles, and birds. Explaining this afterward, the Apostle says: “God has shown me that I should call no human being unclean.”

The dispositions of human beings were therefore represented in different animals. Thus the Pharisees and Sadducees are called “broods of vipers” because of their wickedness, and Herod is called a fox because of his treachery (Luke 3 and 13). The luxurious and pleasure-seeking are called horses, “raging after females” (Jer. 5): “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 32:9).

By contrast, the innocent are called doves and sheep.

Accordingly, in the teaching of the Lord and Savior, who called the cares of this age and the deceitfulness of riches “thorns,” the hedgehog seems to me to be the person who, according to the Apostle, takes pleasure in the uncertainty of riches (1 Tim. 6), and who trusts that he is armed not with God’s armor but with the thorns and sins of this world. To him the Gospel saying most appropriately applies: “Fool, this night your soul will be demanded of you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

Such are the inhabitants of Babylon, desolate of virtues. There is no irrigated field there that produces fruits of various seeds, but infertile, muddy, and filthy marshes, in which animals that delight in the mire crawl.

Therefore the most merciful Lord swept it with the greatest force, rubbing it clean, as though with a kind of broom [elsewhere *everriculum*], until he cleansed it completely, so that Babylon’s seeds might perish and it might be inhabited only by hedgehogs.

Whenever we see someone immersed in the mire of riches, and, as the Septuagint translated, surrounded by a *barathrum*—that is, a deep chasm—or by something like a muddy marsh, let us not hesitate to call him a hedgehog, an inhabitant of desolate Babylon.

### (Verses 24–25)

“The Lord of hosts has sworn, saying: Surely, as I have thought, so shall it be; and as I have purposed in my mind, so shall it happen: I will crush the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains I will trample him. His yoke will be removed from them, and his burden will be taken from their shoulder.”

After the hedgehog has inhabited desolate Babylon and marshes have covered everything in place of irrigated and fertile fields, so that nothing of Babylon’s former seed and abundance remains, the Lord’s oath will be fulfilled. What he has purposed in his mind will happen: the Assyrian will be crushed in his land and trampled on his mountains.

For the reckless enemy hastens to occupy not only God’s land and all the lower places, but also those who have advanced in virtues through God’s service, so that they are compared with mountains. It is said of them: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. 87:1).

Notice the precise distinction: he is crushed in the land, but on God’s mountains he is trampled by the Lord himself.

When all the enemies have been placed under Christ’s feet, so that death, the last enemy, is destroyed, then the saints will have the exceedingly heavy yoke of the Assyrian removed—the yoke by which he had previously weighed them down. His burden, or, as the Septuagint translated it, his **κῦδος** (*kydos*), that is, “glory,” will be taken from their shoulder.

When the Assyrians’ yoke has been removed, they will see that the resting-place is good and that the land is exceedingly fertile. They will place their necks beneath Christ’s yoke for labor and become agricultural workers.

Hence Issachar, whose name is interpreted as “there is a reward,” received his name from virtues. We read in the Prophet: “There is a reward for those who serve the Lord” (Jer. 31:16); and elsewhere: “Behold, the Lord comes, and his reward is with him” (Isa. 40:10), and he will repay each person according to his work.

That the Assyrians—that is, hostile powers—are crushed and trampled is also taught by the Gospel: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). The Apostle’s words bear witness: “God will crush Satan under your feet speedily” (Rom. 16:20).

### (Verses 26–27)

“This is the plan that he has planned concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations. For the Lord of hosts has decreed, and who will be able to weaken it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?”

For “the whole earth,” the Septuagint translated “the whole inhabited world” at the end of the oracle or vision against Babylon.

What was hidden is disclosed: God has planned a purpose concerning the whole earth—that is, the whole world—and not merely against the land of the Chaldeans and the Assyrian and Chaldean king. His hand has been stretched out, or raised up, over all the nations, and not merely over Babylon, one nation.

From this it is shown that everything said does not pertain specifically to one province but generally against the whole world.

When it says, “Who will be able to weaken it?” and “Who will turn it back?” we should not understand these questions as referring to something difficult, as in the words: “Who is wise and will understand these things?” (Ps. 107:43), and: “Who, do you suppose, is the faithful and wise steward?” (Luke 12:42), and other similar passages. Rather, they refer to what is impossible.

No one will be able to weaken the Lord’s purpose or turn back his stretched-out or exalted hand, lest it strike.

### (Verses 28 and following)

“In the year in which King Ahaz died, this oracle came to pass. Do not rejoice, all Philistia, because the rod of your striker has been broken. For from the root of the serpent a basilisk will come forth, and its offspring will swallow the bird. And the firstborn of the poor will feed, and the poor will rest securely; but I will kill your root with famine, and I will slay your remnants.”

The Septuagint: “In the year in which King Ahaz died, this word came to pass: Do not rejoice, all you foreigners, for the yoke of the one who struck you has been broken. For from the serpent’s seed will come forth the offspring of asps, and from their offspring winged serpents will come forth. The poor will feed through him, and the poor will rest in peace. But he will kill your seed with famine and slay your remnants.”

When Ahaz died—his name is interpreted as **κατάσχεσις** (*katáschesis*), that is, “seizure” or “possession”—this burden, or oracle, comes upon the Philistines.

We read that he was an exceedingly wicked king. While he lived and reigned over sinners, neither an oracle against the foreigners nor a word of God could come to the Prophet.

I remember having said the same above, when, after Uzziah’s death, Isaiah saw the Lord seated upon a high and lofty throne. We read in Exodus (Exod. 2) that after the king of Egypt died, the children of Israel groaned because of their labor, cried out, and their cry rose up from their labor; and the Lord heard their groaning.

If what was said were not mystical, they ought rather to have cried out while he was reigning, when they were serving in clay and bricks.

The Philistines are therefore addressed—those whom people now call Palestinians and whom the Septuagint always translates as **ἀλλόφυλοι** (*allóphyloi*), that is, “foreigners.” They are told not to rejoice or be glad, because they have broken the rod or yoke of their striker (Heb. 12:6): “Whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.”

God educates us as sons when he visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges, so that he may not remove his mercy from us (Ps. 89). This is the rod of which another Psalm says: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 23:4).

This is the rod, and this is the yoke that the Savior wishes to place upon everyone’s neck, so that, having laid aside the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, they may carry the yoke of Christ.

But if someone casts it away and breaks it, then immediately from the seed or root of the serpent—the crooked serpent—a basilisk and asps will come forth; and from the asps will come flying serpents, or serpents that swallow birds.

Once God’s yoke has been cast off and the Lord’s discipline broken, the serpent’s seed is first rooted in our thoughts. Second, from the evil seed is born the basilisk, the king of serpents, which is said to kill human beings by its breath and its gaze.

Or there are the offspring of asps, of which it is said in the Psalm: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 14:3; 140:4). These are various sins that burst forth from the evil treasure of thoughts into evil works.

When they have begun to reign in the foreigners—those alienated from God—winged serpents immediately emerge. It is not enough for them to have thought and done what is evil; they must also seek the patronage of evil works and devise various heresies.

I think that the winged serpents are those who exalt and raise themselves against the knowledge of God and set their mouths in heaven; or those who swallow birds—that is, those who, with their poisoned mouths, devour at their throats each person who desires to fly and rise to the heights.

So much for the evil.

But those who have not broken the rod and yoke of their striker, who have subjected their neck to the Lord, and who are poor in spirit, will be fed and will say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing” (Ps. 23:1).

They will hear from the Lord: “I will feed them in the richest pastures” (Ezek. 34; John 10); “they will enter and go out, and find pasture.”

The poor will be fed through him who strikes them in order to correct them, and they will rest in peace.

[Note: Or “with an attentive shepherd.” In the printed editions we read, “without an anxious shepherd,” etc.; this does not seem to me to produce an unsuitable sense. —Martian.]

They themselves will act confidently and, with Lazarus, will rest in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16).

But those who have broken the yoke and rod of their striker will endure perpetual hunger, so that they will not be nourished by the word of God. All their remnants will perish, so that nothing may sprout from the evil seed.

### (Verses 31–32)

“Howl, O gate; cry out, O city. All Philistia has been prostrated. For smoke comes from the north, and there is no one who can escape its ranks. And what answer will be given to the messengers of the nation? That the Lord has founded Zion, and in him the poor of his people will hope.”

For “messengers,” that is, “angels,” which only Symmachus translated in this way, all the others translated “kings,” deceived by the ambiguity of the word. For apart from one letter, **ALEPH**, which is added in the word for angels, the Hebrews call kings and angels by the same name, namely **MALACHE**:

**Kings** — מְלָכִים  
**Angels** — מַלְאָכִים

In the *Book of Hebrew Names* I found that **Philistim** is interpreted as “those falling by the cup.”

[Note: “Philistim,” etc. This passage can refute the critic John Clericus, who reproached Jerome for the etymology of the name *Philistim*, which Jerome himself had found in this form in the *Book of Hebrew Names*. —Martian.]

Those, therefore, who have been intoxicated by Babylon’s cup and have drunk the wine in which there is wantonness, and who, among their other vices, have failed to attain the kingdom of God because of drunkenness, are commanded to howl at their gate and to make their city cry out.

I consider the gate to be the mouth of heretics, with which they blaspheme; the city to be the soul, which is a treasury of evil thoughts.

It must howl and lament because all of it has been prostrated, cast down upon the earth, and contains nothing of sound understanding or of God’s wisdom.

Why does the gate howl? Why does the city cry out? Because all Philistia has been prostrated.

The following verse shows why it has been prostrated: “Smoke comes from the north, and there is no one who can escape its ranks.”

This smoke is stirred up by the burning arrows of the devil. It is harmful to the eyes and opposed to light. It rises from the north, from which the pot in Jeremiah is kindled (Jer. 1:14), and from which evils flare up over all the inhabitants of the earth—those who cannot say, “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 119:19), but dwell in the land.

Hence we read in Proverbs: “The north wind is a harsh wind” (Prov. 25:23; Sir. 43).

By another name it is called “right,” although by itself it is harsh and leftward. It refuses to receive God’s yoke with its exceedingly stiff neck, yet it is called “right” by those who make the sweet bitter and the bitter sweet, who make darkness light and light darkness.

[Note: Another Vatican manuscript omits “by another name,” and thus the text reads in the *Commentary on Jeremiah*, chapter 1: “The north wind is a harsh wind; by another name it is called right,” namely by those who have stiffened under its cold and lost the warmth of faith. The same wording appears in the *Commentary on Jeremiah*, chapter 31.]

No one escapes the ranks of this smoke, for no one is without sin, not even if his life has lasted only one day (Job 25:4–6).

When Philistia has fallen and its smoke has penetrated everything, so that no one can escape it, what will be said to the angels who preside over the individual nations, as they wonder and wish to know why Zion alone, placed on a watchtower and in the heights, has escaped the bitterness of this smoke?

What, then, will be said to them? Surely what follows: “Because the Lord founded it, and he himself is its foundation.”

He founded it upon the foundation of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—names under which Christ is understood. Concerning him the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:11).

But whoever is foolish, speaks foolishly, and whose heart understands vanity builds his house upon sand, which has no foundation.

In this Zion, therefore, which has been founded by the Lord, the poor—or the meek and humble—of his people will hope. Concerning them it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). They have heard the Lord saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

They were humbled before glory and heard the Apostle Peter say: “Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5:6).

These poor are the ones of whom we read above: “The firstborn of the poor will be fed, and the poor will rest securely.”

## Chapter 15

### (Verse 1)

“An oracle concerning Moab.”

The Septuagint: “A word against Moabitis.”

Symmachus and Theodotion: “The taking up of Moab.”

Just as circumcision is both carnal and spiritual, and the Apostle speaks of spiritual circumcision: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the spirit, glory in the Lord, and do not put confidence in the flesh” (Phil. 3:3); and, to distinguish spiritual Israel from the carnal, he says of the latter: “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. 10:18), and, “You Gentiles in the flesh” (Eph. 2:11), so Moab must be understood spiritually.

Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” or “paternal water.” It was conceived through incest and drunkenness, and seemed in some way to have been generated in the father’s absence—or rather, without his knowledge.

[Note: Or “paternal water.” In Egyptian, water is called **MO**; hence Moses may be understood as “saved from water.” Moab, therefore, may be understood as “the father’s water” or “water from the father.” —Martian.]

We read about Moab in many places in Scripture, especially in the Book of Numbers, when Balak, king of the Moabites, invited Balaam the diviner to curse him. Among other things, Balaam also prophesied this mystically against Moab: “A star shall rise out of Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and he shall strike the leaders of Moab” (Num. 24:17).

### (Verse 1)

“Because Ar has been devastated by night, Moab has fallen silent; because the wall has been devastated by night, Moab has fallen silent.”

The Septuagint: “By night Moab has perished; by night the wall of Moab has perished.”

For **AR** [אָר], which Theodotion alone rendered as it is read in the Hebrew, Aquila and Symmachus translated “city.” They did not consider that between the Hebrew letters **AIN** and **RES** there is no letter **JOD**; if it were present, the word would properly mean “city.”

Secular wisdom, concerning which the Lord speaks through the Prophet, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the understanding of the prudent” (Obad. 8; 1 Cor. 1:19), has a sense that is its own author, since it is generated from God’s creation. It seems to be born from a father, which is what Moab means; but because it is adulterous and hostile to God’s people, it is generated from incest, a cavern, and night.

Therefore it perished in the night—that is, in everlasting error.

The Egyptians also were overwhelmed in the Red Sea during the morning watch, which still belongs to the night (Exod. 14). And when the Sodomites perished during the night, Lot came to Zoar, and the sun rose over him (Gen. 19).

Understanding this, the blessed Apostle writes concerning the saints and the perfect (1 Thess. 5:6–8): “We are not of the night or of darkness, but we are children of the day. Those who sleep sleep at night, and those who become drunk are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us remain watchful, clothed with the breastplate of faith and love.”

And because he had left the night and had already begun to be a child of the day, he says to believers: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near; let us walk honorably as in the day, not in reveling and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and wantonness” (Rom. 13:12–13).

When the night of Moab had perished, its wall too—constructed by the art of dialectic—was devastated and destroyed in that same night, and it fell silent in eternal silence.

Ar, which is interpreted as **ἀντίδικος** (*antídikos*), that is, “adversary,” shows that this wisdom, which is hostile to God, has been overcome, with ecclesiastical teaching fighting against it.

### (Verse 2)

“The house has gone up, and Dimon, to the heights in mourning.”

The Septuagint: “Be grieved within yourselves, for Dibon will perish, where the altar is; there you will go up to weep.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript consistently has **Dibon** instead of **Dimon**. Jerome himself discusses the variant reading of this name in the preceding book.]

Every house of hostile wisdom, and Dibon, whose name is interpreted as “their flowing,” goes up to the heights in which it had taken pride—not to offer sacrifices, but to mourn over the things in which it had previously sinned.

Indeed, falsehood passes and flows like a river and can never remain in a stable dwelling. But the word of God, which is compact and joined together, is stable. Hence manna, which appears like ice upon the face of the earth, does not flow away but remains.

According to the Septuagint, however, the Moabites are commanded to mourn and weep—not over others, for that belongs to the perfect, but over themselves—because their Dibon, that is, their composed discourse, which flowed like a torrent, is destined to perish. In it they had what was, as it were, the altar of their consecration and all their worldly riches.

Hence it is said in the Psalm: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them.” The beginning of salvation is to understand what belongs to oneself and to weep over one’s sins.

### (Verses 3 and following)

“Over Nebo and over Medeba Moab will howl; all its heads will be bald, and every beard will be shaved. In its streets they gird themselves with sackcloth; upon its roofs and in its streets everyone howls; it will descend into weeping.

“And Heshbon and Elealeh will cry out; their voice has been heard as far as Jazer. Therefore the armed men of Moab will howl; its soul will howl for itself.

“My heart will cry out to Moab; its bars reach as far as Zoar, the heifer that bellows. For by the ascent of Luhith it will ascend weeping, and on the road to Horonaim they will raise a cry of destruction.

“For the waters of Nimrim will be desolate: the grass has dried up, the shoot has failed, and all verdure has perished.

“According to the magnitude of the work, so will be their visitation. They will lead them to the torrent of the willows, for a cry surrounds the territory of Moab. Its howling reaches as far as Eglaim, and its cry as far as the well of Elim, because the waters of Dimon are filled with blood.

“For I will bring additional afflictions upon Dimon: a lion upon those who flee from Moab, and upon the remnants of the land.”

Because almost the whole of this prophecy has a single sense, I have not torn it apart by presenting it piecemeal, but have set it out all together. I will briefly run through what each part seems to me to signify according to the allegorical interpretation:

- Nebo means “sitting” or “prophecy.”
- Medeba means “from the thicket.”
- Heshbon means “thoughts.”
- Elealeh means “ascent.”
- Jazer means “made” or “command.”
- Zoar means “small.”
- Luhith means “cheeks.”
- Horonaim means “the opening of sorrow.”
- Nimrim means “leopards” or “transgressors.”
- Eglaim means “calves” or “mounds of sand.”
- Elim means “rams” or “strong ones.”
- Dimon means “sufficient sorrow.”

Since every doctrine opposed to the truth, which is born from human thought in the darkness of error without God’s inspiration, has been devastated by night, and its arguments—understood as walls—have been destroyed by ecclesiastical teaching, so that they have fallen silent in eternal silence, and their entire faction has been turned toward repentance and tears, there will be howling and mourning over Nebo—that is, over prophecy and sitting, meaning their teachers—and over Medeba, where there are not fruitful trees but an infertile thicket inhabited by beasts. Concerning it Psalm 29 says: “He will uncover the dense places of the thicket.”

All the ornaments of eloquence will be taken from their heads, so that they will remain naked and deformed. And whatever manliness they seemed to possess in their beard will be shaved away by the ecclesiastical man and proved effeminate and weak.

In their streets as well—that is, in the byways of their errors, where each person invents whatever he wishes according to his own will—they will gird themselves with the sackcloth of repentance.

Upon their roofs and housetops, where they first believed themselves to be exalted, and in their streets—for they do not enter by the narrow way that leads to life but by the broad way that leads to death—there will be howling.

They will no longer ascend in pride but descend into weeping.

Then they will understand all their vain thoughts, which is what Heshbon means, and their empty ascent of pride, which is what Elealeh signifies. Their voice will be heard as far as the evil works they committed and the commandment they thought was from God, condemning themselves by their own confession.

Therefore their bars—that is, those who had been strong in Moab and who have understood their error—will howl, and they will begin to have hope of improvement when their souls have howled for themselves.

Hence the Prophet, speaking with compassionate feeling to those whose soul was howling [elsewhere, “howls”] for itself, says: “My heart will cry out to Moab,” so that I may summon them to repentance.

Their bars and all the strongholds they seemed to possess in their heresies will reach as far as Zoar, that is, as far as something small. They will be shown not to be strong but fragile.

If this Zoar—that is, a small repentance—perseveres, it will lead them to perfect salvation. This is signified by the three-year-old heifer, according to what we read in Genesis, where Abraham is commanded to offer a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old ram, and a three-year-old goat: a perfect sacrifice, by which he may deserve to become the Lord’s heir (Gen. 15).

When they have practiced repentance, through Luhith—that is, through the tears of their cheeks—they will ascend to higher things.

Through this opening and entrance of sorrow they will raise a cry of contrition to the Lord, so that they may say: “The sacrifice acceptable to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 51:19).

This will happen because the waters of Nimrim—that is, the doctrine of the heretics, which is compared with leopards and transgressors—will be desolate and reduced to nothing.

Leopards are those whose variations and spots do not change, as in Jeremiah (Jer. 13:23); transgressors are those of whom we read in the Psalms: “I have reckoned all the sinners of the earth as transgressors” (Ps. 119:119).

Every grass and shoot, and whatever seemed green in their discourse, has also withered.

They were visited by God according to the magnitude of their sins, so that they might recognize through scourges the one whom they had not perceived through benefits.

Finally, they will be led to the valley or torrent of the willows, so that no fruit may remain in them.

They say that this is the nature of the seed of these trees: whoever drinks it in a cup is deprived of children. Hence the saints, who because of their sins have begun to exist in the confusion of this world, hang their instruments upon the willows of the Babylonian rivers (Ps. 137:2).

A cry surrounds all the boundaries of the Moabites, whether from those summoning them to repentance or from those mourning over their error, so that through their howling they may offer “the calves of their lips” and reach the fountain of the Lord’s rams, or of the strong ones, since **Elim** signifies both.

The waters of Dimon, whose name means “sufficient pain” or “sorrow,” had polluted many by their sprinkling. They will be accused before the deceived peoples of having served not for salvation but for blood.

Hence the prophetic word promises that over the flowing tears—which is what Dibon means—not one sorrow but many additions of sorrow will be heaped up in lamentation. After they have performed full repentance and fled from Moab, they may have God—the lion—as their ruler—

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has “may deserve to have as ruler,” followed by the words “whom the Septuagint called …”]

—whom the Septuagint called **Ariel**, which means “lion of God.”

I have refrained here from discussing the Septuagint edition, because in many places it differs from the Hebrew truth; nevertheless, its meaning can also be understood from what we have translated.

## BOOK SIXTEEN

### Chapter XVI

#### Verse 1

“Send a lamb to the ruler of the land, from the rock of the wilderness, to the mountain of the daughter of Zion. And it shall be like a bird fleeing, and like chicks flying from the nest: so shall the daughters of Moab be at the crossing of the Arnon.

“Take counsel; call a council. Make your shadow like night at midday; hide the fugitives, and do not betray the wanderers. Let my fugitives dwell with you; Moab, be their hiding place from the face of the devastator. For the dust has come to an end; the wretched one has been consumed; he who trampled the earth has failed. And a throne shall be prepared in mercy, and one shall sit upon it in truth, in the tent of David, judging and seeking judgment, and swiftly rendering what is just.”

What we have translated from the Hebrew as “send a lamb to the ruler of the land” can also be read: “send a lamb to the ruler of the land.” In that reading, the lamb itself is not the ruler of the land, as we interpreted it according to the historical sense, but a lamb is to be sacrificed to the ruler of the land.

This lamb, therefore—whether it is itself the ruler of the land or is sacrificed to the ruler of the land—is from the nation of the Moabites and from those who have fled from Moab and have deserved to have a lion as their ruler. It signifies Ruth, from whom Christ was born (Matt. 1:5). He calls her “the rock of the wilderness” because, according to God’s commandment, the Moabites and Ammonites, even to the tenth generation and forever, are not to enter the Church of God (Deut. 23:3).

But whoever flees from the wilderness of Moab—if we return from the prophecy to the anagogical sense—and, having despised falsehood, stands upon the mountain of truth, will be “like a bird fleeing,” and “like chicks flying from the nest,” lest they be devoured by the Moabite serpents.

“So,” he says, “shall all the daughters,” that is, the Moabite souls, “be at the crossing of the Arnon,” which is interpreted as “their illumination,” when, having abandoned their errors, they have crossed over to the knowledge of truth.

Thus it is said to Moab itself, or to the one who has escaped from Moab: “Do nothing without counsel” (Prov. 13:10), and “do not be carried about by every wind of doctrine,” but follow him who is “the Angel of the great counsel” (Eph. 4:14). “And call a council,” so that from the wandering and erring you may make the Church of God.

But your shelter and tent, in which you previously thought you were resting—what belonged to night and darkness—place at midday, that is, in the clearest light. In it you must conceal those fleeing from error and no longer betray those who were previously wandering.

“O Moab, my fugitives”—those who had abandoned me and had gone out from the Church, and, abandoning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, followed their own understanding—or those who had dwelt with you: when the devastator, the devil, begins to pursue them, offer them hiding places, with your whole mind turned toward the fear of the Lord. And know that after the coming of the Lamb, who arose from the rock of the wilderness as ruler of the whole earth and came to the mountain of the daughter of Zion, all the devil’s power will have come to an end, for it is compared with dust.

“And the wretched one has been consumed,” he who made many wretched; “and he has failed who trampled the whole earth,” namely, those who were earthly.

When he has been consumed, reduced to nothing, and utterly failed, a throne and an everlasting kingdom will be prepared—first in mercy. For “we are all under sin” (Rom. 3:9) and need [Note: Saint Augustine likewise reads this in Book I, chapter 27, of *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, as does Saint Gaudentius of Brescia, according to the Lyon edition: “the grace of God.” In the Greek text, however, it is τῆς δόξης τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the glory of God,” as the Vulgate translator also renders it. I have no doubt that by the name “glory” Christ is understood, since he is the glory of God the Father, and that the sense comes down to this: Christ the Redeemer is, *κατ’ ἐξοχήν*—“in the eminent sense”—the grace of God. Nevertheless, I think that Jerome and the other Fathers cited here recited the Apostle’s passage from the Latin-edition manuscripts that were then current.] the grace of God—and he will sit in the tent of David, which had fallen and has been raised up. After mercy, he will judge, seek righteousness, and repay each person according to his works.

Let us consider from the beginning either the “burden” or the oracle concerning Moab, in which it says, “By night Ar of Moab was devastated,” and continues to this passage. We shall see how, through the stages and order of repentance, Israelites arise from the Moabites; how they flee like birds and fly like chicks from the nest, so that they cross over by the Arnon and dwell on the mountain of the daughter of Zion; and how, with every power of the devil or Antichrist crushed, Christ reigns in those who have been saved by mercy and righteousness.

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

#### Verses 6ff.

“We have heard of the pride of Moab: he is exceedingly proud. His pride, his arrogance, and his indignation are greater than his strength. Therefore Moab will howl against Moab; everyone will howl. Speak to those who rejoice over the wall of baked brick about his wounds [or: their wounds], because the suburbs of Heshbon are deserted, the vine of Sibmah.”

The Septuagint reads:

“We have heard of the outrage of Moab: he is exceedingly insulting. His pride, his outrage, and his fury are not like your divination. Moab will not howl in this way; for everyone in Moab will howl. But for the inhabitants of Deseth you will meditate, and you will not be put to shame. The plains of Heshbon will mourn the vine of Sibmah.”

How greatly this passage is obscured according to the Septuagint translators is evident from the fact that it can scarcely be read. Let us therefore speak according to the Hebrew.

It is the custom of Scripture that, after lifting the human mind’s despair with a joyful announcement, it again terrifies the negligent and unwilling with a threat, lest God’s goodness harden our heart. Let us give only one example of this.

In Psalm 144 we read: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 145:9). And shortly afterward: “The Lord sustains all who fall, and raises up all who are bowed down. The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord, and you give them their food at the proper time” [or: “at his proper time”]. Having first said, “The Lord preserves all who love him,” so as not to make the hearer careless, he added: “But he will destroy all sinners.”

Since, therefore, after the Antichrist and his parent, the devil who trampled the whole earth, had been brought to an end, he prophesied that a throne was to be prepared in mercy [Note: Previously the text had the awkward and tangled wording, “a throne was, as has been prophesied, to be prepared,” etc.; the Vatican manuscript restored the reading.], and that the one who would sit in the tent of David was to be established, the prophet now speaks from the person of the saints who were saved from Moab and had learned his pride by experience:

“We have heard of the pride of Moab,” or “of the outrage,” as the Septuagint translated it.

For what heretic is not proud? Despising the simplicity of the Church, he regards the people of the Church as though they were brute animals. He is so lifted up by the swelling of pride and outrage that he arms his mouth against the Creator himself, disparaging his prophets as though on the authority of the Gospel testimony in which the Savior says: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers” (John 10:8).

He goes so far as to call Moses, the servant of God, a murderer, and to disparage Joshua the son of Nun as a bloodthirsty man, although he was of such holiness that, at his command, the sun and moon stood still. He calls David, from whose seed Christ was born (Matt. 1), a murderer and an adulterer, failing to consider his repentance and gentleness, by which he is compared with the mercy of God.

But although he is proud and arrogant and exults in fury, he dares more than his strength can endure. Therefore “Moab will howl against Moab,” that is, one against another. All the varieties of the heretics and of secular wisdom will bellow against one another when they are in torment (3 Kings 6).

Therefore, you who possess walls built not of squared stones—the stones from which the Temple was built—and so polished that neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house of God, O teachers of the Church, or you who have been saved from the error of Moab, proclaim his wounds, by which they have been wounded by the darts of the heretics.

For all their thoughts—which is what Heshbon signifies—do not belong to the dwelling of the city of the Lord, of which it is written: “The river’s stream makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 46:4). They are merely suburbs, so that they may be thought to belong to the city of the Lord. These suburbs, however, are deserted of God’s protection, or burned up by divine fire—especially the vine of Sibmah, which is interpreted as “raising up height,” because it lifts itself on high and attempts to build the tower of its pride up to heaven.

What is placed in the Septuagint, “for the inhabitants of Deseth,” is not found in the Hebrew. Instead, we read *ares*, which signifies “baked brick” or “tile.”

#### Verses 9–10

“The lords of the nations have cut off its branches; they reached as far as Jazer. They wandered in the wilderness; its shoots were abandoned; they crossed the sea. Therefore I will weep over the vine of Sibmah with the weeping of Jazer; I will drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh, because a cry of treaders has broken in upon your vintage and upon your harvest. Joy and exultation will be taken away from Carmel; in the vineyards there will be no rejoicing or shouting. The one who used to tread will not tread wine in the winepress; I have taken away the cry of the treaders.”

The suburbs of Heshbon, of which we spoke above, are deserted, as is the vine of Sibmah, which can be interpreted not only as “raising up height,” but also as “a kind of conversion,” because it appears, in the region of the Moabites, to wish in some measure to turn toward the service of the Lord.

The lords of the nations—the Apostles and apostolic men—have therefore completely cut off the branches and shoots of this vine of Sibmah, so that other heresies might not arise from other heresies and an endless multitude of the erring might be produced.

They not only cut off the shoots of Sibmah, but reached as far as Jazer, which is interpreted as “their strength”—that is, to the strongest doctrines of the heretics, constructed by dialectical art, in which they seemed to possess the foundation of their error. Their sword raged so violently that in the end they wandered in the wilderness and had no one left whom they could kill.

Although they cut off its branches, some shoots nevertheless remained because of the vice of the evil root.

The lords of the nations, however, crossed the sea—that is, the temptations of this age, concerning which we read in the Psalm: “I have come into the depth of the sea, and the storm has overwhelmed me” (Ps. 69:3); and elsewhere: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing their work upon many waters, these have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 107:23–24).

They therefore crossed the sea in order to see the works of the Lord and his wonders in the depth of temptations while they were being delivered from them.

Thus the prophetic word mourns the strength of the heretics, that is, Jazer, and the vine of Sibmah, which exalts itself against the knowledge of God.

“And I will drench you with my tears, O Heshbon”—that is, their thoughts—and “O Elealeh,” by which they climb to high places.

But why does he mourn over Jazer and the vine of Sibmah, and drench Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears? So that, while he himself mourns, he may teach them to mourn as well.

“For,” he says, “a cry of treaders has broken in upon your vintage and upon your harvest.”

The vine of the Moabites, because of the region’s proximity, is like the vine of the Sodomites, concerning which it is said: “For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah” (Deut. 32:32). And in Psalm 77 we read about the Egyptian vine, which God struck with hail.

The Moabite harvests likewise grow in the valleys called Rephaim. Their false vintage belongs to the vine of which it was said above: “The lords of the nations have cut off its branches.”

These men crush the most bitter grapes and tread them with their feet, lest the dragon’s poisons be expressed from them and all who drink be killed.

The joy and exultation of the heretics, in which they previously used to rejoice, will also be taken away, so that after they have practiced repentance they may deserve to hear: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:4).

What he added, “from Carmel,” signifies this: not that the heretics truly possess Carmel—that is, knowledge of spiritual circumcision—but that they falsely boast of possessing it.

When the vines have been cut down and joy and exultation have been removed from the falsely named knowledge, then none of the former treaders will remain to tread the grapes that he had previously trodden, and their voice will be silenced in eternal silence.

#### Verses 11ff.

“Therefore my belly will resound for Moab like a lyre, and my inward parts for the wall of baked brick. And it will be, when it appears that Moab has labored over its high places, that it will enter its sanctuaries to plead, but it will not prevail. This is the word that the Lord spoke concerning Moab from that time.”

Once the Moabite error has been destroyed—or rather, once its false joy has been changed into mourning and tears—my belly, that is, the prophet’s belly, which has been arranged like a lyre by musical art and which, conceiving from the fear of God, has produced many children, so that there is no string that does not give forth its own sound, will resound with the mourning of Moab doing penance.

“And all my inward parts” will resound “for the wall of baked brick.” Theodotion translated this as “for the wall that has been demolished.”

All the defenses of contrary things in which they previously trusted will be destroyed and will collapse. These are the prophet’s inward and inner parts, concerning which David also said in the Psalm: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all my inward parts, his holy name” (Ps. 103:1).

For just as a lyre does not emit a vocal and harmonious sound if even one string has been broken, so the prophet’s spiritual belly, if one string of the virtues is lacking in it, cannot resound with a sweet melody or cry out with all its inward parts to the wall of baked brick.

There is also a philosophical maxim that virtues “cling to one another” [Note: Previously, *sibi* was missing; the Vatican manuscript supplies it.]; and the Apostle James teaches that when one virtue is lacking, all virtues are lacking.

When Moab understands that it has labored in vain over those doctrines that it previously thought were lofty, it will enter its sanctuaries—not things holy in themselves, but things that, while wandering, it considered holy—and it will be unable to find help.

Or certainly, having abandoned the error of falsehood, it will attempt to enter the holy places of the Church, to make them its own, and will pray and plead, but it will not prevail. For we cannot immediately possess perfect virtue as soon as we desire it.

As for what follows—“This is the word that the Lord spoke concerning Moab from that time”—we should know that this is an epilogue corresponding to the introduction in which he had said, “the word against Moab,” or “the burden,” so that what he had begun there he completes here.

“From that time” is to be understood as meaning from the time when he began to speak to Moab, so that everything he said may be one word of God, that is, one sentence.

According to the Septuagint, who translated the passage as “the prophet’s inward parts renewed by God like a wall,” and as saying that Moab would be ashamed and enter the altars and the things made by hand, we can explain it as follows: the prophet’s inward parts are always renewed and made stronger by God, so that the adversaries may be confounded and may understand that the things fashioned by human hands are empty and contribute nothing to salvation.

#### Verse 14

“And now the Lord has spoken, saying: Within three years, like the years of a hired laborer, the glory of Moab, with all its numerous people, will be taken away, and it will be left small and insignificant, by no means numerous.”

The three years in which the glory of Moab, with all its numerous people—or, as the Septuagint translated, “with its great riches”—will be taken away are to be understood mystically.

For just as the Lord’s mercy has weights and measures, so torments and punishments have their measure, so that after the three years have passed, during which it will be left small, insignificant, and by no means numerous, then it may cease to be inglorious. [Note: Previously it was wrongly read as two words, *in gloria* (“in glory”), which gave a sense plainly contrary to Jerome’s meaning. We have restored the one-word *inglorius* (“inglorious”), with the correct sense, on the authority of the Vatican manuscript; the same reading occurs a little below.]

And this should be noted: according to the prophecy of Ezekiel, when days are counted as years for Israel (Ezek. 4)—that is, for the ten tribes, which had committed greater sins—the years of punishment amount to three hundred ninety, as the Hebrew contains, not one hundred ninety, as the Vulgate edition has; and for Judah, in which the Temple of God was located, forty years.

“For the one who is small deserves mercy; but the powerful will suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:6). And the servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it “will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

Moab, therefore, because it was an outsider, not from the people of God, but was converted after abandoning its error, will be left small, insignificant, and inglorious not for many years but only for three.

These are the years about which we also read elsewhere: “Remember the days of old” (Isa. 46:9), and again: “I have considered the days of old, and I have had the eternal years in mind” (Ps. 77:5).

For if Israel, according to the flesh, served shadows and copies, and all their solemn observances were a type of future things, why should not the years of the present age also prefigure future times? Concerning them we read elsewhere: “What will you do on the days of assembly and on the days of the feast of the Lord?” (Hos. 9:5).

What is joined to this—“like the years of a hired laborer” (Hos. 9:5)—shows that false doctrine does everything for profit and gain.

For every hired laborer, and one who is not a shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, flees when he sees the wolf coming, because he is a hired laborer and the sheep do not belong to him (John 10:12).

For this reason I think that a stranger and a hired laborer do not eat from the holy things and are not servants who share in the things of the saints. [Note: Vatican manuscript: “A hired laborer of the priest must not eat from the holy things, but servants,” and so forth.]

They do everything not out of love for the Lord but for the sake of payment—those who devour widows’ houses and bring forward their own flocks so that they may clothe themselves with their wool and milk them (Matt. 23:14).

What we have said about hired doctrine should be applied to the rest as well.

If I give alms so that I may be glorified by human beings, I have received my reward, and I must be called a hired laborer.

If I pretend to be chaste while my conscience is otherwise, I possess not the glory of a hired laborer but the punishments of a sinner.

And in comparison between two evils, it is the lesser evil to sin openly than to pretend and feign holiness.

Yet Moab has made progress even in this: the one who previously had many companions in his error will afterward be reduced to a few; or the one who was previously great in the riches of sins will, after repentance, be small and poor in wickedness.

## BOOK SEVEN

[Column 0239]

The seventh book is, according to the anagogical sense, the second—or rather, the final one. In it the tropological exposition of the ten visions comes to an end. When I have completed it, Eustochium, with your prayers and with Christ’s help, I shall come to the eighth book and, following the earlier books, explain both expositions together through the fourth book.

### Chapter XVII

#### Verse 1

“The burden of Damascus.”

Symmachus and Theodotion: “The assumption of Damascus.” The Septuagint: “The word against Damascus,” adding from their own text what they did at the beginning concerning Moab.

We read the name Damascus for the first time in Genesis. Before Isaac, Damascus was Abraham’s household servant, and he was thought to be the heir unless a son of Sarah had been born according to the promise (Gen. 15).

The name is interpreted either as “a kiss of blood,” “drinking blood,” or “the blood of sackcloth.” All these meanings suit the pagan people, who, before faith in Christ, were friends of blood and cruelty and performed deeds worthy of mourning and sackcloth.

The historical book of Chronicles (2 Chron. 24) relates that, when the year had been completed, the army of Syria came up against Joash, king of Judah, and came to Jerusalem. It killed all the princes of the people and sent all the plunder to the king of Damascus, who had come with a few men. God had delivered a very great multitude into their hand because they had abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.

This should be considered according to the anagogical sense and as a type of future things: whether we can refer it to the time of the Lord’s coming.

For after the end of the acceptable year in which the Savior preached the Gospel, an army of the nations came up from Damascus with a few men against Judah and Jerusalem, which had abandoned the Lord. They took away all their riches of the Law and the Prophets and sent them to the king of Damascus—that is, ecclesiastical men and teachers of the Gospel—who at that time were few in comparison with the whole world, which was still unbelieving, and with the Jews scattered throughout the entire world.

Nevertheless, the Lord delivered Jerusalem into their hands because they had abandoned the Son of God, who had previously been foretold through the prophets (Acts 9).

Therefore I think that for this reason Saul—who afterward received the name Paul through the virtue of his calling, because he was a zealot for the Law—went to Damascus and wished to fight against those who believed from the nations. Having been overcome there, he followed those who were dwelling in Damascus, so that from there he might again go up to fight against the Jews in Jerusalem.

Nor should anyone regard it as contradictory that the book of Chronicles announces joyful things about Damascus while Isaiah now proclaims sad things. For even concerning Israel itself, which certainly is God’s portion, sometimes adversity and sometimes prosperity are announced.

And just as it is said to Israel according to the flesh and to the nations, “You nations according to the flesh, who are called uncircumcision by that which is called Circumcision in the flesh,” so conversely there is an Israel according to the spirit, and there are nations according to the spirit. Among the other nations there is also a Damascus according to the spirit, lest we yield only to Jewish fables.

#### Verses 1ff.

“Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city, and it will be like a heap of stones in a ruin. The cities of Aroer will be abandoned to flocks; they will lie down there, and there will be no one to terrify them. Help will cease from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, says the Lord of hosts.”

As was demonstrated in the title, Damascus signifies the calling of the nations—those who loved or drank blood. After they have believed in Christ, their cities will cease to be what they were formerly, and they will become like a heap of stones in a ruin.

For just as heaps of stones scattered through the fields are carried together into one mound, so a heap of believers has been gathered from all the nations amid the ruin of the Jewish people: when they fell, we rose.

The abandoned cities of Aroer, that is, “tamarisk” (*myrice*) [Note: Two of our manuscripts read *myricon*; in others, according to Martianus, the Greek is μυρίκον.], will also belong to ecclesiastical flocks, so that we may inhabit those places which the Jews abandoned; or, when idolatry has been destroyed, the Gospel will be built up.

We see this fulfilled even in our own times: the Serapeum [Note: “The Serapeum of Alexandria.” So our manuscripts read, including the five that Marianus Victor had from Florence. Erasmus reads “Serapis in Alexandria,” and so forth. MARTIANUS.—Concerning the Serapeum, which was the most celebrated temple of Alexandria, see Theophilus’s Synodical Letter among Jerome’s letters, no. 92, section 3, and our notes on that passage. Concerning the temple of Marna, the idol of Gaza, we spoke in the Life of Saint Hilarion, section 14.] of Alexandria and the temple of Marna at Gaza have risen as churches of the Lord, and the cities of Aroer have been prepared for evangelical flocks.

Aroer, that is, the tamarisk, grows in deserted places, in accordance with what is written in the curse of the man who trusts in a human being and whose heart departs from the Lord: “He shall be,” it says, “like a tamarisk in the desert, and he shall not see good when it comes; he shall dwell in parched places, in the wilderness, in a salty and uninhabitable land” (Jer. 17:6).

Others, however, say that from this tree, by magical arts, *místra* (μίστρα), that is, hatreds, are stirred up.

Therefore those who were previously in the wilderness of the nations and in hatred of the Christian name will serve the flocks of Christ. They will rest among them, and there will be no one to terrify them, because the Lord will dwell among them; and with the Shepherd present, they will not be able to fear the wolf.

Then God’s help will cease from Ephraim. In this passage the scribes and Pharisees are understood as Ephraim, according to the prophecy of Hosea, which calls those opposed to the people of God “Ephraim” (Hos. 5; 8).

And the kingdom will cease from Damascus, so that sin and the prince of sin, the devil, will no longer reign in Damascus, which previously loved blood. Rather, the remnant of Syria [Note: Vatican manuscript: “the remnant of those who,” etc.]—that is, those from the nations who believed—will be like the children of Israel formerly were, after the kingdom of God has been taken from them and given to the nations that produce its fruit, as the Lord God of hosts spoke through all his prophets.

#### Verses 4–6

“And it shall be on that day: the glory of Jacob will be humbled, and the fat of his flesh will waste away.” [Note: The same manuscript also reads, “and the fat of his flesh will waste away,” as the text consistently retains below.]

“And it shall be like one gathering what remains at harvest, and his arm will gather ears of grain; and it shall be like one seeking ears of grain in the valley of Rephaim.”

“And what remains in it will be like a cluster of grapes, and like the shaking of an olive tree—two or three olives at the top of a branch, or four or five fruits at the tips of its branches,” says the Lord God of Israel.

After the remnant of Syria has become like the former glory of the children of Israel, and salvation has been given to the nations because of their transgression, then all the glory of the Jews—by which they were glorious throughout the world—will be humbled. Their fat flesh will waste away, since they will have neither prophets, nor signs and mighty works, nor the present help of God, nor the dignity of the priesthood. Their entire national body will wither and be reduced to nothing.

And when it is said concerning the calling of the nations, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9:37), those poor laborers will gather the remnants of the harvest that were saved through the Apostles, and the exceedingly rare ears—not from mountains and elevated places, but in the valley of Rephaim, that is, in the lowliness of the letter.

Consider also that Rephaim, interpreted as “giants,” signifies the Pharisees and scribes, just as Ephraim does above. Accordingly, the Septuagint translated “the valley of Rephaim” as “the hard valley,” in order to express the hardness of the Jewish heart.

From their humility those who are saved are chosen like ears of grain in stubble and like clusters of grapes in a vintage, and like the shaking of an olive tree yielding two or three olives, or four or five. [Note: Some read “of an olive tree” instead of “of an olive.”]

When the striking of the Jewish people came—the olive tree of the people of Israel, which under Moses had six hundred thousand armed men (Num. 26), and under David, when Joab counted it, an innumerable population (2 Sam. 24)—it could scarcely offer a few fruits to the Lord Savior.

The two olives were Paul and Barnabas, and the three olives were Peter, James, and John (Acts 13), who both saw the transfigured Lord on the mountain and deserved to go with the Lord to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Matt. 17).

The four and five olives make up the remaining nine Apostles, among whom Matthias occupied the place of Judas the betrayer. They were divided into four and five olives according to the diversity of graces, which is unknown to us, so that they might display in themselves the number of the Gospels and the volumes of the Law, as preachers of both Testaments (Acts 1).

#### Verses 7–8

“On that day a person will incline toward his Maker, and his eyes will look toward the Holy One of Israel. He will not incline toward the altars that his hands made and that his fingers fashioned; he will not look toward the sacred groves and shrines.”

At that time, when the Lord, hungering because of the dryness of spiritual grace, has scarcely found among the people of Israel—of whom it had formerly been said, “The Lord your God called you a fruitful olive tree” (Jer. 11:16), and concerning whom we read in the Psalms, “Your children are like young olive trees around your table” (Ps. 128:3)—two olives, and three, or four, or five, the fullness of the nations will enter. It will no longer incline toward idols made by hand, but toward its God; looking toward the Holy One of Israel, it will despise altars, sacred groves, and shrines, knowing what is written: “Every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted” (Matt. 15:13).

#### Verses 9–10

“On that day his fortified cities will be abandoned like plows and grainfields that were abandoned before the children of Israel. And it will be deserted, because you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered your strong helper.”

The Septuagint reads:

“On that day your cities will be abandoned, as the Amorites and Hivites abandoned them before the children of Israel. And they will be deserted, because you have abandoned God your Savior and have not remembered the Lord your helper.”

Just as under Moses and Joshua the son of Nun the Amorites, the Hivites, and the other nations inhabiting the land of promise abandoned their plows, grainfields, and heaps in the fields and fled lest they be occupied by their enemies, so the land of Judea and all its strongest cities were abandoned by their inhabitants when the Romans devastated Judea and besieged Jerusalem.

An apostrophe is made to the land of Judea itself—that is, to those who lived in it.

You suffered all these things because you forgot the God of your salvation, whose name is interpreted as Jesus, whom the Law and the Prophets continually announced as one who would come; and you did not remember your strong helper, who had always been your aid.

The cause, therefore, of Judea’s deserted cities is forgetfulness of the Savior, who at the beginning of this prophecy had said: “Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand me.”

### (Verse 11)

Therefore you will plant a faithless planting and sow a foreign shoot. On the day of your planting, there will be a wild vine, and in the morning your seed will bloom: the harvest has been removed on the day of inheritance, and he will grieve grievously.
