**The Septuagint:** Therefore you will plant an unfaithful planting and an unfaithful seed, and on the day when you plant, you will go astray. But if you sow in the morning, it will flower for the harvest on the day of inheritance, when, like a father of a human being, he gives an inheritance to his sons.

For what we have translated, following Aquila, Symmachus, and the Septuagint, as “on the day of inheritance”—which in Hebrew is called *BIOM NEHELA* ()—one may read in Hebrew “on the evil day.” And for what Aquila [Col. 0244B] and Theodotion translated, “and the man will grieve,” we, instructed by the Hebrews, have translated *ANUS* (), that is, “grievously,” instead of “man,” which in their language is called *ENOS*.

Concerning the ambiguity of this word:

> [Note: He later explained it as follows in Jeremiah, chapter XVII, 9: The Hebrew word *ENOS* is written with four letters: ALEPH, NUN, VAU, and SIN. If, therefore, it is read *ENOS*, it means “man”; but if *ANUS*, “inscrutable” or “desperate,” because no one is able to discover the human heart. — “If the span of this life should be …” Jerome, in his discussion of Jeremiah XVII, 9, explains the ambiguity of this word, saying: The Hebrew word *ENOS* is written with four letters, ALEPH, NUN, VAU, and SIN. If, therefore, it is read *ENOS*, it means “man”; but if *ANUS*, “inscrutable” or “desperate,” because no one is able to discover the human heart. Manuscripts in this passage of Isaiah read *ANOS* instead of *ANUS*; but among the ancients *o* and *u* were used interchangeably both in writing and in pronunciation. Even today the French pronounce *u* almost like the diphthong *ou*. Another reading: *Dominous*; G., *Dominus*. MARTIAN., who, as is clear from the following note, entirely agrees with Valesius.]

If the span of this life permits, we shall discuss it more fully in Jeremiah, where, according to the Septuagint, it says: “And he is a man, and who will know him?”

Let me therefore state what I proposed. Because you have forgotten, O land of Judah, the God your Savior, and have not remembered him who always supplied you with strength, therefore you will indeed plant a faithful planting—or, as Aquila and Theodotion translated, a beautiful one; or, as Symmachus has it, a good one—proclaiming one God. But you will sow a foreign shoot, not receiving the Father, because you do not receive the Son. For whoever believes in the Father also believes in the Son.

And because you have sown a foreign shoot of blasphemy against Jesus in the synagogues of Satan, therefore you will not harvest a grape, but a wild vine. And when your shoot seems to flourish and to possess some appearance of piety, while you draw people away from idols, nevertheless, when you come to gather its fruits on the day of inheritance, you will grieve grievously, seeing that the people of the nations have been preferred to you.

Hence the Apostle also says:

> “There is great sorrow for me and unceasing pain in my heart. For I could wish that I myself were accursed and separated from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, the legislation, the glory, the covenants, and the promises; to them belong the fathers,” and so forth (Rom. II, 9 ff.).

Not Paul alone speaks thus, but every saint, wishing that the root also might be preserved together with the branches of the wild olive.

That inheritance, moreover, is the one we receive from the Lord, concerning which the Apostle says:

> “There are varieties of graces, but the same [or: one] Spirit; there are varieties of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of works, but the same God, who works all things in all” (I Cor. XII, 4–6).

Someone may wonder why, instead of “beautiful” and “good plantings,” which Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus translated, we have said “faithful planting.” The Hebrew word *NEEMANIM* (), if written with the letter ALEPH, means *πιστούς*, that is, “faithful”; but if written with AYIN and pronounced *NEAMENIM*, it means “beautiful.” Hence Naomi, whose name is written with this letter, says in Ruth (chapter I, 20): “Do not call me *NOEMI* (), that is, ‘beautiful’; call me ‘bitter.’”

### (Verses 12 ff.)

Woe to the multitude of many peoples, like the multitude of the sounding sea; and the tumult of nations will resound like the sound of many waters. The peoples will resound like the multitude of overflowing waters; he will rebuke it, and it will flee far away; it will be carried off like the dust of the mountains before the wind and like a whirlwind before a storm. In the evening—and behold, disturbance; in the morning—and it will not remain. This is the portion of those who ravaged us and the lot of those who plundered us.

> [Note: Victor: “like a sound,” from the Hebrew , and the Greek ἠχήσει.]

Above, under the name of Damascus, we read of the calling of the nations, the rejection of the Jews, and, through the Apostles—and in the Apostles—the election of the few Jews who believed. And since, in comparison with the whole world and all the nations, only a small part of the people believed as Christians—of whom it was said above, “And the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel” (for “many are called, but few are chosen,” Matt. XXII, 14), and “Faith is not possessed by all” (II Thess. III, 2)—what follows now is not lamentation but a woe against those nations that refused to believe and persecuted the Christian people.

They are compared with masses of waves and a roaring sea, desiring, as far as they can, to crush and seize everything. For the peoples will resound in the spectacles of theatrical luxury, in the cruelty of the amphitheater, and in the madness of the circus, like the sound of overflowing waters, when they blaspheme with a united voice of impiety and say that Christians should be thrown to lions and wild beasts, and things of this kind.

> [Note: The words “and wild beasts should be thrown” are not found in the Vatican manuscript, and apparently more correctly so. “Christians to the lions” was the customary cry of the pagans in the amphitheater and circus. See Tertullian.]

But while they rage like a sea, the Lord will rebuke the author of their sedition and drive him away from his people. And as stirred-up dust on the mountains is carried off the more violently the higher it is, and as a whirlwind rising from the earth is borne aloft by a sudden storm, so he too, seized and separated from the people of God, will flee, lest he be consigned to the abysses.

When the day of consummation arrives—which is interpreted as “evening”—then there will be disturbance for the one who recognizes his sins. And in the morning, namely on the day of resurrection, he will not remain, which the Septuagint translated, “he will not exist.” But if he will not exist, what will those answer who grant the devil repentance and, as far as they can, promise him an archangelic dignity?

“This is the portion of those who ravaged us and the lot of those who plundered us.” Either the Christian people speak these words, or the prophet speaks in the person of the believing people, declaring that their persecutors will possess everlasting destruction—those who oppressed God’s saints with exiles, prisons, and confiscations of their possessions, and who will possess eternal punishments.

### (Chapter XVIII, verses 1 ff.)

Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends ambassadors by sea and in vessels of papyrus upon the waters: Go, swift angels, to a nation torn apart and mangled, to a terrible people, beyond whom there is no other; to a nation awaiting, awaiting, and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land. All inhabitants of the world, you who dwell upon the earth, when a signal has been raised on the mountains, you will see it and hear the sound of the trumpet.

**The Septuagint:** Woe to the land of ships with wings beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, which sends hostages by sea and papyrus letters upon the water. For light-footed messengers will go to a lofty nation, a foreign and exceedingly evil people, which is beyond it: a nation without hope and trampled down, whose rivers now possess the whole land like a region that is inhabited [or: will be inhabited]; their region will be inhabited as when a signal is raised from a mountain and the sound of a trumpet is heard.

I have set down both editions in this exceedingly obscure prophecy, so that nothing might seem lacking to those who wish to understand what has been written.

At the same time, I greatly marvel at those who think that our faith and Christian hope are satisfied with simplicity because it is written, “The commandment of God is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 9), and that we ought to seek nothing more than the fulfillment of what has been commanded. Yet Scripture as a whole, and especially the Prophets, have been wrapped in mysteries of future things precisely so that they may summon us to understanding and to what is said in the Gospel: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”

Since, therefore, I discussed the historical sense and what is contained in the Hebrew in the fifth book, I shall now explain what seems to me appropriate according to the allegorical sense.

Perhaps a prudent reader will inquire what, in the Vision or Burden of Damascus, is meant by “the cymbal of wings” and the other things that follow.

After the prophecy concerning the calling of the nations, the rejection of the Jews, the election of those who believed through the Apostles, and afterward the multitude of the nations and the persecutors who were compared with the waves of the sea, it followed that the prophetic discourse should also announce the heresies that afflicted the Church and continue to ravage it—those which, while the master of the house slept, sowed weeds over the field of the Church (Matt. XIII).

They are called a “cymbal” because they do not possess the love of God, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII, 1).

And they are called not merely a cymbal clanging with a harsh sound, but, because of the lightness of heretical speech running in various directions, “the cymbal of wings”; or, according to the Septuagint, “the wings of ships,” since, promising great commercial ventures, they sail upon the waves of this present age.

Understand the wings of ships as the sails by which they are suspended and drawn along. And beautifully he called them “wings of ships”: every heretic promises lofty things, and although he boasts that he has wings, he nevertheless clings to the salt waves, does not go far from land, and suffers sudden shipwreck in mid-course.

Hence Aquila translated “cymbal” as “the shadow of wings,” for they do not possess wings, but only the likeness of wings.

The statement that it is “beyond the rivers of Ethiopia” signifies that all heretics surpass everyone in impiety. For example, Epicurus says that providence does not exist and that pleasure is the greatest good. Compared with him, Marcion and all the heretics who tear apart the Old Testament are more wicked. For while they accept providence, they accuse the Creator and assert that he made mistakes in many of his works and did not make things as he ought to have made them.

For what benefit to human beings are serpents, scorpions, crocodiles, fleas, bugs, and gnats?

These, therefore, are beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, and they send ambassadors upon the sea of this age—that is, their disciples—who carry their books. They are rightly said to carry papyrus vessels, that is, paper, upon the waters, because these are quickly erased.

For just as books near water and moisture quickly grow dark, are erased, and perish, so their speech and teaching, though at first it may seem to possess some strength, passes away and slips from sight.

Thus, ironically, it is said to them: “O angels of the heretics, go swiftly.” The blessed Apostle Paul calls such people false apostles and deceitful workers who transform themselves into apostles of Christ (II Cor. XI).

“And go to a nation torn apart and mangled”: torn away from God and lacerated by the bites of heretics.

“To a terrible people”: for nothing is more terrible than blasphemy, which sets its mouth against the Most High.

“Beyond whom there is no other people”: for every sin, compared with blasphemy, is lighter.

“To a nation awaiting, awaiting, and trampled down.” All heretics promise themselves heavenly things and make immense promises, yet they are trampled down by demons.

“Whose land the rivers have plundered”: rivers that do not have their waters from heaven but from the earth. For what corner, what remote extremity of the earth is there to which the turbid speech of the heretics does not reach?

Therefore all who inhabit and dwell upon the earth raise their eyes toward the sign of the heretics, which has been raised as if upon the mountains, and hear the sound of their trumpet—that is, their teaching.

This is according to the Hebrew.

According to the Septuagint, however, the wings of the heretics are lamented—wings that flit like ships across the sea of this age and surpass the impiety of the pagans, whom Scripture now calls Ethiopians. And it is said to their teaching and speech:

“You send upon the sea of this age books, pledges of your perversity, and letters to deceive those who will read them.”

Light-footed messengers go to a lofty nation, a foreign and exceedingly evil people. No member of the Church has as much zeal for good as heretics have for evil; they think that they gain profit if they deceive others, and, themselves lost, destroy the rest.

The nation is called lofty because of its pride, and foreign and exceedingly evil because it is alienated from God.

Truly it is a nation without hope and trampled down, whose rivers imitate the dwelling of the Church throughout the whole earth, so that they may find for themselves a lodging and a region in which to raise the sign of their teaching, in which they may sound the trumpet of the Scriptures.

> [Note: The Vatican manuscript has “and as if they sound the trumpet of the Scriptures.” Victor adds “of them,” saying that the sense agrees with what follows, “while the master slept,” and that they sowed over it.]

### (Verses 4 ff.)

For thus says the Lord to me: I will rest, and I will look upon my place, like clear light at midday and like a cloud of dew on the day of harvest. For before the harvest it has flowered completely; its premature perfection will produce shoots, and its little branches will be cut off with sickles; and what has been left will be cut away and shaken off. They will be left together for the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth; and throughout the perpetual summer the birds will be over it, and all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it.

At that time a gift will be brought to the Lord of hosts by a people torn apart and mangled, by a terrible people, beyond whom there was no other, by a nation awaiting, awaiting, and trampled down, whose rivers have plundered its land, to the place of the name of the Lord of hosts, Mount Zion.

God rests and looks upon his place—or, according to Aquila, upon the firmament, that is, the Church, of which the Apostle Paul says, “The pillar and foundation of the truth” (I Tim. III, 15).

He observes what takes place in the Church; and just as the light at midday is clear, so he illuminates everything, according to what is said allegorically in the eighteenth Psalm about the sun of righteousness: “There is no one who can hide from his heat” (Ps. XVIII, 7).

And just as a cloud of dew is most welcome on the day of harvest and in the heat of summer, so the Lord refreshes the inhabitants of his Church; in his presence everything blossoms.

Before the time of consummation arrives—for now we know in part and prophesy in part—many will be found perfect, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Let as many as are perfect think this” (I Cor. XIII; Phil. III, 15).

The little branches that are useless will be cut off with sickles, as the Savior says in the Gospel:

> “I am the true vine, and my Father is the cultivator. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he removes; and every one that bears fruit, he cleanses, so that it may bear more fruit” (John XV, 2).

And what has been cut off will be left to the birds of the mountains and the beasts of the earth: to the birds that devour what is sown beside the road, and to the beasts to which the soul that does not confess God is handed over.

Thus the one who has been cut off and rejected by the Lord, and separated from his body, which is the Church, becomes a dwelling-place for birds and beasts both in summer and winter—that is, in prosperity and adversity.

But just as those who are useless and unfruitful in the Church are cut off and cast out, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump, so, conversely, it can happen that those who had been deceived by heretical error, torn away from the Lord, mangled, and made terrible by blasphemy, waiting in vain for falsehoods, and trampled down by demons, and scattered in various directions by the rivers—when they remember their God and abandon their most wicked teachers—may offer a gift to the Lord of hosts, nowhere except on Mount Zion, “the watchtower,” which is interpreted as the Church.

We say this briefly, since we have already said much in the book of the historical explanation.

### (Chapter XIX, verse 1)

The burden of Egypt.

Symmachus and Theodotion: “The assumption of Egypt.”

The Septuagint: “The vision of Egypt.”

Where the Hebrew has *MASSA MESRAIM* (), which we translated as “the burden” or “weight of Egypt,” Aquila translated ἄρμα Αἰγύπτου, “the burden of Egypt.” We may say that, because the prophet takes up and bears the yoke of the Lord, he proved worthy to see—or bear—the prophecy of Egypt.

> [Note: With the aid of the Vatican manuscript we emend the reading to ἄρμα, which means “burden,” in place of the defective ὅραμα, which means “vision.” Drusius had long ago advised the same correction, both for other reasons and especially because this interpretation better suits Aquila’s manner, since he loved to express even the etymologies. Montfaucon adds that Aquila consistently translated the word in this way wherever it occurs, as in Proverbs XXXI and Isaiah XXI and XXIII and elsewhere, where ἄρμα is always found in the best books and manuscripts. Jerome himself bears witness to this at the end of the fourth book on Jeremiah, chapter XXIII: “The Hebrew word *MASSA*,” he says, “Aquila translates as ἄρμα, that is, burden and weight.”]

Hence I am surprised that the Septuagint translated “vision” in Babylon instead of “weight”; in Philistia, Moab, and Damascus, “word”; and now in Egypt, “vision,” when in Hebrew all these passages contain not “word” and “vision” but *MASSA* (), that is, “burden” or “weight.”

As for the fact that Symmachus and Theodotion always translated λῆμμα, that is, “assumption,” we should understand that the prophet received from the Lord a spiritual grace by which he might know, or behold with the eyes of the mind, the mysteries of Egypt, as the Septuagint translated it.

This is not the Egypt that the Jews think it is, as Josephus supposed, for he records in his books of Antiquities that the priest Onias fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy by building, in the territory of Heliopolis—which the Egyptians call a *νομός*—a temple and an altar like the Temple of God.

> [Note: “Which the Egyptians call a *nomos*.” From this passage the note should be corrected, and the preceding text at column 165, beginning, should be emended to read “which they call *nomoi*,” and so forth. Although “judges” might be meant by *nomoi*, the more accurate meaning seems to be the one that the name *nomos* has among authors. The *nomoi*, therefore, were the prefectures of Egypt. Pliny, Book V, chapter 9, speaking of Thebaid, says: “It is divided into prefectures of towns, which they call *nomoi*, twelve in number.” Diodorus, Book II, divided Egypt into thirty-six *nomoi*. Herodotus used *nomoi* and satrapies in the same sense, dividing the kingdom of Darius into twenty satrapies and as many *nomoi*, that is, regions; their governors were called nomarchs. Thus the district or territory of Heliopolis was a *nomos*, or prefecture, where Onias built the temple. MARTIAN.]

Let us grant, then, that these things were said about Onias and the altar that he built in Egypt. What will be the five cities in Egypt that speak the language of Canaan, one of which, according to the Septuagint, is called ἀσεδέκ, and, according to the other interpreters, the city of ARS or ARES, or the city of the sun?

And who will be the savior who was sent to the Egyptians to save them, so that the Egyptians might know the Lord?

When did they worship him with sacrifices and offerings and fulfill their vows? When did the Lord strike Egypt and heal it? At what time can we show that there was a road from Egypt to the Assyrians, and that the Assyrians entered Egypt and the Egyptians entered Assyria, and that the Egyptians served Assur?

When was Israel the third in Egypt and, among the Assyrians, like a blessing in the midst of the earth, so that the Lord said, “Blessed is my people Egypt, and Assyria, the work of my hands”?

It is clear that these things do not pertain to the Egypt that the Jews imagine. Therefore we may call the place in which we dwell, and the world that lies in the evil one, “Egypt,” especially because *MESRAIM* (), which is called Egypt, is interpreted as ἐκθλίβουσα, that is, “she who afflicts” or “reduces to distress.”

> [Note: The manuscripts read Ἐκθλίβουσα; the printed editions have θλίβουσα.]

It must nevertheless be understood that many things in the burden or vision of Egypt do pertain to the province of Egypt, which is inhabited and seen to this day. But in this and in other passages of Scripture many things are set down that could not stand according to the historical sense, so that the necessity of the subject compels us to seek a higher understanding.

### (Verses 1 ff.)

Behold, the Lord will mount upon a light cloud and enter Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it. I will set Egyptians against Egyptians, and a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend, city against city, kingdom against kingdom. The spirit of Egypt will be torn apart within its midst; I will overturn its counsel. They will consult their idols, their diviners, their Pythonic spirits, and their soothsayers. I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel masters, and a powerful king will rule over them, says the Lord God of hosts.

Much of the prophecy of Egypt that Isaiah lifted up or saw I touched upon in the historical explanation. Therefore we must now gather only its principal points according to the allegorical sense.

The Lord mounts upon a light cloud: the body of the holy Virgin Mary, not weighed down by the burden of human seed; or, certainly, his own body, conceived from the Holy Spirit.

He entered the Egypt of this world, and immediately all the idols of Egypt were shaken, so that divinations and the entire fraud of idolatry, which possessed the deceived world, recognized that it had been broken. Thus the Magi from the East, taught by demons or understanding the prophecy of Balaam (Num. XXIV), recognizing the birth of the Son of God, who would destroy all the power of their art, came to Bethlehem and, when the star showed the way, worshiped the child (Matt. II).

> [Note: Comparable, or even clearer, words occur below in chapter XLVIII: “The Magi,” he says, “came from the East, saying that they had seen the Lord’s star, either through knowledge of their art or through the prophecy of their prophet Balaam, who had said in Numbers, ‘A star will arise from Jacob, and a man from Israel.’” He seems to have learned this from Tertullian’s *On Idolatry*, where he says: “This knowledge”—namely, astrology—“was permitted until the Gospel, so that once Christ had been born, no one thereafter might interpret the birth of anyone from heaven.” The opinion of many other ancient Fathers concerning the Magi is much fairer: they hold that the Magi were honorable men who, without the written Law and the ceremonies of the Jews, worshiped God, who had warned them, like Job.]

Then the whole heart of Egypt melted, and Egyptians rose against Egyptians, according to what the Lord says in the Gospel:

> “Do not think that I have come to bring peace upon the earth. I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matt. X, 34 ff.).

At that time the saying was also fulfilled: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. VII, 6).

“And a man will fight against his brother, and a man against his friend.” For in one house two were separated against three, and three against two; and father was divided against son, and son against father; city against city and kingdom against kingdom: those who did not believe against those who believed, or certainly, the division of those who believed and desired to save their neighbors.

The spirit of Egypt was torn apart within its own midst, so that they no longer thought alike but, separated from one another by a spiritual sword, recognized that all their counsel had been overturned. Nevertheless, remaining in their former error, those who refused to accept the truth of the faith consulted their idols, their diviners, their Pythonic spirits, and their soothsayers.

When they had done this, the Lord delivered them into the hand of cruel masters, according to the Apostle’s saying:

> “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. I, 20),

so that, oppressed by the harshest slavery, they might return to the most merciful Lord.

Beautifully he calls the demons “cruel masters,” for nothing is more cruel than they.

The powerful king, who is their lord, is clearly understood to be the devil, whom the Lord also calls “the strong man” in the Gospel; when he is bound and overcome, his household’s vessels are seized and his spoil is carried off.

### (Verses 5 ff.)

The water of the sea will dry up, and the river will become desolate and dry. The streams will fail; the channels of the banks will grow thin and dry up. The reed and the rush will wither. The bed of the stream will be laid bare from its source, and every sown field that is watered will dry up; it will wither and will not exist. The fishermen will mourn, and all who cast a hook into the river and spread a net over the surface of the water will lament and will wither. Those who work flax will be confounded, plaiting and weaving fine linen, and its irrigated places will become slack—all who made pools for catching fish.

The princes of Tanis are fools; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel.

> [Note: Martianus has *damnatus*; the Vatican manuscript reads *nominatus*. Both are defective. We have restored *dominatus* by changing a single letter, in accordance with the sense of the preceding verse, which Jerome alludes to: “I will deliver Egypt into the hands of cruel masters, and a powerful king will rule over them.”]

When the powerful king has ruled in Egypt, every teaching and all the beauty of secular eloquence will dry up, and the devil himself, the source of all the rivers from which every falsehood arises, will become desolate, so that the remaining rivers and streams, which were filled from the turbid waters of the Nile, will fail.

The reed and the rush, too, will wither through excessive dryness.

In place of “rush,” the Septuagint translated *papyrus*, from which paper is made, adding on its own “green *achi*.”

> [Note: “Green *achi*.” Here too the older editions of Erasmus and Marianus fabricate Greek words that Jerome never mentions, as all the manuscript copies and the actual edition of the Septuagint testify. There we read ἢ Ἀχι τὸ χλωρόν, that is, “green *achi*,” which are precisely the words of the manuscript copies: “green *achi*,” not, as the printed editions fabricate, ἄχυρον τὸ χλωρόν. The name *achi* is also found in the Septuagint at Genesis XLI, 18, and there has no meaning other than the one Jerome gives here. Compare both passages, so that you may learn that among the Egyptians a marsh was called *achi*, and that perhaps the Septuagint should not be blamed in the cited passage of Genesis for reading *achi* instead of *achu*. MARTIAN. —Indeed, “rush” and *achu* are used as synonyms in Job VIII, 11: “Will the rush grow without mud, or *achu* without water?” The Greeks wrote ἄχι or ἄχει, as in Genesis XLI, 2, concerning Pharaoh’s cows: ἐβόσκοντο ἐν τῷ ἄχει, “they were feeding in the *achi*.” In the present passage, however, τὸ ἄχι τὸ χλωρὸν πᾶν τὸ κύκλῳ ποταμοῦ, “the green *achi*, everything around the river,” is not found in the Hebrew, which has “grassy places.” In Jerome, after the words “from which paper is made,” Martianus removed the words that appeared in the earlier editions, “adding on its own ἄχυρον τὸ χλωρόν,” though I would have preferred that they simply be corrected to read ἄχει τὸ χλωρόν.]

When I asked learned men what this word meant, I was told that among the Egyptians the name referred to everything green that grows in a marsh.

According to the allegorical sense, the reed is empty speech, possessing nothing solid within itself. The papyrus appears to have a pith and not to be empty, yet it is fragile and quickly withers.

All the streams, too, when the headwaters of the rivers have dried up, will dry up; and whatever had previously been irrigated by water for the Egyptians, once dried up, will not exist.

Thus the Egyptian fishermen will mourn, for they are very much opposed to the fishermen of the Lord; and those who cast hooks into the river and spread nets over the surface of the water will lament.

Those who deceive individuals cast a hook into the turbid waters. But those who deceive many at once—speaking publicly in the synagogues of Satan and leading away the flocks of peoples—cast a net over the Egyptian waters.

Those also who worked flax, making garments for priests, will be confounded, plaiting it and weaving fine linen. This properly refers to the art of dialectic.

For “fine linen,” the Septuagint translated *byssus*, which likewise is woven into priestly garments.

The statement that follows, “Its irrigated places will become slack, all who made pools for catching fish,” signifies that all the traps of the Egyptian fishermen will be destroyed and perish.

In place of the pools made for catching fish—which we translated according to the sense—in both the Hebrew and all the interpreters, “souls” is found instead of “fish,” so that we may be drawn from the historical sense to the allegorical: namely, that these fishermen made pools and pits for the purpose of deceiving souls in them.

It should be noted that, in place of “pools,” the Septuagint translated ζῦθον, a kind of drink made from grain and water, commonly called *sabaium* in the provinces of Dalmatia and Pannonia, in the language of the native barbarians.

> [Note: One might not improperly derive the name *sabaium* from the Hebrew , meaning “to drink.” Concerning it, Ammianus Marcellinus says in Book XXVI: “*Sabaia* is a poor drink in Illyricum, made from barley or grain converted into a liquid.” *Zythum*, another name for this drink, is mentioned by Pliny, Book XXII, at the end; Dioscorides, Book II, chapter 109; Herodotus, Book II; Hesychius; Suidas; and others.]

The Egyptians make especially frequent use of this, so that they give drinkers not pure waters but turbid ones, resembling waters mixed with sediment, in order that the teaching of heretical depravity may be represented through such a beverage.

Then the princes of Tanis will be fools. Tanis is interpreted as “a humble command.” For all heretics teach a humility opposed to exaltation, drag people down to the underworld, and are princes of a humble and abject command.

The counselors of Pharaoh, who is the king of Egypt and is rightly expressed as the dissipator, the divided one, and the one separated into various parts, will also be convicted of having given foolish counsel, when the Lord destroys the wisdom of the wise and rejects the understanding of the prudent (I Cor. I).

### (Verses 12 and following)

How do you say to Pharaoh, “I am the son of the wise, the son of ancient kings”? Where are your wise men now? Let them announce it to you, and let them declare what the Lord of hosts has planned concerning Egypt. The princes of Tanis have become fools; the princes of Memphis have withered away; they have led Egypt astray, the corner of its peoples. The Lord has mingled within it a spirit of dizziness, and they have made Egypt go astray in all its work, as a drunkard goes astray while vomiting. And there will be no work for Egypt by which it may produce a head and a tail, one that bends and one that restrains.

Heretics commonly say to their king, or Pharaoh: “We are sons of the wise, who from the beginning handed down to us the apostolic teaching; we are sons of ancient kings, who are called kings of philosophers, and we possess knowledge of the Scriptures joined to secular wisdom.” He now asks them—or rather the king of the heretics himself—where his wise men are, those who despised the simplicity of the Church; and he compels him to answer what the Lord of hosts has planned concerning the Egypt of this world, and what he will do at the consummation.

The princes of Tanis, who have held the heretics’ humble command, are shown to have become fools. All the princes of Memphis have withered away, those who have [Col. 0253C] polluted eloquence and speech by boastfulness.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] “To pollute boastfulness.” The manuscript of Silvae Majoris near Bordeaux reads, with suitable sense, “who have caused the boastfulness of eloquence and speech to sprout forth.” MARTIAN. — Martian., “to pollute boastfulness”; manuscripts, “boastfulness.” Elsewhere, “have caused it to sprout forth.”]

For Memphis is interpreted as “mouth,” or “from the mouth,” and metaphorically it signifies speech. And what follows—“They have led Egypt astray, the corner-stone of its peoples,” or, according to the Septuagint, “they will lead Egypt astray by tribes”—means that the kingdom of secular wisdom is demonstrated to be foolish, and that the princes of its individual doctrines, who are interpreted as “tribes,” are charged with having foolish teachers.

For the Lord has mingled among them a spirit of dizziness, or of error, according to what is written: “And because they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a depraved mind” (Rom. 1:24). And just as one who is holy can say with Isaiah, “We shall bring the spirit of your salvation upon the earth,” so one who is a sinner will produce a spirit of error—that is, a spirit of wickedness—according to what we also read in Jeremiah: “Your apostasy shall rebuke you, and your wickedness shall chastise you” (Jer. 2:19).

But if the heretic, who does not accept the Old Testament, is scandalized that the Lord is said to mingle a spirit of error or dizziness, let him hear what is written in the Apostle—that is, in the New Testament: “God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity” (Rom. 1:24). And again: “Therefore God gave them over to dishonorable passions.” And once more: “God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what is improper” [Alternative: “what is not fitting”]. They are handed over to the desires of their hearts because they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, quadrupeds, and reptiles.

We read this not only in the Epistle to the Romans, but also in the Epistle to the Thessalonians concerning the Antichrist: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie and be condemned—all who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in wickedness” (2 Thess. 2:10). I think that the Apostle Paul took this from the present passage of Isaiah, in which he says: “The Lord mingled among them a spirit of error, and they made Egypt go astray in all its works,” just as, he says, a drunkard goes astray while vomiting—one who has become drunk on vices.

[Note: [Col. 0253D] Joel speaks of such drunkards. Thus we read in the manuscript codices, although the contrary is written in Joel, chapter 1—namely, “drunkards from wine,” also according to the Septuagint. Hence Marianus’s conjecture is readily believed: he thought that *idem* should be read instead of the name Joel, so that the sense would be, “concerning whom Isaiah himself speaks.” These words are read in Isaiah 28 according to the Septuagint: ἄνευ οἴνου, “without wine.” MARTIAN. — In place of Joel, in whose writings such a statement is not found, Victorius wishes to restore *idem*, namely Isaiah himself, who, according to the Septuagint, at 28:1, rebukes μεθύοντες ἄνευ οἴνου, “those who are drunk without wine,” although the Hebrew and Latin codices read otherwise.]

And not merely drunkards, but also those vomiting the fury of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, so that after they have vomited out such wine, they may understand their drunkenness and recognize that, so long as they have been drunk, they have had neither beginning nor end—that is, neither head nor tail—but have been an animal truncated at both ends.

In place of “beginning” and “end,” which both Symmachus and the Septuagint translated, Theodotion, as is his custom, inserted the very Hebrew words:

**CHAPHPHE** (חפפה) and **AGMON** (אגמון).

Aquila interpreted the first as “bent” and the second as “perverse.” By “bent” he wished the old men to be understood, and by “perverse,” wanton boys who do everything perversely. Thus the sense is that in Egypt there will be lacking not only head and tail, but also old men and boys—that is, beginning and end.

[Note: [Col. 0254D] The Vatican manuscript reads **CAFFA** and **EGMON**; others prefer **CHEPHPHA**. In Greek it is written κεφφά.]

### (Verses 16–17)

On that day Egypt will be like women; it will be astonished and afraid before the shaking of the hand of the Lord of hosts, which he will shake over it. And the land of Judah will be a terror to Egypt: everyone who remembers it will be terrified before the counsel of the Lord of hosts, which he has planned concerning it.

“At that time”—for, as we have often said, this signifies “the day”—when the Lord has mingled a spirit of error and dizziness, so that Egypt may vomit the wine of dragons and the incurable fury of asps, recognizing its error and former drunkenness, Egypt will fear like a woman. This is not the accidental fear that commonly befalls men, whom Egypt does not love but suffocates and kills, but a feminine fear, since Pharaoh wishes only women to remain alive.

It will fear the shaking, or exaltation, of the hand of the Lord, by which punishments are displayed. He will shake and raise it in order to strike Egypt. Then the land of Judah—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures, the Law and the Prophets, the Gospels and the Apostolic Epistles—will be a festival to Egypt if it comes to know them, or a terror if, by comparison with their teaching and truth, it recognizes that it has possessed falsehood.

Everyone who remembers this land will be terrified with the fear that leads to life, for “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Prov. 9:10). We can understand this not only at the consummation of the world but also in the present time: every heretic fears the ecclesiastical man, the man instructed in heavenly teachings, and is terrified at the recollection of him. He will also fear and dread the counsel of the Lord, which he has planned concerning the Egypt of this world. We have passed over each point briefly in order to proceed to what follows.

### (Verse 18)

On that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts. One will be called the City of the Sun.

The raising or shaking of the Lord’s hand over Egypt is greatly beneficial, so that the land of Judah may be a terror to it, and everyone who remembers it may tremble greatly. At that time five cities in the land of Egypt will speak the language of Canaan. Many of our writers understand these as the five senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

When we look upon a woman in order to desire her, our sight speaks the Egyptian language. When we hear a judgment involving blood, while the Lord says, “You shall not receive a vain report” (4 Kings 12:21, according to the Septuagint), our hearing speaks the Egyptian language. When, according to the prophet, we live in luxury, lie upon ivory beds, and anoint ourselves with the finest [Possibly: “the best”] perfumes, our sense of smell speaks the Egyptian language. When our belly is our god (Phil. 3), our taste speaks the Egyptian language. If we do not heed what the Apostle says—“It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7)—but, on the contrary, join ourselves to a prostitute, our touch speaks the Egyptian language.

But if, conversely, we raise our eyes and see that the regions are already white for harvesting, and are no longer bent down toward the earth, but, like the Gospel woman who for eighteen years could not look toward heaven (Luke 13), raise our eyes and say, “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in the heavens” (Ps. 122:1), then our eye and sight speak the language of Canaan.

If we circumcise our ears and hear the Lord saying, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8), our hearing speaks the language of Canaan. Whoever can say to the Bridegroom, “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song 1:3), and, “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (1 Cor. 2:15), has a sense of smell that speaks the language of Canaan.

Taste too is understood in a good sense in the case of one who eats the bread that descended from heaven, the living and not dead bread, and hears: “Taste and see how sweet the Lord is” (Ps. 33:9). Immediately it speaks the language of Canaan.

Touch also is spiritual. The Apostle John says of it: “Our hands have touched the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). So too does the one who touches Jesus by faith, so that the Savior can say of him: “Someone touched me, for I know that power has gone out from me” (Luke 8:46).

We have learned how many good things the raised hand of the Lord bestows. Let us ask why the five cities of Egypt speak not the Hebrew language but the language of Canaan. We shall try to answer as follows: *Hebrew* signifies **περάτης**, that is, “one who passes through,” who moves from one place to another. Therefore, although we are holy so long as we are in Egypt and dwell amid the darkness of this world, we cannot speak the Hebrew language, but the language of Canaan, which lies between Egyptian and Hebrew and is largely adjacent to Hebrew.

*Canaan* is interpreted as “a shaking,” or “one who answers.” Therefore, when we withdraw from Egypt and wish to leave Pharaoh’s power, so that our land and confession may be terrifying to Egypt, then we are shaken and, as it were, answer the Lord’s will. Yet, because we are still in the present age, we cannot yet speak the Hebrew language.

And what follows—“The five cities will swear by the Lord of hosts”—means that, even while placed here, we should remember not demons but God Almighty. Of these five cities, while the names of the other four are passed over in silence, one is called the City of the Sun. It seems to me to refer to sight. For just as a city requires the sun and moon in order to be seen, so our eyes require the Sun of Justice in order to be illuminated.

### (Verses 19–21)

On that day there will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a monument to the Lord beside its boundary. It will be a sign and a testimony to the Lord of hosts in the land of Egypt. For they will cry out to the Lord because of the oppressor, and he will send them a Savior and a defender who will deliver them. And the Lord will be known to Egypt.

Following what he had said above—“On that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan and swearing by the Lord of hosts”—the text now adds: “There will be an altar of the Lord in the midst of the land of Egypt.” Onias, misunderstanding this according to Josephus (*Antiquities*, book 13, chapter 6), attempted to fulfill it improperly.

And there will be a monument of the Lord containing the Passion, on which was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters, “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19). It is a sign of the Cross and a testimony to all the nations that are now called Egypt.

When persecution has increased because of the Christian name, then they will cry out in their hearts: “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). And the Lord of hosts will send a Savior—that is, Jesus—and a Judge, or defender, who will deliver them. Once delivered, they will know the Lord, and they themselves will be known by the Lord; and “where sin abounded, grace will abound still more” (Rom. 5).

Only one altar of Egypt—that is, of this world—is mentioned, so that we may know that all the altars raised against the altar of the Church are not the Lord’s. Up to the end of the Egyptian vision, in the book of the *Historical Explanation*, since the prophecy was clear, we said that everything referred to Christ.

### (Verse 20)

And the Egyptians will know the Lord on that day, and they will worship him with sacrifices and offerings; they will make vows to the Lord and fulfill them. And the Lord will strike Egypt with a plague and heal it; they will return to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them and heal them.

After the Egyptians have known the Lord, they will worship him with spiritual sacrifices and offerings; they will make vows to the Lord and fulfill them.

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Vatican manuscript: “so that they may say with David.”]

And they will say with David: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Ps. 50:19); and, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140:2). This will occur when, believing in the Nazarene, they themselves become Nazarenes, drinking neither wine nor strong drink (John 19), nor the vinegar offered to the Lord, nor anything made from the grape of Sodom.

When they have fulfilled their vows with Abel, and God has looked upon them, their elder brother Cain—that is, the people of the Circumcision—will be jealous and will pour out Christian blood, which will cry out to the Lord (Gen. 4). Therefore he will go forth from the presence of God, saying of the Savior, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Luke 23:11), and, “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

The one who is holy in body and spirit offers and fulfills a vow to the Lord. Zacchaeus also offered a vow, when he promised half of his property to the poor (Luke 19).

It may be asked: If a Savior and defender was sent to the Egyptians to deliver them from their afflictions, how is it now said, “The Lord will strike Egypt with a plague”? But let us consider what follows: “And he will heal it.” “The Lord disciplines the one whom he loves” (Heb. 12). And the Savior himself says to the Father in Psalm 68: “For those whom you struck pursued them, and they added to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 68:27).

If, therefore, he did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us, so that by his bruising and wounds we might be healed (Rom. 8), the Lord also handed the martyrs over to suffering, but will again heal them in the resurrection, so that by their wounds the faith of believers may be confirmed.

Hence it is also said to Job: “Do you suppose that I spoke to you otherwise than so that you might appear righteous?” For he himself causes pain and restores to former health; and he visits his servants with the rod, so that he may not take away his mercy from them. Therefore the daughters and daughters-in-law who have sinned greatly and spread their legs to every passerby are neither visited nor chastised, since the Lord says: “I will not visit your daughters when they have prostituted themselves, nor your daughters-in-law when they have committed adultery” (Hos. 4:14).

The Lord therefore strikes the Egyptians not with fire or sword but with a rod. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? Once they have been healed, they will return to the Lord, and he will be appeased toward them and heal them again. We always need the mercy of God, and there is no end to his clemency.

### (Verse 23)

On that day there will be a road from Egypt to the Assyrians; the Assyrian will enter Egypt, and the Egyptian the Assyrians, and the Egyptians will serve the Assyrians.

Just as we demonstrated that all the preceding events happened to the Egyptians in a good sense—namely, that five cities in their land spoke the language of Canaan and swore by the Lord; that the altar of the Lord was placed in the midst of the land of Egypt; that there were a monument, a testimony, a sign, and a Savior who delivered them; that the Lord was known by the Egyptians and that they knew him; that they offered sacrifices and gifts, fulfilled their vows, were healed after being struck, returned to the Lord, were reconciled to him, and were healed again—so this also, which follows, namely that the Egyptians will serve the Assyrians, is to be understood in a good sense.

The Apostle also serves believers, so that he may win them (1 Cor. 9). Esau is likewise subjected to his brother Jacob (Gen. 33), so that he may become a participant in his blessings.

Therefore those from the nations who are saved first, and who possess within themselves the altar of the Lord, will save by their service those who persist in hardness. Through their mingling and fellowship, the latter will proceed to the Assyrians, so that they may lead the Assyrians to Egypt and afterward be able to reach the Israelite people.

For this reason, I think, a believing woman also serves an unbelieving husband, so that little by little she may draw him from Egypt and the Assyrians to Judea.

### (Verses 25–26)

On that day Israel will be third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the land, which the Lord of hosts has blessed, saying: “Blessed is my people Egypt, and Assyria, the work of my hands; but Israel is my inheritance.”

Israel will be third with Egypt and Assyria, so that it may mix the whole mass with the leaven of its blessing, and so that those who previously were hostilely divided against one another may be joined by this bond of blessing. Thus Egypt will be the people of God, Assyria the work of his hands, and Israel his inheritance.

The Egyptian is blessed by the Lord because he is blessed through association with Israel. Assyria is the work of his hands because in Assyria he has displayed his mercy. But Israel alone can say: “The Lord is my portion” (Lam. 3:24), Israel which beholds God with the mind and is called his inheritance.

### (Chapter 20: Verses 1 and following)

In the year when Tartan entered Ashdod, when Sargon, king of the Assyrians, sent him, and he fought against Ashdod and captured it, at that time the Lord spoke by the hand of Isaiah son of Amoz, saying: “Go and remove the sackcloth from your loins, and take off your sandals from your feet.” And he did so, going naked and barefoot.

And the Lord said: “Just as my servant Isaiah has gone naked and barefoot, it shall be a sign and portent for three years concerning Egypt and concerning Ethiopia. Thus the king of the Assyrians will lead away the captivity of Egypt and the migration of Ethiopia, young and old, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks uncovered, the disgrace of Egypt. They will fear and be ashamed because of Ethiopia, their hope, and because of Egypt, their glory.

And the inhabitant of this island will say on that day, ‘Was this our hope? To whom did we flee for help, so that they might deliver us from the presence of the king of the Assyrians? And how will we be able to escape?’”

For Tartan, the Septuagint translated Thanatan; and for Sargon, Arna. We cannot know what these names mean. Nor can we invent false etymologies for false names. They are not Hebrew but Assyrian names. From them we have learned that Tartan means “he gave a tower,” or “superfluous,” or “one who lengthens.” Sargon means “prince of the garden.”

This Assyrian king, whom we previously understood as “great in meaning,” has many commanders. One of them is Tartan, exalted in pride, advancing far in wickedness, and greater than the rest. He is sent to attack Ashdod, which is called **ASDOD** in Hebrew (אשדוד), and is interpreted as “fire of generation.”

[Note: [Col. 0259D] In the *Hebrew Questions*: “Ashdod,” he says, “is called Esdod in Hebrew and, according to its former name, has the etymology ‘fire of a kinsman.’” If desired, add Stephen of Byzantium, who says that the city was named from Ἀζᾶ, the wife of its founder, and teaches that a goat is called “Azoti” in their language.]

The commander of the Assyrian king attacks those who serve generation and lust. Appropriately, Sargon, the “prince of gardens,” king of the Assyrians, is said to be devoted to pleasure and luxury. Finally, Ahab, king of Israel, also desired to turn Naboth’s vineyard into a garden (3 Kings 21). Understanding this according to the laws of tropology, Naboth preferred to die rather than do it, lest his ancestral inheritance and ancient possession be turned into the pleasures of an impious king.

The Prophet is commanded to put aside his sackcloth and sandals and walk naked and barefoot, serving as a sign and portent for the Egyptians and Ethiopians who persecuted the people of God and, because of their pride, were made humble.

Egypt is interpreted as “the persecutor” or “the one who afflicts”; Ethiopians as “humble and cast down,” for “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14:11). They are to be led into captivity and endure three years of torment (Exod. 12). Concerning these years we read in the Psalms: “I considered the days of old, and I kept the eternal years in mind” (Ps. 76:6). We should not think that these are minor punishments, but that they are extended over great periods of time.

In the captivity and migration of Egypt itself, young and old will go—those who have grown strong in wickedness and reached the vices of mature age—naked, so that all their crimes may be exposed (“For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed,” Luke 8:7), and barefoot, because they will not be able to eat the Lord’s Passover. Whoever eats it has his loins girded, holds a staff in his hand, and stands with his feet shod, lest, while passing through the wilderness of this age, he be bitten by serpents (Exod. 12).

Then their buttocks will be uncovered, through which dung is expelled, and all the disgrace of Egypt will be displayed. Thus those who placed their hope in Egypt and Ethiopia will be ashamed and will see their glory changed into disgrace. So great will be their shame that the inhabitant of this island—that is, of this world—who is not an alien or sojourner but desired to possess the world permanently, will say in confusion: “Is this Egypt, and is this Ethiopia, from which we hoped for help, so that they might deliver us from the ruler of this world? How, then, will we be able to escape, when those in whom we hoped have been captured?”

This too should be noted: before Ashdod is captured, the Prophet is clothed in sackcloth and wears sandals, so that he may indeed mourn those who have been wounded by the devil’s burning arrows and serve lust, but nevertheless walk shod so that he may trample upon serpents and scorpions and walk securely through the wilderness of this age, where there are serpents and scorpions and thirst for good things.

But after Ashdod has been captured, as a type of the captivity of Egypt and the migration of Ethiopia, he himself walks barefoot and naked. For in the Holy Land to which he hastens, he could neither stand nor walk clothed in sackcloth and with his feet covered in leather, since the Lord says: “Remove the sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:5).

### (Chapter 21: Verses 1 and following)

The burden of the sea-desert.

As whirlwinds come from the south-west, it comes from the desert, from a terrible land. A harsh vision was announced to me: the faithless one acts faithlessly, and the devastator devastates. Go up, Elam; lay siege, Media. I have caused all its groaning to cease. Therefore my loins are filled with pain; anguish has seized me, like the anguish of a woman in labor.

**Septuagint:** “The vision of the desert of the sea. As a storm passes through the desert, coming from the desert, from a terrible land, a harsh vision was announced to me: the transgressor transgresses, and the lawless one acts lawlessly. The Elamites and the Persian envoys are coming against me. Now I shall groan and console myself. Therefore my loins were filled with anguish; pains seized me like a woman in labor.”

We have briefly stated what seems to us according to the historical interpretation. Now let us grasp the chief points of the tropological interpretation.

A vision, or burden, is seen against the sea of this world; and the Prophet sees how full this world is of temptations. That the sea is called this age—to pass over many proofs—I am content with a single testimony from the Psalm: “Those who go down to the sea in ships, doing works upon many waters—they have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep” (Ps. 106:23).

Those who work the work of God in this world and say with the Prophet, “I have come into the depths of the sea,” see his wonders in the deep. Delivered from temptations and afflictions, they say that they have heard a terrible and harsh vision.

This storm itself comes from the desert, where the Lord was tempted (Matt. 4), and where Israel was exposed to the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions (Num. 21). When it comes, it passes through and goes away. Then the one who endures understands that only the transgressor transgresses, and only the lawless person acts lawlessly.

Therefore, if we are overwhelmed by the waves of the sea and a savage storm crushes us, this is the result of our own vice, since before the storm we were transgressors and lawless. And what he says—“The Elamites and the Persian envoys are coming against me”—has this meaning: Elamites are interpreted as “those who despise”; Persians as “those who test.”

Let those who customarily despise, scorn, and test come. But I shall groan, and my groaning will be my consolation. My loins too are filled with anguish, and pains have seized me like a woman in labor, so that I may conceive and give birth to the fear of the Lord and bring his spirit of salvation upon the earth.

According to the Hebrew, it is rightly said that whirlwinds and storms come from the desert and from a terrible land, where God is not an inhabitant and where everything is earthly. Whoever is faithless acts in a manner suited to his faithlessness, and whoever is a devastator lays waste. Thus he speaks boldly against his adversaries: “Go up, Elam; lay siege, Media.” I have caused all the groaning of the sea-desert, of the terrible land, and of the harshest vision that was announced to cease.

For my loins, doing penance, are no longer filled with pleasure as before but with pain; nor will I say any longer, “My loins are filled with illusions” (Ps. 37:7). Anguish and tribulation have seized me, as they usually seize a woman in labor.

The Vulgate edition and the Hebrew differ greatly in this passage. Therefore we shall touch briefly upon both, lest we leave an opportunity for lovers of accusations (**φιλεγκλημῶσιν**) to criticize us.

[Note: [Col. 0261D] “Lest they be lovers of accusations.” I am surprised that Marianus did not correct Erasmus here, as he did in the *Epistle to Evangelus concerning Melchizedek*, where we find the same Greek word. There he preferred to follow a word invented by Erasmus rather than the evidence of the manuscript codices. I therefore found **φιλεγκλημῶσιν**, that is, “to those who love accusations,” not Erasmus’s **φιλεπιτιμῶσιν**. MARTIAN. — That is, “to those who willingly accuse.” The holy Father uses this word with a somewhat different meaning in Epistle 73 to Evangelus, of one who is the father of accusation and slander.]

### (Verses 4–5)

I collapsed when I heard; I was troubled when I saw. My heart withered; darkness stupefied me. Babylon, my beloved, has been set before me as a wonder. Set the table; watch from the watchtower those who eat and drink. Rise, princes; seize the shield.

**Septuagint:** “I acted wickedly so as not to hear; I hastened so as not to see; my heart wanders; iniquity overflowed upon me; my soul persists in fear. Prepare the table; watch from the watchtower; eat and drink. Rise, princes; prepare shields.”

Because of the sound and the exceedingly harsh vision that the Prophet saw coming from the sea-desert, he says that he collapsed and was troubled, and that, with his eyes almost growing dim and his mind stupefied, he did not know what he was seeing.

That Babylon—for which Aquila and Theodotion interpreted “darkness,” signifying this world, which is established in wickedness (1 John 5), and whose rulers, according to the Apostle Paul, are “the rulers of the darkness of this age” (Eph. 6)—which was once beloved either by the Prophet or by God, has become, in its own overthrow, a marvel.

Therefore the Prophet is commanded, while feeding at the Lord’s table and filled with his food, to contemplate more carefully what is going to happen to the world. And through him all believers are told that, eating and drinking the body and blood of the Lord, they should become princes of the Church, and with the Apostles hear, “Rise.” They should seize the shield of faith from the armor of the Apostle Paul (Eph. 6), by which they can extinguish the flaming darts of the devil.

This is according to the Hebrew and the interpretation already begun concerning the world. Let us pass to the Septuagint edition, which differs greatly from what precedes.

The Prophet reproves himself—or rather, under his own persona, confesses the error of others—those who, following the literal meaning that kills, despise the Spirit who gives life. He says that he acted wickedly by refusing to hear the Law spiritually, but instead hastened not to see the mysteries of God, and did not say with David: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. 118:18).

Therefore his heart wanders, and, filled with Jewish superstition, it rests not in the love of God but in fear, so that he has a spirit of slavery in fear and not the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8).

Accordingly, he is commanded to approach the table of spiritual foods, and let all who follow his example eat and drink there. Having despised their former error, let them rise—those who lay in the letter—in the Spirit, become princes, and say with the Prophet: “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5:15).

### (Verses 6–7)

For thus the Lord said to me: “Go, and set a watchman; whatever he sees, let him announce.” And he saw a chariot of two horsemen, a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel; he watched carefully with prolonged attention, and the lion cried out.

**Septuagint:** “For thus the Lord said to me: Go, and set a watchman for yourself; whatever you see, announce. And I saw two mounted riders, a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel. I heard a great sound, and I called Uriah to the watchtower.”

The Prophet is commanded to set a watchman in his heart and carefully observe what is going to happen to the world. He saw two riders: a rider on a donkey and a rider on a camel.

One interpreter understood this as referring to the rider on the donkey, according to the Gospel reading (Matt. 21) and the prophecy of Zechariah (Zech. 9), as Christ; and conversely to the rider on the camel as an opposing power, because of the ugliness of that twisted animal.

Others refer the two riders to the letter and the Spirit, or to the two Testaments.

The Hebrew has **ARIE** (אריה), for which Aquila and Symmachus translated “lion” and “lioness.” I do not know what the Septuagint intended when it placed **οὐρίαν**, which some think should be interpreted as “the light of the Lord,” although “the light of the Lord” is written with different letters, which are not found here, while with other letters it means “lion,” which is what is read here.

The Septuagint wishes this watchman whom the Prophet is commanded to place in his heart to be called Uriah, and by the interpretation of the name refers him to the understanding of Christ, so that, with Christ dwelling in us, we may be able to discern what is going to happen.

This can also be applied to the lion, because the lion is named of Jacob (Gen. 49) and Balaam (Num. 23 and 24) under the mystery of Christ.

### (Verses 8–10)

“I am upon the watchtower of the Lord, standing continually by day, and upon my guard I stand through all the nights. Behold, this one comes, a man riding a chariot of horsemen; and he answered and said: ‘Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all her images of the gods have been shattered upon the earth.’ My threshed grain and children of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.”

The Septuagint reads: “The Lord said: ‘I stood throughout the whole day, and upon the encampment I stood all night. And behold, he himself comes, a rider of a chariot; and answering, he said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen, and all its images and manufactured objects have been shattered upon the earth.” Hear, you who have been left behind and are grieving: hear what I have heard from the Lord Sabaoth; the God of Israel has announced it to us.’”

The Prophet stands upon the watchtower of the Lord and, established in his light, looks out upon what is to come. He has this watch and this duty entrusted to him: to perceive, amid the darkness of this present age, what is to come.

“Behold this one comes,” he says, indicating that he has seen what follows: the Lord and Savior coming, seated upon a chariot and joining two horses—or rather, two living creatures, a donkey and a camel—to one vehicle. The rider of the chariot, in response to the Prophet’s longing and his desire to hear his words, answered and said: “Babylon has fallen, has fallen”—the confusion of the whole world. It has fallen at my coming, when I assumed a human body, and at the consummation of the world it will utterly collapse.

“And all her images have been shattered upon the earth.” In place of this, the Seventy translated “images” and “manufactured objects,” signifying the Scripture of the heretics and the various errors of the heresies, who are makers of idols and worship what they have fashioned from their own hearts.

What follows—spoken in the person of the Prophet—says: “My threshed grain and children of my threshing floor, what I have heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, I have announced to you.” According to the Hebrew, it has this meaning:

“O people, who are to be stored in my granaries, whom I have therefore threshed amid various afflictions so that I might beat the chaff out of you and store the purest grain in my barns: what I heard from the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning what is to come upon the whole world, this I have announced to you—to all of you who are in the world.”

Others, however, say that the preceding speaker is still the Lord and Savior himself, and that he is saying to the Apostles: “What I heard from the Father I have announced to you” (John XV, 15).

And since the Septuagint reads here, “Hear, you who have been left behind and are grieving,” this meaning seems to me appropriate according to their interpretation:

“O Apostles, concerning whom Isaiah writes: ‘Unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah’ (Isaiah V, 9), whose remnant the Apostle also teaches was saved, in his letter to the Romans (Romans IX): you who were left from the Jewish people so that you might be saved, and who grieve over the destruction of your nation, concerning which we also read elsewhere: ‘There is sorrow in my heart, and continual grief for my brothers, who are Israelites according to the flesh’ (Romans IX, 2–3)—what I have heard from God the Father, I announce to you: what the God of Israel foretells is to come upon you.”

### (Verses 11–12)

“Burden of Dumah: He calls to me from Seir: ‘Watchman, what of the night? Watchman, what of the night?’ The watchman said: ‘Morning comes, and also night. If you seek, seek; turn back and come.’”

The Septuagint reads: “Vision of Idumaea: He calls to me from Seir: ‘Guard the fortifications; I guard morning and night. If you seek, seek, and dwell with me.’”

[Note: [Col. 0263] In the Vatican manuscript, as also in the Saint-Germain manuscript cited by Montfaucon, the reading is HELN; I have no doubt whatever that it was written in place of HELH or HELE.]

The Hebrew word **ELAI** (), which all the interpreters have rendered “to me,” may, if one wishes to read it **ELI**, be interpreted as “my God” or “my strong one.”

What we have rendered “he calls” or “he summons”—that is, **καλεῖ**—may, because of the ambiguity of the Hebrew and Greek languages, be understood as “call” or “summon.” The sense is this: God, who is my guardian, calls me day and night to repentance, so that, leaving Seir—which is interpreted as “shaggy” or “hairy”—I may return and dwell with him.

Dumah means either “likeness” or “silence.” Idumaea, however, is translated as “earthly.”

The Lord therefore speaks to the chorus of the Apostles and commands it: “Call to me those who are from Seir,” so that the multitude of the nations may serve me—a multitude which, in the likeness of Esau, has nothing soft, smooth, or shining in itself, but is shaggy, wild, and unmanageable.

“And you, Apostles, after you have called the nations from Seir to me, guard the fortifications of the Church, lest the enemy easily break in; lest the roaring and prowling lion, seeking an entrance by which it may enter, tear apart and destroy the flock shut up within the Church.”

The multitude of the Church answered: “Not only in prosperity but also in adversity—that is, both by day and by night—I will keep your commands, O God.”

God speaks to it: “If you truly seek me, demonstrate by your works that you seek me. Do not let it be enough that you have sought me once; rather, having found me, seek me always. And, in order that you may hold me more perfectly, forget your people and your father’s house, abandon the error of the Gentiles, and dwell with me in the Church.”

This may be said according to the Septuagint, who place “the vision of Idumaea”—that is, “of the earthly”—in the title, to show that those who formerly served earthly works are being summoned.

According to Aquila, however, who rendered **Dumah** as “silence” or “likeness,” we may understand it as follows: the multitude of the nations is summoned to the likeness of the people of Israel; and where previously there had been silence concerning the law of God, there is now the cry of confession. The wild olive is brought into the good olive.

We also read in the Gospel parable that servants were sent to call the good and the evil and to fill the master’s banquet with people from everywhere, because those invited first were unwilling to come (Matthew XXII).

The Church may also relate that the Lord is calling out to it from Seir—that is, from earthly places—and summoning it to salvation, saying to the Lord himself:

“O watchman, why, rising at night, do you move about in darkness? Why are you without sin in sinful flesh? For what reason did you wish to assume a human body?”

The watchman—that is, the Samaritan, who in the Gospel carried the wounded man on his shoulders to the inn (Luke IX)—answered: “Morning comes, and also night.”

The meaning is this: for the multitude of the Gentiles the sun of righteousness has risen, while darkness has come upon the Jews. In accordance with what the Lord says:

“For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John IX, 39).

And that same watchman who had said, “Morning comes, and also night,” speaks to the multitude of the Gentiles: “If you seek me, seek me more diligently. Turn back to me, children who are turning back, and I will heal your wounds; come to me.”

These are difficult passages. Since they are by no means clear according to the historical sense, we are compelled, according to **ἀναγωγή**—the spiritual or higher sense—to follow various opinions.

### (Verse 13)

“Burden in Arabia.”

This is not found in the edition of the Septuagint interpreters. But what follows—“In the thicket, toward evening, you will sleep in the paths of Dodanim”—has been joined to the preceding vision, so that it reads: “If you seek, seek; and dwell with me in the thicket.”

In our language, Arabia signifies “evening,” which is the beginning of night and darkness; and everyone who has the beginning of sins within him moves about in evening. But whoever comes to the extreme end remains in the middle of night.

Hence also, in Egypt, the firstborn are slain at midnight (Exodus XII). And the Apostle Peter, before the cock crowed, denied the Lord three times, which is understood as midnight (Matthew XXVI). But after the night had passed and the day began to draw near, when the darkness of midnight had been overcome and the cock, the messenger of light, had sounded, he wept bitterly and understood his sin. At that time he could say: “In the evening weeping will lodge, and in the morning, joy” (Psalm XXIX, 6).

For the present, let this suffice concerning the passage before us. The name Arabia—meaning “evening” and “the West”—receives different interpretations elsewhere in the Scriptures.

“In the thicket, toward evening, you will sleep, in the paths of Dodanim.”

The Septuagint reads: “In the thicket, toward evening, you will sleep, on the road of Dedan.”

Those who have begun to live in wickedness and are entering the way of sins neither sleep nor remain in cultivated fields and newly ploughed ground, nor in meadows and grainfields which the Savior teaches are white for harvest, nor among fruit-bearing trees. Rather, they remain in barren thickets, where brambles and thorns are found and wild beasts dwell.

Concerning such a thicket we also read in the Book of Kings that the forest or thicket devoured more people than the sword killed, when Absalom rebelled against his father (I Kings XVIII).

And rightly so: since evening is the beginning of evils, they are said to dwell on the road and in the paths—and on the road of Dedan, which is interpreted as “judgments.” For however many kinds of sins they have, they deserve that many judicial sentences. Dedan may also be interpreted as “great judgment.”

### (Verses 14–15)

“Meet the thirsty with water; you who dwell in the land of the South, meet the fugitive with bread. For they have fled from the face of swords, from the face of the impending sword, from the face of the stretched bow, from the face of grievous battle.”

The Septuagint reads: “Bring water to meet the thirsty, you who dwell in the region of Theman; meet the fugitives with bread, because of the multitude of the slain, because of the crowd of wanderers, because of the multitude of the sword, because of the multitude of drawn bows, and because of the multitude of those falling in battle.”

You who are in Theman—which is interpreted as “the South” and “perfection”—and who dwell in that place of which it is written, “God will come from the South” (Habakkuk III, 4), you who are completed and perfected and possess within yourselves the light of knowledge of the Scriptures: meet those fleeing from Arabia and from the thicket with water and bread. Do not wait until they themselves come to you; rather, imitate the father in the Gospel parable, who ran out to meet his returning son.

That father gave him a robe and offered him a ring (Luke XV). You, however, offer water and bread to those who are fleeing, so that those who are weary and exhausted may be sustained by your mercy and may pass more quickly to your dwelling places.

For they have fled the swords of the heretics, the teaching of the Gentiles, and the blasphemies of the Jews. And because they have seen many of their number killed by their darts and many fallen in battle, they themselves desire to be delivered by your help.

This passage may properly be understood against those who, giving themselves over to idleness and indolence and being content with their own salvation, do not extend a hand to the penitent and converted.

### (Verses 16–17)

“For thus says the Lord to me: ‘Still within one year, like the year of a hired laborer, all the glory of Kedar will be removed, and the remainder of the number of the mighty archers among the sons of Kedar will be diminished.’ For the Lord, the God of Israel, has spoken.”

For this reason I tell you to meet with water and bread those fleeing from the thicket and from Arabia: because the Lord has promised that these things will come to pass.

Just as the year of a hired laborer passes quickly—for he expects nothing each day except the wages of his labor, or certainly is always engaged in work and toil in order to receive the wage for his labor—so all the glory of Kedar, which is interpreted as “darkness,” concerning which we also read in the Psalm, “I dwelt with those who dwell in Kedar” (Psalm CXIX, 5), will quickly be removed.

And the whole number of archers—that is, of the various doctrines—which wounded those established in the thicket of Arabia will be reduced to nothing after those fleeing from the thicket have been delivered and have received the water of saving baptism and eaten the heavenly bread.

For the Lord of all things, and especially the God of Israel—that is, of those who perceive God with their mind—has spoken of these future events.

## Chapter XXII

### (Verse 1)

“Burden of the valley of vision.”

The Septuagint reads: “Word of the valley of Zion.”

In the *Book of Hebrew Names* we stated that **Sion** is interpreted as “watchtower,” situated in high places and contemplating from afar what is coming.

Since, according to the laws of tropology—the figurative sense—Zion is referred to the Church, as in the second Psalm, spoken in the person of the Lord and Savior:

“But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm II, 6);

and:

“Those who trust in the Lord are like Mount Zion” (Psalm CXXIV, 1);

and:

“The Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the dwellings of Jacob” (Psalm LXXXVI, 1);

and, more explicitly, the Apostle says:

“You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews X, 22);

we ask why, in the present vision, Zion is called a valley.
