The very sequence of the words draws us toward a spiritual understanding, so that we may recognize all the leaders of perverse doctrines—those who have fallen from the height of their understanding of the holy Scriptures and have rolled down into low places—as dwelling in the valley of Zion.

I think Solomon says something similar in Proverbs:

“Let the eye that mocks its father and despises the old age of its mother be dug out by the ravens from the valleys, and let the young of eagles eat it” (Proverbs XXX, 17).

As soon as the understanding of the heretics mocks the Creator Father and despises the old age of Mother Church, it is dug out by dark and unclean birds, which are understood as hostile powers.

Such people cannot say: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me” (Psalm CXX, 1); rather, they have been pressed down toward earthly things in the manner of irrational animals.

“What is happening to you also, that you too have climbed up, all of you, onto the roofs?”

The Septuagint reads: “What has happened to you now, that you have all climbed onto empty roofs?”

This is the same question that is raised in the Book of Kings according to the Septuagint interpreters, concerning the meaning of Elisha’s words:

“Where is the God of Elijah, **APHPHO**?” (IV Kings II, 14).

[Note: **Aphpho.** This name is found in the Greek Lexicon of Hebrew Names, which I would like to consult. Here, however, with Jerome, we must observe that the word **Aphpho** is more clearly placed in the present passage of Isaiah, namely [the Hebrew form]; whereas in IV Kings II, 14, it is read **aph-hu**, and not **aphpho**. Erasmus and Marianus, understanding this not at all, published Jerome’s text for us in a corrupt and utterly confused form, although in manuscript copies it is clear and distinct. — Martian.]

In the present passage **APHPHO** is more clearly used for what the Septuagint translated as “now.” In Hebrew it has **APHPHO**, which we translated “now also.” Aquila, wishing to preserve the Hebrew idiom, used **καίπερτοι**.

[Note: An old manuscript in the possession of Reinesius, concerning the Punic language, has *ce per tuum*, which readily represents the Greek **καίπερτοι**. The words also indicate **νῦν**, the adverb meaning “now,” as expressed by Aquila. Otherwise, among Latin writers, the conjunction **καίπερτοι** can at least be represented in some fashion. It also seems that Jerome rendered not a simple “also,” but “now also.”]

Latin cannot fully express this conjunction.

When he says, “What is happening to you also?” he asks why she too, among others, is climbing upward and dwelling in low places while imagining herself to be in lofty regions.

The sense is this: when philosophers are puffed up, and all secular wisdom, discussing lofty matters, despises the simplicity of the Church, why do you too pursue lofty things? The Septuagint translated this more significantly as **δώματα μάταια**, that is, “empty roofs,” so that they might show that there is also another roof from which the Savior forbids descending (Matthew XXIV), though that roof is not an empty one.

[Note: **σημαντικώτερον.** Do not confuse the Greek word *σημαντικώτερον*, which Jerome uses, with the following words of the Septuagint interpreters. What he says here in Greek he often expresses elsewhere in Latin by *significantius* (“more significantly”). Thus he teaches that the Septuagint rendered “empty roofs” more significantly, whereas the Hebrew has merely “roofs,” without the word “empty.” — Martian.]

Finally, the Apostle Peter also went up onto a roof at the sixth hour of prayer (Acts X). But here, to display the great variety of heresies, he named not one roof but many roofs.

### (Verse 2)

“Full of shouting, a crowded city, an exultant city.”

The Septuagint reads: “The city is filled with those who cry out, an exultant city.”

The teaching of the heretics is occupied not with understanding but with excessive speech and shouting. Hence, because of the multitude of the deceived, it is called a crowded city, and exultant because of its pride. For they are swollen with conceit and boast that they have discovered things more sacred.

“Your slain are not slain by the sword, nor dead in battle.”

The Septuagint reads: “Your wounded are not wounded by the sword, nor are your dead dead in battle.”

The greater part is overthrown by the deceptions of the heretics without any contest or dispute, and this is a very large crowd.

Therefore the slain—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the wounded—of the valley of Zion were not slain or wounded by the sword, but passed over to the heretics by their own will. Compared with those who were defeated after battle, the person who is wounded and slain by voluntarily surrendering himself is more wretched.

So also in martyrdom: the person who gives in after punishments has been inflicted suffers a lighter penalty than one who, without any necessity or pain of torture, denied Christ.

### (Verse 3)

“All your princes fled together, and they were bound with harsh bonds.”

Here we have followed the Septuagint interpretation, because it does not differ greatly from the Hebrew in meaning. But if I translate the Hebrew word for word, it reads among them as follows:

“All your chiefs departed together; they were bound by the bow.”

The other interpreters also followed this edition.

For all the leaders of the heretics have departed from the Church of Christ to the synagogue of Satan. They passed over together, discordant in their faithlessness but united in their departure, and they were bound by the bow, concerning which it is written in the Psalm:

“Behold, sinners have bent the bow; they have prepared their arrows in the quiver, to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Psalm X, 2),

and to send the fiery darts of the devil, which wound and bind them all together.

Therefore they are bound with harsh bonds, because they have stopped their ears like deaf adders. Having stopped their ears, they do not hear the voices of enchanters, nor even the skillful spell of the sorcerer.

For this reason the Apostle Paul commands that a heretic be abandoned to his perversity after one admonition (Titus III), because he is perverted and condemned by his own judgment.

“For they went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (I John II, 19).

The leader of these fugitive princes is the one whom Isaiah himself calls the fleeing dragon, the crooked serpent. When he has placed deadly words in the ears of the deceived, he binds them with harsh bonds and does not permit them to escape from his chains.

The holy man, delivered from these bonds, rejoiced in the Psalm:

“My soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Psalm CXXIII, 7).

And elsewhere, rejoicing that he had escaped, he says:

“You are my protector and my refuge. My God, I will hope in him. For he himself delivers me from the snare of the hunters and from the harsh word” (Psalm XC, 23),

or, as it may also be translated, “from the turbulent word,” which properly signifies the teaching of the heretics.

“All who were found in you were bound together; they fled far away.”

The Septuagint reads: “And the strong among you fled far away.”

The Prophet’s speech is still directed against the valley of Zion, whose inhabitants climbed upon empty roofs, cried out with confused shouting, and were wounded without battle; whose princes all fled and were bound with harsh bonds; and whose strong men fled farther away.

For the more prudent a person is in heretical perversity, the farther he withdraws from the Lord.

When he says, according to the Hebrew, “All were found in you,” we must note that the heretics also claim to have found those whom they have deceived. But their discovery is destruction.

Finally, they are bound together and flee far away. Nor do I approve the explanation that, according to the diversity of heresies, the distances of those fleeing are also diverse. Holy Scripture says that all who are found by the heretics are bound together and flee very far away, as the Lord says:

“He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke XI, 23).

Hence it is said of Moses:

“Moses alone drew near to God, but the others did not draw near” (Exodus XXIV).

For God is a God who draws near to his saints, and not one who is far away, says the Lord.

### (Verses 4–6)

“Therefore I said: ‘Withdraw from me; I will weep bitterly. Do not press upon me in order to console me over the devastation of the daughter of my people.’ For it is a day of slaughter, trampling, and weeping from the Lord God of hosts in the valley of vision, searching the wall and being magnificent upon the mountain.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Therefore I said: ‘Leave me; I will weep bitterly. Do not contend in order to console me over the ruin of the daughter of my people, because it is a day of tumult, destruction, trampling, and error from the Lord God Sabaoth in the valley of Zion. They wander from the least to the greatest; they wander upon the mountains.’”

Samuel also wept for Saul (I Kings XV), and the Lord and Savior wept over Jerusalem (Luke XIX). The Apostle writes to the Corinthians:

“Lest, when I come again to you, God humble me and I mourn over many who sinned before and have not repented.”

Therefore, moved by compassion, he also says to others:

“Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (II Corinthians XI, 29).

Thus the Prophet, seeing the people who once belonged to the vision climbing upon empty roofs and being absorbed in shouting, and seeing all their princes having fled and being bound in the chains of sins, breaks into tears. He drives away those who offer consolation and testifies that he is weeping with the bitterest grief—not over sons, but over the daughter of his people, who has lost the dignity of manliness.

For the day of judgment, slaughter, and trampling will not belong to Jerusalem, whose name is interpreted as “vision of peace,” but to the ancient name Jebus, which is interpreted as “trampling.”

The day will also be one of weeping—or of error, as the Septuagint translated it—from the Lord Sabaoth. This does not mean that weeping and error come from the Lord; rather, through the opportunity provided by the holy Scriptures, which the Lord gave to be read, an opportunity for error arises in those who are able to say:

“Why have you caused us to wander from your way?” (Isaiah LXIII, 27).

And elsewhere:

“The Lord has mixed into them a spirit of error” (Isaiah XXIX, 10),

so that they might stand not upon the mountain of Vision but in the valley of Zion.

This same day, which arises from the Lord of hosts in the valley of Vision in order to reveal the deeds of individuals, searches out the wall of the heretics, which they have built against the Church like a very strong fortification. It also searches out the magnificent and glorious ones—that is, their teachers—who boast that they stand upon Christ the mountain.

Concerning this we read elsewhere:

“Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce to us his way” (Isaiah II, 3).

As for what the Septuagint translated, “They wander from the least to the greatest; they wander upon the mountains,” we must understand that those who are greater are guilty of a greater crime, yet all, from the least to the greatest, wander—and wander upon the mountains: Moses, Jeremiah, and the other Prophets, the Evangelists and the Apostles.

Although they are in the valley, they wander in a remarkable way upon the mountains.

### (Verses 7–9)

“And Elam took up the quiver, the chariot of the mounted man, and the shield uncovered the wall. And your chosen valleys will be full of chariots, and the horsemen will take their positions at the gate. And the covering of Judah will be revealed, and on that day you will see the arsenal of the house of the forest. And you will see the breaches of the city of David, for they have multiplied.”

The Septuagint reads:

“But the Elamites took up quivers; horsemen, men upon horses, and an assembly of warriors. Your chosen valleys will be filled with chariots, and horsemen will crowd your gates. And they will reveal the gates of Judah; on that day they will look into the chosen houses of the city, and they will reveal the hidden things of the houses of the citadel of David, and they will see that they are many.”

Elam—which is interpreted as “their ascent”—or the Elamites, as the Septuagint translated them, whom we interpret as “those who despise,” took up the quiver in order to shoot in darkness at the upright in heart. They are the mounted men in the chariot of men, so that by their shield and their assault they may strip bare the wall of Zion and the defenses of the Church.

“Your chosen valleys,” he says—and your lowly doctrines, O valley of Zion—“will be full of chariots,” the chariots that the Lord submerged with Pharaoh. Their horsemen and riders will take their positions at your gates, so that they will not allow those besieged and confined within you to escape.

Then Almighty God, through ecclesiastical men, will reveal the coverings of Judah, and all the secrets of those established in the confession of faith. Then you will see, O valley of Zion, on that day and in the clear light of truth, the whole armory of the house of the forest, in which the multitude of the Gentiles dwells.

As it is also sung in Psalm CXXXI:

“Behold, we heard of it in Ephrata; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm CXXXI, 6).

When the covering and secret of Judah—which had previously been concealed because of its mystery—has been revealed, and you have seen the armor of the Church, then you will understand the breaches of the city of David, which you multiplied in order to gather peoples deceived by you.

These Elamites, according to the Septuagint edition, do not have one quiver but many. They are riders of men, riding upon their souls, and they are a very large multitude preparing for battle against the Church, so that all its valleys are filled.

The horsemen block their understanding and, by their fighting, provoke the ecclesiastical man—who is interpreted as “Judas”—to battle. When he brings forward testimonies from the Scriptures and refutes all their lies, the heretics will see the houses of the city of David and will come to know all the secrets that were formerly hidden: how in the citadel of David—which is interpreted as “strong of hand,” that is, Christ—all the doctrines of truth are found.

These are obscure passages, not only according to the historical sense but also according to **ἀναγωγή**, the higher sense. Therefore those to whom our explanation is displeasing ought to bring forward their own, so that, if their explanation proves true, we may accept it.

### (Verses 10–11)

“And you gathered the waters of the lower pool; you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you destroyed houses in order to fortify the wall. And you made a pool between the two walls, and the water of the old pool; but you did not look toward him who had made it, and you did not see its maker from afar.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And they diverted the water of the old pool into the city, and they destroyed the houses of Jerusalem in order to strengthen the walls of the city. And you made water for yourselves between the two walls, within the old pool, but you did not look upon him who made it from the beginning, and you did not see its creator.”

You who will see—or do see—the breaches of the city of David, that is, of the Church, which have multiplied throughout the whole world; you who have gathered the waters of your pool and your doctrine—not of the upper pool but of the lower—and who have counted or destroyed the houses of Jerusalem in order to fortify your wall: you did not dig wells containing living and eternal waters, but broken cisterns that are unable to hold water.

You made them between the two walls of the New and Old Testament. You neglected the water of the old pool and did not consider God, the giver of the law; you utterly disregarded the maker of the world.

This is according to the Hebrew. According to the Septuagint, however, the heretics considered themselves numerous and, trusting in this multitude, diverted the doctrine of the Old Testament from the city of God, which is the Church. They destroyed the houses of Jerusalem in order to build gatherings of the wicked.

Although they reject the Old Testament, they did not follow the New either, because the New Testament is strengthened by the testimonies of the Old.

Therefore, between the two walls—the Old and the New—they made new waters for themselves, which they believe to be more inward and to contain greater mysteries than those contained in the Old Testament. They did not look toward God, who is the founder of the Old Testament, and they did not even wish to see its maker from afar.

### (Verses 12 and following)

“And the Lord God of hosts will call on that day to weeping and mourning, to baldness and the wearing of sackcloth. But behold, joy and gladness: killing calves and slaughtering rams, eating meat and drinking wine: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die.’ And it was revealed in my ears by the Lord of hosts: ‘This iniquity shall not be forgiven you until you die,’ says the Lord God of hosts.”

[Note: Victor adds “voice,” but only from the Vulgate, not from Jerome’s manuscripts.]

Every day the Lord God of hosts calls the heretics to repentance. They have despised the water of the old pool between the two walls, dug a pool for themselves, and gathered the water of the lower pool, which has waters not from heaven but from the earth.

He calls them to weeping, for “blessed are those who weep, for they will laugh” (Matthew V, 5).

He calls them to mourning, lest they later hear: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a lament, and you did not mourn” (Matthew XI, 17).

He calls them to baldness, so that they may shave away all the works of death and remove from their bodies whatever does not live.

And he calls them to the wearing of sackcloth, lest later, in the case of Jerusalem, they be girded with a rope instead of a belt.

But they, on the contrary, made joy and gladness in place of weeping and mourning, baldness and sackcloth. As though everything ended with death, they killed calves and slaughtered rams in order to eat meat and drink wine, speaking words of blasphemy:

“While we are in this present age, let us abound in pleasures. For tomorrow”—that is, the future time—“will be without consciousness.”

When they said these things, the Lord heard their blasphemous words and threatened that he would not forgive this iniquity until they died either to sin and vices or were dragged down to the underworld with their sins.

[Note: Victorius says that *deliciis* (“pleasures”), not *delictis* (“sins”), should be read; Jerome immediately explains it by calling them pleasures.]

This may be understood not only of the heretics but of every sinner who, neglecting his sins, becomes worse through despair and, ensnared by pleasures, joins blasphemy to sin, thinking that all awareness of the living ends in death, saying the words of Epicurus:

“After death there is nothing, and death itself is nothing.”

### (Verse 15 and following)

Thus says the Lord God of hosts: “Go in to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna, the overseer of the temple, and say to him: ‘What are you doing here? Or who are you here, as it were? For you have hewn yourself a tomb here; you have hewn out a memorial on high, carefully making yourself a tabernacle in the rock. Behold, the Lord will cause you to be carried away, as a cock is carried away; and he will lift you up as a garment is lifted. He will crown you with tribulation; like a ball he will toss you into a broad and spacious land. There you will die, and there will be the chariot of your glory, the disgrace of your lord’s house. And I will drive you out from your position, and remove you from your office.

“‘And it shall come to pass on that day that I will call my servant Eliakim, son of Hilkiah. I will clothe him in your tunic and strengthen him with your belt; I will place your authority in his hand, and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; he will open, and no one will shut; he will shut, and no one will open. I will fasten him like a peg in a secure place, and he will be on the throne of the house of his father.’”

**Note:** This passage seems to require supplementation according to the Vulgate: “on the throne of glory for the house of his father,” and so forth. This reading also agrees with the Hebrew and with Jerome’s earlier rendering of the same passage, above, column 224.

“And they will hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house, vessels of every kind, every small vessel, from the vessels of the mixing bowls to every vessel of the musicians. On that day, says the Lord of hosts, the peg that had been fastened in a secure place will be removed, broken, and fall; and what had hung upon it will perish, because the Lord has spoken.”

**The Septuagint:** Thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “Go to the chamber, to Shebna the treasurer, and say to him: ‘What are you doing here? Or what do you have here? For you have hewn yourself a tomb and made yourself a memorial on high; you have inscribed a tabernacle for yourself in the land. Behold, the Lord Sabaoth will cast out and crush the man, and remove your glorious robe and crown; he will throw you into a great and immeasurable region, and there you will die. He will make your excellent chariot a disgrace, and the house of your prince a trampling-place. You will be removed from your stewardship and from your rank.

“‘And it shall come to pass on that day that I will call my servant Eliakim, son of Hilkiah. I will clothe him in your robe, and I will firmly place your crown upon him; I will give your stewardship into his hands, and he will be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to Judah. I will give him the glory of the house of David; he will rule, and there will be no one who contradicts him. I will place the key of the house of David upon his shoulder; he will open, and no one will shut; he will shut, and no one will open. I will appoint him ruler in a secure place and upon the throne of the glory of his father’s house, and every glorious person in his father’s house, from the least to the greatest, will depend upon him—every small vessel, from the vessels of the mixing bowls onward. On that day, thus says the Lord Sabaoth, the man who had been established in a secure place will be moved, removed, fall, and perish, and the glory that had been in him will disappear, because the Lord has spoken.’”

**Note:** In the edition of Martianus, the words “and he will open, and no one will shut” were missing. We have corrected other minor matters above and below.

The prophet Isaiah is commanded to enter the one who dwells in the tabernacle—which in Hebrew is called *SOCHEN* ()—namely Shebna, the overseer of the temple; or, as the Septuagint translated it, *tamias* (ταμίας), that is, treasurer and administrator of the treasures of God’s house. *Sochen* is interpreted either as “tabernacle” or as *pastophorion*, that is, a chamber in which the overseer of the temple dwells.

Who else, then, dwelt in the tabernacle of the Jews and formerly in the house of God except the discourse and meaning of the Jewish Law, which was occupied with the reading of the Old Testament? To this tradition and teaching, therefore, it is said: “What are you doing here? Why do you wish to build yourself a house in the western letter, and to fasten your tabernacle, which has no foundation, in the firmness of a rock—a structure that should be called not so much a tabernacle and house as a tomb and memorial?”

I say this to you because you ought not to labor over the cutting out of a tomb: the Lord will transfer your priesthood, just as *GEBER* () is customarily transferred from one place to another—although everyone has translated it as “man.” The Hebrew who instructed us in the reading of the Old Testament, however, translated it as “cock.” “Just as,” he says, “a cock is carried on the shoulder of its bearer from one place to another, so the Lord will lightly carry you away from your place.”

And you, who once possessed the high priest’s crown and the sanctification on the golden plate on which the name of God was written (Exod. 28), will be crowned with tribulation and distress. Just as, when a sphere is thrown down a sloping and spacious place, it cannot stand still but rolls on without limit, so your entire people will be scattered to the ends of the world. There you will die, together with your letter, all your glory, and the chariots in which you were formerly carried in renown; and the splendor of God’s house will be turned into disgrace.

For the Lord will remove you from your position and from your office—that is, from the ceremonies of sacrifices—in fulfillment of what is written to the Hebrews: “For when the priesthood is transferred, there must also be a transfer of the law” (Heb. 7:12).

But when you have been expelled from your office, I will call my servant Eliakim, to whom I also said elsewhere: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isa. 49:6, according to the Septuagint). Eliakim is interpreted as “God rising” or “the resurrection of God.” This “God rising,” therefore, who is the son of Hilkiah—that is, “of the portion of the Lord”—will take your place. He will be clothed in your robe and strengthened with your belt, so that what you possessed in the letter he may possess in the spirit. He will be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem—that is, to the “vision of peace,” which is interpreted as the Church—and to the house of Judah, where the true confession of faith is found.

Hence he himself says to the Apostles: “Little children, I am with you only a little longer” (John 13:33). And elsewhere: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9:2). And to another: “Daughter, your faith has saved you” (Luke 7:50).

“I will give him,” he says, “the key of the house of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3). This same key will be upon his shoulder—that is, in his passion—in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “Whose rule is upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). What he has opened through his passion cannot be shut; and what he has shut in the ceremonies of the Jews will be opened by no one else.

“For I will fasten him as a peg in a secure place,” where the assembly of the faithful is. Hence those who believe in Christ are also called faithful. “And he will be upon the throne of the glory of his father’s house,” that is, of the Church. “And they will hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house.” Hence it is also written in the Gospel: “All the people were hanging upon him” (Luke 19:48).

This was not done only at that time; it continues to be fulfilled even today, so that upon him may hang, like various vessels of God, wisdom and righteousness and all the things by which Christ is named.

For “vessels of various kinds,” Aquila translated *SASAIM* () and *SEPHOTH* (), which Symmachus rendered “descendants and those mingled together.” Thus the Apostles and all believers—that is, sons of sons and those mingled together from all the nations—will hang upon him.

For “from the vessels of the mixing bowls,” Theodotion placed *AGANOTH* (). Both the small and the great will believe in the Lord. I think that the mixing bowls signify the Apostles, filled with living waters. Concerning them it is said: “Bless God from the fountains of Israel” (Ps. 67:27), in whom Wisdom mixed her wine.

“And every vessel,” he says, “of the musicians”—those who continually resound with praises of God.

What follows appears contrary to our understanding: how can this peg, which had been fastened in a secure place, be removed, broken, fall, and cause what had hung upon it to perish—and all this because the Lord has spoken? The matter can be resolved if we read the Gospel saying that “the love of many will grow cold in the last days” (Matt. 24:12), and if the Lord himself says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

The peg, then, will not be broken, fall, and perish—for it would be impious to say this. Rather, the peg will be removed from the secure place, that is, from the Church, by the impiety that daily increases; and those who had previously hung upon it through faith will afterward be broken, fall, and perish through unbelief. This will happen in the last days, because the Lord has spoken.

For “peg,” which in Hebrew is called *JATHED* () and is pronounced similarly by everyone, only the Septuagint above translated “prince,” whereas here it translated “man.” What we nearly passed over because of the speed of dictation is that *Shebna* is interpreted as “turn now,” or “turning.” It is therefore said to the prince of the Jews that he should turn from the Law to the Gospel and, abandoning the figures of sacrifices, transfer himself to the truth of the spiritual sacrifice.

### (Chapter 23—Verse 1)

The oracle concerning Tyre. What seemed to us, according to the Hebrews, concerning the burden, or word and assumption, of Tyre, we set forth above in the book of historical exposition on the Ten Visions. Now we shall briefly survey the whole prophecy against Tyre according to the spiritual sense (*anagōgē*) and the edition of the Septuagint. In the Hebrew language Tyre is called *SOR* (), which is rendered in our language as “narrowness.” Therefore every soul occupied with vices and perverse thoughts may be called *sor*.

“Wail, ships of Carthage, for they have perished and will come no more. From the land of the Kittim she has been led captive. The inhabitants of the island have become like her: the merchants of Phoenicia, crossing the sea upon many waters, the seed of merchants like imported harvests, merchants of the nations.”

For “Carthage,” the Hebrew has *THARSIS* (), which all likewise translated. *Tharsis* means “contemplation” or “investigation of joy.” Kittim, which in Hebrew is called *CHETIM* (), means “the frozen sea”; and in their text Sidon is read in place of Phoenicia. Accordingly, those surrounded by a multitude of evil thoughts are rebuked: those who, wishing, according to the Apostle, to become rich, fall into temptations and snares of the devil, and into many harmful desires that drag people down into the depths (1 Tim. 6). They are told that they ought to wail, knowing that all the commerce of this world will perish and that contemplation of joy and gladness will be turned into mourning and tears. For this sea will no longer be navigable; rather, everything will freeze, and the colonies of the Tyrians will be led captive for punishments. No others resemble the inhabitants of this island except merchants, or conveyers, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine and pass from one vice to another.

We dwell on an island as long as we are buffeted by the temptations of this age; our island and little ship are struck by the waves of the sea on every side. The merchants of this island are from Sidon, which is interpreted “huntress” and in which very many hunters dwell. Of them it is written: “He will deliver you from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 90:3). And elsewhere the saint rejoices that he has been freed from their traps, saying: “Our soul, like a sparrow, has escaped from the snare of hunters” (Ps. 123:7). All merchants of the nations are compared to crops that quickly wither, or to the harvests of a river which receive rain not from heaven but from the earth, and therefore will perish with the nations. Where we read “the seed of merchants,” the Hebrew has “the seed of *sior*,” with “of the Nile” understood, because it has muddy waters by which the crops of Egypt are irrigated.

**[Column 0276B] (Verses 4–5)**

“Blush, Sidon,” says the sea; and the strength of the sea says: “I have not travailed, nor borne, nor nourished young men, nor raised virgins. When it is heard in Egypt, grief concerning Tyre will seize them.”

The sea of this world, in which small animals dwell with great ones, and the dragon that God formed to sport with it, sees those who had formerly been captured by demons caught by Christ’s hunters, who hunt from every mountain and hill. It speaks to the opposing strength of the hunters, which is interpreted Sidon, and says to it: “Blush, Sidon; for I have not travailed, nor borne, nor nourished the young men captured by you, nor raised the virgins whose folly is condemned in the Gospel” (Matt. 25). For my travail, bearing, nourishment, and raising of virgins have been destroyed by the travail of Christ’s Apostles. One of them said: “My little children, whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19); and: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2); and again: “I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

When Egypt hears this—Egypt is called in Hebrew *MESRAIM* (), which means *ekthlibousa*, that is, “afflicting” and “constraining”—it too will be alarmed, understanding that it will suffer the same things that Tyre has suffered. Though this applies to all vices, it may also be understood of the diversity of heresies: when one heresy is captured, another trembles, and in the confusion of another it perceives that it too will be captured. Just as it is said of Sodom, “If the signs which were performed in Capernaum had been performed in it, it would have remained to this day,” and then added, “Nevertheless, it will be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for you”; so we learn concerning Tyre and Sidon from the Savior’s saying: “Nevertheless, it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for that city” (Matt. 11:21 ff.). Hence the Canaanite woman, who understood that her daughter—that is, her soul—was grievously tormented by a demon, is said to have come out from the borders of Tyre and Sidon for Christ’s entreaty. For she could not otherwise meet the Savior unless she had left the borders of Tyre and Sidon.

### (Verses 6–7)

“Go to Carthage; wail, you who dwell on this island. Is not this your reproach from the beginning, before she was handed over? Her feet will lead her far away to sojourn.”

The words that follow, “Her feet will lead her far away to sojourn,” have been added from the Hebrew and are marked by an asterisk, that is, by illuminating stars. O Tyrians, who dwell in narrowness and live on an island, exposed on every side to the waves of temptations, leave it and go to Carthage—that is, Tharsis—and hasten to true joy, mourning your former sins and the old reproach which you either inflicted on others yourselves or suffered from them. I command this because you see your city Tyre migrating from its abode and purpose to other boundaries, when, having put aside their old error, they bow their necks to the Gospel of the Savior, so that those who formerly dwelt in narrowness may go farther away and become strangers and sojourners in the teaching of the Lord and Savior.

**[Column 0277B] (Verses 8–9)**

“Who has devised these things against Tyre? Is she insignificant, or does she not prevail? Her merchants are princes of Canaan, the renowned of the earth. The Lord Sabaoth has devised to destroy every reproach of those who glory and to dishonor everything renowned upon the earth.”

The word “Canaan” has been added from the edition of Theodotion; Aquila translated it “merchants.” The Holy Spirit therefore asks—or rather, by questioning affirms—that the Lord devised these things against the princes of Tyre, whose entire industry consists in seeking wealth by trade. As in the Gospel we read of dealers in pearls (Matt. 13), who, having sold everything, desire to buy one pearl, and who certainly ought to be called renowned merchants not of earth but of heaven; so, conversely, the merchants of Tyre, that is, of tribulation and narrowness, ought to be called renowned men of earth, because everything they do has regard to earth. They are princes of Canaan, which means “tossing” and “shaken.” For they do not set their feet upon the rock, nor can it be said of them: “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs” (Pss. 39; 103:18), or hares; rather, they suffer what the righteous man nearly suffered: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps nearly slipped” (Ps. 72:2).

The Lord of hosts therefore devised this counsel, to dissolve the most wicked bonds of the merchants—or rather, to scatter the compacted injury through which all who are subject to Tyre are proud. When it adds, “and to dishonor everything glorious upon the earth,” the Lord is not the author of dishonor, but shows to be dishonorable what is manifestly disgraceful in itself. We read the same concerning priests in Leviticus: “He has defiled him by defilement” (Lev. 21), undoubtedly the priest; not because he is the author of defilement, but because he shows to be defiled the one who previously appeared clean to many.

### (Verses 10–11)

“Work your land, for ships no longer come from Carthage, and your hand no longer prevails, which provokes kings upon the sea.”

In this passage the edition of the Septuagint differs greatly from the other interpreters and from the Hebrew itself, but let us pursue our purpose. Above it said: “Go to Carthage; wail, you who dwell on the island.” Now it says the contrary: because ships no longer come from Carthage, work your land. For it benefited Tyre that foreign ships should perish, so that it might be compelled to work its own land. Of this it is said in Proverbs: “He who works his land will be filled with bread” (Prov. 21:11), so that he may live not by the uncertain danger of waves and shipwrecks, but by the fruits of his own labor. Of these fruits the Psalms sing to the righteous: “You will eat the labors of your hands” (Ps. 127:2).

It is written in Hosea that the ways of the harlot were hedged round by the Lord with thorns, so that she could not follow her lovers and, compelled by this necessity, might return to her former husband. We frequently observe this also in worldly affairs: many people who could not perceive the Lord amid prosperity and an abundance of everything come to understand through want and turn to works of righteousness, after their hand has ceased to prevail in enjoying the good fortune of this age, which formerly provoked—or, according to Symmachus, disturbed—kings upon the sea, whose heart is in God’s hand. Would that we too, despising the commerce of this sea, might work our land and no longer await the ships of Carthage, or the ships of Tyre which used to sail to Carthage, lest we be subjected to the power of the dragon who rules in the sea. But let us fix a steady step upon the earth; indeed, hastening toward heaven, let us work our land, so that by sowing here we may reap there. Let our hand also, formerly occupied in the business of the world and able through power and prosperity even to move kings—that is, saints—from their standing, become weak in the affairs of the sea, so that it may be strong in the work of its land.

**[Column 0278C] (Verse 12)**

“The Lord Sabaoth commanded concerning Canaan to destroy its strength, and they will say: ‘You will no longer add to doing injury and iniquity to the virgin daughter of Sidon.’”

We have already shown that Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan, adducing the testimony of the Gospel in which the Canaanite woman, or Syrophoenician, is said to have come from the borders of Tyre and Sidon and to have met the Lord and Savior. Every soul set amid the waves of the world and carried about by every wind of doctrine is to be called Canaan, which means, as it were, “tossing” or “movement.” Hence the aged adulterer is told: “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you” (Dan. 13). It benefits Tyre and its narrowness for Canaanite strength to perish, so that its inhabitants may be told that they can no longer inflict injuries and oppress through iniquity the virgin daughter of Sidon. Whoever is seized by the devil amid the disturbance of diverse vices and given over to shameful dishonors, so that he may defile his body with pleasures and disgrace, is a son or daughter of Sidon. It should be known that *Sabaoth* is not in the Hebrew and, conversely, that “virgin” has been added from the Hebrew.

### (Verse 13)

“If you go to the Kittim, neither will there be rest for you there; and if to the land of the Chaldeans, it too has been laid waste by the Assyrians. Siim founded it; they set up its fortifications; they raised up its tower; its wall has fallen.”

What follows has been added from the edition of Theodotion under asterisks: “Siim founded it; they set up its fortifications; they raised up its tower”; and without asterisks there follows: “Its wall has fallen.” Kittim means “a completed” or “perfect wound”; Chaldeans in this place, “like breasts”; Assyrians, “those who rebuke.” We could not discover an etymology for Siim, and the other interpreters also rendered it by the very name in which it is written among the Hebrews.

Tyre is therefore told that, although it strives to go to the Kittim and avoid the wound of its narrowness, it will be unable to find even there perfect rest. Again, if it wishes to go to the Chaldeans and enjoy their fertility and abundance of all things, it will find them too desolate, the Assyrians rebuking their barrenness, just as the Apostle also delivered sinners to Satan (1 Tim. 1), that they might learn not to blaspheme—those who are delivered to the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved. The Siim laid the foundations of the Chaldeans; I understand them to be most wicked demons, who raised both the fortifications and the most proud towers of the Chaldean city against the knowledge of the Lord. But all their building collapsed into ruins, for it follows: “Its wall has fallen.” “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

We often see some people in the world pass from one pursuit to another; for example, those who have fared badly in military service pass into trade, while advocates in turn take up the arms of soldiers. They change their occupation in order to change their misfortune; yet, by God’s dispensation, all things continue to turn out adversely for those whom he deigns to save, so that through poverty and miseries they may be compelled to place their confidence not in themselves but in their Creator.

**[Column 0279C] (Verse 14)**

“Wail, ships of Carthage, for your strength has perished.”

The ships of Carthage—that is, of Tharsis—are commanded to wail. For it is no longer, as above, that they have perished or will not come; rather, their strength has perished. According to another interpretation, Tharsis is rendered in our language as “the completion of six,” or “of joys.” We read that this world was made in six days, and according to ecclesiastical traditions will afterward be brought to completion. Therefore all the goods of this world and all the labor of mortals are compared to the uncertain course of ships, because they will quickly perish and all the strength of sailors will be dissolved. Hence it is written in Solomon: “The wise man ascended fortified cities and destroyed their strongholds” (Prov. 21:22). Whatever is composed by the art of heretics, worldly wisdom, and contrary doctrines, the ecclesiastical man destroys and teaches to be subject to his feet.

### (Verse 15 and following)

“And it shall come to pass on that day that Tyre will be forsaken for seventy years, like the time of one king, like the time of a man. And after seventy years Tyre will be like the song of a harlot: ‘Take the lyre; wander about, city-harlot, consigned to forgetfulness. Play well; sing many songs, that you may be remembered.’ But after seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she will again be restored to her former state; and her trade will extend to all the kingdoms of the world upon the face of the earth. Her trade and her wages will be holy to the Lord, yet they will not be gathered for themselves, but for those who dwell before the Lord. All her trade will be for eating and drinking and being filled, as a contribution, a memorial before the Lord.”

The phrases “a memorial before the Lord,” “upon the face of the earth,” and “like the time of a man” are not in the Hebrew but have been added in the Greek. Tyre, once confined, is left for seventy years so that, when the time of desolation has been completed, it may turn its formerly harlot’s song into the praises of God and, taking up the lyre, have all its strings sounding together. Thus, after it has played well and sung many songs, it may be remembered by God, though it had been consigned to forgetfulness because of its fornication; it may be restored to its former state; it may possess the riches of all the kingdoms of the world; and the wages of its labor may be gathered not for the Tyrians, but for those who dwell in the presence of the Lord, who may eat and drink and be filled with all the good things contributed by everyone’s labor for the joy of a banquet.

The divine word exhorts Sidon and Tyre to repentance and promises that their labors and wages will be consecrated to the Lord. Who would not have hope of salvation from sins, if only he sings well and all the strings of virtues that were once slack are tuned to the praises of the Lord? In the forty-fourth psalm, which particularly concerns the mysteries of the union of bridegroom and bride—that is, of God the Savior and the Church—we read among other things: “The daughters of Tyre, with gifts, the rich of the people will entreat your face” (Ps. 44:13). Again the bridegroom himself speaks to the Tyrian bride: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and the house of your father, because the king will desire your beauty” (ibid. 11–12). Hence, in the description of her beauty, it is added: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment embroidered with gold, surrounded by variety” (ibid. 10); and again: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (ibid. 14). But if the king desired the beauty of the repentant Tyrian woman, adorned with varied virtues, how much more will her wages and trade belong not to those remaining in Tyre but to those who dwell in the presence of the Lord. After they have repented, they will hear from the Lord and Savior: “Eat, my friends, and drink, and be inebriated, my dearest ones” (Song 5:1). What it means to eat and drink and be filled by the contribution of every virtue, the faithful reader understands.

Jeremiah (ch. 29), Daniel (ch. 9), and Zechariah (ch. 7) teach that the temple was desolate for seventy years. In Ezekiel (ch. 16) we read of Sodom that it will be restored to its former state, and of Egypt that, after the desolation of the land of Egypt and the drying up of the seven rivers, it will receive its former fertility. The number seven and the number seventy, whether consisting of individual days or of seven decades, signify perfect and complete repentance; thus Tyre rightly returns to its former state when the period of repentance has been completed. I think that this harlot is also signified in the mystical discourse of Solomon in Proverbs: “Do not attend to the wicked woman; for honey drips from the lips of a harlot woman, who for a short time fattens your throat, but afterward you will find it more bitter than gall” (Prov. 5:2–4). For from the window of her house she looks out upon the streets (Matt. 7), because broad and spacious is the way that leads to death; and whenever she sees an unwise young man—for she does not dare to tempt the wise—and one passing by the corners, who have lost the straight line, she speaks to him in darkness and gloom and, under the appearance of pleasures, leads him like a victim to death. If she is converted, sings well, and fulfills the period of years of perfect repentance, she will eat and drink and be filled. Let Novatian hear this and be silent.

## BOOK EIGHT

**[Column 0281]**

**[Column 0281A]** Books Six and Seven above contain the allegorical interpretation of the fifth volume, which I once dictated as a historical exposition. The present work, that is, Book Eight, returns to the interpretation already begun, so that it may discuss both the historical and the tropological senses together according to both editions.

If this seems long to you, holy virgin Eustochium, do not attribute it to me, but to the difficulty of Holy Scripture, and especially to the prophet Isaiah, who is enveloped in such great obscurities that, in view of the magnitude of the subject, I consider brief the explanation that is lengthy in itself.

Certainly, we write for diligent students and for those who desire to know Holy Scripture, not for the fastidious, who grow nauseated at every detail. If they desire a river of eloquence and polished declamations, let them read Cicero, Quintilian, Gallio, Gabinianus—and, to come to our own writers, Tertullian, Cyprian, Minucius, Arnobius, Lactantius, and Hilary. Our purpose is that Isaiah should be understood through us, and that our words should by no means be praised under the pretext of Isaiah.

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript reads “Quintilian, Gabinianus,” omitting the name Gallio. Shortly afterward we also supply a conjunction from the same source. It should also be observed that the second part of the Ninth Homily of Origen—or of the work attributed to Origen—on various subjects was often compiled from this book of Jerome on Isaiah, in the same words.

### 329 (Chapter 24: verses 1 and following)

“Behold, the Lord will lay waste the earth, strip it bare, afflict its surface, and scatter its inhabitants. And it shall be: as the people, so the priest; as the servant, so his master; as the maidservant, so her mistress; as the buyer, so the seller; as the lender, so the borrower; as the creditor, so the debtor. The earth shall be utterly laid waste, and it shall be utterly plundered, for the Lord has spoken this word.”

After the specific rebuke of the individual nations—Judah, Babylon, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Israel, Egypt, the desert of the sea, Idumea and Arabia, the Valley of Vision, and finally Tyre—in whose interpretation we have said what we could, the prophetic discourse now describes what the whole world will suffer at the consummation. It no longer prophesies concerning individual nations, but concerning all of them together.

First, it describes the torments that the wicked will suffer, and how, in accordance with the Gospel and the Apostle, heaven and earth and the form of this world will pass away (Matt. 24; 1 Cor. 7), and sinners will be brought down into hell (Ps. 30), concerning whom it is written: “They will enter into the farthest parts of the earth; they will be handed over to the sword; they will become the portion of foxes” (Ps. 63:10).

Then, because there are many dwelling places with the Father according to the quality of merits, it explains how the saints will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air and will always be with him (John 14; 1 Thess. 4).

For “the earth will be laid waste,” the Septuagint translated “the inhabited world will be corrupted.” And for “he will afflict its surface,” that is, the earth, they likewise translated “he will reveal its surface,” so that the dead may come forth from their tombs. Or he will strip it bare, so that all its works may be brought into public view, and its inhabitants may be scattered to different places, destined either for rewards or punishments.

Then there will be no distinction between noble and ignoble, priest and layman, servant and master, maidservant and mistress, rich and poor, lender and debtor, buyer and seller. For all will stand equally before the tribunal of Christ, and there will be no partiality with God (Rom. 14; Col. 3).

Job also speaks of this in almost the same words: “The small and the great are there, and the servant does not fear his master” (Job 3:19). And the Savior, to whom all judgment has been entrusted, bears full witness to it in the Gospel.

The earth, therefore, will be laid waste, and all earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that when the image of the earthly (*χοϊκός*, “earthly”) has been abolished, the heavenly image may remain. “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:47–49).

Hence the same Apostle says: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 15:50). This does not mean, as the heretics suppose, that the nature of bodies will perish; rather, this corruptible nature will put on incorruption, and this mortal nature will put on immortality. All these things will happen because what is to come has been spoken by the Lord through the prophets.

### (Verses 4–5)

“The earth mourned and faded away; it grew weak. The inhabited world faded away; the height of the people of the earth grew weak, and the earth was slain by its inhabitants.”

**The Septuagint:** “The earth mourned; the inhabited world was corrupted; the high places of the earth mourned, but the earth acted impiously because of its inhabitants.”

“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). Hence the first sentence is directed against those who are lofty upon the earth, so that all the things that are now strong may be weakened because of those who mixed blood with blood and, after the manner of the blood of Abel, caused the blood of the slain to cry out to God (Gen. 4).

### (Verse 6)

Because they have transgressed the law, changed the ordinance, and broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse will devour the earth, and its inhabitants will sin; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will rage, and few people will be left.

**LXX:** Because they transgressed the law, changed the commandments, and violated the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse will devour the earth, because its inhabitants sinned; therefore the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, and few people will be left.

Let the Jews hear this—those who boast that they alone received the Lord’s law: the nations as a whole, and the entire world, first received the natural law, and for that reason the law was later given through Moses, because the first law had been broken. Concerning this the Apostle says: “For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves; they show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. II, 14).

Those, therefore, who have observed these laws will receive rewards; but those who have neglected them will endure what the prophetic word now threatens. And just as in the beginning God blessed every creature that he had made (Gen. I), so at the consummation of the world he will curse those who are earthly and have not been strangers here, but inhabitants of the earth, and who have sinned in it—those who, forgetting their own condition, raged against one another in mutual fury. And few will remain who possess the heavenly image; or, according to the LXX, the inhabitants of the earth will be poor, because they have lost spiritual riches.

### (Verses 7 ff.)

The vintage has mourned; the vine has languished; all who rejoiced in their hearts have groaned. The joy of tambourines has ceased; the sound of those rejoicing has fallen silent; the sweetness of the lyre has become mute. They will not drink wine with song; the drink will be bitter to those who drink it. The city of vanity has been crushed; every house is closed, with no one entering. There will be a cry over wine in the streets; all joy has been deserted; the gladness of the earth has been removed. Solitude has been left in the city, and calamity will oppress the gates, because these things will be in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples.

At the consummation of the world, the memory of former pleasures will be the source of torments. Thus that rich man, dressed in purple at his banquet, who had received his good things during his life, raised his eyes from hell and saw Lazarus at rest (Luke XVI). And the Lord, rebuking the rich, the luxurious, and those who laugh, says in the Gospel: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have received your consolation. Woe to you who are now filled, because you will hunger. Woe to you who now laugh, because you will mourn and weep” (ibid., 24–25).

When, therefore, the resurrection of the dead has taken place and the day of judgment has come, then the wine and the vintage will mourn, concerning which Moses says: “Their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their branch from Gomorrah. Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster is one of bitterness. The wine of dragons is their fury, and the fury of asps is incurable” (Deut. XXXII, 33).

Then every drink—or, as it is called in Hebrew, *sicera*, that is, drunkenness, which overturns the mind’s condition and does not allow people to remain watchful—will be changed into bitterness. For a time it deceives those who use it by pretending to be honey, but at the end it will be found more bitter than gall. Then every sweetness of those rejoicing, and the sound of tambourines and lyres, will be turned into lamentation and groaning.

Let us apply this testimony to those who at banquets indulge not only in gluttony and drunkenness but also in their ears, so that through every sense the soul’s strength may become soft.

The city of vanity will be crushed—or every city, or spiritual Babylon, which sits dressed in purple upon seven hills, whose punishments we read in the Apocalypse of John (Apoc. XVIII). He aptly said “the city of vanity.” For if it is said of heaven and earth, and of all things earthly, “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I, 2), how much more must this be said of a single city, which is only a small part of the whole world!

Then the houses whose ceilings are now gilded, and whose walls are covered with marble slabs and shine with the brightness of carved ivory, while the poor die of cold without a roof or hut, will remain empty. There will be a cry in the streets over wine—not in the narrow and confined way that leads to life, but in the broad and spacious way that leads to death (Matt. VII)—over the wine and drunkenness of their error, those who “slept their sleep, and all the men of wealth found nothing in their hands” (Ps. LXXV).

For the gladness of the earth has been transferred to the heavens; and solitude has been left in the once most celebrated city. Calamity will oppress the gates of the well-traveled roads through which the crowds of peoples poured into the city. And so that we might clearly know that the destruction of the whole world is being announced, he added: “These things will be in the midst of the earth,” in the midst of the nations or peoples.

### (Verses 13–15)

It will be as when a few olives that remain are shaken from the olive tree, and as the gleanings after the vintage has ended. These will raise their voice and praise when the Lord has been glorified; they will neigh from the sea. Therefore glorify the Lord in instruction; in the islands of the sea, the name of the Lord, the God of Israel.

How far the LXX translation differs from the Hebrew truth in this passage, the following words will show.

**LXX:** As when someone shakes an olive tree, so they will shake them; and when the vintage has ceased, these will cry out with a shout. But those who have been left upon the earth will rejoice together with the glory of the Lord; the water of the sea will be troubled. Therefore the glory of the Lord will be in the islands of the sea; the name of the Lord will be glorious, the Lord, the God of Israel.

When only a few people have been left, after the curse has devoured the earth, solitude has arisen in the city, and all these things have occurred in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the peoples and nations, the saints will be so few—those of whom the Lord says in the Gospel, “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16)—and the pressure upon the righteous will be so violent that, if possible, even God’s elect will be tested. Their small number will be compared with the very scarce berries of olive trees which, after being shaken and stripped, scarcely leave a few on the tips of the branches. And just as, after the vintage has ended, poor people, compelled by need, customarily go around the empty vines and gather a few clusters of grapes, so those who remain after the vintage and oppression of the world, and who are able to escape the hand of the persecuting Antichrist or the fires of the impending punishment, will raise their voices on high and praise God.

When the Lord comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels, and they see him reigning in majesty, then they will neigh like horses, exulting in the greatness of their joy; they will neigh from the sea of this age.

Therefore, you who are now instructed in the holy Scriptures and know that such joy and such rewards have been reserved for you, glorify the Lord in instruction, hearing what is written: “Whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (II Cor. X, 17). Not in the land of Judea, but in the islands—that is, in the Churches of this sea and age—in which the name of the Lord, the God once of Israel, or of the one who sees God, is blessed and praised.

According to the LXX, everything that we have understood concerning the saints may be referred to the wicked: when the vintage has ended, they will cry out while placed in punishments. But those who have escaped the number of the wicked will rejoice in the glory of the Lord, and the waters of the peoples of this age—or, according to another reading, “of his age”—will be troubled.

### (Verse 16)

From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, “The glory of the Just One”; and I said, “My secret is for me, my secret is for me: woe is me.”

**Note:** In the Vatican manuscript: “And they will say, ‘Woe to the transgressors,’” and the rest; then the words “my mystery is for me” are repeated. Of these readings, the first seems closer to the text of the Septuagint codex, where we find *οὐαὶ τοῖς ἀθετοῦσιν* (“woe to those who reject”); the other agrees with Theodotion’s translation, from which it was taken. We correct certain minor matters above and below.

**LXX:** From other parts of the earth we have heard portents; hope for the righteous; and they will say, “My mystery is for me” **[lacuna or incomplete supplied text]**.

The phrase “my mystery is for me” is not found in the LXX, but has been added in Greek from Theodotion’s translation. Again, where they placed “woe,” so that it might be joined to the following verse, the Hebrew has *OI LI* (), which properly means “woe to me.” For “ends,” moreover, which we rendered more plainly for the sake of the meaning, the Hebrew has *MECCHENAPH* (), which means “wing,” not “end.”

Those, then, concerning whom it was said above, “They will raise their voice and praise,” when they have neighed from the sea, glorified the Lord in instruction, and seen the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, praised in the islands of the sea—these will then sing with one voice and say:

“From other parts of the earth”—that is, from the prophets and saints of the Lord, who, taking up the wings of a dove, hasten toward the kingdoms of heaven—we have heard his praises proclaimed. And we have heard that the glory or hope of the Just One is not futile, but that everything is fulfilled in reality.

While the saints were saying these things, neighing from the sea, raising their voice, and praising, the Prophet speaks to himself: “When,” he says, “I had heard these things and perceived that the prophecy of the Prophets was to be fulfilled in the overthrow of the world, I spoke to myself in the inward feeling of my heart: I cannot recount everything that I see. My tongue clings to my throat; my voice is shut up by grief. Woe is me! What an array of punishments is passing before my eyes! I see the things that are to come as though they were present.”

Those who think that this must be understood as spoken from God’s person are mistaken, because they do not follow the order of the subject.

I also wonder in what sense, instead of “psalms” and “praises,” the LXX translated the Hebrew *ZEMROTH* () as “portents,” unless perhaps it signifies a sign and portent, so that, with the Jewish people excluded, the formerly unbelieving multitude of the nations might be saved.

**Note:** Vatican manuscript: *ZEMIROTH* ().

### (Verses 17–18)

Transgressors have transgressed; with the transgression of the transgressors they have transgressed. Terror, pit, and snare are upon you, inhabitant of the earth. And it will happen that whoever flees from the sound of terror will fall into the pit, and whoever escapes from the pit will be caught by the snare.

**LXX:** Woe to the transgressors who transgress the law. Fear, pit, and snare are upon you who inhabit the earth. And it will happen that whoever flees from fear will fall into the pit, and whoever comes out of the pit will be caught in the snare.

This is the cause of my mourning and groaning, for which I said twice, “My secret is for me, my secret is for me”: because all have transgressed God’s law. The Lord’s punishment is not delayed, nor is it merely foretold as something future; it is imminent and holds the inhabitants of the earth captive. And when they think they have escaped, they will fall from one danger into another, and wherever they turn they will not evade the Lord’s impending wrath.

### (Verses 19–20)

Because the floodgates from on high have been opened, and the foundations of the earth will be shaken. The earth will be utterly broken; the earth will be completely crushed; the earth will be violently moved. The earth will stagger and reel like a drunkard; it will be removed like a tent for one night. Its iniquity will weigh it down; it will fall, and it will not rise again.

Therefore no one will escape the Lord’s terror, snare, and pit, because the floodgates from on high—or, as the LXX translated more explicitly, the windows of heaven—have been opened, so that the Lord might look down upon all human sins, which, because he had not previously punished them, seemed to sinners to be unknown to him.

After he had opened the windows and seen all the works of mortals, the foundations of the earth were shaken, according to what is written elsewhere concerning God’s gaze: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. CIII, 32). Then the earth will be broken, crushed, moved, and agitated in the likeness of a drunkard—not that the earth itself will be reduced to dust or nothingness, but that all earthly things will pass away and another mode of life will succeed them.

And just as a drunkard does not know what he is doing, but when his limbs are dulled by drunkenness neither his foot nor his mind performs its proper function, so the whole earth—that is, all human beings who dwell upon the earth—will be drunk with the magnitude of evils and punishments, and will be stupefied at everything they see.

And just as a tent or shelter for one night is moved from place to place, and the traveler abandons the site of the former tent so that no trace of the previous dwelling remains, so the form of this world will pass away. The earth, weighed down by its iniquity, will be desolate; its weight and exceedingly heavy burden are described in Zechariah: “She who sat upon a talent of lead” (Zech. V, 32).

“And it will fall,” he says, “and will not rise again.” This does not deny the resurrection of human beings, or of all who lived upon the earth. Rather, earthly existence and the condition of the former life will no longer remain, when human bodies rise for this purpose: that their souls may again be clothed with the bodies they previously laid aside, and that they may receive from God either the good or the evil that they did upon the earth.

### (Verses 21 ff.)

And it will happen on that day that the Lord will visit the host of heaven on high, and the kings of the earth upon the earth. And they will be gathered together in the gathering of a single bundle into the pit; they will be shut up there in prison, and after many days they will be visited. The moon will blush, and the sun will be ashamed, when the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified before his elders.

For “the moon will blush, and the sun will be ashamed,” the Septuagint translated “the brick will melt, and the wall will fall.” The reason for this error will be shown by what follows.

In the Hebrew language the sun is called by three names: *SEMES* (), *HAMMA* (), which means “heat,” and *HERES* (), which means *ὄστρακον*—that is, “potsherd” or “dryness.” *MAOR* (), which in Greek is *φωστήρ* and in Latin *luminare* (“luminary”), is common to the sun and the moon.

Again, the moon is called *JAREE* (), which in Greek is *μήνη*, because in a circuit of thirty days it completes a month, and *LABANA* (), that is, “white” or “bright.” In the present passage, therefore, instead of *LABANA*, meaning “moon,” the Septuagint translated “brick”—which in Hebrew is *LEBENA*—having been deceived by the ambiguity of the word.

Again, instead of *HAMMA*, meaning “heat,” by which the sun is understood, they placed “wall,” which in Hebrew is *HOMA* ().

The sense of the whole chapter is this: The windows of heaven have been opened so that, while the Lord looks upon earthly sins, the entire form of earthly works might pass away and fall, and never rise again to its former condition.

On that day—that is, on the day of judgment—the Lord will visit the host, or adornment, of heaven on high, so that he may judge not only earthly things but heavenly things as well. Let us learn what the adornment or host of heaven is from Moses, who writes: “Beware lest, when you look up to heaven and see the sun, the moon, the stars, and all the adornment of heaven, you be deceived and worship them” (Deut. IV, 19).

The Lord will “visit” the host and army of heaven according to the idiom of the Scriptures, as though it were sick and in need of iron and cautery, according to the saying: “I will visit their sins with a rod, and their iniquities with scourges” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 33). For we also read below: “My sword is drunk in heaven” (below, XXXIV, 5); and in Job: “The stars are not clean in his sight,” and, “Against his angels he found something crooked” (Job XXV, 5).

He will also visit the kings and princes of the earth, the rulers of this darkness and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places. Concerning these princes, who preside over different provinces, it is also written in Daniel: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia came to oppose me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes, and the prince of the kingdom of the Greeks” (Dan. X).

These princes, therefore, who did not preserve their own rank, the Lord will gather on the day of judgment as though bound together in a single bundle, and he will send them into the pit of hell, so that in them too what is written concerning the wicked may be fulfilled: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the pit that he made” (Ps. VII, 16). They will be shut up in prison, according to what the Lord says: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

But what follows—“And after many days they will be visited”—seems to favor my friends, who grant repentance to the devil and demons, since they will be visited by the Lord after many ages. Let them consider, however, that divine Scripture did not say explicitly, “They will be visited by the Lord,” or, “They will be visited by angels,” but simply, “They will be visited.” From this ambiguity of the word, both a remedy and a correction may be understood: after the righteous have received their rewards, those others will be visited in everlasting punishments.

It must nevertheless be understood that human frailty cannot know God’s judgment, nor pronounce a decision concerning the magnitude and measure of punishments, which has been left to the Lord’s judgment.

Then the moon will blush and the sun will be ashamed, according to what the Apostle says: “For the creation itself groans and labors” (Rom. VIII, 22), seeing that human beings who enjoyed its light did nothing worthy of God’s goodness—he who makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust (Matt. V).

It will be as when a steward or household manager, at the coming of his lord, sees the household subjected to various torments and having in no way fulfilled his commands.

The Savior teaches more fully about this same passage in the Gospel: “The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken, when the sign of the Son of Man appears in heaven, and all the tribes of the earth will beat their breasts, and they will see the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven in great power and glory” (Matt. XXIV, 29–30).

We have learned of the overthrow of the earth, the visitation of the host of heaven, the gathering of kings and princes into one bundle, their casting into the pit, their confinement in prison, the visitation after a long time of those who have been shut up, the blushing of the moon, and the shame of the sun.

After all these things the Lord of hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in heavenly Jerusalem, concerning which it is also written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “And he will be glorified in the presence of his elders” (Hebr. XII).

What sort of elder was Abraham, who died in a good old age and was gathered to his fathers (Gen. XXV)? What sort of elders Moses is also commanded to choose, whom he knows to be elders (Num. XI): “For a man’s wisdom is his gray hair” (Wis. IV, 8). They imitate the Ancient of Days, whose hair is described as white, so that the length of his age may be indicated (Dan. VII, 9).

This may also be understood of the ecclesiastical rank, provided that they do not destroy their dignity by their works.

**Note:** Martianus reads the clauses in the reverse order: “who imitate the Ancient of Days”; for the gray hair of a man is his wisdom. The reading that we set out is much more harmonious. Vatican manuscript: “Nor should the words ‘who imitate,’ etc., have been distinguished in italic type, as though they were the text of Scripture, as Martianus did.”

## Chapter XXV

### (Verses 1 ff.)

Lord, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will confess your name, because you have done wonderful things, ancient purposes faithful. Amen. Because you have made a city into a heap, a fortified city into a ruin, a house of foreigners, so that it is no longer a city and will never be rebuilt. For this a strong people will praise you; the city of powerful nations will fear you. For you have become a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a hope from the storm, a shelter from the heat; for the spirit of the powerful is like a storm driving against a wall. As heat in thirst, you will humble the tumult of foreigners; and as heat by a scorching torrent beneath a cloud, you will cause the branch of the powerful to wither.

**LXX:** Lord my God, I will glorify you; I will praise your name, because you have done marvelous things, an ancient and true counsel. Let it be. Because you have made cities into a heap—fortified cities, so that their foundations might fall. The cities of the wicked will never be rebuilt. Therefore the poor people will bless you, and the cities of people who endure iniquity will bless you.

For you were a helper to every humble city, and a protection to those who were sorrowful because of poverty. You will deliver them from the most wicked people; a shelter for the thirsty, and the spirit of people who endure iniquity, like fainthearted people thirsting in Zion because of wicked people to whom you handed us over.

There are two interpretations of this passage.

The Jews think it is the voice of the saints and of the believing people: when God has done against the whole world the things stated above, and the prophecies of all the prophets have been fulfilled, they interpret the city that has been overthrown as Rome, which is to be utterly destroyed. They refer the strong people who praise the Lord, and to whom the Lord has become a strength in their tribulation and distress, to Israel, which has been delivered from the persecution of the nations as from the most burning heat and thirst.

Others, however, understand—and more properly—that these words are spoken from the person of the Prophet, giving thanks to the Father for the passion of the Lord and Savior: that he has done marvelous things and fulfilled ancient purposes in truth, when those standing at the right hand will hear: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. XXV, 34).

Understanding this, Paul also said: “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless” (Eph. I, 4). And, desiring that what he prophesies might come to pass, he adds the Hebrew word *AMEN* (), for which the LXX translated “let it be.” The Lord also frequently uses this word in the Gospel: “Amen, amen,” that is, “Truly, truly, I say to you” (John VI, 54).

Why, then, he praises and confesses the Lord’s name, and what these marvelous things and ancient purposes are that he has shown to be true by their fulfillment, follows:

“Because you have made a city into a heap, a fortified city into a ruin, a house of foreigners, so that it is no longer a city and will never be rebuilt.”

The formerly fortified city is understood as Jerusalem, which has become a house of foreigners, concerning whom the Savior says in the psalm: “The sons of foreigners have lied to me; the sons of foreigners have grown old and limped in their paths” (Ps. XVII, 46). When this city has been destroyed, it will never be rebuilt, so that the dreams of a thousand-year kingdom and a golden and jeweled Jerusalem may cease.

When Jerusalem has been destroyed because of its impiety, a strong people will praise the Lord. Who this strong people is, the following verse shows: “The city of powerful nations will fear you.” While those others blaspheme, the people of the nations will fear you. For “the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord” (Prov. IX, 10).

A strong people will praise you, and the city of powerful nations will fear you—that is, the Church gathered from the nations.

“For you have become a strength to the poor,” your Christ, concerning whom we also read in the Psalms: “Blessed is he who understands concerning the needy and poor” (Ps. XL, 1). And in Zechariah, according to the Hebrew truth, the poor man—that is, *EBION* ()—is described as sitting upon a donkey’s colt (Zech. IX).

You are a strength to the needy in the tribulation of his passion, a hope from the storm of the cross, and a shelter from the heat, when he said: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII, 46).
