For just as when wind strikes a wall and passes through it, so the storm of the blaspheming Jews could not harm him.

And, to use another comparison, just as a branch is scorched by extreme heat and withers, so you will make the tumult and outcry of foreigners—that is, of those who have become alienated from you—with­er and perish.

According to the LXX interpreters, I have not been able to discover in this passage—not the sense, but the order and sequence of the words. And instead of the place where we translated “as heat in thirst,” for which the Hebrew has *BASAION* (), which among them is said to mean “impassable place” or “thirst,” why they translated “in Zion” for “impassable place” and “in thirst” is an obvious error, arising from the similarity between the words *SAION* and *SION* (both written with the same letters).

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript inserts the following annotation here: “It should first be noted how appropriate Jerome’s teaching is for the Catholic Church against its detractors, to whom his statements seem worthless.” We soon correct certain minor matters in accordance with the same manuscript.

### (Verses 6–8)

And the Lord of hosts will make for all peoples on this mountain a banquet of rich foods, a banquet of vintage wine, of rich foods full of marrow, of vintage wine well refined. And on this mountain he will destroy the face of the bond bound over all peoples, and the web that he wove over all nations. And he will destroy death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away the tear from every face; and he will remove the reproach of his people from the whole earth, because the Lord has spoken.

**LXX:** And the Lord Sabaoth will make for all the nations upon this mountain a feast of joy; they will drink joy, they will drink wine. They will be anointed with ointment on this mountain. Hand all these things over to the nations, for this counsel is concerning all nations: prevailing death has devoured. And again: “The Lord God has removed every tear from every face, and has removed the reproach of his people from the whole earth. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

For what we translated “the face of the bond bound over all peoples,” Aquila interpreted “the face of darkness over all peoples.” Since Aquila said “darkness” twice, Theodotion named darkness once, with the rest similar. Symmachus translated it, “the face of the Ruler who rules over all peoples.”

What the Septuagint intended to say by “Hand all these things over to the nations” is clear to the reader: they have set down not the words of Scripture but their own interpretation, since all the mysteries of the Law and the Temple are to be transferred to the Churches of the nations.

After the Lord’s passion, therefore, when he has delivered him from thirst, heat, and storm, the Lord will make—not for the Jewish people but for all the nations on Mount Zion—a rich banquet, marrow-filled sacrifices, and refined vintage wine. He will destroy and cause to be swallowed up the face of death and the bond by which all peoples were bound; he will break apart the net of death and the web that had caught all the nations.

And, according to the Apostle, “death will be swallowed up forever” (I Cor. XVI). The Lord will wipe away the tear from every face when, death having been overcome, the kingdom of Christ has come; and the reproach of the human race, which had been created in the image of the Creator, will have escaped the servitude of the devil and death.

It is no wonder if, according to Symmachus, death is called the female ruler, since the blessed Apostle said: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. V, 14).

Some want the Ruler of all peoples—or the face of darkness over all peoples—and the web woven over all nations to be understood as the Antichrist, who is to be destroyed on the Mount of Olives, as we also stated in the final vision of Daniel.

According to the LXX, a feast of joy is prepared for all the nations on Mount Zion. There they will drink wine, which the Lord promised that he would drink with his saints in the kingdom of his Father (Matt. XX; Luke XXII); and they will be anointed with ointment, so that, reborn in Christ, they may become a new people. Hence it is said: “Hand all these things over to the nations,” which Israel once celebrated symbolically and figuratively.

For this is the Lord’s counsel: that everything be transferred to the nations, because death has been swallowed up (I Cor. XV), every tear has been wiped away, and the reproach of the whole earth has been removed as Christ’s rule succeeds.

### (Verses 9 ff.)

And they will say on that day: “Behold, this is our God; we waited for him, and he will save us. This is the Lord; we endured for him. We will exult and rejoice in his salvation.” For the hand of the Lord will rest upon this mountain; and Moab will be threshed beneath him as straw is threshed on a wagon. He will spread out his hands beneath him, as a swimmer spreads them out for swimming; and his glory will be humbled by the striking of his hands. The defenses of your lofty walls will fall, be humbled, and be brought down to the earth, even to the dust.

After death has been swallowed up forever, the people of God, having been delivered from the hand of death, will say to the Lord: “Behold, this is our God,” whom the unbelieving regarded as merely a human being. “We waited for him”—that is, we believed his words, because he would fulfill his promises—“and he will save us.” Therefore, rescued by his aid from the jaws of death, “we will exult and rejoice in him”; and his hand and power will rest upon this mountain.

Concerning it we read above: “When the Lord of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and is glorified in the presence of his elders” (Isa. XXIV, 23).

Moab, which means “from the father,” will be so crushed that it will be like straw customarily crushed by a wagon. This is spoken according to the practice of Palestine and many eastern provinces, which, because of the scarcity of meadows and hay, prepare straw as food for animals. There are wagons plated with iron, whose wheels revolve through the middle in the form of saws; they crush the stalks and reduce them to straw.

Therefore, just as straw is crushed by iron wagons, so Moab will be crushed beneath him—whether beneath God’s power or within himself—so that nothing whole will remain in him. And just as a swimmer customarily extends his entire body, so he will be struck down upon the earth by his own power and, falling, will make a noise.

All his defenses also—the defenses of lofty men, or “walls,” as the Hebrew contains—will fall, be humbled, and be brought down to the earth, crushed even to the dust.

Although the prophetic word generally weaves a prophecy concerning the consummation of the world, nevertheless, so that it may not seem entirely to neglect present matters, it names Moab, who was Israel’s enemy to such an extent that he caused them to fornicate with the Midianites and to consecrate themselves to the idol Baal-peor, which means Priapus. Against him Jeremiah speaks: “Chemosh will go into captivity, his priests and his princes together” (Jerem. XLVIII, 7); and again: “Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel” (ibid., 13), along with other similar passages.

Through one idol and demon who presided over that idol, he indicates that all hostile powers will be humbled, led down into Tartarus, and crushed like dust.

But if this is so, where is the devil’s repentance?

## Chapter XXVI

### (Verse 1)

On that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: “The city of our strength: the Savior will be placed in it as a wall and a bulwark.”

**LXX:** On that day they will sing this song over the land of Judea: “Behold, a strong city, and our salvation will set up a wall and a surrounding wall.”

When Moab has been humbled and brought down to the earth, even to the dust, and all enemies have been placed beneath Christ’s feet, this song will be sung in the land of Judah, or Judea, both of which mean “confession.” Just as we understood Zion and Jerusalem as the heavenly city, so we should understand the region of this city as heavenly confession.

Finally, the saints, unwilling to sing the song of Judea in a foreign land, say: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. CXXXVI, 4).

I think this is the song concerning which the saints are commanded elsewhere: “Sing to the Lord a new song” (Ps. XCV, 1). The song will be the one that follows: “The city of our strength: the Savior” (Matt. V).

What city is this? The one situated on a mountain that cannot be hidden. Concerning it it is also written elsewhere: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 4); and again: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2).

Its founder is the one of whom the Father speaks: “He built my city.” Indeed, the Savior is the city of our strength—that is, Jesus. “And a wall and a bulwark will be placed in it.” The wall is good works, and the bulwark is right faith, so that it may be enclosed by a double defense. For it is not enough to have the wall of faith unless faith itself is confirmed by good works.

This wall and bulwark, or surrounding wall, is built of living stones, which, according to the prophet, roll upon the earth.

For what we translated “bulwark,” Symmachus interpreted “fortification,” so that the walls themselves might be surrounded by defenses, and by a rampart, ditch, and other walls, which in the construction of camps are customarily called *loriculae*.

**Note:** The words “the heavenly confession of the city” are read in manuscripts of Silva Major; they are absent, however, from Erasmus’s edition and from many very ancient manuscript copies. **Martianus.**—These two words, “the heavenly confession,” which Martianus had supplied from a single manuscript of Silva Major, are confirmed by our two manuscripts, Vatican and Palatine.

### (Verses 2–4)

“Open the gates, and let the righteous nation enter, the one keeping faithfulness. The ancient error has passed away; you will preserve peace—peace, because we have hoped in you. You have hoped in the Lord for everlasting ages.”

The Septuagint: “Open the gates; let the people keeping righteousness enter, and keeping truth, grasping truth, and keeping peace—peace, because they have hoped in you, Lord, forever.”

This entire song, which the saints will sing in the land of confession and praise, suddenly changes speakers and is woven together, as it were, through question and answer. The people of God had said: “The Savior is the city of our strength; a wall [Col. 0293C] and a bulwark will be placed in it.” The Lord replied—or rather, he commanded not those who had said this, but the Angels who stood guard over the gates of the Lord’s city—to open the gates, so that a righteous nation might enter through them, keeping faithfulness, or, as it is said in Hebrew, *EMMUNIM* [Al. *EMMONIM*] (), which is rendered in our language as “faith,” in the plural number, not the singular.

What are these gates, which are opened by the Angels so that not the Jewish people, who have been rejected, but the righteous nation may enter—a nation that received the name “faithful” from the faith of believers? Surely they are those of which the saint speaks: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering through them, I will confess to the Lord” (Ps. CXVII, 19). No one, however, will be able to enter these gates unless he has been freed from the gates of death; and the Psalmist says: “You who lift me up from the gates of death, so that I may proclaim all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. IX, 15). For when we have been snatched from the gates of death, then we shall be able to sing all the praises of the Lord in the gates of the daughter of Zion.

And just as I consider the gates of death to be sins, concerning which it is said to Peter, “The gates of hell shall not prevail against you” (Matt. XVI, 18), so I consider the gates of righteousness to be all works of virtue. Whoever enters through them will find one gate, concerning which it is said: “This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. CXVII, 19). And just as one reaches a single pearl through many pearls, so through many roads and gates we arrive at him who says that he is the way and the gate, through whom we enter to the Father.

After the word of God, the people replied in Hebrew, *JESER SAMUCH* (), which Aquila and Symmachus likewise translated as *πλάσμα ἐπηρεισμένον* (“an assailed/afflicted formation”)—

[Note: *Πλάσμα ἐπηρεισμένον.* The manuscripts retain nothing further; therefore Erasmus and Marianus supplied from their own conjecture *τὸ* and *ἡμῶν*, that is, *τὸ πλάσμα ἡμῶν ἐπηρεισμένον*, “our assailed/afflicted formation.” Many similar alterations and additions in Hebrew words will be found above at chapter XXIX if you compare this new edition of ours with the older ones. —MARTIAN.]

Epiphanius, cited by Montfaucon under Aquila, reads *ἐστηριγμένον*, that is, “supported” or “firmly established,” which Jerome himself indicates in the following exposition by the words “either a firmly established thought.” It seemed to the holy Doctor that there was scarcely any difference in meaning between Aquila and Symmachus, even if they differed somewhat in wording; accordingly, he says that they translated similarly.

This means, “Our error has been removed,” or “Our thought has been firmly established,” since previously it fluctuated between you and idols, so that we may no longer be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but may believe in you, the Lord and Savior, with our whole mind. For this reason, to make the meaning clearer, we translated it: “The ancient error has passed away.”

And because our thought has been established, therefore you will preserve peace for us, the peace that you promised to the Apostles when you said: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). And not only once, but twice, so that the recompense may be secure when it is promised in a twofold saying, in accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV, 4).

This is attained by the one of whom it is said in Leviticus: “A man, a man, of the children of Israel” (Lev. XVII). And in the Book of Numbers: “The man, the man whose wife has defiled the marriage-bed” (Num. V, 12), so that the twofold man and the twofold husband may receive a twofold peace.

“We deserve it,” they say, “because with our whole mind we trust in you.”

After the words of the people, the Lord’s response, and then again the voice of the people, the Prophet speaks to believers: “You have hoped,” or “Hope, in the Lord for everlasting ages,” and the rest that follows.

According to the Septuagint, the one who keeps righteousness in good works and preserves, or embraces, truth in the truth of faith enters the gates of the Lord, so that through good works and faith he may arrive at the peace that surpasses all understanding and may deserve to receive that peace, because he has believed in God, who is the eternal rewarder of good works (Phil. IV). Hence it is also written elsewhere: “You desired wisdom; keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to you” (Eccl. I, 33).

### (Verses 5–6)

“In the Lord God, the Strong One, forever, because he will bend down those who dwell on high; he will humble the lofty city, he will humble it to the earth; he will bring it down to the dust. The foot will trample it—the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy.”

The Septuagint: “O great eternal God, who have humbled and brought down those who dwell on high, you will destroy fortified cities and bring them down to the pavement, and the feet of the meek and humble will trample them.”

[Note: We have restored “and brought down” (*detraxisti*) on the authority of the Vatican manuscripts, supported by the Greek text of the Septuagint, *katēgages tous enoikountas en hypsēlois*: “you brought down those dwelling on high.” Previously “you destroyed” (*destruxisti*) stood here incorrectly.]

This is spoken by the Prophet, who responded from the place where he had earlier said, “Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages,” and he joins to it what we have now set forth: “In the Lord God, the Strong One, forever,” and what follows.

For “Lord God, the Strong One,” the Hebrew has three names: *IA* (), *ADONAI* (), and *SUR* (). One signifies the invisible, another the ineffable, and another the strong or mighty; the first of these occurs as the final syllable in *ALLELUIA* ().

Let the careful reader also observe that at times we divide the text in presenting a testimony, because the Septuagint edition produces one meaning, while the translation made literally from the Hebrew produces another. The Prophet therefore says: “Hope in the Lord for everlasting ages—in the Lord God, the Strong One, forever,” whose help is everlasting.

For he will bend down those who dwell on high, because everyone who exalts himself will be humbled—those who boasted that they had Abraham as their father and spoke insultingly against the Lord: “We were not born of fornication” (John VIII, 41).

He will humble the lofty city, which the Jews think is Rome [Al. “the Roman city”]. We, however, rightly understand it to be Jerusalem, which killed the Prophets and stoned those who had been sent to it, and finally killed the son of the householder, so that, once the heir had been slaughtered, the inheritance might perish (Luke XIII).

Nor is the word “city” used here in the Hebrew sense *IR* (), but *CARIA* (), which Aquila translated as *πολίχνη*, a term that we may render “little city,” “village,” or “small town.” Jerusalem is frequently called by this name in Scripture.

He beautifully presents a twofold humiliation: “He will humble it, he will humble it”—first under the Babylonians, when the Temple was destroyed; second under Titus and Vespasian, whose ruin remains until the end.

“The foot will trample it”; and he repeats and joins to this “the feet of the poor,” unquestionably those of Christ. Concerning him we also said above: “He became strength to the poor, strength to the needy in his tribulation.”

“The steps of the needy” are, of course, those of the Apostles, who, imitating the poverty of the Lord, also obtained the privilege of his virtue. When they were not received, they shook the dust from their feet against that city.

And because the Savior is said to have spoken these words—“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV, 11)—we may refer this not only to human beings but also to the opposing powers.

According to the Septuagint, the Prophet sings praises to God because he humbles all the proud, demolishes the fortifications of every city to the ground, and the feet of the saints, the meek, and the humble trample them.

[Col. 0295D]

### (Verses 7–9)

“The path of the righteous is straight; the way of the righteous is straight for walking. And on the path of your judgments, Lord, we have waited for you; your name and your memorial have been the desire of our soul. My soul desired you in the night.”

The Septuagint: “The way of the righteous is straight; the way of the righteous has been made straight and prepared. For the way of the Lord is judgment; we hoped in your name and in the memorial that our soul desires.”

The Prophet is still speaking about Christ, concerning whom he had said above: “The foot will trample it, the feet of the poor.” The path of this righteous one is straight—or, to coin a new word, “straightnesses,” which the Greeks call *εὐθύτητας* and which we may more Latinly call “equities.” In Hebrew they are called *MESSARIM* ().

In the one path of Christ, therefore, all righteousnesses are found; and for this reason he trod and wore it down with his own foot, so that whoever wishes to walk along it may walk with an unhindered course.

On this path of the Lord’s judgments, the saints waited for him and hoped in him, because hope does not disappoint. They held his name and his memorial as the desire of their soul, saying: “My soul desired to desire your judgments at all times” (Ps. CXVIII, 20); and again: “My soul desires and has languished for your salvation” (ibid., 81).

Whoever desires the Lord’s name desires nothing else. It must also be noted that the desire for the Lord is not in the flesh but in the soul, according to what we read in another psalm: “My soul thirsted for God, the strong and living one” (Ps. LI, 2). “For the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). These oppose one another, so that we do not do the things we wish.

The words that follow, “In the night,” are joined to the following chapter according to the Septuagint, but to the preceding one according to the Hebrew. He can say, “My soul desired you in the night,” who speaks confidently with the Psalmist: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with tears” (Ps. VI, 7).

Night and darkness may also be understood as tribulation and distress. Hence in another psalm the Prophet sings of the security of the righteous: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Ps. CXX, 6)—that is, you will never be moved from your course, either in prosperity or in adversity.

But also, “With my spirit within me, I will keep watch for you from early morning.”

The Septuagint: “By night my spirit rises early to you, O God, because your judgments are light upon the earth.”

We wish to follow the Hebrew as well as not entirely pass over the Vulgate edition, and the circumstances of the subject compel us to seek different interpretations in a different order and wording.

Accordingly, the phrase “by night” is, as we said, the beginning of this chapter according to the Septuagint, but the end of the preceding one according to the Hebrew. Yet according to the Septuagint it can also be taken at the end of the preceding testimony, so that the sense is: “My soul desires you at night”; and then begins: “In the morning my spirit rises early to you, O God.”

It rises early because your commandments are light upon the earth. For, keeping your commandments and illuminated by their light—concerning which it is said, “The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 9)—I cannot sleep. Desiring you at every moment, I rise to you in my spirit.

It must also be observed that, while we are still placed in the night, we should desire the Lord in our mind. But after our spirit within us has turned wholly toward God with its entire mind, let us keep watch for him in the morning. To put it more clearly: night and desire belong to the soul, while morning and watchfulness belong to the spirit.

Moreover, the one whose spirit within him keeps watch for God is the one who can say: “From the depths I cried to you, Lord” (Ps. CXXIX, 1).

### (Verse 10)

“When you execute your judgments upon the earth, the inhabitants of the world will learn righteousness. Let us have mercy on the wicked, and he will not learn righteousness. He has acted wickedly in the land of the saints, and he will not see the glory of the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth. For the wicked has ceased, and he will not learn righteousness upon the earth; he will not practice truth. Let the wicked be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord.”

Let us speak first according to the Hebrew, and then, if we wish to express the Prophet’s meaning, let us turn to the Septuagint translators.

As long as you do not execute your judgments upon the earth, and as long as you repay neither good to the good nor evil to the wicked, your righteousness, O Lord God, is unknown on earth. But when, on the day of judgment, you have repaid each person what he deserves according to the quality of his works, then your righteousness will be known throughout the world. Previously it seemed unjust to unbelievers, so that even one of the saints said: “But my feet almost slipped; my steps were nearly poured out, because I was jealous over the wicked, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 2).

To this the Lord replied: “Let us have mercy on the wicked,” which, except for the Septuagint, all the translators rendered similarly. The sense is: “Rather, let the wicked obtain mercy and learn my clemency, while he himself is also being saved.”

[Note: Earlier the text read, “for I myself am the Savior.” We have restored from the Vatican manuscript, “while he himself is also being saved,” a reading that Victorius had long before introduced into the text from five other Florentine manuscripts.]

Again, the Prophet responds to the Lord speaking from the standpoint of human impatience: “And he will not learn righteousness.” The sense is: “How will he be able to know your righteousness if he has experienced only your clemency?” He gives the reasons why he wants him to learn God’s righteousness: because he acted wickedly in the land of the saints and continually fought against your saints; he ought to feel torments.

Again the Lord moderates his sentence: “And he will not see,” or “will not behold,” the glory of the Lord. The meaning is: “It is punishment enough for him that he will not see me reigning with my saints in my majesty.”

Some wish to understand the wicked one—that is, *RESA* ()—as the devil. Concerning him it is written in the ninth psalm: “You rebuked the nations, and the wicked one perished; you blotted out their name forever and for all ages. The swords of the enemies have failed utterly, and you destroyed their cities” (Ps. IX, 6).

We, however, should understand “the wicked” generally, either as the sinner or as one who does not possess the worship of God.

According to the Septuagint, the inhabitants of the earth are commanded to learn righteousness. For every person seems righteous to himself, but God knows the hearts of all and will repay each according to his works (Prov. XXI). And elsewhere in the same book it is said: “There are ways that seem right to a man, but their ends look toward the depths of hell” (Prov. XIV, 12).

Therefore we must learn righteousness and not trust in our own judgment. For there is one who is righteous in his own righteousness (Eccles. VII)—not because he is actually righteous, but because he seems righteous to himself.

But if Christ has been made for us by God “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (I Cor. I), then those who are commanded to know righteousness are commanded to learn and know Christ.

He therefore says: “I command you to learn righteousness because the wicked has been removed, and his kingdom has been destroyed. As long as he reigned on earth, he could neither know righteousness nor practice truth.” Concerning truth it is written elsewhere that “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John XVII).

And because the wicked does not practice truth on earth, he will be taken away; for he does not deserve to see the Lord reigning.

[Col. 0298A]

### (Verse 11)

“Lord, let your hand be exalted, and let them not see; let them see, and let the zeal of the people be confounded, and let the fire devour your enemies.”

The Septuagint: “Lord, your arm is exalted, and they did not know; but when they know, they will be confounded. Zeal will seize the uneducated people, and now fire will consume the adversaries.”

What he had said above, “and he will not see the glory of the Lord,” may be understood in this way:

“You ask, O Prophet, that I not have mercy on the wicked, lest, if I have mercy on him, he begin not to know righteousness, since he acted wickedly in the land of the saints. I answer you: Will he then not see the glory of the Lord? Will he not behold my triumphs, when he ought rather to see me reigning, so that he may know how great a good he is deprived of?”

This should be read more closely as the words of one asking a question.

To this the Prophet replied: “Lord, let your hand be exalted and extended to strike, so that the wicked may not see you or the light of your glory—not even so as to repent.”

The Lord answered him: “Let them rather see and be confounded”—whether “the zeal of the people” or “those who are zealous for the people”—“and let fire devour your adversaries,” that is, the adversaries of the people of the saints, and consume them.

The fire is the fire of repentance, which torments their hearts because they lost such a Lord.

This may also be understood concerning the Jews, who did not know Christ, the arm of the Lord; and when they see and recognize the one whom they had fastened to the cross, they will be confounded.

Then the uneducated people, who do not know the law of God, will be stirred by the goads of jealousy when they see the nations succeed to their place, and will burn with the fire of remorse—or with the pain of punishment—when they hear what is written: “Go into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

### (Verse 12)

“Lord, you will give us peace, for you have accomplished all our works for us.”

The Septuagint: “Lord our God, give us peace, for you have repaid us all things.”

It must be noted that after he has repaid us our works, he will give peace, and that he explains the reasons why he asks for peace.

For, in return for all the works they performed on earth, they say that they endured torments and that it is just for them, after punishments and sufferings, to obtain mercy.

Or alternatively: Since the consummation of the world has come, and all that you spoke through the Prophets has been fulfilled in reality, and you have repaid everything that you promised, grant us the peace that surpasses all understanding.

[Col. 0298D]

### (Verse 13)

“Lord our God, masters besides you have possessed us; only in you may we remember your name.”

The Septuagint: “Lord our God, possess us; Lord, we know no other besides you; we invoke your name.”

For this reason we seek mercy and peace, which are to be granted after all things, because masters besides you have possessed us—namely, idols, or the demons who sit upon idols. We ask nothing else except that, after our many errors, we may be worthy to remember your name.

According to the Septuagint, which says, “Lord God, possess us,” they pray that, after peace has been restored to them, they may become God’s possession.

We read something similar concerning Wisdom, which speaks in Proverbs according to the Hebrew: “God possessed me at the beginning of his ways” (Prov. VIII, 22), although some copies incorrectly have “created” in place of “possessed.”

[Note: This reading has often been attacked elsewhere by certain Latin writers as contrary to the Hebrew. See the Commentary on Micah, chapter IV, and the Letter to the Ephesians, chapter XXII, especially Letter 140 in our recension, to Cyprian, section 6. In the same way Saint Basil, book II, and Gregory of Nyssa, book I, press the Hebrew truth against Eunomius. Accordingly, in the Vatican manuscript, as also in a certain Cluniac manuscript found by Martianay, this praise of Jerome is added here: “You have defeated the impiety of the Arians, who thought that they could overthrow the Catholic truth by this testimony.” Someone diligent may have written these words in the margin; an inexperienced scribe inserted them into the text.]

[Note: Finally, what follows. The passage is interpolated in certain manuscript codices. In the codex of our monastery of Sylva Major it reads: “Although certain copies incorrectly have ‘created’ in place of ‘possessed’: ‘The Lord created me’ in place of ‘possessed me.’ Finally, what follows,” etc. In the Cluniac codex I found the following addition: “Although certain copies—‘You have defeated the impiety of the Arians, who thought that they could overthrow the Catholic truth by this testimony’—incorrectly have ‘created’ in place of ‘possessed.’”]

The passage continues: “Before all the hills he begot me.” For how can the generation of a creature be made to fit here, when the term agrees better with possession? It is written in Deuteronomy: “Is he not your father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?” (Deut. XXXII, 6).

It must also be considered that it does not say, “The Lord,” or “God,” “possessed you, made you, and created you,” but “the Father,” so that the gentleness of the name might temper the severity of power.

The words that follow, “Lord, besides you we know no other,” do not exclude the Son but join him to the Father. For it does not say, “We know no other,” but, “Besides you we know no other.”

When the Son says, “I am in the Father and the Father is in me,” we do not know the Son apart from the Father, because we know him in the Father (John XIV, 10).

Finally, we also name his name when we say in the Lord’s Prayer: “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. VI, 9).

### (Verse 14)

“The dead shall not live; the giants shall not rise again. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and destroyed all memory of them.”

The Septuagint: “For the dead shall not see life, nor will physicians raise them. Therefore you have brought this upon them, destroyed them, and taken away every male of theirs” [Al. “all their masculinity”].

Symmachus, in his customary clearer manner: “The dead shall not give life; the giants shall not raise up. Therefore you have visited and crushed them, and destroyed all memory of them.”

Let us speak first according to the Septuagint. The question seems difficult: how will the dead not see life? It is solved in this way: they do not see life for as long as they are dead.

Just as we say that a blind man does not see light as long as he is blind, but, if he recovers his sight, he will look upon the light, so the one who is dead through iniquity and sins cannot live until he is made alive through righteousness and virtues by the one who says, “I am life” (John XIV).

Hence God is called the God of the living, not of the dead (Matt. XXII). “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII, 4).

We read in the Epistle written to the Hebrews: “Let us not again lay the foundation of repentance from dead works” (Heb. VI, 1). But if sins are called dead works, why should virtues not conversely be called living works?

The following words, “nor will physicians raise them,” have an obvious meaning: the fables of the poets are condemned, for they claim that Aesculapius raised Virbius.

[Note: Martianay had incorrectly read *urbium*. Virbius, however, is a well-known figure from Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*, book XV:

> “You who were Hippolytus,” he said,  
> “now be the same Virbius.”

See the holy Father’s Commentary on the Epistle to the Ephesians, chapter IV, section 16, and Rufinus, who sharply attacks that passage in *Invectives* I, section 42.]

This must be said not only of the dead but of every infirmity: without God’s mercy, the art of medicine has no power to heal. For how is it written? “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain; unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI, 1–2).

Thus, unless the Lord cures an illness, physicians labor in vain when they desire to heal the sick. Unless the Lord preserves health, those who even publish in their own books rules for preserving health guard it in vain.

We must always learn this, not only in bodily health but also in the health of the soul: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases” (Ps. CII, 1, 3).

Those who persist dead in sin and cannot recover the health of their soul through any art of medicine will be destroyed and taken away by the Lord, and whatever is strong in them—what is called “male”—will be completely removed.

Hence Pharaoh does not wish to kill the female sex, which is naturally weak and can easily perish by itself, but every male, which, if grown and brought to manhood, is difficult to kill (Exod. I).

According to Symmachus, “the dead shall not give life,” because those dead through sin cannot make others alive; nor is praise beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.

And “the giants,” that is, *RAPHAIM* (), will not raise up others, because they themselves are called “the fallen” according to the Book of Genesis.

The Lord visits them so that all memory of both the dead and the giants may be erased. For he alone raises the dead, concerning whom it is said: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so the Son also gives life to whomever he wishes” (John V, 21).

We may call the dead images of dead human beings, and the giants demons who sit upon their images.

Nor should we be troubled by the fact that the Septuagint translated the word as “male,” while the other interpreters translated it as “memory,” since among the Hebrews both are written with the same three letters, *ZAI* (), *CHAPH* (), and *RES* ().

[Note: The Vulgate manuscripts read *Zain* according to the more recent pronunciation. The manuscripts, however, both here and in Letter 30 to Paula, concerning the Alphabet, consistently prefer *Zai*, which is also approved by us and by Drusius on the basis of the ancient description of that letter.]

When we say “memorial,” it is read *ZACHAR* (); when “male,” *ZOCHOR* ().

They think that Saul was deceived by this ambiguity of the word when he fought against Amalek and killed all their males (I Sam. XV). For when God commanded him to destroy all memory of Amalek from under heaven, he interpreted the word as “males,” not so much through error as because he was led astray by desire for plunder, not knowing the Apostle’s saying: “Do not be deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal. VI, 7).

### (Verse 15)

“You have spared the nation, Lord; you have spared the nation. Have you been glorified? You have removed all the boundaries of the earth.”

The Septuagint: “Add evils to them, Lord; add evils to the glorious ones of the earth. You have removed all the boundaries of the earth.”

The “evils” that the Septuagint inserted twice are not present in the Hebrew. But because it had said above, “Therefore you have brought this upon them, destroyed them, and taken away all their males,” they followed the same meaning and added the word “evils” on their own, so that those who are glorious on earth might be oppressed by evils doubled.

According to the Hebrews, however, the meaning is quite different and agrees with the preceding discussion. The Lord had said: “Let us have mercy on the wicked.” The Prophet had replied: “Where is your righteousness, especially since he has done such great evils against your saints?”

To this the Lord answered: “He will not see the glory of the Lord.”

Again the Prophet said: “Let your hand be exalted to strike, and let them not see your glory, which they do not deserve to behold.”

To this the Lord replied: “Let them rather see and be confounded.”

Again the Prophet said: “Lord, give us peace and possess us, since we remember your name.”

But let the wicked and proud not live, nor rise again in glory; rather, crush all their memory. He gives the reasons why he desires their destruction:

“You have spared the nation, Lord; you have spared the nation. Have you been glorified?”

The meaning is: “You have often had mercy on the nations—that is, on the human race—and have exercised extraordinary clemency toward them. Have they known you? Have they glorified your name? Have they not, on the contrary, withdrawn far from you?”

For security gives birth to negligence, and negligence to contempt.

### (Verse 16)

“Lord, in distress they sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring, your teaching was given to them.”

The Septuagint: “Lord, in tribulation I remembered you; in little tribulation, your instruction was given to us.”

Because you were often despised when you showed mercy and were not glorified, but, on the contrary, all withdrew from knowledge of you, therefore, Lord, strike them, so that in distress they may seek you, and in the tribulation of murmuring your teaching may be given to them—when so great a burden of evils weighs upon them that they do not even dare to cry out confidently, but silently swallow their pain.

According to the Septuagint, the Prophet remembers the Lord in tribulation, in accordance with what is said in the psalm: “Out of tribulation I called upon the Lord, and he answered me in a broad place” (Ps. CXVII, 5). And elsewhere: “When I was in tribulation, I cried to the Lord, and he answered me” (Ps. CXIX, 1).

Hence the Apostle says: “We are troubled, but not distressed; we suffer persecution, but are not abandoned” (I Cor. IV, 12). And elsewhere: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. VIII, 18).

But if a small tribulation teaches, corrects, and reproves, how much more does a great one, when we are reminded of our condition and remember God’s power?

### (Verses 17–18)

“As a woman who has conceived, when she draws near to giving birth, cries out in pain amid her pangs, so we have become before your face, Lord. We have conceived and, as it were, been in labor; we have given birth to spirit.”

The Septuagint: “And as a woman in labor, when she draws near to giving birth, cries out in her pain, so we have become ÷ to your beloved ** because of your fear, Lord, we received in the womb, and we were in labor, and we gave birth to the spirit of your salvation, which we have wrought upon the earth.”

[Note: In place of “we received in the womb,” the Vatican manuscript has one word, “we conceived,” although the Greek resists this, since it expressly has *ἐν γαστρὶ ἐλάβομεν*, “we received in the womb.” Shortly afterward, however, the relative article is absent according to the Alexandrian exemplar. Victorius continues with “and we suffered” instead of “and we were in labor,” in accordance with the Greek manuscript’s *ὠδυνήσαμεν*.]

Just as a woman approaching childbirth is compelled by pain to cry out, so we seek you in distress; and, because of fear of your presence, we have conceived, been in labor, and given birth—not to children of flesh but of spirit. Thus we may believe in you with our whole mind, so that, although we did not perceive you through benefits, we may learn through torments.

The words added by the Septuagint, “so we have become in your beloved,” in place of which the other translators have “so we have become before your face, Lord,” should be marked with an obelus.

We may understand the Beloved of the Lord to be Christ. Because of his fear we conceive, are in labor, and give birth, and bring forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth.

This may also be said by an apostolic man when he instructs peoples and imitates the Apostle Paul: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV, 19).

Can there be any doubt that the Apostle Paul brought forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth, since he preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum (Rom. XV), and, like a wise architect, laid the foundation, other than which no one can lay, namely Jesus Christ (I Cor. III)?

Therefore, whether we read, “Because of your fear, Lord, we received in the womb,” or, according to the Hebrew, “Before your face, Lord, we conceived and received in the womb,” both expressions amount to this: through fear and remembrance of the Lord, we conceive the word of God, and our heart is illumined as we say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV, 7), and, “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 4).

“We have not performed acts of salvation upon the earth; therefore the inhabitants of the world did not fall.”

The Septuagint: “We shall not fall, but the inhabitants of the earth shall fall.”

A different translation necessarily has a different meaning.

According to the Hebrew, this is said: “Because we have done nothing worthy of your mercy, therefore the wicked have not fallen, but to this day they prevail and possess the earth.”

The Septuagint, however, asserts that, when the saints bring forth the spirit of salvation upon the earth, those who are inhabitants of the earth will fall. There is, indeed, much difference between the “world,” which in Hebrew is *THEBEL* () and in Greek *οἰκουμένη*, and the “earth.”

Therefore all who have given themselves over to dwelling upon the earth and have been rooted and founded in earthly works will fall. Those will not fall who sit in the inhabited world and rest in the Church, which is the dwelling place of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

(Vers. 19.) “May your dead live; may my slain rise again. Awake and praise, you who dwell in the dust, for your dew is the dew of lights, and you will cast the land of the giants down to ruin.” The Septuagint: “The dead will rise, and those in the tombs will rise, and those who are in the land will rejoice. For your dew is healing for them, but the land of the impious will fall.”

When the saints are in labor and give birth to the spirit, and when the inhabitants of the earth fall because they have not brought salvation forth in the earth, those whom the Apostle calls dead in Christ, and who were slain because of the Lord’s name, will rise in glory (I Thess. IV). And because their death is sleep, they are said according to the Septuagint not to rise, but to awake and arise. Hence Lazarus, who was to be awakened [Note: Vatican manuscript: “who was going to awake.”], is called by the Lord “sleeping” (John XI).

All the martyrs, therefore, and holy men who poured out their blood for Christ, and whose whole life was martyrdom, will rise and awake, and will praise God their Creator. They now dwell in the dust, concerning whom it is written in Daniel: “Many of those sleeping in the dust of the earth will rise, these to everlasting life, and those to everlasting disgrace and confusion” (Dan. XII, 1). And in John the Evangelist we read: “The hour is coming, and now is, when those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God; and those who hear will live. And those who have done good will come forth to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

For the Lord’s dew, which according to the tales of the poets surpasses all the Paeonian herbs [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds “and fruits.”], will give life to the bodies of the dead. And just as, when seeds are cast into the earth, dew gradually makes the plants grow and bring forth the crops proper to their kind, so the Lord’s dew—which is used as an image of mercy—will be the dew of many lights, called in Hebrew OROTH (). But the earth—that is, the bodies of the Rephaim, namely, of the giants and the impious—the Lord will cast down into everlasting punishments. Indeed, instead of REPHAIM (), only the Septuagint translated “the impious.”

And since above we read, “The dead will not see life, nor will physicians raise them up,” for which Aquila and Symmachus translated “Rephaim” and “giants,” we ask what has caused the error, so that for the Hebrew REPHAIM some have written “giants,” while others have written “physicians.” If the Hebrew word REPHAIM has, after the first letter RES, the following letter VAU, it is read ROPHAIM [or ROSIM] () and means “physicians.” But if it is written without the letter VAU, it is read RAPHAIM and is translated “giants.” At the same time, because he had said above, “The dead will not see life,” he now makes it clearer that the reference there is not to the dead according to nature, through the separation of soul and body, but to those who are dead through sin. Here, by contrast, he says to God: “Your dead will live,” those who were slain for your sake. They are not simply dead, as the Septuagint translated, but according to the Hebrew, where it says JEJU METHECA (), they are called “your dead.”

“Go, my people; enter your chambers and shut your doors upon yourselves. Hide yourselves for a little while, for a brief moment, until the indignation has passed. For behold, the Lord will go forth from his place to visit the iniquity of the inhabitant of the earth against him; and the earth will reveal its blood and will no longer cover its slain.”

The Septuagint: “Go, my people; enter your chambers and shut your door. Hide yourselves for a little while, for however brief a time, until the Lord’s wrath has passed. For behold, the Lord will bring wrath from the sanctuary upon the inhabitants of the earth, and the earth will reveal its blood and will no longer conceal the slain.”

Above he had said concerning the saints: “The dead will rise, and those who are in the tombs will rise; for the dew from you is their healing.” Conversely, concerning the impious: “The land of the impious will fall.” Now he speaks to the saints, because resurrection has been promised to you, until God’s wrath rages against sinners and the impious: “Enter your tombs and hide yourselves, for it is a brief time until God’s indignation passes.”

Indeed, the Lord goes forth from his place because, although he is merciful, compassionate, and a most gracious Father, he is compelled to strike negligent children. In a certain sense he changes his decision, so that he may visit and bring his wrath upon the inhabitants of the earth, concerning whom it is said in Hosea: “Cursing and lying, adultery and theft have been poured out upon the inhabitants of the earth” (Hos. IV, 2). And in the third chapter of the Apocalypse we read: “Woe upon the inhabitants of the earth” (Apoc. VIII, 13).

The righteous, although they appear to be on earth, nevertheless have their manner of life in heaven; they can say: “I am a sojourner upon earth and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). They enjoy the dwelling of the Most High, concerning whom the holy man says: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. XC, 1).

Then the earth will reveal its blood, concerning which God says to Cain: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hand” (Gen. IV, 10–11). This may also be understood of the martyrs, who poured out their blood for Christ and cry out beneath God’s altar: “How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?” (Apoc. VI, 10). Concerning them Moses also says in the Song: “The blood of his sons will be avenged and repaid, and he will return vengeance to his enemies” (Deut. XXXII, 43).

The earth that had received this blood will reveal it, and will by no means cover the Lord’s slain; rather, it will bring them forth publicly for the condemnation of those who killed the martyrs. Let this be understood of the simple resurrection.

According to the anagogical interpretation, however, the people of God are commanded to enter their chambers or storerooms [Note: “Ταμιεῖα, indeed,” etc. The old editions thrust upon us here the Hebrew word hhadarecha in place of the Greek ταμεῖα, which all manuscript codices retain; for they read TAMEIA and TAMIEIA according to the copies of the Septuagint interpreters. In the Roman manuscript we read ταμεῖα, but in the Alexandrian ταμιεῖα. Greek authors likewise read the noun in different ways: ταμεῖον for ταμιεῖον. See Herodian, book VII; Plutarch, On the Genius of Socrates. MARTIAN.], for ταμεῖα signifies both, so that he may shut the door of his chamber in accordance with the Gospel commandment (Matt. VI), and say with the Prophet: “Set, Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a fortified door upon my lips” (Ps. CXL, 3).

Let him hide himself for a little while, for however brief a time, until the Lord’s wrath passes, doing nothing for the sake of glory, but enjoying the good of conscience and awaiting God alone as judge.

There are also storerooms that must be shut and hidden from those who have become rich in works and words: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The left hand must not know what the right hand does, so that we may enjoy the riches of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel.

That all the days of our life are short and small is stated by Jacob, who lived beyond a hundred years: “Few and evil are the days of my life” (Gen. XLVII, 9). The wrath of the Lord that will pass is the wrath stored up by those who refuse to repent. After it has passed, the storerooms will no longer be shut, but what is written will be fulfilled: “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed, nor concealed that will not be made known” (Luke VIII, 17).

What follows—“Behold, the Lord will bring forth his wrath from the sanctuary”—signifies that God’s wrath begins with the saints, or that all his vengeance is just and holy. It does not arise from mental disturbance, as it commonly does in human beings, but from the purpose of correction.

By “the earth of the inhabitants” I think the Prophet means that of which it is written: “Let the earth hear the words of my mouth” (Deut. XXXII, 1), and: “Give ear, earth” (Isa. I, 2), and again: “Earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord” (Jer. XXII, 29). For just as those who dwell upon the earth cannot please God, so those who are in the flesh cannot please him (Rom. VIII). The earth in this passage signifies the soul that lives carnally.

“And it will reveal its blood,” if it has caused anyone to stumble, and with Cain deserves to hear: “The voice of your brother’s blood cries out to me from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood” (Gen. IV, 10–11). Every blood, therefore, will be required on the day of judgment; the earth will not conceal its blood, but will bring into the midst those whom it has killed, whether willingly or through negligence.

(Cap. XXVII.—Vers. 1.) “On that day the Lord will visit with his hard, great, and strong sword Leviathan the fleeing serpent, and Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will kill the sea-monster.”

The Septuagint: “On that day God will bring his holy, great, and strong sword against the fleeing dragon, the twisting serpent, and he will kill the dragon that is in the sea.”

The Hebrews transmit that the devil—namely, “the accuser,” which is a Greek name—is called in Hebrew SATAN (), that is, “adversary.” Hence in Zechariah it is said: “Satan, that is, the adversary, stood at his right hand to oppose him” (Zech. III, 1).

He is also called BELIAL (), that is, “apostate,” “transgressor,” and “without a yoke.” Hence the Apostle says: “What fellowship has Christ with Belial?” (II Cor. VI, 15). And wherever the Septuagint has “sons of pestilence,” the Hebrew reads “sons of Belial.” Hence also what is sung in the psalm concerning the mystery of the Savior—“The son of iniquity will not again lay harm upon him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 23)—is said in Hebrew as “the son of Belial.”

He is also called by other names, as it is written in another psalm: “You will tread upon the asp and the basilisk; you will trample upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. XC, 13). This dragon is properly called in Hebrew LEVIATHAN ().

He is the great sea-monster concerning whose capture by Christ the mystical account in Job speaks: “He who is going to capture the great sea-monster” (Job XL, 20). There too, in place of “sea-monster,” Leviathan is given. Again: “You will draw out the dragon with a hook; you will put a bridle around his nostrils.” Immediately afterward: “This is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, made for his angels to mock.”

And in the psalm: “This is the great and broad sea; there are creeping things without number, small animals with great ones. That dragon which you formed to be mocked by him” (Ps. CIII, 25–26).

John also writes of him in the Apocalypse: “There was a battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought against the dragon, and the dragon fought, together with his angels; and they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven” (Apoc. XII, 7ff.). And: “The great dragon was cast down, the ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, who leads the whole inhabited world astray. He was cast down to the earth, and his angels with him.” And there it is said: “The accuser of our brothers has been cast down, who accused them before our God” (ibid., v. 10).

It should be noted that in the psalm and in Job he is said to have been made a dragon—that is, Leviathan—in order that he might be mocked by the angels. Hence the Apostles receive power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy (Luke X).

Since, therefore, from the place where it is written, “Behold, the Lord will destroy the earth and lay it bare” (above, XXIV, 1), or according to the Septuagint, “Behold, the Lord will destroy the inhabited world and make it desolate,” down to the present chapter, judgment against the world at the consummation of the age has been proclaimed, and “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed” (I Cor. XV), the final sentence against the devil is accordingly that a holy, great, and strong sword—or, according to the Hebrew and the other interpreters, a hard sword—be brought against him.

For the word is not CADESA (), as the Septuagint supposed; had it been so, it would mean “holy.” Rather, it is CASA (), which is properly translated “hard.” Hence Kish, the father of Saul, is called “hard.”

Some of our writers understand the holy or hard sword, because of the sense that suffers under it, as the Word of God, concerning which the Apostle says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. IV, 12). Hence in another passage we read that a double-edged sword proceeds from the Savior’s mouth (Apoc. XIX).

When at the end of the world the holy, or hard, great, and strong sword has been brought against Leviathan, who at the beginning of Genesis is called the most cunning serpent of all the beasts that were upon the earth (Gen. III, 1), he will flee, although he has never been accustomed to flee, unaware of what is written: “Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 7).

A certain poet beautifully mocked Enceladus in the Gigantomachy:

“Where are you fleeing, Enceladus? Whatever shores you approach,

under Jupiter you will always be.”

[Note: More correctly, at least according to the rules of meter, the old printed editions have “Sub Jove.” The poet is Claudian, whose name Jerome suppresses; he again praises him without naming him in *Amor*, chapter 5 of that poem. The work is also said to have been written in Greek verse, while the final part is missing in Latin. See Macrobius, book I, chapter 20.]

This Leviathan, the fleeing serpent, is called in Hebrew [Note: I suppose Jerome wrote and read BARE, for the ancients customarily pronounced words ending in -e with E. But Latin copyists too readily change this letter to I in pronunciation; hence the surviving manuscripts, both those inspected by us and others, give BARI.] BARI (), which Aquila translated as “bar,” Symmachus as “closing,” and Theodotion as “strong.” I think he is called a bar or one who closes because he has shut up many in his prison and subjected them to his own power. Nothing upright is found in him, and therefore he is called “twisting”; nor can he imitate the Lord’s rod, concerning which it is written: “The rod of uprightness is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV).

The Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth (II Thess. II), him who was once an inhabitant of the sea—that is, of false and bitter waves.

Let those who say that the devil will repent and obtain pardon explain to us how they understand what is written: “And he will kill the dragon that is in the sea,” or “the sea-monster.” For in the second occurrence in the present chapter, the Hebrew does not call him Leviathan, but [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *Thenaim*, and shortly afterward *Thennim*.] THANNIN (), which properly means “sea-monster.”

Hence the Hebrews maintain that Leviathan dwells beneath the earth and in the air, but the Thanniim in the sea. This is a Jewish fable.

As for what is said at the end of this chapter, “on that day,” Eusebius joins it to the preceding chapter, lest the following prophecy be applied to the present time. The Hebrews and the other commentators, however, join it to what follows, which we are now about to set forth.

(Vers. 2, 3.) “On that day the vineyard of pure wine will sing to him. I am the Lord who guard it; suddenly I will give it drink, lest it be visited against it; night and day I guard it.”

The Septuagint: “On that day there will be a beautiful vineyard; its desire is that he should be its ruler. I am a fortified city, a city under siege; in vain will I give it drink. For it will be captured by night, and by day the wall will fall.”

The Hebrew differs greatly in this passage from the Septuagint edition. Therefore let us discuss each point as we have set it forth.

The vineyard of which Isaiah speaks above—“A vineyard was made for the beloved one on a horn, in a fertile place”—must be understood according to the prophet’s own teaching. Let us learn [or, according to another reading, “let us say”]: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. V, 1), concerning which it is sung in the psalm: “You brought a vine out of Egypt,” and so forth (Ps. LXXIX, 9).

To this vineyard Jeremiah also gives a cup of the purest wine (Jer. XXV). For when he had sent him to give drink to all the nations, and the Prophet had willingly offered himself for this service, he is first commanded to intoxicate Jerusalem. Hence he says: “You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived” (Jer. XX, 7).

Jerusalem will therefore drink, and pure wine will be poured out for her, so that she may learn mourning and weeping. The Lord says that he guarded her for a long time, gave her an opportunity for repentance, and, because she was unwilling to turn, that she would suddenly be made drunk. He says that he did this by day and by night, so that she might always be preserved by his help.

The Septuagint, however, calls her the same beautiful vineyard, in which there were the Law and the Prophets, the priesthood and the high priesthood, and knowledge of God, as Scripture says: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. LXXV, 1).

Some think that, according to their edition, this refers to the Church, than which nothing is more beautiful. Concerning it it was said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 3). It is the ruler of its mother and says in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song I, 5).

And it says: “I am a firm city, a city under siege.” Beautifully he says “under siege,” not “conquered.” Immediately he joins what concerns the Synagogue, which has been turned from head into tail: “In vain do I give her the drink of my teachings; she will be captured in the darkness of her error.” And because she did not receive the open light, her wall—that is, everything in which she thought she had help—fell by day. None of the opposing powers will fail to capture her; this must be understood of the hostile powers.

(Vers. 4, 5.) “There is no indignation in me. Who will set me as a thorn and a brier in battle? I will advance against it; I will burn it up altogether. Or rather, will I hold fast to my strength? Let it make peace with me; let it make peace with me.”

The Septuagint: “There is none who has not seized her. Who will set me as a guardian of stubble in a field? Because of this adversary I rejected her. Therefore the Lord did all that he had determined: I have been burned. Her inhabitants will say, ‘Let us make peace with him; let us make peace with him.’”

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: “I, who have always guarded my vineyard day and night, so that the boar from the forest would not destroy it and the beasts would not devour it—do I not have indignation? Do I not know how to strike the sinner and repay each according to what he deserves?”

Where Aquila placed “thorn” and “brier,” the Hebrew has SAMIR () and SAITH (), signifying “adamant” and “places full of thorns.” Hence he says: “Who will teach me to be hard, to overcome my clemency, and to advance savagely in battle and combat? Shall I advance against the vineyard that I previously guarded, and burn the one that I had enclosed with my wall? Or will my strength rather accomplish this: that I delay my anger and save by the mercy of the Gospel those who were not saved by the authority of the Law?”

*Emphatically*, according to the Hebrew, it should be read: “Who will make me hard and cruel, so that I may overcome my nature?” This is signified in the desert and among thorns: that I may crush and burn it as though in battle, the vineyard that I have always guarded with such care.

“Or rather, will I hold fast to my strength”—which is unquestionably Christ, concerning whom we read: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (I Cor. I, 24)—“so that it may itself make peace for me and reconcile the world?”

According to the Septuagint, the sense is this, if we take the words as spoken by the Church: “I am a firm city, a city surrounded by many enemies, which in vain gave the hostile drink to my enemy, the Synagogue. For she will be captured by night, and her wall will fall; none of the opposing powers will fail to seize her.”

Again I will speak: “What advantage is it for me to guard her, since she contains stubble rather than grain, and is so [Note: The adverb *ita* (“so”), which was lacking, we have supplied with the aid of the manuscripts.] uncultivated that she is full of briers and thorns, although I wished to save her? But because she acts hostilely toward me, I withdrew from her.”

The Apostles who were born in me and from me said: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you first; but since you rejected it and judged yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46).

Therefore the Lord will do what he threatened, so that all in her may burn, surrounded by Roman fire. Or certainly, let them burn with vices and sins, so that they may be unable to extinguish the burning arrows of the devil. “For all the adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” [cf. Hos. VII, 4].

And those who previously dwelt in her, after crying out that the city has been captured and burned, will leave her and, reconciling the world [or, according to another reading, “the unclean”] to God, will say: “Let us make peace with him; let us make peace with him”—that is, with Christ—always writing in their Epistles: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord” (I Cor. I, 3).

Concerning them we read in this same Prophet: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace” (Isa. LII, 7)!

Some refer this passage to the Churches: they are indeed guarded by God, but many of them produce no fruit. Therefore they are burned by the ardor of the good teacher, so that they may cry out and confess their error, and afterward make peace with God, who are truly called the sons of Jacob.

(Vers. 6.) “Those who go forth from the root of Jacob will blossom, and Israel will bud; and they will fill the face of the world with seed.”

The Septuagint: “Those who come, the sons of Jacob: Israel will bud and blossom, and his fruit will fill the inhabited world.”

After the Apostles, preaching the Gospel throughout the whole world, have said, “We will make peace with Christ; we will make peace with him,” those who have come from the seed of Jacob and attained apostolic dignity will be called the sons of Jacob.

Then Israel will bud and blossom, seeing that the whole world has been filled with the teaching of its sons and has brought forth the richest fruits, which Israel had not brought forth while remaining in Judea.

(Vers. 7.) “Has he struck him according to the stroke of the one who struck him? Or has he been slain as those whom he slew were slain?”

This passage is understood in two ways.

It may be directed against Jerusalem, saying that she was not struck by God in the same manner in which she herself struck Christ and his Apostles. Or it may be directed against the multitude of the nations: although they persecuted and shed Christian blood, the Apostles and apostolic men nevertheless cared for their salvation and reconciled them to God.

(Vers. 8.) “In measure against measure, when she has been cast away, you will judge her.”

The Septuagint: “Quarreling and reproaching, he will send them away.”

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: As Jerusalem has done, so she will receive; and according to the measure with which she measured, it will be measured back to her. She will then receive a full measure, when the time of judgment arrives and God casts her away.

According to the Septuagint, the statement depends upon what precedes. Israel will not be struck as it struck, nor will it be killed as it killed. It quarreled against the Apostles, reproached its teachers, and ordered them not to speak in the name of Christ. Therefore the Lord will reject them and drive them from his flock.

“He meditated in his harsh spirit throughout the day of heat.”

The Septuagint: “Were you not the one who meditated, with a harsh spirit, to kill them—with a spirit of fury?”

According to the Hebrew, this means that Jerusalem will receive according to the measure with which she measured. Therefore God, in his harsh and vehement spirit, meditated—or spoke—against her on the day of heat, that is, in the time of persecution, when the day of indignation and punishment is more fiercely burning.

According to the Septuagint, the words are addressed to Jerusalem herself, or to Israel: “Were you not the one who, in your most harsh and cruel spirit, and in the fury of your blasphemies, desired to kill the Lord’s Apostles and teachers?”

(Vers. 9.) “Therefore, for these things the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven, and this will be all its fruit: that its sin may be taken away; for he has made all the stones of the altar like stones of crushed ashes. They will not stand—the sacred groves and shrines.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore the iniquity of Jacob will be taken away, and this will be his blessing when I take away his sin, when he has made all the stones of the altars broken like finely pulverized ash; and their trees and idols will not endure.”

He gives the reasons why, after the Jews have laid hands upon the Lord, they may obtain forgiveness if they are willing to repent, so that the Savior’s prayer may be fulfilled: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34).

“Therefore,” he says, “the iniquity of the house of Jacob will be forgiven, and its sin will be taken away,” so that it may deserve God’s blessing, although it had invoked a curse upon itself, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

For through the Apostles, who came from the stock of Israel, the Gospel will be sown throughout the whole world; idolatry will be destroyed; the altars will be shattered to dust; the sacred groves will be cut down; the shrines will fall; and the knowledge of the one God, under the mystery of the Trinity, will be proclaimed.

(Vers. 10.) “For the fortified city will be desolate; the beautiful one will be abandoned and left like a wilderness. There the calf will graze; there it will lie down and consume its branches.”

The Septuagint: “Their idols will be cut down like a grove, and the flock dwelling far away will be left like a forsaken flock. For a long time it will be in pasture; there the flocks will rest, and after a long time there will be no green thing in it, because it has dried up.”

Jerusalem, once a strong and fortified city, because it did not receive the householder’s son but said, “Come, let us kill him, for he is the heir, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matt. XXI, 38), will be desolate.

She who was once beautiful—concerning whom Ezekiel also says, “You ate fine flour, honey, and oil, and became exceedingly beautiful” (Ezek. XVI, 13), and in whom dwelt the one of whom it is written, “Beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3)—will be abandoned and left like a wilderness. The Lord says to the Apostles: “Rise; let us go from here” (John XIV, 31).

There the calf will graze: the Roman army, concerning which it is said elsewhere under the name of a boar: “The boar from the forest will devastate it, and the solitary wild beast will consume it” (Ps. LXXIX, 14). There it will lie down and consume its branches, under the metaphor of a vineyard and its shoots, so that nothing green and no branch will remain in it; the enemy will consume everything.

According to the Septuagint, because they did not receive the good shepherd, they will therefore be like a forsaken flock and will be exposed to the bites of beasts. Nothing green will remain in them, because dryness will possess everything.

(Vers. 11.) “When its harvest is dry, the women who come and teach it will be crushed. For it is not a wise people; therefore the one who made it will not have mercy on it, and the one who formed it will not spare it.”

The Septuagint: “Women coming from the spectacle, come! For it is not a people possessing understanding. Therefore he who made them will not have mercy on them, and he who formed them will not spare them.”

The words, “When its harvest is dry, they will be crushed,” for which the Septuagint translated, “There will be nothing green in it, because it has dried up,” are joined according to the Hebrew to what follows, but according to the Septuagint to what precedes.

Let us first speak according to the Hebrew.

When the time of Jerusalem’s dryness and harvest—and, to speak more plainly, the time of its devastation—has arrived, a crowd from the synagogues will gather from the whole world to mourn Jerusalem and offer consolation for its evils.

Or he speaks openly of women who, with their breasts uncovered, beat their bloodstained arms, and the Lord’s prophecy will be fulfilled: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children” (Luke XXIII, 28).

Great is the people’s misfortune, to learn songs of lamentation from women. Such was Israel’s reproach when, in the Book of Judges (Judg. IV), the Lord brought salvation through the hand of the woman Deborah; and at the time of the impending captivity, while the men were silent, the woman Huldah prophesied (II Kings XXII).

Therefore the women will be crushed on the long journey, exhausted by weakness, hunger, and squalor, and they will teach the pitiable people, because it is not a wise people and did not understand its Creator. Since he was neglected and despised by them, he will not have mercy on the work of his hands and will not spare his creature.

According to the Septuagint, the passage concerns Mary Magdalene, the other Mary, and the remaining women who were the first to see the risen Lord, held his feet, and deserved to hear from him: “Do not be afraid. Go and announce to my brothers that they should go to Galilee, and there they will see me” (Matt. XXVIII, 10).

The prophetic word foretells these women long before they were born, and calls them from the spectacle of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection, so that they may preach the Gospel and, according to the Hebrew, teach Jerusalem—or the land of Israel—that this is the Lord and God.

At that time the people of Israel had no wisdom, when the Lord suffered and the prophetic prediction was fulfilled: “Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed” (Ps. XI, 1), and: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII, 4). The women are called from the spectacle so that they may announce to the Apostles what they themselves saw.

But Israel, of which it was said above, “Israel did not know me, and my people did not understand” (Isa. I, 3), provoked its most merciful Creator and Maker to bitterness, so that he would by no means have mercy on it.

These things are piously said; but how they agree with the rest and can be applied to the times of the world’s consummation is difficult to interpret.

(Vers. 12.) “And it will come to pass on that day that the Lord will strike from the channel of the river to the torrent of Egypt.”

The Septuagint: “And it will come to pass on that day that the Lord will enclose from the trench of the river to Rhinocorura.”

If he had not added “on that day,” by which we are taught that what he is about to say must be joined to what precedes, we could have explained it as the proper sense of this chapter. But now everything must be referred to the preceding passage.

Because the fortified city will be desolate, and the once beautiful city will be left like a wilderness; because the calf will lie there and consume the shoots of the vineyard; because everything will dry up, since there is no people possessing understanding, and because through its folly it has obtained no mercy from its Creator—therefore the Lord will strike, or enclose, from the channel or stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt.

This means that throughout the whole of Judea, which was once the land of promise, no word of teaching and no knowledge of the Scriptures will be found. Concerning these the Apostle also speaks: “That we should not attend to Jewish myths and commandments of men who turn away from the truth” (Tit. I, 14). And again: “For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers, and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision, whom it is necessary to rebuke” (ibid., 10).

Historically, by the channel or stream of the river we may understand the Euphrates, as it is written in the seventy-first psalm: “He will rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends [or, according to another reading, ‘the end’] of the earth” (Ps. LXXI, 8). Others think it means the Jordan.

It should also be noted that within the boundaries of Judea a river is called a river, while within the boundaries of Egypt the torrent has muddy waters and is not permanent.

In place of “the torrent of Egypt,” the Septuagint translated “Rhinocorura,” which is a town on the border of Egypt and Palestine. They express not so much the words of Scripture as the sense of the words.

What we translated as “he will strike,” for which the Septuagint has συμφράξει, that is, “he will enclose,” Aquila and Theodotion translated with ῥαβδήσει. This may be understood either as “he will strike with a rod” or as “he will count with a rod the number of his flock,” so that it may be taken not in a bad but in a good sense.

[Note: The same appears in Amos, chapter VI, and derives from the suggestion of the Septuagint, who translate “to the torrent of Egypt” as ἕως Ῥινοκορούρων, “to the river near Rhinocorura.” Learned men, however, do not contend without reason that by “the torrent of Egypt” no small stream between Rhinocorura and Pelusium is meant, but the Nile itself, which truly existed as the boundary of the Holy Land established by God, although the Israelites, through their own fault, never extended as far as it. On this point they cite the words of Joshua XIII, 2–3, where Sihor is also said to be the Nile itself, and Jeremiah II, 18. They also cite Diodorus Siculus, who seems altogether to deny that any small river existed near Rhinocorura.]

“And you will be gathered, one by one, sons of Israel.”

The Septuagint: “But you, gather one by one the sons of Israel.”
