“O sons of Israel,” for which Symmachus translated “house of Israel”: after your adversaries have been struck from the stream of the river to the torrent of Egypt—that is, from the Euphrates to the Nile—you yourselves will be gathered, one by one, to the faith of the Lord.

For the multitude of the Jews did not believe; by this he signifies that only a few of the Jews would believe in the Lord Savior.

Or certainly, O Apostles and apostolic men, while the multitude of the Jews does not believe, gather from the whole world as many as you can, like diseased sheep, and bring them back to the Lord’s sheepfolds. Gather them together with the people of the Gentiles, so that what the Apostle Paul and Barnabas said to the Jews may be fulfilled: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be announced to you; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46).

(Vers. 13.) And it shall come to pass on that day: a great trumpet shall be sounded; and those who had been lost from the land of the Assyrians shall come, and those who had been driven out into the land of Egypt; and they shall worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

[Note: Victorius restores “from the land” here.]

LXX: And it shall come to pass on that day: they shall sound a great trumpet; and those who had perished in the region of the Assyrians shall come, and those who had perished in Egypt; and they shall worship the Lord on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.

In this passage the Jews make vain promises to themselves: that at the consummation of the world, when Antichrist, as he is called, their ἠλειμμένος (the “anointed one,” that is, the Messiah or Christ) has come, the people scattered from Assyria and from the land of Egypt will be gathered together, come to Jerusalem, build the temple, and worship their Lord God.

[Note: The words “Antichrist, as he is called” are absent in some books. Ἠλειμμένος signifies the Messiah, or the anointed one, or Christ. — Ἠλειμμένος. The manuscript codices read *helimenus* and *helimmenus*; from this it is plainly shown that the reading should be ἠλειμμένος, which is the same as the Hebrew [Messiah], that is, “anointed.” Hence Nazianzenus, cited by Marianus, says that the Jewish people should not be rejected if, in place of “Christ,” it seeks the word ἠλειμμένος. MARTIAN.]

This cannot stand at all according to the literal sense. For they will be called not merely from Assyria and Egypt, but from the whole world—those who will believe in Christ. Therefore this signifies that at the last trumpet, according to the Apostle Paul (I Cor. XV), all who had perished in Assyria and Egypt will come to the Lord. He did not say “all the children of Israel,” but “all who had perished,” by which he signifies the multitude of the nations: those who had been bound by idolatry, magical practices, and philosophical arts will come to faith in Christ and worship him in the Church.

The great trumpet may be understood as the evangelical proclamation, concerning which we also read in this same prophet: “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (below, XL, 9). Therefore that holy mountain and that Jerusalem are the ones of which we have often spoken: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and thousands of angels; and the church of the firstborn, who are written in heaven” (Hebr. XII, 22).

Up to this point the discussion has concerned the consummation of the world, beginning at the place where we began to expound: “Behold, the Lord will lay the earth waste and strip it bare” (above, XXIV, 1), which is contained in the present volume. Now, with Christ helping us—indeed, inspiring us—let us pass to the ninth book, which will have the beginning of another prophecy.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 0313]

[Col. 0313D] 369–370. Occupied with various labors, we dictate our explanations of the prophet Isaiah at intervals. Therefore, having completed the eighth volume, after some passage of time we now proceed to the ninth—not without the bites and slanders of the envious, who, ignorant of what they hear and what they say, dare to judge what they do not know, and despise before they examine; they consider themselves learned and eloquent if they disparage every Writer.

Disregarding their malice and chattering mutterings, let us ask God’s help and say, with the Psalmist’s imprecation: “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII, 32). For the Lord’s place is in peace, which surpasses all understanding. The Prophet also longs for this, crying out: “Lord our God, give us peace; for you have rendered all things to us” (Isa. XXVI, 12).

But now let us set forth Isaiah’s chapter, and with Moses let us enter the cloud and darkness, so that our face may be made radiant and, according to the Hebrew, horned; and let thunderclaps and flashes of lightning be heard and shine forth, which the baser multitude could not see (Exod. XIX).

371 (Chapter XXVIII.—Verse 1.) Woe to the crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim, and to the fading flower of his glorious rejoicing, of those who were on the summit of the very fertile valley, wandering from wine. Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong, like a rush of hail, a destructive storm; like a rush of mighty waters overflowing and released upon a broad land. The crown of pride of the drunkards of Ephraim shall be trampled underfoot. And the fading flower of his glorious rejoicing, which is upon the summit of the fertile valley, shall be like an early fruit before the ripeness of autumn: when the one who sees it has looked upon it, as soon as he takes it in his hand, he will devour it.

LXX: Woe to the crown of insult of the hireling of Ephraim; the falling flower of glory upon the summit of the fat mountain, you who are drunk without wine. Behold, the strong and harsh wrath of the Lord, like hail driven downward, without shelter, which falls violently like a multitude of waters dragging the soil and making room for itself; with hands and feet the crown of insult of the hireling of Ephraim shall be trampled. And the flower that has fallen from the hope of glory on the summit of the high mountain shall be like an early fig, which whoever sees will desire to devour before taking it in his hand.

Let us speak first according to history, then according to tropology, and finally according to prophetic prediction.

The divine word speaks against the ten tribes that reigned in Samaria. Because of Jeroboam, who was from the tribe of Ephraim, they were called Ephraim. He calls them “the crown of pride,” because, compared with the two tribes called Judah, they were superior both in number and in strength.

He calls Ephraim drunkards because they do not understand their Creator but worship golden calves in Dan and Bethel in place of the Lord. These people were once the Lord’s flower and glory, when they were ruled by David and Solomon and were among the twelve tribes worshiping God in the temple of Jerusalem. They were on the summit of the very fertile valley, which in Hebrew is called *GE SEMANIM* [Gethsemane].

[Col. 0315C] It signifies the place where the Lord was betrayed; upon the summit of this valley the Lord’s temple is situated.

These people became drunk with the wine of error and madness that Jeroboam mixed for them. Therefore the Lord threatens them with punishment: just as a storm of hail shatters everything, and the rush of overflowing waters carries away whatever it encounters, so they will be destroyed by the Assyrian army, and whatever remains will be transferred into the mountains or cities of Media.

He compares the glory of the ten tribes to a crown of various flowers, possessing such beauty that, just as someone who sees an early fig (*πρόδρομος*, “premature”) on a tree before summer and autumn arrives devours it as soon as he takes it in his hand, so the Assyrian, when he sees the ten tribes, will lay waste to and devour them, leaving absolutely nothing of the former people in Samaria.

Let this suffice briefly according to history. Let us pass to the allegory.

Following the exposition of the prophet Hosea, in which we referred Ephraim, Joseph, Samaria, and the ten tribes—those cut off from the body of the twelve tribes and who abandoned the Lord’s temple—to the heretics, they are truly, according to the Septuagint edition, “a crown of insult,” blaspheming the Lord and doing everything for the sake of payment. They have fallen from the Lord’s glory and do not follow the thinness of manna or ecclesiastical humility; rather, they live drunk without wine on the very fertile mountain.

Therefore the Lord’s strong and harsh wrath will punish them with precipitous hail, which does not fall upon roofs but rushes upon the heads of mortals, and is compared to floods of many waters, dragging along whatever they encounter.

These are called the crown of insult, the hirelings of Ephraim: according to the Apostle, they have fallen from the flower, hope, and glory of their former faith for the sake of shameful gain, live in pride, and are the devil’s sweetest food; he devours them daily (I Pet. V).

According to prophecy we can say that the “crown of insult” calls the scribes and Pharisees, who blasphemed the Lord.

[Note: Eusebius wrote in the same sense: “He indicates the council of the Pharisees and chief priests, and the remaining rulers of the Jewish people.” He adds: “Judas the traitor was said to have come from the tribe of Ephraim, and he calls him a hireling as one who had been purchased with money to betray the Teacher” (sic). Jerome transfers this together with what follows concerning Gethsemane.]

They were called hirelings of Ephraim because of Judas, who was from the tribe of Ephraim and from a village of that same tribe, Iscarioth.

[Note: Vaticanus: “of that same tribe, Carioth.”]

He sold the Lord for a price. Truly he was the flower of apostolic glory that fell upon the very fertile mountain, concerning which we think it was said: “Jacob ate and drank, and was filled and grew fat, and the beloved kicked” (Deut. XXXII, 15).

Or, according to the Hebrew: “upon the valley of the fertile ones,” that is, Gethsemane, whose name also indicates the place in which Judas betrayed the Lord. It is called the fertile valley, or the valley of the fertile ones, because of its abundance, and because the scribes and Pharisees apprehended the Lord there. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm: “Fat bulls surrounded me” (Ps. XXI, 13).

This valley of the fertile ones, that is, Gethsemane, is called “the fat mountain” in this chapter’s second rendering. I wonder how the LXX first called it the “fat mountain” and afterward the “high mountain.”

The betrayer was drunk not with wine but with greed, with the incurable fury of asps, and with the devil’s food, which entered him after the morsel (John XIII). He was wholly devoured, because his prayer was turned into sin, and even his repentance produced no fruit of salvation.

The Hebrew word *SACCHORE* is ambiguous and may mean either “drunkards” or “hirelings.”

[Note: They differ both in the letters *vau* and *iod*—“drunkards” from “hirelings”—and in the pronunciation of the words themselves. Vaticanus has *Secchore*.]

Thus *Issachar* is interpreted as “there is a wage,” and *SACHAR* as μέθυσμα, that is, “drunkenness”; while the others translated “drunkards,” only the LXX translated “hirelings.”

(Vers. 5 ff.) On that day the Lord of hosts shall be a crown of glory and a wreath of rejoicing for the remnant of his people, and a spirit of judgment for him who sits in judgment, and strength for those returning from battle to the gate. But these too, because of wine, did not know; because of drunkenness they wandered. Priest and prophet did not know; because of drunkenness they were swallowed up by wine; they wandered in drunkenness; they did not know the seer, they ignored judgment, or, wondrously. For all the tables are full of vomit and filth, so that there is no longer any place.

LXX: On that day the Lord Sabaoth shall be a crown of hope, woven together as glory for the remnants of the people. They shall be left in a spirit of judgment over judgment, and strength forbidding the killing. For these were deceived by wine; they wander because of strong drink. Priest and prophet have lost their minds because of strong drink; they have been swallowed up because of wine; they stagger—that is, *φάσμα* [Al. *phasma*]; a curse will consume this counsel, since this counsel is on account of greed.

After the entire land of Samaria, that is, the ten tribes, has been destroyed by the overflowing Assyrian, and the crown of the pride of Ephraim’s drunkards has been trampled underfoot and devoured like an early fig, then the Lord himself will be the crown of victory for the remnant of the people of Israel—that is, for the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin.

He will be the spirit of judgment for the one sitting in judgment, unquestionably King Hezekiah, and their strength, when, after the whole region had been devastated, they returned from battle and shut themselves in the city. We shall read this in the same prophet below (XXXVII), when 185,000 armed men of the Assyrian army were destroyed by the Angel’s striking.

But these too—that is, Judah and Benjamin—were drunk with the wine of idolatry. They had despised the religion of the temple, worshiped images of demons, and did not know the Lord who sees, who observes all things.

For all their tables and their entire religious practice were filled with vomit and filth, so that they filled not only the temple but also the mountain peaks and wooded places with the filth of idolatry, and the Lord had no place of habitation among them.

Let this be said according to the literal sense.

According to tropology, however, let us follow the earlier understanding and not leave the LXX interpreters untouched. For when the heretics have been devoured by the devil’s mouth—those who climbed the very fertile mountain of pride—the Lord will be a crown of glory for those who dwell in the Church and, compared with the multitude of those who wander, are few in number.

He will be a spirit of judgment over judgment, because the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment. But if anyone has blood upon him, he will not be cleansed by the spirit of judgment but by the fire of burning; and he will be strength to the people and prevent them [Al. “him”] from being killed by those who are drunk with the wine of dragons and have wandered because of strong drink.

We have often said that “wine” is what is made from vines. “Strong drink,” however, means every beverage capable of causing drunkenness and overturning the state of the mind.

[Note: Saint Ambrose likewise testifies that this is the Hebrew usage, *On Elijah and Fasting*, chapter 15: “They call every drink that intoxicates by the name of strong drink.” It is perhaps from [a Hebrew root] signifying an intoxicating drink. Saint Basil likewise says, *On Isaiah*, chapter 5: “For it is customary among the Hebrews to call *sikera* every drink capable of producing drunkenness.”]

Aquila specifically translated it as “drunkenness,” whether the beverage is made from wheat, barley, millet, the juice of fruit, the fruit of palms, or any other kind.

Therefore the priests and prophets of the heretics lost their minds because of strong drink and were swallowed up because of wine, such as Prisca and Maximilla and their leader Montanus. They did not know what they were saying.

They become drunk with wine when they misunderstand and distort the holy Scriptures. They become drunk with strong drink when they abuse secular wisdom and the snares of dialecticians, which should be called not so much bonds as *phasmata* [Al. *phantasmata*], that is, certain shadows and images that quickly perish and dissolve.

A curse will possess this kind of counsel: that of those who think gain is godliness and do everything for the sake of greed. The Apostle spoke of this *phasma*: “Paying attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy” (I Tim. IV, 1–2).

There is a third explanation: after the Lord has overthrown the scribes and Pharisees and their associate Judas the traitor, who had been a thief from the beginning—for he himself carried the money box of the poor (John XII and XIII)—then he will be a crown of hope and glory for those among the Jews who believe in the Lord.

There is no doubt that this signifies the apostles, whom he preserved for the preaching of the Gospel and did not immediately permit to shed their blood for Christ.

For all the scribes and Pharisees were drunk with wine and strong drink, as we said above, both priests and false prophets. But their snares and plots were in vain, because Judas himself betrayed him for money, and the priests bribed the betrayer with money because they feared the loss of their own position.

He himself made a whip of cords and drove from the temple those who sold oxen and sheep; by his own authority he overturned the seats of those selling doves and the tables of the money-changers, saying: “It is written: ‘My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you have made it a house of commerce, or a den of thieves” (Matt. I, 13).

According to the anagogical sense, the Hebrew passage in which we said, “For all their tables are full of vomit and filth, so that there is no longer any place,” may be referred to heretics, and to scribes and Pharisees, in such a way that we say their entire doctrine and all their mysteries are full of vomit and filth: they do not digest the food of the holy Scriptures or make it life-giving to the whole body, but expel it undigested and foul-smelling, so that God finds no place in them.

I wonder what Theodotion intended when, in place of the Hebrew word *CISOA*, for which Aquila translated “vomit of filth” and Symmachus simply “vomit,” he said ἑμετὸν δυσαλίας, that is, “vomit of dysalia.” I have not been able to discover this word in the Greek texts available to me, unless perhaps he invented a new name for a new thing.

[Note: Theodotion translated δεισαλία as εἰς δεισαλίαν; this is how it should be read. As for the meaning of the word, Hesychius explains: Δίσαλα, ἀκαθαρσία, “dirt, impurity.” Martinus correctly advises that it should be read *Disalia*. It comes from *deisa*, which in Suidas means ἡ κόπρος, “dung”; and *deisalia* likewise means “dung-like things.” But in the Hexaplaric codex Jerome used, Theodotion’s reading was corruptly written *dysalia*, a word that caused him difficulty, in place of *disalia*, with *iota* at the beginning.]

For the word is also a compound among the Hebrews, since “vomit” is called *CI* and *SOA* means “filthy” [Al. “filth”]. Therefore anything that causes nausea and vomiting may be called *dysalia*.

[Col. 0319A] (Vers. 10 ff.) Whom will he teach knowledge, and whom will he make understand what is heard? Those weaned from milk, torn away from the breasts: for “command, recommit; command, recommit; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there.”

For with stammering lips and in another tongue he will speak to this people, to whom he said: “This is my rest; refresh the weary, and this is my refreshment”; but they were unwilling to hear.

And the word of the Lord will be to them: “Command, recommit; command, recommit; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there,” so that they may go and fall backward, be crushed, ensnared, and captured.

LXX: To whom shall we announce evil, and to whom shall we announce the message? To those who have been weaned from milk, who have been taken away from the breast. “Tribulation upon tribulation, wait; await hope upon hope; still a little, still a little”; because of the mockery of lips, because of another tongue with which they will speak to this people, saying to them: “This is rest for the hungry, and this is crushing,” but they were unwilling to hear.

And the word of the Lord will be to them: “Tribulation upon tribulation: wait, wait; hope [Al. “hope”] upon hope; still a little, still a little,” so that they may go and fall backward, be crushed, endangered, and captured.

“Who,” he says, “is worthy of the Lord’s teaching, so that what he has taken in with his ears he may understand with his heart,” in response to the Savior’s words: “Let the one who has ears to hear, hear” (Matt. XII, 15)?

The following verse shows who they are: those weaned from milk, torn away from the breast, who are not nourished by the milk of infancy but feed on solid food; those who were torn away from the breast with Isaac, for whose joy Abraham made a great banquet (Gen. XXII). These deserve to hear the Lord’s mysteries and to understand what the priest and prophet do not know [Al. “did not know”], having been drunk and swallowed up by wine.

They wandered and did not know the seer, because all their tables were filled with vomit and filth. When the prophets announced future events and threatened torments unless they did what had been commanded, they were accustomed to say mockingly: “Command, recommit; command, recommit”—that is, “Give orders, give orders; command what we ought to do.”

And because they abused God’s patience—since he delays his anger in order to offer mercy—they were also accustomed to say jokingly, in the person of the prophets: “Wait a little; wait briefly. The things we have foretold will come.”

They said all these things among the people because they did not believe God’s words. Immediately the prophet adds: God will by no means speak to you in these words, to command what you ought to do and to tell you to await future events; rather, he will speak to you in his present fury.

He had previously said to the people: “This is my rest; refresh the weary. I have labored for a long time and have found rest nowhere.” “Foxes have dens and the birds of heaven nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX). “And this is my refreshment: that I may at some time rest in you.”

They were unwilling to hear and despised my warnings. Therefore what they used to say mockingly to the prophets—“Command, recommit; command, recommit; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there”—and to mock my patience, thinking that I threatened what I would never do, they will experience fulfilled in events, so that they may go into destruction and fall backward, with an incurable backward pull (*ὀπισθότονος*).

[Note: See Letter 147, to Sabinianus, no. 10, note 2.]

They will never advance toward what came before, nor be able to say with the Apostle: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. III, 13). Instead, they will be crushed and ensnared, and will be captured either by the Babylonian or by the Roman army.

In place of what we said—“Command, recommit; command, recommit; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little there”—the Hebrew reads:

*SAU LASAU, SAU LASAU; CAU LACAU, CAU LACAU; ZER SAM, ZER SAM.*

[Note: Epiphanius also gives and interprets these Hebrew words in *Against Heresies* 25; in Hebrew they are written thus [Hebrew text]. The heresy of the Nicolaitans was accustomed to abuse these words among simple and deceived people. Theodoret, after Epiphanius, reports in *Heretical Fables*, chapter 4, that they revered *Caulacau* and wished by that name to designate Christ as “the awaited one.” Philaster, chapter 33, calls *Caulacau* a man; Epiphanius calls it a certain ruler—perhaps an Aeon or an angel.]

The most filthy heresy is accustomed to abuse these words among the simple and deceived, producing terror by the novelty of its expressions: supposedly whoever knows these words and remembers them in sexual intercourse will pass without any doubt into the kingdom of heaven.

We read in the Apostle: “In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even so they will not hear me, says the Lord” (I Cor. XIV, 21). This seems to me to have been taken, according to the Hebrew, from the present chapter.

We have also observed this in the Old Testament—with a few testimonies excepted, which Luke alone uses, since he possessed greater knowledge of the Greek language: wherever something is said from the Old Testament, they place it not according to the Septuagint but according to the Hebrew, following no one’s interpretation but translating the Hebrew sense into their own language.

Symmachus, Theodotion, and the LXX understood this passage differently. Since it would be lengthy to discuss all of them, let us briefly pass over the Septuagint interpreters, whose version is read in the churches.

Once the Jewish people, the priests, and the prophets have been rejected—those who were drunk with strong drink, wandered, and whose counsel, formed for the sake of greed, was consumed by a curse—to whom shall we announce the tribulations that are to come for Christ, the evils for which the crown of virtues is prepared? To those who have been weaned from milk, who have been torn away from the breast—there is no doubt that this signifies the apostles.

“Tribulation upon tribulation, wait.”

He speaks to the company of the apostles and to all believers, so that they may prepare themselves not for one tribulation but for many. When they have been afflicted and brought low, they should hope again and possess hope upon hope.

If what has been promised is delayed a little, let no one become unbelieving: “A little, a very little, and the promised things will come.” For “tribulation produces endurance; endurance, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not put to shame” (Rom. V, 3–5).

This same tribulation will be doubled by the slander of lips and the blasphemies of persecutors, who rage against God’s people with savage mouths.

But the apostles and apostolic men will speak to the Jewish people, saying: “This is rest for the one who hungers for righteousness, and this is the crushing and anguish that leads to life.” Although they preached these things, the wicked were unwilling to hear.

Therefore what was said to God’s people—“Bear tribulation, bear tribulation; await hope, await hope; still a little, still a little”—will be turned into punishment for those who were unwilling to hear the word of the Lord, so that they may fall, go backward, encounter the danger of siege and death, and be captured without any end to their miseries.

As for the Hebrew word *DEA*, which all translated “knowledge” but the Septuagint alone translated “evils,” the error is obvious. For the first letter, *daleth*, and *resh* are distinguished by a small stroke. If it is read *DEA*, it means “knowledge”; if *REA*, “evil”—not “evil” as opposed to good, but distress.

(Vers. 14–15.) Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men who rule over my people, which is in Jerusalem. For you have said: “We have struck a covenant with death, and made an agreement with hell; when the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and we are protected by falsehood.”

LXX: Therefore hear the word of the Lord, you afflicted men and rulers of this people, which is in Jerusalem. Because you said: “We have made a testament with hell and an agreement with death. If a passing storm should rush upon us, it will not come upon us, because we have made falsehood our hope, and we shall be protected by falsehood.”

As we said above, the rulers of the Jews were accustomed to say mockingly to the prophets, “Command, recommit; wait, wait again,” and other things of this kind. This shows that they did not believe the prophets’ words but held their prophecy in contempt.

The present chapter shows this by calling them “mocking men.” They are the scribes and Pharisees who rule over God’s people in Jerusalem. The LXX calls them “afflicted men” and “rulers of the people of Jerusalem.”

They said not in words but in deeds: “We are like the other nations. We have an agreement and covenant with hell and death. Once and for all we have despaired of salvation.”

“Certainly captivity will come only after a long time,” they said, “since you keep saying: ‘Still a little, still a little; wait, wait again.’ Therefore, when we are dead, we shall not feel this scourge of captivity or this storm.”

For once and for all we believed in falsehood—that is, we placed our hope in God and his Law in vain. And therefore we were protected by falsehood, because, once dead, we escaped the captivity that threatened us.

The Hebrew word *SOT* was translated “scourge” by Aquila and Symmachus, and “storm” by the LXX.

[Note: More correctly, it seems, Vaticanus has *CHZAB*.]

All translated *CHASAB* as “falsehood,” the thing in which the Jews hoped and whose father, according to the Evangelist John, is the devil.

(Vers. 16 ff.) Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, I shall place in the foundations of Zion a tested stone, a cornerstone, precious, firmly founded: whoever believes will not hasten.

And I shall establish judgment by weight and righteousness by measure; and hail shall overturn the hope of falsehood, and waters shall flood the protection. Your covenant with death shall be erased, and your agreement with hell shall not stand. When the overflowing scourge passes through, you shall be trampled by it. Whenever it passes through, it will take you away; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night, and only distress will give understanding to the hearing.

For the bed is too narrow, so that one falls away; and the covering is too short to cover both.

[Note: Victorius repeats “a stone” from the Hebrew and Vulgate editions.]

LXX: Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall cast into the foundations of Zion a precious stone, chosen, a cornerstone, honorable in its foundations; and whoever believes in it will not be put to shame.

And I shall establish judgment as hope, but my mercy by weight; and those who believe in falsehood believe in vain, because the storm will not pass through us and will not take away from us the testament of death, and your hope will not remain in hell.

If the coming storm passes through, you shall be trampled by it. When it passes through, it will take you away morning by morning; it will pass through morning by morning. By day and by night there will be a most evil hope.

Learn to hear, you who are in tribulation: “We cannot fight; we ourselves are too weak to be gathered.”

“I told you,” he says, “to hear the word of the Lord, you mocking men—or afflicted rulers of my people—and not to maintain a covenant with death or an agreement with hell. Despising my commandments, you made falsehood your hope and, boasting—or rather despairing—said: ‘We shall be protected by falsehood.’”

Therefore the merciful and compassionate Lord, patient and very merciful (Ps. CXLIV), says that, whether you wish it or not, he will send into the foundations of Zion a chosen, tested, precious, and cornerstone.

Concerning this the Apostle also says: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation” (I Cor. III, 10); and again: “For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (ibid., 11).

This stone is truly called “stone” twice, just as in Leviticus “man” is said twice. It is also the cornerstone, because he joined together the peoples of the Circumcision and of the nations. Concerning him the Psalm says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. CXVII, 22).

These builders and masons are the ones now called mocking men and rulers of the people who are in Jerusalem.

We also read in Daniel about this stone, that it was cut from the mountain without hands and filled the whole world (Dan. II): for the dispensation of the divine seed assumed a human body, and the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily in it.

Upon this stone, which is otherwise called the rock, Christ built the Church and, firmly—according to the Hebrew—founded it upon a foundation. Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame, or, according to the Hebrew, will not hasten, so that Christ’s coming may not seem slow to him.

For if he delays, according to Habakkuk, no one should despair, because “he who is coming will come” and will fulfill his promises (Hab. II).

God also promises that he will place in him judgment by weight. For “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John V, 22). And he will place righteousness, or mercy, by measure, so that he may repay each according to his works and temper righteousness and mercy with one another, in accordance with what we read in the Psalms: “Mercy and truth have met one another; righteousness and peace have kissed one another” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11).

He also says that your hope and falsehood—that is, the devil, the father of all falsehood—will be overturned by the hail of his punishments.

And the protection under which you thought yourselves safe will be destroyed by a violent storm and a multitude of waters, so that the friendship and covenant you had with death and hell—that is, with the devil—will perish forever.

And the scourge, or storm, of which you had said, “When the overflowing scourge passes through, it will not come upon us,” will come, and you will be trampled by it. That is, you will suffer all the torments that, in your despair, you thought you would never endure.

It will continually assail you; in prosperity as well as adversity you will feel the Lord’s anger, and savage death will ravage you.

What shall I say about the punishments? The mere fear of punishment and dread of torments will correct you toward salvation and make you understand your evils. When you have been afflicted, then you will know that my prophets spoke the truth.

[Note: Vaticanus: “then you will take notice of the prophets,” and so forth.]

As for what follows—“The bed is too narrow, so that one falls away, and the covering is too short to cover both”—it has the sense that we read in the Apostle: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of idols” (II Cor. X, 20–21); and elsewhere: “What participation has righteousness with iniquity? What fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What share has the believer with the unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (II Cor. VI, 14–15).

He speaks under the metaphor of a most chaste husband saying to his adulterous wife: “One little bed cannot contain both me and your adulterer, nor can a short covering cover both husband and adulterer.”

Therefore, O Jerusalem, to whom he also speaks in Ezekiel under the persona of a fornicating wife (Ezek. XVI, 21), and whom he calls a prostitute and adulteress at the beginning of Hosea (Hos. III), if you wish to be joined to my embraces, cast away the idols. If you serve idols, you cannot have me.

This is according to the Hebrew.

[Note: The same applies to the corresponding passage in the LXX. Shortly afterward: “what he said,” and so forth.]

But as for what is read in the LXX—“Learn to hear, you who are afflicted: We cannot fight; we ourselves are weak to be gathered”—I entirely do not know what sense it has or how it is connected with what precedes.

Unless perhaps the divine word is speaking to the rulers of the people and exhorting them to place their hope in God, not in death and hell, and to learn to hear the prophets’ predictions; and they respond that, because of their weakness, they cannot fight against hostile powers, nor be gathered among God’s people.

[Col. 0324B] (Verses 21–22.) For as on Mount Perazim the Lord will stand, so in the valley of Gibeon he will be angry, to perform his work—his strange work—to accomplish his task, which is foreign to him. And now do not mock, lest your bonds perhaps be tightened. For I have heard from the Lord God of hosts a consummation and an abbreviation over the whole earth.

The Septuagint: As a mountain of the ungodly the Lord will rise up, and he will be in the valley of Gibeon; with fury he will perform his works, a work of bitterness, and in his fury he will deal harshly with strangers, and his bitterness is foreign. And you, do not rejoice, lest your bonds be strengthened, because I have heard from the Lord God Sabaoth of completed and abbreviated matters which he is going to perform over the whole earth.

The Lord promised that he would place a precious stone in the foundations of Zion, so that [Col. 0324C] hail might overthrow falsehood and the hope of the ungodly; and that a covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol would be swept away by a violent storm. Because the mocking rulers were unwilling to receive him, as once, in David’s reign, against the Philistines on Mount Perazim—which in Hebrew was called PHARASIM ()—the Lord cut down his adversaries, and from this the place received its name. Likewise in the valley of Gibeon, under Joshua the leader, when he spoke with confidence in the God dwelling within him: “Let the sun stand still at Gibeon, and the moon opposite the valley of Aijalon” [or Elon] (Joshua 10:12); and the sun stood still for the space of one day, while many of the foreigners perished. So against the ungodly and mockers the Lord will be angry, to perform his work.

[Note: Victorius reads this with an interrogative mark and then adds “by no means”; by this distinction and addition of the word he maintains that the defective and contrary sense ought to be restored.]

For it is not the Lord’s work to destroy those whom he created, but to perform a strange work, which belongs more to cruelty than to mercy. Again he repeats the same thing in other words: “to accomplish his task.” It is not his work to punish sinners, but something strange and foreign to him: that he should punish, though he is the Savior.

Therefore, since the Lord is going to rise from his patience and will by no means spare, just as he did not spare on Mount Perazim or in the valley of Gibeon, I warn you, mocking men, not to laugh at my prophets and not to suppose that what they announce will come to pass. For if you persist in mocking, the bonds of your sins may be tightened. “For each person is bound by the cords of his sins” (Proverbs 5:22); or perhaps the time of captivity may come upon you. For what the Lord had postponed—bonds, captivity, and punishments, or the final day of judgment—he is now going to complete in events, bring to an end, and abbreviate. Accordingly, I, the prophet, announce to you what I have learned from the Lord God Almighty is going to happen over the whole earth, so that you may forestall the approaching anger by repentance.

According to the Septuagint, the Lord himself is said to rise like a mountain of the ungodly and to be present in the valley of Gibeon, in order to perform his works, all of which are one work of bitterness. This should not be considered blasphemous. For it does not say that the Lord will become a mountain of the ungodly, but “like a mountain”—one that seems most oppressive to the ungodly and to those who endure it. [Col. 0325B] It is as when a negligent son and another who is ill may regard their father and physician as cruel if they restore them to health through blows and the cautery of discipline.

For the Lord will rise and will be in the valley of Gibeon because of those who, although they remain in a lowly place on account of their sins, are lifted up into pride through the swelling of their spirit. For Gibeon is interpreted as “hill,” so that he may perform his works, which are works of bitterness, when he is compelled to change mercy and becomes bitter instead of sweet.

Therefore, you who will at some time suffer these things, do not now rejoice with the joy with which the rich man, clothed in purple and neglecting poor Lazarus, rejoiced at his banquet (Luke 16). Otherwise your bonds may become stronger. For what the Lord will do, completing his judgment in events, I have both heard and announced to you in its entirety. As for what he added, “over the whole earth,” understand, according to the historical sense, the boundaries of Judea; according to the allegorical sense, the entire world.

(Verses 23ff.) Give ear and hear my voice; pay attention and hear my speech. Does the plowman plow all day in order to sow? Does he continually break up and harrow his ground? Does he not, when he has leveled its surface, sow black cumin, scatter cumin, and put wheat in rows, and barley and millet and spelt within their boundaries? And he instructs it according to judgment; his God teaches him. For black cumin is not threshed with a saw, nor does a wagon wheel revolve over cumin; but black cumin is beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff. Bread, however, is crushed. Yet the thresher does not thresh it forever, nor does he continually torment it with the wheel of his wagon, nor crush it with his hooves. This too has come forth from the Lord of hosts, that he might make his counsel wonderful and magnify justice.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with the Vulgate translator and Jerome’s own version, has “from the Lord God”; this is by no means found in the Hebrew archetype.]

The Septuagint: Give ear and hear my voice; pay attention and hear my words. Does the one who plows plow all day, or prepare the seed before preparing the ground? When he has leveled its surface, will he then sow black cumin and cumin, and again sow wheat, barley, millet, and spelt within your boundaries, and will you be instructed by God’s judgment and rejoice? For black cumin is not cleansed with harshness, nor does a wagon wheel revolve over cumin; but black cumin is beaten out with a rod, and cumin is eaten with bread. For I will not be angry with you forever, nor will the voice of my bitterness trample you; these wonders have gone forth from the Lord. Take counsel; exalt consolation that is vain.

He now speaks to the same people to whom he had earlier said: “Hear the word of God, mocking men, who rule over my people who are in Jerusalem.” He commands them to hear his voice and attend carefully to his speech.

“Does the farmer,” he says, “always plow in order to sow?” Does he not first break up the ground, turn over the furrows with the plowshare, and break the clods that have been cast up with the rake and the hoe, so that, after leveling the surface of the earth and first softening the hard fields, he may then scatter black cumin or cumin, and sow wheat, barley, millet, and spelt within their boundaries, according to the diversity of soil and seasons? For not everything is sown at the same time.

In place of spelt, which the Greeks call ζέα, some understand vetch.

[Note: See what we note on Ezekiel, chapter 4.]

God naturally instructs the farmer himself—that is, the sower—by his judgment and teaches him, so that he may know what cultivation to apply to each seed. Finally, when the time of harvesting arrives, black cumin and cumin, which are weaker seeds, are not crushed by wagon wheels, which are turned and dragged over the reaped crops in the likeness of saws; they are beaten out with a rod and staff, commonly called flails.

Bread—that is, the wheat from which bread is made—is crushed by iron wheels, and all its stalk is broken into chaff. Nevertheless, it is not always tormented and crushed, nor is it at every time broken by the hooves of the wheels. In Hebrew, “their horses” is used in place of this, so that, since he had mentioned the hooves of the wheels, he might preserve the metaphor in what follows.

Some wish to infer from the fact that he mentioned hooves and horses that herds of mares were customarily driven into the threshing floors to thresh the grain. But Scripture could not say this, since the province of Judea did not have such animals.

This, then—that black cumin should be beaten out with a rod and cumin with a staff, while wheat, barley, and spelt, perhaps also millet, are crushed with iron wheels—is not God’s judgment forever. In all things he displays his wonderful counsel and reveals the greatness of his justice.

We have said these things παραφραστικῶς—that is, by way of paraphrase—so that we may more easily understand the meaning for which they are said. God administers the human race in various ways: now he punishes, now he has mercy; now he rebukes, now he defends. That is, now he plows, now he sows, now he harvests ripe crops, and, after they have been reaped, threshes them on the threshing floors; and he governs his world as he wills.

Black cumin and cumin—that is, all the nations that did not receive knowledge of him and did not possess the commandments of the Law—he corrects with a rod and staff. But the wheat—that is, the Jewish people—he will torment with great punishments. For from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more will be required. “The servant who knows his master’s will and does not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47); and elsewhere it is written: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7).

Nevertheless, he will not torment them forever. For it is one thing to be ungodly and another to be a sinner. What we have interpreted concerning the nations and the Jews, others explain concerning the people and the priests: that the unlearned multitude will be corrected on the day of judgment like black cumin and cumin, with rod and staff; but the priests, who possessed the key of knowledge, will be tormented with great punishments. This too will occur by the Lord’s judgment, who displays his wonderful counsel and the truth of his justice in all things, so that more will be required from those who received more.

For what we interpreted as “black cumin will be beaten out with a rod, and cumin with a staff,” the Septuagint, for some reason, translated: “but cumin is eaten with bread.” Thus also the ancient Greek interpreters, explaining the Hebrew, were silent about this statement, perhaps because they had nothing to say about it.

But where, following the Hebrew, we rendered: “Yet the thresher will not thresh it forever, nor will he torment it with the wheel of the wagon, nor crush it with his hooves,” the Septuagint translated not word for word but according to the sense: “For I will not be angry with you forever, nor will the voice of my bitterness trample you.” They thus indicate that future refreshment will come to sinners after their torments, and that these things, as portents and wonders, have gone forth from the Lord.

Hence sinners, who will later be punished, are commanded to take counsel and exalt their consolation—not “vain,” as the Septuagint added, but simply “consolation.” For God would never command them to exalt a vain consolation that would not benefit them.

(Cap. 19.—Verses 1ff.) Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city that David conquered. A year has been added to a year; the festivals have run their course. I will encircle Ariel, and it will be sad and mournful, and it will be for me like Ariel. I will surround you like a sphere, and cast up a rampart against you, and set up fortifications for your siege. You will be humbled; you will speak from the earth, and your speech will be heard from the ground. Your voice will be like that of a python from the earth, and your speech will mutter from the ground. The multitude of those who fan you will be like fine dust, and the multitude of those who prevailed against you will be like passing ash. And suddenly, at once, she will be visited by the Lord of hosts with thunder and earthquake, with the loud voice of whirlwind and storm, and with the flame of devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that fought against Ariel, and all who served in the army, besieged, and prevailed against her, will be like a dream of a nocturnal vision. As a hungry man dreams that he is eating, but when he awakens his soul is empty; and as a thirsty man dreams that he is drinking, but after he awakes he is still weary and thirsty, and his soul is empty—so will be the multitude of all the nations that fought against Mount Zion.

The Septuagint: Woe to Ariel, Ariel, the city that David conquered. Gather up your produce; eat year upon year—for you will eat with Moab. For I will confine Ariel, and its strength and wealth will belong to me; and I will surround you as David did. I will send a rampart around you, and set up towers all around you; your words will be humbled to the earth, and your speech will sink into the earth. Your voice will be like that of those speaking from the earth, and your voice will be weakened down to the pavement. They will be like dust from the wheel—the wealth of the ungodly—and like flying ash will be the multitude of those who oppressed you. And suddenly, in an instant, she will be visited by the Lord Sabaoth. For there will be a visitation with thunder, earthquake, and loud voice, a violent storm, and a devouring flame of fire. The wealth of all the nations that fought against Ariel will be like the dream of one who sees at night, and all who fought against Jerusalem, and all who gathered against and afflicted her. They will be like those who hunger and eat in a dream; when they rise, their dream is empty. And like one who is thirsty and drinks in a dream: when he rises, he is still thirsty, and his soul has hoped in vain. So will be the wealth of all the nations that fought against Mount Zion.

In place of our “Woe,” the Hebrew has OI (), which among them is sometimes used in the vocative case, so that it does not lament Ariel but calls to it, although in the present passage it must be understood as lamentation.

Ariel is also interpreted as “lion of God.” In place of “city,” which Aquila translated as πολίχνην—that is, “little town” or “village”—the Hebrews read CARIATH (), which properly signifies a village; in Syriac it is called [Col. 0328D] Cartha. Hence “the village of the woods” is called CARIATH JARIM (). Likewise, in the preceding passage (on chapter 1:21), where we read, “How has the faithful city, Zion, become a prostitute?” the Hebrew has Cariath in place of “city,” that is, “village.” To express Aquila’s translation literally, we may call it a “little city.”

Accordingly, Ariel—that is, “lion of God”—was once the designation of Jerusalem in its greatest strength; or, as others think, of the temple and altar of God that was in Jerusalem.

As for what follows, “which David conquered,” in place of which Symmachus translated “the fortress of David” and Theodotion “the encampment of David,” the Hebrew reads HANA (), which the most learned of the Hebrews wished to signify “dwelling.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript likewise explains it as signifying “dwelling.”]

If, therefore, we read “which David conquered,” let us refer it to the time when David captured the stronghold of Zion, despite the resistance of the blind and lame, and Joab first climbed the heights of the roofs (1 Chronicles 11). But if, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, we understand that David restored and fortified it, then “a year has been added to a year,” or subtracted, as Aquila translated, and “the festivals have run their course.” For when the temple was overthrown and the Jewish religion abolished, all their festivity perished.

The Lord says that he will surround Ariel with the Babylonian army and that it will be sad and mournful when it has been destroyed by them. Again, under Joshua son of Jehozadak the high priest, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied, it would be like Ariel, because it would possess the likeness of the former temple but would not possess its magnificence and adornment.

A second time the Lord threatens that he will surround Ariel like a sphere, cast up a rampart against it, and set up fortifications for its siege. Thus will be fulfilled what he himself, lamenting Jerusalem, says in the Gospel: “If you had known the things that make for your peace, because days will come upon you when your enemies will surround you with a rampart, besiege you, and humble you to the ground” (Luke 19:42ff.). And Jerusalem will be trampled by the nations until the completion of the times of the Gentiles.

The prophet now says the same thing in other words: that, having been humbled, she will speak from the earth and her speech will be heard from the ground; that her voice will be like that of a python from the earth and that, like sparrows, she will whisper from the ground. By these words he signifies the necromancy of magicians—νεκυομαντείαν—through which they are said to summon souls and hear the faint voices of shades, or rather of demons.

[Note: Previously it read νεκρομαντείαν.]

Finally, in place of “python,” Aquila translated “magician,” which in Hebrew is called CHEB (). For this the Septuagint translated “those speaking from the earth.”

[Note: Our manuscripts and the oldest codex of Saint-Germain, cited by Montfaucon, likewise have this reading. Jerome is therefore not to be understood as meaning that the entire word Cheb, which occurs in the Hebrew, signifies “magician.” The letter ה prefixed to it has the force of the particle “like,” just as; rather, he understands it as expressing the complete Hebrew word which Aquila translated “magician.” Moreover, in modern Bibles the name is written with a full ḥolem, which Jerome does not seem to have found in his exemplar.]

By these words it is indicated that the ruin of the temple will remain until the end of the world: once collapsed into ashes, it will never again be raised up.

Such a vast army of Roman power, O Ariel, will surround you, and it will be compared to innumerable dust, like ash flying through the air. Hence he does not compare to dust and ash the weakness of those who fought against them, but their multitude, which is equated with innumerable grains of sand.

And this will happen suddenly, at once: as though in the midst of peace, sudden wars should arise under Nero. Then the Lord of hosts will visit Jerusalem with thunder, earthquake, whirlwind and storm, and devouring fire, by which he signifies the temple that is to be burned.

But the Romans, after conquering the Jews and overthrowing Jerusalem under Titus and Vespasian, carried the spoils once belonging to God’s vessels to the Capitol [or: removed them], and thought that what they had done was the result of their own strength, the power of their gods, and not the anger of God. In a dream and nocturnal vision they will possess all these riches.

As one who is hungry thinks in sleep that he is eating, and one who is thirsty drinks rivers with a throat parched by thirst, but, when he awakens, his thirst becomes more intense because the drink deceived him with an empty satisfaction, so the multitude of all the nations subject to Roman power that fought against Mount Zion will possess their riches as though in shadow, cloud, and a nocturnal dream; but they will abandon them through a ripe destruction.

Where we rendered “all who served in the army, besieged, and prevailed against her,” the Septuagint translated “all who served against Jerusalem,” which is not found in the Hebrew.

At the beginning of this chapter also, where we said “a year has been added to a year,” or subtracted, they translated: “Gather up fruits, or produce, year upon year; eat, for you will eat with Moab.” The sense is this: before the acceptable year of the Lord, the year of his preaching, arrives—or rather, two years, of which in the Song of Habakkuk, according to the Hebrew, we read, “In the midst of two periods you will be known” (Habakkuk 3)—sow for yourselves in tears, so that you may reap in joy (Psalm 125).

It is written in the Gospel according to John that the Lord came to Jerusalem for three Passovers (John 2:13), which amount to two years. But what follows, “For you will eat with Moab,” is not found in the Hebrew. We may say of this that, unless they gather for themselves the fruits of repentance, they will begin to eat with those who do not enter the Church of the Lord forever.

The remaining points in which they appear to differ are clear, and from what we have explained their interpretation is easy.

I know that I have read that Ariel is interpreted “my light is God,” but this is quite different. For here the first syllable is written with ALEPH and RES (); but the light which in Hebrew is called OR has the letter VAU between ALEPH and RES, and that letter is not present in the name under discussion.

Everything now said against Ariel they refer to heretics, who consider their doctrine the light of God and must be conquered by the true David. All their festivals must be taken away, and their present joy changed into future sadness. God commands them to repent, lest they begin to eat with the Moabites and become like the Gentiles.

For he himself will conquer Ariel and surround all their strength and wealth with his army. With towers—that is, with the teachers of the Church—he will humble their words to the ground, so that they may no longer set their mouths in heaven, but may be written on the earth, speak from the earth, and become like dust shaken from a wheel. All the wealth of the ungodly will be reckoned as nothing in an instant and a moment of time, when he visits them in his majesty, descending in whirlwind, storm, and the fire of punishment. Then they will understand that all their riches, the pomp of their words, and the turns of their arguments are comparable to the empty dream of one who eats and drinks—those who fought against Jerusalem, the vision of peace, or against Ariel, the most powerful lion, and finally against Mount Zion, upon which the city of the Church cannot remain hidden.

(Verses 9ff.) Be astounded and amazed; stagger and reel; become drunk, but not with wine; be shaken, but not by drunkenness. For the Lord has mixed for you a spirit of deep sleep; he will close your eyes and cover your prophets and rulers, who see visions. And the vision of all this will be for you like the words of a sealed book. When they give it to one who knows letters and say, “Read this,” he will answer, “I cannot, for it is sealed.” And the book will be given to one who does not know letters, and they will say to him, “Read”; and he will answer, “I do not know letters.”

In place of “a spirit of deep sleep,” the Septuagint has “compunction”; Theodotion, “ecstasy of mind”; Aquila, καταφοράν—that is, “heavy sleep.” In Hebrew it is called THARDEMA (), the sleep which Scripture records was sent upon Adam by God (Genesis 2), when the woman was made from the rib of his side. Jonah too snored in this same sleep in the ship (Jonah 1).

All the prophecy, after the destruction of Jerusalem and the temple—that is, of Ariel—is directed against the scribes and Pharisees, who, although they possess the key of knowledge, neither enter themselves nor permit those who wish to enter.

They are commanded to be intoxicated with astonishment and wonder—or, according to the Septuagint, with the dissolution of the whole body and ecstasy of mind—and to be shaken and tossed about: staggering not from wine or strong drink, but from the spirit of the Lord’s deep sleep or compunction. Thus, understanding their evil, they may at last repent and say with the prophet: “I was weakened with sickness when a thorn was fastened in me” (Psalm 31:4).

Know, therefore, O scribes and Pharisees, who are the rulers of the Jews, that the Lord will repay you according to your conduct. You heard the Lord the Savior, but you were unwilling to understand; you closed your eyes so that you would not see him and made your ears heavy so that you would not hear. Therefore he too will close your eyes—the prophets, through whom you saw the knowledge of God—or he will close your eyes and those of the prophets who are your rulers.

“For the Law and the prophets were until John the Baptist” (Luke 16:16), so that, while you do not see, those may see of whom the following passage testifies (on verse 18): “On that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see and rejoice.”

[Note: The printed editions add “sealed,” but neither our manuscripts nor the text of Scripture itself has this word. In my opinion it was transferred here by some diligent reader from the exposition that follows, from the Apocalypse.]

For the Lord came for judgment, so that those who saw—namely, the Jews—would not see, and those who were blind—the people of the nations—would see and contemplate the Lord (John 9).

Thus he significantly did not say that the vision of all the prophets was sealed for all readers, but, “For you,” he says, “it will be sealed”—for you to whom I am now speaking, to whom I announce these future things. Or he will close forever the eyes of your rulers, who, according to the Septuagint, boasted that they saw hidden and secret things.

“And all Holy Scripture,” he says, “will be closed and sealed for you, so that you who read the letters of the Law and think that you know the prophecies of the prophets, and who meditate day and night on the volumes of Scripture with tireless speech, will not understand what you read,” as it is written in the Apocalypse of John: “Who is worthy to open the book and loose its seals?” (Revelation 5:2).

[Note: The common text incorrectly had “you who read the letters,” in place of “of the Law,” as we have corrected it from the manuscripts, compelled by the sequence of the argument and its correct meaning.]

When no one was found who could open the seals, he says that he wept; and finally he deserved to hear the word of God addressed to him: “Do not weep. Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has conquered, so that he may open the book and loose its seals.”

The Lion of the tribe of Judah is the Lord Jesus Christ, who looses the seals of the book—not properly of one book, as many suppose, namely the Psalms of David, but of all the Scriptures, which are one through the same Holy Spirit of Scripture, and are therefore called one book.

Ezekiel bears mystical witness to this (Ezekiel 2), saying that it was written within and without—in sense and in letter. Of this the Savior also speaks in the Psalms: “At the head of the book it is written of me” (Psalm 39:9)—not of Jeremiah, not of Isaiah, but in all Holy Scripture, which is called one book.

Therefore, if the teachers of the Jews, even to the present day, are unable to read, open the seals, and disclose the mysteries of the Scriptures, and if you give that book to an unlearned people, who are devoured by their own teachers, they will confess that they do not know letters and therefore cannot read. Of the two evils, it is much lighter to confess ignorance of the Law than to boast of wisdom and yet be unable to understand what is said.

(Verses 13–14.) And the Lord said: Because this people draws near with its mouth and glorifies me with its lips, but its heart is far from me, and they fear me according to the commandment and teachings of men, therefore, behold, I will again act so as to astonish this people with a great and astonishing wonder. For the wisdom of its wise men will perish, and the understanding of its prudent men will be hidden.

The Septuagint: And the Lord said: This people draws near to me with its mouth and honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men. Therefore, behold, I will again remove this people; I will remove them and destroy the wisdom of the wise, and conceal the understanding of the prudent.

The Lord used this testimony against the Pharisees in the Gospel of Matthew, saying: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God because of your tradition?” (Matthew 15:3). And again: “Hypocrites, Isaiah rightly prophesied about you, saying: ‘This people honors me with its lips, but its heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men’” (ibid., 6–9).

Here we must note what we have often pointed out: the Evangelists and Apostles did not translate word for word, nor did they follow the authority of the Septuagint translators, whose edition was already being read at that time. Rather, as Hebrews instructed in the Law, they used their own expressions without harm to the meaning.

The Jewish people draws near to God with its mouth and lips because it boasts that it worships the one God and rejects idols. But its heart is far from him because it does not receive the Lord Jesus Christ. For whoever does not receive the Son does not receive the Father.

Let us at the same time learn how someone draws near to God or becomes distant from him. Through Jeremiah he says: “Am I a God who is near, and not a God from afar?” says the Lord (Jeremiah 23:23, according to the Septuagint).

We draw near to God by the mind, not by the body, just as we read concerning Moses: “Moses alone drew near to God; the others did not draw near” (Exodus 24:2). For he prayed to God in spirit and truth, and approached him in understanding and spirit.

But those of whom it is written that they are taken from the womb and instructed from childhood to old age, and who meditate on the Law of God day and night [or: at midnight], do not draw near to God, because they accept the traditions of the Pharisees and scribes. These make them distant from God. They are whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead; they chose Barabbas and rejected the Lord (Matthew 23:27).

Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he threatens that he will again remove them—not transferring them to the Assyrians and Babylonians, but scattering them throughout the entire world.

According to the Hebrew, he says that he will make a great wonder and an astonishing miracle for the Jewish people: he will destroy the wisdom of those who did not receive the power and wisdom of God, and conceal and hide the understanding of the prudent, so that they may not discover him who is contained in the letter.

The Apostle Paul, writing to the Corinthians, set down testimony from this passage: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (1 Corinthians 1:19). He explains the same meaning in other words—not that God is an enemy of wisdom, whose father he is and through whom all wisdom exists in human beings, but that he added the qualification found in the Hebrew: “the wise men of the people” and “its prudent men,” that is, of the Jewish people.

And truly God performed a great wonder in the people after the coming of the Lord the Savior: at one and the same time Jerusalem burned, the temple collapsed, and all the knowledge of the teachers was removed, in fulfillment of what was said earlier (on chapter 3:1ff.): “Behold, the Lord, the Lord of hosts, will remove from Jerusalem and from Judah the strong man and the strong woman; all the strength of bread and all the strength of water; the giant and the warrior; the judge and the prophet; the diviner and the elder; the captain of fifty; the wonderful counselor; the wise architect; and the prudent hearer,” and the rest which the prophetic word sets forth.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript adds: “It should be noted what is said concerning those who turn religion into profit: ‘Woe…’”]

### (Verses 15–16)

“Woe to those who are deep in heart, so as to hide their counsel from the Lord, whose deeds are in darkness, and who say: ‘Who sees us, and who knows us?’ Your thought is perverse—as if clay were to think against the potter and say to its maker, ‘You did not make me,’ and the molded object were to say to its molder, ‘You do not understand.’”

The Septuagint: “Woe to those who make deep counsels, whose deeds will be in darkness, and who say: ‘Who sees us? Who will know us and the things we do?’ Will you not be reckoned as the potter’s clay? Shall the work say to its maker, ‘You did not make me wisely,’ or the molded object to its molder, ‘You did not make me’?”

Against those same people of whom he had earlier said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise and reject the understanding of the prudent,” or, as the prophet writes, “I will hide it,” God’s word is now also directed—against those who are wise in their own eyes and prudent in their own sight. Of them that saying may most rightly be understood: “Those who search have failed in their searching” (Ps. 63). For it is written concerning God’s wisdom: “For if someone among the children of men is perfect without your wisdom, he will be regarded as nothing” (Wis. 3).

They therefore suppose that God does not know their counsels because their deeds are in darkness, and they say: “Who sees us?” and “Who knows us?” The wise men of this world, the teachers of heretics, and the Pharisees of the Jews say the same thing: that no one understands them. They do not remember what is said to God: “Darkness will not be darkened by you, and night will be illuminated like day” (Ps. 138:12). And: “As is his darkness, so also is his light” (Gen. 3).

Deceived by this error, Adam and Eve, hearing the sound of the feet of the one walking in the paradise of God, hid themselves beneath the tree in which there was the knowledge of good and evil [Note: Compare St. Augustine, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, Book II.] ; and Cain likewise, when he said, “If you cast me away today from your face, I shall be hidden” (Gen. 4:14), in similar folly supposed that God was ignorant.

And through Amos it is said concerning the impious and sinners: “If they hide themselves from my eyes in the depth of the sea, there I will command the dragon, and it will bite them” (Amos 9:3).

Therefore, however wise someone may be and however fervent his intellect, if he does not possess God’s wisdom and teaching, let us say of him: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 12:1–2). We may make a similar statement [Note: Vatican: “For unless the Lord ...”]: “Unless the Lord helps knowledge, the one who thinks himself wise labors in vain. Unless the Lord guards our heart with all vigilance, the one who thinks it can be preserved by his own care keeps watch in vain.”

“Your thought,” he says, “is perverse: you suppose that the maker does not know what he has made, and that the Creator does not know his creature—as though clay and a work might say to the potter and its maker, ‘You did not make me,’ or ‘You did not make me well,’ and ‘You do not understand your work.’”

The Apostle uses this testimony in other words in his Letter to the Romans, where he discusses God’s profound knowledge and wishes to refute the accusation of human beings: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Shall the molded object say to its molder, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the same lump of clay to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

In all these matters that rule must always be observed: the Evangelists and Apostles, without damage to the meaning, rendered passages from Hebrew into Greek as seemed best to them.

### (Verses 17ff.)

“Will not Lebanon, in a little while and in a short time, be changed into Carmel, and Carmel be reckoned as a forest? And on that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see. And the meek will increase their rejoicing in the Lord, and the poor among men will exult in the Holy One of Israel, because the one who prevailed has failed. The mocker is finished, and all who kept watch over iniquity have been cut down—those who caused people to sin by their word, who tripped up the one reproving them at the gate, and who turned the just aside in vain.”

Let the Jews and the friends of a merely literal history answer—those who seek no fruit on the tree, but only the leaves and shade of words, which quickly wither and perish. How, at the coming of the Lord and Savior—for from the time of Isaiah until the dispensation of the assumed flesh, the span of time is short and small in comparison with eternity—was Mount Lebanon, the mountain of Phoenicia, turned and transferred into Mount Carmel? Carmel is called *CHERMEL* in Hebrew [Hebrew term as printed], and overlooks Ptolemais on the border of Palestine and Phoenicia.

There is also another mountain called Carmel in the Holy Scriptures, where Nabal the Carmelite lived (1 Sam. 25), a foolish and wicked man who had Abigail as his wife. After her husband died, she married David; while he was alive, she could not take David as her husband, lest she be called an adulteress if she were joined to another man. How, then, is Carmel reckoned as a forest and as unfruitful wood?

Since they cannot explain this, let them hear that Lebanon, which is interpreted as “whiteness,” refers to the people of the nations, who, washed in the Lord and cleansed of their former filth, ascend as the whole world and, under [or “upon,” *super*] the person of the Church, lean upon the Savior. Concerning them it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this that ascends whitened, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). This people is transferred into Carmel—that is, into knowledge of circumcision—so that it may recognize the mysteries of spiritual and true circumcision and occupy the place formerly held by the people of the Jews.

Those, however, who were unwilling to receive Christ are reckoned as a forest and as sterile trees, which cannot praise the Lord together with fruitful trees.

When Lebanon has been changed into Carmel and Carmel into a forest, then those who were previously deaf and unable to hear the words of the prophetic book will hear. We have already said above that all Holy Scripture is called one book, as Ecclesiastes says: “The words of the wise are like goads and like nails driven deeply; they were given by the councils of one shepherd” (Eccl. 12:11). They will hear and speak, and to them the Savior will say, “Ephphatha” [or “Effatha”], which is interpreted, “Be opened” (Mark 7).

What we render, “Out of darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see,” is easily understood. Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus translated it: “The darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see,” indicating that the mysteries of Christ were to be disclosed to the people of the nations, who had previously been blind, in accordance with the saying: “The dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17:12). In the same psalm it is written concerning God: “He made darkness his hiding place” (ibid. 17:12).

And in Proverbs we read: “When the wise man hears these things, he will become wiser, and the prudent will possess direction; he will understand the parable and the dark saying, the words of the wise and the riddles” (Prov. 1:5–6).

Finally, Moses too, in order to understand and see God (Exod. 20), entered into the cloud and into the gloom, concerning which it is said in the Psalm: “Gloom is beneath his feet” (Ps. 17:10).

When those who were previously blind have either perceived the various mysteries or lifted their eyes from blindness and darkness in order to see, so that the true light may arise for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, then the meek—of whom it is written, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4)—or the poor, whose prince says in the Psalms, “This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him” (Ps. 33:7), and, “He will judge the poor of the people and save the children of the poor” (Ps. 72:4), concerning whom it is said to the Jews, “You have despised the counsel of the poor”—will increase their rejoicing in the Lord, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10).

And poor people—or those despaired of by human beings and despised—who previously had no knowledge of the Law will exult in the Holy One of Israel, who said: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 11:44).

All their exultation is because “the one who prevailed has failed.” The mocker—or the arrogant and proud man—has been finished: the one who said, “By strength and wisdom I will act; I will remove the boundaries of the nations and devastate their strength.” He mocked everyone, so much so that even the holy man said: “My loins are filled with mockery” (Ps. 37:8).

And all who kept watch over iniquity have been cut down, or destroyed. Because of their evil watchfulness, destruction does not sleep. They caused the whole human race to sin by the word of blasphemy, so that people denied the Word of God and set their mouths against heaven.

This signifies the demons, who, being themselves wicked, caused all human beings to sin in speech by blaspheming through various doctrines. They tripped up, as far as lay within them, the one reproving them at the gate and at the judgment, and caused him to turn aside from justice—the one who was at the gates of the daughter of Zion, exalted from the gates of death, and who rebuked those who hated the one reproving them at the gates.

What we have understood concerning the devil and his angels, the Nazarenes think was spoken against the scribes and Pharisees: namely, that the *δευτερωταί*—those who previously mocked the people through their wicked traditions—have failed. They kept watch day and night in order to deceive the simple; they caused people to sin against the Word of God, so that they might deny Christ the Son of God.

### (Verses 22ff.)

“Therefore thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, he who redeemed Abraham: Jacob will no longer be ashamed, and his face will no longer blush. But when he sees his children, the work of my hands, sanctifying my name in his midst, they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and proclaim the God of Israel. Those who err in spirit will know understanding, and the murmurers will learn the Law.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he overcame from Abraham: Jacob will no longer be ashamed, nor will he now change his face. But when his children see my works, they will sanctify my name because of me; [Note: Victorius restores, in accordance with the Greek text itself, “his children see” (*ἴδωσι τὰ τέκνα αὐτῶν*) in place of “he sees his children.”] they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob, and they will fear the God of Israel. Those who err in spirit will know understanding, and the murmurers will learn obedience. The words that follow—‘and the stammering tongues will learn to speak peace’—should be marked with an obelus.”

“When they have heard,” he says, “the deaf will hear the words of the book, and the eyes of the blind will see; when Lebanon has been turned into Carmel and Carmel reckoned as a forest, so that the meek and poor rejoice in the Lord and the proud mocker fails, then Jacob will be ashamed, though for the present he is not ashamed.”

This refers to the times of Isaiah. His face will blush, so that the blush and shame may become an occasion of salvation, especially when he sees his children—that is, the Apostles and apostolic men, who were descended from the Jewish people—performing mighty deeds among the nations of the Lord, proclaiming the name of Christ to the Gentiles, and saying: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9).
