They will sanctify the Holy One who arose from Jacob, and they will teach the God of Israel among the nations, so that, abandoning idols, they may say: “How false were the idols our fathers possessed; there is no one among them who makes it rain.” Then those who now err in spirit will know the understanding of God, and those who once murmured against the Lord in the wilderness will learn the Law, of which previously they had no knowledge.

For if they had received Moses, they would also have received the Lord Jesus Christ, because Moses spoke about him.

What we translated at the beginning of the chapter according to the Hebrew—“Thus says the Lord to the house of Jacob, who once redeemed Abraham, brought him out of the Chaldeans, and led him into the land of promise” (Gen. 11)—is perfectly clear.

What the Septuagint translated as, “Thus says the Lord concerning the house of Jacob, which he separated from Abraham,” may be understood in this way: he separated the scribes and Pharisees, who blasphemed the Lord, from Abraham, who saw the Lord’s day and rejoiced (John 8). For if they were Abraham’s children, they would do Abraham’s works. The Apostle also argues that those should be called children of Abraham who possess a likeness to Abraham’s faith (Heb. 11)—that is, the people of the nations, who are called children of Abraham not on the basis of works but of faith.

### (Chapter 30: Verses 1ff.)

“Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord, who make a plan, but not from me, and weave a web, but not through my Spirit, adding sin upon sin. You are setting out to go down to Egypt, but you have not consulted my mouth, hoping for help from Pharaoh’s strength and trusting in the shadow of Egypt. Pharaoh’s strength will become your shame, and trust in Egypt’s shadow your disgrace. For your princes are in Tanis, and your messengers have reached as far as Hanes” [or “Anes”]. “All are ashamed because of a people that cannot profit them; it has not been for help or any benefit, but for shame and reproach.”

The Septuagint: “Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord. You made a plan, but not through me, and a covenant, but not through my Spirit, adding sins to sins. You go in order to descend into Egypt, but you did not consult me, so that you might receive help from Pharaoh and be protected by the Egyptians. Pharaoh’s protection will become your shame, and for those who trust in Egypt, reproach. For the princes are in Tanis, and the evil messengers will labor in vain for a people that will not benefit them by giving aid—not for benefit, but for shame and reproach.”

After the prophecy against Ariel and the other matters that the preceding exposition has discussed up to this point, this is now the beginning of another prophecy. It is shown to have been fulfilled after the one hundred and fifty years that intervened between Isaiah and Jeremiah.

He foretells the history that we read in the Book of Jeremiah (Jer. 41): when Jerusalem had been overthrown and all its wealth and princes had been transferred to Babylon, Godoliah son of Ahikam, of royal descent, was appointed over those who remained in Judea. After he was treacherously killed together with the Chaldeans who were with him, all the military commanders, Johanan son of Kareah, and Jeconiah son of Josiah, together with the remaining populace from the least to the greatest, came to Jeremiah the prophet and said to him: “Let our prayer fall before you, and pray for us to the Lord your God concerning all these remnants. For we have been left few from among the many, as your eyes see; and may the Lord your God announce to us the way by which we should go and the word that we should do” (Jer. 42:2–3).

When, after ten days, Jeremiah answered them from the word of the Lord, he said: “Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: If you remain quietly in this land, I will build you up and not destroy you; I will plant you and not uproot you, for I have relented concerning the evil that I did to you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you fear in terror” (ibid. 42:11).

And shortly afterward: “But if you say, ‘We will not remain in this land,’ and you set your faces to enter Egypt and go there to dwell, the sword that you fear will overtake you there, and the famine about which you are anxious will cling to you in Egypt; there you will die” (ibid. 42:13, 15–16).

The proud men answered Jeremiah, saying: “You are speaking a lie. The Lord our God did not send you, saying, ‘Do not enter Egypt to dwell there’; rather, Baruch son of Neriah is inciting you against us, in order to hand us over to the Chaldeans, so that they may kill us and lead us away into Babylon” (Jer. 43:2–3).

Finally, after gathering all the leaders of the people together with the remnant, the women, and the children [Note: The words “and the king’s daughters” are absent in the Vatican manuscript], they did not listen to the voice of the Lord. They entered Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them, and came to Taphnas. There Jeremiah prophesied, as a sign of the captivity that was to come, against the disobedient people the things contained in his book.

Thus what was afterward going to happen was foretold many years in advance. They are called rebellious and transgressing children because, having abandoned the counsel of God that they had received through Jeremiah, they followed their own will and wove a web, not through the Spirit of God, which resounded to them through Jeremiah’s mouth.

He used “weaving a web” metaphorically, to indicate a wicked plan. They did this in order to increase their former sins by the sin of contention and pride.

“You are going down,” he says, “into Egypt, and you have not consulted my mouth.” [Note: Vatican: “You have gone down, he says, into Egypt and have not consulted my counsel.”] This does not mean that they did not consult him, but that they were unwilling to hear the prophet’s counsel, hoping for help in Pharaoh’s strength and trusting in Egypt’s protection, or shadow.

In place of “Pharaoh’s strength,” which occurs twice in this passage, the Hebrew has *MAOZ* [Hebrew term as printed]. We have noted this so that, when we read at the end of Daniel (Dan. 11) in the vision of God *MAOZIM* [Hebrew term as printed], we may understand it not, as Porphyry imagines, as the god of the village Modin [or Moden], but as the strong and mighty God.

Among the Egyptians, Pharaoh is the name of royal power. Each king is called by a particular name, such as Pharaoh Neco and Pharaoh Vaphres [or Vaphre], just as if we were to place the names “Caesars” and “Augustuses” before the proper names of kings.

“And Pharaoh’s strength,” he says, “will become your shame, and trust in Egypt’s shadow your disgrace.”

The same Jeremiah writes that in the Egyptian city of Taphnas he buried stones at the gate of Pharaoh’s house and said to the Jewish men: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will send for and take Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant, and I will set his throne upon these stones that I have hidden, and he will establish his seat upon them. He will come and strike the land of Egypt: those destined for death, to death; those destined for captivity, to captivity; and those destined for the sword, to the sword. He will kindle a fire in the shrines of the gods of Egypt and burn them, and he will take them captive. He will clothe himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd clothes himself with his cloak, and he will go out from there in peace” (Jer. 43:10–12).

After the Egyptians were conquered, the Jews who had fled to the Egyptians were also captured.

The following words—“Your princes will be in Tanis, and your messengers have reached as far as Hanes”—should be read with mockery and emphasis: having rejected God’s counsel, they sent their princes to the Egyptian city of Tanis, where Pharaoh’s royal house was situated and where, under Moses, many signs and wonders were performed. The Psalmist says: “He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis” (Ps. 77:43).

Isaiah likewise speaks against Egypt: “Where are your wise men now? Let them announce to you and tell you what the Lord of hosts has planned against Egypt. The princes of Tanis have failed” (Isa. 19:12–13). He recalls that they failed at the time when the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud.

We do not read elsewhere of Hanes as an Egyptian city. But from the statement, “Your messengers have reached as far as Hanes,” we understand it to be the last city of Egypt, near the Ethiopians and Blemmyes [or Blembas]. For this reason the Septuagint translated: “The evil messengers will labor in vain; those who trusted in the people of Egypt, which could not profit them, will be in everlasting reproach.”

Some think that this passage was written against the ten tribes in Samaria, because, while seeking aid from the Egyptians, they were captured by the Assyrians.

According to the figurative interpretation, all who, having despised the worship of God, return to their vomit and, having lost the name of children, are called shameless dogs, make a plan not through the Lord and strike a covenant not through the Spirit of the Lord. They add sins to sins, so that, overcome by flattering vices, they also receive the perversity of doctrines and descend into the darkness of Egypt, seeking the help of Pharaoh, who reigns in Egypt. His protection leads to disgrace and everlasting reproach.

Their princes are in Tanis—that is, in a lowly and degraded command—and they are evil messengers who labor in vain over a people that cannot benefit them. For just as the salvation of disciples assists holy teachers, so the destruction of the deceived destroys the patriarchs of those who fled to the aid of Egypt.

### “The burden of the beasts of the South”

[Note: The Vulgate manuscripts insert here in advance: “The vision of the four-footed creatures in the desert,” the Septuagint version. St. Jerome places this translation shortly afterward in its proper location; in this place its repetition in our manuscripts is superfluous, and the sequence of the exposition is more coherent without it.]

In Hebrew this is called *MASSA BEEMOTH* [or *BEHEMOTH*] *NEGEB* [Hebrew terms as printed], which the Septuagint translated, “The vision of the four-footed creatures in the desert.”

The preceding exposition, which we developed at length by rehearsing the history, is the interpretation of this passage. In accordance with prophetic usage, “burden”—that is, the weight and load of torments and punishments—came not only upon Babylon, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Egypt, the desert sea, Idumea, Arabia, the valley of Zion, and finally Tyre, but also upon the beasts of the South, which the Septuagint translated as “four-footed creatures in the desert.”

This signifies the tribe of Judah, which is situated in the southern region and borders on the wilderness, and those who, rejecting Jeremiah’s prophecy, after Jerusalem had been captured, were unwilling to live in Judea but fled through the desert to the Egyptians.

They are rightly called the beasts of the South, or four-footed creatures in the desert, because they rejected knowledge of God and, despising his command, fled to the images of Egypt, placing their hope in Pharaoh. Whoever leans upon him is like one who leans upon a reed that breaks and wounds the hand of the one relying upon it.

The sons of Korah spoke of such beasts in the Psalm: “When a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13).

The following words—“This way of theirs is a stumbling block to them”—may rightly be understood of the present chapter: the way through the desert became their downfall.

I have recently read that the beasts of the South and the four-footed creatures in the desert—those who, abandoning the boundaries of Judea, fled to the darkness of Egypt—refer to spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places and to the rulers of these darknesses, who lost all their wealth and former riches through their desire for Egypt. That is what he said.

We, following the figurative interpretation, shall discuss matters that we have not yet set forth. We say that all who, abandoning the Creator, have given themselves over to the errors of the world are four-footed creatures in the desert of this world. They may vainly hope for help from it, since they have abandoned the true help of God.

### (Verses 6–7)

“In a land of tribulation and distress are the lioness and the lion; from them come the viper and the flying serpent, carrying their riches on the shoulders of beasts and their treasures on the hump of camels, to a people that cannot benefit them. Egypt will help in vain and to no purpose.”

The Septuagint: “In tribulation and distress are the lion and the lion’s cub; from there come asps and offspring of flying asps, carrying their riches upon donkeys and camels to a nation that will not benefit them. The Egyptians will benefit you with empty and futile things.”

For “lion,” the Hebrew has *LEIS* [or *LEHIS*; Hebrew term as printed]. For “flying serpent,” which the Septuagint translated as “offspring of flying asps,” *ἐμπρηστής* is used; we may call it “the burning one,” and in Hebrew it is called *SARAPH* [Hebrew term as printed]. [Note: The Hebrew term corresponds to Greek *ἐμπρηστής* and means “advancing.” The Erasmian edition, characteristically, intrudes the Hebrew word *meophet* here in place of the Greek *ἐμπρηστής*, which all manuscript codices retain. Marianus, though professing to follow very ancient handwritten exemplars, makes a worse emendation and, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscripts, changes what is entirely correct. Anyone who wishes may compare this passage, corrupted in many ways in the text and notes, and will find this statement true. —Martianus. The passage is sound; Victorius, indulging his conjectures, corrupts it badly.]

Again, where we translated “carrying upon the shoulders of beasts,” all the translators alike rendered “young asses” (*πῶλοι*), that is, foals of donkeys.

The land of tribulation and distress signifies the immense desolation of the wilderness, through which the remnant of Jerusalem, together with Johanan son of Kareah and the daughters of King Zedekiah, fled to Egypt after taking with them everything they could possess.

Understand the lioness and the lion’s cub metaphorically as Jerusalem and its people. Balaam says in Numbers: “Behold, a people will rise like a lioness and lift itself up like a lion. It will not lie down until it devours its prey and drinks the blood of the slain” (Num. 23:24).

It is also written in Ezekiel: “Take up a lament over the prince of Israel and say: Why did your mother, a lioness, lie down among lions? In the midst of young lions she raised her cubs” (Ezek. 19:1–2).

And lest we suppose that Holy Scripture is literally speaking about a lioness and a lion, it speaks contrary to the nature of things when it says that a viper and a flying serpent, or offspring of flying asps, were born from a lioness and a lion. This signifies that worse children were generated from evil parents. Concerning them the Gospel also spoke: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matt. 3:7).

And to the land of Israel it is said: “You are a land upon which no rain has fallen and upon which no shower has come in the day of wrath. Its princes are in its midst like roaring lions, seizing prey and devouring souls by their power” (above, 5).

These offspring of vipers, or flying asps—that is, the princes of the people and the entire multitude of the impious—went to a people that could not benefit them. Jeremiah says that the Lord would deliver Pharaoh Vaphres, king of Egypt, into the hand of his enemies and into the hands of those seeking his life, and that all the men of Judah who were in the land of Egypt would be consumed by sword and famine until their destruction.

The Hebrews report that, before Nebuchadnezzar captured Egypt, Jeremiah and Baruch escaped the imminent captivity by dying.

Some have interpreted the lioness and the lion’s cub as the heavenly Jerusalem and the people deceived from it; the flying serpent, the vipers, and the offspring of asps as the one whom we read of above (chapters 14 and 27) as the twisting serpent, and of whom the Savior spoke in the Gospel: “I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10:18). He is called the dragon in the Apocalypse (Rev. 12), and he dragged down with himself to earth a third of the stars. Through the perversity of their judgment, these lost their former riches, abandoning them in the Egypt of this world.

### “Therefore I cried out concerning this: It is nothing but pride; be still.”

For reasons I do not know, the Septuagint translators rendered this: “Announce these things, because this consolation of yours is vain.”

Symmachus translated it: “There are tumults in which to dwell” [Note: In the Vatican manuscript, *ταραχή* is written in the singular.]

The Hebrew word is *REEB* [or *REHEB*; Hebrew term as printed]. Aquila translated it as *ὅρμημα*, that is, “impetus” and “pride”; Symmachus as “disturbance”; the Septuagint as “vanity”; and Theodotion as “breadth.” It is written with three letters, resh, he, and beth, and it is the same word that is read in the Psalms: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me” (Ps. 86:4).

The sense is this: Since there is vain help among the Egyptians, I commanded it—that is, Jerusalem—or I cried out that the Egyptians possessed only the name of a kingdom and pride without strength, and that Israel should sit or dwell in its own land and not seek help vainly from the weak.

### (Verse 8)

“Now go in, write this before them upon a boxwood tablet; inscribe it carefully in a book, and it shall be for the last day as a testimony forever.”

The Hebrews say that, since there is one Spirit among the prophets and all times are joined together before the Lord, Jeremiah is commanded—and this is God’s command—to enter Egypt and write for them upon boxwood, which is an imperishable wood; or, as Symmachus translated, *ἐπὶ πτυχῇ* [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *ἐπὶ πτυχῆς*], that is, upon a very broad tablet.

“Before them” plainly means before the Jews. He is to explain it carefully in a book, so that there may be no difficulty in reading it, and so that, when the prophecy has been fulfilled by events, they may understand that the word of the prophets is true.

We pass over what is obvious, so that we may linger over what is obscure.

### (Verses 9ff.)

“For this is a people provoking to anger, lying children, children unwilling to hear the law of God. They say to the seers, ‘Do not see,’ and to those who look, ‘Do not look for us at the things that are right. Speak to us pleasing things; see for us errors. Take away from me the way; turn aside from me the path; let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face.’”

It is clear that they provoked the Lord to anger because they were unwilling to hear Jeremiah’s words (Jer. 43). They said to him: “Do not show us what we do not want. Do not forbid us the road to Egypt, and do not proclaim the things that are right; speak instead what pleases us, so that we may go into Egypt,” thereby piling sins upon sins.

“Why do you force upon us what we do not willingly hear? Why do you show us a way by which we do not wish to enter? Why do you repeatedly proclaim in our ears, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel’? Let this preaching cease from us.”

According to the figurative interpretation, all heretics are called lying children. They went out from us, but they were not of us (1 John 2). They do not hear the Law of God with the ears of the inner person, and they say to the teachers of the Churches: “Do not show us what is right, and do not threaten us with the flames of Gehenna. Instead, promise us the kingdoms of heaven, so that after luxury and pleasures paradise may be opened to us.”

“Why do you show me the way of the Lord, by which I do not willingly enter? Why do you repeat the name of the Holy One of Israel, or the word of Israel, which does not penetrate the secrets of my breast?”

This is also said to the people of the Church who are negligent, if they reject the severity of their teachers and favor flatterers.

### (Verses 12–14)

“Therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel: Because you rejected this word and hoped in slander and tumult, and relied upon it, therefore this iniquity will be for you like a breach that falls, a fracture in a lofty wall; for suddenly, when it is not expected, its collapse will come. And it will be shattered as a potter’s vessel is crushed with a mighty breaking, so that no potsherd will be found among its fragments in which to carry a coal from the fire, or [Note: Likewise, “from which a little water may be drawn from the pit”] to draw a little water from a pool.”

“Because,” he says, “you said above, ‘Let the Holy One of Israel cease from before our face,’ or, as the Septuagint translated, ‘Take away from us the word of Israel,’ therefore thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel. Against your will he presses himself upon you, so that you may experience as punisher the one whose warning you neglected.

You trusted in the Egyptians’ slander and falsehood and relied upon their tumult, or contradiction and pride, as Symmachus and Theodotion translated it. Therefore this iniquity, or sin, will be turned upon you, so that you will be like the suddenly collapsing wall of a very strong and captured city whose ruin has suddenly arrived. This is how the Septuagint translated it.

The sense according to the Hebrew is this: Just as a breach in a very high wall, whose collapse has long been in progress, is difficult to restore and return to its former beauty, so sudden destruction will come upon you.

To use another comparison: When a potter’s vessel is broken with a mighty breaking, it is shattered into pieces, so that scarcely a small potsherd remains among the fragments in which a coal may be carried, or a little water drawn from a pool and pit. So you, when you go into Egypt and Nebuchadnezzar pursues you there, will perish completely.

Heretics and every doctrine opposed to the truth likewise trust in slander and falsehood and murmur, according to the Septuagint, against their Creator. Therefore the city of their impiety will be destroyed—the city Cain built—and sudden destruction will come upon it when it has been captured by ecclesiastical men. It will be so destroyed and shattered that nothing will remain in it capable of rekindling an extinguished fire or of offering even muddy and scanty water to thirsty peoples.

(Vers. 15 ff.) “For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: If you return and remain quiet, you shall be saved; in silence and in hope shall be your strength.” But you were unwilling, and you said, “By no means; rather, we shall flee to the horses.” Therefore you shall flee, and you shall mount swift steeds; therefore those who pursue you shall be swift. A thousand men shall flee at the threat of one; and at the threat of five you shall flee.

**LXX:** “Thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel: When you have returned and groaned”—[Note: [Col. 0343D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “when you have returned and groaned.”]—“then you shall be saved, and you shall know where you were, because you trusted in vain things; your strength has become vain. And you were unwilling to listen, but you said, ‘We shall flee upon horses’; therefore you shall flee, and we shall be upon swift riders; therefore those who pursue you shall be swift.” A thousand shall flee at the voice of one, and at the voice of five many shall flee.

The Holy One, he says—the one whose name I had previously left unmentioned—is the Lord God, who speaks to you both through me and through Jeremiah (Jerem. XII): If you repent, whether by abandoning your vices or by abandoning the error of your wicked counsel, and remain in Judaea, fearing not the assault of the Babylonians [Note: [Col. 0344D] Again the same manuscript reads, “the dominion of the Babylonians,” but, etc.] but my commands, you shall be saved. Remain quiet and hope in the Lord, and grasp the strength of faith in my promises. But you, despising the life-giving commands, said in despair, “By no means will it be as you say; rather, we shall flee for refuge to the Egyptian horses, and we shall proceed to them with a rapid and swift step.” Since, therefore, you have said this, you shall indeed flee, and with headlong speed you shall enter Egypt; but the Babylonians, who will pursue you even to Egypt, shall be swifter than you. Such terror and dread will seize Egypt that one thousand Egyptians will be unable to withstand a single Chaldaean, and a great multitude of fugitives will flee before five enemies, in accordance with what we read in Deuteronomy: “The Lord will cause you to fall before your enemies. You shall go out against them by one road, and you shall flee before them by seven roads, and you shall be scattered among all the kingdoms of the earth” (Deut. XXVIII, 25, 32).

According to the allegorical sense and the edition of the LXX, the divine discourse exhorts all sinners to repentance, and especially heretics: when they have turned back from their vices, groaned, and done penance, they shall be saved; and then they shall understand where they previously were, and that they had hoped in vain things. Yet while he exhorts them to repentance, they, on the contrary, trust in false teachers and in the uncertainty of the world. Unwilling to hear the words of God, they desire the Egyptian horses and rejoice in their speed—horses whose multiplication the Lord prohibited (Deut. XVII). Therefore ecclesiastical men will pursue them swiftly, and they will be unable to withstand the voice of one warrior, or of five combatants—which we must refer to the mind and to the five senses—when a thousand men and an undisciplined crowd of fugitives flee.

(Vers. 17.) “Until you are left like a ship’s mast upon the summit of a mountain, and like a signal upon a hill.”

Jeremiah also writes that, after those who had fled into Egypt had been killed by sword and famine, only a few remained who returned to Judaea (Jerem. XLVI). And just as, when a ship has been broken and its framework destroyed, only the pole called the mast remains and is set up as a signal on the top of a mountain or on a high hill, so scarcely one or two will remain as a sign and token, to demonstrate the power of God. “And then,” he says, “all the remnant of Judah who now enter the land of Egypt in order to dwell there shall know, when they have returned to the land of Judah, whose word shall be fulfilled, mine or theirs.”

(Vers. 18.) “Therefore the Lord waits, so that he may have mercy upon you; and therefore he will be exalted, sparing you, because the Lord is a God of judgment. Blessed are all who wait for him.”

Great is the clemency of God, that he waits for our repentance; and until we turn away from our vices, he restrains his powerful hand, lest he be compelled to strike. He has mercy and spares us so that his mercy may be exalted and the goodness of the Creator become known to all. Or certainly, according to what he says in the Gospel—“When I have been lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII, 32)—he is lifted up upon the cross so that he may spare all.

For he is the God of judgment; and blessed are all who wait for the Lord, who waits for their conversion. Whose conversion this is, and what kind it is, the following words will show.

(Vers. 19.) “For the people of Sion shall dwell in Jerusalem.”

The Jews refer this to the time of Cyrus, when the people returned from Babylon to Judaea under Zerubbabel and Jesus the High Priest. But we, as we have often already said, should refer all the promises that exceed the modest scale of that period to the coming of Christ. In him the people who had once been captive, liberated through the Lord’s passion, dwelt in Sion and Jerusalem—that is, in the watchtower and in the vision of peace, namely, in the Church.

Moreover, since the LXX add the word “holy,” saying, “For the holy people dwells [Al. shall dwell] in Sion,” we can interpret this by saying that no one dwells in Sion except one who is holy and hears the Lord say: “Be holy, because I also am holy” (Lev. XI, 44).

(Vers. 20.) “You shall certainly no longer weep; he will surely have mercy upon you. At the voice of your cry, as soon as he hears, he will answer you.”

When you have returned to Sion and dwelt in Jerusalem, you will no longer weep as you wept before, but your mourning will be turned into joy: “Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh” (Luke VI, 21). And after you have cried out and said to the Lord, “I cried with my whole heart; hear me, Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 145); and again, “I cried out: Have mercy on me, and I shall keep your commandments” (Ps. LXXXV); and elsewhere, “I kept watch at dawn and cried out” (Ps. CXVIII, 147)—and your voice has become so clear that it penetrates the heavens—the Lord will immediately answer you, and you will be like Moses, of whom it is written: “Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him” (Exod. XIX, 20).

(Vers. 21.) “And the Lord will give you scant bread and little water.”

If we refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, the interpretation is easy: there was not complete joy under him, since David says, “When the Lord restored the captivity of Sion, we became like those who are comforted,” meaning that they received not full and perfect consolation but only the likeness of consolation.

But if it refers to the coming of the Savior, “scant bread and little water,” according to the Apostle Paul and this same prophet Isaiah, foretells the Gospel proclamation. In place of the many-fragmented observances and commandments of the Law, it gathered everything into one commandment: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” For “the Lord made his word complete and concise upon the earth” (Galat. V).

(Vers. 22.) “And he will no longer cause your teacher to fly away from you”—[Note: [Col. 0345] The words “from you” occur neither in the Hebrew nor in Jerome’s translation of that text.]—“and your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear a word behind you, warning you: ‘This is the way; walk in it,’ neither to the right nor to the left.”

**LXX:** “And those who deceive you shall no longer approach you, because your eyes shall see those who led you astray, and your ears shall hear behind you the words of those who deceive you, who said, ‘This is the way; let us walk in it,’ whether to the right or to the left.”

The edition of the LXX and the Hebrew differ greatly in this passage. We shall therefore first discuss the Vulgate edition, and afterward follow the order of the truth.

When the eyes of the heart have understood and perceived the truth, and when they have recognized with the full reasoning of the mind those who previously deceived them, and with instructed ears have discerned behind them the words of their deceivers—for they are always eager to deceive the blind part of the body, in accordance with what we read in the Psalm: “That they may shoot in darkness at the upright in heart” (Ps. X, 2)—those deceivers assume such authority for themselves that, whether they teach what is right or what is left, that is, whether good or evil, they do not want their disciples to examine matters rationally but want them to follow them as leaders. Then those who previously deceived them will no longer be able to approach them once they realize that they have been understood.

According to the Hebrew, however, the explanation is both easy and true. When the Lord has given believers scant bread and little water, he will no longer cause the one who teaches knowledge to fly away from them. Rather, his eyes will always see his teacher, and his ears will hear the word of the one warning behind him and saying: “This is the straight way; walk in it,” neither to the right nor to the left, in accordance with what is read elsewhere: “We shall not turn aside to the right or to the left; we shall walk by the royal road” (Num. XX, 17).

For in either direction whatever exceeds measure is vicious. Concerning the right-hand ways it is said: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Eccl. VII, 17). Concerning the left-hand ways, there is no doubt that they are assigned to the goats and to those who perish.

(Vers. 23.) “And you will defile the plates of your silver images and the garment of your golden cast image, and you will scatter them like the uncleanness of a menstruating woman; you will say to it, ‘Go forth.’”

**LXX:** “And you will defile your silver-plated and gold-plated idols; you will crush them and scatter them like menstrual water, and you will cast them away like dung.”

When you have understood the truth, and those who deceive you no longer approach you, but your eyes see your teacher and your ears continually hear, “This is the way; walk in it,” neither to the right nor to the left, then you will crush and scatter all errors, idols, and likenesses of the truth that the craftsman-tongue had composed in the splendor of eloquence—which is signified by silver—and in the reasoning of wisdom—which is signified by gold. You will judge them so unclean that you will compare them with the most filthy blood of a menstruating woman, which the Septuagint translated in other words as “menstrual water.”

(Vers. 24.) “And rain shall be given to your seed wherever you sow it in the land, and the bread of the produce of the land shall be exceedingly abundant and rich.” [Note: [Col. 0347D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “The bread of the produce of your land shall be abundant and rich.”]

**LXX:** “Then there shall be rain for the seed of your land, and the bread of the produce of your land shall be abundant and rich.”

It is written in the Book of Kings (III Kings XVIII) that, after Elijah had killed the false prophets, rain was given to the land of Israel; and that the bread of Elisha and afterward of the Savior was exceedingly abundant and rich, possessing such fullness that many thousands of people were satisfied by it (IV Kings IV; John VI).

Thus also in the present passage, spiritual seed will not first receive rain, nor will the bread of the land become exceedingly abundant and rich, unless the silver-plated and gold-plated idols have been crushed and reckoned as dung. For unless vices withdraw, virtues do not enter.

(Vers. 25.) “And the lamb shall feed spaciously upon your possession in that day. And your bulls and the colts of asses that work the ground shall eat a mixed fodder, as it was winnowed on the threshing floor.” [Al. “as it was winnowed on the threshing floor.”]

**LXX:** “And your beasts shall feed in that day in a rich and spacious place. Your bulls and your oxen that work the ground shall eat mixed straw in winnowed barley.”

Amid the abundance of all things, when heavenly rain descends and that bread comes down from heaven—he who eats it shall never hunger—the lambs will feed in a very spacious place. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and they are always on the right.

The bulls, however, are the leaders of the flock, concerning whom we read, “The assembly of bulls among the cows of the peoples” (Ps. LXVII, 31). The colts of asses are those upon which the Lord sat when he entered Jerusalem (Matt. XXI). Since they work the ground, they will eat from the threshing floor after it has been winnowed, so that no straw will be mixed into their food, concerning which it is written in Jeremiah: “What has straw to do with wheat, says the Lord?” (Jerem. XXIII); and which in the Gospel is burned with unquenchable fire (Luke III).

According to the LXX, however, the beasts—who are not yet full of reason and wisdom, and concerning whom one says to God, “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII, 23)—will feed in a very rich and spacious place. It produces neither thorns nor thistles but, like the land of Israel, flows with milk and honey and grants full liberty to those who feed there.

The bulls and oxen who work the ground—that is, the Apostles and apostolic men—are those concerning whom the Apostle Paul interprets the Scripture: “You shall not muzzle the ox that treads out the grain. Is God concerned about oxen?” (I Cor. IX, 9). Rather, he is certainly speaking about those who work their own ground and of whom he says: “We are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (I Cor. III, 9). For the Father is the farmer, and Christ is the vine (John XV).

They will eat mixed straw with winnowed barley. We read that Isaac sowed barley and, because he was among foreigners, received a hundredfold harvest of barley (Gen. XXVI). Hosea also acquired a woman adulterous with a homer and a half-homer of barley (Hos. III). The Savior likewise satisfied five thousand men [Note: [Col. 0347D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “who then [served] the senses,” etc.; and a little later [Col. 0348D], “breaking the five loaves of the Law,” etc.] who still served the bodily senses and followed the Law of Moses with barley loaves (John VI). Elsewhere, breaking seven loaves of the Law and reducing them to fragments, he filled four thousand men with wheat loaves—men who followed the Gospel number (Matt. XV).

Such peoples eat a portion of the straw as well, while in certain matters they follow the letter; yet through the straw [Note: [Col. 0348D] The same manuscript reads, “through the barley straw, little by little,” etc.] and barley they gradually advance so that they may pass over to the wheat.

(Vers. 25.) “And upon every high mountain and upon every elevated hill there shall be streams of running waters in the day of the slaughter of many, when the towers have fallen.”

In this passage the Jews refer the many slain and the falling towers to the power of the Roman Empire, concerning which the Apostle also speaks (II Thess. VII): “Only he who now restrains must continue to restrain, until he is removed from the midst.” They understand that at that time such blessedness will belong to the people of Israel that not only valleys and plains but all mountains and hills will be irrigated by flowing waters.

But we should understand the mountains and hills as those who have been raised on high by their virtues, who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matt. V), and whom the Lord calls to drink. “Whoever drinks of my waters shall never thirst” (John IV). Hence we read in the Psalm: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel” (Ps. LXVII, 27). And in the Gospel it is said that everyone who drinks of the waters of Jesus will have rivers of living water flowing from his belly (John VII).

And the Holy One speaks to God: “For with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10), from which a most pure river proceeds; concerning it Scripture again says: “The rush of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 4). And elsewhere: “The river of God is filled with waters” (Ps. LXIV, 10)—that river, namely, which speaks through Jeremiah: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. II, 13).

This will happen when the many have been killed or have perished. “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX). And when the towers have fallen—whether the powers of demons, or the proud, arrogant, and great ones in this world—concerning whom it is also said in the Psalms: “I saw the wicked man exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon; I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. XXXVI, 35–36).

Those who moved their feet from the East desired to build these towers (Gen. XII); their languages were confused in Babylon, as were those upon whom the tower of Siloam fell (Luke XIII).

(Vers. 26.) “And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, like the light of seven days, on the day when the Lord binds up the wound of his people and heals the stroke of its wound.”

**LXX:** “And the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, on the day when the Lord heals the crushing of his people and cures the pain of your wound.”

I am astonished that in the present passage the Hebrew words *LABANA* (לְבָנָה) and *HAMMA* (חַמָּה), which Aquila interprets as “the white one” and “the heat,” by which he signifies the moon and the sun, were earlier translated by the same LXX as “brick” and “wall” in the passage where it is written, “The moon shall be ashamed, and the sun shall be confounded.” In their place they translated, “The bricks shall melt, and the wall shall fall,” whereas now, following the Hebrew, they have translated “moon” and “sun.” Hence I suspect that they did not err from the beginning, but that the text was gradually corrupted through the fault of scribes. For it is impossible that those who translated the same words correctly in this passage should have erred in the earlier one.

Therefore, on the day of the slaughter of many, when the arrogant and proud have fallen, and those who set their mouth in heaven have learned that they are earth, the light of the moon shall be like the light of the sun. This will be when the Lord gives a new heaven and a new earth, and the form of this world has passed away, so that the moon and the sun may receive the rewards of their labor and course.

“For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God, because creation itself will also be freed from slavery to corruption into the liberty of the glory of the sons of God” (Rom. VIII, 19), although some, understanding these things as instruments of light, maintain that they are insensible.

The moon, therefore, will receive the sun’s radiance. Nor is it strange to think this of that most brilliant element, to which dominion over the night has been given, when it is also written concerning the saints: “The righteous shall shine like the sun” (Matt. XIII, 43). The sun will receive sevenfold light, like the light of seven days, when the world was created in the beginning—although the Septuagint did not translate “seven days”—when the Lord has bound up the wound of his people or healed the crushing of his people.

This will be when what is written is fulfilled: “Pain, mourning, and groaning shall flee away” (Isa. XXXV, 10); when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel shall be saved; or certainly when vengeance comes upon those whose souls cry out beneath the altar: “How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood on those who dwell upon the earth?” (Apoc. VI, 19).

Observe also that he did not say, “when he has healed the crushing of his people Israel,” or “of Jacob,” but simply “of his people,” thereby signifying all who serve God.

Some refer this passage and everything contained in this chapter of promises to the heavenly Jerusalem and to the return of its people, when what is written shall be fulfilled: “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35). Others refer it to the time of Elijah and say that he is the one concerning whom it was written above: “Your eyes shall see your teacher, and your ears shall hear the word of the one warning behind you.” Then, according to the poets’ fables, rivers of milk will flow from the mountains and hills, in the golden age of Saturn, and the purest honey will drip from the leaves of the trees.

Those who accept these things will also accept, through Jewish error, the fable of a thousand years and the earthly reign of the Savior, not understanding that the Apocalypse of John weaves, beneath the surface of the letter, the mysteries of the Church, rich in inner meaning.

**BOOK TEN**

[Col. 0349]

[Col. 0349D] 415–416 The Tenth Book, which we now have in hand, will be shorter than the Ninth and the Eleventh in the number of verses, but not in the greatness of its meaning. For the history of Sennacherib and Rabshakeh and of King Hezekiah follows it. This history could neither be joined to what precedes because of the enormous length of the volume, nor divided because of the continuity of the events.

Therefore, as you wished, virgin of Christ Eustochium, and as we agreed together, just as I dictated the earlier books, I shall dictate this book and the remaining ones, if Christ grants his assent, so that I may join the prophecies together and not tear and rend them apart between the end of one and the beginning of another.

Moreover, I hear that the scorpion, a mute and poisonous animal, is muttering I know not what against the response of my little commentary on the prophet Daniel—indeed, trying to strike, though destined to die in its own pus. [Note: [Col. 0349D] The Vatican manuscript reads, “destined to die in its own work.” “Against the response”: several manuscript copies read “against the pledge”; Erasmus and Marianus followed them, not understanding that there was no pledge of Jerome’s against which Rufinus—the scorpion often compared with him—might mutter, but rather the response in the Preface to the Commentary on Daniel, in which Jerome defends himself, saying: “And I marvel that certain fault-finders are indignant with me, as though I had shortened the book, when Origen, Eusebius, Apollinaris, and other ecclesiastical men and teachers of Greece also admit that these Visions, as I have said, are not found among the Hebrews, and that they ought not to answer Porphyry concerning things that provide no authority for Holy Scripture.” This was the response, not the pledge, which Rufinus was trying to criticize and turn into a charge. MARTIAN.] [Col. 0351A]

The dirge and mournful songs of this scorpion have not yet been revealed to me, and therefore my response has been postponed. Yet I must obey you, and your holy and most learned brother Pammachius, who by letters and with insatiable zeal compels me, once Isaiah is completed, to pass on to Ezekiel. I, however, worn out by weakness of age and body and by the scarcity of secretaries who could assist me with their services, still remain stuck in the same mud, and scarcely expect that I shall finish half of Isaiah in this volume.

But if, with your prayers, I complete it—[Note: [Col. 0351D] The same manuscript reads, “But if, as I think, I complete it.”]—then the remaining books must also be undertaken; they will begin with the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah.

[Col. 0351B] 417 (Vers. 27 ff.) “Behold, the name of the Lord comes from afar: his fury burns, and it is grievous to bear. His lips are filled with indignation, and his tongue is like a devouring fire. His breath is like an overflowing torrent reaching to the middle of the neck, to destroy the nations as nothing, and a bridle of error that was in the jaws of the peoples. [Note: [Col. 0351D] Two manuscripts read, “and a bridle causing error,” which was the earlier reading; a little later, instead of “as the night,” they read “as the voice,” despite the Hebrew text and Jerome’s translation.] You shall have a song, as on the night of a sanctified solemnity, and gladness of heart, like that of one who goes with a flute to enter the mountain of the Lord, to the Mighty One of Israel.”

**LXX:** “Behold, the name of the Lord comes after a long time: his fury burns with glory; the utterance of his lips is an utterance filled with wrath, and the fury of his anger will devour like fire. His breath, like water in a valley, dragging along, shall come up to the neck; and it shall be divided to trouble the nations over their vain error, and error shall be cast away, and he shall take them before their eyes. Must you always rejoice and continually enter into my holy places, as though celebrating festivals and rejoicing, so that you may enter with a flute into the mountain of the Lord, to the God of Israel?”

Let us first discuss the Hebrew. The statements that follow depend upon what has preceded. The prophetic word had rebuked those who, having despised God’s help, fled to the Egyptians out of fear of the Babylonians, and it threatened those who descended into Egypt that they would die there. Again, after the punishments, it promises those who were willing [Al. unwilling] to hear him that they would dwell not only in Jerusalem under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, but would receive a blessedness greater than that of all believers in the word of God at the consummation of the world, when rivers of waters would flow through all the mountains and hills and, after many had been killed, the towers would fall.

The moon and sun also would receive a brighter light when the Lord had bound up and healed the wound of his people. Although some maintain that these things were fulfilled, in a hyperbolical manner, in the time of Cyrus, who released the people from captivity, in the land of Judaea.

Since rewards have therefore been promised to the good and obedient, punishments are now announced, on the contrary, to the wicked and contemptuous: the Lord will fulfill his purpose, come after a long time to punish sinners, pronounce judgment upon all, and kill with the breath of his mouth the impious one whom he calls the bridle of the peoples—not one by which he would govern those subjected to him, but one by which he would drag his subjects to ruin.

He also introduces the likeness of a torrent overflowing as far as the neck, to testify that the end of all things has come. For just as a torrent suffocates the one whose neck it reaches, so the judgment of God will allow no one to depart unpunished.

But when he has destroyed the bridle that was in the jaws of all the nations, together with the nations subjected to it, and has reduced it to nothing, then, he says, there will be for you, the saints who obey my commands, a song like the night [Note: [Col. 0352D] For the same reasons, and as the context itself requires, we restore “night” in place of “voice.”] of a sanctified solemnity, when you came out of Egypt and at the solemnity of Passover cast off the yoke of Egyptian slavery, saying, with Pharaoh drowned in the Red Sea: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified” (Exod. XV, 1).

There will be such joy of heart that you will imitate those who carry the first fruits to the temple and bring gifts to God’s winepresses, proceeding with flutes and displaying the joys of their hearts in song.

I have briefly touched upon these matters according to the Hebrew. In both editions we should note that it is not the Lord but the name of the Lord that comes after a long time. Of this it is said in the Psalms: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; God is the Lord, and he has shone upon us” (Ps. CXVII, 26). And he himself says in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me” (John V, 43).

Beautifully he is said to come after a long time, while human impatience says: “How long, Lord, will you forget me to the end? How long will you turn your face away from me?” (Ps. XII, 1). His burning fury also comes with glory, so that we may fear in his majesty the one whom we despised in his humility.

The same is written in the Psalms: “God will come manifestly; our God, and he will not be silent. Fire will burn before him, and a mighty tempest will surround him” (Ps. XLIX, 3–4). He himself says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled!” (Luke XII, 49).

Again, in another Psalm it is read: “The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire” (Ps. XXVIII, 7), so that the flame may seize and consume whatever in the world is hay, wood, and stubble. [Note: [Col. 0352D] The Vatican manuscript has “a wise flame,” as we observe Jerome wrote elsewhere on more than one occasion.] Hence God is also said to be a consuming fire (Deut. IV).

As for the statement, “The anger of his fury will devour like fire,” many of our people interpret the anger of the Lord’s fury as the devil, to whom we are handed over for punishment, who, according to the Book of Samuel, moved David to number the people of God (II Kings XXIV). The Apostle says: “To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (I Cor. V, 5).

Yet this fury itself, and thus the fury of the Lord, will do nothing according to its own will but only what has been commanded it. Hence it follows: “The utterance of his lips is an utterance filled with wrath.”

His breath also, like water in a valley, dragging along, will come as far as the neck, so that punishments may overflow upon sinners. It will be divided according to the quality of their merits, so that it may destroy and trouble the nations whom vain error had deceived, and so that they may recognize that they have been overthrown.

Hence this is said to such men, who prevailed through the power of this world and delighted in their own error: they will not always continue to do this.

Some of our people think that this passage, and the entire content of the chapter, is spoken against heretics and all doctrines contrary to the truth. When the time of judgment comes, they will not enter his holy places and his mountain—that is, the Church of the Lord—lest under the name of religion they gather riches and abuse themselves with luxury, as though they were celebrating the Lord’s festivals.

The Jews understand these things of the nations Gog and Magog, which they think will come from the north, that is, from the regions of Scythia; Ezekiel speaks about them at greater length (Ezek. XIX).

(Vers. 30 ff.) “And the Lord will cause the glory of his voice to be heard, and he will display the terror of his arm in the threat of fury and in the flame of devouring fire; he will strike in the whirlwind and in the stone of hail. For at the voice of the Lord Assyria will tremble, struck with the rod, and the passage of the rod will be firmly established; the Lord will make it rest upon him with tambourines and lyres, and with mighty battles he will fight against them. For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday, prepared by the king; it is deep and spacious, its nourishment is fire and much wood; the breath of the Lord, like a torrent of sulphur, sets it ablaze.”

**LXX:** “And the Lord will cause the glory of his voice to be heard, and he will display the fury of his arm with fury and wrath. And with a flame of devouring fire he will flash forth violently, and like water and hail descending with force. For at the voice of the Lord the Assyrians shall be overcome by the plague with which he will strike them, and there will be for him, around the place where he had hoped for help and in which he trusted, those very ones who will fight against him with tambourines and lyres, in exchange. For you will be deceived before the days; is a kingdom also prepared for you? A deep valley, wood placed there, fire, and much wood; the fury of the Lord, like a valley set ablaze with sulphur.”

I could indicate to readers, in a continuous exposition according to the Hebrew, what seemed to me to be the meaning. But what shall I do about the zeal of certain people who declare that, unless I also discuss the edition of the Seventy Translators, my work will remain incomplete? I shall therefore follow the order of exposition I have begun.

The voice and command of the Lord will become known to all, and the power of his arm will be revealed to everyone, when the time of retribution comes, with the magnitude of flame, whirlwind, hail, and the weight of stones. Ezekiel writes about this in his prophecy concerning Gog and Magog, as we said, at length (Ezek. XXXVIII and XXIX).

At the command of his voice Assyria will tremble, struck by the rod. Every impious person, every imitator of the hostile nation—not because an Assyrian alone will be struck on the day of judgment, but because by the Assyrian we should understand the devil.

For it follows: “And the passage of the rod will be firmly established, which the Lord will make rest upon him.” The meaning is this: the rod will not strike him and then lift itself again, bringing the punishment to an end in the manner of those who beat someone; rather, as though firmly established and fixed with a deep root, it will make the punishment remain upon him.

But if this is understood in this way, where will the devil’s repentance be—especially since it is said to sinners: “Go into the eternal fire, which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41)?

“With tambourines and lyres and mighty battles he will fight against them”: the Lord will fight against demons and all the impious with the joy of all.

For Topheth has been prepared from yesterday and from ancient time by the Lord the King—[Note: [Col. 0353] Previously the reading was “Theopheth”; the manuscripts, however, read “Thopeth.”—] that is, the broad and spacious Gehenna, [Col. 0354B] which will burn them with everlasting fires. Its nourishment and fuel are fire and much wood—that is, perpetual flame and the punishments of sinners.

And because, as the prophetic word had spoken of a furnace and a blazing kiln, he preserves the metaphor, so that we may know that this place is kindled by the breath, spirit, and will of the Lord, with sulphur mixed in, which intensifies the flames and makes the torments more severe.

But according to the LXX, where it says, “At the voice of the Lord the Assyrians shall be overcome by the plague with which he will strike them, and there will be for him around the place where he had hoped for help and in which he trusted; they themselves will fight against him with tambourines and lyres, in exchange,” the meaning is that those who were once subject to the devil will rise up against him and fight him with joy and gladness, in a sudden exchange, while recognizing their error and destroying the one by whom they had been deceived.

And it is said to him that from the beginning he deceived himself, imagining that his kingdom was eternal, although Gehenna and eternal punishments had been prepared for him.

### (Chapter XXXI.—Verses 1 ff.) Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, placing their hope in horses and trusting in chariots because they may be many—or, alternatively, “are” many—and in horsemen because they are exceedingly strong, but who have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel and have not sought the Lord. Yet he is wise and has brought evil upon them; he has not withdrawn his words, and he will rise against the house of the wicked and against the help of those who practice iniquity. Egypt is man and not God; their horses are flesh and not spirit. When the Lord bends—or, alternatively, has bent—his hand, the helper will fall, and the one who is being helped will collapse; together they will all be consumed.

After the oracle concerning the beasts of the South, and those who were carrying their wealth into Egypt to a people who could not benefit them—those who hoped for help in Pharaoh’s strength and trusted in Egypt’s shadow—the prophetic word had announced, under the appearance of a return to Jerusalem and the release of the captivity under Cyrus, the consummation of the age and the perfect blessedness of the righteous. Now it returns to those to whom it had spoken above, warning them not to go down to Egypt. The difference between the present passage and the earlier one is this: there the tribe of Judah is commanded not to go down to Egypt; here it is prophesied that, having despised the Lord’s command, they will go down. It is also foretold that by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, both Israel and the Egyptians—both the fugitives and those who helped them—will alike be slaughtered. Jeremiah speaks of this at full length (Jer. XLII).

Woe, then, to those who go down to Egypt and, fearing the Chaldeans, despise the Lord’s commands, hoping in idolaters who boast that they possess the worship of God; and who trust in the aid of horses, not knowing what is written: “The horse is deceptive for salvation” (Ps. XXXII, 17). They place their confidence in chariots, wagons, and horsemen, and do not remember that Song: “He cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exod. XV, 1). They have not trusted in the Holy One of Israel, who, through Jeremiah, was promising his help to those remaining in the land of Judah. And they have not sought the Lord—not because they did not seek him, but because, when sought, they despised his words. Hence it is also said of wicked priests: “They devour my people; they have not called upon the Lord” (Ps. LII, 5–6).

But he who is wise—that is, the Lord—has brought evil upon them, and the very worst of men, namely Nebuchadnezzar; or simply “evil,” signifying a thing rather than a person. He has not withdrawn his words, which he had spoken through the Prophets. Therefore he will rise against the tribe of Judah, the house of the wicked, and against the help of the Egyptians who practice iniquity. For Egypt, or “the Egyptian,” as the Septuagint translated it, is man and not God; their horses are flesh and not spirit. Hence it is written in Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He will be like a tamarisk in the desert, and will not see when good things come” (Jer. XVII, 5–6). And elsewhere it is written: “Vain is the salvation of man” (Ps. LIX, 13), or, as it is better rendered in Hebrew, “in man.”

When the Lord stretches out his hand to punish—or bends it, under the metaphor of a charioteer, and loosens the reins of running horses—the Egyptian helper will collapse, together with Israel, for whom help was being provided. This may also be understood of those who, in a time of persecution, tribulation, and distress, do not trust in the Lord but in the help of the Egyptians, that is, worldly people. They do not know that Abraham was endangered in Egypt, and that God’s people served there in clay and bricks, in that region which spiritually is called the iron furnace. Hence it is also read in the Apocalypse of John: “The place where the Lord was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt”—or, alternatively, “the Egyptian” (Apoc. XI, 8).

### (Verses 4–5.) For thus the Lord said to me: As when a lion or a lion’s cub roars over its prey, and a multitude of shepherds comes against it, it will not fear their voice and will not be terrified by their multitude, so the Lord of hosts will descend to fight upon Mount Zion and upon its hill. As birds flying, so the Lord of hosts will protect Jerusalem, protecting and delivering it, passing over and saving it.

In passages that are clear, we present one edition, especially where there is no difference in meaning. After the Israelites and Egyptians in whose help they had trusted have been slaughtered in Egypt, the captives will return—or, alternatively, return— to Jerusalem under Cyrus. By means of two comparisons, the strength of the Lord, who had promised that he would be their helper, is displayed.

As a lion and a hungry lion’s cub, when they see a flock of sheep, are not frightened by any shepherd’s voice and, conscious of their own strength, despise their multitude, so the Lord of hosts will fight—not against Mount Zion and its hill, but upon Mount Zion against its adversaries.

Let us give another comparison. When birds are protecting their young, they fly over their nests; and whether they see a serpent or a man, or other birds approaching their chicks, they forget their weakness and fight with beak and claws, repeating the pain of their breast with their chattering cry. So the Lord will protect Jerusalem, pass over it, deliver it, and save it.

In place of “passing over,” the Hebrew has **PHASE**. In three translators besides the Septuagint, **ὑπερβαίνων** (“passing over”) is used. From this it is clear that Passover—that is, the Lord’s Phase—signifies not passion but passage.

That the Lord was a protector over Jerusalem in the likeness of birds, he himself testifies in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matt. XXIII, 37), “how often”—or, alternatively, “daily”—“I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling?” And in Deuteronomy it is said of the Lord: “He spread out his wings, received them, and carried them upon his shoulders” (Deut. XXXII, 11).

**Note:** In Hebrew, *Phase*. All manuscript codices read this without exception; Erasmus and Marianus, however, preferred to place in Jerome’s text the Hebrew word supplied with the Masoretic points, namely *pasoahh*. **Martianus.** Consult the Commentaries on Micah and on Matthew, chapter XXVI.

### (Verses 6 ff.) Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the deep, O children of Israel. For on that day each man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands made for you as a sin. And Assyria will fall by a sword not of a man, and a sword not belonging to a human being will devour it; it will flee, not from the face of the sword, and its young men will become tributaries. Its strength will pass away in terror, and its princes will tremble as they flee, says the Lord, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

**Note:** Two Vatican manuscripts and one Palatine manuscript of the Septuagint, although they translated the earlier passages in the same way, differ at the end, reading: “Its young men will be overcome,” and so forth. Indeed, you see that they differ from the others only in the final words.

**Septuagint:** Turn back, as you had withdrawn into the deep, O children of Israel. For on that day each man will cast away the idols of his silver and the idols of his gold, which your hands made for you as a sin. And Assyria will fall by a sword not of a man, and a sword not belonging to a human being will devour it; it will flee, not from the face of the sword; its young men will be overcome. For they will be surrounded by a rock as by a rampart, and they will be defeated; but whoever flees will be captured. Thus says the Lord: Blessed is the one who has seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem.

While the Lord fights upon Mount Zion against its adversaries and protects it in the likeness of birds, the words “Turn back, O children of Israel”—or, as Symmachus translated, “Repent, you who have withdrawn from the Lord through deep counsel and sin”—are addressed to them. For if you do this, casting away the golden and silver idols which became a sin for you, and because of which your city was captured, Assyria will fall. The object of your present flight, feared by you, will fall not by the sword of men or the strength of an army, but by the power of God.

This signifies the Angel by whom one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians were destroyed in a single night. The Assyrian king himself will also flee, not from a human sword but from the wrath of God, so that his young and vigorous men will become tributaries to the Medes, of whom it was earlier said against Babylon: “Behold, I will raise up the Medes against you.” The strength of Assyria will pass away and depart before the Lord’s terror, and all its princes will tremble.

For the Lord has spoken and promised, and for him to speak is to accomplish. He is the one who has fire in Zion and a furnace in Jerusalem, so that, like straw and wood, his adversaries may be consumed by the flame issuing from Jerusalem.

Another interprets the words “On that day each man will cast away the idols of his silver,” and what follows, as testifying that from the return from the Babylonian captivity until the coming of Christ the children of Israel never again worshiped idols. He also understands “the Assyrian” in the present passage as one to be overcome not by the Angel but by the Medes: that the ancient and once-powerful kingdom, after offending the Lord, was destroyed and served its conquerors.

The Nazarenes understand this passage as follows: O children of Israel, who by an evil counsel denied the Son of God, return to him and to his Apostles. If you do this, you will cast away all the idols which had previously become a sin for you; and the devil will fall for you, not through your strength but through God’s mercy. His young men, who once fought for him, will become tributaries to the Church, and all his strength and rock will pass away. Philosophers also, and every perverse doctrine, will turn their backs at the sign of the cross.

The Lord’s judgment decrees that this should happen; his fire—or light—is in Zion, and his furnace is in Jerusalem. In Hebrew, “fire” and “light” are written with the same letters: **ALEPH, VAU, RES**. If it is read **UR**, it means “fire”; if **OR**, “light.” This is said because, where Symmachus alone translated “fire,” Aquila and Theodotion translated “light.”

I cannot determine what the words in the Septuagint mean: “They will be surrounded by a rock as by a rampart, and they will be defeated; but whoever flees will be captured.” Unless perhaps we may say that the young men of the Assyrian king, who are to be defeated and captured, will be surrounded by a rock—that is, by the Lord’s strength—as a city is surrounded by a rampart.

As for what follows—“Blessed is the one who has seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem”—we may interpret it as fitting the sense of the present passage: the divine word exhorts those fleeing to Egypt to return to Jerusalem and beget children. Such a person is promised great blessedness, being defended and protected by the Lord’s help. And elsewhere it is written of her: “The glory of this latter house will be greater than that of the former” (Haggai II, 10).

This may also be referred to the Church, the vision of peace and watchtower, of which it is written: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI, 2); and elsewhere: “The river’s rushing makes glad the city of God” (ibid. XLV, 3). In her there is fire and a furnace to devour sinners and consume wood, hay, and straw; or light and a furnace, so that the splendor of the righteous and the punishment of sinners may be displayed.

### (Chapter XXXII.—Verses 1 ff.) Behold, a king will reign with justice, and princes will rule with judgment. And a man will be like one who hides from the wind and shelters himself from the storm, like streams of water in thirst and the shade of an overhanging rock in a desert land. The eyes of those who see will not be dim, and the ears of those who hear will listen attentively. The heart of fools will understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers will speak quickly and clearly. The foolish man will no longer be called a prince, nor will the deceitful be called great. For the fool will speak foolishly, and his heart will practice iniquity, to complete hypocrisy, to speak deceitfully against the Lord, to empty the soul of the hungry, and to take away drink from the thirsty. The weapons of the deceitful are exceedingly evil; for he has devised schemes to destroy the gentle by lying speech, when the poor man speaks judgment. But the prince will think upon things worthy of a prince, and he himself will stand above rulers.

**Septuagint:** Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment. And a man will conceal his words and hide himself as from flowing water; and he will appear in Zion like a running river, renowned in a thirsty land. Those who trust in men will by no means continue, but they will give their ears to hearing, and the heart of the weak will attend to listening. The tongues of stammerers will quickly learn to speak peace. They will by no means say that a fool should be prince, nor will your ministers any longer say, “Be silent.” For the fool will speak foolishly, and his heart will understand vain things, to accomplish iniquity and speak error against the Lord, so as to scatter hungry souls and make thirsty souls empty. The counsel of the wicked will devise iniquity: to kill the humble with iniquitous words and scatter the words of the humble in judgment. But the pious have thought upon wisdom, and this counsel remains.

According to the Septuagint translators, who said, “Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule with judgment,” what follows should be joined to the preceding words, namely those with which the previous chapter ended: “Blessed is the one who has seed in Zion and household members in Jerusalem.”

According to the Hebrew, the preceding prophecy concerning those who went down to Egypt has ended; now begins another prediction, concerning the coming of Christ and his Apostles. This king will reign justly, not showing partiality in judgment, and his princes will rule with truth, considering cases rather than persons.

Whoever is beneath his shelter will be as safe amid tribulations and distresses, and amid the storm of this world, as one who, fleeing wind and whirlwind, hides himself in a secure place; as one who finds the purest springs in the desert; or as one who, when the violent heat of the sun scorches everything, rests beneath an overhanging rock.

Where we said, “like streams of water in thirst,” the Septuagint translated, “and he will appear in Zion like a running river.” The Hebrew word which we discussed above, **BASAION** (ּ), meaning “in thirst,” or “in dryness,” and “in an impassable place,” was translated by the Septuagint and Theodotion as “in Zion.” They read **SION** in place of **SAION**, that is, “thirst,” although the two are written with the same letters.

When Christ has reigned and his princes have ruled in judgment, the eyes of believers will not be dim, and the ears of those who hear will listen attentively—ears that were previously deaf.

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript reads, “the eyes of those who see, and the ears,” and so forth. The heart of those who were once fools will understand knowledge, and the tongue of stammerers and mute persons, which could not proclaim Christ, will confess the Lord in full and open speech.

The one who is foolish will no longer be called a prince (1 Cor. I), for “God made foolish the wisdom of this world.” Nor will the deceitful and perverse teacher be called great among the peoples—namely, the Scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: “Fools and blind men, which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?” (Matt. XXIII, 17).

“For the fool will speak foolishly.” In Hebrew it is written: **NABAL NABALA IDABBER** (נבל נבלה ידבר). We say this in order to explain the words of Abigail concerning Nabal the Carmelite: “As his name is, so is he: a fool” (1 Sam. XXV, 25). Truly the fool will speak foolishly, and his heart will accomplish iniquity—he who feared where there was no fear and used folly in place of wisdom, saying: “If this man were from God, he would not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16).

This is what the teacher of the synagogues does to this day, “to complete hypocrisy,” for which **ONEPH** () is written in Hebrew, that is, **ὑπόκρισις** (“hypocrisy”). Hence it is repeatedly said to the Pharisees: “Woe to you, Scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. XXIII, 14).

“And he will speak deceitfully against the Lord”: “Teacher, we know that you are from God, and that you do not care about men; is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” (ibid. XXII, 16–17). They empty the souls of the hungry people and take drink away from the thirsty crowds, neither entering themselves nor allowing others to enter.

All the vessels and weapons—or, alternatively, “bitter things”—of the deceitful teacher and prince are exceedingly evil. He devises plots to destroy the simple by lying speech, saying to the deceived people: “Search and see, for no prophet will arise—or, alternatively, ‘rise again’—from Galilee” (John VII, 52).

**Note:** In the same manuscript, “poor” is missing.

“When the poor man spoke judgment”—the one who, although rich, became poor for our sake (2 Cor. VIII). Truly Christ was judgment and spoke righteousness to them, saying: “If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works” (John X, 37).

**Note:** Two Vatican manuscripts read, “and if you do not wish to believe me,” and so forth.

This poor man who speaks judgment is prince and Lord. He will think upon things worthy of a prince, saying: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24). He will be concerned to save unbelievers, desiring to save those who do not believe; and he will stand above his rulers, the Apostles, to one of whom he says: “But you are a man of one mind with me, my leader and my acquaintance” (Ps. LIV, 14).

These comments follow the Hebrew, from which the Septuagint differs in many places not only in words but also in meaning. When the righteous king has reigned and his princes have ruled with judgment, there will be a man concealing his words—a man who by nature is God—and he will conceal his words, speaking to them in parables (Matt. XX, 21, 23, 24, and XXV).

He will conceal them as from flowing water, that is, from the Jewish people, who, like water, are carried and dragged here and there according to the will of their teachers. This man, concealing his words from unbelievers, will appear in Zion—that is, in the Church—like a renowned river flowing through a thirsty land.

He will appear to the people of the Gentiles, who previously suffered thirst for the truth; and the river of God will water their thirsty fields, of which it is written: “The river’s rushing makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 4). And elsewhere: “The river of God is filled with waters” (Ps. LXIV, 10). For he himself says in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink. The one who believes in me, as Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII, 38).

Then they will no longer trust in teachers but will offer their ears to hear the Lord. With heart and tongue alike they will confess the Lord’s peace, abandoning the foolish princes and their ministers, who commanded those who believed in Jesus to be silent.

What follows contains nearly the same meaning as the Hebrew and may also be applied to heretics. For they speak falsehood against the Lord, pervert hungry and thirsty souls, and make them depart empty, so that even if they possess anything naturally good, they lose it through the fault of their teachers, whose whole counsel is to destroy the humble with iniquitous words and scatter the words of the humble in judgment. It should likewise be noted that anyone who can be deceived by them is humble and attached to the earth.

### (Verses 9 ff.) Wealthy women, rise and hear my voice; confident daughters, receive my speech with your ears. After days and a year, you too will be disturbed, you who are confident; for the vintage has been completed, and the harvest will not come again. Be astonished, wealthy women; be disturbed, you who are confident; strip yourselves and be ashamed. Symmachus translated this as “make yourselves naked.” It continues: Gird your loins; beat your breasts over the desirable region, over the fruitful vine. Upon the soil of my people thorns and brambles will rise; how much more over all the houses of joy of the jubilant city? For the house has been abandoned; the multitude of the city has been forsaken. Darkness and groping have come upon the caves forever; the joy of wild asses is the pasture of flocks.

Until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high, the wilderness will become Carmel, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest.
