And judgment will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness will sit in Carmel. And the work of righteousness will be peace; and the service of righteousness will be quietness, and security forever. My people will sit in the beauty of peace, in tents of confidence, and in abundant rest.

But hail will fall upon the descent of the forest, and the city will be humbled with utter humiliation. Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, letting the foot of the ox and the donkey enter.

The Septuagint, in place of “darkness and groping have come upon the caves forever,” translated: “Your villages will be caves forever.” In Hebrew this is called **OPHEL** () and **BEEN** (), which the Hebrews believe to have been two towers in Jerusalem, lofty and extremely strong, called by these names. The first is interpreted as “darkness” or “cloud,” because it raised its head as far as the clouds. The second means “proof” and “firmness,” or, as Symmachus translated it, “inquiry,” because when one gazed at its summit the eyes were deceived.

At the end of the chapter they likewise translated: “Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread.”

After the calling of the Gentiles, when Christ the king has ruled with justice and his princes—the Apostles and apostolic men—have presided over believers with judgment, the prophetic word is directed to wealthy women. These may be understood as the cities of Judea, or the synagogues of that time, or, as many think, the matrons of the once-rich Jewish people. To them, as though lying prostrate after their ruin, it is said: “Rise.” Yet they are still called confident daughters, or “hopeful” daughters. They are commanded to hear the Lord’s words and to remember the days and the year, concerning which we shall speak below, with the Savior himself saying:

**Note:** One Vatican manuscript reads, “of which we shall read in what follows.”

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord” (Luke IV, 18–19).

According to the Septuagint, this remembrance itself becomes grief mixed with hope for them, so that they may mourn having denied the Lord and may hope for salvation if they repent.

He says that the vintage has been completed, and that after the final devastation—which occurred under Vespasian, Titus, and Hadrian—no further captivity will come, nor will clusters remain among the peoples to be gathered afterward. Hence they are summoned to mourning and commanded to bare their breasts and gird their loins, because the once-desirable region and fruitful vine, of which it is written, “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true; how have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?” (Jer. II, 21), has been destroyed by the Romans.

“Upon the soil of my people,” he says, “thorns and brambles,” or “grass,” will rise. The meaning is this: If thorns and brambles have filled the land of Judea, which is the land of promise, how much more will they fill the other cities that are full of joy and will experience what is proclaimed in the Gospel: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you will mourn” (Luke VI, 25)!

For the Lord—or, alternatively, “the house”—that is, my temple, has been abandoned, as I said to the Apostles: “Rise, let us go from here” (John XIV, 31); and to the unbelievers: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke XV, 35). The inner chambers of the Temple and its secret mysteries have been possessed by tangible darkness and have become no longer storerooms of the Lord’s vessels but caves forever.

They had heard from the Lord and Savior: “My Father’s house will be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matt. XXI, 13).

“The joy of wild asses,” he says, “is the pasture of flocks.” This may be understood literally, because everything has become deserted; or spiritually, because after Israel was expelled, savage people who do not possess knowledge of God dwell in Judea.

This will continue until the spirit is poured out upon us from on high—the Spirit whom the Savior, ascending to the Father, promised to believers, saying: “Behold, I am going, and I will send you the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John XVI). And again: “Until you receive power from on high” (Luke XXIV, 49).

What he had said above—“For a little while longer, and Lebanon will become Carmel, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest; and on that day the deaf will hear the words of the book, and from darkness and gloom the eyes of the blind will see” (above, XXIX)—he now repeats in other words. The wilderness of the Gentiles will be changed into the riches of Israel, and Israel will be reckoned among the Gentiles.

At that time judgment will dwell in the wilderness: the Lord and Savior, to whom the Father has given all judgment (John III). And righteousness will rest in Carmel. Earlier it was said: “Carmel will become a wilderness,” so that judgment and righteousness might dwell in the wilderness and rest in Carmel, which had previously been called a wilderness.

The work of righteousness will also be peace, which, according to the Apostle, surpasses every understanding (Phil. IV). The service of righteousness will be silence, so that they may worship the Lord not with the many words of the Jews but with the brevity of faith; and, secure in eternal peace, they may rest, with riches in their tents, concerning which the Apostle said: “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge” (1 Cor. I, 5).

When the Christian people sit or dwell in beauty—or, as the Septuagint translated, “in the city of peace”—there can be no doubt that this is in the Church. Then hail, storm, and the Lord’s raging anger will descend upon the forest, concerning which it was said above: “Carmel will be reckoned as a forest.” Jerusalem the city will be humbled, and, according to another Scripture, will speak from the earth.

Since these things are so, and since we have learned through prophetic prediction how many good things the Church will possess and how many evils Jerusalem will suffer, blessed are you, Apostles and other teachers, who sow beside all the waters of Holy Scripture, in which the ox and the donkey tread.

The ox is a clean animal, signifying the election of the patriarchs; the donkey is unclean, signifying the former idolatry of the Gentiles, so that the Lord’s Church may be gathered both from Circumcision and from Uncircumcision.

What is said above, according to the Septuagint—“Upon the soil of my people thorns and grass will rise”—may also be referred to heretics and to those believers who are simple-minded and do not understand Holy Scripture in a manner suited to its majesty. Therefore we have fitted each part to its corresponding subject, so that the soil of God’s people may produce thorns for heretics and grass for the unlearned within the Church.

### (Chapter XXXIII.—Verse 1.) Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered? And you who despise: will you not yourself be despised? When you have finished plundering, you will be plundered; when, wearied, you cease to despise, you will be despised.

**Note:** The Vatican manuscript reads “you will be prey” instead of “you will be plundered,” and consistently retains this reading below.

**Septuagint:** Woe to those who make you miserable; for no one makes you miserable. And those who reject you do not reject you. Those who reject will be captured and handed over, and they will be overcome like a moth in clothing.

**Note:** Another Vatican manuscript reads: “Those who reject you do not reject us,” just as it also reads below, “Those who make you miserable, for no one makes us miserable,” and so forth.

He had spoken of the Apostles and the teachers of the churches: “Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread.” Now he directs a curse against their persecutors—indeed, against their prince, who possesses the hearts of the impious—that whatever they have done they may receive in return, and that their present power may become the material of future torments.

Hence, according to the Septuagint: “Woe to those who make you miserable; for no one makes you miserable.” The meaning is this: As far as their intention is concerned, when they persecute you and afflict you with various torments, they consider those whom they have killed and tortured to be miserable. But no one can make you miserable, for they have no power over the soul, only over the body.

“And those who reject you do not reject you,” but the one who sent you, according to what the Savior says to his disciples: “The one who rejects you rejects me; and the one who rejects me rejects the one who sent me” (Luke X, 16).

The persecutors, therefore, will be captured and handed over to eternal fires. As a moth consumes clothing, so perpetual flame will consume them. The same is written at the end of this prophecy: “Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be extinguished.”

### (Verses 2 ff.) Lord, have mercy upon us; for we have waited for you. Be their arm—or, alternatively, our arm—in the morning, and our salvation in the time of tribulation. At the voice of the Angel the peoples fled; at your exaltation the nations were scattered. Your spoil will be gathered as the locust is gathered, as when ditches have been filled with it. The Lord has been magnified, because he has dwelt on high; he has filled Zion with judgment and righteousness. And there will be faith in your times: the riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge; the fear of the Lord itself is his treasure.

**Septuagint:** Lord, have mercy upon us; for in you we have trusted. The seed of the unbelievers has become destruction, but our salvation has appeared in the time of tribulation. Because of the voice of fear, the peoples were stunned by fear of you, and the nations were scattered. But now your spoil, both small and great, will be gathered. When someone gathers locusts, so they will mock you. The holy God who dwells on high: Zion has been filled with judgment and righteousness. They will be handed over to the law; our salvation is in the treasures. Wisdom and discipline have come, and piety from the Lord—these are the treasures of righteousness.

The Hebrews think that the preceding chapter, in which it says, “Woe to you who plunder: will you not yourself be plundered?” and what follows to the end, was spoken against Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians. After he had overthrown the cities of the ten tribes called Israel and had captured the cities of Judah, except Jerusalem, he himself would be overcome, and his army destroyed when the Angel struck it.

Therefore they contend that the words now before us are spoken in the person of the people giving thanks to God and saying: “Lord, have mercy upon us; we have waited for you.” They belong to the present—or, alternatively, the following—chapter, which says that he himself was the arm and strength of the people surrounded by the siege in the morning, and salvation in need and distress.

At the voice of the Angel, whom Symmachus translated as it is written in Hebrew, **AMUN** (), whom the Hebrews believe to be Gabriel and whose name they take to have the etymology “people,” the Assyrian fled.

**Note:** Alternatively, **HAMON**, a word properly meaning “a multitude”; Jerome interpreted it as “Angel” on the opinion of the Hebrews of his own time. At God’s exaltation, the nations who were with him were scattered here and there. When they had fled, the Jews gathered the spoil, as a multitude of locusts and grasshoppers is usually gathered when they have been heaped into ditches.

In this victory the Lord was magnified; Zion was filled with judgment and righteousness; the faith of the besieged people was confirmed; and they possessed all riches in wisdom, the knowledge of God, and the fear of the Lord, who alone was their treasure.

They say these things according to history, striving by every means to overturn the mysteries concerning Christ and his Apostles. But after the blessedness of the Apostles, of whom it was said above (on chapter XXXI, 20): “Blessed are those who sow upon every water, where the ox and the donkey tread,” and after the lamentation and mourning of those who persecuted them, concerning whom it is said below, “Woe to those who make you miserable; but no one makes you miserable; and as a moth in clothing, so they will be worn away,” we affirm that these words are spoken in the person of those same Apostles and of all believers.

The meaning is this: Lord, we have hoped in your help and trusted in you. The seed of unbelievers has perished forever, and our salvation has appeared in the time of tribulation. With you providing help, the entire multitude of the nations has been scattered and has become prey and an object of mockery to the victors.

This has happened because the holy Lord dwells on high, and Zion has been filled with judgment and righteousness. Of her it was written above: “Judgment and righteousness will rest in the wilderness.” This, then, is Zion, which was previously called the wilderness. Whoever dwells in her will be entrusted with the law of the Gospel, in whose treasure is our salvation, the wisdom of believers, discipline, and piety—or faith, which properly belongs to Christians—and the fear of the Lord, in which the treasures of wisdom are contained.

**Note:** The more accurate reading in two Vatican manuscripts is “as when someone …”; the Greek likewise has **ὃν τρόπον**.

### (Verses 7 and following)

“Behold, those who see will cry out outside; the angels of peace will weep bitterly. The roads have been scattered; the one passing along the path has ceased. The covenant has been annulled; he has rejected the cities and has not regarded human beings. The land has mourned and languished; Lebanon has been confounded and has become deaf. Sharon has become like a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel have been shaken.

“Now I shall arise,” says the Lord; “now I shall be exalted; now I shall be lifted up. You will conceive burning heat; you will give birth to stubble; your spirit, like fire, will devour you. The peoples will be like ashes from a fire; thorns gathered together will be burned in the fire.”

[Note: The Hebrew word *Arellam*, etc. Although I strive to spare Erasmus and Marianus, and everywhere silently pass over many of the errors of those same editors, I cannot remain silent here: nearly all the Hebrew words placed in Jerome’s Commentaries have been corrupted through negligence or ignorance. For here they try to force upon us not what is read in the manuscript codices, but what they themselves have dared to devise or have found in the Masoretic Bibles—namely, *arelam* instead of *arellam*, and *ere lam* instead of *Are lahem*. All the manuscript copies consistently retain the latter readings, in conformity with Jerome’s observation. It is therefore certain and evident to us that before our time no editor had collated the manuscript codices with the printed books for the restoration of Jerome’s text in the Hebrew words. MARTIAN.]

The Hebrew word *ARELLAM* (), which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as “I shall appear to them,” dividing the final syllable and reading *ARE LAHEM* (), the Hebrews believe signifies “angels.” They understand it as a prophecy concerning the destruction of the Temple after the calling of the nations and the riches of the Church: the angels will weep, not dwelling within it but going out, and those who formerly were messengers of peace will weep bitterly.

Or the reference may be to the Apostles themselves, who had been sent to announce peace to Jerusalem, to which the Lord was speaking: “If you had known, even you, the things that belong to your peace” (Luke 19:42). When the Lord appeared to them in order to strengthen them by his presence, they would weep over Jerusalem because it had not received their preaching, since “the roads have been scattered, and the one passing along the path has ceased.”

[Note: In two Vatican manuscripts, the word *justam* is omitted.]

This accords with what is said in the Lamentations of Jeremiah: “The roads of Zion mourn, because there are none who come to the feast” (Lam. 1:4). The covenant also made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has been annulled. He rejected the cities of Judea; he did not regard as human beings those who by their own fault wished to be beasts of burden. “The land mourned and languished” on behalf of those who dwelt in the land (Gen. 15 and 22).

Lebanon was confounded and became deaf—without doubt signifying the Temple, concerning which we read in Zechariah: “Open your doors, Lebanon, so that fire may devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1).

Or it signifies Jerusalem, which is called Lebanon in Ezekiel, when the prophet says: “A great eagle, with great wings, which has the reach to enter Lebanon” (Ezek. 17:3).

[Note: The word *magna*, which had fallen out in the previously published editions because of the similarity of the surrounding text, is supplied by two Vatican manuscripts in accordance with the authority of the sacred text.]

Later the divine discourse interprets this, saying that when Nebuchadnezzar comes into Jerusalem, it plainly explains the eagle as the king of Babylon and Lebanon as Jerusalem.

“Sharon has become like a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel have been shaken.” In place of Bashan, the Septuagint translated “Galilee,” a province, substituting the province for one of its places. Sharon is the whole region around Joppa and Lydda, where very broad and fertile plains extend. Bashan is also the region beyond the Jordan, which two and a half tribes possessed; it is interpreted as “most fertile and rich” (Deut. 3). Carmel is the place about which we spoke above.

Thus the formerly fertile places of Judea will be turned into a wilderness. Through this metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*) is shown that all the wealth of the Jews will be exchanged for poverty and want. Because they refused to receive the Apostles’ preaching, Lebanon was confounded, Sharon was turned into a wilderness, and Bashan and Carmel were shaken.

Therefore the Lord says either that he will rise after an excess of patience, or that he will rise from the dead; that he will be exalted among the nations and lifted up on the cross. He then turns directly to the Jews: “You will conceive burning heat and give birth to stubble, and your spirit will kindle a fire against you,” so that the devouring flame may consume what has been conceived and brought forth.

“And the peoples of the Jews,” he says, “will be like ashes from a fire,” displaying the magnitude of their unhappiness by the remnants of the cinders. Their thorns, gathered together by the multitude of their sins, will be devoured in the fire. Most refer this to the final captivity and destruction of Jerusalem; others more fully and more perfectly affirm that it will take place at the time of judgment.

### (Verses 13 and following)

“Hear, you who are far away, what I have done, and know, you who are near, my strength. The sinners in Zion have been terrified; trembling has seized the hypocrites. Who among you will be able to dwell with consuming fire? Who among you will dwell with everlasting burnings?

“He who walks in righteousness and speaks truth; who rejects avarice gained through calumny and shakes his hands free from every bribe; who stops his ears so as not to hear bloodshed and closes his eyes so as not to see evil—he will dwell on high. The heights of the rocky strongholds will be his refuge; bread will be given to him, and his waters will be reliable.

“His eyes will see the king in his beauty; they will behold a distant land. Your heart will meditate on fear. Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones? You will not see the insolent people, the people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of their language, in which there is no wisdom.”

[Note: In Jerome’s translation from the Hebrew, as also in the Vulgate, *impudentem* (“insolent”) is read; Martianus himself had decided that it should be replaced by *imprudentem* (“foolish”), and this should be retained because of the exposition of this sentence in these Commentaries. Indeed, below, where this passage is explained, one Vatican manuscript prefers *impudentem*; here, however, all agree in reading *imprudentem*.]

The Septuagint reads:

“Those who are far away will hear what they have done; those who draw near will know my strength. The wicked who were in Zion have withdrawn; trembling will seize the ungodly. Who will announce to you that the fire is burning? Who will announce to you the eternal place?

“He who walks in righteousness and speaks the straight way; who hates impiety and iniquity; who shakes his hands free from bribes; who stops his ears so as not to hear a judgment of blood; who closes his eyes so as not to see iniquity—he will dwell in a lofty cave of a very strong rock. Bread will be given to him, and his water will be reliable. Your eyes will see the king in glory; they will see a distant land. Your soul will meditate on fear.

“Where are the grammarians? Where are the counselors? Where is he who counts those who feed the small and the great people, to whom he gave no counsel? He did not know his deep utterance, so that the despised people did not hear, and there is no understanding in the one who hears.

“Because the roads have been scattered, the one passing along the paths has ceased, the covenant with the Jewish people has been annulled, God has rejected their cities and has not counted them among human beings—therefore, you who are far away, hear what I have done, and draw near so that you may know my strength.”

Those who were in Zion, whether sinners or ungodly, have been terrified—or have withdrawn—and trembling has seized the hypocrites, to whom the Lord spoke in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites!” (Matt. 23:14).

Who among you will be able to dwell with him who is consuming fire? Who will dwell with everlasting burnings?

Or, according to the Septuagint: “Who will announce to you that the eternal fire is burning, which God prepared for the devil and his angels?” Who, then, will be able to dwell with God, or announce the punishments that are to come?

Everyone who is such as the prophetic discourse describes—who walks in many acts of righteousness, not once but always loving righteousness, and who speaks truths not on one occasion but continually; who rejects avarice, which is the mother of calumny—for no one accumulates money except at another’s loss and harm—and who shakes his hands free from every bribe.

“Bribes blind the eyes even of the wise.” He stops his ears so as not to hear “the judgment of blood.” Every iniquity, oppression, and injustice is a judgment of blood; even if a person does not kill with the sword, he kills by intention. He closes his eyes so as not to see evil. Blessed is the conscience that neither hears nor looks upon evil.

Whoever, then, is such a person will dwell on high—that is, in the kingdom of heaven—or in the lofty cave of the very strong rock, in Christ Jesus. This is the rock that followed the people of Israel, so that they might drink from it and be protected by its strength.

Bread will be given to him, and his waters will be reliable. The fables of the Gentiles understand these as ambrosia and nectar; we, however, will interpret the most reliable bread and waters as the law of God.

Whoever is such a person will see Christ the King in his glory, of whom it was said above: “Behold, a righteous king will reign, and princes will rule in judgment” (on Isa. 32:1). His eyes will see a distant land, which they had long desired: the land of the meek and gentle, of which it is written in the Gospel, “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4). Or, placed in heaven, they will despise earthly things.

“Your heart will meditate on fear,” so that when you have attained everything, you may say with the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15:9). For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

“Where is the scribe? Where is he who weighs the words of the law? Where is the teacher of little ones?” (Prov. 9:1). “Where,” he says, “are the scribes and Pharisees who, weighing the words of the Law, were deceiving the unhappy people?” Scripture now calls them “little ones”—little in understanding and little in intelligence.

When the eyes of the believer have seen the King in his majesty, and his heart has meditated on fear, then he will not see the foolish people: the Jewish people, or the philosophers and orators of the world, who applaud themselves for their secular learning and eloquence. Concerning them he now says: “A people of deep speech, so that you cannot understand the eloquence of their language.” All their adornment is in words; they possess only the leaves and shade of speeches and do not possess the fruit of truth.

Finally, it follows: “In whom there is no wisdom.” Of such people it is also said elsewhere: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the understanding of the prudent I will reject” (1 Cor. 1:19). Why? Because “God made foolish the wisdom of this world.”

### (Verses 20 and following)

“Look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity. Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich habitation: a tabernacle that can never be moved, whose tent-pegs will not be removed forever, and whose cords will not be broken. For only there is our Lord magnificent.

“It is a place of rivers, of very broad and open streams; no ship propelled by oars will pass through it, nor will a great trireme cross it. For the Lord is our judge, the Lord is our lawgiver, the Lord is our king; he himself will save us.”

Your cords have been loosened, and they will not prevail. Your mast will be such that you cannot spread a sail. Then the spoils of abundant plunder will be divided; the lame will seize the booty. Nor will the neighbor say, “I have grown weak.” The people who dwell there will have their iniquity taken away from them.

[Note: The manuscript of Magnus has *valde magnus* (“very great”); the Hebrew, however, has *magnificus* (“magnificent”).]

The Septuagint reads:

“Behold, Zion, the city of our salvation. Your eyes will see Jerusalem, a rich city, tents that will not be moved; the pegs of its tabernacle will not be removed forever, and its cords will not be torn away. For the great name of the Lord is yours.

“Your place will be rivers and very broad and spacious streams. No ship driven by oars will enter it. For my God”—or, “the Lord”—“is great. The Lord will not cross me, our judge, our ruler, our king; the Lord himself will save us.

“Your cords have been torn”—or, “seized”—“because they did not prevail. Your mast has been bent, so that it may release the sails.”

[Note: In the older Vatican manuscript the contrary sense is found: “and he will not loosen the sails,” which is altogether more faithful to the Greek *οὐ χαλάσει τὰ ἱστία*.]

“He will not raise the standard until it is delivered over to destruction. Many lame people will plunder, and they will not say, ‘I shall labor.’ The people who dwell in them will have their offense forgiven.”

O righteous person, to whom it was said above, “Your heart will meditate on fear,” and “You will not see the foolish”—and who earlier heard, “Your eyes will see the king in his beauty”—look upon Zion, the city of our solemnity; behold the Church of Christ, in which true solemnity exists.

Your eyes will see the vision of peace and unexpected riches, “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man”; and a tabernacle that can never be moved. For the former tabernacle possessed by the Jewish people has been moved and taken away. Its tent-pegs will not be moved forever, and all its cords will be firm, so that the Lord may dwell in it.

This is the place of all rivers and flowing streams, through which no vessel belonging to the opposing side will be able to sail. Nor will a great trireme—which is interpreted as the devil—be able to cross it. For the Lord himself is our judge, ruler, king, and Savior; while he protects us, we will fear no one’s ambushes.

These words have been spoken concerning Zion, the city of our solemnity, and Jerusalem, the exceedingly rich habitation, which the Lord himself will surround and fortify with his rivers.

Now, however, he speaks concerning earthly Jerusalem: its tabernacle cords have been loosened and have not been able to support the tent; its mast, from which once the most beautiful sails hung, has fallen after the cords were broken, so that it is useless not only for sailing but even for displaying a standard.

After their ship has been broken up and their tabernacle destroyed, so that the cords are torn apart on both sides, the booty will be divided among the victors. These victors will be so weak in their own strength that they will be called lame; nevertheless, because God’s anger grants them strength, they will feel no weakness and will not say, “I have labored.”

Whoever among them exists will have his iniquity and sin taken away from him, because he has carried out God’s will.

### (Chapter 34, verses 1 and following)

“Draw near, nations, and hear; pay attention, peoples. Let the earth and its fullness hear, the world and all its offspring. For the indignation of the Lord is upon all the nations, and fury upon all their armies. He has slain them and given them over to slaughter.

“Their slain will be cast out; from their corpses stench will rise. The mountains will melt with their blood. All the army of heaven will waste away; the heavens will be rolled up—or folded up—like a book, and all their host will fall, as a leaf falls from a vine and from a fig tree, because my sword has become drunk in heaven.

“Behold, it will descend upon Idumea and upon the people of my slaughter for judgment. The sword of the Lord is filled with blood; it is fattened with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the blood of the rams rich in marrow. For there is a sacrifice of the Lord in Bozrah and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.

“The wild oxen will descend with them, and the bulls with the mighty. Their land will become drunk with their blood, and their soil will be fat with the fat of the strong.”

After the overthrow of Jerusalem, the ship that had once been exceedingly firm, and the plundering of all its furnishings, the text speaks of the destruction of all nations and the consummation of the world, which will occur on the future day of judgment.

Therefore all the nations and peoples of the earth, its fullness, the world, and all its offspring—both inhabited places and those uninhabitable because of excessive cold or heat—are commanded to hear and to know what is to come with complete trembling of mind.

The indignation of the Lord is described as coming not merely upon one nation, the Jewish people, nor upon the Assyrians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, Moabites, Ammonites, and Philistines, but against all nations and upon their entire army—or, as the Septuagint translated it, their number. It will come to slay them and make the stench of their rotting bodies rise aloft, signifying the sins of all nations, so that the mountains—that is, all the lofty virtues and angels who presided over individual nations—will be filled with their pus, filth, and blood, and all the host or strength of heaven will waste away. The heavens will be rolled up or folded like a book, and all their host and army—or, as the Septuagint translated it, the stars—will fall like leaves that, when the cold approaches, dry up, shrivel, and fall from the vine and fig tree.

The Savior also speaks of this in the Gospel: “The stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Matt. 24:29–30).

It should also be considered that he does not say that the heavens will perish, but that they will be rolled up or folded like a book, so that after all sins have been revealed and read, those heavens that had previously been open may be folded up, so that the sins of many may no longer be written in them.

Daniel speaks of such books in his volume: “The judgment sat, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7:10), in which the deeds of each person had been recorded.

Many think that the falling stars are to be understood according to the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 6 and 8) and according to what is written elsewhere: “All the stars, burning, will be dissolved, and heaven and earth will pass away” (Luke 10:2). For the form of this world is passing away.

[Note: Victorius deletes the words “they think,” and then reads continuously: “they truly believe these stars,” as we shall soon say is also found in the Vatican manuscript. His sense is indeed more correct, since Jerome sets forth only two opinions: one concerning real stars and one concerning mystical stars, and the testimonies he cites apply to only two, not three. Nevertheless, it seemed preferable to alert the reader to these matters with the text kept intact.]

Some think that these are the stars that shine in heaven, so that the part may indicate the whole: namely, that through the fall of the stars the destruction of the heavens also may be shown (2 Cor. 7).

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “They truly believe these stars,” etc.]

Others think that these stars are the ones who will fall, concerning whom the Apostle Paul writes: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6:12).

It is not surprising if demons who live in the air are called heavenly, since Scripture also calls the birds of heaven “heavenly,” although they fly not in heaven but in the air.

Satan is also transformed into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11), pretending to be a star. The Savior saw him “falling from heaven like lightning” (Luke 10). Tropologically, he is spoken of as a great star: “How you have fallen, Lucifer, who rose in the morning!” (Isa. 14:12).

All these things will occur because his sword has become drunk in heaven—that is, in the air, which Scripture commonly calls heaven. His punishment, sentence, and vengeance against sinners are brought forth by the Lord.

This sword is sharpened against the ungodly in Ezekiel (Ezek. 21), and after many have been killed it is commanded to enter its sheath. When it has become drunk and filled in heaven—that is, in the air—then it will descend also upon Idumea, that is, upon earthly things, so that after the punishment of demons the souls of human beings may also be judged.

For *Idumea* in our language signifies “earthly.” The sword is filled with the blood and fat of lambs and goats, of rams rich in marrow, and of bulls, so that it may signify equally the punishment of rulers and people.

“For there is a sacrifice of the Lord in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom.” The same prophet bears witness concerning Bozrah and Idumea below, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, whose garments are red from Bozrah?” (Isa. 63:1).

[Note: As in the Vulgate, the same manuscripts read *tinctis vestibus de Bosra* (“with garments dyed from Bozrah”); they consistently have *Basar* instead of *Bosor*.]

Some believe that because *Bosor* means “flesh,” the phrase “the sacrifice of the Lord in Bozrah” indicates torments in the flesh. They fall into this error from pious motives. In the present passage, however, the word is not written with the letter *sin*, as in *BOSOR* (), meaning “flesh,” but with *sade*, and it is called *BOSRA* (). According to Joshua and Jeremiah, this place is found not in Edom, that is, Idumea, but in the land of Moab (Jer. 48).

*Bozrah* in our language signifies “fortified,” “surrounded,” or “made firm.” Thus it teaches that the world has been solidly established by the Lord’s will, in accordance with what is sung in the psalm: “He founded it upon the seas and established it upon the rivers” (Ps. 23:2); and concerning the firmness of the earth, God says: “I have strengthened its pillars” (Ps. 74:3).

When the sacrifice of the Lord is in Bozrah and his slaughter in Idumea, the wild oxen will descend with the powerful bulls—namely, the kings and rulers of the earth—or, according to another reading, “of it.” Everything will be filled with slaughter and blood, and with the fat once belonging to the rich and powerful.

Through these words, which according to human usage instill terror in those who hear them, torments are shown to await all rulers and powerful people, as well as peoples and the lowly.

The teachers of the Jews wish Bozrah—that is, “fortified” and “made firm”—and Edom, Duma, or Idumea to be understood as Rome, and they wish everything contained in the following chapter to be spoken concerning Rome itself.

### (Verses 8 and following)

“For it is the day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion. Its streams will be turned into pitch, and its soil into sulfur; its land will become burning pitch. By night and by day it will not be extinguished; its smoke will rise forever. From generation to generation it will be desolate; throughout the age of ages no one will pass through it.

“The pelican, the hedgehog, the ibis, and the raven will possess it and dwell there. A measuring line will be stretched over it, to reduce it to nothing, and a plumb line for desolation. Its nobles will not be there; rather, they will call upon a king, and all its princes will be reduced to nothing.

“Thorns, nettles, and buckthorn will arise in its houses—or, according to another reading, its houses—and in its fortifications. It will be a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches.

“Demons will meet onocentaurs, and the hairy creature will call to his fellow. There the lamia will lie down and find rest for herself. There the hedgehog will make its den, raise its young, dig around it, and shelter them in its shade. There the kites will gather, each with the other.

“Search diligently in the book of the Lord and read: not one of them is missing; one has not sought another. For what proceeds from my mouth, he himself commanded, and his spirit, he himself gathered them. He himself cast lots for them, and his hand divided them among them by measure. They will possess it forever; from generation to generation they will dwell in it.”

[Note: Formerly the text read *congregabit* (“he will gather”), and shortly afterward *manus divisit* (“his hand divided”) without the intervening word *ejus*. The manuscripts correct and supply these words in accordance with the sacred text.]

The Hebrews, as we said above, insist that these things were prophesied concerning the Roman empire, and that the former devastation of the most powerful kingdom is proclaimed as vengeance for Zion. Many of our people also think that this is written literally in the Apocalypse of John.

We, however, on the basis of the statement “the day of the Lord’s vengeance, the year of retribution for the judgment of Zion,” understand this to be the year of which the Savior himself speaks: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution for our God, to comfort all who mourn, and to give glory to those who mourn in Zion” (Luke 4:18–19; Isa. 61:1–3).

It is also the year mentioned above: “Rise up, women who are at ease” (Isa. 32:5), and: “Remember the days of the year in sorrow with hope.” Consequently, after the general consummation of the whole world, Scripture returns to Jerusalem, to which it was speaking at that time, and describes its desolation in full discourse.

That is, after the time of the Roman siege has arrived, everything will be filled with pitch, sulfur, and burning flames; its smoke will remain forever; and the pelican, hedgehog, ibis, and raven—animals accustomed to inhabit deserted places—will dwell there.

This will happen because the Lord’s measuring line and plumb line—that is, his sentence—cannot be changed. Its nobles, namely, the Apostles and believers, will not be there, nor will they be joined to the number of the lost; rather, they will call upon Christ the King.

All its princes, namely, the scribes and Pharisees, will be reduced to nothing, and thorns, nettles, and buckthorn will arise in the once most beautifully adorned houses. It will be a lair of dragons and a pasture for ostriches, which are themselves signs of extreme desolation.

According to the Septuagint, various demonic phantoms will meet one another there; or, as all the others translated according to the Hebrew, *SIIM* () and *IIM* (): onocentaurs, hairy creatures, and the lamia, which the fables of the Gentiles and the inventions of poets describe.

The Hebrew word *LILITH* () is translated “lamia” only by Symmachus. Some Hebrews suspect that it means an Erinys (*ἐριννύς*), that is, a Fury.

And indeed, if we consider that colonists from different nations were brought into Jerusalem, and that, according to the customs of their provinces, individual families worshiped monstrous beings belonging to their own demons, we may affirm that all these beings inhabited Jerusalem. There too kites will gather—the most rapacious bird, called *DAJOTH* () in Hebrew—or, as the Septuagint translated, deer, of which we shall speak below.

The Septuagint translation reads: “There the deer met one another and saw one another’s faces; they passed by in number, not one of them perished, nor did one seek another. For the Lord commanded them, and his spirit gathered them. He himself gave them lots, and his hand will divide them among them, so that they may feed forever, possess the land through generations of generations, and rest in it.”

We may interpret this allegorically, teaching that the deer signify the Apostles and all the holy teachers, concerning whom it is written: “As the deer longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God” (Ps. 41:1); and elsewhere: “The voice of the Lord makes the deer give birth” (Ps. 28:9); and again: “Let the deer of friendship and the fawn of your graces speak to you” (Prov. 5); and in Job: “You have watched over the minds of the deer, and you will bring forth their offspring” (Job 39:2); and in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag upon the mountains of spices” (Song 2:9).

They met one another in Jerusalem, saw one another face to face, then passed through and left it, proceeding to different provinces, because the Lord had commanded them: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

His spirit gathered them, gave them lots, and divided them, so that one might go to India, another to Spain, another to Illyricum, and another to Greece; and each might rest in the province assigned to his Gospel and teaching.

What we have said was prophesied concerning Jerusalem, and what the Jews suspect was spoken concerning the Roman empire, some refer to the whole world, so as not to appear to differ from the preceding interpretations.

### (Chapter 35, verses 1–2)

“The desolate and impassable place will rejoice; the wilderness will exult and will blossom like a lily. It will blossom abundantly; it will exult with joy and praise. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Rejoice, thirsty wilderness, and let the desert exult; let it bloom like a lily. The deserts of the Jordan will blossom and exult. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, and the honor of Carmel. My people will see the glory of the Lord and the height of our God.”

Because Jerusalem has been turned into pitch and its everlasting smoke has risen, and because the pelican, hedgehog, ibis, raven, dragons, ostriches, demons, onocentaurs, lamia, and hairy creatures dwell in it, and the Lord’s sentence against it has been fulfilled—“Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35)—therefore the place that had formerly been desolate, concerning which the psalm says, “The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness, and the Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh. The voice of the Lord prepares the deer and reveals the thick places of the forests” (Ps. 28:8–9), will be changed into an abundance of all things.

As the deer contend with one another, the beasts that previously possessed the forests of all the nations will be driven out, so that what the same prophet says may be fulfilled: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1).

This wilderness had formerly been thirsty or impassable, lacking life-giving waters, and the Lord did not walk—or, according to another reading, did not enter—through it. Now it will blossom like a lily, or, as Aquila expressed it more precisely, through *καλύκωσις*.

[Note: We have restored *καλύκωσις*, which Martianus had also conjectured, although he retained *κάλυξ* in the text. Two Vatican manuscripts have *ΚΑΥΚΩϹΙϹ*, supported by the oldest manuscript of Saint-Germain, according to Montfaucon. One Palatine manuscript has *ΚΑΙΚΩϹΙϹ*. The manuscripts examined by Martianus also support the restored reading. In earlier printed books we read *ὡς κάλυξ*, but in the manuscript codices I found *ΚΑΛϹΩϹΙϹ* or *ΚΑΛΙϹΑΣΙΣ*, from which I infer that *καλύκωσις* should be read. Since *κάλυξ* signifies a closed or covered rose, one whose leaves have not yet opened and spread, I did not wish to alter the word found in the text of the older editions. MARTIAN.]

We may call it “a swelling rose not yet expanded with leaves.” It will blossom so that, together with the Apostle, it may proclaim: “We are the good odor of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). And in the Song of Songs: “Flowers have appeared on the earth” [Note: One Vatican manuscript adds “our”]; “the mandrakes have given their fragrance” (Song 7:12–13).

The phrase found in the Septuagint, “the deserts of the Jordan will exult,” is not found in the Hebrew. We can nevertheless say that in the river Jordan the baptism of repentance is signified, which the Lord marked and confirmed by his own washing.

Since the passage speaks figuratively of the wilderness, referring to the nations, in which John was located, the Jordan may appropriately be joined to it, so that through the wilderness of the Gentiles we may come to the Savior’s baptism.

As for what follows—“The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, and the beauty of Carmel and Sharon”—we should understand it according to the earlier explanation, in which we said that Lebanon signifies the Temple or Jerusalem, as Zechariah says: “Open, Lebanon, your gates” (Zech. 11:1), and Ezekiel says:

[Note: Here too, from the manuscripts, we have supplied *magna*, concerning the restoration of this word above, at chapter 33, verse 7.]

“A great eagle, full of great wings and claws, which has the reach to enter Lebanon and Carmel” (Ezek. 17:3).

This signifies the former people, concerning whom it was said above: “And Carmel will become a wilderness, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest” (Isa. 23:9). Sharon has the same meaning, as Scripture says: “Sharon has become like a wilderness.”

Therefore all brightness, the worship of God, the knowledge of circumcision, and the fertile and level places called Sharon—for which Symmachus translated “plains”—will be given to the Church that was formerly desolate. Its inhabitants will see the glory of the Lord and the beauty—or height—of our God.

[Col. 0375B] (Verses 3–4.) “Strengthen the slack hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to the fainthearted (or fearful), ‘Be strong, and do not fear: behold, your God will bring vengeance, the recompense. God himself will come and save you’ (or, as the Septuagint translated it, ‘us’). Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped (or, ‘shall hear’). Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened, because waters have burst forth in the desert, and torrents in the wilderness; and what was dry land has become a pool (or, ‘marshes’), and the thirsty land, springs of water. In the dens where dragons formerly dwelt, verdure of reeds and rushes shall arise” (for which the Septuagint translated: “There shall be the joy of birds, and folds of flocks”). “And there shall be a path and a way (or, ‘a clean way’), and it shall be called a holy way; the unclean shall not pass along it. And this shall be a straight way for us, so that fools shall not go astray upon it” (or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Neither shall there be an unclean way; but the scattered shall pass along it, and they shall not go astray. There shall not be a lion there, he says, and an evil beast shall not ascend upon it, nor shall it be found there; but those who have been delivered shall walk along it. And those redeemed by the Lord shall return, and shall come to Zion with praise, and everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. They shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and groaning shall flee away”).

We have mingled the two editions, lest the length of the books be extended by setting them out individually, since it has already exceeded the limits of brevity.

The Apostles, of whom it was said above, “They shall see the glory of the Lord and the beauty of our God,” are commanded to strengthen the hands that are slack among the nations and to make firm the feeble knees, so that those who formerly could not perform the work of God with slack hands, and had a withered right hand, may extend it toward good works. Those who formerly limped amid various errors among idols are to walk with a firm step upon the truth. And by confirming the fainthearted, or fearful, in the faith of the Lord, they are to make them unafraid; the fear of the one God is to drive out the fears of every error.

The cause of their security and steadfastness is that Christ is coming, to whom the Father has given all judgment; and he will repay each person according to his works (John 5). He himself will come and save you—those to whom it is said, “Do not fear”—or “us,” so that the Apostles may say that salvation is shared by themselves and believers. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped. Then the lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened.

Although this was fulfilled through the greatness of the signs when the Lord was speaking to the disciples of John, who had been sent to him: “Go and report to John what you have heard and seen: the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead rise, the poor are evangelized” (Luke 7:22), nevertheless it is fulfilled daily among the nations, when those who were formerly blind, stumbling against wood and stones, behold the light of truth. Those who could not hear the words of the Scriptures with deaf ears now rejoice in the commandments of God. Those who were formerly lame and did not keep to the straight way now leap like stags, imitating their teachers. And the tongue of the mute is opened—those whose mouths Satan had closed, lest they be able to confess the one Lord.

For this reason the eyes shall be opened, the ears shall hear, the lame shall leap, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened: because the waters of saving baptism of the Church, once a desert, burst forth, or gushed out [Note: [Col. 0376D] Two manuscripts read “the baptism of the Savior.”], and torrents and streams in the wilderness—that is, various spiritual graces. What had been dry land has been changed into a pool and marshes, so that it would not merely lack the burning of thirst but would be navigable and well-watered, and would possess very many springs, for which the stag longs, and from which the one who drinks can bless the Lord, according to what is written: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel” (Psalm 67:27).

In the dens of the souls of the nations, where dragons formerly dwelt, there shall be reed and rush, with which the faith of the Lord may be written, and in which limbs formerly wearied may rest. Or there shall be “the joy of birds, and folds of flocks,” so that they may take up the wings of a dove and, leaving lowly things behind, hasten toward the heights, and may be able to say with the Psalmist: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing. He has placed me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment.”

There shall be a path and an utterly pure way, which shall be called holy, and which itself says of itself: “I am the way” (John 14:6). The polluted person shall not be able to pass along it. Hence it is said in the psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way” (Psalm 113:1).

And this way shall be ours—that is, our God—so straight and level and open that it shall contain no error, and fools and the senseless shall be able to enter upon it. To them Wisdom speaks in Proverbs: “If anyone is little, let him come to me.” And to the foolish she says: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine that I have mixed for you. Leave childishness, and live, and walk along the ways of prudence” (Proverbs 9:4–6).

For God chose the foolish things of the world (1 Corinthians 1), and the prince of these fools says in the psalm: “O God, you know my foolishness.” And “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (Psalm 68:6; 1 Corinthians 1:25).

Hence the Septuagint translated: “And those who had been scattered” (1 Corinthians 2), and who had been separated from the fellowship of the Lord, “shall by no means go astray.”

[Col. 0377A] It follows: “There shall not be a lion there”—our adversary the devil, who prowls about roaring, seeking how he may enter the Lord’s sheepfold (1 Peter 5). “And an evil beast,” his satellites, “shall not ascend upon it.” For the serpent’s track cannot be found upon the rock.

But those shall walk along it who have been delivered from the bonds of sins, redeemed by the blood of the Savior, and have performed repentance. They shall come to Zion, concerning which we have often spoken: “You have drawn near to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). Let us not, in Jewish fashion, seek a golden Zion and a jeweled Jerusalem, which according to the prophecy of Daniel was dissolved into everlasting ashes (Daniel 9).

And everlasting joy shall be upon the heads of those who praise the Lord, so that after they have overcome the age they may be able to say with the Apostle and the Prophet: “I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness” (2 Timothy 4:7–8); and, “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Psalm 5:13). Then, as joy and gladness succeed one another, sorrow and groaning shall flee away, when he comes from Zion who delivers.

All these things we interpret, in accordance with the Apostle Paul, as referring to the first coming of the Savior. But the Jews and our Judaizers refer them to the second coming, relying upon the occasion of a single verse: “They shall return and come to Zion with praise,” while desiring the blood of sacrifices, the servitude of all the nations, and the beauty of women.

# BOOK ELEVEN

[Col. 0377] 451–452

It is difficult—indeed, impossible—to please everyone; nor is there as much diversity of faces as there is of opinions. In my explanation of the Twelve Prophets I seemed to some to have been more prolix than was appropriate. For this reason, in the little commentaries on Daniel I devoted myself to brevity, except in the last and the penultimate vision, in which I was compelled, because of the magnitude of their obscurity, to extend my discourse [Note: [Col. 0377D] Two Vatican manuscripts read more elegantly, “because of the magnitude of the obscurity.”]. Especially in the exposition of the seven, the sixty-two, and the one weeks, I briefly included what Africanus, the chronographer; Origen; Eusebius of Caesarea; Clement, presbyter of the Alexandrian Church; Apollinaris of Laodicea; Hippolytus; the Hebrews; and Tertullian thought concerning them, leaving it to the reader’s judgment which of the many views he should choose.

Thus, what I did out of modesty in passing judgment, and out of respect for those who would read the work, may perhaps displease some who desire to know not the opinions of the ancients but my own view. The answer to them is simple: I did not wish to accept one view in such a way that I might appear to condemn the others. Certainly, if such great and learned men displease fastidious readers, what would they have done to me, who, because of the slenderness of my little intellect, am exposed to the bites of the envious?

But if I have called the men mentioned above teachers of the Church, let them understand that I do not approve the faith of all of them, since they are certainly opposed to one another. I said this to distinguish them from Josephus and Porphyry, who discussed this question at great length [Note: [Col. 0377D] No book of Josephus concerning the Seventy Weeks either exists or appears ever to have existed, unless one should infer that something similar was written by him from what he promises to say about the deeds of Monobazus, king of Adiabene, in Book 20 of the Antiquities, chapter 2, or from what he says in the preface, Book 4, chapter 8, and Book 20, chapter 9, that after completing this work he wished to pursue an allegorical theory of the Jewish laws in a separate work divided into four books.].

If, in the exposition of the statue and its feet and toes, I interpreted the iron and clay over the Roman kingdom as signifying what the Scripture foretells to be first strong and then weak, let them not charge me with it, but the Prophet. For one must not flatter rulers to such an extent that the truth of the holy Scriptures is neglected, nor is a general discussion an insult to one individual [Note: [Col. 0378D] Tillemont appropriately conjectures that Jerome says he wished to bring this reproach upon himself so that his adversaries might represent him as hostile to Stilicho, the barbarian ruler who was bringing barbarian forces against the Western Empire. He said that this slander was suddenly removed by God’s judgment through the death of Stilicho himself, whom Honorius ordered killed near the end of August in the year 408.].

When this was guarded against by the good will of my friends, it was suddenly removed by God’s judgment, so that both the devotion of my friends toward me and the plots of my rivals might be revealed. But these matters belong elsewhere; let us now carry out what we have begun.

The eleventh book on Isaiah, O virgin of Christ, Eustochium, since it will discuss a large part of the history, will be easier at the beginning, and through nearly two-thirds of it. The rest must be dictated in the same manner. We must strive for brevity in such a way that no damage is done to understanding.

## Chapter XXXVI — Verses 1 and following

“And it came to pass in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. And the king of the Assyrians sent Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem to King Hezekiah with a powerful force, and he stood at the aqueduct of the upper pool, on the road to the fuller’s field. And Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, went out to him, together with Shebna the scribe and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder. And Rabshakeh said to them:

‘Say to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians: What is this confidence in which you trust? Or by what counsel and strength do you intend to rebel? In whom do you place your trust, since you have withdrawn from me? Behold, you trust in that broken reed-staff, Egypt, upon which, if a man leans, it will enter his hand and pierce it. Such is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to all who trust in him.

‘But if you say to me, “We trust in the Lord our God,” is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem, “You shall worship before this altar”? And now surrender yourself to my lord, the king of the Assyrians, and I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your own part to provide riders for them. How, then, will you withstand the face of one governor, even the least of my lord’s servants?

‘But if you trust in Egypt, in chariots and horsemen, and now—was it without the Lord that I came up against this land to destroy it? The Lord said to me, “Go up against this land and destroy it.”’

The historical account is clear and requires no interpretation. These same events are reported more fully in the books of Kings and Chronicles: in the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, began to reign. “He was twenty-five years old,” it says, “when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. He did what was good before the Lord, according to all that David his father had done” (2 Kings 18:2).

A little later it says: “He trusted in the Lord God of Israel, and after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those who were before him. He clung to the Lord and did not depart from following him; he kept his commandments, which the Lord had commanded Moses. Therefore the Lord was with him, and in all that he undertook he acted wisely” (2 Kings 18:5–7).

But he rebelled against the king of the Assyrians and did not serve him. In the sixth year of his reign, Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, captured Samaria and the ten tribes called Israel. He transported them to Assyria and settled them by the rivers Halah and Habor, by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17 and 18).

Seven years later—that is, in the fourteenth year of Hezekiah—Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, entered Judah and besieged its fortified cities, wishing to capture them. While he was besieging Lachish, Hezekiah sent messengers to him, saying: “I have sinned; withdraw from me, and whatever you impose upon me I will bear.” When, at the king’s command, he had paid three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, the king of the Assyrians, after breaking the doors of the Temple of the Lord and stripping off its plates, which Hezekiah himself had attached, sent Tartan and Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem with a powerful force.

When they had gone up, they came to Jerusalem and stood opposite the aqueduct of the upper pool, which is on the road to the fuller’s field. They summoned the king to them. Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the prefect of the household, went out to them, together with Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. Rabshakeh said to them: “Speak to Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians,” and so forth, as contained in the historical account.

Here one must observe Rabshakeh’s arrogance. As though imitating a certain opposing power, he adopts the custom of the Prophets, so that just as they usually place in their prologues the words “Thus says the Lord,” displaying the authority and greatness of the speaker, so he now says: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians.”

“Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was prefect of the household, went out to him, together with Shebna the scribe and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder.” This is the Eliakim son of Hilkiah of whom we read above, in the vision of the Valley of Zion (on chapter 22:20–21): “I will call my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe and strengthen him with your belt, and I will give your authority into his hand. And he shall be like a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah,” and so forth.

These words, however, are spoken concerning Shebna, who before Eliakim was prefect of the Temple. Of him it is written in the same vision: “Go and enter to him who dwells in the tabernacle, to Shebna the prefect of the Temple” (ibid., 15). The Hebrews relate that, terrified by Rabshakeh’s threats, he surrendered himself to the Assyrians and betrayed the lower part of Jerusalem to the enemy; except for the citadel of Zion and the Temple, nothing remained that the Assyrian did not hold.

Therefore those who think that the Shebna who now goes out with Eliakim and Joah to Rabshakeh is the same as the man mentioned above are mistaken. There Shebna is presented as prefect of the Temple, and he is said to be destined to be captured by the Assyrians. Here, however, Shebna is a scribe—that is, γραμματεύς (“scribe”)—and in Hebrew is called SOPHER; he is homonymous with the former.

As for Rabshakeh, who spoke in the Hebrew language, the Jews assert that he was the son of the Prophet Isaiah and that he too was a traitor. They say that Isaiah’s other son, who was left behind, was called Jasub, a name that in our language means “left behind.” Others, however, think that Rabshakeh was a Samaritan, and that for this reason he knew the Hebrew language and blasphemed the Lord so boldly and impiously.

Let us therefore consider Rabshakeh’s words. First, when he says, “You trust in that broken reed-staff, Egypt,” he is lying. No history records that Hezekiah sent to the Egyptians or sought Pharaoh’s aid. What he adds—“But if you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’”—is true. Yet again he joins falsehood to truth when he says that Hezekiah had removed the Lord’s high places and altars.

He had done this not against God but for God: after destroying idolatry and the ancient error, he ordered that God be worshiped in Jerusalem, where his Temple was. Nevertheless, we read that, through a very bad custom, after an altar had already been built on the mountains and hills, the people sacrificed victims to God there.

When Rabshakeh wishes to display the small number of the besieged, he promises two thousand horses, for which Hezekiah could not provide riders. This was not because the Jewish people were weak or lacked knowledge of riding, but because they observed God’s commandments. Through Moses God had commanded concerning the king of Israel: “He shall not multiply horses for himself, and he shall not have very many wives” (Deuteronomy 17:16–17).

“If,” he says, “you are unable to withstand me, the servant of Sennacherib, who am the least of his attendants, how will you withstand such royal power?”

To what Hezekiah had said—“If you say to me, ‘We trust in the Lord our God’”—he craftily and cleverly replied that he had come not by his own will but at the Lord’s command: “The Lord said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’” His argument is: “Certainly I could not have come here without the Lord’s will. Since I have come and captured many cities, while part of Jerusalem remains untouched, it is evident that I came by his will.”

I have read in someone’s Commentary that the Sennacherib who captured Samaria was the same man, but this is entirely false. Sacred History relates that the first Assyrian king, Pul, devastated the ten tribes under Menahem, king of Israel. The second, Tiglath-pileser, came against Israel under Pekah son of Remaliah. The third, Shalmaneser, captured all Samaria under Hoshea, king of Israel (2 Kings 15 and 17). The fourth was Sargon, who conquered Ashdod (Isaiah 20). The fifth was Esarhaddon, who, after Israel had been transported away, sent Samaritans as settlers into the land of Judah (2 Kings 17). The sixth was Sennacherib, who, under Hezekiah, king of Judah, after capturing Lachish and the other cities of Judah, besieged Jerusalem (2 Kings 18).

Others, however, think that one and the same man is called by many names.

## Verses 11 and following

“And Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to Rabshakeh: ‘Speak to your servants in the Aramaic language, for we understand it; do not speak to us in Judean in the hearing of the people who are upon the wall.’

“And Rabshakeh said to them: ‘Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you to speak all these words, and not rather to the men who sit upon the wall, that they may eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?’

“Then Rabshakeh stood and cried out in a loud voice in Judean, saying: ‘Hear the words of the great king, the king of the Assyrians. Thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he cannot deliver you. And do not let Hezekiah give you confidence in the Lord, saying, “The Lord will certainly deliver us; this city shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.” Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of the Assyrians:’”

Rabshakeh’s accusation is a testimony to Hezekiah: after all the cities of Judah had been captured, Hezekiah nevertheless trusted in the Lord and said to the people: “Do not fear or be terrified by the king of the Assyrians and all the multitude that is with him, for more are with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh; with us is the Lord our God, who is our helper and fights for us.” And the people, it says, were strengthened by these words of Hezekiah, king of Judah.

Therefore Rabshakeh wishes to destroy what Hezekiah had built. He says to the people: “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you,” and “Do not let him give you confidence in the Lord God.”

As for Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah humbly pleading, “Speak to your servants in the Aramaic language, for we understand it; and do not speak to us in Judean in the hearing of the people who are upon the wall,” their meaning is this: “Why is it necessary to disturb the people with false terrors and to boast of an empty power? Speak the language that the people do not understand. We do understand your language, for we know the Aramaic speech, which is common to both peoples.”

To this Rabshakeh arrogantly replied: “Has my lord sent me to your lord and to you?”—and not rather “to the men who sit upon the wall?” Again increasing the terror of his threat, he says: “That they may eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you.” By this he shows that they are to be captured through hunger, want, and thirst.

At the same time he joins enticement to fear, so that those whom he had not overcome by terror he might deceive through promises and persuasion, speaking in the name of the king of the Assyrians.

## Verses 16–18

“Make a blessing with me, and come out to me, and let each one eat his own vine, and each one his own fig tree, and let each one drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you to a land like your own land: a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards. Do not let Hezekiah disturb you, saying, ‘The Lord will deliver us.’ Have the gods of the nations delivered each one his own land from the hand of the king of the Assyrians?”

In the Book of Kings the corresponding passage reads: “Make with me what is beneficial, and come out to me” (2 Kings 18:31). The sense, therefore, is the same. “Do,” he says, “what will benefit you and advance your welfare.” Or he means: “Bless the king of Assyria and praise him, and confess the Lord, so that you may obtain rewards. Until I return from Egypt—or return after capturing Libnah—remain in your city and enjoy your possessions. Afterward I shall come and transfer you to a land like your own, a land of grain, wine, and olive trees.”

He does not name the region, because he could not find one equal to the Promised Land; instead, he promises a resemblance. Each person longs for the land in which he was born. Some think that Media was promised to them, since it resembled the land of Judah both in situation and in its crops.

As for what he adds:

## Verses 19 and following

“Where is the god of Hamath and Arpad? Where is the god of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand? Who is there among all the gods of these lands who has delivered his land from my hand, that the Lord should deliver Jerusalem from my hand?”

“And they were silent and did not answer him a word, for the king had commanded them, saying: ‘Do not answer him.’”

This shows that Samaria had served all these gods, and for that reason had been captured. “But if,” he says, “with so many gods presiding over them we easily overcame the ten tribes, how much more easily shall we conquer you—or rather Jerusalem alone—with one God as its ruler?”

All the people kept silent and did not answer him anything, for they had received the king’s command not to answer him. Truly Hezekiah was righteous, doing everything faithfully and with complete prudence. He had ordered that the blaspheming Assyrian not be answered so that he would not be provoked to greater blasphemies.

Hence it is written: “Do not stir up the coals of a sinner” (Ecclesiasticus 8:13). And in the psalm we read: “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Psalm 38:2); and again: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a fortified door over my lips; do not incline my heart toward words of wickedness” (Psalm 140:3).

## Chapter XXXVII — Verses 1 and following

[Note: [Col. 0381D] This first verse, which according to the Vulgate division is the last of Chapter XXXVI, is joined by Jerome to this chapter, as often happens with him. Earlier it was indeed cited in its place under the commonly received division of the preceding chapter, but contrary to the evidence of the manuscript codices and to the sequence of Jerome’s following exposition. From that sequence it is wholly clear that the holy Doctor cites it in this second place, especially in the words: “They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming.”]

“And Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their garments torn, and reported to him the words of Rabshakeh.

“And when King Hezekiah heard them, he tore his garments, covered himself with sackcloth, and entered the house of God. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet. And they said to him:

“‘Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of tribulation, correction, and blasphemy, because the children have come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to give birth [Al. ‘for the one giving birth’]. Perhaps the Lord your God will hear the words of Rabshakeh, whom the king of the Assyrians, his lord, has sent to blaspheme the living God and to reproach him with the words that the Lord your God has heard. Therefore lift up a prayer for the remnant that has been found.’

“And the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah. And Isaiah said to them: ‘Thus shall you say to your lord: Thus says the Lord: Do not fear the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of the Assyrians have blasphemed me. Behold, I shall put a spirit in him [Al. ‘in them’], and he shall hear a report, and he shall return to his own land, and I shall cause him to fall by the sword in his own land.’”

Leaving aside what is obvious, let us discuss only those matters in which a hidden meaning is present.

“They tear their garments because they hear Rabshakeh blaspheming” [Al. “because they had heard him blaspheming”]. The king himself also tears his garments, because he believed that the guilt belonged to his own sins and those of the people: Rabshakeh had come as far as the gate of Jerusalem and had spoken such things against the Lord.

Thus the high priest, believing that the Savior had blasphemed, tore his garments (Matthew 26); and Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians offered them divine worship, tore their garments (Acts 14).

Therefore, in place of royal dress, he covered himself with sackcloth. Proceeding from the palace to the Temple, he sent Eliakim the high priest, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests to Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet. Here one must observe the king’s humility and prudence. He himself went to the Temple, while he sent the leaders of the people and the elders of the priests to Isaiah son of Amoz the prophet, not clothed in priestly robes but covered with sackcloth.

In the Book of Kings the corresponding passage reads: “He himself was covered with sackcloth and entered the house of the Lord; and he sent Eliakim the prefect of the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz” (2 Kings 19:1–2).

Here, because Isaiah himself was writing the history about himself, he did not call himself “the Prophet,” but “the son of the Prophet.” There, because another person was the historian, he calls Isaiah “the Prophet.” We read something similar of Matthew the Evangelist: Matthew himself called himself a tax collector (Matthew 9), whereas the other Evangelists omitted the name “tax collector” and recorded only his apostolic dignity. Likewise, in the lists of the Apostles, Matthew is second in his own account but first in the accounts of others.

“And they said to him,” it says: “Thus says Hezekiah”—not “the king,” not swollen with the name of imperial authority: “This day is a day of tribulation, ruin, and blasphemy”—a day of our tribulation, of God’s correction, and of the enemies’ blasphemy.

He introduces the likeness of a woman in labor and suffering, who has reached the point of giving birth but cannot bring forth the child; she cannot say: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived, and we suffered; we gave birth to the spirit of salvation.”

It follows: “Perhaps the Lord your God will hear the words of Rabshakeh” (Isaiah 26:18, according to the Septuagint). They do not dare to call the Lord of all “our Lord,” since they are enduring such things because he is angry; instead, they call him “your Lord.” Yet they possess this confidence of vengeance: the living God is being blasphemed by a worshiper of dead idols.

“And they have reproached him with the words that the Lord your God has heard.” “Lift up,” therefore, “our prayer,” which lies prostrate—not for the whole people, which has already perished, but for the remnant that is under siege.

When the servants of King Hezekiah had come to Isaiah, he again omitted the name “Prophet,” in order to preserve the humility with which he had begun. Isaiah anticipated them. By the same Spirit through which he knew future events, he had also heard of the absent king; and he tells them what they should say to their lord, humbled yet confident in the testimony of his conscience [Note: [Col. 0383] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “confidence of conscience mingled with humility.” We correct some minor matters below.].

“Say,” he says, “to your lord, who is your lord; for my Lord says these things: Do not fear the words by which not you but I have been blasphemed. I shall not state all that I am going to do to the king of the Assyrians, lest I appear to boast of my power; but I will say that a spirit—not God’s, but an opposing spirit—will be given to him.”
