When he hears a report, he will return to his own land and fall there by the sword. Thus Hezekiah would hear two things at once, both what he desired: that he would be delivered from the siege and danger, and that his hostile and angry enemy would die in his own land.

If someone asks why, in the prophetic book, the history written in the books of Kings and Chronicles appears to be mixed in, let him consider that prophecy has been joined to history—both concerning the city’s deliverance and the destruction of the Assyrian, and concerning the sun’s return, with the hours extended by ten and the years by fifteen. This belongs both to prophecy and to history.

## Verses 8 and following

“Rabshakeh returned and found the king of the Assyrians fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that he had departed from Lachish. And he heard concerning Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia: ‘He has gone out to fight against you.’ When he heard this, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:

“‘Thus shall you say to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, saying, “Jerusalem shall not be given into the hand of the king of the Assyrians.” Behold, you have heard all that the kings of the Assyrians have done to all the lands that they overthrew; and you, will you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered those whom my fathers overthrew—Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the sons of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, and the king of Arpad, and the king of the city of Sepharvaim, Ana [Al. ‘Sepharvaim, Anea’], and Ava?’”

The same words and the same sense are written in the Books of Kings and Chronicles: in accordance with the Lord’s will, Rabshakeh abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and went to his lord, whom he had learned was going—after Lachish had either been abandoned or captured—to attack Libnah.

Sennacherib himself, hearing that Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, was bringing war against him, went out to meet him. Nevertheless, he sent messengers and letters to Hezekiah, so that those whom he had not yet conquered by force he might terrify by words. Just as he had said to the people, “Do not let Hezekiah deceive you” (2 Kings 18:29), so he speaks the same blasphemy to the king: “Do not let your God deceive you” (2 Kings 19:10).

He gives examples of former times: just as their gods had not been able to deliver the other lands from the hands of his ancestors, so Jerusalem would not be delivered either.

In his enumeration of the other nations he includes ANA () and AVA (), which the Septuagint conflated, saying “Anavegava.” They inserted the conjunction “and”—that is, the Hebrew waw—between the two nations Ana and Ava, so that to those who did not know the matter it might appear to be one nation or city [Note: [Col. 0385D] One Vatican manuscript has “aneagava”; the Greek manuscripts have ἀναγουγάνα, “anagugana,” and Eusebius reads it in this way. I would have a basis for proving the reading if it said “anagugava,” where the great similarity of upsilon to nu could have deceived the copyist.].

We pass quickly over what is clear, so that we may dwell on what is uncertain.

Herodotus relates that Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium; and that, when embankments had already been constructed for the capture of the city, Tirhakah, king of the Ethiopians, came to the aid of the Egyptians. He also relates that in one night, near Jerusalem, one hundred and eighty-five thousand of the Assyrian army fell through pestilence [Note: [Col. 0385D] Herodotus’ account of Sennacherib’s invasion of Egypt is found in Book 2, chapter 141. Josephus quotes the words of Berossus the Chaldean in Book 10 of the Antiquities, chapter 1, section 4. They are as follows: “When Sennacherib returned from the Egyptian war, he found there that the army which he had left under Rabshakeh’s command had been destroyed by a plague divinely sent. On the first night after he began to attack the city, one hundred and eighty-five thousand soldiers, together with their commanders and tribunes, perished. Terrified by this disaster and anxious about his remaining forces, he hastened by forced marches to his kingdom, to the royal city called Nineveh. A little later, through a plot of his elder sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, he lost his life, being killed and buried in the very temple of Arasci, whom he held in especial veneration. After the parricides had been driven out by the people and fled to Armenia, Esarhaddon, the younger son, succeeded to the kingdom. Such was the outcome of this expedition.” See also Ussher on the year of the world 4004.].

Berossus, a Chaldean writer of history, gives the fullest account. The reliability of both authors must be sought in their own books.

### (Verses 14 ff.)

Hezekiah took the letters from the hands of the messengers and read them. Then he went up into the house of the Lord, spread them out before the Lord, and prayed to the Lord, saying:

“Lord God of hosts, God of Israel, who sit upon the cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the earth; for you made heaven and earth. Incline your ear, Lord, and hear; open your eyes, Lord, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to blaspheme the living God. Truly, Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have laid waste the lands and their territories, and have cast their gods into the fire; for they were not gods, but the works of human hands, wood and stone, and they destroyed them. And now, Lord our God, save us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are God.”

Against the blasphemies of King Sennacherib, Hezekiah took up his customary weapons. He again went to the Temple and spread out Sennacherib’s letters before the Lord. Previously he had remained silent, for, terrified by fear of the Lord, he had not dared to open his mouth in the Temple or pour out unrestricted prayers to God. But now, because he had already heard Isaiah say, “Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, by which the servants of the king of Assyria have blasphemed me,” and so forth, he boldly entreats the Lord and asserts that the living God is one alone. By the idols we understand [Col. 0386A] images of the dead.

As for what follows—“Truly, Lord, the kings of the Assyrians have laid waste the lands and their territories, and have cast their gods into the fire; for they were not gods, but the works of human hands, wood and stone, and they destroyed them”—this is confirmed by many histories, which relate that the kings of the Persians came into Greece and overthrew and plundered the temples of the Greeks. He asks for vengeance, so that through this occasion all kingdoms may learn that he alone is God who is able to rescue his own from danger.

### (Verses 21 ff.)

Isaiah [variant: Josiah], son of Amos, sent word to Hezekiah, saying:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, this is the word that the Lord has spoken against him:

‘The virgin daughter of Zion has despised and mocked you; behind you the daughter of Jerusalem has shaken her head. Whom have you reproached and blasphemed? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes proudly? Against the Holy One of Israel! By the hand of your servants you have reproached the Lord, and you have said:

“With the multitude of my chariots I have ascended [variant: I will ascend] the height of the mountains, the peaks of Lebanon; I will cut down its lofty cedars and its choice fir trees, and I will enter the height of its summit, its forest of Carmel. I dug, and I drank water; and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the channels of the embankments.”’”

Because Hezekiah had prayed to the Lord with such boldness, and had not sent to Isaiah as he had sent previously, the Prophet himself does not go to him but sends messengers to convey God’s words:

“Concerning Sennacherib, against whom you are praying, this is the Lord’s judgment: The virgin of Zion and the daughter of Jerusalem—called virgin and daughter because, while all the nations worship images of dead human beings, she alone preserves the chastity of the worship of God and the devotion owed to one divinity—has mocked and despised you. She did not answer you immediately, lest she provoke you to still greater blasphemy; after you had departed, she shook her head, confident of vengeance and secure of punishment.

“And she said: ‘You have acted arrogantly not against me, but against the Lord; and you did so not personally, but through your servants, so that the arrogance of the blasphemer might be greater.’

[Note: Rabanus formerly read: “so that the arrogance might be greater, you blasphemed the Lord.”]

“For you said that with the multitude of your chariots you would ascend the height of the mountains and the peaks of Lebanon, and would cut down its lofty cedars and its fir trees. This we should understand either metaphorically (*μεταφορικῶς*, metaphorically), as referring to all the nations and their rulers, or as referring to Jerusalem, which is interpreted as ‘Lebanon,’ so that its cedars and fir trees signify all the powerful and the nobles; while ‘the height of its summit’ and ‘the forest of Carmel’ refer to the Temple. For earlier he had said: ‘Have you not heard what the kings of Assyria did to all the lands that they overthrew? Therefore you too will not be able to escape.’

“As for what follows—‘I dug and drank water, and dried up with the sole of my foot all the channels of the embankments’—according to the historical sense, this may mean that, because of the vast number of his army, he dried up all the streams, so that he was forced to dig wells for himself. According to the translation, it means that he devastated with his army all the peoples who are sometimes represented under the names of waters.

“For this the Septuagint alone translated: ‘I set up a bridge’ [variants: ‘a powerful one,’ or ‘power’], ‘and I dried up the waters and every gathering of waters’—that is, no nation was impassable to him, but he set his foot upon all the waters of the peoples.”

### (Verses 26 ff.)

“Have you not heard what I did long ago? From ancient days I formed it, and now I have brought it about: it has become the uprooting of mutually warring hills and fortified cities.” Their inhabitants, their power weakened, trembled and were put to shame; they became like the grass of the field, the green herb of the pasture, and the grass of the rooftops, which withered before it reached maturity. I know your dwelling, your going out and your coming in, and your madness against me when you raged against me. Because your arrogance has risen into my ears, I will put a ring in your nostrils and a bridle in your lips, and I will lead you back by the way by which you came.”

These words are to be understood as spoken by God against the Assyrian’s boasts. The Lord answers his blasphemy as follows:

“Do you not know that you have done these things by my will, and that I foretold them as future and commanded that they be carried out through you? Therefore what I decreed long ago has been fulfilled in its time: the hills—that is, the rulers who had previously fought among themselves—and the most strongly fortified cities were uprooted and destroyed when I withdrew my hand and did not provide my customary aid. They trembled and perished. They were compared not to olive trees, vineyards, or fruitful trees, but to hay, grass, and the vegetation of rooftops, which obstructs crops and withers before reaching maturity.

“Thus I knew beforehand your sitting, your going out, and your coming in, and I spoke through the prophets of the madness with which you were to rage against me. Through them I knew that you would one day say: ‘I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne, and I will be like the Most High.’ Therefore your fury and arrogance have reached my ears, and I will no longer endure you, so that you may understand that what you were able to do you did not accomplish by your own strength, but by my decision.

“For the impious nations and fruitless trees deserved to be cut down and fall through you, as though through my axe and saw. Therefore I will put a ring—or a hook—in your nostrils, so that I may restrain your blaspheming mouth and you may no longer dare to speak such things; and I will put a bridle on your lips, to tame your fierceness and lead you back to Assyria.”

With this same translation Scripture also speaks against the impious in the Psalms:

“Restrain their jaws with bridle and hook, who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:12).

### (Verses 30 ff.)

“But this shall be a sign for you: Eat this year what grows of itself, and in the second year eat fruit; but in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And what has been saved of the house of Judah, what remains below, shall put down roots and produce fruit above, because a remnant shall go out from Jerusalem, and salvation from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall accomplish this.”

Through messengers the Prophet has told Hezekiah all these things: what Sennacherib said and what the Lord answered him. Now he addresses Hezekiah directly, lest he perhaps doubt that what has been said will come to pass. This is especially why the prophets had credibility among the people: they spoke not only of things that would happen many centuries later, but also of things that would be fulfilled immediately or after only a short interval of time—namely, that within two years the king of the Assyrians would perish and security would be restored to the city of Jerusalem.

“This,” he says, “will be the sign of the things I foretell: this year you shall eat what grows of itself”—or, according to the Septuagint, what you previously sowed. “In the second year,” according to Symmachus, “eat fruit”; or, according to the same translators, eat what has sprouted from past crops and from seed that has fallen upon the ground. “In the third year,” once the Assyrian has been driven away and the siege lifted, “sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.”

For the survivors of this small city, now surrounded by an enemy army and not believing that they will escape, will receive such abundance and prosperity in everything that they will be filled with the thickest fruits, like a tree firmly established by a deep root. From Jerusalem and from Mount Zion a remnant will go out and fill the land of Judah—not by its own merit, but by God’s mercy, indeed by the zeal with which he has been zealous for his people against the impious.

### (Verses 33–34)

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not enter this city, nor shoot an arrow there; he shall not occupy it with a shield, nor cast up a rampart around it. By the way by which he came, by that same way he shall return, and he shall not enter this city, says the Lord. I will protect this city and save it, for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.”

He returns to the subject at hand and, after the hope of future events, dispels the present fear. There was not as much joy over what he had promised would happen after a long time as there was concern about what was imminent.

When he says that the Assyrian will withdraw, that he will neither raise a shield against Jerusalem nor shoot arrows, that the city will not be surrounded with fortifications and a rampart, that the enemy will return by the road on which he came, and that the city will be freed from its present siege, he finally adds: “For my own sake and for the sake of David my servant.” This signifies that they are preserved not by their own merit but by God’s clemency—or rather, by remembrance of their father David. By this they are reminded both of their own negligence and of David’s faith and righteousness: God loves righteousness so greatly that he protects even the descendants of holy men, not on account of their own merit but through the virtue of their ancestors.

### (Verses 36 ff.)

Then the angel of God went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand men in the camp of the Assyrians. When they arose in the morning, behold, all were corpses. Then he departed and went away. Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, withdrew and lived at Nineveh. And when he was worshiping in the temple of Nesrach, his god, Adrammelech and Sarasar, his sons, struck him with the sword. They fled to the land of Ararat, and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.

One hundred and eighty-five thousand exceptionally strong men are struck down by one angel in a single night. Without wounds, a savage death moves through them, separating their souls from their bodies by the will of God. Concerning this we read in Chronicles:

“And the Lord sent an angel, who struck every mighty man, warrior, and commander in the army of the king of Assyria; and he returned with shame to his own land” (II Chron. 32:24).

He was spared for this reason: so that he might learn the power of God and restrain his blaspheming mouth; so that he might become a witness to the majesty of the one whom he had shortly before despised.

As for what follows—“And they arose in the morning”—we may understand this of the Israelites or of the remainder of his army, although the Book of Kings says that when the king himself rose at dawn, he saw all the bodies of the dead (III Kings 19).

Pharaoh too is preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt so that he may perish last; and this man too will suffer the same fate. For when he had returned to Nineveh, the chief city of his kingdom, and was worshiping in the temple of Nesrach, his god, as though he had brought back victory over his enemies and were processing triumphantly and joyfully into the shrine of his idol, the contemner of the true God was slaughtered in the sanctuary of a false deity [variant: his own deity]—not by the sword of an angel, which would have been a common fate shared with many, but by the murderous act of his sons.

When they had fled to the land of Ararat, understood as Armenia, Esarhaddon succeeded his father. Scripture testifies that he sent inhabitants to Samaria [Note: More correctly, with Victorius, we read “Samaria”; previously “Samaria” stood here], so that the land would not remain uncultivated.

The region of Ararat in Armenia is a plain through which the Araxes flows. It is extraordinarily fertile and lies at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place.

Therefore the ark in which Noah and his sons were rescued after the Flood had ceased was not carried [variant: destroyed] generally to the mountains of Armenia called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus that rise above the plains of Ararat.

[Note: These mountains were called Ararat because they rise above the plain of Ararat. As for the fact that many ancient writers teach that the Ark adhered to the Gordyaean rather than the Taurus mountains, the holy Doctor in no way undermines this; rather, he explains it more clearly. For Strabo makes clear in Book XI that parts of the Taurus mountains were also called Gordyaean by some. Thus the part of Taurus that rises above the plain of Ararat could have been included under the name of the Gordyaeans. See also the Commentary on Jeremiah, chapter 51, verse 17.]

### (Chapter 38—verses 1 ff.)

In those days Hezekiah became sick unto death. The prophet Isaiah, son of Amos, entered to him and said:

“Thus says the Lord: Set your house in order, for you shall die and not live.”

Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to the Lord, saying:

“I beg you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes.”

And Hezekiah wept with great weeping.

“The Lord reproves the one whom he loves and chastises every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3).

Lest Hezekiah’s heart be lifted up after his unbelievable triumphs and his victory in the midst of captivity, he is visited with bodily illness and hears that he is going to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he may move him to change his sentence. We read the same thing in the prophet Jonah and in the threats spoken against David concerning things that were said to be going to happen but did not happen—not because God changed his decision, but because he summoned the human race to knowledge of himself. For “the Lord repents concerning evils.”

Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall because he could not go to the Temple. He turned toward the wall of the Temple, according to the view that Solomon had built his palace alongside it. Or, more simply, he turned toward the wall so that he would not appear to display his tears to those sitting nearby. Or else, according to Jeremiah, he turned toward his heart: Jeremiah calls *cir*, that is, “wall,” “heart,” so that he might entreat the Lord with his whole mind.

He said: “I beg you, Lord; remember, I pray, how I have walked before you in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done what is good in your eyes.” Hearing that he was going to die, he did not pray for life and many years, but left to God’s judgment what he should grant. For he knew that Solomon had pleased God precisely because he had not asked for additional years of life. But as one who was about to go to the Lord, he recounts his deeds: how he had walked before him in truth and with a perfect heart.

Happy is the conscience that, in a time of affliction, remembers good works. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

And when it is written elsewhere, “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. 20:9), the matter is resolved in this way: the perfection of the heart is here said to consist in the fact that he destroyed the idols, overturned the vessels of the temple of Baal, smashed the bronze serpent, and did the other things that Scripture records.

[Note: In the Vatican manuscripts: “and how elsewhere,” and shortly afterward, “he opened the doors of the temple of Baal.”]

He wept with great weeping because of the Lord’s promise to David, which he saw would perish with his own death. At that time Hezekiah had no children; for after his death Manasseh, who was twelve years old, began to reign in Judah. From this it is clear that Manasseh was born after the third year of the life granted to Hezekiah.

Therefore all this weeping arose from the fact that he despaired of Christ being born from his offspring.

Others maintain [Note: The same manuscripts read: “all holy persons,” and “the uncertainty of judgment.”] that holy men, too, are terrified by death because of the uncertainty of judgment and ignorance of God’s sentence, and of the dwelling they will have.

At the same time, the question of fate is resolved, as are the bonds of necessity and causation: the day of death is by no means fixed for each person, but by God’s will and by causes unknown to mortals a person either lives or dies—especially since a death that now appears to be decreed may be postponed, and we read that many have been raised after death.

### (Verses 4 ff.)

And the word of the Lord came to Isaiah, saying:

“Go and say to Hezekiah: Thus says the Lord God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your days, and I will deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will protect it.

“And this shall be a sign for you from the Lord, that the Lord will do this word which he has spoken: Behold, I will turn the shadow of the lines by which it had descended on the sundial of Ahaz back ten lines in the sun. And the sun went back ten lines by the steps over which it had descended.”

Here the historical sequence is reported in reverse order, as a prophecy; in the Book of Kings it is related more consecutively.

While Hezekiah was weeping bitterly, before Isaiah had gone out into the middle of the courtyard, the word of the Lord came to him, saying:

“Return and say to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: I have heard your prayer and seen your tear. Behold, I have healed you.”

And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: “What will be the sign that the Lord will heal me?” (IV Kings 20:4–5).

The Prophet answered him: “This shall be the sign from the Lord that the Lord will perform the word that he has spoken: Shall the shadow advance by ten lines, or shall it go back by the same number of steps?”

Hezekiah said: “It is easy for the shadow to increase by ten lines, and I do not want that; let it go backward ten steps instead.”

When, at Isaiah’s invocation of the Lord’s power, the sign had been accomplished, Isaiah ordered a lump of fresh figs to be brought. When they had brought it and placed it upon Hezekiah’s wound, he was healed.

The Prophet returns to the king at the Lord’s command, so that he who had struck might himself heal. Hezekiah is called the leader of the Lord’s people and the son of David, whose deeds he followed; for he had done what was right according to all that David his father had done. His prayer is heard and his tears are seen because he had walked before the Lord in truth and with a perfect heart, had wept with great weeping, and had done what was pleasing in his eyes.

Fifteen years are added to his life, although he had not requested them; and, while he is still alive, security for the kingdom is promised.

But if, as some think, living in the body is a condemnation, and according to the saying, “Return, my soul, to your rest” (Ps. 114:7), and elsewhere, “Bring my soul out of prison” (Ps. 141:8), death should be desired so that we may be freed from prison, how does the Lord now grant as a benefit that the one who was to be liberated should remain fifteen more years in prison?

A sign is given: the sun is to go back ten steps, which we have rendered, according to Symmachus, as “lines” and “sundial.” He understood the steps as lines in order to make the meaning clearer to readers.

Or perhaps the steps had been constructed by mechanical art in such a way that, as the shadow descended across each one, it marked the intervals of the hours.

This sign was a type both of the present time and of the future: just as the sun would return to the beginning of its course, so Hezekiah’s life would return to its years already unwoven [Note: Another Vatican manuscript reads: “so that, with years added, it would return also to Hezekiah’s life,” and so forth]. And for us, living in the weeks and the eighth day, the span of life would be extended through Christ’s resurrection.

Those who show the holy places in this province customarily point out, within the Temple enclosure, the steps of the house of Hezekiah or Ahaz, by which the sun is said to have descended. But I would never believe that the house of Ahaz—who was an impious king—not to mention the house of any righteous king, was in the Temple of God. Solomon is said to have offended God among other reasons because he built the Millo on high, from which he was accustomed, while walking in the tower of his palace, to look down upon the Temple courtyard (III Kings 9).

### (Verse 9)

“The writing of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he had been sick and had recovered from his illness.”

The Septuagint: “The prayer of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he was ill and rose from his illness.”

I wonder how the Septuagint alone has substituted “prayer” for “writing,” since “prayer” is called *tephillah*, and not *makhtar*, which is written in the present passage. Otherwise it would properly be called “prayer” if it referred to the present time, and not to the past. For it is clear that, after his health had been restored, rising from his illness, he wrote this account. Therefore it is not a prayer but a thanksgiving for the benefit he had received.

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“I said in the middle of my days: I shall go to the gates of the underworld; I sought the remainder of my years. I said, I shall not see the Lord [Note: From Jerome’s exposition appended below, he appears to have read “Lord” twice, rather than “God” the second time] God in the land of the living. I shall no longer look upon man, nor the inhabitant of rest [Note: The two words “rest” and “ceased” correspond to one word in the Hebrew text, which almost equally signifies both. Victorius states that from the Commentary it is clear that Jerome initially explained the first as “ceased” or “perished” and joined it to the following verse: “my generation has ceased,” and so forth. Shortly afterward, on reconsidering the matter, he changed his view and explained it as “rest,” making it the end of the first verse rather than the beginning of the second, in this way: “I shall no longer look upon man, nor the inhabitant of rest. My generation has been taken away,” and so forth. Compare Jerome himself below, near the end of this section, and what we note there in the annotation immediately following]. My generation has ceased; it has been taken away and folded up from me like a shepherd’s tent. My life has been cut off like a weaver’s; while I was still beginning to weave, he cut me off. From morning until evening you will finish me. I hoped until morning; like a lion, so he crushed all my bones. From morning until evening you will finish me.”

The Septuagint:

“I said at the height of my days: I shall go to the gates of the underworld; I shall leave the remaining years. I said, I shall no longer see the salvation of God in the land of the living, nor shall I see man any longer among the inhabitants. I shall cease from my kindred. He has departed and withdrawn from me, as a tent is taken down by the one who erected it. As a web, my spirit departed when it was cut off from the weaver. On that day I was handed over until morning. Like a lion, so he crushed all my bones. From day until night I was handed over.”

He relates what he silently considered during the time of pressing distress and impending illness:

“I said,” he says, “in my heart, ‘In the middle of my days’”—or, as Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it, “in the weakness and silence of my days.” The Septuagint translated it as “height,” because of the similarity of the letters, reading *rame* for *dame* [Note: “Although we read…” This passage is extremely corrupt in the older editions. In Erasmus’s edition the word *agro* is added, and in the Martianaean edition, “that is, in ἀκρά”; neither expression has any trace in Jerome’s manuscripts. MARTIAN].

Some have translated *dame* as “blood,” so that the sense would be: “In the blood of my days,” when my blood and my death were being sought [variant: awaited].

Thus in despair I said: “I shall go to the gates of the underworld,” either according to the common law of nature or to those gates of which the Psalmist sings that he was delivered:

“You who lift me up from the gates of death, that I may declare all your praises in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 9:15).

I think these are the gates of hell that do not prevail against Peter (Matt. 16), because he “slept in the fullness of his days.”

The saints complete their days, as did Abraham, who died full of days in a good old age (Gen. 25). Sinners and the impious, however, die in the middle of their days. Of them the Psalmist also says:

“Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. 54:25).

For they do not complete works of virtue, nor do they strive to amend their sins through repentance. Therefore, midway through the course of life and amid the darkness of their errors, they are led to Tartarus.

“I sought,” he says, “the remainder of my years,” not thinking that he would live any longer. “I said, I shall not see the Lord, the Lord, in the land of the living.”

In place of “Lord and Lord,” the Hebrew has *Yah* twice, which sounds in the final syllable of *Hallelujah*. The Septuagint translated it: “I shall no longer see the salvation of God in the land of the living.”

Of this it is written elsewhere:

“I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9).

And again:

“I shall please the Lord in the light of the living” (Ps. 55:9).

The land of the saints, therefore, is itself called the light of the living. For God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matt. 22). This is the whole of what he fears: that, having been led down to the underworld, he may no longer deserve to see the salvation of God.

It follows: “I shall no longer look upon man, nor the inhabitant of rest.” Formerly, because of the ambiguity of the word, we had joined this to the following verse. For the Hebrew word *holed*, if it is read [Note: One Vatican manuscript has: “if it is read as it is written.” In fact, *hedel* and *heled* are commonly used interchangeably and are synonymous in usage, although they derive from different etymologies. Here in Isaiah it is [Hebrew text]; in Psalm 49:2, [Hebrew text]. In both places the inhabitants of the world are designated; but in the first passage the future cessation or rest of this age is understood, while in the other its worthlessness or obscurity is intended. It is therefore more correct, and entirely in keeping with Jerome’s meaning, to read in two Vatican manuscripts first *edel*, “rest,” and then *eled*, “the West”], or written *eled*, it means “rest”; if *edel*, it means “the West.”

He therefore fears that he will not dwell with the saints and men of God in rest; that he will not see the Lord in the land of the living; that his generation will be dissolved like a tent; that, like a woven fabric, it will be cut off at the very beginning of the light; and that Christ will in no way arise from his offspring.

That our body is called a tent the Apostle also teaches when he says:

“We who are in this tent groan, being weighed down” (II Cor. 5:4).

“From morning,” he says, “until evening you will finish me. I hoped until morning.” Job also says that he endured this in his distress and bodily torments (Job 4), when during the day he awaited night and looked for light amid darkness, thinking that the punishments might be changed by the change of times.

The one who burns with a high fever knows this truth: his inward fire consumes all his bones like a lion, and because of the magnitude of his pain he does not think that he will live any longer.

### (Verse 15)

“Like a young swallow, so I shall cry out; I shall moan like a dove. My eyes have grown weak as I look upward. Lord, I am oppressed; answer for me. What shall I say, or what will he answer me, since he himself has done it?”

The Septuagint:

“Like a swallow, so I shall cry out; like a dove, so I shall moan. My eyes have failed as I look toward the height of heaven, toward the Lord who delivered me, took away the pain of my soul, and himself did this.”

Death impending and the pain of illness pressing upon him were breaking all the bones of his body like a lion. But, like a swallow and a dove, he joined days and nights in tears and groans; and, raising his eyes on high toward the only God who could help, he awaited assistance.

He said to him: “I suffer more than my merits demand; but if I have gone astray in anything, I shall turn toward what is better. You answer for me.” [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts here read, “You, be surety for me,” and, a little later, “against my Maker, without you.”]

“For it depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

Then he turns back to himself:

“What shall I say, or what shall I plead against you, my Maker? Or what will he answer me who himself has done what he wished?”

Therefore, whatever he has decreed must be endured.

For “young swallow,” or simply “swallow,” as the Septuagint translated it, the Hebrew has *sus agor*, which Aquila translated as “horse of Agor” (*equus Agor*); Theodotion as *sis agur*. For the middle vowel, the letter *waw*, if placed between two *samek* letters, is read *sus* and means “horse”; if it is *yod*, it is read *sis* and means “swallow.”

Symmachus translated it as follows:

“Like a swallow confined, so I shall sing.”

The word *agor* is also found in Jeremiah, where it is written:

“The kite in the sky knows its season; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork observe the times appointed for them” (Jer. 8:7).

(Vers. 16 ff.) I will reckon all my years in the bitterness of my soul. Lord, if this is how one lives, and if such is the condition of my spirit’s life, you will correct me and restore me to life. Behold, my bitterness is most bitter in peace. But you delivered my soul so that it would not perish; you cast all my sins behind your back. For the underworld will not confess you, nor will death praise you; those who descend into the pit will not await your truth. The living, the living—he himself will confess you, as I do today. A father will make your truth known to his children. Lord, save me, and we shall sing our psalms all the days of our life in the house of the Lord.

The Septuagint: Lord, it was announced to you concerning it; and you raised up my spirit, and, having comforted me, you restored me to life. Behold, my bitterness in peace: for you delivered my soul so that it would not perish, and you cast all my sins behind me. For those in the underworld will not praise you, nor will the dead bless you. Those who are in the lower regions will not hope for your mercy; the living will bless you, as I do. From this day onward I will make children who will proclaim your righteousness, Lord, my salvation, and I shall not cease, blessing you with the Psalter, all the days of my life, in the presence of the house of God.

Nothing belonging to mortals is lasting, and every prosperity of this age, while it is held, is lost. For when the time of tribulation arrives, nothing that has passed helps the one who is enduring it. Hence Epicurus’ foolish opinion: he asserts that present evils are alleviated by recalling past goods.

Thus Hezekiah says that he is reckoning all the years of his reign, and of his former happiness—which he supposed it to have been—in his present bitterness. And because he is now secure and is not suffering what he recounts, he philosophizes about the human condition and says: “Lord, if this is how one lives,” and if this is the condition in which we were born, “you corrected me, but you restored me to life,” and gave me peace when the Assyrian had been driven away; but my peace was more bitter to me than every bitterness, because, when tranquillity had been restored to the peoples and the city was secure, I alone entered the thresholds of death.

But you delivered my soul so that it would not perish, whether in the present life or in the future one. For you cast all my sins behind your back, so that I would not look upon them in grief but contemplate your mercy. For the underworld and death will neither confess nor praise you, in accordance with what is written: “But in the underworld, who will confess you?” (Ps. 6:6). Here “confession” is understood not as repentance but as glory and praise, just as we also read in the Gospel: “I will confess [another reading: I confess] to you, Lord, Father of heaven and earth” (Matt. 11:25).

“Those who descend into the pit,” he says, “will not await your truth”—better than the Septuagint’s “mercy.” For the one who is in the underworld does not await the truth of judgment but the mercy of God, especially since the Savior descended to the lower regions in order to free the captives from the underworld. In place of “the pit,” they more explicitly translated “the lower regions.”

“The living, the living—he himself will confess you, as I do today.” Here too “confession” is used for praise. For he is not confessing his crimes but giving thanks to God; and “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). Since the underworld and death neither confess nor praise God, life and the living, by contrast, glorify the Lord.

What follows—“A father will make your truth known to his children”—means what is said in Deuteronomy: “Ask your father, and he will announce it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. 32:7), so that through successions and individual generations God’s mercy may be proclaimed to those who come after.

In place of this the Septuagint has: “From this day onward I will make children who will announce your righteousness.” The causal conjunction connects what follows with what came before: namely, that the living, and he himself as one living, bless God for this reason—that from this day he is going to make children who will proclaim his truth—which certainly was not within his power. For children were not promised to him through the Prophet; rather, the present life was granted to him. This is especially so since he fathered the most impious son, Manasseh, who filled Jerusalem with blood from gate to gate, and did not bless but cursed God while persecuting his holy ones.

We can therefore say, according to the Septuagint, that he did not say, “I will make children,” but παιδία (“little children”), by which we understand little ones, boys, infants, or descendants; so that, because he himself had obtained mercy, every posterity that would come after him, recognizing this, might praise his incredible clemency.

“Therefore save me, Lord”; and all who believe in you and have been delivered by your help will sing of you throughout all the days of our life in the Temple.

### (Vers. 21, 22.)

And Isaiah ordered them to take a lump of figs and apply it as a poultice over the wound, and it was healed. And Hezekiah said: What will be the sign that I shall go up into the house of the Lord?

This must be read before Hezekiah’s prayer, or the passage of Scripture that we have now interpreted. For the poultice was first applied to the wound, and the sign of future healing was requested from him before he gave thanks to the Lord, which he is said to have done after he had been healed.

[Note: At [Col. 0395], Rabanus and the Sangermanensis manuscript in Montfaucon, here and below, read SIM or SIN, with only a single i.] The Hebrews say that the word SIIN (), which the Septuagint omitted, means “ulcer.” For Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion also translated it by ἕλκος (“ulcer”), and they wish the royal disease to be understood by it—a disease for which whatever is sweet, whether taken as food or applied to the body, is thought to be harmful. Thus, in order that God’s power might be demonstrated, health was restored through things harmful and contrary to it.

Others suspect that SIIN means not an ulcer but an abscess: when the swollen body is filled with cooked and putrefying pus. According to medical practice, all suppuration is brought to the surface of the skin by dried and crushed figs. Hence medicine should not be despised when it is established by use and experience, since God also made this medicine.

The prayer and thanksgiving, therefore, have been written out up to this point. As for the sign that was given, the preceding order of the narrative has related it.

### (Chap. XXXIX.—Vers. 1 ff.)

At that time Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah, for he had heard that he had been ill and had recovered. And Hezekiah rejoiced over them and showed them the storehouse of spices, silver, gold, perfumes, and the finest ointment, and all the storerooms of his possessions, and everything that was found in his treasures. There was no matter that Hezekiah did not show them in his house and throughout all his dominion.

Above we read that, in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, came against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them; afterward he besieged Lachish, crossed over to Libnah, and sent part of his army against Jerusalem. One hundred and eighty-five thousand of his army were slain by an angel, and he himself fled to Nineveh, where he was killed by his sons in the temple of his god; and his son Esarhaddon reigned in his place. Hezekiah then fell ill and, at the Prophet’s announcement, received recovery. An incredible sign occurred: the sun returned toward its rising through ten hours, so that the day became almost twice as long.

Now we read that “at that time”—that is, in the same year in which all these events occurred—Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and gifts to Hezekiah; not Esarhaddon, who had succeeded his father Sennacherib to the Assyrian throne, concerning whose death or life Scripture is silent. From this it is clear that at that time the Assyrians had one kingdom and the Babylonians another.

Indeed, the Assyrians captured Samaria, that is, the ten tribes. But afterward we read that the Chaldaeans captured Judah and Jerusalem; their king was Nebuchadnezzar. And because among them the observation of the stars is practiced, and the courses of the stars have been learned through long use and training—as is also shown at the Lord’s birth—they understood that the sun had turned back and the length of the day had been doubled, and that it served the one whom they supposed to be the only God. [Note: The Vatican manuscript inserts, as Rabanus also reads, “that is, the sun.”] When they sought the causes and explanation of this miracle, they learned—since rumor was flying through all the nations—that even the course of the most brilliant sign had been altered on account of the illness of the king of Judah.

That this is not my conjecture but the testimony of Holy Scripture is confirmed by the words of Chronicles, which say afterward: “Hezekiah himself stopped the upper spring of the waters of Gihon and diverted them below, toward the west of the city of David. In all his works he prospered in whatever he undertook; nevertheless, in the matter of the embassy of the princes of Babylon, who had been sent to him to inquire about the portent that had occurred upon the earth, God left him in order to test him, so that all that was in his heart might become known” (2 Chron. 32:30–31).

He was left to temptation for this reason: after such a great victory, the return of the sun, and the congratulations of the most powerful kingdom, his heart was lifted up. In the same book it is written: “Many brought victims and sacrifices to the Lord in Jerusalem, and gifts to Hezekiah king of Judah; and he was exalted before all the nations. In those days he fell ill unto death, and he prayed to the Lord; and he heard him and gave him a sign. But he did not repay according to the benefits he had received, because his heart was lifted up, and wrath came against him, and against Judah and Jerusalem” (2 Chron. 32:23–24).

Again Holy Scripture says that the elevation of his heart was softened by repentance, adding: “Afterward he humbled himself because his heart had been lifted up, both he and the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and therefore the wrath of the Lord did not come upon them in the days of Hezekiah.”

Hezekiah therefore rejoiced at the arrival of Merodach, whom the Hebrews assert to have been the father of Nebuchadnezzar; he rejoiced at the offering of gifts and at the congratulations on his recovery. According to the Septuagint, he showed them the house of NECHOTHA (), for which Symmachus translated “his spices,” and the treasures of silver, gold, perfumes, and the finest ointment. In Hebrew this is written “good oil.” He showed them all the treasures of his vessels of wealth—or, as it reads there, “of his vessels.”

“Gaza” in the language of the Persians means “riches”; it is not a Hebrew word but a barbarian one.

“There was no matter,” he says—according to Hebrew usage, “matter” is often taken for “thing”—“that he did not show them in his house and throughout all his dominion.” Hence God’s anger was entirely just, since he showed them not only his own treasures and those of the palace but also those of the Temple—something that certainly belonged to his authority, since he had already removed the gold plates from its doors. [Note: Conversely, another Vatican manuscript reads, “which certainly was not.”]

### (Vers. 3 ff.)

Then Isaiah the Prophet entered King Hezekiah’s presence and said to him: What did these men say, and from where did they come to you? And Hezekiah said: They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon. And he said: What did they see in your house? And Hezekiah said: They saw everything that is in my house; there was no matter, or thing, that I did not show them among my treasures.

And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. Behold, days will come when everything that is in your house, and what your fathers have stored up until this day, will be carried away to Babylon; nothing will be left, says the Lord. And from your sons who will come forth from you, whom you will beget, they will take them, and they will be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.

And Hezekiah said to Isaiah: Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken. And he said: Let there be only peace and truth in my days.

[Note: This is transferred almost word for word from Eusebius, who says: “The Jewish teacher used to say that Hezekiah fell ill because he had not sung to God a thanksgiving ode upon the fall of the Assyrians, as Moses sang at the destruction of the Egyptians, Deborah at the destruction of Sisera, and Hannah at the birth of Samuel.” Yet Eusebius himself shortly afterward rejects this tale as an ἀναχρονισμός (anachronism).]

The Hebrews relate that Hezekiah fell ill for this reason: after the unheard-of [another reading: celebrated] victory of the Jews and the destruction of the Assyrian king, he did not sing praises to the Lord, as Moses sang when Pharaoh was drowned (Exod. 15), Deborah when Sisera was killed (Judg. 4), and Hannah when Samuel was born (1 Sam. 2). Thus, he was reminded of his frailty.

Again, after the restoration of his bodily health and the greatness of the sign, another occasion for pride was presented to him, which, as a prudent worshiper of God, he ought to have avoided. He should not have shown foreigners the wealth he possessed through God’s generosity.

From this, according to the laws of tropology as well, we learn that pearls must not be cast before swine, nor what is holy given to dogs (Matt. 7). The one who is faithful in spirit conceals his affairs; [Note: Victor reads “a spirit [is] upright,” following the Greek πνοή.] and whoever does not do this has all his virtue weakened. [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts, without the negative particle, read “whoever does this.”] His posterity perishes, and, having lost his masculine strength, he is reduced to feminine softness (Prov. 11:13–15).

Isaiah therefore enters the king and, as though ignorant, asks him: “What did these men say, and from where did they come?” He asks two things: what they said and from where they came. He answered one and passed over the other. This must be read with emphasis and indignation: “They came to me from a distant land, from Babylon.” The more distant the land from which they came, the more glorious he considered himself to be, since they had come on his account.

“They came,” he says, “to me”—when he ought to have said: “They came to glorify God for the greatness of the sign”—“from Babylon,” a city that is the most powerful in the whole world.

Again Isaiah asks: “What did they see in your house?” He answered partly and truthfully that they had seen everything in his house and that there was no thing he had not shown them among his treasures. But he keeps silent about the other matter, concerning which he feared offense: that he had shown them everything he possessed within his authority, unquestionably including the Temple’s vessels.

For these things Isaiah pronounces judgment in God’s words: “Hear the word of the Lord of hosts. The time will come when all these things that are in your house, acquired not by your labor but by that of your fathers, will be carried away to Babylon, and from your offspring eunuchs will be made in the royal court.”

Hence the Hebrews wish Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah, who were of royal descent, to have been made eunuchs; there is no doubt that they served in the household of King Nebuchadnezzar.

Hezekiah therefore said: “Good is the word of the Lord that he has spoken.” For this the Hebrews criticize him: why did he not imitate the goodness of Moses, who said to the Lord: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, blot me out of the book that you have written” (Exod. 32:32)? The Apostle Paul likewise desires to be accursed from Christ for the sake of his brothers, who are Israelites (Rom. 9:3).

For this reason Hezekiah was not approved by the words of God, who speaks in what follows: “Comfort, comfort my people, says your God,” so that those for whom he had not prayed might nevertheless be comforted by the Lord’s mercy.

### (Chap. XL.—Vers. 1 ff.)

“Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, and call to her; for her wickedness has been completed, her iniquity has been forgiven. She has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins.”

The Septuagint: “Comfort, comfort my people, says God: [† priests] speak to the heart of Jerusalem; comfort her, because her humiliation has been filled up. Her sin has been loosed, because she has received from the hand of the Lord double for her sins.”

According to the other translators, some are commanded to comfort God’s people and Jerusalem together. According to the Hebrew, the command is addressed to the people themselves: they are to comfort Jerusalem, speak to her heart, and call to her.

To speak to the heart of Jerusalem is an idiom of Scripture. For one who speaks to a grieving person and, by gentle words, acts as a comforter is said to speak to the heart. Let Shechem, the son of Hamor, teach us this: after violating Dinah, he spoke to her heart and comforted her (Gen. 34). Wherever you find something similar, it has this meaning.

The cause of consolation is the remission of sins; and the cause of remission is that Jerusalem “has received from the hand of the Lord double for all her sins.” For “the one who knows the will of his lord and sins will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47).

Everyone who has within himself the indwelling Holy Spirit—the Spirit whom the Savior promised to the Apostles when he said, “I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Comforter, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17)—and again, “When the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, comes, he will teach you everything” (ibid., 26)—and again, “When the Comforter comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15:26)—and, “It is beneficial for you that I go away; for if I do not go away, the Comforter will not come to you” (John 16:7)—everyone who possesses this Spirit is a comforter, and to him the command is now given to comfort God’s people.

Hence the Apostle Paul also spoke to believers: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we may be able to console those who are in every tribulation, through the consolation with which we ourselves are consoled by God. For just as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so through Christ our consolation also abounds” (2 Cor. 1:3–6). And again: “Our hope for you is firm, knowing that just as you are participants in the sufferings, so also you will be participants in the consolation” (2 Cor. 1:7).

Who this people is who is consoled through the Apostles and ecclesiastical men—not Israel, Jacob, and Judah, as Scripture mentions in other places—the Prophet Zechariah testifies, saying: “Rejoice and be glad, daughter of Zion, because I am coming and will dwell in your midst, says the Lord. And many nations will flee to the Lord on that day, and they will be his people; they will dwell in your midst, and they will know that the Lord Almighty has sent me to you” (Zech. 2:10–11).

This testimony clearly demonstrates that very many nations are to be turned into God’s people. And this is said by the one sent by the Lord, whose name is Almighty.

This too must be noted: our sins are not loosed unless we receive them from the hand of the Lord. Nor is “sins being loosed” the same as “sins being forgiven.” The one whose sins are forgiven has no need of being loosed, hearing the Gospel say: “Take heart, son; your sins are forgiven” (Matt. 9:2). But the one whose sins are loosed is loosed for this reason: because they have been cleansed and released through punishments.

According to the historical interpretation, Jerusalem received double punishment for her sins from the hand of the Lord: once from the Babylonians and a second time from the Romans.

The word added by the Septuagint, “priests,” must be marked with an obelus [†].  
[Note: The obelus † is indeed prefixed to it in the Vatican manuscripts.]

### (Vers. 3 ff.)

“A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight in the desert the paths of our God. Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled; crooked places shall become straight, rough places shall become level roads, and the glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see together that the mouth of the Lord has spoken.”

The Septuagint: “A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be humbled; crooked places shall become straight, and rough places plains. And the glory of the Lord shall appear, and all flesh shall see the salvation of God, because the Lord has spoken.”

Remembering this voice, the scribes, Pharisees, and rulers of the Jews, when they heard John preaching baptism of repentance in the wilderness and teaching the people, sent men to ask him whether he was the Christ, or Elijah, or the Prophet. When he replied that he was none of these, they asked again: “Tell us, then, who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?” And he replied: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” just as the Prophet Isaiah said (John 1:22–23).

Here it must be observed that the straight ways of the Lord and the paths of our God—the filling of valleys and the humbling of mountains and hills, the correction of crooked things, and the transformation of rough rocks into plains—the glory of the Lord and the salvation of our God are preached not in Jerusalem but in the wilderness of the Church and in the deserted multitude of the nations. Concerning this we read above (on chap. 35:1): “Rejoice, thirsty wilderness; let the desert exult and flower like a lily.”

For this wilderness was without knowledge of God. It was held captive by idols, lowly in confession, raised up in pride, rough and unyielding in savagery. But after the glory of the Lord appeared and all flesh saw the salvation of God, everything was suddenly changed and the way of the Lord was prepared, so that the glory of God might appear in the wilderness.

This happened when the Lord was baptized in the Jordan, the heavens were opened, and the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him. The voice of the Father, thundering from above, was heard: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matt. 3:17).

And all flesh saw the salvation of God. It was called “flesh” because previously it did not possess the Holy Spirit. Of it the Lord also says: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3). But that flesh would see the salvation of God of which the same Lord spoke through Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and they shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28).

John was not the only one crying this at that time. Because he was the forerunner and precursor of the word of God, he is rightly called “the voice” (Matt. 3). To this day, however, in the wilderness of the Gentiles, the teachers of the Churches cry out: let us make straight ways and paths for God in our hearts; let us be filled with virtues and bend ourselves through humility; let us change crooked things into straight and turn rough things into smooth. In this way may we deserve to see the glory of the Lord and the salvation of God.

### (Vers. 6 ff.)

“A voice saying: Cry out. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass has dried up, the flower has fallen, because the spirit of God blew upon it; truly the people are grass. The grass has dried up, the flower has fallen; but the word of our God will stand forever.”

[Note: “Because the spirit of God blew upon it,” and the following words are absent from manuscripts of the Septuagint. Hence one may infer that the Roman exemplar was that Greek edition called Κοινή, that is, the Common edition; the same is to be said of the Alexandrian codex, which lacks the asterisks of Origen’s edition. Jerome’s observation that these words are absent because the two verses end alike in “flower” is noteworthy for proving a similar omission in the First Epistle of Blessed John: verses 7 and 8 of chapter 5 end, “and these three are one.” See vol. I of this edition, col. 1674. MARTIAN.]

The Septuagint: “A voice saying: Cry out. And I said: What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the glory of humanity is like the flower of grass. The grass has withered, and the flower has fallen [* because the spirit of God blew upon it; truly the people are grass; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen *]; but the word of our God remains forever.”

The words marked with asterisks—“because the spirit of God blew upon it; truly the people are grass; the grass has withered, the flower has fallen”—have been added from the Hebrew and from Theodotion’s edition. From this it is clear that they were either omitted by the Septuagint or gradually erased through scribal error, since both the preceding and the following verse end with “flower.”

[Note: These words are still absent from the Roman and Alexandrian manuscripts, which are extremely ancient; they were later supplied in the Complutensian edition. See a similar omission of the same words below in the Commentary on Jeremiah, chap. 30:15.]

Above we read the Prophet saying: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people? And I said: Behold, here am I; send me. And he said: Go and say to this people: You shall hear with the ear and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall see and shall not see,” and what follows.

Having endured harsh treatment in that preaching, he now asks, when the Lord’s voice says, “Cry out,” what he ought to cry, fearing similar consequences. Beginning with the general statement, “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass,” he comes to the particular, so that he may also say concerning the people: “Truly the people are grass.”

Indeed, if anyone considers the frailty of the flesh, and how we grow and diminish from hour to hour and do not remain in the same condition—and how even what we speak, dictate, and write flies past as part of our life—he will not hesitate to call flesh grass and its glory like the flower of grass, or like the meadows of the fields.

The one who was recently an infant suddenly becomes a boy; the boy suddenly becomes a young man; and through uncertain stages he changes all the way to old age. Before he wonders that he is no longer young, he understands that he is already old.

A beautiful woman who once drew behind her crowds of young men becomes wrinkled in the furrows of her brow; and the woman who was formerly an object of love later becomes an object of disgust. The distinguished orator among the Greeks likewise writes: “The beauty of the body either time diminishes or illness consumes.”

[Note: In the margin of the Vatican manuscript, Aratus is written. The saying, however, is from Isocrates, near the beginning of his Paraenetic Oration to Demonicus: “For beauty either time has consumed or illness has withered it.”]

The flesh, therefore, has dried up and its beauty has fallen, because the spirit of God’s anger and judgment blew upon it—to return from the general argument to the order of Scripture—the flesh that bears the image of the earthly and serves vices and luxury. It is grass and a passing flower.

But the one who possesses and preserves the image of the heavenly is that flesh which sees the salvation of the Lord. It is renewed daily in knowledge according to the image of the Creator; and, receiving an incorruptible and immortal body, it changes its glory but not its nature.

But the word of our Lord, and those who have been joined to the word, remain forever.

### (Verses 9ff.)

“Climb upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem; raise it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah: ‘Behold your God!’ Behold, the Lord God will come in strength, and his arm will rule. Behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him. Like a shepherd he will feed his flock; with his arm he will gather the lambs, and in his bosom he will lift them; he himself will carry the pregnant ewes.”

The Septuagint: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who proclaim good news to Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem; raise it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah: ‘Behold your God; behold, the Lord God will come with power, and his arm with dominion. Behold, his reward is with him, and his work is in his presence. Like a shepherd he will feed his people, and with his arm he will gather the lambs.’”

[Note: We have deleted the words “and in his bosom he will carry,” which had been inserted here. They are not found in our manuscripts, and it is evident from the translations of Aquila and Symmachus that they were rashly introduced here: *en tō kolpō autou bastaxei* (“he will carry them in his bosom”). They are not found in the present copies of the Septuagint either.]

“And he will comfort the pregnant ewes.”

The choir of the Apostles is commanded to climb to an elevated place for the preaching of the whole human race, which is to see the salvation of God; and, since they are about to speak of great things, they are to dwell in lofty places. The Hebrew, as do the other interpreters, uses the feminine gender, so that the words mean: “you who proclaim good news to Zion,” and “you who proclaim good news to Jerusalem.” Among the Greeks, however, the word is ambiguous, so that we may understand either “the one who announces” or “the one to whom the announcement is made.”

Therefore, whether Zion and Jerusalem proclaim the word of God and the salvation of the Lord—for “the law shall go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. 2:3)—or whether the announcement is made to them through the Apostles, they must climb to elevated places and pass over into the mountains.

In a remarkable way, although Zion itself is a mountain, as Scripture says, “Mount Zion, where you have dwelt” (Ps. 73:3), it is commanded to climb another, higher mountain, from which the prince of Tyre was wounded. And because many things were destined to oppose the Apostles’ teaching, and they were led before governors and tribunals, the words are added: “Raise it up, do not fear; say to the cities of Judah”—that is, to the synagogues and peoples of the Jews, concerning whom the Lord was speaking: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). The Apostle Paul likewise says: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you” (Acts 13:46).

What, then, are they commanded to say? “Behold your God,” whom you were always awaiting. “Behold, the Lord God will come in strength,” whom you despised when he came in humility. “And his strength will rule,” he who had earlier taken the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. 2:8).

“Behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him” (Isa. 40 and 62). In accordance with what he himself says in the Gospel: “For the Son of Man is about to come in the glory of his Father” [Note: The Vatican manuscript adds: “with the angels.” The Greek has *meta tōn angelōn* (“with the angels”).] “and he will repay each one according to his work” (Matt. 16:27).

“Like a shepherd he will feed his flock.” He who will later come in majesty first assumes the form of a shepherd, and says of himself: “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep” [Note: The same manuscript reads: “I know my sheep.” The Greek has only *ginōskō ta ema* (“I know my own”).] “and my own know me, and I lay down my life for my sheep” (John 10:14–15). Concerning him the Father speaks in Zechariah: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7).

“With his arm,” he says, “he will gather the lambs”—not bulls, rams, goats, or large sheep, concerning whom he threatens through Ezekiel (chap. 34), because they feed on the milk and clothe themselves with the wool, while crushing the weak of the flock; rather, he will gather the still-tender lambs, those of an inexperienced infancy in Christ, who have recently been reborn in baptism. Concerning them the Lord himself said to Peter: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:15).

Hence it is also written in the same Ezekiel: “I will raise up over them one shepherd, and he will feed them, my servant David; and he will be their shepherd, and I, the Lord, will be their God, and David will be prince in their midst. I, the Lord, have spoken, and I will establish with David a covenant of peace” (Ezek. 34:23–25).

In this we must observe that, after many ages, he says that he will raise up our Lord, who is descended from David, rejecting the gluttonous shepherds, so that he may gather the lambs, cherish them in his bosom, and himself carry the pregnant sheep—or the sheep with their young—upon his shoulder. Thus we read in the Gospel that he carried back upon his shoulders the wandering sheep that had remained apart from its accustomed flock and folds (Luke 15).

[Note: These words too are drawn in part from Eusebius. After saying that those recently born and regenerated in Christ are called “lambs,” he adds: “In another sense, the souls of his Apostles, conceiving and travailing with those who through them are reborn in Christ, had him as their comforter. You will understand this from the one who says: ‘My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you’” (Gal. 4:19).]

We may call the Apostles, apostolic men, and all the teachers of the Church pregnant sheep, who give birth to the salvation of many and say with the Apostle: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

The Hebrews assert—and among them there is no doubt about this—that the Holy Spirit is called in their language by a feminine noun, namely *RUA CODSA* (). And what is said in Psalm 67, “The Lord will give the word to those proclaiming the good news with great power,” they understand as follows:

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts read this way. In fact, although no difference in the Hebrew reading is apparent here, the holy teacher wished to indicate one, in order to establish that the Holy Spirit is called by the Hebrews with a feminine noun. When he wished to set their reading against the superior Vulgate version, he could easily have written “to the female proclaimers of great power or strength” instead of “to those proclaiming the good news with great power”; for in Hebrew it is feminine, and he himself translated it in this way. They understood the “great strength” that the souls proclaim as the Holy Spirit.]

“The Lord will give the word to those proclaiming the good news with great power” (Ps. 67:12)—that is, to those souls who have received the Holy Spirit. They also interpret the words, “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress,” by understanding the maidservant as the soul and the mistress as the Holy Spirit.

Moreover, in the Gospel written according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, the Lord says: “Just now my mother, the Holy Spirit, took me.” [Note: Origen also cites this same passage in Homily 15 on Jeremiah and in the second volume of his Commentary on John. Jerome himself also cites it elsewhere, including in his commentary on Micah, chapter 7. Nevertheless, Origen does not adequately excuse the statement that the Holy Spirit was called Christ’s mother in that Gospel by arguing that Christ also calls those who do the Father’s will “brother,” “sister,” and “mother.” Learned men have identified the source of the error in Matthew 3:16–17, concerning Christ’s baptism, when the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove together with the voice descending from heaven: “This is my Son,” and so forth. The Nazarenes, through a foolish error, attributed these words spoken by the dove—or by the Holy Spirit—to the dove itself or to the Holy Spirit, as though the Spirit had called Christ its son. Once they had admitted this, however, and recognized that it was absurd to assign two fathers to Christ, they called the Holy Spirit the mother of Jesus.]

No one should therefore be scandalized in this matter because the spirit is feminine in Hebrew, masculine in our language, and neuter in Greek. In divinity there is no sex. For this reason, in the three principal languages in which the title of the Lord’s Passion was written, the word is expressed in three genders, so that we may know that what is different in grammatical gender has no gender in reality.

### (Verses 12ff.)

“Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, and weighed the heavens with a span? Who has held the mass of the earth in three fingers, and weighed the mountains in a balance, and the hills on scales? Who has assisted the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him? With whom did he take counsel, and who instructed him, taught him the path of justice, educated him in knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding? Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are reckoned as a moment on the scales; behold, the islands are like fine dust. Lebanon is not sufficient for burning, nor are its animals sufficient for a burnt offering. All the nations are as though they did not exist before him, and they are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness.”

The Septuagint: “Who has measured the water with his hand, and the heaven with a span, and all the earth with a handful? Who established the mountains by weight, and the rocks by a balance? Who knew the mind of the Lord, or who was his counselor? Who taught him, from whom did he receive counsel, and who instructed him? Or who showed him judgment, and who showed him the way of understanding? If all the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are reckoned as a moment on the scales, and are reckoned as spittle, Lebanon is not sufficient for burning, nor are all the four-footed animals sufficient for a burnt offering; and all the nations are as nothing and are reckoned as nothing by him.”

Lest anyone think the calling of the nations difficult, and lest anyone doubt that all flesh would see the salvation of God, those who proclaim good news to Zion—or, according to another reading, the one who proclaims it—were commanded to climb a high mountain. The Lord himself would come in strength and repay each person according to his work; and, like a shepherd, he would cherish the lambs in his bosom and himself carry the pregnant sheep. His greatness is now described: nothing is impossible for him, and he who established all things and is the Creator of everything can also accomplish these things, which are small by comparison with them.

When he speaks of a handful and a span, he uses words and measurements taken from human custom, so that through our words we may learn God’s power. Where the Septuagint translated, “Who has measured the water with his hand,” or, as we translated it, “Who has measured the waters in a handful,” Aquila translated, “Who has measured the waters with the smallest finger.” This is what *lichas* means: not with the whole hand, but with the little finger, commonly called the “taster,” the entire vastness of the waters is weighed. *Spithamē*, that is, “span,” signifies an extended hand from the thumb to the end of the finger. If, however, we contract the hand, it becomes a handful. Thus, through the span and the handful, we are to understand the extended heavens and the globe of the earth.

In place of “handful,” which the Septuagint translated in the passage about grasping the earth, the Hebrew has *SALIS* (). Symmachus translated it as *triton* (“third”), Aquila as *trisōmon*. [Note: The Vatican manuscript has *TRISŌMA*; the Saint-Germain manuscript has *TRISSŌM*, according to Montfaucon, who rightly suspects that the word *trisōmon* lies hidden beneath the corruption.] We translated it as “three fingers,” to make the sense clearer: he held the mass of the earth and the heights of the mountains and hills as though on three little fingers and the small moment of a balance. Through this, God’s majesty and the Creator’s power are displayed.

“Who,” he says, “has assisted the spirit of the Lord, or who was his counselor and showed him?” and so forth. Symmachus translated this as: “Who prepared the spirit of the Lord, and who showed him the man of his counsel? With whom did he take counsel, and give him understanding, and teach him the way of judgment, and instruct him in knowledge, and show him the path of prudence?”

Through this he more clearly indicates that the spirit was prepared, or that he was established—the one of whom the Apostle says: “The Lord is the Spirit.” And: “Upon whom rested the Spirit of God, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,” and the rest. He says in what follows: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1). He is the Spirit of the Lord and the man of his counsel, in whom “the whole fullness of divinity dwelt bodily” (Col. 2:9). With him he took counsel, concerning whom we spoke above (on chapter 11:6): “Wonderful, Counselor.” And it is written in Proverbs: “God founded the earth by wisdom, but he prepared the heavens by prudence” (Prov. 3:19).

The Septuagint, which said, “Who knew the mind of the Lord, and who was his counselor?” intends this to be understood as the mind, reason, and sense of God, through which all things were made and without which nothing was made. This is the one of whom it is sung in the Psalms: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6).

All the nations, which did not know their Creator—or the whole human race—are, by comparison with God, like a drop from a bucket and like a moment on the scales, which is tipped to one side by a light weight. And just as, if a small drop flows from a bucket, it is disregarded by the one carrying it, so the entire multitude of the nations, when compared with the heavenly ministries and the multitude of angels, is counted as nothing.

The islands too are reckoned as spittle; or, as Symmachus and Theodotion, preserving the Hebrew word itself, give it, as *DOC* (), “that which falls.” In its place Aquila translated *lepton ballomenon* (“a small thing cast down”).
