The Hebrews say that this word signifies the finest dust, which, when carried by the wind, is often blown into the eyes and is felt rather than seen. Thus they call the tiniest and nearly invisible particles of dust by this word—perhaps what Democritus and his Epicurus call atoms.

There are many words which are read in Greek just as they are placed in Hebrew, because of the difficulty of translating and the poverty of both Greek and Latin speech when compared with the Hebrew language.

At the same time, he gradually draws human beings away from idolatry, removes the ceremonies of sacrifices, and teaches that all the trees of Lebanon and the herds grazing there would not suffice for burnt offerings to him. But if all the nations are before him as though they did not exist, and are reckoned as nothing and emptiness—and Israel is included among all the nations—then Israel too is as though it did not exist and is reckoned as nothing and emptiness. We say this in order that its pride may be broken and that it may recognize itself as like the other nations.

### (Verses 18ff.)

“To whom, then, have you likened God, or what image will you set beside him? Has a craftsman cast a statue, or has a goldsmith fashioned it in gold, and a silversmith in plates of silver? Perhaps a skilled craftsman has chosen wood that does not decay, and he will seek how to set up an image that will not move.”

After describing God’s greatness and displaying something of his power, after reckoning the nations and islands as a drop from a bucket, a moment on the scales, and dust, and rejecting the ceremonies of sacrifices, he teaches in the following words why all the nations are as nothing before him and are reckoned as emptiness:

“To whom have you likened God, or what image will you set beside him?”—he who is spirit, who is in all things and moves everywhere, and who holds the earth as though in a handful. At the same time he mocks the foolishness of the nations: a craftsman, whether a bronze-worker, goldsmith, or silversmith, makes a god for himself, joins it together with plates and nails, and fixes it firmly so that it will not be pushed down by the blasts of the winds.

When he adds, “Perhaps a skilled craftsman has chosen wood that does not decay,” the Hebrew says *AMSUCHAN* (). This is a kind of wood that does not decay and from which idols are made above all.

He says these things so that, once idols have been rejected, he may prepare the way for evangelical teaching, all crooked things may be directed into what is straight, valleys may be raised up, hills may be humbled, and the glory of the Lord may be revealed, so that all flesh may see the salvation of God.

According to the tropological interpretation, we may say that he rebukes the rulers of heretics, who fashion various idols out of their own hearts: either through the beauty of eloquence, which is interpreted as silver; or through the splendor of gold, which refers to meaning; or through imperishable wood, which refers to inferior doctrines. Their makers consider these doctrines eternal and establish them by dialectical skill, so that they may neither move nor collapse but stand upon a solid foundation.

### (Verses 21ff.)

“Do you not know? Have you not heard? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not understood the foundations of the earth? He who sits above the circle of the earth, whose inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like nothing and spreads them out like a tent for dwelling; who reduces those who search out secrets to nothing, and makes the judges of the earth as emptiness. Indeed, they are neither planted, nor sown, nor rooted in the earth; suddenly he blew upon them, and they withered, and a whirlwind will carry them away like stubble. And to whom have you likened me and equated me? says the Holy One. Lift your eyes on high and see who created these things: he who brings out their host by number and calls them all by name. Because of the greatness of his strength and power, not one of them was left behind.”

The Septuagint: “Do you not know? Have you not heard? Has it not been announced to you from the beginning? Have you not known the foundations of the earth? He who holds the circle of the earth, whose inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who established the heaven like a chamber and stretched it out like a tent for dwelling; who appoints rulers to reign as nothing and makes the earth as nothing. For they will not be planted, nor sown, nor will their root be strengthened in the earth. He blew upon them, and they dried up, and a storm will carry them away like stubble. Now, then, to whom have you likened me? Shall I be made equal to them? says the Holy One. Lift your eyes upward and see who showed all these things: he who brings out his array according to number, calling them all by name, from the abundance of glory and the strength of his power; nothing is hidden from you.”

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts have: “Nothing is hidden from you.”]

“From the beginning,” he says, “I taught you by the natural law, and afterward, through Moses, I testified in the written Law that idols were nothing, and that the Creator of the world himself was God, who founded such a mass of earth upon the seas and placed it upon the rivers, so that the heaviest element should hang upon the light waters by God’s command. He sits like a king above the circle of the earth”—for this reason some maintain that the earth is like a point and a globe—“and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers.”

If we consider the various nations throughout the whole world, from Ocean to Ocean—that is, from the Indian Sea to the British Sea, and from the Atlantic to the cold of the north, where the waters freeze and beautiful amber forms—we see the entire human race dwelling in the middle like grasshoppers.

What, then, does earth and ashes take pride in? The heavens—or rather, to use the authority of Scripture—are stretched out like a chamber. Or, as the Hebrew contains it, like *DOC*, concerning which we spoke above, for which the Septuagint there translated “spittle.” They translated the same word in one place as “spittle,” in another as “chamber,” that is, “vault.” He stretches out their immense breadth above like a tent and pavilion, so that, in the likeness of a roof, it may cover human beings and make them dwell as though in a vast house. Why should we wonder, then, if the small human bodies are reckoned like grasshoppers, and if living creatures are considered tiny?

Again, in this passage they maintain that a semicircle (*hēmikuklion*) of heaven hangs over the earth and that the heaven is spherical, and they misuse the word “vault,” claiming that half of the sphere covers the earth. But in Hebrew we read not “vault” but *DOC*, that is, the finest dust. In its place, spittle that is cast upon the earth, mixed with dust, and lost shows that the entire magnitude of bodies is reckoned as nothing.

“He who stretches out the heavens and spreads them out,” so that either the multitudes of angels might dwell above or human beings might remain below, and so that he might make a great house for rational creatures—he himself establishes rulers according to the conditions of the times, or those who search out secrets, so that they are as though they did not exist, and makes the judges of the earth as emptiness.

For this the Septuagint translated, “but he makes the earth as nothing.” In the beginning of Genesis also, where it is written, “The earth was invisible and unformed” (Gen. 1:1), the other translators rendered it: “The earth was emptiness and nothing.”

How many kings does Greek, barbarian, and Roman history recount? Where is that innumerable army of Xerxes? Where is Israel’s multitude in the desert? Where is the unbelievable power of kings? Why should I speak of ancient examples? Let present examples teach us that rulers are as nothing and that the judges of the earth are reckoned as emptiness.

Those rulers and judges of the earth—or, as some suspect, of heaven—are neither sown, nor planted, nor established with a firm root. Suddenly, by God’s command, they are removed and perish, just as stubble is snatched away by a whirlwind and storm, in accordance with what is written: “I passed by, and behold, he was not; I sought him, and his place was not found” (Ps. 37:36).

Since the Creator’s power and majesty are so great, to what likeness do you compare God? Why do you not rather understand the Creator from the magnitude of created things? If you do not believe words, at least believe your own eyes, and consider the Lord’s power from the subjection of the heavens and of all the elements.

“He brings out their host by number”—that is, the host of heaven—and calls them all by name, with “stars” understood. Concerning them it is also sung in the Psalms: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Ps. 147:4).

Or let us interpret the host of heaven as the angels, and all the armies of heaven, concerning whom Daniel also speaks: “A thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). Hence the Lord is also called *Sabaoth*, which in our language means “Lord of the army and of the armies,” or “of the powers.”

He brings out the host of heaven according to number, so that the sun, moon, and other stars—which Abraham could not number—are numbered by him and serve in the office assigned to them (Gen. 15). The sun completes the same course of heaven in one year, the morning star and evening star in two years, the moon in individual months, and all the stars complete their courses at fixed times. Some of them are called wandering stars, and we observe their unequal movements with our eyes, though not with our minds; we marvel at them more than we understand them.

The greatness of God’s strength causes all things to serve according to their appointed order. Or, according to the Septuagint, because of the abundance of the glory and power of his strength, nothing can be hidden from him; in the majesty of the Creator he knows the ways, principles, and courses of all things. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “The Creator knows them by his majesty.”]

## BOOK TWELVE

[Col. 0409]

No writer is so unskilled that he does not find a reader like himself; and the number of those who turn over Milesian tales [Note: Two Ambrosian manuscripts have now been added in the course of revising these Commentaries. One of them, quite ancient, marked with the letter S and numbered 45, reads here “Milesian tales and fables.” The ancients used *Milesias* substantivally; thus Jerome, *Against Rufinus*, book 1, no. 17: “The throng of the long-haired men chant the fictions of the Milesian tales in the schools.” The other, of very large format, marked with the letter E and numbered 98, will be used frequently below.] and fables is far greater than that of those who read Plato’s books. In the one there is play and amusement; in the other, difficulty and labor mingled with exertion.

Finally, Cicero himself, who translated the *Timaeus*, when it discusses the harmony of the world, the courses of the stars, and numbers, confesses that he does not understand it.

But crowds of boys in schools, laughing aloud, chant the Testament of Grunnius Corocotta the Pig. [Note: This is how the manuscripts read, as we have also restored the passage elsewhere. Previously it read “Lucius Lavinius.” Concerning the Pig’s Testament, consult Brissonius in his *Formulary*; also Lambecius on book 8, chapter 7 of Apicius.]

Therefore our Luscius Lanuinus too may enjoy his witnesses—or rather, his supporters—and may surpass them in number, since perhaps he surpasses them in talent. For me, the testimony of a few is enough, and I am content with the praise of friends who, in seeking my little works, are led astray by affection for me and by devotion to the Scriptures.

I think that some will claim that even this discourse, which I address to you, Eustochium, is open to criticism, because they do not consider that, while men remained silent, Hulda, Anna, and Deborah prophesied; and that in the service of Christ the distinction of sexes has no force, but only the distinction of minds.

The twelfth book of explanations on Isaiah, therefore, will have this beginning.

### (Verses 27ff.)

“Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God’? Or, ‘Has passed away’? Have you not known, or have you not heard? The eternal God, the Lord who created the ends of the earth, does not grow faint or weary, and there is no searching out his wisdom. He gives strength to the weary, and he multiplies vigor for those who have no strength. Boys will grow faint and labor, and young men will fall into weakness. But those who hope in the Lord will change their strength; they will take up wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not grow faint.”

The Septuagint: “Do not say, Jacob—and what have you spoken, Israel?” [Note: The Vulgate adds “saying,” but neither our manuscripts nor the Greek text contain this word.] “ ‘My way is hidden from God, and my God has taken away my judgment and withdrawn it.’ And now, do you not know, and have you not heard? The eternal God, the God who created the ends of the earth, will not hunger and will not labor, and there is no discovering his understanding. He gives strength to those who hunger, and sorrow to those who do not grieve. For the young men will hunger and labor, the adolescents will grow weary, and the chosen will become weak. But those who await God will change their strength. They will take up wings like eagles; they will run and not labor; they will walk and not hunger.”

Since the greatness of almighty God is so immense that nothing is hidden from him and everything is governed by his will, why do you say, Jacob—that is, the two tribes called Judah—and speak, Israel—the other ten tribes in Samaria, which have already been led captive into Assyria—“My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment will pass away from my God”?

The meaning is this: “You say that earthly matters do not concern God and that he does not consider what each of us does. Hence we are unjustly oppressed by our enemies and, in the likeness of animals and fish, are scattered without any ruler, as in Habakkuk” (Hab. 1).

God answers them: “Do you not know? Have the words of the preceding Scriptures not taught you? Or, according to the Septuagint, are you ignorant because you have not heard that the eternal God and Creator of all, the Lord, knows everything, sustains everything, and governs everything by his majesty? He never grows faint or weary, so that he would not understand your judgment and your ways would be hidden from him.”

“There is no searching out his wisdom,” he says. I think the Apostle took the statement from this passage: “His judgments are incomprehensible, and his ways are unsearchable” [or, perhaps, “inscrutable”] (Rom. 11:33). Or, as the Septuagint translated it, “He will not hunger and will not labor.”

Where there is food, there is often hunger if you remove the food; and where there is hunger, there is also labor. Since these things are not found in God, why do you attribute human passions to him? Rather, he himself gives strength to those who hunger and are weary; and to those who seem in this world to be as nothing, he multiplies strength and vigor.

Or, according to the Septuagint, he gives sorrow to those who do not grieve. For there is a sorrow that leads to death, and there is a sorrow that leads to life. Therefore, to those who have an unrepentant heart he gives sorrow, so that they may understand their sins.

And because many rejoice in bodily health and think that adolescence and childhood will last forever, he adds that blooming age quickly collapses and vigorous bodies wither.

But those who place their trust not in their own strength but in God, and who always await his mercy, will change their strength and go from strength to strength. They will take up wings like eagles and hear: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 103:5). They will run toward the Lord and not grow weary in their desire for him; they will walk and never grow faint.

We have often said that eagles’ old age grows young again through the changing of their feathers, and that they alone can look directly upon the sun’s radiance and behold the brightness of its rays with gleaming eyes. They test their young in this way, to determine whether they are of noble stock.

Thus the saints too become young again; once they have assumed an immortal body, they do not feel the labor of mortals but are caught up in the clouds to meet Christ. According to the Septuagint, they will never hunger, because they have the Lord present as their food.

## Chapter XLI

### Verses 1 ff.

“Let the islands keep silence before me, and let the nations renew their strength. Let them draw near, and then speak; let us approach together for judgment. Who raised up the Just One from the East? He called him to follow him. He will give nations into his presence, and he will subject kings. He will give them like dust to his sword, like straw carried away by the wind to his bow. He will pursue them; he will pass in peace, and no path will appear beneath his feet. Who has performed and done these things, calling generations from the beginning? I, the Lord, I am first and I am last.”

[Column 0412C] “The islands saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were terrified. They drew near and approached. Each one will help his neighbor, and he will say [Al.: “says”] to his brother, ‘Take courage.’ The bronze-worker strengthened [Al.: “will strengthen”] the one striking with the hammer, who was forging at that time, saying, ‘The soldering is good’; and he strengthened him with nails, so that it would not move” [Al.: “so that it would not be moved”].

The Septuagint reads:

“Be renewed toward me, islands, for the rulers will change their strength. Let them approach and speak together; then let them announce judgment. Who raised up righteousness from the East? He called her to his feet, and she will go. He will give nations into her presence; he will throw kings into astonishment. He will give their swords to the earth, and their bows like straw cast away. He will pursue them; he will pass in peace; the way of his feet. Who has performed and done these things? He will call her who calls her from the beginning of generations. I, God, am first, and I am in the things that are to come.

“The nations saw and were afraid; the ends of the earth were terrified and approached. They came together, each one judging that he should help his neighbor and his brother, and he said: ‘The craftsman and smith prevailed, striking with the hammer and producing at the same time. At one point he says, “The soldering is good.”’ They strengthened it; they will place it in nails, and it will not move.”

The nations—that is, the islands—which are battered by the false and bitter waves of this age, are commanded to listen, to close their mouths, and to know what was said to Israel: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.” They are also commanded to change their strength, so that, through their former weakness, they may be able to hear God’s word; so that they may first approach the Lord, and not be content with their own salvation, but may teach others what they have learned and dispute with the Lord whether he has preserved the justice of all things.

[Note: The older Ambrosian manuscript reads: “Whether he himself, who administers these things, is the God of all, or the idols whom they vainly and unjustly served.” It then continues, “He questions them in this way,” etc. I do not know whether this derives from Jerome’s pen or a glossator’s ingenuity.]

He questions them in this way and challenges them to answer, so that by questioning he may teach them what they do not know: “Who raised up the just one from the East,” or “righteousness”? For he is not only the God of the Jews but also of the nations, the one who called Christ the Lord and Savior, who was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption (1 Cor. 1). In him, according to the same Apostle, the righteousness of God is revealed (ibid.).

He called him so that he might follow him in all things, perform the works of the Father, and fulfill what he says: “I desired, O God, to do your will” (Ps. 39:9).

Before his presence kings and nations will bow their necks, and by his sword and arrows the hostile powers will be subjected like straw and dust. He will pursue them—that is, the kings and rulers of the individual nations—and he will pass in peace, calling everyone to peace so that they may be reconciled to God. “No path will appear beneath his feet”: that is, he will not feel the labor of the road or any weariness of human weakness, but will drink from the torrent on the way, and therefore will lift up his head (Ps. 109).

“Who,” he says, “has performed and done these things? Who raised up the just one, or righteousness? Who handed nations and kings over to him? Who subjected everything to his sword and bow?” Surely it was the one who foretold these future things from the beginning of the world, the one who is the Creator of all.

Since he had asked in the spirit of one inquiring, “Who raised up the just one from the East?” and so forth, while all were silent, he answered himself: “I am the Lord; I am first and I am last.” He is the one who also speaks in the Apocalypse of John: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. 1:8; 22:13).

“The islands saw”—that is, the nations, or the Churches gathered from the nations—which endure the storms of this world; and they feared the Lord. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9:10). All the ends of the earth trembled at the words of the Apostles, drawing near and approaching together to the Gospel of Christ.

When they saw that they themselves had been saved, they fulfilled in action what they had heard above: “Let them approach and then speak.” They wished to help their neighbors, to strengthen their brothers in the Lord, and to say to them: “Withdraw from idols; despise the ancient images of demons, which human hands fashioned, which were produced by the hammering smith, which were joined together with glue and secured with nails so that they would not move; and though they stand, they cannot walk.”

What we have interpreted concerning the person of Christ, the calling of the nations, the preaching of the Gospel, and the condemnation of idols, some refer to Cyrus, king of the Persians. They say that he was raised up from the East against the Babylonians, made them obey his command, cast down many nations before him, and subjected everything to his sword and bow. They refer the remaining words to his person as well: namely, that the Babylonian idols did not benefit them, since they were made by human effort and raised up by the skill of the bronze-worker.

Some of the Hebrews think that this was said about Abraham, who was called just from the East—that is, from the Chaldeans—because he alone was found righteous. He followed God, leaving his homeland for a land he did not know, and God delivered into his hand the kings who had come against Sodom and Gomorrah. Before his sword and bow he made them like straw and dust; he pursued them, returned in peace, and felt no weariness from the long journey. He accomplished this not by his own strength but by the mercy of the Lord, who had known these future things from the beginning.

“The islands saw,” he says—that is, the surrounding nations—and were terrified by his power; “and the ends of the earth.” They understand this as Shem, the son of Noah, who at the farthest ends of the earth had escaped the Flood with his father and brothers and had been preserved until that time (Gen. 14).

[Note: Compare Epistle 73 in our recension, especially no. 4.]

They wish Melchizedek to be understood as this figure, saying that he came to meet Abraham returning from battle, received [him], blessed him, and strengthened him with the blessings of God.

They also identify him as the bronze-worker who forged Abraham and brought him forth through the hammer of his craft toward better things, saying to him: “It is good that you be soldered and joined to the fear of the Lord.” He strengthened him, or solidified him, with the nails of the Lord’s commandments, so that he would not be moved but would remain in his fear.

[Column 0414C] ### Verses 8 ff.

“And you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, seed of Abraham my friend. In whom I have taken hold of you from the ends of the earth and called you from its distant places, and I said to you: You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not rejected you. Do not fear, for I am with you; do not turn aside, for I am your God. I have strengthened you and helped you” [Al.: “helped you”], “and the right hand of my righteous one has supported you.

“Behold, all who fight against you will be confounded and put to shame. They will be as though they did not exist, and the men who oppose you will perish. You will seek them and will not find them. Your rebellious men will be as though they did not exist, and the men warring against you will be like destruction.”

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript, together with the Vulgate and Jerome’s own version, reads: “your rebellious men.”]

“For I, the Lord your God, have taken hold of your hand, saying to you: Do not fear; I have helped you. Do not fear, worm of Jacob, you who are dead men from Israel. I have helped you, says the Lord, and your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.

“I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sharp teeth. You will thresh the mountains and crush them; you will make the hills like dust. You will winnow them, and the wind will carry them away, and the whirlwind will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord and glory in the Holy One of Israel.”

The Septuagint reads:

“But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob whom I chose, seed of Abraham whom I loved, whom I took from the ends of the earth and called from its extremities, and said to you: ‘You are my servant; I have chosen you and have not abandoned you.’ Do not fear, for I am with you; do not go astray, for I am your God. I have strengthened you, helped you, and supported you with my righteous right hand.

“Behold, all your adversaries will be confounded and put to shame. They will be as though they did not exist, and all your enemies will perish. You will seek them and will not find them—the men who rage against you. They will be as though they did not exist, and there will be no one fighting against you.

“For I am the Lord your God, who holds your right hand, who says to you: ‘Do not fear, Jacob, little Israel. I have helped you,’ says God, ‘who redeem you, the Holy One of Israel.’

“Behold, I have made you like new wheels of a threshing wagon, in the form of saws. You will thresh the mountains and crush the hills; you will make them like dust and winnow them. The wind will carry them away, and the storm will scatter them. But you will rejoice in the Lord and be glad in the Holy Ones of Israel.”

[Note: Victorius deletes the word “Holy One,” which he found neither in other manuscripts nor in the Septuagint of his exemplar. It was, however, added under an asterisk in the recent edition: ἅγιος, “holy.”]

[Column 0415B] The Apostle Paul teaches that Jacob and Israel are both carnal and spiritual: “See Israel according to the flesh” (1 Cor. 10). From this we understand that there is also another Israel according to the spirit. To the carnal Israel it is said: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.” To them it is also said above (on chap. 40:27): “Why do you say, Jacob, and speak, Israel: ‘My way is hidden from the Lord, and my judgment has passed away from my God’?”

Now, by contrast, God speaks to spiritual Israel, which received the coming of its Lord. He calls it first “servant,” then “chosen,” and finally “seed of Abraham.” Formerly, we received the spirit of slavery in fear (Rom. 8); afterward, having been chosen, we are joined to the friendship of God.

After the calling of the nations, when the islands saw and feared and the ends of the earth were terrified, when they drew near and approached, the remnants are called—the remnants according to the election of grace. Of these the Gospel also writes: “Jesus chose these twelve, whom he also named Apostles” (Luke 6). After the servitude of the pedagogy of the Law, they were chosen in the Gospel and deserved to be the seed of Abraham, the friend of God.

In him he took hold of them from the end of the earth and called Israel from its distant borders—from all the nations—gathering first the Jewish people, concerning whom the Apostle Paul also says: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you; but since you reject it, we are turning to the nations” (Acts 13:46).

To you, therefore, who are both my servant and my chosen one, who are to preach among the nations and endure many persecutions, I say: Do not fear, for I am with you. To you I speak in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

Do not go astray, do not turn aside from the truth, and do not deceive yourself by a false persuasion, imagining that, ignorant and unarmed, you can enter the forest of the nations by your own strength and call the fiercest peoples to gentleness. I am the one who strengthened you and helped you; and the right hand of my righteous one—namely, of the Lord Savior—or, as the Septuagint translated it, my right hand, has supported or protected you.

For behold, your adversaries—the Jewish people and all who fight against you, your persecutors—will be reduced to nothing. You will seek your adversaries and will not find them. The reason is given why you will not find them: “They will be as though they did not exist.” They are said to rage against the Apostles, or, according to the Hebrew, to be consumed.

Therefore you must not fear, because I have taken hold of your hand, I who say to you: “Do not fear; I have helped you. Do not fear, worm of Jacob, you who are dead men from Israel,” or, according to the Septuagint, “you who are very few from Israel.” The words we have set down—“I have helped you; do not fear, worm of Jacob”—are not found in the Septuagint.

The worm, called in Hebrew THOLATH (as printed), is named on account of humility and contempt. The choir of the Apostles imitates the Savior, who speaks in the psalm: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7). Just as a worm penetrates the earth, so the apostolic word penetrated the cities of the nations and first entered their hardest hearts.

They are rightly called “few from Israel,” because, in comparison with the whole world, very few of the Jewish nation believed. To them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke 12:32).

Or, according to the Hebrew, “dead men from Israel”: those who say with the Apostle, “I die daily” (2 Cor. 15:31), and elsewhere: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

What follows—“I have made you like a new threshing wagon, having sharp teeth”—signifies that evangelical preaching crushes hostile powers and spiritual wickedness that raises itself against the knowledge of God. These powers are called “mountains” and “hills” according to the varying degrees of their pride. When they have been removed and scattered like a whirlwind, let Israel rejoice and be glad in the Lord, the Holy One of Israel.

We may also say that the ecclesiastical man, possessing the sharp teeth of evangelical preaching in a new wagon—that is, one that does not operate in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit—crushes the hardest hearts of unbelievers. He separates wheat from chaff and crushes mountains and hills, that is, all the leaders of heretics. Once crushed and broken, they are reduced to dust and shown to be nothing, so that those who had been wrongly gathered may be separated for their own good.

### Verses 17 ff.

“The needy and the poor seek waters, and there are none; their tongue has dried up from thirst. I, the Lord, will hear them; I, the God of Israel, will not abandon them. I will open rivers on the bare hills and springs in the midst of the plains. I will make the wilderness a pool of waters and the dry land streams of waters. I will give in the wilderness the cedar and the thorn, the myrtle and the olive tree. I will set in the desert the fir, the elm, and the boxwood together, so that they may see, know, reflect, and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done this and the Holy One of Israel has created it.”

The Septuagint reads:

“And the poor and needy will rejoice, for they will seek water and there will be none; their tongue has dried up from thirst. I, the Lord God, will hear them, the God of Israel, and I will not abandon them. But I will open rivers in the mountains and springs in the midst of the plains. I will make the wilderness into marshes and the thirsty land into water channels. I will place in the waterless land cedar, boxwood, myrtle, cypress, and poplar, so that they may see, know, think, and understand together that the hand of the Lord has done these things and the Holy One of Israel has shown them.”

The poor and insignificant people of the nations, who did not possess knowledge of the truth, seek health-giving waters through various teachers and the diverse doctrines of philosophers, but do not find them, because they do not exist. Their tongue has dried up from thirst, since they were without the Law and the Prophets.

According to the faith of the Gospel, they had spent all their substance on physicians (Luke 8), yet could not be freed from the blood of idolatry and the blood of sacrifices. Therefore the Lord God of Israel did not wholly abandon them or allow them to perish forever, but opened rivers on the bare hills—or in the mountains—and springs in the midst of the plains.

These rivers took their beginning from that river of which we read in the Psalms: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. 45:4). And in another place: “The river of God is filled with waters.” These waters and springs flowed from that fountain of which Jeremiah speaks: “They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13). Above, in this same prophet, it is said: “They will drink water from the springs of the Savior.” Concerning these the Psalms also sing: “Bless the Lord God from the springs of Israel” (Ps. 67:27).

“And he made,” it says, “the wilderness a pool of waters and the dry land streams of waters.” Concerning these waters the Savior also spoke mystically in the Gospel:

“Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst; but the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14). And again: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:37–38).

The Evangelist adds that he said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.

Since, therefore, the once-deserted multitude of the Church had been irrigated with life-giving waters, the cedar, boxwood, myrtle, cypress, and poplar arise in it according to the Septuagint; according to the Hebrew and the other interpreters, the cedar, the setta, the myrtle, the olive tree, the fir, the elm, and the boxwood together.

These varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace. Since the nature of all the others is well known, let us explain only the Hebrew word SETTA (as printed), which Theodotion translated as “thorn.” It is a kind of tree that grows in the wilderness and resembles a white thorn. From it all the woodwork of the ark and the tabernacle was made; these materials are called Settim (Exod. 37).

[Note: Otherwise, “altars.” The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “all the furnishings of the ark and tabernacle were made.”]

This wood is incorruptible and very light, and among all woods it surpasses them in both strength and brilliance, solidity and beauty.

The cedar, cypress, and myrtle have an excellent fragrance and do not decay. The elm and poplar, or boxwood, are either joined to vines for supporting them or are very suitable for various kinds of work.

All these are placed together in the wilderness, so that not even one string of the Lord’s lyre, nor any spiritual power of the Church’s graces, may appear to be lacking.

Thus all may understand and know together in their minds that the hand of the Lord accomplished all these things: that in the aridity of the nations streams of virtues might be found, and that in a land once deserted and full of saltiness cedar, cypress, and other trees might grow. Their height and summit, hastening toward heavenly things, would be illuminated by the olive tree, which nourishes the light and gives rest to those who labor.

### Verses 21 ff.

“Bring your judgment near,” says the Lord. “Present whatever you may perhaps have. The king of Jacob has said it. Let them approach and announce to us whatever is to come. Announce the former things that have happened, and we will set our heart upon them and know their end; and tell us the things that are to come. Announce the things that are to come in the future, and we will know that you are gods. Whether good or evil, if you can, do it, and let us speak and see together. Behold, you are nothing, and your work is from that which is not; he who chooses you is an abomination.”

[Note: It formerly read “Let them kindle,” incorrectly.]

The Septuagint reads:

“Your judgment is near,” says the Lord God. “Your plans have come and drawn near,” says the king of Jacob. “Let them approach and announce to us the things that are to come; or tell us the former things that were, and we will apply our understanding and know what their end is. Tell us also the things that are to come, and announce what will happen at the end, and we will know that you are gods. Do good and evil, and we will marvel and see together where you are from and where your work is from. From a land of abominations they chose you.”

As we said above that Jacob and Israel are twofold—those who do not believe and those who believe in the Lord Savior—so now, after the nations have been called and rivers and springs have burst forth in the former wilderness of the Church, and after it has wonderfully blossomed with a varied abundance of trees, those among the nations who refused to believe in Christ are summoned to judgment. They must answer why they did not wish to see, know, reflect, and understand that the hand of the Lord had done these things and that the Holy One of Israel had created all.

“Let your idols approach,” he says, “which you think to be very strong. Or present whatever you perhaps have within yourselves, and disclose your plans: by what reasoning and with what understanding you refused to receive the manifest truth.”

At the same time, an apostrophe is made to the idols themselves, which are without sensation and possess no ability either to hear or to answer. “Tell us,” he says, “either the past or the future, and demonstrate your power by the outcome of events.”

This signifies that after Christ’s coming all idols fell silent. Where now are Apollo of Delphi, Loxias, Delius, Clarius, and the other idols that promised knowledge of the future and deceived the most powerful kings? Why could they foretell nothing about Christ, nothing about his Apostles, nothing about the destruction and abolition of their temples?

If they could not foretell their own destruction, how could they announce what belonged to others, whether evil or good? If someone says that many things were foretold by idols, it must be understood that they always joined falsehood to truth and so shaped their pronouncements that, whether something good or evil happened, either interpretation could be accepted.

Such was the oracle of Pyrrhus, king of the Epirotes:

“I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans.”

[Note: In Cicero, On Divination, book 2, from the fragments of Ennius’ Annals: “Whichever of these things had happened, the oracle would have been true.” But why should I ever believe that this was published concerning Croesus? Or why should I consider Herodotus more truthful than Ennius? Could Ennius have invented less concerning Croesus than concerning Pyrrhus?

“‘I say that you, descendant of Aeacus, can conquer the Romans.’ First, Apollo never spoke Latin, and so forth. But he could have said in Greek: Νικᾶν σ’ Αἰακίδη, Ῥωμαίους φημὶ δύνασθαι—‘Descendant of Aeacus, I say that you can conquer the Romans.’

“The other oracle is transmitted in the manuscripts as follows: ‘Croesus, crossing the Halys, will destroy a great kingdom.’”]

There is also the oracle of Croesus: “Croesus, having crossed the Halys, will destroy a great kingdom.”

Another proof that idols are not gods is that they can do neither good nor evil. This does not mean that idols, or the demons sitting beside idols, have often failed to do evil, but that they cannot do it unless power has been granted them by the Lord.

Indeed, in the Gospel they beg to be given power over the herd of swine (Matt. 8). In Job we read that, without the Lord’s command, the Devil could not destroy even the holy man’s animals and possessions (Job 1). Nor is this surprising when the Apostle Paul also says that some are handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. 1).

Or this may be said: mute and insensible images of human beings can do neither good nor evil, know neither the past nor the future, because they are from nothing and from that which does not exist. It is not so much the images themselves as the person who worships them who is worthy of an abomination.

“For the idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands. They have mouths, but they will not speak” (Ps. 113:13). How, then, can they know and announce future things, or recount the past, or do good or evil, when they possess neither human understanding nor that of brute animals? It makes no difference what material they seem to have been made from, since all of it is earthly.

### Verses 25 ff.

“I raised him up from the North, and he will come from the rising of the sun. He will call my name, and he will bring rulers like clay, and like a potter trampling earth” [Al.: “he called”; “he trampled”]. “Who announced from the beginning that we might know, and from the outset that we might say, ‘You are righteous’? There is no one announcing, no one proclaiming, and no one hearing your words. The first one will say to Zion, ‘Behold, they are here,’ and I will give an evangelist to Jerusalem. I looked, and there was no one among them, no one who entered into counsel or, when questioned, gave an answer. Behold, they are all unjust, and their works are empty; their idols are wind and emptiness.”

[Note: Martianus incorrectly read “Behold, I am present,” but many similar corrections have been made above and below.]

The Septuagint reads:

“But I raised up the one who is from the North and the one from the rising of the sun” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts have this according to the Greek κληθήσονται τῷ ὀνόματί μου—“they will be called by my name.” Earlier it read: “they are called by my name.”] “They will be called by my name. Let the rulers come, and as clay of the potter, and as a potter trampling clay, so you will be trampled.

“For who will announce to you the things that are from the beginning, so that we may know the things that are to come, and say that it is true? There is no one who proclaims, nor anyone who hears your words. I will give the beginning to Zion, and I will comfort Jerusalem on the way. For there is no one from the nations, and among their images there was no one who could announce anything. If I ask them, ‘Where are you from?’ they will not answer me. For they are your makers, and they lead you astray in vain.”

He still speaks against the idols and against those who, after Christ’s coming, refused to abandon them. While they remained in error, he says that he himself raised up a people from the nations from the North.

For from the North evils will blaze upon all the inhabitants of the earth. And it is said to Jeremiah: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” He answered: “A boiling pot, and its face from the face of the North” (Jer. 1:13).

They are raised up from the North so that they may believe in the one who has come from the rising of the sun. Concerning him we read above: “Who raised up the just one from the East,” or “righteousness”? And in another place: “Behold, a man; his name is Orient” (Zech. 6:12).

He will call them by his name so that, abandoning their images, they may worship the one God. For he himself speaks in the Gospel: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and you will receive him” (John 5:43).

He will trample rulers and magistrates, and all the pride of the world, and they will be subjected to him like clay for a potter, so that he may make from them one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9).

These things, which according to prophetic custom I say that I have done—as though they were already past—or which, according to Symmachus, I promise as future, no demon or idol can foretell. Therefore all the oracles fell silent, because there is no one who announces and no one who hears, while the formerly brutish hearts of the nations understood their error and abandoned false prophecies.

[Note: With Victorius we read “the first,” where previously it read “before.”]

The Lord will first speak to Zion—that is, to his Church—and say to it: “Behold, your children are present, whom I have given you through my faith.” This signifies the Apostles, who preached the Gospel throughout the whole world.

Zion and Jerusalem differ in name; otherwise, just as there is one city, so there is one Church.

Let all the nations that follow the error of idols be questioned by us, so that they may answer where they are from. Their universal answer will be that they follow vanity and winds and worship the works of their hands.

Whatever we have said about idols and nations, let us apply to the doctrines of depravity and to their leaders, the heresiarchs. Although Christ announces peace to the Church and shows them the way of truth, they themselves follow error and are compared to wind and whirlwind.

The Hebrews interpret the one raised up from the North and coming from the rising of the sun as the Assyrian and the Persian, who came to Jerusalem and trampled all its rulers. None of the idols they worshiped knew that this would happen, except the Lord alone, who avenged them for their sins.

## Chapter XLII

### Verse 1 ff.

“Behold, my servant; I will receive him. My chosen one; my soul has been pleased in him. I have given my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor accept a person’s status, nor will his voice be heard outside. He will not break a bruised reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax. In truth he will bring forth judgment. He will not be sad or troubled until he establishes judgment on the earth, and the islands will await his law.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Jacob, my servant, I will receive him; Israel, my chosen one, my soul has received him. I have given my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations. He will not cry out, nor will he let go; his voice will not be heard outside. He will not break a crushed reed, and he will not extinguish smoking flax, but in truth he will bring forth judgment. He will shine and will not be broken until he establishes judgment upon the earth, and in his name the nations will hope.”

[Note: Martianus prefixed “Behold,” although it is found neither in our manuscripts nor in the Greek text.]

Jacob and Israel are not present in the present chapter, nor did the Evangelist Matthew include them, since he followed the Hebrew truth. We mention this to refute those who despise our text. The matter has been discussed more fully in the little commentaries on Matthew and in the book that we recently wrote to Algasia.

[Note: In our recension, this is Epistle 121, written around the year 406.]

Meanwhile, it should be noted that wherever the choir of the Apostles is described, they are called Jacob and Israel and the seed of Abraham. To them, as human beings and servants, it is accordingly said: “Do not fear, worm of Jacob, and little Israel.”

But where there is a prophecy concerning Christ, it is read without Jacob and Israel: “Behold, my servant; I will receive him; my chosen one, my soul has been pleased in him.” And in what follows: “I have given you as a covenant of the race, as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and bring out those bound from their chains and from the prison house those dwelling in darkness.”

Nor is it surprising that he is called a servant, since he was made from a woman and made under the Law (Gal. 4); and although he was in the form of God, he humbled himself, taking the form of a servant and being found in appearance as a human being (Phil. 2).

In him the soul of God was pleased, seeing in him every virtue—or rather, seeing that he himself was the power and wisdom of God.

“I have given,” he says, “my spirit upon him”: the Spirit who descended in the form of a dove. He will bring forth judgment to the nations, which previously they did not know.

“He will not cry out,” for he will be gentle and meek; and he will not accept a person’s status in judgment, or, with “raise up” understood, he will not raise his voice high. Or, according to Symmachus, “he will not be deceived,” since he understands all the Devil’s ambushes. Or, according to the Septuagint, “he will not abandon,” namely, the Jewish people, calling them to repentance.

“Nor will his voice be heard outside”: for he did not preach the Gospel to other nations beyond Galilee and Judea. If we read that he was in the territory of Tyre and Sidon (Matt. 15), or in the region of Caesarea Philippi, which is now called Paneas, it must nevertheless be understood that Scripture does not say that he entered those cities themselves.

“He will not break a bruised,” or “crushed,” reed. For he will be agreeable to all and will grant forgiveness to sinners, saying to the woman: “Take courage, daughter; your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48).

[Note: Victorius maintains that the words “to the woman” were inserted by an unlearned scribe. He thinks that these words of the Lord, in Matthew 9, were spoken to the paralytic and therefore, after deleting them, substitutes “son” for “daughter.” The manuscripts are silent.]

And he will not extinguish smoking flax, or, as the other translators rendered it, “dark” or “gloomy flax.” Those who were near extinction were preserved by the Lord’s mercy. We have discussed this concerning the Jews and the nations in the works mentioned above.

But he will judge everything with truth, fearing neither the scribes nor the Pharisees, whom he confidently called hypocrites (Matt. 7; 15; 22; 23 throughout, and Luke 6; 12).

As for what follows—“He will shine and will not be broken until he establishes judgment upon the earth”—the Evangelist Matthew did not include it (Matt. 12). Alternatively, words between “judgment” and “judgment” may have been removed through a scribal error.

It signifies that, rising from the dead, he enlightened everyone and was not broken by death until he established judgment upon the earth. He said in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

In place of this we translated: “He will not be sad or troubled,” but will preserve an evenness of countenance at all times. Philosophers falsely boast this of Socrates, that he was never more sad or more joyful than usual.

Aquila and Theodotion translated it instead: “He will not darken, and he will not run, until he establishes judgment upon the earth.” The sense is that no one will be deterred by sadness on his face, nor will he hasten to punishment, since he reserved the truth of judgment for the final time.

What follows—“and the islands will await his law”—the Septuagint expressed more clearly as “in his name the nations will hope.” In Scripture, the nations are called islands because they are exposed on every side to the incursions of persecutors.

Let us understand his law not as the one given through Moses, but as the Gospel: “For a law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (above, chap. 2). Concerning this law Jeremiah also prophesies:

“Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made formerly with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31–32).

### (Verses 5–6 and following)

Thus says the Lord God, who creates the heavens and stretches them out, who establishes the earth and the things that spring from it, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it. I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness; I have taken you by the hand and preserved you; I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light to the nations, so that you might open the eyes of the blind and bring the bound man out of confinement, from the prison house those sitting in darkness.

I am the Lord; this is my name. I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to idols. The former things—behold, they have come to pass; and I announce new things also. Before they arise, I make them known to you.

It was uncertain who had earlier said: “Behold, my servant; I will receive him. My chosen one; my soul has been pleased with him. I have given my spirit upon him; he will bring forth judgment to the nations.” For, after the condemnation of the idols, the speech had suddenly broken forth: “Behold, my servant,” and the rest, which we have interpreted as spoken by the Father concerning Christ. Therefore, lest he leave it ambiguous who had spoken the preceding words, he adds and says: “Thus says the Lord God, who creates the heavens and stretches them out.” Or, as the Septuagint translated: “Who made heaven and fixed it.”

The Creator and Lord of the universe himself promised the advent of his Christ. He not only stretched out and fixed the heavens, but also established the earth with its lofty mass, together with all that is born from it, so that “his invisible things may be understood and seen through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1), as well as his eternal power and divinity. He gave breath to all who dwell upon the earth, according to the first law concerning mortals. For God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and he became a living soul (Gen. 2). But he gave spirit especially to those who tread upon the earth and subject the wisdom of the flesh to his authority.

He, therefore, whose praises are so great, spoke these words to the one whose law the islands and the nations await: “I, the Lord, have called you in righteousness.” Concerning him he himself says in the Gospel: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John 17:25), so that he might be God not only of the Jews but also of the nations.

“And I have taken your hand,” because whatever the Son does, the Father does. “And I have preserved you,” because you preserve all things yourself. “And I have given you as a covenant of the people of Israel,” to whom I had previously promised that you would come. “And as a light of the nations,” which sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, so that you might open the eyes of the blind, who previously did not see God.

“And you might bring the bound man out of confinement” [Another reading: “the bound men”] (Prov. 5), for each person is bound by the cords of his sins. In the Gospel, the Lord releases the one whom Satan had bound (Matt. 8). “From the prison house, those sitting in darkness,” who were living in the night and gloom of error.

The statement that follows—“I am the Lord; this is my name; I will not give my glory to another”—does not exclude the Son. When he said in the Gospel, “Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5), the Father himself answered him: “I have glorified, and I will glorify.” For he did not say, “I will give my glory to no one”; had he said that, he would also have excluded the Son. Rather, he says: “I will not give my glory to another,” apart from you, to whom I have given it and to whom I will give it.

Therefore I greatly admire the precision of Holy Scripture: the word **AHER** all the translators rendered with one voice as “another,” although in many other passages they are accustomed to differ.

That the following words do not exclude the Son but the idols is confirmed by what follows: “Nor my praise to idols.” For this the Septuagint has: “Nor my virtues to images.” Since Christ is the virtue of God and the wisdom of God, he contains in himself all the Father’s virtues.

It follows: “The former things, behold, they have come to pass.” The meaning is: Everything that I have spoken, everything that I promised through Moses and the Prophets, has been fulfilled. But now I announce the Gospel to you—the calling of the nations, the passion of Christ, and the newness of faith—so that, just as you see the former things fulfilled in events, you may believe that what I now promise will likewise come to pass.

### (Verses 10–11 and following)

Sing to God [the Vulgate: “to the Lord”] a new song; his praise is from the ends of the earth; you who go down to the sea and its fullness, the islands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities raise their voice; Cedar will dwell in the houses. Praise, you inhabitants of Petra; from the summits of the mountains they will cry out. They will give glory to the Lord and proclaim his praise in the islands.

The Lord will go forth like a mighty man; like a warrior he will stir up zeal. He will shout and cry aloud; he will prevail against his enemies. I have always been silent; I have kept still and restrained myself. Like a woman in labor I will speak; I will destroy and devour at once. I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their grass. I will turn rivers into islands and dry up the pools.

I will lead the blind along a road they do not know, and I will make them walk on paths they do not know. I will turn darkness before them into light, and crooked things into straight. These are the things I have done for them, and I have not abandoned them. They have turned backward; let those who trust in idols be utterly put to shame, those who say to a cast image, “You are our gods.”

The Septuagint has: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his principality is glorified, and his name is from the summit of the earth; those who go down to the sea and sail upon it, the islands and their inhabitants. Rejoice, desert and its villages; the villages and inhabitants of Cedar shall rejoice. Those who dwell in Petra shall rejoice; from the summit of the mountains they shall cry out. They shall give glory to God and proclaim his virtues in the islands.

“The Lord God of hosts will go forth and crush the war; he will stir up zeal and cry out against his enemies with strength. I have been silent from the beginning—shall I always be silent and endure? Like a woman in labor I have acted patiently; I will burst forth and dry up at once. I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their grass. I will turn rivers into islands and dry up the marshes.

“I will bring the blind along a road they do not know, and I will make them tread paths they did not know. I will make their darkness light and crooked things straight. These are the things I will do for them, and I will not abandon them. But they have turned backward. Be utterly ashamed, you who trust in idols, who say to cast images, ‘You are our gods.’”

The one who had earlier said, “The former things, behold, they have come to pass; and I announce new things also; before they arise, I will make them known to you,” and had promised that he would say what they did not know, testifies in the following speech what those new things are. He commands the Apostles and apostolic men to sing a new song—not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit; not only in the Old Testament but also in the New. His praise must penetrate to the ends of the earth. “His going forth is from the highest heaven, and his meeting reaches to its summit” (Ps. 18). The sound of the Apostles went out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

Or, according to the Septuagint: “Glorify his name at the ends of the earth,” so that Christ’s name might be proclaimed to the nations throughout the whole world.

Who these people are who must sing the new song is shown by the words that follow: “You who go down to the sea,” he says, “and sail upon it,” or “its fullness.” Seeing the Apostles repairing their nets on the shore beside the Sea of Galilee, Jesus called them and sent them onto the great sea (Luke 5), so that from fishers of fish he might make them fishers of human beings. They preached the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum and the Spains, capturing within a short time even the power of the city of Rome.

Or certainly they went down to the sea and sailed upon it, enduring the storms and persecutions of this age. By the islands and their inhabitants understand either the diversity of the nations or the multitude of the churches.

“Let the desert,” he says, “and its cities raise their voice,” concerning which we spoke above. Or, “Let the desert and its villages rejoice,” together with Cedar, which was formerly an uninhabited region beyond Arabia of the Saracens, and the inhabitants of Petra, which is itself a city of Palestine.

This signifies that the people of the nations, formerly deserted of the knowledge of God and bound by the errors of idolatry, should be converted to the praises of the Lord. Or, because Cedar is interpreted as “darkness,” and, according to the Apostle, “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10), all believers are commanded—those who were formerly in darkness and now believe in the Lord the Savior—to cry out from the summits of the mountains and openly preach Christ. Concerning them it was said above (on chapter 40:9): “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem.”

“And I will place his glory in the islands,” concerning which we spoke earlier.

The prophetic speech describes the glorious advent of the Savior. The Apostle Paul likewise speaks of him: “According to the illumination of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Cor. 4; 2 Tim. 1:10). It compares him to a very strong man who is about to fight against his adversaries and stir up zeal. Concerning him it was prophesied in the Song of Deuteronomy: “They made me jealous with what was not God, and provoked me with their idols; and I will make them jealous with a people that is not a people, and with a foolish nation I will provoke them” (Deut. 32:21).

He will also shout and cry out against his enemies, openly condemning their unbelief and proclaiming with a cry: “I have been silent; I have always kept still and endured.” Or, as the Septuagint translated: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Eccl. 3:7), so that the saying spoken through Solomon might be fulfilled: “A time to keep silence and a time to speak.”

The meaning is: For a long time I bore with you as you repeatedly sinned; but because I had previously been silent, I will no longer keep silent. Just as a woman in labor brings forth her child into the light and makes visible what had previously been enclosed in her womb, so I will now bring forth my grief and the concealment I have always maintained concerning your crimes.

[Note: [Col. 0425D] Earlier the text read: “At every time,” etc.]

I will destroy your plans and at one time devour the whole nation, together with all the pride of your mountains and the swelling of your hills.

And the grass concerning which it was said above, “Truly the people is grass”—that is, both the rulers and the insignificant common people—I will reduce to a desert.

What is added in the Septuagint from Theodotion’s edition was omitted by him in this passage. (See above, chapter 4:7.)

When I have dried you up and erased you from head to foot, then I will make the rivers of my teaching flow through the islands of the nations, and I will turn your pools, or marshes, into aridity, so that among the nations there may be knowledge of the Scriptures and in you an aridity of teaching.

I will lead the blind along a road they previously did not know. Concerning them we read above: “I have given you as a covenant of the people, as a light of the nations, so that you might open the eyes of the blind.” They will be led along the road of which Christ speaks: “I am the way”—or the way of the knowledge of God—and I will make them walk along the prophetic paths.

Then their darkness will be changed into light and their crooked things made straight, so that they may understand what they read and see with the eyes of their hearts the clear light of Christ in the Old Testament.

He adds at the same time: “These are the words which I have done,” or “will do,” for he is not promising things that are still entirely future but fulfilling what he had previously promised.

While I say these things, the Jewish people have turned backward, refusing to believe the one who promised, being put to shame in their errors, and neglecting the promise of God, although they had previously believed in idols. Or, when the fullness of the nations has entered, then the people of Israel too will be converted (Rom. II), and will repent of the error by which it had formerly served idols.

Alternatively, after the calling of the nations it will return to the beginning, so that all the nations that refused to believe the Gospel may be said to be put to shame in their idols.

### (Verses 18–19 and following)

Deaf people, hear; and blind people, look up so that you may see. Who is blind except my servant? And who is deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers? Who is blind except the one who has been sold? And who is blind except the servant of the Lord?

You see many things—will you not guard them? You have open ears—will you not hear? The Lord desired to sanctify him, to magnify and exalt the Law. But he himself is a people plundered and devastated; all are a snare to the young, and they have been hidden in prison houses. They have become plunder, and there is no one to rescue them; booty, and there is no one to say, “Restore.”

Who among you will hear this, attend to it, and listen to what is to come? Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to those who devastate him? Was it not the Lord, against whom we sinned? They were unwilling to walk in his ways, and they did not hear his Law. He poured out upon him the indignation of his wrath and the fury of war. It burned him all around, yet he did not know; it set him on fire, yet he did not understand.

The Septuagint has: “Deaf people, hear; and blind people, look up so that you may see. Who is blind except my children, and deaf except those who rule over them? Who is blind (according to the Complutensian edition of the Septuagint) except the one who received? And the servants of God have been blinded. You have seen often, yet you did not guard; your ears were open, yet you did not hear.

“The Lord God desired that he should be justified and magnified in praise. I saw, and the people were devastated and plundered. For there was a snare everywhere in the sleeping places and likewise in the houses where they hid them. They became plunder, and there was no one to rescue the spoil; there was no one to say, ‘Restore.’

“Who among you will hear these things and know what is to come? Who gave Jacob over to plunder and Israel to those who devastate him? Was it not God, against whom they sinned? You were unwilling to walk in his ways or hear his Law. He brought upon them the anger of his wrath; war prevailed against them, and those who burned them all around. Each one did not understand, nor did they take it to heart.”

Lest anyone think that the words, “Deaf people, hear, and blind people, look up so that you may see,” refer to the people of the nations, who had previously been deaf and blind—as the Jews strive to establish by a foolish interpretation—the prophetic speech itself shows who are to be understood as deaf and blind.

“Who,” it says, “is blind except my servant, and deaf except the one to whom I sent my messengers?” There is no doubt that it means the Prophets. “Who is blind except the one who has been sold because of his sins? Who is blind except the one who was previously the servant of the Lord?”

To him it is said: “O Israel, who sees many things and has many Prophets through whom you may know God’s commands, will you not guard what has been commanded to you? You have open ears; will you not hear what is said?” Concerning this we read above: “Hearing you will hear and not understand; seeing you will look and not see; for the heart of this people has become fat” (Isa. 6:9).

“The Lord,” he says, “desired to sanctify him, magnify his Law, and raise up and lift the fallen people.” But he did not wish to do God’s will, and therefore he was plundered and devastated by his adversaries, whom we must understand either as demons or as enemies.

“All are a snare to the young, and they have been hidden in prison houses.” Or, as the Septuagint translated: “A snare is everywhere in the sleeping places, and in the houses as well in which they hid them.” This signifies the scribes and Pharisees, who deceived the pitiable common people and everywhere laid ambushes against the Lord the Savior and his Apostles (Luke 11). They had the key of knowledge, yet did not enter themselves, and prevented those who wished to enter.

He aptly called their breasts, in which evil thoughts dwelt, prisons. Therefore they became plunder and booty; there was no one to free them or speak on their behalf.

At the same time the Prophet exhorts them, so that if all cannot hear, at least a few may know and understand what is to come and from whom they have suffered these things. Let them recognize the causes of their devastation: they were unwilling either to hear or to do what was commanded in the Law.

Therefore the Lord poured out upon them all his anger and the indignation of his wrath, so that he who had previously been silent might no longer keep silent, nor correct them with words but with punishments and torments. A very powerful war seized them, one which they could by no means escape, displaying the ferocity of the Romans.

Although he was burned on every side and had nothing sound left in him, he still did not understand the cause of his punishment: he was punished because he had not received the Son of God.

### (Chapter 43—verses 1 and following)

And now thus says the Lord who creates you, Jacob, and forms you, Israel: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you and called you by your name; you are mine. When you pass through the water [the Vulgate: “waters”], I will be with you, and the rivers will not cover you. When you walk through fire, you will not be burned, and the flame will not consume you; for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I have given Egypt, Ethiopia, and Seba as your ransom. Since you have become honorable in my eyes and glorious, and I have loved you, I will give human beings for you and peoples for your life.

Do not fear, for I am with you. From the east I will bring your offspring, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, “Give them up”; and to the south, “Do not hinder.” Bring my sons from far away and my daughters from the end of the earth—everyone who is called by my name. For my glory I created him; I formed him and made him.

Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears. All the nations have gathered together, and the tribes have assembled. Who among you will announce this and make us hear the former things? Let them produce their witnesses and be justified; let them hear and say: “Truly you are my witnesses,” says the Lord, “and my servant whom I have chosen, so that you may know, believe me, and understand that I am he. Before me no God was formed, and after me there will not be one. I am, I am the Lord, and there is no savior besides me. I announced it, and I saved; I made it heard, and there was no stranger among you. You are my witnesses,” says the Lord, “and I am God; from the beginning I am he, and there is no one who can rescue from my hand. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

The Septuagint has: “And now thus says the Lord who made you, Jacob, and created you, Israel: Do not fear, for I redeemed you; I called you by your name; you are mine. And if you pass through water, I am with you, and the rivers will not cover you. And if you pass through fire, you will not be burned; the flame will not consume you, for I am the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior.

“I made your exchange: Egypt, Ethiopia, and Syene for you. Since you have become honorable and have been glorified in my sight, I loved you, and I will give human beings for you and rulers for your head. Do not fear, for I am with you. From the east I will bring your offspring, and from the west I will gather you.

“I will say to the north, ‘Bring them’; and to the southwest, ‘Do not hinder.’ Bring my sons from a distant land and my daughters from the ends of the earth—all who are called by my name. For in my glory I created him, formed him, and made him. And I brought out the blind people who have eyes, but are blind, and whose ears are deaf.

“All the nations gathered together, and their rulers assembled. Who will announce these things? Or who will announce to you the things from the beginning? Let them bring their witnesses, be justified, hear, and speak the truth. Be my witnesses, and I am a witness,” says the Lord God, “and my servant whom I chose, so that you may know, believe, and understand that I am he. Before me there was no other God, and after me there will not be one.”

[Note: We have retained the reading “God” with Victorius and with the Greek, as found in the oldest manuscript.]

“I am God, and there is no Savior besides me. I announced, and I saved; I reproached, and there was no stranger among you. You are my witnesses, and I am the Lord God from the beginning; there is no one who can rescue from my hands. I will act, and who will turn it back?”

The Hebrews interpret these words as referring to the second advent of the Savior, when, after the fullness of the nations, all Israel will be saved. We, however, by no means think that the promise is made to those concerning whom it was said above: “Who is blind except my children, and deaf except those who rule over them? And the servants of God have been blinded.” And again: “The people became devastated and plundered,” and similar statements. Finally he adds: “He poured out upon him the indignation of his wrath and the fury of war; he burned him all around, yet he did not know; he set him on fire, yet he did not understand.”

Therefore, what we said above—that there are two Jacobs and two Israels, one carnal and the other spiritual, namely those who refused to believe in the Savior and those who received the Son of God—must also be understood here. The chorus of the Apostles and the first Church of Christ, gathered from the Jewish people, is summoned to understand its Creator and Maker, who is the author both of its soul and of its body.

Let it not fear persecutors, since it has been redeemed by the blood of Christ, who called it by its own name and, because of his special familiarity, called the people his own. Rather, let it preach without hesitation and fear no danger.

The references to waters and rivers, fire and flames, describe the attack and fury of persecutors who envy the salvation of the nations and do not want the Gospel to be preached. Although the Jews wish Egypt to be understood by the waters, the Babylonians by the rivers, the Macedonians by the fire, and the Romans by the flame.

He commands them not to fear because the Lord their God and Savior, the Holy One of Israel, is with them; he will make them preach to Egypt, Ethiopia, Syene, and the farthest boundaries of the world.

In place of Syene, the other translators gave **SABA**, from which came the queen of the South, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom (1 Kings 10).

[Note: [Col. 0429] The Septuagint supplied the name. Eusebius likewise discusses comparable matters concerning Saba in this passage.]

Therefore the chorus of the Apostles became honorable in God’s sight and loved by him. They became the salvation of all human beings and peoples who were called through them to the Gospel and who will be reckoned for the salvation of their souls.

Hence he adds: “Do not fear; I am with you,” the one who says to you in the Gospel: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

From the east and from the west I will bring your sons, who will rest in Abraham’s bosom; from every part of the world a people of my sons and daughters will be gathered. They will either invoke my name or be called by my name, so that they may be called Christians, to the glory of their Creator.

What follows—“Bring out the blind people who have eyes, and the deaf who have ears”—many think is said concerning the people of the nations, who began to hear and see through the teaching of the Apostles. But let us understand this also of dispersed Israel, which was called through the Apostles and believed first. To them Paul speaks: “It was necessary that the word of God should first be spoken to you” (Acts 13:46). The Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:6).

Finally it follows: “All the nations have gathered together, and the tribes have assembled”—that is, together with the people who believed from the Jews, so that there might be a twofold calling, of circumcision and of uncircumcision.

The command “Bring out” is addressed to the Son. Or, according to the Septuagint, the Father speaks concerning the Son: he brought out his blind and deaf people, joined them to the nations, and made many of them leaders of the Church.

The Prophet marvels that no one among the nations could have foreknown these things or known the plans of God, but only his people, who had received the Law and possessed the Prophets: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:1).

Or God himself is the witness and accomplisher of his words, together with his child and servant whom he chose. There is no doubt that this signifies Christ, to whom he also says above: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant.”

All these things will happen so that truth may be preached to the world, and so that those whose mind was previously brutish and insensible may know, believe, and understand that there is no other God besides the one God, neither before nor afterward.
