For the Creator of times does not at some point have a beginning, since “at some point” itself belongs to time.

Just as he now says, “I am a witness,” says the Lord God, “and the servant whom I chose,” so the Lord says the same in the Gospel: “The testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness” (John 8:17–18).

The same must be understood concerning his divinity: there is no God except the one who speaks and his chosen servant.

Beautifully, apart from God the Father there is no other God, because Christ is the virtue of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1), and he says in the Gospel: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11). Just as the one Lord Christ does not deprive the Father of being Lord, so the one God the Father does not deprive the Son of being God—he who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God (John 1:1–2).

What follows—“There is no Savior besides me”—shows that in the Father the Son saves all things. Concerning this the same Prophet testifies: “The Lord will send them a Savior, and he will save them” (Isa. IX). For the wise and mighty God cannot exist without his wisdom and virtue.

Since, therefore, I announced from the beginning that these things would come to pass, no one will be able to reject my will—indeed, who could make void what I have done?

These words are spoken to Jacob and Israel, but they refer to the apostolic chorus and to all those from the Jewish people who are willing to believe in Christ.

### (Verse 14)

Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I sent to Babylon, and I brought down all the bars, and the Chaldeans who boasted in their ships. I am the Lord, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King.

The Septuagint has: “Thus says the Lord God, who redeemed you, the Holy One of Israel: For your sake I will send to Babylon and raise up all the fugitives, and the Chaldeans will be bound in ships. I am the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who displayed your king, Israel.”

According to the Hebrew, the prophetic speech is still addressed to Israel. Their Redeemer and the Holy One of Israel, the Lord, has spoken these words to them:

“For your sake—for you who preach the Gospel with me, to whom I said above, ‘Do not fear, for I am with you,’ who are witnesses of my will and proclaim my other servant as a witness to the unbelieving world—I sent my Son into Babylon and into the confusion of this age.

“And I brought down all its bars, which in Hebrew are called **BARIHIM** [another reading: **barichim**] and which Theodotion translated as ‘strong.’ And the Chaldeans,” he says—understand *I brought down* by the common construction—“who boasted in their ships,” namely in those who, like ships, drifted amid idols.

No one doubts that “Chaldeans” signifies demons.

[Note: We have discussed something concerning this etymology in the Book of Names from Genesis. Yet, to conceal nothing, Philo and the other ancient etymologists of Hebrew words seem to be mistaken. Jerome speaks on their authority when they suppose that the Hebrew *Chasdim* is formed from the letter *caph*, expressing likeness, and the word *sedim*, meaning “demons.” The Chaldeans were in fact called *Chasdaei* after Chesed, the son of Nahor, who is mentioned in Genesis 23:20, with the *s* changed into *l* according to the character of the language.]

“I, the Lord, announced these future things, I who am your Creator and the king of Israel.”

According to the Septuagint, however, the meaning is very different: “I am the Lord who delivered you from dangers, the Holy One of Israel. For your sake I will send the king of the Medes and Persians into Babylon and make its inhabitants flee. The Chaldeans who had captured you will be bound and transferred across the Caspian Sea to other nations. I, the Lord, decreed these future things, I who showed that Israel would be the king of believers.”

### (Verses 16–17 and following)

Thus says the Lord, who made a way in the sea and a path in the rushing waters; who brought out chariot and horse, army and mighty force. Together they fell asleep; they will not rise again. They were crushed like flax and extinguished.

Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I am doing new things; now they will arise. Surely you will know them. I will make a way in the desert and rivers in the trackless land. The wild beast of the field, the dragons, and the ostriches will glorify me, because I have given waters in the desert and rivers in the trackless land, to give drink to my chosen people. I formed this people for myself; they will proclaim my praise.

The Septuagint has: “Thus says the Lord, who gives a way in the sea and a path in the violent water; who brings out chariots and horses and a very mighty multitude. But they fell asleep and will not rise; they were extinguished like extinguished flax.

“Do not remember the former things, and do not consider the ancient things. Behold, I will make new things, which will now arise, and you will know them. I will make a way in the desert and rivers in the waterless land. The wild beasts of the field will bless me, the sirens and the daughters of ostriches, because I have given water in the desert and rivers in the waterless land, to give drink to my chosen race, my people whom I acquired, so that they may proclaim my virtues.”

The Lord who destroyed and cast down Babylon, and brought down all its strongest men from their power, together with all the Chaldeans who sailed prosperously upon the waves of this age, made them captives. He himself found a way through the rushing waters of the Red Sea, so that his people, freed from Egypt, might cross.

Or the one who made a way in the Red Sea also found a path through the rushing waters of the Jordan, so that both the departure from Egypt and the entry into the promised land might possess a miracle.

He drowned the chariots, horses, and entire army of Pharaoh in the depths; they fell asleep in perpetual sleep. They were crushed and extinguished like flax within a short space of time, in an instant and moment. For flax not yet seized by fire, because of the lightness of its substance, is immediately extinguished and dissolved into ash.

Therefore I command you: among the signs and miracles by which the most powerful city Babylon was destroyed, and by which a way was opened for my people in the Red Sea and the Jordan, do not remember the former things, because in the Gospel I will do much greater things. By comparison with them, the past ought to be silenced.

For I will no longer find a way in the Red Sea, but in the desert of the whole world. Nor will one river or spring burst forth from a rock, but many rivers, which will refresh not bodies as before but thirsty souls. Thus will be fulfilled what we read above: “You will drink waters from the fountains of the Savior” (on chapter 12:3).

Then what has never happened will occur: all the wild beasts, dragons, and ostriches that dwelt in the wilderness of the nations, and that were like beasts because of the blood of idolatry and the savagery of their ways, will glorify and praise me.

In place of “dragons,” which only Theodotion, according to what is written in Hebrew, called **THANNIM** [another reading: **THENNIM**], the other translators rendered “sirens,” monstrous creatures that, with sweet but deadly song, caused sailors to be torn apart by Scylla’s dogs.

This signifies that those formerly devoted to pleasure and luxury will be converted to the service of the Lord. Yet it is better to understand “dragons,” since they are joined with ostriches: because he was speaking of the beasts of the wilderness, he named animals familiar to the desert.

“They will praise me,” he says, “and the wild beasts of the field, the dragons, and the ostriches will glorify me, because I have given waters in the desert of the nations and rivers in the aridity of the peoples, so that my people might drink—the people whom I chose for myself, or my chosen race, the people whom I acquired with my blood—to proclaim my praises and virtues.”

### (Verses 22–23 and following)

“You did not call upon me, Jacob; nor did you labor for me, Israel. You did not offer me the ram of your burnt offering, and you did not glorify me with your sacrifices. I did not make you serve through an offering, nor did I impose labor upon you with incense. You did not buy me fragrant cane with silver, nor did you satisfy me with the fat of your sacrifices. Yet you made me serve through your sins; you imposed labor upon me through your iniquities.”

The Septuagint: “You did not now call upon me, Jacob, nor did I make you labor, Israel. You did not bring me the sheep of your burnt offering, nor did you magnify me with your sacrifices. I did not make you serve through sacrifices, nor did I impose labor upon you with incense; you did not buy me incense with silver, nor did I desire the fat of your sacrifices. But in your sins I defended you, and in your iniquities.”

While the beasts of the field, the dragons, and the ostriches were praising me, you, Jacob, were entirely unwilling to call upon me, or afterward to labor so as to amend your sin through repentance. But as for your belief that you offered me sacrifices and sacrificed rams, know that they were not accepted by me, because they were common to me and to idols. He repeats the sense of what he had said above: “Why do I need the multitude of your sacrifices?” says the Lord. “I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and of the fat of lambs; I do not desire the blood of bulls and goats.” For, he says, I did not require anything costly from you, so that I might make you labor in preparing these things. I did not demand offerings from you, nor did I seek incense—neither fragrant cane, nor perfume, nor various kinds of spices, with whose smoke you might intoxicate and satisfy me. Rather, I desired and sought obedience, which is superior to sacrifice, and the sacrifice of which David says in the Psalms: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19).

But you made me serve and labor through your sins, so that I was compelled to say: “I have labored in enduring”; and I can no longer bear you. Hence God says the same through Hosea: “What shall I do for you, Ephraim? Shall I protect you, Israel?” (Hos. 11:8). “What shall I do for you?” As though he said: “Shall I make you like Admah and treat you like Zeboiim?”

What the Septuagint rendered, “But in your sins I defended you, and in your iniquities,” can be joined with what precedes, so that God’s labor and weariness consist in defending sinners.

### (Verses 25–26 and following)

“I am he, I am he, who blots out your iniquities for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Recall me, so that we may be judged together; tell me if you have anything by which you may be justified. Your first father sinned, and your interpreters transgressed against me. And I profaned the holy princes; I gave Jacob over to destruction, and Israel to blasphemy.”

The Septuagint: “I am he, I am he who blots out your iniquities, and I will not remember them. But you, remember, and let us be judged. Speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified. Your fathers sinned, and your princes acted wickedly against me, and they profaned my holy things. And I gave Jacob over to destruction, and Israel to reproach.”

“You,” he says, “Jacob and Israel, made me labor through your sins, and I could scarcely bear the burdens of your iniquities. Yet I do not call you my servants or my children, but address you simply by the name Jacob and Israel, in order to expose and accuse sinners. I, however, for my own sake—because I am merciful and patient, rich in compassion—will blot out all your iniquities through the sprinkling and blood of the New Testament. I will erase the old bond that had been written against you; and I will no longer remember your sins, which, if you are willing to believe, I will forgive you in baptism.”

“Recall me,” therefore: if you have anything just that you can answer me, I will gladly accept it, so that we may be judged together and you may accuse me of not having done for you what I ought to have done. We read this sense more fully in Micah: “My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Answer me. For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before you Moses and Aaron and Miriam.” And David speaks to God in the fiftieth Psalm: “So that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6).

“Tell me, then, if you have anything by which you may be justified.” The sense is this: “I will not speak first against you, lest you claim that you have been overwhelmed by the multitude of my words. Rather, if you have anything just, speak for yourself, so that you may appear to be suffering these things undeservedly.”

And so that you may know that I pity you not because of your merit but because of my clemency, I will go back to your fathers and ancestors, so that you may understand that you were born from sinners. “Your first father sinned in the wilderness”—namely, the whole people of Israel.

Or perhaps Abraham, the founder of your race, is shown to have sinned when, although the Lord promised his descendants the land of promise, he replied: “How shall I know that I shall possess it?” And, he says, “your interpreters transgressed against me” (Gen. 15:8): Aaron and Moses at the waters of contradiction, who spoke as mediators between me and you (Exod. 17).

And so that we may understand that this is not a forced interpretation, what follows is: “And I profaned the holy princes,” of whom it is also sung in the Psalm: “Their judges have been swallowed up beside the rock” (Ps. 140:6). He says that he profaned them because they did not enter the land of promise.

“And I gave Jacob over to destruction, and Israel to blasphemy,” so that no one except two of those who had gone out from Egypt would enter Judea; rather, their corpses would lie in the wilderness.

According to the Septuagint, who added on their own: “Speak first of your iniquities, so that you may be justified,” God summons them to repentance, so that they may recognize their crimes and sins and obtain forgiveness. For it is also written elsewhere: “The righteous man is his own first accuser” (Prov. 18:17).

Their princes and fathers are said to have violated the holy things of the Lord by not serving the law of God, but seeking human traditions and commandments. Because of them Jacob perished, and Israel was given over to reproach, expelled from its province and made an exile and wanderer throughout the whole world.

### Chapter XLIV

#### (Verses 1 and following)

“And now hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen. Thus says the Lord, who made and formed you from the womb, your helper. Do not fear, my servant [or: ‘servant’] Jacob, and Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. For I will pour out waters upon the thirsty, and streams upon the dry ground; I will pour out my spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing upon your descendants. And they will sprout among the grasses, like willows beside flowing waters. One will say, ‘I belong to the Lord’; another will call himself by the name of Jacob; another will write on his hand, ‘The Lord’s’; and he will be named by the name of Israel.”

The Septuagint: “But now hear, Jacob my child, and Israel whom I have chosen. I am the Lord God, who made you and formed you from the womb; you shall still have help. Do not fear, my child Jacob, and beloved Israel whom I have chosen. I will still give water to those who walk in thirst and in a waterless place; I will put my spirit upon your offspring and my blessings upon your children. And they will spring up like grass in the midst of water, and like a willow beside flowing waters. One will say, ‘I am God’s’; another will call upon the name of Jacob. Another will write upon his hand, ‘I am God’s,’ and will call upon the name of Israel.”

Where the Jewish people are accused of unbelief and blasphemy, they are addressed without any distinction of name, by plain names: “You did not call upon me, Jacob, nor did you labor for me, Israel”; and again: “I gave Jacob over to destruction, and Israel to blasphemy” (above, 43:22, 28).

But when he addresses the company of the Apostles, which is derived from the Jews, the privileges of their names are joined to the address: “Hear, Jacob my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen,” so that the first designation is servitude and the second election.

“Thus says the Lord, your maker and former, who helped you from the womb” (Gen. 25), so that even in your mother’s womb you might seize your brother’s heel. Or, he is the one who preserved you from persecutors at the beginning of the nascent Church.

“Do not fear their cruelty, my servant Jacob, and Jeshurun, whom I have chosen.” He calls Israel by another name. The Hebrew word *Yeshurun* (ISURUN), however, was interpreted by the others as *euthytaton* or *euthē*—that is, “most upright” or “upright”; only the Septuagint rendered it “most beloved,” adding “Israel” on their own. Properly, according to the Hebrews and the truth of the letters, *Israel* (ISRAEL) means “upright with God.” “A man seeing God” is not present in the letters but in the sound of the word. Hence the book of Genesis is also called *Eutheis*, that is, “of the upright”—Abraham, Isaac, and Israel.

> **Note:** Not in the letters, and so forth. Let the clergy and the other detractors of Jerome now be ashamed, who thought that the holy teacher did not know the Hebrew language sufficiently because he often interpreted the name Israel in his Commentaries with the Greeks as “a man seeing God.” See also the *Questions on Genesis*, col. 357; likewise Book Three *Against the Pelagians*, no. 8; and, if they matter, the notes that we also make there. —Martian.

> **Note:** The Ambrosian manuscripts have *EUTHYS*. Jerome held the same view elsewhere, especially in his commentary on Ezekiel 8, where he says: “Hence also the book of Genesis received its name from the name of these men”—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. This is the opinion of the Jews, who suppose that *Genesis* is designated where the “Book of the Upright” is praised, in Joshua 10:13 and 2 Samuel 1:18.

“Do not fear, therefore, Jacob and Israel, because I will pour out waters upon the thirsty and the dry ground,” of which it has often been said: “And I will pour out,” or “put,” “my spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing upon your descendants,” who will be reborn from water and the Holy Spirit in baptism.

The Savior also promised this in the Gospel, saying: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink.” Immediately it is added: “Now he said this about the Spirit, which those who believed in him were going to receive” (John 7:37–39).

He also compares those reborn in baptism to green grasses and to a willow that grows beside flowing waters. Contrary to the nature of things, it bears fruit, although previously it was barren, or although its seed, when taken as food, makes others barren. This is indeed read in the first Psalm: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall.”

Others understand a twofold calling between the grasses and the newly growing willows: in the grasses, the people of the nations; in the willows, those who believed from Israel. At the same time he describes the variety of believers: “Another will say, ‘I belong to the Lord,’” trusting that works of righteousness are present in him. Another will call—understand, sinners to repentance—in the name of Jacob, so that they too may supplant vices and sins.

Another will write upon his hand, “I am God’s.”

> **Note:** On this first occasion, since the Hebrew text is cited, Victorius changes “I am God’s” to “I am the Lord’s.”

Or, as the Septuagint translated it, he will write upon his hand, “I am God’s,” so that he may boast that he is a soldier enrolled in the new service of Christ.

“And he will be named by the name of Israel.” For not everyone from Israel, but a large portion from the multitude of the nations, will be named by the name of Israel, so that they may receive the Law and the Prophets and all the gifts of the Holy Spirit that were promised to the people of Israel.

### (Verses 6 and following)

“Thus says the Lord, the king of Israel, and its redeemer, the Lord of hosts: I am the first and I am the last, and besides me there is no God. Who is like me? Let him call and announce it, and set forth the order for me from the time when I established the ancient people; let them announce to them the things to come and the things that will happen.”

> **Note:** Martian had read, with a negative particle, “let them not announce,” contrary to the authority of the sacred text, not to mention that of the manuscripts.

“Do not fear, nor be troubled. From that time I made you hear and announced it; you are my witnesses. Is there a God besides me, and a creator whom I do not know? All the makers of idols are nothing, and their most precious works will not benefit them. They are their own witnesses, because they neither see nor understand, so that they may be put to shame.

“Who has formed a god and cast a statue for something useless? Behold, all who share in it will be put to shame; for they are craftsmen from among human beings.”

> **Note:** The preposition *ex* was lacking. I am reluctant to keep reminding the reader of restorations of this kind, which are of minor importance.

“Let them all assemble, let them stand; they will tremble and be ashamed together.

“The smith has worked with the file; he formed it on coals and with hammers, and worked with the strength of his arm. He will hunger and grow faint; he will not drink water and will become weary.

“The woodworker stretches out the measuring line, forms it with the carving knife, makes it with angular tools, and turns it with the compass. He makes the image of a man, like a beautiful human being dwelling in a house.

“He cuts down cedars; he takes holm oak and oak, which had stood among the trees of the forest. He plants a pine, which the rain nourishes. It becomes fuel for human beings: he takes some of it and warms himself; he kindles it and bakes bread. From the remainder he makes a god and worships it; he makes a statue and bows down before it.

“He burns half of it in the fire, and from half of it he eats meat. He cooks a stew, is filled and warmed, and says: ‘Ah! I am warm; I have seen the fire.’ From the remainder he makes a god and a statue for himself; he bows before it, worships it, and entreats it, saying: ‘Deliver me, for you are my god.’

“They did not know, nor did they understand. For their eyes were closed, so that they might not see, and their hearts, so that they might not understand. They do not consider in their mind, nor know, nor perceive, so as to say: ‘I burned half of it in the fire, and baked bread upon its coals. I roasted meat, ate it, and from the remainder shall I make an idol? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?’ Part of it is ashes; an ignorant heart has worshiped it, and it has not delivered its soul, nor will it say: ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand.’”

After the preaching of the Apostles, the calling of the nations, the coming of the Savior, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit—which he promised to give to all believers—when, according to the variety of their merits, one will say, “I belong to the Lord,” another will call upon the name of Jacob, and another will write upon his hand that he belongs to the Lord; and when, although he has arisen from the unbelieving multitude of the nations, he will be named by the name of Israel, so that, having abandoned idols, he may worship the one God, a second section begins. We have set it all out together, so that we might not divide the continuity of a single meaning.

And because the Septuagint in this chapter, except for a few words, does not differ from the Hebrew, we are content with our edition; once it has been understood, the others too will become known. It is a discourse against the idolaters of that time, when the prophet Isaiah was announcing future events to the peoples, and he reproves those who, having despised the worship of God Almighty, bow before wooden images and worship the works of their hands.

Let us therefore proceed through each point.

“Thus says the Lord, the king of Israel,” who is going to believe in me, “and its redeemer,” who will receive the coming of my Son: the Lord of hosts and powers, the Almighty. For this is what *Sabaoth* (SABAOTH) signifies in Hebrew.

“I am the first, and I am the last; I am Alpha and Omega. And besides me there is no God,” because the child whom I have chosen is God in me. Concerning him I said above: “Behold my child, whom I have chosen; my chosen one, in whom my soul has delighted. He will bring forth judgment to the nations, and in his name the nations will hope.”

He does not say that he is alone, but that, apart from his power and wisdom, there is no external god, condemning the belief in many gods and their images: “Who,” he says, “is like me?” Let him call those things that are not as though they were, and set forth the order of my creation, since I have balanced all things by reason and made the human being upon the earth.

Nor do I desire only this; I also seek knowledge of future things. Therefore you, Israel, whose king and redeemer I am, do not fear the images that you learned on Mount Sinai are nothing.

Or is there perhaps another Creator whom I do not know? Or, besides this world, is there another world that displays the power of an unknown god? Indeed, not only the things that are made, but also those who make them, will be regarded as nothing. When the time of vengeance comes, they will in no way be able to free themselves through the works of their own hands—works that are blind and without sensation and that put their craftsmen to shame.

For who could believe that a god is formed by an axe, a file, a drill, and a hammer? Or that images are cast upon coals, or that through a measuring line, carving knife, angular tools, and compass gods suddenly arise? Especially since the hunger and thirst of the craftsman reveal the poverty of his art.

A wooden statue is made, expressing human form; and the more beautiful it is, the more confined the god is thought to be. It is placed in a shrine and shut up in an eternal prison, although it grew for a long time in the forests and, according to the variety of trees, was a cedar, holm oak, oak, or pine.

In a remarkable manner, its fragments and shavings are thrown into the fire to warm the maker of the god and to cook various stews; but another part is fashioned into a god, so that, when the work is completed, its maker may worship it and implore the aid of his own handiwork. He neither understands nor considers—or rather, he does not see with the eyes of either flesh or mind—that something whose part has been burned by fire cannot be a god, nor that divine majesty can be made by human hands.

The prophetic discourse continues more fully in mockery of idols. These matters are easy to understand and do not require a ragged, or rather excessive, exposition. Flaccus also writes about this in his *Satire*, mocking the images of the nations (*Satires* 8, Book 1):

> Once I was a fig-tree trunk, useless wood,
>
> When an uncertain craftsman was deciding whether to make a bench or Priapus.
>
> He preferred to make me a god; from that moment I became a god,
>
> The greatest terror of thieves and birds. [lacuna]

Whatever has been said about idols can also be applied to the leaders of heresies, who fashion images of their doctrines and falsehoods with an artificer’s heart and venerate things they know to have been fabricated by themselves. Their own error is not enough for them unless they deceive the simple by having them worship it.

They think piety is a source of profit and devour widows’ houses (1 Tim. 6:5), and, abusing the ignorance of the common people, they form their god by dialectical art, as though with an axe and a drill, a file and a carving knife; they strike him with a hammer and gild him with the beauty of rhetorical speech. Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame (Phil. 3:19).

### (Verses 21 and following)

“Remember these things, Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant. I formed you; you are my servant, Israel. Do not forget me. I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you.

“Praise, heavens, for the Lord has shown mercy [the Vulgate adds: ‘mercy’]. Shout for joy, ends of the earth; resound with praise, mountains, forests, and every tree in them. For the Lord has redeemed Jacob, and Israel will glory [or: ‘will be glorified’].”

The Septuagint: “Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, because you are my child. I formed you as my child; and you, Israel, do not forget me. For behold, I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud and your sins like darkness. Return to me, and I will redeem you. Rejoice, heavens, because God has shown mercy to Israel. Sound the trumpet, foundations of the earth; cry out, mountains, with joy; hills and all the trees in them, because God has redeemed Jacob, and Israel will be renowned.”

Since these things are so, and you know that idols are human fabrications, Jacob and my child Israel, do not forget your Creator and do not wrong yourself by bowing before the work of your hands.

Because these things must be utterly destroyed at the coming of my chosen child, recognize with the utmost eagerness of mind that, just as a cloud, darkness, and mist are either dissolved by the sun’s heat or thinned by a driving wind, so I will dissolve your iniquities and all the sins by which you previously offended me.

Only return to me and practice repentance, because you are to be redeemed by precious blood. If you do this, know that heaven and earth rejoice over your salvation and that all the elements sing together.

Or understand by the heavens the angels who dwell in heaven and the other powers by which the foundations of the earth are supported. Or certainly understand the Apostles and Prophets, concerning whom the Apostle also spoke: “Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets” (Eph. 2:20).

The mountains and forests, or the hills, which according to the variety of virtues have occupied the first, middle, and last places, are likewise commanded to shout for joy and sound the trumpet, knowing that the Lord has redeemed Jacob and rejoices in Israel’s conversion—or that Israel itself, converted from error, has become renowned.

### (Verses 24 and following)

“Thus says the Lord, your redeemer and your former from the womb: I am the Lord who makes all things, stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth, and there was no one with me. I frustrate the signs of diviners and turn augurs into madness; I turn wise men backward and make their knowledge foolish. I raise up the word of my servant and fulfill the counsel of my messengers.

“I say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be inhabited [or: ‘you shall be rebuilt’],’ and to the cities of Judah, ‘You shall be built’; and I will raise up its desolate places. I say to the deep, ‘Be desolate,’ and I will dry up your rivers. I say to Cyrus, ‘You are my shepherd, and you shall fulfill all my will.’ I say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be built,’ and to the temple, ‘You shall be founded.’”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord who redeemed you and formed you from the womb. I am the Lord who completes all things; I stretched out heaven alone and established the earth.”

> **Note:** We read “I established” from the Greek *esterēōsa*, and Victorius agrees. Previously it read “I formed.”

“Who else has dispersed the signs of the Python-spirits and the divinations of the heart? I turn the prudent backward and make their counsel foolish. I establish the word of my child and prove the counsel of his angels true.

“I say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be inhabited,’ and to the cities of Judah, ‘You shall be built,’ and its desolate places shall arise. I say to the abyss, ‘You shall be desolate,’ and I will dry up your rivers. I say to Cyrus, ‘Let him be wise and do all my will.’ I say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be built,’ and I will lay the foundations of my holy house.”

After the idols and iniquities of Israel have been destroyed and its sins erased, when all creation rejoices together, and, according to the faith of the Gospel (Luke 15), the angels rejoice in heaven over the repentance of sinners, the power of God is described: it is by no means a great thing for him to redeem Jacob and restore Israel, whom he formed from the womb, to a right heart.

And if this seems to anyone to be no small matter, let him not find it difficult for the one who stretched out the heavens alone, according to what is read elsewhere: “Who stretched out the heaven like a skin” (Ps. 103:2). This does not exclude the Son from the stretching out of the heavens: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John 1:3). Rather, as we have often said, this statement excludes idols.

For in Solomon’s Proverbs, Wisdom is also said in the person of Christ, the power and wisdom of God: “When he prepared the heavens, I was with him” (Prov. 8:27). “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5; 32:9); and: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

We repeatedly insist upon these points, so that no opportunity for blaspheming Christ may be left to heretics. Likewise, in establishing the earth, when he was making firm its foundations, no one was with God except the one who was in him.

This one, therefore, so great and so powerful, when the time of the predetermined mystery arrives—so that all idols may be destroyed and knowledge of God alone may be proclaimed throughout the world—will destroy and overturn all the prophecies and signs and portents of diviners, Python-spirits, and augurs by which they had deceived the human race. He will also show the wisdom of the philosophers, which is itself the greatest part of error, to be foolish, since they are not shown to have grasped the wisdom of God through human thoughts.

He will also fulfill in deeds the word of his child, or servant, of whom we spoke above, and the counsel of his messengers—namely, all the Apostles and teachers who will announce the will of their master to the nations.

He, therefore, who is going to accomplish such great things, whose power I have described in a brief discourse, now also says to Jerusalem—which is to be destroyed by the Babylonians, but before its destruction is announced to be inhabited again by the peoples—and to the cities of Judea that they will be restored [or: “would be restored”]. He will also raise up its desolate places, so that everything may be filled with inhabitants.

The one who says to Jerusalem, to Judea, and to its desolate places that they will be inhabited, built, and raised up, says to the deep or abyss—that is, to Babylon—“Be desolate, and I will dry up your rivers,” meaning the whole power of its kings.

Or, because he had mentioned the deep and the abyss, he appropriately added “rivers” by way of metaphor, concerning which the Psalmist also sings: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136:1).

And the one who restores Jerusalem and destroys Babylon also says to Cyrus, king of the Persians, who first destroyed Babylon and the Chaldeans: “You are my shepherd,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “Let him be wise.” The reason for this difference is clear. If we read the Hebrew word *roi* with the letter *resh* (ROI), it means “my shepherd”; if with *daleth* (ROI), it means “my knowing one” or “my understanding one.” Their similarity is distinguished by a small stroke and is therefore often confused.

It is written at the beginning of Ezra that, at the decree of Cyrus, king of the Persians and Medes, the captivity of the people of Israel was loosened, and those who wished to return to Jerusalem were released under Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua, son of Jozadak the high priest. For the Lord inspired him to do his will and fulfill his commands.

He significantly added: “I say to Jerusalem, ‘You shall be built,’ and to the temple, ‘You shall be founded.’” Under Cyrus it was ordered that Jerusalem and the temple be built; only their foundations were laid while he was alive. Later, under Darius, in his second year, when Haggai and Zechariah were prophesying, construction of the temple began.

### Chapter XLV

#### (Verses 1 and following)

“Thus says the Lord to my anointed, Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, so that I may subject nations before him and turn the backs of kings; and I will open doors before him, and the gates shall not be closed. I will go before you, and I will humble the glorious ones of the earth. I will shatter bronze doors and break iron bars. I will give you hidden treasures and secret hoards, so that you may know that I am the Lord who calls you by your name, the God of Israel.

“For the sake of my servant Jacob and my chosen Israel, I called you by your name; I gave you a title, though you did not know me. I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is no God. I girded you, though you did not know me, so that those from the rising of the sun and those from the west may know that there is none besides me [previously ‘God’ was added]. I am the Lord, and there is no other.

“I form light and create darkness; I make peace and create evil. I am the Lord, making all these things.”

I know that in this chapter very many, not only among the Latins but also among the Greeks, fall into serious error, thinking that it is written: “Thus says the Lord to my Christ, the Lord,” so that it may be understood according to what we read elsewhere: “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24), and: “The Lord said to my Lord” (Ps. 109:1).

For it does not say *kyriō*, which means “to the Lord,” but “to Cyrus,” who in Hebrew is called *Chores* (CHORES), the king of the Persians who conquered Babylon and the Chaldeans. It is also stated above that, having joined the Medes, he was the driver of a two-horse chariot—that is, of a camel and a donkey.

He was called “Christ,” that is, “the anointed of the Lord,” because this was a mark of royal power among the Hebrews. Just as among us the diadem and purple are given only to emperors, so among the Hebrews those who were going to reign were anointed with oil. Hence Saul too is called “the Lord’s Christ” (1 Sam. 24:7). And we read in the Psalms: “Do not touch my Christs, and do not harm my prophets” (Ps. 104:15).

He grasped and held Cyrus’s right hand, so that no one could resist his strength. Let us read Xenophon’s history of Cyrus the Great in eight books, and we shall see Isaiah’s prophecy fulfilled. For what city did not open itself to him? What backs of kings did he not subject? What walls, previously impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege?

Hence God addresses Cyrus himself: “I gave you treasures and hidden riches of all the cities,” so that you, who previously worshiped idols, might recognize one God through his benefactions—especially since you know that your name was foretold long before you were born.

Josephus also reports this in the eleventh book of the *Jewish Antiquities*: Cyrus read from Isaiah that he had been prophesied by name with certainty, and for this reason he greatly cherished the Jews as though they were God’s intimate friends.

“These things,” he says, “I granted you for the sake of Jacob my servant and Israel my chosen, and I called you by your name,” just as I called Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and long beforehand I foretold you, as I did Isaac and Josiah, so that you would not be thought to be that Christ to whom you were compared and whose type and image you foreshadowed.

“But you did not know me,” that is, you worshiped images, not God. “I girded you with strength”; I made you victorious over many nations, and you did not recognize your helper.

At this point I cannot sufficiently marvel at the stupidity of readers who refer these words to Christ, through whom the world has been reconciled to God. “I am the Lord, and there is no other; besides me there is none.” For apart from my Word, reason, power, and wisdom, which are in me, there is no other God.

“I did these things so that the whole world, from east to west, might acknowledge that there is no other God besides me. I am the Lord, and there is no other.” For the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father. He says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

It is also written in the book of Ezra that Cyrus wrote to all the nations that there is no God except the one God of Israel. Or it should be understood in this way: the release of the captives and God’s mercy toward his people made God more widely known to all nations.

The one, therefore, who gave you strength and is the one God makes things contrary to one another: light and darkness, that is, day and night; peace and evil, that is, tranquility and war. Through these he signifies that he was angry with his people when they endured the darkness of captivity and the evils of slavery, and again that he showed mercy when they were sent back to their homeland and received peace and joy.

For just as darkness is contrary to light, so war is contrary to peace. Hence the heresy should be confounded that considers God the creator of evils. Here “evil” is not set down as the opposite of good, but for affliction and war, according to what is written in the Gospel: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6:34).

According to the tropological sense, we can also say these things about a churchman, to whom God has given speech and wisdom so that, through his disputation, he may overturn all sects opposed to the truth. Holy Scripture also records this about Stephen (Acts 6): no one could resist his wisdom.

Such a man subjects kings—that is, the patriarchs of the various heresies—to his power; he opens and breaks what previously seemed closed by dialectical art; and he brings forth the secrets of heretics, overcoming and convicting them, so that they may come to know the secrets of Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3).

God calls such a man by his own name because he is the defender of his child Jacob and his chosen Israel. He receives him and conforms him to his word. He must beware of thinking that what he speaks belongs to himself, but must refer everything to the glory of the giver, lest he too deserve to hear: “I girded you, and you did not know me.”

For when, equipped with the armor of the Apostle, he has taught everyone that there is only one God, who is the God of Jacob and Israel, Marcion will be confounded, since he understands two gods: one good and the other just; one the creator of invisible things, the other of visible things. The former, he says, makes light; the latter, darkness; the former, peace; the latter, evil—although one and the same God created both according to the diversity of merits.

## Book Thirteen.

[Col. 0441D] 534–535 Many dangers overwhelm those who sail. If the wind blows with greater violence, the storm is a cause for fear. If a gentler breeze ruffles the surface of the resting element, they fear the ambushes of pirates. And so it happens that those who entrust themselves to a fragile wooden vessel either fear danger or endure it; of these two conditions, one is more grievous than the other: either continually to fear death, or to endure what one has feared. I see this happening to me as I sail upon the sea of Isaiah. For while the sails are being spread on an unhindered course, and the keel glides along cutting through the fields of the sea with the hands of the natural elements at rest, suddenly a storm of illness rises, and with such masses of waves and such a roar of waves crashing against one another [Col. 0443A] that it terrifies the fearful hearts of my friends, so that they are compelled to say: “Master, save us; we are perishing” (Matt. 8:25).

[Note: [Col. 0441D] Thus the Ambrosian manuscripts restore the text; for it is clear that Jerome is speaking of an illness of his body and impaired health, both from the context below and especially from the preface to the following book, where, giving thanks to God for the recovery of his former health, he says: “He who had struck me with a SUDDEN ILLNESS healed me with incredible speed.” Previously, “a sudden storm of sound” could scarcely be understood in any sense, etc.]

Therefore, Eustochium, unique example of nobility and virginity throughout the whole world [Col. 0443D], let not the pupil of your eye be silent, but cry out in your heart: “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15). And speak with the Psalmist: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Ps. 43:23), so that, while you pray and Christ shows mercy, I may complete the work undertaken on Isaiah. For already the thirteenth book of the Commentaries is being forged, and it has not yet reached its end. Meanwhile, until the merciful and compassionate Lord, patient and rich in mercies (Ps. 85 and 145),

[Note: [Col. 0443D] “Restore my former health.” What Jerome suffered while composing his Commentaries, I likewise suffer while restoring them; for my former health is scarcely restored to me by the merciful God, who looks upon the earth and often makes it tremble. Therefore, kind reader, if it is permissible to compare small things with great ones, the complete correction of my edition is reserved for your judgment. MARTIAN.]

restores my former health, I have dictated this little Preface in hurried speech, so that what is here may be copied onto sheets, and the complete correction may be left to the judgment of the reader.

## 535 (Chapter XLV—Verse 8)

“Distill dew, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened and bring forth the Savior, and let righteousness arise at the same time: I, the Lord, have created him.”

The Septuagint: “Let heaven rejoice from above, and let the clouds sprinkle righteousness; let the earth bring forth and let mercy arise, and let it bring forth righteousness at the same time: I am the Lord who created you.”

[Note: [Col. 0444D] Victor prefers “righteousness” in the nominative, whatever the Greek manuscript may say; for in certain copies one reads δικαιοσύνην, “righteousness.”]

This passage has a twofold interpretation. Some think that what is said remains attached to the preceding words, and that when King Cyrus releases the captives, heaven and earth rejoice—by metonymy (μετωνυμικῶς), meaning those who dwell in heaven and on earth. Others separate it from what precedes and regard it as the proper beginning of this chapter, with a prophecy of the Lord’s coming. The clouds are commanded—of them it was written above (on chapter 5:6): “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it,” that is, upon the vineyard of Israel—and to those clouds the truth of God has come, so that they may rain upon the world the righteous one, or righteousness; and that the earth may be opened and bring forth the Savior.

Concerning this it is sung in the Psalms: “Truth has arisen from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. 84:12); or, according to the Septuagint: “The earth has brought forth mercy and righteousness together,” so that sinners may obtain mercy and the righteous their rewards. As for what follows, “I, the Lord, have created him,” or, “I, the Lord who created you,” he will not be scandalized by the name “creature” who has read that he is a worm, a servant, and one brought forth from the earth.

### (Verses 9 ff.)

“Woe to him who contradicts his maker, a potsherd among the earthen potsherds. Does clay say to its potter, ‘What are you doing?’ and, ‘Your work is without hands’? Woe to him who says to his father, ‘What are you begetting?’ and to a woman, ‘What are you giving birth to?’ Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, its potter: Ask me about the things to come concerning my sons, and command me concerning the work of my hands” [Col. 0444D]. “I made the earth, and I myself created the human being upon it; my hands stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. I raised him up for righteousness, and I shall direct all his ways. He himself shall build my city, and he shall release my captivity, not for a price nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts.”

[Note: [Col. 0444D] In the older Ambrosian manuscript, as also in other manuscripts of Jerome’s version, Martian found the reading “you commanded me.”]

“I raised him up for righteousness, and I shall direct all his ways.”

[Note: [Col. 0444D] The same manuscript reads: “I shall raise him up with righteousness.”]

“He himself shall build my city” [another reading: “he built”] “and he shall release my captivity, not for a price nor for gifts, says the Lord of hosts.”

The Septuagint: “What have I made better than the potter’s clay? Does the plowman plow the earth? Will the clay say to the potter, ‘What are you doing?’ because you do not work and have no hands? Woe to him who says to his father, ‘What are you begetting?’ and to his mother, ‘What are you giving birth to?’ For thus says the Lord God, the Holy One of Israel, who made the things to come. Ask me concerning my sons, and command me concerning the works of my hands. I made the earth, and the human being upon it. I established heaven with my hand; I commanded all the stars. I raised him up with righteousness as king; all his ways are straight. He himself shall build my city, and he shall restore the captivity of my people; not with a price nor with gifts, said the Lord God of hosts.”

Those who wish to refer what has been said to the person of Cyrus interpret the passage in this way. Since I make great promises—that for the return of my people to Judea I will subject all kingdoms to Cyrus—woe to him who is unbelieving and does not think that what I say will come to pass, as though clay or a broken potsherd were to accuse its potter of why it had been made or why it had been made in such a way; and as though a work were to speak against the craftsman’s hands; and as though a son were to accuse his father and mother of why he had been poured forth upon the earth according to the law of nature.

Therefore, since I, the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, have fashioned Cyrus, and he has been generated at my command, you do wrong to hesitate about the future. Rather, you ought to know that I distribute my sons, the people of Israel, and the work of my hands, not according to your judgment but according to my will, so that I who formerly created darkness and evil for them may now grant them light and peace.

For I am God, who did not create the earth in vain, so that it should be desolate and waste, but so that human beings might dwell upon it. I stretched out, or established, the heavens, so that they might be the dwelling-place of angels. I distinguished them by the variety of the stars, and commanded each one in what order it should run and complete the different periods of days, months, and years.

Since, then, I made heaven and earth, what great thing is it if I created one king who would preserve my commands and if I directed all his ways? For he will command that my city, Jerusalem, be built and that the captives return to Judea—not for a price nor for gifts, but because of my will, says the Lord God of hosts.

Those, however, who refer the interpretation already begun to Christ regulate the words of their explanation as follows:

Woe to those who contradict God and do not think that Christ will come, as though clay and a potsherd were to contradict their potter. Woe to him who says to the omnipotent Father, “Why do you beget a son?” and to the holy woman Mary, “What are you giving birth to?” Concerning her the Apostle also writes (Gal. 4:4) that Christ was “made of a woman, made under the law.”

Thus says the Lord, the Holy One of Israel, who fashioned the Savior in the virginal womb, saying through Gabriel: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35); “therefore the holy one who will be born in you will be called the Son of God.” Let the potsherd question me and inquire into the secrets of the future [Col. 0445B], and let it command me how I ought to regenerate [Note: [Col. 0445D] In accordance with Jerome’s thought and the context of the discourse, we restore, with the aid of the Ambrosian manuscript, “regenerate,” where the former reading was “rule.”] adoptive sons who will believe in my Son.

The evangelist John also says: “To all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

But if I made the earth so that human beings might inhabit it, and stretched out the heavens above and adorned them with the variety of the stars so that worshipers of God might dwell upon the earth, what is astonishing if I sent my righteous Son, the king, into the world, or raised him from the dead, whose ways are all straight? “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22).

He will build my city upon a rock, against which the gates of hell cannot prevail (Matt. 16:18), and which, being set upon a mountain, cannot be hidden (ibid. 5:14). He will release all those previously bound by demonic chains, not for a price nor for gifts; for we have been saved freely, with the Apostles hearing and doing what was said: “You received freely; give freely” (Matt. 10:8).

Some refer these words to Zerubbabel, who led the captives out of Babylon, built the city, and constructed the Temple, while Haggai and Zechariah prophesied and said: “The hands of Zerubbabel founded this house, and his hands shall complete it” (Zech. 4:9).

But we say more correctly and more truly that Cyrus did not build the city that was later constructed under Nehemiah, nor were all his ways directed. Of him it was said above: “I took you up and girded you, and you did not know me.” Nor can the status of Zerubbabel, who was under the nod and power of the Medes and Persians, encompass everything that is said here. Zerubbabel did not build the city, nor did he release the captivity; nor can he be called king, since he lived under other kings and lacked that title.

What the Septuagint intend, who at the beginning of this chapter translated, “What have I made better than the potter’s clay? Does the one who plows plow the earth?” I cannot determine, unless perhaps I follow the edition of Theodotion, who instead rendered it: “Woe to him who contends against his maker, a plowman plowing the earth”—that is, one who wounds the hearts of mortals in repentance and overturns and subverts them in the manner of furrows.

[Note: [Col. 0445D] We again correct the text from the Ambrosian manuscripts, reading “those who plow,” compelled by the very sequence and meaning of the discourse and by the Greek of Theodotion, ἀροτριῶντας, which Procopius reads. This reading is also confirmed by the Hebrew text and by the most ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain preserved by Montfaucon. Previously the text read “of the one who plows.”]

But this interpretation too is frivolous.

Furthermore, that God is called the potter—that is, our Creator and Maker—is also stated by the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Romans: “Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why have you made me thus?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–21).

And it is written at greater length in Jeremiah, who relates, among other things: “I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work upon the wheel; and the vessel that he was making with his hands was spoiled. And again he made from the same clay another vessel, as it seemed good in his sight. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: ‘If I cannot do with you as this potter does, O house of Israel,’ says the Lord, ‘behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, O house of Israel’” (Jer. 18:3–6).

The statement, “I commanded all the stars,” has given some an occasion to claim that the stars are rational and possess soul and perception. For, they say, he would not command them unless they understood. They do not remember that it is written in Jonah: “The Lord commanded the burning wind” (Jonah 4:8), and again: “He commanded the morning worm” (ibid. 4:7). Nor do they remember that in the Gospel the Savior rebuked the winds and the sea (Luke 8:24), in which it is obvious that there is neither perception nor reason.

### (Verses 14 ff.)

“Thus says the Lord: The labor of Egypt, and the commerce of Ethiopia, and the men of Saba, tall in stature, shall pass over to you, and shall be yours. They shall walk behind you; bound with bracelets, they shall proceed. They shall worship you and entreat you: Surely God is in you, and there is no God besides you. Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior. They have been put to shame and have been confounded, all together; the makers of errors have gone into confusion. Israel has been saved by the Lord with eternal salvation; you shall not be confounded, and you shall not be ashamed for ever and ever.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord of hosts: Egypt has labored, and the commerce of the Ethiopians and of the Sabaeans; tall men shall pass over to you, and they shall be your servants. They shall follow you, bound with bracelets; they shall pass over to you, worship you, and pray to you, because God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it: God of Israel, Savior. Let all his adversaries be confounded and ashamed, and let them walk in confusion. Renew yourselves toward me, O islands. Israel is saved by the Lord with eternal salvation; they shall not be confounded nor ashamed for ever.”

Those who follow the historical interpretation say that Egypt, the Ethiopians, and the peoples of Saba, who live beyond Ethiopia, served Cyrus; that the most distant nations were subjected to him; and that from his marvelous victory they understood that the Lord was in him, and that there was no other God besides the one who dwelt in him.

But how the statement that follows—“Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior”—can fit the person of Cyrus, I do not understand. Perhaps they may use the edition of Theodotion, who translated: “In you is the Mighty One, and there is no other God besides him; therefore you are the hidden Mighty One, God of Israel, Savior.” However they turn the passage, they will not be able to escape the snares of truth. Grant that God is in Cyrus, and that there is no other God besides the one who is in Cyrus: how can it suit Cyrus’s person to say, “Truly you are God, the hidden God, God of Israel, Savior”?

Therefore, the one in whom God is present is more correctly and truly understood as our Lord Jesus Christ, who says in the Gospel: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

[Note: [Col. 0447D] Victor adds from certain manuscripts: “And I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.”]

He is called the hidden God because of the mystery of the body he assumed, and “God of Israel, Savior,” because this is interpreted as “Jesus.” For, according to the angel Gabriel, he will save his people (Luke 1:31).

“They have been confounded and ashamed, all together”: namely, the scribes and Pharisees. “And the makers of error have gone into confusion,” those who spread falsehood throughout the world by saying that he had been secretly removed by the Apostles (Matt. 28:13).

But “Israel saved in the Lord with eternal salvation” signifies the company of the Apostles and those who believed through the Apostles. Hence it is said to them: “You shall not be confounded nor ashamed,” not only in the present age but also in the age to come.

No one doubts that Egypt, the Ethiopians, and the Sabaeans—tall and lofty men—served him, when one sees the world subjected to him and perceives that all the regions of heaven and all the shores of the earth, through the name of a few nations living at the ends of the earth, will believe in him.

Hence “the labor of Egypt” is beautifully said to cease, as though it had been laboring in the error of idolatry. For no nation was so devoted to idolatry, nor worshiped so many monstrous images, as Egypt. Concerning it we read above (19:1): “Behold, the Lord will ascend upon a swift cloud and will enter Egypt, and the idols of Egypt will be shaken before him, and the heart of Egypt will melt within it.”

As for what has been added in the Septuagint, “Renew yourselves toward me, O islands,” we can explain it by saying that the Churches gathered from the nations are renewed in Christ and are called islands because they endure the fury and storms of their persecutors and, founded upon the rock, are shaken by no mass of storms.

The Hebrews, in a foolish dispute, strive to assert that up to the point where it says, “Surely God is in you, and there is no God besides you,” the words are addressed either to Jerusalem or to Cyrus. But when the text continues, “Truly you are a hidden God, God of Israel, Savior,” they say that the discourse suddenly turns in apostrophe to the omnipotent God. Yet it is evident even to fools that the discourse forms a single continuous statement and that its meaning cannot be divided when it is joined by the very order and structure of the narrative.

### (Verses 18 ff.)

“For thus says the Lord, creating the heavens—he himself is God, forming the earth and making it; he himself is its potter. He did not create it in vain, but formed it to be inhabited” [Vulgate: “so that it might be inhabited”]. “I am the Lord, and there is no other. I have not spoken in secret, in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob, ‘Seek me in vain.’ I am the Lord, speaking righteousness and declaring what is right.

“Gather yourselves and come; draw near together, you who have been saved from the nations. They have no knowledge, those who carry the wood of their carved image and pray to a god who cannot save. Declare and come, and deliberate together: Who made this known from the beginning? Who declared it from that time? [Note: [Col. 0447D] Martian read *in recto* (“straightforwardly”), and also “I foretold it” with an affirmative mark, though the sacred text itself rejects this.] Is it not I, the Lord, and is there no other God besides me? There is no just and saving God besides me.

“Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is no other. I have sworn by myself: a word of righteousness shall go forth from my mouth and shall not return, because every knee shall bow to me and every tongue shall swear. Therefore, in the Lord, he shall say: ‘My righteousnesses and my dominion belong to me.’ They shall come to him, and all who oppose him shall be confounded. In the Lord every seed of Israel shall be justified and shall be praised.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord who made heaven: This is the God who displayed the earth and made it; he himself prepared it”—

[Note: [Col. 0447D] From a certain Medicean manuscript Victor reads “distinguished” (*separavit*), a reading also supported by the Greek διώρισεν.]

“not to make it empty did he make it, but he fashioned it to be inhabited. I am the Lord, and there is no other. I did not speak in secret, nor in a dark place of the earth. I did not say to the seed of Jacob, ‘Seek what is vain.’ I am the Lord who speak righteousness and declare truth.

“Gather and come, and consult together, you who are being saved from the nations”—

[Note: [Col. 0448D] The words “and consult” are absent from the Ambrosian manuscript. Symmachus and the Vulgate interpret the phrase as “draw near.”]

“Those who carry the wood of their carved image have not known; they pray to gods who do not save. If they declare it, let them draw near so that they may know together who made these things known from the beginning; then it was declared to you. Is it not I, the Lord God, and is there no other besides me? There is no just and saving one besides me. Turn to me, and you shall be saved from the ends of the earth. I am God, and there is no other.

“I swear by myself: unless righteousness goes forth from my mouth, my words shall not be turned aside, because every knee shall bow to me, and every tongue shall swear and confess to God, saying: ‘Righteousness and glory shall come to him, and all who separate themselves from the Lord shall be confounded.’ Every seed of the sons of Israel shall be justified and glorified in God.”

By calling Egypt, Ethiopia, and Saba, tall men, through whom the salvation of all barbarian nations and the conversion of the entire world to God are indicated, God shows his righteousness: that the Lord belongs not only to the Jews but also to the nations.

For he himself is equally the God of all, maker of heaven and earth, and he created the earth for no other reason than that it should be the dwelling-place of human beings who would worship and understand their Creator and despise all idols.

For even on Mount Sinai, from its lofty summit, he spoke these words to the peoples who were listening: “You shall have no other gods besides me, and you shall not make for yourself an idol” (Exod. 20:3–4).

But it is better to understand this saying as referring to the preaching of the Gospel. For Moses spoke in a hidden wilderness to one people alone. The sound of the Apostles, however, went forth into the whole world, and their words reached to the ends of the earth (Ps. 19:4).

“I did not say,” he says, “to the seed of Jacob, ‘Seek me in vain.’” For I promised them the kingdoms of heaven, and I first spoke to them: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24). Therefore I spoke righteousness and declared what was right, or truth, so that, abandoning the images and ceremonies of the Law, they might follow the truth of the Gospel.

But because they refused to believe and judged themselves unworthy of salvation, I therefore say to the nations: “Gather yourselves from the whole world; come and draw near to me together, you who have been saved from the nations.” By this he shows that not all nations would immediately believe, but gradually and in parts.

Finally, he rebukes those who remained in their former error, saying: “They have not known who lift up the wood [another reading: ‘the sign’] of their carved image, and they pray to a god who cannot save.” The sense is: They did not understand my words, weighed down by the burden of their idols and placing their hope in things in which there is no salvation.

Therefore the Apostles are commanded to proclaim the truth “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2), and to deliberate concerning the salvation of the nations. That many from the nations would be gathered and come, and that they would be saved, God declared from the beginning; and the mouths of all the Prophets sang of it, speaking by the word of the Lord, besides whom there is no other.

For the Son is not God apart from him, but God in him. And beautifully he joins the words, “a just God,” not of one nation but of the whole world, to whom he says: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth,” fulfilling what the Father promised the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

He swears that the sentence of his mouth, and the word that he once uttered concerning the salvation of the nations, will by no means be void, but that his promise will be fulfilled in deed. Above he said: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved, all the ends of the earth.”

He swears, according to the Apostle (Heb. 6:17–18), so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we may have firm consolation. He also swears that, when idols have been abandoned, every knee will bow to him—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and that every tongue of mortals will swear by him (Phil. 2:10–11).

This clearly signifies the Christian people. For it is the custom of the Church to bend the knee to Christ; the Jews, demonstrating the pride of their mind, do not do so at all. Moreover, every tongue of all the barbarian nations confesses God, not in synagogues but in the Churches of Christ.

Every tongue that confesses Christ will speak in the Lord and will say: “My righteousnesses are mine, and my dominion is mine,” not that of the Jewish people. All nations will come to him, and those who previously opposed his Gospel will be confounded. Every seed of Israel will be justified and praised, for their preaching and their most fruitful sowing brought forth abundant fruits throughout the whole world.

Or, according to the Septuagint, every tongue that swears and confesses God will say that the righteousness and glory of the whole world come to him, and that the Jews who separate themselves from him are confounded.

Those, however, who arose from the stock of the sons of Israel, who sprang from the seed of the Apostles, and who believed in Christ, shall possess everlasting righteousness and glory.

## (Chapter XLVI—Verses 1–2)

“Bel is broken; Nabo is crushed. Their images have become beasts and cattle; your burdens are a heavy weight, even to weariness. They have withered and been crushed together; they could not save the one carrying them, and their soul shall go into captivity.”

The Septuagint: “Bel has fallen; Dagon has been crushed. Their carved images have become beasts and cattle. You carry them, fastened together like a burden, for one who labors, fails, and hungers, and is unable to prevail together; they could not save themselves from war, but they themselves were led away captive.”

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Two Ambrosian manuscripts add: “Consequently, after the calling of the nations,” and immediately thereafter testify that he destroyed the idols.]

After the calling of the nations and the election of those who believe from Israel, he testifies that the idols have fallen.

“Bel has fallen, he has fallen,” or “he has been broken.” The Greeks call him Belus; the Latins call him Saturn. So great was his worship among the ancients that they sacrificed to him not only human victims—captives and obscure mortals—but even their own children.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] Compare Tertullian, Apology, chapter 9; also Minucius Felix, among others.]

Nabo too is an idol, whose name means “prophecy” and “divination”; this signifies that after the truth of the Gospel they fell silent throughout the whole world.

Or, according to the Septuagint, Dagon—though he is not found in the Hebrew text. He is the idol of Ashkelon, Gaza, and the other cities of the Philistines.

He moves from the specific to the general: “Their images have become beasts and cattle.” This does not mean that the images of the nations were exposed as prey to beasts and cattle, but that the religion of the nations consisted in images of beasts and irrational animals, which were especially consecrated to divine worship in Egypt.

Concerning these Virgil writes (*Aeneid* 8.698):

> Monsters of gods of every kind, and the barking Anubis.

For many of their towns also bear names derived from beasts and cattle: κυνῶν (*Cynon*), from a dog; λέων (*Leon*), from a lion; θμοῦϊς (*Thmuis*), in the Egyptian language, from a goat; λύκων (*Lycon*), from a wolf—to say nothing of the fearful and dreadful onion and the sound of the swollen belly, which is a Pelusian religious practice.

[Note: [Col. 0449D] The words of Minucius Felix in *Octavius*, chapter 28, belong here: “These same Egyptians, along with many of you” [or, “of the Romans”], “fear not Isis more than the sharpness of onions. Nor do they tremble at Serapis more than at the noises produced through the private parts of the body.” Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, book 1: ἤχους αἰσχύνης, “sounds of shame,” calls them.]

“These images,” he says, “which cannot save those who carry them, are nothing other than burdens of the priests, weighing them down to the point of weariness.” When captivity comes, they are the first to be led away captive, in exchange for the value of the metals from which they were made, and they cannot free either their own soul—or the soul of those who carry them.

This does not mean that mute images possess a soul and some perception of pain, since they are insensible; rather, by an improper use of language (καταχρηστικῶς), the soul and limbs of things that lack both sensation and limbs are spoken of in this way. Otherwise it is also written in Proverbs: “In the power of the tongue are death and life.”

Or this should be understood: among the nations the gravest burden was the error of idolatry, which pressed its worshipers down to the earth and could not save them, but made their souls captives of the devil and demons.

### (Verses 1, 3 ff.)

“Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been carried from my womb, who have been borne from my vulva. Even to old age I am the same, and even to gray hairs I shall carry you. I have made you, and I shall bear you; I shall carry you and save you.

“To whom have you likened me, equated me, compared me, and made me similar? You who bring gold from a purse and weigh silver on a balance, hiring a goldsmith to make a god; and they fall down and worship. They carry him upon their shoulders, bearing him and setting him in his place; he will stand and will not move from his place. When they cry out to him, he will not hear; he will not save them from tribulation.”

The Septuagint: “Listen to me, house of Jacob, and all the remnant of Israel, who are carried from the womb and instructed from infancy to old age. I am he, and until you grow old I am he. I sustain you; I made you and I shall carry you; I shall receive you and save you.

“To whom have you likened me? See and consider, you who wander, who bring gold from a purse, weigh silver on a balance, and hire a goldsmith. They made the works of their hands and, bending down, worshiped. They carry it upon their shoulders and go. But when they have set it in its place, it remains and does not move. Whoever cries out to it, it will not hear him, and it will not deliver him from evils.”

He does not call them “Jacob” or “Israel,” which, as we explained above, is itself said in reproach of the people, without the conjunction of “servant,” “child,” and “elect”; rather, he calls them “the house of Jacob” and “the remnant of Israel,” because of their relationship by flesh and blood and as though they were the dregs of Israel’s remnant.

He teaches that, like children and infants, they were carried by God from Egypt as though from a mother’s womb and the vulva of a pregnant woman. This does not mean that the ineffable and incomprehensible majesty of God possesses a womb or vulva, feet, hands, or other bodily members; rather, through our words we learn of God’s affection toward us.

Otherwise, the same thing is sung in the hundred-ninth Psalm from the person of God. Where the Septuagint translated, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you,” the Hebrew has מֵרֶחֶם (*merehem*), which means “from the vulva.”

Here, however, not only “from the womb” and “from the vulva” are written—that is, מִבֶּטֶן (*mebeten*) and מֵרֶחֶם (*merehem*)—but also מִמֶּנִּי (*menni*), a preposition meaning “from my womb” or “from my vulva.”

The sense is: I who begot you from infancy and carried you in my womb and vulva will protect you even to old age—not my own old age, but yours—so that he may teach that they are to be saved by divine mercy. For the Creator of all things spares his creature, and the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10:11).

But the hired servant, whose sheep they are not, when he sees the wolf, flees. Since, therefore, I made and begot children, I shall bear them, and I myself shall carry them.

According to the Septuagint, who say, “You who are carried from the womb and instructed from infancy to old age,” this signifies that they meditate on the law of God day and night in vain, having no knowledge of God but worshiping images of human beings and beasts. They therefore require prophetic correction, through which God speaks to them: “To whom have you likened me, and equated me?” and the rest.

They brought together gold and silver, hired a sculptor, made idols, and worshiped the works of their hands, which are carried upon shoulders and, once fastened and fixed, cannot move themselves or benefit those by whom they are worshiped.

We pass quickly over what is obvious, so that through Christ’s mercy we may disclose what has been closed.

### (Verses 8 and following)

“Remember this, and be firmly established; return to your heart, transgressors. Remember the former age, for I am God, and there is no God besides me, nor is there anyone like me. I announce the end from the beginning, and from the outset things that have not yet been done, saying: ‘My plan shall stand, and all my will shall be accomplished.’ I call the bird from the East, and from a distant land the man of my will; I have spoken, and I shall bring it about; I have created it, and I shall do it.”

The Septuagint: “Remember these things and groan; repent, you who are going astray. Return in your heart and remember the former things from the beginning, for I am God, and there is no other besides me. I announce beforehand the last things before they happen and are fulfilled, and I said: ‘All my will shall stand, and I shall do all that I have planned.’ I call the bird from the East, and from a distant land those things that I have planned. I have spoken, and I have brought it about; I have created and done it.”

“For I myself begot you, I myself bore you, and from infancy even to old age you are saved—not through your merit but through my compassion. Abandon the idols you have made and return to the worship of the one God.” Repent; groan over the error that held you captive. Rather, be firmly established, lest the sudden storm of idolatry overturn you again. Return to your heart, that is, to your mind, you who, in your madness, worshiping images, stumbled against wood and stones as though you were insane.

Consider from the beginning of the world that there is no God besides me, nor could anyone else know the future except me, who announce through the prophets what I am going to do, so that when I have fulfilled what was foretold, I may prove my divinity through prophecy. For I now declare the mystery that had previously been unknown to all generations; indeed, I declare that my plan will stand, so that when you see it accomplished, you may know that there is no God except the one who knew these future events, or rather, who commanded them to happen.

I am the one who calls the bird from the East—[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “I call the bird.” The Hebrews take this to mean Cyrus, king of the Persians.]—as the Hebrews think, Cyrus, king of the Persians, or Darius, prince of the Medes; and from a distant land the man of my will, who will fulfill all my will against Babylon and the Chaldeans.
