Or, as we prove to be the true interpretation, it refers to the Lord and Savior, concerning whom Balaam also prophesies: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man from Israel” (Num. 24:17), whose name is “Orient” (Zech. 6), whom the Magi worshiped when they came from the East. For he says in the Psalms: “I desired to do your will, O God” (Ps. 39:9), and the Father spoke concerning him; and he confirmed his promise by his deed.

The Septuagint, in place of what we expressed from the Hebrew as “the man of my will,” has “those things that I have planned.” Therefore, according to them, by the birds called from the East we may understand the ministries of the angels, which at the Lord’s command travel throughout the whole world. They are ministering spirits, sent for the salvation of believers. Concerning them the Psalm also sings: “You make your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4).

### 548 (Verses 12–13)

“Listen to me, hard-hearted ones, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness near; it shall not be far away, and my salvation shall not be delayed [another reading: diminished]. I shall give salvation in Zion, and my glory to Israel.”

The Septuagint: “Listen to me, you who have lost your heart, who are far from righteousness. I have brought my righteousness, and I shall not delay the salvation that comes from me. I have given salvation in Zion and glory to Israel.”

To those whom he had earlier said, “Listen to me, house of Jacob and all the remnant of the house of Israel,” and again, “Return to your heart, transgressors,” he now speaks, according to the Hebrew, because of their unbelief, calling them hard-hearted; according to the Septuagint, he calls them people who have lost their heart and mind.

The most learned man, worthy of his name, the martyr Stephen, followed this interpretation when he said in his address to the Jews: “You stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, just as your fathers did” (Acts 7:51).

These people, therefore, are far from the righteousness of God because they did not believe in it, although God, in his clemency, brought it near and made it come to the earth. He did not wish it to be delayed or to remain far away. For he gave Zion its salvation and Israel its glory. Let this be understood as spoken prophetically of future events and of the coming of the Lord and Savior.

Otherwise, according to the historical sense, salvation is given to Zion and glory to Israel, because God brought his righteousness near by calling the bird from the East and the man of his will from a distant land. He would avenge the wrongs done to Israel and to Jerusalem, which had been overthrown, and, when the Medes and Persians conquered, would destroy Babylon and the Chaldeans, as the prophet’s following words testify.

### Chapter 47 — Verses 1 and following

“Come down and sit in the dust, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for you shall no longer be called soft and delicate. Take the millstone and grind flour. Uncover your nakedness; uncover your shoulder; reveal your legs; cross the rivers. Your disgrace shall be uncovered, and your shame shall be seen. I shall take vengeance, and no man shall resist me.”

The Septuagint: “Come down and sit upon the earth, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground. There is no throne for the daughter of the Chaldeans, for you shall no longer be called soft and delicate. Take the millstone; grind flour. Reveal your covering; strip off your gray hair; uncover your legs; cross the rivers. Your disgrace shall be uncovered; your shame shall appear. I shall take from you what is just, and shall no longer hand you over to men.”

Just as in Ezekiel, under the figure of a ship and all its equipment, the adornment of Tyre is described because it is devoted to commerce (Ezek. 26), and because of the abundance of its waters the king of Egypt is called a dragon, while its scales, reeds, papyrus, and little fish are described; and just as the likeness of harlots and a brothel bears witness to Jerusalem’s fornication with idols—so in the present passage, under the person of a captive woman who was once a queen, the slavery of Babylon is indicated. She is told to come down from the pride of her kingdom and sit in the dust.

She is called both virgin and daughter either because we are all creatures of God, and Babylon does not possess a damnable nature, as the heretics claim; or because of the luxury and adornment of that once most powerful city, which, when it had grown old and was approaching its ruin, vaunted itself as a young woman and a maiden.

Although, from the fact that the Septuagint reads “daughter of Babylon,” some interpret not Babylon itself but the city of Rome—which is specifically called Babylon in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 14) and in the Epistle of Peter (1 Pet. 5)—and maintain that everything now said concerning Babylon applies to Rome’s destruction, against which the bird and the righteousness of God must be summoned, so that after Zion, that is, the Church, has been saved, Rome may perish forever.

Babylon is therefore addressed as queen and daughter of the Chaldeans—for she was founded by the Chaldeans—and told that she will no longer be called soft and delicate and overflowing with pleasures, she who was carried in the hands of all the nations, scarcely setting the soles of her feet upon the earth. She is commanded to take the millstone and grind flour, which is an indication of harsh captivity and extreme servitude: she who had once been a queen must afterward serve at the work of grinding flour.

But because it follows, “Uncover your nakedness,” the millstone is also understood figuratively by the Hebrews, namely, that she should be exposed, like a prostitute, to the lust of her conquerors. They also wish the statement in the Book of Judges concerning Samson—that he was condemned by the Philistines to the mill (Judg. 16)—to signify that the strongest of men was compelled to do this for foreign women.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has “the strongest of men.” Some criticize Jerome here, claiming that he unnecessarily interprets Isaiah’s words in an obscene sense, since no one is unaware that, amid the miseries and labors of captivity, there was also the work of the bakery, and that captives were stripped not to disgrace their prostituted bodies but as an insult and as a sign of the basest servile condition. Jerome, however, is not speaking in his own voice but says that this is the Hebrews’ figurative interpretation. Nor is it entirely abnormal, since the well-known passage in Job 31:13 reads, “My wife grinds for another,” meaning “may she become a prostitute for another.” Horace, too, in Book 1 of the *Satires*, line 35, says *alienas permolere uxores*, “to grind other men’s wives.” See Festelius, *Adversaria*, Book 2; Buxtorf, *Catalecta*, chapter 138.]

In the passage where we translated “Uncover your nakedness,” while the Septuagint rendered it “Reveal your covering,” Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself:

[Note: “Samthech. I do not see on what authority the older editions read here, instead of *Samthech*, *Schimlathech*. I will say only this: such a false and fabricated word cannot stand beside Jerome’s text, which expressly teaches us that Theodotion placed Isaiah’s Hebrew word *Samthech*, or *Semmathech*, as Aquila read it. The Greek texts of Symmachus likewise alter it in this way: *tēn siōpēsín sou*, and so forth. —Martianus. The Ambrosian manuscript likewise has *Samtheaec*; Aquila, *Simmathec*. Moreover, the older printed books preferred *tēn siōpēsín sou*—“your silence”—instead of *to siōpēlón sou* (in the Ambrosian manuscript, ΤΟ ϹΙΩΠΕΛΟΝϹΟΥ; in the Sangerman manuscript *apud* Montfaucon, more corruptly, *to siōpōlenón sou*). This may perhaps have been taken from another edition of Symmachus.]

*SAMTHECH*; Aquila: *SEMMATHECH*; Symmachus: *to siōpēlón sou*, which we may express as “your silence,” that is, something that ought to be kept silent out of shame.

We read something similar in the Song of Songs, where the beauty of the bride is described and the passage concludes: “Without your silence” (Song 4). Those who translated the passage were unwilling to render the noun by a word that, in Holy Scripture, would sound like “nakedness.”

He rightly uses shameless terms against Babylon—although there is no shame in calling a bodily member by its proper name—for Babylon is commanded to bare her breasts, uncover her legs and thighs, and go into captivity, so that her disgrace may be seen and she may be exposed to everlasting shame.

The Lord says that he has done this in order to take vengeance on the one who oppressed her people, and that no intercessor will be heard on her behalf who might attempt to soften the Lord’s anger by confronting him.

This signifies the angel who presides over the nation of Babylon, who speaks with the other angels: “We healed Babylon, but she was not healed.”

As for what the Septuagint translated, “I shall take from you what is just, and shall no longer hand you over to men,” “Babylon” is understood; or else it means “what is just,” taken away from Babylon.

The Stoics argue that many things shameful in fact are made respectable in speech by human custom—parricide, adultery, murder, incest, and other such acts. Conversely, they say that things honorable in fact appear shameful in their names: producing children, expelling the inflation of the belly by a fart, relieving the bowels with excrement, and releasing the bladder by the discharge of urine.

Finally, just as we form *rutula* from *ruta*, so we cannot form *mentula* from *menta* as a diminutive (ὑποκοριστικόν).

[Note: Formerly the reading was *mentam a menta*, but Martianus, who entirely failed to grasp the sense of the passage while attempting to emend it, corrupted it through a ridiculous error, substituting *mente*, so that the sense would be that one may not make a diminutive of *mens*. But the facts themselves cry out that the passage concerns the herbs rue and mint. Everyone knows that, just as one may say *rutula* from *ruta*, one may not say *mentula* diminutively from *menta*. Cicero, Book 9 of the *Letters to Friends*, letter 22, to which the holy Doctor alludes, says: “Rue and mint are both correctly said; I wish to call small mint by a form corresponding to *rutula*; it is not permitted.” There is another, obscene meaning of this word in the diminutive. —MARTIANUS. “To make *mente*.” Here too some print *mentam* instead of *mente*, “to make from *menta*.” That reading imposes another and false sense, as will be evident to the reader. —MARTIANUS.]

### 551

Therefore *SEMMATHEC*, which Aquila rendered as we have said, denotes a woman’s private parts. Its etymology among them is said to mean “your thirsty one,” indicating Babylon’s insatiable lust.

### Verses 4 and following

“Our redeemer—the Lord of hosts is his name—the Holy One of Israel. Sit in silence and enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans, for you shall no longer be called mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people; I profaned my inheritance and gave them into your hand. You showed them no mercy. You laid your yoke exceedingly heavily upon the old man, and you said: ‘I shall be mistress forever.’ You did not set these things upon your heart, nor did you remember your end.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the one who redeemed you, the Lord of hosts is his name, the Holy One of Israel. Sit mourning and enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans. You shall no longer be called the strength of the kingdom. I was angry with my people; I profaned my inheritance. I gave them into your hand, but you did not show them mercy. You laid the yoke heavily upon the old man [another reading: upon the old men], and you said: ‘I shall be mistress forever.’ You did not understand these things in your heart, nor did you remember the last things.”

According to the Septuagint, the first verse is joined to what precedes, so that the sense is: “These things will be done by the one who redeemed you, the Lord of hosts, whose name is the Holy One of Israel.”

According to the Hebrew, however, the prophet speaks in the person of the people, saying that the Lord of hosts, whose name is the Holy One of Israel, has done these things against Babylon.

Then speech is again directed to Babylon herself: “Sit in silence,” or “sit mourning,” and remember your crimes. “Enter into darkness,” because through confusion and disgrace you cannot bear the light. You shall no longer be called mistress—not merely of one kingdom, but not even mistress of all kingdoms.

At the same time, because a hidden question arose—why God should be angry with the Chaldeans, whom he himself had sent to capture Israel—he answers that he had been angry with his people and wished to correct them, not destroy them; to chastise them, not kill them.

But the Chaldeans abused their power and imposed more blows than God’s vengeance required. It is a great indication of Babylonian cruelty that they spared not even the aged, whose years are venerable even among enemies.

It is also a sign of pride that, deceived by present prosperity, Babylon gave no thought to the uncertainties of the future.

### 552

Therefore, amid prosperity, we must always beware of what is to come, and we must not oppress those delivered into our hands, who are disciplined for the purpose of becoming better.

### Verse 8 and following

“And now hear this, delicate woman who dwell securely, who say in your heart: ‘I am, and there is no one besides me. I shall not sit as a widow, and I shall not know childlessness.’ These two things shall come upon you suddenly in one day: childlessness and widowhood. All these things have come upon you because of the multitude of your sorceries and because of the great hardness of your enchantments [the Vulgate has: ‘the great hardness’]. You trusted in your wickedness and said: ‘There is no one who sees me.’ Your wisdom and your knowledge deceived you, and you said in your heart: ‘I am, and there is no other.’ Evil shall come upon you, and you shall not know its origin; calamity shall fall upon you, and you shall not be able to avert it; misery shall come upon you suddenly, and you shall not know it.”

Two things shall come upon Babylon together: childlessness and widowhood. She will have neither children—that is, peoples subject to her—nor a husband, whom we may understand as her king. While she does not expect these things, she will suddenly endure them.

For she could not have imagined that the Persians, previously of no great strength, would overcome her under the reign of Cyrus and subject her to their power.

“You have suffered these things,” he says, “not only because of your pride, the abundance of all your wealth, and your luxuries, but also because of the multitude of your sorceries and your enchantments, in which you placed your confidence.”

Evil will come upon you that you previously did not know, whose origin you did not understand.

Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Destruction shall come upon you, and you shall not know it; a pit, and you shall fall into it.” Thus, while Babylon prepared the evil of captivity for all the nations, she herself falls into the pit that she prepared.

We pass quickly over what is clear.

### Verse 12 and following

“Stand with your enchanters and with the multitude of your sorceries, in which you have labored from your youth, if perhaps they may benefit you, or if you may be able to become stronger. You have grown weak amid the multitude of your counsels. Let the astrologers of heaven stand and save you, those who contemplate the stars and calculate the months, so that from them they may announce to you the things that are to come. Behold, they have become like stubble; fire has burned them. They shall not rescue their souls from the hand of the flame. There are no coals with which they may warm themselves, nor a hearth beside which they may sit. Thus have become for you the things over which you labored: your merchants, from your youth, have each gone astray in his own way. There is no one who can save you.”

The Septuagint: “Stand now in your enchantments and in your many sorceries, which you learned from your youth—[Note: The manuscripts have this according to the Greek exemplar: *ha dynēsē ōphelēthēnai*, ‘if they can benefit you.’ Previously the reading was, ‘which cannot benefit you.’]—if they can benefit you. You have labored in your counsels. Let the astrologers of heaven stand and save you, those who contemplate the stars; let them announce to you what is going to come upon you. Behold, they shall all be burned in the fire like brushwood, and they shall not rescue their soul from the flame, because you have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them. These shall be your help. You have labored in your exchange from your youth; a man has gone astray in himself, but for you there will be no salvation.”

That Babylon and all Chaldea devoted themselves to enchanters, augurs, diviners, and *Gazarenes*, whom we call haruspices, is proved by the testimony of the prophet Daniel, who records that the Babylonian kings did everything according to their advice.

In place of what we translated, following Symmachus and Theodotion, as “Let the augurs of heaven stand and save you,” the Septuagint rendered more explicitly, “Let the astrologers of heaven stand and save you.” These are commonly called mathematicians. They think that human affairs are governed by the courses of the stars and the movement and falling of the heavenly bodies.

This is why the Magi came from the East, saying that they had seen the Lord’s star—either through knowledge of their art or through the prophecy of their prophet Balaam, who had said in Numbers: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man from Israel” (Num. 24:17).

Let these people, then, who calculate the months and count the years, weighing the moments of the hours, and who promise knowledge of the future, tell you what the Lord has planned against you.

While they remain silent, the prophet answers what is going to happen: “Behold, they have become like stubble; fire has devoured them,” so that those who promised salvation to others did not know their own punishments. There is no doubt that, when the city was burning, its inhabitants were consumed by the devouring flame.

As for what follows—“There are no coals with which they may warm themselves, nor a hearth beside which they may sit”—the Hebrews explain it in this way: They possess no knowledge of warmth, nor any illuminating understanding capable of dispersing their darkness and driving away the cold of error.

In place of this, I do not know what the Septuagint intended when it translated: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; these shall be your help.” Unless perhaps we can say that fire and burning are much more useful to Babylon than the magi and Gazarenes, the astrologers and enchanters were. Fire calls them to repentance through punishments and torments; the others lead them through error into pride.

All the labor of Babylon and of her merchants—by whom we understand the magi—achieved only this: each went astray in his own way, and the one who himself was lost could not provide salvation to another.

Let us ask those who assert that there are different natures whether Babylon is of an evil nature or a good one. If they say that she is of an evil nature—as there is no doubt they will answer—how is she summoned to repentance and told: “Sit mourning; enter into darkness, daughter of the Chaldeans”? And afterward, following the enumeration of her sins and crimes, how can it be said according to the Septuagint: “You have coals of fire; you shall sit upon them; these shall be your help”?

And what does the statement that follows, according to the same Septuagint, mean: “You have labored in your exchange from your youth”? What is this exchange? Certainly, it is an exchange from good to evil. From this it is clear that beings become evil by their will although they are good by nature.

Finally, the passage concludes: “A man has gone astray in himself”—not by nature, but by the choice of his mind.

### Chapter 48 — Verse 1 and following

“Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel and have come forth from the waters of Judah; you who swear by the name of the Lord and remember the God of Israel, not in truth and not in righteousness. For they are called from the holy city and are established upon the God of Israel; the Lord of hosts is his name.”

I have foretold these things that will happen to the Chaldeans and Babylonians, and what I have spoken through my prophets must necessarily be fulfilled in events.

But you, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel, you who come forth from the water of Judah, and all the rest that follows—listen more attentively to what I am about to say.

It should be noted that he does not call them simply Jacob, but “the house of Jacob”; nor does he call them Israel, since they are falsely called by that name, having no deed worthy of the name.

“And you come forth from the waters of Judah,” he says, calling the waters *semnoterōs* (σεμνοτέρως), “with dignity,” in place of “seed,” so that he might show that they were not children of the virtues of the patriarchs but children of flesh.

[Note: In the same sense, the Ambrosian manuscript has *semnoprepōs* (σεμνοπρεπῶς), meaning “worthily,” “modestly,” or “honorably.” The reading should be *semnoterōs* “waters,” as found in the manuscript copies, not *sōmatikōteron*, as in the printed books. *Semnoterōs* signifies that the waters are spoken of with a certain reverence, modesty, or veneration in place of “seed.” The manuscript copies corruptly read ϹΕΜΝΟΤΙΡΕΤΙΩΣ. —MARTIANUS.]

He rightly called them the waters of Judah because at that time only the tribe of Judah still remained in the land of Judea, and the royal seed of David was preserved.

“You swear,” he says, “in the name of the Lord—not in order to honor the Lord, but in order to commit an outrage by assuming his name, wishing to make him a witness to your lie. You rest in the holy city and lean upon the Lord of Israel, boasting that you are inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem and possess the privilege of the Lord of hosts, while you vainly assume the names of Jacob, Israel, the holy city, and almighty God.”

### Verses 3–4 and following

“I announced the former things long ago; they went forth from my mouth, and I made them known. Suddenly I acted, and they came to pass. For I knew that you are hard, that your neck is an iron sinew, and that your forehead is bronze. From long ago I foretold them to you; before they came, I announced them to you, lest you should say: ‘My idols did these things, and my carved and cast images commanded them.’

“You have heard; behold everything. But you did not announce it. [Note: In the Vulgate this is marked as a question: “Have you not announced it?”] From long ago I made new things known to you, things kept hidden that you did not know. Now they have been created, and not long ago; before this day, and you did not hear them, lest you should say: ‘Behold, I knew them.’

“You neither heard nor knew; from long ago your ear was not opened. For I know that you will transgress grievously, and from the womb I called you a transgressor. For my name’s sake I shall hold back my wrath, and for my praise I shall restrain you, so that you may not perish.

“Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tested you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake, for my own sake I shall act, so that I may not be blasphemed, and I shall not give my glory to another.”

The Septuagint: “I announced the former things beforehand; they went forth from my mouth, and it became known. Suddenly I acted, and they came to pass. I know that you are hard, that your neck is an iron sinew, and that your forehead is bronze. Long ago I announced to you, before they came upon you. I made them known to you, lest you should say: ‘The idols did them for me; the carved and cast images commanded them for me.’

“You heard everything, but you did not understand. Now I have made new things known to you, things that are to come. You did not say, ‘Now they are happening, and not long ago, nor in former days.’ Do not say, ‘Behold, I knew them.’ You neither knew nor understood, nor from the beginning did I open your ears. For I know that you will grievously transgress, and that you will be called unrighteous from the womb.

“For my name’s sake I shall show you my wrath, and I shall bring my glorious deeds upon you, so that I may not kill you. Behold, I sold you, not for silver; but I rescued you from the furnace of poverty. For my own sake I shall act, because my name is being profaned, and I shall not give my glory to another.”

I foretell that the Babylonians will be conquered by the Medes and Persians, and I shall suddenly do what I threatened, lest, when the foretold events come, you should think that they happened either through the will of the gods whom you worship or by chance.

I do not boast of my knowledge of future events; rather, I speak because of your unbelief. From the beginning I knew your unbelieving heart, iron neck, and bronze forehead.

Behold, you have heard everything that is to come, and yet you conceal the truth in silence. I am not recounting the past, by which my power was often proved—how I brought the people out of Egypt, drowned the Egyptians in the Red Sea, gave you the promised land, and subdued various nations beneath you. Instead, I announce the new things that I shall do against Babylon, so that the shameless lie of your mouth may be refuted, since you claim to know what you do not know.

From the beginning you have been a transgressor of my commandments. “From the womb,” God called you a transgressor, when, after being delivered from Egypt, you were conceived, as it were, in my womb, brought forth, and instructed.

You desired the head of the Egyptian ox, saying: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Therefore, not because of your merit but because of my mercy, I delayed my wrath, lest you should perish completely. For the praise of my name I shall restrain you, so that you may follow me unwillingly, like a beast led by a bridle and a horse by reins.

“Behold, I have refined you,” that is, I have tested you as silver is smelted. Or else: I wished to test you not in riches but in the furnace of poverty.

From this it is shown that many are tested both by wealth and by poverty—if they either misuse wealth or do not endure scarcity with virtue.

For my own sake, therefore, I shall act, so that my name may not be blasphemed among the nations and they may not think that you were conquered through the help of their idols rather than through my anger.

As for what follows, “I shall not give my glory to another,” this means that he does not wish the idols to be thought to have overthrown the people of God. Or, certainly, when he says, “I shall not give it to another,” he shows that he has already given it to another, since “another” is said in distinction from the former.

Many of our writers, to touch briefly on a few points according to the Septuagint translators, assert that this prophecy concerns the coming of Christ: that he comes suddenly and unexpectedly and manifests his presence to an exceedingly hard people, to whom God had never opened their ears because their heart had grown fat and they had heard heavily with their ears.

Immediately after the Lord had emerged from the virginal womb, a transgressor and unrighteous man [Note: One Ambrosian manuscript has “and an enemy” instead of “unrighteous”] sought to kill him.

When the passage adds, “For my name’s sake I shall show you my wrath, and I shall bring my glorious deeds upon you,” it makes use of the apostle’s meaning; or the Apostle Paul (Rom. 1) derives his testimony from this passage, so that the wrath of God might be revealed to terrify those who sin and that glory might afterward be given to those who are converted.

“Behold,” it says, “I sold you, not for money, but I sold you in your sins, and I rescued you from the furnace of poverty.”

For this reason Solomon also (Prov. 3) does not wish to possess riches and poverty, but asks only for what is necessary, lest his heart be lifted into pride by riches or he be compelled by poverty to do what he does not wish and, pressed by want, blaspheme God.

Hence the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (1 Tim. 6:8).

### 557

### Verses 12–13 and following

“Listen to me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I myself, I am the first, and I am the last. My hand also founded the earth, and my right hand measured out the heavens. I called them, and they stood together.

“Gather together, all of you, and hear: Which of them announced these things? The Lord loved him; he shall do his will in Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans.

“I, I have spoken, and I have called him. I have brought him, and his way has been made straight.

“Draw near to me and hear these things [the Vulgate has: ‘this’]. I have not spoken from the beginning in secret; from the time before it happened, I was there.

“And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.”

The Septuagint: “Listen to me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call. I am the first, and I am forever. My hand founded the earth, and my right hand established heaven. I shall call them, and they shall stand together. All shall be gathered together and shall hear: ‘Who announced these things to them?’ He who loves you has done your will against Babylon, to remove the seed of the Chaldeans.

“I have spoken, and I have called. I have brought him, and I have made his way prosperous. Come to me and hear these things. I have not spoken from the beginning in secret; when it was happening, I was there. And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.”

Earlier he had said: “Hear these things, house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel and come forth from the waters of Judah.” [Note: Formerly this was printed with an interrogative mark: “perhaps to the same people,” and so forth. Further on, in the most ancient Ambrosian manuscript, “I called you” stands in place of “he heard the Son.”]

Now he speaks to the same people: “Listen to me, Jacob and Israel, whom I call.” For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22). Therefore, because they had not yet received the Savior, he calls them “called,” not “chosen.”

“I am,” he says, “the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, who live and was dead” (Rev. 22), so that you may refer “life” to the beginning and “last” to him who died. He “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and became obedient to the Father; he humbled himself even unto death, and the death of the cross” (Phil. 2).

“My hand founded the earth.” Hence he also speaks in Proverbs: “God founded the earth by his wisdom, and his right hand established the heavens” (Prov. 3:19), or, as the Septuagint translated it, “firmly established heaven.”

He calls the heavens so that they may obey his command and proclaim his glory. But if the heavens obey the Lord’s will and run in their appointed order, why does earth and ashes boast (Ecclus. 10) and fail to recognize its own frailty?

“Gather together, all of you, and hear”—whether the heavens, or the entire creation, or the whole multitude of Israel.

What are they commanded to hear? That the Lord loved him. There can be no doubt that this signifies Cyrus and Darius, who did the Lord’s will against Babylon and exercised his arm against the Chaldeans.

He himself spoke, called him by name, brought him, and made his way straight, so that no one would dare resist his strength.

Therefore he summons them to draw near and listen, so that, with the Lord announcing it, they may know that the king of the Persians and Medes is to come, overthrow Babylon, and destroy the Chaldeans.

And in order to announce these things, he says that he has been sent by the Lord and by his Spirit.

This is according to the Hebrews and their opinion.

According to Symmachus, however, who translated the passage as, “Who announced these things to him? The one whom the Lord loved, who does his will in Babylon,” and according to the Septuagint, “to remove the seed of the Chaldeans,” the passage is referred to the person of the Lord.

He truly was loved by the Father, he did the whole will of the Father, and he overthrew in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this world—the entire seed of the Chaldeans, whom they interpret as demons.

He himself spoke, and he heard the Son; he brought him, the one who speaks to believers: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28).

And hear these things that I have spoken from the beginning in secret—that is, through the riddles and mysteries of the prophets—which had been unknown to all former generations.

When all things were being made by the Father, he was with him, rejoicing with him. Even now he says: “I, who was always with the Father and in the Father, and was never without the Father, even now speak” (John 14).

And according to the weakness of the flesh he assumed, he says: “The Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit.”

In this brief verse the mystery of the Trinity is shown to us.

### (Verses 17, 18 and following)

Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel:

“I am the Lord your God, teaching you what is profitable, guiding you on the way by which you walk. If only you had paid attention to my commandments! Your peace would have become like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea. Your offspring would have been like sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles; they would not have perished, and their name would not have been cut off from before me.” [Col. 0462B]

Because he had promised what would happen to Israel, he gives the reasons why he had previously afflicted them—reasons which, if they avoid them, will prevent them from suffering anything similar. “If,” he says, “you had paid attention to my commandments”—as the Septuagint translated it; or certainly, in the manner of an expression of desire, “If only you had paid attention to my commandments!” If you had done this, your peace would have been like rivers and your righteousness like the waves of the sea, signifying an abundance and plentiful supply of all things.

As for what follows, “Your offspring would have been like sand, and the offspring of your womb like its pebbles,” this seems indeed to remain among the Jewish people, who even to the present day, like worms, produce children and grandchildren in great numbers. But how is this to be understood as a promise, since they do not possess peace and righteousness? Either he is angry with them, or he is reconciled to them. If he is angry, how does their offspring multiply daily? If he is reconciled, how are they enslaved, and why do they not possess peace and righteousness? From this it is clear that the passage now concerns apostolic offspring, of which we also read above (on chapter 1): “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom.” Since this does not seem to have been fulfilled at that time, it is fulfilled at Christ’s coming; and before his face the offspring of Israel remains. [Col. 0462C]

### (Verses 20, 21, 22)

“Go out from Babylon, flee from the Chaldeans! Announce it with a voice of rejoicing; proclaim this; carry it to the end of the earth, and say: ‘The Lord has redeemed his servant Jacob.’ They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out; he brought water out of the rock for them, he split the rock, and waters flowed. There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.” [Col. 0462D]

Those who, at the place where it is written, “I, I have spoken, and I have called her; I have brought him, and his way has been made straight,” understand Cyrus and Darius, refer these verses also to their times: when the people went out from Babylon, fled from the Chaldeans, and were redeemed by the Lord their God.

Although they cannot demonstrate that the statement, “They did not thirst in the desert when he led them out; he brought water out of the rock for them, and he split the rock, and waters flowed,” was fulfilled according to the historical account—for they did not come through the desert under Zerubbabel and Ezra, nor did a split rock provide them with water, as is narrated concerning those who came out of Egypt—they nevertheless testify that it was fulfilled hyperbolically, in imitation of the former happiness, when they came through the desert of the nations into Judaea and were liberated from captivity. [Col. 0463A]

And, they say, so that we may know that the prophecy was not about Christ but about Cyrus, the statement is added: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord.” Its meaning is that complete happiness will not exist except under Christ, which is reserved for the final time.

Those, however, who refer these words more truly and correctly to the Savior’s coming (below, on chapter 61:1)—of whom it is said, “He sent me to announce good news to the poor, to proclaim release to captives” (Luke 4:18–19)—understand this as an exhortation addressed by those who proclaim the Gospel of the Lord himself, the Savior: that we should go out from Babylon, that is, from the confusion of this world, and flee the Chaldeans. Concerning them it has often been said: “For the Lord redeemed his servant Jacob with his most precious blood, and led him through the desert of the age, and split the rock.” [Col. 0463B]

Regarding this the Apostle also speaks: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). The divine word is split and divided into many parts, so that, since we cannot receive it in its entirety, we may take it in portions.

And lest it be thought that this proclamation applies to all the offspring of Jacob, and not only to those who would believe through the Apostles, the statement is introduced and joined to it: “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord”—namely, for those who remained in their former error and did not deserve to drink from the rock.

[Note: The glossator of the Ambrosian manuscript indicates that this also signified the blood of the Lord’s side as baptism and martyrdom, and so forth.] [Col. 0463D]

To speak in a new way about this: when his side was wounded by the lance, water and blood flowed from it (John 19:34), consecrating baptism and martyrdom for us. [Col. 0463C]

### (Chapter 49, verses 1 and following)

“Hear, islands, and pay attention, peoples from afar! The Lord called me from the womb; from my mother’s belly he remembered my name. He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he protected me. He made me like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: ‘You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will glory [or: be glorified].’ And I said: ‘I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for no purpose and in vain. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my work with my God.’”

The Septuagint:

“Hear me, islands, and pay attention, nations. After a long time he will stand, says the Lord. From the womb he called me, and from my mother’s belly he called my name. He made my mouth like a sharp sword, and under the protection of his hand he hid me. He made me like a chosen arrow, and in his quiver he hid me. And he said to me: ‘You are my servant, Israel, and in you I will be glorified.’ And I said: ‘I have labored for no purpose, in vain, and have spent my strength for nothing. Therefore my judgment is with the Lord, and my labor before my God.’” [Col. 0463D]

[Note: Earlier manuscripts read *gloriabor* (“I will glory”). But the more reliable manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek ἐνδοξασθήσομαι (“I will be glorified”), prefer *glorificabor* here and also in the preceding version; this is likewise inferred from Jerome’s exposition below.] [Col. 0464D]

I know that these verses, as well as those that follow, belong to the understanding of a single chapter and must all be understood as spoken in the person of Christ. But I did not wish, by presenting everything at once, to burden the reader’s understanding or to obscure through their magnitude what can more easily be explained in parts. Therefore I have set down both editions, so that what seems obscure in one may be clarified by the reading of the other. [Col. 0464A]

After the calling of the remnant of Israel and the rejection of the people who persist in unbelief—concerning whom he had said, “There is no peace for the wicked, says the Lord” (Isaiah 48:22)—he turns to the churches gathered from the nations and speaks to them under the name of “islands.” They are exposed to the plots of persecutors like waves of the sea, and, with shipwreck raging on every side, they are battered rather than moved.

And lest anyone think that our interpretation is forced, and that what is said does not pertain to the nations but to the synagogues of the Jewish people, the text continues: “And pay attention, peoples, or nations, from afar”—that is, from the remotest boundaries of the earth. Or, as the Septuagint translated it, “After a long time he will stand,” meaning: not at the time in which these things are spoken, but after many ages. [Col. 0464B]

“The Lord,” he says, “called me from the womb, and from my mother’s belly he remembered my name.” What now seems obscure to those who hear it will later become known to all the nations, when Gabriel speaks to Joseph concerning the virgin birth: “And you shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people” (Matthew 1:21).

He also made his mouth like a sharp sword, so that by the breath of his mouth he might slay the wicked. Concerning this sword he himself speaks in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword,” separating the wicked from the good. “For I have come to divide a man against his father, and a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law” (Matthew 10:34–35). [Col. 0464C]

“And in the shadow,” he says, “of his hand he protected me,” so that the lowliness of the flesh might be concealed by the power of divinity, when the angel announced to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

“He made me,” he says, “like a chosen arrow; in his quiver he hid me.” By saying “a chosen arrow,” he shows that God has many arrows, but not all are chosen. These arrows are the Prophets and Apostles, who travel throughout the whole world. Concerning them it is also sung elsewhere: “Your arrows are sharp, O most powerful one; peoples will fall beneath you” (Psalm 44:6); and again: “The sharp arrows of the mighty one, with coals of desolation” (Psalm 119:41). [Col. 0464D]

But Christ, from among the many arrows and the many sons, is one chosen arrow and the Only-Begotten Son. He hid this arrow in his quiver, that is, in a human body, so that the fullness of divinity might dwell bodily in it. Rare indeed is the faith of believers, to whom it is said above also (chapter 45:15): “You are a hidden God, and we did not know it.”

The bride, wounded by this arrow, speaks in the Song of Songs: “I am wounded by love” (Song of Songs 4:9).

“And he said to me: ‘You are my servant, Israel, for in you I will be glorified.’” He is a servant because, although he was in the form of God, he deigned to assume the form of a servant (Philippians 2); and he is Israel because he was born from the Jewish people. [Col. 0465A]

And because this cannot be understood of any other servant, the text adds: “For in you I will glory [or: be glorified].” He himself says in the Gospel: “Father, glorify your name” (John 12:28). In the psalm he speaks to the Son: “Awake, my glory, awake, lyre and harp” (Psalm 56:9)—that is, the chorus of all virtues.

When the Father had said these things to me, as I have recounted them, I answered him: “How have you been glorified in me, Father? For I have labored in vain, and I have not been able to bring a large part of the Jewish people back to you?”

All these things are said to demonstrate the freedom of the human will.

[Note: In the Ambrosian manuscripts, *monstretur* (“may be shown”) is found; the older printed editions have *monstraretur* (“might be shown”).] [Col. 0465D]

For it is God’s role to call, and ours to believe. Nor, if we do not immediately believe, is God thereby powerless. [Col. 0465B]

[Note: Here *impossibilis* is used actively in the sense of “powerless,” not with passive meaning. As to how God can do all things and yet leave his power to our free choice, Augustine, agreeing with Jerome, explains this in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 33, section 58, when he writes that God wills all people to be saved, but not in such a way as to deprive them of free will. Unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel; they will experience in punishments the power of the one whose mercy in his gifts they despised. From this you may infer that Jerome does not approve the omnipotent operation of grace as Quesnell has imagined it in recent times: an operation that compels the will toward the good work for which the power to act is given; an omnipotence which, according to him, belongs so essentially to the nature of every grace that no grace can exist unless it is efficacious. Jerome therefore does not deny God’s omnipotence, either absolutely or with reference to the human heart, if it wills.] [Col. 0466D]

Rather, he leaves his power to our free choice, so that the will of the righteous may receive its reward.

“Because they did not wish to believe in you through me, my judgment is with you,” meaning that I did everything I ought to have done for them. He says in the Gospel: “I have glorified you upon the earth, having completed the work that you gave me to do” (John 17:4); and again: “I have manifested your name to the people.”

“And my work,” or “my labor and my grief”—for this is what the Greek word πόνος (*ponos*) means—“is before you.” He wept over Jerusalem in the Gospel (Luke 19), and in the psalm, because of the multitude of unbelievers, he says in a certain sense that he suffered in vain: “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Psalm 29:10).

According to the Hebrew, while hanging upon the cross he says: “Far from my salvation are the words—” [Col. 0466D]

[Note: “The words of my lamentation.” In his Hebrew Psalter, or in the version translated from the Hebrew truth, he read it as follows: “Far from my salvation are the words of my roaring.” The words retain the same sense. —Martianay. The Pseudo-Jerome, on this passage of the Psalm, has: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins.” Aquila translated the passage: “Far from my salvation are the words of my groaning.” Symmachus: “the words of my groanings.” The Fifth and Sixth Editions: “the words of my outcry.” In fact, no Latin manuscripts seem to have read “lamentations.”] [Col. 0466D]

“—my lamentations” (Psalm 21:1). [Col. 0465C]

### (Verses 5, 6 and following)

“And now the Lord says, he who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself: ‘To bring Jacob back to him, and Israel will not be gathered; and I have been glorified in the eyes of the Lord, and my God has become my strength. And he said: “It is too little for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to turn back the dregs of Israel. I have given [Vulgate: ‘Behold, I have given’] you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”’”

The Septuagint:

“And now thus says the Lord, who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself, that I might gather Jacob to him and Israel. I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord, and my God shall be my strength.

“And he said to me: ‘It is a great thing for you to be called my child, and to raise up the tribes of Jacob and turn back the dispersion of Israel. Behold, I have placed you as a covenant of the race, as a light to the nations, that you may be salvation to the end of the earth.’” [Col. 0466A]

When I said, “I have labored in vain, for no purpose and in vain I have spent my strength,” because the Jews did not wish to believe, and “my judgment is with the Lord,” and my work—which, with his help, I completed—is with the Lord, the Lord who formed me from the womb as a servant for himself answered me.

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts read: “which I completed with the Lord my God, at his command; and he answered,” and so forth.] [Col. 0466D]

From this he shows that the one formed from the womb is called a servant. He also says in the psalm: “From my mother’s womb you are my God” (Psalm 21:10).

What, then, does the Lord say to him? That he should bring Jacob back to him who had gone astray, who, having abandoned the Creator, served idols. Hence he also says to the disciples: “Do not go into the way of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:5); and elsewhere: “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). [Col. 0466B]

The Father’s will, therefore, was that the wicked vinedressers should receive the Son who had been sent and return the fruits of the vineyard—those who killed him, saying: “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Matthew 21:38).

This is what he now says: “And Israel will not be gathered,” that is, it will not return to the Lord.

I am greatly surprised that the Vulgate edition, by another interpretation, has overturned a very strong testimony against Jewish unbelief by saying: “I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord,” since Theodotion and Symmachus agree with our interpretation.

As for Aquila, I am not surprised that this highly learned man in the Hebrew language, who renders word for word, either pretended ignorance in this passage or was deceived by the perverse interpretation of the Pharisees. He wished to translate it: “And Israel will be gathered to him,” that is, to God. [Col. 0466C]

For the Hebrew word LO is not written here with Lamed and Waw (the printed Hebrew form is unavailable in the supplied source), which, if it were so written, would mean “to him” or “to her”; rather, it is written with Lamed and Aleph (again unavailable in the supplied text), which properly means “not.”

[Note: In fact, in contemporary Hebrew copies also, it is not written with the small circle placed above it; in the margin one should read “to him.” Thus the Chaldean paraphrast also formerly read it. Aquila should not therefore be thought to have rashly altered the reading out of hostility toward Christians.] [Col. 0466D]

Because Jacob was not brought back to God, and Israel was not gathered, the Son says to those who did not believe: “I have been glorified in the eyes of the Lord.” For the whole world has believed in me. “And my God has become my strength,” the one who also comforted me in my sorrow over the rejection of my people. [Col. 0467A]

And he said to me: “It is too little if you serve me to raise up the tribes of Jacob, which fell through their own fault, and to turn back the dregs, or remnant, of Israel.”

This is what the Hebrew word NESURE signifies.

“For them I have given you as a light to all the nations, so that you may illumine the whole world and cause my salvation, through which all are saved, to reach the ends of the earth.”

As for what is read in the Septuagint, “I shall be gathered and glorified before the Lord,” it can be understood as meaning that the Lord has been gathered together with believers.

And what follows, “He said to me: ‘It is a great thing for you to be called my child,’” may be understood by referring “great” to the man and the child, who in comparison with God is small.

### (Verse 7)

Thus says the Lord, the Redeemer of Israel, his Holy One, to the despised soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of rulers:

“Kings shall see and arise; princes shall worship, because of the Lord, for he is faithful—the Holy One of Israel, who chose you.” [Col. 0467B]

The Septuagint:

“Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel who delivered you: Sanctify him who despises his soul, who is an abomination to the nations, who is the servant of princes. Kings shall see him, and princes shall arise and worship him, because of the Lord. For the Holy One of Israel is faithful, and he chose you.”

For what we have rendered, “to the despised soul, to the abhorred nation, to the servant of rulers,” Theodotion translated: “to him who despises his soul, who is an abomination to the nation, who is the servant of princes.” This plainly applies to the person of Christ.

For he, the good shepherd, laid down his soul for his sheep (John 10), and despised it; he is an abomination to the nation of the Jews, who curse him in their synagogues three times each day under the name “Nazarenes.” He was the servant of princes and so humble that he stood before Annas and Caiaphas, and, when he was to be crucified, was sent to Pilate and Herod. [Col. 0467C]

Aquila agreed with this interpretation, and partly so did the Septuagint, although they altered and weakened the meaning by translating “nations” instead of “nation,” and “servants” instead of “servant.”

[Note: The earlier text incorrectly had *quae*; the manuscripts correct it to *quod*.] [Col. 0467D]

[Note: There were previously only two words: “servants of princes.” Victorius gives the Greek: τῶν δούλων τῶν ἀρχόντων, “of the servants of the rulers.”]

Others, however, think that this refers to the Jewish nation, which despised its own soul, is an abomination to the whole world, and serves rulers concerning whom it is written: “They devour my people as they eat bread” (Psalm 14:4). [Col. 0467D]

But the better interpretation concerns Christ.

What, then, does the Father—the former Redeemer and Holy One of Israel—say to the Son?

“Kings shall see and princes shall arise and worship,” when he comes in the glory of his Father with his angels, sits upon his throne of glory, and judges the living and the dead. Then all shall worship him because of the Lord his Father, who chose him.

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript inserts: “because he is faithful.”] [Col. 0467D]

Or it may be understood thus: “Kings,” whose hearts are in the hand of God, and the princes of the Church of God, shall worship you because the Lord, the Holy One of Israel who chose you, is faithful.

All these things refer to the one who despised his soul, who is abhorred by the nation, and who is the servant of rulers.

### (Verses 8 and following)

Thus says the Lord:

“In an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you. I have preserved you and given [Vulgate: ‘Behold, I have given’] you as a covenant of the people, to raise up the earth and possess desolated inheritances; to say to those who are bound, ‘Come out!’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Be revealed!’

“They shall feed along the roads [Vulgate: ‘upon the roads’], and their pastures shall be in every level place. They shall not hunger or thirst, and heat and sun shall not strike them, because their merciful one will guide them and will give them drink at springs of water. I shall make all my mountains into a road, and my paths shall be raised up.

“Behold, these shall come from afar; and behold, those from the north and the sea; and these from the southern land.

“Praise, heavens, and rejoice, earth; mountains, shout for joy and praise, because the Lord has comforted his people and will have mercy on his poor.” [Col. 0468A]

The Septuagint:

“Thus says the Lord: At an opportune time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you. I formed you and gave you as a covenant of the nations, to establish the earth and possess desolated inheritances.

“You shall say to those who are in bonds, ‘Come out!’ and to those who are in darkness, ‘Be revealed!’ They shall feed along all the roads, and their pastures shall be in every path. They shall not hunger or thirst, nor shall heat or sun strike them; but the one who has mercy on them will comfort them and lead them by springs of water.

“I shall place every mountain as a road and every path as pasture for them.

“Behold, these shall come from afar; these from the north and the sea; others from the land of the Persians.

“Rejoice, heavens, and let the earth exult; let the mountains burst forth in joy, because God has had mercy on his people and has comforted the humble of his people.” [Col. 0468B]

The Apostle Paul used this testimony in the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, saying: “At an opportune time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time,” and so forth (2 Corinthians 6:2). [Col. 0468C]

If, then, the chosen vessel refers these words to the meaning of the first coming, let us follow the traces of his interpretation and, like little children, impress letters upon the master’s outlined lines.

The acceptable and opportune time and the day of salvation are the Savior’s passion and resurrection, when he prayed upon the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

And he preserved him—or formed him—after death had been conquered, and gave him as a covenant to the people of the Jews, namely, to those among them who wished to believe. He did this so that he might raise up the earth, which lay in the errors of idolatry, and possess desolated or deserted inheritances, which had no inhabitant, God. [Col. 0468D]

He would say to those who were in bonds, “Come out”—those who were held fast by the bonds of sins, since each person is bound by the cords of his own sins (Proverbs 5)—and to those who were in darkness, “Be revealed.” These were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death and could not see the light.

After they have been converted and have looked upon the clear light of Christ, they will feed along the roads and paths of the Holy Scriptures, and will say: “The Lord shepherds me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture; he has led me beside waters of refreshment” (Psalm 22:2). [Col. 0469A]

Whoever has been fed and nourished along such roads and paths will neither hunger nor thirst, nor feel the sun’s heat. In him will be fulfilled what is written: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120:6), so that he may feel neither the adversities nor the prosperities of this age.

For the merciful and compassionate Lord himself will comfort and guide them and lead them to springs of water.

Or he will give them drink at the springs concerning which it is written: “Bless the Lord from the springs of Israel” (Psalm 67:27); and elsewhere: “Draw water from the springs of the Savior” (Isaiah 12:3).

[Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts read, “or he will carry them,” and so forth.]

These springs are found in the Old and the New Testament.

All the obstacles that could impede the steps of believers the Lord will turn into level ground for them. He will humble the lofty and raise up the lowly, so that they may have a level and open road. [Col. 0469B]

Who these are for whom the way is prepared, he states more clearly: “Behold, these shall come from afar; and behold, those from the north and the sea; and these from the southern land.”

He indicates the four regions of the world: east, north, west, and south. Instead of the east he says “from afar”; instead of the southern region, the Hebrew reads *sinim*, which the Septuagint translated as “Persians.”

The others expressed the word as it is in Hebrew, *sinim*, which we translated “from the south [or: from the south wind].” We conjecture that Mount Sinai is situated in the southern region, in accordance with the prophet Habakkuk: “God will come from the south, and the Holy One from Mount Paran, shadowy and dense” (Habakkuk 3).

But if we understand *sinim* as “Persians,” as the Septuagint translated it—Persia being situated in the east—we can refer the earlier statement, “Behold, these shall come from afar,” to the south. [Col. 0469C]

He commands the heavens and the earth—or the powers dwelling in heaven and on earth, or angels and human beings—to sing together the praises of God. Those placed in the heights of the virtues are to testify to the joy of their mind with jubilation and exultation.

“For the Lord has comforted his people,” namely, those among the Jews who wished to believe. “And he has had mercy on his poor and humble”—or on all his people, who have been called to him from east and west, north and south, possessing neither the Law nor the Prophets nor spiritual riches, but abandoned, poor, and humble, subject to all demons.

### (Verses 14 and following)

“And Zion said: ‘The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.’

“Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget [Vulgate adds: ‘yet’], I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you upon my hands; your walls are always before my eyes.

“Your builders have come; [Vulgate: ‘Those who destroy and devastate you shall go out from you.’] And those who destroyed and devastated you shall go out from you.

“Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together; they have come to you.

“As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them around you like a bride. For your deserted places, your solitudes, and your land of ruins will now be too narrow because of the inhabitants, and those who devoured you will be driven far away.

“Still they will say in your ears, the children [or: to the children] of your barrenness: ‘The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell.’

“And you will say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and did not give birth, exiled and captive; and who raised these? I was abandoned and alone; and where were these?’” [Col. 0469D]

The Septuagint:

“And Zion said: ‘The Lord has forsaken me, and God has forgotten me.’

“Will a woman forget her child, so as not to have compassion on the offspring of her womb? And even if a woman should forget these, yet I will not forget you, says the Lord.

“Behold, upon my hands I have painted your walls, and you are continually before me.

“You shall quickly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed, and those who had devastated you shall go out from you.

“Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered together; they have come to you.

“As I live, says the Lord, you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them around yourself like a bride’s necklace; for your deserted places, your devastated places, and your fallen places will now be too narrow because of the inhabitants, and those who humbled you will be far from you.

“For they will say in your ears, your children whom you lost: ‘The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell.’

“And you will say in your heart: ‘Who has begotten these for me? I was childless and a widow; and who raised these for me? I was abandoned and alone; and where were these?’” [Col. 0470A]

We have often stated that Jerusalem and Zion must be understood in four ways in the Holy Scriptures.

First, according to the Jews, it is the Jerusalem which the Lord laments in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the Prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matthew 23:37). And elsewhere: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its desolation has drawn near” (Luke 21:20). [Col. 0470B]

Second, it is the assembly of the saints, who, established in the peace of the Lord and on the watchtowers of the virtues, are rightly called Zion. Concerning it is said: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob” (Psalm 86:1). For the foundations of the Jewish Zion, which we see to have been destroyed, were not loved by the Lord; nor could what is loved by the Lord be destroyed.

Third, Jerusalem is called the multitude of angels, Dominions, and Powers, and everything established in the service of God. Concerning this Jerusalem the Apostle also spoke: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Galatians 4:26). And elsewhere: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22). [Col. 0470C]

Fourth, Jerusalem is the city which the Jews and our Judaizers, in accordance with the Apocalypse of John—which they do not understand—think will be brought down from heaven, golden and adorned with jewels (Revelation 21). Its boundaries and immeasurable breadth are also described in the final part of Ezekiel.

[Note: It formerly read, “I have described it”; for this reason Tillemont thought that these words had been added by Jerome when, after the year 413, having already completed his Commentary on Ezekiel, he reread this work. If this is not accepted, the text should be restored to: “Ezekiel described it in the final part.” The reading restored by Martianay is now also confirmed by our manuscripts, and the sense strongly supports it.] [Col. 0470D]

Since these things are so, we must now examine more carefully which of the four Zions says: “The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.” [Col. 0471A]

There is no doubt that this refers to the assembly of the saints, which previously existed among the Jews and was abandoned by the Lord. It makes this complaint and laments in a tearful voice that it has been deserted and deprived of the Lord’s help.

God answers it, using a natural comparison: If it can happen that a mother forgets her infant and is not moved by compassion toward the child of her womb, then I too will forget you. I will say something more: even if she should forget, overcoming through hardness of mind the laws of nature, I nevertheless will not forget my creature, and I will always retain the souls of the saints in my heart.

For know that you, who think yourself completely abandoned, have been engraved and painted upon my hands, and that your walls continually remain before my eyes. [Col. 0471B]

From this we learn that Jerusalem is not to be sought in the region of Palestine, which is the poorest part of the whole province, roughened by rocky mountains and afflicted by a shortage of water, so that it depends on heavenly rains and ordinarily compensates for the scarcity of springs by constructing cisterns. Rather, it is to be sought in the hands of God, concerning which it is said: “Your builders have hastened.”

Or, according to the Septuagint: “You shall quickly be built by those by whom you had been destroyed.” For it was destroyed by Jews and built by Jews. Deserted because of the guilt of the scribes and Pharisees, it was gathered together at the preaching of Christ’s Apostles from both Jews and nations.

The text continues: “And those who destroyed and devastated you shall go out from you”—the evil teachers—so that you may no longer follow the commandments and traditions of human beings (Matthew 15), but the law of God. [Col. 0471C]

She is told to lift her eyes round about and see the children who have been gathered to her. Concerning them the Lord also spoke: “Lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35).

And to make us secure, he says: “As I live,” says the Lord—for according to the Old Testament this is the customary formula of an oath—“you shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament, and you shall put them around yourself as a bride puts on a necklace.”

Happy is the one who possesses such merit and virtue that he may be called the ornament of the Church. I think that these signify the various spiritual graces by which the bride’s adornment is embellished.

Concerning her it is also sung in the forty-fourth psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied colors” (Psalm 44:10). [Col. 0471D]

Those places which had previously been deserted and had fallen into solitudes and ruins will be restored when Christ’s Gospel arrives. They will have such a multitude of inhabitants that they will not be able to contain them.

This is so only insofar as the persecutors are driven far away—or those of whom we spoke above: “Those who destroyed you and devastated you shall go out from you.”

The children of your barrenness, whom you thought you had completely lost and from whom you believed yourself widowed, will say in your ears: “The place is too narrow for me in the synagogues; make room for me in the churches, so that I may dwell more widely, so that I may not be compressed by the blasphemies of the Jews, and so that the breadth of your expanse may contain the whole world with me.” [Col. 0472A]

But you, unable to express the greatness of your joy with your mouth, will silently ponder in your heart and say: “Who has begotten these for me? I was barren and widowed, deserted and captive among the Jewish people; I had ceased to have children and had not given birth for a long time. After Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, I had seen no other Prophets until John the Baptist. How, then, have I, who was alone and deprived of the help of a husband, now begun to have so many children?”

And so that we may know that Zion is built upon Christ the rock and foundation from both peoples, Paul says to believers: “Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the chief cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20).

From this it is evident that the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets is one: our Lord Jesus Christ. [Col. 0472B]

(Verses 22–23.) “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I will raise my hand toward the nations, and toward the peoples I will lift up my standard; and they will carry your sons in their arms, and bear your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and queens your nursing mothers. With face lowered to the ground they will adore you, and lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, upon whom those who await him shall not be put to shame.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I lift my hand over the nations, and over the islands I will raise my standard; and they will bring your sons in their bosom, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. And kings shall be your foster fathers, and female princes your nursing mothers. They will adore you upon the face of the earth, and lick the dust of your feet; and you shall know that I am the Lord, and those who await me shall not be put to shame.”

To what the Church had said—“I am barren and captive; who has borne these children for me? I was abandoned and alone, and where were these?”—the Lord replies: “Are you astonished that these things have happened? You will certainly not be astonished when you hear that I have raised my hand toward the nations.” Of this the Holy One also speaks: “You formed me and placed your hand upon me” (Ps. 138:4). And the Savior himself says: “No one can snatch anything from the hand of my Father” (John 10:29). The Apostle Peter likewise says: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Pet. 5:6).

This hand raised toward the nations is the same of which the same Prophet speaks: “There shall be a root of Jesse, who will arise to rule the nations; in him the nations will hope” (Isa. 11:10). Nor will he raise his hand only toward the nations; he will also exalt his standard among the peoples. There is no doubt that this is the banner of the cross, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “The earth is full of his praises.” And again: “His name is marvelous in all the earth” (Ps. 8:1).

Then they will carry the sons of Zion in their arms, or in their bosom, and bear her daughters upon their shoulders. Such was Lazarus, and all the saints who rest in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16), as well as the souls of believers, to whom the Apostle Paul was speaking: “I gave you milk to drink” (1 Cor. 3:2). And elsewhere: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). And in another place: “As a nursing mother cherishes her own children, so, longing for you, we desired to share with you not only the gospel of Christ but also our own souls” (1 Thess. 2:8).

Otherwise, it is absurd, in the Jewish manner, for fully grown sons and daughters to be carried in arms and upon shoulders. But “kings as foster fathers, and queens, princes, and female rulers as nursing mothers” clearly indicate the Apostles and apostolic men. Such was Abraham, to whom it is said: “You are a king from God among us” (Gen. 23:6).

[Note: Earlier the text was corruptly “from your God” instead of “you”; the manuscripts, as does the Greek text, prefer the latter.]

And such also are those whose heart is in the hand of God (Prov. 21), who say to believers: “As newborn infants, desire the rational, guileless milk” (1 Pet. 2:2).

The word “prince” also signifies ἄρχουσα, which is what the name Sarah means; and the queen—or “the queen”—of whom it is sung in the forty-fourth Psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold,” daily nourishes Christ’s little ones and leads them to mature age. Every age, sex, and rank will adore Zion because of him who dwells in her.

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript reads “will enter” for “will adore.”]

If Christ is the head of the Church, the head is adored in the body. And if it is said to certain people, “Exalt the Lord our God and adore the footstool of his feet” (not because the footstool itself ought to be adored, but because the majesty of his feet is indicated), why should the Church not be adored, since she embraces the whole body of Christ? Thus what is written in Zephaniah may be fulfilled: “Each one will adore him from his place; all the islands of the nations” (Zeph. 2:11).

[Note: Following the Greek more closely: “Each man will adore him from his place, all the islands,” etc.]

Thus they will no longer come to Jerusalem three times a year in the Jewish manner, but, adoring the Lord in their own place, they will possess Jerusalem.

And what follows—“and they will lick the dust of your feet”—signifies that kings and princes will cleanse and lick away with their speech whatever earthly work has clung to the feet of the Church. Hence the Apostles are also commanded to shake the dust from their feet. And Peter is told that one who has been washed once has no need except to wash his feet (Matt. 10; John 13).

Through all this the Church learns that there is no other Lord besides him; those who await him will possess eternal glory.

(Verses 24 and following.) “Can booty be taken from the strong, or can what has been captured by the mighty be rescued? For thus says the Lord: Indeed, the captive will be taken from the strong, and what has been carried away by the mighty will be saved. But I myself will judge those who judged you, and I myself will save your sons. And I will feed your enemies their own flesh, and they will be drunk with their own blood as with new wine; and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord, your savior and your mighty redeemer, the Strong One of Jacob.”

The Septuagint: “Can anyone take spoils from a giant? And if someone unjustly leads away a captive, will he be saved? Thus says the Lord: If someone captures a giant, he will take his spoils; and the one who takes them from the strong will be saved. But I will execute my judgment. And I will rescue my sons, and those who afflicted you will eat their own flesh and drink their own blood like new wine, and they will be drunk; and all flesh shall know that I am the Lord who rescued you, and the helper of the strength of Jacob.”

[Note: Again, following the Greek: “and I am the helper of the strength of Jacob.”]

Our Lord and Savior, who had previously spoken through Isaiah, repeats the same meaning in the Gospel: “How can anyone enter the house of a strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then he will plunder his house” (Mark 3).

The strong man and the giant are the devil, who had subjected all nations to his dominion, daring to say to the Savior: “All these things have been handed over to me, and I will give them to you if you fall down and adore me” (Matt. 4:9). For “the world is placed in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5), and none of the righteous was able to conquer him, nor, according to Amos, “snatch prey from the mouth of the lion” (Amos 3).

After the question had been proposed—namely, that no one could conquer the strong man and the giant, nor save what had been snatched away by him—the Lord replied that all this would be accomplished at his coming: namely, that the nations previously captured by the giant would be taken from him, and all his possessions and his entire household would be divided among the Apostles.

When what is written had been fulfilled—“The King of the armies of the beloved, and the beauty of the house, divides spoils” (Ps. 67:13)—this is the one who, ascending on high, “led captivity captive and gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. 68:19; Eph. 4). That is, he received into life those who had previously been captives unto death.

Hence Symmachus translated the passage more explicitly: “Even the captivity of the strong man will be taken away, and the terrifying booty will be saved.” He wished the devil to be understood as the strong and terrifying one, who was overcome by the Lord’s power.

Therefore the Lord, judging those who had oppressed Zion—or judging its judgment—will free and save her children, who had been captured by the giant. He will feed the hostile powers their own flesh and make them drunk as with new wine, so that they may be satiated not by the death of others but by their own death. And because they are flesh, having lost the Spirit of God, let them feed upon their own flesh.

The Holy One also speaks of this in the Psalms: “When those who afflict me drew near to eat my flesh” (Ps. 27:2). For it is not the spirit, which is incorporeal, that is eaten, but the flesh, exposed to the bites of savage beasts.

Then Zion will say—or rather, all flesh that will see the salvation of God—that her Redeemer and Savior is the one who wrestled with Jacob, or was the helper of Jacob’s strength, so that, when he was exalted in his passion,

[Note: In Ambrosianus, apparently with better sense, “overcome” instead of “exalted above.”]

he might bless those crucifying him: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

575 (Chapter 50.—Verse 1.) “Thus says the Lord: Where is this bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her? Or who is my creditor, to whom I sold you? Behold, you were sold because of your iniquities, and because of your crimes I dismissed your mother. For I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who would listen.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: What kind of bill of divorce is this of your mother, by which I dismissed her? Or to which creditor and exactor of mine did I sell you? Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and because of your iniquities I dismissed your mother, for I came, and there was no human being; I called, and there was no one who would obey.”
