After the calling of the nations, and after kings and princes—foster fathers and nursing mothers—and after the captivity of the strong and mighty one, whose booty was distributed among the Apostles, and after the madness of the demons, who were satiated with their own flesh and drunk with their own blood—when all flesh had recognized that the Redeemer and the Strong One himself was the God of Jacob—he speaks to the Jewish people concerning Zion, which had earlier said: “The Lord has forsaken me, and the Lord has forgotten me.”

Do you suppose that, because of my harshness, your earthly mother Jerusalem was cast away, and that I, hard of mind, gave her a bill of divorce? Do you not rather understand what is true: that she departed from me through her own fault? For when I said to her, “Cease to act wickedly; learn to do good,” she refused to hear me, but turned her shoulder away from me as she departed. Therefore I said to her children: “Woe to them, for they have departed from me. Those who have acted impiously against me are manifest.” And to her herself: “Your apostasy will discipline you, and your wickedness will rebuke you; and you will know that it is evil and bitter for you to have abandoned me.”

But perhaps you cannot produce the bill of divorce, and perhaps some creditor of mine, demanding money, received you in payment of a debt because I had nothing with which to repay him? It is not so. Rather, I will show you why I abandoned the mother together with her children.

Your crimes and sins sold you to the demons, so that, ensnared by the pleasures of the present age, you abandoned your parent and she abandoned her husband. Therefore I could no longer keep your adulterous mother, but permitted her to depart willingly.

The Apostle Paul also teaches that each person is sold because of his sins, when, abandoned to his own free will, we are led by our own choice either toward good or toward evil: “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7:14). “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). And just as the greedy and robbers are slaves of mammon, so every sin rules over sinners. To them it is said: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6:12).

But so that you may know that your mother was not repudiated by me but departed by her own will, after many benefits I assumed a human body and spoke not through the Prophets but in person. I came, and there was no man, or human being. For all, abandoning the image of man and humanity, took on the images of beasts and serpents.

Hence, because of his wickedness, he is told concerning Herod: “Go and tell that fox” (Luke 13:32). And to the Pharisees: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. 23:33). And to the lustful: “They became frenzied horses toward women” (Jer. 5:8). And concerning the pleasure-loving: “Do not cast your pearls before swine.” And to the shameless: “Nor give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7:6). And generally concerning all: “The vision of the four-footed creatures that were in the wilderness” (Isa. 30).

Thus the Lord came and found no human being. For “when man was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 49:13). “I called them,” he says, “as rational animals, and said: Incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 78), “but my people did not hear my voice.” I cried out and said: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And elsewhere: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28). Yet there was no one who would listen. Hence in the Gospel I said to them: “You have neither seen the form of God nor heard his voice, because you do not have his word abiding in you” (John 5:37–38).

(Verses 2.) “Has my hand become shortened and small, so that I cannot redeem? Or is there no power in me to deliver? Behold, at my rebuke I will make the sea desolate; I will turn rivers into dry land. The fish will rot for lack of water and will die of thirst. I will clothe the heavens with darkness and make sackcloth their covering.”

The Septuagint: “Is my hand not able to save, or does it not prevail to deliver? Behold, at my threat I will make the sea desolate and turn the rivers into deserts; their fish will dry up because there is no water, and they will die of thirst. I will clothe the heavens with darkness and make its covering like sackcloth.”

Against those who thought that the Lord could not deliver his people from captivity, he sets forth reasons and very complete examples: the one who made the Red Sea passable for his people (Exod. 14), dried up the waters of the Jordan, and, when the rivers in Egypt dried up, turned the fish into corruption (Exod. 7); the one who caused palpable darkness to exist in Egypt for three days, so that the sky seemed covered as with sackcloth and darkness—surely he was also able to free his people from danger.

Or, because he had said above, “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who would listen,” we can say that the one who performed such great signs, and makes heaven, earth, and seas obey his command, could himself also have escaped the cross, saying in the Gospel: “Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he would immediately provide me with more than twelve legions of angels?” (Matt. 26:53).

[Note: Victor, from the sacred text, rewrites this as “Or do you think,” and “and would provide,” instead of “that I cannot ask” and “so that he would provide.”]

According to the allegorical interpretation, at the Lord’s rebuke the sea becomes desolate when all the bitterness of this world is dried up and the rivers are laid waste—those rivers of which the spiritual dragon said in Egypt: “My rivers are mine, and I made them” (Ezek. 29:9). Concerning them we read elsewhere: “What have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the waters of the rivers?” (Jer. 2:18).

The fish, too, after the net has been cast into the sea, will rot if they have been separated from the good fish.

And what follows—“I will clothe the heavens with darkness, and its covering will be like sackcloth”—we may understand as referring to everything above us, which we call heaven, just as the birds in the air are called heavenly creatures. The hostile powers are also said to be heavenly, moving between heaven and earth.

Or certainly heaven is clothed with darkness when it is covered with clouds, according to what is written: “He covers the heavens with clouds and gives rain to the earth” (Ps. 147:8). And in a threat of drought God says: “I will make the heaven like bronze and the earth like iron” (Deut. 28:23). This does not mean that the nature of the elements is changed, but that the greatness of the punishments is shown through bronze and iron.

Philosophers say that clouds are not lifted more than ten stadia above the earth, and that they conceal the brightness of the sun. Therefore it is not the sky that is wrapped in sackcloth; rather, when the light of the sky is shut out, the air beneath it is darkened by the darkness of the cloud.

We can interpret the heavens wrapped in darkness and covered with sackcloth by saying that all are under sin, and that even the saints need the mercy of God.

BOOK FOURTEEN

[Col. 0477]

[Col. 0477B] 577–578 The Lord, who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; who touches the mountains and they smoke [Alt. “smoke”] (Ps. 104); who says in the song of Deuteronomy, “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal” (Deut. 32:39), caused my own earth also to tremble through frequent illnesses. To it was said: “You are earth, and to earth you will go” (Gen. 3:19). And, forgetful of the human condition, he repeatedly reminds me that I am a man and an old man, and one who will very soon die. Of me it is written: “What does earth and ashes boast of?” (Sir. 10:9).

Therefore the one who had struck me with sudden illness healed me with incredible speed, so that he might terrify rather than afflict me, and correct rather than chastise me. Knowing, therefore, whose everything is that I live by, and that perhaps my sleep is delayed for this reason, so that I may complete the work I began on the Prophets, I devote myself entirely to this study. And, as though placed upon a watchtower, I contemplate the storms and shipwrecks of this world—not without groaning and sorrow—thinking not at all about present things but about those to come, and fearing not human reputation and rumors but the judgment of God.

[Note: “My own earth through frequent illnesses,” etc. Every day I also suffer the same things with Jerome; nor do I doubt that my sleep is delayed so that I may complete the edition of the holy doctor’s works that I have begun. Therefore I give myself wholly to this study, fearing not at all the murmurs of critics and heretics but the judgment of God. MARTIAN.]

And you, Virgin of Christ, Eustochium, who assisted me in my illness by your prayers, implore the grace of Christ also for me now that I am healed [Alt. “holy”], so that, by the same Spirit with which the Prophets sang of future things, I may enter into their cloud and darkness and know the word of God, which is heard not by the ears of the flesh but by the heart, and say with the Prophet: “The Lord gives me a disciplined tongue, so that I may know when it is necessary for me to speak.” This testimony is the beginning of the fourteenth book on Isaiah, which I now wish to expound.

[Note: Martianus reads “who,” masculine, instead of “who,” feminine.]

579 (Chapter 50.—Verses 4 and following.) “The Lord God has given me a learned tongue, so that I may know how to sustain the weary with a word. He awakens me morning by morning; morning by morning he awakens my ear, so that I may hear as a teacher. The Lord God has opened my ear; but I do not resist; I did not turn back. I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them. I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked and spit upon me. The Lord God is my helper; therefore I have not been put to shame. Therefore I set my face like the hardest stone, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord gives me a disciplined tongue, so that I may know when it is necessary for me to speak a word. He placed me in the morning and added an ear to me for hearing; and the discipline of the Lord opens my ears. But I do not refuse, nor do I contradict. I gave my back to scourges and my cheeks to blows. I did not turn my face away from the disgrace of spitting. And the Lord is my helper; therefore I was not put to shame. Rather, I set my face like a very strong stone, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”

The Jews, separating this chapter from what precedes, wish to refer it to Isaiah’s person. They say that he declares that he received from the Lord the word by which he might sustain the weary and wandering people and recall them to salvation; and that, like little children who are instructed in the morning hours, he heard from the Holy Spirit what he should say. They say that he did not contradict the Spirit’s command, but that when the Lord asked, “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?” he replied: “Behold, here I am; send me” (Isa. 6:8).

And because he said, “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:10), they say that he suffered such harsh treatment that he was exposed not only to verbal insults but also to the pain of blows. Nevertheless, they claim that he was not at all terrified by the consciousness of the God who commanded him, but, in accordance with what is said to Ezekiel—“Behold, I have made your face stronger than their faces, and your forehead harder than their foreheads; I have made your face like adamant and flint” (Ezek. 3:8–9)—that he crushed all their assaults.

Let those who use every means to overturn the prophecies concerning Christ and twist them by perverse interpretation toward an erroneous understanding say this—as though, if these things were written about Isaiah, they could remove other testimonies concerning Christ, which are so clear that they pour forth the unmistakable light of their meaning into everyone’s eyes.

These things, therefore, must also be referred to the person of the Lord, in whom the preceding book also ended: namely, that, according to the dispensation of the body he assumed, he was instructed and received a disciplined tongue, so that he might know when he ought to speak and when to remain silent.

Indeed, the one who was silent in his passion now speaks throughout the whole world through the Apostles and apostolic men. It is a sign of great knowledge to give provisions to fellow servants at the proper time and to take into account the character of one’s hearers.

Hence the Apostle Paul, speaking to those who did not accept the faith of the Prophets, uses the testimonies of their own authorities. Thus certain of their poets said: “For we are indeed his offspring” (Acts 17:28), referring to Aratus. Again, from the comic poet: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33). And he quotes the hexameter of Epimenides: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies” (Tit. 1:12).

[Note: Compare Epistle 70 to Magnus in our recension, no. 2. The words of Aratus are τοῦ γὰρ καὶ γένος ἐσμέν (“For we are indeed his offspring”). The comic poet Menander’s iambic line is Φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρησθ᾽ ὁμιλίαι κακαί (“Bad associations corrupt good morals”). Finally, the hexameter of Epimenides is Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται, κακὰ θηρία, γαστέρες ἀργαί (“Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies”).]

If they do not preserve the order and measure of the meters in translation, one should know that in Greek they proceed according to metrical feet. He did this because he had received a disciplined tongue, so that he might know when it was necessary to speak the word.

An ear was added to him through grace, which he did not possess by nature, so that we may understand that bodily ears are not intended, but those of the mind. Concerning these the Lord also spoke in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

This discipline and instruction opened his ears, so that he might transmit to us the knowledge of the Father. He did not contradict him, but “became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (Phil. 2). Thus he gave his body, or his back, to blows; and the breast capable of receiving God endured the scourges. He did not turn his cheeks away from blows.

There is no doubt that he endured this from the servant of the chief priest, while the Jewish people also mocked him in rivalry with one another. Struck and spat upon, he was not ashamed, but was led like a lamb to sacrifice; and like a sheep before its shearer, he did not open his mouth.

That the Son, according to the mystery of the body he assumed, heard from the Father what he should say, we learn more fully in the Gospel, where he himself says: “The Father who sent me gave me a command concerning what I should say and what I should speak.” And again: “As I hear, I judge” (John 8:28; 5:30).

(Verses 8–9.) “He is near who justifies me; who will contend with me? Let us stand together. Who is my adversary? Let him approach me. Behold, the Lord God is my helper; who is he who will condemn me? Behold, all of them will be worn out like a garment; the moth will consume them.”

The Septuagint:

[Note: Victor insists that, in accordance with the Greek ὅτι ἐγγίζει δικαιώσας μου, the text should be restored as “For he is near who justifies me.”]

“He who is near justifies me; who is he who will be judged with me? Let him resist me together with me. And who is he who will enter into judgment against me? Let him approach me. Behold, the Lord is my helper; who will afflict me? Behold, all of you will grow old like a garment, and the moth will eat you.”

“If anyone,” he says, “thinks that I was justly condemned to the cross and that I committed some sin, let him resist me. Who is he who will be judged with me, so that he may be overcome not by the power of my majesty but by reason?”

One is judged with the Lord not by the authority of the ruler but by comparison of virtues. Thus the Apostles judge the twelve tribes of Israel, and the Ninevites and the queen of Sheba judge the Jewish people. In accordance with this interpretation it is said to Jerusalem: “Sodom was justified in comparison with you” (Ezek. 16:52).

Since, then, no one can be justified in the presence of the Lord, all will grow old like a garment (Ps. 102). Whatever grows old is near destruction. “And like a moth,” he says, “it will consume them”: namely, the conscience of sinners and the zeal of the nations that have been saved.

Concerning this it is said at the end of this volume: “Their worm shall not die.” And in Micah against perverse rulers: “I will take away their goods like a moth that consumes them, walking upon the measuring line on the day of visitation” (Mic. 7:4, according to the Septuagint). And in Proverbs: “An understanding heart is a moth to the bones” (Prov. 14:30, according to the Septuagint). In the present passage, instead of “moth,” Symmachus translated “rust,” and Aquila “worm.”

(Verses 10–11.) “Who among you fears the Lord, hearing the voice of his servant? Whoever walks in darkness and has no light, let him hope in the name of the Lord and rely upon his God.”

The Septuagint: “Who is among you who fears the Lord? Let him hear the voice of his servant. Those who walk in darkness have no light. You trust in the name of the Lord and rely upon God.”

“You scourged me; you spat upon my face. Yet I summon my persecutors to repentance. For I do not desire the death of the sinful people, but only that it should turn back and live” (Ezek. 33).

And I say: Who among you fears the Lord and hears the voice of his servant or servant-child, that is, of his Son? In the one case we are speaking of the flesh he assumed, in the other of his nature.

Nor should we think it a small thing to fear the Lord, in accordance with what is said in Proverbs: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9:10). Perfect love casts out fear, because fear has punishment; and whoever fears is not perfect in love.

But here “fear” is used for timidity and εὐλάβεια, that is, reverent caution. Elsewhere also we read: “Blessed is the one who fears everything” (Prov. 28:14), because of εὐλάβεια, that is, because of timidity—the sort whom people commonly call devoutly God-fearing. For the Lord protects their way and guards the path of those who fear him.

Of this fear it is written: “The fear of the Lord surpasses everything.” And elsewhere: “There is no want for those who fear him” (Sir. 25:14; Ps. 34:10).

Finally, one reaches this kind of fear of the Lord after many stages of virtue. The divine word speaks in the person of a teacher and father instructing a disciple and son: “If you call for wisdom and give your voice to understanding, and if you seek it like money and search for it as for treasures, then you will understand the fear of the Lord and discover the knowledge of God” (Prov. 2:3).

This is the fear that preserves the souls of the saints whole, chaste, and pure. Concerning it is said: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever.” To this the divine words exhort us: “Fear God and give him glory” (Rev. 14:7).

Let the one who thus fears the Lord hear the voice of his servant or servant-child, who walked in darkness and had no light; who had neither outward appearance nor glory, but assumed the form of a servant in the likeness of sinful flesh, in order to overcome sin in the flesh.

Concerning him it is said that he should hope in the name of the Lord and rely upon his God, so that whatever belongs to human weakness may be strengthened and supported by divine majesty.

This is according to the Hebrew. But according to the Septuagint, the statement concerns sinners who refused to obey the voice of his Son, walk in the darkness of error, and therefore have no light. For it could not happen that wisdom should enter a perverse soul. They did not know or understand, and therefore they walk in darkness.

They did not perform the works and commandments of the Lord; they did not sow righteousness for themselves, nor gather grapes from the vine, so as to kindle for themselves the light of knowledge. Whoever desires wisdom should keep the commandments, and the Lord will grant it to him.

Hence it is said to God: “Your commandments are light.” And elsewhere: “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. 19:9). And the impious are commanded to trust in the Lord and, falling because of their sins, to rely upon and be supported by his help.

(Verses 11.) “Behold, all of you who kindle a fire, girded with flames, walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled. This has happened to you from my hand; you will lie down in sorrows.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, all of you kindle a fire and strengthen the flame; walk in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled. These things have happened to you because of me. You will sleep in sorrow.”

The exhortation is of no benefit, nor is there hope of salvation after crimes. “All have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 14). All kindle a fire for themselves and strengthen the flame. For within themselves they have hay, wood, stubble, thorns, thistles, and weeds, which are destined for eternal burning.

Hence it is written in Proverbs: “In a multitude of wood the fire grows strong” (Prov. 26:20). But if a small fire seizes a great quantity of material, how much will a great flame consume?

It is also said in the Epistle attributed to the Hebrews concerning the earth, which produces thorns and thistles, that it is rejected and near a curse, and that its end is burning (Heb. 6:8).

Therefore those who are girded with flames and surrounded by them, and who have strengthened the fire for themselves, are summoned to salvation, and it is said to them: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flames that you have kindled,” so that through punishments and torments they may learn the power of God and return to salvation.

This signifies the devastation of the Jewish people, by which they were handed over to the Romans and continue to endure the yoke of captivity to this day. For all these things were done by the hand of Christ, and they will sleep in sorrow and pain, because they were unwilling to receive the Son of God either through benefits or through torments.

Hence he says to them: “Go into the eternal fire that God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). This is what the Apostle also says: “For wrath has overtaken you to the end” (1 Thess. 2:16).

From this chapter we learn that, in proportion to the quality of his sin, each person kindles a fire for himself. Just as, while remaining in the same place—and, if it may be said, on the same couch—some are healthy while others burn with the heat of fevers, experiencing different sufferings because of the differing humors and phlegms, so the fire kindled by sinners has its fuel in their sins and iniquity. Concerning this it is written: “Iniquity will burn like fire, and like dry grass it will be consumed by the flame” (Isa. 9:18).

### Chapter LI

#### Verses 1ff.

“Listen to me, you who pursue what is just and seek the Lord. Look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the hollow of the pit from which you were cut. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who bore you: for I called him when he was one, blessed him, and multiplied him.

“Therefore the Lord will comfort Zion; he will comfort all her ruins and make her wilderness like delights, and her solitude like the garden of the Lord. Joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Listen, you who pursue what is just and seek the Lord. Look to the solid rock which you hewed out, and to the pit of the cistern which you dug. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you, because he was one and I called him, blessed him, loved him, and multiplied him. And now I will comfort you, Zion. I have comforted all her deserts like paradise, and the regions toward the west like the paradise of the Lord. Exultation and gladness will be found in her, confession and the voice of praise.”

While those who kindled a fire for themselves and made its flames exceedingly strong sleep in perpetual mourning and pain, you who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord—for this signifies the company of the Apostles and of those who through the Apostles have believed—are told to look to the rock, that is, Abraham your father, from whom you were hewn, and to the hollow of the pit from which you were cut, that is, Sarah who bore you.

Consider also that, when he was [Note: Victorius emends this to “when Abraham was one hundred years old,” rather than “when he was one and one hundred.”] one and one hundred [585] years old and had a barren wife, I multiplied his children like the stars of heaven, so that their multitude surpassed counting. If, then, so many thousands of peoples arose from one man, what is so great for me in restoring the ruins of Zion and changing her deserts into a paradise of delight, into the garden of the Lord which God planted in Eden toward the east? In her, instead of various trees, joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise will be found.

The Jews refer this to the time of Zerubbabel, because after the devastation of Babylonia Zion was restored, the Temple was built, and the ancient religion was restored. But just as above (on chapter XLIX, verses 22–23) it is said to Zion, “They will bring your sons in their arms, and carry your daughters upon their shoulders. Kings will be your foster-fathers, and queens your nurses. Behold, these will come from afar, and those from the north and the sea, and these from the southern land,” when Zion will say, “The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell”—statements which exclude the limited circumstances of those times and are not known to have been fulfilled in the earthly Jerusalem—so here also the Lord speaks to those who pursue what is just, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “Seek peace and pursue it” (Psalm XXXIII, 5), and again: “Pursuing hospitality” [Alternative reading: “following hospitality”] (Romans XI, 13).

They seek the Lord, so that from the former things he may infer the present ones; and since what is promised has already become much more difficult, they should not doubt that these things will be future.

According to the Septuagint, however, the persecutors of righteousness are told to look upon the strongest rock which they hewed out, and the pit of the cistern which they dug—that is, the Lord and Savior, of whom the Apostle says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians X, 4). Elsewhere it is written: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Psalm XXXIX, 3). And again: “He exalted me upon a rock.”

For they pierced his side with a lance; from it came blood and water. They dug through his hands and feet, as the Lord and Savior himself says: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Psalm XXI, 18).

We may understand the rock that was hewn out as the Savior’s tomb, in which he was buried and, rising from the dead, begot innumerable children. He was called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations.” Just as Sarah, formerly barren, is interpreted as the Church, which is also called by another name, Zion, so the Lord comforted her and made her deserts like paradise. “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband.”

When it is said, “I will make the regions toward the west into the paradise of the Lord,” or “into the garden of God,” this signifies that light suddenly arose for those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

In place of paradise, which we have rendered as “delights,” the Hebrew has [Col. 0483C] *EDEN* (אָדֶן), concerning which it is written at the beginning of Genesis.

It should also be noted that in Zion, which is compared with the paradise of God, there ought to be nothing except joy and gladness, confession and the voice of praise, so that what the saints will do in heaven with the angels of God, they may also practice continually on earth in the praise of the Lord.

#### Verses 4–5

“Attend to me, my people, and my tribe; listen to me: for a law will go forth from me, and my judgment will rest as a light for the peoples. My righteous one is near; my savior has gone forth; and my arms will judge the peoples. The islands will wait for me, and they will hope in my arm.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Listen to me, listen to me, my people, and kings; attend to me: for a law will go forth from me, and my judgment as a light for the nations. [Note: The word “nations” was lacking; we supply it from the Ambrosian manuscripts, as the Greek text itself, εἰς φῶς ἐθνῶν, requires.] My righteousness is quickly approaching, and my salvation will go forth like light; and in my arm the nations will hope. The islands will wait for me, and they will hope in my arm.”

In the Hebrew there is one “Attend,” whereas according to the Septuagint there are two, “Listen to me, listen to me,” so that he may teach us that we ought to listen both with the ears of the body and with the understanding of the soul.

The multitude of the nations, which is the people of God, is summoned to listen carefully to what is said. Concerning this Zechariah says: “Many nations will flee to the Lord, and they will be his people” (Zechariah II, 11).

Or, as some wish, “people” refers to the remnant of believing Israel, while “tribe,” or “nations,” refers to those who believed from the multitude of the nations, in accordance with Moses’ words to the nations in the Song of Deuteronomy: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 43).

Instead of “tribe,” which we have translated, Theodotion rendered “race,” Symmachus “nation,” and the Septuagint “kings.”

We are the tribe, nation, and race of the Lord, a royal and priestly people, as was Abraham, who was called a king, and the other saints concerning whom it is written: “Do not touch my anointed ones” (Psalm CIV, 15).

What are they commanded to hear? “For,” he says, “a law will go forth from me, and my judgment as a light for the peoples,” or nations.

Here the spiritual law of the Gospel is indicated, which will go forth from Zion—not the law of Moses, formerly given on Sinai. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “and his judgment as a light,” etc.] My judgment will proceed as a light for the nations, by which he has established and decreed that all nations are to be saved.

And lest we perhaps think that what he promised would come only after a long time, he adds: “My righteous one is near,” or “my righteousness.” For Christ was made for us by the Father “wisdom and redemption” (1 Corinthians I), holiness and righteousness, and everything designated by the names of virtue.

Beautifully it says that righteousness will proceed, so that not one nation alone but the whole world may be saved.

As for the Savior, or salvation—which in Hebrew is called [Note: Earlier editions printed *Jeschua* for the name Jesus. In the Hebrew text of Isaiah at this passage, LI, 5, we read *Jischi*, meaning “my salvation” or, according to Jerome, “my savior”; below, in verses 6 and 8, Jerome translates *Jesehuathi* as “my salvation.” The Septuagint everywhere renders it *σωτήριόν μου*, “my salvation.” —Martian.] *Jesus*—being called the Son of God, who was sent by the Father, Simeon, holding the child in his arms, says: “Now dismiss your servant, Lord, because my eyes have seen your salvation, which you prepared in the sight of all the peoples, a light for revelation to the nations” (Luke XI, 29ff.).

What follows—“And my arms will judge the peoples,” or, according to the Septuagint, “and in my arm the nations will hope”—may signify either that all will be judged by his power, or that all the nations will believe in Christ, who is the arm and strength of God.

It is also said elsewhere: “Your arm is with power; let your hand be strengthened and your right hand exalted” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 14). And again: “Sing to the Lord a new song: his right hand and his holy arm have saved him” (Psalm XXVII, 1–2).

The Lord’s right hand and arm is himself: he formerly saved those who were lost, so that none of those whom the Father had given him might perish (John XVII).

We have frequently explained that the islands, or the souls of the saints who in the persecutions of this world have been made firm in God by solid faith, or the multitude of the churches from the nations, are meant here.

Just as the arm of the Lord signifies the Savior, so we may understand his arms, which will judge the peoples, as all the saints, through whom God will judge the world.

#### Verse 6

“Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look down beneath the earth: for the heavens will melt like smoke, and the earth will be worn out like a garment; and its inhabitants will perish in the same way. But my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will not fail.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Lift up your eyes to heaven, and look upon the earth below, because heaven has been strengthened like smoke. But the earth will grow old like a garment, and its inhabitants will die like these things. But my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will not fail.”

This is what the Lord says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew XXIV, 35).

David also sings in the psalm: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all will grow old like a garment; and like a cloak you will wrap them, and they will be changed” (Psalm CI, 26).

From this it is shown that the destruction of the heavens does not mean annihilation, but transformation for the better. Concerning them it is said: “There will be a new heaven and a new earth, which I will make to remain in my sight” (Revelation XXI, 2).

For if it is written concerning the saints, “We shall all indeed sleep, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Corinthians XV, 51) [Note: Victorius here prefers another reading, likewise attested by Jerome as the Apostolic reading in his Letter to Minervius and Alexander, as more suitable to the context and the saintly doctor’s meaning: “We shall not all indeed sleep, but we shall all be changed.”]—and in the titles of four psalms we read, “For those who will be changed”—how much more must this be believed concerning heaven, the sun, and the stars, when the moon will receive the sun’s light and the sun will shine with sevenfold brilliance?

Hence the whole creation groans and labors, awaiting the revelation of the children of God, so that it may be changed for the better (Romans VIII). Not only will the souls of human beings, which are immortal, be changed, but their bodies also will be changed into a glorified substance. “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians XV, 53).

When heaven and earth grow old, consequently the things contained within the circle of heaven, and human beings who inhabit the earth, will die like these things—not into their own annihilation, but into the removal of their ancient baseness [Note: We restore “removal” (*abolitionem*) for “absolution” (*absolutionem*) from several Victorian manuscripts.] and the renewal of future glory, when “the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew XIII, 43), and when past and ancient things have departed, all things will have become new.

Some understand “perish” and “grow old” as referring to abolition and death, in accordance with what we read in the Catholic Epistle: “The heavens that now are and the earth have been reserved by the same word for fire.” And again: “The elements, burning, will be dissolved” (2 Peter III, 7).

This is also the opinion of the philosophers of the world: that everything we see will perish by fire.

Hence the Apostle says: “The form of this world is passing away,” while we contemplate not the things that are seen but those that are unseen. “For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal” (1 Corinthians VII, 32).

The apostle John also writes something similar: “The world is passing away, and its desire” (1 John II, 17).

In Hebrew it says: “The heavens will melt like smoke.” According to Aquila and Symmachus, however, they “will be crushed into nothing” and “will be ground down and vanish like salt.”

The former said *ἡλίσθησαν*; the latter, *ἁλίσουσιν*. It is clear that these words derive their etymology from the crushing and dissolving of salt.

[Note: Until this point, the reading had been based not on manuscript evidence but on Erasmus’ conjecture, which the others copied: *μειωθήσεται* and *ἁλιώσονται*. An older Ambrosian manuscript, however, expressly has, in uncial letters, *ΗΛΙϹΘΗϹΑΝ* and *ΑΑΛΛΗϹΟΥϹΙΝ*. We alter or correct only the second of these by changing the double alpha and lambda to *ἁλίσουσιν*. These forms mean “to be destroyed and vanish like salt,” although the first is passive in termination and the second active. Jerome notes that both translators derived their etymology from the dissolution of salt. We therefore consider that reading less satisfactory than the one Montfaucon draws from other manuscripts, restoring *ἠλοηθήσαν* from the verb *ἀλοάω*, which means “to crush” or “to break,” but derives its etymology not from the word for salt. —Martian.]

But I wonder what the Septuagint intended by saying, “Heaven has been strengthened like smoke.” For if “strength” is understood as power, how can what is firm be compared with smoke? Perhaps we can say that all the firmness, strength, and power of the heavens are compared with the emptiest wind and with smoke, which dissolves into the air, in accordance with Ecclesiastes: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes I, 2).

It must also be said that if heaven and earth will perish and grow old, how can their inhabitants consequently die and perish like them, when we know that souls are everlasting and that bodies will rise again?

From this it is clear that heaven and earth do not perish and become nothing, but are changed for the better.

#### Verses 7–8

“Listen to me, you who know what is just, my people [the Vulgate adds: ‘my people’]: my law is in their hearts.” Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not dread their blasphemies. For as a garment, so the worm will consume them; and as wool, so the moth will devour them. But my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness through generation after generation.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Listen to me, you who know judgment, my people, whose law is in their hearts. Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not be overcome by their contempt. For like a garment they will be consumed by time, and like wool they will be eaten by the moth. But my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation through generation after generation.”

The one who earlier said, “A law will go forth from me, and my judgment as a light for the nations,” now speaks to the same people, who know his judgment and have his law in their hearts, so that they may do everything with judgment and possess the law which the Lord promises through Jeremiah, saying (Jeremiah XXXI, 31ff.):

“I will establish a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers; but I will establish a covenant, giving my laws in their minds, and I will write them upon their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people.”

Thus they should no longer live according to the letter but according to the spirit, restoring the natural law in their hearts. Concerning this the Apostle also writes: “When the Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do what belongs to the law, these, though they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Romans II, 14).

This law is signified in the psalm: “The mouth of the righteous will meditate wisdom, and his tongue will speak judgment. The law of his God is in his heart, and his steps will not be shaken” (Psalm XXXVI, 30–31).

And because the prophetic Spirit knew that many persecutions would come upon believers, he exhorts them to courage, indeed to contempt for those who would persecute them.

The Lord also spoke this in the Gospel: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna” (Matthew X, 28). And elsewhere: “Rejoice when they speak every evil against you falsely” (ibid., V, 11).

For just as a garment is consumed by the worm or by time, and as wool is devoured by the moth, so every reproach of the persecutors will pass away together with the persecutors.

Hence the Apostles rejoiced that they had been considered worthy to suffer insults for the Lord (Acts V). They rejoiced because the Lord’s salvation and righteousness, which had promised them victory and rewards—that is, the Lord and Savior—remain forever, whether in the two generations of the former and the later people who received his coming. Concerning him it is also said above: “My righteous one is near; my Savior has gone forth.”

#### Verses 9ff.

“Awake, awake; put on strength, arm of the Lord. Awake as in the ancient days, as in the generations of ages. Are you not the one who struck down the proud, who wounded the dragon? Are you not the one who dried up the sea, the water of the mighty abyss, who made the depths of the sea a road for the redeemed to cross?

“And now those redeemed by the Lord will return and come to Zion, praising; and everlasting joy will be upon their heads. They will possess joy and gladness; pain and groaning will flee.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Awake, awake, Jerusalem [the obelus and the word ‘Jerusalem’ are discussed below], and put on the strength of your arm. Awake as at the beginning of the day, as an everlasting generation. Are you not the one who cut down the breadth and dissolved the dragon? Are you not the one who made the sea desolate, the many waters of the abyss, who made the depths of the sea a passageway for those who had been liberated and redeemed? For they will be brought back by the Lord and will come to Zion with eternal joy and exultation. Praise and gladness will seize them upon their head. Pain, sorrow, and groaning will flee.”

The name “Jerusalem,” which is added here by the Septuagint, is found neither in the Hebrew nor in any of the three translators; therefore it should be marked beforehand with an obelus, and the following chapter should be joined to the preceding sense.

The Lord had exhorted those who believed in him, saying: “Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not dread their blasphemies.” He had promised them his everlasting salvation and righteousness as an aid; this is none other than Christ, the arm of the Lord, concerning whom he had said above: “In my arm the nations will hope.”

Therefore the people speak to the arm of the Lord, entreating his coming and imploring the promised aid:

“Awake, awake; put on strength, arm of the Lord. Awake as in the ancient days, and exercise all your strength, so that just as through many ages you have delivered your saints from dangers, you may also protect us by your strength.

“For you are the one who struck down the proud and wounded the dragon”—namely, the king of Egypt, Pharaoh, who is also called “the great dragon” in Ezekiel (Ezekiel XXIX).

“You dried up the Red Sea, so that through the strongest waters and the depths of the sea your people might find a road and escape the Egyptians who pursued them.

“Since you did these things, now also bring back those redeemed and liberated by your blood to Zion, and to the heavenly Jerusalem, or to the Church which you prepared for yourself with your blood. When they are there, they will rejoice with everlasting joy and say: ‘Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will’” (Psalm V, 13).

They will possess joy and gladness, while pain and groaning flee.

This is according to the Hebrew. According to the Septuagint, however, Jerusalem—that is, the sinful soul—is summoned to put on the strength of her arm and to take up her former works, as she was before she fell, when she moved in the day and in the light.

“You are,” he says, “the one who overcame the broad and spacious way that leads to death, and dissolved the dragon, the crooked serpent.” Concerning him it is also read in the Psalms: “You crushed the heads of the dragons in the waters” (Psalm LXXIII, 13).

Remember your former strength: that you trampled the sea of this world, made it desolate, and found a road in the midst of the waves. Hence the Apostle Peter also passed through the sea of this world to the Lord; and although he was walking by faith, he began to sink through unbelief—except that the Lord’s right hand supported him.

Therefore, just as the earlier victory was granted with the Lord’s help, so, after repentance, to those who return and hear, “If one falls, shall he not rise?” says the Lord (Jeremiah VIII, 4), and, “Turn back to me, returning children, and I will heal your brokenness” (ibid., III), he himself will extend his hand and lead them back to Zion, the watchtower and summit of virtues, with everlasting joy and gladness. He will place praise and gladness upon their head.

“For the eyes of the wise are in his head”; they will have this crown and be protected by this diadem, so that they may always rejoice and praise the Lord, because joys will have succeeded pain, sorrow, and groaning.

#### Verses 12–13

“I, I myself will comfort you. Who are you, that you should fear a mortal human being, and a son of man who will wither like grass? And you have forgotten God your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and founded the earth; and you have continually feared all day long before the face of the fury of him who afflicted you and prepared himself to destroy you. Where now is the fury of the one who afflicts you? Soon he will come, striding forth to open, and he will not kill to the point of annihilation; nor will his bread fail.

“But I am the Lord your God, who troubles the sea, so that its waves swell; the Lord of hosts is my name. I have placed my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, so that you may plant the heavens and found [Note: The erroneous reading was “pour out” (*effundas*).] the earth, and say to Zion: ‘You are my people.’”

The Septuagint reads:

“I am, I am he who comforts you. Know who you were and whom you feared: a mortal human being and a son of man, who have withered like grass. And you have forgotten God your Maker, who made heaven and founded the earth; and you were always afraid, all your days, of the face of the fury of the one who afflicted you, as he planned to remove you. And now where is the fury of the one who afflicts you? For when you have been saved, he will not stand or remain [lacuna]; he will not kill unto corruption, and his bread will not fail [lacuna]. For I am your God, who troubles the sea and makes its waves resound. The Lord Sabaoth is my name. I will place my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you, in which I established heaven and founded earth; and he will say to Zion, ‘You are my people.’”

The people of believers, who had entreated the arm of the Lord—which is itself the power of God and the wisdom of God—to arise and provide them aid, so that while it fought for the saints they might possess joy and gladness once pain and groaning had been put to flight, now receive the answer.

Thus either the arm of the Lord or the Lord himself replied:

“I am, I am; and I will comfort you myself, not through the prophets: the God of mercies and the Father of all consolation.”

I wonder, however, how it is that, when I had said above, “Do not fear the reproach of human beings, and do not dread their blasphemies,” you feared the rage of your persecutors and did not know that they were mortal, withering suddenly like hay and perishing.

Certainly, at the time when you feared them, you had forgotten the Lord your Maker. For if the memory of me had always remained in your heart, you would never have feared human beings, who are to be dissolved into ashes.

And whom did you forget? God, who by his immeasurable power suspended the heavens and founded the earth upon a stable mass.

You feared your adversaries, not for a short time—a fear that might have been conceded to you in some measure—but continually and all day long, so that although you possessed the light of faith, the darkness of fear possessed you, and you feared the one who thought you were going to perish.

Where, then, is the arrogance of the persecutors? Where is the secular power by which, with rabid mouth, they raged against you?

“Soon my Son will come,” he says, “striding forth and trampling down your adversaries, to open for you the way of victory,” or to open the underworld. He will not kill unto annihilation, but will wish to save those who have turned back.

Finally, his bread—which, as the Gospel proves, is interpreted as doctrine—will never fail, but will always be open to those who wish to eat.

At the same time he turns his speech toward the Son, whom he promises will soon come and whose bread he says is everlasting. According to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, he is himself the Lord his God, who makes the sea troubled and its waves swell, so that the arrogance of the persecutors may be puffed up against his servants and then, with the Lord’s help, subside again.

He says also that he has placed his words in his mouth. Whatever the Son speaks is the Father’s words. And he protected him in the shadow of his hand.

He was protected for this reason: so that he might plant new heavens, found a new earth, and say to Zion—that is, to the Church—“You are my people.”

Therefore Zion is none other than the people of God.

In the passage where we said, according to the Hebrew, “Soon he will come, striding forth to open, and he will not kill unto annihilation,” Symmachus translated:

“Soon the underworld will be opened, and he will not die unto corruption,” with “Christ” understood. In the fifteenth psalm he says: “You will not abandon my soul in the underworld, nor will you allow your holy one to see corruption.”

In the passage where, according to the Hebrew and Aquila, we translated, “I have placed my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I have protected you, so that you may plant the heavens and found the earth, and say to Zion, ‘You are my people,’” he translated as follows:

“I will place my words in your mouth, and in the shadow of my hand I will protect you, in which I planted heaven and founded earth, and so that I may say to Zion, ‘You are my people.’”

According to the Septuagint, this is addressed to every soul of believers, because although created in the image and likeness of God, it has failed to recognize its dignity. Instead, it feared a human being and a son of man, who can kill only the body, and did not know that it was immortal, nor did it say with the Prophet:

“The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the protector of my life; from whom shall I tremble?” (Psalm XXVI, 1–2).

And again:

“The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what a human being can do to me. The Lord is my helper, and I will look down upon my enemies” (Psalm CXVII, 6–7).

What a human being is is demonstrated by another verse:

“I will hope in the Lord; I will not fear what flesh can do to me” (Psalm LV, 5).

Hence it is now said: “You feared a mortal human being and a son of man, who have withered like grass.”

“For all flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass” (Isaiah XL). Terrified by the power of the judge, you forgot that he himself was your protector, who made heaven and earth and all the elements that we see—or those heavens which bear the image of the heavenly, and that earth which multiplies the Lord’s seed.

The statement above, “He will not kill unto corruption, and his bread will not fail,” has been added from Theodotion’s edition, from the Hebrew. [Col. 0490C]

He himself troubles the sea and makes its waves resound; of him it is sung also in the Psalms: “You rule the power of the sea; you still the swelling of its waves” (Psalm LXXXVIII, 10).

It is also written in Jeremiah: “Will you not fear me, says the Lord, and not tremble before my face, who set the sands as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting commandment which will not pass away?” (Jeremiah V, 22).

The seas were troubled when the Lord’s dragnet drew out a multitude of fish (Matthew XIII).

The Lord placed his words in the mouth of the believer and protected him in the shadow of his hand. He also says in the Gospel:

“When they hand you over, do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew X, 19–20).

And elsewhere he says to the righteous: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm LXXX, 12).

Again: “Open your mouth with the word of God; for the Lord will give speech to those who evangelize with great power.”

Hence God speaks to the inner person of Jeremiah, after touching his mouth: “Behold, I have given my words into your mouth” (Jeremiah I, 9). He could sing with the Psalmist: “He put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Psalm XXXIX, 4).

Who, then, has done all these things except the Lord and Savior, who made heaven and earth and says to Zion, “You are my people”?

This properly applies to the Church gathered from the nations. In Hosea he promises this to believers, saying: “I will call ‘Not my people,’ ‘My people’; and he will say to me, ‘You are my God’” (Hosea II, 24).

### (Verses 17 ff.) [Cols. 0491B–0492D; pp. 596–597]

“Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his wrath. You have drunk the cup of stupor to the very bottom, and you have drained it to the dregs. There is no one to support her, among all the sons whom she has begotten; and there is no one to grasp her hand, among all the sons whom she has raised. Two things have confronted you—who will grieve over you? Desolation and ruin, famine and sword—who will console you?”

**Note:** In the Ambrosian manuscript: “There is no one to raise her up from among you, her sons,” etc.

The Septuagint has: “Arise, arise; lift yourself up, Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury. For you have drunk to the dregs and emptied the cup of ruin, κόνδυ, of fury; and there was no one to console you among all your sons whom you begot; and there was no one to grasp your hand, neither among all your sons whom you exalted. These two contrary things have happened to you—who will grieve with you? Ruin and destruction, famine and sword—who will console you?”

I have often shown that Jerusalem and Zion are a *dyōnymon* (δυώνυμον), that is, a place with two names. Of these, Zion—which is interpreted as “watchtower,” because it is situated on a mountain—is called the citadel; the remaining part of the city, however, is called Jerusalem. It was previously called Jebus and Salem. The Prophet now exhorts it to rise, since it had previously fallen through denial, saying during the Lord’s Passion: “Crucify, crucify such a man! We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). He exhorts it to repent and to experience the evils of captivity, because it offended its Creator.

Physicians commonly give a very bitter antidote—whose name derives from its taste—to a nauseated stomach, so that it may vomit out harmful humors and be able to pass cooked and digested foods into the bowels, which the quantity of phlegm had prevented it from digesting. Likewise, Jerusalem, which drank from the cup of the Lord’s fury and from his κόνδυ, which Symmachus translated as “mixing bowl,” and which, according to the Book of Genesis, Joseph ordered to be hidden in the sack of his brother Benjamin (Genesis 44), is commanded to rise from its drunkenness, because it drank, emptied, and drained the cup to the dregs. These three expressions indicate the same thing in one statement: Ἐξεστράγγισας—“you drained completely.”

**Note:** Up to this point, Ἐξεστράπησας had been transmitted erroneously in place of Ἐξεστράγγισας; we restored the latter from an older Ambrosian manuscript. Montfaucon also noted it, and the authority of Procopius’s commentary on Isaiah confirms this reading. The word occurs frequently among the Greek interpreters. It means “you drained completely.”

This is the cup of which we read in the Psalms: “A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine. He poured from this into that; yet its dregs were not emptied: all the sinners of the earth shall drink” (Psalm 74:9–10).

God also says to Jeremiah concerning this cup: “Take the cup of unmixed wine from my hand, and you shall give it to all the nations to which I send you. And they shall drink, vomit, and become mad because of the sword which I shall send among them” (Jeremiah 25:15–16). And when he says that he has given it to the other nations, to Jerusalem, and to the cities of Judah, he adds: “Thus says the Lord Almighty, the God of Israel: Drink, become drunk, and vomit; fall before the sword which I shall send among you” (Jeremiah 25:27).

It must be observed that this cup of the Lord’s fury is his sword, which is sent into the midst of sinners. Here a question arises: how, after drinking, drunkenness, vomiting, and falling, is Jerusalem said in Jeremiah to be unable to rise, while Isaiah now speaks to it: “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem”? The answer is this: as long as someone is drinking the cup, becoming drunk and deranged, vomiting, and collapsing, he cannot rise, for he has not yet drained the Lord’s cup, nor reached the dregs, so as to have drunk it to the bottom. But here he speaks to Jerusalem of the past: “You who have drunk from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury,” not “you who are drinking.”

At the same time, it must be considered that from that time onward there was neither prophet nor apostle in Judea who consoled Jerusalem, grasped its hand, and raised it when it lay fallen. It is therefore clear that these words refer to the period after the final captivity. Otherwise, history tells us that during and after Babylon it had Ezekiel and the other prophets.

As for the statement, “Two things have confronted you,” or, “These two contrary things have happened to you—who will grieve over you?” and then, instead of two, four are introduced—“desolation and ruin, famine and sword”—it resembles what is sung in the Psalter:

“God has spoken once; I have heard these two things: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, belongs mercy; for you will repay each according to his works” (Psalm 61:12–13).

There also God speaks once, saying that he is almighty, while the Prophet hears two things: that his omnipotence prevails in both directions, so that he grants mercy to the penitent and repays those who persist in sin with the punishments they deserve.

In accordance with this, two things have also confronted Jerusalem elsewhere, each of which has two aspects. Ruin, or desolation, is followed by destruction; famine is followed by the sword of death.

**Note:** More accurately, one Ambrosian manuscript reads, “which is sung in the Psalm: ‘Once,’ etc.” The remainder entered the text from the margin.

We can also understand these things allegorically of the sinful soul, which, unwilling to drink the cup of the Lord’s fury, says in the Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Psalm 6:1). But if it drinks, it is good for it to experience its punishments and to hear the Lord saying: “When the anger of my fury has passed, I will heal again.” And elsewhere: “Does one who falls not rise again?” says the Lord (Jeremiah 8:4).

### (Verse 20) [Cols. 0492D–0494D; p. 598]

“Your sons have been cast down; they have slept at the head of every road, like a snared oryx, full of the indignation of the Lord, the rebuke of your God.”

The Septuagint has: “Your sons are needy and sleeping at the head of every road, like a half-cooked beet, full of the fury of the Lord and failing because of the Lord God.”

In place of “half-cooked beet,” the other interpreters translated “an oryx captured and snared.” In Hebrew it is called **THO**, a species of beast born in the wilderness and counted among the clean animals.

**Note:** Ambrosian manuscripts read “among the unclean animals.” Martianay also noted that *Tho* is numbered among the clean animals in Deuteronomy 14:5. A little later, the same manuscript has *Thorib* as two words in place of *Thoreth*.

**Note:** The word *Tho* does not occur in Leviticus but in Deuteronomy 14:5. Nor did Saint Jerome intend to say this: rather, the animal called *Tho*—that is, the oryx or wild ox, which chews the cud and has a divided hoof—is numbered among the clean animals in Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14. Jerome teaches us that the Syrians call the beet *Thoreth*, though I was unable to find this word in the *Pentaglot Lexicon*. —MARTIANAY.

Instead of this, the Septuagint, in the Syrian language, supposed *thoreth*, which means “beet.”

Let us pass from the name to the meaning. Your sons, like an oryx entangled in hunters’ snares, have slept in the crossroads and streets; laying their naked limbs upon the bare earth, they have manifested through their own miseries the indignation of the Lord and the rebuke of their God.

According to the Septuagint, those who refuse to possess spiritual riches in every word, knowledge, and good work, but are poor and unable to endure the threat, will by no means dwell in houses built of virtues. Rather, they will remain at the beginnings of roads and, touching everything at the exit, will abandon everything. They are rightly said to sleep with that sleep of which it is written: “They slept their sleep and found nothing” (Psalm 75:6). The king of the Assyrians lulled them into this sleep.

They are compared to half-cooked beets, a vegetable of the lowest quality and extreme fragility. I think the following passage in the Psalms refers to such vegetables: “Do not be jealous of evildoers, nor envy those who practice iniquity. For they will quickly dry up like grass, and like the vegetables of herbs they will quickly wither” (Psalm 36:1–2). It is food for the sick.

Someone who is simply unbelieving is called an uncooked beet. One who, content with a simple faith and without reason or the truth of doctrines, performs works of righteousness may be called a cooked beet. But one who wavers between vices and virtues, and approaches the service of God with a divided heart, is most rightly called a half-cooked beet. To him God also speaks in the Apocalypse of John: “Would that you were either hot or cold! But because you are lukewarm, I will vomit you out” (Revelation 3:15–16).

Those who are lukewarm and sleeping are full of the Lord’s fury, and are dissolved or fail through the Lord God. This does not mean that the Lord is the cause of their dissolution, since he did not make death and does not delight in the destruction of the living. Rather, those who have sinned under the Law are judged through the Law, which works wrath against those who are its transgressors.

### (Verses 21 ff.) [Cols. 0493D–0494D; pp. 599–600]

“Therefore hear this, poor one and drunk, but not from wine. Thus says your Lord, the Lord and your God, who fought for his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of stupor, the bottom of the cup of my indignation; you shall not continue to drink it any longer. And I will place it in the hand of those who humbled you, who said to your soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you’; and you placed your body like the ground, and like a road for those passing over you.”

The Septuagint has: “Therefore hear this, humbled one and drunk, but not from wine. Thus says the Lord God who judges his people: Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of ruin, the κόνδυ of my fury; you shall not continue to drink it any longer. And I will give it into the hands of those who unjustly oppressed and humbled you, who said to your soul, ‘Bend down, so that we may pass over you’; and you made your middle parts level with the ground for those passing outside.”

O Jerusalem, to which I said, “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, and repent,” because you drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury and drained it to the dregs, and your sons—scattered throughout the whole world and led away captive—lay in the streets and at the heads of the roads: know that you are poor, humbled, and drunk, not with wine but with the fury of the Lord.

Therefore, if you repent and, having been lifted up, arise, you will know that the cup of stupor and ruin—or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, of laceration and disturbance—is to be taken from your hand. And the κόνδυ, which Symmachus here too translated as “mixing bowl,” you will no longer drink; rather, it is to be handed over to your adversaries, who said to your soul, “Bend down, so that we may pass over you.” When they said this, you bent down of your own will. And you placed your body, or your back, like the ground—or, according to the Septuagint, your middle parts and your necks—for those passing outside.

This may be understood historically: if Jerusalem wishes to lift itself up and arise, it must no longer drink the cup of the Lord’s fury or suffer what it previously endured.

But, to proceed according to the Septuagint toward the spiritual meaning, this is said of the soul humbled by vices and drunk with disturbances, so that it may know that the Lord is its judge and that it must render an account of everything. If it turns toward better things, the cup of ruin must be taken from its hands, as must the mixing bowl of the Lord’s fury, which contained punishments. Ezekiel also says of this to Jerusalem: “You shall drink the cup of your sister Samaria, deep and broad, so that you may become drunk” (Ezekiel 23:32).

This cup is to be handed over into the hands of those who had humbled it. There is no doubt that this signifies hostile powers, which said to its soul, “Bend down, so that we may pass over you.” At the same time, it must be noted that they did not bend it down or use force, so that it might first stand upright and then be bent toward the earth; rather, they left it to its own will. It was by its own choice that it placed its neck, back, or entire body—not inside but outside—for those who trampled upon it.

We read something similar in the Gospel (Luke 13): Satan had bent a woman over for eighteen years, but the Lord restored her to her former posture, so that she could say: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where help will come to me” (Psalm 120:1); and, “To you I lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 122:1).

### (Chapter 52, verse 1)

“Arise, arise; clothe yourself with your strength, Zion; clothe yourself in the garments of your glory, Jerusalem, city of the Holy One, for the uncircumcised and the unclean shall no longer pass through you.”

The Septuagint has: “Arise, arise, Zion; clothe yourself with your strength, Zion, and clothe yourself with your glory, Jerusalem, holy city. The uncircumcised and the unclean shall by no means continue to pass through you.”

Here again the name Zion has been added by the Septuagint, as above, and therefore the obelus has been placed before it. To the one whom he had said above, “Lift yourself up, lift yourself up; arise, Jerusalem” (chapter 51:9), he now speaks the same words: “Arise, arise; clothe yourself with your strength, Zion.”

The following verse shows who Zion is: “Clothe yourself in the garments of your glory, Jerusalem.” We have said this to prove that Jerusalem and Zion are one city. It is commanded to lay aside its mourning garments and to clothe itself in those which it possessed before it drank from the hand of the Lord the cup of his fury.

It is called the city of the sanctuary, for this is what *CODES* means, on account of the temple that was built in it. Or it is called “of the Holy One” because of the knowledge of God; or “holy,” because it alone in the world had received the Law. Hence, after the resurrection of the Savior, the bodies of the dead appeared in the holy city. Certainly, because of its blasphemy and the hands stretched out against the Lord, it could not truly be holy (Matthew 27).

The promise that, if it rises after its fall and is clothed in its strength and glory, the uncircumcised and unclean shall no longer pass through it signifies what the Apostle Paul also says: “What fellowship has righteousness with iniquity? What communion has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? What portion has a believer with an unbeliever? What agreement has the temple of God with idols?” (1 Corinthians 6:14–15).

As we have begun to explain, all these things may also be referred to the condition of the soul. If, through repentance, it recovers its former strength, let it be called the dwelling place of the Holy One and become the temple of God, and let no uncircumcised and unclean λογισμός—“thought”—pass through it.

Concerning these things it is said: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden sins, and spare your servant from those belonging to others. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless, and I shall be cleansed from the greatest offense” (Psalm 18:13–14).

All the things promised to Zion and Jerusalem are not spoken, as the Jews dream, of those stones, ashes, and embers, as though the city were to be restored to its former condition. Rather, they are spoken of the people of Jerusalem, who killed the Prophets and stoned those who were sent to them (Matthew 23), and finally also laid hands upon the Son of God. Having fallen in the Passion of Christ, it was raised in his resurrection, when many thousands of Jews believed and the remnant was saved.

We can say the same about the Church, which is both “vision of peace” and “watchtower.” If it falls into heresy, it is commanded to come out and take up again the ornaments of its former faith. And if it is raised up, the rewards of holiness and continence are promised to it, so that no uncircumcised and unclean thing may pass through it.

This does not refer to the cutting of the flesh and the foreskin, but to the uncleanness or purity of works, so that we call uncircumcised and unclean those who serve bodily pleasure and lust.

Thus Jeremiah speaks to those circumcised in the flesh but not in spirit: “All the nations are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the sons of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts” (Jeremiah 9:26).

And the blessed Apostle, discussing virginity, continence, and marriage, inserted this statement: “Was anyone called circumcised? Let him not draw back his foreskin. Was anyone called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised” (1 Corinthians 7:18).

It seems to me that he says the same thing in other words: “Was someone called without a wife, and did he believe? Let him not take a wife.” Or conversely: “Someone who had a wife believed in Christ; let him by no means divorce her.”

He preserves this meaning not only in circumcision and uncircumcision but also in freedom and servitude, calling virgins and the continent “free,” and those who render to their wives the debt owed to them “slaves.” For it is not within our power to draw back the foreskin after circumcision, according to those who are said in the Book of Maccabees to have made foreskins for themselves—though this concerns children at birth, not fathers.

Or he who was called free is rather Christ’s slave, although in Christ’s baptism there is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, Greek and Barbarian, man and woman, free and slave (ibid., 7:22).

**Note:** Jerome was evidently unaware of the procedure of restoring the foreskin. Accordingly, he denies that this can be done and twists the Apostle’s meaning into an allegory. See also Book 1 of *Against Jovinianus*, no. 21, where, speaking of the circumcision repeated by Joshua, he says: “For if we understand that literally, it cannot stand at all, since the skin, once cut away, does not grow again.” Shortly afterward he also inadequately explains away what is written in the Books of the Maccabees about the sons of Tobias, namely, that they made foreskins for themselves so as to be like the Greeks.

Josephus, however, a most reliable authority, clearly states that Menelaus and the sons of Tobias, when they went to Antiochus, “ἀπεκάλυψαν τὴν τῶν αἰδοίων περιτομήν, ὡς ἂν εἶεν καὶ περὶ τὴν ἀπόδυσιν Ἕλληνες”—“they undid the circumcision of their private parts, so that, even in being naked, they might be like the Greeks.”

Nor do the Hebrews themselves deny this; they attribute the invention of the procedure to Esau. I say nothing of the testimony of the celebrated physicians, both ancient—Celsus, Book 7, chapter 25; Galen, *Method of Medicine*, Book 14, chapter 16; Dioscorides, Book 3, chapter 51—and more recent, whose testimonies we recorded in our notes on the cited passage from *Against Jovinianus*.

### (Verses 2–3) [Cols. 0496B–0497C; pp. 602–603]

“Shake yourself free from the dust; arise, sit up, Jerusalem. Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and without silver you shall be redeemed.”

The Septuagint has: “Shake off the dust and arise, Jerusalem. Loose the bond of your neck, captive daughter of Zion. For thus says the Lord: You were sold for nothing, and without money you shall be redeemed.”

The following verse shows that the Prophet’s speech is not addressed to Jerusalem—that is, to the ruins of its stones, ashes, and embers—but to the people who dwell in it; and it shows why the people are called “daughter,” on account of the effeminacy of their spirit: “Loose the bonds of your neck, captive daughter of Zion.”

The Jewish people truly are captive. To this day they bear the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar and are bound by the cords of their sins and blasphemies. They were sold for nothing and did nothing deserving by which they could be redeemed.

To them it is also said above: “Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and in your iniquities I dismissed your mother.” He gives the reasons why they were sold and why they were rejected: “Because I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who heard.”

From this it is clear that they were handed over to error and demons because they had not listened to the one crying: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11:28).

Those who wish to believe will be redeemed—not with silver or money, but with the precious blood of Christ—so that they may hear through the Apostles: “Grace to you and peace” (Romans 1:7). We have not been reconciled to God because of our merits, but because of the grace and faith of Christ.

The same is said of the soul that, polluted by the filth of its vices, had lost the brightness of its former way of life: let it shake off the dust that clung to its feet, as the Apostles did (Matthew 10).

For it could not be that one who had prostrated itself and exposed its neck to those passing outside, had joined its middle parts to the earth, and had said, “My soul has been humbled in the dust; my belly has clung to the earth” (Psalm 43:25), had not received the image of the earthly.

The Apostle recalls us from this condition, saying: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, so let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

Hence those who are in the flesh cannot please God (Romans 8). This does not mean that the nature of the flesh is condemned, for God is its creator, and many have pleased God in the flesh and now reign with Christ. Rather, it means that the works of the flesh are rejected, concerning which the same Apostle says: “But I am carnal, sold under sin” (Romans 7:14).

Finally, to such people he says: “Where there is jealousy and rivalry among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human standards?” (1 Corinthians 3:3).

Conversely, he says to the saints: “But you are not in the flesh, since the Spirit of God dwells in you.”

Therefore the dust is shaken off, of which it is written: “Will the dust confess to you, or announce your truth?” (Psalm 29:10), so that the bonds of our necks may be loosed and we may no longer hear: “Your neck is an iron sinew.” Instead, with the bride, may we deserve to hear: “How beautiful are your cheeks, like those of a dove; your neck is like necklaces” (Song of Songs 1:9).

And again: “I surrounded your hands with bracelets and your neck with a necklace.” Thus, freed from a heavy burden and receiving our former ornaments, we may cease to be captives—redeemed by the one who came to proclaim release to captives.

Of him it is written above (45:13): “He will build my city and restore the captivity of my people, not with a price or with gifts.”

The Apostle Peter agrees with this meaning: “Knowing that you were redeemed from your empty way of life, handed down from your ancestors, not with corruptible silver and gold, but with the blood of an unblemished lamb” (1 Peter 1:18).

### (Verses 4 ff.) [Cols. 0497D–0499D; pp. 604–606]

“For thus says the Lord God: My people went down into Egypt at the beginning, to dwell there as a colonist; and Assyria oppressed him without cause. And now, what have I here? says the Lord. For my people have been taken away for nothing; their rulers act unjustly, says the Lord, and my name is continually blasphemed all day long. Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, for I am the very one who was speaking—behold, here I am.”

The Septuagint has: “For thus says the Lord: My people first went down into Egypt to sojourn there, and they were violently carried away to the Assyrians. And now, what will happen here? says the Lord. For my people have been taken away; for nothing you admire and howl. Thus says the Lord: Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations. Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, for I am the very one who was speaking; I am present.”

He rebukes the Jewish people and foretells what is to come. Those who voluntarily went down with Jacob to the Egyptians and, in a time of necessity and famine, sojourned in the land of Goshen (Genesis 47) later suffered oppression from the Assyrians, whom they had injured in no way, and were carried away captive to Babylon (4 Kings 17:25).

Therefore he adds: “And now, what have I here? says the Lord.” The meaning is: I have nothing remaining that would cause me to remain in this region, from which my people have been taken away for nothing, sold to their sins, and, like an oryx caught in a net, seized either by the strength of the Romans or by the snares of the devil, by which they have been bound and held until now.

They suffered these things because their rulers and teachers acted unjustly. According to Symmachus and Theodotion, they will howl; according to Aquila, they will weep, when they have been handed over to torments.

They themselves are the ones who stirred up the people against the Savior, so that they cried out with one voice: “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (John 19:15).
