Concerning them he had already said: “The Lord himself will come with the elders of the people and with its rulers. But why have you set my vineyard ablaze and taken the spoil of the poor into your houses?” (Isaiah 3:14).

Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he says to them: “Because of you my name is continually blasphemed among the nations.”

It must be understood that “among the nations” is not found in the Hebrew, but that the text simply reads, “My name is continually blasphemed,” with “in your synagogues” understood. Day and night they blaspheme the Savior and, under the name—as I have often said—of Nazarenes, heap curses upon Christians three times a day.

While they blaspheme and curse the Lord, his people—of whom we have already spoken frequently, namely, the Christian people—will know the name of the one who is to come in the name of the Father.

They will know it because the very one who formerly spoke through the Prophets will teach the peoples by his presence.

According to the Septuagint, God says to Israel that it went down into Egypt voluntarily. Moses says in Deuteronomy: “Your fathers went down into Egypt with seventy souls” (Deuteronomy 10:22), and they were violently carried away captive by the Assyrians.

Therefore it is said to them: “And now, what are you doing here? What are you doing in the land of Judea, you who, after the murder of the Prophets, laid hands on the Son of God?”

Or else God speaks to the angelic powers and the angels who preside over the Temple: “What are you doing here? Why do you not leave the blaspheming people?” Josephus also reports this (*Jewish Antiquities*, Book 6, chapter 12): when the doors of the Temple suddenly opened and were spontaneously unbarred—though many men could scarcely close them—a voice was heard from the inner sanctuary saying, “Let us pass from these dwellings.”

In this we must consider the precision of the wording: they did not say, “Let us withdraw,” but “Let us pass over to the people of the nations.”

Hence the veil of the Temple was torn from top to bottom into two parts, so that all the ceremonies of the Jews might be exposed, and so that what is said in this same Prophet might be fulfilled: “From Zion the Law shall go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. And he shall judge among many nations, even to the farthest places” (Isaiah 2:3–4).

“For their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 18).

And in every place incense and a pure sacrifice are offered to God (Micah 3), when the prophetic word has been fulfilled: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and return to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:28 ff.).

Therefore he says to the rulers of the Jews: “Admire and howl, because you are the cause of the people’s ruin.”

According to the allegorical meaning, we can say that God’s people descend into the Egypt of this age by their own will when they are lovers of pleasures more than of God and do not heed the prophetic word: “Woe to those who go down into Egypt for help” (Isaiah 31:1).

When such a person has been enticed by vices and dwells in a place of waters and rivers, where there is no dryness of chastity, then he will be violently handed over to the Assyrians, so that they may rule over him and afterward accuse and convict him of sin.

These are both enemies and avengers, concerning whom he says to Israel: “And now, what have you to do with the way of Egypt, to drink the water of Gihon? And what have you to do with the way of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the rivers?” (Jeremiah 2:18).

Therefore, whoever has descended into Egypt and fallen from the heights of Jerusalem to lower things, and, going to Jericho—another Egypt—has received many wounds from robbers, is told: “And now, what are you doing here? What are you doing in the land and in the Church of God, pretending to be there, when with zeal and every desire you have descended into Egypt and are possessed and captured by the Assyrians? You ought rather to howl and mourn, because on account of your vices and sins the name of God is blasphemed among the nations.”

To them it is said in Ezekiel: “You profaned my name among the nations” (Ezekiel 36:20).

And just as the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16), so conversely, when we perform evil works, the name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of us.

Therefore whoever possesses knowledge of the name of God, and knows that he was created in God’s image and likeness, will live in the light.

He will be in the day of which Abraham rejoiced that he had seen it (John 8), and of which the holy David also says: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalm 117:24).

Those who have illuminated themselves with the light of knowledge and possess the everlasting light promised to believers—“The Lord will be your everlasting light” (Isaiah 60:20)—walk honorably in the day and are children of light and of the day.

They know the one who says to Moses: “Go, say to the children of Israel, ‘The One who is has sent me’” (Exodus 3:14); and they will recognize that the one whom they had previously known among the holy ones is also present with them.

(Verses 7–8.) How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace, who announces good things, proclaims salvation, and says to Zion, “Your God will reign” [Alternative: “has reigned”]. The voice of your watchmen: they have raised their voice; together they will praise, because they will see eye to eye when the Lord has restored Zion.

The Septuagint: “As an hour upon the mountains, so are the feet of him who evangelizes the report of peace, who evangelizes good things; for I will make my salvation heard,” saying, “Zion, your God will reign.” The voice of those guarding you has been exalted, and together they will rejoice with their voice, because they will see eye to eye when the Lord has had mercy on Zion.

Consequently, concerning him who above had said, “I myself, who was speaking, behold, I am here,” the Prophet now testifies that he himself proclaimed the Gospel upon the mountains—that is, upon the Apostles, of whom it is written, “Draw near to the everlasting mountains” (Micah 2:9, according to the Septuagint), and whose teaching is the illumination of God. Hence it is said to him in the Psalms: “Illuminating wondrously from the everlasting mountains” (Psalm 75:5).

He announced and proclaimed peace to those who were far away—that is, to the Gentiles—and to those who were near, namely, the Jews, reconciling the world to God. Concerning this, under Solomon’s name, the Psalm sings: “In his days righteousness shall arise, and an abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away” (Psalm 71:7). And in this same Prophet, concerning the child who was born and the son who was given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulder and who will be called the Angel of the Great Counsel, it is said after the other things (above, 9:7): “And of his peace there shall be no end.”

For he himself is our peace, who made peace through the blood of his cross, both in heaven and on earth. He is the one who said to the Apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27).

And he announced good things to us—not those which the Philosophers call indifferent, but those which are truly good, which the Father gives to those who ask him, namely, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Accordingly, another Evangelist writes in the same place: “How much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11:13).

These are the good things that the Lord promises to believers: “Hear me, and you shall eat good things; and your soul shall delight in good things.” And he announced not only good things, but salvation to all—the salvation provided by him who says to Zion, that is, to the Church: “Your God will reign” [Alternative: “has reigned”].

Hence the Apostle also says to the saints: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Romans 6:12). And, writing about sinners, he says: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses” (Romans 5:14).

What follows—“The voice of your watchmen,” or “of your guardians”—signifies the Apostles, concerning whom God also speaks elsewhere to the Church (below, 62:6): “Upon your walls I have appointed guardians, who shall never be silent, remembering the Lord,” who will raise their voice, speaking from the heights.

Hence it is said to them (above, 40:9): “Ascend upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion. Lift up your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem.”

These will praise God with one voice, and they will see eye to eye. The Apostle expresses this in other words: “Face to face” (1 Corinthians 13). At that time the saint sings: “My eyes are always toward the Lord” (Psalm 24:15), and: “To you I have lifted up my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 20:1). And the Lord will answer him: “For the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayer” (Psalm 33:16).

What the Septuagint translated as “as ὥρα, that is, an hour, upon the mountains, so are the feet of him who evangelizes the report of peace,” and the rest, Paul, following the sense of the Hebrew Truth, places in his Epistle to the Romans: “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize good things, who evangelize peace” (Romans 10:15). He wishes the Apostles to be understood—those whose feet the Lord washed (John 13), so that they might be clean and beautiful for preaching and might travel throughout the whole world, filling it in a short time with the teaching of Christ.

Now ὥρα, that is, “hour,” according to the Septuagint and the ambiguity of the Greek expression, signifies either time or beauty. If it means “time,” the following passage will suit it: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you” (Isaiah 49:8). Hence the Apostle concludes: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

For at the opportune time he poured out his blood on behalf of all, when all had turned aside and together had become useless. “There was none who did good, not even one” (Psalm 13), so that he might taste death for all, because all had sinned and lacked the glory of God (Romans 3).

But if we refer it to beauty, in accordance with what is said in the Psalm, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3)—for what is more beautiful than that the form of a servant should become the form of God, and that he should sit and reign with Christ in the heavenly places?—then, according to the breadth of the Greek language, ὥρα may be understood as care and solicitude, in accordance with what the saint says: “You will multiply me in my soul, in your strength” (Psalm 137:4).

For “you will multiply me,” the Greek has πολυωρήσεις με, meaning, “You will consider me worthy of much care and solicitude.” And elsewhere: “According to your greatness, ἐπολυώρησας the sons of men” (Psalm 11:9), which in Greek is expressed in other words as πολλῆς ὤρας, that is, “you considered them worthy of much care”—that is, of solicitude.

**Note:** Until now the Vulgate had τὴν ὤραν ὠράσω, with a very tangled sense and no regard for what follows. We have restored from the Ambrosian manuscript πολλῆς ὤρας as the third expression, which is absent from the manuscripts and had caused difficulty, deleting the offending word. A true and harmonious sense thereby emerges: “you made them worthy of much care,” that is, of solicitude.

But these matters are superfluous. The feet of Christ, or of the Apostles, are to be understood as beautiful, since, apart from the Septuagint, all the translators rendered the passage similarly, and Paul approved their interpretation.

(Verses 9–10.) Rejoice and praise together, desolate Jerusalem, because the Lord has comforted his people; he has redeemed Jerusalem. The Lord has prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the nations, and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

The Septuagint: “Let the desolate places of Jerusalem burst forth together in joy, because the Lord has had mercy on her and has delivered Jerusalem. The Lord will reveal his holy arm in the sight of all the nations. And all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.”

After the Jewish people had been led into captivity and the city had been burned, Jerusalem had few, or no, inhabitants. But after he who had previously spoken through the Prophets, who was in the beginning with God—God the Word—dwelt among us and became flesh, the desolate places of Jerusalem were restored. He came of whom it is written: “He will build my city, and he will bring back the captivity of my people,” so that Jeremiah’s lament would no longer be heard: “How the city that was full of peoples sits alone; she has become like a widow, though she was multiplied among the nations” (Lamentations 1:1). Instead, she hears David singing: “When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted” (Psalm 125:1, 4). A little later: “We became rejoicing.”

And so that we may know that these words are spoken not about the Jewish people but about all who through the Apostles would believe in the Lord, he adds and says that the one who comforted her, or had mercy on her, and who delivered or redeemed her, himself prepared, or revealed, his holy arm in the sight of all the nations; and all the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God.

It is therefore clear that, after spiritual Jerusalem—that is, the Church, which had been abandoned by the Jews—was built through the Apostles, the Lord’s arm was revealed to all the nations, and all the ends of the earth saw his salvation.

This is understood in two ways. Either the Father reveals his arm to all the nations, or the Son reveals his strength. Concerning him it is written: “Power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke 6:19). And again: “I perceived that power had gone out from me, which healed the woman with the flow of blood” (Mark 5:30).

That the Son of God is called the Father’s right hand and arm is supported by many testimonies, of which we shall mention a few: “His right hand and his holy arm saved him” (Psalm 97:2). And elsewhere: “In my arm the nations will hope” (Isaiah 51:5). Concerning this Jacob says: “He will be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10). And the eighty-eighth Psalm: “Your arm with power.”

By this arm the Lord led the people of Israel out of the land of Egypt. Concerning this he spoke to the chief of the Apostles: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17).

And the Apostle Paul says of himself (Galatians 1:15): “When it pleased God, who separated me from my mother’s womb, to reveal his Son in me.”

By joining all the ends of the earth with all the nations that will see the salvation of God, he shows what is also said elsewhere: “Turn to me from the ends of the earth, and you shall be saved” (Isaiah 45:22); and through Jeremiah: “The nations shall come to you from the ends of the earth” (Jeremiah 16:19); and again: “All the families of the nations shall remember and turn to the Lord, because the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule the nations” (Psalm 21:28 and following). Thus it is foretold that not only the diversity of individual nations but also all the quarters of the world will believe in Christ.

This agrees with his own words: “When this Gospel has been preached throughout the whole world, then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14).

Others wish the summits and ends of the earth to be understood as those who do not stand in the middle of the earth but, stationed at its outermost boundaries like the ends of wheels, abandon lowly things and hasten toward what is exalted.

[Col. 0503A] (Verses 11–13.) Depart, depart, go out from there; do not touch what is polluted. Go out from its midst; purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord. For you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight. For the Lord will go before you, and the God of Israel will gather you.

The Septuagint: “Depart, depart, go out from there, and do not touch what is unclean. Go out from its midst; separate yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the Lord, because you shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you go in flight. But the Lord will go before you, and the one who gathers you is the God of Israel.”

The Jews attempt to explain this passage as follows: “Go out from Babylon, and abandon their idols. Go out from its midst, and bring back to the Temple the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried away when he captured Jerusalem” (2 Kings 15), when Cyrus released the captives under Zerubbabel and Ezra (Ezra 1). Do not leave Babylon as you previously fled from Egypt, amid tumult and fear, but with peace and with the consent of the king of the Persians and Medes, in which the Lord’s will appeared: he protected and gathered you.

Others interpret what we have said about Babylon as referring to the Roman kingdom, maintaining that all these things will be fulfilled at the coming of Christ, who will liberate them.

But we, hearing above, “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who announces and proclaims peace,” and, “The Lord will reveal his arm in the sight of all the nations,” and, “All the ends of the earth shall see the salvation of our God,” understand this not at all of the Jews but of the chorus of all the Apostles and Saints.

They are commanded to depart from Jerusalem and preach the Gospel throughout the whole world, as the Lord and Savior says: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). They must not remain with the blaspheming Jews, against whom the Roman army is being prepared for their destruction, but must abandon the polluted and separate themselves from them and purify themselves—those who carry the vessels of the Lord.

For they are the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 3), and the golden and silver vessels of a great house. Such was the Apostle Paul, who is called a vessel of election (Acts 9); for he had prepared himself as a precious vessel, suitable for the service of God.

Or certainly this must be said: the vessels of the Lord are the spiritual armor of God. Concerning this the Apostle Paul also spoke: “Put on the armor of God” (Ephesians 6:11), and he enumerates its parts: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is interpreted as the word of God. To these he adds the belt of truth and feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace. And elsewhere: “Therefore, laying aside the works of darkness, let us put on the weapons of light” (Romans 13:13).

The passage continues: “You shall not go out in tumult, nor shall you hasten in flight.” They did not withdraw from Jerusalem as defeated people, but as conquerors. Having preached the Gospel of God daily in the Temple and subjected many thousands of Jews to the faith of Christ, they would also subject the world to his Gospel.

They had the Lord going before them, the God of Israel who would gather them—that is, who would make one flock from the whole world—so that what the Lord says to the Father in the Gospel might be fulfilled (John 17:21): “Grant that, just as I and you are one, so these also may be one in us.” In the same sense and with the same purpose, abandoning mutually opposing and contrary vices, they would grasp one single virtue.

For vices and disturbances do not follow one another in harmony. The opposite is said of virtues, in which there are neither ὑπερβολαί, “excesses,” nor ἐλλείψεις, “deficiencies”—that is, neither too much nor too little—but all things are balanced.

In vices, however, everything is mutually contrary: fear is opposed to boldness, superstition to impiety, and luxury to thrift.

Behold, my servant shall understand; he shall be exalted, lifted up, and shall be very high. Just as many were astonished at you, so his appearance shall be without glory among men, and his form among the sons of men. He shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths because of him. For those to whom nothing had been told about him shall see, and those who had not heard shall contemplate.

The Septuagint: “Behold, my servant shall understand, and he shall be exalted, and shall be greatly glorified” [Note: With Victorius, I prefer “and shall be glorified,” in accordance with the Greek δοξασθήσεται.] “Just as many shall be astonished at you, so your appearance shall be in glory among men, and your glory among the sons of men. Thus many nations shall marvel at him, and kings shall shut their mouths, because those to whom nothing has been announced about him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand.”

So that no ambiguity may remain for readers concerning who it is that said, “I who was speaking, behold, I am here,” and what the holy arm of the Lord is that has been revealed to all the nations, God the almighty Father clearly teaches: “Behold, my servant,” or “my child,” concerning whose distinction we spoke above.

He shall understand—not as the Word of God and Wisdom, but as a servant and child. Although he was in the form of God, he deigned to take the form of a servant, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even the death of the cross (Philippians 2). Therefore God exalted him and gave him a name above every name.

He is the one who speaks in the Psalm: “I will bless the Lord, who has given me understanding” (Psalm 15:7), and concerning whom David sings: “He made the heavens in understanding” (Psalm 135:5). For he himself is Wisdom and Understanding, who advanced as a child in age and wisdom.

Concerning him Peter also speaks: “The God of our fathers glorified his Son Jesus, whom you indeed delivered up and denied before Pilate’s face, when he wished to release him. But you denied the Holy and Righteous One” (Acts 3:13–14).

And above we showed that it is written concerning him: “I am a witness, says the Lord, and the child whom I chose; many shall be astonished at him” (Isaiah 43:10), when they have seen his signs.

The greater wonder will be that his appearance among men will be without glory—not because this signifies deformity of form, but because he came in humility and poverty. Though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, and he said to believers: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:29).

The apostolic man Clement, who governed the Roman Church after Peter, writes concerning him to the Corinthians: “The scepter of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, did not come in boastful pride, although he can do all things, but in humility.”

[Note: Clement’s words are from the First Epistle to the Corinthians through the word “humility,” but not through the following phrase “they should obey,” as Martianaeus supposed.]

So completely was this his manner that, when struck by a servant of the high priest, he replied: “If I have spoken wrongly, testify concerning the wrong; but if rightly, why do you strike me?” (John 18:23), although he had twelve thousand angels who would obey his commands.

He shall sprinkle many nations, cleansing them with his blood and consecrating them to the service of God in baptism.

Kings and the princes of this world shall shut their mouths because of him, for all their wisdom has been overturned by the preaching of the cross. Those who had not possessed the Law and the Prophets, and to whom nothing had been announced about him, will themselves see and understand.

Concerning them the Savior also says: “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John 20:29).

By comparison with them, the hardness of the Jews is condemned. Though seeing and hearing, they fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy in themselves: “You shall hear with hearing and shall not understand; and seeing, you shall look and shall not see. For the heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears” (Isaiah 6:9–10).

(Capítulo 53.—Verse 1 and following.) Who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he shall rise like a young shoot before him, and like a root from thirsty ground. He has no appearance or beauty; and we saw him, and he had no aspect, and we desired him: despised and last among men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness; and as one whose face is hidden and despised, so that we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our sicknesses and carried our pains [the Vulgate repeats “he himself”]; and we considered him as though he were a leper, struck by God and humbled.

The Septuagint: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced him as a little child before him, like a root in thirsty ground. He has no appearance or glory, and we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty; but his appearance was dishonored and deficient in comparison with the sons of men. A man under a blow and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face was turned away, despised and not esteemed. He bears our sins, and he suffers for us, while we considered him to be in pain, under a blow and in affliction.”

After the Father’s words, by which he had announced to the world that his Son would come, and before the scandal of the cross, concerning which he was going to say, “His appearance shall be without glory, and his form among the sons of men,” he had already proclaimed the glory of the resurrection: “He shall be exalted, lifted up, and shall be very high.” Thus, by preceding the humility of the cross with the glory of the resurrection, the chorus of the Prophets replied that it had fulfilled its office and, insofar as it was able, had announced his arm and power to all.

In the statement, “Who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” he signifies the small number of believers from among the Jews.

What follows, “He shall rise like a young shoot before him,” for which the Septuagint translated, “We announced him as a little child before him,” Symmachus rendered “a branch” instead of “a young shoot,” so as to show that the man who proceeded from the virginal womb had been assumed.

Concerning him it adds: “Like a root from thirsty ground.” Instead of “thirsty,” Aquila translated “impassable,” in order to demonstrate the privilege of virginity: he was created from ground previously impassable, without any human seed.

He is the one concerning whom we read above: “A shoot shall go out from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isaiah 11:1), so that it may signify his birth and his rising in the world.

But if he had neither appearance nor glory, and his form was ignoble and deficient in comparison with the sons of men—or, as it is found in the Hebrew, “despised and last among men”—how is it said in the Psalms: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one, in your beauty and your splendor” (Psalm 44:4)?

The matter is easily resolved. He was despised and ignoble when he hung upon the cross and, having become a curse for us, bore our sins. He spoke to the Father: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46).

But he was renowned and beautiful in appearance when the earth trembled at his passion, the rocks were split, and, as the sun fled, the elements feared an everlasting night.

Concerning him the Bride also says in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands” (Song of Songs 5:10). White in the fullness and purity of his virtues, ruddy in his passion, concerning which we shall later read: “Who is this who comes from Edom, whose garments are red from Bosor?” Chosen out of thousands in the resurrection, so that he who was the firstborn of all creation might become the firstborn from the dead.

What follows—“A man in pain and knowing how to bear weakness,” or “a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts also insert the word “to bear” here]—demonstrates a true human body and a true soul. Knowing how to bear weaknesses, he overcame them all through his divinity.

His face was hidden and despised so that divine power might be concealed within a human body. Concerning him it was said above: “You are a hidden God, and we did not know.”

He truly bore our sicknesses and sins and truly suffered for us—not merely apparently, as the old and new heresies imagine. He was truly crucified. He truly suffered, saying in the Gospel: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38), and: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12:27).

We considered him to be unclean, or “in pain,” as the Septuagint translated it; Aquila and Symmachus rendered the word “leprous,” and Theodotion, “scourged.”

The Hebrew idiom understands this as leprosy in accordance with what is written in the Psalm: “And scourging shall not come near your tabernacle” (Psalm 90:10).

The sense is: We considered him struck by God on account of his sins, though he was humbled for our sake and crucified with thieves.

Instead of what Symmachus translated, Ἐν ἁφῇ ὄντα, “being in leprosy,” Aquila used ἁφημένον, “leprous.” Many who do not understand this think it means “abandoned,” while others read καθήμενον, “sitting.”

[Note: “Being in leprosy,” and so forth. In his Sacred Criticism, explaining this chapter of Isaiah, Capellus thought he had detected a double error and hallucination on Jerome’s part, but the learned man labored in vain, as I have shown in the Prolegomena to volume III. Moreover, the Erasmian edition, against the testimony of all the manuscript codices, changed the words ἁφῇ and ἁφημένον into ἀλφῇ and ἀλφήμενον. Martianaeus. Indeed, as Montfaucon also noted, according to the meaning assigned to it here, the word ἁφημένον is scarcely found anywhere. It is derived from ἅπτομαι, from which come ἁφή and then ἁφημένος, that is, “struck with a blow” or “with leprosy.” This derivation conforms to no rules of grammar. There seems to be no obstacle to reading ἀφήμενον, “set apart,” from the preposition ἀπό and the participle ἥμενον; for everyone knows that lepers were customarily forbidden intercourse with other people. —Editor.]

At the beginning of the chapter, where according to the Septuagint it says, “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Romans 10), a testimony which the Apostle Paul also employs in Romans when expounding the Lord’s passion, “Lord” is not found in the Hebrew. It has been added to clarify the person to whom the statement is addressed.

[Col. 0507B] (Verses 5–7.) But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was crushed for our crimes. The discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruise we were healed. All of us, like sheep, have gone astray; each one has turned aside into his own way [the Vulgate: “his own path”]; and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all. He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth.

The Septuagint: “But he was wounded for our sins, and he was weakened for our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep; a man went astray in his own way. And the Lord handed him over because of our iniquities, and he, because of his affliction, did not open his mouth.”

“We,” he says, “considered him a man of sorrows,” or, according to the Septuagint, “to be in pain,” and “struck by God,” bearing his own sins. But he was wounded for our iniquities, saying in the Psalm: “They pierced my hands and feet” (Psalm 21:18), so that by his wound he might heal our wounds.

He was crushed, or weakened, for our crimes, so that, having become a curse for us, he might free us from the curse. “Cursed is everyone who hangs upon a tree” (Deuteronomy 21; Galatians 3).

Hence the discipline of our peace was upon him. What we ought to have endured for our crimes, he suffered for us, making peace through the blood of his cross, whether the things on earth or those in heaven. For he himself is our peace, who made both one and, in his flesh, destroyed the middle wall of the barrier, abolishing hostility (Ephesians 2).

It is therefore clear that, just as a scourged and lacerated body bore the marks of injury in its bruises and livid wounds, so also the soul truly suffered for us, lest Christ be believed to be truth in one respect and falsehood in another (Romans 3).

“All of us,” he says, “like sheep have gone astray,” and we needed the mercy of God, saying in the Psalm: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost” (Psalm 118:176). In the Gospel’s parable of the good and attentive Shepherd, this sheep was carried back upon his shoulders (Matthew 18).

The following verse shows who these sheep are. “A man went astray in his own way,” or “each one turned aside into his own way,” so that he might follow his individual error; abandoning the straight path, he formed a different opinion concerning the Crucified One.

But the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all, or handed him over for our sins, so that what we could not bear because of the weakness of our strength, he might bear for us—the one who was offered because he himself willed it.

He did not endure the cross by necessity but by his will, saying in the Gospel: “Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (John 18:11).

And to Peter, who was scandalized by the mention of the cross because he did not understand its mystery and was trembling with human fear, he said: “Get behind me, Satan; you are a scandal to me, because you do not understand the things of God but those of men” (Matthew 16:23).

Otherwise, if he had not been offered by his own will—though he could identify and foretell the betrayer, and said to the Apostles, “All of you will suffer scandal because of me on this night”—he could have avoided those who had been sent against him. Instead, he met them fearlessly and offered himself voluntarily, saying: “Whom do you seek?” (John 18:4, 6). Immediately they fell backward, for they could not endure the voice of the present God.

He fittingly added: “And he did not open his mouth.” When Pilate said to him, “Do you not speak to me?” he refused to answer.

Or, according to the Septuagint: “Afflicted, he did not open his mouth.” Or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion: “Hearing, he did not open his mouth.”

### (Verses 7 ff.)

“He will be led like a sheep to slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer [the Vulgate adds “itself”] he will be silent, and he will not open his mouth. From distress and judgment he was taken away. Who will declare his generation? For he was cut off from the land of the living; because of the crime of my people he struck them.”

[Note: The Hebrew text agrees; Jerome’s version, however, has “he struck him,” while the Vulgate reads “I struck.”]

“And he will give the impious for his burial, and the rich man for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in infirmity.”

The Septuagint: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb mute before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth. In humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will declare his generation, because his life is removed from the earth? Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death; and I will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death. Because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit in his mouth; and the Lord wills to cleanse him from the blow.”

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript reads, “and he will give”—and indeed the ancient Greek translators rendered δώσει (*dōsei*, “he will give”) rather than δώσω (*dōsō*, “I will give”).]

This testimony was understood by the eunuch of Queen Candace when, in the Acts of the Apostles, he was riding in a chariot and, while reading, did not understand. When Philip interpreted it for him concerning the passion and name of the Savior, he understood; and, being immediately baptized, he merited to be called a man in the blood of the Lamb about whom he was reading, and was sent as an apostle to the Ethiopian nation.

[Note: Jerome received this from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* II.1, who likewise learned from Irenaeus, *Against Heresies* III, that the eunuch was sent into the regions of Ethiopia to preach what he himself had believed. Add the testimonies of the apocrypha: *Apostolic Constitutions*, ch. XLVII, and pseudo-Abdias.]

The one who was offered to Pilate because he himself willed it, and who did not answer, so that, condemned for us, he might ascend the cross, was led like a sheep to slaughter and, like a lamb before its shearer, became silent. For “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5), whom John the Baptist pointed out, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). He is also often mentioned as the slain Lamb in the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist (Rev. 5). He speaks of himself in Jeremiah (Jer. 11): “But I was like an innocent lamb, and was led to sacrifice; I did not know.”

[Col. 0509B] 618

Since he knew no sin, he was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5). And just as a lamb, when it is led to slaughter, does not resist, so he suffered willingly, in order to destroy him who held the power of death (Heb. 2), humbling himself unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2).

This is the Lamb in whose type the lamb was sacrificed whose blood, smeared on the doorposts, drove away the destroyer from Egypt (Exod. 22). He redeemed us not only with his blood but also covered us with his wool, so that, cold with unbelief, we might be warmed by his garment, and might hear the Apostle speaking to us: “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27). And elsewhere: “Put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 13:14).

What follows—“From distress and judgment he was taken away”—or, as the Septuagint translated it, “In humiliation his judgment was taken away,” means either that he ascended victoriously from tribulation and judgment to the Father, or that, although he was the judge of all, the truth of judgment was not found in his case; rather, without any fault, he was condemned by the sedition of the Jews and the voice of Pilate. Hence the Prophet marvels that the God of all surrendered himself to suffering. Paul speaks of him: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

[Note: Victorius reads *cognovissent* (“had understood”), from the Greek text ἔγνωσαν.]

It follows: “Who will declare his generation?” This is understood in two ways. It must either be understood of his divinity, since it is impossible for us to know the mysteries of divine birth—of which he himself speaks in Proverbs: “Before all the hills he begot me” (Prov. 8:25)—in accordance with what we read elsewhere: “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:34), that is, no one; or it must be understood of the Virgin’s childbirth, which can scarcely be explained.

Accordingly, when the Angel said to Mary: “You will conceive and bear a son,” she replied: “How can this be, since I have not known a man?” The Angel answered her in turn: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:31, 34–35). Thus the mysteries of this birth are spoken of only by the Angel or by the Evangelist. Its narrator is exceedingly rare, in accordance with the saying: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Who is discerning, and will know them?” (Hos. 14:10).

But if a prudent reader should answer silently in thought: “How, then, is it written: ‘No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him’?” And whoever knows the Father and the Son can surely declare the mystery of the generation. Let him hear that knowing is one thing and expressing is another, since often we cannot explain in speech what we conceive in the mind. Thus the saints may know the mystery of the divine birth in the flesh more through faith than through speech.

Otherwise, even the Apostle, caught up into the third heaven and into paradise, heard words that the human tongue could in no way utter (2 Cor. 12). Moreover, the Spirit intercedes for us with ineffable groanings.

[Col. 0510B]

The life, therefore, of this one—whose generation either no one or very few can declare—was taken from the earth, so that he might live not on earth but in heaven. Or he was cut off from the land of the living, so that what is written in the Apocalypse of John might be fulfilled: “I am the first and the last, who was living and became dead; and behold, I am alive forever” (Rev. 17:18). Thus, after the life he lived on earth, dead to the earth, he would live eternally in heaven.

What is joined to this—“Because of the crime of my people he struck them,” or, according to the Septuagint, “Because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death”—has a twofold meaning. Either by his death he struck the persecutors and criminals of his people, or, because of the magnitude of the sins of the people whom he had always regarded as his own, he was led to death so that by his death he might call them back to life.

[Col. 0510C]

“He himself gave the impious for his burial, and the rich man for his death”; or, “the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death.” In both cases the two peoples are signified: in the wicked and most evil, who formerly had no knowledge of God (Rom. 9), the multitude of the Gentiles is displayed; in the rich, to whom belonged the Testament, the Law, and the Prophets, the Jewish people are indicated. Therefore the Lord suffered and was buried for this reason: that from both peoples he might gather an Church for himself.

Or this must be said: God delivered the scribes and Pharisees, and the Sadducees, priests and high priests who formerly ruled among the people and abounded in excessive wealth, to the Romans after the Lord’s passion, and subjected them to perpetual slavery.

[Note: More probably, as it seems, the Ambrosian manuscripts omit the name of the Sadducees.]

The one for whose burial and death the impious and the rich were delivered committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. This cannot be understood of any human being at all, as though he had sinned neither in deed nor in speech, since Scripture says: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life has been but one day,” and: “We have all gone astray like sheep; each has turned aside into his own way” (Job 25)—unless it is understood of him who carried our sins, who suffers for us, and was wounded for our iniquities and afflicted for our crimes, by whose bruise we were healed.

Concerning him the chief of the Apostles, Peter, explaining this testimony, says: “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:21 ff.).

The Lord, however, willed to cleanse him from the wound which he had received when pierced by the soldier’s spear. Or, “to crush him in infirmity and wound,” concerning which he himself also said: “For they persecuted the one whom you struck” (Ps. 68:27). And through Zechariah God says: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7).

Therefore it was not necessity but the will of the Father and of the Son that he should suffer. To the Father he himself said: “God, I willed to do your will” (Ps. 39:9). Concerning him we also read above: “He was offered because he himself willed it.”

### (Verses 10–11)

“If he makes his soul an offering for sin, he will see a long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord will prosper in his hand. Because his soul has labored, he will see and be satisfied; in his knowledge the righteous one himself will justify my many servants [another reading: ‘my servant’], and he himself will bear their iniquities.”

The Septuagint: “If you give your soul for sin, it will see a long-lived offspring; and the Lord wills to take his soul away from pain, to show him light, and to form understanding; to justify the righteous one who serves many well; and he himself will bear their sins.”

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript reads, “If you give your soul for sin, you will see a long-lived offspring”; and certain Greek manuscripts, including the Aldine and several others, read δῶτε τὴν ψυχήν (“if you give the soul”).]

According to the Hebrew, the sense is this: If the one whom the Lord willed to crush—or cleanse—makes his soul an offering for sin, he will see the long-lived offspring that he sowed in good soil. Concerning this it is written in the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow”; and again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field” (Matt. 13:3).

And the will of the Lord will prosper in his hand, so that whatever the Father willed might be accomplished through his powers. He says to the Father: “I have guarded those whom you gave me in your name. I kept them, and none of them perished except the son of perdition” (John 17:12).

He will see eternal offspring, and the will of the Father will prosper in his hand because his soul labored for a long time, finding no rest among the Jews, and saying in the Gospel: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:10). And in this same Prophet: “I have labored while enduring” (Isa. 1:14).

Because he labored, he will see Churches arising throughout the whole world, and he will be satisfied with their faith. Thus, when he was hungry and thirsty and sat beside Jacob’s well at midday beneath the burning sun (John 4), he refused to eat the food that had been bought, because he was already satisfied by the faith of the Samaritan woman and of the city of Shechem as it came out to him.

In accordance with this meaning he said among the eight beatitudes: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6).

“In his knowledge,” that is, in his teaching, the righteous one himself—who committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth—and the Father’s servant, who had taken the form of a servant and served the Lord’s will, will justify the many believers from the whole world. And he himself will bear their iniquities, which they could not bear and beneath whose weight they were crushed.

According to the Septuagint, this is said: “O you, because of whose sins the Son of God was led to death, you who were most wicked and rich in evil, given over for his burial and death: if you wish to repent and offer for your sins a sacrifice pleasing to God, a contrite spirit, your soul will see the offspring of long duration—the Lord and Savior himself.”

Of him it is sung in Psalm 88: “His offspring will endure forever,” and again: “I will establish his offspring forever, and his throne like the days of heaven.” Gabriel speaks the same thing in other words to the Virgin: “Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son; he will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:31–32).

The Lord wills to take away from pain the soul of him who had said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38), so that the dishonor of the cross might be tempered by the glory of the resurrection. And he wills to show him light, so that he may see all people enlightened through him. And “to form understanding”—the understood object is “him”—upon whom the spirit of wisdom and understanding has descended.

And to justify the righteous one who served many well: for he did not come to be served but to serve (Matt. 20), washing the sins of all the Apostles in Peter’s feet (John 13). He appeared in the flesh and was justified in the Spirit.

Concerning him Judas the betrayer also confesses: “I have sinned by betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). And Pilate’s wife says: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man, for I have suffered many things today in a dream because of him.”

It must be noted that he was not justified as though he had been unrighteous and then became righteous. Rather, the righteous man is justified—not so that he might begin to be what he was not, but so that what he was might become apparent to all.

This righteous man suffered for the unrighteous, so that he might offer all of us to God. Concerning him it is said to the Jews: “You denied the Holy and Righteous One and asked that a murderer be granted to you” (Acts 3:14).

“And he himself bore their sins,” like a physician bearing the illnesses of the sick, of whom the healthy have no need (Luke 5).

### (Verse 12)

“Therefore I will allot him many, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because he gave his soul over to death and was reckoned among criminals; and he himself bore the sins of many and prayed for the transgressors.”

The Septuagint: “Therefore he himself will possess many, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was defiled in death, and he was reckoned among the unrighteous; and he himself received the sins of many, and for their iniquities he was delivered up.”

He gives the reasons why Christ will receive many rewards after his passion. “Because,” he says, “he suffered, did all that the preceding discourse described, and himself bore the iniquities of many, therefore I will allot him many,” so that those coming from East and West may believe in him as the portion of the Lord Jacob and the allotment of his inheritance, Israel, and may recline in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matt. 8). Thus what is written may be fulfilled: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

Concerning him we also read in this same Prophet: “There will be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the nations—in him the nations will hope” (Isa. 11:10).

These many were formerly held by the strong. Under the appearance of the donkey and its colt, they had many masters, to whom the Apostles said: “The Lord has need of them” (Matt. 21:3). These were strong before Christ assumed a human body and, after overcoming the strong man, plundered his house.

Therefore he handed over and divided the spoils of the strong among his Apostles, so that Peter, James, and John might become leaders of the circumcised people, while Paul and Barnabas were sent to the Gentiles. Separated by place but not in spirit, they stood in different battle lines under one Lord, so that the victory of both armies might raise a triumph for the Savior.

Those who therefore truly say that the administrative dispute between Peter and Paul (Acts 15) was a quarrel and a contest, in order to satisfy Porphyry when he blasphemes, and who assert that the ceremonies of the old Law must be observed in the Church of Christ by the believing stock of Israel, must also await a golden Jerusalem during the thousand years, so that they may sacrifice victims, be circumcised, sit on the Sabbath, sleep, be filled, become drunk, and rise up to play—play which offends God.

I have said this because of what is now prophesied: “He will divide the spoils of the strong” (Isa. 53:12).

In accordance with what is written elsewhere: “When the Heavenly One scattered kings in it.”

[Note: For “kings,” which the manuscripts restore, “nations” was previously read, although, so far as we know, it occurs in no text or book of the ancient versions.]

And again: “The King of hosts is of the Beloved, and it is the beauty of the house to divide spoils” (Ps. 67:13).

Accordingly, concerning the Apostle Paul, who was of the tribe of Benjamin, it is said according to the Hebrew: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat prey, and in the evening he will divide spoils” (Gen. 49:27).

[Note: Victorius adds “prey,” from the sacred text.]

Concerning these things we have already spoken: “They will rejoice before you as those who rejoice at harvest, and as those who divide spoils” (Isa. 9:3), dividing Christ’s Churches throughout the whole world among themselves.

Therefore he will receive very many nations, who came to preach release to captives; and he led captive the captivity previously held by the devil and demons, and gave it as a gift to human beings and believers, because he gave his soul over to death and was reckoned among criminals or unrighteous people (1 Cor. 9).

For if his Apostle became as one without the law to those who were without the law, although he was not without the law but was under the law of Christ, why should Christ not also have been reckoned among the unrighteous, so that he might redeem the unrighteous from sin and become all things to all, in order to save all?

He bore our sins in his body upon the wood of the cross (1 Pet. 2), affixing them there, so that he might erase the record of debt that we had made for the devil and his angels, written by the hands of the soul—that is, by its deeds.

The Apostle Paul speaks of these things: “And when you were dead in sins and in the desires of the flesh, he made you alive with Christ, forgiving us all our sins. He erased the record of debt that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, fastening it to the cross. He stripped the principalities and powers, disgraced them, and openly triumphed over them” (Eph. 1:2; Col. 2:14–15).

The unrighteous among whom he was reckoned are understood by Mark the Evangelist as the robbers, when he writes: “And they crucified with him two robbers, one on his right and the other on his left. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says: ‘And he was reckoned among the unrighteous’” (Mark 15:27).

[Note: One Ambrosian manuscript reads, “which can also be understood otherwise,” and so forth.]

This can also be understood more profoundly, since the Lord says of himself: “I am reckoned among those who descend into the pit; I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. 87:4).

For he truly was reckoned among sinners and unrighteous people, so that he might descend into hell—which is called a pit in many passages of Scripture—and free those bound in prison.

He was delivered up for our sins and rose again for our justification (Rom. 4). His clemency was so great that on the cross he prayed for the transgressors, indeed for his very persecutors, saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

## BOOK FIFTEEN

[Col. 0513] 625–626

I know that I have often said, Eustochium, that whenever the Apostles and Evangelists cite testimonies from the Old Testament, if there is no difference between the Hebrew text and the Septuagint, they customarily use either their own words or those of the Septuagint translators. But if the sense is one thing in Hebrew and another in the old edition, they follow the Hebrew rather than the Septuagint translators.

In short, just as we have shown that they frequently set down passages from the Hebrew that are not found in the Septuagint, so let our opponents demonstrate that some testimonies have been taken from the Septuagint which are not found in the books of the Hebrews; and the dispute is ended.

I have said this because the present chapter, although one in meaning, differs in wording. The fifteenth book on Isaiah begins with its explanation.

### (Chapter 54—Verse 1)

“Sing praise, barren woman who do not give birth; break into praise and cry aloud, you who did not labor in childbirth; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who had a husband,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

[Col. 0515A]

For the Lord has spoken.

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: “Rejoice, barren woman who have not given birth. Rejoice with exultation and cry aloud, you who have not labored in childbirth; for the children of the scattered woman are more numerous than those of her who was under a husband.” Theodotion and Aquila do not differ from him except in a few words.

After the Savior’s birth, the order of his life and virtues, the passion of the cross, and the glory of the resurrection—when, having laid down his soul, he saw a long-lived offspring, and in his knowledge the righteous one himself justified many, divided the spoils of the strong, and prayed for the transgressors, granting a place for repentance—he turns to the calling of the Gentiles and describes at length those who will believe in him.

The Apostle Paul refers this passage to the Church under the names of Sarah and Isaac (Gal. 4:27 ff.): the former people, from Mount Sinai and Hagar, serves with her children, while the later people are free. Isaiah says of them: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not labor in childbirth; for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.” Immediately he adds: “But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac.”

“But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, so also it is now. But what does the Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman will not be heir with the son of the free woman.’ Therefore, brothers, we are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman, with the freedom with which Christ has set us free” (Gal. 4:27 ff.).

If, therefore, the chosen vessel, taking from Isaiah the testimony now before us, applied it to the children of the promise and to the Church from the Gentiles—or gathered from both peoples—which had been deserted and abandoned among the Jews, and which had not had God as a husband, nor received the Law or the Prophets, we are compelled by the very argument to follow the footsteps of our predecessor and call her deserted, concerning whom we read above (on chapter 36): “Rejoice, deserted woman,” and other similar passages.

Of her it is also written in Jeremiah in the person of God: “She who bore seven has become empty; her soul has failed. Her sun has set while it was still midday” (Jer. 15:9).

And in the book of Samuel: “The barren woman has borne seven, and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Sam. 2:5).

And in the Psalms: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. 112:9).

The synagogue is said to have borne seven children because of the mystery of the week and the Sabbath, to which the former people had been bound. Or “seven” should be understood as “many,” in accordance with the ambiguity of the Hebrew word, by which both the Sabbath and multiplicity are signified. This is explained more fully in the book of *Hebrew Questions* that we wrote on Genesis.

Therefore, while this woman had God as her husband, was joined to the divine Word and to the Law, she bore many children for God. But when she received a bill of divorce, refused to answer the husband who called her, and heard: “You are the daughter of your mother, who abandoned your husband” (Ezek. 16:15); and again: “You did not call me, ‘My father,’ nor ‘Guide of my virginity’” (Jer. 3:4), for this reason she is lamented in this same Prophet: “How the faithful city has become a prostitute, Zion full of judgment! Righteousness once lodged in her, but now murderers” (Isa. 1:21).

It must also be noted that when he says, “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband,” the synagogue is not altogether excluded from childbirth; rather, the multitude of the Gentiles is preferred to it. For she herself, in the Apostles and through the Apostles, first brought forth the people of the Jews.

Hence the two leaders of the Apostles divided among themselves the two armies of those believing in Christ—the Circumcision and the Gentiles—so that from both peoples they might build up Jerusalem, previously deserted and poor.

The fact that the Hebrew has “a cry of joy” as “a neighing” signifies the greatness of the joy, like a horse neighing toward victory. This is written about more fully in Job (Job 39).

The Jews and our Judaizers refer this passage and what follows to Jerusalem, which they say will be restored during the thousand-year kingdom. They say that she is the same woman who first had a husband and later ceased to have one, and that after her divorce she will have many more children than she previously had with her husband.

Yet the text plainly compares two women: one who had a husband and was dismissed, and one who was always deserted and without a husband.

Nor is it surprising that the Jews, whose eyes and ears are closed, do not see the obvious truth. What shall I say about Christians? I do not know. Although the Apostle, referring to Sarah and Hagar, teaches that these things are allegorical and pertain to the two Testaments, old and new, they extend their hands to the Jews and surrender to the desire for earthly pleasures during the thousand years.

[Col. 0516C]

### (Verses 2–3)

“Enlarge the place of your tent, and stretch out the skins of your tabernacles; do not spare. Lengthen your cords and strengthen your pegs. For you will penetrate to the right and to the left, and your offspring will inherit the nations and inhabit deserted cities.”

The Septuagint: “Enlarge the place of your tabernacle, and fasten the skins of your curtains; do not spare. Stretch out your cords and strengthen your pegs still further. Enlarge to the right and to the left, and your offspring will possess the nations, and you will cause deserted cities to be inhabited.”

To the woman to whom he had said, “Sing praise, barren woman who do not give birth,” and who had no children, he now commands—after she has broken the bonds by which she was formerly held fast and cried out in confession of the Lord—that, in the likeness of Moses’ tabernacle, which it once had in the desert (Exod. 36), she enlarge her tent and stretch out its skins, make her cords longer, and drive deeply into the ground the pegs by which every tent is formed and strengthen them, lest the blasts of the winds scatter it.

She is to penetrate to the right and the left and no longer imitate the narrowness of the Jewish tabernacle, which enclosed one hundred cubits in length and fifty in width, nor be confined by the smallness of the Temple, which was sixty cubits long and twenty wide. Rather, she must continually make room to the right and the left (Exod. 27).

And lest we think that this is said, according to the Jews’ frivolous argument, of Zion, which is to be restored by the Lord to its former condition, he makes what was hidden more explicit: “And your offspring will inherit the nations.”

[Col. 0517A] 629

Concerning this we also read in the Gospel: “The sower went out to sow” (Matt. 13:3); and again: “Did you not sow good seed in your field?” (ibid., 27). This seed will also cause deserted cities to be inhabited, so that Churches of the Gentiles may arise throughout the whole world.

Or certainly the seed should be understood as the Apostles and the remnants of the Jewish people. Concerning this it is said in the same Prophet: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have been like Sodom and become like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9). And the Apostle says: “The remnant has been saved” (Rom. 11:5).

This concerns the greatness of the Churches, which, instead of the one territory of Judea, and that a very narrow one, will extend their boundaries throughout the whole world.

Let us come to the spiritual understanding. Whoever is in a tabernacle does not possess a firm and perpetual dwelling, but continually changes places and hastens onward, saying in the Psalm: “I will pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle” (Ps. 41:5), forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what is ahead until he reaches the prize of the heavenly calling.

Concerning this tabernacle we also read elsewhere: “How beloved are your tabernacles, Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:1). Then he adds: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (ibid., 6).

For the end of tabernacles is possession of the eternal house, whose foundations do not change and which is not transferred from one place to another. Those who are planted in the house of the Lord first blossomed in his courts, so that from flowers they might come to fruit and be able to say: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Ps. 51:10).

Thus the holy man, hastening to pass beyond the tabernacles and desiring to see the house of God, says that he has one request: never to leave the house of God: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:1).

Therefore the tabernacle must be enlarged, its curtains and skins stretched out, the cords of manifold and varied discourses extended farther, and the pegs strengthened by reason, on the right and on the left, so that the seed of the word—that is, the teaching of God—may possess the nations and make habitable the cities received by the one who had doubled the mina.

The right and the left are understood positively in the Holy Scriptures when we understand them both according to the spirit and according to the letter, “by the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left” (2 Cor. 6). Thus the humbler understanding preserves the discipline of life and the examples of our predecessors, while the spiritual and sublime understanding transfers us from present things to future ones.

This is what the Lord also said when the Pharisees questioned him: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21). Thus we are subject to the powers of this age, which justly bear the sword for the punishment of those who do evil—this is understood as the left—and we give to God what belongs to God, fearing no one else except him who has authority over both soul and body—this is understood as the right (Matt. 10).

Accordingly, it is said of the wisdom of God, with which nothing precious can be compared, that in her right hand she has length of life and many years, while in her left are riches and glory. The riches are understood as those present in knowledge and good works; the glory is that which is received by the one through whose works God is glorified among the nations; while length of life and many years signify eternal life, which neglects present things and hastens toward the future.

### (Verses 4–5)

“Do not fear, for you will not be put to shame; do not be confounded, for you will not blush. For you will forget the shame of your youth and will remember the reproach of your widowhood no longer. For he who made you will rule over you; the Lord of hosts is his name. And your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel, will be called the God of the whole earth.”

The Septuagint: “Do not fear, because you have been confounded; do not be confounded, because you have been reproached. For you will forget eternal shame and will remember the reproach of your widowhood no longer, because the Lord who made you—the Lord of hosts is his name—and he who redeemed you, the God of Israel, will be called the God of the whole earth.”

A question arises: if this is said to the Church gathered from the Gentiles—“Rejoice, barren woman who do not give birth,” and “The children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband”—that is, if she had no husband and afterward produced more children, while the woman who previously had a husband became barren, how can it now be said to the woman who had no husband: “You will remember the reproach of your widowhood no longer,” and “You will forget the shame of your youth”?

For this reason the Jews wish everything that is said to be understood of Jerusalem, which, after being deserted by God, is to be restored by him. They can easily be refuted when they are reminded that the Lord speaks in Zechariah in the following terms: “And I took for myself two staffs; one I called Beauty, and the other I called Cord; and I pastured the flock” (Zech. 11:7). We have discussed this more fully in its proper place, and something will now be said about it.

The two staffs are the two peoples, the Gentiles and the Jews. The first was called the multitude of the Gentiles, which received the natural law fixed in their hearts, concerning which Paul argues most powerfully in writing to the Romans (Rom. 1). Nothing is more beautiful than this staff, since every creature is equally called to worship its Creator.

The second, that is, the Jewish people, was called “Cord.” After the offense of the Gentiles, it is called the Lord’s portion and “the cord of his inheritance, Israel” (Deut. 32).

Accordingly, after Israel was called in Abraham, the Lord says: “I took my staff, which was called Beauty, and cut it off, to annul my covenant which I made with all the nations” (Zech. 11:10).

Therefore, at the coming of Christ, the following is said to the staff that had been cut off: “Do not fear, do not blush, and do not cover your face with shame. You will no longer be confounded as you were before; you will not remember the shame of your youth, nor will you remember your widowhood, through which you were abandoned by God. For your Maker himself will rule over you, whose name is Almighty, who reigns not over one Jewish nation but throughout the whole world.”

Thus it follows: “He who made you has himself redeemed you with his blood, and he will be called the God of the whole earth,” that is, of all who dwell on the earth.

From this it is plainly evident that the words are not addressed to Jerusalem, which never ruled over the whole world, but to the Church of Christ, whose inheritance is the possession of the world.

### (Verses 6, 7)

“For as a woman forsaken and grieving in spirit the Lord has called you, and as a wife rejected from her youth, your God has said. For a brief moment I abandoned you; but with great mercies I shall gather you. In a moment of indignation I hid my face from you for a little while; but with everlasting mercy I have pitied you, says your redeemer, the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Not as a forsaken and fainthearted woman has the Lord called you, nor as a woman who has been hated from her youth has your God said so. For a short time I forsook you, but with great mercy I shall have mercy on you. In a little anger I turned my face away from you; but with everlasting mercy I shall have mercy on you, says the Lord who redeemed you.”

Here the friends of the Jews disparage the forsaken woman and the wife rejected from her youth, whom the Lord abandoned for a moment and for a short time, saying that she is Jerusalem. He who had hidden his face from her for a little while, they say, will receive her in everlasting mercies and will change her former grief into joy. This is according to the Hebrew.

But according to the Septuagint, he does not say that she was like a forsaken woman, or that she was called fainthearted by the Lord; nor does he say that she was like a wife who had been hated from her youth. Rather, he says that for this reason he left her for a short time and turned his face away from her, so that he might have mercy on her forever. If, therefore, the Jews and our Judaizers say that Israel was abandoned for a short time so that, at Christ’s coming, God might have mercy on it, and if they interpret “a short time” in comparison with the whole of eternity, why do they not also allow us to say that the nations were abandoned for a short time, so that those who had in their youth been cast out from the midst of God might afterward, in their old age, obtain everlasting mercy? [Note: The order, impeded by Paul’s wording, seems to require restoration thus: “so that those who had in their youth been cast out from the midst of God …”]

This is especially so since, during the period of Israel’s calling, the multitude of the Gentiles was never excluded; rather, through proselytes, the door of return was always open to them. Thus, just as we seem to have been excluded for a short time by their calling, so, through their perpetual exclusion, return to God may be granted to us. We have called that exclusion perpetual if they do not repent. Otherwise the apostle Paul says: “God has shut up all things under sin, so that he might have mercy on all” (Gal. 3:22).

We have interpreted these words as referring to the Church gathered from both peoples, whereas the Jews understand them of Jerusalem. Those who follow only the tropological interpretation, and who avoid questions by an excursion into unrestricted debate in the most difficult passages, refer them to the sinful soul, which has been rejected by God—not through hatred, but as part of his providential ordering—so that, oppressed by the weight of evils, it may return to its former husband, and, having squandered its substance, may not despair of its father’s clemency (Luke 15).

Is it not great mercy to run out to meet the returning son, to offer him the ring, the robe, and a kiss, and to say to the envious brother, in accordance with the likeness of the other parable: “Friend, if I am good, why is your eye evil?” (Matt. 20:15).

### (Verses 9, 10)

“As in the days of Noah, this is for me: I swore that I would no longer bring the waters of Noah over the earth; so I have sworn that I will not be angry with you or rebuke you. For the mountains shall be shaken and the hills shall tremble, but my mercy shall not depart from you, and the covenant of my peace shall not be shaken, says your compassionate Lord.”

The Septuagint: “As the water that was under Noah was for me, so I swore to him at that time that I would never again be angry with the earth because of you, nor, in your rebuke, would I move the mountains; nor would your hills be moved. So neither shall my mercy fail, nor shall the covenant of my peace be removed, says the Lord who has been gracious to you.”

So that the congregation of the saints may believe in the Lord’s everlasting mercy, and therefore understand that we were abandoned for a moment and for a brief time so that they might be joined to God in friendship through an everlasting covenant, he sets forth examples from ancient times, saying:

When the whole world had sinned, after all the earth had corrupted the way of the Lord, the flood was brought upon it. When all sins, together with their perpetrators, had been destroyed, the human race was preserved in one man, Noah. To him God swore that he would never again bring a flood upon the earth; and his promise has remained in force to this day and will never be annulled (Gen. 8–9). So I swear to my Church, which I redeemed for myself with my blood, that I will never be angry with those upon whom I have had mercy, nor will my clemency be changed by any severity of rebuke. The mountains will be moved more easily than my decision will be changed.

Accordingly, he also says in the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35). “This,” he says, “is my mercy: that the covenant of peace by which the world has been reconciled to me may be preserved, not through the merit of those to whom it was given, but through my clemency.”

According to the Septuagint, the sense is confused, and everything is so disordered that it is difficult to understand what is being said—not that I fail to understand what that most prudent man said in this chapter, but that it does not satisfy my mind. He introduces a tropological flood, which is interpreted as the Savior’s baptism, collecting very many examples, such as: “The Lord makes the flood dwell” (Ps. 28:10). And again: “The Lord is gracious to those who await him in the day of tribulation; and, knowing those who fear him, he brings the completion of the journey in the flood” (Nah. 1:7, according to the Septuagint). That is, he wiped away all sins in baptism, saying elsewhere: “I am he, I am he, who wipes away your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25).

“For all have turned aside; together they have become worthless” (Ps. 13:3). There was no one who practiced mercy or truth; there was no knowledge of God upon the earth. Curse, falsehood, murder, adultery, and theft had occupied everything, and they had mingled blood with blood. Therefore he speaks through the Prophet: “Alas for me! For the faithful person has perished from the earth. There is no one who does what is right among human beings; all are judged in my blood. Each one afflicts his neighbor with affliction, and they prepare their hands for evil” (Mic. 7:2, according to the Septuagint), and other similar things.

Among these is: “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life upon earth should be only a single day” (Job 15:14). Therefore the Lord caused the flood—he who, according to the apostle Peter, “was put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Pet. 3:18), and preached to the spirits imprisoned when God’s patience was waiting in the days of Noah, bringing the flood upon the ungodly. As an image of this, water cleanses us—not by washing away the filth of the flesh, but by the appeal of a good conscience toward God.

By the mountains and hills that are not shaken, although they had been shaken in such a flood, he wishes the saints to be understood, having received an everlasting covenant. They had been shaken in the earlier flood and had abandoned their former firmness. By the mountains he also means demons and hostile powers, who saw that the daughters of human beings were beautiful, were wounded by the dart of love, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose, and lost their former strength; they will certainly not be present in this flood (Gen. 6). Let this be said by him whose explanation I leave to the reader’s judgment.

### (Verses 11, 12)

“Poor little woman, shaken by the storm, without consolation. [Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts, as also Jerome’s own version and the Vulgate, read “without any consolation.”] Behold, I shall arrange your stones in order and lay your foundations in sapphires. I shall set your battlements in jasper, your gates in carved stones, and all your boundaries in precious stones. All your children shall be taught by the Lord, and great shall be the peace of your children; and you shall be founded in righteousness.”

The Septuagint: “Humble and unstable, without consolation. Behold, I prepare your carbuncle as your stone, and your foundations as sapphire; I shall set your battlements in jasper, your gates as crystal stones, and your walls as chosen stones. All your children shall be disciples of God, and great shall be the peace of your children; and you shall be built in righteousness.”
