Where we said, “I shall arrange your stones in order,” the Hebrew has **BAPHPHUCH** (), which all translators except the Septuagint have rendered alike: “I shall arrange your stones in antimony,” after the likeness of a well-adorned woman who paints her eyes with antimony, signifying the beauty of the city.

And where, following the Septuagint, we said “jasper,” the Hebrew has **CHODCHOD** (), which Symmachus alone translated as **chalcedony** (Greek: *chalkēdónion*).

In place of “crystal,” for which the Hebrew reads **ECDA** (), Symmachus and Theodotion put “of carving,” that is, **γλυφῆς** (*glyphēs*), while Aquila put **τρυπανισμοῦ** (*trypanismoû*).

[Note: Martianay and other printed editions incorrectly read *τρήπτανισμοῦ*; the Ambrosian manuscript rightly corrects this, using the uncial letters **ΤΡΥΠΑΝΙϹΜΟΥ**, which means “of engraving.” The word conveys the sense of gems that have been pierced and carved.]

We have spoken of the diversity of the translations; let us come to the meaning.

He is still speaking to the Church, formerly humble and poor, which had neither the Law nor the Prophets nor the word of God, and which had been shaken by the storm, or was unstable, having endured many tempests of the world and having fluctuated amid various errors concerning idols. She had no comforter and had vainly spent all her substance on physicians. He himself will come, he himself will descend, and he will build upon earth the heavenly Jerusalem, which in John’s Apocalypse is called the bride and wife of the Lamb. It has a light like a precious stone, like jasper and crystal, a great wall, and twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel—three toward the east, three toward the north, three toward the south, and three toward the setting sun (Rev. 21). Its wall is supported by twelve foundations; its entire construction is of jasper, and each foundation of the walls has its own stone: the first jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius [or sardine], the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh hyacinth, and the twelfth amethyst.

When we read this, we exclaim and say: “O depth of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. 11:33–34). And again: “Who is wise, and will understand these things? Intelligent, and will know them?” (Hos. 14:10).

Let those who love only the letter that kills answer—those who prepare delicacies for the throat and luxury during a thousand years, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. 3). After the Savior’s second coming in glory, they hope for weddings, for little children one hundred years old, for the injury of circumcision, for the blood of sacrifices, and for an everlasting Sabbath. In their perverse manner they say with Israel: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” [Note: The same is found in the Ambrosian manuscript: “for tomorrow we shall die.” A few lesser matters are corrected below.]—what, then, is this heavenly Jerusalem to which it is now said:

“Behold, I shall arrange your stones in order,” or, according to the Septuagint, “Behold, I prepare your carbuncle as your stone,” so that the entire city may be full of carbuncles, have sapphire foundations, jasper or chalcedony battlements, crystal or embossed gates, and a wall all around made of precious stones; so that all its children may have not human teachers but God, and may be called disciples of God; so that everlasting peace may be in it, and its construction may be righteousness.

From this it is clear that, under the pretext of righteousness—which is the name of a virtue—we ought also to seek the other virtues for the building of the Church, and not follow Jewish deliriums. Let them explain what is said about wisdom in Proverbs: “She is more precious than all the most precious stones” (Prov. 3:15). For if Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24), it is foolish to compare Christ with insensible stones.

Again, we read concerning the judgments of God: “The judgments of the Lord are right, justified in themselves, more desirable than gold and much precious stone” (Ps. 18:10–11). From this it is evident that the “stone” compared with the other stones is the one of which, earlier in this same Prophet, God says in his own person: “Behold, I am laying in the foundations of Zion a cornerstone, a chosen and precious stone; whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame” (Isa. 28:16).

“This stone the builders rejected” (Ps. 117:22)—namely, the scribes, Pharisees, and rulers of the Jews—and it became “the head of the corner” (Matt. 21:42). Concerning it the apostle Peter also says: “Honor, therefore, belongs to us who believe in the chosen, precious, and cornerstone; but to the unbelieving it is a stone of stumbling and a rock of scandal” (1 Pet. 2:7–8). In the Acts of the Apostles he also says to the chief priests and rulers: “This is the chosen and precious stone which you rejected when you disapproved of it” (Acts 4:11); it became the head of the corner and holds together two peoples, the Gentiles and Israel.

He built the city whose architect and founder is God. Concerning this city the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: “You are God’s building.” And: “Like a wise architect I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one see how he builds. For no one can lay another foundation apart from the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 3:9–11). “But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, precious stones, wood, hay, straw, each one’s work will become manifest.”

Concerning this foundation he also speaks in the other Epistle: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the cornerstone” (Eph. 2:20). And again: “In whom you also are all being built together as living stones into a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices” (1 Pet. 2:5).

Of these stones it is mystically said: “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth” (Zech. 9:16). With these stones Christ builds the Church upon the rock, saying in the Gospel: “Upon this rock I shall build my Church” (Matt. 16:18). Whoever is worthy to enter that city speaks joyfully to the Lord: “As we have heard, so we have seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God; God founded it forever” (Ps. 47:9).

Of the builder of this city it is said elsewhere: “He will build my city and restore the captivity of my people” (Isa. 45:13).

It is not for the present occasion to speak about the nature of the twelve stones and gems, since many Greek and Latin writers have written about them. Of these I shall name only two: Epiphanius, a bishop of holy and venerable memory, who left us a notable volume as a monument to his talent and learning, entitled **Περὶ λίθων** (*Peri lithōn*, “On Stones”); and Pliny Secundus, likewise among the Latins an orator and philosopher, who in the splendid work of his *Natural History* devoted Book Thirty-Seven, which is also the final book, to a discussion of stones and gems.

These twelve stones are listed in order in Exodus and in Ezekiel—that is, in the **λογεῖον** (*logeion*, “breastpiece”) of the high priest [manuscripts: *in logio*], and in the crown and diadem of the ruler of Tyre.

Let us speak first of Exodus: “Four rows of stones were woven in” (Exod. 28). The first row had a sardius, topaz, and emerald. The second row had a carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper. The third row had a ligure, agate, and amethyst. [Note: Up to this point the reading *lyncurium* has prevailed; it is a kind of amber rather than a gem. See our note on this in Epistle 64 to Fabiola, §17. The Ambrosian manuscripts correct it.] The fourth row had a chrysolite, beryl, and onyx, set in gold. They were engraved with the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel.

Here it should be noted that the second row of stones is also placed in the present passage: carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper. For we do not yet possess perfection, nor have we reached the beginning, because now we see through a mirror in an enigma.

In Ezekiel we find the following written:

“You are the seal of likeness and the crown of beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God. You were clothed with every precious stone: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver, gold, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. with gold you filled your treasures and storehouses within you.” [Note: Two manuscripts read: “your storehouses on the day on which you were created.”] “From the day on which you were created, I placed you with the Cherubim upon my holy mountain, you were in the midst of fiery stones, blameless in your ways from the day on which you were created, until your iniquities were found in you” (Ezek. 28:12ff.).

Who could be so foolish and dull-witted as to believe that the ruler of Tyre, whoever he may have been, was placed in the paradise of God, created among the cherubim, and dwelling among fiery stones—which we undoubtedly understand as angels and heavenly powers—and to suppose that he was adorned with earthly stones and possessed a likeness and a seal?

It is therefore not the time to speak about the nature of all the stones and of each one individually; for not everything must always be said. Let us now discuss only the carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper.

The carbuncle that is prepared, or arranged in order, seems to me to signify the fiery word of teaching which, when the error of darkness has been driven away, illumines the hearts of believers. This is the stone which one of the Seraphim took with tongs and brought to cleanse Isaiah’s lips (Isa. 6). According to the account in Genesis, it is born in the land of Havilah, where there is excellent gold (Gen. 2), as well as carbuncle and prase.

[Note: Victor reads “carbuncle and prase” in the opposite order, according to the sacred text. Shortly afterward, in place of “above us air,” he has “the air above us.”]

The sapphire, which is placed in the foundations, bears the likeness of heaven and of the air above us. It is such that one might say with Socrates, in Aristophanes:

**Ἀεροβατῶ καὶ περιφρονῶ τὸν ἥλιον**

which we can render into Latin as: “I walk upon the air and despise the sun” (see Suidas under *περιφρονεῖν*).

Or one may say with the apostle Paul: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Ezekiel’s Scripture also records that the place where God’s throne is has the likeness of sapphire, and that the glory of the Lord consists in this color, which bears the image of the heavenly.

The battlements of the Lord’s city—that is, the defenses of its walls—are also strengthened by jasper. They can destroy and refute every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God and subject falsehood to the truth (Ezek. 1; 2 Cor. 10:5). Whoever, therefore, is strongest in debate and fortified by testimonies from the holy Scriptures is a battlement of the Church.

There are many kinds of jasper:

[Note: Here he transfers Epiphanius almost word for word. For comparison, we shall record his Greek words:

**Ἔστι τῷ εἴδει σμαραγδίζων· παρὰ δὲ τὰ χείλη τοῦ Θερμώδοντος ποταμοῦ εὑρίσκεται καὶ περὶ Ἀμαθοῦντα τὴν ἐν Κύπρῳ· τοῦτο δὲ ἄκος εἶναι φαντασμάτων οἱ μυθολόγοι λέγουσι· ἄλλη δὲ ἔστι γλαυκοτέρα θαλάσσης, ἄλλη δὲ βαθυτέρα τῷ ἄνθει τῆς βαφῆς, ἐν τοῖς σπηλείοις, ἐν τῷ ὄρει τῷ ἐν τῇ Φρυγίᾳ, ὁμοιάζουσα πορφύρᾳ, τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος κόχλου διαυγεστέρα μᾶλλον, ὥσπερ οἴνῳ ὁμοιάζουσα, ἢ ἀμεθύστου ξανθοτέρα· οὐ γὰρ μιᾶς χροιᾶς, οὐδὲ τῆς αὐτῆς δυνάμεως· ἀλλ᾽ ἡ μὲν ἐστὶ χαυνοτέρα καὶ λευκοτέρα, οὔτε πάνυ στίλβουσα, οὔτε πάλιν ἀποδέουσα· ἄλλη δὲ κρυστάλλου ὕδατι ὁμοία· εὑρέθη δὲ καὶ παρ᾽ Ἴβηρσι καὶ ποιμέσι Ὑρκανῶν τοῖς κατὰ τὴν Κασπίαν γῆν· καὶ ἄλλος ἴασπις ὁ παλος καλούμενος** [The reading appears to be: **ἄλλη ... παλαιὰ ... καλουμένη**], **οὐ πάνυ λάμπουσα, χλωρὰ, ἥτις ἔχει γραμμὰς μέσας· καὶ ἄλλός ἴασπις, ὅμοιος** [perhaps **ὁμοία**, and above **ἄλλη**] **τῇ χιόνι ἢ ἀφρῷ θαλάσσης**,” and so forth. In English: “It is emerald-like in appearance; it is found beside the banks of the Thermodon River and around Amathus in Cyprus, and mythographers say that it is a remedy for apparitions. Another kind is bluer than the sea; another is deeper in the bloom of its dye, found in caves on the mountain in Phrygia, resembling purple but more translucent than purple drawn from the blood of the murex, like wine, or yellower than amethyst. For it is not of one colour or of the same potency: one is duller and whiter, neither especially gleaming nor deficient; another resembles crystalline water. It has also been found among the Iberians and among Hyrcanian shepherds in the Caspian region. Another jasper, called *palos* [the reading perhaps should be *palaia*, ‘ancient’], is not very brilliant, greenish, and has lines across its middle; and another jasper resembles snow or the foam of the sea.”]

For one kind has the appearance of emerald; it is found at the sources of the Thermodon River and is called **Grammatias**, by which, they say, all apparitions are driven away.

[Note: In the Ambrosian manuscript it is not *Grammatias*, but **ΑΜΑΦΟΥϹΙΟϹ**, written in Greek letters. Perhaps **Ἀμαθούσιος** is the true name of this stone, since the Epiphanius just quoted teaches that it is found *περὶ Ἀμαθοῦντα*, “around Amathus,” which is in Cyprus. See our Pliny, Book 37, chapter 29, where he mentions *Grammatias* jasper, also called *Polygrammos* by several others.]

Another is greener than the sea and as though dyed with flowers; they report that it grows on Mount Ida in Phrygia, in its deepest caves. Another is found near the Iberians, the Hyrcanians, and the Caspian Sea,

[Note: Dionysius calls this a dark or blackish jasper, that is, **ἠερόεσσαν ἴασπιν**.]

especially near Lake Neusis.

There is also another jasper resembling snow and the foam of sea waves,

[Note: In place of “and gently,” the older Ambrosian manuscript has “and elementally,” that is, “mixed with the element of water.”]

and faintly reddish as though mixed with blood.

We have said this so that we may recognize all the spiritual gifts in the battlements of the Church. Whoever possesses them drives away empty fears and can say with the bride: “My beloved is white and red” (Song 5:10).

The gates of this city are made of crystal stone, which is carved in various ways; nothing is purer than this stone. Indeed, in the intense cold of the Alps and in caves inaccessible to the sun, water is said to congeal into crystal: to the touch it is a stone, but to the sight it is water. Through this is shown that those who are at the gates of the Church ought not to be stained by any impurity, but should possess the purest faith and say with the Prophet: “From your commandments I have gained understanding” (Ps. 118:104). They should also hear: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

The walls of the city—or its boundaries and **περίβολος** (*peribolos*, “enclosure”)—are built of chosen stones. By these we can understand the remaining stones, and all its children as taught by God, or as disciples of God. The Lord uses this testimony in the Gospel of John, saying: “No one can come to me unless my Father who sent me draws him; and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me” (John 6:44–45).

A little later it is written in the Prophets: “They shall all be taught by God.” He also speaks through Jeremiah: “I shall give my laws in their minds, and I shall write them upon their hearts; and they shall no longer teach each one his neighbor and his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord.’ But all shall know me, from the least to the greatest. For I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more” (Jer. 31:33–34).

The teaching of the disciples of God possesses a multitude of peace, which has been left to them by the Lord. The building of the most beautiful city is completed by righteousness, so that God may belong not to one nation but to the whole world, calling to his faith servants and free persons, Greeks and barbarians, rich and poor, noble and ignoble, men and women, children and old people, and all those who appear to be opposites in the world (John 14).

We have exceeded the limits of brevity, which are useful in everything that must be said, since, unlike the Jews and our half-Judaizers, we seek the city of God not on earth but in heaven—the city that, situated upon the mountain in Christ, cannot remain hidden.

### (Verse 14)

“Depart far from slander, for you shall not fear; and from terror, for it shall not come near you.”

The Septuagint: “Depart from the wicked, and you shall not fear, and trembling shall not come near you.”

The order is most beautiful. He had consoled the poor and humble woman, promising her spiritual gifts. Now he teaches what she must do if she does not wish to fear the attacks of her adversaries. The sense is:

Do you not wish to fear your enemies? Do what I say. Depart far from slander, or from iniquity—for every iniquity and robbery arises from slander—and you shall not fear. Trembling and terror shall not approach you, so that you may fear not human beings but God, saying with Moses: “I am trembling and fearful” (Deut. 9:19); and with one of Job’s friends: “Horror and trembling came upon me, and greatly shook my bones” (Job 4:14); and with the Prophet: “At the sound of my prayer trembling entered my bones” (Hab. 3:16); and: “Upon whom does the Lord rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at his words?” (Prov. 10:24).

The trembling of the ungodly, however, is something different; it arises from fear of punishment. Of this it is written: “Trembling has seized the ungodly” (Ps. 47:7).

### (Verse 15)

“Behold, the sojourner shall come who was not with me; your former stranger shall be joined to you.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, proselytes shall come to you through me; they shall be your settlers, and they shall flee for refuge to you.”

The Jews think that this is said to Jerusalem, meaning that many proselytes from the nations will come and accept the Law of Moses and its ceremonies. We, following the interpretation we have begun, refer it to the Church, which has been gathered from both peoples through the apostles. It has neither stain nor wrinkle; it is free and the mother of all believers (Eph. 5; Gal. 4).

To gather these proselytes and strangers, the Lord sent his disciples, saying: “Teach all nations” (Matt. 28:19), so that they might flee for refuge to the Gospel and receive the new Law, and so that those who had formerly inhabited idolatry might become settlers of the Church.

Of these it is said in the Psalms: “The Lord makes the blind wise.” Or, as it is read in the Latin manuscripts: “The Lord gives light to the blind; the Lord loves strangers” (Ps. 145:8–9). Once the blind have received the light of truth and the foolish have learned wisdom, they pass over to the Church and are loved by the Lord. Then they hear through the Prophet: “I shall call ‘Not my people,’ ‘My people’” (Hos. 2:24). When this people enters the temple of God, jealousy seizes the unlearned people.

### (Verses 16, 17)

“Behold, I created the smith who blows upon the coals in the fire and brings forth a vessel for his work; and I created the slayer for destruction. Every vessel that has been fashioned against you shall not prosper, and every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge. This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord, and their righteousness is from me, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “Behold, I created you—not as a smith blowing upon coals in the fire and bringing forth a vessel for its work. But I created you not for destruction, to kill. Every vessel that has been made against you shall not prosper, and every voice that rises against you in judgment—you shall overcome them all, and they shall be liable to you in it.” [The words marked with the obelus appear to have been added.] “This is the inheritance of those who serve the Lord, and you shall be righteous for me, says the Lord.”

Let us first speak according to the Hebrew.

If you do not wish to fear, and want dread to be far from you, do what the preceding discourse related. For I am the one through whom you will have proselytes. I am the one who created the smith blowing upon coals in the fire—that is, the devil, the craftsman of all evils—not by necessity of nature but by the choice of his mind. He kindled fires and will bring vessels against you, such as Simon and Elymas the magicians, who resisted the apostles Peter and Paul (Acts 13).

I created the slayer of those who will be unbelieving—not that I am the cause of their destruction, but because the adversary was created for battle, and destruction is the lot of those who are defeated, while victory becomes the cause of rewards for those who conquer. All those who have been fashioned against you by the smith who blows upon the fire shall not prosper; they shall experience both present and future punishments.

What had first seemed hidden is stated more clearly in what follows: “And every tongue that resists you in judgment you shall judge,” destroying the wisdom of the wise and rejecting the prudence of the prudent. You will condemn all the leaders of the heretics, the teachers of the Jews, and the philosophers of the world whom that smith had forged. Thus the Queen of Sheba condemned the unbelievers, as did the Ninevites; and, conversely, Sodom will be justified in comparison with the worse Jerusalem (Matt. 12).

After this, the rewards of the future are introduced, so that they may not think the contest empty or that it ends with present death. [Note: The older Ambrosian manuscript adds: “lest those enduring the contest should suppose that it ended in present death.”]

“This is the inheritance of the servants of the Lord”—that is, the kingdoms of heaven, everlasting life, and the recompense of their labors, which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9). But if for those who love him, then also for those who serve him, since they have no other Lord except God.

“And this is the righteousness of those who are with God,” says the Lord: that present tribulation may be compensated by future joy.

According to the Septuagint, this seems to me to be the sense:

“I, your Creator, did not make you in the manner in which the devil, the worst of smiths, fashions vessels of iniquity with an unclean spirit and brings them forth for destruction. He ought to know that vessels of this kind do not have a prosperous course, but are broken in the middle of their journey.”

What these vessels are, he demonstrates in the following discourse: “And every voice that rises against you in judgment—you shall overcome them all.”

The vessels of iniquity have a voice; that voice rises against the Church when heretics exalt their mouth on high and their tongue passes through the earth. As for what follows—“and they shall be liable to you in it”—we have marked it with an obelus, since it appears to have been added not so much by the Septuagint as by bad scribes.

When the Church has overcome every voice rising against her, then those who serve and obey the Lord shall have an inheritance: everlasting possession. Concerning this it is said in Jeremiah in other words: “There is a reward for your works” (Jer. 31:16).

The inhabitants of the Church shall be righteous before the Lord. For everyone who practices righteousness has been born of God. To them the Lord says: “Be holy, because I am holy” (Lev. 20:26).

## Chapter LV

### Verse 1

[Col. 0528C] “All who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no money [Vulgate: silver], hasten, buy, and eat. Come, buy without silver and without any exchange, wine and milk. Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread, and your labor for what does not satisfy?”

[Printed numeral 643.] **Septuagint:** “You who thirst, go to the water; and all who have no money, going, buy and eat. Go and buy without money and without price wine and fat. Why do you buy with money [Note: [Col. 0527D] Victorius adds “not for bread,” following the Greek [οὐκ ἐν ἄρτοις] [Col. 0528D], and your labor not for satisfaction?”

The Hebrew word *OI* (אוי), concerning which I had said above in the prophecy against Ariel (see chapter 29) that it was ambiguous and signified either the interjection of one calling or “woe,” is placed here at the beginning of the chapter. It is read not as an expression of lamentation, but with the feeling of one calling.

Since, therefore, he had said that every earthen vessel fashioned against the Church was to be shattered, and that every voice and tongue which had armed itself against the knowledge of God was to be overcome, he summons believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters and whose rushing makes glad the city of God, so that they may drink waters from the fountains of the Savior. He says to the Samaritan woman:

“If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you water.” [Note: [Col. 0528D] The same text adds: “He would have given you living water. For whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain,” and so forth.]

“The water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:10, 14).

Concerning these waters he cried out in the Temple:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (ibid., 7–8),

signifying the Holy Spirit, whom believers were to receive, and concerning whom the Prophet resounded in mystical language:

“My soul has thirsted for the living God” (Psalm 41:2);

and again:

“With you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 35:10).

He himself spoke concerning himself:

“They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jeremiah 2:13).

The clouds upon which the truth of God has come scatter these waters. As it is written:

“Let the clouds rain down righteousness” (Isaiah 45:8, according to the Septuagint).

The thirsty are commanded never to drink the turbid waters of the Shihor or the swollen torrents of the Assyrians, but to proceed to the waters of Siloam, which go quietly. Nor are they to fear poverty of expression if they perhaps do not have silver (Isaiah 45; Jeremiah 2), but let them hear the Apostle saying:

“By grace you have been saved” (Ephesians 2:8),

and the Lord saying to the disciples:

“You received freely; give freely” (Matthew 10:8).

And, wondrously, they buy the waters without money; and they do not drink them but eat them. For he himself is both water and bread, who descended from heaven (John 6).

Therefore, what is read in certain copies—“Buy and drink”—has been altered by inexperienced scribes, who thought it more fitting that the waters should be drunk rather than eaten. [Printed numeral 644.] Yet there is also a very bad kind of money, or silver, which Scripture rejects, saying:

“Money given deceitfully will be reckoned as a potsherd” (Proverbs 26:23, according to the Septuagint);

and elsewhere:

“Your silver is rejected” (Jeremiah 6:30).

There is also silver which is compared with the words of God:

“The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11:7).

[Col. 0529C] Having therefore rejected that silver and those monies with which we cannot buy the waters of the Lord, let us proceed to him who, holding the cup of the Sacrament, said to the disciples:

“Take and drink; this is my blood, which will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:27–28).

This is the wine which Wisdom mixed in her cup, summoning all the fools of the world and all who lack the wisdom of the world to drink. And so we are to buy not only wine but also milk, which signifies the innocence of little children. This custom and type is still preserved today in the churches of the West, so that those reborn in Christ are given wine and milk. [Note: [Col. 0529D] From this passage the custom of the ancient Church should be noted, as well as the differing discipline of Westerners and Easterners. For the churches of the East offered milk and honey to the newly baptized, whereas those of the West offered wine and milk. Compare what learned men have collected concerning the Epistle of Barnabas, and Rosweyde on the Life of Saint Pachomius [Col. 0530D], and Edmund Martene, book 1, *On Rites*.]

Paul also spoke of this milk:

“I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3:2).

And Peter:

“Like newborn infants, desire rational milk” (1 Peter 2:2).

Therefore Moses too, understanding wine and milk in relation to Christ’s passion, bears witness in mystical language:

“His eyes are graceful from wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk” (Genesis 49:12). [Note: [Col. 0530D] The older Ambrosian manuscript, more coherently with the argument, reads “possession” instead of “passion.”]

In the present passage the Septuagint translated “milk” as “fat.” Concerning this the holy David says in the psalm:

“May my soul be filled as with fat and richness” (Psalm 62:6);

and elsewhere:

“He fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Psalm 80:17).

[Col. 0530A] These fats signify nothing other than mystical flesh. To this the Lord urged his disciples, saying:

“Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

For this reason he was also handed over in Gethsemane, a name which signifies “fat valley” or “very rich valley.”

At the same time he reproves those who follow worldly wisdom, the perverse and counterfeit teachings of heretics, the traditions of the Pharisees, and every knowledge falsely so called that exalts itself against God. They weigh out silver for such instruction at great prices and with continual labor, although it contains no bread [Printed numeral 645.], and they sweat for these foods in which there is no satisfaction. From this it is shown that the wisdom to be pursued is not in the leaves and blossoms of words, but in the marrow and fruits of meanings: wisdom that does not merely pass over the ear but refreshes the mind. To learn it, we do not cross the seas and do not need great expense; rather, “the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.”

### Verses 2–3

[Col. 0530A] “Listen, listening to me, and eat what is good, and your soul will delight in abundance. Incline your ear and come to me; listen, and your soul will live. And I shall make an everlasting covenant with you: the faithful mercies of David.”

**Septuagint:** “Listen to me, and eat good things, and your soul will delight in good things. Attend with your ears and follow my ways; listen to me, and your soul will live in good things. And I shall establish with you an everlasting covenant, the holy faithful things of David.”

[Note: [Col. 0530D] In the same Ambrosian manuscript: “you eat”; I would certainly prefer “you will eat,” in accordance with the Greek φάγεσθε.]

Lest anyone think that the hearing to which the divine word exhorts them is bodily hearing rather than that of the mind, he promises good things not to their flesh but to their souls. For he says:

“If you listen to me, you will eat the good things of the land” (Isaiah 1:19).

Or else he speaks of the Good One, who says:

“I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11).

“And your soul will delight in good things and in abundance.”

Therefore, the good things promised to the soul are not riches, bodily health, or worldly dignities—things which even philosophers call *indifferents*, that is, neither good nor evil, and which vary according to the character of those who use them. Rather, we must understand as good those things to which God exhorts us:

“Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36:27).

But if the good things of the soul are called integrity and virtues, then the evils too are not to be understood as poverty, bodily weakness, or low birth, but as all the vices that are truly evil.

Thus Abraham did not possess good things because he was rich, but because he used his riches well (Genesis 13). Lazarus, who afterward rested in Abraham’s bosom, did not suffer evils because he endured the torments of diseases together with poverty; rather, through what were considered evils in the world he obtained true good things.

Therefore that rich man dressed in purple received “his good things in his lifetime”—the things that were good to him because he considered them good (Luke 16). Of Lazarus, conversely, it is not said, “He received his evils in his lifetime,” but rather that he received evils in his lifetime which seemed evil not to the one who suffered them but to others.

[Col. 0531A] Blessed Job gives us an example of both matters. He was overcome neither by the good things nor by the evils of the world, but endured everything with equal firmness of mind (Job 2). [Printed numeral 646.]

For this reason Solomon prays to God:

“Do not give me riches or poverty. Appoint for me what is necessary and sufficient for my sustenance, lest, when I am filled, I become a liar and say, ‘Who sees me?’ or, when I am needy, steal and swear falsely by the name of the Lord” (Proverbs 30:8–9).

If he prays not to have riches or poverty, but only the necessities of sustenance—concerning which the Apostle also says, “Having food and clothing, with these we are content” (1 Timothy 6)—it is clear that riches and destitution, health and sickness, pleasure and suffering are neither good nor evil in themselves, but become good or evil according to the diversity of those who endure them.

Therefore, the Lord does not promise the abundance of wealth, delicate foods, bodily fatness, Phasian birds and stuffed turtledoves, honeyed wine, the beauty of wives, or swarms of children, as the chiliasts suppose. [Note: [Col. 0531D] The same manuscript adds: “birds and fat turtledoves,” and so forth.]

Rather, he promises those delights to which he mystically summons us, saying:

“Delight yourself,” or “enjoy delights,” “in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Psalm 36:4);

and elsewhere:

“I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13);

and in another psalm:

“Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. He fills your desire with good things” (Psalm 102:1, 5).

Finally, he adds:

“Listen to me, and your soul will live” (Isaiah 55:3).

The promise of all good things is eternal life. If you are willing to listen, and your soul lives forever, “I shall make an everlasting covenant with you, the faithful mercies of David.”

Concerning these the same Psalmist sang:

“I shall sing the mercies of the Lord forever. From generation to generation I shall proclaim your truth” (Psalm 88:1–2).

And so that we may know what these mercies are, he demonstrates it in what follows:

“Once I swore by my holiness: If I lie to David, his offspring will remain forever, and his throne will be like the sun before me, and like the full moon forever, and like a faithful witness in heaven.”

He is called faithful because he fulfilled his promises.

For “the faithful mercies of David,” the Septuagint translated “the holy faithful things of David” (Acts 13:34), which can be understood as firm and strong. [Printed numeral 647.] Thus:

“All his commandments are faithful, established forever and ever” (Psalm 110:8);

and elsewhere:

“God is faithful, and there is no injustice in him” (Deuteronomy 32:4).

The Apostle Paul likewise says:

“If we deny him, he remains faithful; he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13).

And elsewhere, writing to Timothy:

“Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance” (1 Timothy 1:15).

The covenant which the Lord promises will not be brief or last for only one period, as was the covenant of the Jewish people, but will remain forever, so that the true David may come and the promises made in the person of God may be fulfilled in the Gospel:

“I have found David my servant; with holy mercy I have anointed him” (Psalm 88:21).

He is the one whose hand he placed upon the sea and whose right hand upon the rivers. Through Ezekiel, while David has already been sleeping for many ages, he calls him his servant and shepherd, saying:

“I shall raise up for you one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23).

### Verses 4–5

[Col. 0532A] “Behold, I have given him as a witness to the peoples, a leader and commander to the nations. Behold, you will call a nation that you did not know, and nations that did not know you will run to you, because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, for he has glorified you.”

**Septuagint:** “Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, as a ruler and commander of the nations. Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples that did not know you will flee to you, because of the Lord your God, the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you.”

[Note: [Col. 0531D] Victor places a second “Behold” before “nations,” following a Greek manuscript: ἰδοὺ ἔθνη. Likewise, shortly afterward he adds “all” to the testimony from Genesis: “all nations will be blessed.” [Col. 0532D]]

He had summoned the Jewish people to believe, urging them to incline their ear and receive the everlasting covenant which the Lord had promised to David and to Abraham and his offspring, saying:

“In your offspring all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

The Apostle Paul explains this:

“He did not say ‘in offspring,’ as of many, but ‘in your offspring,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3:16).

And because he knew that, if the Jews did not believe, the peoples of the nations would believe, he turns to the nations and says that he sent his Son as the witness or testimony of all nations, to announce his precepts and commandments to the peoples. He speaks of himself:

“This gospel must be preached in the whole world as a testimony to all nations” (Matthew 24:14).

Finally, with this saying he refutes the proud Pilate:

“For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37).

Concerning him the Apostle Paul writes to Timothy:

“There is one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all, a testimony in its proper times, in which I was appointed a herald and an apostle” (1 Timothy 2:5). [Printed numeral 648.]

[Col. 0532C] Everything that is said, therefore, must be referred to him who was led to the slaughter like a sheep and, like a lamb before its shearer, did not open his mouth. Concerning him it was said above:

“We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isaiah 53:2);

and:

“He himself bore our sins and suffered for us.”

Those who formerly did not know him fled to him or ran to him, saying:

“God is our refuge and strength” (Psalm 45:1);

and again:

“Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation” (Psalm 89:1).

Concerning their faith we also read above:

“Those to whom nothing was preached about him will see, and those who had not heard will understand.”

[Col. 0532D] He is the witness of everything that the Father promised and accomplished for the world. Paul briefly embraces his mystery in his words to the Ephesians:

“The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory” (Ephesians 1:3).

Of him it is also now written:

“Because of the Lord your God and the Holy One of Israel, who has glorified you,”

and with the glory that he possessed before the world existed. The Prophet also bears witness to this:

“The glory of God will appear” (Hebrews 1),

who is “the radiance of his glory and the form of his substance,” when every tongue will confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Philippians 2).

He answered the Son when the Son asked for the glory which he had previously possessed:

“I have glorified, and I shall glorify.”

The Apostle John also says concerning him:

“We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 12:28; 1:14).

Therefore, when he speaks of the one who “was God the Word and was in the beginning with God,” he is called “the Father of glory.” But when he speaks of the one who says in the Gospel, “Why do you persecute me, a human being who speaks the truth to you?” (John 8:40), he is called “the God of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

This does not mean that one is one person and the other another person—which is the worst error of many—but that one and the same Son of God speaks now according to the glory of his divinity, now according to the affections of our nature, which he deigned to assume [Note: the Ambrosian manuscript adds, “and preserve”].

[Col. 0533B] [Note: [Col. 0533D] The words “one” and “another,” which were lacking, were supplied by the Ambrosian manuscript.]

### Verses 6–7

“Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the impious person leave his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.”

[Printed numeral 649.] **Septuagint:** “Seek the Lord; and when you have found him, call upon him. And after he has drawn near to you, let the impious person leave his ways and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord; he will obtain mercy, because he will greatly forgive your sins.”

Since, therefore, as we have already said, you were unwilling to receive the everlasting covenant and the faithful mercies of David—which, because you were unwilling to accept them, the multitude of the nations accepted—I, the Prophet, your fellow countryman, admonish and testify to you: while there is time, do penance.

Turn to him who now speaks to you through the Prophets and who afterward will speak in person. Seek him while he may be found, while you are in the body, while opportunity for repentance is granted. Seek him not in a place but in faith.

How God is to be sought is stated more fully elsewhere:

“Think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart, because he is found by those who do not test him, and he appears to those who are not unbelieving toward him” (Wisdom 1:1–2). [Note: [Col. 0533D] Two manuscripts read: “who are not unbelieving toward his word.”]

Therefore, knowing what is said concerning sinners—“Those who depart far from you will perish”—let us speak to the Lord:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8).

And let us call upon him while he is near, lest through our vices and sins he depart far from us. For he draws near to those who draw near to him, and he gladly runs to meet the son returning after a long time.

Therefore the saint sings in the psalm:

“But for me, to cling to God is good” (Psalm 72:28).

And Moses alone drew near to the Lord (Exodus 20).

Through Jeremiah God says:

“I am God who draws near, and not from far away” (Jeremiah 23:33).

He draws near to those who approach him in faith and withdraws far from those who depart from him through unbelief.

For this reason it is said to believers:

“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.”

And lest we think that this alone could suffice, he immediately adds:

“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:8).

Concerning him he had said above:

“Your adversary the devil, like a lion going about, seeks someone to devour. Resist him, strengthened by faith” (1 Peter 5:8–9).

Nor is it enough to seek the Lord and, while there is time for repentance, to find and call upon him while he is near, unless the impious person leaves his former ways and his former thoughts by which he had turned away from the Lord.

Then we shall return to the Lord, who will have mercy on us, and to the most compassionate Father [Printed numeral 650.], who is abundant in mercies and ready to forgive, when we have abandoned our former thoughts and ways, so that afterward we may deserve to hear:

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Psalm 31:1).

[Col. 0533C] [Note: [Col. 0533D] The printed tradition immediately continues in this way. All our manuscript copies and the edition of Erasmus read it thus; Marianus Victorius, however, emends it without manuscript authority and establishes the following reading: “And lest we think that this alone could suffice, he immediately adds above: ‘Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.’ Concerning him Peter had also said: ‘Your adversary the devil,’” and so forth. Anyone who compares the cited testimonies will find this restoration consonant with Scripture. But since nothing in the manuscript copies supports that reading, we have not altered the ancient text, contenting ourselves with notifying the reader both of the corruption and of the necessary restoration. —Martianus.]

[Note: [Col. 0534D] Our manuscripts have nearly the same reading; they differ only in joining by this one word where the text has “adds immediately.” Victorius’s version is somewhat more coherent, but does not follow the manuscript evidence. He restores: “he immediately adds above”; then follows, “Concerning him Peter had also said: ‘Your adversary,’” and so forth.]

### Verses 8–9

[Col. 0534B] “For my thoughts are not your thoughts, nor are your ways my ways, says the Lord. For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts.”

**Septuagint:** “For my thoughts are not like your thoughts, nor are my ways like your ways, says the Lord. But as heaven is distant from earth, so is my way distant from your ways, and your thoughts from my thought.”

“Do not think,” he says, “that what I promise is difficult or seem to yourselves that it is incredible that the impious and unjust can be saved, whether the Jewish people or all those among the nations who did not know God. Consider that there is a great difference between my plans and yours, and that the difference in will is as great as the difference in nature” (Proverbs 19).

“For many are the thoughts in a man’s heart, but the counsel of the Lord remains forever.”

You, as human beings, often repent of what you have promised and overturn an old will with a new will. [Note: [Col. 0534D] Two Ambrosian manuscripts read: “You repent of what you have promised, and overturn an old will with a new will.”]

But the Lord destroys the plans of the nations, rejects the thoughts of the peoples, and makes void the wills of rulers (Psalm 32). The thoughts of his heart, however, endure from generation to generation; and whatever he has decreed cannot be changed.

Do you wish to know the difference between my counsel and yours? As far as heaven is separated in place from earth, and the dwelling place of angels differs from that of human beings, so far are my thoughts separated from your counsels.

Concerning my thoughts it is said:

“His judgments are unsearchable and his ways inscrutable” (Romans 11:33).

But concerning yours:

“They devised a plan which they were unable to establish” (Psalm 20:12);

and elsewhere:

“Whatever counsel you take will be dispersed, and whatever word you speak will not remain among you” (Isaiah 8:10).

They require no clear interpretation; for that reason they are compressed rather than explained.

### Verses 10–11

[Col. 0535A] [Printed numeral 651.] “And just as rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth, soak it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be, which will go forth from my mouth. It will not return to me empty, but it will do whatever I willed, and it will prosper in the things for which I sent it.”

**Septuagint:** “As if rain or snow descends from heaven and does not return until it has watered the earth, made it bring forth and sprout, and given seed to the sower and bread for eating, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth. It will not return until it completes what I willed, and I shall make its ways and my commandments prosper.”

[Col. 0535B] What is said depends upon the preceding passage, and the meaning is briefly this: the people of the nations should not disbelieve that, after such great crimes, an impious person can suddenly be saved. For my thoughts are not like human thoughts; and as far as heaven is distant from earth, so far are my thoughts separated from human thoughts. For I am most merciful and abundant in forgiveness.

Do you wish to receive another comparison? Just as rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water and soak the earth and cause various seeds to sprout, so that loaves may be produced for human use from full crops, so the word of my promise, which I once promised and which went forth from my mouth, will not be void; rather, everything will be accomplished in deed.

According to the allegorical interpretation, there is a twofold understanding. The word of the Lord is either the one of whom it is written:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1),

who will not return to him empty unless he has done the Father’s will, completed everything for which he had been made flesh, and reconciled the world to God.

He is said to proceed from the mouth, and from the womb and vulva—not because God possesses these bodily members, but because we learn the nature of the Lord through our own words.

Or certainly this must be said: the word of evangelical teaching is called rain, and the rains which spiritual clouds pour upon good earth are those to which the truth of God has come.

Moses promises this rain and these showers in the Song of Deuteronomy:

“Let the earth hear the words of my mouth; let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew” (Deuteronomy 32:1–2),

so that those who sow in tears may reap in joy (Psalm 125).

And those who sow in righteousness and in the Spirit may reap the fruit of eternal life and receive the bread of evangelical teaching, concerning which it is written in Proverbs and Ecclesiastes [Printed numeral 652.]:

“Open your eyes, and fill yourself with bread” (Proverbs 20:13);

and again:

“Send your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it” (Ecclesiastes 11:1).

Nor should we believe that those who eat are commanded to open their eyes in order to eat this bread by which bodies are nourished, and thus be filled with the loaves which the poor man secretly eats in Habakkuk (Habakkuk 3). Rather, God exhorts us to the bread of teaching, which we cannot eat unless we open the eyes of our hearts.

Paul often writes concerning this to those who are nourished by the words of faith and truth (2 Corinthians 9).

The teacher is commanded to cast the bread of his teaching upon every water, to pour spiritual grace into all, and to know that, if he does what has been commanded, he will receive a reward at the last time.

It would seem most unjust if one who gives alms from unrighteous mammon makes friends for himself who will receive him into eternal dwellings (Luke 16), while one who distributes spiritual food and gives his fellow servants their portion of food at the proper time does not find them after many ages, which Ecclesiastes calls “the multitude of days” (Ecclesiastes 11).

### Verses 12–13

[Col. 0536A] “For you shall go out in joy, and be led forth in peace. The mountains and hills shall sing praise before you, and all the trees of the country shall clap their hands. In place of the rush the fir tree shall rise, and in place of the nettle the myrtle shall grow. And the Lord shall be named as an eternal sign, which shall not be taken away.”

**Septuagint:** “You shall go out in joy, and be led forth in gladness. The mountains and hills shall leap, awaiting you in gladness, and all the trees of the field shall applaud with their branches. In place of στοιβή—that is, very worthless stalks [or stems]—the cypress shall rise; and in place of the fleabane the myrtle shall rise. And the Lord shall be for an everlasting name and sign, and it shall not fail.”

[Col. 0536C] “My word,” he says, “will not return empty; but after it has fulfilled everything I willed and accomplished my will on earth, then it will come to me. And what is written will be fulfilled:

‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet”’” (Psalm 109:1–2).

You shall go out in joy from the blood of idolatry, and be led forth in peace, so that you may hear from the Apostle:

“Grace to you and peace” (Romans 1:7).

Or, “you shall be led forth in gladness,” so that after the shadow of the Law you may learn the truth of the Gospel.

The mountains and hills—which we may understand as angels and the souls of the saints, who according to the variety of their virtues are called mountains and hills—will rejoice over those who repent and express the gladness of their minds by leaping. [Printed numeral 653.]

The Lord also says this in the Gospel:

“There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7).

Likewise, all the trees of the field, whether with branches or hands, will applaud—those trees planted beside the streams of water, which will yield their fruit in its season and whose leaves will not fall (Psalm 1).

One of these trees spoke in the psalm:

“But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of the Lord” (Psalm 51:10).

Let us ask those who follow only the literal history and eat boiled flesh of the lamb [Note: [Col. 0537D] Victorius long ago restored this reading; our manuscripts clearly confirm it. Martianus, however, from other copies preferred the nonsensical reading “they eat boiled flesh with blood.” —Martianus. Another note reads: “They eat boiled flesh of the Lamb. Marianus changed this passage, for he read, ‘and they eat boiled flesh of the Lamb.’ This reading has an excellent sense and would seem preferable if the manuscript copies supported it.” —Martianus.] in what sense the trees applaud with branches and resound with hands, and how the saying about rivers is to be understood:

“The rivers will clap their hands” (Psalm 97:8).

Not only will the mountains and hills leap and sing, and all the trees of the field, which the Lord has blessed, applaud with their branches and resound with their hands; but στοιβή and κονύζη—whether “rush” and “nettle”—will also be transformed [variant: are transformed] into fir and myrtle and cypress.

According to Symmachus and the Septuagint, στοιβή is written in Hebrew as *NESUS* (נסוס); Aquila and Theodotion translated it as κονύζη. Κονύζη is a very worthless and bitter herb with a most foul smell.

Where the Septuagint translated κονύζη, which in Hebrew is called *SARPHOD* (סרפד), Symmachus translated “nettle.”

Whatever may be the precise identity of these names, this must be said: evil things are changed into good, and virtues grow in place of vices—that is, righteousness in place of iniquity, courage in place of rashness, self-control in place of luxury, and prudence in place of folly.

Let us give examples from the great ones. Matthew, Zacchaeus, and the tax collectors were rushes, στοιβή, useless stalks, and κονύζη of bitter taste and most foul smell, saying:

“My wounds have become foul and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37:6).

Suddenly transformed into apostles, they became cypress, fir, and myrtle: of excellent fragrance and useful for various works.

Paul too, the persecutor of the Church, when he heard the Lord saying:

“Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me? It is hard for you to kick against the goad” (Acts 9:4–5),

was a nettle, possessing the stings of persecution. [Printed numeral 654.]

But when he preached the Gospel throughout the whole world and could say:

“We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15),

he is rightly called cypress and myrtle.

Prostitutes and tax collectors go before the Pharisees into the kingdom of God, and the thief passes from the cross into paradise (Matthew 21).

Therefore, what is said in the Gospel—

“A good tree cannot produce bad fruits” (Luke 6:43; Matthew 7:18)—

does not at all refer to the properties of nature, as heretics wish, but to the choice of the mind.

Finally it adds:

“Either make the tree good and its fruit good.”

From this it is clear that each person, by his own will, makes his soul [variant: the soul] a good or bad tree, whose fruits are various.

It follows:

“And the Lord shall be for an everlasting name and sign, which shall not fail.”

For those who have been changed from evil into good, the Lord will be an eternal name and sign, so that they may be called Christians from his name and branded with the mark of his cross.

Concerning this sign Simeon, holding the little child in his arms, said:

“This child is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and as a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34).

Concerning it also it was said above:

“The Lord himself will give you a sign” (Isaiah 7:14).

And the holy man sings in the psalm:

“Make with me, Lord, a sign for good” (Psalm 85:17).

And he himself is the sign. He says:

“When you see the sign of the Son of Man”—

a sign that will not fail or be changed by any end, but will pass from the present way of life into the future.

## Chapter LVI

### Verse 1

[Col. 0538A] “Thus says the Lord: Guard judgment and do righteousness, for my salvation is near to come and my righteousness to be revealed.”

The Septuagint translated “mercy” in place of “righteousness”; otherwise it is similar.

With the prophecy concerning the nations concluded—the nations which, at the coming of the Word of God, are to be changed from rush and nettle into cypress and myrtle—Isaiah speaks to the hearers of that time, urging them to do everything that is right and to prepare themselves for the coming of the Savior, because he himself is the righteousness and mercy of God.

If the thoughts of the saints are judgments, and we ought to have trained senses for the discernment of good and evil [Note: [Col. 0538D] Two Ambrosian manuscripts read: “judgments which we ought to possess with trained senses for discerning good and evil”], why should we not guard judgment at all times? We must not despise the person of the poor in judgment, nor be frightened by the power of the rich; rather, we must judge the great as the small, knowing according to Moses that judgment belongs to the Lord, who judges those who judge (Deuteronomy 1). [Printed numeral 655.]

Accordingly, it is read in the psalm:

“God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Psalm 81:1).

What is now said—“Guard judgment and do righteousness”—is like this:

“Blessed are those who guard judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Psalm 105:3),

so that they may pursue justly what is just.

Although under the name “righteousness” the whole sphere of virtue seems to me to be signified: whoever practices one act of righteousness is said to have fulfilled all the virtues, which follow one another and cling together, so that whoever possesses one possesses them all, and whoever lacks one lacks them all.

Something similar is expressed by the fourteenth psalm:

“He who walks blamelessly and practices righteousness” (Psalm 14:2).

And elsewhere it is written:

“Learn righteousness, you who dwell upon the earth” (Isaiah 26:9).

That the Savior, who has become for us righteousness, holiness, and redemption, is himself the mercy of God (1 Corinthians 1), the words of the saints bear witness:

“God sent his mercy and his truth” (Psalm 56:4).

(Vers. 2.) “Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who takes hold of it: who keeps the Sabbath, so as not to profane it; who guards his hands, so as not to do any evil” [Col. 0538D]. The Septuagint reads: “Blessed is the man who will do these things, and the man who holds fast to them, who keeps the Sabbaths so as not to profane them, and who keeps his hands from committing iniquity.”

He who, with the Apostle Paul, can say, “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I destroyed the things that belong to a child” (I Cor. XIII, 11), attains the blessedness of the present passage, forgetting what lies behind [Col. 0539A] and reaching forward to what lies ahead [Note: [Col. 0539D] The same manuscripts read, “and reaching forward to what lies ahead.”], until he arrives “at the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at a perfect man, at the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ”; so that this psalm may be applied to him: “Blessed is the man who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. I, 1).

This man, therefore—the son of the inner man, concerning whom it is repeatedly said in Leviticus, “Man, man” (Lev. XVII, 8)—is blessed in that he first does these things and takes hold of them: namely, the judgment and righteousness and salvation of the Lord, which is near and is to be revealed to all the nations. Thus he not only does what has been commanded, but holds it firmly in his hand; and he keeps the Sabbath, so as not to profane it.

What the Sabbath is that he commands to be observed, the following verse shows: “Guarding his hands, so as not to do any evil.” For it is of no benefit to sit on the Sabbath, or to sleep, or to long for banquets. Rather, if he does good, let him rest from evil and keep a perpetual Sabbath of iniquity—that is, leisure from it—and let him do only those things that pertain to the salvation of the soul, and let him not engage in any servile work. “For whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (John VIII). But we have been called into freedom, the freedom with which Christ has endowed us (Gal. IV), so that we should by no means labor for food that perishes; but, cleaving to the Lord, let us say with the Prophet: “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28).

Let us become one spirit with him, and let us fulfill the dedicated Sabbaths [Note: [Col. 0539D] In accordance with the Greek of the Septuagint below, chapter LVIII, σάββατα τρυφερά, “delicate Sabbaths,” Victor writes “dedicated” instead.], so that we may not belong to the six days in which the world was made, the days of which the Apostles were not, and to whom the Lord said: “If you were of this world, the world would love what is its own. But because you are not of this world, since I chose you, therefore the world hates you” (John XV, 19).

(Vers. 3.) “And let not the son of the foreigner who clings to the Lord say, ‘The Lord will surely separate me from his people’; and let not the eunuch say, ‘Behold, I am a dry tree.’” The Septuagint reads: “Let not the foreigner who has been joined to the Lord say, ‘Will the Lord surely separate me from his people?’ And let not the eunuch say, ‘Because I am a dry tree.’”

Those who understand this passage in a humble sense refer what is said to proselytes from the nations and to actual eunuchs. Thus foreigners, if they receive the law of the Lord and are circumcised, and eunuchs—such as the eunuch of Candace, that queen (Acts VIII), who could not even remain idle on his journey, and who, while seeking an interpreter of the reading, found Christ whom he was seeking—are not to be excluded [Col. 0539D] from the salvation of God.

They say that this is spoken against the Jews, who boast of the nobility of their descent, call themselves children of Abraham, and consider blessed those who have “seed in Zion” and “household members in Jerusalem” (John VIII). But we understand those whom above we interpreted as saliunca (a saltwort), nettle, κονύζη (*konýzē*), and στοιβή (*stoibē*) (above, on chapter LV), transformed into fir, cypress, and myrtle, to be summoned now to the faith of the Gospel: they must not despair if they cling to the Lord, nor think that they are separated from the people of God. “For all who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. V).

There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither circumcision nor uncircumcision. To them the Song in Deuteronomy commands: “Rejoice, nations, with his people”—that is, with the people of God, who formerly had the Jewish people (Deut. XXXIII, 43). Those coming from the east and from the west will rest in Abraham’s bosom.

This is also what John the Baptist said: “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For I tell you that God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9). And just as among proselytes there is no difference, but men and women alike are called equally to salvation, so among eunuchs who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven both sexes are understood: those who have put to death their members upon the earth—sexual immorality, impurity, passion, and evil desire—until all arrive “at a perfect man” and say with the Apostle: “We know no one according to the flesh. Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him thus no longer” (II Cor. V, 16).

[Note: [Col. 0540D] Victor supplies *ergo*—“therefore”—from the Hebrew.]

Therefore, by “eunuchs” we are by no means to understand those whom the fiery poet describes, saying (Lucan, book X):

> Nor the unhappy youth, mutilated by the sword,  
> and the man cut off . . . . . . . .

Rather, they are those of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “Those who have castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XIX, 12). Such were also the Apostles, who, when they were astonished and said, because of the difficulty of the matter, “Who then can be saved?”, received the Savior’s reply: “The one who can receive it, let him receive it.”

Thus the Apostle testifies concerning such eunuchs—that is, virgins—that he has no command of the Lord, but gives advice as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord, wishing all to be as he himself is: “The time is short; it remains that those who have wives should live as though they had none” (I Cor. VII, 29). For whoever has been called free from the bondage and duty of marriage is truly a servant of Christ.

(Vers. 4, 5.) “For thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: If they keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast to my covenant, I will give them a place in my house and within my walls, and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not perish.”

The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: Those who keep my Sabbaths, choose what I desire, and hold fast to my testament, I will give them a place in my house and within my wall, a named place, better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name, and it shall not fail.”

He had proposed two groups, proselytes and eunuchs. He first speaks about the eunuchs, giving them rules for living [658] and promising them rewards in the future. After them he comes to the proselytes, promising them similar things.

He therefore speaks to the eunuchs who said in despair, “Behold, I am a dry tree” (Exod. XXIII), so that they should not think themselves subject to the curse pronounced against the sterile: “Cursed is the sterile person who does not make offspring in Israel” (Deut. VII). “If,” he says, “they keep my Sabbaths, and from my commandments choose those that I desire—not those that I granted because of the weakness of those who heard—and retain my covenant, or testament, with complete faith, I will give them a place in my house, in my Temple, and within the walls of my most firmly established city, and a name better than sons and daughters, a name that no forgetfulness will erase.”

We have explained above who the eunuchs are: those who are concerned with the things of God. Wisdom, too, which is inscribed under Solomon’s name, speaks to them:

> “Blessed is the barren woman who is undefiled, who has not known a sinful marriage-bed; she will bear fruit at the visitation of souls. And the eunuch who has not worked iniquity with his hand, nor imagined evil against the Lord. For a chosen gift will be given to his faith, and a most desirable portion in the temple of the Lord” (Wis. III, 13–14).

This barren woman is fruitful through virginity [or: made fruitful]; this eunuch does violence to the kingdom of heaven and seizes it forcibly. He is the keeper of the Sabbaths, so that he never performs the works of marriage (I Cor. VII). He chooses what the Lord desires, offering more than what is commanded, considering not the Apostle’s concession but the Lord’s will.

He holds the Lord’s everlasting covenant, so that he does not devote himself to prayer for a time and then return again to the same things, but knows that he will receive in the house of the Lord, which is his Church, an excellent place. “For there are many dwelling places with the Father” (John XIV).

And whoever is a eunuch and does everything that is written will have an excellent place within his walls, so that he may become a tower of the Lord, stand in the priestly rank, and, in place of physical children, have many spiritual children.

Ecclesiastical histories report that such a eunuch was the Evangelist John, whom Jesus loved greatly: he reclined upon Jesus’ breast (John XIII); when Peter was walking more slowly, he, borne on the wings of virginity, ran ahead to the Lord (John XX); and, plunging himself into the mysteries of the divine birth, he dared to say what all the ages had not known: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God” (John I, 2).

Let every Jewish quibble therefore cease, and let it stop exposing itself to ridicule by opening the kingdom of heaven to those who are half-men, since chastity lies not in bodily weakness but in the will of the mind.

(Vers. 6, 7.) “And the sons of the foreigner who cling to the Lord, to worship him and to love his name, so that they may be his servants—everyone who keeps the Sabbath, so as not to profane it, and holds fast to my covenant, I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer.”

The Septuagint reads: “And to the foreigners who have been joined to the Lord, to serve him and to love his name, so that they may be his servants ÷ and maidservants **—and all who keep my Sabbaths, so as not to violate them, and hold my testament, I will bring them to my holy mountain, and I will make them joyful in my house of prayer.”

[Note: [Col. 0541] Victor reads: “to his holy mountain.”]

After the eunuchs he passes to the foreigners, whom he had mentioned earlier, and promises them rewards as well: if they serve him, and pass from servitude to love of his name, they are to be his servants. Such was the Apostle Paul, who wrote at the beginning of his letters: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ” (Rom. I, 1). And Moses was “the servant of God” (Heb. III).

We have marked with an obelus what has been added in the Septuagint, “and maidservants.” For there can be no difference of sex in spiritual gifts, since in Christ Jesus there is neither male nor female, but we are all one in him (John XVII).

We have spoken above about the Sabbath and the everlasting covenant. Whoever therefore does these things, God will bring him to his holy mountain and gladden him in his house of prayer.

The holy mountain is either the doctrines of truth and the confession of the Trinity, or the Lord himself, to whom in the last time—according to this same Isaiah and the prophet Micah—many nations will stream (Isa. II; Mic. IV).

The house of prayer is the Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, and not the Temple of the Jews, which was confined within the narrow limits of the land of Judea.

(Vers. 8, 9.) “Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be pleasing to me upon my altar, for my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples, says the Lord God, who gathers the dispersed of Israel: I will still gather to him those already gathered to him. All the beasts of the field, come to devour; all the beasts of the forest.”

The Septuagint reads: “Their burnt offerings and their sacrifices will be acceptable upon my altar. For my house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations, says the Lord, who gathers the dispersed of Israel, because I will gather an assembly to him. All the wild beasts, come and eat; all the beasts of the forest.”

We learn more fully in Leviticus the difference between sacrifices and burnt offerings. Burnt offerings are those that are wholly consumed upon the altar. Sacrifices and offerings are those of which one part is offered upon the altar and another part is given to the priests.

We must not therefore suppose that the offerings of foreigners and eunuchs are sought according to the Jewish rite. Rather, we must understand that the eunuchs offer burnt offerings, since they consecrate themselves wholly to God, while the foreigners offer sacrifices, since they devote themselves to prayer for a time. Concerning these the Lord says: “The sacrifice of praise glorified [or: will glorify] me”; and in another place: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. XLIX, 14).

Concerning these sacrifices and burnt offerings the Lord speaks through Hosea: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings that are offered upon the altar of the Lord” (Hos. VI, 6).

This is what John testifies that he saw in heaven in the Apocalypse, beneath which were the souls of the martyrs (Rev. VI). From this altar one of the Seraphim took a coal with tongs and brought it to Isaiah’s lips to purify them (Isa. IV, 6). This is the altar and this is the tabernacle, after whose pattern everything in Exodus was made, and upon which spiritual sacrifices were offered to God (Exod. XXXVIII).

Otherwise, concerning bodily sacrifices and burnt offerings God himself testifies above [Note: [Col. 0541] Some manuscripts read: “God himself testifies through the same [prophet].”]: “Why do I need the multitude of your sacrifices?” says the Lord. “I am full of the burnt offerings [or: burnt offerings] of rams, and I do not desire the fat of lambs, or the blood of bulls and goats.” For “my house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples”—not for one Jewish nation, nor in one place, Jerusalem and its city, but throughout the whole world: a house not of bulls, goats, and rams, but of prayer.

The Lord used this testimony when he spoke against those who, under the name of the Holy Spirit, were selling gifts of doves in the Temple, sitting in the seats of pestilence and keeping the tables of the money-changers (Matt. XXI; John II), doing everything for the sake of shameful profit and not knowing what is written: “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matt. X, 8).

The Lord promised these future things, he who gathers the dispersed of Israel. To them the Apostle Peter also writes a letter [Col. 0543B]—concerning them the Evangelist speaks: “He did not say this from himself; but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered” (John XI, 7). Thus what was said would be fulfilled: “The assembly of the peoples will surround you; because of this, return on high” (Ps. VII, 8) [Note: [Col. 0543D] Two Ambrosian manuscripts read, “for this, return on high.”]

But when the remnants of Israel had been gathered through the Apostles and those who had previously been scattered had been brought together into one flock, all the beasts are summoned to come and devour Israel—that is, those who refused to believe. Concerning them the Apostle says: “The end will come upon them” (Phil. III). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army, then know that its consummation has come” (Luke XI, 20).

Or this may be understood as follows: they were handed over to beasts for devouring, the beasts whom the Prophet detests when he says: “Do not give the souls confessing you to the beasts” (Ps. LXXIII, 19). These are the beasts in the tropological sense, which devoured a certain portion of the Lord; above, too (on chapter IX), we read of Syria from the rising of the sun and the Greeks from the west, who devour Israel with their whole mouth.

And in Jeremiah: “Israel is a wandering sheep; lions drove it away. The king of Assyria first devoured it, and the king of Babylon, the last, will crush its bones” (Jer. L, 17).

It may also be said that, when the previously savage nations are summoned to faith together with the people of Israel, they come to the Church after leaving the forests—those who killed many from Absalom’s army—and eat the heavenly bread and are filled with the flesh of the Lamb.

[Col. 0543D] (Vers. 10–12.) “His watchmen are all blind; they all lack knowledge. They are mute dogs, unable to bark; seeing vain things, sleeping, and loving dreams. And the most shameless dogs do not know satiety; the shepherds themselves have no understanding. They have all turned to their own way, each one to his own greed, from the highest to the last. Come, let us take wine and fill ourselves with drunkenness; and as it is today, so shall it be tomorrow, and much more besides.”

The Septuagint reads: “See, for they have all been blinded; they have all failed to understand. They are mute dogs, unable to bark, dreaming on a couch and loving slumber. And the shameless dogs in soul have not known satiety [or: have failed to know satiety].” [Note: [Col. 0544D] Victor reads “shameless,” from the Greek ἀναιδεῖς τῇ ψυχῇ, “shameless in soul.”]

The Septuagint continues: “And they are evil, lacking understanding; they have all followed their own ways. Each one together from his highest point [or: from his summit]. Come, let us take wine and become drunk, and let tomorrow be like today, exceedingly great and much more **.”

“Let all the beasts of the forest come,” he says, “and devour those who have been gathered.” Or, if the crowds of the nations are to take the place of the Jews, their watchmen are responsible: namely, the scribes and Pharisees. For they were all blind and did not know the Lord Savior, nor did they wish to see the light that was present.

To them the Lord said: “Fools and blind! Which is greater, the gold, or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” (Matt. XXIII, 17); and again: “Blind guides, who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel” (ibid., 24); and: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. XV, 14).

That teachers are called watchmen we have also read above. For in the passage where the Septuagint reads, “The voice of your watchmen has been raised” (Isa. LII, 8), the Hebrew has: “The voice of your watchers.” One of these was Ezekiel, to whom God says: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watcher for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III, 17).

But those watchmen were not blind. Indeed, they were called seers. These, however, of whom the Prophet now speaks, are called not only blind watchmen but also mute dogs, unable to bark. They ought to guard the Lord’s flock, drive away wolves, and bark on behalf of the Lord, but they love dreams and delight in demonic visions.
