The meaning is: they cannot speak the truth, but only every kind of falsehood. Nor are they content with this. They slept while guarding the Lord’s flock, were unable to bark, and loved the bed—by which bodily pleasure is signified. Among their own people, however, they were shameless in soul and knew no satiety, since they are never satisfied with their error.

They devour the Lord’s people as though they were bread, and they devour widows’ houses; they serve their appetites and lust. For they cannot say, “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. XVIII, 9), nor do they know what is written: “The wisdom of a man illuminates his face” (Prov. XVII, 24).

They are mute dogs toward their enemies, concerning whom it is written: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII, 6). They are sleeping dogs who do not know that the commandment says: “Do not give sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids” (Ps. CXXXI); and again: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. XXIV, 42).

And therefore, giving place to the devil, they are the most shameless dogs, who are never satisfied. For they vomit what they have eaten and return to their vomit (Prov. XXVI). The Apostle Peter also speaks of them: “The true proverb has happened to them: ‘The dog returns to its own vomit,’ and ‘The sow, after washing, returns to wallowing in the mire’” (II Pet. II, 22).

That these watchmen and dogs are the same as the shepherds, the following words demonstrate: “The shepherds themselves lacked understanding.”

The Hebrew word רועים (*ROIM* [or *ROEM*]), written with four letters—resh, ʿayin, yod, and mem—means “shepherds” if read *roim*, but “worst” if read *raim*. We have said this to show the causes of the differing interpretation.

For they all sought their own interests and not the things of God, and they did not walk in the way of the Lord (Phil. II), concerning which it is written: “Ask what the good way is, and walk in it” (Jer. VI, 16). But, according to what is read in the Book of Judges, “There was no king in Israel; each person did what seemed right to him” (Judg. XVII, 6), and they followed their own errors.

What follows—“Each one to his own greed, from the highest to the last: Come, let us take wine and fill ourselves with drunkenness, and as it is today, so shall it be tomorrow, and much more”—is not found in the Septuagint interpreters, but has been added from the Hebrew and marked beforehand with stars.

Indeed, none of the ecclesiastical interpreters has expounded these verses; as though they were leaping over and passing by a plainly open pit in the middle.

What he says means this: because they have turned away from the way of the Lord and followed their own paths, they therefore burn with greed from the highest to the last, from the leaders to the people. After they have begun to strike their fellow servants and to eat and drink with the drunkards, they say: “Come, let us take wine and fill ourselves with drunkenness. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. And as it is today, so shall it be tomorrow, and much more” (I Cor. XV, 2).

This is what he said above: “They have not known satiety.” They are not satisfied with past pleasure [Note: [Col. 0545D] With the Victorian manuscripts, we read “they were satisfied” instead of “they are satisfied.”], but prepare future delights, much greater than those they had previously enjoyed.

If this is said about the leaders of the Jews, on account of whom the Lord’s people were devoured by beasts, let us avoid the examples of the wicked. Let us not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery; let us not be overwhelmed by pleasures; let us not be mute in speech yet rabid dogs against our adversaries [Note: [Col. 0545D] One Ambrosian manuscript, with a very different sense, reads: “nor mute in speaking against adversaries, and rabid against our own people,” etc.]. Rather, let us follow the ways of God instead of our own, and let us hear Scripture admonishing us: “Think of the Lord in goodness” (Wis. I, 1). And again: “Understanding is excellent for those who practice it.”

And if we have been dogs, let us not despair of salvation, hearing the words of the Canaanite woman who said to the Lord: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table” (Matt. XV, 27).

[Note: [Col. 0546D] The same manuscript reads: “For this utterance she obtained mercy.”]

For this reason, having obtained mercy, she hears from the Lord: “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” For she could have said with the Prophet: “I ran in the way of your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 32). And again: “Lead me in the straight way.”

(Cap. LVII.—Vers. 1, 2.) “The righteous has perished [Vulgate: is perishing], and there is no one who considers it in his heart; and men of mercy are gathered away, because there is no one who understands. For the righteous has been gathered away from before evil. Let peace come; let him who walks in his uprightness rest in his bed.”

[Note: [Col. 0546D] Two manuscripts have a different reading: “and no one considers it in his heart.”]

The Septuagint reads: “See how the righteous has perished, and no one takes it to heart; and righteous men are taken away, and no one considers it. For the righteous has been removed from before iniquity; his burial will be in peace; it has been taken away from the midst.”

Because of the blind watchmen and mute dogs who are themselves shepherds, lacking understanding and never satisfied with present pleasures but always preparing themselves for future ones, the righteous has perished. Of him Pilate’s wife says: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matt. XXVII, 19). Having washed his hands, he says: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.”

Here we must consider that the word of perdition, concerning which heretics often make accusations, as though it signified destruction and eternal abolition, is applied to Christ. His “perdition” plainly indicates the magnitude of the persecution, not the end of his substance.

“And there is no one,” he says, “who considers it in his heart,” or “stores it up.” For it was impossible that the blind and mute, who saw vain things and loved dreams, and who lacked understanding and wisdom, should consider the things that belong to God.

What follows—“And men of mercy,” or “the righteous,” “are gathered away and taken away”—signifies the Apostles, who are killed by the ungodly and gathered by the Lord.

He gives the reasons why the righteous man was killed and taken away, saying: “For the righteous has been gathered away from before evil,” so that he might not see the evils of the world. Or, because of the evil of human beings, whose sins he himself bore, he ascended victoriously to the Father.

As for what is said according to the Hebrew, “Let peace come; let him rest in his bed; let him walk in his uprightness,” the meaning is clear, but the sequence of the words—which stands in the idiom of its own language—seems disordered in ours.

What it says is this: “Let the peace of the Righteous One come,” the peace that, when he ascended to the Father, he left to the Apostles, saying: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV, 27). When the peace of Christ, which surpasses all understanding, has come, his Apostles will rest in their beds, and their death will be a rest.

Thus he shows that the martyrs do not perish but conquer, and rest in an eternal dwelling. But he whose peace it is, and whose Apostles rest in their beds, walks in his uprightness, ascending victoriously to the Father by a straight path.

The Septuagint’s reading—“The righteous has been removed from before iniquity; his burial will be in peace; it has been taken away from the midst”—refers everything to Christ, without mixing in the persons of the Apostles. His burial is in peace, and it has been taken away from the midst. For his flesh did not see corruption, nor did he remain in the tomb; he is the one “free among the dead.” The angel said to the women: “You seek Jesus; he is not here. Come and see the place where the Lord was laid” (Matt. XXVIII, 5–6).

The Jews think that these things, and what follows, are to be understood either generally of all the righteous, whose blood Manasseh shed and with which he filled Jerusalem from gate to gate, or certainly of Isaiah prophesying about his own death: that he would be sawn apart by Manasseh with a wooden saw. This is an absolutely certain tradition among them.

Therefore many of our writers refer to Isaiah’s martyrdom the passage about the sufferings of the saints in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “They were sawn apart” (Heb. XI, 37).

SIXTEENTH BOOK.

[Col. 0547]

[Col. 0547A] 665–666. It is an outstanding saying of the most eloquent orator: “The arts would be happy if only craftsmen judged them” [or: “if craftsmen alone judged them”]. And lest I seem to take an example only from profane sources, this is surely what the Prophet demonstrates in other words: “Blessed is he who speaks into the ears of those who hear” (Ecclus. XXVI, 12).

By this blessedness you, daughter Eustochium, have made me a participant. For when you read the preface to the preceding book, in which I asserted that the Apostles and Evangelists cite from the Septuagint translators or from their own words only those testimonies that agree with the Hebrew, while completely disregarding anything added by others, you immediately brought me a not insignificant question.

The question was this: the eight verses read in the churches and absent from the Hebrew text of the thirteenth Psalm were nevertheless used by the Apostle when he wrote to the Romans:

> “Their throat is an open tomb;  
> with their tongues they dealt deceitfully;  
> the venom of asps is under their lips.  
> Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.  
> Their feet are swift to shed blood.  
> Destruction and misery are in their ways.  
> And they have not known the way of peace.  
> There is no fear of God before their eyes” (Rom. III, 13 ff.).

[Note: [Col. 0547D] “Their throat is an open tomb.” Concerning these eight verses, see our edition, vol. I, cols. 843 and 1336, both in the text of the Psalms and in our annotations. MARTIAN. Pseudo-Jerome, in the *Breviary*, adds also the testimony from Deuteronomy which the Apostle drew upon in part; I do not know how truly. But certainly the verses “Their feet are swift,” etc., are composed not only from Isaiah LIX, 7, as Jerome notes, but also from Proverbs I, 16.]

When I heard this, I was as though struck by a very powerful boxer. I began to burn inwardly in silence and to mark my mental stupor by the pallor of my face.

I said: “A Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee according to the law, and instructed at the feet of Gamaliel—either he did not know these things, or he abused the ignorance of those who were going to read them” (Phil. VI; Acts XXII, 3).

The former alternative is characteristic of the unlearned; the latter, of one clever in wickedness. Neither is appropriate to one who said: “Even if I am unskilled in speech, I am not in knowledge” (II Cor. XI, 6); and again: “In simplicity and sincerity I proclaimed the word to you” (II Cor. I, 12).

At last, returning to myself, I asked for the space of one day, so that my answer might not be an argument produced by human ingenuity, but the fruit of continual reading.

Thus, reviewing all Scripture in my mind, I observed that, just as nearly the whole Epistle to the Romans is constructed from the Old Testament, so this testimony also is composed from the Psalms and Isaiah (verse 11).

The first two verses—“Their throat is an open tomb; with their tongues they dealt deceitfully”—are from the fifth Psalm (verse 11).

What follows—“The venom of asps is under their lips”—is from the one hundred thirty-ninth Psalm (verse 4).

Again, “Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness,” is taken from the ninth Psalm (verse 29).

The three verses that follow—“Their feet are swift to shed blood; destruction and misery are in their ways; and they have not known the way of peace”—I found in the prophet Isaiah. I will expound them in the sixteenth book of his commentary, which I now wish to dictate.

But the final verse, the eighth—“There is no fear of God before their eyes”—is found at the beginning of the thirty-fifth Psalm.

No one should think it strange in this matter if something said in the singular number in its original setting is spoken by the Apostle in the plural, since he was writing to many people and joining together many examples into a single meaning.

I believe that your question has been resolved, and that our rule concerning the translation of the Old Testament has been shaken rather than overturned. It was not so much the Apostle who took from the thirteenth Psalm something that is absent from the Hebrew as those who did not know the Apostle’s skill in weaving passages of Scripture together who sought a suitable place in which to insert the testimony he had taken, since they did not think that it could be placed in Scripture without authority.

Finally, all the Greek commentators who have left us commentaries on the Psalms as evidence of their learning mark these verses with a spit and pass them by, plainly admitting that they are absent from the Hebrew and are not found in the Septuagint translators, but are found in the common edition, which in Greek is called κοινή (*koinē*, “common”), and which differs throughout the world.

But now it is time for us to apply ourselves to the work we have begun and proceed with what remains.

(Vers. 3, 4.) “But you draw near here, children of the female diviner, offspring of an adulterer and a prostitute: over whom did you make sport? Over whom did you enlarge your mouth and thrust out your tongue?”

The Septuagint reads: “But you draw near here, wicked sons, offspring of adulterers and a prostitute. In whom did you make sport? Against whom did you open your mouth and against whom did you thrust out your tongue?”

The righteous has been taken away, whose burial is in peace—indeed, he has been taken away from the midst. You who are sons of iniquity, draw near to me and hear what I shall say (John VIII).

For just as the one who commits iniquity is the slave of iniquity, so the one who, like Judas the betrayer, is a son of perdition may be called a son of iniquity. Thus it is written concerning the Lord Savior: “And the son of iniquity shall not add to afflict him” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 23).

In place of “iniquity,” or “the wicked,” which the Septuagint translated, Theodotion retained the Hebrew word ONENA [the Hebrew characters are not supplied in the text]. We, following Symmachus, translate it as “female diviner,” evidently because Jerusalem, which is the mother of those who hear, was always devoted to idolatry.

For this reason he calls them the offspring of an adulterer or adulterers—concerning whom it is said, “They committed adultery with wood and stone” (Jer. III, 9)—and of a prostitute. There is no doubt that he signifies the same woman of whom we read above: “How the faithful city, Zion, has become a prostitute!” (Isa. I, 21).

[Note: [Col. 0549D] An Ambrosian manuscript reads: “This prostitute, without doubt …”]

“Over whom,” he says, “did you make sport,” spitting in his face and plucking his beard? Over whom did you enlarge and open your mouth and thrust out your tongue, saying to him: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John VIII, 48)? And again: “He does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Matt. XII, 24).

And later, during the Passion: “Crucify him, crucify such a man!” (Luke XXIII, 21). And again: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25).

And elsewhere: “Ah, you who destroy the Temple and rebuild it in three days! He saved others; he cannot save himself. Let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe in him” (ibid., 40).

### (Verses 4–5)

“Are you not wicked children, a lying seed, you who take comfort in gods beneath every leafy tree, sacrificing little children in the ravines beneath overhanging [Vulgate: lofty] rocks?” The Septuagint reads: “Are you not children of destruction, an unrighteous seed, you who call upon idols beneath leafy trees, sacrificing your children in the valleys amid the rocks?”

[Note: The same manuscript reads, “you who call upon idols”; according to the Aldine Greek exemplar, ἐπὶ τὰ εἴδωλα, “upon the idols.”]

“You,” he says, “have done these things that the preceding passage recounted. You are wicked children—or children of destruction, such as the traitor Judas was, who was called ‘the son of destruction’ (John 17)—and an unrighteous, or lying, seed, a seed of falsehood. You delight in gods beneath every leafy tree, and sacrifice your children in the ravines (Acts 8). The history of Kings and Chronicles also relates that they sacrificed their children to the gods and consecrated them in fire (2 Kings 16 and 17). There is no doubt that King Ahab of Israel and King Manasseh of Judah did this; from the murder of their children they proceeded to the shedding of the prophets’ blood. Concerning this, Hosea also says: ‘Sacrifice human beings, for the calves have failed’ (Hosea 13:2).

“Or, as it is written in the Hebrew: ‘Sacrificing human beings, you worship calves.’

[Note: Ambrosianus reads, “He said, ‘You sacrificed human beings.’” Compare this passage in Jerome’s version. Victorius has, “Sacrifice human beings who worship calves,” from the Hebrew, and compare Jerome’s commentary on Hosea.]

“And in the Psalms it is written more fully: ‘They mingled with the nations and learned their works; they served their carved images, and it became a stumbling-block to them. They sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, and poured out innocent—or guiltless—blood, the blood of their sons and daughters; and they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan. And the land was defiled by blood, and polluted by their works’ (Psalm 105:35 ff.).”

Since the history plainly shows that the children of those who did these things were Christ’s murderers [variant: “murderer”], the question arises how they can be called children of destruction, against those who want there to be different natures: one that is lost and evil and cannot be saved, and another that is good and cannot perish. For if, as they think, the children of destruction are of the worst nature, how was what had previously been lost found? Indeed, in the parables concerning penitents, both the lost sheep from the hundred sheep and the drachma that had been lost from the ten are found; and the lost son is found, of whom the father said to his elder son: “This brother of yours was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32). For nothing ever perishes unless it was previously safe, and nothing ever dies unless it had previously lived.

Therefore these people, who are now called children of destruction, or of unrighteousness and wickedness, abandoned the Lord through their own fault and from being the Lord’s children began to be children of destruction. The same prophet says to them: “You have abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger” (Isaiah 1:4).

We can also understand this allegorically of the heretics, who are children of destruction and a most evil seed, or a seed of falsehood. From the beginning they are liars, like the devil, who is their father and the father of all falsehood. They call those whom they have deceived to idols—or to images of their own doctrines—beneath leafy and wooded trees, promising them pleasures and delights, or concealing their impurities from them. Hence Adam, after he had sinned, hid himself in paradise beneath a tree, lest he be exposed to God’s gaze (Genesis 3).

There is no doubt that such children of destruction and an unrighteous seed have many children, namely all whom they deceive. They kill them in deep valleys and in the abyss of ungodliness, beneath overhanging rocks that always threaten collapse. These rocks are called many because of the diversity of their falsehood and the variety of their perverse doctrines. We, however, have one Rock, which always follows God’s people, from which the people of Israel once drank when they enjoyed the Lord’s friendship.

### (Verse 6)

“In the parts of the ravine is your portion; this is your lot. To them you have poured out a libation; to them you have offered sacrifice. Shall I not be indignant at these things?” The Septuagint reads: “This is your portion; this is your lot. To them you poured out libations, and for them you prepared victims. Shall I not be angry at these things?”

What is said corresponds to the time of Isaiah. All the mountains, valleys, and ravines were full of the worship of demons. Jeremiah speaks of these things: fathers and sons carried wood and kindled fire in order to make *chavonas* for the army of heaven, while women kneaded flour and mixed in fat, provoking the Lord to anger (Jeremiah 7). There is no doubt that these words signify cakes, or little pastries, prepared by the hand of a craftsman. For in our language *chavonim* has this meaning.

Concerning these things Moses, in the Song of Deuteronomy, had sung beforehand in the prophetic spirit, speaking in the person of the Lord: “They provoked me with foreign gods, and angered me with their abominations; they sacrificed to demons and not to God” (Deuteronomy 32:16–17).

They did this by their own will, since it lies within our choice to select good or evil. Thus it is said of those who offered themselves to God through virtues: “He chose our inheritance for us, the beauty of Jacob, whom he loved” (Psalm 46:5). And elsewhere: “The Lord’s portion is his people Jacob; Israel is the lot of his inheritance” (Deuteronomy 32:9). The Acts of the Apostles also reports that many gave themselves to be Paul’s and Silas’s portion and lot.

Those who are the Lord’s portion and lot, like the Levites, will have the Lord as their portion and will be able to say with David: “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm 72:26).

We can also apply this to the person of the heretics. For, having abandoned the worship of God, they venerate the images of their errors, offer victims to them, and pour out libations, secretly doing things that it is shameful even to mention. They take captive little women burdened with sins, driven by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3). Since the wicked do these things in both forms of impiety, is it not just that God’s anger should be provoked against them?

### (Verse 7)

“Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed, and there you have ascended to sacrifice victims. And behind the door and behind the doorpost you have set your memorial.” The Septuagint is the same.

The sacred history relates that Israel sacrificed victims to the gods of the nations on high mountains and hills, and, like a most shameless prostitute, spread her legs to all the demons. There was no place that was not polluted by the filth of idolatry, to such an extent that they placed idols behind the doors of their houses. They call these household gods *Lares*, and they poured out the blood of their souls both publicly and privately.

[Note: Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 13: “Household gods, whom you call Lares, you handle with household authority.” Compare Augustine, *City of God*, book 4, chapter 8, concerning the goddess Tutela, and elsewhere.]

Many provincial cities suffer from this error and the worst ancient custom; even Rome herself, mistress of the world, venerates in every apartment building and house an image of Tutela with candles and lamps. They call her by this name for the protection of their dwellings, so that both those entering and those leaving their houses may constantly be reminded of the error to which they have grown accustomed.

The heretics also, whose hearts are lifted up in pride, and who despise the humility of the Church while promising themselves lofty things, climb the highest mountains of their doctrines and there prostitute their bed to demons. Since, according to the prophet, they have turned backward, imitating Lot’s wife (Genesis 19), they are changed into a pillar of salt. They possess the appearance of ecclesiastical seasoning but have none of its flavor; they are cast outside and are useful for nothing except to be trampled under everyone’s feet.

Therefore the Lord warns in the Gospel that whoever holds the plow-handle must not look behind him (Luke 8).

### (Verse 9)

“Because beside me you uncovered yourself and received an adulterer; you enlarged your bed and made a pact with them [the Vulgate adds: ‘a covenant’]; you loved their bed with an open hand; you adorned yourself for the king with perfume [the Vulgate: royal perfume], and multiplied your cosmetics. You sent your envoys far away, and you were humbled even to the underworld.”

The Septuagint reads: “You thought that if you departed from me you would have something more. You loved those sleeping with you, multiplied your fornication with them, made many far away from you, and sent your envoys beyond your boundaries; and you were humbled even to the underworld.”

First let us discuss the Hebrew, which differs greatly from the Septuagint at this point. Above he had said: “Upon a high and lofty mountain you have set your bed,” and had accused her, like a prostitute, of having been exposed at the entrances of houses and in dark places, behind doors, so that whoever wished to enter a house would have pleasure displayed before his eyes. Now he accuses and rebukes that same woman as an adulterous wife, because, while lying [variant: “while she lay”] with her husband, she secretly received an adulterer and uncovered her cloak—or rather enlarged her bed—and made a pact, as though drawing up a marriage contract with adulterers.

He says this to show that they not only worshiped idols in the fields and houses, but also placed an image of Baal in the Temple, which Ezekiel says he saw after breaking through a wall.

“You loved their bed with an open hand,” he says (Ezekiel 8), so that you were not ashamed of your sin, nor wished to conceal the disgrace of your fornication, but sinned with complete freedom. “You adorned yourself for the king with perfume, and multiplied your idols.” The meaning is: You sought various ornaments so that, by sight and smell alike, you might entice the adulterers.

The statement “you adorned yourself for the king with perfume” can be understood in two ways: either for the King, God, when you adorn yourself with the things he had given and prostitute yourself to idols; or for the idol-king of the Ammonites, who is called Molech and whose name in our language means “king.” According to the Septuagint, we read *Melchom* in other passages (Zephaniah 1).

“And you sent your envoys far away,” so that you might not only devote yourself to fornication with the idols of neighboring peoples, but also with those of peoples living far away. This signifies the gods of the Babylonians and Egyptians.

“And you were humbled,” he says, “even to the underworld”—not with the humility that is praiseworthy, but with the kind by which Ammon humbled his sister Tamar (2 Samuel 13). Truly, it is a great humiliation, or rather a descent even to the underworld, to be hurled from the light and summit of chastity into the darkness of a brothel, indeed into the abyss of lust. To her it is said elsewhere: “You will be brought down to the underworld.”

According to the Septuagint, in the places where it differs, this seems to me to be the meaning: “You thought, prostitute, that if you departed from me and joined yourself to your lovers, you would find something more.” God also says to her through Ezekiel: “Wages are given to all prostitutes, but you gave your wages, and this happened perversely in your case” (Ezekiel 16:33). For you not only received nothing from your lovers, but also lost what you had received from your husband.

The following words, “You enlarged your bed and made a pact with them,” are not found in the Septuagint. She loved those sleeping with her—blind watchmen and mute dogs—who see dreams of vanity while sleeping. And she multiplied her fornication, so that she did not have intercourse once with one person, but frequently and with many.

Therefore she made many withdraw far from her: angels who had been in her defenses, or holy men who withdrew from the companionship of such a prostitute.

We can also say this about the heretics.

[Note: Earlier the text read, “having abandoned their God”; what follows, etc.]

Having abandoned God, they follow their own errors and think that they possess something more, although by following falsehood they have lost the truth. They have multiplied their fornication, not in one doctrine but in many, and have caused the angels who guard the Churches to withdraw from them. Not content with nearby fornication, they send envoys beyond their boundaries to the doctrines of the pagans and the errors of barbarian peoples, so that by the novelty of their language they may deceive their hearers.

### (Verse 10)

“You grew weary in the multitude of your ways, and you did not say, ‘I will cease.’ You found the life of your hand; therefore you did not ask me” [the Vulgate omits “me”]. The Septuagint reads: “You grew weary in your many journeys and did not say, ‘I will stop.’ You made these things strong; therefore you did not ask me.”

Whoever walks in the one royal way does not grow weary. Concerning it God commanded through Moses: “You shall walk on the royal road and shall not turn aside to the right or to the left” (Deuteronomy 5:32).

There is one way of truth, which says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6); and there are many ways of falsehood, along which Jerusalem is now accused of having walked. God, knowing the difference between these ways, says above to those who err: “My ways are not like your ways” (Isaiah 55:8). Those who confess to the Lord say: “You have made our ways turn aside from your ways” (Psalm 43:19).

Having recognized the one royal way, let us see what are the right and left ways on which we are forbidden to walk. The royal way is moderate [variant: “is moderation”], possessing neither more nor less than is proper.

For example, the straight and royal way is prudence. We turn to the right if we are wiser than we ought to be and love cunning instead of prudence, because [variant: “for which”] the serpent was more prudent than all the beasts in paradise (Genesis 3), and “the children of darkness are more prudent than the children of light” (Luke 16). We turn to the left when we are foolish and have less understanding than necessary. Of such people it is said: “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 13:1).

Piety and true religion are also a royal way.

[Note: The manuscripts read: “from which he turns aside,” etc.]

He turns to the right who is superstitious and deserves to hear: “Do not be excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes 7:17). He turns to the left who neglects the worship of God and is numbered among the kids and goats.

Generosity and proper distribution are also a great virtue. He turns to the right who is miserly and gives what is necessary not only to others but not even to himself. He turns to the left who consumes his substance with prostitutes and says with Israel: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isaiah 22:13).

Courage and steadfastness are likewise a royal way. He turns to the right who is rash and obstinate; to the left, he who is fearful and timid. Therefore the holy man, wishing to walk along the straight way, prays: “Lead me, Lord, in the straight way” (Psalm 138:24). And elsewhere: “Make known to me, Lord, the way in which I should walk, for to you I have lifted up my eyes” (Psalm 142:8).

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “To you I have lifted up my soul.”]

Scripture also speaks elsewhere of this kind of way: “Seek the good way, walk in it, and you will find purification for your souls” (Jeremiah 6:16).

Jerusalem was therefore humbled even to the underworld because she grew weary in many ways [one Ambrosian manuscript: “grew weary in many wandering ways”] and did not say, “I will correct my error through repentance.” Instead she said, “I will strengthen what I have begun,” and paid no attention to the admonition of the one who warned: “Turn your foot away from the difficult way and your throat from thirst” (Jeremiah 2:25).

Then it follows: “But she replied, ἀνδρίσομαι,” that is, “I will act manfully,” which is now expressed by another word: “I will be strengthened.”

[Note: Earlier Vulgate editions read, “Turn your foot,” and so forth, incorrectly, contrary to the manuscripts and the sacred text. Shortly afterward, instead of ἀνδρίσομαι, the Ambrosian manuscript has ἀνδριοῦμαι.]

Because she did the things that the preceding passage recounted, she did not entreat the Lord, placing her confidence more in her own strength than in God.

Moreover, the Hebrew wording, “You found the life of your hand; therefore you did not ask,” has this meaning and interpretation: Because you abounded and overflowed with all things, therefore you neglected the Lord. Solomon also refuses to have such riches, lest he forget God (Proverbs 30 and 31). And Ezekiel says to Sodom that because she was filled with bread, she became proud (Ezekiel 16).

It is not only riches that test a person; poverty does so as well. Hence it was written above: “I tested you in the furnace of poverty” (Isaiah 48). Lazarus too was tested as a poor man, enduring both want and bodily weakness (Luke 15).

### (Verse 11)

“On whose account were you anxious and afraid, because you lied and did not remember me, nor considered it in your heart? Because I was silent and as though I did not see, you forgot me.” The Septuagint reads: “Whom did you fear, so that you were terrified? You lied to me and did not remember me. You did not set me in your mind or in your heart. And I, seeing you, will despise you, and you did not fear me.”

Because you place your confidence in riches and in full storehouses, you did not wish to ask me; therefore you feared many people. You could not say: “The Lord is my helper, and I shall despise my enemies” (Psalm 117:7); and again: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 26:1).

Even if at some point you wished to say this against the testimony of your conscience, you lied. How could you invoke me, when you had no remembrance of me and never considered the commandments of the one who says: “Honor the Lord, and you will be strengthened, and fear no one apart from him” (Ecclesiasticus 38)?

I am the one who, according to Symmachus and Aquila, always kept silent about your sins and, as though I did not see, disregarded whatever crimes you were committing, so that, if not through fear of me, at least through my patience, you might return to me. I question human children not with my eyes but with my eyelids.

But, on the contrary, you forgot me and deserved to hear: “You have forgotten the law of your God, and I will forget your children” (Hosea 4:6). And again: “They walked perversely against me, and I will walk against them with perverse fury.”

The word “mind,” which in the Septuagint is joined with “heart,” is not written in the Hebrew; it has been added almost as an interpretation of what the heart is understood to mean in Scripture.

### (Verse 12)

“I will announce your righteousness, and your works will not profit you. When you cry out, let your assembled companions deliver you.” The Septuagint reads: “I will announce your righteousness and your evils, which will not profit you. When you cry out, let them rescue you in your tribulation.”

I, who was always silent and, as though I did not see your sins, disregarded them, will no longer remain silent. I will say what I said before: “I was silent; shall I always be silent?” I will announce your righteousness and your works. This should be read ironically, as when someone caught in crimes is told, “Look at your good works.”

Therefore, whenever a time of tribulation comes upon you, and you begin not to stretch out your hands to the idols that you worshiped, but toward heaven, imploring God’s help, let those whom you worshiped in security hear you and rescue you from danger. God also says to her through Jeremiah: “Where are your gods that you made? Let them arise and save you in the time of your troubles” (Jeremiah 2:28).

In place of the Septuagint’s “Let them rescue you in your tribulation,” we have rendered, “Let your assembled companions deliver you.” Symmachus translated: “Let your synagogues rescue you.” Thus he is speaking specifically to the Jews, since the multitude of their synagogues would not be able to deliver them at the time of the siege.

### (Verses 13–14)

“And a wind will carry them all away; a breath will take them. But the one who trusts in me will inherit the land and possess my holy mountain. And I will say, ‘Make a way; provide a road; turn aside from the path; remove the obstacles from the way of my people.’”

The Septuagint reads: “For the wind will carry all these people away, and a storm will take them. But those who hope in me will possess the land and inherit my holy mountain, and they will say, ‘Clear the ways before him and remove the obstacles from the way of my people.’”

The Jews assert that this is prophesied concerning the Babylonians: once they have been overcome by God’s power, the people will return to Judea, possess Mount Zion, and have every obstacle removed from the journey, suffering no ambush from any nation, because the Lord will have made the way level for his people. They contend that this was fulfilled under Zerubbabel and Ezra.

We, however, joining these words to what precedes, maintain that all the idols that could not deliver them will be carried away by wind and storm and will become like dust that the wind casts from the face of the earth.

But those who have placed their trust in the Lord will possess the land, concerning which we shall read in this same prophet: “He will raise you up to the good things of the land.” From this it is clear that this land is not below but above. The holy person will ascend to it when the Lord raises him up. We have often spoken of it in the words: “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land” (Matthew 5:4); and, “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Psalm 26:13).

The holy mountain of God is to be understood as that of which the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews speaks: “You have approached Mount Zion, the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, many thousands of angels, and the assembly of the firstborn who are written in heaven” (Hebrews 12:22).

We can also understand the land and the Lord’s mountain, which the saints will possess, as the holy Scriptures. The Lord threatens that these will be taken away from the Jews when he says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew 21:43). Thus they may find in them that mountain of which we read in this same prophet Isaiah (chapter 2) and in Micah: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be revealed” (Micah 4:5).

The Lord himself also commanded the Apostles and all the teachers of the Church to dissolve by their interpretation whatever seemed harsh and difficult, to provide a way to understanding, and to remove every stumbling-block from the midst, so that the Lord’s people might understand what they read without any impediment and advance in the fear of God.

John the Baptist also spoke of these ways: “Prepare the ways of the Lord,” and so forth (Matthew 3:3).

Where we have placed the words “And I will say” as spoken in the person of God, the Septuagint has “And they will say”—namely, those who will possess the land and inherit God’s holy mountain. They will not be content with their own salvation, but will also summon others to teach the peoples.

Symmachus interpreted this passage as follows: “But the one who trusts in me will possess the land and inherit my holy mountain, and he will say: ‘Make a straight way,’” and so forth. The meaning is that the one who has possessed the land and the mountain will instruct the others, so that they may prepare the way for the Lord.

### (Verse 15)

“For thus says the One who is high and exalted, who inhabits eternity, whose name is holy: ‘I dwell in a high and holy place, and also with the contrite and humble in spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble and revive the heart of the contrite.’”

The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the One who is high and dwells in the heights forever: holy is his name among the holy. The One who is high, resting among the holy, gives patience to the fainthearted and life to those whose hearts are contrite.”

The prophetic discourse had begun against the Jewish people, whose teachers he called blind watchmen, mute dogs, and shepherds lacking understanding, and whom he called wicked children and the children of adulterers and a prostitute. After this he came to Jerusalem, reproving her fornication because she had enlarged her bed for her lovers, received them with an open hand, adorned herself with every idol, and sent envoys far away so that she might enjoy even foreign lovers.

When this rebuke has been completed, he comes to those who trust in the Lord, to whom he had promised possession of the land and the mountain, and for whose return he had ordered a road to be prepared. There is no doubt that these are the Apostles, through whose preaching people from both nations believed.

Therefore he begins with praises of God and bears witness in the following discourse to what he had promised concerning the return of his people. For this is what the Lord, the high and exalted one, says: he dwells in the heights, and is holy among the holy—not because of a place, but because of the merit of those in whom he dwells. One of them says in the Psalm: “I will exalt you, Lord, for you have received me” (Psalm 29:1). And again: “Be exalted, Lord, who judge the earth” (Psalm 93:2).

This does not mean that God is elevated by human words; rather, according to the statement found elsewhere, “The Lord became my salvation” (Psalm 117:21), he becomes exalted even to the humble. He resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James 4), so that he may raise them up and dwell in the heights.

“For the Lord is exalted, and he looks upon the humble” (Psalm 137:6). In the Gospel the angels cry out: “Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth” (Luke 2:14). And again in the Psalms: “Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise him in the heights” (Psalm 148:1).

The One who is exalted not only dwells in the heights but is also holy among the holy. He says elsewhere: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus 11:44). Just as wisdom does not enter a perverse soul nor dwell in a body subjected to sins (Wisdom 1), so the holy one dwells among the holy. Wherever there is filth, purity cannot dwell, as the holy man says to the Lord: “But you dwell in the holy place, the praise of Israel” (Psalm 21:1).

Hence in prayer we dare to say: “Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name.” And in the second Psalm we read: “He who dwells in heaven will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them” (Psalm 2:4).

Christ does not dwell in those who are earthly, but in those who are above the heavens, who declare the glory of the Lord. Of them it is said: “May he hear him from his holy heaven” (Psalm 19:7). And again: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 113:16).

Moses, the servant of God, agrees with this meaning in the same words: “Behold, to the Lord your God belongs heaven and the heaven of heaven” (Deuteronomy 10). We must not understand this in a Jewish manner, as though God were enclosed in some place and dwelled only in heaven, since he is spread everywhere and contains all things. Rather, we should understand the heights and the heavens as the saints and the Virtues, according to their merit.

He is the one who dwells in heaven, concerning whom it is written in the Gospel: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

He rests among the holy and dwells in the humble and in those who are contrite in spirit. Concerning them it is said: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 50:19).

He gives patience to the fainthearted, so that those placed in distress may endure tribulation through hope of future things. He gives life, especially to those who were dead through sin. Concerning him it is said: “With you is the fountain of life” (Psalm 35:10). He says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

### (Verse 16)

“I will not contend forever, nor will I be angry to the end, because the spirit will go forth from my face, and I will make the breath.”

The Septuagint reads: “I will not avenge you forever, nor will I always be angry with you. For the spirit will go forth from me, and I made every breath.”

The Lord, who dwells in the heights and looks upon the humble, whose name is holy and who rests among the holy, who sustains the afflicted and grants life to the oppressed (Psalm 112), has spoken these words: “I will not always be angry, nor will I be continually indignant.” I strike in order to correct; I kill in order to make alive. For I have mercy on my creation, and I will not allow those whom I myself created to perish forever.

My spirit also, which will go forth from me—or which, according to the Hebrew, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, surrounds all things—for this is the meaning of περιειληθήσεται and περιβαλλεῖ—is the giver of life to all.

[Note: Until now, these two words had incorrectly been represented by a single word. The older Ambrosian manuscript writes them in uncial letters as ΠΕΡΙΕΙΛΗΘΗϹΕΤΑΙ and ΠΕΡΙΒΑΛΛΕΙ. Erasmus, conjecturing, obtained περιελεύσεται, and the recent edition of the *Hexapla* likewise imposes this single form, as though all three interpreters had used the same word. Now, however, from the Ambrosian manuscript we understand that, although they convey the same meaning, the interpreters did not use the same word. Aquila and Symmachus agree in the first form; elsewhere, for example in Job 38:9 and Psalm 142:4, they also use the verb περιειλέω. The second form, περιβαλλεῖ, must be attributed to Theodotion. Both words mean what Jerome notes: to surround all things, to wrap around, or to encircle on every side.]

“And I made the breath,” or, in the plural, “the breaths”—for this is what *nasamoth* means. Concerning this it is written elsewhere: “Let every breath, or everything that breathes, praise the Lord” (Psalm 150:6).

Concerning this spirit and breath it is also written at the beginning of Genesis: “God breathed into him the breath of life, and the man became a living soul.” Job says something similar: “The spirit of God, which is in my nostrils, and the breath of the Almighty, which teaches me” (Job 27:3).

Since the spirit goes forth from me, and all things are enlivened and live by my breath and inspiration, it is not just that those who are sustained by my breath and spirit should perish forever.

Some of our writers say that this is the spirit by which the whole world is inspired and governed, and through which all things possess knowledge of God. The distinguished poet, writing according to the Stoics, says this of it (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6):

> In the beginning, heaven and earth and the watery plains,  
> and the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars,  
> an inward spirit nourishes; infused through their limbs,  
> Mind moves the mass and mingles with the great body.

And so forth.

Others understand this as the Holy Spirit, who in the beginning was borne over the waters and gave life to all things; who proceeds from the Father and, because of the communion of nature, is sent by the Son, who says: “It is advantageous for you that I go. For if I do not go, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you” (John 16:7).

Concerning him he says again: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

No one should be scandalized if the Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, since the Son also said of himself: “I came forth from the Father and have come; for I did not come forth from myself, but he sent me” (John 16:28).

It was concerning this Spirit that he said: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16).

This is the Spirit of whom Moses also writes: “Would that all the Lord’s people were prophets, and that the Lord would place his Spirit upon them!” (Numbers 11:29).

Joel speaks in the person of God: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). Zechariah says: “Yet receive my words and my statutes, which I command through my Spirit to my servants the prophets” (Zechariah 1:6). And again: “I will pour out upon Jerusalem the Spirit of grace and mercy” (Zechariah 12:10).

There are many other passages from both Testaments that it would now take too long to repeat. We say only this: the same prophet has spoken equally of this Spirit and breath: “Thus says the Lord God, who made heaven.” And shortly afterward: “He gives breath to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isaiah 42:5).

(Vers. 17 ff.) “Because of the iniquity of his greed I was angry, and I struck him; I hid myself, and was indignant; and he went mourning on the way of his heart” [Vulgate: “he departed as a wanderer”]. “I have seen his ways and healed him; I led him back and restored consolations to him and to his mourners. I created the fruit of the lips: peace, peace to him who is far off and to him who is near,” says the Lord, “and I healed him. But the wicked are like the tossing sea, which cannot rest, and its waves overflow into trampling and mire. There is no peace,” says God, “for the wicked.”

The Septuagint: “Because of sin I grieved him for a little while, and I struck him; I turned my face away from him, and he was grieved and walked sadly in his ways. I saw his ways and healed him; I consoled him and gave him true consolation, peace to those who are far off and to those who are near, says the Lord, and I will heal them. But the lawless will be tossed about and will not be able to rest. There is no joy for the wicked, says the Lord God.”

After the rejection of the Jewish people and of those who refused to believe in the Savior, he had promised those who placed their trust in him the land of the meek and the mountain of the saints, and he had commanded the Apostles: “Make a way for the people who are returning, and remove all stumbling-blocks from their midst.” And lest this seem unbelievable, he explains his power: the exalted and great one can easily grant forgiveness to those who repent, and it is right that the Creator should have mercy on his creature.

For this reason he adds that he had been angry and had grieved his people; that he had done this because they had sinned and possessed the greed of iniquity, and had not been content with a single iniquity but had continually added sins to sins. “And I struck him,” he says, “for a short time, in order to heal him; and I hid”—namely, my face—“so that he would desire me more and say: ‘Show us your face, and we shall be saved’” (Ps. 79:4).

“And I was indignant.” When he perceived this, he walked sadly, saying: “All day long I went about mourning” (Ps. 37:7). “And he went mourning,” or “turned in the way of his heart,” so that he might do penance not before the face of human beings but in his heart. Therefore, seeing the ways of his conversion, I healed the wounds with which I had previously struck him. I led back to myself the one whom I had earlier cast out, and I restored true consolation to him. For there are many false consolations by which the human race is deceived.

Or, “I consoled his mourners,” saying in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

The following statement—“I created the fruit of the lips”—has this meaning: I fulfilled what I had promised when I said: “As I live, says the Lord, I prefer the repentance of the sinner to his death” (Ezek. 33:11). Or else, I bestowed everything that I had previously promised.

What is the Lord’s promise? “I give you my peace; my peace I leave you” (John 14:27). This is what he now says: “Peace upon peace,” not to one nation alone but to the whole world—to those, namely, who were far off and to those who were near: first to the Gentiles, and afterward to those from Israel who wished to believe. [Note: The manuscripts read: “peace to those who are far off, and peace to those who are near,” and so forth.]

The Apostle also speaks of them: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you; but since you judged yourselves unworthy of salvation, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). Writing to the Ephesians and discussing at length the people of the Circumcision and the Gentiles, he adds: “But now in Christ Jesus you who were once far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the dividing barrier, abolishing hostility in his flesh, and so forth” (Eph. 2:13–14); and again: “And coming, he announced peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near” (ibid., 17).

For through him we both have access to the Father in one Spirit: he gives peace upon peace to those who had been far off and to those who were near, both to those who had not possessed the Law and the Prophets and to those who had previously received them; he received both and healed them. [Note: With Victorius, we supply the previously missing words: “and those who are near.”]

But “the wicked,” or “the lawless,” will be tossed about like a raging sea and will never be able to rest. Although this can be understood of every wicked person, it refers especially to the Jewish people, who cried out with one voice and persisted in their wickedness, saying: “Crucify him, crucify him!” and “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15).

Just as the raging sea cannot rest, but its waves overflow, roll back toward the shores, and are again swallowed up, breaking upon themselves and becoming mud that is trampled underfoot, so the wicked will be subjected to eternal trampling. They have no joy and find no rest in any peace, because they persist in wickedness.

Some understand this passage specifically of the Savior: because of the sins of the world, he was grieved for a little while, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38). The Father who speaks through Zechariah struck him: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Zech. 13:7). He himself also said of himself in Psalm 68: “For the one whom you struck, they pursued” (Ps. 68:27).

God turned his face away from him so that he might for a little while assume the form of a servant, walk sadly, and mourn the sins of the people, lamenting and weeping over Jerusalem. And when the Father saw his ways, he therefore healed him—him who was free among the dead—and his flesh did not see corruption, so that the one who was struck on the cross might be healed in the resurrection.

“And I consoled him,” he says, giving him the whole world in place of the one Jewish nation. “And his mourners”—the words “I consoled” are understood. There is no doubt that this signifies the Apostles.

And he fulfilled the fruit of his lips, since he had said to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8): “peace upon peace,” reconciling the world to God, so that he might call both peoples to himself and be healed by the Father.

But the wicked, of whom we spoke above, he compares to the sea, which can never rest. Even in perfect calm its waves, broken against the shores, roll onward; and its end is mud and trampling.

### Chapter LVIII

(Col. 0561A) **(Vers. 1.)** “Cry out; do not cease. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins.”

The Septuagint: “Cry out with strength, and do not spare. Raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to the people their sins and to the house of Jacob their iniquities.”

Having finished the preceding chapter, in which peace is announced for the righteous and no rest for the wicked, God commands the prophet Isaiah to cry out with strength, to raise his voice like a trumpet, and not to fear proclaiming the sins and crimes of the people of Israel—not fearing death, nor the threats and insults of the wicked [Note: The same manuscripts read “nor the savage insults of the wicked”], but rather considering the Lord who commands him.

And because they have deaf ears and can scarcely hear, according to Symmachus and Aquila he is to turn his throat into a trumpet, which in Hebrew is called *SOPHAR* [Hebrew text not preserved here], and which they translated as κερατίνη (*keratinē*), that is, “a horn.”

Above, where the Apostles were told, “Go up onto a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem; raise it, do not fear” (Isa. 40:9), neither a horn nor a trumpet is mentioned, but they are commanded to ascend the mountain. Here, however, because the people were sinners to whom the message had to be announced, and because they remained below, the Prophet is not commanded to ascend the mountain; he is only commanded to raise his voice like a trumpet and announce to them the wars that were coming.

Otherwise, on the day of judgment, when the resurrection of the dead and the final trumpet are spoken of, it is written: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible.” Just as they are to be judged at the sound of the trumpet, so Israel, dead in sin, is to hear its crimes; and at the same time it is called the people of God, so that it may learn what kind of father it has lost—one who nevertheless calls even the sinner his people.

**(Vers. 2.)** “For day after day they seek me, and they wish to know my ways, like a nation that has done justice and has not abandoned the judgment of its God.” The Septuagint is similar.

This applies especially to the Jews, who run to the synagogues every day and meditate on the law of God, wishing to know what Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did, and what the other saints did. Rehearsing the books of the Prophets and of Moses from memory, they chant the divine commandments. To them the statement most aptly applies: “The wicked will seek me and will not find me.” For it is written: “Everyone who seeks finds” (Matt. 7). Whoever does not find is shown to have sought wrongly. The Lord is found by those who seek him in goodness, and he is revealed to those who are not unbelieving toward him.

Since they have abandoned the justice and judgment of God—by which names Christ is revealed, as the psalmist says: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your justice to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1)—for Christ has become for us redemption, holiness, and justice (1 Cor. 1), they boast of knowing the Law in vain. The holy person does not glory in knowledge of the Scriptures but in works, saying: “I ran in the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32).

(Col. 0562A) **(Vers. 3.)** “They ask me for judgments of justice, and they wish to draw near to God. ‘Why have we fasted, and you have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known?’ Behold, on the day of your fasting your will is found [Alternative: ‘is discovered’], and you have exacted [Alternative: ‘you exact’] all your debtors” [Note: The oldest Ambrosian manuscript does not contain the added word “your”; nor is it present in the Hebrew]. “Behold, you fast for quarrels and disputes, and strike with the fist wickedly.”

The Septuagint: “Now they ask me for just judgment, and they desire to draw near to God, saying: ‘Why have we fasted, and you have not seen? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known?’ For on the days of your fasts your desires are found, and you afflict all those subject to you, fasting for judgments and quarrels, and you strike the humble with your fists.”

This is another instance of the Jews’ presumption, as though they trusted in a good conscience: they demand just judgment and imitate the words of the saints who say: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. 25:1–2). And again: “Test me, O Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart.” And elsewhere: “Judge my cause and redeem me” (Ps. 118:154).

They desire to draw near to God, although this does not take place in a location but in the disposition of the heart—not through an idle mind but through laborious work. Scripture accordingly teaches what it means to draw near to God, saying: “Seek the Lord.” And when he has drawn near to you, “let the wicked abandon his ways, and the lawless man his thoughts.” For the Lord draws near to those who draw near to him, to those who justly pursue what is just, and who can say: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28).

If Almighty God is the Father of truth and justice, no liar or unjust person can draw near to God, of whom it is written: “The evil man shall not dwell near you, nor shall the unjust remain before your eyes” (Ps. 5:6).

“Why have we fasted,” they say, “and you have not looked upon us? We have humbled our souls, and you have not known?” [Note: Earlier the text read: “They accuse [him] unjustly.”]

They accuse the Lord of injustice because he does not regard their good works. They offer God only the hunger of the belly, without any work of virtue—not eating the foods that God created for the faithful and for those who know the truth, to receive them with thanksgiving, but those of which it is written in Proverbs: “For they feed on the bread of wickedness and drink the wine of iniquity” (Prov. 4:17).

Filled with such banquets, the Pharisee boasted among his other words of pride that he fasted twice a week (Luke 18). He had not drunk wine from the vine of Sorek but from the vine of Sodom, whose wine is the fury of dragons and the incurable rage of asps, and whose grapes are grapes of gall. God reproves such people through the Prophet: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8). And again: “Why did you keep silent about their wickedness, and harvest and eat the grain of falsehood?” (Hos. 10:13) [Note: Victor remarks: “It is astonishing how everything becomes corrupted through time and carelessness. For *frumentum* one should read *fructum*, ‘fruit’; the passage is Hosea 10, and the Septuagint has καρπὸν, while the Hebrew and the Vulgate themselves have ‘fruit.’”]

Since they had put their question to God, wishing to know why they had fasted and humbled their souls and God had not looked upon them, they had forgotten the ancient history: why he had not looked upon Cain’s offerings, who indeed offered rightly but did not divide rightly with his brother (Gen. 4). They did not perceive the love of God, when Scripture says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 22:39).

Therefore God answered that he did not reject fasting itself, but the works performed during the fasts, saying: “On the days of your fasts your desires are found”—so that they do not do the will of God but their own will, which Paul condemns when writing to the Ephesians: “According to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our thoughts. And we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:2–3).

As for the following words, according to the Septuagint, “And you pierce or afflict all those subject to you,” Theodotion and Symmachus translated them more accurately—and we have followed them here—as: “And you exact all your debtors.” This shows that it is not without danger to exact payment from a poor person who cannot pay, and to refuse to return to a freezing debtor the cloak that one has taken as a pledge, lest his cry reach God. “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to God” (Prov. 19:17). Conversely, whoever exacts from one who has nothing commits violence against God.

And so that we may know that this is the meaning in the present passage, we shall read in what follows in this same chapter: “Undo the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress.” There is no doubt that this signifies written bonds. For what benefit is there in making one’s face pale through fasting, and fasting for quarrels and disputes, when Scripture says: “Whoever loves sins rejoices in quarrels” (Prov. 17:11)?

The servant of the Lord must not quarrel but must be gentle (2 Tim. 2), and imitate the one who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29), so that humility may not be affected but arise from the heart, seeking not human glory but the conscience of the soul.

“You fast,” he says, “and strike the humble with your fists, and beat them with slaps” (1 Tim. 3). Hence a bishop must not be a striker. For how can one restrain lust who cannot restrain either his hand or his tongue?

The Lord also condemns such fasts at the beginning of this prophecy, saying: “Fasting and idleness, new moons and Sabbaths, and your other festivals, my soul hates” (Isa. 1:13). Therefore Joel commands: “Sanctify a fast; proclaim a healing” (Joel 2:15), so that we may fast from vices and, through good works and healed sins, make our fasts holy.

Finally it follows: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber and the bride from her bridal room,” so that during the time of fasting we may devote ourselves to prayer, lest our inner person feed on the flesh of the dragon that was given as food to the peoples of Ethiopia.

We say these things not to reject fasting. Through fasting Daniel, the man of desires, learned future events (Dan. 9); the Ninevites appeased the wrath of God (Jonah 3); Elijah (1 Kings 19) and Moses (Exod. 34), nourished by intimacy with God after forty days of hunger, were filled with God; and the Lord himself fasted for the same number of days in the wilderness (Matt. 4), leaving us the solemn days of fasting. Rather, we say this because it is of no benefit to carry an empty stomach while doing other things that displease God.

To say nothing of the rest: those who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting [Alternative: “fasting”] will, although they receive glory in the present, be excluded from the kingdom of God, because they have received their reward (Matt. 6).

Hence the Apostle also says that even if he gives his body to martyrdom, so that it may burn—or “so that he may boast,” for both readings are found in the manuscripts—without the love of God (1 Cor. 13), which resides in the conscience of the heart, he claims in vain to shed his blood.

**(Vers. 4–5.)** “Do not fast as you have done until this day, so that your cry may be heard on high. Is this the kind of fast that I have chosen: for a person to afflict his soul for a day? Is it to twist his head like a circle, and to spread out sackcloth and ashes? Will you call this a fast and a day acceptable to the Lord?”

The Septuagint: “Why do you fast for me as today, so that your voice may be heard in a cry? I have not chosen such a fast, nor a day for a person to humble his soul. Nor if you bend your neck like a circle and spread sackcloth and ashes beneath you; you shall not call such a fast acceptable.”

[Note: The manuscripts read this way. The Greek text has ἵνατί μοι νηστεύετε, ὡς σήμερον ἀκουσθῆναι—“Why do you fast for me, so that today your voice may be heard,” and so forth. Earlier editions of the Vulgate had “you fast, so that today it may be heard,” and so forth.]

[Note: Victor inserts *hominem*, “a person,” from the Greek ἄνθρωπον.]

[Note: Martianay and other printed editions read: “Nor if you call a fast and a day acceptable.” We have corrected the text according to the Greek with the aid of the older Ambrosian manuscript. The Septuagint plural καλέσετε, “you shall call,” is certainly written, not καλέσεις, “you shall call” in the singular. Moreover, the words “and a day” (καὶ ἡμέραν) do not belong to the Septuagint version but to Theodotion and Symmachus.]

Lest he appear to condemn the fast that he himself had commanded, he teaches how one ought to fast. Indeed, before teaching what they should pursue, he instructs them what they must avoid: “So that your cry,” he says, “may be heard on high.”

Do not bring your cry into prayer, praying in synagogues and at the corners of the streets so that you may be seen by people (Matt. 6), nor raise your voice on high and, with the Pharisee who is condemned by the Lord’s judgment, proclaim your fasts and works (Luke 18).

For this reason, while rejecting the prayer of the Pharisees, the Lord teaches his disciples how they ought to pray (Matt. 6), in the closed chamber of their breast, so that they may speak to God alone, who can hear the silence of the heart; so that they may cry out in their hearts, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15), and not disfigure their faces but wash with water and anoint their heads with oil.

John the Evangelist also writes concerning this: “And you have an anointing from the Holy One” (1 John 2:20), so that when they have been anointed, they too may become holy.

For God does not seek only the affliction and humiliation of the soul through injury to the body: he does not seek that one should twist the body like a circle, bend the neck, and walk sadly, in accordance with what is said in the Psalms: “I was afflicted and bowed down to the end; all day long I went about mourning” (Ps. 37:9).

Nor does he seek merely that someone should be clothed in sackcloth and sleep in ashes, as we read of David and Ahab (2 Sam. 3; 1 Kings 21), but that, together with these things, he should do what follows.

Otherwise the Apostle also frequently says that he fasted (2 Cor. 6 and 11), and the Lord teaches that when the bridegroom has been taken away from his disciples they will fast (Matt. 6). In the Psalms the penitent says: “I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Ps. 101:10). And: “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Ps. 34:13).

From this we learn that these things must first be done as the Lord wills, and that the other things must not be omitted.

**(Vers. 6–7.)** “Is this not [Vulgate adds: ‘is’] rather the fast that I have chosen? Undo the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress; set free those who have been broken, and break every burden. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor and homeless into your house [Vulgate adds: ‘your house’]. When you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise your own flesh.”

The Septuagint: “Is this not the fast that I have chosen, says the Lord? But loosen every bond of iniquity. Undo the bonds of violent securities. Set the broken free for release, and tear up every unjust document. Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the poor without shelter into your house. If you see the naked, cover him, and do not despise the members of your own seed.”

After teaching what kind of fasting he rejects, he shows what kind he gladly accepts. “Undo,” he says, “the bonds of wickedness; loosen the bundles that oppress”—or, as the Septuagint translated more explicitly, “the bonds of violent securities,” which our translators, deceived by the ambiguity of the word συναλλάγματα (*synallagmata*), “exchanges,” interpreted as written bonds.

It signifies bundles of documents containing the creditors’ accusations, by which the poor are oppressed through debt. These are the cause—or often the greatest cause—of sedition in every city.

Hence the Roman people also occupy the neighboring hills, and there are the “new tablets,” which the Greeks call χρεῶν ἀποκοπάς (*chreōn apokopas*), “cutting off of debts.” [Note: The older Ambrosian manuscript has “or of ruin.” Then, with the order reversed: “Hence also the new tablets,” and so forth. “New tablets” were called those occasions when, with injury and loss to the creditors, all debts contracted up to that point were simultaneously erased and abolished, as though they had already been paid. As Jerome notes, the Greeks called these χρεῶν ἀποκοπαί; among them was Diodorus Siculus, book 19.]

The Prophet therefore does not command that each person refuse to collect what is owed—especially what he has justly given and justly seeks to recover; otherwise he would be an advocate of tribunician sedition. Rather, where the security is unjust and the poor are oppressed by accusation, the bundles of securities and all the bonds of iniquity must be broken.

Or certainly this must be said because the subject is fasting, and fasting involves the affliction and humiliation of the soul. The affliction of the body, however, seeks forgiveness for sins. Divine Scripture teaches us to forgive our debtors, so that our heavenly Father may also forgive us our debts (Mark 11).

Ancient history relates that in the seventh year of remission, or in the fiftieth year, which is the true Jubilee, all possessions returned to their owners, the servants’ former freedom was restored, and all records—which are commonly called securities—became void (Lev. 25 and 27).

If [Alternative: “But if”] this was commanded in the Old Law (Exod. 21), how much more in the Gospel, where everything good is doubled (Matt. 5), and we are no longer commanded to exact “an eye for an eye” and “a tooth for a tooth,” but to offer the cheek to the one who strikes us!

And so that we may understand that what we said above—“You exact all your debtors”—is written concerning creditors, while what follows speaks more clearly of debtors: “Set free those who have been broken,” that is, those who have been broken by poverty, whom want has afflicted. Do not allow them, once set free, to beg.

“And break every burden” by which they are weighed down. The Septuagint translated this more clearly: “And tear up every unjust document.” Symmachus translated it: “And break every false security.”

But someone might say: “I have no debtors. What should I do so that my fast may be accepted?” The answer follows: “Break your bread for the hungry.” Not many loaves, so that you may not plead poverty, but one loaf. Nor the whole loaf, but a portion of bread—the portion you would have eaten had you not been fasting—so that your fast may not be a profit for your purse but nourishment for your soul.

Beautifully he adds “your,” so that you do not make an alms-offering from robbery: “A man’s wealth is the ransom of his soul” (Prov. 13:8). And elsewhere: “Honor the Lord from your just labors” (Prov. 3:9).

Certainly, if you have no bread and there is a great multitude of hungry people, offer something from which you suffer no loss. Where there is no expense, bring the poor without shelter into your house.

Or, as it is written in the Hebrew, simply “into a house”: if you do not have your own house, bring him into a small lodging that you possess either by renting it or through someone’s kindness.

“If you see the naked, cover him.” The Lord also said this in the Gospel: “Whoever has two tunics, let him give one to the one who has none” (Luke 3:11).

He did not command that one tunic be cut up and divided, as many do for the sake of popular applause, but that the second not be kept in reserve. Thus he enlarges the commands of justice, so that he even says that a cup of cold water given will have its reward.

“And do not despise your own flesh.” Every human being is our flesh. And according to the Gospel parable of the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and was wounded by robbers, the one who did good is called his neighbor (Luke 10).

Or, according to the Septuagint, which says, “Do not despise the members of your own seed,” let us understand as members of our own seed those of whom the Apostle teaches that alms should be given to all, but especially to the members of the household of faith (Gal. 6). They are our flesh and our seed, because they are born from the same parent together with us.

The Savior also extended his hand toward them, saying: “These are my mother and my brothers, those who do the will of my Father” (Mark 3:34–35).

And so that we may know that there is one Lord, and that the Lord speaks the same things in the New and Old Testaments, he says in the Gospel concerning those who will stand at the right hand on the day of judgment: “Come, blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was sick and in prison, and you came to me; I was a stranger, and you welcomed me into your house; I was naked, and you clothed me” (Matt. 25:34 ff.).

When they humbly said that they had done nothing for the Lord and Savior, he replied: “As long as you did it for one of the least of my brothers, you did it for me.”

According to the tropological interpretation, we may say this: Whoever fasts from every evil and wishes his fast to be regarded must not only turn away from evil but also do good, so that he may break every bond of iniquity by which the simple among believers have been bound through the deceptions of heretics.

And the στραγγαλίαι (*strangalíai*), “bonds of violent dealings,” which the Prophet also identifies in the Psalm when he says: “But those who turn aside into bonds, the Lord will lead away with the workers of iniquity” (Ps. 124:5).

For all who are bound by the chains of heretics turn aside from the Lord, like an ox led to sacrifice; they choose and exchange truth for falsehood.

The ecclesiastical man should therefore release and loosen such people, who have been broken by judgment; and he should undo and tear apart every writing of the heretics, concerning whom this same Prophet says: “Woe to those who write iniquity; for in writing they write wickedness, robbing the poor of my people of judgment” (Isa. 10:1–2), so that they may no longer hold the simple entangled in their snares.

And when he has done this, he should break for the hungry the bread of ecclesiastical teaching. The Lord did this as well, giving broken loaves to the Apostles, which he left to them in the seven baskets and twelve hand-baskets—not whole, as they had existed in the Law, but broken and fragmented in the Gospel, so that they would have something to distribute to the poor (Matt. 15).

Those whom you see without the warmth of faith, chilled outside the Church by the cold of unbelief, poor and homeless—bring them, he says, into the house of the Church, and cover them with the cloak of incorruption. [Note: An old Brixian manuscript, owned by Victorius, reads: “bring [them] into your house,” that is, into the house of the Church; he approves this reading.] Clothed in Christ’s tunic, let them not remain in the tombs, as we read concerning the one possessed by a legion of demons, who lived naked among the memorials of the dead.
