“And when you have done these things,” he says, “and your generosity has been made available to all, do not especially despise the members of the household of faith.”

**(Vers. 8–9.)** “Then your light will break forth like the morning, and your healing will quickly [Vulgate: ‘more quickly’] arise; your justice will go before your face, and the glory of the Lord will gather you. Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry out, and he will say: ‘Here I am.’”

The Septuagint: “Then your morning light will break forth, your healings will quickly arise, your justice will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, he will say: ‘Here I am.’”

When you have not done the things described in the preceding passage, and have done the things of which we have just spoken, then your fast will be acceptable, and your morning light will break forth: namely, the sun of justice, of which the prophet Malachi speaks in the person of God the Father: “For you who fear my name the sun of justice shall rise, and healing is in its wings” (Mal. 4:2).

What is there called the sun is here called the light. Just as morning light dispels darkness, so the light of knowledge and truth drives away every error.

“And your healings,” he says, “will quickly arise.” Instead of this Aquila, translating word for word, wrote: “And the scar of your wound will quickly be closed,” so that the wounds of our sins may be closed by the scar that quickly forms at the rising of the sun of justice.

In place of what the Septuagint translated as τὰ ἰάματά σου (*ta iamata sou*), “your healings,” the Latin translators, led by the similarity of the words, wrote ἱμάτια (*himatia*), “garments.” Hence many, deceived by the falsity of the translation, use this testimony to prove the resurrection of the body, wishing to understand the body as the garment of the soul that will arise on the day of resurrection.

“And your justice,” he says, “will go before you” (Gen. 30:33, according to the Septuagint). This accords with Jacob’s statement: “Tomorrow my justice will answer for me.” And what is written will be fulfilled: “Behold the man and his works.”

“And the glory of the Lord will surround you,” like a most beautiful garment, so that you may be glorified with God and with human beings.

“Then you will call, and the Lord will answer; you will cry out, and he will say: ‘Here I am’”—not by voice but by action, not by a verbal response but by benefits.

This is confirmed literally in the Gospel also, when the leper said to the Lord, “If you will, you can make me clean,” and the Lord replied: “I will; be cleansed.”

[Col. 0568C] **(Verse 10.)** If you remove from your midst the chain, and cease extending the finger and speaking what is unprofitable; when you pour out your soul for the hungry and satisfy the afflicted soul, then your light will rise in darkness, and your darkness will be like midday.

> **Vulgate:** “then” is absent.

**The Septuagint:** If you remove from yourself the bond, and the ordinance, and the word of murmuring, and give your bread to the hungry from your soul, and satisfy the humbled soul, then your light will rise in darkness, and your darkness will be like midday.

The Hebrew word *MOTA* (), which in Jeremiah is interpreted as “iron collars” (Jer. XVIII), occurs twice in the present chapter. In the passage where above, according to the Septuagint, we said, “Dissolve the bonds of violent [Col. 0567D] exchanges”—

> **Note:** Victor replaces *commutationum* (“of exchanges”) with *cautionum* (“of securities”), and says that the error is evident from the words themselves and from the Greek text of the Septuagint. Yet it should not be denied that *συνάλλαγμα*, according to the propriety of the Greek language, may also be interpreted by Jerome as “exchange” in the following exposition.

—for the one Hebrew word *MOTA*, let us know that they rendered it “violent securities”; Aquila rendered it “error,” Symmachus “deviation,” and Theodotion—

> **Note:** Our manuscripts, and those consulted by Martianay, read *κλυόν*.  
> **[Col. 0568D]** The holy Doctor, in his book *On Hebrew Names*, writes concerning Joshua: “Luz; some interpret it as *κλειόν*, namely, the collar of the condemned, which is commonly called a *boia*.” He has the same statement below in Jeremiah, chapter XXVII. —Theodotion: *κλοιόν*, etc. Manuscript codices read ΚΑΥΟΝ, as we previously observed in the book *On Names*, under the entry *Luz*, which some have interpreted as *κλοιόν*, namely, the collar of the condemned, commonly called a *boia*. Consult the passage and our scholia. MARTIAN.

—*κλοιόν*, that is, “collar.”

Again, in the present passage, where we translated, “If you remove from your midst the chain,” and where, instead of “chain,” the Septuagint translated *σύνδεσμον*, that is, “bond” or “tie,” Aquila, as above, interpreted it as “error”; Symmachus, agreeing with Theodotion’s judgment—

> **[Col. 0569A]** **694** *Aliter*: “collapsing”—

placed “collar.” Let this suffice concerning the variety of translations.

Otherwise, the sense is joined to what precedes in this way: “Your morning light will rise, and your healings will quickly spring up; your righteousness will go before you, and the glory of the Lord will crown you.” He will immediately hear the one who entreats, and will show himself to be present. This will happen only if you add these things also to your former works: that you remove from yourself the bond and chain by which your soul is fettered. Concerning this Peter also spoke to Simon: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity” (Acts VIII, 23). Paul likewise grieved when he saw the city of the Athenians bound by idolatry. “Each person,” it says, “is bound by the cords of his sins” (Prov. V).

For these bonds of the soul David also prayed in the psalm: “Cleanse me from my secret faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from those belonging to others” (Ps. XVIII, 13). It is difficult to find anyone who is not bound by these chains. Rarely is a soul found that does not have this exceedingly heavy collar around its neck, dragging it downward toward earthly works, so that it looks not toward heaven but toward the earth. The same is reported concerning the woman in the Gospel whom Satan had bound for eighteen years, so that, bent over, she could not see heavenly things (Luke XIII).

“If, therefore,” he says, “you remove this chain from the midst of your heart, disperse such bonds, and remove the *χειροτονία*—for which the three other interpreters, using a corresponding expression, translated ‘the extended finger’—

> **[Col. 0569C]** namely, so that you not only neither think nor do evil yourself, but do not slander your neighbor either, nor point your finger at individuals as though marking them, nor speak what is unprofitable to your soul, considering not your own evils but the errors of others—then you will receive what the following statement adds.”

Most of our people understand *χειροτονία*, that is, the ordination of clergy—which is fulfilled not only by the pronouncement of a formula but also by the laying on of hands, so that, as we once laughed at in certain cases, a secret verbal imprecation might not ordain clergy who were unaware of it—in this way: they apply Paul’s testimony when he writes to Timothy, “Lay hands hastily on no one, nor share in the sins of others” (1 Tim. V, 22).

For it is no slight sin to cast pearls before swine and give what is holy to dogs (Matt. VII), and to confer clerical ordination not upon holy men, and those most learned in the law of God, but upon one’s own hangers-on and ministers of base offices; and what is more shameful than this, to confer it at the entreaties of little women. Here we must consider the wisdom of Christ’s Apostle, who, to demonstrate the danger of ordination, joined it to the punishment of sinners: “Nor share in the sins of others.”

Just as, therefore, in the ordination of wicked men, the one who appoints such people becomes a participant in their sins, so in the ordination of holy men, the one who chooses good men becomes a participant in their righteousness.

It follows: “And the word of murmuring”—understand, by a common construction, “if you remove it from yourself.” The word of murmuring occurs when God speaks against us: “Let the murmuring of this people cease from me, and they shall not die.” We refer our sins to God in order to make excuses for our sins, saying: “The heat of my body overcame me; the impulses of youth conquered me; I was created such by God; poverty compelled me to steal.”

Therefore, if we do not do the things just mentioned, but do the things that are about to be mentioned—giving our bread to the hungry not as above, but giving our soul, so that we may help him in whatever ways we can, and giving not as though from sorrow or necessity, but from the heart, receiving the benefit more than giving it—for “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. IX, 7)—so that we do not refresh the hungry or afflicted soul only in part, but satisfy it; and if we grieve with those who grieve and mourn with those who mourn (Rom. XII), then our light will rise in darkness: he who says, “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness, but may have the light of life” (John XII, 46).

“For the eye is the lamp of our body: if it is simple, our whole body will be luminous. But if what ought to be light has been turned into darkness, then the whole body will be dark, and it will be said to us: ‘If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!’” (Matt. VI, [Col. 0570C] 23).

Let us consider through how many virtues we reach the light of God, so that darkness may be turned into midday; and let us say with the bride: “Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday?” (Song I, 6).

**(Verse 11.)** And the Lord will always give you rest, and will fill your soul with splendors, and will deliver your bones. And—

> **Note:** Formerly, “and it will be.” The Hebrew, however, has . See Jerome’s following exposition.

—you will be like a watered garden, and like a spring of waters whose waters will not fail.

**The Septuagint:** And your God will be with you always; and you will be filled as your soul desires, and your bones will grow fat. And they will be like a drunken garden, and like a spring whose water will not fail.

> **Note:** In the Alexandrian copies, etc. The Alexandrian manuscript, printed in the London Polyglots, preserves nearly the whole of this passage. After the final word *ὕδωρ* (“water”) of the eleventh verse, it reads: “And your bones will rise like grass and grow fat; and generations of generations will inherit.”  
> **[Col. 0570D]** From this it is clear that it is one of the Alexandrian exemplars of which Jerome speaks at this point. MARTIAN.

What has been added in Alexandrian copies at the beginning of this chapter—“And still my praise will be in you always”—and at the end, “And your bones will rise like grass and grow fat, and they will inherit for generation [Col. 0570D] and generations”—

> **Note:** In the copy called Alexandrian, as also in the Aldine, this other portion of the verse is found: *καὶ τὰ ὀστᾶ σου ὡς βοτάνη ἀνατελεῖ καὶ πιανθήσεται, καὶ κληρονομήσουσι γενεὰς γενεῶν* (“and your bones will rise like grass and grow fat, and they will inherit generations of generations”), which Cyril and Procopius also read.

—is not found in the Hebrew, nor even in the corrected and genuine copies of the Septuagint. It should therefore be marked beforehand with an obelus.

“When,” he says, “the darkness of your breast has been dissolved by the rising light, and midday has arisen in place of palpable night, then you will always have God as an inhabitant, and he will fill your soul with splendors.” Concerning these it is written in the psalm: “With you is dominion in the day of your power, amid the splendors of the holy ones; from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 4).

Or you will be satisfied with all that your soul desires, because you yourself have satisfied the hungry soul, and you will be able to say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who fills your desire with good things” (Ps. I, 5). And your bones will be delivered from destruction and everlasting fire.

Or they will grow fat, recovering their former thickness, which had been attenuated by hunger for the word of the Lord. This may indeed be understood literally of the resurrection of those bodies that are destined to fall, and of the virtues of the soul, concerning which the holy man speaks meaningfully in the psalm: “All my bones will say, O Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. XXXIV, 10).

Concerning these things it is also written in Proverbs: “A good reputation makes the bones fat” (Prov. XV, 30); and to them rewards are promised: “It will be health to your body and healing to your bones” (Prov. XVI, 24). Again it is written concerning them: “The Lord keeps all their bones; not one of them will be broken” (Ps. XXXIII, 21).

By contrast, the sinner, who has lost the strength and virtue of his soul, mourns and says: “Our bones have been scattered beside the grave” (Ps. CXL, 7). For we cannot believe that the bones of sinners are not in hell but merely beside hell. Nor does “a good reputation makes the bones fat” (Prov. XV, 30) refer to bodily fattening.

It follows: “And you will be”—or “it will be,” that is, either you or your soul—“like a watered garden.” Concerning it, it is written: “A spring went out and watered the whole face of paradise” (Gen. II, 6); in place of “paradise,” the Hebrew reads “garden.”

We can identify this spring as none other than the one of which it is said: “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. XXXV, 10). It continually waters his Church and the hearts of all believers.

**(Verse 12.)** And the ancient ruins will be rebuilt in you; you will raise up the foundations of generation and generation; and in you will be called—

> **Vulgate:** “And you will be called”—

—the builder of walls, turning [Vulgate: “averting”] paths into rest.

**The Septuagint:** And the ancient ruins will be rebuilt for you, and your foundations will be everlasting, through generations and generations—

> **Note:** Our manuscripts supply the missing “and generations” according to the Greek archetype.

—and you will be called the builder of a wall, and you will cause paths to rest in the midst.

“Not only,” he says, “will your light rise in darkness, and your darkness be like midday; the Lord will always give you rest, and you will be like a watered garden, and so forth; but what had long been desolate will be rebuilt in you. The foundations of your buildings will be laid so as to remain through many generations, so that either you yourself will be called the builder of walls and fortifications, or there will arise in you—

> **Note:** Formerly, less correctly, “as though he were,” instead of the reading preferred by the manuscripts: “who is.”

—one who is the builder of walls and turns paths into rest, or, according to the Septuagint, causes roads to rest in the midst.”

The Jews, and those who are merely friends of the Western interpretation, refer this to the restoration of the cities of Palestine. They argue that it either took place under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, or will occur at the end of time; that the foundations of Jerusalem and the surrounding cities must be restored and laid exceedingly deep; and that walls must be built so high that no enemy can enter and the access of all hostile forces to them can be barred.

We, however, following the order of the explanation we have begun, say that what had been desolate among the Jews is rebuilt in the Church—not for a short time, but forever—and that its foundations are to be raised from both peoples, that is, in two generations. Hence the Apostle said: “As a wise architect I laid a foundation, and another builds upon it; but let each one take care how he builds upon it” (1 Cor. III, 10). And elsewhere: “We are God’s agriculture, God’s building”; and again: “Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets” (Eph. II, 20).

She is to be called, or the one who has been born in her is to be called, the builder of walls. Concerning him we read in the psalm: “A man was born in her, and the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. LXXXVI, 5).

Scripture records that fields and vineyards are enclosed by such walls and fortifications—for this is what the Greek word *φραγμούς* signifies: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it”; and shortly afterward: “Why have you destroyed its wall, so that all who pass along the way pluck it?” (Ps. LXXXIX, 9, 13).

And in this same Prophet: “A vineyard was made for the beloved.” Describing it in beautiful language, he continues: “I built a tower and surrounded it with a wall” (Eccles. II, 4). According to Ecclesiastes, the serpent will bite the one who destroyed it.

It was enclosed for this reason: to prevent all wild beasts from gaining access to God’s vineyard. This is the crooked serpent who deceived Eve in paradise. Because she had destroyed God’s commandments, she was exposed to his bites, and she heard from the Lord: “You will watch his head, and he will watch your heel” (Gen. III, 15).

In the passage where, following the Septuagint, we translated, so as not to appear to innovate—because the testimony is widely known—“And you will be called the builder of walls,” in Hebrew it reads: “And he will be called in you, *GODER PHERES* [repairer of the breach].” Aquila translated this as—

> **Note:** This passage was so corrupt that the distinguished Montfaucon did not dare restore it even conjecturally. The older Ambrosian manuscript returns it to its former and certain reading. In uncial letters it is written ΠΕΡΙΦΡΑΚΤΗΣΑΙΑΚΟΠΗΣ. Dividing these into two words and correcting one or two letters, which are particularly liable to be interchanged, we read *περιφράκτης διακοπῆς*. From the meaning of the words themselves—“one who places a barrier against an interruption”—for which Symmachus translated “one who places a wall against the one cutting down”; from the context and sequence of the discourse; from its agreement with the Hebrew; and finally from Jerome’s exposition according to the sense, the authenticity of the restored reading is evident. Nor should the fact that *περιφράκτης* is almost unknown to lexicographers disturb anyone, since it can rightly be derived, according to the analogy of the Greek language, from the verb *περιφράττω*, “to enclose”; and Aquila’s contentious temperament is well known, as he devised many other words not used by Greek authors in order to render word for word. Moreover, what Erasmus wrote by conjecture was monstrous, and has rashly passed into later editions down to the present day: *πεφράκτισμα χολῆς*. The ancient manuscripts consulted by Montfaucon were no less corrupt; from them he could scarcely print even the second word, *διακοπῆς*.

[Col. 0573A] **699**—*περιφράκτης διακοπῆς*, which according to the sense we may render, “one who opposes himself to the fury of God’s anger.”

Finally, Symmachus translated it, “one who places a wall against the one cutting down” (1 Sam. VII), such as Moses, Aaron, and Samuel were. They resisted the Lord’s anger and, as though they had built a wall, set a limit to his indignation.

The same is said to Jeremiah: “Do not oppose the Lord, nor seek to resist his wrath,” and so, by prayers as by a kind of wall, to shut off his indignation (Jer. VII). And to Moses, as though the Lord were being restrained by him, he says: “Let me go, and I will strike this people” (Exod. XXXII, 10).

Such a builder of walls, fortifications, and enclosures, therefore, will turn paths into rest, so that God’s anger will no longer rage, but the Lord will be appeased toward them, and all the paths of his indignation will come to rest.

**(Verse 13.)** If you turn your foot away from the sabbath, from doing your will on my holy day; and if you call the sabbath delightful, holy and glorious to the Lord, and glorify him by not following your own ways, and your will is not found, so that you may speak a word—

> **Vulgate:** “And your will is not found.”

**The Septuagint:** If you turn your foot away on the sabbaths, so as not to do your wills on the holy day; and if you call the sabbaths delightful and holy to the Lord; you will not move your foot for work, nor speak a word in anger from your mouth.

> **Note:** The words “in anger from your mouth” do not occur in the Hebrew.

To the one to whom he had earlier said, “Is this not rather the fast that I have chosen: dissolve the bond of impiety, loosen the bundles that oppress,” and so forth, he now also promises rewards, if he is willing to do what follows (Exod. XX): namely, to restrain his foot on the sabbaths, not do his own will, and not defile the Lord’s holy day with his own desires—

> **Variant:** “pleasures.”

The Law commands that on the sabbaths we do no servile work, that we do not kindle a fire, that we sit in one place, and that we perform only those works that pertain to the salvation of the soul.

If we take this literally, it cannot be fulfilled at all. Who can manage to sit throughout the entire day and night of the sabbath without moving from one place—or even stirring slightly? Yet if he does stir, he becomes a transgressor of the Law.

From this one commandment, therefore, which is impossible according to the letter, we are compelled to understand the other matters spiritually as well: we must not perform servile work or lose the soul’s freedom, for “everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII).

We must not carry a burden on the sabbath, such as the one carried by him who says: “My iniquities have risen above my head; like a heavy burden they have been made heavy upon me” (Ps. XXXVII, 5). We must not allow the iniquity that sits upon a talent of lead to have power over us; we must not allow bodily pleasure and lust to set us ablaze (Zech. V). “For all adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hos. VII); and the fiery darts of the devil are set alight to shoot at the upright in heart in darkness (Ps. X).

We are also commanded, after taking up the plow, not to look back; and, when climbing to the height of roofs, not to wish to descend in order to retrieve the garments of the world (Luke IX). Rather, we should hear Moses say, “But stand here with me” (Exod. XXXIV, 2), and sit with the Lord, weary on the road of this world, beside the well of the Samaritan woman and thirsting for the conversion and salvation of those who err (John IV).

We should hear the Apostle admonishing us: “Stand firm and immovable” (1 Cor. XV, 58), lest we suffer what Judas the betrayer suffered: he lost the place of his ministry and became a transgressor. We should always remember the saying: “If the spirit of one who has power rises against you, do not leave your place” (Eccles. X, 4).

The one who thus rests on the sabbath washes his hands among the innocent and does not move his feet to do his own will. This person celebrates the Lord’s delightful sabbaths. This sabbath rest is promised to us in the heavenly places, according to the Epistle written to the Hebrews, and glory is prepared for us (Heb. IV).

Thus, when we do not follow our own ways on the sabbath, nor is our will found so that we speak a word—that is, when we sin neither in deed nor in speech—we fulfill the command.

Otherwise, if these things alone are forbidden on the sabbath, then liberty to sin is granted to us on the other six days. Since it is foolish to believe this, it remains that the sabbath—which is interpreted as “rest”—must be sanctified by the faithful at all times, while they do not the will of the flesh but the will of the soul.

The addition found in the Septuagint, “in anger from your mouth,” is not present in the Hebrew.

To this sabbath, which is to be celebrated at every festival, the Savior summons us in the Gospel, saying: “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest” (Matt. XI, 28). This is what *ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς* means, namely, that, laying down the burdens of sins, we may keep sabbath in Christ and say: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX, 3).

Let us avoid what the holy man says he almost suffered: “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. LXXII, 2).

**(Verse 14.)** Then you will delight in the Lord—

> **Vulgate:** “in the Lord”—

—and I will lift you up over the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

**The Septuagint:** And you will be confident in the Lord; and he will lift you up over the good things of the earth, and will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.

**701** After you have called the sabbaths delightful, and have not moved your foot on the sabbath to perform servile work, and have spoken no word—that is, have maintained perpetual silence—and have fulfilled what is commanded, “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit” (Ps. XXXIII, 14), then you will delight in the Lord, and you will see fulfilled in yourself: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI, 4).

Or you will have confidence in the Lord, according to what is written: “The one who trusts in the Lord is blessed.” And in Jeremiah: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope” (Jer. XVII, 7). And elsewhere: “It is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man” (Ps. CXVII, 8).

And the Lord will raise and lift you over the heights and good things of the earth. The land of the meek, and the land of the living, is not below but above. Accordingly, to Lot, fleeing from the valley of Sodom and Gomorrah, it is said: “Save yourself on the mountain” (Gen. XIX). After he reached it, the sun rose for him in Segor.

Concerning this land the Lord said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. V, 4). There are many other passages that we have often used, including: “Honor your father and your mother, and you will be long-lived upon the land that the Lord your God will give you” (Exod. XX, 12).

This cannot stand literally at all. Many honor their parents and die young, while others who murder their parents live for a long time. To know more certainly that this land is in the heights, let us briefly recall Psalm XXXVI, in which it is written: “The meek shall possess the earth, and shall delight in the abundance of peace.” After this comes: “Wait for the Lord and keep his ways, and he will lift you up, so that you may possess the earth” (Ps. XXXVI, 11).

> **Note:** The repeated occurrence of the word “earth” caused ancient scribes, as commonly happens, to omit the words between the two passages, where it is sung: “The righteous shall possess the earth.” We have supplied them from an older Ambrosian manuscript.

Elsewhere it is sung: “The righteous shall possess the earth, and shall dwell upon it forever and ever” (ibid., 34). This too is impossible. For if the earth will pass away, how will the righteous dwell forever and ever upon this earth that we inhabit? From this we learn that there is an earth situated in the heights.

After this comes: “And I will feed you”—or “the Lord will feed you”—“with the inheritance of Jacob your father.” Just as the one who has Abraham’s faith is called a son of Abraham, so the one who supplants vices and sins is called a son of Jacob. Whoever imitates the virtue of someone is called that person’s son.

The good things of the earth, situated in the heights, with which the son of Jacob is satisfied, must be understood as those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. II).

Concerning these things it is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Those who say such things show that they are seeking a homeland. If indeed they had been thinking of that from which they had gone out, they had time to return to it. But now they desire a better homeland, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. XI, 14 ff.).

From this we learn that the fable of a thousand years, in which marriages, food, and the conduct of earthly life are again promised, must be rejected. For if in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but will be like the angels because they are children of the resurrection (Matt. XXII); and if the Apostle speaks concerning the belly and food, “Food is for the belly and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI, 13), how shall we again seek, in an incorruptible, spiritual, and immortal body, the vices of our former mortal and corrupt flesh?

We say this not to deny the substance of the glorified body, but to remove entirely the former works in those who are made like the angels. Otherwise, even in this present body, through fasting, self-restraint, perpetual chastity, and love, we imitate the virtues of the angels, yet we do not lose the substance of our bodies.

To believe all these things as future, let us know that they have been promised by God, whose mouth has spoken. Thus, just as the hand signifies work, the feet walking, the belly generation, and the ears and eyes hearing and seeing, so let us understand speech to belong to the mouth of God.

**(Chapter LIX—Verses 1, 2.)** Behold, the hand of the Lord is not shortened, so that it cannot save; nor is his ear burdened, so that it cannot hear. But your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you, so that he would not hear.

**The Septuagint:** Is the hand of the Lord unable to save? Or is his ear burdened, so that he cannot hear? But your sins separate you from God; and because of your sins he has turned his face away from you, **703** so that he may not have mercy.

I could have completed earlier what I said I would now do: “You will be confident in the Lord, and he will raise you to the good things of the earth, and will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father.”

For my hand is not shortened or contracted, so that I cannot extend it to deliver my people; nor do I have deaf ears, so that I cannot hear. From this it is shown that the ears of the Lord, which hear the righteous and do not hear sinners, are by no means like our ears, which hear equally whatever voice is uttered, whether of righteousness or unrighteousness.

But your sins, he says, like a wall set in the middle, divide you from God. Hence the Savior in his passion made both one (Eph. II), and, destroying the dividing wall of the enclosure, abolished hostility in his flesh, so that those whom the wall of sins had separated might be joined by the blood of Christ.

He opened the gate of paradise, which had long been closed (Gen. III), and extinguished the flaming sword with his own blood, so that the thief might hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

What follows—“And because of your sins he has turned his face away from you, so that he would not hear,” or “so that he would not have mercy”—shows that he could not endure the stench of their sins and iniquities, but turned his face away so that he would not see their shame and immediately be compelled to strike them.

Therefore the sinner, desiring to see the Lord’s face, says in the psalm: “How long, O Lord, will you forget me forever? How long will you turn your face away from me?” (Ps. XII, 1). And elsewhere: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. LXXIX, 4).

**(Verses 3, 4.)** For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with iniquity; your lips have spoken falsehood, and your tongue utters iniquity. There is no one who invokes righteousness, nor anyone who judges truly; but they trust in nothingness—

> **Vulgate:** “in nothing”—

—and speak vanities.

**The Septuagint:** For your hands are defiled with blood, and your fingers with sins. Your lips are defiled with iniquity, and your tongue meditates injustice. No one speaks what is right, nor is there a righteous judgment. They trust in vain things and speak empty words, iniquities and sins.

What he earlier named in general he now explains in its parts. It must be considered that he does not accuse them here of the idolatry by which they were held in Isaiah’s time, but of the shedding of blood, concerning which he had already said: “The righteous man perishes, and no one takes it to heart. Men of righteousness are taken away, and no one understands. The righteous man is taken away from the face of iniquity; his burial will be in peace, and he will be removed from the midst” (Isa. LVII, 1–2).

> **Note:** Victor reads: “The righteous man perished, and no one takes it to heart. And righteous men are taken away, and no one understands … and immediately removed from the midst,” from the preceding chapter, chapter 5.

Although they themselves did not lay hands on the Lord and Savior, nevertheless, by crying out with a voice consonant with their impiety, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII, 25), they are guilty of his death and have polluted hands.

The same Prophet testifies concerning them, saying: “When you stretch out your hands toward me, I will not hear; your hands are full of blood” (Isa. I, 15). Their lips and tongue likewise speak iniquity and falsehood, so that in place of Christ they may promise themselves the Antichrist; and there is no one among the people who invokes righteousness and judges truth—or, as it is found in the Hebrew, “faith,” namely, who believes in Christ.

But they trust in nothingness and speak vanities. Hence the Apostle commands us not to attend to Jewish fables and commandments of people who turn away from the truth (Tit. I). Truly they trust in nothingness and follow vanities, fulfilling the Lord’s prophecy: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V, 43).

**(Verses 5, 6.)** They have conceived labor and brought forth iniquity; they have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. Whoever eats from their eggs will die, and what has been incubated will break out as a basilisk. Their webs will not become clothing, nor will they cover themselves with their works.

**The Septuagint:** For they conceive pain and give birth to iniquity. They have broken the eggs of asps and woven a spider’s web—

> **Note:** Two Ambrosian manuscripts read “they weave,” in accordance with the Greek *ὑφαίνουσι*.

—and whoever wishes to eat from their eggs, breaking one, will find it rotten, and in it a basilisk. Their web will not become clothing, nor will they be covered by their works.

Those who await the coming of the Antichrist, and cannot say, “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and were in labor; we gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI, 18), rightly conceive pain and bring forth iniquity, so that they receive in iniquity the one whom they seek with great labor. Concerning their father it is written: “He conceived pain and brought forth iniquity” (Ps. VII, 15).

They break and shatter the eggs of asps so that they may receive their poisons into their minds. To them it is said in the Gospel: “Serpents, offspring of vipers” (Matt. III, 7). Fittingly he speaks of the eggs of asps and serpents, which are said first to produce eggs.

**705** And because they not only retain the poisons of malice in their hearts, but meditate day and night upon the law of the Lord, muttering old-wives’ tales, therefore it is said: “And they weave spiders’ webs.” With these they catch flies, gnats, and small creatures; and when something happens to come upon them, it passes through as though through empty air.

“Whoever eats,” he says, “from their eggs will die,” that is, whoever agrees with their counsels, as Abel agreed with Cain when he said, “Let us go out into the field” (Gen. IV, 8), will immediately be killed.

Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Whoever wishes to eat from their eggs, breaking one, will find it rotten, and in it a basilisk.” For someone deceived at first glance, who thinks the eggs are those of hens or other birds, whose eating is harmless, will, if he breaks one before eating it, immediately recognize its foul decay and most offensive stench, and what has been incubated will prove to be a basilisk.

Or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, an asp. Aquila, however, used “viper,” for which the Hebrew reads *EPHEE* ().

Therefore, whoever, hearing Jewish traditions, wishes to prepare himself for the foods of the thousand years and, ensnared by the delights of their promises, stretches out his hand toward the egg—

> **Note:** The same manuscripts read “to extend the hand toward the food.”

—if, before eating it—that is, before assenting to deadly words—he wishes first to examine what is being said and to scrutinize each statement and investigate its reasoning, will immediately discover that the Antichrist is being prepared within those very traditions.

Thus, according to the Hebrew, “whoever eats from their eggs will die.” But whoever, according to the Septuagint, wishes first to break them and look more carefully to see what lies hidden will discover the most dreadful stench and the prince of all serpents, the devil, lurking in their traditions.

And because he had said above, “They weave spiders’ webs,” he explains that the weaving of these webs is of no benefit. Their entire labor and doctrine, he says, does not produce the clothing of Christ, nor a cloak by which the nakedness of the soul may be covered; rather, they sweat through futile labor. The same Prophet says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me. In vain do they worship me, teaching doctrines and commandments of men” (Isa. XXIX, 13). By following these, they neglect the law of God.

And so that we may know that works are signified by the web, he adds: “Nor will they be covered by their works.”

Some explain this passage in the following way: “They cut or broke the eggs of asps,” that is, by biting, they rejected all the words of the Prophets, and wove for themselves the flattering—

> **Note:** One Ambrosian manuscript reads: “and they took the flattering and fawning speeches of the false prophets, concerning whom,” etc.

—speeches of false prophets. Whoever eats from these will be struck by the serpent and will understand that the words of falsehood have profited him nothing.

### (Verses 7, 8)

Their works are works of uselessness, and the work of iniquity is in their hands. Their feet run toward evil, and they hasten to shed innocent blood. Their thoughts are useless thoughts; devastation and destruction are in their ways. They did not know the way of peace, and there is no judgment in their footsteps. Their paths are crooked for them; whoever treads upon them does not know peace.

The Septuagint has: “For their works are works of iniquity, and their feet run toward wickedness. They are swift to shed innocent blood; their thoughts are the thoughts of fools. Destruction and misery are in their ways, and they did not know the way of peace; there is no judgment in their ways. For their paths are crooked, and those who travel them do not know peace.”

Therefore they are not covered by their works, because their works are works of iniquity, which the Apostle calls unfruitful—that is, bearing no fruit (Ephesians 5). Their feet run toward evil, and they hasten to shed innocent blood (Proverbs 1). For they had this same habit even in the killing of the prophets. To them Stephen said: “Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?” (Acts 7:52). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you” (Matthew 23:37); and again: “All the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth will come upon you, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Barachiah, whom you killed between the Temple and the altar” (ibid., 35).

Hence it is also said to them above: “For your hands are polluted with blood, and your tongue speaks iniquity” (Isaiah 1:15). Through this practice of cruelty and blasphemy they came to the death of the Lord. Judas likewise came to murder by way of avarice—or rather, to murder joined with the sacrilege of avarice.

What follows—“Their thoughts are the thoughts of fools; destruction and misery are in their ways, and they did not know the way of peace”—together with the earlier statement, “Their feet are swift to shed blood,” the Apostle placed in Romans, chapter 3. Many people, being unaware of the matter, suppose that these words were taken from Psalm 13; they were added in the Vulgate edition and are not found in the Hebrew text. We discussed this more fully at the beginning of this volume.

They rightly did not know the way of peace, because they refused to accept its author. For he is our peace, who says to the Apostles: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” [Col. 0579C] (John 14:27). And to Jerusalem: “If you had known the things that are for your peace, for now they will come upon you: your enemies will surround you with a rampart, besiege you, and dash your children to the ground” (Luke 19:42–43).

Those who have not received peace consequently have no judgment in their ways either—the one of whom it was said above: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has delighted; he will bring forth judgment to the nations” (Isaiah 42:1).

It follows: “Their ways are crooked,” not by nature but by their own will. For whatever is perverted and bent is twisted from what is straight into what is wrong. The whole teaching of the Pharisees is a subversion of truth; whoever walks by it not only fails to find peace but does not even recognize it, so as to know what he ought to seek.

### (Verses 9 and following)

For this reason judgment has withdrawn far from us, and righteousness will not overtake us. We awaited light, and behold, darkness; brightness, and we walked in darkness. We groped like blind men along a wall, and, as though without eyes, we felt our way. We stumbled at midday as though in darkness; in dark places, as though dead. We shall roar like bears, all of us, and we shall moan like doves, meditating. We awaited judgment, and it will not come; salvation, and it has withdrawn far from us.

The Septuagint has: “Therefore judgment has departed from them, and righteousness has not overtaken them. While they awaited light, darkness came upon them. While awaiting it, they will walk in darkness; they will grope like blind men along a wall, and, as though they had no eyes, they will feel their way. They will fall at midday as though in the middle of the night; as dying men they will groan; they will walk together like a bear and like a dove. We awaited judgment, and it is not here; salvation has withdrawn far from us.”

After the accusation of the Jewish people, the Prophet responds in their person, telling them what penitents ought to say, if indeed they wish to receive healing after their wounds. I am astonished that the Septuagint, as though the Prophet were speaking about them rather than their replying to the Prophet’s words, has woven this speech together, since in what follows, overcome by the truth, they do the same thing, saying: “We awaited judgment, and it is not here; salvation has withdrawn far from us. For our iniquity is great in your sight, our sins have resisted us,” and so forth.

Everything, therefore, is being fulfilled in the present time. Judgment has withdrawn far from the Jews—the judgment that was announced to the nations. Righteousness, which was grasped by the nations, will not overtake them. They awaited light, saying: “Send forth your light and your truth” (Psalm 42:3), which had been promised to them through the prophets, but they were seized by the darkness of error. They awaited brightness, yet walked in darkness.

Thus they handle the Holy Scriptures like blind men groping along a wall, seeking in them only words and leaves, not the meaning and fruit that are held within the letters. Finally, he joins this to what follows and says: “We stumbled”—or, “we shall fall”—at midday, as though in darkness; in dark places, as though dead. For throughout the whole world, while the Sun of righteousness shines forth in splendor, they remain in darkness, clearly dead through sin.

“We shall roar,” he says, “like bears, all of us, and like doves, meditating, we shall moan,” so that they may be at once cruel and miserable: fierce and savage toward the humble and submissive, but fearful and trembling before those who are stronger, whom they dread like hawks. We read also in another place: “Like a bear robbed of her cubs.” And in Daniel, the bloodstained kingdom possessing three rows of teeth is compared with a most savage bear (2 Kings 17:8; Daniel 7).

“And like doves, meditating, we shall moan”: without the sense and understanding of the Scriptures, merely meditating upon the words that they recite from memory. But why doves, concerning which it is written: “Ephraim is like a dove without understanding” (Hosea 7:11); and why, in the Gospel, is the simplicity of doves set against the malice of serpents (Matthew 10)? In the present passage, likewise, simplicity without prudence—which is close to foolishness—is displayed in the mere meditation of words.

“They will await”—[Note: [Col. 0579] From this Victor concludes that the reading in the preceding text should be *Exspectabimus* (“we shall await”) rather than *Exspectavimus* (“we awaited”). In Hebrew, …]

“judgment, and it will not come;” that is, they will await salvation, and it will not come, because it has migrated far away to the nations. Here it should be noted that everything is spoken in the future tense, so that what the Jews now endure may be indicated.

### (Verses 12 and following)

Our iniquities have multiplied before you, and our sins have answered us, because our crimes are with us, and we have acknowledged our iniquities. We sinned and lied against the Lord; we turned away, so as not to follow behind our Lord, to speak slander. We conceived and spoke words of falsehood from the heart. Judgment turned backward, and righteousness stood far away, because truth fell in the street, and equity could not enter. Truth was turned into forgetfulness, and the one who departed from evil was exposed to plunder.

The Septuagint has: “For our iniquity is great before you, and our sins have resisted us. Our iniquities are within us, and we have acknowledged our injustices. We acted impiously and lied, and we departed from our God. We spoke iniquity and were disobedient. We conceived and meditated words of iniquity in our hearts. We departed from judgment, and righteousness stood far away, because truth was consumed in their ways, and they could not pass along the straight path. Truth was taken away, and they turned their mind aside so that they would not understand.”

He gives the reasons why they roared like bears and meditated like doves, and why they awaited judgment that was not present and salvation that had passed to the nations: because their iniquities had multiplied. They said, “Our iniquities are before you”—from them you had turned your face away for a long time, so as not to see them or strike them. “Our sins have answered us,” so that we might receive what we deserved. “Our crimes are with us, and we have acknowledged our iniquities,” which, though we had long been committing them, we thought were righteousness.

What, then, are these iniquities? To sin and lie against God—or, according to the Hebrew, as Aquila translated it, to deny God—which refers to the Savior. “And we abandoned our God,” they say, declaring: “We know that God spoke to Moses, but as for this man, we do not know where he is from” (John 9:29), in order “to speak slander”: “If this man were from God, he would not break the Sabbath” (ibid., 16); and: “He casts out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons” (Luke 10:15).

“And transgression”—which in Greek is more expressively called ἀπόστασις (*apostasis*, “apostasy”), when someone denies God and is charged with defection.

“We conceived and spoke words of falsehood from the heart,” despising the law of God and following human traditions, which they call δευτερώσεις (*deuterōseis*, “second traditions”), and which we fabricated in our heart.

“Judgment turned backward, and righteousness stood far away.” For what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? What agreement is there between Christ and Belial? Righteousness stood among the nations and departed from us, because truth fell in the street. For broad and spacious is the way that leads to death (Matthew 7), and they did not wish to enter the narrow way in which truth dwells.

“Truth was turned into forgetfulness,” concerning which it is written: “Truth has sprung from the earth, and righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Psalm 84:12). Here it should be observed that truth is repeatedly named so that the person of Christ might be revealed. After abandoning him, they followed falsehood.

“And the one who departed from evil was exposed to plunder.” Although this may seem obscure, it can be explained as follows: while we invented falsehood from our own heart and abandoned the law of God, righteousness stood far away, truth fell in the streets, equity could not enter among us, and the Son of God, who is truth, was turned into forgetfulness. This happened to such an extent that whoever wished to withdraw from the traditions of the Jews was immediately exposed to plots and persecutions, so that they expelled from the synagogues the man blind from birth who had received his sight (John 9). After the resurrection of the Lord and Savior, they also persecuted and stripped all who believed in him; to them the churches throughout the whole world sent supplies, to be distributed by the hands of the Apostles.

### (Verses 16, 17)

The Lord saw, and evil appeared in his eyes, because there was no judgment. He saw that there was no man, and he was astonished because there was no one to intervene. His own arm will save him, and his righteousness itself strengthened him. He put on righteousness like a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon his head. He put on garments of vengeance and covered himself like a cloak with zeal. As for vengeance, like repayment of indignation against his enemies, and recompense to his adversaries, he will repay the islands in kind.

The Septuagint has: “The Lord saw, and it did not please him, because there was no judgment. He saw, and there was no man. He considered, and there was no one to defend. He avenged them with his arm, and mercy sustained him. He put on righteousness like a breastplate and placed a helmet of salvation upon his head. He wrapped himself in a garment of vengeance and a cloak, as though repaying retribution and reproach to his adversaries.”

Up to this point the prophetic speech has been composed in the person of the people; now the Prophet speaks in his own person. While they were saying these things, the Lord saw that they were proclaiming repentance with their mouths but were not practicing it in their hearts, and it did not please him. He sought in them the truth of judgment, which had been transferred to the nations, but did not find it. He desired some righteous man who could intervene with him while he was angry, but found none—he who had also said above: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who would hear” (Isaiah 50:2).

Because, while they remained in their crimes, not even one righteous man was found—but all had turned aside and together become worthless, and “there is no one who does good, not even one” (Psalm 13)—he strengthened himself by his own arm and righteousness, or mercy, so that those who wished to turn away from error might be preserved, not by their own merit but by God’s clemency.

Finally, he put on the breastplate of righteousness and the helmet of salvation, was surrounded by garments of vengeance and a cloak of zeal, and thus armed went forth to war, to repay vengeance to his enemies. There is no doubt that this signifies the Jews, who persisted in blasphemies, and recompense to his adversaries when the Roman army encircled them. When the Romans conquered, the Lord is shown to have fought.

Paul used this testimony when writing to the Ephesians and wishing us to put on the armor of Christ, so that we might be able to resist the flaming darts of the devil (Ephesians 6).

What is not found in the Septuagint translators—“He will repay the islands in kind”—signifies the cities of Judea that the Roman army devastated. For above also (chapter 20) the Lord speaks through the Prophet to the inhabitants of the island, that is, Jerusalem.

### (Verses 19, 20)

Those from the West will fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his glory, when he comes like a violent river driven on by the spirit of the Lord. And the Redeemer will come to Zion and to those who turn back from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord. This is my covenant with them, says the Lord: My spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have placed in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed—

[Note: [Col. 0583D] The Ambrosian manuscripts consistently have the word *seed* only once here and below, although the Hebrew archetype rejects this reading. Victor restored the reading, “from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed, and from the mouth of the seed of your seed,” according to the Hebrew, in accordance with the commentary of the holy Father; the Louvain correctors also approve this reading.]

—says the Lord, from now and forever.

The Septuagint has: “Those from the West will fear the name of the Lord, and those from the rising of the sun his illustrious name. For he will come like a violent river, the wrath of the Lord—÷ he will come with fury **—and he will come from Zion, the one who delivers. He will turn away impieties from Jacob, and this will be my covenant with them, says the Lord. My spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have given into your mouth, shall not fail from your mouth and from the mouth of your seed, says the Lord, from now and forever.”

After the Lord has put on the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, the garments of vengeance, and the cloak of zeal for battle, and has come to the contest and to vengeance, to repay his enemies, recompense his adversaries, and overthrow their islands—that is, their cities and villages—then the foreigners who are to come from the West and the East, to rest in the bosom of Abraham (Matthew 8), will fear the Lord. Concerning them it was also said above (on chapter 49:12): “Behold, these will come from far away, some from the West, others from the North, and others from the land of the Persians.” They will fear the Lord with that fear which is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclesiasticus 1).

We read of this in many places, of which let us quote a few: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Psalm 111:1); and: “There is no want for those who fear him” (Psalm 33:10); and: “The fear of the Lord is discipline and wisdom” (Proverbs 15:33); and: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12); and: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Psalm 127:4); and: “The fear of the Lord adds days” (Proverbs 10:27).

That, after Israel has been rejected, a multitude of the nations would succeed to its place, the prophet Malachi teaches more fully. There it is said to the Jews: “I have no will in you, says the Lord Almighty, and I will not accept an offering from your hands” (Malachi 1:10–11). Again, concerning the multitude of the nations: “For from the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name has been glorified among the nations.”

The author of this blessedness is the one who will come like a violent river driven on by the spirit of the Lord. Or, as Aquila translated it, “like a narrow stream; the spirit of the Lord is his seal.” Theodotion has: “like a river attacking; the spirit of the Lord has been sealed.”

Accordingly, in the final part of this testimony, which the Septuagint translated, “Like a violent river, the wrath of the Lord will come with fury,” the Hebrew does not contain the words “with fury.” For wrath and fury ought not to be placed among God’s promises, since in all the other things that follow there is a promise of future blessedness and a threat of punishment for sinners.

According to Aquila and Theodotion, the spirit of the Lord, sealed in Christ, confirms the example recorded in the Gospel of John: “For this one the Father, God, has sealed” (John 6:27). Concerning him it was already said: “A rod will go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower will rise from his root; and the spirit of the Lord will rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety—and the spirit of the fear of the Lord will fill him” (Isaiah 11:1 and following).

Hence we also say: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7). And in Ezekiel, the foreheads of the men who groan are marked by the impression of *THAV*, a Hebrew letter that is the last among them (Ezekiel 9).

But if we wish to know how the Holy Spirit is a violent river, let us reread the Acts of the Apostles, where it is written: “When they had assembled together, suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a violent wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, and it rested upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:2–4).

It follows: “The Redeemer will come to Zion and to those who turn back from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord.” In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “He will come from Zion, the one who delivers, and he will turn away impieties from Jacob.”

If, then, the one who turns away the impieties of Jacob will come from Zion, we understand that he was born as a man in Zion and that the Most High founded it—the one who turns away the crimes of Jacob.

But if the text reads, “The Redeemer will come to Zion and to those who turn back from iniquity in Jacob, says the Lord,” its meaning is: Christ will come, who will redeem Zion with his blood. Or, according to the Hebrew idiom, he is the one who is a kinsman of Zion and was born from the stock of Israel; for this is what *GOEL* means, namely, ἀγκιστεύς (*ankisteus*, “kinsman-redeemer”).

And lest we think that all Zion is redeemed and liberated from its crimes—Zion which was stained, or, according to another reading, made bloody, by the Lord’s blood—he significantly added: “to those who turn back from iniquity,” if they are willing to practice repentance. In them the Lord’s prayer is fulfilled: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Their redemption, therefore, is in Zion; and he promises to those from Jacob who receive him that he is their kinsman. He says to them: “This is my covenant with them,” or “pact,” as all the others translated it, or “testament,” as the Septuagint rendered it.

What this covenant, pact, or testament is, the following verse shows: “My spirit,” he says, “which is in you, and my words which I have placed in your mouth, shall not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouth of your seed, from now and forever.”

This is addressed either to Isaiah, as I think, or to the Lord, as most judge. Accordingly, if it is addressed to Isaiah, the sequence runs as follows: This is the eternal covenant of the Gospel: that my spirit, which is in you, and my words, which I have placed in your mouth, through which you proclaim what is to come, should not depart from your mouth, nor from the mouths of your sons and grandsons, nor from your seed, so that every generation in succession may be indicated. This means that the grace of the prophets would come upon the Apostles and, through them, upon those from Israel who would believe through the Apostles.

What follows—“from now and forever”—corresponds to the testimony: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matthew 24:35).

Paul carefully explains this passage when writing to the Romans: there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, but the Lord himself is Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him (Romans 10); and the nations did not believe in such a way that Israel was completely rejected. “For I myself,” he says, “am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Romans 11:1–2).

A little later, after giving the example of Elijah, who complained to the Lord that he alone had been left, and after hearing from him that the Lord had preserved for himself seven thousand men who had not bent the knee before Baal (1 Kings 19), he adds: “So therefore at this present time also there is a remnant saved according to the election of grace. But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace. What then? What Israel was seeking, it has not obtained; but the election has obtained it, while the rest have been blinded. If they do not remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again” (Romans 11:5 and following)—not contrary to nature from the wild olive, as the multitude of the nations was grafted in, but according to nature into the good olive, that is, into their own olive.

Finally, he brought the matter to the present chapter: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation: that blindness has occurred in part to Israel, until the fullness of the nations enters; and thus all Israel will be saved, as it is written: ‘He will come from Zion, the one who delivers, and he will turn away impieties from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins’” (Romans 11:25 and following).

We have pursued these matters at greater length so that we may understand that whatever promises we have read and will read concerning Zion and Jerusalem are not spoken generally of all Jews, but specifically of those from Israel who were chosen in the Apostles and through the Apostles.

## BOOK SEVENTEEN

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585B] 715–716

I would like, virgin of Christ Eustochium, to run briefly through how many mysteries the number seventeen, which the present book of the *Commentaries on Isaiah* has now reached, contains in the Holy Scriptures. But since I cannot speak of everything in every place, I will give this brief reminder: the psalm marked by the title of this number belongs to David, the servant of the Lord, and he sang the words of the Song on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and said: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength,” and what follows.

That servant of the Lord is the one to whom the Father speaks in Isaiah: “It is a great thing for you to be called my servant” (Isaiah 44). And in another place: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved in whom my soul has been well pleased” [or, according to another reading, “in whom my soul has pleased itself”] (Isaiah 42:2).

This servant, whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of Saul—for *Saul* in our language signifies “desired” or “hell”—and from all his enemies, who cried out against him, “Crucify, crucify such a one!” (Luke 23), when he ascended victorious to the Father, spoke among other triumphant words, clothed in tawny garments from Bozrah: “Deliver me from the contradictions of the people; you will appoint me as head of the nations. A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Psalm 17:44–45).

Again, concerning the Jewish people: “The foreign sons lied to me; the foreign sons grew old and limped from their paths” (ibid., 46). To them Elijah had also said: “How long will you limp on both feet?” (1 Kings 18:21).

Finally, something difficult to find elsewhere: this psalm is contained both in the history of Samuel and in the history of Chronicles (2 Kings 22).

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Victor reads: “This psalm is also contained in the history of Samuel, or Kings.” To support this reading—which, as far as I know, has the support of no manuscript—he argues as follows: “He is speaking,” he says, “of Psalm 17: ‘I will love you, O Lord, my strength.’ But it would be false to say that this psalm is found in the history of Chronicles, since only Psalm 104, ‘Give thanks to the Lord and call upon his name,’ is found there, in 1 Chronicles 16; whereas Psalm 17 is found in 2 Kings 22.”]

Advancing by increments from the number one to the number seven, it comes to Psalm 28, which is likewise inscribed “of David,” for the completion of the tabernacle, when the angels are commanded: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.” All the mysteries of saving baptism and of the Church are sung there: “The voice of the Lord is over the waters; the God of majesty has thundered; the Lord is over many waters; the voice of the Lord is in strength” (Psalm 28:1 and following). And a little later: “The voice of the Lord prepares servants, and he will reveal the dense forest; and in his Temple all will say, ‘Glory’” (ibid., 3, 10).

And to demonstrate the multitude of believers, he added: “The Lord made the flood to dwell,” and: “The Lord will sit as king forever.”

Again, by adding the mystery of the eighth, it produces Psalm 36, an alphabetical psalm, whose beginning is: “Do not be jealous of evildoers, and do not envy those who commit iniquity.” Its exposition belongs not to this preface but to its own volume.

And not to repeat many things now, as it grows by increments up to the number fifteen—the number of the Songs of Ascents—and the chosen vessel dwells with Peter at Jerusalem, it produces the number 120, the number of those who were the first believers in Christ and ascended with the Apostles to the upper room of faith (Acts 5); and the Holy Spirit descended upon them (Galatians 1).

Then, proceeding in order up to the number seventeen and possessing evangelical dignity, when the Lord commanded from the right-hand side, it caught 153 large fish and placed them in the Church (John 21). To this number Isaiah the prophet also now speaks.

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Victor reads “he will reveal,” and shortly afterward “makes dwell” instead of “made dwell.”]

[Note: [Col. 0585D] A more recent Ambrosian manuscript adds “the sacrament of the eighth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0586D] “The chosen vessel,” and so forth. Concerning this number fifteen and the number 120 he wrote the same things to Paulinus. See the letter beginning: “Brother Ambrose,” and so forth. Moreover, Marianus, contrary to the testimony of all the manuscript codices, alters the preceding text marked with an asterisk, lest we say that Jerome erred in so small a matter. MARTIAN.]

[Note: [Col. 0586D] Compare letter 53 in our recension, where he speaks about the numbers fifteen and 120.]

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Victor reads: “This psalm is also contained in the history of Samuel, or Kings.”]

[Note: [Col. 0585D] Earlier the word “testimony” was lacking.]

## Chapter LX

### (Verses 1 ff.) [p. 717]

“Arise, shine, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you. For behold, darkness will cover the earth, and gloom the peoples; but over you the Lord will arise, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations will walk in your light, and kings in the splendor of your rising.”

**The Septuagint:** “Shine, shine, Jerusalem; for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you. Behold, darkness will cover the earth, and gloom the nations. But over you the Lord will appear, and his glory will be seen upon you. And nations will walk in your light, and kings in your splendor.”

What we think concerning the restoration of Zion and Jerusalem, and all that is promised to it in prophetic prediction, we explained more fully at the end of the preceding book, where we interpreted what was signified by the verse: “The Redeemer will come to Zion, and to those who turn back from iniquity in Jacob.”

Now we must briefly indicate what many people think about this passage, so that, once the error has been recognized, we may more easily embrace the truth.

The Jews and our semi-Judaizers, who expect a golden and jewel-encrusted Jerusalem descending from heaven, contend that these things will take place in the kingdom of a thousand years, when all nations will serve Israel; when the camels of Midian and Ephah, coming from Sheba, will bring gold and frankincense; when all the flocks of Kedar will be gathered, and the rams of Nebaioth will come to be sacrificed upon the altar of the Temple that will have been built.

They say also that the daughters of Jerusalem will fly from the islands, and especially from the ships of Tarshish, like doves, bringing riches of gold and silver; that the walls of Jerusalem will be built by foreigners, over whom the kings of the nations will preside; and that the gates of the city will always remain open, so that by day and by night the riches of Jerusalem and sacrificial victims may be brought in.

They maintain that everything now desolate will be constructed from cypress, pine, and cedar cut in Lebanon—especially the Temple of the Lord, in which there will be everlasting joy—so that it will suck the milk of the nations and consume the riches of kings. There will be such abundance of all things that, instead of bronze, they will have gold; instead of iron, silver; instead of wood, bronze; and instead of stones, iron.

They say also that its princes will enjoy eternal peace, that bishops will govern the peoples in righteousness, and that its gates will be embossed. And, greater than all this, that in place of the sun and moon the Lord himself will shine with everlasting light; that for one man it will have a thousand mighty men, and that in place of little children it will possess the strongest nations.

Such are the claims of those who desire earthly pleasures, seek the beauty of wives and the number of children, whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Philippians 3). Whoever follows their error, under the Christian name, confesses himself similar to the Jews.

Others, however, assert that all these things were promised carnally to the Jews, if they had received him who says in the Gospel, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), which enlightens everyone coming into the world. They argue that, just as sacrifices were granted to the people of Israel—not because they were good in themselves, but so that they would not be offered to demons—so the Lord promises these things to the gluttonous Jews, who seek nothing but bodily pleasures, so that at least for the sake of carnal desires and an abundance of riches they might receive the Son of God sent to them. Since they did not receive him, the promises also became void.

Finally, when the Canaanite woman pleaded for her daughter, he said: “I did not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). And to his disciples: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; go rather to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:5–6).

For this reason the Apostles first proclaimed the Lord in the synagogues. When the Jews did not receive the Gospel, they said to them: “It was necessary that the word of God should be spoken to you; but since you rejected it, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46).

The light came into the world, but the Jews loved darkness more. Therefore, after the Lord had wept over Jerusalem, he added: “If you had known—even you—the things that make for your peace” (Luke 19:42). Because Jerusalem did not receive them, he continued: “But now they will come upon you, and your enemies will surround you with a rampart; they will hem you in and bring you down to the ground, together with your children” (ibid., 43).

But according to the earlier interpretation, let us understand that all these things are spoken concerning the Church. She was first gathered from the Jewish people, and through the Apostles transmitted to the nations the light that had risen over her.

To her it is said: “Arise, shine,” so that she who fell among unbelievers may rise among the faithful; she who fell in the synagogues may rise in the churches. After she has risen, let her be enlightened, so that she may no longer possess the darkness of error.

“For your light has come,” he says—the light promised by all the Prophets, which you continually awaited. “And the glory of the Lord,” which formerly rested over his tabernacle and Temple, “has risen over you.” Concerning this it is written: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86:2).

“For behold, darkness will cover the earth,” namely, those who set their minds on earthly things; “and gloom the peoples,” or, as it is read in Hebrew, “the tribes.” This properly refers to the Jews, concerning whom it is written in another psalm: “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony for Israel” (Psalm 122:4).

“But over you the Lord will arise,” the sun of righteousness, “and his glory will be seen upon you.” Of this it is written: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

“And nations will walk in your light.” We shall all walk in the light of the Apostles, which shines in the world, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

“And kings,” he says, “in the splendor of your rising,” when you were first born in Christ. This is fulfilled both spiritually and carnally: kings whose heart is in the hand of the Lord, and in whose mortal body sin does not reign (Proverbs 21; Romans 6), walk in the splendor of the nascent Church—or in him who was born in the Church—and submit the necks of true kings to the faith of Christ.

We see this fulfilled daily, when, after the error of idolatry and the fury of persecution have been removed, Roman rulers pass over to the faith and peace of Christ.

There are some who expect all these things—which we remember as partly fulfilled after the first coming of the Savior and partly still to be fulfilled until the consummation of the world—to take place in the future, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved (Romans 11). Their opinion is by no means to be rejected, provided that we understand these things to be fulfilled spiritually, not carnally.

Moreover, the names “Jerusalem” and “nations,” which are found here in the Septuagint, are not present in the Hebrew and should be marked with an obelus [†], against those who assert that everything said here is spoken concerning Jerusalem. [p. 720]

### (Verse 4)

“Lift up your eyes round about and see: all these have gathered and come to you. Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will suck at your side.”

**The Septuagint:** “Lift up your eyes round about and see all your sons gathered together. All your sons have come from afar, and your daughters will be carried upon the shoulders.”

[Note: Victor prefers the reading “your daughters will suck milk,” based on three manuscript copies of the Bible and on Jerome’s own commentary, both here and below in the same chapter, at the words “Because you were forsaken,” verse 16.]

This is spoken to the Church, which was first gathered through the Apostles as Zion. Concerning them we read in the Acts of the Apostles that devout men from the whole world were in Jerusalem; they received the word of God and, in the languages of their own and foreign peoples, either heard others speaking or themselves spoke to the rest (Acts 2).

She is commanded to lift up her eyes round about. The Lord also commanded this to the Apostles, saying: “Lift up your eyes and see, for the fields are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35).

For from Zion, and no longer from Mount Sinai, the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.

She is commanded, with her eyes lifted, to see her sons gathered together, who come from afar. Elsewhere she is told: “Rejoice greatly, daughter of Zion; proclaim it, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, I am coming, and I will dwell in your midst, says the Lord” (Zephaniah 3:17); and: “Many nations will come to the Lord, and they will be my people, and I will be their God” (Zechariah 2:11).

We are the sons who came from afar to the Lord—formerly strangers to the covenant of God and his promises, without hope and without God in the world. But what does the Apostle say? “You who were once far away have now been brought near” (Ephesians 2:13).

What follows—“And your daughters will suck at your side”—signifies that souls suckling in Christ, and the little ones in baptism, of whom the Apostle Peter also speaks, “Like newborn infants, desire rational and guileless milk” (1 Peter 2:2), suck the milk of the Apostles.

Paul also spoke to these little ones and sucklings: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4:19). And elsewhere: “Like a nursing mother cherishing her children, so we desired to impart to you not only the Gospel of Christ, but also our own souls” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8).

What is said in the Septuagint in place of this—“Your daughters will be carried upon the shoulders”—must be considered more carefully. The sons, who are strong, come from afar by their own strength and are gathered into the Lord’s faith. But the daughters, who are weaker and, because of the fragility of their sex, have not yet come to mature manhood, are carried upon the shoulders of the Apostles, so that they may be borne into the bosoms of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. [p. 721]

### (Verse 5)

“Then you will see, and overflow, and your heart will wonder and expand, when the abundance of the sea has turned toward you, and the strength of the nations has come to you.”

**The Septuagint:** “Then you will see, and fear, and be astonished in your heart, because the riches of the sea, and of the nations and peoples, will be transferred to you.”

[Note: The commonly printed editions add “and you will rejoice,” although this is found neither in our manuscripts nor in the Greek text.]

When you have lifted up your eyes and seen your sons and daughters—either coming swiftly by themselves or carried upon the shoulders of the saints—then you will rejoice. You will be flooded, as by sudden waters, in the manner of rivers; your heart will wonder and be astonished, indeed will expand, as you hear the Apostle: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians.” And again: “Be enlarged, and you also” (2 Corinthians 6:11).

Otherwise, through the narrowness of your heart you might be unable to receive Christ as a guest, though he says in the Gospel: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

As for what is added in the Septuagint, “and you will fear,” this is not found in the Hebrew. Perhaps fear entered after the greatness of joy, lest she be deprived of so great a good.
