Or is it not joy to see riches and the multitude of the sea transferred and turned toward oneself, and the strength of the nations come to oneself, so that whatever exists in the world and throughout the earth may be one’s own, and, strengthened by the faith of the nations, one may say: “I can do all things through him who strengthens me, Jesus Christ” (Philippians 4:13)?

### (Verses 6–7)

“The multitude of camels will cover you, the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah. All those from Sheba will come, bringing gold and frankincense, and proclaiming the praise of the Lord. All the flocks of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will minister to you. They will be offered upon my acceptable altar, and I will glorify the house of my majesty.”

**The Septuagint:** “And flocks of camels will come to you, and the camels of Midian and Gephar [or Ephah] will cover you. All those from Sheba will come, bringing gold and frankincense, and they will proclaim the salvation of the Lord. All the sheep of Kedar will be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth will come, and they will be offered as acceptable sacrifices upon my altar, and the house of my prayer will be glorified.”

After the riches of the sea and the strength of the nations, flocks of camels and the dromedaries of Midian and Ephah are also promised to Jerusalem. All these will come from Sheba, carrying gold and frankincense—and, greater than these, proclaiming the Lord’s salvation.

All the sheep of Kedar will likewise be gathered to the Church, and the rams of Nebaioth will come—or, as it is written in Hebrew, they will “minister”—and they will be offered, or will offer victims, upon the altar of the Lord, so that his house may become renowned.

Midian and Ephah are regions beyond Arabia, fertile in camels, and the whole province is called Sheba. From there came the queen of Sheba, who came to hear Solomon’s wisdom, herself bringing gold and frankincense, carrying many gifts to the peaceful king and receiving greater gifts from him (1 Kings 10).

Kedar is a region of the Saracens, who are called Ishmaelites in Scripture. Nebaioth is one of Ishmael’s sons. From their names the wilderness is called—a wilderness lacking crops but full of livestock.

Through the familiar names of barbarian nations neighboring Israel, the conversion of the entire world is proclaimed.

In this passage Midian is interpreted as “iniquity”; Ephah as “loosed” or “pouring out”; Sheba as “conversion” or “captivity”; Kedar as “darkness”; and Nebaioth as “prophecies.”

Thus the flocks of camels, loosed from the bonds of iniquity and pouring out their souls before God, will cover Jerusalem with gifts. All will come from captivity, bringing, through their conversion, the gold of faith and the frankincense of sacrifice.

Through these gifts, not content with their own salvation, they will advance so that they may proclaim God’s salvation also to others.

That rich man who, like a camel, carried the burden of his riches in the Gospel, did not wish to hear the Lord’s counsels or to be unloaded, so that, throwing off his burden, he might fly to heaven on the wings of a dove; therefore he went away sorrowful.

Concerning such a camel the Savior says: “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:24). He set forth the difficulty of the matter, not its impossibility.

Finally, your mother Paula, of blessed memory, and your brother Pammachius passed through the eye of the needle—that is, through the narrow and constricted way that leads to life—into the kingdom of heaven, leaving behind the broad way with its burdens, which leads to Tartarus.

Indeed, whatever they possessed they carried as gifts to the Lord, fulfilling what is written: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 13:8). For what is impossible with human beings is possible with God (Matthew 19).

Possessing in their gifts the chief things—gold, [p. 723] gold in the sense of understanding, and frankincense of the finest fragrance—and saying: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight”; and: “We are the good fragrance of Christ in every place” (2 Corinthians 2:15)—through the example of their virtue they proclaim the Lord’s salvation daily, so that all the sheep of Kedar may be gathered into the Church and pass from the darkness of error into the light.

[Note: Formerly the text had *aurum, incensum* in a single word, instead of the two words required by the sense. We have corrected it after Victor, whose arguments we entirely accept, although no manuscripts support him. His arguments are these: Jerome interprets gold as understanding and silver as eloquence a thousand times. Above, in chapter 3: “Necklaces woven with rods of gold and silver,” that is, with the understanding and words of Scripture. Jeremiah 4: “If you adorn yourself with a golden necklace,” that is, if you possess meditation on meaning and spiritual understanding. And chapter 10: “They utter grand things, and, to deceive individuals, as though with golden meanings and eloquence shining with the splendor of silver,” and so forth. Ezekiel 38: “Do you think that you will possess silver and gold,” understood as eloquence and understanding, “of the Church?” Daniel 5: “Those seem golden to me who are composed according to secular reasoning; silver are those who possess beauty of eloquence.” Therefore it was wrong formerly to read: “gold, incense, and frankincense of the finest fragrance.” What place would the word *incense* have here, since it is identical in meaning with frankincense, when the passage concerns only gold and frankincense, namely the words “bringing gold and frankincense”? He therefore spoke of the gold of understanding, just as below, in chapter 65, he called it “the grain of understanding,” when he said that through much labor and diligence they finally managed to arrive at “the grain of understanding.”]

And the rams of the Prophets, concerning whom it is sung in Psalm 28: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams”—let them come and be offered, or, according to Theodotion, “let them offer themselves” as a sacrifice to the Lord, and become acceptable victims, so that the Church of Christ may be glorified.

[Note: In the more recent Ambrosian manuscript, the words “themselves” are absent.]

Concerning such sheep the Savior spoke to the disciples: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 10:3). And again: “My sheep hear my voice” (John 10:3).

And in Ezekiel more fully: “Behold, I myself will seek my sheep and visit them, as a shepherd seeks his flock. Thus says the Lord: I will seek the lost, bring back the straying, bind up the broken, strengthen the sick, and guard the strong; and I will feed them with judgment” (Ezekiel 34:11–12).

And so that we might know which sheep these were, he states it more clearly: “And they shall know that I am the Lord their God; and these are my people, the house of Israel, says the Lord God. And you are my sheep, and you are all sheep of my flock, and I am the Lord your God” (ibid., 27–28).

Therefore, if someone among the nations is rich, let him be saved like a camel—not without gifts and offerings, but in such a way that he can preach the word of the Lord.

If someone possesses the simplicity of sheep and the authority of rams, let him ascend to the altar of the Lord, or be offered upon it by those who have the power, so that his house may be glorified.

As for what we noted as written in Hebrew—“The rams of Nebaioth will minister to you, and they will offer upon my acceptable altar”—this is properly understood of those chosen from the nations for the priesthood, who are ministers of the Savior.

But if anyone is contentious and insists that these promises must be understood carnally, let us answer him: “We have no such custom, nor the Church of God” (1 Corinthians 11:16).

Let us also say that, even if these things were promised carnally to the Jews, they were nevertheless promised conditionally: if they had received their light, which had been sent to them, then these things too would have followed. In other words, through the desire for gold, an abundance of riches, and carnal possessions—pleasures by which that people was always ensnared—they would receive the Son of God sent to them.

Since they did not receive him, all these things were taken away and the inheritance was given to those who received it spiritually. [p. 724]

### (Verses 8–9)

“Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows? For the islands await me, and the ships of the sea at the beginning, so that I may bring your sons from afar; their silver and their gold with them, for the name of the Lord your God and for the Holy One of Israel, because he has glorified you.”

**The Septuagint:** “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves with their young to me? The islands awaited me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your sons from afar, and their silver and gold with them, because of the holy name of the Lord, and because the Holy One of Israel has been glorified.”

Because the Lord entered Egypt upon a light cloud, and commanded the clouds of the Prophets not to rain upon Israel—the people to whom the truth of God came—the Church, first gathered from the people of the Circumcision, wonders to see the throng of the nations from throughout the world flying to her.

Taking the wings of the Holy Spirit, they hasten, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, to their windows; according to Aquila, to their sluices, so that they may enter the Church.

Or these may be teachers with their disciples—that is, doves with their young—flying to the Church from the islands of the nations, which, in accordance with the predictions of the Prophets, will await the Lord.

The ships of Tarshish—that is, of the sea—of which we spoke more fully in the vision concerning Tyre, will bring the sons of the Church at the beginning of faith, carrying gold and silver.

“For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Concerning this gold and silver it is written in Psalm 68: “The wings of the dove are silvered, and her hind parts gleam with the brightness of gold” (Psalm 68:14). And in Psalm 71: “The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts, and the kings of the Arabians and Sheba will bring presents” (Psalm 72:10).

All these things are brought for the name of the Lord God and the Holy One of Israel, who glorified him.

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“The sons of foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will minister to you. For in my indignation I struck you, but in my reconciliation I had mercy on you. Your gates will be opened continually; by day and by night they will not be closed, so that the strength of the nations may be brought to you, and their kings may be led in. For the nation and kingdom that will not serve you will perish, and the nations will be laid waste in desolation.” [p. 725]

**The Septuagint:** “Foreigners will build your walls, and their kings will attend you. For because of my anger I struck you, and because of my mercy I loved you. Your gates will always be opened; by day and by night they will not be closed, so that they may bring to you the strength of the nations and their kings who are to be led in. For the nations and the kings who will not serve you will perish; the nations will be desolated into desolation.”

Among the other things by which the Church is enriched and the city of the Savior is built, foreigners and the sons of sojourners also build her walls, so that the enemy may neither enter nor find a place for unbelief.

Foreigners and sojourners properly signify the people of the nations, who truly built the Church of Christ—to such an extent that their kings and princes minister to her, or attend her.

This may be understood either carnally or spiritually.

If carnally, we see Roman emperors submit their necks to the yoke of Christ, build churches at public expense, and establish legal decrees against the persecutions of the nations and the attacks of heretics.

If spiritually, all who are leaders among them in self-control, eloquence, and holiness, and who subject the flesh to the rule of the soul, minister to her, attend her, and assist her—her whom negligence often abandons, or whom the rod of persecutors strikes, so that afterward, because of his mercy, he may love her again.

Or certainly this should be said: the Lord reconciles to himself the Church, once afflicted and delivered into captivity among the Jewish people, through the calling of the nations, so that her gates may always be open and never closed by day or night, and may continually stand open to those who desire salvation—that is, so that entrance may not be denied to those who wish to believe in joy and in tribulation.

And let the strength, or riches, of the nations be brought into her; let their kings minister to her, or be led to her as captives.

You will understand this when you see the most eloquent being brought to the faith of Christ, the wisdom of the wise made foolish, and the understanding of the prudent rejected (1 Corinthians 1), so that “the foolishness of God is wiser than men.”

But the nation and its kings who refuse to serve the Church with a good and useful service, so that they may be transferred into apostolic dignity, will perish with the destruction prepared for the impious. Whatever is found in them will be reduced to desolation, because they did not wish to have God as their guest.

[Note: Another reading is “by which the Church is built,” which Victor preferred, since it better suits the words being interpreted: “The sons of foreigners will build your walls.” For a city cannot be enriched before it is built.]

[Note: The same editor reads “may be transferred” with a more polished sense.]

### (Verses 13–14)

“The glory of Lebanon will come to you, the fir tree, the box tree, and the pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctuary; and I will glorify the place of my feet. The sons of those who humbled you will come to you bent low, and all who slandered you will worship the traces of your feet; and they will call you the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.”

**The Septuagint:** “The glory of Lebanon will come to you, with cypress, pine, and cedar together, so that my holy place may be glorified, and I will glorify the place of my feet. And the sons of those who humbled you—and provoked you—will go to you in fear, and all who provoked you will worship the traces of your feet; and you will be called the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel.”

[The text of the Septuagint has many omissions; I have inserted from the Hebrew what is marked with asterisks, while what they added I have marked with an obelus.]

Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, planted with lofty trees. Describing them, the Psalmist says: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 36:35). And elsewhere: “The Lord will break the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 28:5). There are many other passages, which I pass over for the sake of brevity.

Formerly Hiram, king of Tyre, sent timber from there to Joppa for Solomon, for the building of the Temple of God (1 Kings 5).

Now Scripture likewise promises from there fir, box, and pine—or, according to the Septuagint, cypress, pine, and cedar—or, according to Aquila, fir, *thaadaor*, and *thaassur*; or, according to Theodotion, *Brais*, *Thadaar*, and *Theassur*—all to be cut together for the construction of the temple of Zion (2 Chronicles 2).

[Note: Instead of *Thaassur*, some also read *Thadaar* in Aquila, and apparently more correctly; Theodotion likewise has *Thaassur* instead of *Theassur*. We suspect that *Brais* contains a textual error and should be read *Brathi*. Symmachus renders the word βραθύ as *brathi* in Isaiah 55:13, and the oldest manuscript at Montfaucon here has *Brati*, which comes close to the reading of the ancient editions—namely *Prati*, which Martianaeus calls inept.]

If this is so, where will the golden and jewel-encrusted Jerusalem be? Where will the Bride of the Lamb be? Where will the twelve gates distinguished by the variety of their jewels be? Unless perhaps it will have jewel-encrusted walls and foundations, while the Temple, which ought to be more splendid, will be built of wood.

For this reason we are compelled to understand everything spiritually: the fir, cypress, pine, and cedar, formerly the lofty trees of Lebanon, glorify the Temple of God and the place of his feet, and make it renowned.

And, not to prolong the exposition, do not the holy and most eloquent martyr Cyprian and Hilary, the confessor of our own time, seem to you to be formerly lofty trees in the world who built the Church of God?

What follows—“The sons of those who humbled you will come to you bent low,” or “returning,” “and all who slandered you will worship the traces of your feet”—we should understand of those who are Christians not by their will but by necessity, and who, out of fear of offending rulers, bow with fearful hearts.

Or certainly it may refer to those who were formerly persecutors and afterward came to believe. Such was the Apostle Paul, who persecuted the Church of God and afterward was called a chosen vessel (Acts 9).

When these things have been fulfilled, so that the fullness of the nations enters, then all Israel will be saved.

And she will truly be called the city of the Lord, Zion of the Holy One of Israel, which stands upon a watchtower and has been gathered from both peoples.

### (Verses 15–16)

“Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was no one who passed through you [the Vulgate: ‘through you’], I will make you an eternal pride, a joy from generation to generation. You will suck the milk of the nations, and you will be nursed at the breast of kings. And you will know that I am the Lord, your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.”

**The Septuagint:** “Because you were forsaken and hated, and there was no one to help you, I will make you an eternal exultation, a joy from generation to generation. You will suck the milk of the nations, and you will eat the riches of kings. And you will know that I am the Lord who saved you, and who delivered you, the God of Jacob.”

She who had formerly been forsaken and hated, her branches broken because they had borne no fruit—broken for this reason, that there was no one passing by who would offer assistance—is now restored. Concerning these branches it is said in the Psalms: “And those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Psalm 128:8).

Therefore I will make you an everlasting pride, or exultation and joy for two generations. In place of the former branches, other branches will be grafted from the wild olive of the nations; contrary to nature, they will bear fruit—not the former bitterness, but the sweetness they received from the root.

You will also suck the milk of the nations and be nursed at the breast of kings.

We explained the meaning of this passage more fully above, when discussing the verse: “Your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will suck at your side.”

[Note: “And your daughters will suck at your side.” This is a persistent error in the previously printed books, which always read, both in the sacred text and in the Commentaries, “And your daughters will suck milk.” We have restored “will suck at your side” everywhere in accordance with the manuscript copies.]

Or, according to the Septuagint, “you will eat the riches of kings.”

According to the Hebrew truth, these riches are the breasts of kings and teachers, by which infancy newly born in Christ is instructed and nourished.

When you have sucked them and reached solid food, so that you also eat the riches of such kings, then you will know that I am your Savior, who redeemed you with my blood—or the mighty God of Jacob. [p. 728]

### (Verses 17 ff.)

“Instead of bronze I will bring gold; instead of iron I will bring silver; instead of wood, bronze; and instead of stones, iron. I will appoint your visitation as peace, and your overseers as righteousness. No longer will iniquity be heard in your land, devastation and destruction within your borders; salvation will occupy your walls, and praise your gates.”

**The Septuagint:** “Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; instead of iron I will give you silver; instead of wood I will give you bronze; and instead of stones, iron. I will give your rulers in peace, and your bishops in righteousness. No longer will iniquity be heard in your land, nor destruction and misery within your borders; but your walls will be called salvation, and your gates sculpture.”

The same reality is expressed according to the character of the passages: one text gives the genus, another the species.

And lest I seem to say anything about the arts, rhetoric, or dialectic, I will give common examples that can instruct the simple reader.

My son, who is a species in relation to me, and has me as his genus, is a genus in relation to his own son.

I will give another example, in which one thing is greater for one person and lesser for another. A centurion is greater than a common soldier and less than a tribune. Five are few in comparison with ten, but many in comparison with one.

Therefore, in the restoration of spiritual Jerusalem, wood will be changed into bronze and stones will be changed into iron—that is, people who were formerly brutish and without understanding will be changed into materials that provide some usefulness to the city.

Bronze and iron themselves, through the growth of virtues, will be changed into gold and silver, so that they will possess not merely the appearance of usefulness but also value and beauty.

We have often explained what gold and silver signify in the holy Scriptures.

“I will appoint,” he says, “your rulers in peace, and your bishops in righteousness.” Instead of this, the Hebrew reads: “I will appoint your visitation as peace, and your overseers as righteousness.”

Here the holy Scripture displays admirable majesty: it calls the future rulers of the Church “bishops,” whose entire visitation is in peace and whose title of dignity is in righteousness, so that they neither show partiality in judgment nor allow anything unjust to be heard in the land of the Church, nor destruction and misery within its borders.

For wherever there is iniquity, righteousness is not preserved, and peace is lost, all these things will follow.

“But in place of these things,” he says, “salvation will occupy your walls,” or the Savior, who in Hebrew is read as *Jesus*, which properly sounds the name of the Lord.

He himself is the strength of the walls of the Church, whose gates are in the praise of the Lord, so that those who enter her may first learn to praise the Lord and confess his name.

As for the fact that the Septuagint translated “praise” as γλύμμα (*glymma*), that is, “sculpture,” we may say that the gates of the Church ought to be engraved with every virtue, through which we enter her.

(Verses 19–20.) “You shall no longer have the sun to shine for you by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon illumine you; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. Your sun shall no longer set, and your moon shall not wane, because the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed.”

The Septuagint: “Your sun shall no longer be your light by day, nor shall the rising of the moon provide you light at night; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light, and your God your glory. For your sun shall not set for you, and your moon shall not fail you. The Lord shall be your everlasting light, and the days of your mourning shall be completed.”

From this chapter we are compelled to refer everything that has been said and is to be said to the final time, when, as heaven and earth pass away, the service of the sun and moon will cease. The Lord himself will be the perpetual light, so that we may believe that what the χιλιασταί [“millenarians”] assert is to be fulfilled carnally is to be fulfilled spiritually, differing not in the character of the promises but in their timing.

To them we must briefly reply: if the sun sets at midday for false prophets and sinners, while, conversely, the sun of righteousness rises for those who fear the Lord, why should that sun of righteousness not continually arise for the saints—the one who says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), who shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend him (John 1)? “By day the sun shall not burn us, nor the moon by night” (Ps. 120:6). Since we possess the Lord as perpetual light, and the days of our mourning shall be completed, this does not mean that those who weep over the overthrow of Jerusalem will continue to mourn, but that they will rejoice because of the Church’s instruction. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. Blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh. Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5). After they have been filled with the Lord’s flesh, they will pour forth the Lord’s word and “declare their works to the king” (Ps. 44).

[Note: For χιλιασταί, the Ambrosian manuscript reads “Jews.”]

[Note: “To them we must briefly reply: for false prophets …” This passage is found corrupted in various ways in Erasmus and Marianus. Erasmus seems to introduce an impious sense when he reads, “To them we must briefly reply: for false prophets,” and so on. Therefore, “Why should the sun of righteousness not continually arise …?” Marianus, overcome by the difficulty of the reading, removes four words from the middle so that he can read it according to his own sense: “The sun of righteousness always rises, the one who says,” and so on. MARTIAN. The same is found in the Ambrosian manuscript: “for false prophets and sinners the sun always sets at midday. Conversely, for those who fear God the sun of righteousness rises; therefore, for the saints always …” Erasmus differs in this one respect: with the negative particle he reads, “therefore, why not always …?” Victorius reads, “the sun of righteousness always rises, the one who says …”; nevertheless, with the help, as he says, of the Brixian codex, he removes these four words, “therefore, why not always for the saints” (then “the Saint”), and reads “let the sun set” without the particle *si* (“if”). Much more correctly, and without introducing any alteration into our edition, understand it as follows, with an interrogative mark: “Why should that sun of righteousness not immediately arise for the saints …?”]

(Verses 21–22.) “But your people shall all be righteous; they shall inherit the land forever, the shoot of my planting, the work of my hands, for glorification. The least shall become a thousand, and the smallest a mighty nation. I am the Lord; at its time I shall suddenly accomplish this.”

The Septuagint: “Your people shall all be righteous; they shall possess the land forever, preserving the planting, the work of their hands, for glory. The one who is small shall become thousands, and the one who is least a great nation. I am the Lord; at the appointed time I shall gather them.”

When the days of mourning have ended and have been completed, when sorrow has been turned into joy, the entire people of Zion will be righteous—not for a short time, but forever. And because it is righteous, it will possess the land of the meek. It is not surprising that, in receiving the good things promised, it should possess the land of the meek and the living, for which the Prophet sighs, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13), since it is the shoot of the Lord’s planting and the work of his hands for the glorification of God. For, he says, “Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. 15).

Or, according to the Septuagint: the people that preserves God’s planting and the works of the Lord’s hands will be preserved in the glory of the Creator. Through Jeremiah God speaks of the good planting: “I planted you as a choice vine, wholly true,” which in Isaiah is called the vine of Sorek (Isa. 5). And because Paul, conscious of the virtues of Christ speaking in him, could say, “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11:1), he therefore said to the Corinthians: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6). “Those planted in the house of the Lord shall flourish in his courts” (Ps. 91).

Then the one who was small will become thousands, hearing from the Lord: “Have authority over five or ten cities” (Luke 19:17, 19), so that he may be called a χιλίαρχος [“commander of a thousand”]. And the one who, with the Apostle, had said, “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Eph. 3:8), will be ruler of a great nation in the heavenly places, when, at the appointed time, the Lord sends his angels and they gather to him all the saints, from the summit of heaven to its highest point (Matt. 24)—not only from Israel, but also from the people of the nations, of whom he spoke representatively: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; I must gather them also, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

He will do this suddenly, so that when all hope has been abandoned they may then be gathered into a mighty nation. Although we see this fulfilled in part every day in the Church, it will nevertheless be fulfilled more fully at the consummation of the world and at the Savior’s second coming.

(Cap. LXI.—Verses 1 ff.) “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and opening to prisoners, and to announce an acceptable year to the Lord and a day of vengeance for our God, to comfort all who mourn; to appoint for those who mourn in Zion and give them a crown instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, the garment of praise instead of a spirit of sorrow.”

The Septuagint: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to call the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense, to comfort all who mourn, to give to those who mourn in Zion, to give them glory instead of ashes, anointing of joy to those who mourn, and a garment of glory instead of a spirit of sorrow.”

[Note: Victorius adds, “to release the broken into freedom,” not from the Greek text of the Septuagint, in which those words are entirely absent, but from Luke the Evangelist, who, when citing these words in chapter 4, has them in the Septuagint; and, as he thinks, Jerome added them here in his Commentary.]

The one who had earlier said, “I am the Lord; at the appointed time I shall gather them,” or, according to the Hebrew, “I am the Lord; at its appointed time I shall suddenly accomplish this,” now goes on to say: “The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me.” This does not mean that the Lord God has a Lord God, but that, according to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed, he speaks of things that are humble.

To him the Psalmist had already said: “You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44:8). Whenever “companions” are mentioned, understand the nature of the flesh, since God has no companions of his substance. And because this was a spiritual anointing, not an anointing of the human body such as existed among the Jewish priests, he is therefore said to have been anointed above his companions—that is, above the other saints.

His anointing was fulfilled at the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained upon him (John 1). Concerning him this same Prophet also said: “A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of God shall rest upon him—the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isa. 11:1–2).

Therefore, when the Savior came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up after his baptism in the Jordan, he entered, according to custom, their synagogue on the Sabbath day. When he rose to read, the book of the prophet Isaiah was given to him. Opening it, he found written: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to release the broken into freedom, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.” When he returned the rolled-up book to the attendant and sat down, the eyes of all who were in the synagogue were fixed upon him, and he began to say to them: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” All bore witness to him and marveled at the words of grace that proceeded from his mouth.

If, then, the prophecy was fulfilled at that time, how do some refer what is said to the time of the consummation? Unless perhaps we can say that it was then fulfilled in part, but will be fulfilled more fully when all God’s people are righteous. “For now we know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, what is in part will be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13).

He was therefore anointed with the Holy Spirit in order to announce good news to the poor, or the meek, saying to them in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3), and: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (ibid., 4). He was sent to heal those whose hearts are broken (Luke 4), who say: “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise” (Ps. 50:19).

Or, according to Symmachus and Theodotion, he was sent “to bind up the wounds of sinners,” to proclaim release to captives, sight to the blind, or opening to prisoners—something Symmachus translated more clearly as “release for the bound.” Concerning him, or rather to him, it was said above: “Behold, I have appointed you as a light to the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out those bound from fetters, and those sitting in darkness from the house of prison” (Isa. 42:6–7).

Understand “the acceptable year” and “the day of recompense” as the entire period of his proclamation while he lived in the flesh. The Apostle Paul also interprets this as referring to the Savior’s first coming, saying: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (1 Cor. 6:2). We have spoken more fully about this above (on chapter LX).

But if “recompense” is understood not in the merits of the good but in the punishments of sinners, according to the expression “day of vengeance,” it must be understood as referring to the Jewish people, upon whom, after his Passion, the wrath of God immediately came.

He also comforted all who mourn, saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5), so that he might appoint for those who mourn in Zion and give them glory and a crown instead of ashes. The Apostle Paul was among these mourners; he mourned for Zion and said: “I have great sorrow and continual pain” (Rom. 9:2), and again: “I could wish that I myself were accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers and my kinsmen according to the flesh, who are Israelites” (ibid., 3). Therefore, those who mourned and wept received the oil of joy instead of ashes, seeing that very many among the Jews had believed and received an immaculate robe instead of mourning apparel.

(Verses 3–5.) “And they shall be called strong ones of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, for his glorification. They shall build the ancient ruins and raise up the former devastations; they shall restore the deserted and devastated cities from generation to generation. Strangers shall stand and pasture your flocks, and the sons of foreigners shall be your farmers and vinedressers.”

The Septuagint: “And they shall be called generations of righteousness, the planting of the Lord for glory. They shall build the everlasting deserted places, which had previously been desolate; they shall raise them up and renew the deserted cities, desolated for generations. Foreigners shall come and pasture your sheep, and farmers and vinedressers from other nations.”

After the Apostles and apostolic men have received the oil of joy and the garment—or, according to the Septuagint, the robe—of glory and praise instead of ashes and a spirit of sorrow, then they shall be called generations of righteousness, the glorious planting of the Lord. Or, according to the Hebrew, *ELE*, with both syllables drawn out, “strong ones,” “of God’s righteousness,” or “the planting of the Lord for glorification.”

When they have been glorified, or when they themselves have glorified the Lord, they will build the cities deserted from ancient times and raise up the ancient ruins: both the peoples of the Jews and all the nations. They will possess not only the skill to build and restore cities, but will also be excellent shepherds, so that, once the former shepherds have been rejected, concerning whom God had said through Ezekiel, “O shepherds of Israel, do shepherds feed themselves, and not rather the sheep?” (Ezek. 34:2), they may hear with the Apostle Peter: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:17).

And, wonderfully, they will pass from being builders and shepherds to being farmers—that is, plowers and vinedressers—so that with the Apostle they may say: “We are God’s building, God’s cultivation” (1 Cor. 3:9). Finally, the Savior asks the scribes and Pharisees, the vinedressers and farmers of the Jews, what he will do to the wicked vinedressers and farmers. When they answer, “He will destroy those wicked men miserably and will give the vineyard to other farmers” (Matt. 21:41), he adds: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (ibid., 43).

The matter requires no interpretation. For how many rulers of the Churches are there from the Jews, rather than from foreigners and people of the nations abroad? These people formerly served idols, were alienated from God’s covenant, strangers to his promises, without hope, and without God in the world; now they preside over the Churches and tame the hard and previously untamed hearts of the nations with the plow of faith, so that they may multiply the seed of the Lord’s teaching through the abundance of good works.

(Verses 6–7.) “But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be named ministers of our God. You shall eat the strength of the nations and glory in their glory. Instead of your double shame and disgrace, they shall praise their portion; therefore, in their land they shall possess double, and everlasting joy shall be theirs, because I am the Lord, who love judgment and hate robbery in a burnt offering.”

The Septuagint: “But you shall be called priests of the Lord; you shall be called ministers of our God. You shall eat the strength of the nations, and you shall be admired in their riches. Thus they shall possess the land a second time, and everlasting joy shall be upon their head. For I am the Lord, who love righteousness and hate robberies arising from iniquity.”

[Note: Neither in the Ambrosian manuscript nor in the Greek exemplar is the pronoun “our” added.]

The builders of the deserted cities and the shepherds of the flocks, who themselves are farmers and vinedressers—that is, the sons of foreigners—are also the priests of God. To them the Prophet now says: “You shall be called priests of the Lord, and you shall be called ministers of our God.” There is no doubt that this signifies the rulers of the Churches.

Or certainly it should be understood of the Apostles, so that the order is as follows: When builders, shepherds, farmers, and vinedressers from the nations have been placed over the Churches, you, concerning whom it was said, “The remnant shall be saved” (Rom. 9:27), and, “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah” (Isa. 1:9), shall be called priests and ministers of God, such as the sons of David also were. Concerning them Scripture says: “The sons of David were priests of God” (2 Sam. 8:18).

These will eat the strength of the nations and be admired in their riches. For “the glory of fathers is their children,” and the progress of the people is the priests’ feast (Prov. 17). Paul wrote to the Corinthians about such riches: “I give thanks to my God through Jesus Christ, because in everything you have been enriched in him, in every word and in all knowledge, just as the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, so that you lack nothing in any grace” (1 Cor. 1:4 ff.).

The strength of the nations, however, is the triumph of the martyrs. We glory in their glory—not with the pride that is a vice, which God resists while giving grace to the humble, but with the pride that is understood as power and glory (Jas. 4). Hence Moses’ face was horned [or radiant] (Exod. 34), and he could say: “In you we shall gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. 43:6).

Instead of “you shall glory in their glory,” Aquila translated: καὶ ἐν δόξῃ αὐτῶν πορφύρᾳ ἐνδύσεσθαι, that is, “you shall be clothed in purple,” displaying the insignia of royal splendor.

What follows—“Instead of your double shame and instead of disgrace, they shall praise their portion”—which is not found in the Septuagint, seems to me to be explained as follows. Instead of the double shame that you had, both over the Jewish people who had withdrawn from God and over the nations that served idols, you will see them converted to the fear of God and praising their portion. There is no doubt that this means the Lord, concerning whom the holy man also said: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26). No one can say this unless he has no other portion.

Since, therefore, you had a double shame and disgrace over them, because of their sin over which they themselves did not blush, for this reason they will possess double in their land—that is, in the land of the meek and the living—since they will have believed both in present things and in future things. And they will have everlasting joy.

For this the Septuagint reads: “Thus they shall possess the land a second time.” And everlasting joy shall be upon their head, so that those who had possessed the land within the narrowest boundaries of Judea may afterward possess the entire world. Concerning this land the Father speaks to the Savior: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

The Lord accomplished this, for he loves the truth of judgment and hates robbery in a burnt offering. For this the Septuagint translated, “robbery from iniquity,” as though there were any robbery that did not consist in iniquity. Therefore, what he says is this: The God of the righteous loves poverty more than the gifts of the rich, which arise from robbery and iniquity.

(Verses 8–9.) “And I will give their work in truth, and I will make an everlasting covenant with them. Their seed shall be known among the nations, and their offspring in the midst of the peoples. All who see them shall recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed.”

The Septuagint: “And I will give their labor to the righteous, and I will establish an everlasting covenant with them. Their seed shall be known among the nations, and their descendants in the midst of the peoples. Everyone who sees them shall recognize them, because they are the seed blessed by God.”

God, who loves righteousness and judgment and detests violent burnt offerings—for whatever comes from robbery he counts as the price of a prostitute and the price of a dog [or “flesh”]—will give the labor to the righteous, those who will possess the land a second time and whom he will crown with double joy. Or, as it is better expressed in the Hebrew, he will give it “in truth,” so that it will no longer be, as in the Law, a shadow of the truth, but the truth itself.

And he will make an everlasting covenant, not like the one he gave to Moses, which has passed away, but the covenant of the Gospel, concerning which Christ says: “Heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away” (Matt. 24:35).

Then the apostolic seed will be known among the nations, and all future generations will receive the seed of God’s teaching. They will no longer say what the former circumcised people said in error: “For what else does God seek except seed?”

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads: “saying, ‘For what else does God seek except the seed of God?’”]

Everyone who sees them will recognize at first sight that they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed. For who would not recognize the people of God by their manner of life, meekness, self-restraint, hospitality, and all their virtues? And who, conversely, would not detest the bloodstained hands of Israel, against whom the Prophet invokes the words: “Fill, O Lord, their faces with disgrace” (Ps. 82:17)?

(Verses 10–11.) “I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God, because he has clothed me with garments of salvation and covered me with the vestments of righteousness, as a bridegroom adorned with a crown and as a bride adorned with her jewels. For as the earth brings forth its shoot, and as a garden germinates its seed, so the Lord God will cause righteousness and praise to germinate before all the nations.”

The Septuagint: “They shall rejoice with joy in the Lord; let my soul exult in the Lord. For he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and surrounded me with a tunic of joy. As a bridegroom with a turban, and as a bride he has adorned me with feminine ornament, and as the earth brings forth its flower and as a garden germinates its seeds, so the Lord God brings forth righteousness and praise in the presence of all the nations.”

According to the Septuagint, the beginning of the chapter, which reads, “They shall rejoice with joy in the Lord,” is joined to the end of the preceding chapter. According to the Hebrews, however, it is the beginning of another chapter, in which the Church is introduced as responding to Christ’s words: “I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my soul shall exult in my God.”

She does not glory in the fathers, as the Jews gloried, saying, “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone” (John 8:33), but in God, since Scripture says: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

She gives the reasons for her joy: “Because he has clothed me with a garment of salvation and adorned and covered me with a vestment, or tunic, of righteousness and joy,” which in Hebrew is called *MAIL*. For as many as have been baptized in Christ, we have put on Christ and possess the tunic of righteousness—he who became for us holiness, righteousness, and redemption (Gal. 1).

He sets forth the likeness of two groups in the Church, the perfect and those who are beginning (1 Cor. 1). He compares the perfect to the beauty of a bridegroom and beginners to the adornment of a bride.

Paul was perfect: like a bridegroom adorned with a crown, and one who was to be crowned, or, as Aquila translated it, ἱερατευμένος στεφάνῳ, which in our language means “bearing a crown as a priest.” Speaking with the authority of Christ in him, he said: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4:7). And elsewhere: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way” (Phil. 3:15).

But he was a beginner in comparison with fullness when he spoke in the person of beginners: “When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I reasoned as a child” (1 Cor. 13:11). And again: “We see in part and we know in part, until the perfect comes” (ibid., 9). Therefore she is compared to the adornment of a bride, who is adorned with feminine ornament, or, as the others translated it, with her vessels or jewels.

He gives examples of another comparison, the first of which refers to the bridegroom and the second to the bride. “As the earth brings forth its shoot and is watered by heavenly rains, and as a garden germinates its seed, longing for the waters of springs and rivers, so,” he says, “the Lord will cause righteousness and joy to germinate before all the nations”—not before Israel, so as to humble the pride of the Jews, but before all the nations gathered into the Church.

(Cap. LXII.—Verses 1 ff.) “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until her righteous one goes forth like brightness and her savior is kindled like a lamp. The nations shall see your righteous one, and all kings your renowned one, and you shall be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord has named. And you shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.”

The Septuagint: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not cease, until her righteousness goes forth like light and her salvation burns like a lamp. The nations shall see your righteousness, and all kings your glory, and he shall call you by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name. And you shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.”

[Note: It seems that *nominabit* (“shall name”) should be restored from the sacred text; Victorius prefers it.]

The Lord and Savior had said: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Luke 4:18), continuing to the place where it is written: “All who see them shall recognize them, because they are the seed whom the Lord has blessed” (Isa. 61:1).

After this promise, the Church responded: “I will rejoice greatly in the Lord.” In the third of the Gradual Psalms, speaking in the person of the repentant people, she joyfully sang: “I rejoiced in those things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. 121:1). Now the person of the Prophet is introduced, saying: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest.”

“By day and by night,” he says, “I will not close my mouth, nor will my prayer ever be silent. I will cry out continually and join prayer to prayer until the promised one comes and illumines the whole world with his radiance.”

He makes clearer who it is whom he seeks and desires to come: “Until her righteous one goes forth like brightness and her savior is kindled like a lamp.”

Or, according to the Septuagint: “Until her righteousness goes forth like light and her salvation burns like a lamp.”

He was the one who said in the Gospel: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). When she has been kindled in Zion and Jerusalem, she will not shine in Judea alone, but it will be said to her: “The light that is in you has been kindled; the light that came forth from the Father began to burn within your borders and will illumine all the nations” (Matt. 6).

And all kings shall see your renown, O Jerusalem and Zion: he who was born from your stock, who, exalted upon the cross in you, drew all people to himself, so that the nations might see his righteousness, by which the Creator of all had mercy upon the nations, and kings might see his glory, by which he was glorified on the cross and subjected all kingdoms to his authority.

Finally, Jerusalem and Zion will no longer be called by those names, but will receive a new name that the Lord will impose upon it, saying to the apostle Peter: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I shall build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. 16:18). He derived this title from the Lord’s name, so that it may be called “the Lord’s own” (*Dominicum*).

Nor shall his people be called by the old name, Israel, but by the new name, Christian. And it shall be like a crown of beauty in the hand of the Lord and like a royal diadem in the hand of its God, when the multitude of believers has crowned it, and the diadem of imperial power, which the martyrs have adorned with the variety of their jewels, is in the hand of God, so that he may crown his Son with their victories. Hence the Apostle Paul also spoke to the saints: “My joy and crown.”

(Verses 4.) “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate; but you shall be called ‘My Will Is in Her,’ and your land ‘Inhabited,’ because the Lord has been pleased with you, and your land shall be inhabited.”

The Septuagint: “You shall no longer be called Forsaken, and your land shall no longer be called Desolate. For you shall be called ‘My Will,’ and your land ‘Inhabited.’”

In place of Zion and Jerusalem you shall be called the Church and the Lord’s own; in place of Jews, they shall be called Christians. Nor will you be content with this limit of names. You, who were formerly called “Forsaken,” which in Hebrew is *AZUBA*, will be called *EPESI-BA*, which means “my will is in her.” And your land, which was formerly called *SEMEMA*, “desolate” or “deserted,” will afterward be called *BULA*, which Aquila translated as ἐσχημένη, Symmachus and Theodotion as συνωκισμένη, and the Septuagint as οἰκουμένη. All these terms signify “inhabited” and “possessed.”

This is characteristic of Hebrew usage: names are always assigned to things from their outcome. Thus Abram, who was formerly called “exalted father,” when he heard the promise, “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 12:3), was called “father of many nations,” that is, Abraham.

A name is likewise imposed above upon the Lord and Savior: “Swiftly take away the spoils; quickly plunder” (Isa. 8:1). The sons of Zebedee, one of whom could utter the voice of thunder (Mark 3), were called *BANEREEM*, which means “sons of thunder,” because of the words: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

What follows—“because the Lord has been pleased with you, and your land shall be inhabited”—has been omitted by the Septuagint; instead, it gives the reasons why she is called *EPHSI* and why she is called *BULA*: because the Lord has been pleased with Zion and has made its land inhabitable, whereas previously it had been desolate through Jewish error.

Or we may refer the same words to the Church, which, after having previously been possessed by idols, had been deserted by God.

(Verses 5.) “For a young man shall dwell with a virgin, and your sons shall dwell in you. And as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God shall rejoice over you.”

The Septuagint: “And as a young man dwelling with a virgin, so your sons shall dwell. And as a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so the Lord shall rejoice over you.”

The Apostle also says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. 5:25). And when elsewhere he had introduced the example, “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh,” he added: “This mystery is great; but I speak of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5:31–32).

If, therefore, because the time is short and constrained, husbands must have their wives as though they did not have them, how much more holy will the union between bridegroom and bride be? This is the bridegroom of whom the eighteenth Psalm sings: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber” (Ps. 18:6). And this is the bride who is repeatedly described in the Song of Songs, who has neither wrinkle nor blemish (Song 4). Paul desires to present her to one man as a chaste virgin, holy in body and spirit (1 Cor. 2).

Under the name of the Beloved, the forty-fourth Psalm also sings of her: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” (v. 10). Therefore, just as a bridegroom rejoices in a bride, and a young man in a virgin—examples in which there is a holy union—so the Lord will rejoice in her whose names have been changed.

(Verses 6–7.) “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never be silent. You who remember the Lord, do not be silent, and do not give him silence until he establishes and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

The Septuagint: “And upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen, all day and all night, who shall never be silent, remembering the Lord. For there is none like you when he corrects, and he will make Jerusalem a joy upon the earth.”

The Prophet had said: “For Zion’s sake I will not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest,” and so on, up to the place where the chapter now ends: “As a bridegroom rejoices over a bride, so your God shall rejoice over you.”

He had promised to plead day and night that the promised Savior and Righteous One might come and, like a lamp, illumine the whole world. After this, the person of God speaking to Jerusalem—that is, to the Church of the first believers, which was built in and through the Apostles—is introduced: “Upon your walls I have appointed watchmen.” We may understand these to be angels, or Apostles, or all its rulers and teachers.

They guard the walls of the Church so that our adversary, the devil, who prowls about like a roaring lion and seeks how he may enter (1 Pet. 5), may not find an opportunity to devastate the Lord’s flock. These watchmen must not be silent by day or by night, neither in times of joy nor in times of sorrow; rather, they must continually implore the Lord’s mercy, so that his flock and the walls of Jerusalem may be guarded and fortified by his assistance.

Therefore the word is addressed to these same watchmen and teachers: “O you who remember the Lord and weary out his mercy with prayers by day and night, take care that prayer never be silent in your mouth. Do not give him silence”—that is, do not give the Lord silence—but always trouble him, in season and out of season, and imitate the persistent petitioner of the unjust judge.

If that judge laid aside the fierceness of his mind through continual entreaty,

[Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript reads, “through continual entreaty he laid aside.”]

how much more will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask him?

You must ask for so long that Jerusalem, which fell among the Jews and became an example and a curse, may be turned into the praise of the whole world.

I marvel at what the Septuagint intended when, instead of the Hebrew text, “Do not give him silence until he establishes and until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth,” it says something whose sense does not cohere with what precedes: “For there is none like you when he corrects, and he will make Jerusalem a joy upon the earth.”

Unless perhaps we fit this together by an artful turn of expression, so that it is addressed to the Church’s watchmen: none of them will be like the one who, through his preaching, causes Jerusalem to be corrected and made the joy of the whole earth.

### (Verses 8–9)

“The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the arm of his strength: If I give your grain any longer as food to your enemies, and if foreigners drink your wine for which you have labored—for those who gather it shall eat it and praise the Lord, and those who carry it away shall drink it in my holy courts.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord has sworn by his right hand and by the strength of his arm: If I give my grain any longer to be food for your enemies, and if foreigners any longer drink your wine for which you have labored—but those who gather it shall eat it, and they shall praise the Lord; and those who gather it shall drink it in my holy courts.”

Almighty God, who had said to the Church, “Upon your walls I have appointed watchmen,” who will never be silent, and to whom he will command that they never cease praying unless they obtain what they ask, now swears by his right hand and by the arm of his strength. We have often said that this means our Lord and Savior, who, according to the Apostle, is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1).

He swears that Jerusalem’s grain and wine will in no way become food for its enemies, nor will foreigners be nourished by its labor. Rather, whoever has sown in tears shall reap in joy; and those who have harvested, cast away the chaff, and gathered the pure grain into barns shall themselves eat the labor of their hands, raise up the Lord with everlasting praise, and drink wine in his holy courts.

We may understand these courts either as the many dwelling places with the Father, if we take the passage as referring to the future blessedness in the kingdom of heaven, or certainly as the Churches dispersed throughout the whole world, in which, after being planted, we shall later flourish in the house of the Lord.

When he says, “I will no longer give your grain to your enemies, and foreigners will not drink your wine for which you have labored,” he shows that formerly the labor of the Jews and all their works had been possessed by demons, when they wavered between God and idols, when Elijah said to them: “How long will you limp with both feet? If the Lord is God, follow him” (1 Kings 18:21).

According to the typological history narrated in the Book of Judges, the Midianites came and devastated its produce as far as Gaza, so that human food was turned into food for beasts (Judg. 6). This grain and this wine, however, will be eaten only by those who praise the Lord, and will be drunk only in his holy courts. Concerning this wine the Lord said during his Passion: “Amen, amen, I say to you, I shall not drink of the fruit of this vine until I drink it new in the kingdom of my Father” (Mark 14:25).

These things are partly fulfilled in the Church, when the Lord says to his disciples: “Drink, my friends, and be drunk, brothers”—that wine “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. 103). And Joseph drinks it with his brothers in full light and at midday (Gen. 43). It will be fulfilled more completely when the earth is drunk with the blessings of the Lord.

The grain, too, from which heavenly bread is made, is that of which the Lord says: “My flesh is truly food.” And again concerning the wine: “My blood is truly drink” (John 6).

### (Verses 10–12)

“Pass through, pass through the gates; prepare the way for the people; make the road level, and choose out the stones; raise up a signal for the peoples. Behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard to the ends of the earth. Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior is coming; behold, his reward is with him, and his work is before him. And they shall call them a holy people, redeemed [the Vulgate: *redeemed ones*] by the Lord. But you shall be called a sought-out city and not forsaken.”

The Septuagint: “Go through my gates, and make a way for my people; cast the stones out of the way. Raise a signal among the nations; for behold, the Lord has caused it to be heard to the end of the earth. Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your Savior is coming, bearing his reward with him and his work before his face. And he shall call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord. But you shall be called a sought-out city and not forsaken.”

He commanded the watchmen of Jerusalem’s walls—those whom he had previously commanded not to be silent and never to cease praying—to pass through the gates of Jerusalem and make a way for the people. The semi-Jews claim that this will happen at the end of time, when, after the fullness of the nations, Israel will be saved and return to the Lord.

Others think that it is to be fulfilled in the kingdom of heaven, when there will be true joy and each person will receive according to his merit, and they will no longer behold the Lord in humility but recognize him in the appearance of the judge, when he comes upon the clouds with a multitude of angels to repay each person according to his work.

According to the explanation we have begun, however, we can understand these things also of his first coming: namely, that the Apostles and apostolic men are commanded to enter and pass through the gates against which hell does not prevail, and to remove all obstacles from the way, so that the people may enter the Church of the Savior without any stumbling block.

Hence John also cried out in the wilderness: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness,” as Isaiah said: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low” (John 1:23; cf. Isa. 40:3–4).

The same meaning is now expressed in other words: “The ecclesiastical man chose stones,” for he softens all hardness from the hearts of believers. Concerning these stones the same Baptist said: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9).

Or, according to the Septuagint, he casts the stones from the way that separate unbelievers from believers. And lest the Jews think that this was said about them, it is added: “Raise up a signal among the nations”—that is, for the peoples of the nations—so that salvation may no longer be summoned within the narrow bounds of a single Jewish land, but may be heard to the ends of the earth, so that the whole world may hear the Passion of the Creator.

“Say,” he says, “to the daughter of Zion.” She is called the daughter of Zion either because she first arose from the Jews, concerning whom it says in the Song of Songs: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song 1:5), or certainly because she is called a daughter because she received from God the name of adoption. “For as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God” (John 1).

What is it, then, that the teachers and instructors are commanded to announce to the daughter of Zion? “Behold, your Savior is coming”—he who in Hebrew is called *Jesus*. Hence Gabriel also says to Joseph: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

This Savior is the judge of all believers, so that he may repay each according to his works: rewards to the righteous and eternal punishments to sinners (Matt. 16). “And he shall call them,” he says—the Lord and Savior himself.

Or, according to the Hebrew, the Apostles and apostolic men shall call them a holy people, redeemed by the Lord, who have been redeemed by Christ’s blood.

The city itself will no longer be called forsaken, as it was previously called—either among the Jews, because of commerce [Note: Victor corrects this from the Medicean manuscript, reading the negative *non* in place of *negotiationem* (“commerce”), which he says is plainly a false reading]—or among the nations, because of idolatry—but sought out, as it is said in Hebrew, **DRUSA** (דרושה), so that, in accordance with the increase and variety of virtues, it may always receive new names.

### Chapter 63

#### (Verse 1)

“Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one beautiful in his robe, proceeding in the multitude of his strength.”

The Septuagint: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with tawny garments from Bosor?” [Note: Victor says that “Thus” is corruptly written instead of “This,” even in the commentary, since the Hebrew reading is not displayed here, while the Greek has **οὗτος** and the Latin *iste*.] “Thus beautiful in his robe, violence with strength.”

From the place where, according to the Septuagint, it says, “Arise, arise, Jerusalem, for your light has come, and the glory of the Lord has risen over you” (chap. 60:1), up to the present chapter, where it says, “Who is this who comes from Edom, with garments dyed from Bozrah?”, many of our writers refer the whole passage to the end of the world. They insist that it will then be fulfilled either carnally or spiritually—for the opinions of many differ.

But because above, in this same book, we read: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the poor”—which the Lord and Savior, after reading the scroll of Isaiah in the synagogue of the Jews, showed to have been fulfilled in himself when he said, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your ears” (Luke 4:21)—and because it is now said of the same one that after his Passion he ascended to the Father covered in blood, we are compelled to understand everything that is said as referring to the Savior’s first coming.

For it cannot be that, as many of our writers attempt, the events joined together in their works should be assigned to different times. Nor do we deny that it is exceedingly difficult to join all these things together and show that they are to be spiritually fulfilled at the consummation, so that we may teach that in Christ they have already been completed both according to the flesh and according to the spirit.

Since, then, the Savior has come to the daughter of Zion, whose reward is with him and whose work is before him; since the righteous has gone forth like splendor, and the Savior has been kindled like a lamp; and since the bridegroom rejoiced over his bride, the Church—indeed, her God exulted over her, he who is himself both bridegroom and Lord—therefore, with reference to the assumption of the flesh and the Passion of the cross, it is said to him: “That your foot may be dipped in blood” (Ps. 67:24).

Under the name of Judah it is prophesied in Genesis: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hand shall be upon the necks of your enemies; the sons of your father shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; from the prey, my son, you have gone up; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness—who shall rouse him?” (Gen. 49:8–9). And again: “Binding his colt to the vine, and his she-ass to the vine, O my son, he shall wash his robe in wine and his mantle in the blood of the grape” (ibid., 11).

This is the one whom the angelic powers, seeing him ascend to the Father covered in blood, command the other angels; and from them they hear: “Lift up the gates, princes”—[Note: From the Greek **ἄρατε πύλας οἱ ἄρχοντες ὑμῶν**, and the Vulgate edition’s *vestras* (“your [gates]”), Victor substituted *vestri* (“of you”).] “and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the king of glory shall enter. Who is this king of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23:7–8). And again: “The Lord of hosts, he is the king of glory” (ibid., 10).

We have prefaced these remarks so that we may show that this present chapter agrees with the other testimonies as well. Hence it is also said in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is ruddy and white” (Song 5:10)—ruddy in his Passion, white in his resurrection.

The angels therefore ask, terrified by the novelty of the event. For the mystery of Christ’s Passion and resurrection, according to the Apostle Paul, had been unknown to all former generations (1 Cor. 2).

“Who is this who comes bloody from the land of Edom?” [Note: The name *Edom*, which was missing here, is supplied from the Ambrosian manuscript, in which *adveniat* (“may he come”) occurs shortly afterward instead of *advenit* (“he has come”).] **EDOM** (אדום) is expressed in our language by both “earthly” and “bloody.”

“With garments dyed from Bozrah?” Many, falling into a pious error, think that this is to be understood of the Lord’s flesh—that is, **BASAR** (בשר). But if that word signified “flesh,” it would be written with the medial letter **SIN**; whereas it is now written with **SADE**, and is interpreted as “firm” and “fortified.” We may understand this either of Jerusalem (Ps. 59:11), which was formerly surrounded by extremely strong walls and in which the Lord suffered, or of hell, concerning which it is written in the fifty-ninth and one-hundred-seventh Psalms: “Who will lead me into the fortified city?” (Ps. 107:11)—the place in which the souls of the dead are enclosed and surrounded by the strongest guards.

It should also be known that, according to the historical account, **BOSRA** (בצרה) is not in Edom but in Moab.

It follows: “Thus beautiful in his robe, proceeding in the multitude of his strength.” Concerning him the forty-fourth Psalm also sings: “Beautiful beyond the sons of men in appearance. Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty. [Note: Some manuscripts read “O most powerful”; compare the remarks on this verse of the Psalm in Letter 106 to Sunnias and Fretela.] In your appearance and your beauty, advance, prosper, and reign” (Ps. 44:3–5). In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “Violence with strength.” Let the prudent reader inquire what sense this has.

“I am the one who speaks righteousness and am a defender for salvation.”

The Septuagint: “I am the one who speaks righteousness and judgment of salvation.”

The Lord answered the angels who were asking: “You ask who I am, who shall ascend bloody to the heavens, and whose blood, with which I have been sprinkled, has not brought me deformity but beauty. I am the one to whom the Father has entrusted all judgment” (John 5). Concerning him the Psalmist also said: “Give your judgment to the king, O God, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Ps. 71:1).

“I am the one who speaks righteousness”: so that I may repay evil to the wicked and good to the good; I am the one who came to fight against hostile powers, to proclaim release to captives, and to free the bound from prison, so that both the enemies may experience punishment and the captives freedom.

#### (Verse 2)

“Why, then, is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has: “as though of those who tread the winepress.”]

The Septuagint: “Why are your garments red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress, full and trampled?”

Where our text says “red,” the Hebrew reads **EDOM** (אדום). Therefore, above too, where *Edom* is written, it is not the name of a place but the name of blood.

Again the angels inquire and say: “We have learned that you are the one who speaks righteousness, and that the salvation of all has been established in your judgment. Now we wish to know why your garments are like those dyed in must, or what cause there was for you to stain with blood the tunic woven from above, which cannot be torn and which had received from the virgin womb a whiteness such as no fuller on earth could produce. Mercy suits you more than cruelty; whiteness more than bloodshed.”

The Lord answered them not in one verse, as before, but in many words, so as to teach everything to those who were ignorant and prevent them from being compelled to ask again.

#### (Verses 3ff.)

“I have trodden the winepress alone, and no man from the nations was with me. I trod them in my fury and trampled them in my wrath; their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my clothing [the Vulgate: ‘defiled’]. For the day of vengeance was in my heart; the year of my redemption has come. I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist. My own arm saved me, and my indignation itself assisted me. I trampled peoples in my fury, made them drunk in my indignation, and brought their strength down to the earth.”

Instead of our “I have trodden the winepress alone,” the Septuagint translated, “the full one has been trampled,” which belongs more properly with the preceding chapter than as the beginning of what follows. They translated the rest as follows:

“There was no man from the nations with me; I trampled them in my fury, crushed them as earth, brought their blood down to the earth, and stained all my garments. For the day of retribution has come upon them, and the year of redemption is at hand. I looked, and there was no helper; I considered, and there was none to offer assistance. My arm delivered them, my wrath came, I trampled them in my anger, and brought their blood down to the earth.”

In place of “winepress,” which in Hebrew is called **GETH** (גת), Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself, **PHURA** (φουρά). But Symmachus is better in this passage, and we have followed him. For the word **PHURA** is ambiguous and generally signifies both a winepress and a small flask.

We must therefore speak of a winepress which, according to the usage of Holy Scripture, is sometimes used for the vengeance and punishments of sinners, and sometimes for the gathering of new fruits.

It is used for punishments and torments when Jeremiah, lamenting the destruction of Jerusalem in the Lamentations, says: “The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; therefore I weep” (Lam. 1:15–16).

The eighth and eighty-third Psalms are inscribed in a favorable sense, “For the winepresses.” Concerning these, if life accompanies us, the Lord permitting, we shall speak in their proper places. [Note: See the general preface placed at the beginning of the first volume, no. 21ff.]

This is the winepress in which the Savior alone treads both punishments for the wicked and rewards for the good; he alone trod it, and had no helper. For neither angel nor archangel, thrones, dominions, nor any of the heavenly powers assumed a human body, suffered for us, and trampled and crushed the hostile powers—except the one who says in the Psalm: “Save me, O Lord, for the holy one has failed” (Ps. 11:1).

So completely was he alone that even the most confident and most steadfast apostle in the truth of faith, Peter, terrified by fear, fled—indeed, denied the Lord (Matt. 26).

The following statement, “Their blood was sprinkled upon my garments, and I stained all my clothing,” must not be understood as though we should believe that demons and hostile powers possess blood. Everything must be understood tropologically, when the most merciful God is compelled to strike the enemies in order to educate his people and free them from the bonds of captivity.

“For the day of vengeance,” he says, “was in my heart; the year of my redemption has come.” Concerning this we also read above (on chap. 61), in a favorable sense, of “proclaiming the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution of our God”; here the expression is used both in an unfavorable and in a favorable sense.

In an unfavorable sense: “The day of vengeance was in my heart.” In a favorable sense: “The year of my redemption has come”—so that at the time when the adversaries are punished, God’s people might be freed, or rather redeemed by the precious blood of the Lamb who is said in John’s Apocalypse to have been slain.

Concerning this day of retribution Moses also prophesied in the Holy Spirit: “He will repay vengeance to his enemies and render recompense to those who hate him. I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist” (Deut. 32:41).

He had also said in the Psalm: “I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none, and for one who would comfort me, and I found none” (Ps. 68:21).

For although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross—and therefore God gave him the name above every name, so that he might save believers by his right hand; and his indignation against the adversaries delivered God’s people.
