Alternatively, he rescued believers by his arm, and did not delay his fury any longer. He brought their blood down to the earth—either tropologically, the blood of demons, or certainly the blood of the Jews. In place of this, the other interpreters translated “contention,” since they were striving with all their strength to release the bound people.

#### (Verse 7)

“I shall remember the mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord for all that the Lord has repaid us, and for the abundance of good things bestowed upon the house of Israel according to his mercy and according to the abundance of his mercies.”

The Septuagint: “I remembered the Lord’s mercy; I shall remember the Lord’s mighty deeds in all that he has repaid us. The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel; he will repay us according to his mercy and according to the abundance of his righteousness.”

When, as we think, the Savior’s first coming has ended—or, as many judge, his second coming—in which [Note: Victor ingeniously recast this passage as: “in which, under the guise of a judge, or rather a combatant, and [slaying] his own, etc.” Yet, according to the manuscripts and printed books, the sense is either not at all, or not quite correctly, fulfilled.] the voice of the judge, or rather of the warrior who slaughters his own adversaries and those of his people, is implied, and he is described as bloody and victorious, another section begins. In it the Prophet speaks in the person of the people, recounting God’s benefits toward them and the hardness of their heart, because of which Jerusalem was handed over to fire and Israel to captivity.

The Jews refer this to the time of Babylon. We, however, have shown by order and reason that the passage speaks of the present time, in which they serve the Romans and, with Israel excluded, a multitude of nations has taken its place.

Let us therefore run through the individual members of the discourse and explain them briefly, lest the exposition become drawn out.

Pressed by the weight of evils, I have hope in no one except the mercy of God, who shows mercy for thousands to those who love him and extends his mercy to those who know him. From this it is shown that the Lord’s mercy comes to the aid of those who love and know God.

“For it is not of him who wills or of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9). And unless the Lord builds the house and guards the city, the one who builds and guards watches in vain (Ps. 126).

For he himself will grant strength, so that we may perform acts of courage and be able to say: “My strength and my help and my refuge in the day of my troubles” (Jer. 16). In the present passage we must understand these words not of vices and sins but of hardships.

According to the Septuagint, what follows is: “I shall remember the mighty deeds of the Lord in all that he has repaid us.” In place of this, the Hebrew contains “the praises of the Lord.” We should understand signs and miracles, for which “mighty deeds” is often used, as in: “I shall not give my glory to another, nor my mighty deeds to carved images” (Isa. 42:8).

And elsewhere: “They shall announce his mighty deeds in the islands”—either to the nations of the whole world or to the Churches founded upon a firm mass, which are struck rather than overturned.

Sometimes *virtue* is by no means understood as strength and miracles, but as good conduct, as in the words of the Apostle Peter: “Supply virtue in your knowledge” (1 Pet. 1:5), and of Paul: “If there is any virtue and if there is any praise” (Phil. 4:8). Likewise, it is said elsewhere: “Sterility with virtue is better.”

The first understanding of virtue belongs to God; the second applies to human beings.

In place of what we translated, “for all that the Lord has repaid us”—which can be understood in either a favorable or unfavorable sense—Symmachus more clearly placed it in the context of benefits, saying: “For all the things in which he benefited us, and for the abundance of goodness that he exercised toward the house of Israel.”

In its place the Septuagint translated: “The Lord is a good judge to the house of Israel; he repays us according to his mercy and according to the abundance of his righteousness.”

No one can say this unless he understands that he is justly enduring what he suffers. Thus, in the seventy-second Psalm, whose beginning is, “How good is the God of Israel to those who are upright in heart,” the Prophet speaks in the person of those who are troubled by God’s judgments: “But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped,” when he saw the peace of sinners, and so on to the end of the Psalm.

Hence the Apostle Paul, who had recognized the Lord as a good and just judge, speaks confidently: “The crown of righteousness is laid up for me, which the righteous judge will repay me—not only to me, but also to all who love the coming of our Lord and Savior” (2 Tim. 4:8).

Nor is there any difference between “good” and “just,” as the heretics maintain, since the same writer says: “Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good” (Rom. 7:12), so that goodness is understood in general and justice in particular.

For this reason he writes to the Romans: “Scarcely does anyone die for a righteous person; perhaps someone might dare to die for a good person” (Rom. 5:7).

#### (Verses 8ff.)

“And he said: ‘Surely they are my people, children who will not deny; and he became their Savior. In all their tribulation he was not afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his mercy he himself redeemed them, carried them, and lifted them up all the days of the age. But they provoked him to anger and afflicted the spirit of his holy one [variant: ‘the Holy One’]; and he became an enemy to them, and he himself fought against them.’”

The Septuagint: “And he said: ‘They are not my people; children will certainly not reject.’ And he became their salvation from all their tribulation. Not an envoy, nor an angel, but he himself saved them, because he loved them and spared them. He himself redeemed them, received them, and exalted them all the days of the age. But they did not believe, and they embittered his Holy Spirit; he became an enemy to them, and he himself fought against them.”

Where we translated, “In all their tribulation he was not afflicted,” the Hebrew has **LO** [Note: *Lo* is a negative particle, etc. Because of this single negative particle *LO*, older editions print the entire Hebrew verse and consequently impose another word for which there is no trace in the manuscript codices and which obstructs the understanding of Jerome’s words. This will be evident to a prudent critic who carefully compares the new edition with the others. As for how it can be read in the opposite sense, “he himself was afflicted,” the answer is easy from the Hebrew context: it reads *lo tsar*, which is ambiguous and can be translated either “to him, distress” or “no distress”—“In all their tribulation, distress to him,” or “In all their tribulation, no distress.” MARTIAN.]—a negative adverb meaning “not.” It can also be read as “he himself,” giving the sense: “In all their tribulation he himself was afflicted,” that is, God, so that he might bear not only our sins but also our tribulations. For he himself bears our weaknesses and suffers for us.

The Septuagint, moreover, inserted something not found in the Hebrew: “Not an envoy nor an angel, but he himself saved them.” We shall speak of this in its proper place.

God, then, who is the righteous judge of the house of Israel and who tempers the severity of the judge’s justice with mercy, said: “I fathered children and exalted them, and they despised me. Nevertheless, because they are my people and, once named children, they will not perish forever, if they cease despising and denying me, they will experience the Savior”—because in all their tribulation he himself was afflicted.

Or: “He was not afflicted,” so that he might abandon them for a little while and, stripped of his help, compel them to pray.

Or certainly: “He did not afflict them at all”; on the contrary, while others persecuted them, he was their helper and sent his angel to free them from danger.

Or, according to the Septuagint, he did not wish to save his people through angels and prophets and other holy men; rather, he himself descended to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, so that he might carry the sick sheep upon his shoulders, find the drachma that had been lost, and joyfully meet the returning prodigal son.

Therefore the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth.” Let him no longer act through patriarchs, Moses, and the prophets; let him assume my body, dwell in my flesh, let the Word become flesh, and thus let him kiss me by dwelling in me, so that he may be Emmanuel.

Therefore he will save not as an envoy or as an angel, but he himself will save those who have received salvation—not through the merit of works but through God’s love. For “God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

If the prudent reader should silently respond: “Why, then, have many not been saved, if he himself saved them, loved them, spared his children, redeemed them with his blood, received them, and exalted those whom he assumed?”, the cause is made perfectly clear:

“But they did not believe, and they embittered his Holy Spirit,” or “the Spirit of his Holy One”—which in Hebrew is called **CADESO** (קדשו).

God therefore wished to save those who desired salvation and summoned them to salvation, so that their will might receive its reward; but they did not wish to believe.

Otherwise it is also written concerning John: “There was a man sent by God, whose name was John. He came as a witness, to bear witness to the light, so that all might believe through him” (John 1:6). It is not immediately a fault if many refused to believe; rather, the will of the one who came was that all should believe and be saved. [Note: Some prefer to read *vocantis* (“of the one calling”) instead of *venientis* (“of the one coming”), but there is no reason to alter the reading.]

But if the one who has embittered and afflicted the Holy Spirit—or his Holy One, that is, Christ—provokes God, then the Holy Spirit is of the same nature as the Father and the Son. Therefore the Apostle commands: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed” (Eph. 4:30).

The Holy Spirit departs from a body subjected to sins, and wisdom does not enter a wicked soul (Wis. 1). Hence David, conscious of his sins and fearful of losing the Holy Spirit, prayed: “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:13).

To show that everyone who provokes the Holy Spirit offends God, and that one becomes from a friend an enemy and adversary, the Apostle Peter speaks more explicitly in the Acts of the Apostles: “Why has it been agreed among you to lie to the Holy Spirit? You have not lied to human beings but to God” (Acts 5:9).

This is the Holy Spirit of whom the Lord said in the Gospel: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:15–16).

Concerning him we also read in the Wisdom written under Solomon’s name: “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from foolish thoughts” (Wis. 1:5).

#### (Verses 11ff.)

“And he remembered the days of the age, Moses and his people. Where is the one who brought them up from the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is the one who placed in their midst the Spirit of his Holy One? He who led Moses at his right hand by the arm of his majesty; who divided the waters before them to make for himself an everlasting name; who led them through the abysses like a horse in the wilderness that does not stumble. As an animal descending through the plain, the Spirit of the Lord was his guide. Thus you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name.”

The Septuagint: “And he remembered the ancient days, the one who brought up from the earth the shepherd of the sheep. Where is the one who placed the Holy Spirit among them? He who led Moses by the right hand, the arm of his glory. Thus he led his people through mighty water before his presence, to make for himself an everlasting name. He led them through the abyss like a horse through the wilderness, and they did not labor. And as beasts descend through a plain, the Spirit from the Lord was their guide. Thus you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name.”

The Lord, who from being the protector of the Jewish people became their adversary because they provoked his Holy Spirit and he fought against them, himself remembered the ancient days, when Moses prayed for them in the wilderness, saying: “Either forgive them this offense, or, if you will not, erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. 32:31–32).

Isaiah, therefore, remembering ancient history, says: “Where is that Moses who brought them out of the Red Sea? Where is the shepherd of sheep? Where is the one who labored with the other shepherds of the Lord’s flock? Who obtained and placed the Spirit of God in the Lord’s flock by his prayer and supplications?”

Or certainly it should be understood in this way: “Where is that mercy of the Lord by which he formerly had compassion on his people, so that he also granted them the grace of the Holy Spirit: he who led Moses his servant to the right hand, not to the left, by the arm of his majesty; who divided the waters before them to make for himself an everlasting name”—so that his power might be proclaimed even to the present day?

For he led his people through the immense abysses of the waters like a horse through the wilderness and like beasts across a plain, and the Spirit of the Lord was his guide—that is, the guide of the Lord’s flock (Exod. 14).

Here we must understand “Spirit” as an angel, who was the guide of the people of Israel, in accordance with what is written: “He makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. 103:4). And in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Are they not ministering spirits, sent into service for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1:14).

Let us consider what is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more” (Acts 8:39)—whether we should understand this as referring to an angel. There are those who assert that the angel did these things in the Holy Spirit.

We have passed rapidly over the obvious matters so that we may linger over the more obscure.

*(Verses 15ff.)* “Look down from heaven and see, from the dwelling-place of your holiness and your glory. Where are your jealousy and your strength? The multitude of your inward affections and your mercies have restrained themselves from me. For you are our father, and Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us. You, O Lord, are our father; our redeemer is your name from eternity.”

The Septuagint has: “Turn back from heaven and see, from your holy house and your glory. Where are your jealousy and your strength? Where is the multitude of your mercies and your compassion, by which you sustained us? For you are our father, because Abraham did not know us, and Israel did not acknowledge us. But you, O Lord, are our father; deliver us. From the beginning your name has been upon us.”

You who bestowed such benefits upon the people, as the preceding passage recounted, so that you also considered us worthy to share in your Spirit, now likewise look down from heaven and see our deeds—if indeed they are worthy of you. Why do you turn your face away from us?

Heaven is called the holy dwelling-place and house of his glory (Psalm 43), according to the statement: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isaiah 66:1); and elsewhere: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them”; and: “To you I lifted my eyes, who dwell in heaven” (Psalm 112:1). This does not mean that the almighty God, who holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist, is enclosed in any place; rather, whatever things are holier are called his place and dwelling.

Thus Solomon, who built the house of God, speaks to him in prayer: “The heavens of heavens and the earth are not sufficient for you” (Ecclesiasticus 16:18). And in the Lord’s Prayer it is said: “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). Wherever, therefore, God’s will is done, there is his dwelling-place and the house of God.

As for what follows, “Where are your jealousy and your strength?” let us explain it by the testimony in which God says through Ezekiel to Jerusalem, which had followed her lovers: “I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you” (Ezekiel 16:42). The meaning is this: Because we sinned and you began to hate us, your jealousy has departed from us—the jealousy that does not depart when he speaks through Zechariah: “I have been jealous for Zion and Jerusalem with great jealousy” (Zechariah 1:14). Therefore he also says in what follows: “And I will be angry with the nations that have gathered against her round about.”

When jealousy departs, the strength of God also departs, and the affection of a father’s inward compassion is overcome, when the magnitude of sins conquers the incredible clemency of God, so that he restrains himself from helping me, though he could not bear to see me oppressed.

“For you,” he says, “are our father,” who are the creator of all. Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us, because we have offended you; and they do not recognize as sons those whom they understand not to be loved by their God.

A sudden question arises: why did he mention Abraham and Israel—that is, Jacob—and remain silent about the name of Isaac (Genesis 32)? We shall answer that when the beginning and the end are given, the middle is also named. Or we may explain it this way: Abraham was called from the Gentiles to faith, and, according to the differing character of his former and subsequent condition, received a change of name. Jacob likewise attained the name Israel only after much labor. Hence Abraham had three wives and Jacob four, whereas Isaac retained his ancient name from beginning to end; and, signifying the chastity of the Church, he was content with one wife.

These men, therefore, who pray for sinners to be changed into a better condition, take on the likeness of those whose joy followed sorrow. This is all that they ask: since he is their father and has granted them this name, that he not forget his sons, lest through them the name of God be blasphemed among the nations.

*(Verses 18, 19.)* “Why have you made us stray, O Lord, from your ways? You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you. Turn back for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your inheritance. Our enemies have possessed your holy people as though they were nothing; they have trampled your sanctuary. We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your name was not invoked upon us.”

The Septuagint has: “Why have you led us astray, O Lord, from your holy way? You have hardened our hearts, so that we would not fear you. Turn back for the sake of your servants, for the sake of the tribes of your inheritance, so that we may possess a little of your holy mountain. Our adversaries have trampled your sanctuary. We have become as at the beginning, when you did not rule over us and your name was not invoked upon us.”

[Note: “From your holy way”—Victorius says, “I do not know who inserted this word ‘holy’ here; for it is absent not only from the Septuagint but also from the Hebrew and the Vulgate edition, nor does Jerome include it. Moreover, below, at the beginning of chapter 65, he cites this testimony without it.”]

The Epistle that Paul writes to the Corinthians, although addressed to the single population of one city, because of the differing character of its inhabitants—that is, the holy and the sinful—now praises them, now rebukes them, now teaches, now reproves, and urges them to continence; he does not reject marriage; he draws them away from idolatry; he instructs them concerning the resurrection; and he extends a hand to those who marry a second time, so as not to give fornication an opportunity.

We have said this so that we may understand the present chapter also, which is composed entirely from the prayer of a people entreating God, as belonging either to the righteous or to sinners: now praising the Lord, now raising a question against the Lord, and now attributing their own fault to God. Thus, after the other things, they also say: “Why have you made us stray, O Lord, from your ways,” or, “Why have you led us astray from your way? You have hardened our heart, so that we would not fear you.”

This does not mean that God is the cause of error and hardness, but that his patience, while he awaits our salvation and does not punish the transgressors, may appear to be the cause of error and hardness. Thus, when he was exceedingly angry with certain people, he withheld his hand from striking and said: “I will not visit your daughters when they have committed fornication, nor your brides when they have committed adultery” (Hosea 4:14).

“For he scourges every son whom he receives,” and he strikes for the purpose of correction (Hebrews 12). Accordingly, concerning those who have by no means lost the name of sons but are recalled to repentance through punishments, he says: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with scourges; but I will not remove my mercy from them” (Psalm 88:33). There is a sorrow that leads to life, and there is a sorrow that leads to death.

Therefore the sinner also says in the psalm: “You have turned our paths away from your way, and you have humbled us in a place of affliction” (Psalm 43:19). For forty years the people wander in the wilderness, so that they do not find their former way and do not return to the Egyptians (Numbers 32). In Hosea, too, the paths of Jerusalem are hedged in and closed with thorns, so that she will not follow her lovers and, compelled by necessity, return to her former husband (Hosea 2).

It is also said that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart, so that he would not release his people and would be afflicted with ten plagues (Exodus 4). Paul discussed this question most carefully in his Epistle to the Romans (Romans 9).

[Note: “We touched upon this in a certain work.” He means the Epistle written to Hedibia, for in question 10 he discussed this difficulty. Moreover, in the first epistle of the Church of Lyon concerning Predestination, written against three letters of the same monk who had raised the question, it is said that the monk supported his opinion by the authority of blessed Jerome, in the book *On the Hardening of Pharaoh’s Heart*, and proved from this passage that the book was genuine. This letter, written around the year of the Lord 855, is found in the *Library of the Fathers*. — Martian.]

“Turn back,” he says, “O Lord,” or “turn us back,” for the sake of your servants Abraham and Israel, who did not know us, or whom we believe to be present among the people. For our enemies have possessed your holy people as though for nothing and without any labor.

Or turn us back so that, according to the Septuagint, we may possess a little of your holy mountain, since we cannot possess the whole of your mountain; so that, once we have a part, we may come to its fullness and behold the glory of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth (John 1). Concerning him it is said in this same prophet: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord will be made manifest” (Isaiah 2:2).

As for the statement above, “Why have you made us stray?” (Isaiah 63:17), Jeremiah teaches fully in what sense it should be understood: “You deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you prevailed, and you were able” [or, according to another reading, “you set me”] (Jeremiah 20:7).

For while you promise me clemency, and, like a merciful father, conceal your severity, and, like a skilled physician, hide the sharpest iron lest you frighten the sick person before you cure him, you made me negligent. Therefore God also says concerning Jerusalem: “Behold, I will deceive her, and I will make her like a wilderness, and I will set her like a land without water, and I will speak to her heart. And from there I will give her possessions, and the valley of Achor for the opening of understanding” (Hosea 2:14–15).

[Note: “Victorius judges the words ‘I will set her like a land without water’ to have been added as an explanation of the preceding words, since they are absent not only from the Septuagint but also from the Hebrew and the Latin Vulgate; accordingly, he emends ‘and’ to ‘that is.’”]

Let us consider the order of each expression. He deceives her and makes her desolate and without water, so that she suffers thirst for virtues. After she has said, “My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh thirsted for you” (Psalm 41:2), he will then speak to her heart and console her in her mourning. And he will give her possessions from there—that is, from repentance and the grief that produces salvation. The humility of her troubled heart—for this is what the valley of Achor signifies—opens understanding, so that she may not remain ignorant of her Creator.

“Our enemies,” he says, “have trampled your sanctuary.” There is no doubt that this signifies the Temple, which the victorious Romans trampled.

“And we have become as at the beginning,” before we were called in Abraham, and while we were in Egypt, having neither God, nor kings, nor rulers, nor prophets, nor the Law of God’s commandments (Hosea 3). All these things were fulfilled after the Lord’s Passion and are still being fulfilled today.

For when they said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25), an everlasting curse remains, and their God does not rule over them, nor is his name invoked upon them, since they are no longer called the people of God.

*(Chapter 64—verses 1ff.)* “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down; the mountains would melt away before your face. As at the burning of fire they would melt, the waters would burn with fire, so that your name might be made known to your enemies; the nations would be troubled before your face. When you do marvelous things, we shall not endure them; you came down, and the mountains melted away before your face.”

The Septuagint has: “If you open heaven, trembling will seize the mountains because of you; and they will melt as wax melts before fire, and fire will burn the adversaries; and your name will be made manifest among the adversaries; the nations will be troubled before your face. When you do glorious things, trembling will seize the mountains.”

Because our enemies have trampled your sanctuary and we have become as at the beginning, when your name was not invoked upon us, therefore we entreat you and say: “Would that you would rend the heavens and come down,” and that you, who are always promising, would at last fulfill your promises.

This was said at a time when the Savior had not yet come and had not yet assumed from the virgin’s womb a human being of our nature and substance whom he might save, so that, “as we have borne the image of the earthly, we may also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15).

“If you did this,” they say, “and the heavens, or heaven, were opened at the coming of your majesty, the mountains would melt away—or trembling would seize the mountains—and they would be consumed as wax is consumed before fire.”

The heavens were opened also to Ezekiel, and he saw a great vision (Ezekiel 1). Moses likewise, in the blessings of Deuteronomy, invokes this blessing: “May the Lord open for you his good treasury, heaven, to give you blessing” (Deuteronomy 28). And in the Gospel (Matthew 3), John the Baptist is said—or, according to another reading, testifies—to have seen the heavens opened and the Holy Spirit descending upon the Lord in the form of a dove.

The mountains that at the Lord’s coming—for it is written, “God is a consuming fire” (Deuteronomy 4:24)—will be consumed and melted like wax are the hostile powers and all who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. Concerning them the ninety-sixth psalm also sings: “He saw, and the earth was shaken. The mountains melted like wax before the Lord, before the God of the whole earth” (Psalm 96:4–5).

For if you descended and fulfilled your promises, the waters of the sea, according to Symmachus, would waste away, and that fire would consume all their saltiness. Concerning it another psalm also says: “As smoke vanishes, so may they vanish; as wax melts before fire, so may sinners perish before the face of God” (Psalm 68:2).

It should also be noted that when the waters of the sea have been consumed by divine fire, then the name of the Lord the Savior will be made known to his enemies. Concerning them the sixty-seventh psalm says: “The tongue of your dogs is from the enemies themselves,” so that those who had not recognized him through his benefits might recognize him through the overthrow of their city and their own captivity.

And the nations will be troubled before his face, or, as it is expressed more significantly in Hebrew, they will be moved, so that those who were previously immovable may come to salvation.

When he has performed marvelous deeds and displayed in the Gospel the signs that he once displayed in Egypt and in the wilderness, they will confess that they cannot bear the glory of his coming—or, alternatively, that trembling has seized the mountains.

Beautifully, according to the Hebrew, as though those who had earlier prayed had been heard—“Would that you would rend the heavens and come down; the mountains would melt away before your face”—they then add: “You came down.” The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, truly Emmanuel, which is interpreted, “God with us.” Therefore all the mountains melted away before your face, concerning which we spoke above.

The Hebrews explain this passage as follows: “Thus fire will burn the wicked, as waters boil from the heat of fire.” For they wish the term AMASIM () to be understood not as “consumption” and “melting away,” as the others interpreted it, but as “the wicked.”

*(Verses 4, 5.)* “From eternity they have not heard, nor perceived with their ears; the eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who await you. You met the one who rejoices and practices righteousness in your ways; they will remember you.”

The Septuagint has: “From eternity we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen a God apart from you, and your works, which you will do for those who await mercy; for he meets those who practice righteousness, and they will remember your ways.”

The apostle Paul, as though a Hebrew from the Hebrews, takes a paraphrase of this testimony from the authentic books in the Epistle that he writes to the Corinthians. He does not render it word for word—for he utterly despises doing that—but expresses the truth of the meanings, which he uses to strengthen whatever point he wishes to establish (1 Corinthians 2).

[Note: “He appears here to be attacking Origen, who in *Homily 35 on Matthew 27* teaches that the words found in 1 Corinthians 2:9 were taken from the apocryphal *Apocalypse of Elijah*. Rufinus renders his opinion into Latin as follows: ‘The apostle brings forward certain secret Scriptures, as he says somewhere: What the eye has not seen nor the ear heard; for this is found in no canonical book, except in the secrets of the prophet Elijah.’ For this reason Hegesippus also accuses Stephen Gobarus, according to Photius, of having considered this testimony false. Gobarus had either done so out of contempt for the apocryphal volume, or, while not denying that such a thing had once existed, had argued that it was no longer true that the things God had prepared for his own were unseen, unheard, and unknown, after the incarnation of Christ and the sending of the Holy Spirit, since Paul adds: ‘But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit,’ and so forth. Jerome most rightly attacks the Gnostics and the disciples of Basilides, as we note in the letter to Desiderius prefixed to the Pentateuch. See that letter and compare it with the one to Pammachius on the best method of translation.”]

Let the ravings of the apocrypha, which are introduced into the churches of Christ on the occasion of this testimony, therefore fall silent. Of them it may truly be said: “The devil sits in ambush with the rich in the apocrypha, to kill the innocent.” And again: “He lies in wait in the apocrypha like a lion in his den; he lies in wait to seize the poor” (Psalm 9:8).

The *Ascension of Isaiah* and the *Apocalypse of Elijah* contain this testimony.

[Note: “Thus Epiphanius calls it *ἀναβατικὸν Ἠσαΐου* in *Heresy 40*, section 2, and *Heresy 67*, section 3. The work that he calls the *Apocalypse of Elijah* is called *The Prophecy of Elijah* by Anastasius the Librarian in the Latin version of Nicephorus’s *Stichometry*.]

On this account, and through many similar things, the women of Spain, especially those of Lusitania, have been deceived—women burdened with sins, led by various desires, always learning and never coming to a knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 3)—so that they accepted the monstrosities of the names Basilides, Balsamus,

[Note: “We have explained these names as far as was possible from Hebrew sources in Letter 75, to Theodora, section 3. We also discussed the testimony of Irenaeus, which appears below, in which the holy Doctor seems to have been mistaken. See the notes there, page 449, and also the letter to Hedibia, Question 10.”]

Thesaurus, Barbelon, Leusibora, and the rest of the names.

The apostolic man Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon and martyr, writes about these matters with the greatest care, explaining the origins of many heresies (αἱρέσεων), and especially of the Gnostics, who through Marcus the Egyptian first deceived noble women of Gaul around the Rhône and afterward those of Spain, mingling pleasure with fables and arrogating to the name of knowledge what was in fact their ignorance (Irenaeus, Book 1, *Against Heresies*).

But what the people say at present is that they have never known, either through their ears or their eyes, what God is preparing for his holy ones in the future, and that he meets those who practice righteousness and remember his ways.

According to the Septuagint, however, they say that they have never known any other God apart from the one who is truly God, nor have they seen such great works of another as those he will perform for those who await his mercy, practice righteousness, and remember his ways.

And how is it written: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)? And again: “No one sees my face and lives” (Exodus 33:20)? Therefore God cannot be explained in words, nor can he be contemplated with the eyes; but he is seen by those concerning whom it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

*(Verse 6.)* “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; we were always in them, and we shall be saved. And we have all become as an unclean thing; all our righteousness is like a menstruating woman’s cloth. And we have all fallen like a leaf, and our iniquities have carried us away like the wind.”

The Septuagint has: “Behold, you were angry, and we all sinned; therefore we went astray, and we have all become like the unclean, and all our righteousness like the cloth of a woman who sits; and we have fallen like leaves because of our iniquities; the wind will carry us away.”

The order is reversed. It is not because you were angry that we sinned; rather, because we sinned, you were angry. And because we sinned, you were angry with us, O Lord; therefore we went astray and abandoned the right way.

Or, according to the Hebrew, since we have always been in sins, we shall be saved only by your mercy; for by ourselves we are unclean, and whatever righteousness we seem to possess is compared with the cloth of one who sits, or with a menstruating woman’s cloth.

For this reason Theodotion retained the Hebrew word itself, EDDIM (), which Symmachus translated as κυουσῶν, that is, “of women in labor”; Aquila as μαρτυριῶν, that is, “of testimonies,” referring to the time when blood in the first marital intercourse gives proof of virginity.

[Note: “Martian has κυουσῶν, and shortly afterward μαρτυριῶν.”]

“And we have fallen,” he says, “like leaves from trees, which, because of our iniquities, are scattered by blasts of wind.”

In this we must consider that the righteousness found in the Law is called uncleanness in comparison with evangelical purity. For “what was formerly glorified was not glorified” because of the surpassing glory.

Accordingly the apostle Paul, who had fulfilled everything according to the righteousness that is in the Law, says that he counted it all as loss in order to gain Christ (Philippians 3), and, because of the surpassing knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake he considers everything as dung, in order to gain Christ and be found in him—not having his own righteousness, which is from the Law, but the righteousness that is through the faith of Christ, which is from God.

“There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness” (Ecclesiastes 7), if, after the truth of the Gospel, he wishes to practice the shadows of the Law and does not pursue what is just in a just manner.

Hence, according to the wisest Solomon, every man seems righteous to himself when he is occupied with the Law. To such people the Lord speaks in the Gospel: “You are those who justify yourselves before men” (Luke 16:15). Fleeing this, Paul says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, yet I am not thereby justified” (1 Corinthians 4:4).

There is, moreover, a righteousness of God, concerning which the same Solomon says: “Understand true righteousness.” Therefore there is another righteousness that does not possess truth, and there is this true righteousness, concerning which it is again said in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6).

Many prophets and righteous people desired to see it, and did not see it (John 8). Abraham, however, saw this righteousness and rejoiced, no longer following the letter that kills but the Spirit that gives life.

Nor is it surprising to say this about human beings, since even the stars are not clean when compared with God’s righteousness, and he devised something perverse against his angels (Job 4, 15).

If, therefore, after the Gospel of Christ and the coming of the Son of God, anyone observes the ceremonies of the pedagogical Law, let him hear the people confessing that all that righteousness is compared with a most filthy cloth. Esther likewise compares her diadem, which was the emblem of royal power and which she wore not willingly but under compulsion, to such a cloth: “You know my necessity, for I detest the sign of my pride that is upon my head on the days of my display; I abhor it like a menstrual cloth, and I do not wear it on the days of my rest” (Esther 14:16).

*(Verse 7.)* “There is no one who invokes your name, who rises up and takes hold of you. You have hidden your face from us and have crushed us in the hand of our iniquity.”

The Septuagint has: “There is no one who invokes your name, or who, remembering, takes hold of you. For you have turned your face away from us and handed us over because of our iniquities.”

Because we have fallen like leaves from trees, which the wind dries and scatters, therefore no one was found who invoked your name and, rising from the ruin of his iniquities, took hold of you or held you fast, saying with the bride: “I found him whom my soul sought; I will hold him and will not let him go” (Song of Songs 3:4).

In Scripture, “wind” is used in three ways: either for the magnitude of temptations, or for the perversity of doctrine, or simply for the wind by which clouds are gathered and the air is compressed into clouds.

Of temptations: “The rivers came, the winds blew, and struck against that house, and they could not overthrow it, because it had been firmly founded upon the rock” (Matthew 7:27).

Of the perversity of doctrine: “So that we may no longer be carried about by every wind of doctrine in the wickedness of men” (Ephesians 4:14).

Of wind simply: “They could not sail, for the wind was against them” (Mark 6:48). This does not mean that this too cannot be understood tropologically, but only that in the present sense it serves merely as an illustration.

When the Lord turns his face away from us, we are crushed in the hand of our iniquity, or handed over to temptations because of our sins. From this we learn that iniquity also has a hand, and that all sins desire to hold us tightly in their grasp.

Thus “in the hand of the tongue are death and life” (Proverbs 18), and the holy man prays: “Let not the foot of pride come against me” (Psalm 35:12).

But because the Lord has turned his face away from us, let us, knowing what is written—“Everyone who invokes the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32)—invoke his name and say: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the impiety of my heart” (Psalm 31:5–6).

Immediately we shall have the Lord responding: “I have blotted out your iniquities like a cloud, and your sins like a mist” (Isaiah 44:22).

[Note: “Victorius: ‘to whom this reading, “and,” gives a considerably better sense.’”]

And we shall say: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 79:4), so that we may no longer be servants of sin but your servants. For everyone who commits sin is its servant (John 8).

*(Verses 8ff.)* “And now, O Lord, you are our father, while we are clay; you are our fashioner, and we are all the work of your hands. Do not be angry, O Lord, beyond measure, and do not remember iniquity forever. Behold, look upon us, for we are all your people. The city of your holy one has become a desert; Zion has become a desert; Jerusalem has been desolated—the house of our holiness and our glory, where our fathers praised you, has become a burning of fire, and all our desirable things have become ruins. Will you restrain yourself over these things, O Lord? Will you remain silent and afflict us exceedingly?”

The Septuagint has: “And now, O Lord, you are our father; we are clay, and we are all the work of your hands. Do not be angry with us, O Lord, exceedingly, and do not remember our sins in time. And now look, for we are all your people. The city of your holy one has become desolate, Zion; Jerusalem has become like a wilderness. The house of our sanctuary and glory, which our fathers blessed, has become burned with fire, and all our glorious things have fallen.”

“And over all these things you have endured, O Lord, and have remained silent, and you have humbled us greatly.”

[Note: “The Ambrosian manuscript has ‘we shall endure you, O Lord’; likewise the Complutensian copy has ἀνέξομεν (‘we shall endure’) instead of ἀνέσχου (‘you endured’).”]

If we consider our merits, we must despair. But if we consider your clemency—since you scourge every son whom you receive—we dare to pour out prayers (Hebrews 12).

For you are our father, who deigned to say: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). Although we are clay, and the work of your hands, and you are our fashioner, and although the vessel cannot answer the potter as to why it was made this way or that, yet, knowing that we are sons, we dare to say: “Do not be angry, O Lord, beyond measure.”

We do not forbid anger, nor do we ask for your patience any longer, through which we have stored up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath. But this we ask: do not be angry with us beyond measure; do not remember our iniquity at the time of vengeance and retribution. Rather, look upon your people, who were once called your people.

And have mercy on the city of your sanctuary, in which your name was invoked. It is called Zion and Jerusalem, the city made glad by the river’s stream, and in which there was once a watchtower of virtues and a contemplation of peace (Psalm 43).

Your house also—that is, the Temple of our sanctification and glory, in which our fathers praised you—has fallen into ruins and ashes and has been destroyed by a consuming fire, so that sacrifices are no longer offered there, Passover is no longer celebrated, and none of the ceremonies that you commanded is performed. All our desirable things have become ruins.

Since these things are so, will you, O Lord, restrain your mercy over them? Will you remain silent while your adversaries blaspheme, and will you afflict and humble us—not in the customary manner, but exceedingly?

The Jews think that all these things were fulfilled in the times of the Assyrians and Babylonians. But we, in accordance with what follows from the person of the Savior—“I appeared to those who did not ask for me; I was found by those who did not seek me” (Isaiah 65:1)—refer everything to the time of the Roman victory.

Josephus, the historian of the Jews, explains this in seven volumes, to which he gave the title *The Captivity of the Jews*, that is, περὶ ἁλώσεως, “On the Capture.”

It is superfluous to discuss in words things that are evident to the eyes, since all their desirable things have become ruins, and the Temple celebrated throughout the whole world has become a dung-heap in the new city, which its founder called Aelia, and has become a dwelling-place for owls.

In vain they say daily in their synagogues: “Over all these things, O Lord,”

[Note: “Again the Ambrosian manuscript has ‘we shall endure,’ and ‘afflict us.’”]

“will you endure and afflict us, and humble us exceedingly?”

We can refer these things to the Church, or to the soul of a holy man, which may rightly be called a watchtower and a vision of peace when the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit have dwelt in it.

But if, through the fault either of ourselves or of the people, such a Zion has been abandoned by the Lord, it will immediately be exposed to the burning of the devil’s fiery arrows: “For the hearts of all adulterers are like an oven.”

When the cold of chastity has been driven out, the flame of lust will rage in the temple of God, so that whatever was formerly glorious and renowned in us may fall, be destroyed, and perish.

And what is written in the Psalms will be fulfilled: “They burned your sanctuary with fire; they profaned on the earth the dwelling-place of your name.”

Only he can extinguish this—the one from whose belly flow rivers of living water.

**BOOK EIGHTEEN**

[Col. 0627]

[Col. 0627A] 767–768 The Twenty-Second Book on Isaiah—or rather, the final book—is dedicated to your name, O Eustochium, and to that of your holy mother Paula, so that I may now recall those whom I honored equally with equal remembrance. This is especially fitting since, while she was alive, she repeatedly requested this work together with you, and your most learned brother Pammachius never ceased urging me, both then and afterward, through frequent letters. For me, too, the same religious devotion is owed to present and absent friends, and to men and women sleeping in Christ—that is, love of souls, not of bodies.

Nor am I unaware how great is the diversity of opinion among human beings. I do not speak of the mystery of the Trinity, whose correct confession is ignorance of knowledge, but of other ecclesiastical doctrines: the Resurrection, namely; the condition of souls and of human flesh; the promises of future things, how they ought to be understood; and the manner in which the Apocalypse of John should be interpreted. If we take it according to the letter, we must become Jews; if we explain it spiritually, as it was written, we may appear to contradict the opinions of many of the ancients: among the Latins, Tertullian, Victorinus, and Lactantius; among the Greeks—to pass over the others—I shall mention only Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons.

[Note: [Col. 0628D] At this point Valesius charges the holy Doctor with saying that the book written by Dionysius against Nepos was written against Irenaeus. Jerome himself, however, carefully enumerating Dionysius’s writings in the Catalogue, mentions none against Irenaeus, but two books against Bishop Nepos, who affirmed in his writings a corporeal kingdom of a thousand years. Yet Jerome may here be understood to call the book written against Irenaeus in the sense that, although Irenaeus’s name did not appear in its title, the work nevertheless frequently refuted his opinion.]

Against him the most eloquent Dionysius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church, wrote an elegant book, ridiculing the fable of the thousand years; Jerusalem on earth, golden and adorned with jewels; the restoration of the Temple; the blood of sacrifices; the leisure of the Sabbath; the injury of circumcision; marriages; childbirth; the upbringing of children; the delights of banquets; and the enslavement of all nations; and again, wars, armies, and triumphs, the slaughter of the defeated, and the death of the sinner who has reached a hundred years.

[Note: [Col. 0627D] I presume that the book which has been lost is the one On the Hope of the Faithful, which he explicitly praises below in chapter 36 of Ezekiel. Nevertheless, what his opinion there was concerning Christ’s thousand-year reign, Tertullian presents most clearly in another work which he later wrote against Marcion, the same Tertullian whom he cites in chapter 24. From this you may learn that he by no means approved the pleasures, marriages, childbirths, Jewish sacrifices, and so forth which Jerome here attributes to others, but only the restoration of the city of Jerusalem and the abundance of all good things, spiritual in particular. Compare Saint Augustine, City of God, book XX, chapter 7.]

Apollinarius replied to him in two volumes. Not only the members of his own sect but also a very large number of our people follow him, at least on this point; so much so that I already foresee, with prophetic awareness, how much fury will be stirred up against me. I do not envy them if they love the earth so much that they desire earthly things in Christ’s kingdom, and, after abundance of food and the gluttony of throat and belly, seek the things that belong below the belly. Of these the apostle Paul says: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. VI, 13). And: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Rom. XIV, 17). The Lord and Savior likewise says: “You are mistaken, because you do not know the Scriptures or the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but they will be like the angels” (Matt. XXII, 29–30).

Nor, in saying this, do I remove the reality of bodies, which I confess will rise incorruptible and immortal, so that they may change their glory, not their substance. We must therefore proceed along the straight path, turning neither to the left nor to the right—that is, following neither Jewish nor heretical error. Some, being carnal, love only flesh; others, ungrateful for God’s gifts, refuse to possess what Christ had both when he was born and when he rose again.

For when the Apostles thought he was a spirit—or, according to the Gospel according to the Hebrews, which the Nazarenes read, an incorporeal demon—he said to them: “Why are you troubled, and why do thoughts arise in your hearts? See my hands and my feet, for it is I myself. Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.” And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and feet (Luke XXIV, 38–39). Again, he spoke to Thomas, who was doubtful: “Put your finger here and see my hands; extend your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving but believing” (John XX, 27).

Finally, to prove the reality of his body, he is reported to have taken food, just as he had commanded food to be given to the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue whom he raised from the dead. Lazarus also, so that his resurrection would not be thought a phantom, is said to have dined with the Savior (Mark V; and Luke XIII; John XII). This was not so that we should eat and drink after the resurrection, as our Millenarians wish, and so that immortal and incorruptible bodies should have to be sustained by earthly nourishment. Otherwise, where there is food, there are illnesses; where there are illnesses, a physician is needed; where there are physicians, there is often death; and then again resurrection and a new way of life from the beginning. Rather, he took food so that the reality of the resurrection might be confirmed by eating.

We are exceedingly cautious about these matters and speak with particular care, knowing that we must walk among serpents and scorpions, which bite and strike in secret (Ezek. II). Concerning them Ecclesiastes also says: “If a serpent bites in silence, he who secretly slanders is no better than it” (Eccles. X, 11). Their father David says: “You sat and spoke against your brother, and you placed a stumbling-block against your mother’s son. You did these things, and I was silent; you thought, wickedly, that I would be like you. I shall rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX, 20–21), so that you may be taught to possess yourself the faults which you accuse in others.

If anyone dislikes the length of my explanations of the Prophets, let him hear plainly that I have said much less than the obscurity of the subject demands, and that anyone can make brief little commentaries for himself from the breadth of my work—though they will not suffice for a complete understanding. The Prophets do not simply narrate history and the sequence of events; everything is full of riddles. Their words sound one thing, while their meanings hold another, so that what you may have thought clear and moving along without difficulty in reading is again wrapped in the obscurities of what follows.

[Col. 0629B] But it is time for me to bring the prophetic volume to an end. If, in explaining it, I have been more prolix than usual, this must be granted to its final portions, which I did not wish to divide, lest the number of books be increased.

### Chapter LXV

**(Verse 1.)** “They sought me who previously did not ask; they found me who did not seek me. I said: Here am I, here am I, to a nation that did not call upon my name.”

The Septuagint: “I appeared to those who were not seeking me; I was found by those who were not asking me. I said: Here am I, in a nation that did not call upon my name.”

In response to the people’s prayer mingled with complaints, in which they had said, “Why have you made us wander, O Lord, from your way? You have hardened our hearts, so that we would not fear you” (Isa. LXIII, 17), God the Father answered, as the Jews wish; but, as we understand it, the Lord and Savior answered. He is not so harsh and cruel that he does not prefer the sinner’s repentance to his death; nor does he reject repentant children who have preserved the dignity of his name, since he wishes to save even strangers (Ezek. XXXIII).

Those who did not seek me, and could not say, “We have found him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the Prophets” (John I, 45), are the very people to whom I appeared. Of them the Prophet also testified elsewhere: “Those to whom he was not announced will see, and those who have not heard will understand” (Isa. LII, 15). But you, who meditate on God’s Law day and night, boast in vain of repentance whose works you do not perform.

Therefore the Evangelists and Apostles, always wishing to strengthen the Lord’s coming by testimonies from the Old Testament, said: “So that what was spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled” (Matt. I, 22). The centurion was not seeking the Lord, yet he heard the Lord say: “I have not found such faith in Israel” (Luke VII, 9; Matt. VIII, 10). The Syrophoenician woman did not know the utterances of the Prophets, yet she was praised by the Lord’s voice: “O woman, great is your faith.” The royal official (John IV), who in Greek is called *basilikos* (βασιλικός), whom we may more accurately interpret as “palatine,” found healing not only for his son but for his entire household.

As for what is said according to the Hebrew: “They sought me who previously did not ask,” it refers to the same meaning: those who previously did not possess knowledge of God afterward seek the Lord and come to know him through revelation. He was revealed even to Paul while he was persecuting the Church (Acts IX). To the apostle Peter he said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 17).

Moses also sought him when he spoke to God: “If I have found favor with you, show yourself openly to me, so that I may see you” (Exod. XXXIII, 13). Considering Christ’s reproach greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, while desiring the recompense of future things, he contemplated the invisible God in his mind as though he saw him. Concerning him it is also read in the Psalms: “The hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea” (Ps. LXIV, 6). And in Genesis: “He himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10).

The following words, “I said: Here am I, here am I, to a nation that did not call upon my name” (Exod. III, 14), agree with the sense: “He who is has sent me to you.” Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, and so forth (Phil. II). Yet, summoning all the nations of the world, he made one nation bearing his name: the Christians.

**(Verse 2.)** “I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving people who walk in a way that is not good, after their own thoughts.”

The Septuagint: “I stretched out my hands all day to an unbelieving and contradicting people, who did not walk in a good way, but after their sins.”

The words stated above—“I appeared to those who did not ask me; I was found by those who did not seek me”—the apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, explained with reference to the person of the Gentiles. Then he added: “But to Israel he says: I stretched out my hands to an unbelieving and contradicting people” (Rom. X, 21). Although they were overcome by the Lord’s benefits and saw signs surpassing anything human, they said: “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul, the prince of demons” (Luke XI, 15). And again: “You are a Samaritan and have a demon” (John VIII, 48). And again: “Although you are a man, you make yourself God” (John X, 33). And elsewhere: “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the Sabbath” (John IX, 16). There are many other examples, which it would take too long to list.

Finally, when he stretched out his hands on the cross toward the unbelieving people and said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34), they, on the contrary, said: “Ha! You who destroy the Temple and build it in three days, come down now from the cross, and we will believe him.” He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matt. XXVII, 40).

Simeon also prophesied of him while holding the child in his arms: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke II, 34). At Rome the Jews said to Paul: “We know concerning this sect that it is opposed everywhere” (Acts XXVIII, 22).

We may also understand his outstretched hands as signifying the generosity of the giver, since he denied them nothing when they asked: he immediately restored health to the leper who begged him (Matt. VIII), and gave sight to the man blind from birth (John IX), and in the desert thousands of people, apart from children and women, were satisfied when they were hungry (Matt. XIV).

The outstretched hands also signify a parent’s mercy, eager to receive his children into his embrace. But they, on the contrary, “walked in a way that is not good” and followed their own thoughts. Through the Prophet the Lord says to them: “Turn your foot away from the difficult path” (Prov. IV, 27). For they had loved strangers and, like a prostitute, had said: “I shall go after my lovers” (Hos. II, 5).

Abandoning the good way, which says in the Gospel, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6), they walked along the broad and spacious way that leads to death. They followed their own thoughts, which the Prophet sought to avoid when he entreated the Lord: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my secret faults, and spare your servant from strangers. If they do not rule over me, then I shall be blameless” (Ps. XVIII, 13–14). The Apostle teaches that those who did not possess knowledge of God were handed over to a debased mind and evil works, so that they might do what is unfitting (Rom. I).

Let us instead say in the Psalmist’s words: “Lead me in the right way” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 24).

**(Verse 3.)** “A people who provoke me to anger, always before my face; who sacrifice in gardens and burn incense upon bricks” (from Exod. XX, 4).

The Septuagint: “This people provokes me in my sight; they always sacrifice in gardens and burn incense upon a brick—[to] demons who do not exist.”

When the Lord said, “You shall not make an idol for yourself, nor any likeness of all that is in heaven or upon the earth,” and Moses rebuked those who made such things: “They provoked me with foreign gods and angered me with their abominations. They sacrificed to demons and not to God” (Deut. XXXII, 16–17), these people, in their deliberate eagerness to sin—as though they were irritating and provoking God—not only did what was forbidden, but did it continually and without interruption. They sinned in the sight of the Lord, whose eyes see everything, or in his Temple, sacrificing victims to idols.

And, so that nothing might be lacking from their sacrilege, they sacrificed in gardens and burned incense upon bricks, joining the luxury of idolatry to pleasure in sacrifices. Instead of the one altar which God’s Law ordered to be constructed from unhewn stones, they stained baked bricks and clods of earth with the blood of victims.

This is the literal meaning. Otherwise, according to the spiritual understanding, every heretic provokes the Lord to anger and offers unclean sacrifices in the falsity of his doctrines. These are by no means firm or destined to endure forever, but flourish briefly like gardens, providing for the pleasures of the flesh. To such a person it is said: “All flesh is grass, and all its glory is like the flower of grass. The grass withers and the flower falls, but the word of the Lord, which is preached in the churches, remains forever” (Isa. XL, 6–7).

Naboth, unwilling to allow his vineyard to become such gardens, shed his blood under the most wicked king Ahab (III Kings XXII). It was not fitting that the ancestral inheritance should perish, and that, once the vineyards which produce fruit that gladdens the heart of man had been cut down, vegetables of pleasures and vices should grow in the place of virtues.

A saying celebrated and praised among the Greeks, attributed with good reason to a very wise man, is said to call all the pleasures of the world, the pomp of the age, and rapidly passing luxury “the gardens of Adonis.”

Heretics also sacrifice upon stones when they strive to establish their errors and carefully fashioned lies through the art of dialectic, building them into a square and strengthening them with what they call *linear necessities* (γραμμικαῖς ἀνάγκαις), that is, with lines cut and drawn upon the surface of dust on a brick.

[Note: [Col. 0631D] “Linear necessities,” and so forth. Let fair-minded and prudent readers now concede to me that the true and genuine Jerome has not previously been published. For here he uses Greek words which were unknown to Erasmus and Marianus, who were not greatly trained by reading manuscript codices. Instead of mathematical demonstrations, or compelling arguments and reasons, which are signified by γραμμικαὶ ἀνάγκαι, they inserted “lines drawn in the dust,” reading as follows: “and with, as they say, angular lines” (ἐγκονίοις ... γραμμαῖς), that is, “with lines cut and drawn on the surface of dust,” and sought to strengthen them. Although this may seem to fit the sense of the passage, it is false and an interpolation, because it is found in no manuscript copy, whereas all copies—not even one excepted—retain the reading which we have published. MARTIAN.]

[Col. 0632D] Thus geometers call their demonstrations “linear necessities” (γραμμικαὶ ἀνάγκαι); hence Quintilian also said *grammatikai apodeixeis* (γραμμικαὶ ἀποδείξεις) in book I, chapter 10, and book V, chapter 10, and *grammikōs apodeiknysthai* (γραμμικῶς ἀποδείκνυσθαι), “to demonstrate by lines.” Sextus Empiricus uses this expression against the geometers, since it properly means to demonstrate by lines, as Jerome explains: “to strengthen what has been cut and drawn in lines upon the surface of dust.” Some, however, read “upon bricks.” Since Erasmus did not understand the Greek reading, he nevertheless ingeniously supplied “with, as they say, angular lines” (ἐγκονίοις, ὡς φασίν, γραμμαῖς), and Victorius followed him.]

As for the reading in the Septuagint, “to demons who do not exist,” which is not found in the Hebrew, it should be understood in this sense: both literally and spiritually, demons do not remain, because they have already fallen away from God, who truly exists; nor do the sects of heretics remain, since they retain no truth but pass away and perish in the likeness of shadows.

Thus Esther says to the Lord: “Do not hand over your inheritance to those who do not exist” (Esther XIV, 11). And the saint prays in the Psalm: “Forgive me, so that I may be refreshed before I depart and cease to exist” (Ps. XXXVIII, 14). For one who, while living in this body, does not obtain forgiveness of sins and thus departs from life is lost to God and ceases to exist, although he continues to exist for himself in punishments.

**(Verses 4–5.)** “Those who dwell in tombs and sleep in the shrines of idols; who eat swine’s flesh and broth that is profane in their vessels; who say, ‘Withdraw from me; do not come near me, for you are unclean.’”

The Septuagint: “They sleep in tombs and caves because of dreams; they eat swine’s flesh and the broth of sacrifices; all their vessels are profane; they say, ‘Go far from me; do not come near me, for I am clean.’”

There was no form of sacrilege which the people of Israel omitted. Not only did they sacrifice in gardens and burn incense upon bricks, but they also sat or lived in tombs and slept in the shrines of idols. They were accustomed to lie upon the skins of victims spread there, so that through dreams they might learn future things.

This error is practiced to this day in the temple of Aesculapius by many pagans and others; such places are nothing other than the tombs of the dead.

Nor were they satisfied with this limit of impiety. They also ate the flesh of pigs, which the Law had forbidden, and eagerly swallowed yesterday’s broth, which the Greeks call *heōlon* (ἕωλον) (Lev. XI).

[Note: [Col. 0633D] That is, food or drink from the previous day, or yesterday’s food. Exodus XVI, 23 commands that on the day before the Sabbath food should be cooked and set aside for the following day, to be eaten on the Sabbath itself; and in chapter XXXV, 3, lighting a fire throughout the houses on the Sabbath is forbidden. The Greeks call it ἕωλον; hence Saint Ignatius, in his Letter to the Magnesians, says, “not eating stale food” (οὐχ ἕωλα ἐσθίων). See the Talmudic treatise on the Sabbath, where the furnace in which hot foods are preserved is also discussed.]

Thus both they and their vessels were unclean. They increased daily in shamelessness and arrogance to such an extent that they considered anyone who was not led by the same error unclean and avoided his touch. This is what the Samaritans and Jews do to us, and all heretics, such as recently sprang up under a deranged teacher in Gaul.

[Note: [Col. 0633D] The reference is certainly to Vigilantius, against whom Jerome wrote. He says: “They endure in Gaul a native enemy, a man of unsettled mind, who ought to be bound in Hippocrates’ chains. They see him sitting in the church and saying, among other blasphemous words, this also: ‘Why is it necessary for you not only to honor with such great honor but even to adore that object—I do not know what it is—which you carry about and venerate in a small vessel?’ And again, in the same book: ‘Why do you kiss and adore the dust wrapped in linen?’” See what we have said about his heresy and homeland in the preface to Jerome’s books against him. MARTIAN.]

These people avoid the basilicas of the martyrs and shun us, who customarily celebrate prayers there, as though we were unclean. Yet it is not so much they who do this as the demons inhabiting those places, who cannot endure the power and scourges of the holy ashes.

Which heretic does not rest in memorials or sleep in the caves of his teachers? Such were Marcion and Valentinus, and recently Eunomius, who displayed the uncleanness of his mind through leprous flesh. They abandoned the light of the Holy Spirit and the upper room in which the Apostles dwelt, remain in the darkness of the devil, and love the caves which Jeremiah condemns in mystical language: “My inheritance has become for me like the cave of a hyena” (Jer. XII, 8), an animal which our people call a beast. This creature always pursues corpses and lives on the fluid and corruption of dead bodies.

Against those who dwell in caves, Habakkuk also spoke in a lamentable voice: “Woe to him who gives his neighbor drink of turbid potion and intoxicates him, so that he may look upon his caves” (Hab. II, 15).

[Note: [Col. 0634D] The word “friend” was added, although it is superfluous here, and was transferred from the Latin version. Then “his neighbor” will be superfluous. Victorius, however, reads: “who gives his neighbor his own overturning as a turbid drink,” following the Septuagint, who translated the Hebrew word as ἀνατροπήν, “overturning.”]

Concerning these caves the Lord also spoke: “It is written, ‘My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a cave of thieves” (Matt. XXI, 13). In them you kill the souls of the deceived, so that they do not see in them the visions of which the same Savior says: “I multiplied visions, and I was represented by the hands of the Prophets” (Hos. XII, 10). Another says to him: “You spoke in a vision to your sons” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 20).

But they believe in dreams and phantoms, although the Lord commanded that such things should not be believed.

These people eat the flesh of pigs, concerning whom it is said: “Do not cast your pearls before pigs” (Matt. VII, 6). They also eat profane broth, prepared by heretical skill in their books. All their vessels are unclean, both their bodies and their doctrines, and they fall into such madness that they detest as lost anyone among them who is not like them.

**(Verses 6–7.)** “These will be smoke in my anger, a burning fire all day. Behold, it is written before me: I will not be silent, but I will repay and recompense into their bosom your iniquities and the iniquities of your fathers together, says the Lord, who sacrificed upon the mountains and upon the hills and reproached me; I will measure out their former work into their bosom.”

The Septuagint: “This is the smoke of my anger; fire burns in it all the days. Behold, it is written in my sight: I will not be silent until I repay and recompense into their bosom their sins and those of their fathers, says the Lord. They burned incense upon the mountains and upon the hills; they reproached me. I will repay their works into their bosom—or, according to another reading, ‘into his bosom.’”

Because of your works and the incredible arrogance of your mind, by which, though unclean, you considered the clean unclean, you will be smoke and a burning fire—or, according to another reading, “of burning fire”—kindled from my anger.

Anger, forgetfulness, wrath, and repentance must be understood in God in the same manner as feet, hands, eyes, ears, and the other limbs which the incorporeal and invisible God is said to possess. This does not mean that he is subject to these passions, for by the gift of his grace he extinguishes them in us; rather, through our language we understand God’s attitude toward us.

For the anger which is defined as a desire for vengeance is not understood in God as it is in human beings. In us it has its source in our vices, not in the Lord’s will. We store up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, so that his wise flame may consume our thorns, briars, and weeds—which we have brought forth instead of God’s seed—as well as the wood, hay, and straw which we have built upon Paul’s foundation (1 Cor. III).

Of this perpetual fire we also read in Moses’ song: “A fire has been kindled from my anger, and it will burn to the depths of hell below. It will devour the earth and its crops; it will burn the foundations of the mountains, and my arrows will consume them” (Deut. XXXII, 22–23). The meaning of this testimony is that God’s fire and vengeance always burn against sinners and pursue them even to the underworld.

Such was the rich man in the Gospel, dressed in purple (Luke XVI), who, while Lazarus rested in Abraham’s bosom, was tormented by eternal flames.

The same fire will also burn the earth—that is, our flesh—and its crops—that is, the desires of the flesh—and the foundations of the mountains that raise themselves against the knowledge of God. God’s arrows will destroy the mountains themselves, so that, humbled in punishments, they may cease to be mountains.

“Behold,” he says, “it is written before me.” All our sins are open to God’s eyes and are written in the books of which we read in Daniel: “Thrones were set, and the books were opened” (Dan. VII, 9–10). Of these books it is said elsewhere: “Let them be written upon the earth” (Jer. XVII, 13).

He will no longer remain silent who previously said, “I was silent.” “Will I always be silent?” says the Lord (Isa. XLII, 14). He will repay each person what he has done, “into his bosom”—that is, into the secret place of his heart—so that his own conscience may torment him.

Of this the prophet Hosea also prophesies: “Their princes will fall by the sword because of the indiscipline of their tongue” (Hos. VII, 16). This is their slander returning into their bosom, proceeding from each person’s heart.

Something similar is written in Proverbs: “All the wicked receive their iniquities into their own bosom” (Prov. V, 22). This bosom, because of the ruling part of the soul—*the hegemonikon* (ἡγεμονικόν)—is elsewhere called by another name, “the head”: “I have given their ways into their heads” (Ezek. IX, 10). And elsewhere: “His sorrow will return upon his head, and his iniquity will descend upon his crown” (Ps. VII, 17).

There is also a good bosom, which enjoys the holiness of conscience, of which the Psalmist said: “My prayer will return into my bosom” (Ps. XXXIV, 13). “Bosom” may also be understood as any affection and love, as when speech is addressed to a husband: “The wife who is in your bosom”; or to a parent: “They will bring your children into your bosom” (Luke XVI).

Hence all who have Abraham as their father and have been worthy to resemble his virtues rest in his bosom.

We must not understand the fathers whose iniquities and sins are now repaid to us as those from whose seed our bodies were born. Otherwise Moses himself, who had said that the sins of fathers are repaid to their children to the third and fourth generation, namely, to those who hate God (Exod. XX, 5), interprets his own statement by saying: “The children shall not die for the sins of their fathers, but each person shall die in his own sin” (Deut. XXIV, 16).

Ezekiel confirms the same judgment, so that the proverb is not said: “The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (Ezek. XVIII, 2), but only the teeth of the one who ate should be set on edge; the sinful soul itself perishes, and does not suffer for the sins of others.

From this we understand that the fathers must be taken either in a good or in an opposing sense: they are those whom each person joins when he departs from this life.

Israel sacrificed upon mountains and hills when it set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan. It reproached God concerning his commandments when it neglected his ceremonies and gave the worship due to God to demons. Their works will be repaid into their bosom (Hos. IV).

Every heretic likewise, despising ecclesiastical simplicity, sacrifices upon mountains and reproaches God by disregarding his commandments.

(V. 8.) Thus says the Lord: “As when a grape-cluster is found and it is said, ‘Do not destroy it, because there is a blessing in it,’ so I shall act for the sake of my servants, so that I may not destroy everything.” The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the Lord: As when a grape is found in a cluster and it is said, ‘Do not touch it, because there is a blessing in it,’ so I shall act for the sake of my servant, so that I may not destroy them all.”

The Lord had said that Israel would perish, that all its sins lay open to his sight, and that he would repay each person’s deeds in his own bosom. After this he introduces a likeness and an example of comparison, by which he teaches that each person perishes through his own sin and that, even if the multitude of sinners is very great, one righteous person does not perish through the fault of all.

“If someone,” he says, “finds in a grape-cluster—or in a grape that has not been able to reach maturity, has produced sour fruit, or has been spoiled by some defect of air or earth—one sound grape-seed that still has hope of growing larger and reaching its customary maturity, he may say to another, ‘Do not touch it, but leave it so that it may grow, because it is the Lord’s blessing’: so, he says, from the innumerable multitude of the Jews, who have offended God, if I find a few righteous people, I shall rescue them from the destruction of the many.” And I shall do this for the sake of my servants Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, to whom the promise was made—or for the sake of those who serve me amid the many sinners.

We read something similar in Genesis, when righteous people are gradually sought out, from fifty down to ten, who might deliver the city from sin (Gen. XVIII), and Lot alone, together with his daughters, is rescued as righteous from Sodom (Gen. XIX). Concerning him it is written in the [Note: [Col. 0635D] In the Catholic Epistle. On the authority of Victorius, from the Ambrosian manuscript, we have restored *Catholica* (“Catholic”). Martianus, together with Erasmus, retained *canon­ica* (“canonical”). Much will have to be said about this word in its proper place. —Contrary to his usual practice, Jerome calls the Second Epistle of Blessed Peter “Canonical,” although elsewhere he always calls the seven Epistles of this kind “Catholic.” Nevertheless, Marianus Victorius ought not to have altered this reading, since he had no manuscript to support its restoration at this point.
