But I, who can do nothing against the truth and everything on behalf of the truth, did not think that I should conceal the agreement of all the manuscript copies, even though it appears somewhat contrary to the conjecture that I proposed in my Annotations on the Prologue prefixed to the Seven Canonical Epistles in the first volume of our edition. MARTIAN.] Catholic Epistle it is written (II Pet. II), that his soul was tormented when he saw unspeakable acts being committed, and that the judgment of his soul was demonstrated by the condition of his body. Enoch also, amid the very great multitude of sinners, was alone taken up to God (Gen. V). And the Flood could not destroy Noah together with his children, although all flesh had turned away from the Lord’s service (Gen. VII). Abraham, too, was preserved from the fire of the Chaldeans through the integrity of his faith (Gen. XI).

To the same meaning agree the words of Jeremiah, spoken in the person of the Lord: “As a warm thing in the wilderness, I found Israel among those slain by the sword” (Jer. XXXVIII, 2 according to the Septuagint; in the Vulgate XXXI, 2). For when, he says, the whole world lay lifeless, wounded by the swords of idolatry, I found Israel in Abraham possessing the warmth of faith—like a physician who, after a battle, among the corpses of the dead, when he senses that one person has some life remaining in him through the beating of his veins, applies care to his wounds [Col. 0637A] in order to restore health.

For what is written as *ὡς θερμὸν*—that is, “as warm”—the Latin translator, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, translated *lupinum* (“lupine”), and many of the Greeks also err in this. Nevertheless, it must be known that in Hebrew *THODA* is written for “warm” [Note: [Col. 0637D] The earlier printed books retain not *thoda* according to the evidence of all the manuscript copies, but the word *hoda*, which cannot mean “grace,” as Jerome intended when he said that Israel was saved by God’s grace, and not by the merit of its works. In this sense, however, *thoda* does not mean grace, that is, mercy, but rather thanksgiving and praise. Nor do we read the word *thoda* in the Hebrew of Jeremiah XXXI, 2, as Jerome expressly observes; instead we read *hen*, which properly signifies grace and mercy. This passage, then, is a reef against which the holy Doctor’s arguments and commentaries run aground, when he accuses the Latin translator and most of the Greeks of error. Yet no critical judge should be appointed over this mistake, since Jerome himself later corrected it in his commentary on Jeremiah. For he says: “Ridiculously, the Latin books, because of the ambiguity of the Greek word, translated *lupine* in this passage instead of *warm*. For the Greek *θερμὸν* signifies both. This word itself, however, is not found in the Hebrew. It is written *HEN* (), which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as *χάριν*, that is, ‘grace.’ The Septuagint alone rendered it ‘warm,’ thinking that the final letter was *M*. For if we read *HAN* with the letter *N*, it means grace; if with *M*, it means warmth.” Jerome wished to say the same thing here in Isaiah, but he did not remember the word *HEN*, because, while reading the Hebrew text of Jeremiah, the preceding word *thoda*, which occurs in Jeremiah XXX, 19, may perhaps have been before his eyes. MARTIAN.] *THODA* (), which is interpreted as “grace”—namely, that Israel was saved by God’s grace and not by the merit of its works.

(V. 9.) “And I shall bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah one who will possess my mountains; and my chosen ones shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. And the plains shall become sheepfolds, and the valley of Achor a resting-place for cattle, for my people who have sought me.” The Septuagint reads: “And I shall bring forth offspring from Jacob and from Judah; and he shall inherit my holy mountain. And my chosen ones shall inherit it, and my servants shall dwell there. And in the forest there shall be sheepfolds, and the valley of Achor a resting-place for cattle, for my people who have given me rest.”

The one whom above he called the grape-cluster, or grape-seed—or, as many wish, the bunch of grapes—he now calls the offspring of Jacob and Judah, who will possess the mountains, or his mountain. Most understand the offspring of Jacob and Judah as Christ, concerning whom it is said in Genesis: “Judah, your brothers shall praise you” (Gen. XLIX, 8), and so forth. No one doubts that the Savior was born from the tribe of Judah.

Others, however, wish the Apostles to be understood, concerning whom we have often spoken: “The remnant shall be saved” (Isa. I, 9); and: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (Rom. IX, 29). These possessed the Lord’s mountain through the consciousness of Christ dwelling in them, saying: “We have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. XII, 22). Or his mountains, concerning which it is sung in the Psalms: “The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. CXXIV, 2); and: “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI, 1).

The Lord’s chosen ones will possess Zion, and his servants will dwell in it. Concerning them it is written in the same volume: “The offspring of Abraham his servant, the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones” (Ps. CIV, 6). Therefore, whoever is still offspring and has not yet been formed into a son is the Lord’s servant, to whom he says in the Gospel: “I know that you are Abraham’s offspring, but you are not yet sons” (John VIII). For if they were Abraham’s offspring, they would certainly do Abraham’s works. But whoever is a son is also the Lord’s chosen one. Hence the chosen one possesses Jerusalem, and the servants dwell in it; and concerning the distinction between sons and servants it is said: “You have not received again the spirit of slavery unto fear, but the spirit of adoption” (Rom. VIII, 15).

“And they shall be,” he says, “the plains—or the forest—in sheepfolds.” In place of “plains,” the Hebrew has *SARON* (). The whole region around Lydda, Joppa, and Jamnia is suitable for grazing flocks. Concerning this it is also written in the Acts of the Apostles: “The forests shall be turned into sheepfolds” (Acts IX), in accordance with what is sung in the Psalm: “The voice of the Lord perfecting the stags, and he will uncover the forests” (Ps. XXVIII, 9)—or the dense parts of the woods—so that robbers may cease to lurk there, and wild beasts and venomous creatures, and places once given to ambushes and bloodshed, may pass into the churches of the Lord, where flocks may be pastured by him who laid down his life for his sheep. Concerning him it is written: “He himself will feed us forever” (Ps. XLV, 15).

This is the voice of the Lord, perfecting the stags and uncovering the dense parts of the forests, which through John cries out in the wilderness: “Now the axe has been laid at the root of the trees. Every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. III, 10). And again: “Every valley shall be filled” (Luke III, 5). Concerning this valley it is now also said: “And the valley of Achor shall be a resting-place for cattle and for my people who have sought me.”

In the book of Joshua son of Nun we also read that Achan was killed there, the man who stole from the devoted things and from the spoils of Jericho; and, since he had troubled the people, the place where this occurred received from that event the name *ACHOR* (), that is, “of trouble and tumult” (Josh. VII). Therefore the valley of Achor, where formerly there was a curse and punishment, will become a resting-place for cattle.

Explaining this, Paul says: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned?” (I Cor. IX, 9), or does he certainly speak about us, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes the threshing-floor ought to thresh in hope, so that he may share in it? Concerning this valley it is also written mystically in Hosea: “I shall speak to her heart”—without doubt meaning Jerusalem—“and I shall give her those who possess her from there, and the valley of Achor, so that she may open her understanding” (Hos. II, 14).

For this reason the valley of Achor is given as a possession to the cattle of God’s people, and the forests are changed into sheepfolds, so that understanding may be opened and the Lord’s truth may be known.

(Vv. 11, 12.) “But you who have forsaken the Lord and forgotten my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it: I shall number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter.” The Septuagint reads: “But you who have forsaken me and forgotten my holy mountain, who prepare a table for Fortune and fill a drink-offering for the demon: I shall hand you over to the sword; you shall all fall slain.”

In places that were formerly wooded and full of disturbances, in gentile places, there will be sheepfolds—that is, churches of believers from the whole world. But you, O people of Israel, who have forsaken the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger, who have forgotten his holy mountain—about which we have often spoken, either the Lord the Savior, who is the mountain of mountains and the holy one of all the holy ones, or Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem—you who do these things, I shall hand over to the sword, so that you may all fall together, slain. What the sword is, we shall say later.

“You set,” he says, “a table for Fortune and pour libations upon it”; or, according to the Septuagint: “You prepare a table for Fortune and fill a cup for the demon,” or *κέρασμα*, which they all translated similarly, namely, “a mixed drink.”

There is an ancient custom of idolatry in all cities, and especially in Egypt and Alexandria: on the last day of the year and of their final month, they set out a table filled with various kinds of food and a cup mixed with honey-wine, making omens for the fertility either of the past year or of the coming year. The Israelites did this while venerating the monstrous forms of all the idols together; they poured libations not upon an altar with sacrifices, but upon such a table.

What the Septuagint translated as “demon” is *MENNI* () in Hebrew. Symmachus interpreted it as “apart from me,” so that the sense is: “You prepare a table for Fortune and fill a drink-offering apart from me”—to show that it is made not for God but for a demon.

The sword by which they are killed is understood as punishment. For the whole people of Israel was not handed over to the sword, since we see how many thousands of them are scattered throughout the whole world; rather, they were handed over to punishments and torments, captivity, and the ultimate slavery, in accordance with what is said elsewhere: “All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword”; and in the Song of Deuteronomy: “I shall make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour the flesh of the wounded” (Deut. XXXII, 42).

It cannot be believed that the Lord’s arrows become drunk with blood and that his sword is filled with the flesh of the wounded. He speaks of those arrows by which Job was punished at every moment: “The arrows of the Lord are in my body; their fury drinks up my spirit; when I begin to speak, they pierce me” (Job VI, 4) [Note: [Col. 0639D] The Ambrosian manuscript alone reads “blood” in place of “spirit,” and this agrees better with the Septuagint.].

According to the allegorical sense, however, this must be said: all who abandon the Church and forget God’s holy mountain, and give themselves over to spirits of error and doctrines of demons, prepare a table for Fortune, believing that nothing pertains to God but that everything is governed either by the course of the stars or by the variability of Fortune. Paul rebukes them, saying: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons” (I Cor. X, 20–21). For they will be handed over to eternal punishments, so that none of them will be able to escape slaughter and ruin.

(V. 12.) “Because I called and you did not answer; I spoke and you did not listen. But you did evil in my sight, and you chose what I did not want.” The Septuagint reads: “Because I called you and you did not listen; I spoke and you despised me; you did evil in my sight, and you chose what I did not want.”

“You have been handed over to the sword,” he says, because you not only abandoned me, forgot me, and mixed the cup of Fortune, but, when I was Emmanuel—that is, “God with us,” of whom John also writes, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14)—I called you while present: “Return, returning children” (Jer. III, 14); and: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. XI, 28). Yet you did not wish to answer.

I spoke in parables, and I did everything that I ought to do, but you did not listen to me; indeed, you even despised me. For I am the one of whom I said above: “I came, and there was no man; I called, and there was no one who obeyed” (Isa. L, 2).

Nor was this impiety sufficient for you: to despise me when I was present and to kill the heir sent to you. You did evil in my sight and chose what I did not want, and you blasphemed the Son of God, so that you might ask for Barabbas, a robber and the instigator of murder and rebellion. And still you dare to say: “Why did you make us wander from your way?” (Isa. LXIII, 17).

For if those who did not know me found me, and those who did not call upon me received me, what torments are you worthy of, who refused to receive the one sent to you, who said: “I have not come except for the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV, 24), and who, in addition, fastened him to the cross?

We must consider what he means when he says, “And you chose what I did not want,” and what the will of the Son of God is, who says in the Gospel: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII, 21). Concerning this will God himself also says: “I desired to do your will” (Ps. XXXIX, 9).

This is the will of which the Lord himself also spoke: “I have found David, son of Jesse, a man according to my heart, who will do all my wills” (Acts XIII, 22). Hence the saint prays and says: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God” (Ps. CXLII, 10).

Everything is lawful, but not everything is beneficial. Concerning virgins, the Apostle says that he does not have a commandment from the Lord, yet he wishes us to be as he is himself (I Cor. VI). From this he shows that we should by no means follow the teacher’s permission, but his will (I Cor. VII), and that we ought to choose what is beneficial, not what is merely lawful. Such is the matter of second marriage: “I want the younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households” (I Tim. V, 14). He gives the reasons why he permits this: “For some have already turned back after Satan.” Therefore the will concerning a second marriage is not pure; it becomes less honorable by comparison with fornication [Note: [Col. 0640D] The same Ambrosian manuscript has “which, as a cause of fornication, is rendered less honorable by comparison.”].

(Vv. 13, 14.) “Therefore thus says the Lord God: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall praise because of the exultation of their heart, but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart, and because of the brokenness of your spirit you shall howl.” The Septuagint reads: “Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry. Behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. Behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. Behold, my servants shall exult in joy, but you shall cry out because of the pain of your heart, and because of the brokenness of your spirit you shall howl.”

You who have forsaken the Lord, done evil in his sight, and refused to listen to him while he was present will not merely fall by the sword; you will also see a great distinction between yourselves and the multitude of the nations.

Those who will be my servants will eat and drink, rejoice, and praise because of the exultation of their heart. You, on the contrary, will be hungry and thirsty, put to shame, and because of the pain of your heart and the brokenness of your spirit you will howl.

The *chiliasts* think that all these things will be fulfilled in a thousand years. They believe that food and drink constitute the kingdom of God, without understanding what is written: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for the bread of life and truth” (John VI, 27). They desire to eat the flesh of Christ and the fruit of the tree of life. Concerning this the Savior says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI, 33). Ecclesiastes says: “Open your eyes, and be filled with bread” (Prov. XX, 13). And the Psalmist says: “I was young, and then I grew old, and I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread. All day long he shows mercy and lends, and his offspring shall be in blessing” (Ps. XXXVI, 25).

Concerning this bread and spiritual banquet he instructed the disciples: “You who have remained with me in my temptations shall eat at my Father’s table in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke XXII, 28).

But if we understand this as ordinary bread, how shall we explain: “The Lord will not kill the righteous soul with hunger” (Prov. X, 3)? And again: “The Lord knows the ways of the blameless, and their inheritance shall be forever. They shall not be put to shame in the evil time, and in days of famine they shall be satisfied” (Ps. XXXVI, 18–19).

For how many holy people die in persecution, exhausted by hunger and poverty? How many righteous people hunger while the wicked are swollen with excess? The drink, however, must be understood as that which is drawn from the springs of Israel. Whoever drinks it will have within himself a spring of water leaping up into eternal life (John IV; Luke XXII). The Savior promises that he will drink of it with the Apostles in his Father’s kingdom. It “makes the heart of man glad” (Ps. CIII, 14), so that those who drink can say: “You have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. IV, 7).

Of this food and drink it is said among the eight beatitudes: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. V, 6). The mother of the Lord, filled with the Holy Spirit, prophesied: “He has filled the hungry with good things” (Luke I, 53)—those who previously did not possess the Lord’s food—and “he has sent the rich away empty,” those who were handed over for his burial and rejected the one whom the Prophets had promised.

Concerning them the Psalmist also sings elsewhere: “The rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII, 11)—that is, the Jewish people. But those who seek the Lord, that is, the multitude of the gentiles, “shall not lack any good thing.”

When those who serve Christ and believe in him have rejoiced and praised God because of the exultation and joy of their heart, then the others will be put to shame, seeing that others have succeeded to their place. They will cry out because of the pain of their heart, fulfilling what is written: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XIII, 50), when the lambs of the gentiles and the righteous stand at the right hand, and the goats of the Jews and the impious at the left—when some receive eternal rewards and others eternal punishments.

The brokenness of the spirit because of the pain of the heart must be understood as occurring in the conscience of sinners, in accordance with what is written: “Those who wander in spirit shall know understanding” (Isa. XXIX, 24); and: “A contrite and humbled heart you will not despise, O God” (Ps. L, 19).

The spirit is broken when it has been lifted up. Concerning the hostile king of Israel it is written: “The Lord hardened his spirit” (IV Kings XVII, 14). The same is said of the ruler of the Babylonians, when his heart was lifted up and his spirit hardened, so that in his pride he said: “This is Babylon, and I made it” (Dan. IV, 27).

(Vv. 15, 16.) “And you shall leave your name for an oath to my chosen ones, and the Lord God shall kill you, but he shall call his servants by another name. Whoever is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in the God Amen; and whoever swears upon the earth shall swear by the God Amen.” The Septuagint reads: “For you shall leave your name as a fullness for my chosen ones. But the Lord shall kill you, while those who serve me shall be called by a new name, and he shall be blessed upon the earth; for they shall bless the true God, and those who swear upon the earth shall swear by the true God.”

In place of “fullness,” the Hebrew has *SABAA* () [Note: [Col. 0641D] This is the Hebrew word *Sabaa*, and so forth. Jerome did not read *Sebaa* according to modern practice, because in his time the Hebrews rarely had vowel letters in the middle of words, as he himself elsewhere bears witness. The manuscript copies consistently retain *Sabaa*, which we have followed, although we have placed *Sebua* in the margin according to modern pointing. Consult the Questions on Genesis concerning this word. MARTIAN.], while the others interpret it as “oath.” This word has many meanings and varies according to the different accents [Note: [Col. 0642D] See Genesis XLI, 29, and what we have noted concerning the meaning of the Hebrew accent in the commentary on Ecclesiastes II, 23 and XII.]. It may mean an oath, fullness, satiety, many, or seven. We discussed this in the book of Genesis and in this volume, where seven women seized one man (on chapter IV).

Again, in place of what the Septuagint translated as “true,” and what is *AMEN* () in Hebrew [Note: [Col. 0642D] Aquila translated it as *πεπιστωμένως*, “faithfully.” Jerome asserts the same. The printed editions incorrectly read *πιστομένως*. MARTIAN.], Aquila translated *πεπιστωμένως*, that is, “faithfully.”

The meaning is this: when others succeed to your place, your name will be an oath for my chosen ones, so that they may take you as an example of evil and detest suffering such things, swearing, “I shall not endure what the Jewish people endured.”

Or your name will become fullness, as is customary to say of those whose recollection and memory are hateful, and who have proceeded as far as fullness and nausea.

Or, certainly, this may be said: they will leave their name to the Lord’s chosen ones, so that the multitude of the gentiles may succeed to their place, and they themselves may be called the sons of Abraham and Israel. Concerning them Paul says: “Peace upon them and upon the Israel of God” (Gal. VI, 16). For not all who are from Israel are Israel, nor are all who are Abraham’s offspring sons (Rom. IX, 7). To them it is said: “If you were Abraham’s sons, you would do Abraham’s works” (John VIII, 39).

Because they are Abraham’s offspring and not sons, concerning whose distinction we spoke above, John the Baptist rebukes them, saying: “Do not wish to say, ‘We have Abraham as father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III, 9). For how can they be his sons who said to wood and stone, “You gave birth to me,” when, on the contrary, those who are from faith are called Abraham’s sons?

“But you,” he says, “the Lord shall kill, so that you may no longer be called circumcision but mutilation” (Gal. III)—so that you may lack eternal life and not possess the one who says: “I am life” (John XIV, 6).

“But his servants,” he says, “he will call by another or new name,” which will be celebrated throughout the whole world. And it will be blessed, to such an extent that whoever is called by that name will be blessed in the Lord and will receive the sign of true circumcision, *Amen*, a word the Lord often uses in the Gospel to confirm what has been said: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John V, 19).

The new or other name is none other than that which derives from the name of Christ, so that God’s people may no longer be called Jacob, Judah, Israel, Ephraim, or Joseph, but Christian. For whoever swears upon the earth will no longer swear by idols and false gods, but by God; and this statement is again confirmed by the seal of *Amen*.

According to the Septuagint, however, which translated *Amen* as “the true God”—so that God may be blessed as the true God and those who swear upon the earth may swear by the true God—we do not refer this, in accordance with the error of the Arians, only to the person of God the Father, concerning whom it is written: “That they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3), but also to the Son, who himself is true God. The evangelist John says: “The Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know the true one and be in his true Son Jesus Christ” (John V, 20). “This is the true God and eternal life.”

For if the Savior says of himself, “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6), then, consequently, the true God received his name from truth, so that he may not be called God according to the false gods, but according to the true God the Father, and may himself be the true God. Otherwise, if he is not true, he will be like an idol—a conclusion that rebounds upon the heads of those who deny that Christ is true God.

This is the new name that is written for him in the Apocalypse upon the little stone (chap. II), and by which he is blessed throughout the whole world.

(Vv. 17, 18.) “For the former troubles have been forgotten, and they have been hidden from my eyes. For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered, nor shall they rise upon the heart. But you shall rejoice and exult forever in the things that I create.” The Septuagint reads: “For they shall forget the former tribulation, and it shall not rise upon their heart. For there shall be a new heaven and a new earth, and they shall not remember the former things, nor shall they come upon their heart; but they shall find joy and exultation in it.”

The cause of joy and confession of the true God is that eternal forgetfulness of former troubles will follow, so that they will no longer remember idols and their former error, but will pass from darkness into light and enjoy eternal blessedness.

They will forget their former evils—not through the forgetfulness of memory, but through the succession of good things, in accordance with what is written: “On a good day there is forgetfulness of evils” (Eccles. XI, 27); and elsewhere: “The affliction of an hour causes forgetfulness of pleasures” (ibid., 29), because those placed in distress do not enjoy their former pleasures according to the error of Epicurus.

It is also possible to say that in the new heaven and the new earth all memory of their former way of life will be erased, lest even the recollection of former distress should be part of their evils.

Those who think that everything we see will perish interpret “new heaven and new earth” according to the testimony of the Gospel: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. XXIV, 35), and according to the Apostle Paul: “The things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV, 18).

Those, on the other hand, who understand the newness as a change for the better [Note: [Col. 0643D] Saint Augustine, in *The City of God*, chapter 16, says for all: “Then the form of this world will pass away through the conflagration of worldly fires . . . so that the world, renewed for the better, may clearly be adapted to human beings renewed for the better.”], and not as the destruction of the elements, use this example: “In the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and all things will grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will wrap them up, and they will be changed” (Ps. CI, 26–27).

This plainly demonstrates that “perishing” and “destruction” do not mean abolition into nothingness, but change for the better. For what is written elsewhere, “The moon will shine like the sun, and the sun will receive sevenfold light” (Isa. XXX, 16), does not signify the destruction of the former things, but their change for the better.

To make this intelligible, let us set forth examples from our own condition. When an infant grows into a boy, a boy into a young man, a young man into a man, and a man into an old man, he does not perish through the successive ages. He is the same person who was there before; but he is gradually changed, and is said to have perished with respect to his former age.

Understanding this, the Apostle Paul also said: “For the form of this world is passing away” (I Cor. VII, 31). Let us consider what he said: the form passes away, not the substance.

Peter signifies the same thing: “They willingly overlook this: that the heavens existed from the beginning, and the earth was formed from water and through water by the word of God; through these the former world, being flooded with water, perished. But the heavens and earth that now exist are preserved by the same word for fire” (II Pet. III, 5 ff.). He subsequently teaches the sense in which this must be understood: “But we see new heavens and a new earth, and his promise” (ibid., 13) [Note: [Col. 0645D] *Nos* was printed corruptly for *Novos*, “new”; Greek *καινοὺς δὲ οὐρανοὺς*, and so forth.]. He did not say, “We shall see other heavens and another earth,” but rather the old and ancient ones changed for the better.

We may also say that those who have been converted from idolatry and have abandoned their former error see new heavens and a new earth, no longer believing that the elements are gods or that the things born from the earth are divine.

Now we confess that heaven and earth are the works of God’s hands. At that time, however, we worshiped servants and creation with the service due to God. David, perceiving this, sings in the Psalm: “I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers” (Ps. VIII, 4). This does not mean that he had not seen the heavens at the time when he said these words, but that, through successive increases in virtue and knowledge of future things, he sees as new those heavens that he already saw as old [Alt. “growing old”].

What is said at the end of this testimony, “the things that I create,” is omitted by the Septuagint.

(V. 19.) “For behold, I create Jerusalem as exultation and its people as joy; and I shall exult in Jerusalem and rejoice in my people.” The Septuagint reads: “For behold, I make Jerusalem an exultation and my people a joy; and I shall exult over Jerusalem and rejoice over my people.”

You ought to rejoice and exult with everlasting joy in the creation of the new heavens and the new earth, and not remember the former things at all, lest any sadness from the ancient memory arise for you. For I shall create not only new heavens and a new earth, but also Jerusalem in exultation and its people in joy.

There is no doubt that this refers to the whole earth, so that what was formerly joy for one nation may become new joy for all the nations. The exultation and joy over the city and people of God will be so great that I, their creator, shall also exult and rejoice over Jerusalem and over my people, who shall eat, drink, rejoice, and exult in it, and who shall be called by the new name.

### (Verse 20)

“And no longer shall the sound of weeping be heard in it [Vulgate: “in him”], nor the sound of crying out; there shall no longer be there an infant who lives only a few days, nor an old man who does not complete his days. For the child shall die at a hundred years, and the sinner who is a hundred years old shall be accursed.”

The Septuagint: “And no longer shall the sound of weeping be heard in it, nor the sound of crying out; neither shall there be there one untimely born, nor an old man who does not fulfill his time. For the child shall be [variant: “is”] a hundred years old, and the sinner who dies at a hundred years shall be accursed.”

For it will not be fitting that, in the city of Jerusalem and among the people of God, who will receive the eternal creation of exultation and joy, the sound of weeping and crying should still be heard, when pain, sorrow, and groaning have passed away. For contrary things cannot exist together. And where there is exultation and joy—which is the fruit of the Holy Spirit—there weeping and lamentation cannot remain, since these belong to those who lament and mourn, and especially crying out, which Paul drives from the Church of believers, lest, in the manner of the Jews, we raise a cry for judgment (Ephesians 4).

In such a city there will not be different ages: infant and old man, small and great, one who does not complete his days. Rather, like children of the resurrection, all will attain maturity, to the measure of the full age of Christ, so that no one will lack the span of years, nor will anyone exceed it; one will not yet possess firm strength while another ceases to be what he was and withers in decrepit age. All will reach the number one hundred, as did Abraham, who at that age received the promise of his son Isaac (Genesis 21).

It is unnecessary to say very much about the praises of this number, lest the discussion become superfluous. We say only this: ten decades have equal sides and possess the stability of a square. In the promises also, instead of what we have consumed [or: despised], the Lord promises us a hundredfold increase; and the seed falling on good soil first yields the number of a hundredfold harvest. Finally, Isaac too, sowing one seed of faith, received in this number the multiplied work of his labor.

At that time, therefore, when there is one age for all, both the holy and the sinner will be perfected in a similar resurrection, and they will not differ from one another in time; but one will be dragged to rewards and another to punishments. The sinner will be accursed in this respect: that, though possessing an incorruptible body, he will suffer eternal punishments.

That which we read in the Apocalypse of John (chapter 20)—that after the resurrection the small and the great are brought before the presence of the Judge—signifies differences not of ages but of merits. For one who is small according to Solomon’s judgment is worthy of mercy: “The mighty will suffer mighty torments” (Wisdom 6:7). To the same meaning agree the Lord’s words: “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12:47). But the one who does not know and does things deserving of blows will be beaten with few.

The blessed apostle Paul, explaining the ancient Scripture with Christ speaking in him, asserts that the patriarch Abraham was the father not only of circumcision but also of uncircumcision (Romans 4)—that is, that two peoples were generated from him. He declares that the one who was born according to the flesh, “a hundred years old” on account of Christ, who was generated from Abraham’s stock, and against whom that man laid hands, is subject to perpetual cursing.

[Note: Victorius explains this somewhat obscure passage as follows: “S.”—he says—“the Father explains the Prophet’s words: ‘The child of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed.’ He says that the hundred-year-old sinner who will be accursed signifies the Jewish people, who was Abraham’s son according to the flesh, and that it is therefore subject to perpetual cursing because it laid hands upon Christ, who was born from Abraham’s lineage. He interprets the child of a hundred years as Christ.”]

The Gospels teach this figure (Mark 5), where it is reported that the woman with the hemorrhage began to suffer when the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born, and that when the former was healed, the latter immediately died: within one and the same period of twelve years, the new people persists in youth while the old dies in unbelief and is accursed.

[Note: Victorius also notes that Jerome says this because the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was twelve years old when she died (Luke 8), while the woman with the hemorrhage had been ill for twelve years when she was healed (Matthew 9; Luke 5). Thus, when the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue was born, the woman began to suffer; and when the woman was healed, the girl died. With divine ingenuity he draws this comparison to the two peoples, namely the Jews and the Gentiles: when the Jews were rising to faith, the Gentiles began to suffer; but the Gentiles were healed and came to faith when the Jews lost the faith in which they had been born. Thus, when one ceased, the other began.]

We have said this according to the Septuagint interpreters, whose edition is spread throughout the whole world, lest, in so famous a passage, we seem to take refuge in the citadel of the Hebrew language. Whether you understand it as referring to the time after the resurrection, at the Savior’s second advent, or as referring to the time after baptism, in the first resurrection, it does not conflict with the faith of the Church.

The Hebrews contend that these things will occur before the resurrection, in the thousand-year reign upon the earth, and that such long spans of future life are promised that one hundred years will be counted as infancy; but the sinner will die in the hundredth year of his life, so that he may not enjoy the possessions prepared for him, but may recognize that he is accursed because of his sin. But if this is so, where will perfect blessedness be, since it is violated and corrupted by sin, and sin is punished by untimely death?

### (Verses 21–22)

“And they shall build houses and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruits. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat.” The Septuagint likewise.

[Note: Victorius writes “all things” instead of “houses”; for, he says, that psalm speaks not only about houses but about everything that is explained here in the Prophet.]

Concerning these houses, prophetic speech also promises in Psalm 68, saying: “For God will save Zion, and the cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there, and they shall acquire it as an inheritance, and the seed of his servants shall possess it; and those who love his name shall dwell in it.”

The Jews understand all these things carnally, so that Jerusalem and the cities of Judea may be restored to their former condition. But if we grant them this, let them hear that not only Jerusalem but also Sodom is promised restoration, as Ezekiel says: “Sodom shall be restored to its former state” (Ezekiel 16:55).

Therefore the houses in which those who build them will dwell are to be understood either as Virtues or as the various dwelling places with the Father, which the one who has built them will possess continually. Such houses are also said to have been built for themselves by the midwives in Exodus, because they feared God—although it is written in Hebrew that God built houses for them because they feared him (Exodus 1).

And because Jacob was simple—or, as it is said in Greek, ἄπλαστος (*aplastos*), that is, “not at all deceitful,” and not like those condemned in Peter’s Epistle, of whom he says, “Through covetousness they will exploit you with fabricated words” (2 Peter 2:3)—therefore he dwelt in the house that Esau, who delighted in wild animals and forests, could not possess.

The Savior’s words in the Gospel describe such a house also: “Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them will be like a prudent man who built his house upon a rock” (Matthew 7:24), and so forth.

Otherwise, according to the literal sense, many holy people build houses but do not inhabit them, being deprived of them by exile, another person’s robbery, or death. Such was Job, who, rich in flesh and spirit, was reduced to such poverty that he sat upon a dung heap outside the city gate (Job 2).

Conversely, that rich man in the Gospel, clothed in purple, built a house and inhabited it; to him it could most rightly be said: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20).

He says not only, “They shall build houses and inhabit them,” but also, “They shall plant vineyards, and they themselves shall eat their fruit,” in accordance with what is said in Micah: “Each one shall rest beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree, and there shall be no one to make him afraid” (Micah 4:4).

This is the vine that spoke in the Gospel: “I am the vine, and you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator” (John 15:5). “Everyone who does not bear fruit shall be cut off and cast into the fire” (Matthew 3:10).

Its fruits are eaten and drunk; they gladden the human heart, make the bridegroom’s friends drunk, and are drunk daily in the kingdom of God. Beneath the fig tree rests and fears no one’s ambush the one who enjoys the sweetness of the Holy Spirit and is filled with its fruits: love, joy, peace, faith, self-control, and patience.

Of such a person the planter is told: “He who plants a fig tree shall eat its fruit” (Amos 9:14). Whoever builds such houses and plants such vineyards—concerning which the Apostle also says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6)—“shall eat the labors of his hands” (Psalm 127), and, “sowing in the Spirit, from the Spirit shall reap eternal life” (John 4); nor shall he be overthrown by the deceits of the devil and his attendants.

### (Verses 23 and following)

“For as the days of a tree shall be the days of my people, and the works of their hands shall grow old for my chosen ones. [Note: In the Vulgate and Jerome’s version: “shall grow old; my chosen ones shall not labor,” less correctly in relation to the Hebrew.] They shall not labor in vain, nor shall they beget in turmoil, because they are the seed blessed by the Lord, and their descendants are with them. And it shall be that before they cry out, I shall answer; while they are still speaking, I shall answer [Vulgate: ‘I shall hear’]. The wolf and the lamb shall feed together, and the lion and the ox shall eat straw, and dust shall be the serpent’s bread. They shall not harm or kill on all my holy mountain, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint: “For as the days of the tree of life shall be, so shall be the days of my people; my chosen ones shall cause the works of their labors to grow old. They shall not labor in vain, nor shall they beget children for a curse, because they are a seed blessed by the Lord, and their descendants are with them. And it shall be that before they cry out, I shall hear them; while they are still speaking, I shall say, ‘What is it?’ Then wolves and lambs shall feed together; but the lion shall eat straw like an ox, and the serpent shall eat earth like bread. They shall not harm or destroy on my holy mountain, says the Lord.”

The dwelling and planting of the righteous will be eternal, so that the days of the life of my people may be compared with the days of the life of a tree, concerning which it is said in the Psalms: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm tree” (Psalm 91:13), triumphing daily over adversaries and displaying the emblem of victory.

But if we read according to the Septuagint, “the days of the tree of life”—which translates the sense from the Hebrew more than the words—we understand the tree of life that was placed in paradise. Adam was expelled from paradise so that he would not stretch out his hand to it and live (Genesis 3). Cherubim—that is, a multitude of knowledge—and a flaming sword were set to guard it, to preserve the way to the tree of life, lest Adam, while he remained in sin and did not yet recognize his transgressions, eat from it and die the death of impenitence, despair, and pride.

What this tree of life is, Solomon explains more clearly. Speaking about the wisdom of God, he says: “She is a tree of life to all who approach her, and to those who rely upon her, as upon the Lord, she is firmness” (Proverbs 3:18). There is no doubt that this signifies the Word of God, who is himself the way and wisdom, and who says of himself: “I am life” (John 11:25).

Of this the Prophet sings: “You made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your creation” (Psalm 103:24), and the apostle Paul says: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24).

The works of the people of God also will not grow old, but will be renewed daily, so that they may not walk in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit (Romans 7). Just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many will be made righteous.

Or certainly this should be said: their works grow old whose house, founded upon the rock, remains forever, and who built upon Christ’s foundation with gold, silver, and precious stones (1 Corinthians 3); whereas the works of those whose house was founded upon sand perish, and whose house is overturned by a sudden storm, and who built upon Christ’s foundation with wood, hay, and stubble.

Does he not seem to you to make his works grow old daily who, forgetting what is behind, stretches forward to what is ahead? Hence the Testament is called both old and new—not because the old perishes, but because another does not succeed the new.

This also may be said according to the Hebrew: the works of the people and of those who believe in Christ are the fruits of the Apostles, that is, of God’s chosen ones, and are stored in their treasures. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20).

These will not labor in vain, as the Jews once labored, but will eat the labors of their hands. Nor will they beget in turmoil or in a curse; and, as it is expressed more clearly in Hebrew, εἰς ἀνυπαρξίαν (*eis anyparxian*), which in their language is called LABALA [variant: LABAALA]—that is, “so that they cease to exist and reach the end of their substance.” For this Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion interpreted “hastening”: they should not hastily believe without reason, but imitate Nathanael, who was praised by the Lord’s voice: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” (John 20:47). He was seeking Christ on the authority of the Scriptures and desired to recognize him from the Prophets, saying: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

The sense is: “How are you bringing me the Messiah from Galilee and Nazareth, whom I know to have been promised from Bethlehem of Judah?”

The Apostles and apostolic men, therefore, will beget children in such a way that they instruct them from the Holy Scriptures, so that they do not imitate the curse of the Jews, but say with the Prophet: “Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, and we were in labor and gave birth” (Isaiah 26:18).

Of these it had been said: “Blessed shall be the offspring of your womb” (Deuteronomy 28:4). Such are the children of Abraham, who do his works; in the ancient history they are called “sons of the Prophets” (John 8). Such children the Apostles begot in the New Testament (Acts 16): Paul begot Timothy, Luke, Titus, and many others; Peter begot Mark the Evangelist; and the others begot the others. Their seed is blessed and continues to be blessed, and their children’s children remain.

Concerning them the Prophet says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he will greatly delight in his commandments. His seed shall be mighty in the land; the generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Psalm 111:1–2). And elsewhere: “Your children are like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord” (Psalm 127:4–5).

Conversely, concerning Judas the traitor and all who resemble him, it is said: “Let his children be orphans, and his wife a widow. Let his children be shaken and removed, and let them beg; let them be cast out of their houses” (Psalm 108:9–10).

For the end of an evil generation is exceedingly bad: “They conceive pain and give birth to iniquity.” Of their leader it is written: “Behold, he was in labor with injustice, conceived pain, and gave birth to iniquity” (Psalm 7:15).

But if this is said about the ungodly, how did Samuel, a blessed and righteous man, beget exceedingly wicked sons who did not walk in their father’s way (1 Samuel 8)? And David, from whose seed Christ was born, begot two sons, Amnon and Absalom, one of whom became a murderer of his brother and the other of his father (2 Samuel 13, 15–16)?

From all this we learn that sons and descendants must be understood according to what we have said. In this sense Paul also gives birth to children until Christ is formed in them, and in chains he begets Onesimus (Galatians 4).

When they cry out, they will immediately be heard, and while they are speaking the Lord will say, “I am present.” All these things we also see fulfilled literally in the Acts of the Apostles. For all the nations could not have believed in so short a time unless their faith had in some way been compelled by the miracles of signs.

While the Apostles and apostolic men were speaking and crying out, the Lord answered with the greatness of his signs: Dorcas rose at Peter’s prayers (Acts 9); Publius’s father on the island of Malta, suffering from fever and dysentery—diseases contrary to one another—was healed through Paul’s prayers; and the whole world called them gods walking among human beings (Acts 28).

Then the wolf and the lamb fed together: the persecutor Paul and the disciple Ananias (Acts 9). He was the wolf of whom it is written: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he shall devour the prey, and in the evening he shall divide the spoil” (Genesis 49:27), or, as it is said in Hebrew, “he shall divide the spoils.” His teaching became food for believers, and throughout the world he triumphed over conquered adversaries.

The lambs are to be understood as all those who, clothed in white garments, follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Revelation 14), whom the Lord entrusted to Peter for feeding, saying: “Feed my lambs” (John 21:16).

The lion also will eat straw like an ox when men most eloquent and once powerful in the world surrender themselves to the rustic simplicity of the Scriptures. They will no longer feed upon worldly eloquence, which drips like honey from the lips of the prostitute, but will follow the lowliness and straw of the historical sense until, through much labor and diligence, they deserve to reach the grain of spiritual meanings.

Jeremiah speaks of this straw and grain: “What has straw to do with wheat? says the Lord” (Jeremiah 23:28). And it must be considered that it is not the ox who becomes enraged, but the lion who is changed into gentleness.

The serpent, which watched the human being’s heel and whose head was watched by the human being, will no longer be nourished by the destruction of others, but will eat earth or dust as bread (Genesis 3).

Or certainly this should be understood in the following way: the devil, who was previously nourished by the deaths of human beings, will eat only those who are dust and earth. Through all these things the transformation of the wicked into good is demonstrated: they will be harmless, having laid aside their ancient ferocity—not outside, but on the holy mountain of the Lord, that is, in the Church and in the confession of that mountain from which the prince of Tyre was wounded, and which, cut from the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the world (Daniel 2).

Let us ask the Jews, and all who still eat the straw of the Scriptures under the Christian name, which will be separated from the grain by the Lord’s winnowing fan and given over to wind and flames, what blessedness is to be thought present if, in the thousand-year kingdom, on Mount Zion, in the city of Christ’s presence, Jerusalem, and in the most august Temple, wolves and lambs, lions and oxen, serpents and human beings eat and dwell together, and only those who have dwelt on the Lord’s holy mountain are harmless.

From this we understand that all who are outside the mountain will be killed. Therefore the whole world will be exposed to wolves, lions, bears, leopards, serpents, and the other beasts; and the immense forests and the Egyptian vastness of the desert, fertile in poisonous animals, and the holy city, as the supreme happiness, will be the dwelling place not only of human beings but also of beasts and serpents, so that, according to the earlier prophecy, the wolf may dwell with the lamb, the leopard with the kid, the calf and the lion together, and sheep with bears (Isaiah 11); and a little child may rule them, and an infant weaned from the breast may put his hand into the hole of an asp and kill the basilisk in its den.

The cause of such great happiness will be that the whole earth is filled with the knowledge of the Lord.

### (Chapter 66, verse 1)

“Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet. What is this house that you will build for me, and what is this place of my rest? My hand made all these things, and all these things came to be, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint likewise.

Lest we understand the holy mountain as Zion and cover it with the Jewish error—for they think that Jerusalem must be rebuilt and that everything the Lord promises must be fulfilled there in a carnal manner—this passage removes that suspicion from us and provides the testimony used by Stephen, the first martyr in Christ, against the Jewish contention (Acts 7).

Solomon built a house for him, undoubtedly for God; but the Most High does not dwell in things made with hands, as the Prophet says: “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet.” And Paul says in the same book: “God, who made the world and all that is in it, does not dwell in temples made with hands” (Acts 17:24).

For if, like one seated upon a throne and reigning, heaven is his throne and earth the footstool of his feet, how can he who fills all things, and in whom all things exist, be enclosed in a small place?

Hence Moses also says: “Do not say in your heart, ‘It is far away’; for God is in heaven above and upon the earth below, and there is no other God besides him” (Deuteronomy 4:39).

And the Psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend to the underworld, you are present” (Psalm 138:7).

Jeremiah likewise agrees with him, speaking in the person of God: “I am God who is near, and not a God from far away. Can anyone hide himself in secret places so that I will not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:23–24).

“For in him we are and move” (Acts 17). He says this to refute the Jewish error, which thinks that the invisible, incorporeal, and incomprehensible God can be enclosed in the temple of Jerusalem.

Solomon himself, the builder of the Temple, also confesses this at length in his prayer to the Lord (1 Kings 8). And lest we think that God’s greatness can even be measured by heaven and earth, we read of him elsewhere: “He holds heaven in his palm and the earth in his fist” (Isaiah 40:12).

Through these words God is shown to be both outside and inside, both infused into and surrounding all things: he is not enclosed by the throne that surrounds him, but he encloses heaven and earth in his fist and palm.

He is the creator not only of heaven and earth but also of the invisible angels, archangels, dominions, powers, and all human beings, concerning whom the Apostle speaks (Colossians 1). All these things the hand of God has made.

Job and the Psalmist also recall this hand: “Your hands made me and fashioned me” (Job 10:18; Psalm 118:73). “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” John again says of him: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1).

“He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 32). Scripture also demonstrates this in the mystical language of Genesis: “God said, and God made” (Genesis 1).

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.” There is no place of the Lord’s rest except the one that the Prophet next mentions.

### (Verses 2–3)

“But upon whom shall I look, except upon the poor and contrite in spirit, and the one who trembles at my words? He who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a human being. He who slaughters a sheep is like one who brains a dog. He who offers an offering is like one who offers swine’s blood. He who remembers incense is like one who blesses an idol” [Vulgate: “to an idol”].

The Septuagint: “And upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet, and the one who trembles at my words? ÷ But the unjust one **: he who sacrifices a calf is as one striking a man; he who sacrifices from the flock, as one killing a dog; he who offers fine flour, as one offering swine’s blood; he who gives incense as a memorial, as a blasphemer.”

Once the altar and the earthly Temple that human hands had built have been removed, the sacrifices of the Jews are rightly removed as well, lest they perhaps say: “We are not so foolish as to think that God can be enclosed in a place; rather, in a separate place intended for sacrifice, we offer to God the victims prescribed by the Law.”

The inhabitant of heaven—or rather, the Creator of all things, who denies that he has a temple on earth—gladly takes as a temple the humble and quiet person who trembles at his words, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you. If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him. For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:16–17).

Therefore, whoever is humble and quiet and trembles at God’s words is the one upon whom the Lord looks. Of him it may be understood that the following is prophesied under the name of earth: “The earth trembled and was still when God arose for judgment” (Psalm 75:9–10).

Its inhabitants—on whose account the earth is spoken of metaphorically—considering God’s judgment, cease from evil works. Sitting in the house, they rest in an eternal Sabbath [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript reads *serreno* instead of “eternal” (*aeterno*)], so that they do not move themselves toward the servile work of sin, as the builders of the tower once moved their feet from the East and abandoned the rising of the true light.

They did not heed what was said to Cain: “You have sinned; be still” (Genesis 4). Rather, according to Solomon’s Proverbs: “He who hears God will dwell confidently, and he will rest without fear from every evil” (Proverbs 1:33). [Note: Victorius alternatively notes “confidently”: in the Greek of Proverbs 1, ἐπ’ ἐλπίδι means “in hope,” followed by καὶ ἡσυχάσει ἀφόβως ἀπὸ παντὸς κακοῦ, “and he shall rest without fear from every evil.” The text had earlier been corruptly read, “he shall rest without fear and from every evil.”]

This is the humble and poor person, contrite in spirit and trembling at the Lord’s words, of whom it is written in the Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3).

And elsewhere: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor” (Psalm 40:1). And again: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Isaiah 61:1).

The clause that follows in the Vulgate edition, “But the unjust one,” is not found in Hebrew. Rather, the text simply joins the words and says: “He who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a human being.”

The same is written elsewhere: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice; the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hosea 6:6). And through Malachi: “You did everything that I hated, covering my altar with tears. Is it worthy that I should look upon your sacrifice and accept anything favorable from your hands?” (Malachi 2:13).

Let the Jews hear that God does not seek sacrifices but the intention of those who offer them. “He who slaughters,” he says, “a sheep is like one who brains a dog.”

Hence it is written through Moses: “You shall not offer the wages of a prostitute, nor the price of a dog, in the house of the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 23:18). Dog and prostitute are aptly joined together, because each animal is inclined to lust.

Let us also consider that he did not say, “He who sacrifices a ram is like one who sacrifices a dog,” but “he shall kill a dog.” This word is not used for sacrifices but for things slaughtered unlawfully.

“He who offers an offering and a sacrifice is like one who offers swine’s blood.” This too is prohibited by the Law; such are the ceremonies of the Jews (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14).

“He who offers incense is like a blasphemer,” or rather, like one who blesses an idol.

This passage may also have the following meaning: “After my Son came, meek and poor, seated upon a donkey’s colt, I do not want meats; I reject the victims and sacrifices of the Jews and repudiate the shadows of the Law, because the truth of the Gospel is pleasing to me” (Zechariah 9; Matthew 21; Luke 19; John 12).

But if this is said to mean that, after the lightning flash of the Gospel, the ancient religion ceases in the cloud, what answer will those give who believe that converts from the Jews can offer sacrifices carnally without harm?

### (Verse 4)

“All these things they chose in their ways, and their soul delighted in their abominations. Therefore I also shall choose their mockeries [Note: It previously read “their mockers,” contrary even to the manuscripts of Jerome’s own version], and I shall bring upon them the things they feared. For I called, and there was no one who answered; I spoke, and they did not hear. They did evil in my sight, and they chose what I did not desire” [Vulgate: “they did what I did not desire”].

The Septuagint: “They themselves chose their ways, and their soul desired their abominations; and I shall choose their mockeries, and I shall repay them according to their sins. For I called them, and they did not obey; I spoke, and they did not hear. They did evil in my sight, and they chose what I did not desire.”

To sacrifice an ox, slaughter a ram, offer a sacrifice, and burn incense—things that God regards as murder, an offering of a dog, swine’s blood, and blasphemy—they themselves chose. It was their own decision to worship such things, according to what he says through Ezekiel: “I gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances that were not good” (Ezekiel 20:11).

“And in their ways,” he says, “they walked,” not in the way of the Lord. Their soul desired their abominations, so that they would be lovers of themselves rather than lovers of God.

For this reason, while they were choosing their own ways and not the one who says, “I am the way” (John 14:6), the Lord also chose their mockeries—or their mockers—who are called in Hebrew THALULE [uncertain/variant form], that is, ἐμπαῖκται (*empaiktai*), “mockers,” so that he might appoint exceedingly wicked rulers and bring upon them all their evils, or all the things they feared. [Note: Victorius reads *quae* and accordingly substitutes ἐμπαίγματα (“mockeries”) from the Septuagint for ἐμπαῖκται (“mockers”); he notes that the Septuagint also uses the word in Psalm 37: “My loins were filled with ἐμπαιγμάτων, mockeries.” Nevertheless, the printed reading is more correct and more consistent with the sequence of the argument and with the manuscripts.]

He gives the reasons why they were handed over to their mocking scribes and Pharisees, concerning whom the first psalm sings according to the Hebrews: “He did not sit in the seat of mockers.” The Septuagint calls them “pestilent men.” Such were the sons of Eli, “sons of pestilence”; for this, in Hebrew, is written BELIAL [variant: BLIAL], that is, “of the devil.”

“For I called,” he says, “and there was no one who answered; I spoke, and they did not hear. They did evil in my sight, and they chose what I did not desire.”

He places these verses a second time in the present passage, and earlier also, where it is said: “I shall number you for the sword, and you shall all fall in slaughter, because I called and you did not answer” (Isaiah 65:12), and the rest similarly. In what sense this testimony should be understood has been explained there.

### (Verse 5)

“Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brothers who hate you [Note: Victor says that *abjiciunt* (“they cast off”) should be read, rather than *abjecerunt* (“they cast off” in the perfect tense); the Vulgate edition likewise preserves this tense, reading: “Your brothers, hating you and casting you off for my name’s sake.” Jerome also says: “Who hate and separate you.” The Septuagint has: “Who hate you and abhor you.” Nor is this surprising, since the Hebrew likewise reads [reading not present in the supplied text].] and cast you off for my name’s sake have said: ‘Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy’; but they themselves shall be put to shame.”

The Septuagint reads: “Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Say to your brothers who hate you and abhor you, so that the name of the Lord may be glorified and may appear in their joy; and they shall be put to shame” [some copies: “may they be put to shame”].

Concerning these people he had already said: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble and quiet one, who trembles at my words?” He commands them, despising the sacrifices of the Jews and rejecting all the arrogance of the scribes and Pharisees, to pass over to the worship of the one whom those people refused to hear when he called them, and whom they despised, doing evil in his sight.

Nor is he content with this end of his commands; rather, he orders them to keep the Gospel commandment [Luke VI]: that they love their enemies, do good to those who hate them, pray for their persecutors, and imitate the clemency of the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the just and the unjust: “So that, when they see your works,” he says, “they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16).

After the general sense, this is specifically commanded to the Apostles and to apostolic men [Note: Previously, *spiritualiter* (“spiritually”) stood corruptly in place of *specialiter* (“specifically”)]:  that they love their Jewish persecutors and regard those who abhor them as brothers, saying with Peter: “Men, brothers and fathers, hear”; and with the Apostle Paul: “I have great sorrow and continual pain in my heart for my brothers, who are Israelites” (Rom. IX, 2).

The name of the Lord is glorified when people see the ferocity of our persecutors broken by our patience, and the striking hand confounded by the turning of the other cheek. To such people the Gospel gives this command: “Let your light shine before men, so that, when they see your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V, 16); and in the Apocalypse of John: “Fear God and give him glory” (Apoc. XIV, 7).

Paul likewise writes to the Corinthians, urging them to self-restraint: “That you may glorify God in your body” (I Cor. VI, 20). And again: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (I Cor. X, 31). Therefore the Lord did not revile those who reviled him (I Pet. II), and he prayed for his persecutors.

But when he commands: “Say to your brothers” (Matt. XXVIII, 10), this must not be understood in a simple or superficial sense. Otherwise, many call others brothers but do not retain charity in their hearts. Of them the Apostle writes: “They profess that they know God, but by their works they deny him” (Tit. I, 16). Concerning them the Lord also said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but he who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. VII, 21).

Thus that other saying can stand: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (I Cor. XII, 3). For although heretics say “Lord Jesus,” and many at the resurrection will say: “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and perform many miracles in your name?” (Matt. VII, 22), the Lord will answer them: “Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity.”

Therefore, saying is not proved by speech—which is easy—but by affection and works. From this we learn that the Lord of both Testaments is one and the same: he commands that, if we see our enemy’s beast fallen beneath its burden, we should not pass by but help to raise it with him; and if we find his ox or donkey wandering, we should return it to him (Luke XV; Matt. XVIII).

This is the sense according to the Septuagint. According to the Hebrew, however, the following seems to me to be the meaning:

“Hear, Apostles; hear, my disciples, you who tremble at the word of the Lord. I shall tell you what your brothers have said—those who hate you, separate you, and consider you outsiders—not on account of your evils, but on account of my name. They regard as unclean all who believe in me from their own people, and they say: ‘Depart from me, for you are unclean.’”

What, then, is the meaning of their reported words: “Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy”? The sense of this verse is:

“Why do you introduce to us a humble God? Why one who was crucified, a man of sorrows and acquainted with bearing infirmities? We want to see him reigning in his own majesty, as you say; we will look upon him triumphing in his glory. We cannot see him humble and cast down.””

Immediately he adds: “But they themselves shall be put to shame”—that is, those who speak such things, who do not understand the mysteries of the Scriptures. Through their own evils they will experience the power of the one whom, because of his humility, they had despised.

### (Verse 6)

“A sound of uproar from the city, a sound from the Temple, a sound of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies.”

The Septuagint has “a cry” instead of “an uproar,” and is otherwise similar.

We wish to know what the Jews’ shame will be—the Jews who said: “Let the Lord be glorified, so that we may see your joy and behold with our eyes the triumphs of your king, not as empty promises.” “A sound,” he says, “of a cry from the city.” There can be no doubt that this signifies Jerusalem, surrounded by the Roman army and divided within by sedition into three factions: one faction occupied the Temple and possessed everything that had previously been holy, fighting the enemies outside and the citizens within.

At that time, both in the city and in the Temple, the wailing of priests and Levites, of the common people, of women, and of children was heard, when the Lord rendered recompense to his enemies, fulfilling the threat in which he had said: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke XIII, 35), as well as that prophecy: “I have forsaken my house.”

Then the officials of the Temple said with one voice, like that of an angel: “Let us depart from these places.”

Concerning them, not only Josephus, the writer of Jewish history, but also the Psalmist many centuries earlier bears witness, saying: “I saw iniquity and contradiction in the city” (Ps. LIV, 10). These surrounded its walls day and night, so that the city was overturned (Mic. III), and another prophecy was fulfilled: “Sion shall be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem shall be left like a hut in a cucumber garden” (Isa. I, 8).

[Note: See what we have noted in Letter 18 to Damasus, no. 9, and in Letter 46, Paula and Eustochium to Marcella, no. 4, and elsewhere. In these passages we have shown that Jerome was misled by Eusebius. Here, however, he at least agrees more correctly with Josephus. See the Chronicle under the year A.D. 33, and what we observe there.]

### (Verse 7)

“Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her labor came, she gave birth to a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing? Who has seen anything like it? Shall the earth bring forth in one day, or shall a nation be born all at once? For Sion was in labor and gave birth to her sons. Shall I, who cause others to give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord. If I, who grant generation to others, shall be barren, says the Lord your God.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Before she who is in labor gave birth, before the labor pains of the woman in labor came, she escaped, and she gave birth to a male child. Who has heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? If the earth gave birth in one day, or if a nation was born all at once, for Sion was in labor and gave birth to her little ones. But I gave this expectation, and you did not remember me, says the Lord. Did I not make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman? says your God.”

When a cry resounded from Jerusalem and its Temple, when the city was besieged and overturned, and the enemies of Christ—who refused to receive God as king [Note: Victor preferred to restore *eum* (“him”) with the help of the Brixian manuscripts, rather than *Deum* (“God”), referring specifically to Christ.]—received eternal punishments for their impiety and blasphemies, the Church, gathered in the name of the Lord, gave birth before she was in labor; before her labor came, she brought forth a male child.

For the whole world did not conceive, labor, and give birth to the male child over a long period, as the Jewish people grew through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the twelve patriarchs, and again through their children and grandchildren. Rather, at the preaching of the Gospel the whole world immediately conceived, was in labor, and gave birth to the male child whom Pharaoh and Herod attempted to kill, and who was saved in Egypt both in Moses and in Christ.

In the end, Abraham and Isaac had male children, and Jacob, the father of many sons, had one daughter, on whose account he suffered harshly (Gen. XXXIV). If the daughters of Zelophehad, by God’s decision, receive their father’s inheritance (Num. XXVII), it must be considered that their father died in his sin: he had fathered no son, and Moses dared not make any judgment concerning them but referred the matter to the Lord, who commanded that they be joined to their brothers so that they might not remain destitute.

The book of Genesis also relates (chap. VI) that, after human beings began to multiply—a number that is always associated with sin—and daughters were born to them, they took them, not angels but sons of God, from whom giants were born; or, as it is written in Hebrew, *ἐπιπίπτοντες* (*epipíptontes*), that is, “falling upon” or “attacking.”

Conversely, it is said to the holy man: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine within your house; your sons like olive shoots around your table” (Ps. CXXVII, 3). And again: “May you see your children’s children” (ibid., 6).

Thus Sion—that is, the remnant of Israel and the faith of the believing Apostles—gave birth to the male child, the Lord and Savior, who was born at once throughout the whole world. No one had ever heard this; no history or teaching had ever related it: that all the nations should believe in so short a time. [Note: Victor supplied the word *est* (“is”) from Florentine manuscripts; without it the passage seemed to him mutilated and unintelligible. From the same manuscripts he also substituted “or any teaching” for “or from them.”]

From all the nations one Christian people was formed. Of this Paul also speaks: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, new things have come” (II Cor. V, 17). In accordance with what is written elsewhere: “All the families of the nations shall worship before him, because the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he shall rule over the nations. All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, and they shall glorify your name” (Ps. XXI, 28 and following).

Jacob says of him: “He is the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX, 10). The Psalmist says: “The hope of all the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXIV, 6). And the same Isaiah whom we are now explaining says: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who shall arise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI, 10).

The Apostles fulfilled the command: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII, 19), so that a new people might be born. Concerning this the twenty-first Psalm also sings: “The heavens shall declare his righteousness to a people who shall be born, whom the Lord has made” (Ps. XXI, 32). And again: “The people that shall be created shall praise the Lord” (Ps. CI, 19).

This people was created in a single day, illuminated by the sun of righteousness, as Scripture says: “The Lord shall be your everlasting light” (Isa. LX, 19).

We can also refer the statement, “A nation shall arise at once, for Sion was in labor and gave birth to her sons,” to the time when three thousand and five thousand from the Jewish people believed in a single day (Acts II). [Note: The Ambrosian manuscripts do not contain the words “and five thousand.”] The same book of the Acts of the Apostles also says that people from all the nations under heaven were in Jerusalem, hearing them speak of the mighty works of God in various languages (ibid.).

What follows according to the Septuagint—“But I gave this expectation, and you did not remember me, says the Lord. Did I not make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman? says your God”—is stated more clearly in the Hebrew, and the other interpreters agree with it:

“Shall I, who cause others to give birth, myself not give birth? says the Lord. If I, who grant generation to others, shall be barren, says the Lord your God.”

This accords with what is said elsewhere: “He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? He who formed the eye, shall he not see?” (Ps. XXXIX, 9). The one who created all human beings from nothing can surely make from all the nations one Church consisting of those who believe in him.

Finally, in the twenty-eighth Psalm, where we read: “The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness” (Ps. XXVIII, 8), the Hebrew has: “The voice of the Lord causes the wilderness to give birth” (according to the Hebrew), so that the formerly deserted Church may give birth and the hinds may be made complete amid open and broken glades.

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is that, at one time, in response to the preaching of the Gospels, one nation arises throughout the whole world.

“I repeatedly promised this through many prophets, but you did not remember my promise, O city filled with cries; O Temple abandoned by the Lord; O people to whom I have repaid what was due. Did I not,” he says, “make the woman who gives birth and the barren woman”—that is, the one who was previously barren afterward went into labor and gave birth?

Of her it is written in the Psalm: “He makes the barren woman dwell in a house, a joyful mother of children” (Ps. CXII, 9).

Or certainly the order of events has been reversed: the woman who was in labor became barren, and the formerly barren woman gave birth to many, because this is the Lord’s declaration.
