[Note: Victor argues that *id est* (“that is”) should be inserted for clarity of meaning.]

### (Verse 10)

“Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love her. Rejoice with her in joy, all you who mourn over her, so that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, so that you may milk her and abound in the abundance of her complete glory.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Rejoice, Jerusalem, and gather together, all you who love her. Rejoice with joy, all you who mourn over her, so that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation; so that, after you have suckled, you may delight in the entrance of her glory.”

The Apostles and apostolic men are commanded—those who love both Jerusalems, mourning and grieving over the one that has fallen, and awaiting with every desire the one that will rise again—to rejoice with her and in her, the city built of living stones. These stones roll upon the earth and, in the likeness of the wheels of the Cherubim, follow the spirit that goes before them—not among those who have been dissolved into everlasting ashes.

Concerning these the Lord said: “Truly I say to you, not one stone shall remain upon another until all these things are fulfilled” (Matt. XXIV, 2).

“Rejoice,” he says, “with her in joy, all you who mourn over her.” Such people, as we have shown above, were the Apostles Peter and Paul and all who awaited the redemption of Israel, so that they might suck and be filled from the breasts of her consolation.

For it could not be that she who had given birth to a male child and was a woman in labor should lack an abundance of milk for the nourishment of that nation and of the little ones who had been born together with it. She would offer them two breasts—not as formerly in Egypt, broken and lying useless, but whole and standing in virginal beauty—the breasts of the Old and New Testament, to provide rational milk.

Concerning these the bridegroom says to her: “Your breasts are better than wine” (Song I, 1).

These were the people of whom it was specifically said: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5).

It should also be noted that those who are little ones need the milk of consolation, since they are still situated in a mortal condition. But those who, after the milk of consolation, have advanced to solid food will abound in the delights of truth and in the knowledge of complete glory, which in Hebrew is called *ZIZ* (). For this the Septuagint translated “entrance”; Symmachus, “fatness”; and Theodotion, “multitude.”

We have said this in order to explain the ambiguous word in the eightieth Psalm, where it is written: “The boar from the forest has ravaged it, and the solitary wild beast has devoured it” (Ps. LXXIX, 14). For where our Latin and Greek books read *μόνιος ἄγριος* (*mónios ágrios*), that is, “the solitary wild beast” [Note: The conjunction *et* (“and”), which is entirely necessary for the sense, was lacking previously.], the Hebrew has *ZIZ SADAI* ().

Aquila translated this as *παντόδαπον χώρας* (*pantódapon chṓras*), that is, “every kind of the region,” signifying that Israel was devastated not only by the Romans but by all the nations. [Note: Previously *παντοδαπὴν* was printed, against the manuscripts and Eusebius, who also reads Aquila’s *παντῶδαπον χώραν*, “a land of every kind.”] [Note: One Ambrosian manuscript has “that Jerusalem was devastated.”]

The glorious entrance of the Church is to be understood as that of which the Apostle John writes: “At the twelve gates were twelve pearls, and the streets of the city were pure gold, like transparent glass” (Apoc. XXI, 21).

The Lord forbids these pearls to be cast before swine (Matt. VII). The good merchant, when he finds them in the Prophets and Apostles, goes on to the one pearl of great price—not throwing away the earlier ones, but seeking the more precious through them (Matt. XIII).

### (Verse 12)

“For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bend over her like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck. You shall be carried to the breast, and upon the knees they shall caress you.”

[Note: Victor reads *declino* (“I bend over”) and immediately afterward *ad ubera* (“to the breasts”) rather than *ab ubere* (“from the breast”), and discusses the reading at length. This passage troubled me for a long time, since the reading formerly found was: “You shall be carried from the breast.” Many manuscripts of the sacred Scriptures retain this reading. But all the old printed editions consistently read: “You shall be carried to the breasts.” The difficulty was increased by the fact that Jerome in his Commentary seems to acknowledge neither reading, but rather the reading of the Septuagint, which adheres more closely to the Hebrew truth and which we too initially followed: “You shall be carried upon the shoulders,” corresponding in Hebrew and Greek to *ἐπ’ ὤμων ἀρθήσονται* (*ep’ ṓmōn arthḗsontai*), “they shall be carried upon the shoulders.” Finally, after a long internal debate, it seemed preferable to retain the common edition of Jerome. It may be that Jerome placed in his Commentary not what he himself translated, but what the Septuagint translated. Nor does this interpretation conflict with the fact that *latus* (“side”) rather than *uber* (“breast”) is the proper meaning, since the latter word is used. Although I am not unaware that Jerome everywhere translated it as “side”—for example, in Genesis VI, Exodus XXV and XXVI, and I Kings XX—nevertheless the preceding word, which means “to suck,” may have moved the holy man here to understand “side” as “breast,” just as he did above, in chapter LX, where he translated the words “he shall be nourished at the side” as “he shall suck milk.” To be carried to the breasts is more natural than to be carried from the breast. The word itself does not oppose this meaning. For *ad* (“to”) sometimes also has that force, as in Psalm XVII: “They cried to the Lord, and there was no one who saved them, and he did not hear them.” I do not think he would have translated *ab ubere* (“from the breast”) unless he had joined *uber* to the preceding word, saying: “which you shall suck from the breast.” “You shall be carried,” and so forth.]

The Septuagint reads:

“For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall bend toward them like a river of peace and like an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations. Their little ones shall be carried upon shoulders, and upon knees they shall be comforted.”

After Jerusalem has been built and restored to its former condition through the Apostles, and after her children and inhabitants have been comforted by her breasts and have reached the delights of truth through the abundance of milk, by which one arrives at the glory of God [Note: The Medicean manuscript reads “one enters,” a better reading than “one arrives,” since he is mystically expounding the Septuagint’s words, “that after you have suckled, you may delight in the entrance of her glory.”], then the Lord will bend over her like a river of peace. Concerning this we have often spoken: “The river of God is filled with waters” (Ps. LXIV, 10); and: “The rushing of the river makes glad the city of God” (Ps. XLV, 5).

When peace possesses everything and the wars of the nations have ceased—concerning which Scripture says, “Scatter the nations that desire wars” (Ps. LXVII, 32)—the torrent of God’s teachings will water the fields of believers.

Then her children—or little ones, as the Septuagint translated it—will be carried upon shoulders and will receive consolation upon knees.

These are the shoulders concerning which it was also said in the earlier prophecy, and which Jacob invokes upon his son Issachar: “He placed his shoulder toward labor” (Gen. XLIX, 15), and he was called a farmer. [Note: This reading, *imprecatur* (“invokes”), is retained by the manuscripts and printed books. Victor preferred *interpretatur* (“interprets”), calling the other reading unsuitable: Jacob, he says, interprets the saying “he placed his shoulder,” namely, for labors, as Jerome explains at length.]

By sweat and great labor we arrive at the abundance of fruits. Therefore it is said to Sion through Jeremiah: “Give your heart to your shoulders” (Jer. XXIV, 7), so that he may understand the Lord from his commandments, imitating him of whom it is written: “Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts I, 1). Thus faith must not be idle but must advance through works toward its reward.

What the knees and the bosom signify I explained briefly above, and Abraham can now teach us by his example: Lazarus rests in his bosom, as do all who come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

### (Verses 13–14)

“As one whom his mother caresses, so I shall comfort you; and in Jerusalem you shall be comforted. You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like grass. And the hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant against his enemies.”

The Septuagint has “those who fear” instead of “servants,” and “the unbelieving” instead of “enemies”; otherwise it is similar.

We learn the Creator’s mercy toward his creatures by the example of mothers, who nourish their children lovingly in their bosom and surpass every other form of affection.

Therefore, wishing to show how he loves those whom he created, God says: “Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have mercy on the child of her womb? And even if she should forget, I nevertheless shall not forget you” (Isa. XLIX, 15). [Note: Victor inserts the negative particle, “so as not to have mercy,” without altering the sense.]

The same meaning is found in the Gospel passage in which the Lord says to Jerusalem: “How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling” (Matt. XXIII, 37).

There is also a similar passage in Deuteronomy: “As an eagle protects its nest and longs for its young, spreading its wings, it received them and carried them upon its shoulders” (Deut. XXXII, 11).

Those who have written about the natures of animals say that all beasts, cattle, livestock, and birds possess an innate affection for their offspring and young, but that the love of eagles is greatest. They place their nests in lofty and inaccessible places, lest a serpent harm their young.

They also say that a stone called amethyst is found among their chicks, by which all poisons are overcome. [Note: The same Ambrosian manuscript has *videat* (“may see”) instead of *violet* (“may harm”), and *Anethitem* instead of *Amethisten*. I suspect that the latter is corrupt.]

If this is true, God’s affection for his creatures has rightly been compared with that of eagles. He protects his children with every form of vigilance, lest the dragon and the ancient serpent—the devil and Satan—creep upon the newborn young, so that, in accordance with the name of the stone placed in the foundations of Sion, all the adversaries’ plots may be broken.

The Jerusalem in which the children will be comforted by their mother and caressed upon her knees is the one of which the Apostle writes: “But the Jerusalem above is free, which is the mother of us all” (Gal. IV, 26).

Filled with the milk of this consolation, he comforted others who needed his words, saying: “Blessed be God, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, who comforts us in all our tribulation, so that we may also be able to comfort those who are in every tribulation, through the consolation with which we ourselves are comforted by God” (I Cor. I, 3).

[Note: The recurrence of the same name, “Father,” easily deceived the copyist, who, with a hurried glance, omitted these intervening words from the testimony: “the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Victor supplies them from the Apostle’s text, but they are found in none of our manuscripts. He immediately supplies the word *nostra* (“our”) from the same text, where it says “in all our tribulation.”]

After they have been comforted, it will be said to them: “You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like grass,” or “shall spring up,” or, according to Symmachus, “shall blossom” (John XVI, 22).

They will see—there can be no doubt that they will see God—for this is true joy. Concerning them the Lord said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V, 8). The vision of God is perfect joy, which dwells in a heart possessing complete faith. The flourishing of the bones follows, concerning which we have already spoken. If the reader has forgotten what was said, let him return to the earlier explanation. It is better for him to reread what we wrote than for us to repeat what we have already said.

“And the hand of the Lord,” he says, “shall be known to his servants,” or to those who fear him, “and he shall threaten his enemies,” or his unbelievers.

The hand is understood either as power—that God is able to do everything he promises—in accordance with what Moses says to Pharaoh in God’s person: “Now I shall send my hand, and I shall strike you and kill your people, and you shall be destroyed from the earth” (Exod. III, 20). And again, to the same tyrant: “Behold, the hand of the Lord shall be upon your cattle” (Exod. IX, 4). Concerning this the Psalmist said to God: “Your hand destroyed the nations, and you planted them” (Ps. XLIII).

Or certainly the hand of the Lord must be understood as Christ, concerning whom we also read above: “My hand made all these things.”

The Lord will make this hand known to his servants and to those who fear him, and he will threaten the unbelieving and his enemies, promising rewards to some and threatening punishments to others.

In this we must consider the precision of the words: he did not say, “He will inflict punishment upon his enemies,” but “He will threaten them,” so that, terrified by the threat, they too may pass over to the service of the Lord.

### (Verses 15–16)

“For behold, the Lord shall come in fire, and his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his fury in indignation and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For the Lord shall judge in fire [Vulgate: “shall judge”] and with his sword all flesh, and those slain by the Lord shall be many.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Behold, the Lord shall come like fire, and his chariots like a storm, to render his vengeance in fury, and his rebuke in a flame of fire. For in the fire of the Lord the whole earth shall be judged, and by his sword all flesh shall fall; many shall be wounded by the Lord.”

The hand of the Lord, which will be made known to his servants and to those who fear him, threatens the unbelieving—or his enemies—so that, unless they repent, they may endure what follows:

“Behold,” he says, “the Lord shall come in fire, and his chariots shall be like a whirlwind or storm.”

These chariots must be understood as the angelic powers, when the Lord will come in the glory of his Father with his angels to judge the living and the dead—not because the Lord is literally fire, but because he appears as fire to those who endure punishments.

Although Moses said—and the Apostle confirms the same thing—“God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV, 24; Heb. XII, 29), the Savior, expressing the substance of divinity, said: “God is spirit” (John IV, 24). Between spirit and fire, according to bodily understanding, there is much difference.

If he is fire or spirit, how is he said to have eyes, ears, hands, feet, a belly, and the other members of a body, since neither spirit nor fire possesses these things?

God is therefore called a consuming fire so that he may consume whatever vices are in us—hay, wood, and stubble—and also the thorns, that is, the cares of this world, which infertile soil produced instead of good seed. Concerning this it is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “That which brings forth thorns and thistles is rejected and near to being cursed; its end is burning” (Heb. VI, 1).

Concerning this fire the Lord also spoke in the Gospel: “I came to send fire upon the earth” (Luke XII, 49). And above we read: “Wickedness shall burn like fire, and like dry grass it shall be consumed by fire” (Isa. IX, 18), together with all the weeds that the enemy sowed while the householder slept (Matt. XIII).

Of this fire the Epistle of James also says: “How great a forest a little fire sets ablaze!” (Jas. III, 5). And in Proverbs: “In many pieces of wood the fire grows strong” (Prov. XXVI, 20). Although, in the proverb, another meaning may be understood (Ecclus. XXVIII).

I think that this fire sat upon the tongues of the Apostles and of all believers when they spoke in various languages. It drove away all the darkness of error and illuminated the hearts of those who received the word of the Lord (Acts II).

What follows—“His chariots are like a storm,” or “like a whirlwind”—we shall explain by examples from the Psalms. There it is written: “God shall come manifestly, our God, and he shall not be silent. Fire shall burn before him, and a mighty storm shall surround him” (Ps. XLIX, 3–4). And elsewhere: “The chariots of God are ten thousand multiplied by thousands of those who rejoice” (Ps. LXVII, 18).

Elisha was surrounded by these chariots and horses, which his servant could not see. Therefore he said: “Lord, open this boy’s eyes, so that he may see.” And when his eyes had been opened, he saw chariots, and quadrigas, and horses all around (IV Kings VI, 17).

Elijah was also carried to heaven in a fiery chariot, when Elisha cried out: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” (IV Kings II, 12).

All these things are narrated not because God actually possesses a chariot, quadrigas, or horses and is carried by their speed—although elsewhere it is written: “He walks upon the wings of the winds” (Ps. CIII, 3)—but because, just as he is said to sit upon a throne when he assumes the role of judge, so when he comes for vengeance, to conquer his adversaries, he is shown in the guise of a victor and triumphant ruler.

We have often discussed the fury of the Lord: it must be understood in the same way as his forgetfulness, repentance, grief, and other emotions that do not properly belong to the divine majesty.

Thus, in this fire and fury, in these chariots and in the flame of fire, all flesh shall be judged—or the Lord himself together with his creatures—so that he may be seen to pronounce judgment not by power but by the truth of judgment, in accordance with the saying that is expressed at greater length in Micah and more briefly in the fiftieth Psalm: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L, 5).

The sword by which all flesh is to be judged is the sword of which we spoke earlier and will now discuss in part: “Unless you turn back, he will brandish his sword” (Ps. VII, 13).

This is the sword that punishes sinful flesh and every vice. The Israelites complain that it has been given into Pharaoh’s hand, and they say to Moses and Aaron: “May God see you and judge you, because you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh, so that he might put a sword in his hand and kill us” (Exod. IV, 21).

Concerning this sword it is also written in Amos: “All the sinners of my people shall die by the sword” (Amos IX, 10), although there are certainly other kinds of punishments as well.

Whatever pierces, strikes, tortures, or torments is called a sword in the Holy Scriptures. By this sword those who have not done the will of God will be wounded or killed, because they have abandoned the light of truth and wrapped themselves in the darkness of error.

Concerning them it is written in Jeremiah: “Can an Ethiopian change his skin?” (Jer. XIII, 23). And in Zephaniah: “You too, Ethiopians, shall be wounded or killed by my sword” (Zeph. II, 12).

The Apostle explains at greater length the entire meaning of this passage when he writes to the Romans:

“According to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will render to each according to his works: eternal life to those who, by patient continuance in good work, seek glory, honor, and incorruption; but wrath and fury, tribulation and anguish upon all human beings who work evil, upon the Jew first and also upon the Gentile” (Rom. II, 5 and following).

### (Verse 17)

“Those who sanctified themselves and considered themselves pure in the gardens, one after another within” [Note: Martianaeus, who had annotated the Canon of the Hebrew Truth, observed that in all corrected manuscript books *unam* (“one”) is found in place of *januam* (“door”), although here he rather carelessly retained *januam*. We, on the contrary, although aided by no manuscript testimony, have restored *unam* in accordance with Jerome’s version. For the exposition of the holy Father appended below also shows that he read—or rendered it in Latin—in this way, since immediately afterward he explains it according to the sense of Symmachus and Theodotion as referring to those who sanctify themselves in the gardens, one after another. This is still clearer at the end of the chapter, where, after explaining *unam* inwardly of Christ, he says: “He is eaten not outside, but in one house and within.” Moreover, we know that the Hebrew archetype also reads *post unum* (“one after another”), although the Masoretic note in the margin records that the Jews read it with a less suitable sense; nevertheless, the feminine form *unam* is signified.]

“who eat the flesh of swine, and the abomination, and the mouse, shall all be consumed together,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “Those who sanctify themselves and purify themselves in the gardens and vestibules, eating swine’s flesh, abominations, and the mouse, shall all be consumed together,” says the Lord.

Symmachus and Theodotion interpreted this passage as follows: “You who sanctify and purify yourselves in the gardens, one after another, among those who eat swine’s flesh, the abomination, and the mouse, shall all perish together,” says the Lord. They wished to show that those who sanctify themselves in the gardens, one after another, do not themselves eat swine’s flesh, the abomination, and the mouse; rather, those who purify themselves associate with people who eat what is forbidden.

The divine word reproves the Jewish people—indeed, the scribes and Pharisees, whom the Lord also reproved, saying: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts, because what is exalted among men is an abomination before God” (Luke 16:15). Therefore he rebuked them and said: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who cleanse the outside of the cup and dish, but inside you are full of uncleanness” (Matthew 23:25). And again: “You are like whitewashed tombs, but inside you are full of the bones of the dead and of every impurity” (ibid., 27); they blessed with their mouth but cursed in their heart (Psalm 61); they spoke peaceably to the Lord and softened their words more than oil, yet they themselves were arrows. Of them it was rightly said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13).

God had commanded through Moses (Numbers 19) that if anyone had been overtaken by sin, he should return to the Temple after being sprinkled with the ashes of the red heifer and undergoing the other rites of purification through sacrifices and offerings. But these negligent people, in places of pleasure and luxury—that is, in the most delightful gardens—constructed either baptisteries or pools for irrigating garden plots, thinking that they could wash away adulteries and every disgrace of lust with ordinary water. To them the saying of Horace may most aptly be applied: “And they cleanse the night with a river” (Horace).

No one should think it inappropriate if disgraceful practices are explained more openly, for the correction of those who are not ashamed to commit such things—things that are shameful even to mention—while they cling to prostitutes like dogs and males practice disgrace with males, receiving the recompense of their sin in themselves.

Those who perform these deeds are, by their will and crimes, associated with those who eat swine’s flesh and everything prohibited by the Law, as well as the mouse, which we call a dormouse (*glis*), or, in the eastern provinces, a *myoxos* (μυωξός). Therefore both those who eat these things and those who practice every kind of disgrace—doing things that perhaps even the Gentiles do not do—shall alike be consumed (Leviticus 11).

In the tropological sense we may say that all who are lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God sanctify themselves in gardens and vestibules, because they are unable to enter the mysteries of the truth; and they eat the food of impiety because they are not holy in body and spirit. They do not eat the flesh of Jesus, nor drink his blood. Concerning this he himself says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life” (John 6:55). “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5). He is eaten not outside, but in one house and within.

### (Verses 18–19)

“But I am coming to gather their works and thoughts together with all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my glory. And I shall set a sign among them, and I shall send from them those who have been saved to the nations—to the sea [variant: *to the sea*], to Africa, to Lydia” [Note: *tenentes* (“holding”) was formerly printed instead of *tendentes* (“drawing”), an obvious error of ancient copyists, which is ruled out by the Hebrew exemplar and Jerome’s version and is incompatible with the exposition of this passage that follows. “Lud” means the Lydians, whose colonists are the Etruscans, now called Tuscans. They were once highly skilled at shooting arrows, and they are now called “drawing the bow”—that is, “shooters.”]

“to Italy and Greece, to distant islands, to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory.”

The Septuagint: “And I know their works and their thoughts, and I am coming to gather all nations and all tongues; and they shall come and see my glory, and I shall set a sign upon them. And I shall send from them those who have been saved to the nations, to Tarshish and Phud, Lud and Mosoch and Thobel, and to Greece and distant islands—to those who have not heard my name and have not seen my glory.”

Before explaining what the enumeration of so many nations signifies, something brief must be said about the differences among the translations.

In the Hebrew language, *Tarshish* means “sea” and, as they say, refers to a region of India. Josephus, however, changing a letter, thinks that *Tarsus* is meant instead of *Tarshish*: the city of Cilicia to which Jonah wished to flee from Joppa (Jonah 1).

*Phud*, or *Phul*, refers to the Libyans and all Africa as far as the sea of Mauretania. There is presently a river called Phud there, and the entire surrounding region is called Phutensis.

They call *Lud* the Lydians, whose colonists are the Etruscans, now called Tuscans. They were once highly skilled at shooting arrows and are now called “shooters.” In Hebrew, instead, we read *MOSCHE CESETH* [the Hebrew text is incomplete or uncertain as printed], which all the translators, apart from the Septuagint, have rendered alike as “shooters of the bow.” The Septuagint wrote *μοσὸχ* (*Mosoch*), interpreting a noun in place of a verb. If it is taken as a proper name, it signifies the Cappadocians, whose capital was Mazaca, later given the name Caesarea by Caesar Augustus.

For reasons I do not understand, they also rendered in Genesis (chapter 10) the last son of Aram—that is, of Damascus in Syria—who is called Mes, as *Mosoch*. We more correctly translate it as “Maeonians.”

*Thubal*, or *Thobel*, is interpreted either as Italy or as Iberia—that is, Spain—from the river Iberus; hence even today a region of Spain is called Celtiberia. Concerning them Lucan writes beautifully (Lucan, book 4):

> The Celts of Gaul, mingling their name with the Iberians—

whom we may call “Gallo-Spaniards.”

The Greeks, who are called *Javan* in the Hebrew language, signify the Ionians; hence the Greeks are called *Iones*, and the Ionian Sea bears the same name.

It should also be considered that he placed among the nations chiefly the peoples of the East descended from Japheth, one of Noah’s sons, although in *Tarshish* and *Phud* he also remembered Shem and Ham—that is, the names of India and Africa—in order to indicate the whole world.

The Lord therefore comes to gather the works and thoughts of each person. From this we learn that not only deeds but also thoughts are to be judged on the day of judgment. For “whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

Of these thoughts it is said: “Now their thoughts have surrounded them,” when the Lord judges the hidden things of human beings according to the Gospel of Jesus Christ, so that what the Apostle writes may be confirmed by the truth of the judgment: “Their thoughts alternately accusing and defending them, on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings” (Romans 2:15). Thus all our thoughts, gathered together at one time, are proved by the just judge, while either our conscience accuses us or makes satisfaction for the offense: whether our sins are more numerous than our good works; whether they are old or new; whether they have been erased through repentance or renewed by fresh crimes. For the Lord says: “I have given them their ways upon their heads, and I will repay their thoughts to them” (Hosea 4:9). He “formed their hearts individually and understands all their works” (Psalm 32:15).

Elsewhere also we read: “You alone know the hearts of human beings” (2 Chronicles 6:30). For “no one knows what is in a person except the spirit of the person that is in him” (1 Corinthians 2). Hence God speaks through Jeremiah: “I am God who is near and not far away, says the Lord. Can a person hide himself in hidden places, and shall I not know?” (Jeremiah 23:23).

Finally, it is said to the scribes and Pharisees: “You are those who justify yourselves before men, but God knows your hearts” (Luke 16:15). Here we must note that he did not say “the Father,” in accordance with the blasphemies of the heretics, lest he appear to exclude the Son, but “God,” which is common to the Father and the Son. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God” (John 1:1–2).

Of him the same John writes: “Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people and had no need for anyone to testify concerning a human being; for he himself knew what was in a human being” (John 2:24–25). To this also belongs the statement: “Jesus, knowing their thoughts” (Luke 6:8). Elsewhere: “Jesus, knowing their wickedness” (Matthew 22:18).

And so that there may be no doubt, when heretics make accusations against the Word of God because he knows all things, the Epistle written to the Hebrews says at greater length: “For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, piercing even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart. No creature is invisible in his sight, but all things are naked and open to his eyes, concerning whom our discourse is” (Hebrews 4:12).

When all thoughts have been gathered into one place, accusing or defending us, then all nations and tongues, together with their thoughts, will likewise be brought forth for judgment. According to the Apostle Paul, we read of tongues not only among human beings but also among angels (1 Corinthians 13). From this it may be understood that all creatures will be judged by the Lord—not only those upon the earth, but also those in the air and in the heavens—according to what he had said above: “My sword is drunk in heaven; it shall descend upon the earth” (Isaiah 34:5).

All will come to see the glory of God, and he will set a sign among them, as is shown at the beginning of Ezekiel under the interpretation of the Hebrew letter *tau* (Ezekiel 9). Whoever bears this sign will escape the hand of the one who strikes. The doorposts of the houses in Egypt were also marked with this sign when Egypt perished and Israel alone remained unharmed (Exodus 12).

Concerning this sign, which King Ahaz of Judah did not wish to accept, the prophet Isaiah testifies: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7:14). Hence the Prophet prays concerning what had been promised: “Give me a sign for good” (Psalm 85:17). Elsewhere: “You have given a sign to those who fear you, so that they might flee from before the bow” (Psalm 59:4).

When the Lord ascended to the Father, he left this sign to us, or placed it upon our foreheads, so that we might freely say: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7).

What follows—“And I shall send from them those who have been saved to the nations”—and the enumeration of the individual nations appears contrary to our interpretation. For if this refers to the day of judgment, how does the Savior return again to his first coming, when the Apostles are sent to the nations and hear the Lord say: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19)?

The answer is this: the day of judgment is proclaimed, indeed threatened, so that, through fear of the future punishment, they may receive the coming of the Savior and the Gospel of the Apostles, who are to be sent beforehand.

He beautifully says: “And I shall send from them those who have been saved” (Isaiah 66:18). For unless the Lord had left us a seed, we would have been like Sodom and made like Gomorrah. The Apostle says: “A remnant has been saved” (Romans 9:27).

These people are sent to the nations—to Tarshish, Phud, Lud, Mosoch, Thobel, Greece, and the many distant islands—which have not heard the name of the Lord and have not seen his glory. Concerning them we spoke above according to the historical sense (on chapter 12). Now the allegorical interpretation must be stated briefly.

*Tarshish* is interpreted as “the exploration of joy” [Note: One Ambrosian manuscript has “plantation of joy.” In the book of Hebrew Names from Genesis, *Tarshish* means “explorers of joy,” or “joy.”]. Thus we should consider not the things that are present but those that are future, and deserve to hear: “Because you were faithful in a few things, enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25:21). The Apostle Peter likewise writes: “Rejoice with ineffable and glorious joy” (1 Peter 1:8), so that we may praise God, saying: “Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Psalm 125:2).

What follows, *Phud* [Note: In the same book of Names, *Fud* means “Libya,” or “the turning away of the mouth.”], is interpreted as “the exclusion of the mouth”: so that, excluding every blasphemy, we may speak what is good and say: “My mouth shall proclaim your righteousness, O Lord, your salvation all the day” (Psalm 70:15). Again: “I have not hidden your truth in my heart; I have declared your salvation” (Psalm 39:11).

*Lud* also, in our language, is translated as “usefulness”; *Mosoch* as “extension” [Note: In the book of Names, *Mesech* is interpreted as “extension,” or “failure,” or, alternatively, “compressed.”]; and *Thubal*, or *Thobel*, as “led toward mourning,” or “turned” [Note: Previously, under a single etymology, it was incorrectly read as “turned toward all things.” The words we have restored are Jerome’s own in the book of Names from Genesis: “Thobel, or Thubal, led toward mourning, or turned, or all things.”], or “all things.”

All these meanings accord with the calling of the nations: they should pursue usefulness through confession of their soul, forget the past, and stretch themselves toward the future. Let them mourn their former sins and be drawn toward mourning and sorrow, which lead to life. “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall laugh” (Matthew 5).

Let all be converted to the Lord, so that afterward they may pass over into grace and know what the Apostle said: “Glory, honor, and peace to everyone who does good, to the Jew first and to the Greek” (Romans 2:10), because he is God not only of the Jews but also of the nations.

As for the statement, “And to the distant islands, which have not heard my name and have not seen my glory,” it applies to those of whom we read above: “Those to whom it was not announced concerning him shall see, and those who have not heard shall understand” (Isaiah 55:5). Again: “I became manifest to those who were not asking for me; I was found by those who were not seeking me” (Isaiah 65:1). “I said, ‘Here I am,’ to those who were not calling upon my name.” We have often said that the islands signify either the nations of the whole world or the churches scattered throughout the world.

### (Verse 20)

“And they shall announce my glory among the nations” [Note: The Vulgate reads “my glory to the nations,” without the preposition *in*.] “and they shall bring all your brothers from every nation as a gift to the Lord, on horses, in chariots, in litters, on mules, and in wagons, to my holy mountain, Jerusalem,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “And they shall announce my glory among the nations, and they shall bring your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the Lord, with horses and carriages, in mule-litters, with canopies, to the holy city Jerusalem,” says the Lord.

Those who have been saved and sent to various nations, to those who had not previously heard or seen the glory of the Lord, will announce it among all the nations. They will bring the brothers of the Jewish people—those remnants who have been saved—as a gift to the Lord from every nation. These may be either the people who, having rejected the error of idolatry, have followed knowledge of the true God, or those from the people of Israel throughout the whole world who have believed. The Apostle Peter writes to them as well (1 Peter 1).

They will bring them on horses, in chariots, litters, mules, and wagons. In place of *carrucae* (“wagons”), which Symmachus alone translated and whom we have followed here, Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated “mules.” Where the Septuagint rendered “with canopies”—which we may interpret as covered sleeping couches or litters—others, with the same word, translated *φορεῖα* (*phoreia*), which we interpret as “vehicles of various kinds” [Note: The Ambrosian manuscript has *φορίους*; other manuscripts examined by Martianaeus have *φορίοις*.]. Where the Septuagint and Theodotion said “mule-litters,” Symmachus translated “litters,” while Aquila wrote *σκεπαστά* (*skepasta*), which likewise signifies litters covered with skins.

This may suffice concerning the variations among the translations.

We may understand the horses, chariots, litters, mules, wagons, and vehicles of various kinds as angelic ministries. Elsewhere it is said to God: “Mount upon your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3:8). Elijah was taken up to heaven by these horses, chariots, and quadrigas; and Elisha showed that he was surrounded and protected by them, although the boy with him did not know it (2 Kings 2).

Zechariah also saw this by night: “Behold, a man riding upon a red horse, and he stood among two shaded mountains. Behind him were red, sorrel, variegated, and white horses. And I said,” he says, “‘What are these, Lord?’ And the angel who spoke with me said to me, ‘I shall show you what these are.’ And the man who stood among the mountains answered and said to me, ‘These are those whom the Lord sent to traverse the earth’” (Zechariah 1:8–10).

John likewise testifies in the Apocalypse that he saw these things: “I saw heaven opened, and behold, a white horse; and the one sitting upon it was called Faithful and True, judging and making war in righteousness. His eyes were like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems. He had a name written that no one knows except himself, and he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood; and his name was called the Word of God. The armies in heaven followed him on white horses, clothed in white and pure linen, and from his mouth proceeded a sharp sword, so that with it he might strike the nations” (Revelation 19:11 ff.).

The Lord and Savior sat upon a red horse when he assumed a human body, of whom it is said: “Why are your garments red?” and, “Who is this who comes from Edom, with crimson garments from Bozrah?” (Isaiah 63:2). Horses of various colors followed him: red in martyrdom, starling-colored in flight, variegated in virtues, and white in virginity.

He sat upon a white horse when, after the resurrection, he assumed an immortal and incorruptible body. Whoever followed him likewise rode white horses—that is, incorruptible and immortal bodies.

It would take too long to explain both testimonies in full. I shall say only this: the different vehicles by which human beings are brought to the faith are angels, or holy men who have advanced from humanity into angels [Note: Do not suppose that this is being said in the Origenist sense, as though human beings, having stripped off their human nature, put on an angelic nature—a view Jerome often rejects and dismisses with a hiss. He states the matter most clearly in Letter 75 to Theodora, section 2: “When it is said, ‘They will be like the angels in heaven,’ the nature and substance of bodies are not taken away; rather, the greatness of their glory is shown. For it is not written, ‘They will be angels,’ but ‘like angels’: where likeness is promised, identity is denied. ‘They will be like angels,’ he says—that is, similar to angels; therefore they will not cease to be human beings. They will indeed be illustrious and adorned with angelic splendor, but they will remain human beings, so that the Apostle remains the Apostle and Mary remains Mary. Thus the heresy is confounded— that heresy which makes uncertain and grand promises in order to take away what is certain and moderate.”].

Many passages of Scripture teach that each of us has angels, among them this one: “Do not despise one of these little ones, for their angels continually see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 18:10). When the girl Rhoda announced that Peter was at the door, some believed that it was his angel (Acts 12).

But if this is said concerning the little ones, and concerning one human being, how much more must it be understood of all the saints, and especially of the Apostles, whose angels continually see the face of the Father, according to what is written: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him” (Psalm 33:8). Jacob also says of himself: “The angel who delivered me.”

These are the angels who ascend and descend upon the Son of Man. Those who are swift in faith are carried on horses; those who abound in grace are carried in chariots; those who need consolation are carried in roofed litters and under canopies, so that they may deserve to hear: “By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120:6).

In the Holy Scriptures we understand mules in two ways: either in the sense of sterility and continence, such as those upon which David and Solomon sat—the one whose name is interpreted as “strong of hand,” the other as “peaceful”; or in the negative sense, concerning which it is said: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9). Doeg was set over such people (1 Samuel 21).

The wagons, for which—as we said above—the Septuagint translated “covered vehicles,” while the others translated simply “vehicles,” should be understood as referring to those about whom the Apostle speaks: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2).

The mule-litters, moreover, are to be understood as the shining bodies of the saints and the souls illuminated by faith in the Lord, to whom it may be said: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14).

All this equipment serves the purpose of our entering the holy city of God, or the holy mountain of the Lord, Jerusalem—not that Jerusalem which kills the Prophets and stones those sent to it, but the heavenly Jerusalem, of which we have often spoken: “The Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (Galatians 4:26). Again: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Hebrews 12:22).

We may understand this either of the present Church, gathered throughout the world through the Apostles, or of the future Church, so that what the Apostle prophesied through the Holy Spirit may be fulfilled: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16).

The Jews and the Ebionites, heirs of Jewish error, who assumed the name of “poor” on account of the humility of their understanding [Note: See above, in the commentary on Isaiah 1:3, what we observed concerning the name of the Ebionites.], and who await all the pleasures of the thousand years, understand the horses, chariots, wagons, litters or mule-litters, sleeping couches, mules and she-mules, wagons, and vehicles of various kinds exactly as they are written.

They suppose that at the consummation of the world, when Christ comes to reign in Jerusalem, the Temple has been restored, and Jewish sacrifices have been offered, the children of Israel will be brought back from the whole world [Note: The earlier printed books add: “not at all upon horses, but upon mules of Numidia; nor, indeed, taken up with wings; but upon Gallic *sarraca*, Belgian *covini*, and Cappadocian and Spanish horses, and in Italian wagons; and their matrons will be carried back in litters and mule-litters.” This passage is found in no manuscript exemplar and therefore seems to us adulterated. Marianus Victorius thought that *sarracum* and *covinus* were kinds of horses, although *sarracum* is a kind of vehicle, a French *haquet* (a type of cart), while *covinus* is also a known type of vehicle, not only among the Britons but among the Belgians and Germans. A *covinus* was a scythed chariot. See Pomponius Mela and Lucan, book 1. These types of vehicles do not at all suit the sense and clearly show that the words are additional and spurious. MARTIAN.], “not at all upon horses, but upon Numidian mules.”

Those who have senatorial rank and hold the place of rulers will come in wagons from the Britons, Spaniards, Gauls, and the remotest Morini of mankind—Virgil so calls the Morini (Aeneid 8)—and from the place where the two-horned Rhine is divided. All the nations prepared for their servitude will come to meet them.

### (Verse 21)

“As if the children of Israel were bringing a gift in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord. And I shall take some of them as priests and Levites,” says the Lord.

The Septuagint: “As if the children of Israel were offering their sacrifices to me with psalms in the house of the Lord; and from them I shall take priests and Levites,” says the Lord.

Those who have been sent to the nations and have announced my glory to them will thus bring your brothers from all the nations as a gift to the Lord, with horses, chariots, litters, mules, wagons, and various vehicles, to the holy mountain Jerusalem, just as the children of Israel, while their religion still stood and the rites of the Temple were observed, used to offer sacrifices with psalms in the house of the Lord.

Or, as it is found in the Hebrew and as all the translators rendered it with one voice, “in a clean vessel”—which even today the children of Israel who behold God with the mind offer in the house of God, which is the Church: spiritual sacrifices with the fruits and virtues of their souls in clean vessels, that is, in holy bodies.

Concerning them the Apostle writes: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Holy Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16).

“And I shall take some of them as priests and Levites,” says the Lord, so that those who have been saved may preach to the nations. One of them said: “Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God” (1 Corinthians 4:1). The evangelist Luke likewise says: “Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us.”

Concerning them we also read above: “You shall be priests of the Lord for me” (Isaiah 61:6).

For just as there is a hidden Jew who is circumcised in spirit (Romans 2), of whom it is written, “We are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit” (Philippians 3:3), and who offer spiritual sacrifices pleasing to God, singing psalms in spirit and understanding, so also there are hidden priests and Levites who do not follow a sequence of descent but the order of faith.

Or certainly he is not speaking of the Apostles and apostolic men, who were leaders of the Church and came from the Jewish people, but of the nations enumerated above—those from the sea, Africa, Libya, Cappadocia, Italy, Greece, and all the islands whose inhabitants had not first heard the Lord or seen his glory. These peoples will later be turned into priests, so that those who had been the tail may become the head, and those who had been the head may be turned into the tail.

### (Verses 22–23)

“For just as the new heavens and the new earth that I am making shall stand before me,” says the Lord, “so shall your seed and your name stand. And it shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath; all flesh shall come to worship before my face,” says the Lord [Note: The word *mea* (“my”)—which is also present in the Hebrew [Hebrew word omitted in the supplied text]—was absent from Martianaeus’s edition. The Ambrosian manuscripts, together with Victorius, supply it.].

The Septuagint: “For just as the new heaven and the new earth that I make shall remain in my presence,” says the Lord, “so shall your seed and your name stand. And it shall be month after month and sabbath after sabbath; all flesh shall come to worship the Lord before me in Jerusalem.”

When he says, “I shall take some of them as priests and Levites,” he shows that the former priesthood has been set aside—the priesthood that belonged to the tribe of Levi, in which there was not election but natural order and a succession of family descending through offspring.

Since the priesthood has been transferred, it is necessary that there also be a transfer of the Law, and that election belong to those to whom the priesthood is conferred not according to blood but according to merits and virtues. They will come from the islands of the nations and announce the glory of the Lord. They will be brought on horses, chariots, litters, mules, and wagons.

But how will there be a new heaven, a new earth, and a new Jerusalem, so that it may no longer be said, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35), and again, “Heaven will be rolled up like a scroll, and the earth will be destroyed by corruption” (Revelation 6:14)? In the same way, when all things are made new, the people of God will also become new, as Scripture says: “The old things have passed away; behold, everything has become new” (Isaiah 43:19). Elsewhere: “If anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

There will also be a new people: “Christ the firstfruits, then those who belong to Christ at his coming.” There will be a new heaven and a new earth, concerning which it is said among the eight beatitudes: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matthew 5:3–4).

Indeed, every creature is now subjected to vanity in hope, because of him who subjected it (Romans 8). But they will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the glory of the children of God. Human beings will become his children, stand forever in his presence, and their name will continually remain, so that no other nation may succeed them, as happened among the Jews; rather, they will remain forever.

“And it shall be,” he says, “month after month and sabbath after sabbath,” so that from carnal sabbaths and months there may arise spiritual and delightful sabbaths, the sabbath-rest reserved for the people of God.

There will also be a spiritual month, when the moon is completed from point to point and runs its appointed course to form a month—that is, the kalends, which in Greek are called νεομηνίαι (*neomeniai*), meaning “the beginning of a new month.” Among them the beginning of the kalends does not commence and end according to the course of the sun and the varying lengths of the months, but according to the circuit of the moon.

This is the moon of which it is said in praise of the true Solomon: “He shall endure with the sun and before the moon, throughout all generations” (Psalm 71:5). In the Song of Songs she is called “chosen”: “Who is this who comes forth like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, awesome?” (Song of Songs 6:9).

Physicists, and those whose concern is to discuss heavenly matters, say that the moon does not possess its own light but is illuminated by the rays of the sun. For it is always completed and shines on that side of its sphere by which it is nearer to the sun, and it is not darkened by the shadow of the earth. The poet also demonstrated this in a single verse (Virgil, *Georgics* 1):

> Nor does the moon rise subject to the rays of her brother.

If this is true, then we too may say tropologically that the Church, which grows and declines amid peace and persecutions and, when oppressed by the darkness of temptations, again takes up its former light, receives its radiance from the sun of righteousness; and that this is what is said: “The moon will shine like the sun” (Isa. XXX, 26). Its inhabitants likewise—those who are righteous—will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Through these months, too, the seed of the Lord, which has been established forever, comes to its festivals, of which the holy man spoke with mystical utterance: “I have kept the eternal years in mind, and I have meditated” (Ps. LXXVI, 6).

Concerning the Sabbath, which signifies rest, we have treated at length in the prophecy concerning the eunuchs and foreigners (On chapter LVI). Now it must be said briefly that those come at the new moons and on the Sabbaths who, after crossing and passing beyond the six days in which the world was made, hasten toward the seventh day—that is, the Sabbath—in which true rest exists.

With respect to these festivals, the apostle Paul instructed believers, saying: “For the law, possessing a shadow of the good things to come” (Heb. X, 1). And again: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast day, or of a new moon, or of Sabbaths, which are shadows of things to come” (Col. II, 16). But if these things preceded as shadows of future good things and as an image, the whole Law must be understood spiritually. Concerning it the same Apostle said: “We know that the law is spiritual” (Rom. VII, 14). David, too, desired to know its mysteries: “Open my eyes, and I shall consider the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII, 18). “The things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (II Cor. IV).

To run through all these matters in a brief discussion is not appropriate here. For if “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II), how can we attempt, on a little tablet, to display a description of the whole Law, as though it were the entire world?

As for what follows—“All flesh shall come to worship before me in Jerusalem”—it must be known that the Hebrew does not contain “Jerusalem.” Let us therefore strike down the arrogance of the Jews: it says only “before me,” so that the word of the Lord may be fulfilled, who says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John IV, 21). And again: “God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (ibid., 24). And the Apostle says: “Lifting up holy hands in every place” (I Tim. II, 8).

“All flesh” does not signify the Jewish people but the whole human race, in accordance with what was said above: “All flesh shall see your salvation” (Isa. XL, 5). And in Joel: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel II, 28). And in Zechariah: “Let all flesh fear before the face of the Lord” (Zech. II, 13). And in the Psalms: “To you all flesh shall come” (Ps. LXIV, 2). The same thing is expressed in other words in another psalm: “All the nations that you have made shall come and worship before you, and they shall glorify your name, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXV, 9).

The Chiliasts (χιλιασταί), whom we may call the Millenarians, absurdly interpret “month after month” and “Sabbath after Sabbath”—on which all flesh shall come to worship God—as follows: those who are near will come to Jerusalem every Sabbath; those who are farther away, by months, that is, when the cycle of the new moons has been completed; and those who are very far away, once each year—that is, on the days of Easter or of the Tabernacles—according to what is said in Zechariah: “Going up from year to year to worship the Lord, the King of hosts, and to celebrate the festival of Tabernacles” (Zech. XIV, 16).

And, to provoke even greater laughter among their hearers, they interpret what is written in the final book of that same prophet—“And there shall no longer be a merchant in the house of the Lord of hosts on that day”—to mean that merchants will cease to exist for a thousand years, because everything will grow in every place, so that we will not need the leaf of amomum or pepper, nor will the Indians desire pennyroyal from us.

**(Verses 24.)** “And they shall go out, and they shall see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched. And they shall be, to the satisfaction of the sight, for all flesh.”

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** These words are likewise found in the Septuagint; we have supplied them from the Ambrosian manuscript. The Septuagint differ from the Hebrew in this one respect: they omit “to the satisfaction,” if indeed the one word—which properly signifies nausea—may be circumscribed by so extensive a periphrasis as “to the satisfaction of the sight.”]

The Septuagint likewise read: “All flesh that is to worship before the Lord,” either in the heavenly Jerusalem or in every place where pure hands are lifted up, “shall go out” to see the corpses of men who have transgressed against God. This may be understood either of the Jews, concerning whom it was said: “I begot and exalted sons, but they themselves despised me”; or of all who, possessing knowledge of God in their hearts, turned aside into vanity, so as to worship the creature rather than the Creator.

They shall go out, not in place but in understanding. For corpses of the dead cannot be within with the Lord. If, then, all flesh is to worship the Lord, while, conversely, the corpses of men who have transgressed against the Lord are to be handed over to eternal fires, there will be a resurrection of true flesh on both sides.

The worm that will not die and the fire that will not be quenched are understood by many as the conscience of sins, which torments those placed in punishments because, through their own fault and sin, they have been deprived of the good of the elect, according to what is said: “I was turned in misery while the thorn was fixed in me” (Ps. XXXI, 4). And in Proverbs: “An understanding heart is a moth to the bones” (Prov. XXV, 20). And again, under the obelus: “As a moth to a garment, and a worm to wood, so sorrow tortures the heart of a man” (ibid.).

**[Note: [Col. 0675D]** Compare this exposition with the one immediately following, [Col. 0676D], which people commonly and maliciously misrepresent as though the holy Doctor had believed that the punishments of transgressors and impious men would eventually come to an end. I say nothing meanwhile of the many other, frequent, and far clearer testimonies of his—such as the one shortly above: “In this the accursed sinner will be punished, because he will suffer eternal penalties in an incorruptible body.”]

This is so, at least, provided that they do not deny the eternal punishments of transgressors and of those who deny the Lord, since the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41). And in another place: “Bind his hands and feet, and cast him into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. XXII, 13).

If we have heard of hands [variant: “we bind”] and feet, of the outer darkness—which is the punishment of the eyes that do not see the light of God—of weeping, which certainly also pertains to the eyes, and of the gnashing of teeth, I am astonished that some introduce an aerial body after the resurrection, to be gradually dissolved into thin air. For the Lord, by the power of his majesty, entered to the Apostles through closed doors (John XX). He had certainly already walked before the resurrection with a floating step upon the sea, and he granted this very thing to the apostle Peter: so that he who walked by faith might afterward sink through unbelief. To him he said: “Why did you doubt, O you of little faith?” (Matt. XIV, 31).

The fire, too, must be understood in the same way as the worm: it burns for as long as it has material on which the devouring flame may feed. If anyone therefore has in his conscience the weeds that the enemy sowed while the master of the house was sleeping, when the fire consumes them, the conflagration will devour them (Matt. XIII). Before the eyes of all the saints, the punishments will be displayed of those who, instead of gold, silver, and precious stone, built upon the Lord’s foundation hay, wood, and straw—the fuel of everlasting fire.

**[Note: [Col. 0677C–0678C]** Clearly, therefore, those do Jerome an injury who slanderously claim that he agrees with those who dream—and have tried to prove—that the torments of evil men will someday have an end. For it is evident that here he repeats these testimonies in that direction not as his own view, but solely in fulfillment of a commentator’s duty. That he himself held the orthodox view is shown both by these very words and by the context below: he carefully distinguishes, as it were, two classes of the condemned, one to be tormented by eternal punishment, the other by temporal punishment; but which lot belongs to whom, we must leave to the knowledge of God alone, who knows whom, how, and for how long he ought to judge. This he accordingly adds at the end. When he judges the Judge’s sentence to be measured and mingled with clemency concerning sinners and impious persons who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified by fire, it is clear that he speaks of those who have repented of their crimes and whom purgatorial fire will cleanse. Conversely, concerning the Devil and all deniers and impious persons who have said in their heart, “There is no God,” he does not doubt that the torments are eternal; and that impious Christians who have denied God by their works will also fall into that condemnation if they are overtaken in sin. Nor did he teach otherwise in Dialogue I against the Pelagians, no. 28: that the Devil and his followers, and all the impious and transgressors, perish forever; but that Christians, if they are overtaken in sin (that is, a lighter sin, capable of being cleansed by purgatorial fire, in accordance with the Pauline testimony to which he alludes, I Cor. III, 13–14), are to be saved after punishments. See also what we have noted on this passage, in order to show him free from the error into which he too was being drawn, namely, that the sufferings of the condemned will someday end. For what some say—that Augustine had these Commentaries of Jerome on Isaiah before his eyes when he attacked that error, though he kept the great man’s name silent out of reverence, in *On Faith and Works* and in the *Enchiridion, on Faith, Hope, and Charity*—is far removed from every appearance of truth. The arguments and scriptural testimonies which the bishop of Hippo there dismantles and refutes as belonging to that wicked opinion are altogether different from those Jerome here rehearses as the opinions of others. Thus it is clear on this ground also that Augustine never found anything in Jerome’s writings consonant with this error.]\n\nBut those who wish punishments eventually to end, and, even if only after many ages, to have a limit to their torments, use the following testimonies: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI, 25). And again: “God has confined all things under sin, so that he may have mercy on all” (Gal. III, 22). And in another place the holy man says: “I will bear the wrath of the Lord, because I have sinned against him, until he justifies my cause, removes my judgment, and brings me into the light” (Mic. VII, 9). And again: “I will bless you, Lord, because you were angry with me. You turned your face away from me, and you had mercy on me” (Isa. XII, 1).

The Lord also says to the sinner: “When the wrath of my anger has passed, I will heal again” (Ps. XXX, 20). And this is what is said in another place: “How great is the abundance of your goodness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you.”

They repeat all these passages, wishing to assert that after punishments and torments there will be future reliefs. These things must now be hidden from those for whom fear is useful, so that, while they dread punishments, they may cease to sin. We must leave this to the knowledge of God alone, whose mercy—and whose punishments also—are measured, and who knows whom, how, and for how long he ought to judge.

Let us say only what suits human frailty: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger” (Ps. VI, 1; XXXVII, 1).

And just as we believe that the devil and all who deny him, as well as the impious who have said in their hearts, “There is no God” (Ps. XIII, 1), suffer eternal torments, so we judge that there is a measured sentence, mingled with clemency, from the Judge concerning sinners and impious persons who are nevertheless Christians, whose works must be tested and purified in fire (I Cor. III, 13).

**[Note: [Col. 0678D]** In the older Ambrosian manuscript the reading is: “So concerning sinners, even Christians, whose works, and so forth.” This is, I think, more faithful to Jerome’s meaning and to the sense of what has just been discussed concerning the torments of the condemned.]

**[Col. 0679]**

# THE SIX BOOKS OF COMMENTARIES ON THE PROPHET JEREMIAH BY SAINT EUSEBIUS HIERONYMUS, PRESBYTER OF STRIDON

**[Note: [Col. 0679B]** We have edited these books of Explanations on Jeremiah chiefly on the authority of two manuscripts: one Vatican manuscript, marked number 250, and another exceedingly accurate Cistercian manuscript, namely, that of the library of Santa Croce in Jerusalem at Rome. We also consulted Rabanus, who copied Saint Doctor’s Commentaries word for word from the finest exemplars of his own age and continuously incorporated them into his work; from him we corrected many passages.]

**(C)**

## Prologue

**[Col. 0679A] 833–834** After the explanations of the Twelve Prophets, Isaiah, Daniel, and Ezekiel, we finally set our hand to Jeremiah, dedicating these little commentaries to you, brother Eusebius,

**[Note: [Col. 0679B]** Understand this to mean the man of Cremona, to whom he had dedicated the Commentaries on Matthew eighteen years earlier. He calls him an evangelical man because of his virginity; Martianaeus also observes this from Jerome’s Preface to his translation of the same prophet.]

so that you may join the evangelical man to the evangelist Matthew, whom many years ago, at your urging, I explained in concise interpretations.

And because the volume is very long, and because in most places a clear historical narrative is woven into it, I urge your prudence not to seek an extensive explanation, especially of matters already stated in the other Prophets and which are self-evident to the understanding. Thus I shall try to write in the manner of a notary, so that nothing will be lacking in meaning, although much will be lacking in words.

I shall prepare for you the warp, the woof, and the threads; you yourself must make the most beautiful garment, so that you may be able not only to hear us but also to teach others.

As for the little book of Baruch, which is commonly joined to the edition of the Septuagint and is not found among the Hebrews, and the pseudepigraphic Letter of Jeremiah, I have judged that they should not be discussed. Rather, I shall arrange Jeremiah’s order, which has been confused through the error of copyists, and supply from the Hebrew sources the many things that are missing, so that you may possess the Prophet newly drawn from the old, and the true in place of the corrupted and falsified text.

**[Note: [Col. 0679C]** And the pseudepigraphic (ψευδεπίγραφον) Letter, and so forth. The printed editions falsely read ψευδόγραφον, along with a few more recent manuscript copies, which have “Pseudographon” through the ignorance of ancient copyists. All the other manuscript codices consistently preserve the genuine word ψευδεπίγραφον. In one beautiful and excellent manuscript of the Abbey of Cluny, and in another of Saint Albinus of Angers, I found written ΨΕΥΔΟΕΠΙΓΡΑΦΟΝ. Let prudent and fair-minded readers now marvel at the judgment, good faith, and learning of the critical slanderer who, after recently seeing the Royal manuscript number 3990, formerly 569, containing Jerome’s Commentaries on Jeremiah and reviewed by Abbot Peter, began to cry out in his notorious pamphlets: “O fraud! O reckless Benedictine monks! O corrupters of the most excellent ancient books!”

But if you ask what he proclaims worthy of such a wide-mouthed outcry, he answers, with grief of heart and pain of stomach: “Peter, abbot of the monastery of Micy, removed the Greek word Pseudographon from his copy. Oh, wickedness! Come, let us erase all the monks of Saint Benedict from the land of the living, because they too have erased one Greek word from the Prologue of Saint Jerome’s Commentaries on Jeremiah.”

But now spare your tongue and spare your pen, crushed and exorcised serpent; reread the Preface of the holy Doctor, so that you may feel yourself pierced by Jerome’s words as though by Thracian goads. And if your rage for slander permits it, consult the manuscript codices and enjoy the libraries of all the monasteries of Gaul, Italy, Germany, and Spain, so that unwillingly you may become a witness to the faith and integrity of all the monks who, in two thousand manuscript copies, distinctly wrote the Greek word whose removal from a single copy provoked you to such calumny. MARTIAN.]

I have disregarded the fury of detractors, who slander not only our words but even our syllables, imagining that they know something if they disparage the works of others.

**[Note: [Col. 0680C]** He means Pelagius, whom shortly afterward he calls the forerunner of Grunnius, namely Rufinus.]

Thus recently an unlearned slanderer broke out against me, thinking that my Commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Ephesians ought to be censured. He does not understand, snoring in excessive stupidity, the laws of commentaries, in which many opinions of different people are set forth, with their authors’ names either suppressed or stated, so that it is left to the reader’s judgment to decide what he ought chiefly to choose. Although, in the first book of that same work, I prefaced the statement that I would speak either my own words or those of others, and that the Commentaries themselves belonged as much to ancient writers as to me.

Not seeing this, his forerunner Grunnius once tried to attack me.

**[Note: [Col. 0681B]** His Grunnius. By this name he means Rufinus, as also below in the Preface to the Fourth Book of these Commentaries. See the letter to the monk Rusticus, where he vividly portrays Grunnius. MARTIAN.]

I answered him in two books, in which what he puts forward as his own, and what another slanderer had already attacked, has been cleared up. I pass over the volumes Against Jovinianus, in which he laments that virginity was preferred to marriage, marriage to bigamy, and bigamy to polygamy.

**[Col. 0682A]**

That utterly foolish man does not remember, weighed down by the porridge of the Scots,

**[Note: [Col. 0681B]** From this passage and another in Book III below, it is established that Pelagius was born in Scotland. If he is commonly called a Briton and a Briton among writers of that age, the reason is that in Latin Britannia was the name of the whole island, including the northern region itself, which was later called Scotland. In this sense he is called a Briton by Marius Mercator in the Commonitorium, by Orosius in the Apology, “our British serpent” by Prosper in the Carmen de ingratis, and, before all of them, “the Briton” by Augustine in Letter 186.]

that we ourselves said in that very work: “I do not condemn those married twice, nor even those married three times; and, if it can be done, those married eight times. I shall go further: I also receive a fornicator who repents. Whatever is equally permitted must be weighed in an equal balance.”

Let him read the Apology of that same work, which Rome gladly received many years ago against his master.

**[Note: [Col. 0682B]** “Against his master.” We read the plural “masters” in our ancient manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. MARTIAN.]

Then he will perceive that he blasphemes with the voices of others, and is so ignorant that he does not even possess insults of his own, but uses against us the fury of enemies long since buried.

But now we must undertake the work we have begun.

# BOOK ONE

**[Col. 0681]**

**[Col. 0681C] (Chapter I—verses 1 and following.)** “The words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The word of the Lord came to him in the days of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign. It came also in the days of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the completion of the eleventh year of Zedekiah, son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the deportation of Jerusalem, in the fifth month.”

The other prophets—Isaiah, Hosea, and Joel—lived before the captivity of the ten tribes of Israel, or of the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin. Others came after the captivity, such as Daniel, Haggai, and Zechariah.

Jeremiah and Ezekiel, however, composed their prophecies when the captivity was imminent: one of them in the land of Judah, the other in Babylon.

Jeremiah began to prophesy while he was still a boy, in the thirteenth year of Josiah, son of Amon, king of Judah. He prophesied for nineteen years during Josiah’s reign; afterward for eleven years under his son Jehoiakim; and under Zedekiah, the last of the kings of Judah, for eleven years, until the fifth month, when Jerusalem was captured by the Babylonians.

The three months of Jehoahaz and Jeconiah—one of whom was taken to Egypt, the other to Babylon with his mother—are counted within the years mentioned above. Thus, from the beginning of his prophecy until the captivity of Jerusalem, in which he himself was captured, he prophesied for forty-one years, apart from the period when he was taken to Egypt. There he prophesied at Tahpanhes, as this very book relates.

In place of “the words of Jeremiah,” the Septuagint put: “The word of God which came to Jeremiah” (Jer. XLIII, 8), with the evident meaning that the words of Jeremiah are the word of the Lord.

He belonged to the priestly family that lived opposite the north side of Jerusalem, at the third milestone, in the little town of Anathoth.

**[Note: [Col. 0681D]** Formerly it incorrectly read “by a bond.”]

At the same time, the Lord’s remarkable mercy is evident: although the captivity was near and the Babylonian army was besieging Jerusalem, he nevertheless summoned the people to repentance, preferring to save those who turned back rather than destroy those who sinned.

In place of “deportation,” which all the others translated with one accord, the Septuagint put “captivity.”

After the beginning of Jeremiah’s prophecy, in the thirty-fifth year of his prophecy, Ezekiel began to prophesy in Babylon to those who had been captured with him.

**(Verses 4, 5.)** “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you: I made you a prophet among the nations.”

**[Note: [Col. 0681D]** Vatican manuscript 520 does not recognize here the clause “I made you a prophet among the nations.”]

This does not mean that Jeremiah existed before conception, as the heresy supposes,

**[Note: [Col. 0681D]** He means the disciples of Origen, as we have often said elsewhere. MARTIAN.]

but that the Lord foreknew that he would exist. For to him things not yet made are already made, in accordance with what the Apostle says: “He calls those things that are not as though they were” (Rom. IV, 17).

As for being sanctified in the womb, we should understand it according to the Apostle’s words: “When it pleased him who separated me from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me, so that I might preach him among the nations” (Gal. I, 15).

John the Baptist, too, is sanctified in the womb, receives the Holy Spirit, moves in the womb, and speaks through his mother’s mouth (Luke I).

When he said, “I made you a prophet among the nations,” he wished it to be understood that we shall later read in the Prophet himself that he prophesied not only to Jerusalem but also to many surrounding nations.

Some understand this passage of the person of the Savior, who was properly the Prophet of the nations and, through the Apostles, called all peoples.

He truly was sanctified before he was formed in a virginal womb and before he came forth from his mother’s womb; he was known to the Father, since he is always in the Father and the Father always in him.

**(Verse 6.)** “And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God, behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a boy.”

The Septuagint: “And I said: O Lord God, I do not know how to speak, for I am young.”

He rejects an office that, because of his age, he cannot sustain, with the same modesty by which Moses also said that he was slow and weak of speech (Exod. IV and 6). Moses, as though he were of a strong and mature age, is rebuked; to Jeremiah, because of his boyhood, pardon is granted—a boyhood adorned with modesty and shame.

**(Verses 7, 8.)** “And the Lord said to me: Do not say, ‘I am a boy,’ for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak everything that I command you. Do not fear their faces, for I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.”

“Do not consider your age,” he says. From another prophet you have learned: “The wisdom of a man is his gray hairs” (Wis. IV, 9).
