Let your will alone be sufficient for you to go; with me as your companion, and with my help in all things, you will complete your task. “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. LXXX).

Do not consider the multitude of those to whom and against whom you will speak; consider me, who am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.

The Lord delivers him—not by removing the Prophet from persecutions and afflictions, since we read that he suffered many things—but by enabling him to overcome everything through endurance and not to yield to distress.

**(Verse 9.)** “And the Lord stretched out his hand and touched my mouth; and the Lord said to me: Behold, I have given my words in your mouth.”

It should be noted that here the hand of God is stretched out to touch the Prophet’s mouth, and he is told: “Behold, I have given my words in your mouth.” In Isaiah, however, it is written: “One of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he held a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs; and he touched my mouth and said: Behold, this has touched your lips, and it will remove your iniquities and cleanse your sins” (Isa. VI, 6–7).

There, because Isaiah was of mature and perfect age, and because he himself simply confessed that he had unclean lips and lived among a people with unclean lips, one of the Seraphim was sent to touch his mouth—not with his hand but with tongs and a coal—to remove his iniquities and cleanse his sins.

Here, however, the hand of God himself is sent—the hand through which he made all things, and which elsewhere is called his arm—not to remove sins, since Jeremiah had committed few because of his boyhood, but to grant him the grace of speaking.

Ezekiel, moreover, devours a book written inside and outside, containing both divine mysteries and the plain historical account. Jeremiah’s mouth is touched and the Lord’s words are given to him so that he may gain confidence in preaching.

Beautifully, according to the literal sense, the hand is sent, so that, seeing the likeness of human limbs, he will not shrink from the touch of a hand.

**(Verse 10.)** “Behold, I have appointed you this day over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and to destroy, to ruin and to overthrow, to build and to plant.”

What we have added from the Hebrew—“to overthrow,” or “to bring down”—is not found in the Septuagint. It should be considered that four gloomy things are followed by two joyful ones. Good things could not be built unless evil things had been destroyed, nor could the finest things be planted unless the worst had been uprooted.

“For every planting that my heavenly Father has not planted will be uprooted”; and a building that has no foundation upon rock but has been constructed on sand is undermined and destroyed by the word of God.

The one whom Jesus will consume with the spirit of his mouth and destroy by the appearance of his coming—namely, every sacrilegious and perverse doctrine—he will destroy forever.

Whatever is raised against the knowledge of God and trusts in its own wisdom, which is foolishness with God, he will overthrow and bring down, so that humble things may be built in their place, and in the place of the higher things that have been destroyed and uprooted there may be constructed and planted what accords with the truth of the Church.

Thus may be fulfilled what the Apostle says: “You are God’s building, God’s cultivation” (II Cor. III, 9).

Many understand this passage of the person of Christ. Jeremiah means “the exalted one of the Lord”: he destroyed the kingdoms of the devil, which the devil had shown him on a high mountain; he overthrew the opposing powers, erasing the record of errors on the cross.

Concerning these things, after the historical truth, he speaks tropologically (τροπικῶς) in the Psalm: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples meditate on vanities? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together” (Ps. II, 1–2).

In place of these things uprooted, destroyed, ruined, and dragged down to lower regions, the Church of God is built and planted.

There is no doubt, however, concerning the person of Jeremiah. For in what follows we read (On chapter XXV) that he receives in his hand a cup full of unmixed wine and is ordered to give it to all the surrounding nations.

**(Verses 11, 12.)** “And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see, Jeremiah? And I said: I see a watching rod. And the Lord said to me: You have seen well, for I will watch over my word to perform it.”

In place of “a watching rod,” the Septuagint translated “a rod of almond wood.” We must therefore labor so that the Latin reader may briefly understand the Hebrew etymology.

**SECED**

**[Note: [Col. 0683D]** Refer here to what we noted on the final chapter of Ecclesiastes; from that passage you may conclude that in both places “Sacod” is preferable, which is also the reading of some ancient codices. It is called an almond rod because, as Pliny testifies, the almond is the first of all trees to flower in January.

Chrysostom, in this passage, differs from Jerome’s exposition only in Greek words: “As for the word ‘of walnut,’ some have translated it ‘of almond,’ but the Hebrew has it thus: ‘I see a watching rod.’ For ‘watching’ and ‘almond’ are expressed by the same words in Hebrew.” He then adds: “You have seen well,” and so forth.]

is the word for “nut.” “Vigilance,” “watching,” or “to watch” is called **SOCED** (סֹקֵד). Hence, because of the similarity of the word for nut, the name was applied to the sense of watching. The same term is also used later for the watching leopard.

Accordingly, from the word “nut,” by the similarity of the word, the name alluded to the meaning of watchfulness. The same thing is written in Daniel according to Theodotion: from trees of holm oak and terebinth—namely, ilex and mastic—splitting and sawing was decreed for the adulterous elders.

Otherwise, at the beginning of Genesis, from the man who is called **IS** (אִישׁ), the woman is called **ISSA** (אִשָּׁה), as a kind of “manly woman” or “virago,” because she was taken from the man.

In place of “a rod of almond wood,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “a watching rod”; Theodotion translated “an almond rod.”

The rod watches, considering all the sins of the people so that it may strike and correct the offenders. Hence the Apostle writes to sinners: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. IV, 23).

This is the rod, or staff, of which David speaks: “Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me” (Ps. XXII, 5). He beautifully added, “They have comforted me.” For the Lord corrects in order to amend.

And just as a nut, or almond, has an extremely bitter husk and is enclosed by a very hard shell, so that, after the harsher and harder parts have been removed, the sweetest fruit may be found, so every correction and the labor of self-restraint seem bitter at present but produce the sweetest fruits.

Hence the old saying: “The roots of literature are bitter, its fruits sweet.”

**[Note: [Col. 0685D]** Compare Letter 22 to Eustochium and Letter 125 to Rusticus, number 12.]

Some understand the watching and almond rod as the Lord, of whom Isaiah says: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse” (Isa. XI, 1). Thus Aaron’s rod, which was thought to be dead, is said to have blossomed in the Lord’s resurrection.

**(Verses 13, 14.)** “And the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: What do you see? And I said: I see a boiling pot, and its face is turned from the face of the north. And the Lord said to me: From the north evils shall be opened”—or “shall blaze”—“against all the inhabitants of the land.”

Through successive stages, punishments are assigned to sinners, so that they may gradually come to salvation. Those who do not wish to be corrected when struck by the rod are cast into a bronze and burning pot, about which Ezekiel writes more fully: it is kindled from the face of the north (Ezek. XXIV), signifying the king of Babylon [variant: “of the Babylonians”] and the city of Jerusalem.

It is beautifully inserted: “From the north evils shall blaze against all the inhabitants of the land”—either of the land of Judah, or certainly of the whole earth, concerning which it is written in the Apocalypse: “Woe to all the inhabitants of the earth” (Apoc. VIII, 13).

For the saints are not inhabitants of the earth but strangers and pilgrims. One of them says: “I am a stranger upon the earth, and a pilgrim like all my fathers” (Ps. XXXVIII, 13). Another says: “Few and evil are my days, the days of my pilgrimage upon the earth” (Gen. XLVII, 9).

Hence Peter also writes the Catholic Epistle to the strangers and pilgrims of Pontus, Galatia, and Cappadocia (I Pet. I).

According to mystical interpretations, Solomon says: “The north is a harsh wind” (Prov. XXV, 23). But among those who have grown stiff from its cold and lost the warmth of faith, it is called by the name “right hand.”

**[Note: [Col. 0686D]** See the notes above on Isaiah, chapter XV, column 263.]

(Verses 15–16.) “For behold, I shall summon all the clans of the kingdoms of the North,” says the Lord, “and they shall come, and each shall set up his throne at the entrance of the gates of Jerusalem, and upon all its surrounding walls, and upon all the cities of Judah. And I shall speak my judgments with them concerning all their wickedness, those who abandoned me, poured libations to foreign gods, and worshiped the work of their hands.”

There is no doubt that many nations, and the kings of individual nations, were subject to the king of Babylon. When Jerusalem was besieged, they stationed themselves around it, and especially at the exits of the gates they set up their throne and tents, so that none of those who were shut in might break out. And not only Jerusalem, but all the cities of Judah, were likewise surrounded by siegeworks. “And when,” he says, “the city has been captured, then I shall speak to them, showing that my judgments were right, and that each received what he deserved”—not on account of the other vices to which human nature is subject, but especially on account of idolatry, through which, abandoning me, they worshiped the works of their hands.

Some interpret this passage in a favorable sense: namely, that those who have been boiled in the bronze cauldron, previously cleansed through torments, will afterward become rulers of Jerusalem; and that, after the Lord has had mercy on them, he will then reproach them because, having abandoned him, they venerated images. But this is a forced and perverse interpretation, lest an unlearned commentator should make a false accusation.

(Verses 17.) “You, therefore, gird up your loins; rise and speak to them everything that I command you.” Job, too, is commanded to gird up his loins (Job 4); and the Apostles are told (Luke 12), with their loins girded, to hold lamps in their hands—that is, the lamps of evangelical preaching. Those, therefore, who are about to speak the words of God must gird up their loins, knowing that all the strength of the devil is in the loins (Job 40), and let the righteous say in the Psalms: “My loins are filled with illusions” (Psalm 37:8). And when he has girded his loins, let him hear what is written: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14), so that, always watchful and rising from sleep, he may speak what God has commanded him.

“Do not be afraid before them; for I will not make you afraid of their faces.” Or, according to the Septuagint and the other interpreters: “lest perhaps I make you afraid.”

[Note: One Cantabrigian manuscript has μήποτε πτοηθῆναι σε ποιήσω, “lest I make you afraid”; the others have μηδὲ πτοηθῆς, “and do not be afraid.”]

According to our translation, the meaning is: “Do not be afraid before them; for, with me as your helper, you will not be able to fear them.” According to the Septuagint: “Do not be afraid before them; have confidence in my command. For if you do not offer what you possess, so that you may cease to be afraid, I shall abandon you and hand you over to fear; and in a certain sense I shall appear to make you afraid, when I leave you to dread.”

This signifies that the truth must always be loved, and that one must not fear the multitude of people who, when reproved, do not endure correction but lay snares for the one who reproves them. What follows according to the Septuagint—“because I am with you to deliver you,” says the Lord—is not found in the Hebrew. The meaning is: “I shall rescue you,” not by ensuring that no one lies in wait for you, but by ensuring that, although subjected to ambushes, you do not sin.

(Verses 18–19.) “For behold, I have made you today”—or, “Behold, I have set you on this day”—“as a fortified city, and as an iron pillar, and as a bronze wall over all the land: against the kings of Judah, its princes, its priests, and the people of the land. And they shall fight against you, but they shall not prevail, because I am with you,” says the Lord, “to deliver you.”

The divine word explains why the Prophet ought not to fear. “I,” he says, “have set you—or given you—today,” that is, in the present life, as long as the day is called “today,” “like a most firmly fortified city.” Not as one house, nor a tower, nor some particular walls (Matthew 5), but as the whole city that is situated upon a mountain and cannot be hidden. Of this it is written: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 86:2). And: “I am a fortified city, a city under attack” (Isaiah 27:3).

“And as an iron pillar,” he says, concerning which the Apostle writes: “The pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). Hence Peter and John, who were regarded as pillars of the Church, gave the right hands of fellowship to Paul and Barnabas. Nor is this enough; but, he says, “as a bronze wall,” which is not injured by rust, nor destroyed when struck by rains, but becomes stronger with age.

You will be such a one against kings, princes, and the people—not of any particular place, but of the land: against those who set their minds on earthly things and do not know heavenly things, who bear the image of the χοϊκός, the “earthly man,” and not of the heavenly one.

“These,” he says, “will fight against you, but they will not prevail.” Why, I ask? What is the cause of such great strength that neither kings, nor princes, nor priests, nor peoples can prevail against one man? The answer follows: “Because I am with you,” says the Lord, “to deliver you.”

If at any time the kings of Judah—which is interpreted as “confession”—and its princes and priests, that is, bishops, presbyters, and deacons, together with the base and ignoble common people, wish to rise up against a holy man, let him possess the firmness of faith and cease to fear, because, with the Lord’s help, he will overcome.

(Chapter 2.—Verse 1.) “And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Go, and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying…”

This is not found in the Septuagint, but has been added under asterisks from the edition of Theodotion, who interpreted the Hebrew word CARATH, for which we have said “cry,” or “preach,” as “read.” For because of its ambiguity, it signifies both reading, crying out, and preaching. We must understand “the ears of Jerusalem” as referring to the ears of its inhabitants.

(Verses 2.) “Thus says the Lord: I remember you, showing mercy to your youth and to the love of your betrothal, when you followed me in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown.”

The Septuagint has: “Thus says the Lord: I remembered the mercy of your youth and the love of your perfection.”

This is stated more fully in Ezekiel (Ezekiel 1), when the Lord joins Jerusalem to himself in marriage and, under the person of a wife, binds her to his embraces. Or, to show a more ardent affection, he calls her a girl, a young woman, and a betrothed bride. For what we have not yet possessed, we desire more eagerly to possess.

“When,” he says, “you followed me in the wilderness,” and, like the ornaments and dowry of a betrothal, “I distributed to you the adornments of the Law and necklaces of words.” He refers the whole of this not to her merit, but to his own mercy, through which she also obtained love.

The words we have rendered, “in the wilderness, in a land that is not sown,” are not found in the Septuagint.

(Verses 3.) “Israel was holy to the Lord, the firstfruits of his produce. All who devour him will offend; evil will come upon them,” says the Lord.

When Israel is called the firstfruits of the Lord’s produce, it is shown that the people gathered from the nations came after the firstfruits, in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “Remember your congregation, which you possessed from the beginning” (Psalm 73:2). Firstfruits are always owed to priests, not to enemies.

What follows—“All who devour him will offend; evil will come upon them,” says the Lord—has this meaning: just as those who devour the firstfruits (Numbers 5), being in no way of the priestly stock, are guilty of a crime, so those who defile Israel will be subjected to evils, in accordance with what holy David says in the twenty-sixth Psalm: “When evildoers draw near against me, to eat my flesh, those who trouble me, my enemies, they themselves became weak and fell” (Psalm 26:3–4).

Nor, because they carry out God’s sentence, will they be exempt from punishment; evil will come upon them. For scandals must come, but woe to the one through whom scandals come (Matthew 18).

(Verses 4–5.) “Hear the word of the Lord, house of Jacob, and all the clans of the house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: What injustice did your fathers find in me, that they went far from me and walked after vanity and became vain?”

Another prophet attests to this meaning: “My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Answer me: for I brought you up from the land of Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery” (Micah 6:3–4).

Both names, Jacob and Israel, are used—not with reference to the two tribes and the ten tribes, but concerning the whole people, since Jacob himself was afterward called Israel (Genesis 32).

He brings the accusation against the fathers—not because the sins of the fathers are imputed to their children, but because the children, possessing the likeness of their fathers, are punished both for their own crime and for that of their parents. We often read that, on account of holy fathers, God has mercy on their children.

The fathers of the sinful people abandoned God, and not briefly, but over a long period of time. Instead of God, they followed vanity—that is, idols—which profit their worshipers nothing; and they became like them, according to what is written: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 113:16).

(Verses 6.) “And they did not say, ‘Where is the Lord, who brought us up from the land of Egypt, who led us through the wilderness, through an uninhabited and pathless land, through a land of thirst and the image of death, through a land in which no man walked and no human being dwelt?’”

For “man,” the Septuagint interpreted “son of man”; and for “the image of death,” “the shadow of death” has been added from Theodotion.

Although this is clear according to the historical sense, we must consider, according to the allegorical sense, that as long as we are in this world and are being led out of Egypt, we gradually ascend. First we pass through deserts and an uninhabited land, which a holy person ought not to inhabit, and through a pathless land, to show the difficulty of the journey.

We pass through a land of thirst, where we always desire greater things and are not content with what is present, and through the image—or shadow—of death. For we are always in danger, and everywhere the devil stretches out his snares.

We pass through a land in which no man has walked—that is, no one who has reached perfect maturity in Christ. For we shall all rise as a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ’s maturity. Nor does the one who is a man of God, or a son of man, ever dwell in that land; rather, he is always hastening toward greater things.

From this it is evident that perfection is not on the way, but at the end of the way and in the dwelling prepared for the saints in the heavenly places. To them it is said: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 134:1).

Therefore a new heresy, derived from an old one, wrongly imagines that perfect victory exists here, where there is struggle and conflict and the outcome of future things is uncertain.

[Note: This refers, of course, to the Pelagians, who had taken ἀπάθεια—“freedom from passions”—from the Stoics, Origen, and Jovinian, and asserted that a person living in this life could attain perfection in righteousness, indeed without God’s grace, and security from every temptation and danger of sinning. Jerome calls this perfect victory.]

(Verses 7.) “And I brought you into the land of Carmel, so that you might eat its fruit and its good things; and you entered and defiled my land, and you made my inheritance an abomination.”

In place of the labor of an extremely difficult journey, I gave you abundance of all things. This is signified by Carmel, which in Hebrew is called CHERMEL, and in our language means “knowledge of circumcision.”

Just as that people polluted and violated the holy land, fertile in every kind of produce, through idolatry, so we, having received knowledge of true circumcision, eat its fruits; and if negligence creeps in, we defile God’s land and make his inheritance abominable.

(Verses 8.) “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ And those who held my Law did not know me; the shepherds transgressed against me; the prophets prophesied by Baal and followed idols.”

[Note: Victor deletes “my,” since it is found neither in Jerome’s edition nor in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint.]

After such great benefits, they turned the privileges of their dignity into contempt: the priests did not seek the Lord; the teachers of the Law did not know the one whom they ought to have taught others; the shepherds—or preachers—became transgressors through negligence; and the prophets, who dispute among the peoples, spoke not for God but for an idol and worshiped their own inventions.

These words should be used against the teachers of our own order, who devour God’s people as though they were bread and, through evil works, do not call upon the Lord.

(Verses 9.) “Therefore I shall still contend with you in judgment,” says the Lord, “and I shall dispute with your children.”

[Note: A manuscript of the Holy Cross at Jerusalem reads: “So that he may not seem to strike by power, he contends in reason with equals,” and so forth.]

So that he may not seem to strike by force, as though he were contending in reason with equals, in accordance with what David sings and the Apostle employs: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Psalm 51:6; Romans 3:4).

By saying “still,” he testifies that he has often done this; and by adding “with your children,” he shows that the same obstinacy also exists in the children of the wicked.

He secretly indicates that their children, at the coming of the Lord, also followed their ancient denial of God.

(Verses 10–11.) “Cross over to the islands of Cethim and see; send to Cedar and consider carefully, and see whether anything like this has happened: whether a nation has changed its gods”—or “its own gods.” “And certainly they are not gods. But my people has changed its glory for an idol”—or “for that which will profit it nothing.”

He compares something incomparable and sets the true God against false ones. “Go,” he says, “to the islands of Cethim,” which we should understand either as Italy or the western regions, because the island of Cyprus, in which a city bearing this name is situated, is close to the land of Judea.

[Note: The city is evidently Citium, or Cittium, or Cetium. Hence Zeno is called Κιτιεύς or Κιττιεύς by Diogenes Laertius, Book 7, and Citieus or Cittieus by Latin writers. Our Jerome says in his Questions on Genesis: “Cetim are the Citians, after whom the city of Cyprus is still called Citium.” Recall what we noted concerning this passage, and also Book 2 Against Jovinian, no. 21.]

Zeno, the founder of the Stoics, was also from there.

Cedar is a region of the wilderness and of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens. Against it, at the end of this very prophet’s book, a prophecy is woven (below, at chapter 49); David also mentions it, saying: “I dwelt with the inhabitants of Cedar; my soul was long a sojourner” (Psalm 120:5).

The meaning is: Either go toward the West, or send into the wilderness, and see whether any nation has done what you have done. None of them has despised its gods, nor exchanged wooden and stone gods for golden ones; rather, following its ancient error, it retained what it had received from its ancestors.

And this, although none of them is God, but only images fashioned by human hands.

But my people has exchanged truth for falsehood and preferred an idol to me—an idol that will not be able to help them in time of need.

We can also say this against those who pursue vices with greater zeal than virtues, whom the Apostle warns, saying: “I speak in human terms, because of the weakness of your flesh. Just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and iniquity for iniquity, so now present your members as servants to righteousness for sanctification” (Romans 6:19).

(Verses 12–13.) “Be astonished, heavens, at this, and let its gates be desolate and utterly horrified,” says the Lord. “For my people have committed two evils: they have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cisterns, broken cisterns that cannot hold water.”

The Septuagint has: “The heaven was astonished at this, and was exceedingly and vehemently horrified,” and the rest similarly.

The heaven to which it was said, “Give ear, O heaven, and I shall speak” (Deuteronomy 32:1), and, “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (Isaiah 1:2), seeing the commandments of God trampled underfoot, is horrified and cannot conceal its astonishment. For all creation groans and grieves over human sins.

But the people of God committed two opposing acts. First, they abandoned God, who is the fountain of life, although he gave the commandment: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exodus 20:2). Second, they did what is written in the same place: “You shall have no gods before me”; instead, they followed demons, whom he calls broken cisterns, because they cannot preserve God’s commandments.

We must also note that the fountain is perpetual and has life-giving waters. Cisterns and reservoirs, however, are filled either from torrents or with muddy waters, earth, and rain.

He calls the gates those of heaven, concerning which it is also written in the twenty-third Psalm: “Lift up your heads, O gates, and the king of glory shall enter.” In place of this, the Septuagint translated: “Lift up your gates, O rulers.” These matters will be discussed more fully in their proper place.

No one should be troubled by the fact that Aquila and Symmachus translated “heavens,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated “heaven.” For the Hebrew word SAMAIM is common in number, and both “heavens” and “heaven” are called by the same name, as are Thebes, Athens, and Salona.

(Verses 14.) “Is Israel a slave, or a servant born in the household?”

I think that, on the basis of this passage, the Jews, lifted up in pride, said to the Savior: “We are Abraham’s offspring and have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?” (John 8:33).

They did not know that everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, and that each person serves the one by whom he is conquered.

Thus, although they were born from Abraham, God’s friend, they became through their own fault like the sons of Ham, concerning whom it was said: “Cursed be Canaan; he shall be a servant to his brothers” (Genesis 9:25).

(Verses 15.) “Why, then, has he become plunder? Lions roared over him and gave forth their voice; they made his land a desolation; his cities were burned with fire, and there is no one who dwells in them.”

The divine word asks the question so that it may answer for itself.

By “lions” it means the princes of Babylon, who made his land desolate and destroyed his cities by fire.

Or certainly, according to the allegorical sense, we should understand the lions as hostile powers, or the leaders of heretics, who, laying waste the land of the Church, devastated all its cities with heretical fire—that fire of which it is written: “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hosea 7:4).

They truly give forth their voice; and in this same prophet, under the figure of a partridge, they cry out: “They gather what they did not produce; they make riches without judgment” (Jeremiah 17:17).

Therefore his cities have been devastated and destroyed, because they have no inhabitant, God, as Scripture says: “And there is no one who dwells in them” (ibid., 4).

(Verses 16–17.) “The sons also of Memphis and Tahpanhes violated you to the crown of your head. Has this not happened to you because you abandoned the Lord your God at the time when he was leading you on the way?”

What we have rendered, “at the time when he was leading you on the way,” is not found in the Septuagint.

He names the two great cities of Egypt, Memphis and Tahpanhes, and says that their sons violated Israel to the crown of its head, in the sense in which Isaiah says: “From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isaiah 1:6).

For such was the lust of the Egyptians, who are large in the flesh, that they spared no member but violated them all.

According to the literal sense, this refers to the idols of Egypt; according to the spiritual understanding, to teachers of perverse doctrine, who pollute the purity of the Church with their own depravity.

These things happen to it because it abandoned the Lord its God, and especially at the time when it ought to have followed him as its guide.

(Verses 18.) “And now, what do you want on the road to Egypt, to drink the water of Sior? And what have you to do with the road of the Assyrians, to drink the water of the river?”

In place of Sior, we translated “turbid,” which is what the Hebrew word signifies.

[Note: Sior and Gion are ancient names of the Nile, as is clear from the book On Place Names and from Josephus, Antiquities, Book 1, chapter 1, and Book 19, section 26. The common edition, which Jerome notes, paid greater attention to the meaning: for the Nile is known to have been called by this name because of its blackness; hence Greek authors call it μέλας, “black,” and Ausonius calls papyrus “the white page of Melon.”]

In its place, the common edition has Gihon.

Since he had previously mentioned the sons of Memphis and Tahpanhes, who violated Israel to the crown of its head, he now names Egypt itself more explicitly.

There is no doubt that the Nile has muddy waters, and that “the river of the Assyrians” signifies the Euphrates, since Scripture says that the land of promise extends from the torrent of Egypt to the great river Euphrates.

Those who have abandoned Christ, the fountain of life, and dug for themselves the reservoirs of heretics, which cannot hold the waters of their teachings, must necessarily fall under the power of lions, who reduce their land to desolation and destroy all their churches. They are polluted to the crown of their head and drink turbid waters, the streams of the Assyrian river and of the North, from which evils blaze forth over the earth.

(Verses 19.) “Your wickedness will rebuke you”—or “your transgression will instruct you”—“and your apostasy will reprove you. Know and see that it is evil and bitter for you to abandon the Lord your God, and that the fear of me is not in you,” says the Lord God of hosts.

We must note that wickedness, or transgression, after it has sated the transgressor and, like quail, has reached the point of nausea, may instruct the one who is doing penance. He is commanded to see what he has abandoned, what he has followed, and how, scorning good and sweet things, he chose evil and bitter ones.

All this happened because he abandoned the Lord his God, and his fear is not in him. For “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9). Since he did not possess it, he is handed over to evil and bitterness.

(Verses 20.) “From ancient times you broke my yoke”—or “your yoke”—“and tore my bonds”—or “your bonds”—“and you said, ‘I will not serve.’ For on every high hill and under every leafy tree you lay prostrate as a prostitute”—or “there you spread yourself out in fornication.”

He speaks to Israel as to a prostitute, because it broke its marital covenant and said, “I will not serve,” with “the lord” or “the husband” understood. But on every high hill and under every leafy tree it lay prostrate in idolatry. Pleasant and elevated places are always dedicated to idols.

This can also be said of someone who was a Christian from the beginning and, having been partly instructed in the sacred Scriptures, later, through a desire for secular literature—signified by the hills—and for pleasant eloquence—represented by leafy trees—prostrates himself before demons. Under the pretext of learning and lofty knowledge, they pollute the souls of believers and make them spread their feet before every passerby.

(Verses 21.) “But I planted you as a choice vine, all of it true seed. How have you been changed for me into the perverse vine of another?”

The Septuagint has: “But I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you been changed into a bitter vine of another?”

In place of “fruitful vine,” or “choice vine,” the Hebrew has SOREC, which appears in Isaiah’s song (Isaiah 5). It is a kind of excellent vine.

With this vine-shoot, the Lord says that he planted Israel, and he marvels that the true seed and choice vine have been changed into bitterness and have therefore become a vine belonging to another.

Let no one, therefore, be secure if the Lord’s planting, the true seed, and the Sorec vine can be so altered by its own fault that, becoming bitter, it departs from the Lord and becomes a foreign vine.

Here too the Savior’s clemency must be considered: he who said in the Gospel, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), also granted to his disciples and to the people who believe in him that they might be a choice or true vine, if they wished to remain in that in which they had been planted.

(Verses 22.) “Though you wash yourself with natron and multiply for yourself the herb Borith, you are stained in your iniquity before me,” says the Lord God.

In place of the herb BORITH, which we translated as it stands in the Hebrew, the Septuagint translated πόα, “herb,”

[Note: Since it was not readily possible to call it by its proper name, they used the general word πόα, “herb.” Theodoret, commenting on this passage, says: “He calls the cleansing agents that grow from the earth πόα.” He calls it an herb endowed with the power of cleansing, which grows from the earth. Compare the book On Names under the word Fua.]

to signify the herb of fullers, which, according to the custom of the province of Palestine, grows in green and moist places and has the same power for washing away dirt as natron.

Our natron and the fuller’s herb signify repentance. Ecclesiastical speech, which rebukes, reproves, and corrects sinners, also resembles sharper natron.

But the one stained by a light defilement of sins is cleansed by lighter admonitions. Serious sins, however, which drag a person toward death, can be washed away neither with natron nor with the herb Borith; they require more severe torments. For “each person’s work, whatever it may be, will be tested by fire, and it will be revealed in fire” (1 Corinthians 3).

He added beautifully: “You are stained in your iniquity before me,” because even if you appear clean to human beings, you are not clean to me, who know the consciences of individuals. Hence it is said elsewhere: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 143:2).

(Verses 23.) “How can you say, ‘I am not polluted; I have not gone after the Baals’? Look at your ways in the valley”—or “the valley,” which in Hebrew is called GE and is translated by the Septuagint as πολυάνδριον, which in our language may be called “a burial place of a multitude.”

[Note: The manuscript of the Holy Cross does not recognize the little word se; immediately afterward, together with two other manuscripts, it has adscribit, “he adds,” in place of describit, “he describes.”]

“In vain,” he says, “you refuse to confess your crimes and boast of your purity, although you have been polluted by the filth of idolatry; and shamelessly deny that you worshiped the idol Baal” (below, chapter 19).

Look at the valley of the sons of Hinnom, which is watered by the springs of Shiloah, and there you will see the shrine of Baal, whom, abandoning God, you venerated.

The addition, “Know what you have done,” opens the closed eyes of the denier, so that he may see what he is ashamed to look upon.

According to the tropological sense, let us prove by their works the shamelessness of those who refuse to confess their vices. Such people do not walk on the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, but on the broad and spacious one through which the multitude enters, which leads to death (Matthew 7).

Therefore it is significantly called πολυάνδριον, “a burial place of a multitude,” either because, according to the historical sense, a multitude was killed and destroyed there by the evil of idolatry.

(Verses 24.) “A swift runner, spreading out her ways; a wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness, in the desire of her soul, drew in the wind of her love; no one will turn her away. All who seek her will not fail. In her menstruation they will find her.”

The Septuagint has: “Toward evening her voice howled; she spread out her ways over the waters of the wilderness; in the desire of her soul she was carried along by the spirit. She was handed over; who will turn her back? All who seek her will not labor, and in her humiliation they will find her.”

The Septuagint’s edition differs greatly from the Hebrew truth in this passage; nevertheless, each has its own meaning.

Since he had said above, “I am not polluted,” and was speaking as though to a woman who had behaved shamefully, he describes her fornication.

“How,” he says, “a light-footed doe”—which we have rendered by the more general term “runner,” while Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion more precisely translated δρομὰς κούφη, “a swift runner”—

[Note: Until now the printed editions had read δρομεύς instead of δρομάς, but the manuscripts, with remarkable agreement and more correctly, prefer δρομάς, dromas.]

“spreads out her ways and rushes swiftly to pasture; and just as a wild donkey accustomed to the wilderness draws in, in the desire of her soul, the wind or spirit of her love”—for among the Hebrews one word, RUA, means both “wind” and “spirit”—so Israel, or Jerusalem, was carried with all its force toward the desire of lust and burned with every love of idols.

There is no one who can turn her from this impulse by his admonitions—not because the prophets lacked the power to do so, but because of the perverse malice of the one who desires it.

“Whoever,” he says, “has sought her will not labor greatly. In her menstruation and impurity they will find her.”

In place of this, Aquila translated νεομηνία, that is, “new moon” or “the first day of the month”; Symmachus, “month”; and the Septuagint and Theodotion, “humiliation.”

According to the Septuagint, the meaning is this: prostitute Jerusalem, like the woman described in Proverbs, howled toward evening with her voice, provoked lovers to lust, opened the paths of her shame, and spread her feet before every passerby (Proverbs 5 and 6).

There was a place possessing the beauty of flowing waters, made more delightful when the wilderness surrounded it, so that no one might see the fornicator.

“In the desire,” he says, “of her soul she was πνευματοφορεῖτο”—either “carried along by a perverse spirit,” or “she drew in the refreshing breath of her love”; or certainly she sang the songs of her shame.

“She was handed over,” he says, “to her vices and lust. No one will be able to turn her back. All who wish to find her will find her in the humiliation of her shame, so that she can never be satisfied with the love of pleasure.”

(Verses 25.) “Keep your foot from nakedness and your throat from thirst.” And you said, “I have despaired; I shall not do it. For I have loved foreigners, and I shall walk after them.”

The Septuagint has: “Turn your foot from the rough road and your throat from thirst”; and she said, “I shall act manfully, because I have loved foreigners and have walked after them”—or “I shall walk after them.”

Those who were about to celebrate Passover were commanded to have sandals on their feet (Exodus 12). The Apostle also says that the feet of those who are prepared for the Gospel are shod (Ephesians 6), so that, while they walk through the wilderness of this age, they may not be exposed to poisonous creatures, which ought to be trampled and crushed by the evangelical foot.

We keep the throat from thirst when we fulfill the Savior’s command: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7:37).

[Note: Three manuscripts have “we receive” in place of “we fill”; and shortly afterward they have “in despair of better things” in place of “in despair of evil things.” Victor also approves this reading and praises a similar passage in Cyprian’s letter to Donatus: “I used to comply with vices that clung to me, and, in despair of better things, I embraced my evils as though they were already my own and native to me.”]

She, however, who in despair of evil things denied that she would do what the Lord commanded, explained her reason by saying: “I have loved foreigners, and I shall follow them,” thinking that by this shameless confession she could avoid her crimes.

According to the Septuagint, the road of sinners is rough, and the Lord turns it into a level road.

Whoever follows heretics should be marked by the reproach of these verses: she said, “I have despaired,” or “I shall act manfully in my evil purpose and grow strong in my error.”

It is necessary that anyone who follows a doctrine foreign to the Church should love foreigners and follow in their footsteps—whether demons or the leaders of heretics, who are alienated from God.

(Verses 26–27.) “As a thief is ashamed when he is caught, so the house of Israel has been ashamed: they, their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets.”

Although the face of thieves is shameless and brazen, they nevertheless blush when they are caught in theft.

Thus Israel also, saying to the wood, “You are my father,” and to the stone, “You gave birth to me,” calling as its parents those whom it itself fashioned, is ashamed when it is caught in its idolatry.

[Note: This sentence, beginning “And lest we think that he says this about the people” and continuing through “their prophets,” is found in none of the manuscripts we use, nor in Rabanus at this point; rather, it is appended below to the text of Zechariah. The immediately following passage also varies in the Cistercian manuscript: “Let us use this testimony whenever our princes, and those who are regarded as leaders in the Church, are caught in shameful sins.”]

And lest we think that he is saying this about the common people, he names their kings, princes, priests, and prophets.

Let us use this testimony against our own princes and against those who are regarded as leaders in the Church, whenever they are caught in shameful sins.

“They turned their backs to me and not their faces.”

Those who cast God’s words behind them turn their backs toward him and not their faces.

For when a teacher gives a command, it is a sign of obedience if the listener hears it with head bowed. But if he turns his back, it is a sign of contempt, as it is written elsewhere: “They turned their shoulder to me in retreat” (Zechariah 7:11).

God says that they despised his commandments to such an extent that they were unwilling even to listen, but displayed the arrogance of their spirit through the gesture of their bodies.

“And in the time of their affliction they will say: ‘Rise and deliver us.’”

Those who did not recognize God through his benefits will recognize him through torments.

### (Verse 28)

“Where are your gods, which you made for yourself? Let them arise and save you in the time of your affliction” [Alt.: “on the day”]. An impudent request: in a time of need and distress to seek help from one whom they had despised in prosperity. It should be read with the tone of one rebuking: “Let your gods, whom you made for yourself, save you”—so that, since God is the Creator of human beings but a human being has made a god, necessity may prove what power those gods possess whom you formerly worshiped in security.

“According to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah.” Either the same gods, or individual and diverse gods, were worshiped by the individual cities, so that they might not even seem to share in impiety; rather, superstition, fighting against itself, followed a different error. The words that follow, “and according to the number of the roads of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal,” were added by the Septuagint.

[Col. 0696D] (Verse 29.) “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord.” Human perversity is inclined to excuse itself, so that whatever it deservedly suffers it may appear to suffer unjustly, and may refer its own guilt to God’s judgment. “In vain, therefore,” he says, “do you put forward complaints and an unjust case against the judge, since what you suffer is the consequence of your own impiety.” [Col. 0697A] 854 The words that follow, “And you have all acted wickedly toward me,” were added by the Septuagint.

[Note: [Col. 0697D] Two Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts add: “likewise.”]

(Verses 30.) “In vain I struck your sons: they did not accept correction.” In place of this the Septuagint read, “You did not accept correction.” The sense in Hebrew is: “Those who were struck refused to accept correction.” In the Septuagint, however: “Therefore I struck your sons, so that you might be instructed by their death.” And lest you perhaps say, “You were unwilling to correct sinners,” learn from the blows inflicted on your sons how I wished to treat you with a harsher remedy.

“Your sword devoured your prophets.” Not my prophets, but your prophets: it was not my sword but your sword that devoured them—the sword which you endured because of your sins. The Septuagint, moreover, does not have “your”; they translated simply, “The sword devoured your prophets,” so that the reference may be either to the hostile sword or to my sword, by which your sins were pierced.

[Col. 0697B] “Your generation was like a ravaging lion.” The Septuagint: “Like a ravaging lion—and you did not fear.” He says: The sword that devoured your prophets—there is no doubt that he means the diviners of Baal and of the idols—ravaged everything like a lion. Yet your generation, which ought to have been corrected by the killing of a few, continued wholly in its crime.

According to the Septuagint, however, the sense is this: Thus the sword of the Lord, which displayed [Note: [Col. 0697D] The same manuscripts read, more correctly, it seems, “which was displayed in the sword of the adversaries”; or, according to others, “which was displayed,” without the addition.] the sword of the adversaries, devoured and tore apart your false prophets like a lion, which, being exceedingly greedy, tears apart the prey it has found; yet even by the punishment of your prophets you could not be converted to better things.

(Verses 31.) “See the word of the Lord: Have I become a wilderness for Israel, or a land of late sowing? Why then did my people say, ‘We have withdrawn; we will come to you no more’?” The Septuagint: “Hear the word of the Lord: Thus says the Lord: Have I become a wilderness for Israel, or a land full of thorns? For my people says, ‘We will not serve, nor will we come to you’?”

Moses also saw the voice of God (Exod. 33), and the Apostle John says that he saw and touched the word of God (1 John 1). He wonders how the people of Israel could have regarded God as a wilderness, while they pursued idols as though they were the crowded centers of cities. A land of late sowing is one that receives no showers of teaching and no rain of the gospel’s discipline; it is full of thorns because it had not been cultivated. The people, therefore, once God’s own, are all the more criminal because they withdrew from the Lord and do not wish to return any longer to their Lord. It is a great offense not to wish to appease the one whom you have offended.

(Verses 32.) “Will a virgin forget her ornament, or a bride the band around her breast? Yet my people have forgotten me for innumerable days.” By this we learn that Christ is the bridegroom of the virgin Church, which has neither spot nor wrinkle. If he is the bridegroom, then these are his words, concerning whom John the Baptist says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). Therefore the one who withdraws from the Lord loses her ornament and forfeits the understanding of the teachings, which is signified by the breast. Hence the Evangelist John reclines upon the Lord’s breast (John 13), and among the portions of the victims the breast is separated for the priests (Num. 18). The greater the number of days during which we forget the Lord, the greater is the punishment of the sin—one that even the length of the ages cannot subdue.

(Verses 33–34.) “Why do you strive to display your good way in order to seek love, when you have even taught your ways your wickednesses? And on your wings [or: hands] the blood of the souls of the poor and innocent has been found. I did not find them in trenches [or: pits], but in all these places [or: beneath every oak].”

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Again, the same two manuscripts mentioned above add this.]

“In vain,” he says, “do you wish to defend yourself by verbal skill and, as though to earn love, display your good works—when you have also taught others your ways and have been an example to all in evil works. For on your wings [Alt.: evils], or indeed on your hands, the blood of the innocent has been found: those whom you sacrificed to idols, or whose souls you destroyed by the likeness of sacrifices. We have supplied ‘the poor’ from the Hebrew; the Septuagint does not have it.

“These poor and innocent people,” he says, “I did not find murdered in pits, as usually happens through the ambushes of robbers, but in all the places I have mentioned above—or beneath the oak, which in Hebrew is called ELLA: a word that also signifies these things. The sense is: ‘In all these places, or beneath the oak and terebinth, under whose shade and foliage, as in pleasant places, you were enjoying the crimes of idolatry.’”

[Note: [Col. 0698D] The Vatican manuscript reads: “idolatry and crimes.”]

(Verses 35–36.) “And you said: ‘I am without sin and innocent; therefore let your anger turn away from me.’ Behold, I will contend with you in judgment because you have said, ‘I have not sinned.’ How utterly vile you have become [or: how greatly you have despised], repeating your ways.”

[Note: [Col. 0698D] Three manuscripts read: “or, when you despised.”]

These words should be used against those who refuse to acknowledge their sins but, in a time of affliction and distress, say that they suffer unjustly what they suffer. They provoke God’s anger all the more, since it is a greater sin not to mourn what they have done but to put forward empty excuses for their sins. “I will contend with you in judgment,” he says, “because you have said, ‘I have not sinned’”—as though it were a greater sin to have one thing in the conscience and to say another in speech.

Let the new heresy hear from the Old Testament that the greatest possible anger of God is to be unwilling humbly to confess one’s sin, but shamelessly to boast of one’s righteousness:

(Verses 37.) “And from Egypt you will be put to shame, just as you were put to shame by Assyria. For you will also go out from there, and your hands will be upon your head, because the Lord has shattered your confidence [or: hope], and you will have nothing prosperous in it.”

To avoid the assault of the Egyptians, they fled to the Assyrians, whose protection proved futile; for we read that they were defeated by the Egyptians. Again, to escape the anger of the Assyrians, they used the assistance of the Egyptians, whom history reports to have been overcome by the Assyrians.

[Note: [Col. 0699D] The manuscripts read “relied upon” instead of “used,” and, consistently a little later, “may they rely upon” instead of “may they use.”] They are therefore rebuked because, abandoning hope in the Lord, they use human help—help that has all been shattered and so overturned that they can find no benefit in it.

Hence he says: “And from there you will go out,” that is, from Egypt, just as you went out from the Assyrians; “and your hands will be upon your head,” and you will mourn in vain that you had expected assistance from the Egyptians. Let us recall the historical event when Tamar, after being criminally violated by her most wicked brother Amnon, scattered ashes upon her head and placed her hands upon it, and thus returned to her house (2 Sam. 13).

### Chapter 3

#### Verse 1

“It is commonly said” (for which the Septuagint translated only “it is said” [Col. 0699B]).

[Note: [Col. 0699D] In the present copies of the Septuagint there is nothing corresponding either to the two words “it is commonly said” or to the single word “it is said.” Moreover, I think the latter is incorrectly printed in italics as though it came from the Septuagint’s translation, whereas Jerome seems to have written it to teach either that the Septuagint alone, unlike the other translators, rendered merely “it is said,” or, more probably, that in place of the two words “it is commonly said” they supplied only “it is said.”]

“If a man divorces his wife, and she leaves him and marries another man, will she return to him again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled [or: that land]? And you have prostituted yourself with many lovers [or: shepherds].”

The word REIM (רֵעִים), written with four letters—RESH, AYIN, YOD, and MEM—signifies both “lovers” and “shepherds.” If we read REIM, it means “lovers”; if ROIM, “shepherds.”

“Nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” [or: “You were returning to me, says the Lord”]. In Hebrew, even after fornication he receives the penitent and urges her to return to him.

[Note: [Col. 0700D] We explained in the notes to Letter 122, to Rusticus, section 2, what the sense of this passage is in the Hebrew archetype. For although the present copies of the Hebrew text have nothing beyond “and return to me, says the Lord,” he himself, as guarantor of his own faith, clearly states in the cited letter: “It is written according to the Hebrew truth, which is not found in the Greek and Latin manuscripts: ‘Nevertheless convert yourself, AND I WILL RECEIVE YOU, says the Lord.’” Nor, I think, are those words inserted without reason in certain copies of Jerome’s own translation.]

In the Septuagint, however, he does not invite her to repentance but reproves the shamelessness of the prostitute, since after adultery she dares to return [Col. 0699C] to her husband. The words “and will that woman be defiled,” for which we read “land” in the Hebrew, leave an example and speak more plainly of the land of Israel, which is compared with an adulterous woman.

Let us use this testimony against those who abandon the faith of the Lord and, impeded by the errors of heretics, after many acts of fornication and deceptions of souls, pretend to return to the former truth—not to lay aside the poisons in their hearts, but to commend themselves to others.

(Verses 2.) “Lift up your eyes straight ahead, and see where you have not been cast down. You sat beside the roads waiting for them, like a robber in the wilderness [or: like a deserted crow].”

In place of “robber,” or “crow,” the Hebrew has ARABE, which can also signify the Arabs. That people, devoted to robbery, still attacks the borders of Palestine and lies in wait on the roads for those descending from Jerusalem to Jericho; the Lord also recalls this event in the Gospel (Luke 10).

Therefore lift up your eyes, O Jerusalem, and look around in every direction, and see where you have not been cast down through fornication. For just as robbers customarily lie in wait for travelers toward evening and in deserted places, so you, like the adulterous woman of Proverbs, sat beside the roads toward evening in order to kill through your intercourse the souls of those who fornicated (Prov. 7). Therefore the whole land was polluted by your fornications (Eccles. 9).

Significantly, according to the allegorical sense, those who promise that they are abandoning heretical errors are commanded to lift up their eyes straight ahead. Unless they begin to see what is straight, they cannot condemn their former crookedness.

(Verses 2–3.) “And you polluted [or: killed] the land with your fornications and with your wickednesses [or: evil deeds]. Therefore the drops of rain were withheld, and there was no late rain [or: ‘and you had many shepherds to offend you’].”

The land was killed—or polluted—because of the killing of those who perished through the fornication of idolatry. Therefore the blessing of all things was removed, so that they suffered a drought of the word of God. Or else it had shepherds through whom it offended God: those who ought to have been teachers, preventing others from error, became the authors of impiety.

“You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed.” The Septuagint: “You have acquired the face of a prostitute; you have become shameless toward everyone.”

Because above (at chapter 2:35) she had said, “I have not sinned,” and had sinned even more by denying her crimes, he now accuses her as a shameless woman of extreme impudence—not one who displays a bold face toward one or another person, but one who is ashamed before no one. [Col. 0700C] Let us use this saying against the assembly of heretics, who glory in their errors.

(Verses 4–5.) “At least from now on call me, ‘My Father’; you are the guide of my virginity. Will you be angry forever, or will you persist to the end?”

Let the heretics be ashamed who refuse to turn to better things and do not wish to return to their Father and Creator, and let them hear: “At least from now on call me, ‘My Father’; you are the guide of my virginity.” He himself betrothed your soul in his embraces, and he teaches how it ought to pray and perform repentance. The more merciful he is who shows the way of salvation after fornication, the more wretched is the prostitute who refuses to receive healing after her wounds.

“Behold, you have spoken and done evil, and you were able.” In place of words of repentance, you blasphemed with words of pride; you fulfilled your evil intention and displayed your strength against your husband, so that you could do what you had discussed in speech.

(Verses 6 and following.) “And the Lord said to me in the days of Josiah the king: Have you seen what apostate Israel has done? She went for herself upon every high mountain and beneath every leafy tree, and there she fornicated. And I said, when she had done all these things: ‘Return to me’; but she did not return. And her treacherous sister Judah saw that, because apostate Israel had committed adultery, I had sent her away and given her a bill of divorce. Yet treacherous Judah, her sister, was not afraid, but went and herself also fornicated, and by the ease of her fornication polluted the land

[Note: [Col. 0701D] Two manuscripts read: “and by the difficulty of her fornication.”], and committed adultery with stone and wood. And in all these things her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me with her whole heart, but in falsehood, says the Lord.”

The sufferings of some are remedies for others. When a murderer is punished, he receives what he has done, but others are deterred from crime. Thus, when the ten tribes called Israel had been captured by the Assyrians and transferred to Media (2 Kings 17), the two tribes of Judah and Benjamin, which ought to have feared a similar fate and turned wholly to God, surpassed the crimes of the ten tribes. They followed idols so completely that they set up a statue of Baal in the Temple of God, which in Ezekiel is called an idol placed there to provoke the Lord to jealousy and rivalry (Ezek. 8).

He speaks figuratively of two sisters because they were descended from the one stock of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he calls the earlier one “apostate” and the later one “treacherous.” The former wholly turned away from God, immediately worshiping the golden calves at Dan and Bethel. The latter, among whom were the Temple and the worship of the true God, gradually withdrew from the Lord by imitating her sister (1 Kings 12). Therefore she is called “treacherous.”

[Note: [Col. 0701D] One Cistercian manuscript reads: “therefore she is called co-treacherous.”]

According to the allegorical sense, the prophecy concerns heretics. While they imagine that they excel in the knowledge of a false name and consider themselves distinguished by heretical subtlety, they ascend into the mind of pride; and, enticed by the pleasures of this flesh, beneath every leafy and pleasant tree they display their fornication. When they are handed over to the devil for the destruction of the flesh, it often happens that the house of Judah—that is, confession and the true faith—is not at all terrified by the example but commits much greater crimes and, through the ease of its fornication, pollutes the land of the Church. It commits adultery with stone and wood, following doctrines that are hostile to God.

But if an ecclesiastical man wishes to correct the one who has gone astray, cut away the rotten flesh, and draw back to repentance those who have followed falsehood, yet they nevertheless continue to follow their ancient error under the appearance of ecclesiastical truth, it may be said of them: “In all these things her treacherous sister Judah did not return to me [Note: [Col. 0701D] The two words ‘her sister’ are absent from all the Florentine copies, according to Victorius.] with her whole heart, but in falsehood.”

This prophecy took place in the days of Josiah, a righteous king, under whom Jeremiah began to prophesy.

(Verses 11.) “And the Lord said to me: Apostate Israel has justified her soul in comparison with treacherous Judah.” “Israel,” he says, “is more righteous in comparison with Judah,” because the former perished at the beginning, while the latter could be corrected by the sufferings of the former.

Let the new heresy hear from the Old Testament that Israel is said to have been justified in comparison with Judah.

[Note: [Col. 0701D] The Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts read “in comparison with the worse one” instead of “in comparison with Judah.”]

Nor is it surprising that this is said of sisters of one nation, since Sodom also receives the name of righteousness in comparison with Jerusalem, when the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Sodom was justified by you” (Ezek. 16:55); and the tax collector becomes righteous in comparison with the Pharisee (Luke 18).

(Verses 12 and following.) “Go and proclaim [or: read] these words toward the north, and say: ‘Return, apostate Israel, says the Lord, and I will not turn my face away from you [or: establish my face against you], because I am holy [or: merciful], says the Lord, and I will not be angry forever. Nevertheless, know your iniquity, because you have acted treacherously against the Lord your God [or: acted impiously], and you have scattered [or: poured out] your ways among strangers beneath every leafy tree, and you have not listened to my voice, says the Lord.’”

[Note: [Col. 0701D] The Hebrew word is Carath. Today they read it in the future tense because of the conversive Vav, vecharatha, “and you will cry out.” See the same word above, chapter 2, MARTIAN.]

The Hebrew word CARATH (כָּרַת) signifies “call,” “cry out,” and “read.” Hence Aquila and Symmachus translated it, “cry out repeatedly”; the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it, “read.”

[Note: [Col. 0702D] The same manuscripts: “and ‘call,’ or ‘cry out,’ and ‘read’ are understood.”]

The word is directed toward the north and against Babylon and the Assyrians, toward the ten and the two tribes; and their return is foretold. “I will not turn my face away from you,” he says—or, “I will not establish my face against you”—so that I may receive you not with the severity of judgment but with a merciful countenance. For I am holy and merciful, so that I will no longer remember your iniquity, nor remember that you withdrew from the Lord, that idols pleased you in his place, and that you fornicated beneath every shady and leafy tree.

This may also be said to heretics and to the negligent within the Church, who are daily summoned to repentance by ecclesiastical men; and to them the words especially apply: “You have not listened to my voice.” Every heretic dwells in the north, has lost the warmth of faith, and cannot hear the Apostle’s command: “Fervent in spirit” (Rom. 12:11). Because he has surrendered himself to pleasures, he has withdrawn from the Lord, scattered his ways among alien doctrines, and pursued pleasure.

No heresy is constructed except for the sake of the belly and the appetite, so that it may seduce “little women weighed down with sins, always learning and never able to arrive at knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3), of whom it is truly said: “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. 13:8); and whom Christ marks out as “devouring widows’ houses” (Matt. 12).

“And when,” he says, “I have shown you mercy, do not think that you are righteous. But always remember your iniquity, and know that you have fornicated against the Lord; lower the neck of your pride, so that you who offended the Lord through arrogance may please him through humility.”

The words mentioned above—“I will not establish my face against you”—correspond to the prophetic saying: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Ps. 50:11).

(Verses 14 and following.) “Return, returning sons [or: wandering and departing ones], says the Lord, because I am your husband [or: your ruler]. And I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and I will bring you into Zion. And I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and teaching.

“And when you have multiplied and increased in the land, in those days, says the Lord, they will no longer say, ‘The ark of the covenant [or: Testament] of the Lord.’ It will not ascend upon the heart; they will not remember it, it will not be visited, and it will not be made again.”

[Note: [Col. 0703D] Victorius deletes the words “to me,” which are found neither in the Vulgate edition nor here or below, and neither in the Hebrew nor in the Septuagint.]

The Jews think that this was fulfilled after the return from Babylon under Cyrus, king of the Persians, and Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel (Isa. 1), even though not all returned; and that this is signified by “I will take one from a city and two from a family.”

But it is better understood as referring to the coming of Christ, when the remnant was saved, as the Apostle says and explains: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (Rom. 9:29). Then they were brought into Zion, of which it is written: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:2).

And shepherds according to his heart were given to them: the Apostles and apostolic men. They fed the multitude of believers, not with Jewish ceremonies but with the knowledge and teaching of Christ, after the preaching of the Gospel had been sown throughout the whole world. They would no longer place their confidence in the ark of the Lord, which had been the guardian of the Mosaic law; rather, they themselves would be the temple of God. Nor, like the mistaken Nazarenes, would they serve abolished sacrifices, but would pursue spiritual worship.

Others understand this of the end of time, when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved (Rom. 11).

(Verses 17.) “At that time they will call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will be gathered to it in the name of the Lord, to Jerusalem, and they will no longer walk after the perversity of their evil heart.”

The Lord will no longer sit upon the ark of the Testament and the cherubim, to whom that people formerly said: “You who sit upon the cherubim, manifest yourself” (Ps. 79:2); rather, all who believe with a perfect mind will be the throne of God.

Or, certainly, the whole passage is better understood of the Church: when all the nations are gathered in the name of the Lord to Jerusalem, in which there is a vision of peace, and they no longer walk after the perversity of their evil heart, doing what they desire or following their own errors. Instead they say with the Prophet: “My soul clung after you; your right hand received me” (Ps. 62:9).

(Verses 18.) “In those days the house of Judah will go to the house of Israel, and they will come together from the land of the north to the land that I gave to your fathers.”

This is fulfilled specifically in the coming of Christ, when people from all twelve tribes believed the Gospel together, leaving the land of the north, of the harshest cold. Having withdrawn from the dominion of the devil, they then received the promised land that had been promised to their fathers, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

I recently published a small book on the promised land.

[Note: [Col. 0703D] In our recension, Letter 129, to Dardanus, written around the year 414.]

(Verses 19.) “But I said: How shall I place you among sons, and give you a desirable land, a splendid inheritance of the hosts of the nations? And I said: You will call me Father, and you will not cease to walk after me.”

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Here, with Victorius, we restore “among sons,” from the Vulgate edition and the Greek, as well as from Jerome’s own Commentary; previously it read “among the sons.” Immediately afterward, we also corrected “of the armies” from “of the army,” in agreement with the Hebrew manuscript.]

In place of “a splendid inheritance, an inheritance of the armies of the nations,” which the Septuagint translated “a named inheritance of God almighty of the nations,” Theodotion translated more meaningfully: “a renowned inheritance of the strength of the most powerful of the nations,” signifying Christ, who is the leader and Lord of all the nations that believe in his name and passion.

He himself said to Israel: “You will call me Father.” And: “Whoever believes in me believes in the Father” (John 2:19). He himself promised: “I will place you among sons”—that is, among the number of my sons who believed in me from the people of the nations—and to whom I gave a desirable land. For “as many as received him, he gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1).

[Note: [Col. 0704D] Jerome appears to have read among the Septuagint the word ὀνομαστήν, “renowned,” which is absent from the present copies.]

(Verses 20.) “But just as a woman despises her lover, so the house of Israel has despised me, says the Lord.”

This is the voice of Christ concerning the Jewish people, to whom he had said: “I will place you among sons; and I will give you a desirable land; and you will call me Father, and you will not cease to walk after me.”

“How,” he says, “does a woman despise not her husband but her lover, once she has been joined to him, when she sees him serving her lust and recognizes that the law of nature has been changed in her—the law by which she had formerly been subject to a man—according to the Lord’s saying, ‘Her turning shall be toward you’? So the house of Israel, that is, the Jewish people, despised the Lord Savior to its own destruction.”

(Verses 21–22.) “A voice was heard on the roads [or: on the lips], weeping and the wailing of the sons of Israel, because they made their way wicked; they forgot the Lord their God.

“Return, returning sons, and I will heal your apostasies [or: wounds].” In place of this Symmachus translated, “your conversions.”

God willingly receives penitents and runs to meet the son exhausted by poverty and filth; immediately he clothes him in his former garments and restores glory to the one who returns—provided only that he return with weeping and wailing. For through his own fault he made his way wicked and forgot the Lord his God and Father, to whom he speaks through the prophetic word: “Return, returning sons.”

I call them sons for this reason: because, recognizing your sins, you return with weeping and wailing to your parent. And when you have returned to the Lord, he says, he will heal all your wounds or apostasies by which you had withdrawn from the Lord—or, certainly, your conversions.

Although we return to the Lord by our own will, nevertheless, unless he draws us and strengthens our desire by his aid, we cannot be saved. Let us understand this both of the Jewish people returning to the Lord and of heretics who have abandoned the Lord.

(Verses 23.) “Behold, we have come to you, for you are the Lord our God. Truly the hills were deceitful, and the multitude [or: strength] of the mountains; truly, in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.”

Let the penitent say this, abandoning all pride and the multitude or height of the mountains and hills by which he had exalted himself against God. Prostrate in humility, let him say: “Truly, in the Lord our God is the salvation of Israel.”

(Verses 24.) “Shame has devoured the labor of our fathers from our youth: their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters.”

[Note: [Col. 0705D] Two manuscripts read: “All heretics, their labors.”]

All the labors of the heretics, of whom it is written, “They failed while searching with careful investigation” (Ps. 63:7), our shame has overwhelmed—from the youth of those whom they deceived, their sons and daughters who had advanced in heresy, or those who were merely held captive by luxury.

[Note: [Col. 0705D] In Rabanus: “as herds oppressed by shame.” And Vatican manuscript 91 reads: “or, held fast by lust, they were covered with shame.”]

Therefore they add:

(Verses 25.) “We will lie down in our shame, and our disgrace will cover us, because we have sinned against the Lord our God, we and our fathers, from our youth to this day; and we have not listened to the voice of the Lord our God.”

Let Israel, which did not listen to its Lord, say this; let every heretic who performs repentance say it. Yet confessing and knowing one’s sins is part of salvation. “First declare your iniquities,” he says, “so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26).

For truly Israel abandoned Christ, its Lord and God, and sinned against him—not only at the time when he was seen in the flesh but also before his coming. Therefore they say, “We and our fathers, from our youth to this day, have not listened to the voice of our God,” who spoke to our fathers: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

### Chapter 4

#### Verse 1

“If you return, Israel, says the Lord, return to me.”

In place of this the Septuagint translated: “If Israel turns back, says the Lord, it will return to me.”

The sense is: If it has returned to me, it will return from captivity. Or otherwise: when he has offered what he has—“For to everyone who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. 25:29).

According to the Hebrew, however, the sense is this: If you return to me, Israel, and, desiring salvation once and for all, say that you have sinned and have not listened to the voice of the Lord your God, turn fully, believe the one whom you denied, and then your conversion will be complete.

[Col. 0706A] “If you remove your stumbling-blocks from my sight, you will not be shaken.” When we are shaken and say, “But my feet were almost moved” (Ps. 72:2), we suffer this not from weakness of nature but because we set up stumbling-blocks and place our idols against the Lord.

(Verses 2.) “And you will swear, ‘The Lord lives,’ in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness; and the nations will bless him, and they will praise him.”

How does the Gospel prohibit us from swearing? Here, however, “you will swear” is said of confession and of the condemnation of the idols by which Israel used to swear. The stumbling-blocks are removed, and he swears by the Lord.

Moreover, when it says, “The Lord lives,” this is an oath in the Old Testament, for the condemnation of the dead beings by whom every idolater swears. At the same time, we should observe that an oath has these companions: truth, judgment, and righteousness. If these are absent, it will not be an oath but perjury.

“And when,” he says, “Israel has done this and has become a teacher of the nations through the Apostles, then all the nations will bless—or will be blessed—in him, and they will praise him because salvation has proceeded from Israel.”

(Verses 3 and following.) “For thus says the Lord to the man of Judah and Jerusalem: ‘Break up new ground for yourselves, and do not sow upon thorns. Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest perhaps my indignation go forth like fire and be kindled, with no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness [or: inventions] of your thoughts.’”

In place of what we said, “Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts,” Symmachus wrote, “Purify yourselves for the Lord, and remove the wickednesses of your hearts,” understanding circumcision as cleansing and foreskins as vice.

This is commanded to the men of Judah and Jerusalem who follow the true faith and dwell in the Church: they must not sow upon thorns, which the Gospel word signifies, since thorns choke the seed of God. Rather, they must first break up new ground, dig up all the brambles, and remove the thorns, so that clean seeds may be received by clean fields.

This is what is said elsewhere: “Do not cast your pearls before swine, and do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7:6). For how can one hear the word of God, conceive the seeds, and produce fruit when one’s mind is filled with the anxieties of the world?

The words that follow, “Circumcise yourselves for the Lord, and remove the foreskins of your hearts,” are commanded to no one else except the man of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that they may abandon the killing letter and follow the life-giving Spirit.
