“For if you do not do this,” he says, “my indignation will go forth like fire; it will be kindled, and there will be no one to extinguish it.” He warns and foretells this in advance so that he may not be compelled to do it—which we also see in the case of the Ninevites, to whom the sentence was announced beforehand so that they might avert the approaching wrath through repentance.

All these evils will come because of the wickedness of your thoughts—or inventions [or: our inventions]. [Note: [Col. 0707D] The words “or inventions” are recognized neither by Rabanus nor by the Vatican manuscript.]

Where are those who say that there is no sin in thoughts, when, according to the truth of the Gospel, all vices proceed from the heart (Matt. 15)?

### (Verses 5–6)

“Announce in Judah, and make it heard in Jerusalem; speak out: sound the trumpet in the land, cry aloud, and say: Gather yourselves, and let us enter the fortified cities.”

Let Judah hear this, and Jerusalem, in which there is confession of faith and in which the peace of Christ dwells, and to which it was said through Isaiah: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion. Lift up your voice, you who evangelize Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:9). Let it cry aloud and thus command: “Let us enter the fortified cities.”

The battles of the heretics are rising up; let the fortifications of Christ hold us. Raise the standard of the cross upon the watchtower, upon the exalted height of the Church [Alternative: “of the Church’s exaltation”]. Take courage, you who are afraid; do not remain standing, but run to the aid of Christ.

“I am bringing evil,” he says, “from the north, and great destruction”—namely, Nebuchadnezzar, who is permitted by me to exist in this world for this reason: that your strength and victory may be proved.

[Col. 0707B]

### (Verse 7)

“A lion has gone up from his lair, and the ravager of nations has risen; he has gone out from his den to make your land a desolation” [Vulgate: “destruction”]. “Your cities shall be laid waste, remaining without an inhabitant.”

This is, as we have said, the true Nebuchadnezzar, concerning whom blessed Peter the Apostle also speaks: “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8).

He has gone up either from the abysses [Col. 0707C] into which he is to be bound, and from which he pleads not to be sent; and the ravager, or destroyer, of the nations has risen—that is, he of whom it is said: “He shall rule over all his enemies” (Psalm 9:5), and who boasts in the presence of the Lord: “I have gone around the whole earth, and trampled it” (Job 2:2).

For who is there whom the devil’s poisons do not touch, except the one who can say: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30)?

This one repeatedly makes the whole land of the Church desolate, so that those who have gone out from the Church fight against the Church. Of these the Evangelist John speaks: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

The cities of the land of Judea are laid waste, while the assemblies of the heretics flourish. Therefore, if someone is a supporter and originator of perverse doctrines, this may be said of him: “A lion has gone up from his lair, and the ravager of nations has risen,” and what follows.

[Note: With the Vatican manuscripts, Rabanus reads: “is the supporter and author of perverse doctrines.”]

[Col. 0707D]

### (Verse 8)

“For this reason gird yourselves with sackcloth; mourn and howl, because the anger of the Lord’s fury has not turned away from us”—or, as the Septuagint translated, “from you.”

We cannot otherwise avoid the lion and the most savage beast unless we do penance and turn back to the Lord, not only in mind but also in deed. For as long as he lays waste to the Church and the land of Judah, and also devastates Jerusalem, the anger of God is evident.

### (Verse 9)

“And it shall be on that day, says the Lord: the heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests shall be stupefied, and the prophets shall be dismayed.”

[Col. 0708A]

While the ravager is laying waste to the Lord’s Church and the Lord’s anger remains against us, every aid will be useless.

The heart of the king shall perish—although his heart ought to be in the hand of God—and the heart of the princes, who were thought to be wise. “For God made foolish the wisdom of the world, because through it they did not know God” (1 Corinthians 1).

The priests themselves, who ought to have taught the Lord’s law and defended the peoples subject to them from the lion’s fury, being stupefied by a certain bewilderment, will be turned to madness. For this is how the Septuagint translated it, expressing mental derangement by “stupefaction.”

“And the prophets shall be dismayed”—or, as Aquila translated the Hebrew word *IETHMAU* (), “they shall be mad.”

For who would not go mad, who would not lose heart, when he saw the princes, kings, priests, and prophets—once his own—under the lion?

[Col. 0708B]

### (Verse 10)

“And I said: Alas, alas, alas, Lord God” [for which the Septuagint had translated, “O Lord God”], “surely you have deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying: Peace shall be yours? And behold, the sword has reached as far as the soul.”

Because above he had said: “At that time they shall call Jerusalem the throne of God, and all the nations shall be gathered to it upon the mountain of the Lord, in Jerusalem”; and now he says: “The heart of the king shall perish, and the heart of the princes; the priests shall be stupefied, and the prophets shall be dismayed,” the prophet is troubled and thinks that God has deceived him. He does not understand that the former promise was made for a time far in the future, whereas this is to occur in the near future, in accordance with what the Apostle also says: “Has God rejected his people? Certainly not” (Romans 11:1).

[Col. 0708C]

The sword reaches as far as the soul when nothing vital is left in the soul. At the same time, this also shows that unless the sword comes first—one that cuts away and purifies the soul’s vices—neither peace nor the promise will follow.

### (Verses 11–12)

“At that time it shall be said to this people and to Jerusalem: A scorching wind” [or “of dew”] “is on the roads that are in the wilderness, the roads of the daughter of my people—not for winnowing, and not for cleansing. A spirit full of these things shall come to me.”

When the sword has reached as far as the soul and the threshing floor has been completed, then a scorching wind shall come from the wilderness—one that does not cleanse and winnow it, so that, with the chaff scattered here and there, the grain may be stored in barns; rather, a full spirit shall come, not to the people but to me, so that my wheat may be scattered.

Among the Hebrews, “wind” and “spirit” are called by the same name, *RUA* (). According to the character of the passages, we must understand it either as wind or as spirit.

[Col. 0708D]

Others explain this passage in such a way that, after the threshing floor has been cleansed, the survivors may be saved. Hence it is also written: “The spirit of fullness shall come to me,” as the Evangelist says: “From his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16), and we shall receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Understand the scorching wind, according to the historical sense, as Nebuchadnezzar, who consumes everything. According to the tropological sense, understand it as the hostile power which, coming from the wilderness and the solitude—where there is no dwelling of God—strives to overthrow his Church.

[Col. 0709A]

“And now I shall speak my judgments with them.”

This is an *ἀποσιώπησις*—a breaking off in speech—in accordance with Virgil’s line (*Aeneid* 1):

> “Whom I … but it is better to calm the troubled waves.”

About to speak of prosperity, he restrains himself and joins sorrow to sorrow. For these are the judgments about which God speaks with his former people, so that they may know that they justly endure what they endure.

### (Verse 13)

“Behold, he shall ascend like a cloud, and his chariots like a storm; his horses are swifter than eagles. Woe to us, for we have been laid waste.”

[Col. 0709B]

He sees things to come as though they were present, and describes the Babylonian army. The clatter of its chariots and wheels is compared with a most savage storm, and the speed of its horses is likened to that of eagles.

When the prophet had said this and pointed out with his finger the enemies as they approached, the people groan and feel not what is future but what has already happened, saying: “Woe to us, for we have been laid waste.”

The same may be referred to the Church: every day the army of the true Nebuchadnezzar attacks us, and the chariots of Pharaoh and all his cavalry surpass the assault of eagles. If the ecclesiastical man understands this, believing the saying, “When you turn and groan, then you shall be saved,” he will say: “Woe to us, for we have been laid waste” (Ezekiel 33:11).

### (Verse 14)

“Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem, so that you may be saved. How long shall harmful thoughts remain within you?”

[Col. 0709C]

To the people who say, “Woe to us, for we have been laid waste,” the prophet—or rather, God through the prophet—responds: “Wash your heart from wickedness, Jerusalem,” with that water of which Isaiah also speaks: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isaiah 1:16)—the water of saving baptism, the water of repentance.

He speaks to the metropolis of the Jews, so that through the city the peoples may be understood: “How long will you remain subject to wicked thoughts that proceed from your heart?” In the holy Scriptures, we must understand “heart” as meaning the mind and the soul.

### (Verse 15)

“For a voice announces from Dan and makes known an idol” [or “a sorrow”] “from Mount Ephraim.”

[Col. 0709D]

In accordance with the situation of the land of Judea, the divine word now speaks. For the tribe of Dan, situated beside Mount Lebanon and the city now called Paneas, faces the north, from which Nebuchadnezzar is to come.

It describes the idol Bel—or sorrow or iniquity—as coming from Mount Ephraim. For after the tribe of Dan comes the land of Ephraim, through which one travels to Jerusalem.

Dan is interpreted as “judgment”; Ephraim as “fruitfulness.” Therefore the judgment of the Lord shall come upon the land that has offended the Lord, together with an abundance of punishment.

### (Verses 16–17)

“Tell the nations: Behold, it has been heard in Jerusalem that keepers are coming from a distant land, and they have raised their voice against the cities of Judah. They have become like keepers of fields around her, because she provoked me to anger, says the Lord.”

[Col. 0710A]

He wishes all the surrounding nations to know the sentence of God, and, when Jerusalem has been scourged, to receive instruction.

“It is widely proclaimed,” he says, “in Jerusalem that adversaries are coming from a distant land and that the roar of a howling army is rising against her. They besiege the city and close it in with fortifications so carefully that you would think them not so much enemies as keepers of fields and vineyards.”

All this happened not through the strength of the enemies but because of Jerusalem’s guilt, since she provoked God to anger. For if hostile powers have no authority over pigs, how much more do they have authority over human beings—and over human beings who were once citizens of God’s city?

### (Verse 18)

“Your ways and your thoughts have done these things to you; this is your wickedness, because it is bitter” [the Vulgate adds “because”]; “it has touched your heart.”

[Col. 0710B]

He turns his address toward the city of Jerusalem, saying that her ways and thoughts—by which she sinned both in deed and in speech—caused everything that happened to come upon her. Her wickedness, which is bitter in itself, touched her heart and penetrated the inner parts of her soul.

Whatever therefore happens to us happens through our own fault: we turn the sweet Lord into bitterness and compel him to rage, though he is unwilling to do so.

### (Verses 19–20)

“My belly, my belly—I am in pain; the senses of my heart are troubled within me. I shall not be silent, because my soul has heard the sound of the trumpet, the cry of battle. Destruction upon destruction has been called; the whole land has been laid waste. Suddenly my tents have been laid waste, in an instant my coverings.”

[Col. 0709D]

Where we have rendered “have been troubled” according to Symmachus, the Hebrew has *HOMA* (). The Septuagint and Theodotion set down *μαιμάσσει*, a word whose meaning I do not know to this day.

[Col. 0710C]

[Note: In our manuscripts the Septuagint reads *μαιμάσσει*, without the intervening words, and Theodotion also has it. What Jerome says he does not know about the meaning of this Greek word is easily explained if one takes it to have the same sense as *μαιμάζει* in Nobilius, namely, “is agitated.”]

Aquila, however, wrote *ὀχλίζει*, which itself also conveys tumult. Let this be said about the word, concerning which I know that there is great disagreement among many.

The voice of the prophet—and through the prophet, of God speaking—is introduced: he grieves over the destruction of his people, and his inward organs are torn asunder like those of a human being.

So too the Savior grieved over the death of Lazarus (John 11) and wept over Jerusalem, lest he conceal his grief by silence (Luke 19). Every blast of the trumpet and roar of battles disturbs his affection, while evils are piled upon evils and the entire land of the two tribes is laid waste.

[Col. 0710D]

“While I did not expect it,” he says, “my tents of former times and my coverings were ravaged while the Babylonian army raged; and my former dwellings fell as spoil to the enemy.”

God says this same thing when he sees the disturbances and dissensions of sedition in the Church, and in its assemblies hears them cry out “partridge” [Alternative: “by day”], while God’s rest is turned into wars. Hence it follows:

### (Verse 21)

“How long shall I see those fleeing” [Vulgate: “the one fleeing”] “and hear the sound of the trumpet?”

Either those fleeing from the Babylonian king, or those fleeing from me and withdrawing from my service.

### (Verse 22)

“For my people are foolish; they have not known me. They are foolish children and without understanding. They are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good.”

[Col. 0711A]

The cause of their destruction, devastation, flight, and trumpet blast is that the people have become foolish—not by nature, but through the deliberate choice of their will.

Their foolishness is proved by this: they did not know God, and instead of becoming wise children, they became foolish and senseless children.

For what greater foolishness can there be than that, while the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master’s manger, Israel should not know the Lord and should despise the one whom it always desired to see present?

As for what follows—“They are wise in doing evil, but they have not known how to do good”—here “wisdom” must be understood as wickedness, in accordance with the saying that the children of this age are wiser than the children of light; and the unjust steward is said to have acted wisely in certain matters (Luke 16); and the serpent in paradise is read to have been more prudent than all the beasts (Genesis 3).

[Col. 0711B]

True wisdom, therefore, is that joined to the fear of God. Otherwise, where there are ambushes and evasions, it should be called not wisdom but cunning and craftiness.

For what we have rendered, “My people are foolish; they have not known me,” the Septuagint translated: “The rulers of my people have not known me,” so that the blame may fall more upon the teachers than upon the people who lack knowledge of God.

### (Verses 23 and following)

“I looked upon the earth, and behold, it was empty and void; and at the heavens, and there was no light in them. I saw the mountains, and behold, they were shaken, and all the hills were disturbed. I looked, and there was no human being, and every bird of heaven had departed. I looked, and behold, Carmel was a desert, and all its cities were destroyed before the Lord and before the face of his wrathful anger.”

[Col. 0711C]

The prophet sees in the spirit what is to come, so that the people, hearing it, may be terrified and, having done penance, may not endure what they fear.

The earth is empty, its inhabitant having been destroyed. The heavens have no light because of the enormity of the terror, since the people do not see.

The mountains and hills themselves have no secure hiding places, and through *ὑπερβολή*—hyperbole—they appear to be shaken and disturbed.

He looked and gazed around in every direction, and not even a bird could be found. For the mute elements also perceive God’s anger, and irrational animals are terrified.

The truth of this is now demonstrated by the whole world: when a multitude of human beings has been slaughtered, even the birds, which ordinarily follow inhabitants, have gone away and perished.

[Col. 0711D]

Carmel itself, which overlooks the great sea and is planted with olive trees and shrubs and thick with vines, shall come to such a desolation that it will have the devastation of a wilderness.

All the cities also shall become deserted, and the cause of all these evils is that the Lord’s anger has been stirred up by the fault of the sinful people.

Whatever we have said historically about Jerusalem and Judea, let us refer to the Church of God when it has offended God and has been devastated either by vices or by persecution. Where once there was a chorus of virtues and joy, let there be a multitude of sins and sorrows.

[Col. 0712A]

### (Verses 27–28)

“For thus says the Lord: The whole land shall be desolate, yet I shall not make a complete end. The land shall mourn, and the heavens above shall grieve, because I have spoken” [Alternative: “because I have said”]. “I have determined, and I have not repented; nor have I turned away from it.”

God’s mercy is mingled with his anger. The whole land is deserted, but no complete end is made, so that there may be people who understand his clemency.

The heaven also will appear sad above, and the earth itself will mourn, because the Lord’s sentence has reached its end, and he has not repented of what he determined and spoke.

God’s repentance is spoken of when the announced sentence is withdrawn and the raging anger does not reach its full conclusion. He threatened through Jonah, but the multitude of tears and groans overcame the sword that hung over them (Jonah 3).

[Col. 0712B]

### (Verse 29)

“At the sound of the horseman and of the one shooting arrows” [Note: Two manuscripts read, “At the sound of the cavalry”] “or drawing the bow, every city” [or “region”] “flees. They entered the steep places and climbed the rocks.”

As for what follows—“And they entered the thickets,” or “the caves”—the Septuagint added: *καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄλση ἐκρύβησαν*, “and they hid themselves in the groves.” The rest corresponds to the Hebrew text.

[Note: The Septuagint added *καὶ εἰς τὰ ἄλση ἐκρύβησαν*, “and they hid themselves in the groves.” The rest corresponds to the Hebrew text. It is remarkable, however, that the other part of this verse—“All the cities were abandoned, and no one dwelt in them”—is cited by Rabanus and two manuscript codices as though it were something the Septuagint had added on its own.]

The divine discourse describes the army of the raging Babylonian: because of its terror the whole people abandoned the city and climbed every steep place, yet could not evade the Lord’s anger.

Whatever, as we said above, is understood historically against Jerusalem is referred to the Church when it has offended God and has been handed over to its adversaries, whether in a time of persecution or certainly through vices and sins.

[Col. 0712C]

### (Verse 30)

“But you, who have been laid waste, what will you do?”

For “laid waste,” the Hebrew word is *SADUD* (), which Aquila alone translated; the others rendered it “wretched” and “miserable,” because of its own guilt, by which it offended the merciful God.

Then it follows:

“When you clothe yourself in scarlet, and [Alternative: “when”] adorn yourself with a golden necklace, and paint your eyes with antimony, you adorn yourself in vain. Your lovers have despised you; they seek your life.”

He speaks under the figure of an adulterous woman: once you have offended God and, as though abandoning your husband, have left the Creator, you seek adornments in vain.

Your lovers, the demons, have despised you, and they seek not the impurity of fornication but the destruction of your soul.

This same passage must be understood spiritually against those who have lost conjugal affections and the modesty of true faith.

[Col. 0712D]

“If you clothe yourself in scarlet,” he says—that is, if you assume faith in the blood of Christ; “if you adorn yourself with a golden necklace”—that is, if you devote yourself to the contemplation of spiritual meaning and understanding; “and if you paint your eyes with antimony”—that is, if you apply yourself to learning the mysteries and secrets of God—you adorn yourself in vain.

For you had prepared these things even for your lovers; and therefore the narrow bed cannot contain both, nor does God receive the ornaments by which you previously pleased your lovers.

### (Verse 31)

“For I heard a voice like that of a woman in labor, anguish” [or “groans”] “like that of a woman giving birth. The voice of the daughter of Zion, dying and spreading out her hands: Woe is me, for my soul has fainted because of the slain.”

[Col. 0713A]

We have restored *intermorientis* (singular “dying”) and *expandentisque* (“and spreading out”), as Martianus also noted in the book’s margin from the Vulgate; the earlier reading was *intermorientes exscandentesque* (“dying and climbing out”).

[Note: We have restored *intermorientis* (singular “dying”) and *expandentisque* (“and spreading out”), as Martianus also noted in the book’s margin from the Vulgate; previously the text had *intermorientes exscandentesque* (“dying and climbing out”).]

By the likeness of a woman in labor—that is, one giving birth to her first children—he describes the city of Jerusalem lamenting and crying out.

For just as a woman giving birth, who has not yet experienced the pain of labor, nearly dies and, enduring anguish, can scarcely breathe, collapsing with outstretched hands, so the daughter of Zion, when she sees her children slain, will break out in these words and say [Alternative: “breaks out and says”]: “Woe is me, for my soul has fainted because of the slain.”

[Note: The manuscripts read: “having experienced it, she dies.”]

[Col. 0713B]

Two examples are compared in one chapter: a woman giving birth to children and a woman mourning. Thus whatever a woman suffers in bearing children, or through the deaths of her children, Jerusalem suffers in its peoples.

## Chapter 5

### (Verses 1–2)

“Go around the streets of Jerusalem, and look and consider, and seek in its squares whether you can find a man who practices justice and seeks faithfulness; and I shall be merciful to it. But even if they say, ‘As the Lord lives,’ they will swear falsely.”

Great is the love of justice: God would not, as in Abraham’s question and God’s answer, spare the city for the sake of ten righteous men (Genesis 18); but if he should find even one in Jerusalem, already on the point of perishing, who practices justice and seeks faithfulness—or, as Symmachus translated, “truth”—God would nevertheless have mercy on Jerusalem.

And because it could happen that some among the people would be found who pretended to worship God and swore by God, he forestalls this by saying that God is pleased not by empty words but by the truth of faith. He says: “I do not love those who swear by me and swear falsely, but those whose hearts and lips agree.”

### (Verse 3)

“Lord, your eyes look upon faithfulness. You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction. They hardened their faces like rock and refused to return.”

[Col. 0713C]

After the words of the Lord, in which he had commanded, saying, “Go around the streets of Jerusalem,” and what follows, the prophet speaks to the Lord:

“Lord, your eyes look upon faithfulness,” which in Hebrew is called *EMUNA* (). Not upon the works of the Jews, in which they rejoiced according to the ceremonies of the Law, but upon the faith of Christians, through which we have been saved by grace.

From this chapter we learn that punishments are inflicted so that vices may be corrected. Accordingly he says: “You struck them, and they did not grieve; you crushed them, and they refused to accept correction.”

[Col. 0713D]

Through every torment and scourging Jerusalem is corrected, yet even after all this they did not have the slightest shame over their vices. Instead, hardening the insolence of their forehead like rock [Note: Victor reads, “the shamelessness of their foreheads”], they refused to turn to better things.

### (Verses 4–5)

“But I said: Perhaps they are poor and foolish” [or “unable”; our manuscripts do not attest the words “unable”], “ignorant of the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God. I shall go to the nobles and speak to them, for they know the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God.”

Here he speaks of the poor and the nobles not in terms of poverty and riches, but by comparing the people with their leaders.

[Col. 0714A]

The meaning is this: Seeing the obstinacy of the unbelieving people, and that, with hardened faces, they refused to receive correction, I reasoned with myself:

“Perhaps the lowly masses cannot know the teaching of God, and therefore are excusable, because through ignorance they are unable to know the commandments. I shall therefore go to the priests and those who rule the people, and I shall speak to them; for they know the Lord’s will and understand the judgment of their God.”

He says this in the language of one who doubts, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “I shall send my son; perhaps they will respect him” (Matthew 21:37), so that through the ambiguity of the sentence and the suspension of the words the freedom of the human will might be demonstrated.

[Col. 0714B]

### (Verse 6)

“And behold, these have altogether broken the yoke even more; they have burst the bonds. Therefore a lion from the forest struck them, a wolf at evening ravaged them, a leopard watches over their cities; everyone who goes out from them shall be captured. For their transgressions have multiplied; their apostasies have grown strong.”

Those whom I thought to be teachers were found to be worse than the disciples. And the greater the authority of the wealthy, the greater the insolence of their sins.

For they broke the yoke of the Law, as the Apostle says: “Now therefore, why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the neck of the disciples which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are” (Acts 15:10–11).

[Col. 0714C]

They also burst the bonds of God’s commandments—not those of the Pharisees, concerning whom it is said in the second psalm: “Let us burst their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm 2:3).

Because they did these things, a lion from the forest struck them—namely, the Babylonian kingdom. A wolf at evening ravaged them, signifying the Medes and Persians; for this, in Daniel’s vision, a bear is set down, with three rows in its mouth (Daniel 7).

A leopard watching over their cities prefigures Alexander’s assault and his swift advance from the West to India [Note: With Victor, we read “advance,” as required by the sequence of the sentence and by the Brixian manuscripts. Previously the reading was “striking”].

[Col. 0714D]

He calls him a leopard because of his variegated character, and because, with many nations subjected to him, he fought against the Medes and Persians.

“And,” he says, “there were four heads on the beast, and authority was given to it.”

And because he is not prophesying about the future but has clothed the history in terms as though it were already present or just about to occur [Note: In the Cistercian manuscript and in Rabanus: “or already about to occur, he said,” and so forth], he is silent about the Roman empire, concerning which perhaps it is said: “Everyone who goes out from them shall be captured.”

He gives the reasons why they suffered these things: “For their transgressions have multiplied,” and they have persisted in their violations. Hence it is said: “Their apostasies have grown strong.”

The Hebrew word which we placed at the beginning, *SOCED* (), is shown in the present passage to mean “watching.” For where we said “a leopard watching,” the Hebrew has *NEMER SOCED* ().

[Col. 0715A]

[Note: The manuscripts prefer either *Saced* or *Sachad*. See what we noted above concerning this word in chapter 1.]

According to the tropological sense, those who are considered great in the Church, because they break the yoke and burst the bonds, are therefore handed over to shameful passions, so that they may do what is unfitting.

### (Verses 7 and following)

“On account of what can I be merciful to you? Your children have abandoned me and swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery, and they luxuriated in the house of a prostitute. They became lustful horses, stallions; each one neighed after his neighbor’s wife. Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord? And shall my soul not avenge itself upon such a nation?”

A *κατάλογος*, a catalogue, of Jerusalem’s sins: God says that he does not know on what basis he can show mercy toward it.

[Col. 0715B]

“Your children,” he says, “have abandoned me”—not my children, but yours—“and swear by those who are not gods. I filled them, and they committed adultery.”

Let those who, after receiving riches from the Lord, lie upon them and serve luxury hear this.

“They became lustful horses, stallions.” [Note: The same editor notes that the words “unto women” are absent from the Hebrew, as likewise is the word “to me” in the Septuagint.]

For “stallions,” the Hebrew has *MOSECHIM* (), which all the translators rendered with the concordant word *ἕλκοντες*, that is, “drawing” or “pulling,” so that the size of the genitals may be indicated, in accordance with Ezekiel: “Their flesh was like the flesh of donkeys” (Ezekiel 23:20).

[Col. 0715C]

This is what is written elsewhere: “They have been made like senseless beasts and have become like them” (Psalm 48:13).

At the same time he displays such madness of lust that he calls not only the appetite for pleasure but also *χρεμετισμός*, that is, “neighing,” preserving the metaphor of horses raging with desire.

“When you have done these things,” he says, “are you not worthy of visitation?”

Note that here “visitation” signifies punishment and penalties, in accordance with what is written: “I shall visit their iniquities with a rod.”

“And shall my soul not avenge itself upon such a nation?” (Psalm 88:33).

After it has been bound by sins, it is no longer called the people of God, but a nation from which God’s soul has withdrawn, according to what is written: “Your new moons and your Sabbaths and your feast days my soul hates” (Isaiah 1:13).

[Col. 0715D]

What is said in the Old Testament in terms of affection is written in the New Testament as a reality, when the Savior says: “I have power to lay down my soul, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18).

### (Verses 10–11)

“Go up upon its walls” [or “fortifications”] “and destroy them, but do not make a complete end. Remove its branches” [or “supports”], “for they are not the Lord’s. For the house of Israel and the house of Judah have acted faithlessly against me, says the Lord.”

He commands the nations—of whom he had said above, “A lion from the forest struck them, a wolf ravaged them, and a leopard was in their cities”—to climb the walls of Jerusalem, or its fortifications, and destroy it. But he commands that they not make a complete end, so that survivors may be saved and there may be someone who announces the glory of God among the nations. Thus he mingles clemency with severity.

As for what he adds—“Remove its branches,” or “supports”—he commands that all the aids which it lost through its own fault be taken away, because the house of Israel and the house of Judah acted faithlessly against God [Alternative: “the Lord”], signifying the ten tribes and the two.

[Col. 0716A]

Let the Church hear this: the walls and fortifications of those who have no hope in the Lord and act faithlessly against him will quickly be destroyed. Yet no complete end will be made, because of the clemency of the judge, not because of the merits of the sinners.

### (Verses 12–13)

“They denied the Lord and said: He is not” [or “these things are not”], “and evil shall not come upon us; we shall not see the sword or famine. The prophets have spoken into the wind” [the word “spoken” is missing in Jerome’s Vulgate verse], “and the word” [or “declaration”] “was not in them. Therefore these things shall happen to them.”

Because they denied the Lord—or lied to the Lord—and said, “He is not,” meaning that all things do not happen by his judgment but have occurred by chance; and because they said that the things threatened by the prophets’ voices would not come upon them, that they would not see the sword or suffer the famine of a siege; and because whatever the prophets said was spoken into the wind and all passed away ineffectually, and they received no answer—that is, no oracle, or word of God, was in them—they shall therefore suffer what the following discourse describes.

[Col. 0716B]

Let the negligent Church hear this: if it rejects God’s providence, it will endure both sword and famine unless it believes the things that are said are going to come.

### (Verse 14)

“Thus says the Lord God of hosts: Because you have spoken this word, behold, I am making my words in your mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them.”

[Col. 0716C]

You said: “The prophets have spoken into the wind, and the things they threaten will not come.” Therefore, O prophet, I place my words in your mouth, words possessing the power of fire, and I will turn this people into wood, so that by your speech and prophecy the unbelieving may be burned up.

Thus God is called a consuming fire, so that, if we build upon the foundation of Christ, he may consume in us the wood, hay, and straw (Deuteronomy 4).

### (Verses 15 and following)

“Behold, I am bringing against you a nation from afar, O house of Israel, says the Lord: a strong nation, an ancient nation, a nation whose language you will not know, and you will not understand what it says. Its quiver is like an open tomb; all its men are mighty. It shall eat your crops and your bread; it shall devour your sons and your daughters; it shall eat your flocks and your herds; it shall eat your vine and your fig tree; it shall crush your fortified cities, in which you trust, with the sword. Nevertheless, in those days, says the Lord, I shall not make a complete end of you.”

[Col. 0716D]

Not after a long time, nor—as you falsely believe—will the prophets speak to you into the wind. Rather, even now I shall bring against you the nation of the Babylonians, which will come from afar: a strong nation, for which the Hebrew has *ETHAN* (), an ancient nation, whose ruler was once the giant Nimrod (Genesis 10).

“A nation whose language you will not know” [Note: Victor prefers another sense, reading “just as,” instead of “or,” since both are written in Hebrew and Jerome’s Vulgate retains both: “whose language you will not know, and you will not understand what it says.” He wishes “just as” to be stated because the Septuagint translated differently—that is, “whose voice in its language you will not hear”].

Or, as it is written in Hebrew: “You will not understand what it says.” It is a consolation amid evils if you have enemies whom you can address, and who understand your prayers.

[Col. 0717A]

As for what follows—“Its quiver is like an open tomb”—and the fact that this is not said in the Septuagint edition, it signifies the Babylonian weapons. There is no doubt that the kingdoms of the Assyrians, Babylonians, Medes, and Persians were highly skilled in archery.

At the same time, he describes the devastation of the land of Judea, the slaughter of many, the driving away of livestock, and the overthrow of cities and walls: all things are seized by the hostile sword. Yet amid such great evils he does not destroy them utterly; rather, he preserves survivors—either those who were led into Babylon and then left behind for the cultivation of the land of Judea [Alternative: “the cultivation of the fields”], or those who, after the heat of persecution, preserved faith in the Lord either by flight or by confession.

[Col. 0717B]

### (Verse 19)

“And if you say: ‘Why has the Lord our God done all these things to us?’ you shall say to them: ‘Just as you abandoned me and served a foreign god’” [or “foreign gods”] “in your land, so shall you serve foreigners in a land that is not yours.”

It is great foolishness not to know why they suffered these things, when they had committed such great sins. The answer to those who ask is brief:

“Just as you served a foreign god”—that is, Baal—or the foreign gods of all the nations in the land of Judea, “so shall you serve foreign gods in a land that is not yours,” unquestionably the land of Babylon and Chaldea.

[Col. 0718A]

If foreign religion delights you, why is it necessary to undertake a distant error? Live with such people—indeed, serve those whose gods you worship.

This may also be understood concerning the heretics, of whom it is written: “They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

The Lord casts out from the Church the heretics who, for a long time under his name, worshiped the idols of their lies [Note: The Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts insert a negative particle], so that outside they may worship what they previously worshiped within, and so that the chaff may be separated from the wheat.

[Col. 0718B]

## Book Two

[Col. 0717]

[Col. 0717C] 877–878 Secondly, brother Eusebius, we are dictating the second book of our commentary on Jeremiah in a rapid style, turning our ears aside for a little lest we hear the judgment of blood and lament the souls of the slain—those who, in the opinion that they possess virtues, fall daily into pride and think themselves equal to God, so that they grant to all human beings the equality which the impious heresy of the Arians denies in the Son, and set their mouth in heaven, leaving nothing more to the future blessedness of the saints. We answered their fury, as best we could, in our letter to Ctesiphon (Epistle 133): [Note: [Col. 0717D] These words, “and, if the Lord grants life, we shall answer more fully,” are absent from the manuscripts mentioned above. Saint Jerome is evidently alluding to his books of Dialogues against Pelagius.] and, if the Lord grants life, we shall answer more fully. Now we must begin the path already undertaken and the dictation of this little commentary, neither extending the work through excessive length nor removing its meaning through excessive brevity—the former burdens the understanding of readers, the latter [Note: [Col. 0718D] Vatican manuscript: “the latter cuts short.”] hinders the desire of students.

(Verse 20, 21.) “Announce this to the house of Jacob, and make it heard in Judah, saying: Hear, foolish people, who have no heart; you have eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear.” In many ways he draws sinners back to salvation. He calls foolish the people who have abandoned the author of wisdom, and compares them with idols, of which it is written: “They have eyes and do not see; they have ears and do not hear. May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Psalm 113:5–6). But he speaks specifically to Judah and to the house of Jacob. Israel had already for a long time been exulting in the Assyrians [Note: [Col. 0718D] Two manuscripts read: “was feasting in Assyria.”] and at the same time he gives the understanding that, even without a commandment, we ought by natural instinct to understand what is right.

(Verses 22 ff.) “Will you not then fear me,” says the Lord, “and will you not tremble before my face? [or: fear]—I who placed the sand as a boundary for the sea, an everlasting ordinance which shall not pass away. And they will be moved, and will not be able [or: it will be troubled, and will not be able]; its waves will swell [or: roar], and they will not pass over it. This people has acquired an unbelieving and embittered heart; they have turned away and gone off, and have not said in their heart: Let us fear the Lord our God, who gives us the early and late rain in its season, preserving for us the fullness of the annual harvest.”

He recounts his benefits in order to convict the ungrateful. “Will you not fear me,” he says, “who have bestowed such things upon you? I do not seek the love of the perfect, but the fear of beginners—I who placed the sand as a boundary for the sea, who restrained by my command so powerful an element and the immense masses of its waters at the shores,” according to what is written: “He gave a command, and it shall not pass away” (Psalm 148:6). They hear and perceive me, although they have no faculty of hearing; but my former people, made foolish through their own fault, not only despise God but also embitter the gentle God. “They have turned away,” he says, “from me, turned their backs upon me, and gone away with hurried steps.” Their silent conscience did not draw them back so that they might say in their hearts: “Let us fear him who gives us the early and late rain.” Through all this he shows the goodness [variant: “good”] of the fullness of the annual harvest, for which Aquila’s [Note: [Col. 0719D] Aquila is known to have undertaken the work of translating Scripture into Greek twice, as our Jerome especially testifies in Ezekiel, chapter 2, where he praises Aquila’s second edition, which the Hebrews called κατὰ ἀκρίβειαν, “with precision.” Therefore the manuscripts falsely read, with the word “and” inserted, “Aquila and the first edition.”] first edition and Symmachus translated “weeks.” For in Hebrew it is written SABAOTH (), which, because of the ambiguity of the word, signifies both “weeks” and “fullness” [Note: [Col. 0719D] In both the Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts the following gloss is appended here: “It should be noted what he says about heretics, who strive only to plot against our people and say: ‘Our iniquities have turned these things aside, and our sins have withheld good from us.’”].

(Verses 25.) “Your iniquities have turned these things aside, and your sins have withheld good from you.” Therefore, whenever the sea also crosses its boundaries and the rain is held back, the hand of the Lord has by no means been shortened so that he cannot do these things; rather, our sins have diverted these things, which were coming to us, so that they might go to others who did not sin. “And they have withheld,” he says, “the good that was already coming to us,” according to what is written literally: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5:6). We can, however, understand the early and late rain as the Law and the Gospel, and the various callings from the first hour until the eleventh, in which the workers of the vineyard are promised one reward of eternal life (Matthew 20).

(Verses 26.) “For wicked men have been found among my people, lying in wait like bird-catchers, setting traps and snares for catching men; as a cage full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit.” The reasons are supplied for why the early and late rain should be diverted from them and all good should not come: because wicked men have been found among his people. He did not say “the unrighteous and sinners” (as the new heresy wishes), but “the impious.” Impiety openly denies God; iniquity and sin, if they confess their error, easily incline God toward mercy.

And what we translated as “lying in wait like bird-catchers,” which is not found in the Septuagint, Aquila and Symmachus translated as JASIR (), “like a bird-catcher’s net” [Note: [Col. 0719D–0720D] Most manuscripts, both ours and those consulted by the Benedictines, prefix here a word which, although retained also by the old editions, is further erroneous in reading Jasur from the Masoretic text instead of Jasir. Drusius rightly deleted the word τῷ, which had plainly been wrongly inserted, and substituted for the Hebrew Jasir the Latin equivalent of that word. Jerome teaches that Aquila and Symmachus gave Jasir itself in translation: namely, Ἰασίρ, ὡς δίκτυον ἰξευτοῦ, “Jasir, like a bird-catcher’s net”; although that word, which derives from an omitted or uncertain form in the printed text, could suitably have had the appellative sense “upright.” Martianay maintained, from the Sancygirannus manuscript, the printed reading, which is closer to the truth, as is clear from Jerome’s own exposition.]. Thus even the one among them who appears good and upright lays snares like a bird-catcher, while they hunt one another to the death and fill their houses with the losses and expenditures of others, so that the philosophers’ saying may be fulfilled [Note: [Col. 0720D] That saying of the philosophers. In the Letter to Hedibia, question 1: “Hence that common saying seems to me most true: Either a rich man is unjust or he is the heir of an unjust man.” MARTIAN.]: “Every rich man is either unjust or the heir of an unjust man.”

And would that such things were done only by those who appear to be outside and whom the Lord judges, and that they were not carried out in our own assemblies, which avarice—the root of all evils—possesses (Colossians 3), so that we look not upon the faces of those who come to us but upon their hands.

(Verses 27 ff.) “Therefore they have become great and rich; they have grown fat and sleek, and they have passed beyond my words most wickedly. They have not judged the cause [Note: [Col. 0720D] Three manuscripts add “of the widow,” although this conflicts with the sacred text.]; they have not directed [variant: “declared”] the cause [or: judgment] of the orphan; they have not judged the judgment of the poor [or: widow]. Shall I not visit these things,” says the Lord, “or shall my soul not avenge itself upon such a nation?”

If I wished to note individually what has been omitted in the Septuagint edition, it would take too long. “Those who lay snares,” he says, “and rejoice in the nakedness of others have therefore become great and rich,” because they have done the things mentioned above. “They have grown fat and sleek,” according to what is written: “The beloved grew fat and sleek and kicked” (Deuteronomy 32:15). And they passed beyond my words because, in the consciousness of their riches, they said of the Gospel: “Soul, you have many good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12:19). They passed beyond them to their own harm, and, despising all people [Note: [Col. 0720D] The same manuscripts read “deceiving” instead of “despising.”], they did not set God’s judgment before their eyes.

They despised the orphan and the poor; for this the Septuagint said “widows,” although this is not found in the Hebrew. For EBIONIM () properly means “the poor,” not “widows.” What follows—“Shall I not visit these things,” says the Lord, “or shall my soul not avenge itself upon such a nation?”—has already been explained above.

[Col. 0720C] (Verses 30, 31.) “Astonishment and marvels have occurred in the land. The prophets prophesied falsehood [or: wicked things], and the priests clapped their own hands; and my people loved such things. What, then, will you do at the end [Vulgate: ‘what will happen at its end’] [or: after these things]?”

Earlier he had said: “I will go to the great men and speak to them; perhaps they know the way of the Lord”; and behold, these very men have together broken the yoke and torn the bonds even more. Now he describes who the great men are: namely, the prophets and priests. Some proclaim future events; others determine from the Law what must be done. “And behold,” he says, “while they were prophesying falsehood, the priests clapped their hands.” And to show that the people too are not without blame when they are led astray by such men, it is written: “And my people loved such things.” They were once mine; but after they loved such things [Note: [Col. 0721D] Several manuscripts, on Victor’s authority, supply the word “such.”], they ceased to be mine. What, then, will they do when the final time of judgment arrives—or the necessity of captivity? Hence there are astonishment and marvels: no one was found among either the rulers or the people who thought rightly.

(Cap. VI.—Verse 1.) “Strengthen yourselves, sons of Benjamin, in the midst of Jerusalem; blow the trumpet in Tekoa; and raise a signal [or: banner] over Beth-haccerem, because evil has appeared [or: been seen] from the north, and great destruction.”

No one is unaware that Jerusalem lies in the tribe of Benjamin. We also see daily with our own eyes that Tekoa is a little village situated in the hill country, twelve miles from Jerusalem. Between these there is another village which in the Syriac language [Note: [Col. 0721D] And in Hebrew it is called Bethacharma. This name is read differently in Greek and Latin exemplars: in the Septuagint, Βαιθαχαρμὰ, Bethacharma, and Βηθθαχὰρ, Beththachar; in Jerome’s manuscript, the Sancygirannus, Bethacharem; in one Regius and another Cluniac manuscript, Bethacharma; finally, in our Saint-Germain manuscript, Bethacharem in the first hand and Bethacharim in the later hand. Jerome rightly observes, however, that the name is called Bethacharma in the Syriac and Hebrew languages, because “vineyard” is karma or karmo in both languages. MARTIAN.] is called BETHACHARMA, and it too is situated in the hill country (). What he therefore says amounts to this: Because Nabuchodonosor is about to come from the north and captivity is close at hand, O inhabitants of Jerusalem, take up arms, blow the trumpet loudly in Tekoa, and raise a banner in Beth-haccerem, he says, so that you may be able to resist the enemies.

Benjamin is interpreted as “son of the right hand”; Tekoa as “trumpet”; Beth-haccerem as “village of the vineyard.” Let us refer all these things to the Church: if it sins and the assault of persecution comes, let it prepare itself to resist.

(Verses 2, 3.) “I have compared the daughter of Zion to a beautiful and delicate woman; shepherds will come to her with their flocks. They have fixed [or: will fix] their tents around her; each one will pasture those who are under his hand. Consecrate [or: prepare] war against her; arise, and let us go up at midday.”

The beauty of Jerusalem, which is Zion itself, is described, so that one phrase may indicate the whole city and another the citadel of the city [Note: [Col. 0722D] Vatican manuscript: “so that some may occupy the whole city and others the citadel of the city.”]. For Zion is interpreted as “watchtower,” and is compared with a beautiful woman. Just as lovers are said to gather around her, so shepherds are said to gather around this city. In Hebrew, the word written with four letters—RES, AIN, JOD, MEM—if read REIM (), means “lovers”; if read ROIM (), it means “shepherds.” Thus, either according to the metaphor, the lovers of a beautiful woman, or according to the city’s overthrow, shepherds are understood: some hasten to violate the prostitute, others to besiege and overthrow the city.

In the shepherds and their flocks let us understand the rulers and armies of the Chaldeans. They will fix their tents around the city in a siege, and each one will pasture those who are under his hand—namely, his own companies and divisions [variant: “innumerable divisions”]. These rulers, or shepherds, will say to their flocks: “Consecrate war against Jerusalem,” for it is the Lord’s command. “Arise, and let us go up at midday”—not by night and through ambushes, but let us fight in full daylight, for no one can resist us.

(Verses 4, 5.) “Woe to us, for the day has declined, for the evening shadows have grown longer [or: have failed]. Arise, and let us go up by night and destroy her houses [or: her foundations].”

They say: “Arise, and let us go up at midday and fight in the clear light.” These reply: “Woe to us, for the evening shadows have grown longer.” In accordance with Virgil’s lines (Eclogue 1):

“And now from afar the rooftops of the farmhouses smoke,

and the shadows fall longer from the high mountains.”

The meaning is: If we suffer these things by day, what will we suffer by night? Again, those who had earlier said, “Consecrate war against her, and arise,” now challenge one another to battle, saying: “Arise, and let us go up by night,” so that the adversaries may know that victory depends not on the time but on strength; “and let us destroy the houses,” which are uselessly enclosed by the strength of their walls.

(Verses 6.) “For thus says the Lord of hosts: Cut down wood [or: its wood] and pour out [Vulgate: heap up] [or: carry] a mound around Jerusalem.”

Therefore, they say, we are confident of victory, because it is the Lord’s command, issuing orders to the Chaldeans: “Cut down wood and carry earth for the future fortifications.” This shows that, before the crown of victory comes, the city will not immediately be captured, but only after a long siege, as we read later.

(Verses 7.) “This is the city of visitation [or: falsehood]; all calumny [or: oppression] is in its midst. As a cistern [or: pool] makes its water cold, so she has made her wickedness cold.”

The Lord commanded that the trees be cut down and that siege mounds be heaped around the city, because the time of its visitation had arrived, so that it might receive according to its sins. The greatest of these is συκοφαντία, “false accusation,” by which an innocent person is oppressed through calumny. Just as a cistern or pool makes its water cold, so the wickedness in the midst of Jerusalem has lost all the warmth of life. It should also be noted that those inflamed by the Holy Spirit are called fervent, whereas evil things are cold. Hence it is written (Matthew 24) that in the last days, when iniquity has multiplied, the love of many will grow cold.

I think this is also expressed by: “I have become like those who go down into the pit” (Psalm 27:1). The Latin reader should understand this once and for all: among the Greeks, lacus does not mean a pond but a cistern, which in the Syriac and Hebrew language [Note: [Col. 0722D] In Hebrew it is called Gubba. Erasmus and Marianus alter Jerome’s Hebrew reading here, inserting the purely Hebrew word gever; for they do not understand that, according to Saint Jerome, “cistern” is called gubba in Syriac and Chaldean—that is, in the common Hebrew language [Col. 0723D]. Thus, in Saint Jerome’s time, “Hebrew language” meant the Syriac-Chaldean dialect, as is clear from the present testimony and from the earlier name Beth-haccerem, which, as the same Jerome testifies, was called Bethacharma in Syriac and Chaldean. The earlier editors, paying no attention to this, everywhere thrust purely Hebrew names upon us in place of Syriac-Chaldean words, giving us a different, corrupt, and fictitious Jerome instead of the real one. MARTIAN.—In the manuscripts it is read Caba or Cab. Jerome himself says in the Life of Saint Paul the Hermit, no. 6: “Another was sustained each day by five figs in an old cistern which the Syrians, in their gentile language, call GUBBAM.” Therefore, when he says here that “cistern” is so called in the Syriac language, he indicates the pronunciation of the Syrians of his own time, or more correctly the Syriac-Chaldean language. See what we have noted on that passage.] is called GUBBA (). In the present passage, however, the Hebrew word for the pool, which all have translated in the same way, is BOR ().

(Verses 8.) “Iniquity and devastation will be heard in it continually before me, weakness and plague. Be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul withdraw from you, lest I make you desolate, an uninhabitable land.”

The Septuagint: “Impiety and misery will be heard in it before his face. Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem, lest my soul withdraw from you, lest I make you an impassable land that is not inhabited.”

Through these words we learn that the Lord scourges every son whom he receives. Jerusalem is therefore instructed through blows and torments so that she may be corrected, God’s soul may not withdraw from her, and she may not be reduced to solitude. Whenever, then, we are subjected to repeated hardships, let us recall this verse for our consolation: “Through every pain and scourge you will be instructed, Jerusalem.”

(Verses 9.) “Thus says the Lord of hosts: They will gather Israel’s remnant as one gathers the gleanings of a vineyard. Turn your hand like a grape-gatherer to the basket.”

The Septuagint: “For thus says the Lord of hosts: Glean, glean as a vineyard the remnant of Israel. Return like a grape-gatherer to his basket.”

Some receive these words in a good sense, others in a bad sense. In the good sense, when Jerusalem has been devastated, the remnant is saved. In the bad sense, it means that not even a single grape or small cluster will remain in the vineyard, but everything will be gathered; whatever you find, collect it like a grape-gatherer into a basket, so that just as he drags the grapes to the winepress, you may drag the captives to Babylon.

(Verses 10.) “To whom shall I speak, and whom shall I warn, so that he may hear? Behold, their ears are uncircumcised [or: your ears], and they cannot hear.”

They cannot hear because they refused to circumcise their ears. Yet this inability is not free from punishment, since it proceeds from contempt and unbelief. Therefore, if someone does not receive the words of God and does not possess an understanding of his commandments, he has uncircumcised ears.

At the same time, it should be noted that circumcision is called by three names in Scripture: of the foreskin, of the heart, and of the ears. Hence the Lord says: “Let the one who has ears to hear hear” (Matthew 11:15). Thus, by our own will, we do not receive the word of God; and therefore what was given to us for salvation is turned by our own fault into punishment [Note: [Col. 0724D] I would prefer: “that circumcision”; in two manuscripts it reads: “that uncircumcision.”].

(Verses 11.) “Therefore I am full of the fury of the Lord; I am weary of enduring.”

The Septuagint: “And I have filled my anger, and I have endured, and I have not consumed him.”

According to the Hebrew, this is said in the person of the prophet, who foresees the approaching wrath of God, is full of the Lord’s fury and anger, and can endure no longer; nor does he dare to entreat the Lord on behalf of sinners.

According to the Septuagint, however, a new meaning is introduced: that the Lord himself has fulfilled his anger by striking the sinful people, yet has restrained it and not poured it out entirely, so that the remnant may be saved. This seems to me contradictory to itself. For if he has fulfilled his anger, how did he restrain himself so as not to fulfill it?

(Verses 12.) “Pour it out [or: he pours it out] upon the child outside [Note: [Col. 0724D] For “outside,” restored from the Hebrew and from Jerome’s own version, “wrath” has hitherto been read erroneously. Either similarity of the words or the following exposition deceived some pedantic copyist.], and upon the gathering of young men together; for man with wife shall be taken, the old man with the one full of days. And their houses shall pass to others, and their fields and wives likewise.”

Either the prophet, in the spirit, commands the coming Chaldean to pour out the Lord’s fury upon the children, sparing no age, even the innocent; or else he reports what happened to the assembly of young men together, who had taken up arms to resist. “Man with wife shall be taken”: together they will experience captivity, although they possess the sweetest names for one another. “The old man with the one full of days.” Therefore, old age is not simply the final period of life, but refers to those who are full of days, whom in our language we call aged or decrepit.

It follows: “And their houses shall pass to others,” through the evil of captivity, and their fields and wives together, so that both the wife and the property pass to the enemies. Whatever we understand literally concerning Jerusalem, let us refer spiritually to the Church, if it offends God.

(Verses 13 ff.) “For I will stretch out my hand over the inhabitants of the land,” says the Lord. “For from the least to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice; and from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. And they treat the brokenness of the daughter of my people with disgrace, saying: Peace, peace, when there is no peace.”

In Hebrew it is said: “I will stretch out my hand over the sinners,” or “over the inhabitants of the land.” In the Septuagint it is consistently written “I will raise up,” both of which are attitudes of one who strikes. In accordance with what is written: “And still the hand of the Lord is stretched out,” or “raised high” (Isaiah 5:25).

The inhabitants of the earth are always in a state of vice. Hence also in the Apocalypse it is said more than once: “Woe to the inhabitants of the earth” (Revelation 8:13). From the least [variant: “from the smallest”] to the greatest, all are devoted to avarice, according to the apostolic saying: “The root of all evils is avarice” [Col. 0724D] (1 Timothy 6:10). And from prophet to priest, all practice deceit: some by prophesying falsehood, others by interpreting God’s law perversely. For the prophet says elsewhere: “Seek the law from the priests” [Col. 0725A] (Jeremiah 18).

“And when,” he says, “they were doing such things, they announced every prosperity to my people and seemed to wish to cure the wound and disgrace of my daughter, saying: ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace at all.” This is to be understood especially of priests and teachers, who promise prosperity to the rich and to those whom they see established in the highest honor, and proclaim God merciful, thereby preparing them all the more for punishment and wrath.

(Verses 15.) “They were confounded because they committed abomination; indeed, they were not confounded by confusion, and they did not know how to blush.”

This should be read more closely according to the Hebrew. “When,” he says, “they had done such things, were they confounded? Did they blush at their crimes? On the contrary, they increased their sin through contempt and did not know how to blush.” Here “did not know” means “did not wish to,” or else, through their excessive contempt and their vice, which had become ingrained, they were unable even to understand.

“Therefore they shall fall among those who fall; at the time of their visitation they shall collapse,” says the Lord.

Because, he says, they did not know how to blush, and had not only no good works but not even knowledge or a sense of repentance, therefore those who formerly stood will fall among those who collapse through their vices. When the time of their visitation and punishment arrives, they will join the general ruin. Great, then, is the impiety—not merely failing to avoid sins, but refusing even to understand them, and possessing no distinction between good and evil works.

(Verses 16 ff.) “Thus says the Lord: Stand upon the ways and see, and ask about the ancient paths, which is the good way, and walk in it, and you will find refreshment [or: purification] for your souls. And they said: We will not walk [or: go]. And I set watchmen over you: Listen to the sound of the trumpet. And they said: We will not listen. Therefore hear [or: they heard], nations, and know [variant: “know, you who pasture flocks”], O assembly [or: you who pasture flocks]; or, according to Symmachus: “And know the testimony that is in them, how great are the things I shall do to them.” Hear, O earth.”

If the evangelical parable is understood, it will provide the meaning of this passage. In it, the good merchant is said to sell all his pearls in order to buy one exceedingly precious pearl with their price (Matthew 13). This means that through the Patriarchs and Prophets we should come to him who says: “I am the way” (John 14).

We must therefore stand upon the prophets, contemplate them with the greatest care, and ask about the ancient or everlasting paths, which have been worn by the footsteps of many saints. These are more significantly called in Greek τρίβοι, “paths.” We must ask which is the good way in the Gospel (Matthew 7) and walk in it. When this way has been found, it offers refreshment, or purification, to the souls of believers.

But they, on the contrary, answered that they would not walk in the way of the Gospel—this being said specifically by the prophet concerning the unbelief of the Jews. Immediately he adds: “And I set watchmen over you.” There is no doubt that the chorus of the Apostles is indicated, according to Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 3:17).

And he commanded them to hear the sound of the trumpet: either the commandments of the Gospel or the teaching of the Apostles, according to Isaiah: “Go up upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; lift up your voice like a trumpet, you who announce Jerusalem” (Isaiah 40:9).

They said: “We will not hear,” and, when invited to the banquet, refused to come. Therefore it is said: “Hear, nations.” The Apostles followed this course when they spoke in Lycaonia: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the nations” (Acts 13:46).

“And know, O assembly”—not the Jewish assembly but that of all nations—or “you who pasture flocks,” namely bishops, presbyters, and the entire ecclesiastical order. Or: “Know the testimony that is in them.” For “the testimony of God is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Psalm 18:8). To them also the Lord says: “Do not fear, little flock” (Luke 12:31), and: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me” (Isaiah 8:18).

Know, then, how much I will do to the unbelieving people. What follows—“Hear, O earth”—calls the whole world to hear, just as at the beginning of Isaiah we read: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth” (Isaiah 1:2). The things which the Lord is going to do to the Jewish people are meant.

(Verses 19.) “Behold, I will bring evils upon this people, the fruit of its thoughts [or: aversion], because they have not heard my words and have rejected my law.”

He calls the punishments and penalties suffered by them “evils”—not evils upon the nations that are called to the truth of the Gospel, but upon the people who answered: “We will not hear.” They will receive the fruit of their thoughts, or of their turning away, as David says: “You shall eat the labors of your hands” (Psalm 127:2). The reason is evident: they did not hear the words of the Lord and cast away his law.

(Verses 20.) “Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba and fragrant cane from a distant land? Your burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me.”

No one doubts that frankincense comes from Sheba; hence Virgil’s line:

“And a hundred altars glow with Sabaean incense” (Aeneid 1).

As for the cane, which is called CANE () in Hebrew, and which the Septuagint and Theodotion translated as “cinnamon” [Note: [Col. 0725D] Victor has “cinnamon,” following the Septuagint reading.], the prophetic word testifies that it comes from a distant land, so that we may understand India, from which many spices arrive by way of the Red Sea. Physicians call this kind of aromatic substance κασία σύριγγος, “cassia reed,” [Note: [Col. 0725D] Perhaps “a reed of cassia”; Galen uses this expression for what we commonly call cinnamon. I see that learned men also approve this, and here understand, instead of India, the much more distant region of the Chinese.]

The meaning is: In vain do you bring me the most fragrant spices for preparing the unguents prescribed by the Law and burn your burnt offerings, when you do not do my will in the Law, according to what was said above: “They did not hear my words, and they rejected my law.”

This applies specifically to those who offer sacrifices from robbery and the stripping of the poor, and think that they can redeem their sins through almsgiving, although Scripture says: “The ransom of a man’s soul is his own riches” (Proverbs 13:8)—riches gathered not from iniquity but from labor and righteousness.

(Verses 21.) “Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will place ruins before this people, and they will fall among them [or: weakness, and they will become weak]; fathers and sons together, neighbor and near one, and they will perish.”

We see fulfilled everything that the Lord threatened against that people. Every day they fall through their blasphemies, possessing nothing strong within themselves; all among them is weakness. The sons of the fathers follow their blasphemies and daily receive that imprecation: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27:25). And not only they themselves, but also their neighbors and those near them, and all who follow the Law and the Prophets according to the letter that kills rather than according to the life-giving spirit, will all perish together, because all have sinned together.

(Verses 22, 23.) “Thus says the Lord: Behold, a people is coming from the land of the north, and a great nation will arise from the ends of the earth. It will take up arrow and shield [or: zebynna]; it is cruel [or: shameless] and will not show mercy. Its voice will roar like the sea, and they will mount horses, prepared like a man for battle against you, daughter of Zion.” [Note: [Col. 0727D] Two manuscripts read “upon” instead of “against.”]

This is specifically prophesied concerning the Babylonians, who are going to come against the people of Jerusalem. The entire order of their armor and the assault of the combatants are described so that, shaken by the terror of the voice, they may repent and appease the most merciful God. Finally, he provides an occasion for prayer when he says: “Against you, daughter of Zion.” We may misuse this testimony in a time of persecution, when all the fury of the devil is stirred against us and there is no mercy, and when the attackers overwhelm those who resist like the waves of a most violent sea.

(Verses 24.) “We have heard its report; our hands have become weak; tribulation has seized us, pains like those of a woman in labor.” [Note: [Col. 0727D] The same manuscripts read, as does Rabanus: “and pains like those of a woman in labor.” A little later they read: “because before they come.”]

The people reply, whom the prophet—or rather, through the prophet, the Lord—has threatened with the Babylonians: before they come, they have already been overcome by fear and cannot raise their hands, and anguish has seized them like the pain of a woman in labor. They affirm that they have felt nothing more grievous than that pain.

[Col. 0727D] (Verses 25.) “Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, because the sword of the enemy is terror all around.”

The Gospel teaches (Matthew 24) that one must not go out into the field or descend from the height of the roofs, but must heed the command: “Save yourself upon the mountain” [Col. 0728A] (Genesis 19:17). In Isaiah and Micah (Isaiah 2; Micah 4) we are commanded to run to and ascend that mountain. Literally, however, it is commanded that they not go outside or abandon the walls, but defend themselves within the strongest fortifications.

(Verses 26.) “Daughter of my people, gird yourself with sackcloth and sprinkle yourself with ashes; make mourning like that for an only child [or: beloved child], a bitter [or: lamentable] lament, because the destroyer [or: misery] will suddenly come upon us [or: you].”

Because he had said above, “Do not go out into the fields, and do not walk on the road, because the sword of the enemy is terror all around,” and had also forbidden flight, he now teaches what they must do: namely, turn to repentance and possess in it their firmest and safest armor.

Where we translated, “Make mourning like that for an only child,” the Hebrew writes JAID () [Note: [Col. 0727D] Jaid. This Hebrew name is somewhat corrupted, together with the following one, in many manuscript copies, where ancient scribes, through ignorance of the Hebrew language, wrote Aid without the initial yod, and used ididae, idida, or idide instead of IDID, which means “beloved.” If ididia had been written, it would mean “the beloved of the Lord,” not merely “beloved,” as Jerome observes. MARTIAN.]. This more properly means “solitary” than “only-begotten.” For if the meaning were “beloved” or “lovable,” as the Septuagint translated it, IDID () would have been written—the name God also gave to Solomon. Nothing is more painful than to lose one’s only or solitary son (2 Kings 12).

What we translated as “because the destroyer, or misery, will suddenly come upon us,” the Septuagint rendered “upon you.” God has spoken more mercifully by saying this, so that whatever is going to come upon his people, he may testify will also come upon himself. The destroyer properly signifies either Nabuchodonosor or the devil.

### (Verses 27ff.)

“I have appointed you as a tester among my people, a strong one, and you shall know and test their way. All these princes are turning aside [or: disobedient], walking deceitfully [or: perversely]. Bronze and iron: they are all corrupted; the bellows have failed in the fire” (which the Greeks more significantly call *physētēr*, φυσητήρ); “the lead has been consumed; the smelter has smelted in vain” [or: the silversmith]. “For their wickednesses have not been consumed. Call them rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away.”

[Note: In the Cistercian manuscript together with the Vatican manuscript, “because I have cast them away.”]

A strong tester is given by the prophet to an unbelieving people. In Hebrew this is called *Mabsar*, which, according to Aquila, means “fortified,” or, according to Symmachus and the Septuagint, “shut up and enclosed,” [Note: Yet the Septuagint, at least in the copies that have survived to our time, reads ἐν λαοῖς δεδοκιμασμένοις, “among tested peoples,” which scarcely—or not even scarcely—agrees with this comparison to a most strongly fortified city.]

like a very strongly fortified city, so that he fears none of the people’s ambushes. “When you have tested,” he says, “and have learned the way of the sinful people, then you will understand that silver mixed with bronze cannot in any way be purified.”

For just as lead is mixed with adulterated and defiled metals so that the foreign material may be separated, and, if it has perhaps not been purified, all the lead is consumed and reduced to nothing, so every utterance of instruction and prophetic speech perishes in those who disdain to listen (Psalm 57). Let us say this also concerning those who, like deaf adders, stop up their ears so that they may not hear the voices of the charmers. For the silversmith, or smelter, has smelted in vain: their wickednesses have not been consumed. Therefore they are called not silver, but rejected silver, because the Lord has cast them away. The princes are those who depart from the Lord, or who are disobedient, and who walk perversely and deceitfully.

### (Chapter 7—Verses 1, 2)

The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: “Stand in the gate of the house of the Lord, and proclaim [or: read] there this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, all Judah, you who enter through these gates to worship the Lord.”

This is not found in the Septuagint edition, but it was added from the Hebrew according to Theodotion.

[Note: In a certain Parisian Jesuit manuscript of the *Hexapla*, according to Montfaucon, Theodotion reads Ἰουδαία, “Judea,” instead of *Juda* (“Judah”).]

The Prophet is commanded to stand in the gate of the Lord, through which the multitude of the people enters to worship the Lord, so that on this occasion they may be able to hear what the Lord commands. From this we understand the hardness of the Jewish people: they regarded the prophets as liars and madmen, since they were compelled to hear the words of the Lord because of the occasion and the public nature of the place, and not because the words were the Lord’s.

### (Verse 3)

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: “Make your ways good [or: direct your ways] and your practices [or: your inventions], and I will dwell with you in this place” [or: “I will make you dwell in this place”].

The most merciful physician desires to heal all the wounded with medicine. When he says, “Make your ways good,” or “correct your ways,” he shows that they are perverse and possess nothing good in themselves. And because it is natural for each person to love his native soil and to consider nothing sweeter than his homeland, he promises rewards to those who obey. “I will dwell,” he says, “with you,” so that he may make you secure concerning his dwelling; or, according to Symmachus, “I will establish you in a firm dwelling,” as he says: “And I will make you secure in this place.”

### (Verses 4ff.)

“Do not trust in deceitful words [or: words of deceit], saying: ‘The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.’ For if you bless [or: direct] your ways and your practices; if you execute judgment between a man and his neighbor [or: between a man and his fellow]; if you do not wrong [or: oppress] the stranger, the orphan, and the widow; if you do not shed innocent blood in this place; and if you do not go after foreign gods to your own harm; I will dwell with you [or: I will make you dwell] in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers from age to age.”

[Note: It seems that, with Victorius, *bene direxeritis* (“you have directed well”) should be restored from the Vulgate edition and Jerome’s own Commentary. Jerome probably added *bene* (“well”) because the word is repeated in this way in Hebrew.]

The addition that the Septuagint placed at the beginning of this chapter—“in words of deceit, which will not profit you at all”—is not found in the Hebrew.

He commanded both the Jewish people then and us today, who seem to be established in the Church, to place no confidence in the splendor of buildings, in gilded ceilings, or in walls clad with marble panels. Let us not say: “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this.” That is the temple of the Lord in which true faith, holy conduct, and the chorus of all virtues dwell.
