Finally he adds: “If you make your ways straight, and your thought does not go after error; if you follow justice, do no evil, and shed no innocent blood, causing no simple people to stumble; and if you do not go after foreign gods, worshiping perverse doctrines that you have fabricated from your own heart to your own harm, then I will dwell with you in this place which you call the temple of God, and in the land that I gave to your fathers”—that is, to the Apostles and apostolic men—or certainly: “I will make you dwell in a firm station from beginning to end.”

This can also apply to those virgins who boast of their modesty and display their chastity with an impudent face, although their conscience says otherwise, and who do not know the Apostle’s definition of virginity: “that she may be holy in body and spirit.” For what does bodily chastity profit a mind that has been defiled, if it does not possess the other virtues described by the prophetic word?

### (Verses 8ff.)

“Behold, you trust in yourselves in deceitful words [or: deceitful sayings] that will not profit you. To steal, to kill, to commit adultery, to swear falsely, to offer libations to the Baals, and to go after foreign gods whom you do not know. And you have come and stood before me in this house in which my name has been invoked, and you have said: ‘We have been delivered’ [or: ‘We have ceased’], because we have done all these abominations.”

The sins that follow demonstrate how futile it is for them to trust in the temple. For what does it profit them boldly to cross the threshold of God’s house and stand there with necks held high, while not only their hearts but also their hands are polluted by theft, murder, adultery, perjury, sacrilege, and the worship of gods whom they do not know?

No one doubts that these things occur spiritually in the Church, when people, considering the prosperity of the present time, do not reckon with their sins and think that God remains hidden because punishment does not immediately follow. Rather, they burst into such madness that they consider themselves delivered because, after their evil deeds, they have also withdrawn from the worship of the Lord.

### (Verse 11)

“Has this house [or: my house], in which my name has been invoked, become a den of robbers in your eyes? I, I am he; I have seen it, says the Lord.”

I think that this passage was taken up in the Gospel: “It is written: ‘My Father’s house shall be called a house of prayer’; but you have made it a den of robbers” (Matthew 21:13); or, as it is written in another Gospel, “a house of commerce” (John 2:16).

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “what is written”; this is also how it is written in Rabanus.]

The Church of God is turned into a den of robbers when thefts, murders, adulteries, sacrileges, perjuries, the invention of heresy, and every kind of crime are practiced in it; when its leaders burn with the torches of greed, and a worthless—or at least not worthless—little cloak possesses the wealth of former kings.

Therefore he adds: “I, I am he; I have seen it, says the Lord.” My eyes have observed what you think is hidden; the darkness of your treasures does not escape my knowledge. Although he was rich, he became poor for our sake; now he is ashamed of our riches (1 Corinthians 8), and says: “Woe to you who are rich, because you have your consolation” (Luke 6).

### (Verse 12)

“Go to my place at Shiloh, where my name dwelt at the beginning, and see what I did to it because of the wickedness of my people Israel.”

He teaches the present from the past. To those who say, “The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord is this,” and who rejoice in the splendor of precious buildings, he recalls Shiloh, where God’s tabernacle first stood. Concerning it the Psalm says: “And he rejected the tabernacle of Shiloh” (Psalm 77:60).

Just as that place collapsed into ruins and ashes, so also the Temple will fall when it has become the dwelling of sinners of the same kind. Therefore, just as Shiloh is an example of the Temple, so the Temple is an example for us when the time of that testimony arrives: “Do you suppose that, when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke 18:8).

### (Verses 13ff.)

“And now, because you have done all these works, says the Lord, and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, and you did not listen; and I called you, and you did not answer, I will do to this house, in which my name has been invoked and in which you trust, and to the place that I gave to you and to your fathers, as I did to Shiloh. And I will cast you away from my presence, as I cast away all your brothers, the whole seed of Ephraim” [or: Israel].

The phrase that we have rendered “rising early and speaking” is not found in the Septuagint. God rises early—not because any period of time is absent from him before dawn, but because, after the rest of night and the restoration of bodily strength, the human soul is more vigorous and, no longer occupied by pleasures or the desire for food, is able to hear and do what is said.

Therefore we also read in the Psalm: “In the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you and see” (Psalm 5:4–5). And in Isaiah: “At night, or at dawn” [Note: Victorius, supported by four manuscripts and by the Greek ὀρθιάζει, reads “rises”] “my spirit rises to you, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth” (Isaiah 26).

Thus the Apostle Paul calls them children of light (Ephesians 5), not of night or darkness, nor sleepers as the others sleep—those who do not perceive the commandments of God.

[Note: The printed editions insert “glorious,” a word unknown to the old books.]

Since God therefore called them, rising at night or at dawn, in order also to free them from darkness, he threatens that he will do to the Temple in Jerusalem what he did to the place of Shiloh, where the tabernacle first stood, so that similar sins may receive an equal sentence.

And just as the Lord rejected the seed of Ephraim—that is, the ten tribes called Israel, which had rulers because of Jeroboam son of Nebat, from the tribe of Ephraim, which was also called the tribe of Joseph—so he testifies that he will likewise reject Jerusalem and the tribe of Judah together with Benjamin. He rejected Shiloh and will reject the Temple; he rejected the ten tribes and will reject the two. Whatever is said to that people, let us understand also as spoken concerning us, if we commit similar acts.

### (Verse 16)

“Therefore you must not pray for this people, nor take up praise and prayer on their behalf” [or: “nor ask that they obtain mercy”]. “And do not oppose me, because I will not hear you.”

So that the Prophet might not appear to be praying without obtaining what he requests, God commands him not to intercede for a sinful people that practices no repentance. When he says, “Do not oppose me,” he shows that the prayers of the saints can withstand God’s anger.

Thus the Lord also says to Moses: “Let me alone, so that I may strike this people, and I will make you into a great nation” (Exodus 32:10). And in the Psalms we read: “Phinehas stood and made atonement, and the plague ceased, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Psalm 105:30). Aaron likewise took a censer and stood between the burning fire and the people; and God’s anger ceased.

And lest we think God cruel because he does not even permit himself to be entreated, he gives the reasons why he will not hear them (Numbers 16), saying:

### (Verses 17ff.)

“Do you not see what these people are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem? The sons gather wood, and the fathers kindle the fire; and the women knead the fat so that they may make cakes [or: *Chavonim*] for the queen [or: the host] of heaven, and offer libations to foreign gods, provoking me to anger. Are they provoking me to anger? says the Lord. Are they not rather provoking themselves to the shame of their own faces?”

“Do you wish,” he says, “to hear, O Prophet, why I told you, ‘Do not pray for this people’? They do the following: inside and outside, in the streets and in the exits of Jerusalem, the sons carry wood, the fathers kindle the fire, and the women knead fat with flour in order to make *Chavonim*, which we have interpreted as ‘cakes,’ or ‘preparations,’ so that the expression may indicate every kind of sacrifice to the queen of heaven, whom we should understand as the moon; or certainly to the host of heaven, so that we understand all the stars.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read *Chavonum*. The old printed editions have Χαυώνας.]

“And after these things they offer libations to foreign gods”—not because such gods exist, but because under their names they burn incense to demons—and by doing these things they provoke me to anger.

The wretched do not understand that this conflict does not injure me, whom anger never changes, but brings shame upon their own faces and everlasting disgrace. Whatever we do, therefore, we do not injure God, who can never be injured; rather, we prepare destruction for ourselves, storing up wrath for the day of wrath.

He placed the various duties of sons, fathers, and mothers—or wives—in order to show that no age was free from impiety.

### (Verse 20)

Therefore thus says the Lord God: “Behold, my fury and my indignation have been poured forth” [Vulgate: “are poured forth”] [or: “have dripped”] “upon this place, upon human beings and animals, upon the trees of the countryside, and upon the fruits of the earth; and it shall burn, and shall not be extinguished.”

The one who earlier said, “Are they provoking me to anger?” now says, “Behold, my fury and my indignation have dripped upon this place.” The meaning is: “I do not naturally become angry, but they act in such a way that they provoke me to anger and seem to change my nature. Let them therefore experience me as angry, which they attempt to bring about as far as lies within them.”

He fittingly does not say, “My fury has been poured out upon this place,” but “has dripped,” to signify a measured punishment. But if such severity exists in a single drop of fury, what will happen if the whole rain is poured out?

The outpoured indignation can also be understood in this way: what he long refused to do, he is compelled to do by the multitude of their sins.

[Note: The same two manuscripts read *coguntur* (“are compelled”), though incorrectly, for *conantur* (“attempt”); shortly afterward they read *conflatio* (“pouring forth”) for *conflata indignatio* (“outpoured indignation”).] When God is angry, human beings and the things belonging to human beings will suffer a similar destruction.

“And it shall burn,” he says—clearly, the Lord’s fury—and it shall not be extinguished, because the people do not do the things by which it could be extinguished.

### (Verses 21ff.)

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat the meat. For I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning the matter of burnt offerings and sacrifices. But this word I commanded them, saying: ‘Listen to my voice, and I will be your God; and you shall be my people. Walk in every way that I have commanded you, so that it may be well with you.’”

Since he rejected their Temple, he consequently rejects their sacrifices as well. Indirectly he accuses them of sacrificing not out of reverence for him but from a desire for feasting.

When he says, “I did not speak with your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices,” this is clearly understood to mean that he first gave the Decalogue on tablets of stone, written by the finger of God; and then, after the offense of idolatry and the making of the calf (Exodus 31),

[Note: I would prefer *ea tantum* (“only these things”) instead of *postea* (“afterward”). Compare the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 10.]

he later commanded that sacrifices be made to him rather than to demons, removing the pure religion of God’s commandments and permitting the shedding of sacrificial blood and the desire for meat.

### (Verses 24, 25)

“And they did not listen or incline their ear, but went after the desires [or: the will] and the perversity of their evil heart. They became backward and not forward” [Vulgate: “and not even forward”], “from the day when their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day.”

When I said, “Listen to my voice, and I will be your God,” and the rest, they did not listen or incline their ear, but followed the desires of their own heart. Contrary to the Apostle’s teaching—he forgot what lay behind and stretched out toward what lay ahead—they did the opposite: they desired the past and despised the future.

When he says, “From the day when their fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day,” he means that they spent the whole intervening time in offense against the Lord. Hence the grace of the Gospel was necessary, which preserved them not through their own merit but through the Lord’s mercy.

### (Verse 26)

“And I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early day by day and sending them. Yet they did not listen to me or incline their ear, but hardened their neck and acted worse than their fathers.”

The Lord’s anger, therefore, is just: it has been poured forth—or has dripped—upon a contemptuous people, hard of neck and unwilling to hear the words of God. We have explained above how God sends prophets at night, at dawn, and during the day.

### (Verses 27, 28)

“And you shall speak all these words to them, but they will not listen to you; and you shall call them, but they will not answer you. And you shall say to them: ‘This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God, and did not accept discipline. Faith has perished and has been removed from their mouth.’”

“Do not doubt,” he says, “that they have hardened their neck and acted worse than their fathers. Behold, I am giving them an opportunity for repentance. I do not speak in order that these things may happen, but because they are going to happen, and therefore I foretell them. At least now speak to them my words; yet they will not listen to you. Call them, and they will not answer you.”

Such will be their arrogance that, when you call them to hear, no one will deign to answer. And you shall say to them: “This is the nation that did not listen to the voice of the Lord its God and did not accept discipline.”

Fittingly, as I have already said, he does not call them his people but a nation. Although this was partly fulfilled in the time of the prophets, and preceded in shadow and in image, it is more fully completed in Christ, when they refused to accept discipline and despised the voice of their Lord.

Therefore the statement is elegantly added: “Faith has perished”—faith which properly belongs to Christians—“and has been removed from their mouth,” namely, every confession of the Son of God and of faith.

### (Verse 29)

“Cut off your hair and cast it away, and take up lamentation on the heights” [or: “upon your lips”], “because the Lord has rejected and abandoned the generation of his wrath.”

We read that Job, after hearing of the death of his sons and daughters, cut his hair (Job 1). Among the ancients it was customary for all mourners to cut their hair. Now, by contrast, letting one’s hair grow long is a sign of mourning.

Every lamentation and prophetic mourning is therefore taken up because “the Lord has rejected and abandoned the generation of his wrath.” There is no doubt that this refers to the Jewish people. More specifically, it must be referred to the time of Christ, when faith perished and was removed from the mouth of the people blaspheming the Lord.

### (Verses 30, 31)

“For the sons of Judah have done evil in my sight” [Vulgate: “in my eyes”], says the Lord. “They have set up their abominations in the house in which my name has been invoked, in order to defile it. And they have built the high places [or: an altar] of Topheth, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, in order to burn their sons and their daughters with fire—something I did not command and never conceived in my heart.”

We learn at the beginning of Ezekiel that the sons of Judah set up a statue of Baal in the Temple of God. The high places, which in Hebrew are called *Bamoth*, or the altar of Topheth, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom,

[Note: Here and below Victorius, on the basis of the Brixian manuscripts, restored “the sons of Hinnom.”]

signify the place watered by the springs of Siloam. It is pleasant and wooded, and even today offers the delights of gardens.

This error of paganism took possession of all provinces, so that they sacrificed victims on mountain peaks and in most beautiful groves, and every form of perverse superstition was maintained.

*Topheth* is interpreted in the Hebrew language as “breadth.” It is said to be written in the book of Joshua son of Nun concerning this place, which is in the valley of the sons of Hinnom and is called in Hebrew *Ge-Hinnom*.

[Note: In Hebrew it is “the valley of the son of Hennom,” which is more briefly called *Gehennom*, and, in the archaic form, *Gehenna*. The letter O has been changed into A in accordance with the character of the Syriac dialect.]

For *Ge* means φάραγγα (*pharanga*), “a ravine,” that is, a valley; and *Hinnom* either means a man’s name or signifies “grace.” The Hebrews relate that Gehenna was named from this place because the whole Jewish people perished there by offending God.

In that place they also consecrated their sons to idols by fire, or offered them as burnt offerings—things that he had not commanded them, and that no sanction of the Law had ordered (2 Kings 17). If Jephthah offered his virgin daughter to God, it is not the sacrifice that is pleasing, but the intention of the one offering it (Judges 11). For if a dog, or a donkey, or any unclean animal had been the first to meet the father returning from the slaughter of his enemies, he ought not therefore to have offered it to God.

### (Verses 32, 33)

“Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, when it will no longer be called Topheth or the valley of the sons of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. And they will bury in Topheth, because there will be no place.”

[Note: The same manuscripts, following the form of the sacred text, read “and they will bury.”]

“And the corpses of this people will become food for the birds of heaven and the beasts of the earth, and there will be no one to drive them away.”

He signifies the time of the siege, which they endured from the ninth year of King Zedekiah to the eleventh year (2 Kings 25). The valley itself will no longer be called *Gehenna*, that is, the valley of Hinnom or of the sons of Hinnom, but, because of the slaughter of so many, the valley of slaughter.

The carnage will be so great that, in a place formerly devoted to religion, there will be countless graves; and those whom they cannot bury will be torn apart by birds and devoured by beasts. There will be no one to drive them away, since everyone will fear a similar fate and be prevented from performing the duties of burial.

We pass rapidly over what is clear, so that wherever there is an obscure point we may linger. The size of the book itself can weary its readers—how much more if we were to discuss it at greater length.

### (Verse 34)

“And I will cause to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of joy, the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride. For the land will become a desolation.”

When the place of idolatry has been turned into graves, so that in the very place where they offended God their unburied corpses lie, every joy will be removed from the city once called Jerusalem [or: from Jerusalem, which was once such], and from the other cities that were under its authority. Everything will be filled with sorrow, lamentation, and desolation.

## (Chapter 8—Verses 1ff.)

“At that time,” says the Lord, “they will bring out of their graves the bones of the kings of Judah, the bones of its princes, the bones of the priests, the bones of the prophets, and the bones of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And they will spread them out before the sun, the moon, and all the host of heaven, which they loved, served, followed, sought, and worshiped. They will not be gathered up or buried; they will be like dung upon the face of the earth. And all the remnant of this evil family, in all the places where I have driven them, will choose death rather than life, says the Lord of hosts.”

Everything described by the prophetic word we see happening in our own time—not only to Jerusalem, which suffered these things at the hands of the Chaldeans and Romans, but to the whole world, so that tears have dried up and everything has been filled with the bones of the dead.

And because, according to ancient custom, they used to place gold and certain ornaments of women or men in graves, greed also broke open and dug up these things, so that they might be exposed to the sky and the daylight.

[Note: In the Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts, the words “these things,” and certain ornaments belonging either to women or to men, are missing. We correct some less important matters below from the same manuscripts.]

Therefore the bones of the kings of Judah first, and of their princes, priests, prophets, and the whole people who had been in Jerusalem, were brought out from the tombs and exposed to the sight of the sun, moon, and all the stars, so that they might lie open to the sight of those whom they had served after abandoning God, and, consumed, be reduced to dung and ashes.

But if anyone from the multitude could escape, wherever he came he would prefer death to life and consider destruction the remedy for his wretched soul.

### (Verse 4)

“And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Does one who falls not rise again? And does one who has turned away not return?” [or: “not turn back?”]

After so many evils he calls those who might remain to repentance; or, before the threatened events arrive, he urges them to conversion and grants an opportunity for repentance.

According to the Hebrew text, “And he who has turned away, will he not turn back?” signifies that one who has turned away from God, if he wishes to turn toward better things, can also turn God’s anger toward better things, withstand what is coming, and avoid the blows through prayer.

### (Verse 5)

“Why, then, has this people in Jerusalem turned away with a contentious turning away? They have grasped deceit and have refused to return.”

[Note: The same manuscripts read “has turned away.”]

The more, he says, I called them to repentance, the more they withdrew from me—not so much from a desire to sin as from a desire to defeat me. They have firmly grasped deceit, whether idols or anything perverse and contrary to truth and justice, and they have refused to return. He did not say, “They could not,” but they pursued evil with every effort.

### (Verse 6)

“I paid attention and listened: no one speaks what is good. There is no one who repents of his sin and says, ‘What have I done?’ All have turned to their own course, like a horse rushing headlong into battle.”

Recalled to repentance, they disdain listening. Nor is it enough for them to have sinned against the Lord and spoken blasphemy; like horses plunging into battle at a furious pace, they do not reflect upon their sin or say, “What have I done?”

We may understand this either of the whole human race, because it is inclined toward vices, or of the time of the Savior, when all turned aside together and became useless: “There was no one who did good, not even one” (Psalm 13).

[Note: The same manuscripts again read: “they turned aside together and became useless.”]

Hence he himself cries out mystically [or: cried out]: “Save me, Lord, because the holy one has failed” (Psalm 12:1).

But if these things are so, where are those who say that it lies within our will to be entirely free from sin? “No one,” he says, “speaks what is good” (Matthew 11), because even for an idle word we shall have to give an account on the day of judgment.

### (Verse 7)

“The kite in the sky knows its appointed time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork observe the time of their coming; but my people do not know the judgment of the Lord.”

In place of the kite, which Symmachus translated, the Septuagint and Theodotion have retained the Hebrew word itself, *Asida*, while Aquila has *herodion*.

Again, in place of “swallow,” Symmachus translated “cicada,” which in Hebrew is called *Sis*. In place of what we have rendered “stork,” Aquila and Symmachus translated *Agur*, as it is written in Hebrew; instead of this, the Septuagint translated “sparrows of the field.”

[Note: All our manuscripts read *herodiona*; one manuscript from Saint-Germain, according to Montfaucon, has *erodion*.]

The meaning is one and the same as that found at the beginning of Isaiah: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel does not know me, and my people does not understand” (Isaiah 1:3). Even small birds know their seasons and understand when, hastening toward warm regions, they must escape the cold of winter, and again, at the beginning of spring, return to their customary regions.

Here “heaven” should be understood as the air above us.

[Note: Two of our manuscripts read “the heaven that is above.” We should understand this as the air that is above.]

### (Verse 8)

“How can you say, ‘We are wise, and the Law of the Lord is with us’? Truly, the lying stylus of the scribes has worked deceit.”

He speaks to the scribes and Pharisees, who boast of their knowledge of the Law and, in writing, write iniquity.

And when he says:

### (Verse 9)

“The wise have been put to shame, terrified, and captured. For they have rejected the word of the Lord, and what wisdom is in them?”

He does not mean that those who do these things are wise; rather, he calls them wise so that they may be condemned under judgment. Conversely, their wisdom is convicted of folly, as the Apostle Paul says: “You who teach another, do you not teach yourself?” (Romans 2:21).

And because they rejected the word of the Lord, there is no wisdom in them. They therefore boast in vain of their knowledge of the Law, since by their deeds they destroy its teaching.

### (Verses 10, 11)

“Therefore I will give their wives to foreigners [or: strangers], their fields to heirs, because from the least to the greatest all pursue greed; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit” [or: iniquity]. “And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people to their disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace.”

They have received the wages of their deeds: those who rejected the word of the Lord have themselves been rejected by him.

“I will hand over,” he says, “their wives and possessions to their enemies.” And lest my judgment be thought cruel, let the listener recognize the reasons: “From the least to the greatest, all pursue greed” (1 Timothy 6). For greed is the root of all evils.

From prophet to priest—those who ought to restrain others from sinning are themselves the first to submit to crimes—and all either practice iniquity by plundering what belongs to others, or at least practice deceit, so that there is no truth in their mouths.

After these things, like good physicians, they wished to heal the wounds of others with words, although they themselves were pierced by the wounds of every disgraceful act. We see this daily also among our own people, as the blessed Apostle Paul says: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Romans 2:21), and so forth.

When they see sinners and the rich, they wish to heal the brokenness of the daughter of God’s people—that is, of the Church—to the disgrace either of those who are deceived or of those who deceive others, so that they may say to people covered by every crime, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace and the war of sins threatens them.

### (Verse 12)

“They were put to shame because they committed abomination; indeed, they were not ashamed with shame, and they did not know how to blush.”

This should be read interrogatively in Greek (*erōtēmatikōs*), so that the meaning is: “Did they feel shame over their crimes and understand the abominations they had committed?” Certainly not; rather, they burst into such madness that they neither wished to correct their vices through shame nor confess their crimes in hope of pardon.

Therefore they will fall among those who are falling [or: rushing headlong]; at the time of their visitation they will fall, says the Lord.

These are the rewards of those who did not know how to feel shame: those whose dignity was higher than that of the people will be mixed with the people’s ruins. From the least to the greatest, all pursue greed; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. The time of visitation is the approaching captivity.

### (Verse 13)

“I will surely gather them,” says the Lord. “There are no grapes on the vines, and there are no figs on the fig tree; the leaf has fallen, and I have given them what has passed away.”

He explains more clearly what the time of visitation is, in which sinners will fall, saying: “I will surely gather them.” There is no doubt that this means in Jerusalem, so that they will be besieged for a long time and endure the evils of famine.

“When the seasons pass,” he says, “when autumn follows summer and the leaves of the trees fall in winter, you will see everything from afar but will obtain no food from it. There is no grape on your vines, since you will not take the fruit of the vines; and there are no figs on the fig tree for the besieged people, who see the fruit of their trees devoured by their enemies.”

[Note: All the old books read “to be plundered,” instead of “to be devoured.”]

“The leaves,” he says, “will fall after summer and autumn have passed. For I have given them things that they would see passing away, and they would lose the abundance of everything with greater pain because they were not permitted to touch it.”

(Verses 14–15.) Why are we sitting here? Gather together, and let us enter the fortified city (or: fortified cities), and let us be silent there (or: let us be cast there), because our Lord has made us be silent [Note: [Col. 0739D] In place of “has made us be silent,” there formerly stood “has cast us away,” according to the Greek ἀπέῤριψεν ἡμᾶς (“he has cast us away”). I think, indeed, that Jerome customarily included both interpretations; but since all the manuscripts now prefer the former, which comes from the Hebrew, it seemed better to restore it, and he also repeats it in the exposition that follows, while excluding the other, of which no mention is made. In Jerome’s own version, “God” is added: “because the Lord God has made us be silent.”] and has given us water of gall to drink. For we have sinned against the Lord; we hoped for peace, and there was no good; for a time of healing—and behold, terror.

The voice of the people responding, confessing their own faults, and mutually exhorting one another to enter the fortified cities (or: walled cities), or the single city, Jerusalem, is introduced; for the others had already been captured. “And let us be silent,” he says, “there, because our Lord has made us be silent.” For we have no confidence to implore him—or else, let us be cast there, or thrown there like dung. He himself gave us water of gall to drink, because we turned God, who is sweet, into bitterness. And the reason why we should drink such waters is evident: “For we have sinned against the Lord,” and we hoped for peace, although we had done no good work; and we thought that the time of healing had come, while everything was being filled with fear and terror. [Col. 0739C] The change of persons, especially in the Prophets, makes interpretation difficult; but if the persons are restored to their proper places, causes, and times, what seemed obscure will become clear.

(Verses 16.) From Dan the snorting of his horses is heard; at the sound of the neighing of his warriors (or: cavalry) the whole land is shaken. And they came and devoured (or: they will come and devour) the land and its fullness, the city and its inhabitants.

Therefore, as the Septuagint translated above, the people did not say, “Let us enter the fortified cities,” but “the fortified city,” so that Jerusalem might be signified. Accordingly, he now adds: “the city and its inhabitants.” The approach of Nebuchadnezzar with his army from Dan through Phoenicia is described; it is the place where the Jordan River rises. What the Septuagint presents as future, the Hebrew, in accordance with the truth of the event, records as already accomplished.

(Verses 17.) For behold, I shall send against you basilisks (or: most evil serpents, or, as the Septuagint translated, deadly serpents), for which there is no enchantment. And they shall bite you, says the Lord, incurably; you shall faint from the anguish of your heart. [Note: [Col. 0740D] See what we have noted concerning this reading in the annotations to Jerome’s version. Victor, to be sure, preferred “when they are failing,” with certain manuscripts.]

Who those are who come from Dan, whose snorting is heard, and who reduced the whole land [Col. 0740A] to desolation, the same prophetic speech demonstrates under another figure, calling them most evil or deadly serpents; and, as Aquila translated, “basilisks,” which are called in Hebrew SAPHPHONIM (). Why his second edition chose to say “watchers,” I do not understand, unless perhaps because of the similarity of the word. “For which,” he says, “there is no enchantment.” For those who have despised God’s commandments pour out prayers against the ancient serpent, the crooked serpent, in vain. Let us use this passage against those who, despising the sayings of the Savior, are handed over to hostile powers.

(Verses 18.) My pain is beyond pain; my heart within me mourns.

As we said above, the Septuagint joined these words to the preceding sentence, rendering them: [Col. 0740B] “And they shall bite you, says the Lord, incurably; you shall perish amid the anguish of your heart.” In the Hebrew, however, the word is not so much “pain,” which in Greek is called ὀδύνη, as μειδιάμα, which we may interpret as “the grimace of a mouth contracted by pain and bearing the appearance of laughter.” These words are to be read emphatically as spoken in the person of God, mourning the overthrow of Jerusalem and unable to endure her sufferings.

(Verses 19.) Behold, the voice of the cry of the daughter of my people from a distant land.

He describes the weeping and wailing of the city of Jerusalem when the enemies have entered it.

“Is the Lord not in Zion, or is her king not in her?” Or: “The Lord himself is king.” Or certainly, “Lord” refers to the Father and “king” to the Son, according to what is written under the name of Solomon: “O God, give your judgment to the king, and your righteousness to the king’s son” (Psalm 72:1).

But why should there be a voice of crying in Jerusalem, and why should the cry itself come from a distant land? The reason is clear: the Lord is not in her, and her king has departed from her.

“Why, then, did they provoke me to anger with their carved images and with foreign vanities?” “The Lord,” he says, “has departed from them, because they provoked me, who was their Lord and king, to anger by the worship of idols.”

(Verses 20.) The harvest has passed, the summer has ended, and we have not been saved.

Again the people speak, enclosed in Jerusalem by a prolonged siege, because the seasons have changed, the circle of the year has run its course, and all their hope has proved vain and passed away.

[Col. 0740D] (Verse 21.) Over the breaking of the daughter of my people I am broken and sorrowful; astonishment has seized me.

God answers that, in Jerusalem’s affliction, he himself appears afflicted, and, in human likeness, is crushed by astonishment.

(Verses 22.) Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why, then, has the wound of the daughter of my people not been bandaged?

Not only in the present passage but also in many other testimonies of Scripture, we find the balm of Gilead used to signify repentance and medicine. God now wonders why Jerusalem’s wounds have by no means been healed and why scars have not yet covered the skin, because there are no prophets or priests whose medicine ought to heal them.

(Chapter IX.—Verse 1.) Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, that I may weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people?

“If I should be wholly turned into weeping,” he says, “and there should be not drops of tears but an abundance like a river, nevertheless I could not sufficiently mourn the slain of the daughter of my people.” For the evils are so great that by their magnitude they surpass all the grief that could be felt for them. This may be understood both from the person of the Prophet and from that of the Lord. [Col. 0741B]

(Verses 2.) Who will give me a lodging for travelers in the wilderness (or: in a travelers’ lodging), that I may leave my people and depart from them?

The Septuagint: “Who will give me in the wilderness a final dwelling, that I may leave my people and depart from them?” “It is better,” he says, “to dwell in the remotest wilderness than to remain amid such great crimes of human beings.” Hence the Savior also said in the Gospel: “How long shall I endure you?” And elsewhere it is written: “At that time the one who understands (or: will understand) shall sit and be silent, because it is an evil time” (Lamentations 3; Micah 2).

(Verses 3.) For all are adulterers, an assembly of transgressors. They stretched out their tongue like a bow of falsehood, and not of truth. They have grown strong in the land, because they went out from evil to evil [Note: [Col. 0741] Formerly it read “they entered,” contrary to the manuscripts and the sacred text], and they did not know me, says the Lord.

Sinners pass from evil to evil when they exchange one idol for another and advance from sins to sins—or certainly when they pass from the evil of siege into captivity. Of the saints it is said: “They shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 84:7). But of sinners: “They went out from evil to evil.” And the cause of all their miseries is that they did not know the Lord; they are an assembly of transgressors, arming their tongue like a drawn bow for blasphemy. They have grown strong in the land, so that they deserve to hear: “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Genesis 3).

905 (Verses 4 and following.) Let each one guard himself from his neighbor, and let him not trust any of his brothers, because every brother will utterly supplant (or: supplants and proceeds), and every friend will proceed deceitfully; a man will mock his brother, and they will not speak the truth. For they have taught their tongue to speak falsehood (or: their tongue has learned to speak falsehood); they have labored to act wickedly (or: they have acted wickedly and have not ceased from turning back). Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit, in deceit (or: usury upon usury, and deceit upon deceit); they refused (or: were unwilling) to know me, says the Lord.

This passage is to be used in a time of persecution and distress, when faith is either rare or nonexistent; when one must trust neither brother nor neighbor, and a man’s enemies are his own household (Micah 7); when, according to the Gospel, “the father will hand over the son, and the son the father,” and “two will be divided against three, and three against two.” The statement that follows, “They have taught their tongue to speak falsehood,” or “their tongue has learned to speak falsehood” (Matthew 10), shows that the habit of lying is somehow turned into nature, and that they act deliberately in order to do what is wicked. The next statement, “Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit, in deceit,” is addressed specifically to the Prophet: he dwells in the midst of a lying people. Or, as the Septuagint translated it: “Usury upon usury, and deceit upon deceit”—that is, they daily increase their crimes and do not repent of what they formerly did, but heap new offenses upon the past. In doing these things, they act with every effort so that they may not know the Lord, who commanded that these things not be done. [Col. 0742B]

(Verses 7.) Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I shall smelt them (or: test them with fire) and examine them. For what else shall I do because of the daughter of my people (or: what shall I do because of the wickedness of the daughter of my people)?

Whenever we are subjected to distress, receive evils from God, and are tested by persecutions, whatever adulterated material there is in us is burned away by the heat of tribulations and miseries (or: is boiled away): “The silver of the Lord, tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified seven times” (Psalm 12:7).

(Verses 8–9.) Their tongue is a wounding arrow; it has spoken deceit. With his mouth he speaks peace with his friend, but secretly lays ambushes for him. Shall I not visit them for these things, says the Lord? Or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?

Every heretic who wounds the hearts of hearers and of those who do not know the written command, “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Proverbs 4:23), possesses a wounding arrow and speaks deceitfully. Although with his mouth he promises peace to his neighbor, he secretly lays ambushes.

906 In the verses that follow, where he says, “Shall I not visit them for these things, says the Lord? Or shall my soul not avenge itself on such a nation?” this Prophet frequently uses the expression, so that after enumerating each of their evil deeds he may add that he acts justly in doing what he does (or: that he will act justly).

(Verses 10.) Over the mountains I shall take up weeping (or: lamentation), and over the beautiful places (or: paths) of the wilderness, mourning, because they have been burned (or: have failed), since there is no man (or: human being) passing through; and they did not hear the voice of the possessor (or: substance). From the bird of the sky to the cattle they have migrated and departed.

When the Babylonian army arrives and lays everything waste, the desolation of the province is prophesied: there will be mourning on the mountains and weeping in the wilderness, or on the paths of the wilderness; everything will have failed and been burned, and there will be no one walking through the land, since all have been slaughtered and nothing remains that can breathe or live.

Hence, instead of “possessor,” the Septuagint translated “substance,” which in Hebrew is called MACNE (). Here “substance” does not mean οὐσία, that is, essence, but resources and riches. The statement that follows, “From the bird of the sky to the cattle they have departed and gone away,” shows what we have often said: that all things feel the anger of God, and not only the birds of the air but also the fish of the water fail.

According to the tropological interpretation, weeping is taken up over the mountains and lamentation over the beautiful places of the wilderness when the leaders of the Church sin [Note: [Col. 0743D] The words “and nothing of substance is found in it” are absent from two of our manuscripts], and no substance of God is found in her, nor is the voice of the Lord heard—the Lord who possesses the Church through holy and apostolic men. From the bird of the sky to the cattle, that is, from those able to ascend on high to the irrational and simplest people, they have departed from the assembly of God.

(Verses 11.) And I shall make Jerusalem into heaps of sand (or: into exile) and into a dwelling-place of dragons, and I shall make the cities of Judah a desolation, because there is no inhabitant.

When ecclesiastical men and all the teachers have failed, Jerusalem is given over to exile, or to heaps of sand, so that heretical speech may prevail in her; she becomes a dwelling-place of dragons, and her cities are reduced to solitude. There is no dwelling in her of the divine word, nor of the one who says: “I shall dwell and walk among them, and I shall be their God” (Leviticus 26:12).

(Verses 12 and following.) Who is the wise man who understands this, and to whom the word of the Lord’s mouth may come, so that he may declare it: Why has the land perished and been burned like a wilderness, because there is no one passing through it?

907 And the Lord said: Because they abandoned my law that I gave them, and they did not hear my voice, and they did not walk in it, but went after the perversity of their heart and after the Baals, which they learned from their fathers.

The Prophet asks whether he can find any wise man in Jerusalem, or any of those to whom the word of God may come, who could declare the Lord’s will and explain why Judea had been reduced to desolation, and why, after all had been killed, no one remained to pass through it.

He then introduces the Lord responding and explaining the causes: because they abandoned his Law, which he had given them; they did not hear his voice, nor did what had been commanded; instead, they went after the perversity of their heart. Therefore confession must be made not in our own will but in the Lord. “The heart is perverse in all things” (below, 17:9). And: “From our heart evil thoughts proceed” (Matthew 15:19).

“And after the Baals,” he says, “they went, which they learned from their fathers.” [Col. 0743D] Baal is the idol of the Sidonians, and is singular in number, whereas Baalim is plural. Therefore neither the error of parents nor of ancestors (or: evils) is to be followed, but the authority of the Scriptures and the command of God who teaches.

(Verses 15–16.) Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I shall feed this people with wormwood [Note: [Col. 0743D] Three manuscripts, as well as Jerome’s version as edited by Martianay, do not recognize the intervening word “them,” although it is present in the Hebrew], and I shall give them water of gall to drink, and I shall scatter them among nations that neither they nor their fathers knew; and I shall send the sword after them until they are consumed.

This may be prophesied of the near time, when they were captured by the Chaldeans, and specifically of the time when they were scattered among nations that neither they nor their fathers knew. Divided throughout the whole world, they were fed with wormwood, or with necessities and distresses. They received water of gall to drink, which either signifies the magnitude of their evils and the everlasting yoke of captivity, or else that, through ignorance of God’s law, they will receive Antichrist in place of Christ. The sword is sent after them so that they may be consumed even unto destruction. Or else it is the sword that divides them and does not allow them to consent to evil, so that they may perish in what they are evil.

(Verses 17–18.) Thus says the Lord of hosts: Consider (or: understand), and call for the mourning women [Col. 0744B] and let them come; and send for the wise women, and let them hasten (or: speak), let them hurry, and let them take up a lament over us (or: over you); and let our eyes (or: your eyes) pour forth tears, and let our eyelids (or: your eyelids) flow with water. For the voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion (or: in Zion).

Because of the future captivity and overthrow of Jerusalem, he commands that mourning women be called, who customarily, in mourning, provoke the people to tears with a plaintive voice and by striking their arms with their hands. This custom continues even to the present day in Judea, so that women, with their hair unbound and their breasts uncovered, stir everyone to weeping with a measured voice.

God—or the Prophet—joins himself to them in compassionate feeling, so that he says that he himself bears and experiences whatever the people endure. The statement that follows, “For the voice of lamentation has been heard from Zion,” immediately explains what that voice is.

(Verses 19.) How devastated we are, and utterly confounded! Because we have abandoned the land, because our tents have been cast down (or: we have cast down our tents).

This is the voice of those lamenting in Zion: “How devastated we are, and utterly confounded!” Immediately they answer themselves and explain the causes of their devastation, saying: “Because we have abandoned the land,” through our own fault and sin; “and our tents have been cast down,” tents that, like passing travelers, they once possessed. Let the crowds of those who once believed say this also during persecution, because they were devastated and confounded for this reason: they abandoned the land of the Lord and deserted their tents.

(Verses 20–21.) Therefore hear, women, the word of the Lord, and let your ear receive the word of his mouth; teach your daughters lamentation, and each one her neighbor mourning. For death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses, to destroy the children outside and the young men from the streets.

In the preceding chapter he had said: “Call the mourning women, and let them come; and send for the wise women, and let them hasten.” Now, as though speaking to women who are present, he condemns the priests, teachers, and all the men, so that, when those men cease teaching, the women may hear the word of the Lord, receive the words of his mouth, and teach their daughters and neighbors the causes of mourning and tears.

“For death has climbed through our windows; it has entered our houses.” Although this may be understood spiritually, in that death enters through all the senses for the destruction of the sinful soul, it may also be understood of the Babylonian assault: such is the strength and speed of their warfare that they do not wait for the doors to be opened, but climb through windows and over roofs in order to lay waste the houses of Jerusalem.

The children who are outside perish, those who go out from Jerusalem; and the young men, to whom John also writes, are those who do not enter by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life, but walk through the streets, of which it is written: “How broad and spacious is the way that leads to death!” (Matthew 7:13).

(Verses 22.) Speak these things, says the Lord, and the corpse of a man (or: the corpses of men) shall fall like dung upon the face of the land (or: field), and like hay behind the one who reaps, and there shall be no one to gather it.

The Hebrew word, written with three letters—DALETH, BETH, RES—for it has no vowels in the middle—may, according to context and the reader’s discretion, be read DABAR (), meaning “word”; DEBER, meaning “death”; or DABER, meaning “speak.” Hence the Septuagint and Theodotion joined it to the preceding chapter, saying: [Note: [Col. 0745D] The Cistercian manuscript together with the Vatican reads “that they might destroy”; in Rabanus, “to destroy.” We often pass over evident scribal errors in the manuscripts.] “They shall destroy the children outside and the young men from the streets by death.”

Aquila and Symmachus, however, translated λάλησον, that is, “speak,” so that God commands the Prophet to speak what follows: “Speak these things, says the Lord,” and the rest.

The sense is this: When death has climbed through our windows and entered the houses of Jerusalem, and the children and young men outside have perished in the streets, then their slaughter, or the corpses of the dead, will be like a dung heap upon the face of the earth and like stubble left behind the reapers and not gathered as useless. Through this he wishes to show that such a great slaughter will occur in Jerusalem and around the city that there will be no one to bury those who fall.

(Verses 23–24.) Thus says the Lord: Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches. But let the one who glories glory in this: to know (or: understand) and to recognize me, that I am the Lord who exercises mercy, judgment, and righteousness on the earth. For these things please me (or: because in these is my will), says the Lord.

All human pride is removed when their wisdom, strength, and wealth are regarded as nothing. This alone is the true boast: to know and understand that he is the Lord who exercises mercy, judgment, and righteousness upon the earth; that all things are governed by God’s providence and justice; and that what seems to us to have no reason is nevertheless full of justice and reason. [Col. 0745D]

For these alone please God, [Col. 0746A] and in these is his will. Where, then, are those who say that a human being can be governed by his own will [Note: [Col. 0746D] Three manuscripts and Rabanus read “can be governed by his own will” without the verb “to be able”], and that the power of free choice has been given in such a way that God’s mercy and justice are removed? Hence the Apostle, taking up this testimony, gives the example: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (2 Corinthians 10:17).

(Verses 25–26.) Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall visit everyone who has the foreskin circumcised: Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all those who shave their hair, dwelling in the wilderness, because all the nations have a foreskin. But the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.

Among many nations, especially those neighboring Judea and Palestine, peoples are circumcised even to the present day, particularly the Egyptians, Idumeans, Ammonites, and Moabites, as well as the whole region of the Saracens, which dwells in the wilderness, and concerning which it is said: “Upon all those who shave their hair, dwelling in the wilderness.”

Therefore Judah, who is mixed with the nations mentioned above, should not glory because he does not have a foreskin and has been circumcised according to the Law of God, since others also do these things who do not keep the commandments of the Law and do not know the God of Israel. Circumcision, which was given as a sign, is of no benefit unless the Lord’s commandments are fulfilled—just as hair, which signifies a nation, does not signify bodily strength or the power of warriors [Note: [Col. 0746D] Victor adds “strengthen” from the Brixian manuscripts. Similarly, shortly afterward, for “for the most part,” he more correctly reads “the greater part” from a single Medicean manuscript.]

The statement that follows, “All the nations have a foreskin; but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart,” has this meaning: Apart from the Egyptians, Idumeans, Ammonites, and Moabites, and the Ishmaelites dwelling in the wilderness, most of whom are circumcised, all other nations throughout the world are uncircumcised in the flesh; but the whole house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart, not in flesh. This uncircumcision leads to death. The former is of the flesh; the latter, of the spirit.

(Chapter X.—Verse 1.) Hear the word that the Lord has spoken concerning you, house of Israel. Thus says the Lord: Do not learn the ways of the nations, and do not fear the signs of heaven, which the nations fear, because the laws of the peoples are vain.

He speaks specifically against those who venerate celestial things and judge the human race to be governed by those things that have been appointed as signs of years, seasons, months, and days, and who believe that earthly affairs are regulated by the causes of heavenly things. 911 The statement, “The laws,” or “statutes,” of the peoples are vain (or: vain things), demonstrates that all human wisdom is futile and has no usefulness in itself.

(Verses 3–5.) For a tree is cut from the forest, the work of the hands of the craftsman with the axe. He adorns it with silver and gold; he fastens it with nails and hammers, so that it may not come apart (or: move). They are fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree, and they do not speak; they are carried when they are lifted up (or: they are carried about), because they cannot walk. Therefore do not fear them, because they can do neither evil nor good.

A description of the idols that the nations worship. “He cuts,” he says, “a tree from the forest.” The material of idols is therefore cheap and corruptible: “the work of the hands of a craftsman.” Since the craftsman is mortal, those things that he fashions are mortal as well. “He adorned it with silver and gold,” so that by the brightness of both materials he might deceive the simple. This error has passed even to us, so that we think religion consists in riches.

“He fastened it with nails and hammers, so that it might not come apart,” or “so that it might not move.” What power do idols have, since they cannot stand by themselves unless they are fastened with nails and hammers? Fashioned in the likeness of a palm tree, they possess the beauty of metals and are adorned by the art of painting; but they do not possess the usefulness by which they might provide any fruits to their craftsman.

And they do not speak, for they have nothing living within them. Concerning them it is written: “They have mouths, and they will not speak; they have ears, and they will not hear. They are carried when they are lifted up” (Psalm 115:5–6). The one who carries is stronger than what is carried; indeed, in the one there is sense, while in the other there is a figure without sense.

Therefore do not fear them, because they can do neither good nor evil. Many of the gentiles customarily worship demons so that they may not harm them, and entreat others to grant benefits. Hence also comes that Virgilian line (Aeneid 1):

“A black sheep for winter, a white one for favorable Zephyrs.”

Whatever we have said about idols can be referred to all doctrines that are contrary to the truth. They too make enormous promises and fashion from their own heart an image of vain worship. They boast of great things and, as though shining with golden senses and eloquence gleaming with the brilliance of silver, bind the minds of the unlearned in order to deceive the simple; they are exalted by their inventors, although they have no usefulness, and their worship belongs properly to the nations and to those who do not know God.

(Verses 6 and following.) There is none like you, O Lord; you are great, and great is your name in strength. Who will not fear you, O King of the nations? For yours is the glory among all the wise men of the nations, and in all their kingdoms there is none like you.

Likewise, the foolish and the wise will be proved; their doctrine of vanity is wood. Silver beaten (or: spread out) from Tarshish is brought, and gold from Ophaz, the work of a craftsman and the hands of a metalworker. Hyacinth and purple are their clothing; all these are the work of craftsmen (or: wise men). But the Lord [Col. 0747D] God is the true God, this God is living and the everlasting king (or: he himself is king). At his indignation the earth shall be shaken, and the nations shall not endure his threat.

These words are not found in the Septuagint, but have been added in most copies from Theodotion’s edition. Although they appear clear according to the literal sense, they have great difficulty according to the allegorical sense. For there is none like the true God among those gods fashioned by heretical art. All will fear him, because he is king of the nations. “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10), and from it we progress toward true love.

“Yours is the glory,” he says. In truth there is beauty; in falsehood, disgrace. Although heretics, according to the wisdom of the world—which will be destroyed—may seem wise in their own eyes, yet in all the kingdoms by which they tear the Church apart there is none like you, as the divine word says: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the intelligent” (1 Corinthians 1:19).

They are at once wise and foolish. Their doctrine, according to the quality of their intellect, is either cheap and comparable to wood, or like silver because of the beauty of their eloquence. It is brought from Tarshish. Tarshish is either a region of India, as Josephus says, or certainly the whole sea is called Tarshish, and it bears a likeness to the sky; yet it is wrapped up in an artifice of words, or spread out. [Col. 0748B] For if it wishes to deceive, it will not be able to do so.

And gold from Ophaz. Among the Hebrews gold is called by seven names, one of which is OPHAZ (), which we may call refined gold, so that it may shine on the surface of the idols, although within they are wood and cheap material. They are covered with hyacinth and purple so that, by their outward appearance, they may deceive the eyes, while promising themselves the color of heaven and heavenly kingdoms. Yet all these are the works of the wise, who are thought wise in the world; but before God they are fools.

But the Lord our God is the true God. Therefore all those things are lies. And he is the living God; therefore those things that are fashioned are dead. [Note: [Col. 0747D] The Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts read: “and God is king.”] And he is the everlasting king. The shadows of heretics prevail for a time but are corrupted over the course of time.

At his indignation the earth shall be shaken: those who have earthly works and fashion earthly images. And the nations shall not endure—not the people of the Lord, but the multitude of the nations, which cannot bear his threat.

(Verses 11.) Thus you shall say to them: The gods who did not make the heavens and the earth shall perish from the earth and from the things that are beneath the heavens.

These words are to be said to false gods, who have been artfully fashioned. For they made neither the heavens nor the earth. [Note: [Col. 0748D] The same manuscripts read: “Nor are they fellow workers with Christ, who are called gods,” and so forth.]

Those who are fellow workers with Christ are called gods; and, through ecclesiastical teaching, the Lord’s servants in large part build the house.

(Verses 12 ff.) He who makes—or, “who made”—the earth by his strength, prepares the world by his wisdom, and by his understanding stretches out the heavens. At his voice he gives the multitude of waters in the sky, and raises—or, “leads forth”—the clouds from the ends of the earth; he makes lightning for the rain, and brings forth the wind—or, “winds”—from his treasuries.

Every human being has become foolish through his knowledge; every craftsman is confounded by the graven image, because what he has cast is false, and there is no spirit in them. They are vanity, and a work worthy of ridicule. At the time of their visitation they will perish.

[Note: In two manuscripts: “works worthy of ridicule”; but Rabanus has rashly read, “worthy of the workmen who made them.”]

The portion of Jacob is not like these. For he who formed all things is himself, and Israel is the rod of his inheritance. The Lord of hosts is his name.

“He who makes the earth by his strength” is God the Father. Yet he makes it by his strength, the Lord Savior. For Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24). He himself is also the understanding by which he stretches out heaven. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created (Ps. 32:9), speaking to the Son: “Let us make man according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26).

“At his voice he gives the multitude of waters in the sky.” For all the Lord’s teaching flows down from heavenly things, as David says: “You will set apart a willing rain, O God, for your inheritance, and it was weakened, but you perfected it” (Ps. 67:10). “And he raises”—or, “leads forth”—“the clouds from the ends of the earth.” The clouds, or clouds of mist, concerning which God commanded that they should not rain upon Israel with rain (Isa. 5), are led forth from the extremities of the earth. One of these clouds was speaking: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last, appointed to death, because we have become a spectacle to this world, and to angels, and to men” (1 Cor. 4:9).

“He makes lightning for the rain.” For when the rain of teachings has come from heaven and has satisfied the parched hearts of human beings, then you will find flashes and bright lightnings of wisdom.

“And he brings forth the winds from his treasuries,” in which are “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden” (cf. Col. 2:3).

“Every human being has become foolish through knowledge.” Even if Paul, Peter, Moses, and Abraham are wise, in comparison with God all their wisdom will be reckoned as nothing. Hence, “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1:25).

“Every craftsman is confounded by the graven image,” whoever fashioned idols from his own heart; and what he cast is false. But if every human being is foolish through knowledge, then everything false and foolish that he has made is so as well (1 Cor. 1).

“And there is no spirit in them.” It should be noted that in this chapter also “wind” and “spirit” are called by one name among the Hebrews, RUA (רוח). He calls it the Spirit of sanctification, which cannot be found in the minds of heretics.

“They are vanity and a work worthy of ridicule.” For who would not laugh when he saw the idols of heretics? Either what is said is rustic and consists of wood; or it is composed in beautiful language, and silver is found beneath it; or else it is fabricated from their own imagination, and in vain they promise the likeness of gold.

“At the time of their visitation they will perish.” Heresy is effective for a time, so that the elect may be revealed and tested. But when God’s visitation has come and his eye has perceived the foolish things, everything falls silent (1 Cor. 11).

“The portion of Jacob is not like these”: the portion of those who supplanted the Jews and daily destroy heretics. But the portion of the saints is God, concerning whom the prophet says: “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72:26).

“He who formed all things is himself that portion”: he who made and fashioned all things, both in soul and in body.

“And Israel is the rod of his inheritance.” Everyone who is upright in God, or who sees God with understanding, is the scepter of his inheritance.

His name is “the Lord Almighty,” or “of hosts”—for this is what *Dominus exercituum* signifies—which is written in Hebrew as “the Lord Sabaoth.”

(Verses 17–18.) Gather from the earth your possessions—or, “your confusion”—you who dwell under siege; for thus says the Lord: “Behold, this time I will cast far away the inhabitants of the land, and I will trouble them so that they may be found.”

The Septuagint: “He gathered from outside his possessions, which dwells in the fortress. For thus says the Lord: ‘Behold, I will overthrow the inhabitants of this land, and I will trouble them so that they may be found.’”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript, together with most other manuscripts of the Hieronymian version, has “so that they may not be found,” repeating the negative particle also in the Septuagint translation. But the authority of the sacred text, as well as that of other manuscripts and Jerome’s following exposition—“I will confine them, so that all may be found in the city and unable to escape the evil”—stands against this reading.]

Jerusalem is commanded to gather into the most strongly fortified city whatever possessions it has outside, and to prepare provisions for a long siege. For he is no longer threatening them, as before, with something future and far off, but with a captivity that is already near and about to come. “Gather,” he says, “both from outside and from the land,” that is, from the fields, “your possessions,” or “your confusion.” For whatever you have is worthy of confusion. Although you prepare these things, understand what the Lord has said concerning them.

“Behold, this time”—at this moment—“I will cast far away,” or “hurl as with a sling,” the inhabitants of this land. For this the Septuagint translated, “I will overthrow and cause to fall.” For the Hebrew word [Note: In the manuscripts it is written in Greek letters, ΚΩΛΗ.] *COLEA* (כּוֹלֵעַ?), Aquila and Symmachus translated with σφενδονήσω, “I will hurl with a sling.”

The sense is: “Like a sling, with every force, I will cast them away, and in this way I will cause them to be besieged; and I will trouble and confine them, so that all may be found in the city and be unable to escape the evil.”

(Vers. 19.) Woe is me because of my crushing, my grievous wound.

The Septuagint: “Woe because of your crushing, your grievous wound.”

According to the Hebrew, Jerusalem herself is speaking, saying that she has been grievously afflicted and is suffering an incurable wound. According to the Septuagint, however, the prophet speaks to Jerusalem and laments her crushing and her wound.

“But I said: Surely this is my infirmity”—or, “my wound”—“and I will bear it”—or, “it has seized me.”

Jerusalem herself is speaking: “Whatever I suffer, I suffer through my own fault. I understand my wound that has seized me; or, I will endure the Lord’s anger, because I have sinned against him.”

(Vers. 20.) My tent has been devastated [Note: The Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts have “has been abandoned”]; all my cords have been broken—or, “all my skins have been torn”; my children have gone out from me—or, “my sheep”—and they are no more [another reading: “they do not remain.”] There is no one who will stretch out my tent any farther—or, “there is no longer room for my tent”—or who will raise up my skins.

Jerusalem laments the destruction of her city as though it were so easy that one might think not that her walls and defenses had been uprooted from their foundations, but that her tabernacle and tent had merely been removed.

“My tent,” she says—that is, “my dwelling”—“has suddenly been taken away. All my cords have been broken.” She preserves the metaphor of the tent; or, “all my skins have been torn.”

“My children have gone out from me,” or “my livestock,” which the Septuagint added, though it does not fit the historical account. During a long siege, how could sheep and livestock have been taken away from Jerusalem? Even if they had remained, famine had consumed them.

“And they are no more,” he says, or “they do not remain.” For they were not transferred to Chaldea; rather, a great part of them was killed and utterly destroyed.

“There is no one who will stretch out my tent any farther”: there is no one who will restore me and lay the foundations of my walls, which had been thrown down to the ground.

(Vers. 21.) For the shepherds acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord; therefore they did not understand, and their whole flock was scattered.

Through the metaphor of shepherds and sheep, the guilt of the rulers and the scattering of the people are described. Since the rulers acted foolishly and did not seek the Lord, whom they ought to have pursued with their whole heart, they consequently did not see—or did not understand—the evils that were coming upon them; and the whole multitude of Jerusalem was scattered here and there.

(Vers. 22.) A sound of report—behold, it comes!—and a great commotion from the land of the north, to make the cities of Judah a desolation and a dwelling-place of dragons—or, “a lair of ostriches.” As Symmachus translated it, “of sirens”; for the Hebrew has *THANNIM* (תַּנִּים).

The prophet’s words are: “Behold,” he says, “the sound and roar of the approaching Babylonian is heard, and a great commotion, or earthquake, from the land of the north, so that he may reduce all the cities of Judea to desolation after killing their inhabitants, and make dragons dwell there instead of human beings, together with every poisonous creature; or ostriches, which are likewise creatures familiar to the desert and are born and nourished in wastelands. Or certainly we may understand sirens, certain monsters and phantoms of demons.”

Let us refer all these things, which both the preceding and the present discourse have described, to the times of the Church’s persecution, when the Lord’s tents are overthrown and every dwelling-place of the Church is reduced to desolation. And the fault lies with the shepherds, who acted foolishly, did not seek him, and did not understand him; therefore the whole flock was scattered.

(Vers. 23.) I know, O Lord, that a person’s way is not his own; nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps.

Let the new preachers be ashamed, who say that each person is governed by his own free choice, when here too the prophet says: “A person’s way is not his own” (Ps. 36:23). And David sings in a lyric song: “The steps of a man will be directed by the Lord, and he will greatly desire his way.”

Or the sense is this: “What we suffer at the hands of the Babylonians is not due to their strength, but to our merit and to your indignation.”

(Verses 24–25.) Correct me, O Lord, but nevertheless with judgment, and not in your anger, lest you reduce me to nothing.

Pour out your indignation upon the nations that have not known you, and upon the provinces—or, “generations”—that have not called upon your name, because they have devoured Jacob, consumed his place, and laid waste his honor—or, “pasture”—or, “reduced it to desolation.”

[Note: More correctly, according to the Hebrew exemplar, Rabanus reads: “because they ate Jacob, devoured him, and consumed his place and his honor,” etc. We were permitted to restore from the manuscripts only *consumpserunt*, “they consumed,” in place of the former reading *contempserunt*, “they despised.”]

We read this passage also in the psalm: “O Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:1; 38:1).

The sense is: “We certainly deserve everything that we suffer, and deserve much more than we endure. Nevertheless, I ask this: correct me as a father, not as an adversary; amend me as a son, and do not punish me as an enemy” (Heb. 12). For you chastise every son whom you receive, and through every pain and scourging you correct Jerusalem.

But the enemies who have not known you, and the provinces or regions that have not called upon your name, ought not to experience your judgment, but your indignation (Ps. 87). You handed us over so that we might be corrected. They, however, made their yoke heavier: they did not spare the old and afflicted the young; they ate us and utterly devoured us; and they reduced Jerusalem to such desolation that they destroyed everything belonging both to public and private buildings and killed your people.

## Book Three

(Vers. 1–3.) The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Hear the words of this covenant—or, “testament”—and speak to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and say to them: Thus says the Lord God of Israel.

It is not stated in the title under what circumstances, or under which king, or in what year of his reign, this prophecy was made. But we understand either that it should be joined to the preceding prophecy and period, or certainly that, after some interval of time, this word of the Lord came to the prophet.

It should be noted that Aquila and Symmachus always translated the word *BERITH* (בְּרִית) as “covenant,” while the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as “testament.” Properly, the discourse is now addressed to Jerusalem and to the men of the tribe of Judah.

(Vers. 4.) Cursed is the man who does not hear the words of this covenant, which I commanded your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace, saying: Hear my voice and do everything that I command you, and you shall be my people, and I shall be your Lord [another reading: “God”].

It is not on account of privileges of ancestry, nor because of the injury—or, “offense”—of circumcision, nor because of the leisure of the Sabbath, but on account of obedience, that God becomes the God of the people of Israel and Israel becomes his people.

Here he speaks as to servants, so that they may please God. In the Gospel, however, the Lord says to the disciples: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you. I will no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15:14–15).

And when they have become his friends, they pass from friends into sons: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). Hence he commands friends and sons: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48), commanding likeness, not equality. In the former passage there is obedience to commandments; here there is likeness to God.

When he says, “On the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, from the iron furnace,” he gives us to understand that the furnace and the iron furnace, heated by fire, signify the greatness of tribulation and punishment, not a particular place of punishment prepared from iron.

(Vers. 5.) So that I may establish the oath that I swore to your fathers, that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is today.

The fathers appear to receive the promise when their children receive it, and the promise made to Abraham is fulfilled in his descendants.

We should understand the land flowing with milk and honey hyperbolically as signifying an abundance of all things, as in Virgil (*Eclogue* 3):

> May honey flow for them, and may the rough bramble bear amomum.

And again:

> And everywhere he held back wines running through the streams.

Or, certainly, tropologically, let us understand the land flowing with milk and honey as the Church of Christ, in which infants and sucklings are raised through faith, so that we may be able to receive solid food.

And I answered and said: Amen, Lord.

For this the Septuagint translated, “May it be, Lord”—for this is what *amen* signifies. The Lord had said: “I swore to your fathers that I would give them a land flowing with milk and honey, as is confirmed today by the events themselves” (Exod. 3).

The prophet, who loves his people, anticipates the Lord’s words and desires what has been given to be true and to remain forever. Hence he says: “Truly, Lord, you have fulfilled what you promised”; or, “May it be, Lord”—that is, “May what you have given always remain.”

[Note: Two manuscripts have “what has been said.”]

(Vers. 6.) And the Lord said to me: Proclaim—or, “read”—all these words in the cities of Judah and outside Jerusalem, saying: Hear the words of this covenant and do them.

The most merciful God frequently foretells the future, so that at last a mind slow to believe may be softened. He foretells it both in the city of Jerusalem and outside it in the countryside, so that those whose danger is shared may also share the same repentance.

(Verses 7–8.) For I earnestly warned your fathers on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt, even to this day. Rising early, I warned them and said: Hear my voice. But they did not hear and did not incline their ear; instead, each went after the stubbornness of his evil heart. And I brought upon them all the words of this covenant, which I commanded them to do.
