[Note: On the authority of three manuscripts and Rabanus, we have removed from this point the words “and they did not do,” which in earlier editions were added in continuous sequence, contrary to the intention of the holy Doctor. He recites them shortly afterward in their proper place, so that it may be immediately clear which words were omitted by the Septuagint interpreters.]

Up to this point the Septuagint does not contain the following words. They placed “and they did not do” after this passage and joined it to the end of the preceding chapter, where it is written: “Hear the words of this covenant and do them; and they did not do them.”

We have already explained what it means that God rises early, repeatedly presses his words upon them through the prophets, brings them out of Egypt, and repeatedly admonishes them, saying, “Hear my voice”; and that they went after the stubbornness of their heart, after which he gives them what they deserve—

[Note: Victor says that it should be read, “what they deserve to receive,” without the conjunction *et*, “and.”]

—and what they deserve to receive.

(Verses 9–10.) And the Lord said to me: A conspiracy has been found among the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They have returned to the iniquities of their former fathers, who refused to hear my words. They too have gone after foreign gods, to serve them. The house of Israel and the house of Judah have made my covenant void, which I made with their fathers.

For “conspiracy,” which we have translated according to Symmachus, Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated σύνδεσμον, which we may call “a binding together.” Hence Athaliah, when she discovered that an ambush was being prepared for her in the Temple, used the same word: “Conspiracy, conspiracy!” (2 Kings 11:14).

Properly, Scripture uses this word when the offense is not pursued through a sudden and accidental sin, but through prepared ambushes and conspiracy, and when they act with one mind and one purpose to despise God’s commandments.

It says that fathers and sons, with one mind and in agreement, neglected God and worshiped idols—both Israel, namely the ten tribes, and the house of Judah, namely the two tribes whose rule was in Jerusalem—so that, since they shared one purpose in despising God, their punishment in enduring captivity might also be the same.

(Verses 11–12.) Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I am bringing evils upon them from which they will not be able to escape, and they will cry out to me, and I will not hear them.

And the cities of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem will go and cry out to the gods to whom they burn offerings, but they will not save them in the time of their affliction.

God does not hear in a time of need and distress, because they themselves refused to hear the voice of the Lord. Saul also experienced this. When he feared the armies of the Philistines and had not deserved to receive the word of the Lord, he turned to the witch, so that he might learn from idols what he ought to have obtained from the Lord through persistent prayer and tears (1 Sam. 21).

[Note: In several manuscripts, mostly: “we learn.”]

From this we learn that even if the Lord does not hear, we must by no means cease praying, nor flee to demons, who cannot help their worshipers, but rather to the Lord’s aid. He is quickly moved when angry and changes his decision if those with whom he is angry also change.

Everything now being said concerns the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, for whom captivity is imminent.

(Vers. 13.) For according to the number of your cities were your gods, O Judah; and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem you set up altars of shame—or, “again, altars”—to burn offerings to the Baals.

Let us read the books of Kings and Chronicles (2 Kings 21; 2 Chron. 33), and we shall find that Judah and Jerusalem did far worse things than Israel, so that as many cities as they had, they had just as many kinds of idols; and as many streets and street-corners as there were in Jerusalem, so many altars they had for their own disgrace, on which they sacrificed victims to the idols of the Baals.

(Vers. 14.) Therefore do not pray for this people, and do not take up praise and prayer on their behalf, because I will not hear them when they cry to me in the time of their distress.

Jeremiah is commanded not to wish to entreat the Lord on behalf of those against whom the sentence has already been completed, lest his prayer appear ineffective and go unheard because of their own crimes.

“Do not pray for them,” he says, “nor take up praise,” so that by recalling the mercy of the former history, through which I always pitied them, and by praising me, you may strive to change my decision.

Even if you do this, I will not hear those who are compelled to entreat me in the time of their need. From this we learn that it is useless for someone to pray on behalf of another when the person for whom God is asked to intervene does not deserve to receive what is requested.

(Verses 15–16.) What has my beloved done in my house, that she has committed so many crimes? Can sacred flesh take away your wickedness, in which you have gloried?

The Lord called your name “a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful, splendid olive tree.” At the sound of great speech, fire blazed against it, and its thickets were burned.

He calls the people of Judah beloved and dearly loved because they placed themselves in his Temple and worshiped idols there, thinking that they could appease God’s anger by offering many victims and boasting in the multitude of their sacrifices, which cannot remove the wickedness of sins.

He compares Jerusalem, or the entire Jewish people, to a beautiful and fruitful olive tree. Raised up through pride, it did not act humbly and did not understand its Creator and Lord. But lifted up through pride and speaking arrogantly, it was set ablaze by the Lord’s fire, so that its branches—or thickets—were burned and reduced to nothing, that is, the whole people was destroyed by the sword of its enemies.

The same sense appears elsewhere (chap. 2), where it is said to Jerusalem: “I planted you as a fruitful vine, wholly true. How have you been changed into the bitterness of a foreign vine?”

When its walls are destroyed, and the boar from the forest lays it waste, and all the beasts devour its fruit (Ps. 78), let us say this chapter to the leaders of the Churches: “What has my beloved done in my house, that she has committed so many crimes?”

Or certainly let us say it to the rich, who, while they seize what belongs to others and do not remove the wickedness from their own hearts, think that they deserve God’s mercy: “Can sacred flesh take away your wickedness, in which you have gloried?”

But now the names of those who make offerings are publicly recited, and the redemption of sins is changed into praise. Nor do they remember that widow in the Gospel who, by putting two small coins into the treasury, surpassed the gifts of all the rich (Mark 12).

(Vers. 17.) And the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has spoken evil against you, because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah committed against themselves by offering sacrifices to the Baals in order to provoke me.

“The Lord your God,” he says, “called you a luxuriant, beautiful, fruitful olive tree, and planted you. But because at the sound of great speech the flame of God descended upon you and consumed all your branches, therefore he who had planted you has now spoken evil against you—not through an unjust sentence or sudden perversity of speech, but because of the evil that the house of Israel and the house of Judah committed against themselves, deliberately offering sacrifices to the Baals in order to provoke me to anger.”

Although God can do whatever he wishes, he gives reasons so that he may not appear to act unjustly, according to what is written: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. 50:6).

(Verses 18 ff.) But you, O Lord, made it known to me, and I understood; you showed me their designs. And I was like a gentle lamb being led to the slaughter, and I did not know that they had devised plots against me.

“Let us put wood into his bread, and let us cut him off”—the Vulgate: “erase him”—“from the land of the living, so that his name may no longer be remembered.”

But you, Lord Sabaoth, who judge justly and test the kidneys and the heart, let me see your vengeance upon them, for to you I have revealed my cause.

There is agreement among all the Churches that these words are understood to be spoken by Christ under the person of Jeremiah: the Father showed him how he ought to speak, showed him the designs of the Jews, and he himself, like a lamb led to the slaughter, did not open his mouth and did not know—understand “sin”—according to what the apostle says: “He who knew no sin was made sin for us.”

And they said: “Let us put wood into his bread,” namely, the cross into the body of the Savior. For he is the one who says: “I am the bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). And, “Let us erase,” or “crush,” “him from the land of the living.” For they devised this crime in their minds, so that they might destroy his name forever.

But, conversely, according to the mystery of the assumed body, the Son speaks to the Father and invokes his judgment while praising his justice. He calls upon God as the examiner of the kidneys and the heart, so that he himself may repay the people what they deserve. He says: “Let me see your vengeance upon them,” namely upon those who persist in their crime, not upon those who turn—or, “are converted”—to repentance.

Concerning the latter he said on the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

And he reveals and opens his cause to the Father, because he was crucified not for any merit of his own but through the crime of the people, saying: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he has found nothing in me” (John 14:30).

The Jews and our Judaizing opponents understand these words as spoken under the person of Jeremiah. They maintain that, because of the prophecy of future events and the evils of the approaching captivity, Jeremiah endured these things from the people. But I do not know how they can prove that Jeremiah was crucified, since Scripture does not mention it—unless perhaps they think that the Jews devised it but did not carry it out.

(Verses 21 ff.) Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the men of Anathoth who seek your life and say: “You shall not prophesy in the name of the Lord, and you shall not die by our hands.”

Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will visit punishment upon them. Their young men will die by the sword; their sons and daughters [Note: Victor here too, following the Vulgate, writes “their sons.” The difference is not clear from the Hebrew or Greek text.] will die of famine, and no remnant will remain of them. For I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth, the year of their visitation.

This appears to contradict the preceding interpretation, in which we wished—or, “wish”—to establish that the words were spoken under the person of Christ and not of Jeremiah, who actually lived in the village of Anathoth, three miles from Jerusalem.

But if we understand the etymology of the town *ANATHOTH* (ענתות), which is interpreted as “obedience,” it will clearly be shown that “the men of Anathoth” refers to all the Jews who once obeyed the Lord’s commands, and especially to the inhabitants of the city of Jerusalem, upon whom the final sentence has come: they were to perish through the evils of siege, sword, famine, and plague.

To free ourselves from all the difficulty of interpretation, let us follow this rule: all the prophets enacted many things as types of the Lord Savior, and whatever was fulfilled in Jeremiah in relation to the present time was prophesied concerning the Lord in the future.

## Book Three

[Col. 0757]

[Col. 0757B] 923–924

[Note: The Lernaean serpent. Lake Lerna is in the Argive territory and is especially famous for the labor of Hercules; for he is said to have killed there the Lernaean Hydra, which so afflicted the neighboring region that it gave rise to the proverb, “Lerna of evils.” Jerome indicates the Lernaean serpent in these words. —MARTIAN.]

The myths relate that the Lernaean serpent produced many snakes from the middle of its head, and that Scylla, the monster of the Sicilian strait, had a maiden’s face but was girded with dogs and tore apart the shipwrecks of wretched people. On the same shore was joined the deadly song of the Sirens; to avoid it, the Homeric Ulysses is said to have stopped his ears and, by prudent counsel, escaped an evil that could not otherwise be overcome.

When I wanted to do this—to avoid the madness of heretics—and, following Ismenias, to sing “for me and mine,” while turning over that prophetic passage, “When the sinner stood against me, I was silent and humbled myself, and kept silent concerning good things” (Ps. 38:2–3), the devil did not allow me to remain content with the rest I desired, devote myself to the explanation of the holy Scriptures, and transmit to people of my language the learning of the Hebrews and Greeks.

[Note: Two manuscripts have “following the poet Maenius.” The famous saying of the flute-player Antigenides to his pupil Ismenias is: “Play for me and for the Muses,” which Jerome elsewhere repeatedly adapts for himself. See Cicero, *Brutus*; Plutarch, *Pericles*; Valerius Maximus, book 3, chapter 7, and others. Victor here reads “and for the Muses” instead of “for mine,” as the saying was addressed to Ismenias, but the manuscripts do not support this.]

Rather, the devil works day and night, openly and by ambushes, mixing falsehoods with truths—indeed, coating every lie with deceptive honey—so that the one who hears the sweetness of the words may not fear the poison in his breast. He promises peace in order to wage heavier wars; he laughs in order to bite; he offers his hand in order suddenly to kill the innocent Abner (2 Sam. 3).

Surely this is what the apostle also said: “For we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Cor. 2:11).

[Note: The manuscripts praised above have “you are ignorant.” In these words, I believe Rufinus is chiefly being indicated, since he had already died. The lower context of the discourse can also suitably be understood as referring to Rufinus’s death.]

He is silent here and accuses elsewhere. He sends letters about the Scriptures throughout the world, formerly golden and now slanderous, and interprets our patience, which comes from the humility of Christ, as a sign of a bad conscience.

And while silent, he barks through an Alban dog—

[Note: We have restored “Albinum,” where the Vulgate editions had hitherto read “Alpinum.” The reading is preferred by the Corbie manuscript, which the Benedictine editors of Augustine cite in the second appendix to volume 10; Garnerius had earlier conjectured that it should be restored in this way, with considerable learning. He is taunting Pelagius by this name, for Pelagius was of Scottish birth, from the vicinity of Britain. The ancient Scots called their homeland Albion or Albin, as can be found in the author of the book *On the World*, attributed to Aristotle. The words that follow, “large, stout,” etc., fit Pelagius very well; Paul Orosius calls him a man with broad shoulders, a thick neck, and a very large face, while Jerome in the first *Dialogue against the Pelagians* turns his shoulders into a jest resembling Milo’s.]

—a large and corpulent dog, one better able to rage with his heels than with his teeth.

For he has the offspring of the Scottish race, from the vicinity of the Britons. According to the myths of the poets, he must be struck down like Cerberus with a spiritual club, so that he may fall silent forever with his master Pluto.

[Note: Two manuscripts, and the Cistercian manuscript in a later hand, prefer “Plato” to “Pluto.”]

But that belongs elsewhere. Now I shall undertake the third book on Jeremiah, in which I shall attempt, brother Eusebius, to compress the broad fields of explanation into the narrow path of commentaries.

(Chapter 12, verses 1 ff.) You are just, O Lord, if I dispute with you—or, “if I make answer to you”—yet I shall speak judgments to you. Why does the way of the impious prosper? Why is it well with all who transgress and act unjustly? You planted them, and they took root; they advance—or, “they have begotten sons and produce fruit.” You are near their mouth, but far from their kidneys.

This disputation is directed against all who act unjustly, and the thought of the seventy-second psalm is briefly contained in it, where the prophet says: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But my feet were almost moved; my steps almost slipped, because I was jealous of sinners when I saw the peace of sinners,” and so forth (Ps. 72:1–2).

But it is said specifically against heretics, whose way prospers although they are impious. They beget sons whom they have deceived into heresy; they transgress and act unjustly, so that they strip the Church. While they persist in the perversity of their doctrine, they boast that they have been planted by God, have taken root, have begotten sons, and have produced fruit.

Although they frequently repeat the name of Christ, they do not have God as their inhabitant, according to Isaiah: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart”—or, “their hearts”—“is far from me” (Isa. 29:13).

### (Verse 3)

And you, Lord, know me; you have seen me and tested my heart with yourself. [Note: Thus in the manuscripts and in Rabanus; it is also the reading of Jerome’s version. Previously it read “I shall gather”; the Hebrew likewise has [a corresponding form].] Gather them like a flock for sacrifice, and sanctify them for the day of slaughter.

“There is no scandal,” he says, “in the fact that the wicked—or all heretics—flourish for a time. For you, Lord, know me; you have seen me and tested my heart with yourself.” How does God the Father know him in this way? “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matthew 11:17). “Even if,” he says, “the heretics prosper, even if they produce children and bear fruit, and even though you are near their mouth but far from their kidneys—that is, from their conscience—there is nevertheless no small consolation in the fact that they are being fattened like sheep for sacrifice. Gather them into the city of Jerusalem, or into their own assemblies, so that, like sacrificial victims, they may be slaughtered for death; and then let them be sanctified when they have been cut down by an ecclesiastical sword. For the killing of heretics is the salvation of those who had been deceived.”

### (Verse 4)

How long will the land mourn, and every plant of the countryside wither because of the wickedness of those who dwell in it? The animals and the birds have perished, because they said, “He will not see our end” (or, “God will not see our ways”).

Whatever good or evil happens in the world does not happen without providence or by chance, but by God’s judgment. The land is now barren; the vegetation withers. Do you wish to know the reason? The wickedness of its inhabitants causes this, so that the animals on the earth and the birds of the sky perish, because all these things were created for human use. Yet they have risen to such blasphemy that they say God is ignorant of their ways and does not know what each person will suffer.

The expression “How long?” signifies that God’s anger continues, because the mind of sinners has not been moved toward repentance. [Note: Previously the reading was “which”; in other books it is changed. [The phrase] “was bent” occurs in place of “was turned.”]

### (Verse 5)

If, running with foot soldiers, you have grown weary, how will you compete with horses? If you have trusted in the land of peace, what will you do in the pride (or, tumult) of the Jordan?

“If,” he says, “the frequent captivity imposed by neighboring nations has wearied you—the Moabites and Ammonites, the Philistines and Edomites—what will you do in the face of a long captivity that will carry you as far as Chaldea?” [Note: The Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts read: “by which you are to be led as far as Chaldea.”] He compares foot soldiers with horsemen, because in fact, both according to history and according to the character of those regions, all Persia, all Chaldea, and the armies of those lands rejoice in cavalry. The nations I mentioned above, because of the difficulty of their terrain, are suited less to battle than to banditry.

He preserves the metaphor and says: “If, running with foot soldiers, you have failed through weariness, what will you do if you wish to match your course with horses? And if you had some confidence in your own land, what will you do when you have crossed the Jordan and endured its torrents?”

### (Verse 6)

For even your brothers and your father’s household themselves have fought against you, and they have cried out after you with a full voice: Do not believe them when they speak good things to you.

“To such an extent,” he says, “will you be covered by the most grievous floods of the Jordan, and the multitude of horsemen coming from far away will devastate you, that even your brothers, the Edomites, and your father’s household—those born from Lot’s stock, Moab and Ammon—will themselves, in the time of necessity and distress, fight against you and insult you” (Genesis 19). Therefore beware of wishing to believe them or to place hope in kinship, by which they rage against you with greater hatred than your enemies.

This may also be understood of the Savior: that his brothers and his father’s household fought against him and cried out with a full voice, saying, “Crucify him, crucify him! We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15).

### (Verses 7–8)

I have abandoned my house; I have left my inheritance. I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies. My inheritance has become for me like a lion in the forest; it has raised its voice against me; therefore I hated it.

He who spoke in the Gospel, “Rise, let us go from here” (John 14:31), and again, “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35), here threatens the same thing through the Prophet and says that he has already done what he is going to do. For the Lord’s inheritance is Israel, and it is the cord of his inheritance.

When he says, “I have given my beloved soul into the hand of its enemies,” this means: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18). The people of the Jews, once the Lord’s inheritance, became against him like a lion in the forest when, in his passion, it cried out against him with a united voice. And because it raised its voice against him, he therefore hated and rejected it; what was once beloved and most dear is now called hateful.

### (Verse 9)

Is my inheritance for me a many-colored bird? Is it a bird dyed all over? [Note: Victorius, from the Hebrew and the Vulgate edition, supplies “come against it.”] Come, gather yourselves, all the beasts of the earth; hasten to devour.

The Septuagint has: “Is my inheritance for me a hyena’s den, or a den surrounded by her? Go, gather all the beasts of the field, and let them come and eat it.”

[Note: The previous reading was *tectamque*, which the manuscripts correct.] According to the literal sense, he calls it a many-colored and wholly dyed bird—namely, a peacock. “Israel,” he says, “possessed such beauty, and Jerusalem was adorned with such virtues, that no good thing could be seen which was not present in it. Since, therefore, my former inheritance—that is, the people of Israel—has become like a lion in the forest, raised its voice against me, and incurred my utter hatred, come, therefore, and gather yourselves against it, all the beasts of the earth: the multitude of various nations. Devour the one that did not know its Lord.”

But if, as the Septuagint and other translators rendered it, we read, “Is my inheritance for me a hyena’s den?” we should refer it to the uncleanness of the nocturnal beast that lives on corpses, commonly digs bodies out of graves, and eats every kind of filth. Such is Israel, offending its Lord and delivered over to the bites of all the beasts.

### (Verse 10)

Many shepherds have destroyed (or, broken up; others: corrupted) my vineyard; they have trampled (or, polluted) my portion. They have made my desirable portion into a desert of desolation (or, an impassable place). They have set it (or, it has been set) as a devastation. [Note: Two manuscripts, the Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts, add the opening of the following verse: “And it mourned over me,” or “it perished.” The words that follow in the earlier exposition also seem to refer to this.]

Let those who wish to be rulers of peoples hear this: they will render an account on the day of judgment not only for themselves but also for the flocks entrusted to them. Because of them, the Lord’s portion is trampled and polluted, so that where there was once a lodging place, there is now a dwelling place of beasts.

Others understand by the shepherds not the leaders of the people and the priests, but the leaders of the enemies who devastated Jerusalem, that is, the Lord’s vineyard.

### (Verses 11–12)

It mourned over me; the whole land was utterly desolated, because there is no one who considers in his heart. Destroyers have come over all the paths of the wilderness, because the sword of the Lord has devoured from one end of the land to the other; there is no peace for any living creature.

The Septuagint has: “Therefore the land was utterly devastated,” and so forth.

The words “and it mourned over me,” which we have placed here, are joined to the preceding verse according to the Hebrew, so that the sense is: “They set it as a devastation”—that is, my inheritance—“and it mourned over me,” deprived of my help.

According to the Septuagint, however, God says that the land was devastated and reduced to a wilderness because of him, because there is no one who considers in his heart, and there is no peace for any living creature.

[Note: The entire passage that follows, almost twelve verses to the end of this section, was missing from the books previously published. This is the customary error of copyists when the same words occur twice: the eye is deceived, and the intervening material is omitted. The same thing happened here, since the passage begins immediately after the words with which the preceding section ends, “there is no peace for any living creature.” The lacuna is supplied by the most ancient books, except the Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts, which we are using continuously; also by two other Vatican manuscripts, numbered 323 and 324, and by several others in different libraries of Italy, which we consulted for this passage. Rabanus also read precisely the same words in his copy, and the sequence and structure of the wording clearly show that it proceeds from Jerome’s pen. In addition to the fairly long passage that we have restored, Victorius appended the following words in continuous sequence: “For the flesh cannot receive the peace of God. For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.” We found these words in none of our manuscripts.]

For the flesh cannot receive the peace of God. For the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, and those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

According to the Hebrew, all Judea is desolate for this reason: there is no one who considers God in his heart, nor anyone remaining who can escape. For destroyers have come along every wilderness path—that is, the hostile army—and the sword of the Lord has devoured from boundary to boundary. There was no respite for those fleeing from the city. Hence it is said: “There is no peace for any living creature.”

### (Verse 13)

They sowed wheat and reaped thorns; they received an inheritance, and it will not benefit them.

The Septuagint has: “You sowed wheat and reaped thorns; their allotments will not benefit them.”

“They expected better things,” he says, “and the worst came upon them. They hoped for prosperity and suffered adversity. They received from the Lord an abundance of all things, which will not benefit them.”

According to the Septuagint, however, all heretics sow as though they were sowing wheat, but reap thorns. The Lord expected them to produce fruit, but they produced no judgment, only a cry.

This is also said of ecclesiastics who dissipate the Lord’s words and teaching through bad conduct. Of them it is added: “Their allotments will not benefit them.” For what can the title of bishop or presbyter, or the remaining ecclesiastical order, profit them, when they are weighed down all the more by their dignities, and the powerful suffer powerful torments? The more has been entrusted to them, the more will be required of them (Wisdom 6).

### (Verses 14–15)

Be ashamed because of your fruits (or, because of your boasting), because of the anger of the Lord’s fury (or, because of reproach before the Lord).

Thus says the Lord against all my evil neighbors who touch the inheritance that I distributed to my people Israel: Behold, I will tear them away from their land, and I will tear the house of Judah from their midst (or, cast it out).

And when I have torn them away, I will turn back (or, return) and have mercy on them, and I will bring each man back to his inheritance, and each man to his land (or, make each man dwell there).

This is said to those for whom their own allotments and ecclesiastical order will be of no benefit, so that they may be ashamed of their boasting and of their reproach before the Lord.

When it adds, “against all my evil neighbors,” the literal sense refers to the neighbors of the Holy Land: Edom, the Philistines, Moab, and Ammon. In the tropological sense, however, it refers to all heretics who are reckoned under the name of Christ. They are neighbors rather than inhabitants of the Holy Land; they touch God’s inheritance and devastate it. It is said of them that they will be removed from the midst of the land, and that the house of Judah will be taken away from their midst.

When they have been torn away and liberated from the jaws of heretics, they will obtain God’s mercy and will be brought back into their inheritance and their land.

### (Verses 16–17)

And if, having been instructed, they learn the ways of my people, so that they swear by my name, “As the Lord lives,” just as they taught my people to swear by Baal, they will be built up in the midst of my people. But if they do not listen, I will tear that nation away with tearing away and destruction, says the Lord.

If, having been transferred from heresy into the Church, they learn the ways of God’s people and swear by the Lord’s name, and not by the names of idols that they fashioned from their own hearts, they will be built up by the Lord and will be part of his people.

But if, having been transferred into the Church, they retain the remnants of perverse doctrines and do not listen to the Lord’s words, that nation will be torn from the midst of God’s people with an everlasting tearing away and destruction, so that no place for repentance will be left to them.

We see this daily and prove it by events: heretics pretend to possess the truth of the faith in order to deceive the simple. They do not themselves convert to the faith; rather, they draw the faithful into unbelief.

## Chapter XIII

### (Verses 1 and following)

Thus says the Lord to me: Go and acquire for yourself a linen loincloth (or, girdle), and put it around your loins; you shall not put it in water (or, it shall not pass through water).

And I acquired the loincloth according to the word of the Lord and put it around my loins.

Then the word of the Lord came to me a second time, saying: Take the loincloth (or, girdle) that you acquired, which is around your loins, and arise, go to the Euphrates, and hide it for yourself in a hole in the rock.

And I went and hid it in the Euphrates, as the Lord had commanded me.

And it happened after many days that the Lord said to me: Arise and go to the Euphrates, and take from there the loincloth (or, girdle) that I commanded you to hide there.

And I went to the Euphrates, dug, and took the loincloth from the place where I had hidden it. And behold, the loincloth (or, girdle) had rotted, so that it was fit for no use.

And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Thus says the Lord: So will I make the pride (or, injury) of Judah rot, and the great pride of Jerusalem, and this most evil people, who do not wish to hear my words and walk in the perversity (or, according to the direction) of their heart. They have gone after foreign gods in order to serve them and worship them; and they will be like this loincloth, which is fit for no use. [Note: The added word “most evil” is found neither in the Hebrew nor in Jerome’s version.]

For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me, says the Lord, so that they might be my people, my name, my praise, and my glory; but they did not listen.

The girdle, or loincloth, that is joined to God’s loins is the people of Israel. Like linen taken from the earth, unwashed, it possessed neither softness nor whiteness; yet, through his mercy, it clung to God.

When it sinned—for such linen and such a loincloth possess reason—it was led across the Euphrates, that is, among the Assyrians, and was hidden there: in other words, it was in some manner swallowed up and rendered worthless by the multitude [variant: magnitude] of great and innumerable nations.

After a long time, the same Prophet, in the figure of God, liberated the people from captivity. Yet after their return they still did not carry out God’s commands. Instead, they followed foreign gods, and in the end even laid hands on the Son of God; thus they wasted away in eternal destruction.

Every holy man, too, is God’s loincloth. Taken from the earth and from the earth’s [Note: Victorius suspects that “linen” should be read, since the discussion concerns a linen loincloth.] clay, he is joined to fellowship with God. In a certain sense he covers and surrounds with greater care those things that appear shameful in God’s Church, so that they may not be exposed to the bites of pagans and heretics.

If this loincloth touches water and crosses the currents of the Euphrates, becoming soaked with the moisture of the Assyrian region, it loses its former strength, rots, and falls apart. Although it returns to God’s service, it cannot possess its former beauty—not because of any harshness on God’s part, but through its own fault, because it does not wish to hear his words and walks in the perversity of its heart, or does whatever seems right to itself.

The divine word itself explains why it used this comparison, saying: “For just as a loincloth clings to a man’s loins, so I made the whole house of Israel and the whole house of Judah cling to me and remain attached to me”—namely, the ten and the two tribes—“so that they might be my named people, my praise, and my glory.” Yet for all this they did not listen to me; they followed their own vices.

Therefore let anyone beware who can say, “But for me it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28), lest through negligence he be separated from God’s loins, cross the Euphrates, be handed over to the power of the king of Assyria, and be occupied not in the most solid rock but in a hole of a corrupted and damaged rock—that is, in the filth and vices of heretics—and come into such great rottenness that he can no longer return to the Lord’s service or be his girdle.

### (Verses 12 and following)

Therefore you shall speak this word to them (or, to the people). Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Every flask (or, wineskin) will be filled with wine.

And they will say to you: “Do we not know that every flask (or, wineskin) will be filled with wine?”

And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings who sit from the stock of David (or, the sons of David) upon his throne, and the priests, and the prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem with drunkenness. And I will scatter them, each man from his brother, fathers and sons alike, says the Lord. I will not spare (or, desire), nor grant, nor have mercy, so as not to destroy them.

The Hebrew word is NEBEL [the Hebrew form is not preserved in the supplied text]. Aquila’s first edition translated it as “flask”; his second retained the word *nebel* itself. Symmachus translated it as “mixing bowl,” the Septuagint as “wineskin,” and Theodotion as “vessel.” Every such vessel is filled not with oil, water, honey, milk, or any other liquid substance, but with wine and drunkenness.

This shows that we are fragile vessels, in accordance with the Apostle who says, “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7). Nor can it happen that what is written is not fulfilled in us: “For I know that nothing good dwells in my flesh.” And again: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, that I practice” (Romans 7:18). And afterward: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid., 19).

By this drunkenness, through which we forget God’s commandments and the whole human condition is filled with vices and sins, the Prophet’s saying is fulfilled: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm 142:2). This is not meant in comparison with God, as ancient and modern heretics and the defenders of heretics wish, but in relation to his knowledge. Human beings look at the face, but God at the heart (1 Samuel 16:7); and what sometimes appears clean to us is found filthy in his eyes.

This applies not only to the obscure masses and the worthless common people, but also to the kings of the Churches, descendants of David or sons of David, who sit reclining with raised necks and with their bellies thrust forward upon his throne. The priests also—the second rank in ecclesiastical honor—and the prophets, who seem to possess knowledge of the Scriptures, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, are filled according to the variety of their sins; or, as the Septuagint added, all of Judah.

When they have become drunk, they are scattered from one another’s company; fathers are separated from sons and sons from fathers, so that they may be polluted by different heresies, fight among themselves under the name of Christ, and wage war against their mother, the Church that gave them birth.

Hence he says: “I will not desire them,” but “I will hate them with everlasting hatred. I will not spare, nor grant, nor have mercy”—not through cruelty of judgment, but through the truth of judgment. For those who slaughtered my peoples will themselves perish forever.

This may also be understood simply according to history: the kings, priests, prophets, and whole people of Jerusalem would be made drunk with the Babylonian cup and overwhelmed by the evils of captivity.

### (Verse 15)

Hear and perceive with your ears; do not exalt yourselves, because the Lord has spoken.

Since he had said above, “Every wineskin will be filled with wine,” so that the kings, priests, prophets, and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem would be filled with drunkenness, he therefore joins this statement and says: “Hear and perceive with your ears”—both outwardly and inwardly, both in mind and in body—“and do not exalt yourselves through pride.”

Consider your fragility, and recognize that no one is free from this drunkenness in proportion to his sin. Therefore the one who raises himself against God through pride is destroyed and corrupted and becomes unworthy of God’s mercy.

### (Verses 16–17)

Give glory to the Lord your God (or, our God), before it grows dark and before your feet stumble against the dark mountains (or, shadowy mountains). You will await the light, but there will be the shadow of death, and they will be placed in darkness (or, according to the Hebrew, “and he will place it in the shadow of death and in darkness”). [Note: Since the interpretation marked “according to the Hebrew” is Jerome’s, while Jerome’s own rendering immediately precedes the Septuagint’s, Victorius, deleting the words *sive juxta Hebraicum*, rearranges the passage on his own initiative as follows: “You will await the light, and he will make it into the shadow of death and into gloom; or, there will be the shadow of death, and they will be placed in darkness.”] But if you do not listen, your soul will weep secretly [the Vulgate: “my soul”] because of pride (or, injury).

The divine word now calls those to repentance to whom it had said, “Hear and perceive with your ears, and do not exalt yourselves.” Before they are led to Babylon and their feet stumble against the dark or shadowy mountains, they are to give glory to God. Hence sinners are often told, “Give glory to God” (Psalm 67:35).

That Babylon and the whole region of the Chaldeans are called dark or shadowy mountains is clear from the beginning of Isaiah’s vision against Babylon, where it is written: “Raise a banner upon the dark mountain” (Isaiah 13:2), which in Hebrew is called NESEPHA [the Hebrew form is not preserved in the supplied text].

He therefore commands them to repent before they are led into captivity and experience the evils of servitude. Although they await light, they will sit in darkness. But if, he says, they do not wish to hear him secretly—or, according to Aquila, “in darkness”—their soul will weep; or, according to the Septuagint, “because of pride,” so that even their groans and lamentations will not be free, lest they offend the eyes of their conquerors.

We can also interpret this passage in the following way. The Savior speaks: “Work while it is day; night is coming, when no one can work any longer” (John 6:27). Isaiah prophesied concerning this time: “The stars of heaven and Orion, and all the array of heaven, will not give their light; the sun will be darkened at its rising, and the moon will not give its light” (Isaiah 13:10). Zephaniah also agrees in the same words, saying: “A day of tribulation and distress, a day of misery and destruction, a day of darkness and storm, a day of cloud and gloom” (Zephaniah 1:15).

Before the time of judgment arrives, therefore, and our feet stumble against the dark mountains—that is, the hostile powers appointed over torments and sufferings—let us repent, lest, while awaiting light, we be enveloped in the darkness of night. Let us know that, unless we do this, the soul either of God or of the Prophet will weep because of the pride of those who refuse to hear God’s words. Hence the Prophet himself says:

Jerusalem will weep bitterly (or, “weeping, my eye will shed a tear”), because the Lord’s flock has been taken captive (or, “I cannot conceal my grief in silent groans”). [Note: Because he found this latter interpretation, “or, I cannot conceal my grief,” in no sacred manuscript, Victorius removed it as a rashly inserted gloss.] The whole cause of its sufferings is that the Lord’s flock has been taken captive.

Let us say to the Jews and to those among us who Judaize, who follow only the simple and death-dealing historical sense: unless you listen secretly—that is, in mystery—or in the darkness which God made his hiding place (Psalm 17), and, according to Solomon, understand the proverb and the dark saying, the Prophet’s soul—or their own soul—will weep because of their pride, while in their stubbornness they resist God.

Hence there will be continual weeping and perpetual tears, because the Lord’s flock has been captured and corrupted by the true Nebuchadnezzar.

### (Verses 18–19)

Say to the king and the mistress (or, say to the king and the powerful): Humble yourselves; sit down, because the crown of the glory of your head has descended (or, been taken away).

The cities of the South are closed, and there is no one to open them. All Judah (or, all Judaea) has been transferred in complete migration (or, captivity).

The Prophet is commanded to speak to King Jeconiah and to his mother, whom he calls mistress and ruler, or queen, so that they may humble themselves and sit in the dust. They have lost their royal dignity and are about to be handed over to the king of Babylon.

“The cities of the South are closed” means the tribe of Judah and Jerusalem, which faces southward near the wilderness; they are surrounded by siege, and there is no one to open them.

“All Judah has been transferred in complete migration,” or “all Judaea has been transferred in complete captivity”: it has received what it deserved, and what the Septuagint translated has been fulfilled in it.

Anyone who understands the king as Christ and the powerful as angels or apostles, so that they are to assume a body of humility, sit in the dust, and lose the crown from their heads—whether the king or the powerful—and who understands Judah’s glory as having been transferred when the following was fulfilled in the passion, “All have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is no one who does good, not even one,” is raving in this passage.

The Hebrew word is GEBIRA [the Hebrew form is not preserved in the supplied text]. Aquila and Symmachus translated it as “mistress” and “lady”; the Septuagint understood it as GEBUROTH [the Hebrew form is not preserved in the supplied text] and translated it as “the powerful.”

### (Verses 20–21)

Lift up your eyes and see those who are coming from the North. Where is the flock that was given to you, your illustrious sheep? What will you say when he visits you? For you yourself teach them against you and instruct them for your own head.

The Vulgate has “you taught and instructed them,” which is more correct.

The inhabitants of Jerusalem are commanded to lift up their eyes and see the Chaldeans coming from the northern region. The city itself is questioned, and it is said to her: “Where is the flock that was given to you, your illustrious sheep? Where is your people, whom you had received from God? Where is that great and illustrious multitude, so large that you thought the population of the entire province had been gathered into one place?”

“What will you say when the Lord visits you with his rod and hands you over to the enemies of Babylon—those whom you yourself taught, either against you or for your own head, from the beginning, so that you might flee to their aid and follow their idols? Under the pretext of your friendship, they learned by which road they ought to come against you.”

Let the negligent Church hear this: it teaches its adversaries how they can seize it in spiritual captivity and tear its flock apart with the cruelty of beasts.

### (Verse 22)

Will pains not seize you like a woman in labor? But if you say in your heart, “Why have these things happened to me?” because of the multitude of your iniquity your shameful parts have been exposed, and your feet have been defiled (or, dishonored).

While you are unaware, sudden captivity will seize you like labor seizes a woman. If you wish to complain and ask why you have been handed over to your enemies, hear plainly: the multitude of your iniquity has done this to you. Like the shame of a prostitute whose clothes have been removed, your disgrace has been exposed and your fornications publicly displayed.

From this we learn that, as long as sins are minor, the Lord acts patiently and awaits our repentance. But if we wish to join sins to sins and heap up a mass of offenses, our shameful parts will be exposed and our feet displayed to everyone, either in the present age or in the future.

For nothing is hidden that will not be revealed (Matthew 10), when Daniel’s saying is fulfilled: “These will rise to everlasting life, and those to everlasting disgrace and everlasting confusion” (Daniel 12:2).

### (Verse 23)

Can an Ethiopian change his skin, or a leopard its spots? Then you also will be able to do good, having learned evil.

Those who wish to assert different natures use this testimony against the Church. They say that the blackness or variety of sins is so great that it cannot pass into whiteness and beauty of a single color. They do not attend to what follows: “Then you can do good, having learned evil.”

Whatever is learned belongs not to nature but to effort and the will of the individual. Through excessive habit and love of sinning, however, it is transformed, in a certain sense, into nature.

But what is impossible for human beings is possible for God (Matthew 19; Luke 18): the Ethiopian and the leopard do not appear to change their nature, but the one who works in the Ethiopian and the leopard does so, as the Apostle says: “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:13).

Hence, in another passage, he says: “I labored more abundantly than all of them—not I, however, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). And: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Again we read: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

For these reasons, let the wise man not boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, nor the chaste man in his chastity, knowing that in all these things it is Christ’s power, not the power of those who boast in their own virtues.

### (Verses 24–25)

I will scatter them like straw carried off by the wind in the wilderness. This is your lot and the portion of your measure from me, says the Lord (or, “and the portion of your disobedience against me”).

Because, through their excessive habit of evil, they could not change their nature—not through any fault of the Creator, but through their devotion to an ingrained wickedness—I will therefore scatter them into the wilderness like straw carried off by the wind, according to what is written elsewhere: “Like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth” (Psalm 1:4).

He then turns in direct address to Jerusalem: this is her lot and this is the portion she chose for herself, a measure heaped up and complete and overflowing (Luke 6), or the portion of her disobedience, by which she refused to obey God. “With whatever measure you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matthew 7).

### (Verse 26)

Because you have forgotten me and trusted (or, hoped) in falsehood, therefore I also have uncovered (or, will uncover and reveal) your thighs and your buttocks before your face, and your disgrace, your adulteries, and your neighing will appear, along with the crime (or, estrangement) of your fornication.

The cause of Jerusalem’s dispersion is that she forgot God and trusted or hoped in falsehoods. Whoever trusts in worldly things apart from God forgets God.

Therefore her thighs or buttocks are exposed, so that she may see her disgrace; what ought to be behind becomes what is in front. She sees what she has done, and her disgrace appears not only to her but to everyone.

“Your adulteries and your neighing,” he says, show not only lust but the madness of lust, after the manner of mares that eagerly desire intercourse, as in Virgil:

> Hippomanes, which shepherds say by that name  
> Drips slowly from the groin.

Let us ask Jesus that, neither in the present age nor in the age to come, he reveal our thighs [variant: “our private parts”] and our buttocks, but erase all our iniquities and not make all our crimes appear.

### (Verse 27)

Upon the hills in the countryside I saw your abominations. Woe to you, Jerusalem! You will not be cleansed (or, because you have not been cleansed) after me. How long still?

I saw your idols not only in the middle of the city of Jerusalem but on every hill and in every region. Hence it is said to her: “Woe to you, Jerusalem, because you have not been cleansed after me.” Although you boasted that you followed in my footsteps and proclaimed your confession of my name, you were never purified, because you forgot me and hoped in falsehoods.

Therefore he rebukes her and says, “How long still?” The sense is: How long shall I wait for you? How long shall I endure you? How long will you forget me to the end and despise my commandments?

The one who commits fornication on hills and in the countryside and is never cleansed is the one who, with neck held high in pride, is not humbled under the mighty hand of God but trusts in his crimes and vices.

## Chapter XIV

### (Verse 1)

The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words about the drought.

All things agree with God’s anger. Hence the sun sets upon sinners at midday, and the moon, stars, and other heavenly bodies do not give their light (Amos 8). It should be supposed that during the siege there was no rain, so that those under siege would endure a shortage of water.

The city uses one spring, Siloam, and not even that continually; to the present day, the scarcity of rain causes a shortage not only of crops but also of drinking water.

### (Verses 2 and following)

“Judah mourned (or, Judea), and its gates collapsed (or, were emptied), and they were darkened (or, enveloped in darkness) over the land, and the cry of Jerusalem went up. Their nobles sent their lesser ones (or, their younger men) for water. They came to draw (or, to the wells), but found no water. They carried back their vessels empty; they were confounded and distressed (or, they were ashamed), and they covered their heads because of the devastation of the land (or, and because the works of the land had failed), since rain did not come (or, was not present) upon the land. The farmers were confounded and covered their heads.”

In a time of drought, when the multitude suffers from a hunger for hearing and [Note: [Col. 0769D] Alternative manuscripts read: “and knowing the word of God.” Below we correct certain minor matters.] learning the word of God, Judah mourns, though previously boasting that it possessed the worship of God and the confession of the true faith. Its gates are either emptied or collapse; these we ought to refer to the senses, through which instruction is conceived in the soul. [Note: [Col. 0769D] Alternative manuscripts read: “and knowing the word of God.” Below we correct certain minor matters.]

Then everything is darkened and wrapped in shadows; and in Jerusalem reason and the word of instruction no longer reign, but rather clamor and confusion. The nobles also, who ought themselves to go to draw water, send the younger men, in whom there are no gray hairs of wisdom. They therefore come to the wells and do not find the waters which history relates that the patriarchs found (Genesis 26). They carry back their vessels empty—the younger men, that is—not because there had been no water, but because they had been unable to find it.

They were confounded and distressed, or ashamed, and covered their heads, because they could not say with the Apostle: “But we all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord” (2 Corinthians 3:18). They covered them because of the devastation of the land, or because the works of the land had failed—those works through which we proceed to the knowledge of God. The reason is clear: “because,” he says, “rain did not come upon the land.” For the clouds were commanded not to rain showers upon it (Isaiah 5).

The farmers also—one of whom says, “You are God’s agriculture, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9)—and elsewhere, “We are God’s fellow workers,” [Note: [Col. 0770D] Victor prefers “that these words be joined together with one another” at this place.] cover their heads and are confounded, understanding that without God’s grace and help they strive in vain.

### (Verses 5–6)

“For even the hind (or, hinds) gave birth in the field (or, gave birth), and abandoned (or, abandoned them), because there was no grass. And the wild asses stood upon the rocks, drew in the wind like dragons, and their eyes failed, because there was no grass (or, hay).”

There is great barrenness when even hinds give birth in the field and abandon their young, because there is no grass or hay. Thus those who by the scent of their nostrils draw serpents out of their caves and kill poisonous creatures do not partake of the food of grace.

The wild asses also, of whom it is written in Job, “Who let the wild ass loose in the wilderness?” (Job 39:5), abandoning the level and open country, stand upon the rocks; they cannot run, but draw in the wind like dragons, and their eyes fail, so that they cannot see the clear light, because rational foods have been withdrawn.

This drought often occurs in the churches, when hinds and wild asses are found among the peoples and waste away from lack of teachers: there are those who can learn, but there are none who can teach.

“If our iniquities answer us (or, resist us), Lord, act for the sake of your name, for our apostasies are many (or, our sins). We have sinned against you, O hope of Israel, its Savior in the time of trouble.”

If we wonder why rains do not descend upon the land, why everything withers in dryness, let us listen. Our iniquities have resisted us; therefore, Lord, conquer our many apostasies, not according to our deeds, but according to your holy name. For we have sinned against you, whom the secrets of the heart do not deceive, and we await you, who are the true hope and expectation of Israel; you save them in time of trouble, according to what is written: “To the Lord, when I was in trouble, I cried, and he heard me” (Psalm 119:1).

Let us also say in a time of drought and scarcity of water: “We have sinned against you and done evil before you” (Psalm 51); we await your coming, who save Israel, not through its own merit, but through your mercy.

### (Verse 9)

“Why are you to be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay? Why are you to be like a wandering man, or like a strong man who cannot save?”

The Septuagint reads: “Why have you become like a stranger in the land, and like a native turning aside to stay? Will you be like a sleeping man, and like a man who cannot save?”

The Jews understand this passage as follows: Why do you separate yourself from your people? And, like a traveler who, because of refreshment for a single hour, does not care what kind of lodging he uses, since he is about to pass on elsewhere, why do you not save your people, and abandon the once-renowned Temple?

Our writers, however, think that this is spoken concerning Christ’s future dispensation: that he would be a stranger in the land, would use the land’s hospitality for a short time, and, like a man passing through and strong, would leave Israel and turn toward the multitude of the nations, passing from place to place, from people to people, and from the Temple to the Church.

But when, according to the Septuagint, it says, “Will you be like a sleeping man, and like a man who cannot save?”, it gives a likeness, not the reality of the matter, in accordance with what is written: “Awake; why do you sleep, O Lord?” (Psalm 44:23). This does not mean that the Lord sleeps, of whom it is said: “He will neither slumber nor sleep who keeps Israel” (Psalm 121:4), but that he appears to sleep to those whom he abandons. Accordingly, in what follows it does not say, “a sleeping man who cannot save,” but “like a man”; in both places ἀνθρωποπαθῶς is written, that is, in humanly figurative language.

“But you are among us, Lord, and your name has been invoked over us; do not forsake us” (or, do not forget us).

You who, among the Jews, are to be a stranger and a traveler, a wandering man, abandoning your ancient dwelling, dwell among us. Your name has been invoked over us (Proverbs 31), so that we are called Christians. Therefore do not forsake us and do not forget us, concerning whose future coming the mouths of all the prophets have sung.

### (Verse 10)

“Thus says the Lord concerning this people: Because they loved (or, because they have loved) to move their feet, and did not rest (or, they did not spare), and the Lord was not pleased (or, God did not please himself in them), now he will remember their iniquities and visit their sins.”

When the people say, “Why have you become like a stranger, a traveler, and a wanderer, so that you abandon your dwelling?”, the Lord answers his former people: Do you wish to know the reason? Listen to what is said: The people loved to move their feet and did not remove them from the fetters of sins; or, they did not rest and were unable to stand. Therefore I abandoned them, and I have no pleasure in them.

He who for a long time delayed punishment and, in his patience, did not wish to punish sinners, because they persisted in their crime, will remember their iniquities. Like people who are sick and do not perceive God, he will visit their sins, so that they may cease sinning thereafter.

It should be noted in the Holy Scriptures that the feet of sinners are always moved, while it is said to the saints with Moses: “But you, stand here with me” (Deuteronomy 5:31). And elsewhere it is written: “Praise the Lord, you servants who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 134:1–2).

### (Verses 11–12)

“And the Lord said to me: Do not pray for this people for their good. When they fast, I will not hear their prayers; and if they offer burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not accept them, for with sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them.”

It is foolish to pray for one who has sinned unto death, as John says: “There is sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray concerning it” (1 John 5:16). Every iniquity is sin, and there is sin not unto death. [Note: [Col. 0771D] Victorius rejects the negative particle here, because it is not present in the text of John to which he alludes.]

Fasts, prayers, sacrifices, and burnt offerings are beneficial when we withdraw from vices and weep over former sins. But if, while remaining in our crimes, we think that we can redeem ourselves by vows and sacrifices, [Note: [Col. 0771D] In Rabanus: “to redeem ourselves by the ears of God, vehemently,” and so forth. In the Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts: “that we may be redeemed, as hearers of God.”] we greatly err, judging God to be unjust.

For whoever has once been destined for sword, famine, and pestilence can be rescued by no prayers. Hence the prophet is also told not to ask in vain for what he cannot obtain.

### (Verses 13–14)

“And I said: Ah, ah, ah, Lord God” (or, “who are, Lord God”). [Note: [Col. 0772D] Printed books add “my,” but the manuscripts do not recognize the pronoun here.]

“The prophets say to them: You shall not see the sword, and famine shall not be among you; rather, he will give you true peace in this place.”

And the Lord said to me: “The prophets prophesy falsely in my name. I did not send them, nor did I command them, nor did I speak to them. They prophesy to you a false vision, a fraudulent divination [the Vulgate: “fraudulence”], and the deceit of their heart.”

Let teachers who promise prosperity to sinners who persist in their vices hear this. They say to the rich: “You shall not see the sword of God’s punishments, and famine shall not be among you.” You will indeed be filled with the words of God, and the Lord will give you the truest peace in the place of the Church, or Jerusalem.

As for the fact that, according to the Hebrew, he says “ah, ah, ah” three times, this responds to what came before, where the Lord had threatened, saying: “By sword, famine, and pestilence I will consume them.” Since the prophets, or rather the false prophets, had made false promises, the Lord therefore spoke through Jeremiah: “Do not listen to the words of the false prophets, who were not sent by me but came by their own will.” Accordingly, they should not be called prophets at all, but diviners, since they speak deceit to the people.

It is much better to correct sins through fear of punishments than, through hope of prosperity, to become subject to the divine judgment.

### (Verses 15–16)

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning the prophets who prophesy in my name, whom I did not send, and who say: ‘There shall be neither sword nor famine in this land’: By sword and famine those prophets shall be consumed. And the peoples to whom they prophesied [the Vulgate: “to whom they prophesy”] shall be cast out upon the streets of Jerusalem because of famine and sword, and there shall be no one to bury them: them, their wives, their sons, and their daughters; and I will pour out their evil upon them” (or, their evils).

Let the false prophets beware, who, by promising prosperity, overthrow the people of God, lest they themselves perish and the deceived people likewise be destroyed in the same catastrophe. Let them lie in the streets of Jerusalem, trampling upon the Lord’s commandments, and perish from famine and sword, with no one to bury them; nor will the dust of repentance cover their disgrace.

For the prophets themselves, the people, their wives, their sons and daughters—in fact, the entire generation—will be in the refuse heap without any undertaker [alternative: “promiser”]. How many lie in the streets of Jerusalem! How many do we see unburied, receiving the evils which they suffer as the Lord pours them out!

### (Verse 17)

“And you shall say to them this word: Let my eyes shed tears (or, let your eyes shed tears) day and night, and let them not be silent (or, let them not cease), because the virgin daughter of my people has been crushed with a great crushing, with a grievous wound.”

This passage is understood in two ways: either that God himself weeps for his people and his eyes do not cease to shed tears, or that he commands the eyes of the peoples to flow with tears, since what must be mourned is no slight matter: the virgin daughter of his people has been struck with the greatest crushing and an intolerable wound. Others think that these words are spoken in the person of the prophet.

### (Verse 18)

“If I go out into the fields, behold, those slain by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, those weakened by famine (or, by the pain of famine). Both prophet and priest have gone into a land they did not know.”

There is just cause for mourning, because the virgin has been crushed, the daughter struck, and the people destroyed. For he says: If I wish to go outside, I shall see the slain; if I enter the city, I shall behold people weakened and scarcely clinging to their bones from the necessity of famine.

And why is it surprising to say this about the common people and the insignificant multitude, when even the prophets and priests—who prophesied prosperity to others and ought to have disclosed the commandments of the Law—have gone into a land they did not know and suffered the evil of captivity?

Let our prophets and priests hear this: because, through their negligence, there is no security either within or without; they scandalize those who are outside and allow those who are within to perish from famine; and those who have been the authors of sinning become participants in the punishments.

### (Verse 19)

“Have you utterly rejected Judah? Or has your soul abhorred Zion? Why then have you struck us, so that there is no healing? We hoped for peace, but there is no good; and for a time of healing, but behold, turmoil.”

The prophet marvels that the Lord has so suddenly rejected Judah and Jerusalem—that is, the kingdom of the two tribes, in which the worship of God and the ceremonies of the Temple existed—and has struck it with so great a wound that no medicine can be applied.

“We hoped,” he says, “for peace and a time of healing, but there is no good; on the contrary, there is turmoil.” Where previously there had been the worship of God and tranquility, everything was filled with seditions and the hostile roar of war.

[Note: [Col. 0773D] The printed editions read: “If therefore at some time…”]

If, then, our Zion and our Judah are rejected, and God’s soul abhors them, let us not be surprised, but rather let us say what follows:

### (Verse 20)

“We acknowledge, Lord, our impieties and the iniquity of our fathers, because we have sinned against you.”

We and our fathers, he says, in the same madness neglected God’s commandments. The measure of our ancestors has been filled in us, so that whatever was lacking in them might be completed in our accumulated guilt.

Hence it is also said concerning Judah: “Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered before the Lord, and let not the sin of his mother be blotted out. Let them be continually before the Lord, and let their memory perish from the earth” (Psalm 108:14).

### (Verse 21)

“Do not give us over to reproach for your name’s sake, and do not disgrace us. Remember the throne of your glory; do not annul your covenant with us.”

Let us not think that the throne of God’s glory is only the Temple of Judea, which has often been destroyed, but every holy person, in whom, according to what is written, “You have struck his throne down to the ground,” it is cast down and destroyed when, through the multitude of sins, he has offended God. [Note: [Col. 0774D] We have supplied the words “in which” from the manuscripts and Rabanus.] Nevertheless, the one who has perished through his own fault is sustained by the Lord’s mercy; that mercy is changed into the severity of judgment if the Lord annuls his covenant, by which he promised that we would be saved.

### (Verse 22)

“Are there among the idols of the nations those who can bring rain? Or can the heavens give showers? Are you not he, Lord God, whom we have awaited? For you have made all these things.”

After many and varied speeches, he returns to the title of the prophecy, in which it is written: “The word of the Lord that came to Jeremiah concerning the words of the drought.”

Therefore what he says is this: Since the images of demons cannot bring rain, nor can the heavens of themselves give their own shower, you, Lord our God, whom we have always awaited, in whom we have placed our hopes and turned our prayers, give your rain. For all things are yours, and whatever is good cannot be given without you, to whom it belongs.

Let us also say this against heretics, who cannot bestow the rain of doctrines. Although they promise that they are heavens and proudly apply to themselves what is written, “The heavens declare the glory of God” (Psalm 19:1), nevertheless they cannot give the showers of teaching. For God alone instructs his people and grants varieties of grace to those who await him.

## (Chapter 15)

### (Verse 1)

“And the Lord said to me: Even if Moses and Samuel stood before me (or, against me), my soul is not toward this people.”

We read that these men stood against the Lord’s anger on behalf of the people and turned aside the sentence that was already impending. “Even if they stood,” he says, either in my presence or against me—one of them being told by God, “Let me alone, and I will strike this people” (Exodus 32:10)—nevertheless I will not hear them, because the crimes of the offending people have reached completion.

“Cast them out (or, send them forth) from my presence, and let them go.”

Sinners do not depart from God spatially but by their will, although we also read that Adam and Cain were cast out from the presence of God (Genesis 3 and 4).

### (Verses 2–3)

“If they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Those destined for death, to death; those for the sword, to the sword; those for famine, to famine; and those for captivity, to captivity.

“And I will appoint over them four kinds of punishment, says the Lord: the sword for slaughter, and dogs for tearing apart (alternative: barking), and the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the earth for devouring and scattering.”

The four punishments to which the Jewish people were delivered are also shown by the prophecy of Ezekiel: sword, pestilence, famine, beasts, and captivity (Ezekiel 14). Among the beasts understand also the dogs and birds, to which the bodies were delivered to be torn apart, devoured, and scattered. For it could not happen that, when the Creator was neglected, the whole of creation would not rise against sinners.

### (Verse 4)

“And I will make them a terror (or, a commotion and distress) to all the kingdoms of the earth, because of Manasseh the son of Hezekiah, king of Judah, for all that he did in Jerusalem.”

We read in the Book of Chronicles that Manasseh, after captivity and repentance, returned to Jerusalem and reigned again (2 Chronicles 33). But just as the merits of the saints descend to their descendants, as in the case of David and others, so the crimes of sinners reach their descendants if their children and grandchildren commit similar deeds.

When he says, “I will make them a terror, or a commotion and distress, to the whole earth,” this was partly fulfilled under the Babylonians and is now completely fulfilled, when the impious people imitated the worst king, who filled Jerusalem from gate to gate with the blood of the righteous.

From this we learn that peoples are often destroyed because of the crimes of kings, rulers, and governors.

### (Verse 5)

“For who will have pity on you, Jerusalem? Or who will grieve for you? Or who will go to ask about your peace?”

When God has been offended, no one can plead for sinners because of their crimes. A creature cannot be as merciful as the Creator, nor can anyone be as unconcerned with outsiders as the Lord is merciful toward his own.

### (Verse 6)

“You have abandoned me, says the Lord; you have gone backward.”

The reason is given why no one will pity Jerusalem, grieve for it, or plead for its peace: although, according to the Apostle (Philippians 3), it ought to have forgotten what lies behind and stretched toward what lies ahead, it instead turned backward and desired the meats of Egypt.

“And I will stretch out my hand over you and destroy you. I have grown weary of being entreated” (or, of entreating); for this the Septuagint translated: “I will by no means release them any longer.”

An outstretched hand indicates one who is striking; the destruction of sinners signifies completed anger. The statement “I have grown weary of being entreated,” or “of entreating,” has a double meaning: God has now grown weary from repeatedly forgiving them, and weary from continually urging them toward salvation.

### (Verse 7)

“And I will scatter them with a winnowing fork at the gates of the land (or, of my people). I have killed and destroyed [the Vulgate: ‘utterly destroyed’] my people, yet they have not turned back from their ways.”

What benefit is there in being entreated so often when they do not turn back from their most evil ways and do not repent? I scattered them like a winnowing fork, in order to cleanse my threshing floor. I scattered them at the gates of the land, so that they might, in a sense, tread upon the thresholds of hell. I killed and destroyed my people so that, compelled by the necessity of evils, they might avoid the evils that were threatening.

### (Verse 8)

“Her widows have become more numerous for me than the sand of the sea. I brought upon them, against the mother of the young man, a destroyer at midday; I sent sudden terror upon the cities.”

God seeks to save sinners by various remedies, so that those who despised him when he was wooing them may fear him when he threatens. Widows became more numerous than the sand of the sea when their husbands were killed. Mothers, deprived of their children, experienced the destroyer—not at night and by ambush, but in broad daylight—so that he might show the open force of a stronger adversary.

“I sent,” he says, “sudden terror upon the cities,” plainly meaning Judah and the sinful people, so that the more sudden the evil was, the more difficult escape would be.

### (Verse 9)

“She who bore seven (or, many) has grown weak (or, has been cast down, or become empty); her soul has failed. Her sun has set while it was still day (or, midday). She has been confounded and ashamed; and I will give what remains of her to the sword before their enemies, says the Lord.”

We have often said that the Hebrew word *SABA* can mean either “seven,” “an oath,” or “many.” Hence the interpretation differs: Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translate “seven”; Symmachus, “many.”

She who was rich in children was suddenly made childless, perished in broad daylight, and was confounded in the solitude of her desolation. “The remnant,” he says, “I will hand over to the sword,” so that no one may escape death and God’s anger.

Others refer this to the synagogue, which was weakened so that the multitude of the Church might grow, according to what is written: “The barren woman has borne seven, or many; and she who had many children has grown weak” (1 Samuel 2:5). Hence the sun of righteousness, in whose wings there is healing (Malachi 4:2), has also set for her; and therefore she has been covered with eternal confusion, losing her people through the spiritual sword.

### (Verse 10)

“Woe is me, my mother, why did you give birth to me, a man of strife (or, of judgment), a man of discord (or, one who judges), throughout the whole earth?”

This may be understood *synecdochically* concerning Jeremiah, since he was judged not throughout the whole world but in the land of Judah. But it truly applies to the Lord and Savior, who says in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

Concerning him it is written: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be opposed” (Luke 2:34). For which philosopher, which pagan, which heretic does not judge Christ, imposing upon him laws concerning his birth, passion, resurrection, and substance? [Note: [Col. 0777D] The manuscripts and Rabanus read “and his substance,” with the conjunction.]

Nor is it surprising that, according to the reality of the assumed body, Christ says, “Woe is me, my mother,” since in another passage the following clearly suits his person: “Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers straw at harvest and like one who gathers grapes at the vintage, with no cluster to eat of the first fruits” (Micah 7:1).

And lest we think that the lowliness of these groans refers to the Word of God, who is it who mourns? Immediately it follows: “Woe is my soul, for the one returning from the earth has perished.” This does not mean that we divide the Persons, as the impious do, but that the one and same Son of God speaks now according to the flesh and now according to the Word of God.

“I have not lent, nor has anyone lent to me; everyone curses me.”

For this the Septuagint reads: “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me.” Theodotion: “I have not owed, nor has anyone owed me.”

The meaning of all these versions, spoken in the person of Christ, is this: No one has offered himself who could worthily receive my money; no one has lent to me by caring for the saints and the poor, making me his debtor.

Or, “I have not benefited, nor has anyone benefited me”: no one wished to receive as much as I desired to give. “Nor has anyone benefited me,” because the salvation of the creature is the profit of the Creator.
