Or certainly, “I have not owed, nor has anyone owed me”: no one gave me as much as I desired to receive, nor did anyone make me his debtor in anything. And the statement that follows, “Nor has anyone owed me,” has this meaning: How could anyone owe me interest who did not deign to accept a loan?

“Everyone,” he says, “curses me.” For which heretic or misguided person does not curse Christ by believing perversely and blaspheming still more perversely?

### (Verse 11)

“The Lord says: If your remnant is not for good; if I do not meet you in the time of affliction, and in the time of tribulation and distress [the Vulgate omits ‘and distress’], against the enemy.”

These words can also be understood as spoken in the person of Jeremiah, who was compelled to prophesy at the worst time, when captivity was already imminent, and to endure harsh treatment from an unbelieving people.

To what he had said above—“Woe is me, mother! Why did you give birth to me as a man who is judged and distinguished throughout the whole earth?” and the rest—the Lord answered: Do not consider the present, but the future. Your remnant and your end will be for good.

Indeed, even at present, when your enemies desired to oppress you, I was present with you, and you were protected by my help. This can refer both to Jeremiah and, according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, to the Savior.

For what we have translated according to the Hebrew, from “Everyone curses me” up to the place where it says “in the time of tribulation against the enemy,” the Vulgate edition reads as follows:

“My strength has failed among those who curse me. Let it be, Lord, for those who direct them, if I did not stand before you in the time of their affliction and in the time of their tribulation, for good against the enemy.”

The meaning is: “My strength has failed among those who curse me.” They do not understand my power, which is perfected in weakness; and the more they curse me, the more my strength fails among them.

Then either the prophet or the Lord joins the words and says, “Let it be, Lord” [alternative: “Let the Lord”], “for those who direct them”—that is, let the curses spoken by the enemies come upon me, and let them be directed toward good—if, in the time of their tribulation and distress, when the enemy was ravaging them and hastening to capture them, I did not stand before you, plead for them, and say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

We also often find Jeremiah in this book pleading for the people.

### (Verse 12)

“Can iron be joined with iron from the north, and bronze?”

Symmachus: “Can iron harm iron from the north, and bronze?”

The Septuagint and Theodotion: “If iron and a bronze covering will know?” [Note: [Col. 0777D] *Jare.* Jerome did not read the middle letter *vau*, or *ḥolem*, in this Hebrew word, as is clear to us from the testimony of all the manuscript codices: they read *Jare*, not *Jaroa*, according to the current pointing of the Hebrew text. Martianus. —Martianus writes *with vau*, although in his notes he himself does not approve the current pointing of the Hebrew text. Moreover, the Hebrew exemplar which he criticizes reads without *vau*.]

The reason for the variation is clear. The word *JARE*, which is written in the present passage, means both friendship and hostility because of the ambiguity of its pronunciation. If, in place of the letter *res*—which resembles the letter *daleth*—*daleth* is read, it signifies knowledge and understanding. [Note: [Col. 0778D] That is, if you read *JADE*. Otherwise the Septuagint differs from Theodotion in this one respect: the former translates εἰ γνωσθήσεται, “if it will be known,” while the latter interprets it as “if it knows.” Some minor matters are corrected below.]

What is said should be understood as follows: Do not grieve because the people are your enemy. Since you announce harsh things, one who is harsh cannot love you.

Or the Babylonians, who come from the north and are iron—exceedingly hard—cannot be joined in friendship to this people, which is harder still and untamable like bronze.

Or the exceedingly hard iron, that is, the people of Israel, is unworthy of the knowledge of God. It has reached such wickedness that it is enclosed by bronze, a harder metal.

### (Verses 13–14)

“I will give your riches and your treasures for plunder, freely (or, without payment), because of all your sins and throughout all your boundaries. And I will bring your enemies (or, make you serve your enemies) from a land you do not know, because a fire has been kindled in my anger; it will burn against you.”

I will hand over all your substance to your enemies without any payment, because of the sins you committed throughout all your boundaries. Therefore I will bring your enemies, or make you serve them in the land of the Chaldeans, because my fire, once kindled in my anger, will burn against you and cannot be extinguished.

You yourself supplied the material for your burning, so that my fire might consume the wood, hay, and stubble that are in you. Thus the cause of the burning is not in the Lord but in those who supplied fuel for the fire.

### (Verses 15–16)

“You know, Lord; remember me, visit me, and protect me from those who persecute me. Do not receive me in your patience; know that I have borne reproach for you. Your words were found, and I ate them” (or, “consume those who reject your words”). “And your word became for me the joy and gladness of my heart, because your name was invoked over me, Lord God of hosts.”

The words “You know, Lord” are not found in the Septuagint. Blessed is the conscience that bears reproach for God. Hence he says: “Your words were found,” the words that you spoke through my mouth. “And I ate them”—that is, they became food for me.

Or, according to Symmachus, “I received them,” so that they might be turned into joy for me, though previously they had been a reproach. Hence the Babylonians confess that what Jeremiah had foretold would happen was fulfilled.

Or this is the meaning: I experienced distress and endured the misery inflicted by the persecuting people; nevertheless I rejoiced that I had obeyed your commandments and suffered harsh things for your name.

### (Verses 17–18)

“I did not sit in the assembly of those who play, and I rejoiced (or, feared) before the face of your hand. I sat alone, because you filled me with bitterness [the Vulgate: ‘with threatening’]. Why has my pain become perpetual (or, why are those who distress me strengthened), and my wound is incurable and refuses to be healed (or, my wound is strong—how shall I be healed)? It has become for me like deceptive waters that cannot be trusted (or, like lying water that keeps no faith).”

The Hebrews think that this is spoken in the person of Jerusalem: it sat alone, was filled with bitterness, and its pain became perpetual; and just as waters pass away, so the words of the prophets, by which they falsely promised it prosperity, passed away.

It is better, however, to understand these words as spoken in the person of the prophet, a holy man who did not sit in the assembly or secret company of those who play, because he feared the hand of God impending over him; or rather, who rejoiced that he had no fellowship with the wicked. [Note: [Col. 0779D] The Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts read: “but with the words of the holy man,” and omit “which did not.” Rabanus has “or from the words,” and so forth.]

“I sat alone,” according to what is written: “I did not sit in the council of vanity, and I will not enter with those who act unjustly. I hated the assembly of evildoers, and I will not sit with the impious” (Psalm 26:4–5). And elsewhere: “I am solitary until I pass away.”

“Before the face of your hand,” he says, “I sat alone” (Psalm 141:10), while I fear you and continually await the hand that threatens me. I did not wish to sit in the assembly of those who play, but I swallowed my bitterness in order to prepare joy for myself in the future.

I did not have intervals of relief from my pain, but was weighed down by continual misery, so that I expected no remedies. Those who distressed me prevailed, and my wound became strong.

Yet I had this consolation: that it had become like deceptive and passing water. For just as passing waters are seen and then disappear as they flow, so, with your help, the whole force of the enemies passed away.

May the Lord grant that we also not sit in the assembly of those who play and of those who give no thought to the future; that we neither yield to adversities nor withdraw from them [alternative: “yield”], but always fear God’s judgment and say with the prophet: “I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness.”

Let the present age rejoice—not in the counsel of the wise, but in the hidden and secret assembly of those who play. For me, may it be good to cling to God, to place my hope in God, to be filled with reproaches, and to await the sentence of my judge. When the end has come, that sentence will show by its work that all sadness and bitterness have passed away like flowing waters. [Note: [Col. 0780D] The same manuscripts read “of works”; immediately afterward they have “to have withdrawn” instead of “to have passed through.”]

**(Verses 19 ff.)** Therefore the Lord says:

“If you return, I will restore you, and you shall stand before my face. And if you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth. They shall turn to you, but you shall not turn to them. And I will make you for this people a strong bronze wall; they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail, because I am with you to save you and to rescue you, says the Lord. And I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked, and redeem you from the hand of the strong [or: pestilential].”

It is clear that the preceding words were spoken not at all about Jerusalem, but by the Prophet. The Lord answers him: If you turn the people away from their sins, I too will turn you from tribulation into joy, and you shall stand before my face, just as the angels stand in God’s presence, seeing his face every day. “And if you separate what is precious from what is vile, you shall be as my mouth.” Do not think, he says, that a good work has no reward. If by your words you separate my saints from the number of sinners, you shall be as my mouth and shall be joined to my commandments. They ought to imitate you, not you them.

Do not shrink back and say: “Why has my pain become perpetual, and my wound strong—or incurable—so that I despair of being healed?” For I will make you like a bronze wall, exceedingly strong, so that you may resist the adversary with all your strength. Have me as your helper, and I will deliver you from the hand of the wicked—or pestilential—and redeem you, either by my blood or, for the present, by my help. Let us consider how great a reward belongs to a teacher’s speech if he succeeds in freeing someone from error and leading him out of the number of sinners.

**(Chapter 16—verses 1 ff.)** And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Do not take a wife, and do not let there be sons or daughters for you in this place. For thus says the Lord concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them, and concerning their fathers from whose stock they were born in this land: They shall die deaths of sickness [or: of the sick]. They shall not be mourned, nor buried; they shall be like dung upon the face of the earth. They shall be consumed by sword and famine, and their corpses shall be food for the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth.”

If, at the time of an impending captivity, the Prophet is forbidden to marry, lest he have the tribulation of the flesh and be tormented not only by his own suffering but also by the misery of his wife and children, how much more does the Apostle command (1 Cor. 7), because “the time is short” and the consummation is imminent, that even those who have wives should be as though they had none!

Hence the criticism of the new heretics, the Jovinians, is superfluous. We have taught that digamy and trigamy do not proceed from the law but from concession. For it is one thing to do what is good in itself, and another thing for something to be conceded lest we do worse. He himself gives the reasons why he wants young widows to marry, adding: “For some have already turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. 5:15). At the same time, while teaching continence and perpetual chastity, and blasphemously making himself equal to God, he praises threefold and fourfold marriages—which I would not call marriages so much as consolations amid misery and the final plank of shipwrecked men [or: of shipwreck]—unless perhaps he grants indulgence to his Amazons, so that even into decrepit old age they may wage the wars of lust.

[Note: Compare St. Basil, canon 4, where he calls third marriages “punished fornication” (πορνείαν κεκολασμένην) and considers them unworthy of being given the name of marriage. In canon 50 he calls them “filth of the Church” (ῥυπάσματα τῆς ἐκκλησίας). St. Gregory Nazianzen, too, in Oration 31, calls trigamy “lawlessness” (παρανομίαν), not to mention others who call it adultery in explicit terms. From these examples those who slander Jerome as an enemy of marriage may understand how much milder his judgment was than that of others.]

But why the Prophet is forbidden to take a wife is perfectly clear: siege, pestilence, sword, and famine are near, and everyone will perish. So great will be the number of the dying that the work of burial will be overwhelmed; their corpses will lie like dung, to be torn apart by birds and beasts. We should also note that wasting away through sickness and prolonged illness is a manifestation of God’s anger. Thus Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, is consumed by illness (2 Chron. 21). The Apostle likewise teaches that those who have violated holy things become sick, waste away, and die (1 Cor. 11).

**(Verses 5 ff.)** For thus says the Lord:

“Do not enter the house of feasting, nor go to mourn, nor console them, because I have taken my peace from this people, says the Lord—mercy and compassions. And great and small shall die in this land; they shall not be buried, nor mourned, and they shall not cut themselves, nor make themselves bald for them. They shall not break bread among them in mourning, to console someone over the dead, nor give them the cup to drink in consolation for their father or mother. And you shall not enter the house of feasting, to sit with them and eat and drink.”

The Apostle commands that one should not even eat with those who reject God (1 Cor. 5). And further: “Do not even say a greeting to such people” (2 John 10). The Savior likewise forbids the Apostles to greet anyone on the road (Luke 10). Hence Elisha also forbids Gehazi to offer a greeting when he is going to heal the boy (2 Kings 4).

It is customary to bring food to mourners and prepare a feast, which the Greeks call περίδειπνα, and which among us are commonly called *parentalia*, because funeral rites are celebrated for parents.

[Note: St. Gaudentius uses this name for the days and festivals of the *Inferiae*, and counts them among the practices of idolatry. See Ausonius, *Parentalia*.]

Divine Scripture also says elsewhere: “Give wine to those who are in mourning” (Prov. 31:6), so that they may forget their grief. The Prophet is therefore commanded not to console anyone from the people, not to mingle in the banquets of God’s enemies, and not to perform funeral rites over the burials of the dead. For it is one thing to die according to the common law of nature, and another for God’s judgment to have killed someone.

“I have taken my peace from this people,” he says, and they are unworthy of mercy. I will spare no age; great and small alike shall perish, so that they will lack even burial. “They shall not cut themselves,” he says, “nor make themselves bald for them.”

This was a custom among the ancients, and continues to the present day among certain Jews: in mourning they cut their arms and make themselves bald. We also read that Job did this (Job 1 and 22). The Prophet is therefore told not to break bread among them, nor enter to console anyone over the dead, nor give drink, nor enter the house of feasting, and not to mingle with those who have been prepared for God’s judgment.

But if this is said of mourners, what will become of heretics, whose word spreads like cancer, and who every day lay low funerals of the deceived within the Church?

**(Verses 9 ff.)** For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel:

“Behold, I will remove from this place, before your eyes and in your days, the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride. And when you have announced all these words to this people, and they say to you: ‘Why has the Lord spoken against us all this great evil? What is our iniquity, and what is our sin that we have committed against the Lord our God?’ you shall say to them: ‘Because your fathers forsook me, says the Lord, and went after foreign gods, served them, and worshiped them; they forsook me and did not keep my law. But you have acted worse than your fathers.’”

When the Church sins, all joy and complete gladness are taken away from it, of which the Apostle says: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4). “The voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride”—of whom it is written: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29).

But if the people ask you why they suffer these things and seek the causes of their misery, you will answer them: “Because your fathers forsook me,” says the Lord—those who preside over you in the churches—and they went after foreign gods, whose god is their belly, and avarice and luxury, and whose glory is in their shame; and they served them. For whoever is overcome by someone is that person’s servant.

“And they worshiped them.” Each person worships what he loves. “And they forsook me, and did not keep my law.” It is especially the duty of priests not only to teach the law but also to practice it, so that they may teach the peoples subject to them and the flock entrusted to them not merely by words but by examples.

And lest they perhaps say, “The sentence is unjust: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge” (below, 31; Ezek. 18), he adds: “But you have acted worse than your fathers,” so that just punishments may be imposed upon those who have sinned worse than their fathers.

**(Verse 13.)** “For behold, each one walks after the perversity of his evil heart, so as not to listen to me. And I will cast you out from this land into a land that neither you nor your fathers have known, and there you shall serve foreign gods day and night, who will not give you rest.”

Once they have abandoned the Lord, they do what is unfitting: they follow the desires of their evil heart, from which the worst thoughts proceed (Matt. 15). Therefore they are separated from the Church, so that they may go into a distant land, which neither they nor their fathers knew before they sinned, and there serve foreign gods who are not gods, but are thought to be gods through the error of those who worship them.

By adding “day and night,” he shows the sinners’ perpetual persistence in crime: during the day they serve their offenses, and at night their lust. “Who will not give you rest,” he says. There is no doubt that he means the false gods, of whom he said: “And there you shall serve foreign gods.” Whatever we sin, whatever we do day and night, whatever evil works we commit, is the dominion of demons. They never give us rest, but always drive us to increase sin upon sin and heap up offenses.

**(Verses 14, 15.)** Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and it shall no longer be said: “As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel up from the land of Egypt,” but: “As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel up from the land of the north and from all the lands to which I had driven them”; and I will restore them to their land, which I gave to their fathers.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “and it shall not be said, ‘As the Lord lives,’” and so forth.]

The future restoration of the people of Israel is plainly foretold, and mercy after the captivity. Literally, this was partly fulfilled under Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest, and Ezra; in the spiritual sense, it is described as being more truly and perfectly fulfilled in Christ.

A time will come, he says, when it will no longer be said that the people were brought up from Egypt by Moses and Aaron, but that they were brought up from the land of the north, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, released the captives. And “from all the lands,” he says—a thing that was not fulfilled in the time of Cyrus, but will be completed at the final end, when the Apostle says: “After the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11:25–26).

We can also speak of the persecutions that have befallen our people from the days of Nero—of whom the Apostle writes, “I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (1 Tim. 4:17)—up to the time of Maximian: how the Lord had mercy on his people and brought them back into their land.

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “up to the time of Maximian.”]

There is no doubt that this means the Church, which he gave to their fathers, the Apostles and apostolic men.

**(Verses 16 ff.)** “Behold, I will send many fishermen, says the Lord, and they shall fish for them. And after this I will send them many hunters, and they shall hunt them from every mountain, from every hill, and from the caves of the rocks, because my eyes are upon all their ways. They have not been hidden from my face, and their iniquity was not concealed from my eyes. And I will repay first their double iniquities and their sins, by which they polluted my land with the carcasses of their idols, and filled my inheritance with their abominations.”

There are various interpretations of this chapter. The Jews think that the Chaldeans are signified under the name of fishermen, and afterward the Romans, who are compared with hunters and hunted the unhappy people from the mountains, hills, and caves of the rocks. The Lord says that he himself did this because he looked upon their ways and repaid the iniquities with which they had polluted the land by venerating images and defiling his inheritance with the abominations of idols.

Our own interpreters, however, more rightly and more suitably think that the Prophet prophesied these things about the future. Since he had said above, “I will restore them to their land, which I gave to their fathers,” he now shows how they are to be restored: first he will send Apostles, to whom the Savior said, “Come after me, and I will make you become fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19). And afterward hunters, whom we may understand either as ecclesiastical men or as angels, who, when the time of the consummation has arrived, will hunt the saints from the mountains of lofty doctrines, from the hills of good works, and from the caves of the rocks—that is, from the Apostles and apostolic men.

For not only is Christ a rock, but he also granted to the Apostle Peter that he should be called Rock (1 Cor. 10; Matt. 16). Resting in his understanding, they are rightly said to have been transferred from the rock.

He also shows that either the Apostles or those who hunted afterward had sins and received their double iniquities. “The servant who knows the will of his master and does not do it will be beaten severely” (Luke 12:47).

It should be known that the Hebrew has the word “first,” which was omitted in the Septuagint edition. When he says, “I will repay first their double iniquities and their sins,” he subtly indicates that after they have received evil, they will also receive good.

Those who are afterward to be transferred polluted the Lord’s land with the carcasses of their idols and filled his inheritance with their abominations, so that the whole world might become subject to God and be preserved not by its own merit but by his mercy.

[Note: The words we have placed here from the Hebrew—“They have not been hidden from my face”—are not found in the Septuagint.]

**(Verse 19.)** “Lord, my strength and my stronghold and my refuge in the day of tribulation [or: of evils].”

All human strength, without the power of God, which is Christ, is considered weakness and nothing. Therefore one must flee to the Lord and say: “Lord, you have become our refuge from generation to generation” (Ps. 89:1). And elsewhere: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High will abide under the protection of the God of heaven” (Ps. 90:1).

The day of tribulation, or of evils, is to be understood as that of which the Apostle also says: “That he might rescue us from the present evil age”; and: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Gal. 1:4; Eph. 5:16).

**(Verse 20.)** “To you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth and say: ‘Truly our fathers possessed a lie, vanity that did not profit them.’”

The Septuagint: “To you the nations shall come from the ends of the earth and say: ‘How falsely our fathers possessed idols, and there is no benefit in them.’”

After Israel has been cast out and transferred by the fishermen and hunters, the multitude of the nations is consequently summoned to faith and confesses that it—or its fathers—had lived in former error. Those who say, “How falsely our fathers possessed idols, in which there is no benefit,” confess that the things to which they pass are true and supported by every protection.

“Can a man make gods for himself, and they are not gods?”

The nations that came to the Savior from the ends of the earth speak these words, reproaching both their own ignorance and that of their ancestors, because they thought that gods could be made by a human being, although it belongs to God to make human beings.

**(Verse 21.)** “Therefore, behold, I will show them this time; I will show them my hand and my power, and they shall know that my name is the Lord.”

[Note: The same manuscripts read: “that I am the Lord.”]

God’s hand, through which he accomplished all things, and his power, of which the Apostle said, “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), are shown to the nations when the suffering of the Son has been completed.

Beautifully he says, “I will show them this time.” I will show them openly, and not as before, in shadow, image, and prophecy of future things, so that after they have come to know, they may know my name and hear from the Son: “Father, I have manifested your name to the people” (John 17:6).

**(Chapter 17—verse 1.)** “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point, engraved upon the breadth [or: height] of their heart [or: upon the breast of their heart], and upon the horns of their altars [or: hearths].”

It was said above concerning the nations that had been converted to the Lord: “Behold, I will show them this time; I will show them my hand and my power.” Now he speaks about Israel, which has been rejected: “The sin of Judah is written with an iron stylus, with a diamond point,” and so forth.

Why this was omitted by the Septuagint, I do not know, unless perhaps they spared their own people, just as it is evident that they did the same in Isaiah: “Cease, then, from the man whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” (Isa. 2:22), and many similar passages. If I wished to arrange them all, the work would require not merely a book but books.

[Note: Origen attributes this to the rashness and faithlessness of later Jews, from whom he complains that many copies of the Septuagint had been corrupted, *Homily 16 on Jeremiah*: “Since it is harder for someone to confess himself wicked and say that these things are written concerning the Jews: ‘their sin is written.’” Jerome translates this as follows: “Because it is difficult for anyone to confess himself wicked, therefore the Jews, who falsified certain copies, in this passage too wrote ‘their sin’ in place of ‘the sin of Judah.’” He then reports that this verse was entirely absent from the Septuagint, which the Jews had corrupted in their own, not Greek, copies: “There is another prophecy which, I do not know why, we do not find among the Seventy; but we find it in the other editions,” and so forth. Eusebius also adds, in *Demonstration of the Gospel*, book 10: “Although we do not find these things among the Seventy, nevertheless we find them in the Hebrew and in the editions of the other translators, indeed even under asterisks in the more accurate copies of the Septuagint.” See also Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho*.]

The sins of the nations have been erased, because, converted to the Lord from the ends of the earth, they heard: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. For his mercy has been confirmed upon us, and the truth of the Lord endures forever” (Ps. 116:1–2). These are the people concerning whom he had said to Moses: “Let me alone, that I may destroy this people and make you into a great nation” (Exod. 32:10).

But Judah’s sin, indelible and, so to speak, incapable of being erased by any means, is written with an iron stylus on a diamond point, which in Hebrew is called *SAMIR* (). It is not that there is some point called *Samir*, but that the diamond stone—so named because it is unconquered and unbreakable—has such brilliance and smoothness that it can be written upon with an iron stylus without any obstruction. Thus the hard substance of iron writes upon a harder diamond tablet, and what has been written endures forever.

For they themselves said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25). Therefore it has been engraved or inscribed upon the horns of their altars or hearths, so that their sacrilegious deeds may endure in eternal memory.

But if this is so, where is the claim invented by a senile old woman that a person can be without sin if he wishes, and that God’s commandments are easy?

**(Verses 2, 3.)** “When their sons remember their altars and their groves and leafy trees upon the high mountains, sacrificing in the field, I will give your strength and all your treasures for plunder, your high places because of your sins throughout all your borders. And you shall be left alone, separated from your inheritance that I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know, because you kindled a fire in my anger; it shall burn forever.”

These words are not found in the Septuagint, for the same reason, I believe, which we mentioned above: namely, lest the sentence against them remain eternal.

“You shall be left alone,” he says, “separated from your inheritance that I gave you, and I will make you serve your enemies in a land that you do not know”—either under the Babylonians or, more truly, under the Romans. For they themselves kindled the fire and provoked the most merciful Lord to anger; the fire of his fury will burn forever.

I am ashamed of the dispute among our own people, who accuse the Hebrew truth. The Jews read these words against themselves, and the Church does not know what supports its own cause. Therefore we, who are sons of the Apostles, remember the iniquities of the former people and testify that they suffered these things justly.

The high places, which in Hebrew are called *BAMOTH* (), can also be understood against the heretics, who have set their mouths on high, and whose tongue has traversed the earth. They have rushed into such madness that they alone have remained without the grace of the Holy Spirit and have lost the Lord’s inheritance—that is, the former truth of faith. Therefore eternal fire and slavery to demons, who are their enemies and avengers, are prepared for them.

**(Verses 5, 6.)** Thus says the Lord:

“Cursed is the man who trusts [or: hopes] in man, who makes flesh his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord. He shall be like a tamarisk in the desert, and shall not see good when it comes; he shall dwell in parched places in the desert, in a salty and uninhabited land.”

If every person who trusts in man is cursed, then Paul of Samosata and Photinus, although they proclaim the Savior as holy and exalted above all virtues, nevertheless confess him to be a man. Therefore they will be cursed, placing their hope in a man.

If someone objects that we too believe in the one who says, “Now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken the truth to you, which I heard from God. Abraham did not do this; you do the works of your father” (John 8:40), we will answer with the words of the Apostles: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16).

Finally, the same Apostle writes at the beginning of his Epistle to the Galatians: “Paul, an Apostle not from men [or: not from a man], nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead, and all the brothers who are with me” (Gal. 1:1–2).

If death has been swallowed up in victory (Hos. 13:14), why should not the lowliness of the flesh, assumed for the salvation of humanity, have passed into the majesty of divinity, so that the two might become one? Let us not worship the creature, but the Creator, who is blessed forever.

Therefore cursed is not only the one who places his hope in man, but also the one who makes flesh his arm—that is, his strength—and whatever he does, thinks is due not to the Lord’s mercy but to his own power. Whoever does this has a heart that departs from the Lord, claiming that he can do what he cannot.

He shall be like a tamarisk, which in Hebrew is called *AROER* (), or, as Symmachus translated it, “an unfruitful tree in the wilderness.” He shall not see the good things that the multitude of the nations will see, but shall dwell in parched places in the desert.

This is said concerning the Jewish people, who dwell in the desert and produce no fruit. They are in a salty land, which produces no fruit, and in an uninhabited land, which has neither God as its inhabitant, nor the protection of angels, nor the grace of the Holy Spirit, nor the knowledge of teachers.

**(Verses 7, 8.)** “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord shall be his hope [or: confidence]; and he shall be like a tree transplanted [or: fruitful] beside waters, sending its roots toward moisture. He shall not fear when the heat comes; his leaf shall be green [or: his branches shall be leafy]. In the year [or: season] of drought he shall not be anxious [or: afraid], nor shall he ever cease to produce fruit.”

Let this be understood as spoken concerning the Jews and heretics who place their hope in man—namely, in their Christ, whom they think will come not as the Son of God but as a mere man.

In contrast, the ecclesiastical man who trusts in the Lord hears: “Know that the Lord himself is God” (Ps. 99:3). He trusts in the Lord and will be compared to the tree of which the first psalm also sings: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf shall not fall.”

The waters mean the grace of the Holy Spirit and his various gifts.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript supplies, “understand: who also shortly afterward has ‘healing’ instead of ‘persecution.’”]

“Sending its roots toward moisture,” so that it may receive abundance from the Lord.

We can also say in another way that we have been transferred from Jewish drought into the everlasting grace of baptism.

“He shall not fear,” he says, “when the heat comes”—whether the time of persecution or the day of judgment. “His leaf shall be green,” or, “there shall be leafy branches in him,” so that he may never fear drought but may produce the grace of every virtue.

When the time or year of drought comes, he will not fear, when the angry Lord commands the clouds not to rain upon Israel (Isa. 5). The following words, “nor shall he cease to produce fruit,” may be explained by the passage written in Mark: the Lord came to the fig tree and found no fruit on it, because it was not yet the season, and he cursed it so that it would never produce fruit (Mark 11).

For whoever trusts in the Lord, and whose confidence is the Lord, will not fear even in the time of Jewish drought. He will always bear fruit, believing in him who once died for us and dies no more (Rom. 6), and who says: “I am life” (John 14:6).

**(Verses 9, 10.)** “The heart of all [or: of all human beings] is perverse and inscrutable; who can know it? I, the Lord, search the heart and test the kidneys, giving to each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.”

The Septuagint: “The heart is deep above all things, and it is man; who can know him?” and the rest similarly.

The Hebrew word () *ENOS* is written with four letters: *aleph*, *nun*, *vav*, and *shin*. If it is read *ENOS*, it means “man”; but if *ANUS*, “inscrutable” or “desperate,” because no one can discover the human heart.

Symmachus translated this passage as follows: “The heart of all is inscrutable; but who is the man who can find it?”

Some of our own writers, with good intention but not according to knowledge, customarily use this passage against the Jews to say that the Lord and Savior was a man, according to the dispensation of the assumed flesh, and that no one could know the mystery of his birth, in accordance with what is written: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8)—except God alone, who examines hidden things and repays each person according to his works.

It is better, however, to understand the passage simply: no one knows the secrets of thoughts except God alone. For he had said above: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man.” In contrast: “Blessed is the man who trusts in the Lord.”

Therefore, lest we think that human judgment is certain, he adds that the hearts of nearly all are perverse, as the Psalmist says: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others” (Ps. 18:13)—clearly referring to thoughts.

And in Genesis: “When God saw that the wickedness of human beings was great on the earth, and that every inclination of the thoughts of their heart was directed toward evil all the time” (Gen. 6:5). And again: “The sense and thought of the human heart are inclined toward evil from youth” (Gen. 8:21).

Through these passages we learn that God alone knows their thoughts. But if it is said of the Savior, “Jesus, seeing their thoughts” (Luke 9:47), and no one can see their thoughts except God alone, then Christ is God, who searches hearts and tests the kidneys, and repays each person according to his works (Ps. 7:9).

**(Verse 11.)** “The partridge brooded over [or: gathered] what it did not hatch. (As the Septuagint translated it: ‘The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch.’) It made its riches without judgment. In the middle of its days it will leave them [or: in the middle of his days they will leave him], and at his end he will be a fool.”

The writers of natural history—of beasts and birds, as well as of trees and plants—whose leading authorities among the Greeks are Aristotle and Theophrastus, and among us Pliny the Elder, say that it is the nature of the partridge to steal the eggs of another partridge, that is, eggs belonging to another, and brood over and warm them. When the offspring has grown, it flies away from it and abandons the alien parent.

[Note: Drusius emphatically denies that Aristotle, Theophrastus, or Pliny attributed this care and brooding of other birds’ eggs to the partridge, accusing Jerome of error. But the holy Father did not say that those writers specifically recorded it, only that it was reported by writers of natural history, among whom those authors hold the leading place. Indeed, very many ecclesiastical authors affirm it: Hippolytus the Martyr in the *Catena on Jeremiah*; Epiphanius in *Physiologus*, chapter 9; Ambrose, book 6 of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 3, and formerly Epistle 48; Philastrius in the preface to his book *On Heresies*; Augustine, *Against Faustus*, book 13, chapter 12; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book 12, chapter 7; and others. More recent critics, however, think that ambiguity was caused by the Hebrew name used by Jeremiah, which the Septuagint, and from them the Latins, rendered as “partridge.” Since they had no word for that bird, unknown to Europeans, they used the name of the most similar and closely related bird. See Bochart, *On the Animals of Scripture*, and Huet in his notes on Origen, where he observes that all that the Hebrews and Arabs report agrees with the *pico*.]

Such are the rich: they seize what belongs to others and, without considering—or reconsidering—God’s judgment, make riches without judgment. They leave these riches in the midst of their life, taken away by sudden death, when it is said to them: “Fool, this night they will demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?” (Luke 12:20). Nothing is more foolish than failing to provide for one’s end and considering what is brief to be everlasting.

Others, both because of the preceding account and because of another tradition according to which the partridge is extremely combative and unclean, so that it pollutes even the one it defeats, interpret the devil under the name of the partridge: he gathered the riches of others for himself, saying to the Lord, “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4:9).

His riches, which he had wickedly gathered, will abandon him, and through the Apostles they will return to the Lord. He who seemed wise to himself will, in the judgment of all, be a fool.

As for the Septuagint’s wording, “The partridge cried out,” this should be referred to the person of the heretics: that this partridge—the devil—cried out through the leaders of the heretics, gathered what it did not hatch, and assembled for itself a multitude of the deceived, whom it will afterward abandon and, in the judgment of all, be proved the greatest fool.

(Verses 12–13.) The throne of glory, exalted from the beginning, the place of our sanctification. O Hope of Israel, Lord, all who abandon you will be put to shame; those who withdraw [Note: Manuscripts add “from you,” as it is found in the Vulgate and in Jerome’s own version, although the Hebrew text rejects it.] will be written in the earth [Al. “be erased”], because they have abandoned the vein—or fountain—of living waters, the Lord.

With the partridge abandoned because of its own folly, the Hope of Israel—that is, the hope of God’s people and of the believer in the Lord—is he who made all things, whose throne is glorious and exalted from the beginning, and the place of sanctification of all believers—not so that the Lord is contained in a place, but so that wherever he is, that place is sanctified. Conversely, those who abandon the Lord will be put to perpetual shame; those who withdraw or turn away from him will be written in the earth, erased from the book of the living. For just as the one who can say with the Apostle, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3), is written among heavenly things, so the one who abandons or turns away from the Lord will be written in the earth with those who set their minds on earthly things. The reason why they are written in the earth is evident: they have abandoned the fountain of life, the Lord, or the Lord, the fountain of living waters, who says in the Gospel: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink; whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed were going to receive (John 7:37–38).

(Vers. 14.) Heal me, Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my praise. Many physicians in the Gospel (Matt. 9) had treated the woman with the issue of blood, who had spent all her resources on them, and yet she could be healed by none except him who is the true physician and whose healing is in his wings. Therefore the Prophet now, having suffered reproaches from the people and having often been surrounded by plots, desires to be healed and saved by him whose praise and medicine are true.

(Verses 15 and following.) Behold, they themselves say to me: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.” But I have not been troubled [Col. 0791B] by following you as shepherd [or: “I have not labored by following you”], and I have not desired the day of man; you know. What came forth from my lips was right in your sight [or: “is before your face”]. Do not become a terror to me; you are my hope in the day of affliction [or: “Do not become alien to me; spare me in the evil day”].

Those who do not believe that the things spoken will come to pass say to the Prophet: “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come,” treating the sentence as a pretense or delay. But while they say these things, he says, I have not been troubled, nor have I labored by following you as shepherd, or by walking in your footsteps. Nor was I content with this alone, but I did not desire the day of man, whether a longer life or any prosperity of this age. He calls him both witness and judge: “You know.”

It follows: “What came forth from my lips was right in your sight,” so that he had never lied or spoken anything contrary to the Lord’s will. “Do not become,” he says, “a terror to me; you are my hope in the day of affliction.” This is clear according to the Hebrew. According to what the Septuagint translated—“Do not become alien to me; spare me in the evil day” [Note: The words “to me” were lacking; the manuscripts supply them, with whose help other similar matters of lesser importance have been corrected above.]—the sense is: Do not spare me in the present age, which is evil, but repay me according to my sins, so that I may have everlasting rest. For I know that it is written: “Whom the Lord loves, he chastens; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). The evil day is either the whole age or the day of judgment, for those who are tormented because of their sins.

(Vers. 18.) Let those who persecute me be put to shame, and let me not be put to shame. Let them be afraid, and let me not be afraid. Bring upon them the day of affliction, and crush them with a double crushing.

The Prophet invokes this against those who reproach him concerning the word of the Lord and say, “Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come,” so that those who persecute him may be put to shame, blush, and return to salvation; so that those who lie may be afraid, and not he who foretells the truth. When the day of vengeance arrives, may he crush them with a double crushing [Al. “crush them”], through famine and the sword.

(Verses 19–20.) Thus says the Lord to me: Go and stand in the gate [or: “gates”] of the sons of the people, through which [or: “through which gates”] the kings of Judah enter and depart, in all the gates of Jerusalem, and say to them: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah, and all Judah [or: “Judea”], and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem who enter through these gates.

Because, he says, they disdain hearing your words and do not come to you to inquire what the judgment [Al. “wisdom”] of God may be, proceed to the most frequented place, whether the gate of the Temple or of the city, through which the kings and the entire populace enter and depart, so that they may be compelled by necessity to hear, and preach the word of the Lord “in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4). Thus no excuse may remain among them that they failed to do so because they had not heard.

(Verses 20 and following.) Thus says the Lord: Guard your souls, and do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day, nor bring them through the gates of Jerusalem. Do not cast burdens out of your houses on the Sabbath day; do no work, and sanctify the Sabbath day, as I commanded your fathers. But they did not listen, nor incline their ear; they stiffened their neck more than their fathers—the words “more than their fathers” not occurring in the Hebrew—so that they would not hear me and would not accept instruction.

And it shall be, he says, if you listen to me, says the Lord, so that you do not bring burdens through the gates of this city on the Sabbath day, and if you sanctify the Sabbath day by doing no work on it, kings and princes sitting on the throne of David will enter through the gates of this city. They will ride in chariots and on horses, they and their princes, the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and this city will be inhabited forever. They will come from the cities of Judah, from the region around Jerusalem, from the land of Benjamin, from the lowlands and the hill country [Al. “mountainous country”], and from the south, bringing burnt offerings and sacrifices [or: “incense offerings”], offerings [or: “manna”], and frankincense; and they will bring an offering [or: “praise”] into the house of the Lord.

But if you do not listen to me, to sanctify the Sabbath day, to carry no burden, and to bring no burden through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day, I will kindle a fire in its gates, and it will devour the houses of Jerusalem, and it will not be extinguished.

So that I might not tear apart in fragments the Sabbath commandment restored through Jeremiah, I have thought it worthwhile to set down the whole passage, so that we may understand everything together. Whoever does not carry the burdens of sins on the day of rest and the Sabbath guards his soul; nor does he bring them through the gates of Jerusalem, which we ought to understand as the virtues. “Do not,” he says, “cast burdens out of your houses.” They are not to be carried, but utterly cast away. “Do no work”—whether servile work or that of which it is written, “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food; God will destroy both the one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13)—but perform the work of which the Savior speaks: “Work for the food that does not perish” (John 6:27).

“Sanctify,” he says, “the Sabbath day,” so that we may spend the whole time of our life in sanctification, as our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did. Although God had commanded these things, they did not incline their ear—that is, the ear of the mind, not of the flesh—but stiffened their neck, rejecting the yoke of the Law and, by metaphor, bearing the likeness of untamed animals.

Let us see what reward belongs to those who do not carry burdens on the Sabbath day and sanctify it. “Kings,” he says, “will enter through the gates of this city,” kings whose heart is in God’s hand and who rule their own bodies (Prov. 21), and princes sitting on the throne of David, so that they may imitate Christ’s example. They will ride in chariots and on horses, of which it is written: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands upon thousands of rejoicing ones; the Lord is among them at Sinai, in the holy place” (Ps. 67:18). And elsewhere: “Your riding is salvation” (Hab. 3:8).

Every man who confesses God and dwells in Jerusalem, of which it is said, “His place has been made in Salem [Al. Jerusalem], that is, in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:2)—the Church of God will be inhabited forever—will come from the cities of Judah and from the region around Jerusalem, of which we have already spoken; from the land of Benjamin, who is the son of strength and of the right hand; from the lowlands, which is called SEPHELA in Hebrew () and signifies a plain understanding of the historical sense; from the hill country, that is, from lofty doctrines; and from the south, of which it is written: “God will come from the south” (Hab. 3:3). From there come heat and full light, and every cold thing is driven away.

“They will bring,” he says, “burnt offerings,” consecrating themselves to God, and a sacrifice—or incense—so that they may say: “The sacrifice to God is a broken spirit” (Ps. 50:19). “We are the good odor of Christ in every place” (2 Cor. 2:15). And elsewhere: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140:2).

And the offering for which the Septuagint set down the Hebrew word MANAA ()—which through a very bad custom, or rather through the negligence of scribes, is read as “manna” in our books [Note: The Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts insert it into the books. The same error is still found here, and also at chapter 48:5 and Baruch 1:10. In Theodoret you will sometimes find μαναὰ written, and sometimes μαννὰ: namely, at Jeremiah 41:5 and in the cited passage of Baruch. Chrysostom likewise reads μαναὰ in the first Exhortation to Theodore, chapter 3, and μαννὰ in Daniel, chapter 2. See in the following volume, in the commentary on Ezekiel, chapters 45 and 46, the explanation of this name.]—and frankincense, of which it is written: “Why do you bring me frankincense from Sheba?” (above, 6:20).

“They will bring an offering,” which is called THODA in Hebrew (), and may be rendered “thanksgiving,” and which the Septuagint translated as “praise,” into the house of David, plainly meaning the Church.

These are the rewards of those who sanctify the Sabbath and are weighed down by no burden. But if, he says, you do not listen to my commands [Note: In the Vatican manuscript: “and do not do what I have commanded to be done.”], and do what I commanded not to be done, I will kindle a fire in its gates—that is, in Jerusalem—the fire of which it is said: “All the adulterers are like an oven; their hearts” (Hos. 7:4). This fire devours the houses, or streets, of Jerusalem, which the Septuagint call ἄμφοδα, while Aquila and Symmachus call them βάρεις, that is, “towered houses”; in Hebrew they are called ARMANOTH () [Note: The Septuagint have Ἄμφοδα. Beware the false opinion introduced here by Erasmus and Marianus, who say that the Septuagint, together with Aquila and Symmachus, translated βάρεις, that is, “towered houses.” Nor should you think that Jerome affirmed this with Nobilius in the notes on the Septuagint version, because from the testimony of all the manuscript copies of the holy Doctor it is clear that he read Ἄμφοδα in the Septuagint and said that it meant “crossroads,” not “towered houses.” MARTIAN.] [Note: More clearly, in Letter 65 to Principia, he says: “Βάρις is a local word of Palestine, and even today houses enclosed on every side and built in the form of towers and public walls are called βάρεις.” Recall what we have noted on this passage and in the Commentary on Amos, chapter 1:2.]

And this fire will never be extinguished [Note: We have supplied “this fire” from the manuscripts; the noun had dropped out of the Vulgate], as the Apostle says: “The fire will test the quality of each one’s work” (1 Cor. 3:13). And again: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire” (ibid., 15).

But if our Judaizers reject the allegorical explanation, they will either have to become Jews and circumcise their foreskin while observing the Sabbath, or at least condemn the Savior, who commanded the paralytic on the Sabbath to carry his bed, as the Evangelist says: “For this reason the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his own Father, making himself equal with God” (John 5:18).

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0793]

[Col. 0793D] 965–966 The devil is always watching for a good work [perhaps: “envies it”], and everywhere lays snares for those who walk, as the Prophet tells of the plots of his minions: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling-block for me” (Ps. 139:6); and the Gospel (Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 8) teaches this more fully, saying that the birds of heaven snatch away and scatter the seed cast beside the road.

Why I have used this as my opening, brother Eusebius, the following discourse will show. Occupied by the crowds of many people flocking here from the whole world and by the cares of the holy brothers and the monastery, I dictated my Commentaries on Jeremiah at intervals, so that what was lacking in leisure might be supplied by diligence. Suddenly the heresy of Pythagoras and Zeno—ἀπαθεία and ἀναμαρτησία, that is, impassibility and impeccancy—which was once slaughtered in Origen and, not long ago, in his disciples Grunnius and Evagrius [Note: “Ponticus” was added, though it is not found in the manuscripts, perhaps by some diligent student; I would rather reject it again to the margin of the page.] Ponticus and in Jovinian, began to revive. It began to hiss not only in the regions of the West but also of the East, and to defile many in certain islands, especially Sicily and Rhodes, growing day by day while secretly teaching and publicly denying.

I was compelled to answer it after remaining silent for a long time and devouring my grief in silence, because of the frequent complaints of the brothers. Yet I have not burst forth to the point of naming its authors, preferring that they be corrected rather than disgraced [Al. “imitated”]. For I am not the enemy of men but of error. When they tried to strike me in return with the law of retaliation and the sting of their own pain [Al. “sweat”], composing the old slanders of their teachers against me, they proved so speechless [Al. “bilingual”] and wretched that they could not even curse in their own words.

At that time, when books had been published against them, their dirges were refuted. Those who wish to read them will clearly see that, according to Isaiah, these men are mute dogs unable to bark: they have the will and madness to lie, but lack the skill to fabricate and bark (Isa. 56).

To them I shall speak briefly: Either the things you teach are good or they are bad. If they are good, defend them openly; if they are bad, why do you secretly slaughter wretched people with error and parade an exposition of the true faith before the simple in order to deceive them? If it is true, why is it hidden? If it is false, why is it written? I ask, what madness is this? The Apostle commands us to be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks for a reason concerning the hope that is in us (1 Pet. 3), and the Prophet cries: “I spoke of your testimonies before kings, and I was not put to shame” (Ps. 118:46). Yet these men flee the public and whisper in the corners of the lost, grieving as though for things that belong to them, when they fear confessing them as their own.

Whenever we speak generally against vices and heretics, they complain that they themselves are being attacked, and, after concealing their indignation for a long time, they announce the evil of their conscience.

If we must be careful not to appear to injure an old relationship by cutting down a most arrogant heresy with the spiritual sword [Note: It may be that some relationship intervened between Pelagius and Jerome, while both were living in Rome or while both were friends of Paula, Demetrias, or other holy women. More probably, however, John of Jerusalem is indicated: Jerome had until recently used him as a friend, but was already accusing him as a patron of the Pelagians.], then we must endure the crosses of the betrayed faith, and say with the Prophet: “I was plunged into misery while a thorn was driven into me” (Ps. 31:4).

Rather, let them hear the apostolic saying: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29; Gal. 1). And again: “If I were pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ.” But if they do not keep silent, we shall discuss these matters more fully in a work of their own [Note: He seems here to threaten the three books of Dialogues that he wrote shortly afterward against the Pelagians. What he had just said—“when books had been published against them, their dirges were refuted”—should not be understood of the Pelagians but of their teachers, as he himself calls them: Rufinus, Jovinian, and others.].

Now let us resume the journey we began in Jeremiah, and, passing briefly through the fourth volume on him, let us linger only over those matters that are obscure.

(Chapter 18—Verses 1 and following.) The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down to the potter’s house, and there you will hear my words. And I went down to the potter’s house, and behold, he was making a work on the wheel [or: “stones”]. And the vessel that he was making from clay with his hands was spoiled. And turning [or: “again”], he made it into another vessel, as it seemed good in his eyes to make it. And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Can I not [Vulg.: “shall I be able,” according to the Hebrew] do with you, house of Israel, as this potter does? says the Lord. Behold, as clay is in the hand of the potter, so are you in my hand, house of Israel.

Suddenly [or: “at the conclusion”] I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot [or: “remove”], destroy, and annihilate it. If that nation repents of its evil, concerning which I have spoken against it, I too will repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it. And suddenly [or: “at the conclusion”] I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build and plant it. If it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent of the good that I had spoken of doing to it.

By every sense one reaches the judgment and understanding of the mind—by hearing, smell, taste, and touch—but what is seen by the eyes is retained more firmly in the mind. Therefore the Prophet is commanded to go to the potter’s house and there hear the Lord’s commands.

“When I had gone and descended,” he says, “to the potter’s house, he was making a work on the wheel.” The Septuagint, misled by the ambiguity of the word, translated “stones.” For ABANIM () means, according to the nature of the place and the difference of pronunciation, both the instrument—that is, the potter’s wheel—and stones.

“And when I saw,” he says, “a vessel being made from clay, it was suddenly spoiled.” God’s providence brought this about, so that the craftsman’s hands, without his knowing it, might represent the parable through their mistake. Again the potter, who had lost the clay vessel while the wheel was turning, made another for himself, as seemed good to him.

Immediately the Lord said to the Prophet: If the potter has such power that from the same clay he can make again what had been spoiled, “shall I not be able to do this with you,” who, so far as depends on you, seem to have perished? To signify free will, he says that he announces both evil to that nation and kingdom or to another, and again good; yet what he has foretold does not necessarily come to pass. On the contrary, good comes to the wicked if they repent, and evil to the good if, after receiving promises, they turn back to sins.

We say this not because God is ignorant of what this or that nation or kingdom will do, but because he leaves a person to his own will, so that by his own will and merit he may receive either rewards or punishments. Yet what happens will not belong wholly to the human being; it will belong also to the grace of him who has bestowed everything. Free will must indeed be preserved in such a way that the grace of the giver excels in all things, according to the prophetic saying: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it keeps watch in vain” (Ps. 126:1–2). For it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9).

(Verses 11–13.) Now therefore say to the man of Judah and to the inhabitant [Manuscripts: “inhabitants,” more correctly] of Jerusalem, saying: Thus [or: “so”] says the Lord: Behold, I am forming evil against you and devising a plan against you. Let each one turn back from his evil way, and direct your ways and your purposes.

But they said: We have despaired [or: “we shall be strengthened”]; for we will follow our own plans, and each of us will do the perversity [or: “what pleases”] of his evil heart [Al. “what pleases his evil heart”]. Therefore thus says the Lord: Ask among the nations who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly.

The Lord fulfills the parable that he had taught both by words and by sight, and says: “Behold, I am forming evil against you,” like a potter forming clay. The evil is understood according to Isaiah, who says: “Making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45:7). It is not that evil is evil in itself, but that it appears evil to those who suffer it. “And I am devising a plan against you,” that is, I am imposing a sentence according to your merit. Change your works and direct your ways, so that punishment may likewise be changed into prosperity.

They, he says, answered in opposition: “We shall be strengthened”—namely, in evil works—or, according to Aquila, “We have despaired,” and according to Symmachus, “We have failed.” Both responses offend God: either one thinks oneself unable to be saved, or one has failed in spirit to appease God. “We will follow,” he says, “our own plans.” [Note: Two manuscripts insert this gloss: “To be noted against the Pelagians.”] Where, then, is the power of free will without God’s grace and the judgment of one’s own will, when it is a grave offense against God to follow one’s own plans and do the will of an evil heart?

Therefore he adds: “Ask among the nations,” and among all the surrounding peoples, “who has done or heard of such a thing while serving idols as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly?” He calls her a virgin because she had served one God, as the Prophet says: “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2).

(Vers. 14.) Will the snow of Lebanon fail from the rock of the field? Or can the waters that burst forth, cold and flowing down, be torn away? The Septuagint: Will breasts fail from the rock, or snow from Lebanon, or will water forcibly carried away by the wind turn aside?

Something similar is conveyed by that Virgilian passage (Eclogue 1:60 and following):

> Before the swift stags will feed in the air,  
> And the sea leave fish naked upon the shore,  
> Than his image slip from my heart.

And elsewhere (Aeneid 1:611 and following):

> While rivers run into the sea, while shadows wander over the mountains,  
> While the sky feeds the stars in its vault,  
> Your honor, name, and praises will always remain.

“How,” he says, “can snow fail from the summits of Lebanon, or be overcome by any heat of the sun so that it all melts? Nor do streams flowing down from the mountains dry up at their sources. In the same way my name, which is stable and everlasting in itself, cannot be changed. Yet while the other things of nature preserve their order, my people have forgotten me.”

It follows:

(Vers. 15.) For my people have forgotten me, offering sacrifices in vain and stumbling in their ways, in the paths of the age [or: “everlasting paths”], so that they might walk along them on an untrodden road.

Whoever forgets God and abandons him, who says, “I am the way” (John 14:6), sacrifices to foreign gods and stumbles in his own ways—not in God’s ways but in his own—and abandons the ancient and everlasting paths worn smooth by the footsteps of all the saints who worship God. But these people walked on an untrodden road. Having abandoned the worship of God, they venerated idols, and because of them the punishment that follows is imposed.

(Vers. 16.) So that their land might become a desolation and an everlasting hissing, and everyone who passes through it will be astonished and shake his head.

Because, he says, they abandoned the worship of God and followed the crooked paths of idolatry, their land was reduced to solitude and to a wonder and hissing for all, so that those who had once seen the land and city flourishing, then collapsed into desert and ash, might marvel and be astonished and indicate the confusion of their soul by a gesture of the body. For this is what shaking the head means: to display the astonishment of the mind by silent gesture [Note: Our manuscripts and Rabanus read “by hissing” instead of “by silence.”]

We understand this more fully and accurately as having been fulfilled after the Lord’s coming, when no Jew is permitted by law to enter the land that was once theirs or the holy city; but when they come to lament, they marvel and mourn over the prophecies of the Prophets, fulfilled in reality.

(Vers. 17.) Like a burning wind I will scatter them before the enemy [or: “enemies”]; I will show them my back and not my face on the day of their destruction.

To this day God’s sentence remains upon the Jews. They have been scattered throughout the whole world before the enemy, the devil, or before hostile demons. Although day and night they invoke God’s name in the synagogues of Satan, God shows them his back and not his face, so that they may understand that he is always departing from them and never coming toward them. The day of the Jews’ destruction is the entire period after the Savior’s Passion, until the end of the age, so that after the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11).

(Vers. 18.) And they said: Come, let us devise plans against Jeremiah; for the Law will not perish from the priest, nor counsel from the wise man, nor speech from the prophet. Come, let us strike him with the tongue, and let us pay no attention to all his words.

This was then the thought of the Jews against Jeremiah, or against the Lord and Savior, and it is today the thought of heretics against his servants: to construct calumnies, forestall holy men with accusations, and give no thought to what truth they speak, but only to what falsehood they themselves construct. For they boast that among their priests, wise men, and false prophets the Law and counsel of God and his utterance remain, although Scripture says: “Wisdom will not enter into a perverse soul” (Wis. 1:4).

(Verses 19 and following.) Attend to me, Lord, and hear the voice of my adversaries. Is evil repaid for good, because they dug a pit for my soul? Remember that I stood in your presence, to speak good on their behalf and turn away your indignation from them.

Therefore give their children over to famine, and deliver them into the hands of the sword. Let their wives be childless and widowed, and let their husbands be put to death. Let their young men be pierced by the sword in battle; let a cry be heard from their houses.

In a type of the Savior, Jeremiah suffers all these things from the Jewish people, who are afterward devastated when Babylon comes. But they are fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ: when the city was overthrown, they were slaughtered by the Roman sword, not because of idolatry, which did not exist at that time, but because of the killing of the Son of God, when the whole people cried out together: “Take him away, take him away; we have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). Their imprecation was fulfilled in eternal condemnation: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

For they had dug a pit for Christ and said: “Let us remove him from the land of the living” (Isa. 53:8). Yet he showed such great mercy toward them [Note: The same manuscripts read: “and stood in the presence of the Father, to speak good on their behalf and turn away his indignation from them.”] that, standing in the presence of the Father, he spoke good on their behalf to turn away his indignation from them, and even on the cross said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

We pass quickly over what is evident, so that we may linger over what is more obscure—not interpreting the ravings of certain people and the captivity of the heavenly Jerusalem, but pursuing the transparent history and clearest prophecy with complete confidence in every word and meaning.

(Verses 22–23.) For you will bring a sudden robber upon them, because they dug a pit to seize me and hid snares for my feet. But you, Lord, know all their counsel against me for death. Do not forgive their iniquity, and do not erase their sin from your sight. Let them become stumbling [or: “falling”] before you; in the time of your wrath, deal with them [or: “act against them”].

If we understand this of Jeremiah, let us refer the sudden robber to Nebuchadnezzar; if of the Savior—which is both truer and better—to the Roman army. And lest God’s sentence appear unjust, he explains what they did against Christ, the Son of God, and what they suffered.

What follows—“Do not forgive their iniquity, and do not erase their sin from your sight”—is by no means contrary to the earlier sentence in which he intercedes with the Father for the people. But after the time granted for repentance had passed, and they persisted in their crime, the people and elders [Note: The words “of the people and elders” are absent from the Cistercian manuscript.] were punished not so much for themselves as for others, lest an unpunished sin harm others by its example.

The statement “Let them become stumbling, or falling, before you” resembles that of Isaiah and the Apostle Peter: “And you will not stumble as against a stone of offense and a rock of scandal” (Isa. 8:14; 1 Pet. 2:8). The Prophet also recalls him in the Psalms: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. This is the Lord’s doing” (Ps. 117:22).

(Chapter 19—Verses 1 and following.) Thus says the Lord: Go [Note: The Vulgate reads: “Take a clay flask of the potter from the elders,” etc.] and take a clay flask of the potter, and take some of the elders of the people and of the elders of the priests; go out to the valley of the son of Ennom, which is beside the entrance of the Potsherd Gate [or: “Charsith”]. And you shall proclaim [or: “cry out,” or “read”] there the words that I shall speak to you, and you shall say: Hear the word of the Lord, kings of Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem.

For the potter’s flask, which is called BOCBOC in Hebrew (), the Septuagint translated “little jar.” For the Potsherd Gate, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion retained the Hebrew word HARSITH (). The Septuagint, according to their custom, added the Greek chi for the aspiration of the Hebrew letter heth, saying Charsith instead of Arsith, just as they say Chebron for Hebron and Jericho for Jericho.

Divine Scripture wishes the people to be taught not only through the ears but also through the eyes. For, as we have already said, what reaches the mind through sight is retained more firmly than what comes through hearing. “Take,” it says, “a clay flask, or little jar, and take some of the elders of the people and of the priests, and go out to the valley of the son of Ennom,” about which we spoke above. There was a shrine of Baal there, as well as a grove and wooded sanctuary watered by the springs of Siloam.

“The valley itself,” it says, “is beside the gate called HARSITH in Hebrew (), that is, ‘Potsherd.’ And you shall proclaim, or read, there the words that I shall speak to you,” so that what I am going to say may be heard there. The reason why “you shall proclaim,” “cry out,” and “read” are all given is that the Hebrew word CARATH () has all three meanings.

He wishes both the kings of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to hear what he is going to say—that is, both the royal line and the entire people—so that those who refuse to hear may be without excuse.

(Verses 4–6.) Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will bring affliction [or: “evils”] upon this place, so that everyone who hears of it will have ringing ears, because they abandoned me, made this place foreign, and offered sacrifices in it to foreign gods whom neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah knew. They filled this place with the blood of the innocent, and built high places for the Baals, to burn their sons with fire as a burnt offering to the Baals—things that I did not command [or: “conceive”], nor speak of, nor did they enter my heart.

Certain foolish people refer this place to the heavenly Jerusalem. To avoid having to warn against this repeatedly, it is enough to say this once: such an explanation—or rather, such a heresy—that overturns clear meanings and attempts to introduce certain deceptions into the Churches of Christ must be avoided.

No one doubts that they placed the idol of Baal in the Temple of God, or in the shrine that was in the valley of the son of Ennom, where there was also a grove of Baal and his altar, upon which they sacrificed and burned their sons. These things the Lord neither conceived nor spoke of, nor did they enter his heart. This does not mean that God did not know the future, but that he says he is ignorant of things unworthy of his knowledge, according to the Gospel saying: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Luke 13:27). For “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19), and “whoever is ignorant will be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38). Or certainly these statements about God are to be understood ἀνθρωποπάθως—that is, figuratively according to human affect—as are other such statements.

Every heretic abandons God and makes the place of God’s dwelling foreign by polluting it with his deceit. He offers sacrifices to foreign gods whom neither he himself knew nor his fathers, namely, the Apostles and apostolic men. The kings of Judah—that is, the patriarchs of the heretics—fill the former place of God with the blood of the deceived and innocent. For unless someone is foolish and simple, he is not easily overthrown. They build high places for the Baals while claiming to debate lofty matters. They burn their sons to an idol, those whom they have begotten in heresy. The Lord says that he knows none of these things and that they have never entered his thoughts.

**(Verse 6.)** Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter.

**The Septuagint:** “Therefore, behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and this place shall no longer be called ruin and the *polyandrion* (“multitude of men”) of the son of Hinnom, [Col. 0801B] but the *polyandrion* (“multitude of men”) of slaughter.””

We have explained above what the valley of the son of Hinnom is, which in Hebrew is called *GEENNOM* (), and from which Gehenna is also thought to have received its name. [Note: [Col. 0801D] See above. Below we restore a passage whose sense is impaired by faulty punctuation.] I wonder what the Septuagint intended by rendering *TOPHETH* () as διάπτωσιν, that is, “ruin,” and “valley” as πολυάνδριον, which signifies “a multitude of men”—unless perhaps because the people fell there and a multitude of men was slain, either spiritually, through the error of idolatry, or literally, by the Babylonian army, as is made clearer in what follows.

**(Verses 7 ff.)** “And I will dissipate the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place, and I will overthrow them by the sword before their enemies and by the hand of those who seek their lives; and I will give their corpses as food to the birds of the sky [Col. 0801C] and to the beasts of the earth; and I will make this city a cause of astonishment and a hissing. Everyone who passes by it will be astonished and will hiss over all its plague. And I will feed them the flesh of their sons and the flesh of their daughters, and each one will eat the flesh of his friend, during the siege and distress in which their enemies and those who seek their lives will confine them.”
