Although we know that these things also happened to the people in the Babylonian captivity, they refer more fully to the times of the Savior, when they were besieged by Vespasian and Titus, and when, in the time of Hadrian, their city collapsed into eternal ashes. Thus those who had offered their sons to idols later, compelled by the necessity of famine, turned them to the use of food, and the flesh of all was given to the birds of the sky and the beasts of the earth: [Col. 0801D] so that those who had abused the Lord’s gifts for impiety and had sacrificed their own entrails to idols made their bellies the tombs of their children.

**(Verses 10, 11.)** “And you shall break the flask in the sight of the men who will go—or depart—with you. And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: So will I break this people and this city, as a potter’s vessel is broken, which cannot be restored again.”

Clearly this is spoken not of the Babylonian but of the Roman captivity. After the Babylonians, the city was rebuilt, the people were brought back to Judea, and restored to their former prosperity. But after the captivity that occurred under Vespasian and Titus, and afterward under Hadrian, the ruins of Jerusalem are to remain until the consummation of the age [Alternative: “remained”], although the Jews think that a golden and jewel-adorned Jerusalem is to be restored, together with sacrifices, the offerings of victims, the marriages of the saints, and the earthly reign of the Lord and Savior. Although we do not follow these beliefs, we cannot condemn them, because many ecclesiastical men and [Note: [Col. 0801D] I have no doubt that Justin Martyr in particular is indicated, in whose mind this opinion took root in the *Dialogue with Trypho*. Nor is there any need to mention the other ecclesiastical writers: Irenaeus, Book V of *Against Heresies*, chapter 32; Tertullian, *On the Hope of the Faithful* and Book III of *Against Marcion*; Lactantius, Book VII, chapters 24 and 26; and others who held the same opinion, which Papias of Hierapolis first introduced. Jerome, with great moderation, advises that, out of regard for their holiness, one should beware of this doctrine of theirs.] martyrs have expressed these views. Let each person abound in his own judgment, and let all things be reserved for the judgment of the Lord (Romans XIV).

But just as an earthen vessel, a clay vessel, when it has been broken, cannot be restored to its former shape, so the Jewish people and Jerusalem, once overthrown, will not possess their former condition. Indeed, today the name of the city itself has been annulled: it is called Aelia after Aelius Hadrian, and along with its former habitation it has also lost its former name, to humble the pride of its inhabitants. The names of the Holy Cross and the Resurrection, however, signify not a city but a place; nor do they signify the former greatness of wealth through which the Jewish people perished, but the glory of holiness, which our poor little Bethlehem possesses—not having gold and jewels, but the bread that was born in it.

**(Verse 12.)** “And they shall bury in Topheth” [or: “they shall bury”], “because there is no other place for burial. So will I do to this place,” says the Lord, “and to its inhabitants, and I will make this city like Topheth” [or: “like ruin”], “and the houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah shall be like the place of Topheth” [or: “of ruin”].

The words inserted in the Septuagint—“All the houses of the kings of Judah shall be like the place of Topheth”—are not found in the Hebrew. And it continues:

**(Verse 13.)** “All the houses are unclean, on whose roofs [or: “terraces”] they sacrificed to all the host of heaven and poured out libations to foreign gods.”

What he had said above—“This place shall no longer be called Topheth and the valley of the son [Alternative: “sons”] of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter”—he now states more explicitly: such slaughter is to occur in that very place that the people will be buried there in heaps, and that the grove [Alternative: “place”] once devoted to worship will become a tumult of the dead. The city itself, which overlooks this place, will become like Topheth, for which the Septuagint translated “ruin.” The houses of Jerusalem and the palaces of the kings will likewise be turned into similar ruins. The reason is given: they were unclean and polluted by the crime of idolatry, because on their roofs and terraces they sacrificed to the sun, moon, and stars of heaven and burned incense; nor were they content with this error, [Col. 0803A] but sacrificed to demons and poured out libations to foreign gods (Zephaniah I).

**(Verses 14, 15.)** Then Jeremiah came from Topheth, where the Lord had sent him to prophesy, and stood in the court of the house of the Lord and said to all the people: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I am bringing upon this city and upon all its towns all the evils that I have spoken against it, because they have stiffened their neck, so as not to hear my words.”

After Jeremiah had broken the flask, or little jar, in Topheth in the presence of the elders of the people whom he had brought with him, and had prophesied in the words of the Lord concerning the crushing of the people and the city of Jerusalem, he returns and stands in the court of the house of the Lord and speaks to the whole multitude, which [Col. 0803B] had not wished to go to Topheth, saying that the Lord would bring upon the city of Jerusalem and upon all its towns all the evils that he had spoken against it. And lest we think the sentence cruel, he gives the reasons why he will bring the evils. “Because,” he says, “they have stiffened their neck, so as not to hear my words”—not even wishing to repent after so many acts of impiety.

**(Chapter XX.—Verses 1, 2.)** “And Phassur, son of Emmer, the priest who had been appointed chief in the house of the Lord, heard Jeremiah prophesying these words. And Phassur struck the prophet Jeremiah and put him in the stocks that were at the upper gate of Benjamin, in the house of the Lord.”

For *Phassur*, the Septuagint translated *Phascor*, which is interpreted as “blackness of mouth”; and for the stocks, as we have called them, the Septuagint and Theodotion rendered *cataracten*, while Symmachus used βασανιστήριον [Note: [Col. 0803D] This suggests that Symmachus’s version existed in two forms.] or στρεβλωτήριον, both of which signify instruments of torture.

We have used “stocks” according to common usage, because we also read of this kind of torment in the Acts of the Apostles, when the apostles Paul and Silas were placed in the custody of the prison (Acts XVI). This man was the high priest of the Temple, and, having been entrusted with the dignity of the priesthood, he abuses it perversely—not to teach and rebuke by speech, but to terrify by tortures (John XIX). Hence both the Savior and the apostle Paul are beaten at the high priest’s command (Acts XVI). Nor is it surprising if today the servants of God are killed [Alternative: “beaten”] by Phascor, sent into prison, and kept in a horrible confinement. For this power is given by God, so that the faith of the prophets may be displayed. [Col. 0803D] Yet the one who beats is not greater; rather, the one who is beaten is stronger. The Prophet patiently accepts God’s judgment and does not protest against the blows, but considers the one giving the command.

*EMMER* () means “word,” from which blackness often arises—not through the fault of the parent, but through the crime of one who has degenerated. The instrument of torture by which the Prophet is tormented appears to be on the right side, which is interpreted as Benjamin; and at the high gate, which indicates not truth but the unjust power of the priest.

**(Verse 3.)** When morning came, Phassur brought Jeremiah out of the stocks, and Jeremiah said to him: [Col. 0804A] “The Lord has not called your name Phassur, but Terror on every side.”

Here, too, all have interpreted both the priest’s name and the kind of torture in the same way as above. The priest’s name is changed so that the future punishment may be indicated by the name. [Note: Victor: “the future punishment”; and shortly afterward, “will have the name ‘blackness of mouth.’”] “You shall no longer,” he says, “have blackness of mouth and the rule of unjust power; instead, you will be led captive to Babylon.” For this is what “terror on every side,” or “all around,” signifies: that, trembling and uncertain of your own safety, you will look about in every direction and fear the enemies advancing against you.

For “terror,” which is written in Hebrew *MAGUR* [Alternative: *Magor*] (), the Septuagint and Theodotion translated μέτοικον, that is, “one who migrates”; the second edition of Aquila, “a stranger,” and the first, “one who looks around”; Symmachus, “removed,” or “gathered and compelled.” [Col. 0804B]

**(Verses 4–6.)** “For thus says the Lord: Behold, I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends, and they will fall by the sword of their enemies, and your eyes will see it. And I will give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will lead them away to Babylon and strike them with the sword. And I will give all the wealth [or: “strength”] of this city, all its labor, and all its value [or: “glory”], and all the treasures of the kings of Judah, into the hand of their enemies; and they will plunder them, take them, and lead them to Babylon. But you, Phassur, and all the inhabitants of your house, shall go into captivity; you shall come to Babylon, and there you shall die and there be buried—you and all your friends to whom you prophesied falsely.”

According to the interpretation given above, by which Phassur’s name was changed so that he would be called *Magur* [Alternative: *Magor*], all have likewise translated the word to signify either terror, or migration, or removal and transfer, and [Note: [Col. 0804D] I would prefer *commigration*, following the Vatican manuscript. On this matter compare what the holy Father repeats concerning Phassur at the end of this book and of chapter 23.] gathering.

He threatens him and his friends, who are now on the point of being captured and handed over to the enemies, and the entire people of the tribe of Judah, who are to fall into the hands of the king of Babylon. Some will be killed by the sword, others led into captivity; all the wealth both of the city and of the royal treasuries will be seized by the enemies. Phassur himself, with his entire kin and household, will be led into captivity and will die in Babylon, because he deceived his people with a lie, promising them through falsehood not true and grievous things but prosperity.

At the same time, the Prophet’s patience and prudence must be observed: although sent into prison, he remains silent and overcomes the injury by silence. Yet he does not conceal what he knows is going to happen, so that perhaps the false-prophet priest may cease from sinning and implore God’s mercy.

**(Verses 7, 8.)** “You have deceived me, Lord, and I have been deceived” [or: “You enticed me, Lord, and I was enticed”]. “You were stronger than I and prevailed” [or: “overcame and were able”]. “I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me. For long ago I have spoken, crying out against iniquity, and I proclaim devastation” [or, according to the Septuagint: “Because with my bitter word I shall laugh at transgression, and I shall call for misery”].

The Prophet says that he was deceived by the Lord because, hearing at the beginning, “I have appointed you as a prophet to the nations” (above, I, 5), and again, “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and overthrow, to build and to plant” (ibid., 10), he supposed that he would say nothing against the people of the Jews, but against the various nations surrounding them. For this reason he gladly accepted the prophetic office. But the opposite occurred: while proclaiming the captivity of Jerusalem, he endured persecutions and afflictions.

As for what he adds, “I have become a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me,” this is because they think that he has lied about everything and that all the things he foretold would happen were false. The Prophet had immediately supposed that what the Lord threatened would come to pass, while the people thought that what had not come immediately would never come.

I cry out about the Babylonian devastation and the iniquity of the enemies by which my people are to be oppressed. But if we follow the Septuagint in what they said—“With my bitter word I shall laugh at transgression, and I shall call for misery”—the sense is this: I know that present sadness will be changed into future joy, according to what is written, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall laugh” (Matthew V, 5). Therefore I willingly endure misery, iniquity, and affliction, so that I even desire and call for them, and compensate for the brevity of the injury with the eternity of happiness.

**(Verses 9, 10.)** “For the word of the Lord has become for me a reproach and a mockery all day long. And I said: I will not remember it” [or: “I will not name the Lord”], “and I will no longer speak in his name. And it became in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones, and I grew weak” [or: “I was dissolved”], “unable to bear it. For I heard the insults [or: “reproach”] of many and terror on every side” [or: “of those gathered from every side”]. “Persecute, and let us persecute him.”

When I cried out and said that the Babylonian army was already coming and that the hostile sword was plundering everything, the word of the Lord became for me a reproach and a mockery, because they thought the delay in the prophecy proved it false. Therefore I resolved in my mind to speak no further to the people of God and to name his name no longer.

When, overcome by shame, I had made this timid but foolish decision, “it became,” he says, “in my heart like a burning fire, shut up in my bones”; or, “I was dissolved on every side,” so that I could not bear it. For once the divine word has been conceived in the mind but not uttered by the mouth, it burns in the breast.

Hence Paul also says: “If I preach the gospel, this gives me no ground for boasting, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship” (1 Corinthians IX, 16–17). And in Athens, seeing a city devoted to idolatry, “his spirit was stirred within him,” and he burned with his whole mind (Acts XVII). A little later in the same book we read: “When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ” (Acts XVIII).

Many teachers in the Church likewise endure similar things to this day, hearing the reproach of many gathered against them on every side and saying: “Persecute, and let us persecute them.”

**(Verse 11.)** “All the men who were at peace with me” [Alternative: “By all the men who were at peace with me”] “and who guarded my flank: perhaps he may be deceived, and we may prevail against him and take revenge upon him. But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior.”

When adversaries rise up, and former friends and those who were once peaceful turn to warfare and wish to lay ambushes for us, let us not be overly concerned; rather, let us desire to say what the Prophet says: “But the Lord is with me like a mighty warrior.”

[Col. 0806B] “Therefore those who persecute me will fall and become weak” [or: “Therefore they persecuted, but could not understand”]. “Let them be greatly confounded, because they did not understand everlasting disgrace” [or: “shame”], “which will never be erased.”

Because they persecuted him, they were unable to understand the prophetic word, and profound confusion followed their ignorance. They did not understand the everlasting disgrace that will possess them and never be erased by any forgetfulness.

Let those who were once peaceful, who guarded my flank and desired to deceive me, say what they wish, provided that after the persecution the just man and teacher of the Church receive such vengeance and such rewards.

**(Verse 12.)** “But you, Lord of hosts, tester of the righteous” [or: “who tests what is just”], “who see the kidneys and the heart, let me, I beg you, see your vengeance upon them, for to you I have revealed my cause” (Luke VI).

The Lord alone knows how to test righteousness, just as he alone sees the inner things of the heart. Hence Jesus, knowing human thoughts, is not God by progress, as some think, but by nature. Something similar also sounds in the Psalms: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Psalm CXLII, 2). If one who lives in virtues will not be justified, how much less one who is dead because of sins?

Although he knows that God is the defender of the righteous, nevertheless, through the impatience of human weakness, he already desires to see what he knows will come. He has revealed his cause to the one who says elsewhere: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord” (Deuteronomy XXXII, 35). Blessed is the conscience whose cause is revealed to the Lord (Hebrews X, 30), since the Apostle says: “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Ephesians V, 13).

**(Verse 13.)** “Sing to the Lord, praise the Lord, because he has delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of the wickedest” [Vulgate: “the wicked”].

The one who is poor in spirit and does not possess the riches that have received their consolation in this world—concerning which Paul also says, “Only that we should remember the poor” (1 Corinthians XIII)—when he has obtained vengeance from the Lord, praises the Lord in spirit and glories in having been rescued from the hand of the wickedest.

All this happens not through our merit but through the grace of him who has delivered the poor man, who does not possess the wealth of collapsing pride but the humility of the poor man who has been delivered.

[Col. 0807A] **(Verses 14 ff.)** “Cursed be the day on which I was born; let not the day on which my mother bore me be blessed. Cursed be the man” [or: “the human being”] “who announced to my father, saying, ‘A male child has been born to you,’ and gladdened him as though with joy. Let that man be like the cities that the Lord overthrew and did not repent of; let him hear a cry in the morning and a wailing at midday—because he did not kill me in the womb, so that my mother might be my tomb and her womb an eternal conception. Why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in confusion?”

Those who think that souls existed in heaven and were cast from a better into a worse condition use this and similar testimonies, arguing that it was better to remain in heaven than to dwell on earth and assume a body of humiliation. They seek new arguments—or rather, already old ones—for their heresy.

But we, reading that of blessed Job, “Cursed be the day on which I was born, and the night on which they said, ‘Behold, a male child’” (Job III, 3), and, “Cursed be the man who announced to my father, saying, ‘A child has been born to you,’” adapt this testimony to the meaning that it is better not to exist than to live in punishments, according to what is written: “Death is rest for a man whose way God has closed” (Ecclesiasticus XXII, 11). And again: “Why was light given to the miserable, and life to those who are in bitterness of soul?” (Job III, 20). And in the Gospel we read simply: “It would have been better for him if he had not been born” (Matthew XXVI, 24)—not that there is anyone who has not been born, but that it is better not to exist than to exist badly.

For it is one thing to be altogether nonexistent and another, while existing, to be tortured without any interruption. In this way we prefer a peaceful death to a miserable life. Hence Amos calls the day a day of darkness, a day of affliction (Amos V). And Jacob, because he lived in labor and distress, calls the days of his life few and evil (Genesis XLVII). The apostle Paul says, “To deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians I, 4), and again, “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (Ephesians V, 16).

The Hebrews, by certain intricate and unbelievable arguments, reckon the fifth month—the month in which Jerusalem was captured and the Temple overthrown—as belonging to Jeremiah’s birth. If they can prove this, I do not know how they will be able to interpret the testimony of Job—unless perhaps they also claim that that day, through a certain prefiguration and prophecy of future events, referred to the overthrow of the Temple.

As for the imprecation that the man should be like the cities that were overthrown, I think this refers to Sodom and Gomorrah, and to a time wholly given to mourning, so that there would be a cry in the morning and a wailing at midday. As for the words, “Who did not kill me in the womb,” they think that God is signified. “So that,” he says, “my conception might be eternal”—all of which is spoken hyperbolically. Finally, he explains the reasons why he prefers death to life, and nonexistence to an evil existence, adding: “Why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow, and for my days to be consumed in confusion?”

**(Chapter XXI.—Verses 1 ff.)** The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord when King Zedekiah sent to him Phassur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, saying: “Inquire of the Lord for us, because Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is warring against us. Perhaps the Lord will act toward us according to all his wonders, and withdraw from us.”

Above, the priest Phassur, or Phascor, who struck Jeremiah, had Emmer as his father (above, XX). But this Phassur is the son of Malchiah. This is stated so that no one may think they are the same person.

King Zedekiah sends to the Prophet, not wishing either the people or the princes to know, so that through messengers he may secretly discover what judgment the Lord holds concerning the city of Jerusalem and the people of the Jews. The statement, “Because Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, is warring against us,” shows that Jerusalem was already under siege and that Zedekiah asked the Prophet about this.

It should be noted that in the Prophets, especially in Ezekiel and Jeremiah, the order of kings and times is by no means preserved. Rather, what happened later according to history is sometimes related earlier, and what happened earlier later. For it is one thing to write history and another to write prophecy. Thus in the present passage Zedekiah, who was captured with the city of Jerusalem, is said to have sent to Jeremiah at the time when Jerusalem was under siege; afterward the history of his brother Jehoiakim, who was king before him, is related, and then that of Jehoiachin—that is, Jeconiah—who was the son of Jehoiakim. These matters will be discussed below.

**(Verses 3 ff.)** And Jeremiah said to them: “Thus you shall say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel: Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war [or: “the instruments of battle”] that are in your hands and with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans, who are besieging you around the walls. And I will gather them” [or: “these things”] “in the middle of this city, and I will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm” [or: “an exalted arm”], “in fury, indignation, and great wrath. And I will strike the inhabitants of this city; men and animals will die of a great pestilence.”

“You struggle uselessly,” he says, “against the Chaldeans who are besieging you, and you prepare weapons of war whose only use you will have in the middle of the city, so that you may appear to be armed. But while they besiege you, I will fight against you with an outstretched hand and a strong arm, and I will strike you with my fury and indignation, so that both you and every living thing will die in the middle of the city from famine and pestilence.”

We read that this indeed happened. For without any crown or clamor of combatants, so great a city was captured by siege that there were none for the conquerors to defeat, but only people for them to seize. “Better,” he says, “were those pierced by the sword than those slain by famine.”

**(Verse 7.)** “And after this, says the Lord: I will give Zedekiah, king of Judah, and his servants and his people, and those who remain in this city after the pestilence, the sword, and the famine, into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies, and into the hand of those who seek their lives. And he will strike them with the edge of the sword, and he will not turn aside, nor spare, nor have mercy.”

The words that we translated, “into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and into the hand of their enemies,” are not found in the Septuagint. And for what we said, “He will not turn aside, nor spare, nor have mercy,” the Septuagint translated, “I will not spare, nor will I have mercy.”

The Hebrew is better, so that the cruel and inflexible sentence may appear to belong more to the king of Babylon than to the Lord. First the prophecy was made concerning the whole city; now it is pronounced specifically against Zedekiah and his people who remain after the pestilence, sword, and famine: they will be captured by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and killed with the sword together with their friends. They should expect no mercy from one whose covenant and relationship they abandoned through perjury.

**(Verses 8 ff.)** “And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death. Whoever remains in this city will die by the sword, famine, and pestilence. But whoever goes out and defects to the Chaldeans who are besieging you will live, and his life will be like spoil to him. For I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good, says the Lord. It will be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire.”

To those who had been sent by the king and had come to the Prophet to implore him to inquire of the Lord on their behalf, he had given the preceding answer, telling them what they should report to King Zedekiah. Now he urges them to reply to the people and gives the advice that they should defect to the Chaldeans, against the king’s wishes—a course whose danger to the Prophet no one is unaware of. Hence he also imprecates death upon himself and says, “Cursed be the day on which I was born” (Jeremiah XX, 14), and, “Why did I come forth from the womb, to see labor and sorrow?” (ibid., 18).

This is not because it is easy, while they have not yet been captured, to advise them to hand themselves over voluntarily to captivity—as though those who are about to suffer shipwreck were ordered, before the shipwreck and the breaking apart of the ship, to seize the oars and planks and commit themselves to the waves—but because it is more bearable, however captured, to remain alive than to be consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence.

Some explain this passage allegorically in the following way: it is better to hand oneself over to secular disciplines, and especially to philosophy, than to remain in that Church in which there is a famine of the word of God, and in which the whole people are dying through the sword of heretics’ teaching, the scarcity of doctrine, and the pestilence of heresy.

**(Verses 11, 12.)** “And to the house of the king of Judah: Hear the word of the Lord, house of David. Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor, lest perhaps my indignation go forth” [or: “so that my indignation may not go forth”] “like a fire and be kindled, and there be no one to extinguish it, because of the wickedness of your practices.”

[Note: [Col. 0809D] I would prefer, following the Cistercian and Vatican manuscripts, that the words “because of the wickedness of your practices” be silent here, since they are superfluous here and immediately afterward are given in their proper place, in a sense entirely consonant with Jerome’s thought.] The words that follow, “because of the wickedness of your practices,” are not found in the Septuagint.

Since he had said above, “And to this people you shall say: Thus says the Lord,” he now appropriately adds, “and to the house of the king of Judah.” The words “you shall say, Thus says the Lord” are to be understood; for by a common construction [ἀπὸ κοινοῦ], the preceding and following clauses are joined. The sense is: “And to this people you shall say, Thus says the Lord.” The speech is now directed specifically to the royal house, chiefly because of whose guilt the city is under siege, so that it may correct its error through repentance and obtain the Lord’s mercy.

“Judge,” he says, “judgment in the morning”—not in the darkness of iniquity but in the light of righteousness. “Rescue the oppressed from the hand of the oppressor,” so that you do not show partiality in judgment, but so that when the rich oppress the poor, God’s command may have greater force with you than the power of the persecutor.

“And if,” he says, “you do this, the fire of my fury will not be kindled among you, nor will it find material to consume.”

In this passage the incredible mercy of God is shown: although he had said above, “I have set my face against this city for evil and not for good; it will be handed over to the king of Babylon, and he will burn it with fire” [Alternative: “the fire”], now, with the sentence of the Lord already impending, he calls them to salvation.

This is not because he does not know that the city of Jerusalem is to be captured, but because human freedom of choice is preserved, so that they may appear to perish not through ignorance of the future but through their own will. In the same way the Savior knew that the Apostle would deny him and that he would be crucified—for he had often foretold this to the Apostles—and nevertheless warned them, wishing to correct them toward repentance, so that whatever they afterward suffered might happen through their own fault and not through the harshness of the one who threatened.

**(Verses 13, 14.)** “Behold, I am against you, inhabitress of the solid and level valley,” says the Lord, “you who say, ‘Who will strike us?’” [or: “Who will terrify us?”] “And who will enter our houses? And I will visit upon you”—the words that follow, “according to the fruit of your practices, says the Lord,” are not found in the Septuagint—“and I will kindle a fire in her forest, and it will devour everything around her.”

For “inhabitress of the solid and level valley,” the Septuagint translated, “Behold, I am against you who dwell in the valley of *SOR* (), in the plain.” For this Symmachus used “rock,” Theodotion “besieged,” Aquila’s first edition “solid,” and the second “Tyre.” For *Sor*, or *Sur*, in the Hebrew language signifies both Tyre and flint and [Note: [Col. 0810D] In the Vatican manuscript: “and it signifies ‘constrained.’”] a constrained place.

He speaks against Jerusalem, which has been surrounded by a siege; or, in the likeness of Tyre, it is enclosed as though by a great sea, so that it is surrounded by the Babylonian army and cannot escape. Or perhaps it is a city that thinks itself, like a very hard rock, impregnable and strong because of the solidity of its walls and its size, and says, “Who will be able to terrify us? And who will enter our houses?” Yet God speaks in opposition: “I will visit you; you will not be able to escape my eye.”

“I will visit you,” however, “for destruction, and I will repay you according to the fruit of your wickedness. And I will kindle a fire in your forest. Not the Babylonian, as you suppose, not the king of the Chaldeans, but my wrath will accomplish all these things.”

He calls Jerusalem and the entire surrounding region a forest because it has no fruit-bearing trees of good works and has been prepared for burning. Beautifully he calls it a level valley because it is accessible to enemies, and not a lofty mountain, which is difficult to climb, according to what is also said in Isaiah: “The vision of the valley of Zion” (Isaiah XXII, 1).

Whatever is prophesied concerning the royal house and the metropolitan city, let us refer to the ecclesiastical order and to the rulers of the Churches—those, at least, who have given themselves over to pride, riches, and licentiousness. Let them not immediately be freed from destruction merely because theirs is a royal house. Likewise, among those descended from David, very few are found who pleased the Lord as David himself did—Hezekiah and Josiah—while a large part of the rulers and royal lineage provoked the Lord’s wrath against the whole people.

## Chapter XXII

### Verses 1 ff.

“Thus says the Lord: Go down to the house of the king of Judah, and there speak this word, and say: Hear the word of the Lord, O king of Judah, who sit upon the throne of David—you and your servants and your people, who enter through these gates.

“Thus says the Lord: Do justice and righteousness, and rescue the oppressed from the hand of the slanderer; do not grieve the resident alien, the orphan, or the widow, and do not oppress them unjustly [or: impiously]; and do not shed innocent blood in this place. For if you truly do this word, kings sitting upon David’s throne and descended from him will enter through the gates of this house, riding in chariots and upon horses—they and their servants and their people. But if you do not heed these words, I swear by myself, says the Lord, that this house will become a desolation.”

This vision—or rather, this word of the Lord—is either given to the Prophet before Zedekiah sent messengers to him, or certainly, after he instructed the messengers what they ought to report to the king, Jeremiah is commanded not to speak to the king through messengers, but to go himself to the palace and speak to him there. At the same time, let us observe the divine wisdom: through messengers he commands that grievous things be announced, mixed with promises of prosperity if the king should wish to repent.

[Note: The Cistercian text has, conversely: “through messengers he forbids grievous things,” and so forth.]

Here, however, because Jeremiah himself is ordered to go, he does not announce grievous things and the captivity that is already at hand; rather, he warns him what he must do in order to avert the sentence of God that threatens him. It is proper to kings to do justice and righteousness, to rescue those oppressed by violence from the hand of slanderers, and to offer assistance to the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow, who are more easily oppressed by the powerful. And in order to impress upon them a greater concern for God’s commands, he adds: “Do not grieve them”—so that they should not merely refrain from rescuing them, but should not even allow them, through their own connivance, to be grieved by others.

“And do not shed innocent blood in this place.” For punishing murderers, sacrilegious persons, and poisoners is not the shedding of blood but the administration of the laws.

“If,” he says, “you do these things, O kings of Judah, you will retain your former power, and you will enter the gates of Jerusalem with pomp. But if you do not wish to do them, O royal house, it will not be so much the Lord’s cruelty as your own will that reduces the entire city to a desolation.”

Whatever was said to the royal house, bishops, their fellow presbyters and deacons, and the entire ecclesiastical order should understand as applying to themselves: if they do what has been commanded, and among other things do not shed innocent blood by scandalizing the least and striking the consciences of individuals, let them retain the dignity entrusted to them by the Lord. But if they do not wish to do these things and despise them, let them themselves reduce the Church of God to a desolation.

Those descended from David enter through the gates of Jerusalem and sit upon his throne—he is interpreted as “strong of hand”—and they ascend chariots and horses when they restrain both their own disturbances and those of the people, enter the Church with ordered step, and are accompanied by a choir of many virtues singing harmoniously on every side.

And so that we may believe this to be true, he swears by himself, because, according to the Apostle, he has no greater by whom he might swear (Hebrews 6).

### Verses 6–8

“For thus says the Lord concerning the house [or: to the house] of the king of Judah:

“‘Gilead, you are to me the summit [or: the beginning] of Lebanon. If I do not make you a desolation, uninhabited cities! And I will consecrate [another reading: build] against you a destroyer, a man and his weapons; and they will cut down your choice cedars and cast them [another reading: throw them] into the fire. And many nations will pass through this city, and each person will say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord done this to this great city? And they will answer: Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord their God, worshiped foreign gods, and served them.’”

Scripture recalls Gilead, possessed by half the tribe of Manasseh, as lying beyond the Jordan. On this mountain Laban overtook Jacob as he fled, and, according to Genesis, the mountain received the name *sōros* (σωρός), that is, “heap” or “mound of testimony,” because Jacob and Laban swore there after gathering stones into a heap (Genesis 31).

It is the summit—or beginning—of Lebanon, the lofty mountain planted throughout with cedars, in accordance with David’s song: “The Lord will shake the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 28:5). And elsewhere: “I saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon” (Psalm 36:35). And in Zechariah we read: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars” (Zechariah 11:1).

Therefore, in the present passage, because he was speaking to the royal house, he speaks metaphorically to the Temple—or to the house of the tribe of Judah—either because it itself is on high, or because from the Temple and sanctuary remedies for all sins were sought. Hence this same Prophet also says: “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there? Why has healing not risen for the daughter of my people?” (above, 8:21).

He therefore threatens the royal house, the city of Jerusalem, and the Temple—which he calls the summit of Lebanon—that it will be reduced to a desolation together with all its cities. This will happen not through the power of the king of Babylon but at the Lord’s command, who says: “I will consecrate against you a destroyer.”

Nebuchadnezzar and his entire army are called “holy,” because they execute the sentence of God. “And they will cut down,” he says, “your choice cedars”: the powerful and the rulers of the city. “And they will cast them into the fire,” so that the all-devouring flame may consume everything.

When everything has been destroyed, many nations will pass through the city and the Temple, which previously they were not permitted to enter. Each person will say to his neighbor: Why has the Lord brought such a sudden and such great overthrow upon this famous and great city? Those who are questioned will answer and explain the causes of the ruins, saying: Because they abandoned the covenant of the Lord their God and worshiped idols instead of God.

Let the royal house of our own city hear this also, along with its rulers and its cedars, which raise their crowns to the clouds and speak in their pride: “Who will see?” Let them understand that they will quickly be consumed by the Lord’s flame if they refuse to submit to his commands.

The sanctification [another reading: sacrifice] of the destroyer and his weapons is one thing; that of the priests and those who minister to the Lord is another.

### Verses 10–11

“Do not weep for the dead, nor mourn over him; weep bitterly for the one who goes away, because he will not return again, nor will he see the land of his birth.

“For thus says the Lord concerning Shallum, son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father, who went out from this place: He will not return here again, but in the place to which I have transported him, there he will die, and he will not see this land again.”

[The Vulgate reads “of the king” rather than “king.”]

Josiah, the righteous king, had three sons: Jehoahaz, Jehoiakim, and Zedekiah. The first of these was taken captive to Egypt by Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, and died there; in his place he established Eliakim [another reading: Jehoiakim], his brother, as king (2 Kings 23–25).

After Jehoiakim’s death, his son Jeconiah reigned. He was taken into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, together with his mother and the rulers. In his place his uncle Zedekiah reigned. After Jerusalem was captured, Zedekiah was taken to Babylon.

The question therefore arises: who is this person for whom one should not weep, who is to be led into captivity and will not return again, when three were captured and deported?

The Hebrews think that this applies to all of them—to Jehoahaz, Jeconiah, and Zedekiah—and that all are called sons of Josiah, “Sellem” or “Sellum” (), which is interpreted as “completion” or “consummation,” because the kingdom of Judah ended in them.

I, however, think that this is properly said of Zedekiah, concerning whom the prophecy of both the present and the preceding chapter is given. Under him the kingdom of Judah truly ended, and under him the city was captured; he was taken to Babylon, where he is recorded as having died.

This is Shallum—that is, “completion” and “consummation”—son of Josiah, king of Judah, who reigned in place of Josiah his father. Jeconiah, however, was not Josiah’s son but his grandson, the son of Jehoiakim. Thus, from the beginning of the vision, when King Zedekiah sent to Jeremiah Pashhur son of Malchiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest, down to this chapter, we should understand everything as being said to the king and about King Zedekiah (above, chapter 21).

### Verses 12 ff.

“Woe to him who builds his house in injustice and his upper rooms without justice; who oppresses his friend for nothing [the Vulgate adds: ‘and does not pay him’] and does not give him his wages; who says, ‘I will build myself a spacious house and airy upper rooms,’ who opens windows for himself, makes cedar-paneled ceilings, and paints them with vermilion. Will you reign because you compete with the cedar? Did not your father eat and drink, and do justice and righteousness? Then it was well with him. He judged the cause of the poor and needy for their good. Was this not because he knew me? says the Lord. But your eyes and your heart are directed toward greed, toward the shedding of innocent blood, toward oppression, and toward the pursuit of evil action.”

The Septuagint reads:

“O you who build your house without justice and your upper rooms without judgment! Your neighbor works for him without payment, and he does not give him his wages. You built yourself a small house, upper rooms open to the wind, distinguished by windows, ceiled with cedar, and painted with vermilion. Will you reign because you contend against your father Ahaz? They will neither eat nor drink. It would have been better [another reading: ‘it will be better’] for you to do good justice and righteousness. They did not know; they did not judge the judgment of the humble, nor the judgment of the poor. Is this not your failure to know me? says the Lord. Behold, your eyes are not right, nor is your heart good, but they are directed toward your greed, toward shedding innocent blood, toward wickedness and murder, so that you may do these things.”

I have set down both editions in full, so that both the Hebrew truth and the difficulty of the Vulgate edition may more easily be recognized.

The passage is directed against Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah. We spoke above about him: Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, established him in place of his brother Jehoahaz, whom he had taken bound to Egypt.

We read—as the history narrated both in Kings and in Chronicles relates (2 Kings 23–24; 2 Chronicles 36)—that Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, reigned eleven years in Jerusalem, that he reigned cruelly, was wicked, and later died. Yet his burial is not recounted, although Sacred Scripture has the custom of reporting all kings both as dead and as buried. In his case, however, it specifically reports that he died but was not buried. We shall speak of this in what follows [another reading: “in the subsequent discussion”].

He therefore laments the king mentioned above because he trusts in injustice, thinks that royal dignity is perpetual, builds upper rooms for himself, oppresses his friends, does not pay those who work for him their wages, and considers the construction of his palace eternal.

“Will you be able to reign forever,” says the divine word, “because you wish to make yourself comparable to the lofty cedar—to your father Josiah, that is, the righteous king?”

“Your father,” he says, “ate and drank and enjoyed royal wealth; yet he did not offend God by possessing riches. Rather, he pleased him because he did justice and righteousness. Therefore it was well with him both in the present age and will be well with him in the age to come.

“He judged the cause of the poor and needy,” and for the refreshment of those whom he heard, and specifically for his own good. All these things prospered for him because he knew me, says the Lord.

But your eyes, O Jehoiakim, turn toward greed, toward shedding innocent blood, toward oppression, and toward the pursuit of evil action.

As for the Septuagint, I cannot understand what sense they have. Although the remaining elements agree with them to some extent, the statement that follows—“Will you reign because you contend against your father Ahaz?”—for which the Hebrew has *Araz* (), and this word means “cedar,” plainly has no intelligible sense.

The following statement likewise—“They will neither eat nor drink”—and the other words, which are so scattered and confused among themselves, have no intelligible meaning apart from the truth of the Hebrew reading.

We can understand this passage, according to the allegorical sense, as directed against heretics. They build for themselves not a great house, broad with the abundance of the Church, but a small one. They build it not with justice and judgment, desiring to seize what belongs to others.

Hence it says: “You built yourself a small house, upper rooms open to the wind,” rooms carried about by every wind of doctrine and distinguished by windows. They do not possess a lasting structure or solid firmness.

“And ceiled with cedar,” it says. They seem indeed to have a most beautiful ceiling, but in the rains and storms of persecutions it quickly rots and collapses.

“And painted with vermilion.” They too promise the Lord’s passion and blood; yet they do not reign forever, because they contend with and provoke to anger *Araz*, that is, their father, the cedar.

Every heretic is born in the Church, but is cast out from the Church; he contends and fights against his parent.

And when it adds, “They will neither eat nor drink,” the Body and Blood of the Savior are understood, along with other things of the same kind.

It says that the entire error arises from their not having known God and from their not having straight eyes, while their heart is inclined toward greed, so that they may seize what belongs to others and shed the blood of those whom they have deceived. For this is to commit murder.

Obscure matters must be discussed at greater length.

### Verses 18–19

“Therefore thus says the Lord concerning Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah:

“They will not mourn for him, saying, ‘Alas, brother!’ or ‘Alas, sister!’ They will not cry out for him, saying, ‘Alas, lord!’ or ‘Alas, illustrious one!’ He will be buried with the burial of a donkey, rotting and cast away outside the gates of Jerusalem.”

The words that we have placed from the Hebrew—“They will not mourn for him, saying, ‘Alas, brother!’ or ‘Alas, sister!’”—are not found in the Septuagint.

The passage is specifically directed against Jehoiakim, king of Judah, and the riddle that previously seemed hidden and uncertain among three brothers is disclosed: the passage is not about Jehoahaz, nor about Zedekiah, but specifically about Jehoiakim. The Hebrew history says that he was killed by bands of Chaldeans, Syrians, Ammonites, and Moabites.

Hence in the Books of Kings he is written of as dead, while his burial is left unmentioned (2 Kings 24). In the Book of Chronicles we read that he was bound with chains and taken to Babylon (2 Chronicles 36), and nothing further is reported about him.

Appropriately, it says that he will be buried with the burial of a donkey, signifying in other words that he will remain unburied—that is, he will be torn apart by beasts and birds. For this is the burial of a donkey.

[Note: We have removed here the word “is resolved,” which was superfluous; neither the Vatican manuscript nor Rabanus reads it.]

### Verses 20 ff.

“Go up to Lebanon and cry out; raise your voice in Bashan, and cry out to the passersby, because all your lovers have been crushed. I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, ‘I will not listen.’ This has been your way from your youth, because you did not listen to my voice. The wind will pasture all your shepherds [or: lovers], and your lovers [or: friends] will go into captivity. Then you will be ashamed and embarrassed because of all your wickedness.

“You who sit in Lebanon and nest among the cedars, how you have groaned when pains came upon you, pains like those of a woman in labor!”

By the metaphor of Lebanon and Bashan—regions and mountains beyond the Jordan—the word is directed to Jerusalem: it had trusted in Egypt in vain. Or it is directed to Jehoiakim himself, who at that time reigned in Jerusalem and had been appointed king by the Egyptians: he hoped in vain for Egyptian aid, since they too would be overcome by the king of Babylon and led into captivity (2 Kings 23).

When it says, “I spoke to you,” this means that God himself spoke through the Prophets. Or it may mean, “They spoke to you,” with my Prophets understood. And you, in your prosperity, said, “I will not listen.” He accuses her of arrogance and of having abused the abundance of her wealth in contempt of God.

He relates that she had not listened to God’s voice not only at this time but from the beginning, when she was brought out of Egypt. Hence all her shepherds and rulers were scattered here and there and submitted their necks to Babylonian captivity.

The statement that follows—“You who sit in Lebanon and nest among the cedars”—rebukes the arrogance that had grown out of the abundance of all things, and indicates that, like a woman in labor, sudden pain and unexpected captivity would come upon her.

What we have rendered, “Cry out to the passersby,” is written in Hebrew as *MEABARIM* (). The Septuagint and Theodotion translated it “across the sea”; Symmachus, “from the opposite side,” indicating that the Prophet’s voice should reach from Jerusalem as far as Mount Lebanon and Bashan.

### Verses 24 ff.

“As I live, says the Lord: Even if Coniah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, were a signet ring on my right hand, I would tear him away from there [or: you]; and I would give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of those whose face you fear, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon”—this is not found in the Septuagint—“and into the hand of the Chaldeans.

“And I will send you [or: cast you] and your mother who bore you into a foreign land in which you were not born; there you will die. And to the land to which they lift up their soul, desiring to return, there they will not return.”

[Note: Two manuscripts read “Jeconiah,” a reading also preferred by most Latin books. But Jerome himself orders that “Coniah” be read here somewhat below: “Jeconiah,” he says, “is interpreted ‘preparation of the Lord.’ In the present passage the first syllable—that is, the name of the Lord—is removed, and he is called Coniah, so that ‘prepared for destruction and ruin’ may be understood.]

[Note: Previously there was a serious error, “without you,” which was also printed in italic type, lest one think it was merely a typographical error—“without” having been placed for “or.” It is now clear that this was marked according to Jerome’s customary practice, since the Septuagint differs here, interpreting σέ, “you,” rather than “him.”]

Above he had said: “To the house of the king of Judah you shall speak.” Then: “Go down to the house of the king of Judah.” Again: “Thus says the Lord concerning the house of the king of Judah.” And now, in reverse order, after speaking about Zedekiah, who was the last of the kings in Jerusalem, he returns to his brother Jehoiakim, who reigned before him.

After this prophecy had been fulfilled, he now speaks to Jehoiakim’s son, Josiah’s grandson, Jeconiah, king of Jerusalem, who is also called by another name, Jehoiachin. He was captured by Nebuchadnezzar together with his mother, rulers, craftsmen, and many nobles, and was taken to Chaldea, where he died.

This is therefore what is said: just as a signet ring does not leave the hand of its bearer and is removed from the finger only with difficulty, so Jeconiah was in God’s hand. Yet God would tear him away and hand him over to the king of Babylon, where he would die with his mother and all his companions, and would no longer see the land of Judah, which he desires.

The wretched Grunnius—who opened his mouth to slander holy men and taught his tongue falsehood—translated into Latin one book of Sextus the Pythagorean, a most pagan man. He divided it into two volumes and dared to publish it under the name of the holy martyr Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome.

[Note: In the Preface to that book Rufinus had written, as though reporting the opinion of others: “I translated Sextus into Latin. They say that this same Sextus is the one who among you in the city of Rome is called Sixtus, distinguished by the glory of bishop and martyr.” Saint Augustine also tried to interpret in a favorable sense testimonies drawn from that book by the Pelagians, as long as he believed it to be the work of the martyr Sixtus; later he retracted this. See the Letter in our recension, 133, to Ctesiphon, section 3, and what we note there.]

In this book there is no mention of Christ, the Holy Spirit, God the Father, the Patriarchs, the Prophets, or the Apostles. With his customary recklessness and madness, he called the book *The Ring*—a book read throughout many provinces, especially by those who preach *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια), “freedom from passions,” and impeccability.

Therefore, just as the Lord threatens to cast Jeconiah away from his hand and finger like a ring, so I beg the reader to cast away that wicked book. Let him read it, if he wishes, as he reads the other books of the philosophers, but not as an ecclesiastical volume.

In commentaries and explanations, whose custom is to set forth the various opinions of interpreters, I usually introduce such language as: “Some say this; others maintain that; others think this.” The wretched Grunnius—and, many years later, the disciples of Jovinianus—have accused and continue to accuse me of placing my own opinions under the names of others. I do this out of goodwill, so that I may not seem to attack anyone by name.

Since goodwill has been turned into slander, I now say to both him who has died and him who is alive and attempts to revive his heresy: their teacher Origen applies this passage to Christ. He says that Christ was torn from the hand of God the Father like a ring, sent into a land of captivity, into the valley of tears, and handed over to the cross; and that his mother—undoubtedly meaning the Synagogue—was likewise captured and cast away.

In making these claims, he is not afraid to understand the following words—“Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man as abominable [or: sterile],” and the rest—as referring to the Lord of majesty.

He writes this so that his disciples may not dare to deny it, in the fifth book of the *Stromata*.

[Note: The manuscripts and Rabanus read “before,” whereas previously the text had “disciple.”]

[Note: It is beyond doubt that “the one who has died” must be understood as Rufinus, who had already died in the year 410. But I think that “the one who lives” refers not to Anianus, as Martianay thinks, but to Pelagius himself.]

### Verse 28

“Is this man Coniah [another reading: Jeconiah] a clay vessel, crushed and broken? Is he a vessel without any pleasure [or: usefulness]? Why have he and his offspring been cast away and thrown into a land they did not know?”

For what we have rendered, “a clay vessel, crushed and broken,” Symmachus translated: “a refuse heap,” or “cheap and discarded rubbish.” The Septuagint contains nothing corresponding to this, but translated only: “Jeconiah is dishonored, like a vessel in which there is no usefulness.”

And when this is said about Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, someone dares to refer it typologically to Christ. Because the Apostle says that the Lord Savior is the image of the invisible God (Colossians 1), the firstborn of all creation—that is, wisdom, the Word, truth, life, and righteousness—he calls him a ring that is cast away or torn from the Lord’s hand and handed over to King Nebuchadnezzar.

“He and his offspring,” it says, “have been cast away and thrown into a land they did not know.” No one doubts that this happened to Jeconiah.

Jeconiah is interpreted as “preparation of the Lord.” In the present passage the first syllable—that is, the name of the Lord—is removed, and he is called Coniah, so that “prepared for destruction and ruin” may be understood.

### Verses 29–30

“Earth, earth, earth, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord: Write this man as sterile, a man who will not prosper in his days. For none of his offspring will be a man who sits upon the throne of David and has authority any longer in Judah [another reading: Judea].”

If I wished to note individually all the things that the Septuagint either omitted or changed, the discussion would become lengthy, especially since a diligent reader can examine both editions and see what has been changed, added, or removed.

For “sterile,” the Hebrew has *ARIRI* (). Aquila’s first edition translated it “sterile”; his second, ἀναύξητον, that is, “not growing”; Symmachus, “empty”; the Septuagint and Theodotion, “abominable” and “rejected.”

The question arises how the prophecy can stand that none of his descendants would be born who sat upon David’s throne or ruled any longer in Judah, since the Lord and Savior was born from this lineage. Concerning his birth Gabriel says to Mary:

“Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you will call his name Jesus. He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High. And the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:31–33).

We can therefore say that the difficulty arises from the words missing in the Septuagint, namely, “he will not prosper in his days,” or “he will not grow.”

The Septuagint translated: “Write this man as rejected, a man [another reading: ‘of men’], because no man from his offspring will grow who sits upon the throne of David, a ruler any longer in Judah.” This statement is placed twice in the Hebrew. Those who copied the text at the beginning, thinking that it had been added in the Greek books, removed it.

Let us therefore answer that in the days of Jeconiah no man succeeded him who sat upon his throne; but after a long time someone was born from his offspring who obtained his throne.

The passage can also be resolved in this way: no ordinary man will sit upon the throne of David, but God will sit there; and his kingdom will not be earthly and brief, as David’s was, but eternal and heavenly, as Scripture says: “He will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32).

Thus Jeconiah was born from Jehoiakim, Shealtiel from Jeconiah, Zerubbabel from Shealtiel, and in due order one comes to Christ.

But in the days of Jehoiakim no royal son succeeded him, as he himself had succeeded his father. Rather, both Shealtiel and Zerubbabel were in captivity, and until Christ no one from the royal line possessed royal power.

This was because the Hebrew reads: “in his days and in his time”—that is, during the time when he himself existed—“there will be no man who sits upon the throne of David.”

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “in that very time, when he himself existed.”]

For all were captives, and thereafter no one from the line of David held authority in the land of Judea.

Hence Josephus also reports that the rulers were from the priestly class and the tribe of Levi, until Herod, son of the proselyte Antipater, succeeded them. Later, under Vespasian, the kingship of this lineage—or rather, the semblance of imperial power—was completely destroyed.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verses 1 ff.

“Woe to the shepherds who destroy and tear apart the flock of my pasture [or: O shepherds, you who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture], says the Lord.

“Therefore thus says the Lord God of Israel to the shepherds who pasture my people: You have scattered my flock, driven them away, and not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your endeavors, says the Lord. And I will gather the remnant of my flock from all the lands to which I had driven them, and I will bring them back to their fields [or: restore them to their pastures], and they will grow and multiply. And I will raise up shepherds over them, and they will pasture them. They will no longer fear or be afraid, and none will be missing from their number, says the Lord.”

The prophetic word is directed to the shepherds, or concerning the shepherds.

Because we read that concerning Jeconiah, the penultimate king of Judea, who was descended from David, it was written: “Earth, earth, earth, hear the words of the Lord; write this man as rejected or sterile, and there will be no man from his offspring who sits upon the throne of David” (above, 22:29–30), and because every hope of the Judean kingdom had been cut off, the discourse turns to the leaders of the Church.

After the Synagogue with its shepherds has been abandoned and condemned, the word is directed to the Apostles, concerning whom it is said: “I will raise up shepherds over them, and they will pasture them; they will no longer fear or be afraid, and none will be missing from their number, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 34:23).

The Apostles will pasture the ecclesiastical flock confidently and without any fear, and the remnant of the people of Israel will be saved from all the lands and will return to their fields, or pastures; they will grow and multiply.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript and others read: “that the people, entrusted to others …”]

But against the wicked shepherds—the Scribes and Pharisees—the Lord will visit the wickedness of their endeavors.

We can also understand this according to the tropological sense as referring to the leaders of the Church who do not govern the Lord’s sheep worthily. Once they have been rejected and condemned, the people will be saved after being entrusted to others who prove worthy, and the remnant will be saved.

Shepherds destroy the sheep when they teach heresy. They tear apart and scatter them when they create schisms. They drive them out when they separate them from the Church contrary to justice. They do not visit them when they withdraw their hand from penitents.

The Lord will have mercy on all of them, restoring their former pastures to them and removing the wicked shepherds.

### Verses 5–6

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous branch [another reading: king] [or: a righteous rising one]. He will reign as king and will be wise [or: understand], and he will do justice and righteousness in the land.

“In those days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is the name by which they will call him [or: by which he will call him]: ‘The Lord our righteous one’ [or: ‘our righteousness’], which in Hebrew is called *SADECENU* ().”

The phrase improperly added in the Septuagint—“among the Prophets”—must be completely removed. Another chapter follows, which they omitted; after it is finished, there is a heading, “To the Prophets,” or “Against the Prophets.” We shall discuss it in its proper place.

After the shepherds of the Synagogue—the Scribes and Pharisees—have been rejected, after the remnant of Israel has been saved, and after the Apostles of the Gospel have been appointed in the place of the former leaders, the shepherd of shepherds, the prince of princes, the King of kings, and Lord of lords is introduced: Christ, our Savior.

He is properly the righteous branch, or the righteous rising one, concerning whom we read: “In his days righteousness will arise” (Psalm 71:7). And elsewhere: “Behold the man; ‘Rising’ is his name” (Zechariah 6:12), and “under him he will arise, and he will build the temple of the Lord.”

Thus, just as in Isaiah he is called Emmanuel—that is, “God with us” (Isaiah 7:14)—so in Jeremiah he receives the name “our righteousness.”

Hence the Apostle says: “He was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

His adversary, the Antichrist, with the devil dwelling in him, is called the foolish shepherd in Zechariah (Zechariah 11).

“And he will do,” it says, “justice and righteousness in the land.” For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22).

In those days both the two tribes of Judah and the ten tribes of Israel will be saved together. According to Ezekiel, the two rods will become one rod (Ezekiel 37).

As for his name: according to the Septuagint, if it reads “the Lord will call him,” he will be called *Josedec*, that is, “the righteous Lord.” According to the Hebrew, which reads “they will call his name,” he will be called “the Lord our righteousness.”

For this is what *ADONAI SADECENU* () means. Symmachus translated it: “Lord, justify us.”

### Verses 7–8

“Therefore, behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, when they will no longer say: ‘As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel up from the land of Egypt,’ but: ‘As the Lord lives, who brought up and led the offspring of the house of Israel from the land of the north and from all the lands to which he had driven them’; and they will dwell in their own land.”

This entire chapter is absent from the Septuagint.

Its meaning is that the people of God will no longer be liberated through Moses from Egypt, but through Jesus Christ from the entire world into which they had been scattered.

This is partly being fulfilled now throughout the world, and will be fulfilled completely when they come from east and west, north and south, and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Matthew 8), so that after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel may be saved (Romans 11).

## To the Prophets

[Or: “In the Prophets,” or “Against the Prophets.”]

As we said above, in the edition of the Septuagint this heading is placed as the conclusion of the preceding chapter, where we read: “And this is the name by which the Lord will call him: Josedec, among the Prophets.”

Many people, not understanding this, fabricate various delirious explanations. It would have been much better simply to confess ignorance than to make others heirs of one’s incompetence.

The passage is in fact directed against the Prophets—or rather, the false prophets—of Jerusalem and Samaria, whom it now calls by the common and familiar name “Prophets.” Concerning them it is written in what follows: “Among the Prophets of Samaria I saw wickedness,” and immediately afterward: “Among the Prophets of Jerusalem I saw horrifying things.”

When he places the conjunction “and,” he shows that the preceding words were spoken about the Prophets of the Lord, who themselves also proved to be like the false prophets.

### (Verse 9)

“My heart is broken within me (or, in me); all my bones tremble (or, are shaken); I have become like a drunken man and like a man drenched (or, overcome with sleep) with wine, because of the Lord and because of the words of his holy ones (or, because of the face of the splendor of his glory).”

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript here and below has *superatus* (“overcome”) for *soporatus* (“put to sleep”). The Greek reads συνεχόμενος, “held fast” or “constrained.” The Hebrew also has [blank in supplied text].]

When the Prophet considers the face of almighty God—that is, of the Father—and considers the face of the Son, who, according to the Apostle, is called “the radiance of his glory and the form of God’s substance” (Hebrews 1), he shudders in soul and body and understands that he is nothing, in accordance with what is also said elsewhere: “I became like a beast before you” (Psalm 72:23). Or he offers to God the victim of his conscience and humility, according to what is read in the Psalms: “A sacrifice to God is a broken spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

As for the bones that trembled, or were shaken, let us understand them as those of which the same David sings: “All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 34:10). He became like a drunken man, and like a man drenched—or overcome with sleep—with wine, possessing no understanding and no wisdom. For “the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93:11). But if this is so, where are those who proclaim perfect righteousness in a human being? If they answer that they say this of the saints, not of themselves, I certainly think that no one is holier than Jeremiah, who, being a virgin, a prophet, and sanctified in the womb, prefigures the Lord and Savior even by his name. For *Jeremiah* is interpreted as “the exalted one of the Lord.”

### (Verse 10)

“Because the earth is filled with adulterers [another reading: adulteries], because the earth has languished before the curse (or, oath), the fields (or, pastures) of the wilderness have dried up, and their course has become evil, and their strength unlike [what it was].”

What we have rendered from the Hebrew—“because the earth is filled with adulterers”—is not found in the Septuagint, which has “oath” in place of “curse.” He gives the reasons: because of adulteries and curses, or excessive oath-taking—indeed, perjuries—barrenness of crops has followed.

Whatever you understand literally about the land of Judea, refer it to the congregation of believers, since because of adulteries and lies, or perjuries, there is barrenness of virtues and of God’s gifts in the churches. [Col. 0822B]

### (Verses 11–12)

“For both prophet and priest have been polluted, and in my house I found their evils [the Vulgate: evil], says the Lord. Therefore their way shall be like a slippery path in darkness. For they shall be pushed and fall upon it, because I shall bring (or, inflict) evils upon them, the year of their visitation, says the Lord.”

When evils are found in the Church of God, and especially among its leaders, let us understand that this has been fulfilled: “Prophet and priest have been polluted; in my house I found their evils, says the Lord.” The house of Christ is the Church, of which the Apostle also writes to Timothy: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15).

In the prophet, understand the teacher; in the priest, the dignity of ministry. If they agree with an evil mind, their way will be a slippery path and in darkness; nor will they have the Lord saying: “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46). Hence the saint speaks, fleeing all darkness [another reading: fleeing darkness]: “The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord; you have given gladness in my heart [another reading: in my heart]” (Psalm 4:7).

But when they are in darkness and on a slippery path—that is, in heretical error—they will be pushed and fall at every movement. And the Lord inflicts evils upon them, not because they are evils in such a way that the Lord himself inflicts evil, but because they are evils for those who endure punishments. Otherwise the same things are both evil and good: evil for those whom they torment, good for those whom they correct.

This too should be noted: the year of the Lord’s visitation is called the correction and torment of sinners, in accordance with what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with blows; but I will not remove my mercy from him” (Psalm 88:33–34).

### (Verse 13)

“And in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly (or, iniquity [the Vulgate: stupidity]); they prophesied in Baal [one manuscript adds: and deceived in Baal], and they deceived my people Israel.”

According to mystical interpretations, I think that the prophets of Samaria properly mean heretics, and all who boast of knowledge falsely so called. Just as the prophets of Samaria, whatever they said, prophesied in Baal—that is, in the idol consecrated to demons—so heretics, whatever they say in the Church or outside the Church in order to overthrow the people of Israel, who once saw God, speak through demons.

Therefore he significantly says: “And in the prophets of Samaria I saw folly” (1 Corinthians 1:24). For they do not possess him of whom it is said: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

### (Verse 14)

“And in the prophets of Jerusalem I saw a likeness (or, dreadful things), adultery and a way of falsehood, and they strengthened the hands of evildoers, so that no one would turn from his military service (or, from his most evil way). They have all become for me like Sodom, and its inhabitants like Gomorrah.”

[Note: In one manuscript and in Rabanus, together with the Vulgate and the Hieronymian edition: “of those committing adultery.” Hebrew: [blank in supplied text].]

He says: These things were found not only in the gatherings of heretics, but also in the prophets of Jerusalem—that is, in the teachers of the Church. I saw similar things, or dreadful things: they adulterated the word of God and entered upon the way of falsehood, so that they might assent to the deceptions of heretics and strengthen the hands of evildoers, adding their evils to their own crimes and leading to destruction those whom they ought to have corrected.

Those who do this should not consider themselves immune from punishment. They themselves, and those whom they favor, will be like Sodom; and all who dwell with them and do not withdraw from such people will be like Gomorrah.

Let wicked teaching exult as much as it wishes, and let the prophets of Jerusalem boast that through falsehood they have prevailed and strengthened the hands of evildoers: their end will be like that of Sodom and Gomorrah.

### (Verse 15)

“Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts to the prophets: Behold, I will feed them wormwood (or, pains; according to Symmachus, bitterness), and I will give them gall to drink (or, bitter water), because pollution has gone forth from the prophets of Jerusalem into all the earth.”

Let us use this testimony against those who send throughout the world letters full of lies, deceit, and perjury, polluting the ears of their hearers and harming the reputation of the simple, so that what is written may be fulfilled in them: “From the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth into all the earth.”

For it is not enough for them to swallow their own iniquity and harm their neighbors; those whom they have once hated they attempt to defame throughout the world and to sow blasphemies everywhere.

### (Verses 16–17)

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you and deceive you; they speak the vision of their heart and not from the mouth of the Lord. They say to those who blaspheme me (or, reject my word), ‘The Lord has spoken: peace shall be yours.’ And to everyone who walks in the perversity of his heart they say, ‘Evils shall not come upon you.’”

So that the people might not think themselves free from guilt if they listened to perverse teachers, he says: “Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy falsehood to you and deceive you.” For the punishment will be the same for teacher and disciple. They do not speak from the mouth of the Lord, but the things they have fabricated in their own heart.

They say to those who blaspheme me—that is, to heretics and the perverse—or to those who reject my word: What do they say? “The Lord has spoken: peace shall be yours.” Do not fear harsh punishments or be terrified by empty threats: peace and tranquility shall be yours, and whatever we say and announce to you, the Lord has spoken. The evil that you fear because of your evil conscience will not come upon you; rather, the good that the Lord has spoken to you will come.

“For who has stood in the council of the Lord, and seen and heard his word? Who has considered his word and heard it?”

Where we have translated “in the council,” the Hebrew has *BASOD* ([Hebrew term absent or illegible in the supplied text]). Aquila translated it as “secret”; Symmachus as “word”; the Septuagint and Theodotion as “substance,” or “subsistence.” The sense is:

“Do not believe, O unlearned multitude, the prophets who announce falsehoods to you and say, ‘The Lord has spoken this: peace shall be yours; evil shall not come upon you.’ For how can they know God’s secrets, or through whom have they learned God’s council? How has the word of the divine disposition reached them?”

Some of our writers think that they have discovered in this passage a description of God’s substance.

### (Verses 19–20)

“Behold, the whirlwind (or, storm and upheaval) of the Lord’s indignation shall go forth, and an erupting storm shall come upon the head of the impious. The anger of the Lord shall not turn back until he acts and until he accomplishes the thoughts of his heart. In the last days you shall understand his council.”

Those who had said above, “The Lord has spoken to us: peace shall be yours,” and whom he had rebuked because they could not know what was to come or understand God’s judgment, he now shows, by contrast, to know nothing at all.

Instead of peace and security, a Babylonian storm will come; and it will come not upon just anyone, but upon the heads of the impious—whether the whole people or those who announced falsehoods to the people. Nor will God’s anger and fury be something to be appeased as in former times; what he foretold and repeatedly threatened will be fulfilled in action, and his thought and judgment will be confirmed by the punishments of the impious.
