“When,” he says, “the final time of captivity has arrived, when the triumphant victor has prevailed over you and bound your hands with the clatter of chains, then you will understand his council, which you now falsely boast that you know.”

### (Verses 21–22) [Col. 0824D]

“I did not send the prophets, yet they ran; I did not speak to them, yet they prophesied. If they had stood in my council and had made my words known to my people, I would surely have turned them away from their evil way and from their most evil thoughts.”

The Apostle also explains this meaning in his letter to the Romans: “And since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting, filled with all iniquity, wickedness, fornication, and depravity, avarice” (Romans 1:28–29), and the rest.

Once false teachers have surrendered themselves to lies, perjuries, and the deaths of those whom they have deceived, they rush headlong—not gradually or with measured steps—to destruction, both their own and that of those whom they have deceived.

Nor does the Lord speak to them; they themselves speak as though from the mouth of the Lord. Of such people it is said: “If they had stood in my council”—that is, if they had wished to submit to my will—and “had made my words known to my people,” not flattering them and destroying them through adulation by saying, “You have no sins; you possess perfect righteousness; holiness, chastity, and justice are found only in you,” then I would not have handed them over to impurity and disgrace, so that they might do what is not fitting and follow their worst thoughts.

Let us observe heretics: once they have despaired of salvation, they surrender themselves to gluttony and pleasures; they eat meat, frequently visit the baths [another reading: frequently], smell of musk, and, anointing themselves with various perfumes, seek bodily beauty. For once they cease to hope for the future and do not believe in the resurrection. Although they do not proclaim this in words, they show it by their deeds. If they believed, they would not do these things.

In this passage also, where it is written, “If they had stood in my council,” Aquila, Symmachus, Theodotion, and the Septuagint have translated it in the same way as above.

### (Verses 23–24)

“Am I a God nearby [the Vulgate: perhaps nearby], says the Lord, and not a God far away? If a man hides himself in hiding places, will I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.”

The Septuagint has: “I am a God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God far away. If a man is hidden in hiding places, will I not see him? says the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord.” [The manuscripts supplied the verse, “Do I not fill heaven…”]

Aquila and Symmachus likewise translated: “Am I a God from nearby, or near at hand, and not a God from far away?” The Septuagint and Theodotion, however, translated the sense in the opposite way, saying: “I am a God who draws near, says the Lord, and not a God far away.”

The former interpretation asserts that God knows not only what is near but also what is far away, and that he sees not only the present but also the future. The latter holds that God is present everywhere and that there is no place where God is absent.

God draws near to everyone, and especially to the saints, as though a garment clung to the skin. But sinners, who withdraw far from him, will perish. We read this meaning also in the Psalms:

“Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face? If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present. If I take my wings at dawn and dwell at the farthest limits of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me” (Psalm 118:1 ff.).

Amos also agrees with this, saying:

“If they descend as far as hell, from there my hand [another reading: your hand] shall bring them out; and if they ascend into heaven, from there I shall drag them down. And if they hide themselves on the summit of Carmel, from there I shall search them out and remove them. And if they conceal themselves from my eyes in the depths of the sea, there I shall command the serpent, and it shall bite them” (Amos 9:2–3).

Again, in the preceding Psalm:

“For darkness,” he says, “shall not be darkened from you, and night shall be illuminated like day; as its darkness, so also is its light” (Psalm 138:12).

Whenever it is frequently said in the Prophets, “Thus says the Lord,” it is always added for this reason: so that the words may not be despised as merely the words of prophets, but so that people may continually be reminded that the words they speak are God’s.

### (Verses 25 ff.)

[These preceding words—“I have heard what the prophets said”—are absent from the Cistercian manuscript.]

“I have heard what the prophets said, prophesying falsehood in my name and saying, ‘I dreamed’ (or, ‘I saw a dream’). How long will this be in the heart [another reading: in the hearts] of the prophets who prophesy falsehood and prophesy the deceptions (or, desires) of their own heart? They intend (or, think) to make my people forget my name because of their dreams, which each one recounts to his neighbor, just as their fathers forgot my name because of Baal (or, in Baal).”

Since the preceding heading is “Against the Prophets,” or “To the Prophets,” and we clearly understand these to be false prophets—and since there are many kinds of prophesying, one of which is through dreams, as in the case of Daniel—the prophetic word is directed against those who believe in dreams and think that everything they see is a divine revelation, which is properly disclosed to the saints and servants of God.

If we read that Pharaoh (Genesis 41) and Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 2), impious kings, saw dreams that were true, the merit did not belong to those who saw them. Rather, it was so that through them the holy men Joseph and Daniel might become renowned, and that the tyrants’ harsh and untamed hearts might recognize the Lord’s majesty through their own consciences.

Even today there are dreamers in the Church, especially in our own flock, who boast that their errors are the Lord’s prophecy and repeatedly declare, “I dreamed, I dreamed.” The Lord rebukes them, saying: “How long will this be in the heart of those who prophesy, who prophesy falsehood and the deceptions of their own heart?”

They do this so that, just as the ancient people who came out of Egypt forgot the name of God [another reading: my name], so their descendants too may forget me.

Such prophecy is not in the name of the Lord, but in the name of Baal, which is properly the idol of the Sidonians, or Babylonian, and is called Bel by a closely related name.

### (Verses 28–29)

“Let the prophet who has a dream recount the dream, and let the one who has my word speak my word truthfully. What has straw to do with wheat? says the Lord. Are not my words like fire? says the Lord, and like a hammer (or, an axe that shatters a rock)?”

Those who deserve to possess God’s word should explain a dream and say, “Thus says the Lord”—those to whom the Lord has spoken, in whom there is truth and not deceitful falsehood.

What have the straw of heretics to do with the wheat of the Church? John the Baptist speaks more fully about this (Matthew 3): the Lord will cleanse his threshing floor and, with a winnowing fork, scatter the chaff [two manuscripts: the chaff of words] in the blasts of the winds, leaving it to be burned in the fires; but he will gather the wheat into barns, so that it may become heavenly bread. Then each believer may say: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9).

Doctrine that is perverse is aptly compared to straw, which has no marrow and cannot nourish believing peoples; it is made from empty stalks.

And because heretics always promise prosperity and open the kingdoms of heaven to sinners, saying, “The kingdoms of heaven are prepared for you; you can imitate God’s majesty so that you may be without sin. For you have received the power of free will and knowledge of the law, by which you may obtain whatever you wish,” they deceive the wretched with flatteries—especially “little women burdened with sins, carried about by every wind of doctrine, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth”—and they deceive all their hearers through adulation (Ephesians 4).

Therefore, comparing his words with the straw of heretics, the Lord says: “Are not my words like fire? says the Lord, and like a hammer that shatters a rock?”

“My word,” he says, “announces future punishments, so as to deter people from sinning; and it threatens sinners’ straw with burning, so that the hard hearts of heretics, untamed like flint, may be shattered by the hammer of my word.” It removes the heart of stone in order to put a heart of flesh in its place—that is, a soft heart capable of receiving and feeling God’s commandments.

The Lord says something similar through Ezekiel (Ezekiel 13): the false prophets plaster their wall with their flatteries without tempering material, and afterward it is overthrown by a violent rain and by the truth of judgment. The false prophets sew cushions under every elbow, so that they may make sinners rest and prevent them from appeasing God’s anger with tears.

In place of “hammer,” the Septuagint translated “axe,” namely the one of which John the Baptist speaks: “Even now the axe has been placed at the roots of the trees” (Matthew 3:10). This axe cuts down unfruitful trees, and this hammer shatters the hardest stones.

Hence the prophet Nahum also says: “His fury—undoubtedly God’s—will consume the rulers, and the rocks will be shattered by him” (Nahum 1:6).

This is directed against heretics. As for ecclesiastical men, it is written that neither hammer nor axe was heard in the house of the Lord (1 Kings 6).

### (Verses 30 ff.) [Col. 0827D]

“Therefore, behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who steal my words, each one from his neighbor [another reading: to his neighbor]. Behold, I am against the prophets, says the Lord, who take up their tongues and say, ‘He says’ (or, ‘they drowse a drowsing’). Behold, I am against the prophets who dream falsehood, says the Lord, who recount them and deceive [another reading: recounted them and deceived] my people with their falsehoods and with their miracles (or, with their stupors and terrors), although I had not sent them and had not commanded them. They have benefited this people nothing, says the Lord.”

Falsehood always imitates truth; and unless it possesses some likeness of what is right, it cannot deceive the innocent.

Thus, just as the prophets among the earlier people lied and said, “Thus says the Lord,” and “I saw the Lord,” and “The word of the Lord that came to him” or “to him,” so heretics take testimonies from the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. Each one steals the words of the Savior from his neighbor—from the prophets, apostles, and evangelists—and takes up his tongue to utter the poisons of his heart with his mouth. They drowse a drowsing, of whom it is truly said: “They fell asleep in their sleep and found nothing” (Psalm 76:5).

Or, according to the Hebrew: “And they say, ‘He says,’” with “the Lord,” or perhaps “the divine word,” understood.

The Lord therefore threatens that he himself will come against such teachers, who deceive his people with their falsehoods and with stupors and miracles. They promise great, unbelievable, and enormous things—or, according to another reading, senseless things—in order to deceive the wretched; yet they have benefited God’s people nothing.

They fulfill the apostolic saying by “teaching what they ought not, for the sake of shameful gain.” They are accustomed to announce prosperity to the wicked and adversity to the good.

### (Verses 33 ff.) [Col. 0828D]

“If this people, or a prophet, or a priest asks you, saying, ‘What is the burden of God?’ (or, ‘What is the assumption of the Lord?’), you shall say to them: ‘You are the burden’ (or, ‘the assumption’). For I will cast you down (or, dash you to pieces), says the Lord.

And the prophet and priest and people [another reading: the prophet, priests, and people] who say, ‘The burden’ (or, ‘the assumption’) ‘of the Lord,’ I will visit (or, punish) that man and his house.

Thus shall each one say to his neighbor [the Vulgate: close companion] and to his brother: ‘What has the Lord answered?’ and ‘What has the Lord spoken?’ The burden (or, assumption) of the Lord shall no longer be mentioned, because each person’s own word shall be his burden (or, assumption) [another reading: his].”

The Hebrew word *MASSA* ([Hebrew term absent or illegible in the supplied text]) is translated by Aquila as ἅρμα (*harma*), that is, “burden” and “weight”; Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translate it as “assumption.”

Therefore, wherever what the Lord threatens is grievous, full of weight and labor, and unbearable, the title too is called ἅρμα, that is, “weight.” But wherever the Lord promises prosperity, or after a threat promises better things, it is called a vision, or simply the word of the Lord. Thus it was clear from the title itself—whether of weight, vision, or the word of God—what kind of prophecy would follow.

Since the prophets were accustomed to announce sad things to the sinful people and threaten punishments in order to draw them back to repentance, while the merciful and compassionate Lord delayed his sentence for a long time, the deceived people, led astray by the fraud of the false prophets, thought that what the Lord threatened would not come. They turned the matter into a joke and mockery and, jeering at the prophets who prophesied, said: “Again this one sees the burden and weight of the Lord.”

Thus it happened that “vision” was no longer used, but, in jest and derision, “burden” and “weight” were used instead.

The Lord therefore commanded that if either the people, or a prophet, or a priest asked Jeremiah what the burden or assumption of the Lord was, he should answer them and say: “You are the burden, and you are the assumption. For I will assume you, cast you down, dash you to pieces, and destroy you.”

If anyone thereafter, whether of the prophets, priests, or people, dared to speak of the burden and weight of the Lord, he says: “I will visit that man and his house,” and I will erase him forever.

Therefore let each one say to his neighbor and friend, not “What is the burden of the Lord?” but “What has the Lord answered?” and “What has the Lord spoken?” Let the old expression be forgotten: let “burden,” “weight,” or “assumption” no longer sound from your mouths, because each person’s word and deed will be reckoned as a burden and weight for him, in accordance with what is written: “By your mouth you will be justified, and by your mouth you will be condemned” (Matthew 15).

### (Verses 37 ff.)

“And you pervert the words of the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God.”

“Thus you shall say (or, ‘Thus you shall say’ [plural]) to the prophet: ‘What has the Lord answered you?’ and ‘What has the Lord spoken?’

But if you say, ‘The burden of the Lord’—”

[This clause, “Up to this point it is not found in the Septuagint,” did not originally stand here but was deferred to the end of the sacred text. It was therefore wrongly asserted that verses 38, 39, and 40, which follow from this point, were absent from the Septuagint version, since they plainly appear in the present text as: “Therefore thus says the Lord,” and so forth. Only the preceding passage is missing; the annotation restored here concludes it. The manuscripts also warned us to restore the passage in this way.]

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Because you have said this word, ‘The burden’ (or, ‘the assumption’) ‘of the Lord,’ although I sent to you saying, ‘You shall not say, “The burden” (or, “the assumption”) ‘of the Lord,’ therefore, behold, I will take you up (or, assume you), carrying you, and I will cast you away [the Vulgate: abandon you], together with the city that I gave to you and to your fathers, away from my face. And I will give you over to everlasting reproach and eternal disgrace, which shall never be erased by oblivion.”

The Lord commanded that the language of burden, weight, and assumption should no longer be used among the people, but the language of response and the word of God. Because the people had refused to fulfill this command, he interprets the very word against them and says:

“Because you have said what I did not want you to say, even though I repeatedly sent prophets and commanded you not to say it, I will therefore fulfill upon you in action your word of assumption, burden, and weight. I will assume you, take you up, carry you, dash you to pieces, and make you fall from the heights to the ground.

“And not only you, but also your city, which I gave to your fathers. And I will give you,” he says, “over to everlasting reproach and disgrace, which shall never be erased by oblivion.”

We know that this happened at the time of the Babylonian captivity; but it is fulfilled more fully and perfectly after the passion and resurrection of the Savior, when the Lord said: “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Luke 13:35), and his sentence will remain until the end.

Let us also interpret the passage differently, at least according to the Septuagint: λῆμμα (*lemma*) signifies not only “assumption,” but also “gift” and “present.” Since the people were always promising themselves prosperity, he says that they must no longer say this. For they are unworthy of God’s gifts and presents; rather, they must be cast away and entirely abandoned by God’s help.

Things are often revealed through words and the interpretation of names: the changed names of Abraham, Sarah, Peter, and the sons of Zebedee signify a change in circumstances. Likewise, in this same prophet (above, chapter 20), Pashhur [another reading: Phasor and Phascor] is interpreted as “terror,” or “transference,” and “settler,” or “sojourner.”

It should be noted that the words “the living God, the Lord of hosts, our God” are not found in the Latin and Greek manuscripts; and that the Hebrews read in their books against themselves. This properly signifies the mystery of the Trinity.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0829]

The fifth book of the Commentary on Jeremiah, brother Eusebius, will begin with the two baskets, one of which will display the sweetness of right faith and the other the bitterness of the heretics’ faithlessness.

Although Hananiah son of Azur resists Jeremiah, and Shemaiah the Nehelamite wishes the prophet to be sent to prison [two manuscripts and older editions: orders him to be sent], and the priest Zephaniah conspires in the words of the false prophets (Jeremiah 28–29), truth can be shut up and bound, but it cannot be conquered. It is content with the small number of its own and is not frightened by the multitude of its enemies.

Therefore, with Moses, raise your hands to heaven, and suspend the ancient serpent in the wilderness; immediately Amalek too will be destroyed, and the poisonous bites will not prevail. The secure people of the Lord will cross the streams of the Jordan with Jesus, and after the vast solitude they will eat the bread that was born in our little village of Bethlehem (Exodus 17; Numbers 21).

(Cap. 24.—Verses 1 ff.) The Lord showed me, and behold, two baskets (or hampers [Note: [Col. 0829D] Our manuscripts, one older manuscript in Montfaucon’s possession, and several printed books insert, following Symmachus, these words; I have not admitted them into the text]) full of figs, full, set before the Temple of the Lord, after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had deported Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with his officials, the craftsmen, and the metalworkers, from Jerusalem and brought them to Babylon. One basket contained very good figs, such as figs of the first season usually are; and one basket contained very bad figs, which could not be eaten because they were bad.

[Col. 0831A] And the Lord said to me: “What do you see, Jeremiah?” And I said: “Figs—very good figs, and very bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are bad.” And the word of the Lord came to me, saying:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: As these figs are good, so I will regard the deportation of Judah, whom I sent from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good. And I will set my eyes upon them [Note: [Col. 0831] One Vatican manuscript reads ‘to appease’ instead of ‘for good’] for good, and I will bring them back to this land; and I will build them up and not overthrow them; and I will plant them and not uproot them. And I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord; and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, because they will return to me with their whole heart.

“And as for the very bad figs, which cannot be eaten because they are bad, thus says the Lord: So I will give [Al. ‘I will cry out’] (or ‘deliver over’) Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem [Col. 0831B] who remained in this city, and those who live in the land of Egypt. I will make them a terror and an affliction (or dispersion) to all the kingdoms of the earth, a reproach, a proverb, a byword, and a curse in every place to which I have driven them. And I will send among them the sword, famine, and pestilence, until they are consumed from the land that I gave to them and to their fathers.”

Some interpret the two baskets—or baskets—of good and bad figs [Al. ‘of good and bad female figs’] as the Law and the Gospel; the Synagogue and the Church; the Jewish people and the Christians; Gehenna and the kingdom of heaven, one of which pertains to the punishment of sinners, the other to the dwelling of the saints. But, knowing with the Apostle Paul (Rom. 7) that the Law and the commandment are good and holy, and that the God of both Testaments is one, let us refer them rather to those who believed and did not believe at the coming of the Lord and Savior. Those who, stirred up by the scribes and priests, cried out, saying, “Crucify, crucify such a man!” (Luke 23:21), are the basket of bad figs; but those from the people who believed after his ascension should be referred to the good figs, the excellent basket.

Let us follow the simple and true historical account: that he called Jeconiah the basket of good figs, because he had surrendered himself to the Babylonian king at Jeremiah’s counsel and by God’s command; and to him the Lord promises prosperity. The basket of bad figs, however, is Zedekiah, who, contradicting God’s decision, was captured, blinded, and led to Babylon, where he died [Col. 0831D] (2 Kings 25).

To such an extent did God set his eyes for good upon those who obeyed his command (below, 42), that he brought them back to their land, built them up and did not overthrow them, planted them and did not uproot them, and gave them a heart to know him, that he was the Lord. They became his people, and he became their God. Thus, even in captivity, he set his eyes upon them and permitted them to cultivate the land, build houses, and plant orchards [Al. ‘fruit gardens’] in the Babylonian region. Daniel, through the miracles of his signs, suddenly became a prince from a captive (Dan. 5), and the three boys were gloriously delivered from the fire of the furnace [Col. 0832A] (Dan. 3). When the seventy years had been completed, under Zerubbabel, Jeshua the high priest, Ezra, and Nehemiah, a very large part of the people returned to Jerusalem; their number is contained in the book of Ezra itself (1 Esd. 2).

It should also be noted that this vision was given to the Prophet in the time of Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been led into exile. He did not say “captivity,” because Jeconiah had surrendered himself voluntarily. By “craftsmen” and “metalworkers” we should understand either interpreters and teachers of the Law, or artisans and craftsmen in gold and precious stones, an art that is extremely esteemed among barbarian nations. Instead of “metalworkers,” the Seventy translated “the bound,” to indicate the evil of captivity, and added from their own text “the rich,” which is not found in the Hebrew.

He compares the basket that contained good, very good figs with the figs of the first season, which in Greek are called πρώϊμα (*prōïma*): namely, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, Moses and Aaron, Job, and the other holy men, concerning whom one of the Twelve Prophets says: “Like grapes in the wilderness I found Israel, and like figs on a fig tree I found their fathers” (Hos. 9:10). Hence we too are called children of Abraham. Conversely, it is said to the Jews: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham” (John 8:39).

These baskets, which contained good and bad figs, were not outside and beyond the Church, but before the Temple of the Lord, because all the elements of its knowledge are openly displayed. Nor do the figs that are outside have as much bitterness as those that, after confessing the faith, have been changed by apostasy. And the good figs that are not before the Temple of God—such as the philosophers of the world, who, through their natural goodness and understanding of the Creator, seemed less to follow virtues than to praise them—do not have as much sweetness as the figs that are in the Temple of God, of which the Prophets and Apostles were examples. One of these figs said: “I gave you milk, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:2); and: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

Hence it is said that, in the sight of the Temple of God, the good figs were very good, and the bad figs were very bad. And lest we seem to be imposing our own interpretation, Scripture itself unfolds the meaning:

“As these figs are good,” it says, “so I will regard the deportation of Judah, whom I sent from this place into the land of the Chaldeans, for good,” signifying Jeconiah and the officials who were taken captive with him. Conversely, concerning the basket that contained bad figs: “As the very bad figs,” it says [Al. “the very bad ones”], “which cannot be eaten because they are bad, so I will give Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials, and those who fled to Egypt, and those who remained in this city, as a terror and an affliction to all the kingdoms of the earth” (below, 42). This happened when they were also captured in Egypt, and Nebuchadnezzar set up his throne at Tahpanhes. The Lord sent against them the sword, famine, and pestilence, until they were consumed from the land that he had given to their fathers.

What he said about the good figs—“I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the Lord”—is like the Apostle’s statement: “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2:13). Not only our deeds, but also our will, depends upon God’s assistance.

At this point the allegorical interpreter is always delirious, seeking to do violence to the historical truth. He says that those who were captured and transferred to the land of the Chaldeans came from the heavenly Jerusalem, and that they would return again to their former place, like Jeremiah and the other holy prophets; while others, who had been sinners, would die in this land and in the valley of tears. I have set down the whole vision together as a περικοπή (*perikopē*, “section”), so that I would not divide its meaning in the exposition.

(Cap. 25.—Verse 1.) The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the people of Judah (or “against all the people of Judah”) in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah.

This earlier passage follows the preceding vision. That vision occurred under Zedekiah, after Jeconiah had been transferred to Babylon; this one occurred under Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah. The Prophets were not concerned—as I have already said—with preserving the chronological order required by the laws of history. They knew that it was useful to write in whatever manner was suitable for those who heard and read. Hence some people wrongly seek in the Psalter, according to the historical sequence, an order among the psalms that is not observed in lyric poetry.

(Verses 2.) “This is the first year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon” [Note: [Col. 0833D] Victor deletes these words, enclosing them in parentheses, since the statement is false and the comma is not found in the Seventy] (which is not found in the Seventy. The text continues):

“What Jeremiah the Prophet spoke to all the people of Judah and to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying.”

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah and father of Jeconiah, Nebuchadnezzar assumed power in Babylon. Thus it happened that the year that was Nebuchadnezzar’s first year in Babylon was the fourth year of King Jehoiakim in Jerusalem. Finally, in the eighth year of his reign, he led Jeconiah, together with his mother and the officials, into captivity. Jeconiah had reigned for only three months after his father Jehoiakim’s death. Jehoiakim was killed in the eleventh year of his reign in Jerusalem (2 Kings 24).

(Verses 3.) “From the thirteenth year of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah, to this day—this is the twenty-third year—the word of the Lord has come to me, and I have spoken to you, rising and speaking throughout the night, and you have not listened.”

In the thirteenth year of King Josiah [Al. “of the reign of”], who reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years [Note: [Col. 0833D] The Cistercian manuscript reads “twenty-one years”], Jeremiah began to prophesy. He prophesied under him for nineteen years, after which his son Jehoahaz succeeded him in the kingdom. When Jehoahaz was immediately led into captivity by Pharaoh Neco, king of Egypt, his brother Jehoiakim obtained the kingdom (2 Kings 23).

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim’s reign, this word of the Lord came to Jeremiah. Accordingly, it was the twenty-third year of Jeremiah the Prophet since he had begun to speak to the people. He never ceased preaching, but rose every day at dawn and during the night and spoke to the people. “And you did not listen,” he says.

But if, as the new heretics claim from the old, the Law was once given as an aid, and commandments were established that we either do or do not perform by the choice of our own will, how is it that the Prophet is always presenting himself and repeating daily the commandments of God? Those who received them would certainly have been sufficiently instructed once, unless this shows that we always need God’s assistance, and that what was once given can never be sufficient unless it is renewed daily by the Lord’s admonition.

“And the Lord sent to you all his servants the Prophets, rising early and sending them; and you did not listen.”

God continually admonished his people, not through one Prophet but through all of them. He rose early, as it were, himself stationed on watch and guard, to admonish his people. “And you did not listen,” he says, so that the more frequent the warning, the greater would be the sins of those who despised it.

(Verses 4–5.) “Nor did you incline your ears to hear, when I said [Vulg. ‘when he said’]: Return, each of you, from his evil way and from your very evil thoughts, and you shall dwell in the land that the Lord gave to you and to your fathers, from age to age.”

Such was the hardness of the people that they did not even assume the posture of one who listens, nor incline their ear, especially when the Lord was admonishing each person to return from his evil way and from his very evil thoughts. And, O infinite mercy! He did not impose punishment for the crime, but summoned them to repentance—for evil deeds, which he signifies by “the evil way,” and for very evil thoughts, which are also reckoned as sin even without an action.

He promises a reward if they do what has been commanded: that they will dwell in the land given to their fathers and taken away on account of their children’s sins. When he says “from age to age,” or “from eternity to eternity,” he shows that God’s gifts are perpetual, if those to whom they have been given prove worthy.

(Verses 6–7.) “And do not go after foreign gods to serve and worship them; nor provoke me to anger by the works of your hands, and I will not afflict you. And you did not listen to me [Note: [Col. 0834D] The words of the sacred text that follow are absent here in the Cistercian manuscript, since they are recited shortly afterward in their proper place], says the Lord, provoking me to anger by the works of your hands, to your own harm.”

“These things,” he says, “I warned you about along with the preceding matters: that you should not serve foreign gods and worship them, and that by doing these things you should not provoke me to anger through the works of your hands, so that I might do what I did not wish and afflict you. Yet you did not listen to me.”

The following words—“says the Lord, provoking me to anger by the works of your hands, to your own harm”—are not found in the Seventy.

(Verses 8.) “Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts: Because you did not listen to my words, behold, I will send and take all the tribes of the north, says the Lord, and Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant.”

Because you provoked me to anger, did evil to your own destruction, and trampled under your proud foot the one who was calling you to repentance, “I will send,” he says, “to all the tribes—or nations—of the north, and I will bring their leader, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant.”

The Lord sends either angels to stir up the nations, or, certainly, he moves such tribes to carry out the Lord’s will. When he calls Nebuchadnezzar his servant, he is not calling him a servant in the same way as the Prophets and all the saints, who truly serve the Lord; rather, he is calling him a servant because, in the overthrow of Jerusalem, he serves the Lord’s will. Thus the Apostle also says: “Whom I delivered to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20). No one doubts that the Chaldeans are situated in the northern region, in relation to Jerusalem.

(Verses 9.) “And I will bring them against this land, and against its inhabitants, and against all the nations surrounding it; and I will kill them, and make them an astonishment, a hissing, and everlasting desolations.”

These are the rewards of those who despise God and refuse to hear his words. Whatever evil, therefore, is brought upon us is caused by our sins. And just as then all the nations were brought against Jerusalem, so today they are brought against the negligent Church, to kill them and make them an astonishment, a hissing, and everlasting desolations, so that they may be an example and a marvel to everyone. A hissing is an indication of marvel and astonishment; and everlasting desolation is found in those who do not have God as their ruler.

(Verses 10.) “And I will destroy from them the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstone and the light of the lamp. And all its land [Vulg. ‘this land’] shall become a desolation and an astonishment.”

This is also demonstrated today in the assembly of the wicked: their teachers do not teach the word of God, but hiss like a serpent. The voice of joy and the voice of gladness perish among them, so that they never hear the Apostle’s words: “Rejoice; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4).

The voice of the bride is the voice of ecclesiastical faith, and the voice of the bridegroom is that of the Lord and Savior: “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3:29). The sound of the millstone is absent, so that grain may not be ground in it and distributed to feed the people [Col. 0835D]. The light of the lamp is the teaching and knowledge [Al. “doctrine and knowledge”] of the Prophets. Finally, John the Baptist is also called “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35). And another Prophet says: “Your word, O Lord, is a lamp to my feet and a light to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

“All the land,” he says, “of the heretics will become a desolation and an astonishment, when its final fool has been exposed.”

(Verses 11 ff.) “And all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. When the seventy years are completed, I will visit the iniquity of the king of Babylon and of that nation, says the Lord, and of the land of the Chaldeans, and I will make it everlasting desolations. And I will bring upon that land all my words that I have spoken against it: everything written in this book, whatever Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations.”

Just as Jerusalem receives back its former inhabitants after seventy years and, once its punishments have been completed because it obeyed God’s decision, enjoys its former prosperity, so the king of Babylon, who was lifted up in pride and attributed his rule over the nations to his own strength rather than to the will of the Lord, will be destroyed when the Medes and Persians arrive. Indeed, to this day only the ruins of the city of Babylon remain. The Lord made it an everlasting desolation and fulfilled all the words contained in this very Prophet’s book. For in what follows Jeremiah describes the evils Babylon will suffer.

(Verses 14.) “For they served them, although they were many nations and great kings; and I will repay them according to their works and according to the deeds of their hands.”

This is not found in the Seventy. It signifies that Jeremiah prophesied not only against Babylon, but also against the other nations that had been in the Babylonian army and had fought against the Lord’s people. Indeed, what follows speaks against Egypt, the Philistines, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, the kingdoms of Hazor, Elam, and finally against Babylon and the land of the Chaldeans.

(Verses 15 ff.) “For thus says the Lord God of Israel to me [Vulg. adds ‘of hosts’ and omits ‘to me’]: Take this cup of the wine of fury (or unmixed wine) from my hand, and give it to drink to all the nations to which I send you. They shall drink and become drunk [Vulg. ‘become disordered’] (or vomit), and they shall go mad because of the sword that I will send among them.”

And I took the cup from the hand of the Lord and gave it to drink to all the nations to which the Lord sent me.

The giving of the cup, and of the cup of unmixed or unblended wine [Al. “mixed”], which in Greek is called ἀκράτου (*akratou*, “unmixed”), is an indication of the Lord’s fury: all the nations that fought against God’s people are to drink from the cup of the Lord’s fury. Concerning this Isaiah writes against Jerusalem: “You have drunk the cup of his fury, the cup of ruin; you have drained it. Therefore rise up” (Isa. 51:17).

This cup is drunk by all the nations so that they may vomit and go mad. A certain perverse interpreter takes this in a favorable sense, as though, like a purgative potion, it forces out whatever bile, phlegm, and harmful humor is in the breast and restores the former health. In place of Jeremiah he understands the Savior [Note: [Col. 0836D] Compare Origen’s Homily on this passage], on the grounds that he gave the cup to all the nations to which he had also been sent, so that, casting away idolatry, they might devote themselves to the worship of God.

The following passages will show that this is contrary to Holy Scripture. They are given the unmixed cup not as a remedy, as he wishes, but as a punishment.

(Verses 18.) “Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, and its kings and its officials, to make them a desolation, an astonishment, a hissing, and a curse, as they are today.”

“I thought,” he says, “that I was giving the cup only to the nations, and therefore I had gladly offered myself for this ministry. But among the other nations—indeed, before the other nations—I gave it to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, to its kings and officials, to make them an astonishment, a desolation, a hissing, and a curse, as the present example also proves.”

Hence he says above: “You deceived me, O Lord, and I was deceived; you prevailed and overcame” (above, 20:7).

(Verses 19.) “To Pharaoh king of Egypt, his servants, his officials, and all his people, and all the peoples generally.”

After Jerusalem, Pharaoh king of Egypt and his associates drank; the officials and the entire people drank, as did everyone who was not Egyptian but lived in his regions. The Seventy translated these people as συμμίκτοι (*symmiktoi*), that is, “mixed peoples”: not the common people of the Egyptian region, but foreigners and newcomers.

“And to all the kings of the land of Ausitis.”

In Hebrew this is called Uz (), concerning which the history also says that Job came from there: “There was a man in the land of Ausitis, whose name was Job” (Job 1:1). Nevertheless, it should be known that this verse is not found in the Seventy, and that Theodotion translated Uz as “island.”

(Verses 20.) “And to all the kings of the land of the Philistines, and to Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and the remnant of Ashdod.”

[Col. 0837C] He has named the Philistines generally—that is, the land of the Palestinians—and specifically their cities: Ashkelon, Gaza, Ekron, and Ashdod. He mentioned only Gath indirectly, since it is included among the remnant. This is the meaning of the words: “and the remnant of Ashdod.” For Gath is nearby and contiguous with Ashdod; in Hebrew it is called ESDOD (), the territory of the city of Gath. Isaiah records that the Palestinians were captured and devastated by the Babylonians.

(Verses 21.) “To Edom, Moab, the sons of Ammon, all the kings of Tyre, and all the kings of Sidon.”

Edom is the region containing Mount Seir, and in Hebrew it is called EDOM (). Moab and Ammon are the sons of Lot, near the Dead Sea. Tyre and Sidon are chief cities on the Phoenician coast. They too were conquered when the Babylonian army arrived [Note: [Col. 0837D] The Vatican manuscript adds “army”]. Carthage was their colony. Hence the Carthaginians are called Poeni, as though Phoeni, through corruption of the term “Phoenicians”; their language is largely related to the Hebrew language.

(Verses 22.) “And to the kings [Note: [Col. 0837D] The Vatican manuscript again adds “of the land,” a term retained here by the Hieronymian version; in Hebrew there is only [the corresponding word]] of the islands that are beyond the sea.”

Beyond Cyprus, Rhodes, and the islands called Κυκλάδες (*Kyklades*, “Cyclades”). These too were occupied by the Babylonians.

(Verses 23.) “And Dedan, Tema, Buz, and all who shave the hair of their heads.”

These nations are in the desert, near to and mixed with the regions of the Ishmaelites, whom they now call Saracens, and concerning whom it is said: “those who shave the hair of their heads.”

(Verses 24.) “And all the kings of Arabia, and all the kings of the west who dwell in the desert.”

This is not found in the Seventy. After Dedan, Tema, Buz, and the Ishmaelites, he therefore follows the geographical order of the regions.

“And all the kings of Zamri.”

This too is not found in the Seventy.

(Verses 25.) “And all the kings of Elam, and all the kings of the Medes.”

Because Elam and the kings of the Medes follow Zamri, we think that Zamri is also a region of Persia, unless perhaps, because Arabia has just preceded it, these kings are to be understood as kings of the desert. Elam is a region of Persia beyond Babylon; hence the Elamites. The Medes also, and the Persians, were the people by whom Babylon was captured and destroyed. They too drank the unmixed cup when Alexander, king of the Macedonians, gave it to them.

“And all the kings of the north, near and far.”

Because he had enumerated the regions of Persia and Babylon—Elam and the Medes—he now speaks generally of all the kings of the north, both those who are near and those who are far away. Instead of “north,” which in Hebrew is called SAPHON (), the Seventy translated ἀφηλιώτης (*aphēliōtēs*), which we may call “the east wind.”

(Verses 26.) “Each against his brother, and all the kingdoms of the earth that are upon its face” [Note: [Col. 0838D] The Vatican manuscript appropriately supplies the other half of the verse: “And King Sheshach shall drink after them”].

To avoid the length of enumerating separately all the regions of the eastern province, he spoke generally of all the kingdoms of the earth that are mentioned in the land. When he said “each against his brother,” the unstated meaning is: “I gave them unmixed drink,” so that they might all rage, vomit, go mad, and fight among themselves in mutual battles.

“And King Sheshach shall drink after them”—which is not found in the Seventy—has this meaning: “All the surrounding nations shall be subjected to the rule of Babylon, and he will subject everything to his power, so that all the nations named in the preceding passage will serve him and drink from his cup.” Hence, in the vision against Babylon, it is also written: “Babylon was a golden cup, making all the earth drunk” (below, 51:7).

Finally, the king of Babylon will drink this potion when Cyrus, king of the Medes and Persians—the rider of the chariot, camel, and donkey—offers it to him [Col. 0838D]. But whoever has even a small knowledge of the Hebrew language will have no great difficulty understanding how Babylon, which in Hebrew is called BABEL (), is understood as SESACH ().

Just as among us the Greek alphabet is read in order through its final letter—Alpha, Beta, and so on up to ω—and then, for the memory of children, we customarily reverse the order of reading and mix the first letters with the last, saying Alpha, O, Beta, Psi, so among the Hebrews the first letter is ALEPH, the second BETH, the third GHIMEL, and so on through the twenty-second and final letter, THAU, whose penultimate letter is SIN.

Thus we read ALEPH, THAU, BETH, SIN. When we come to the middle, the letter LAMED corresponds to CHAPH. If we read correctly, we read BABEL (); but with the order changed, we read SESACH ().

The vowel letters between BETH and BETH, and LAMED [Note: [Col. 0839D] Between BETH and BETH. “And CHAPH” is added superfluously in all the manuscript copies; the text reads, “between Beth and Beth, Lamed and Chaph,” though it concerns the name [Sesach], whose consonantal letters, according to Hebrew idiom, do not include vowel letters. They call these *Boias*. Consult the book of Names under the entry “Luza.” MARTIAN.] are not written in this name, according to Hebrew idiom. [Materially uncertain because the printed Hebrew-letter sequence is absent.] [Note: [Col. 0839D] In the Cistercian manuscript, as also in the manuscripts consulted by Martianay, “and Chaph” is added. The meaning is that, just as in the name Babel the two Beths—which are the second letter of the Greek alphabet—correspond in the name Sesach to the two Sins, which are the penultimate letters, so in the same order Lamed corresponds to Chaph. Some therefore think the passage should be supplied as follows: “between Beth and Beth and Lamed; between Sin and Sin and Chaph.” The full rationale of this Kabbalistic permutation, current among the Jews and commonly called Athbash from its first letters, is as follows:]

I think the holy Prophet prudently concealed this, lest he openly provoke the madness of those who were besieging Jerusalem and were already on the point of taking possession of it [1020]. We also read that the Apostle did the same thing against the Roman Empire when he wrote concerning the Antichrist:

“Do you not remember that, when I was still with you, I used to tell you these things? And now you know what restrains him, so that he may be revealed in his own time”—that is, the Antichrist. “For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only let the one who now restrains hold back, until he is removed from the midst. And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the manifestation of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:3 ff.).

He indicates that the one who restrains is the Roman Empire. Unless it is destroyed and removed from the midst, according to the prophecy of Daniel, the Antichrist will not come beforehand. If he had wished to say this openly, he would foolishly have stirred up the rage of persecution against Christians and the Church then coming into being.

We have spoken about this chapter at greater length than the brevity of commentaries permits—something that the Greeks and Latins may perhaps find tiresome, since it is not found in their manuscripts. But what benefit would there be in this, when the same Prophet says in what follows: “How Sheshach has been captured, and the glory of the whole earth has been seized! How Babylon has become an astonishment among the nations”?

The allegorical interpreters refer this entire passage to all the nations whom the devil has intoxicated with the unmixed cup of sins. They say that he himself will finally drink punishments and torments, concerning whom the Apostle writes: “The Lord Jesus will kill him with the breath of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). And elsewhere he says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Cor. 15:26).

It requires great ingenuity to be able to transfer the names of various nations beneath their etymologies and to fit individual vices to individual names.

(Verses 27.) “And you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Drink and become drunk, vomit and fall, and do not rise [Vulg. ‘nor get up’] from before the sword that I will send among you [Al. ‘against you’].”

“After you have given the cup to all the nations and fulfilled the Lord’s command, you will again command them in the Lord’s words [Note: [Col. 0840D] The Cistercian manuscript reads ‘you will reproach’ instead of ‘you will command’], saying: Drink and become drunk, vomit and fall, and do not rise.”

If drinking and becoming drunk, vomiting and falling were an indication of salvation, so that harmful things might be expelled like a purgative potion, how does the text continue, “and do not rise”? What the potion is that causes them to fall forever, he states more clearly: namely, “from before the sword that I will send among you.”

(Verses 28.) “And when they refuse to receive the cup from your hand and drink, you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord of hosts: You shall certainly drink. For behold, in the city over which my name has been invoked I begin [Vulg. ‘I will begin’] to afflict, and will you be regarded as innocent and exempt (or, ‘will you be completely cleansed’)? You shall not be exempt (or, ‘you shall not be clean’).”

He subtly shows that those who refuse to carry out God’s command willingly will receive it by necessity and hear the words: “You shall certainly drink.” Whether you wish it or not, he says, God’s sentence must be fulfilled.

For if the city of Jerusalem, in which God’s name was known—according to the Prophet’s words, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:1)—drank the unmixed cup of fury, how much less will you be clean, who worship idols in place of God’s name?

(Verses 29.) “For behold, I call the sword upon all the inhabitants of the earth, says the Lord of hosts.”

This is the unmixed potion, this is the cup of the Lord’s fury, which is summoned not only against Jerusalem but against the whole earth and all the surrounding nations. Concerning it he had said above: “I will send for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, my servant, and I will bring him against this land, against its inhabitants, and against all the nations surrounding it.”

### (Verses 30–31)

“And you shall prophesy to them all these words, and say to them:

‘The Lord will roar from on high (or, will give an answer), and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice. Roaring, he roars over his beauty (or, he will answer over his place); a battle-cry like that of men treading the winepress will be sung against all the inhabitants of the earth. The sound (or, destruction) reaches to the ends (or, over the extremity) of the earth, because the Lord has a judgment with the nations; he is judged with all flesh. I have handed over the wicked to the sword (another reading: He has handed over the wicked to the sword), says the Lord.’

First, let us give the meaning according to the truth of the interpretation. “You shall prophesy,” he says, “to all the nations, and say that the Lord roars from on high”—that is, that he gives a sign of his fury—in accordance with what is written: “The lion has roared, and who will not fear? The Lord has spoken, and who will not prophesy?” (Amos 3:8). “And from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice,” so as to terrify all who hear.

He will roar over his beauty, that is, over the Temple. And when he has roared, a battle-cry like that of men treading in winepresses will be sung. [Note: Others prefer *celeusma*, but *celeuma* is also good. Rutilius, Book I: “While a lowly *celeuma* resounds in varied rhythms” [reading uncertain]. It is Greek κέλευμα, in place of κέλευσμα. This was the name of a song uttered with a great shout. Thus Macarius, Homily 6, comparing those who shout while praying to *celeustae* (boatswains), says: “For those who employ cries are like boatswains.” In the Acts of Saint Genevieve the Virgin, ch. 7: “And all together with him, singing in the manner of a *celeuma*, glorified God in heaven, raising a cry.”] And amid the shedding of one another’s blood (another reading: mutually), a mournful song will be sung. Symmachus calls this a κατάληγμα; Aquila, an ἰασμός.

[Note: Montfaucon explains what ἰασμός is from the Syriac interpretation of Jeremiah 48:33, where the Hebrew words [Hebrew text not reproduced in the source] are rendered by the Syriac interpreter: οὐκέτι οἱ ληνοβατοῦντες κελεύουσι λέγοντες ἴα, ἴα—that is, “No longer do those treading the winepress command, saying, ‘Ia, ia.’” I would render it, “they will sing, saying ‘ia, ia,’” so that just as the noun κέλευμα signifies a song, so the verb κελεύω signifies “to sing.” Thus ἰασμός is a song of jubilation consisting of the cries “ia, ia,” which was customary among those treading the winepress and was produced by their voices. Moreover, Lambert Bos has rather learnedly emended this entire passage of Jerome, which had formerly been suspected by the distinguished Drusius of containing an error. First, in place of κατάληγμα, he restores κατάλεγμα with ε, a word signifying a mournful song, from καταλέγεσθαι, which Hesychius explains as “to mourn for the dead”; and thus this word is correctly read in Origen’s commentary on Ezekiel 11:10, where he says that Symmachus translated “mourning, song, and woe” (θρῆνος καὶ μέλος καὶ οὐαί) as “mournful songs, a κατάλεγμα, and a mournful melody” (θρῆνοι καὶ ΚΑΤΑΛΕΓΜΑ καὶ μέλος πενθικόν). In place of the latter ἰασμός, however, he wishes αἰασμός to be read, which likewise signifies lamentation and a mournful song, from αἰάζειν, “to lament,” itself derived from αἴ, “alas.” In this way the two corrupted words, which have also entered the lexicons on the basis of this one testimony of Jerome, are restored to their integrity.]

The sound of this battle-cry and song will reach to the ends of the earth, because the Lord has a judgment with the nations. But if the Lord has a judgment with the nations, their merits are also different (Hosea 4). This may be explained according to what some wish to understand in the passage, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). He has indeed been judged in that he did not believe; yet those who do not believe will suffer different punishments among themselves. “He is judged with all flesh,” so that no one departs without judgment. But the wicked—that is, those who do not believe in the Lord (another reading: in God)—he hands over to the everlasting sword.

The allegorical interpreters, following the Septuagint, explain this passage in such a way as to refer the Lord’s plainly expressed threat to a good outcome. “The Lord,” they say, “will give an answer from on high”—namely, to those whom he is going to save. “And from his holy place he will utter his voice”; he will answer with a word in his place. But they, like harvesters filled with fruits, will answer that sentence: “Destruction will come upon all the inhabitants of the earth”—not upon the whole earth, but upon a part of the earth, namely, those who do not believe. There will be judgment among the nations, and he himself will be judged with all flesh. But the wicked will be handed over to the sword.

### (Verses 32–33)

“Thus says the Lord of hosts:

‘Behold, affliction (or, evil) will go out from nation to nation, and a great whirlwind (or, storm) will go out from the summits (or, extremities) of the earth. And those slain by the Lord (or, wounded by the Lord) will be on that day from one end of the earth to the other. They will not be mourned; they will not be gathered up or buried. They will lie as dung upon the face of the earth.’”

Let those be ashamed who attempt to do violence to Holy Scripture by explaining in a favorable sense things that are full of threats. I think that the Lord also spoke of this passage when he said: “Nation will rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom” (Luke 21:10), together with the other things contained in the meaning of that Gospel.

We should understand these things (another reading: these very things) according to the historical account, when all the surrounding nations were subjected by the Babylonian king and experienced his cruel rule; or according to the prophecy, as events that will occur after a long time, at the consummation of the world. They are called “slain by the Lord,” not because the Lord himself strikes them, but because, in the destruction of the worst men, the Lord’s will and command are fulfilled.

### (Verses 34–35)

“Howl (or, rejoice), shepherds, and cry out, and sprinkle yourselves with ashes, leaders of the flock (or, lament, rams of the sheep), because your days have been completed for you to be slaughtered, and your dispersions; and you shall fall like precious vessels (or, like chosen rams). Flight will perish from the shepherds, and deliverance from the leaders (or, rams) of the flock.”

It should be noted that only here the Septuagint has used “rejoicing” in a negative sense; for it, the other interpreters translated “howling,” as it is written in the Hebrew. The distinction between shepherds and rams, or leaders of the flock, is that shepherds are understood as rulers of rational beings, whereas rams and leaders refer to the rich, who themselves are also called part of the flock.

As for the statement, “Your days have been completed for you to be slaughtered,” their days will then be completed when their sins have been completed. They will be scattered and fall like precious vessels, so that, once shattered, they cannot be restored; and the more precious they were before (another reading: precious), the greater will be their loss in being broken. Or, “like chosen rams,” so that they may be a fat victim for those eager to devour them.

“Flight,” he says, “will perish from the shepherds,” when they have not practiced repentance. Thus it is said to the Pharisees: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke 5:7). And we read in the Psalms: “Flight has perished from me” (Psalm 141:5). “And deliverance,” he says, “from the leaders of the flock,” or from the rams; by a common construction, “will perish” is understood.

### (Verse 36)

“The sound of the cry of the shepherds, and the howling of the leaders of the flock (or, the rejoicing of the rams), because the Lord has devastated their pasturelands. And the peaceful fields (or, beautiful places) have fallen silent before the face of the anger of the Lord’s fury.”

Here too it should be noted that among the Septuagint “rejoicing” has been used for “howling.” The difference between shepherds and rams is that shepherds are thought to be those in the Church who preside over the flock with wisdom, learning, and teaching. Rams, however, appear to be leaders among the people, but possess no learning or wisdom; through excessive simplicity they are almost akin to foolishness.

When we have peace but do not understand either the good things or the beautiful things of peace, and instead give ourselves over to luxury, idleness, and pleasures, then the good things of peace will cease—or fall silent—and will be taken away from us because of the anger of the Lord’s fury. What is written will then be fulfilled: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thessalonians 5:3); and when it comes, everything will fall silent.

### (Verses 37–38)

“He has abandoned his shelter like a lion (or, his lair).” More accurately, “his tabernacle,” for this is what the Hebrew *succho* signifies. “Because their land has become a desolation (or, an impassable place) before the face of the wrath of the dove (or, before the face of the great sword), and before the face of the anger of the Lord’s fury.”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript supplies the word “wrath,” in agreement with the Hebrew text, [Hebrew text not reproduced in the source].]

The Lord is the one of whom he had said above: “He will roar from on high, and from his holy dwelling he will utter his voice. Roaring, he will roar over his beauty.” He himself will abandon his tabernacle, of which it is written: “His place has become in peace, or in Salem, and his dwelling in Zion” (Psalm 75:2). He himself will abandon his seat and fulfill what he spoke through this same prophet: “I have forsaken my house; I have abandoned my inheritance” (Jeremiah 12:7).

He abandoned his lair like a lion, so that all the beasts might have power to ravage his land. When the lion is its guardian and ruler, no one dares approach it. “Their land,” he says—plainly meaning either the land of the Jewish people or, certainly, the land of all the nations—has become a desolation and an impassable place before the face of the dove’s wrath.

No one will be surprised that the Lord’s dove is understood as Nebuchadnezzar, since above he was called the Lord’s servant. In its place the Septuagint translated “great sword.” Although we may also understand the dove as representing Jerusalem, in that she is angry and sorrowful because she has lost the protection of her lion and because her land has been reduced to desolation.

### (Chapter 26: Verses 1 ff.)

“At the beginning of the reign (the Vulgate: ‘of the king’) of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord, saying:

‘Thus says the Lord: Stand in the court of the house of the Lord, and speak to all the cities of Judah, from which they come to worship in the house of the Lord, all the words that I have commanded you to speak to them. Do not withhold a word. Perhaps they will listen, and each one will turn from his evil way, and I will repent of the evil that I am considering doing to them because of the wickedness (the Vulgate: ‘wickednesses’) of their practices (or, I will cease from the evil that I am considering doing to them because of the wickedness of their practices).’”

[Note: The Vatican manuscript has the more harmonious reading: “The preceding is first.”]

This prophecy is earlier than the preceding one, although it was made under the same king. The former occurred in the fourth year of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah; this one, however, occurred at the beginning of the same king’s reign, as Scripture says: “At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord.” Therefore, as we have often said, the order of history is not to be woven together in the prophets, since here, under the same king, earlier events are reported later and later events earlier.

Whoever is going to proclaim the word of the Lord must stand with Moses (Deuteronomy 5) and hear with the Psalmist: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Psalm 134:2). He is commanded to speak to all the cities of Judah. Although the Septuagint did not translate “cities,” perhaps lest it seem inappropriate to speak in the court of the Lord’s house to cities that were not physically present, when he speaks to the people and citizens, he speaks to the cities themselves.

Beautifully, he stands in the court and vestibule of the Lord’s Temple, so that, under the pretext of the Lord’s prayer and worshiping him, they may be compelled to hear the prophet’s words.

“Do not withhold a word,” he says. Although it is sad, although the fury of the hearers may be stirred against you, nevertheless speak what has been commanded you—not fearing the persecutions of those who will be provoked against you, but fearing the command of the Lord who orders you.

“Perhaps,” he says, “they will listen and turn.” The word “perhaps” cannot properly be applied to the majesty of the Lord, but he speaks according to our human feeling, so that free will may be preserved for man, lest, because of God’s foreknowledge, he be compelled by necessity either to do or not to do something.

For something does not happen because God knows that it will happen; rather, because it will happen, God knows it, as the foreknower of future things. Yet we should understand, according to this same Jeremiah, that if the Lord predicts evil and the people repent, he too will repent concerning what he threatened to do. And if he promises prosperity and the people act negligently, God changes his judgment and brings evil instead of good.

Something similar appears in the Gospel: “I will send my son; perhaps they will respect him” (Luke 20:13). This is certainly spoken from the person of God Almighty. Finally, here too he says: “Perhaps they will listen and each one will turn from his evil way,” so that, when they have turned, I may repent of my judgment and not do what I am considering doing to them.

He is considering doing it because of the wickedness of their practices; if those practices are changed, his judgment will also be changed. Let us read the history of Jonah and Nineveh.

### (Verses 4 ff.)

“And you shall say to them:

‘Thus says the Lord: If you will not listen to me, and (another reading: so as to) walk in my law, which I gave you, and to listen to the words of my servants the prophets, whom I sent to you, rising early and sending them, and you have not listened, I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.’”

It lies within our power either to do something or not to do it, provided that whatever good work we desire, seek, and complete, we attribute to the grace of God, who, according to the Apostle, gave us both the will and the accomplishment (Philippians 2).

But if it is enough, as the foolish heresy supposes, to walk once in the law given to us through Moses, how did he add: “So as to listen to the words of my servants the prophets”? They were sent after the law, and not once but frequently—not carelessly and from a position of security, but always and with earnest concern.

“I sent,” he says, “my servants the prophets to you daily, rising early and sending them.” If you refuse to listen to them, “I will make this house”—that is, the Temple of God—“like Shiloh,” where the tabernacle was. Once the Temple has been destroyed, consequently the city too will become a curse to all the nations of the earth.

But just as, when the Temple was built on Ornan’s threshing floor and on Mount Moriah—that is, the mountain of vision, where Abraham is said to have offered his son Isaac—the worship of Shiloh ceased and sacrifices were no longer celebrated there, so, when the Church was built and spiritual sacrifices were offered in it, the ceremonies of the Law ceased (2 Chronicles 3). And the city of the Jews was made a curse to all the nations (another reading: kings) of the earth. From this curse the Lord delivered us, as the Apostle says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13).

### (Verses 7–9)

“And the priests and the prophets (or, false prophets) and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the house of the Lord. And when Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the Lord had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets (or, false prophets) and all the people seized him, saying:

‘He must be put to death, because (the Vulgate: “why”) he prophesied in the name of the Lord, saying: This house will be like Shiloh, and this city will be desolated, because there is no inhabitant.’”

The priests and prophets—whom the Septuagint more explicitly translated as false prophets—are angry with Jeremiah because he proclaims the truth: that, with the Temple overturned and the city deserted, the worship will perish, along with the profits that come from religion. Therefore they seize him and, with the people agreeing, condemn him to death, because he said in the name of the Lord that this house would be like Shiloh and the city would be desolated because it had no inhabitant.

Therefore, whenever, because of the commandments of the Lord and the truth of faith, either priests, false prophets, or a deceived people become angry with us, let us not be greatly concerned; let us carry out the judgment of God, thinking not about present evils but about future goods.

### (Verse 10)

“And all the people gathered against Jeremiah in the house of the Lord. The princes of Judah heard these words, and they went up from the king’s house to the house of the Lord, and sat at the entrance of the new gate of the Lord (the Vulgate: ‘of the house of the Lord’).”

Jeremiah was prophesying the Lord’s words in the Temple, and had said: “I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.” Immediately, when an uprising had been stirred up by the priests, prophets, and people, the whole crowd gathered against the prophet in the Temple, where the prophet was being held in the hands of the priests, prophets, and populace. [Note: Victorius supplied the word *dabo* (“I will make/give”).]

When the city’s princes, who were in the royal palace, heard this, they crossed over, or went up, from the king’s house to the house of the Lord. It should be noted that going to the house of the Lord is always an ascent.

They sat at the entrance of the Lord’s new gate. It was the duty of the princes to sit at the gate of the Lord’s house and there investigate the truth of the dispute and uprising. It is called the new gate because those who sat there and presided over judgment resisted the accusations of the priests and false prophets.

### (Verse 11)

“And the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes and to all the people, saying:

‘Judgment of death belongs to this man, because he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your own ears.’”

While the city’s princes sat at the gate of the Temple and at the new gate, having hurried from the royal palace to the Temple so that the people’s uprising might be quieted, and while the assembly of the people was gathered, the priests and false prophets accused Jeremiah.

The prophet would have perished, so far as the priests and prophets were concerned, if the accusers themselves had possessed judicial authority. From this we understand that those who appeared devoted to religion were more savage toward the prophet, out of envy of his holiness, than those who were in charge of public affairs.

### (Verses 12 ff.)

“Then Jeremiah said to all the princes and to all the people:

‘The Lord sent me to prophesy against this house (or, over this house) and against this city (or, over this city) all the words that you have heard. Now therefore make your ways and your practices good, and listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and the Lord will repent of the evil that he has spoken against you (or, the Lord will cease from the evils that he has spoken against you).

‘But as for me, behold, I am in your hands. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes (or, what is expedient for you). Nevertheless, know and understand that if you kill me, you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its inhabitants. For in truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears.’”

While the princes sat at the city gate in the presence of the people, and the priests and prophets accused Jeremiah the prophet and brought a charge worthy of death against him, Jeremiah spoke to the princes and to all the people whom the faction of the priests and false prophets had stirred up—wisely, humbly, and steadfastly.

He spoke wisely in saying that he had been sent by the Lord to speak against the Temple and the city, and in giving them the counsel that, if they were willing to listen to him and repent, the Lord too would change his judgment.

He spoke humbly when he said: “Behold, I am in your hands; do with me what is good and right in your eyes.” And he spoke steadfastly in saying: “In truth the Lord sent me to you, to speak all these words in your ears.”

In other words, he says: “If you are angry because (another reading: ‘why’) I have spoken against the Lord’s Temple and city, and if the safety of the city and Temple matters to you, why do you add sins to sins and make both the city and its inhabitants liable for my blood?”

Therefore, whenever we too need humility because of the pressures of necessity, let us assume it in such a way that we do not abandon truth and steadfastness. It is one thing arrogantly to insult the judge, which is a sign of foolishness; it is another thing to avoid an impending danger in such a way that you subtract nothing from the truth.

### (Verse 16)

“And the princes and all the people said to the priests and the prophets:

‘This man does not deserve the judgment of death, because he has spoken to us in the name of the Lord our God.’”

The people, who had previously been led astray by the priests and false prophets, join the city’s princes and speak on Jeremiah’s behalf, saying that he is by no means guilty of death, but that he prophesied in the name of the Lord and from his mouth.

The uneducated crowd quickly changes its judgment once it has grasped the reasoning. But the anger of the accusers—especially the priests and false prophets—cannot be changed. Thus, while those men continue accusing and persist in their accusation, the people change, because the Lord had given them the hope of pardon if they made their ways good and listened to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord too might bend his judgment.

### (Verses 17 ff.)

“Then men from the elders of the land arose and spoke to the whole assembly of the people, saying:

‘Micah of Moresheth was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he said to all the people of Judah:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts: Zion will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house a wooded height.”

‘Did Hezekiah king of Judah and all Judah condemn him to death? Did they not fear the Lord and entreat the face of the Lord? And the Lord repented of the evil that he had spoken against them.

‘Therefore we are doing great evil against our own souls.’”

The city’s princes and the people understand the truth of the judgment. The elders—whose particular duty it was to know ancient things—repeat the history and compare the prophecy of Micah of Moresheth, who prophesied under King Hezekiah, with Jeremiah’s prophecy, on account of which he is threatened with death.

They show that Micah spoke more severe words, yet suffered nothing from the righteous King Hezekiah. Instead, the people turned to repentance, and the Lord changed his judgment for the better. Micah said: “Zion will be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem will become a heap of stones, and the mountain of the house a wooded height” (Micah 3:12).

Jeremiah, however, said: “I will make this house like Shiloh, and I will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth” (above, 24:9).

They give this counsel because they think that what Micah had foretold would by no means happen, since it had not happened for a long time because of the people’s repentance. Likewise, what Jeremiah has spoken will not happen if, following his counsel, they make their ways and practices good and listen to the voice of the Lord their God, so that the Lord will not bring upon them the evil with which he threatened them.

At the same time they break the fury of the accusers and join themselves to them, saying: “Therefore we are doing great evil against our own souls”—not because they ought to do evil, but because, if they do so, they will not harm the accused; rather, they will harm their own souls, which they could free by changing the judgment.

### (Verses 20 ff.)

“There was also a man prophesying in the name of the Lord, Uriah son of Shemaiah from Kiriath-jearim. He prophesied against this city and against this land, according to all the words of Jeremiah. And King Jehoiakim and all his mighty men and his princes (Vatican manuscript: “and all the princes”) heard these words, and the king sought to kill him. When Uriah heard this, he was afraid, fled, and entered Egypt.

The statement that follows—‘King Jehoiakim sent men to Egypt, Elnathan son of Achbor and men with him, to Egypt’—is not found in the Septuagint. Then the account continues:

‘They brought Uriah out of Egypt and brought him to King Jehoiakim. He struck him with the sword and threw his corpse into the graves of the common people.’

Nevertheless, the hand of Ahikam son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah (the Vulgate: “was”), so that he was not handed over to the people to be killed.

The question arises why, when Uriah son of Shemaiah from the town of Kiriath-jearim prophesied the same things as Jeremiah, he was terrified and fled to Egypt, was brought back from there, and killed, while Jeremiah was able to escape—even though he had not fled, but had courageously persevered in his former declaration—and was delivered, both by the judgment of the people and princes and by the counsel of the elders against the accusers, priests, and false prophets.

The answer must briefly be that God’s judgment cannot be known: in the same cause and under the same sentence one person is punished and another delivered. Unless perhaps we can answer that Uriah was slain as a condemnation of the accusers and the people, while Jeremiah was preserved for God’s judgment, so that he might preach to the remnants of the wretched people and lead them back to repentance.

We read something similar in the Acts of the Apostles: the Apostle James immediately suffered Herod’s sentence and was crowned with martyrdom (Acts 12), whereas blessed Peter and the other apostles were preserved for the teaching of the Lord.

We should also observe the prophet’s steadfastness: even when Uriah was brought back from Egypt, he did not change his judgment, but, seeing that death was being prepared for him, nevertheless spoke what the Lord had commanded.

That he was afraid, fled, and entered Egypt is not a sign of unbelief but of prudence, lest we needlessly expose ourselves to danger. Otherwise, we also read that the Savior escaped from the hands of those pursuing him (Luke 4; John 8), and that he commanded the apostles: “When they persecute you in this city, flee to another” (Matthew 10:23).

It is also asked how Jehoiakim, king of Judah—a ruler of little power, already weakened and on the point of perishing—could have had the authority to send men to Egypt and bring Uriah out from there.
