This is easily resolved if we consider that he had been appointed prince by Necho, king of Egypt, and that this prophecy was made at the beginning of his reign.

Although Jeremiah was delivered by the Lord’s help, the one through whom the Lord delivered his prophet is also credited with this as a reward—namely, Ahikam son of Shaphan, as we shall read later, when Jeremiah is delivered from the danger of death from the cistern of mud through the counsel and protection of Abdemelech the eunuch (below, 38).

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “if at some time he is delivered from the cistern …”]

### (Chapter 27: Verse 1)

“At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying.”

This is not found in the Septuagint edition. Many think that it is the beginning of the following chapter, but this is not so. Rather, it must be joined to what precedes, so that we understand everything reported as said and done to have been done at the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign.

Hence he also had the authority to send men to Egypt, as to a friendly king. It seems to me, however, that the Septuagint omitted this heading for the following reason: they did not wish to appear to say it twice. For they had already placed at the beginning: “At the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the Lord to Jeremiah.”

### (Verse 2)

“Thus says the Lord to me:

‘Make for yourself bonds and chains.’”

Or κλοιοί, which in Hebrew are called *mutoth* [Hebrew term not reproduced in the source], and in ordinary speech are called *boiae*.

[Note: In the old glossaries κλοιός is rendered *boia* and *equuleus*. In the same place, under *boia*, one finds κλοιὸν περιτίθημι. We have often discussed this word. See the Book of Numbers under “Luz.”]

### (Verses 3–4)

“And you shall place them upon your neck, and send them to the king of Edom, to the king of Moab, to the king of the sons of Ammon, to the king of Tyre, and to the king of Sidon, by the hand (the Vulgate: ‘in the hand’) of the messengers who came to Jerusalem to Zedekiah king of Judah. And you shall command them to speak to their masters:

‘Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel. Thus shall you say to your masters.’”

The preceding vision occurred at the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, king of Judah. This one, however, occurred under Zedekiah, who was the last to reign in Jerusalem, and under whom the city was captured and destroyed.

Jeremiah is commanded to place upon his neck chains, or wooden yokes, which in Hebrew, as we said, are called *mutoth*, and to send them by messengers to the kings of Edom, Moab, the sons of Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon—messengers who had come to Zedekiah. He is to command them to announce to their masters that they must serve King Nebuchadnezzar and hear what the prophet’s following speech continues to say.

And lest perhaps the messengers and kings of these nations should reply, “Why do you not command this of your own people?” he speaks similarly to Zedekiah as well, and to the priests and prophets.

The allegorical interpreter (Origen) always interprets this passage while fleeing from the truth of history, saying that it concerns the heavenly Jerusalem: its inhabitants must voluntarily assume bodies and descend into Babylon—that is, into the confusion of this world, which is set in evil—and serve the king of Babylon, plainly meaning the devil.

If they refuse to do this, he says, they will not carry heavy bodies but will perish by sword, famine, and pestilence; and they will no longer be human beings but demons.

Let him say this, so that his defenders do not bring accusations against us. For our part, let us follow the simple and true history, lest we be enveloped in certain clouds and illusions.

### (Verse 5)

“I made the earth, and man, and the beasts that are upon the face of the earth, by my great strength and my outstretched arm, and I gave it to whomever seemed good in my eyes” (another reading: “who was pleasing in my eyes”).

Although Scripture speaks here ἀνθρωποπάθως—that is, in human terms, as we human beings can speak and understand—the strength of God and his arm are the one of whom the Apostle also speaks: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:14). Isaiah too says: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1). The Evangelist John writes: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). David likewise says in his song: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Psalm 32:6).

When he says, “I gave it to him who was pleasing in my eyes,” this signifies that all things have been granted to the human race through the grace of God. “I,” he says, “made the earth, and man, and beasts” (Psalm 35). The order is reversed. In Genesis the animals are made first and man last (Genesis 1), but here he names man first and then the things subject to man.

### (Verses 6–7)

“Now therefore I have given all these lands into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, my servant. Moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field, so that they may serve him. And all nations will serve him, and his son, and his son’s son.”

What misery is Israel’s, when by comparison with him Nebuchadnezzar is called God’s servant? It is written in the Gospel: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him” (John 1:10–11).

Rightly, therefore, the Creator gives his creation to whomever he wishes. Indeed, the devil too, whose type Nebuchadnezzar prefigures, confesses: “All these things have been handed over to me.”

When he adds, “Moreover, I have given him the beasts of the field, so that they may serve him,” we should either understand simply every kind of animal—for together with man those things subject to him are also handed over—or else understand “beasts” as savage nations, since even those serve who previously did not know how to serve.

By “his son” and “his son’s son,” according to the Hebrew, he names Belshazzar and Evil-merodach, about whom Daniel writes.

“Until the time of his land and of him comes.”

Beautifully, lest Nebuchadnezzar’s rule be thought everlasting, he says that he too will be captured by the Medes and Persians. This is what the phrase signifies: “Until the time of his land and of him comes.” But this too is not found in the Septuagint.

“And many nations and great kings will serve him.”

He did not say “all,” for this belongs properly to the rule of Christ. Yet according to Symmachus the reading is not, “Many nations and great kings will serve him,” but rather, “Many nations and great kings will subject him to servitude,” so that he too may serve the Medes and Persians—he whom all the nations had previously served.

This passage, which we have inserted from the Hebrew—“I gave [them] to him that they might serve him, and all nations will serve him, and his son, and his son’s son, until the time of his land and of him comes; and many nations and great kings will subject him to servitude”—is not found in the Septuagint edition, as we have already said.

### (Verse 8)

“But the nation and kingdom that will not serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and whoever will not bend his neck beneath the yoke of the king of Babylon, I will punish that nation with sword, famine, and pestilence, says the Lord, until I consume them by his hand.”

The Lord not only subjects sinful nations to Nebuchadnezzar; the Apostle also speaks of sinners: “Those whom I have handed over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20). And elsewhere: “I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (1 Corinthians 5:5).

He also teaches that we must obey authorities, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience, lest we be condemned by them.

(Verses 9 ff.) “Therefore do not listen to your prophets, diviners, dreamers, augurs, and sorcerers, who say to you, ‘You shall not serve the king of Babylon,’ for they prophesy falsehood to you, so that they may remove you far from your land, drive you out, and cause you to perish. But the nation that submits its neck beneath the yoke of the king of Babylon and serves him, I will leave in its own land,” says the Lord; “and it shall cultivate it and dwell in it.”

The allegorical interpreter raves in this passage as well, urging those placed in the heavenly Jerusalem not to listen to their prophets, diviners, dreamers, augurs, and sorcerers, but rather to serve Nebuchadnezzar and assume the body of our humiliation: the cries of infants and the swaddling clothes of little children. For if they do this, then, once their servitude and the condition of human mortality have been completed, they will return to their own land, dwell in it, and perform the works they previously performed. He says that he suspects those who have despised God’s commands will become demons weighed down by human bodies, and unclean spirits, and will by no means recover their former dwelling.

Let us, however, explain the passage simply. There are prophets among the nations who pretend to foretell the future by divine inspiration; and diviners, of whom there is also a common proverb: “The wise claim to divine”; and dreamers who imitate Joseph and Daniel; and augurs who announce, from the flight of birds and the cries of birds, whether something should or should not be done; and sorcerers, whom we may call poisoners or those who serve the phantasms of demons, who in Hebrew are called CASSAPHE (). “All these,” he says, “deceive and ensnare you, so that you do not serve the king of Babylon.” For it is much better voluntarily to accept servitude, to have as a friend the one whom you serve, and to cultivate your native land, than to serve as captives by force and necessity.

(Verses 12, 13.) “And I spoke to Zedekiah, king of Judah, according to all these words, saying: Submit your necks beneath the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why should you and your people die by the sword, famine, and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that refuses to serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you, ‘Do not serve the king of Babylon,’ because they speak falsehood to you, for I have not sent them,” says the Lord; “and they prophesy falsely in my name, so that I may drive you out and you may perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you.”

After all the nations, he turns to Zedekiah, king of Judah, and addresses him in the same words with which he threatened the nations; for the Israelite nation does not deserve a privilege when it has sinned either similarly to the other nations or more grievously than they. Finally, because the rebellious people refused to listen, they were consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence.

It should be observed in Holy Scripture that it calls “prophets” those who prophesy falsely in the name of the Lord, instead of calling them false prophets. “But they do this,” he says, “so that I may drive you out and you may perish, both you and the prophets who prophesy to you.” Thus the destruction of those who are deceived and of those who deceive is alike.

This passage, which we have rendered from the Hebrew—“Beneath the yoke of the king of Babylon, and serve him and his people, and you shall live. Why should you and your people die by the sword, famine, and pestilence, as the Lord has spoken concerning the nation that refuses to serve the king of Babylon? Do not listen to the words of the prophets who say to you”—is not found in the Septuagint. I therefore give this warning, so that the prudent reader may understand how much is lacking, one passage at a time, in the Greek and Latin codices.

(Verses 16, 17.) “And I spoke to the priests and to this people, saying: Thus says the Lord: Do not listen to the words of your prophets who prophesy to you, saying, ‘Behold, the vessels of the Lord will soon be brought back from Babylon’; for they prophesy falsehood to you.”

The words “soon”—which we have included—are not found in the Septuagint. Nor is what follows found there: “Do not listen to them, but serve the king of Babylon, so that you may live. Why should this city be given over to desolation?”

After addressing the nations and the king, he speaks to the priests and the people, to whom he had already announced the destruction, saying that he would drive them out and they would perish, both they and the prophets who prophesied to them. He repeats to them what he had said to the king and to the nations: they must not listen to the words of their prophets or say that the vessels of the Lord’s temple were soon to be brought back—those vessels that had been carried away with Jeconiah, the princes, and his mother.

[Note: [Col. 0851D] In the Cistercian manuscript: “were soon to be brought back now, which …,” etc.]

He urges them to serve the king of Babylon and live, so that the city, voluntarily subjected, may not be handed over to the flames. Here too the Lord’s clemency is evident: he wishes to hand them over to a lighter punishment, so that they may not suffer a more severe one.

(Verses 18.) “But if they are prophets, and the word of the Lord is in them, let them intercede.”

What follows, which we shall append through the end of this chapter, is not found in the Septuagint.

(Verses 19 ff.) “Let them intercede with the Lord of hosts, so that the vessels that had been left in the house of the Lord [the Vulgate does not have ‘in the house of the Lord’], and in the house of the king of Judah, and in Jerusalem, may not come to Babylon. For thus says the Lord of hosts concerning the pillars, the sea, and the bases—for which the Hebrew has MECHONOTH—and the remaining vessels that were left in this city, which Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, did not take when he transferred Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, from Jerusalem to Babylon, together with all the nobles of Judah and Jerusalem.

“For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning the vessels that were left in the house of the Lord and in the house of the king of Judah and in Jerusalem: They shall be carried to Babylon, and there they shall remain until the day of their visitation, says the Lord; and I will bring them up and restore them to this place.”

As we have said, these words are not found in the Septuagint but have been translated from the Hebrew truth. In their place they inserted something else that was not written, saying: “For this is what the Lord said to me,” and the rest. [Note: [Col. 0853D] The Vatican manuscript has: “It is for me, because thus said the Lord,” etc.]

And the other vessels that the king of Babylon did not take when he transferred Jeconiah from Jerusalem to Babylon “shall enter,” they say, “the Lord said,” setting down the meaning rather than the words. Perhaps they considered it irrational for God to speak to pillars, the sea, bases, and the remaining vessels left in Jerusalem, as though we did not read that the Lord rebuked the morning worm and spoke to the sea: “Be silent and be still” (Jonah 4).

When he says, “Let them intercede with me,” or “with the Lord of hosts” [Col. 0853B] (Mark 4:39), he shows that a true prophet can resist the Lord through prayers, just as Moses also stood against the Lord in the plague, to turn away the anger of his fury. Samuel did the same (1 Kings 8). And the Lord says to Moses: “Let me alone, so that I may strike this people” (Exodus 32:10). When he says, “Let me alone,” he shows that he can be restrained by the prayers of the saints.

“Let the prophets,” he says, “intercede, and let them demonstrate by deeds that whatever they proclaim is fulfilled; then the prophecy will be proved true.” We read about the pillars, the sea, the bases, and the remaining vessels in Malachim and at the end of this prophet’s book (2 Kings 24). The vessels that were carried off to Babylon are enumerated there, when Zedekiah was captured, the city burned, and the temple overthrown.

(Cap. 28—Verses 1 ff.) And it came to pass in that year, at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the fourth year, in the fifth month, that Hananiah, son of Azur, a prophet from Gibeon, spoke to me in the house of the Lord, in the presence of the priests and all the people, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon. Within two years of days I will bring back to this place all the vessels of the Lord” [the Vulgate has “of the house of the Lord”].

The Hebrew word for prophets, namely NEBEIM, was rendered by the Septuagint as “false prophets,” so that they might make the meaning clearer. Indeed, in the present passage he too is called a prophet, namely NEBIA (), and not a false prophet.

The word of the Lord comes during the reign of Zedekiah, in the fourth year of his reign and in the fifth month—Ezekiel not yet prophesying in Babylon to those who had been carried away with Jeconiah. Hananiah has the confidence to speak in the temple against the prophet because he promises prosperity to the people, and falsehoods are gladly heard, especially those that promise happiness.

Jeremiah had said that the remaining vessels, whether of the temple, the royal house, or the whole people, which Nebuchadnezzar had left behind, were to be carried off to Babylon. Hananiah, on the contrary, promises that even the vessels already carried away will be brought back.

(Verses 3, 4.) “The vessels that Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, carried away from this place and transferred to Babylon, and Jeconiah, son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with all the exiles of Judah who entered Babylon, I will bring back to this place,” says the Lord. “For I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon.”

[Note: [Col. 0853D] The manuscripts, together with the Vulgate, have: “The vessels that Nebuchadnezzar took.”]

For this the Septuagint reads: “Jeconiah and the exile of Judah, because I will break the yoke of the king of Babylon,” briefly setting down the meaning of the Hebrew truth rather than its words.

Hananiah, who at that time appeared to the people to be a prophet [Note: [Col. 0853D] The same manuscripts: “Hananiah the prophet, as he then appeared to the people”], promises that not only the vessels but also King Jeconiah will be brought back to Jerusalem, and that the yoke of the king of Babylon—that is, his rule—will be broken or destroyed. He promises that this will happen before the completion of two years, thereby increasing the people’s joy by making the time of fulfillment seem near.

(Verses 5, 6.) And the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah in the presence of the priests and in the presence of all the people who were standing in the house of the Lord. And the prophet Jeremiah said:

“Amen; may the Lord do so. May the Lord raise up your words which you have prophesied [another reading adds “you”], so that the vessels may be brought back to the house of the Lord and all the exiles from Babylon [another reading: “of Babylon”] to this place.”

He wishes what the false prophet falsely promises to come to pass; this is what “Amen” signifies, a word the Lord often uses in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you” (John 5:19). And he desires, for the sake of the people’s prosperity, that Hananiah rather than himself should speak the truth.

Hence another prophet also testifies, saying: “Would that I were not a man possessing the spirit, and that I spoke falsehood instead” (Micah 2:11). Jonah, on the contrary, is saddened that he has been proved false, and is rebuked by the Lord: it is more advantageous for a prophet’s prediction to prove false than for so great a multitude to be destroyed (Jonah 3).

[Note: [Col. 0853D] In Rabanus: “He is rebuked by the Lord because he does not wish that prophecy to prove true rather than [wish] the destruction of so great a multitude. This statement too should be weighed by those who discuss the so-called ‘useful lie’ in many different ways and on both sides. Nor would I conceal what Saint Hilary says in Psalm 14, number [.....]: ‘Sometimes falsehood is useful, when we lie about a hidden wound, or frustrate testimony on behalf of one in danger, or deceive a sick person concerning the difficulty of his cure.’”]

And lest he seem to approve the false prophet’s prediction, he asserts the truth by means of another example, without doing injury to the liar.

(Verses 7 ff.) “Nevertheless, hear this word that I speak in your ears and in the ears of all the people: The prophets who were before me and you from the beginning, and who prophesied against many lands and against great kingdoms concerning war, affliction, and famine—the prophet who prophesied peace, when his word comes to pass, will be known as the prophet whom the Lord has truly sent.”

Jeremiah could have said to Hananiah: “You are speaking falsely; you are deceiving the people; you are not a prophet but a false prophet.” If he had said this, the false prophet could have thrown the same accusation back at Jeremiah. Therefore he does not insult him, but speaks to him as to a prophet.

“Not only,” he says, “are you and I prophets, but many others came before you and me, among them Isaiah, Hosea, Joel, Amos, and the rest. They prophesied against many lands and kingdoms—not insignificant ones but great ones—announcing war, adversity, and the lack of all things. Conversely, there were others who promised peace and prosperity. The pronouncements of both groups were confirmed not by the flattery of falsehood but by the outcome of events.”

Thus, by the example of others, he speaks about himself and Hananiah: when the end of events arrives, the truth of the prophets will then be revealed. The Lord also spoke this same thing through Moses (Deuteronomy 23): a prophet is demonstrated by the outcome of his prophecy.

It should also be noted that he rebukes the liar neither threateningly nor harshly, but with confidence in the truth, and postpones the matter to the future, so that those who hear may await the outcome of events.

[Col. 0855B] (Verses 10, 11.) And the prophet Hananiah took the chain—or yoke—which in Hebrew is called MUTOTH (), from the neck of the prophet Jeremiah and broke it. And Hananiah said in the presence of all the people:

“Thus says the Lord: So I will break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, from the neck of all these nations within two years of days.”

And Jeremiah went on his way [the Vulgate adds “the prophet”].

The Septuagint did not translate “two years.” Nor did it call Hananiah a prophet, lest it seem to call a man a prophet who was not a prophet—although many things in the Holy Scriptures are spoken according to the opinion of the time in which the events are related, and not according to the truth of the matter.

Thus Joseph too is called the Lord’s father in the Gospel. And Mary herself, who knew that she had conceived from the Holy Spirit and had answered the angel, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” [another reading: “since I have not known a man”] (Luke 1:34), says to her Son: “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I were seeking you in sorrow” (Luke 2:48).

At the same time, Jeremiah’s prudence, humility, and patience should be considered. The false prophet insults him by taking the yoke from his neck and breaking it—a thing he could not in fact have done if it had been made of iron. Jeremiah remains silent and conceals his grief, for the word of the Lord had not yet been revealed to him. Thus Holy Scripture clearly shows that prophets do not speak solely on their own authority but according to the Lord’s will, especially concerning future events, which are known only to God.

“He went away,” it says, “and departed on his way,” as though defeated, fulfilling the prophetic word: “I became like a man who does not hear, and who has no rebukes in his mouth.”

(Verses 2 ff.) And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah after the prophet Hananiah had broken the yoke—or chain—from the neck of the prophet Jeremiah, saying:

“Go and say to Hananiah: Thus says the Lord: You have broken wooden yokes, and you will make—or I will make—in their place iron yokes.”

[Note: [Col. 0855D] Victor has “in their place iron yokes,” adding from the Hebrew the word “yokes,” and enclosing in the customary parenthesis “yokes,” the Septuagint’s translation, “chains.”]

“For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: I have placed an iron yoke upon the neck of all these nations, so that they may serve Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.”

[Note: [Col. 0855D] In accordance with the manuscripts, we have removed from this point the final words of the verse, “and they shall serve him,” and so forth, which you find immediately afterward in a more coherent arrangement [Col. 0856D]; their repetition was pointless.]

What follows—“And they shall serve him; moreover, I have given him the beasts of the earth”—is not found in the Septuagint.

In the present passage, according to the Septuagint, Hananiah is not called a prophet, nor is he so called in what follows, lest, as I said earlier, they seem to call a false prophet a prophet.

[Note: [Col. 0856D] From the Brixian manuscripts Victor reads: “Let us follow the Hebrew truth,” and argues that the reading should be restored according to the sequence of the context.]

But what of the Hebrew truth? After the prophet Jeremiah had gone away on his way and silently swallowed the insult, the word of the Lord came to him, so that the prophet would not address the false prophet boasting in his lie with his own words, but would say: “Thus says the Lord.” Hananiah too, breaking the wooden yoke, had spoken with the same authority in the presence of the Lord: “Thus says the Lord.” For falsehood always imitates truth.

When he added, “You have broken wooden yokes, and you will make—or I will make—in their place iron yokes” [another reading: “you have made”], he showed that Hananiah, by refusing the lesser punishment, had become the cause of a greater punishment for the people.

The allegorical interpreter raves here as well, calling the wooden yokes and chains ethereal and brazen bodies—namely, those of demons and hostile powers. But the iron yokes or chains he calls our denser bodies, woven together from nerves, bones, flesh, and veins, so that those who, because of the measure of their sin, were unwilling to undergo lesser torments in the heavenly Jerusalem might be condemned to the chains of our bodies, endure the cries of infancy, and bear the bonds and filth of swaddling clothes; and might serve the devil, the king of Babylon—that is, of this world—since Scripture says: “The world is set in the power of the evil one” (1 John 5:19), together with the beasts of the earth, which are bound within the bodies of brute animals [another reading: “which are bound”].

An unlearned commentator and follower of Grunnius’s slander have compelled me openly to set forth the faults of others, which previously I mentioned only discreetly, leaving them to the reader’s judgment.

(Verses 5 ff.) And the prophet Jeremiah said to the prophet Hananiah:

“Hear, Hananiah: The Lord did not send you, and you have caused this people to trust in falsehood” [the Vulgate has “that people”]. “Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will send—or drive—you from the face of the earth. This year you shall die.”

What follows—“because you have spoken against the Lord”—is not found in the Septuagint. Instead, it has only: “And he died in the seventh month.”

Here too the Septuagint does not call Hananiah a prophet, although according to the Hebrew the Holy Scripture calls him a prophet, even though, when Jeremiah rebukes him by saying, “Hear, Hananiah, the Lord did not send you,” it does not use the word “prophet.” For how could Jeremiah call him a prophet whom he denied to have been sent by the Lord?

But the truth and sequence of the history are preserved, as we have said, not according to what he was, but according to what he was then thought to be.

“You deceived,” he says, “the people with a lie, so that they would not submit to God’s judgment. Therefore know that you are going to die this year.”

If, whenever we die, we are released from the prisons of our bodies, according to the testimony which heretics wrongly interpret—“Bring my soul out of prison” (Psalm 141:8)—how is death now inflicted upon the false prophet as a punishment?

In this passage, however, it should be noted that Jeremiah, after suffering an insult from the false prophet, remains silent because the word of the Lord had not yet come to him. Later, when sent by the Lord, he boldly rebukes the liar and announces his imminent death.

As for the fact that he died in the seventh month, those who habitually interpret this number as signifying rest may perhaps say that he died in the seventh month so that he might be freed from the evils of the body.

[Col. 0857B] They cite the saying: “Death is rest for a man” [another reading: “the saying is quoted”].

But we know that the bodies of believers are temples of God, provided that the Holy Spirit dwells in them (Ecclesiasticus 22:11).

(Cap. 29—Verses 1 ff.) [1041] These are the words of the book that the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the remnant of the elders of the exile, to the priests, to the prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon.

After King Jeconiah had departed, together with the lady—or queen—the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem—or the nobles—and the craftsmen [the Vulgate has “the craftsman and the smith”—from Jerusalem, by the hand of Elasah, son of Shaphan, and Gemariah, son of Hilkiah, whom Zedekiah, king of Judah, sent to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to Babylon, saying:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and dwell in them;

[Note: [Col. 0857D] The Vatican manuscript reads this way, and Victor formerly restored it in the same manner, reading “and” instead of “or.” Erasmus considers “or” corrupt, while Martianay retained it improperly, taking the word away from Jerome’s version in order to attribute it to the Septuagint translators.]

“plant gardens—or orchards—and eat their fruit. Take wives and beget sons and daughters; give wives to your sons, and give your daughters to husbands, so that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply [the Vulgate likewise has “multiply”], and do not become few in number. Seek the peace of the city—or land—to which I have carried you [the Vulgate has “to which I made you migrate”], and pray to the Lord for it, because in its peace you shall have peace.”

This letter—or rather, this little book—of the prophet Jeremiah was sent to Babylon by the envoys of Zedekiah, Elasah and Gemariah, to those who had been carried away by Nebuchadnezzar with Jeconiah and his mother. Through the occasion of the royal embassy, the prophet might also complete his own task and admonish the exiles concerning what had been commanded them by the Lord.

Beautifully he said: “King Jeconiah and the lady, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah, and the rest departed.” And: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom he carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon,” so that they might seem to have been carried away not by the power of the king of Babylon but by the will of the Lord.

First the word is addressed to the elders, then to the priests, third to the prophets, and fourth to all the people of God, so that, according to the order of age, the prophet’s letter might reach those who were being admonished.

He admonishes them, not in his own words but in the Lord’s, to build houses and dwell in them; to plant gardens or orchards and eat their fruit; to take wives and beget sons and daughters; to multiply in the place of their exile and not become few in number; to seek the peace of the city or land to which the Lord had carried them, and to pray to the Lord for them [another reading: “for it”]. He gives the reason, saying: “Because in the peace of that land there shall be peace for you.”

Because the captivity of Jerusalem was soon to follow, Jeremiah was commanded not to take a wife or beget children. Hence the Apostle also says to us: “The time is short” [another reading: “shortened”]; “it remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” [another reading: “should thus be as though they did not have them”] (1 Corinthians 7:19). If, because of the shortness of time, the use of wives is taken away from those who have them, how much more is it commanded that those who do not have them should not take them!

The whole of this prophetic passage commands them not to listen to the false prophets who were promising them a return to Jerusalem after a short time, but to understand that they would remain in Babylon for a long period—so long that they ought to take wives, plant orchards and gardens, build houses, and beget children.

What he adds—“Seek the peace of the city or land”—and again, “Because in its peace there shall be peace for you”—may be compared with the apostolic command in which he urges: “Therefore I ask first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and for all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity” (1 Timothy 2:1–2).

According to the mystical meanings, after we have been cast out of Jerusalem—that is, the Church—because of our sins and handed over to Nebuchadnezzar, of whom the same Apostle says, “I have handed such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 5:5), and again, “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:20), we must not be secure, sluggish in idleness, or utterly despair of salvation.

First, we must build houses, not upon sand but upon rock, and such houses as the midwives built in Exodus because they feared the Lord (Exodus 1). Next, we must plant gardens or orchards, such as the Lord planted in Eden, placing in it the tree of life, of which it is written: “She is a tree of life to those who take hold of her, and blessed is the one who holds her” (Proverbs 3:18).

Third, we must take wives, one of whom is Wisdom, concerning whom Solomon writes: “Love her, and she will preserve you; embrace her, and she will exalt you” (Proverbs 4:6). And elsewhere: “I sought to take her as a bride for myself, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wisdom 8:2).

One wise wife is not enough for us unless we also possess the other virtues: strength, temperance, and justice, so that we may beget many children from them. Let us also give our daughters to husbands, so that the truth of faith, which is signified by sons, may be joined to good works, which are signified by daughters, and good works may be joined to sound faith.

Begetting such sons and daughters, let us multiply in number, so that, destroying the things that belong to childhood and growing into a perfect man, we may deserve to hear: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2:13); and with the Apostle say to our children: “For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15).

Let us also seek the peace of the Church, our city and land, so that we may deserve to return to it, from which by the Lord’s judgment we were carried away, in order to dwell in the confusion of error. For if it receives us, we have peace.

At the same time, the Lord’s clemency must be considered: he commanded us to pray for our enemies and to do good to those who persecute us, so that we may not be content with our own salvation alone but may also seek the salvation of our enemies (Luke 6).

(Verses 8, 9.) “For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Do not let your prophets who are among you and your diviners deceive you; and do not attend to your dreams that you dream, because they prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them,” says the Lord.

That there were prophets—or rather false prophets—diviners, and dreamers in Babylon among those whom Nebuchadnezzar had brought away with Jeconiah and his mother is testified by the prophet Ezekiel, who wrote against them; Jeremiah too commands that they not be believed (Ezekiel 13). At the time when this letter was sent, however, Ezekiel had not yet begun to prophesy in Babylon. For this message was sent at the beginning of the reign of King Zedekiah. Ezekiel began to prophesy in the fifth year of Jeconiah’s exile, which was the same year of Zedekiah’s reign.

According to the tropological interpretation, we should understand as false prophets those who interpret the words of Scripture otherwise than the Holy Spirit speaks them. Diviners are those who, without the authority of divine words, announce the conjecture of their own mind and uncertain future events as though they were certain.

Dreamers are those who do not heed what is written: “Do not give sleep to your eyes or slumber to your eyelids” (Proverbs 6:4). The Apostle Jude speaks of them: “Likewise, these dreamers defile the flesh and reject authority” (Jude 8). Their mind is never vigilant but, sunk in the slumber of arrogance [Note: [Col. 0859D] Formerly it read: “and in the slumber of error,” the manuscripts differing], is surrounded by the horror of night. To them the Apostle Paul also says: “Rise up, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14).

(Verses 10 ff.) “For thus says the Lord: When seventy years begin to be completed in Babylon, I will visit you and raise up over you my good word, to bring you back to this place. For I know the thoughts that I think concerning you,” says the Lord—“thoughts of peace and not of affliction, to give you an end [another reading adds “a good end”] and patience—or hope. And you will call upon me, and you will go [or, according to Symmachus, ‘you will find’], and you will pray—or worship—me, and I will hear you. You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart, and I will be found by you—or I will appear to you,” says the Lord.

“Do not,” he says, “believe your false prophets, diviners, and dreamers, who promise you a return to Jerusalem in the near future. For unless the seventy years have been completed, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, releases the captives [Note: [Col. 0860D] The Vatican manuscript has “before releasing the captives”; shortly afterward: “then in the fulfillment of that promise,” etc.], you will by no means return to your homeland. Then I will fulfill my promises and bring you back to this place: ‘For I know the thoughts that I think concerning you,’ says the Lord.”

He says that he knows what he is thinking, whereas they, together with their prophets, diviners, and dreamers, do not know. Knowledge of future events therefore belongs to God alone.

“To give you,” he says, “an end and patience”: an end to captivity and patience amid present labors, or hope for the future [Note: [Col. 0860D] In the Cistercian manuscript the noun “hope” is lacking].

Then you will call upon me and go to Jerusalem; you will pray, and I will hear you. Certainly, even without the invocation and prayer of the captives, the Lord could have fulfilled what he had promised. But he urges them to pray, so that they may deserve to receive what has been promised.

“You will seek me and find me when you seek me with all your heart,” in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7).

According to the anagogical interpretation, we remain for as long in the confusion of this world as it takes for us to deserve to receive the rest signified by the number seven. Once we have received repentance, God will fulfill what he promised, and we shall be brought back to our place, the Church.

For this reason the Lord seemed to strike us, so that he might heal us. He will give us an end to our labor and patience; we shall call upon him, return to the Church, pray, and be heard. We shall seek him and find him when we seek him with all our heart, and then he will appear to us.

Some interpret the seventy years according to what is written: “The days of our years are seventy years” (Psalm 89:10). When these have been completed, let us return to the Lord with all our heart, be heard by him, and let the end of our labor and patience arrive. For now we possess everything in shadow and in image.

### (Verses 14 ff.)

“And I will restore your captivity, and gather you from all the nations and from all the places to which I scattered you,” says the Lord. “And I will bring you back from the place to which I caused you to be carried away. For you said: ‘The Lord has raised up prophets for us in Babylon.’ For thus says the Lord to the king who sits upon the throne of David, and to all the people who inhabit this city, and to your brothers who did not go out with you into captivity. Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will send among them the sword, famine, and pestilence; and I will make them like bad figs that cannot be eaten, because they are exceedingly bad. And I will pursue them with sword, famine, and pestilence; and I will give them [variant: you] for vexation to all the kingdoms of the earth, for a curse, astonishment, hissing, and reproach among all the nations to which I shall cast them out [variant: have cast them out], because they did not listen to my words,” says the Lord, “which I sent to them through my servants the prophets, rising by night and sending them; and you did not listen,” says the Lord. “You, therefore, hear the word of the Lord, all you exiles whom I sent from Jerusalem to Babylon.”

Up to this point the Septuagint does not contain what I have marked with asterisks. As for the rest—passages in which either individual verses or a few words have been omitted by them—I did not wish, overcome by weariness, to note them, lest I cause boredom to the readers.

The Lord promises those who were in captivity that, after seventy years of captivity, he will bring them back from all the nations and from all the places to which he will have driven them; and, when their captivity has been released, he will restore to them their former condition and homeland. And since, he says, I shall do these things of my own will, and have determined that you will return at the appointed time [Note: Victorius adds the word “determined”; shortly afterward the Cistercian manuscript has *despair* instead of *hope*], you are deceiving yourselves in vain and think that you have prophets in Babylon who make false promises to you.

Know, then, that you ought by no means now to hope for a return; instead, you should build houses, plant orchards, take wives, beget children, increase in number, and await the promised time. Hear what the Lord says to Zedekiah, who now reigns in Jerusalem, and to all its inhabitants—that is, to your brothers who were unwilling to obey my decision and migrate with you to Babylon: they will certainly be unable to escape captivity, but will die by sword, famine, and plague.

“And I will make them like bad figs”—which Theodotion translated as *sudrinas*; the Second [edition]: “exceedingly bad”; Symmachus: “last”; these in Hebrew are called **SUARIM** (סורים), but through scribal error a Greek delta has become established in place of the middle syllable, or letter alpha, so that instead of **SUARIM** one reads **SUDRIM**. Just as the basket or hamper that contained the good figs is said to have contained the first fruits, so the other basket, which contained the bad figs, is said to have contained the last figs [Note: Here again Martianaeus read *alter* incorrectly as *aliter*].

“And I will pursue,” he says, “those who now dwell in the city of Jerusalem with sword, famine, and pestilence; so that first, after the siege, those who will have been able to remain and escape may be scattered through all lands [Note: The sense appears defective here; I suspect *confecti* should be read instead of *confestim*], and may become an example to all of curse, astonishment, hissing, and reproach—to whom I shall cast them out [variant: you], because they did not listen to my words,” says the Lord, “which I spoke to them through my servants, rising by night and sending them; and I never ceased warning them to imitate you who now enjoy secure leisure in captivity, until the Lord’s promise is fulfilled.”

“But you who obeyed my decision and surrendered yourselves to the Babylonian king, hear what I am about to say.” At this point the deranged Interpreter dreams of the ruin of the heavenly Jerusalem and supposes that the prophecy is directed at those who dwell in the Babylonian region of this world. He thinks that these people did well to descend voluntarily into these bodies, build houses in the land of the Chaldeans, plant orchards, take wives, beget children, and, after seventy years, be restored through good works to their former place and to the heavenly Jerusalem.

But those who were unwilling of their own will to descend to earthly things will suffer what the Lord threatens against Zedekiah and his people: those who were unwilling to imitate their brothers or come to Babylon—against them he will send sword, famine, and pestilence, that is, scarcity of all things; and he will make them like exceedingly bad figs, which cannot be eaten at all. He will pursue them with an everlasting sword and give them for vexation to all the kingdoms of the earth, so that, plainly, they will become not human beings but demons, aerial powers; and among all the angels who preside over the individual provinces they will be for a curse, astonishment, hissing, and reproach among all the nations.

They will suffer these things because they were unwilling to listen to the words of the prophets in the heavenly Jerusalem, who urged them to descend to earthly things and assume a body of humility; and, after repentance, to possess their former place after the true sabbatical rest.

So he has spoken. When his disciples and the filth of the Grunnian sect hear these things, they think they are hearing divine mysteries. But us, who despise such doctrines, they regard as brute animals and call us **πηλουσιώτας** (*Pelousiōtas*, “people of the mud”) [Note: That is, men of coarse intelligence and leaden minds. The allusion concerns no less the character of the inhabitants of Pelusium than the etymology of the name: according to Strabo, **Πηλούσιον παρὰ τὸ πηλός**, “Pelusium is named from *pelos*, mud”—just as one might say that Lutetia is derived from *lutum*, mud], because, being placed in the mud of this body, we are unable to perceive heavenly things.

### (Verses 21 ff.)

Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy falsely to you in my name: “Behold, I will deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them before your eyes. And from them a curse shall be taken up by all the exiles of Judah who are in Babylon, saying: ‘May the Lord make you like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire, because they committed folly [Vulgate: iniquity] in Israel, and committed adultery with the wives of their friends [variant: fellow citizens], and spoke a false word in my name which I had not commanded them. I am judge and witness,’ says the Lord.”

The Hebrews say that these men were elders who committed folly in Israel and committed adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens. To one of them Daniel says: “You who have grown old in evil days”; and to the other: “Seed of Canaan and not of Judah, appearance has deceived you and desire has overturned your heart. Thus you acted toward the daughters of Israel, and they, fearing you, spoke with you; but the daughter of Judah did not endure your iniquity” (Dan. 13:56–57).

What the Prophet now says—“And they spoke a false word in my name which I had not commanded them”—they think signifies that these men deceived wretched little women who were carried about by every wind of doctrine, persuading them that, since they belonged to the tribe of Judah, Christ was to be born from their offspring. Ensnared by desire, the women offered their bodies as though they were to become mothers of Christ.

But the statement made here—“whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire”—appears to conflict with the narrative of Daniel. Daniel asserts that, at his judgment, they were stoned by the people; here, however, it is written that the king of Babylon roasted them in the fire. Consequently, this story is rejected as almost a fable and is not read by many, indeed nearly all, of the Hebrews in their synagogues. For, they say, how could it have happened that captive rulers and prophets would have had the power to stone their own leaders? They affirm instead that what Jeremiah writes is more likely to be true: the elders were indeed convicted by Daniel, but the sentence was imposed upon them by the king of Babylon, who, as victor and master, exercised authority over the captives.

How many like Ahab and Zedekiah there are even in our own flock, who prophesy falsehood in the Lord’s name, commit folly in Israel, and commit adultery with the wives of their fellow citizens—men who were born in that same city of the Church! The true Nebuchadnezzar roasts them in the fire of sin [Note: See the *Commentaries on Daniel*, at the end], as the prophet Hosea says: “All adulterers are like a furnace heated by the baker” (Hos. 7:4).

Blessed is the one who takes up his yoke from his youth and sits alone, because he is filled with bitterness (Lam. 3); and he can say with David: “I have not sat in the council of the wicked, and with those who act unjustly I shall not enter” (Ps. 25:4).

What the Prophet now adds—“I am judge and witness,” says the Lord—has this meaning: These things that I say about the two false prophets, who speak a false word in my name which I had not commanded them, I did not learn merely by hearsay; I myself know that they are true, I whom no one can conceal from or escape the truth of whose judgment [Note: Formerly the text read, “which no one can conceal,” etc.].

### (Verses 24 ff.)

“And to Shemaiah the Nehelamite you shall say.” What follows—“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Because you sent letters in your own name to all the people who are in Jerusalem”—is not found in the Septuagint. They have again added on their own account: “I did not send you in my name.” Then, in its proper order: “And to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest.” And again, from the Hebrew: “And to all the priests” [Vulgate adds: “saying”].

Then the narrative continues: “The Lord made you priest in place of Jehoiada the priest, so that you might be leader”—or “teacher and bishop”—“in the house of the Lord over every frenzied man and prophet, so that you may put him in fetters and in prison”—or “in custody”—“and in the cataract,” which Symmachus rendered **μόχλον** (“bar”), while Aquila retained the Hebrew word itself, **SINAC** [Note: Some manuscripts and editions, including the Sinaitic and Sangerman manuscript in Montfaucon, have *Sinas*, doubtless incorrectly for *SINAC*].

“And now, why have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite, who prophesies to you? For on this account he sent to us in Babylon, saying: ‘The time is long; build houses and inhabit them, and plant gardens’”—Victor inserts “or orchards”; he says that this word was omitted from earlier editions and therefore assigned to the Septuagint [Note: The priest Zephaniah therefore read this book aloud in the hearing of Jeremiah the prophet].

Shemaiah from Nehelam, which means “torrent,” had been led into Babylon with King Jeconiah and was prophesying falsely to the people, saying that they would soon return to Jerusalem. That he was a false prophet is shown by the words that follow from Jeremiah: “Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah prophesied to you, although I did not send him.”

Since Jeremiah had sent letters to those who were in Babylon, saying: “Build houses and inhabit them; plant gardens and eat their fruits; take wives and beget sons,” and had added afterward: “Do not let your prophets who are among you [variant: among you all] and your diviners deceive you”; and then: “For they prophesy falsely to you in my name, and I did not send them,” says the Lord—Shemaiah, understanding that what had been written under the general name of false prophets was directed against him, sent letters from Jerusalem to Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest and to the other priests, asking why Jeremiah was not rebuked by the priest Zephaniah, whose office it was to distinguish between prophets who spoke by the Holy Spirit and those who spoke by the opposite spirit [Note: “And should be ordered to be confined in prison.” From this passage and the one immediately following, in which Jerome uses *recludere* in the sense of shutting up, the prudent reader should judge the learning of Jean Le Clerc, who dared accuse me of ignorance because I had said that a certain scholion could genuinely be Jerome’s even though it contained the word *recludere* in the sense of confining. — Martianaeus].

He asks why Jeremiah should not be confined in prison [variant: is ordered to be confined], so that he might suffer the punishment of his falsehood and cease further misleading the people.

Jehoiada was the priest who, after Athaliah was killed [Note: Two Vatican and Cistercian manuscripts have “of Athaliah” instead of “of Godoliah”], handed the rule over to Joash and killed the priests of Baal (2 Kings 11; 2 Chron. 23). This, then, is what he writes: “Why do you not imitate Jehoiada the priest and kill Jeremiah the false prophet? For the Lord appointed you in place of Jehoiada, so that you might have charge of the Temple and, above all, distinguish those who speak by the Holy Spirit from those who speak by a demonic spirit.” The Apostle too recalls that the discernment of spirits is a divine grace (1 John 4).

“Why,” he says, “have you not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite?” What he himself deserved as a false prophet, he transfers to the prophet and anticipates the truth with a lie. Thus the sons of darkness are considered wiser than the sons of light in this generation.

While we act patiently and await the salvation of the wretched, heretics anticipate us and call us by their own name, leading the blind into a pit along with the blind. “He sent to us,” he says, “in Babylon, saying: ‘It is far away.’” This is the whole source of his grief: why Jeremiah had written the truth against his falsehood—that the return was far off, and that they would return to Jerusalem only after seventy years. Therefore they ought to build houses, plant orchards, eat their fruits, take wives, and beget children, as the preceding discussion related.

When the priest Zephaniah received this letter, which had been written specifically in his name [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “the letter of Jeremiah had been written,” etc.], he read it to Jeremiah, in a sense taunting him and rebuking him by the very act of reading it: why had he dared to write such things to Babylon?

### (Verses 30 ff.)

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying: “Send to all the exiles, saying: Thus says the Lord to Shemaiah the Nehelamite: Because Shemaiah prophesied to you, although I did not send him, and made you trust in a lie, therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit punishment upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite and upon his offspring. He shall have no man sitting in the midst of this people, and he shall not see the good that I will do for my people,” says the Lord, “because he spoke rebellion against the Lord.”

The false prophet Shemaiah, truly a Nehelamite, who had drawn foreign and turbid waters from a torrent, becomes angry because Jeremiah wrote the truth against his falsehood and sends letters to the priest Zephaniah, asking why the Prophet had dared to write the truth and seeking to have him confined in prison [variant: in a prison], so that he might not speak.

Zephaniah too secretly accuses the prophet, when he reads the letter of the liar and boasts that he has obtained his accusation. How much more guilty are those who defend false prophets, encourage liars, and make the wicked inventions of others their own sins!

Let the false prophet therefore hear, and let the priest understand what he himself deserves to hear through him: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will visit punishment upon Shemaiah.” The Lord speaks this, not the prophet: he will visit punishment upon Shemaiah the Nehelamite—not for the liar’s healing but for his punishment, according to what is written: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod, and their sins with scourges” (Ps. 88:33).

And he visits punishment not only upon the false prophet but also upon his offspring—all the disciples whom he deceived by his error. “There shall not be,” he says, “a man sitting in the midst of this people.” Let the evil stock be erased from the assembly of the saints; let him not sit in the midst of those who rest, who could not stand with those who stand and did not hear: “If he had stood in my substance” (Jer. 23) [Note: In Greek: **εἰ ἔστησαν ἐν τῇ ὑποστάσει μου**. Hence Victorius wishes it to be read in the plural, “if they had stood”].

And since the Lord promises the perfection of all virtues after the completion of the period of seven, he will not see the good that he claimed for himself in the present age. This entire thing will happen because he spoke rebellion against the Lord, saying that, once the captivity of sins had already been released, they would return to Jerusalem. To them the Apostle threatens: “Already you are filled; already you have become rich; you have reigned without us—and would that you had reigned, so that we also might reign with you!” (1 Cor. 4:8).

## BOOK SIX

The length of the book of the prophet Jeremiah exceeds our purpose, so that although we speak briefly, we must nevertheless say many things. Accordingly, this present sixth book of the *Commentaries on Jeremiah* will contain the mystical promises that the Jews, and our Judaizing Christians, think are to be fulfilled at the consummation of the world; for they cannot yet prove that they were fulfilled under Zerubbabel.

But, following the authority of the Apostles and Evangelists, and especially of the Apostle Paul, we show that whatever is promised to the people of Israel in a bodily sense has been fulfilled—and continues to be fulfilled—spiritually in us. There is no other dispute today between Jews and Christians except this: while both they and we believe that Christ, the Son of God, was promised, they say that the things destined to occur under Christ are still to be fulfilled by them, whereas we say that they have been fulfilled by us [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “so that we may believe with them,” etc.].

Since, therefore, we already believe that Christ has come, we must demonstrate that the things said to occur under Christ have been fulfilled. We must also show that we are children of Abraham, of whom it is written: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:9), to whom the promise was made: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

Teaching that this blessing was fulfilled in Christ, the vessel of election says: “He did not say ‘in seeds,’ as of many, but ‘in your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

Pray, therefore, brother Eusebius, to the Lord Jesus Christ, that by the same labor and grace of the Spirit by which we have interpreted the promises of the other prophets, and especially of Isaiah, we may also be able to explain those of this prophet. For to the extent that he appears simple and easy in his words, he is equally profound in the majesty of his meanings.

### (Chapter 30: verses 1 ff.)

This is the word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, saying: “Write for yourself in a book all the words that I have spoken to you. For behold, days are coming,” says the Lord, “and I will restore the fortunes of my people Israel and Judah,” says the Lord [Note: Other books add “God.” Moreover, Victorius maintains that *to the land* should be read instead of *in the land*, in agreement with the Vulgate, since the Hebrew also has this reading and it agrees with the verb “I will restore.” He also adds another version, namely, “I will restore and make dwell,” produced by the word **ושב**; he says that both renderings belong to Jerome, since the Septuagint likewise had **ἐπιστρέψω**, “I will restore”], “and I will restore them—or make them dwell—in the land that I gave to their fathers, and they shall possess it.”

In opposition to the false prophets who were promising that the people taken captive with Jeconiah would soon return from Babylon, and to Hananiah son of Azzur, who was proclaiming the same things in Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah asserted that this would indeed happen, but not within two years, as they falsely claimed; rather, it would happen after the completion of seventy years. He is then commanded to write in a book and commit to memory what the Lord foretells will come.

From this it is clear that the time of the prophecy is by no means near, but that these things are to be fulfilled after many ages, when Israel and Judah will return to their land and what Ezekiel prophesied will be fulfilled: that the two rods will be joined together and that David will reign. Of him he writes: “My servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for all of them” (Ezek. 37:24).

Therefore, if we have said anything about that prophecy, it should also be understood in the present passage, especially since Ezekiel was prophesying in Babylon and Jeremiah in Jerusalem at the same time.

### (Verses 4 ff.)

And these are the words that the Lord spoke to Israel and Judah, for thus says the Lord: “We have heard a voice of terror”—or “fear”—“dread, and there is no peace. Ask and see whether a male gives birth. Why, then, have I seen every man’s hand upon his loins like a woman in labor [Vulgate: giving birth], and have all faces turned yellow?”

First, sorrowful things are announced, so that after the magnitude of evils, joyful things may follow. Health is more pleasing when sickness has been driven away, and the magnitude of pain is transformed into the magnitude of joys.

What he says means this: there will be such great fear and dread that, with peace driven away, everything will be filled with wars and bloodshed; and even men, whose proper task is to fight against adversaries, will be seized by womanly fear. Their hands will be applied not to weapons but to holding their loins, as though a woman in labor were clutching her sides and loins. Hence the faces of all will be turned yellow, their pallor bearing witness to the fear of the heart.

Some interpret this passage tropologically, thinking that it may be compared with the testimony: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and were in labor, and gave birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth” (Isa. 26:17–18), and with the Apostle’s statement: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). It is clear, however, that this does not concern terror but joy, whereas the present Scripture signifies the time of Israel’s devastation and ruin.

### (Verse 7)

“Woe, for great is that day, and there is none like it; it is a time of tribulation for Jacob, and he shall be saved from it.”

He predicts a time of misery in order to introduce a time of joy. When, he says, such evils have preceded that the pain of all men is compared with the pain of a woman in labor, nevertheless the time of Jacob’s tribulation—that is, of God’s people—will be changed into prosperity; and he too will be saved from it, meaning from the time about which the discourse had been speaking.

Understand Jacob as the twelve tribes, which were not saved under Zerubbabel, as some falsely think, but through the evangelical calling.

### (Verses 8–9)

“And it shall be in that day,” says the Lord of hosts, “that I will break his yoke from your neck and tear apart his bonds; and strangers shall no longer rule over them [Vulgate: him], but they shall serve—or work for—the Lord their God and David their king, whom I will raise up for them.”

This is the David whom the Gospel also mentions (Luke 1), saying that he will give us the opportunity, delivered without fear from the hand of our enemies, to serve him in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

For just as the first Adam and the second Adam are written of according to the truth of the body, so also David is the Lord and Savior: for according to the flesh he is from David, with holy Mary contributing to him everything that came from David’s stock; and he has his origin and conception from the Holy Spirit.

When he says, “I will break his yoke from your neck and tear apart his bonds,” there is no doubt that, under the type of Nebuchadnezzar, this is to be understood of the devil.

### (Verses 10–11)

“But you, my servant Jacob, do not fear,” says the Lord; “and do not be afraid, Israel. For behold, I will save you from a distant land, and your seed from the land of their captivity. And Jacob shall return and rest, and shall abound in all good things, and there shall be none whom he fears; for I am with you,” says the Lord, “to save you. For I will bring an end to all the nations among which I scattered you; but I will not bring an end to you. I will chastise—or instruct—you in judgment, so that you may not appear innocent [or: I will not utterly cleanse you while cleansing you].”

This **περικοπή** (“section”) is not found in the Septuagint, and in most manuscripts of the Vulgate it has been added under asterisks from Theodotion.

The divine word promises, and addresses familiarly as its servant, Jacob and Israel, just as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are called servants of God—along with Moses, the other prophets, and the Apostle Paul, who at the beginning of his letters takes pride in this title. Thus the ten and two tribes—that is, the twelve—may know that they will be saved from a distant land, that their captivity will be released, peace restored, and they themselves filled with every abundance, according to what is said in the psalm: “Let there be peace in your strength and abundance in your towers” (Ps. 121:7).

This will happen because they will enjoy the Lord’s presence, when the hostile nations that had captured them will perish and they themselves will be liberated from among the nations. He teaches that they have been handed over not to punishment but to instruction, so that they may be judged as his own and not destroyed as strangers. “The one who does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18), that is, he has already been sentenced to destruction.

What he adds—“so that you may not appear innocent,” or, according to Symmachus, “and while cleansing you I will not cleanse you”; or, according to Aquila, “when I instruct you through judgment, I will not make you innocent”—signifies that every human being, even the purest [variant: impurest], needs the mercy of God, and that no one, however holy, proceeds securely before the Judge.

This stands against the new heresy arising from the old one, which thinks that in this age and in this mortal flesh—before this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality—anyone can possess perfection and completely fulfill all virtues.

### (Verses 12 ff.)

For thus says the Lord: “Your fracture is incurable, your wound exceedingly grievous. There is no one to judge your judgment in order to bind it; there is no usefulness of remedies for you. All your lovers have forgotten you; they will not seek you. For I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel [or: severe] chastisement, because of the multitude of your iniquity; your sins have become hard [or: multiplied]. Why do you cry out over your fracture? Your pain is incurable because of the multitude of your iniquity, and because of your hard sins I have done these things to you” [Note: The Vatican manuscript inserts “to me”].

He speaks as though to a beautiful woman, to whom he had earlier said: “I will chastise you in judgment, so that you may not appear innocent,” or “innocent woman.” By metaphor he speaks of Jerusalem, which has been most grievously wounded by God’s judgment and can be healed by no one except the one who struck her.

“There is no one,” says the Lord, “to judge your judgment,” nor anyone capable of laying the skin of a scar over a very deep wound. Wherever you turn, there is no remedy for you, because you have offended the one who is the true and only physician.

“All your lovers have forgotten you”—whether priests, rulers, or indeed the angelic protections by which you were surrounded before you offended the Lord. “They will not seek you,” acting contrary to the Apostle, who sought believers and not what belonged to believers (2 Cor. 12).

“For I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement.” A friend strikes differently from an enemy; a father differently from a hostile person. One beats in order to correct, the other strikes in order to kill (Ps. 6). Hence the Prophet also says tearfully: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger” (Ps. 37:1).

This happened because, on account of the multitude of your iniquity, your sins became hard. What follows—“Why do you cry out over your fracture? Your pain is incurable because of the multitude of your iniquity, and because of your hard sins I have done these things to you”—is not found in the Septuagint. Evidently it is omitted because “because of the multitude of your iniquity” and “your hard sins” are said twice; those who copied the text from the beginning thought that the repetition had been added [Note: Jerome notes this kind of omission, caused by the recurrence of the same letters, above in the *Commentary on Isaiah*, column 482].

The meaning is this: The multitude of your iniquity and your hard sins caused me to strike you with the wound of an enemy and beat you with cruel chastisement—sins that could not be healed except by the most biting powder, a burning cautery, and the sharpest iron, with which I had to cut away the putrid and incurable flesh. Nevertheless, because of the multitude of your iniquity and your hard sins I did these things to you, not by my will but because the requirements of medicine compelled me.

### (Verses 16–17)

“Therefore all who devour you shall be devoured, and all your enemies shall go into captivity. Those who ravage you shall be ravaged, and I will give all your plunderers for plunder. For I will apply a scar to you and heal you of your wounds,” says the Lord, “because they called you ‘the outcast’”—or “the dispersed”—“Zion, whom no one seeks.”

We know that these things occurred under Zerubbabel, when the Babylonians and Chaldeans devastated the Assyrians—that is, Nineveh—and then the Medes and Persians captured the Babylonians and Chaldeans, and Babylon was destroyed. Then Zion began to have the Lord seeking her; a scar was applied to her wounds, and she was healed of her blows. This is fulfilled more fully and perfectly in Christ [variant: will be fulfilled].

### (Verses 18 ff.)

Thus says the Lord: “Behold, I will restore the fortunes of the tents of Jacob, and I will have mercy on his dwellings [Vulgate: captivity]. And the city shall be built upon its height, and the Temple shall be founded according to its order. And praise shall go forth from them, and the voice of those who play. And I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished.”

What follows—“And I will glorify them, and they shall not be weakened”—is not found in the Septuagint [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “and I will not weaken them”].

“And,” he says, “his children shall be as at the beginning, and his assembly shall endure before me; and I will visit punishment upon all who afflict him. And his leader shall be from him, and his prince shall be brought forth from his midst. And I will draw him near, and he shall approach me. For who is this who applies his heart, so as to draw near to me?” says the Lord.

Again, “and this is not found in the Septuagint” [Note: Martianaeus, following Erasmus, had read: “and this is not found in the Hebrew”; Victorius changed the reading to “in the Septuagint,” since the verse is found in the Hebrew but absent from the Septuagint Greek text. He says that the passage is corrupt, as is also clear from what precedes. Jerome had said above: “What follows, ‘And I will glorify them, and they shall not be weakened,’ is not found in the Septuagint,” and afterward added: “Again, this is not found in the Septuagint”; the words agree in this reading, but not if one reads, “Again, it is not found in the Hebrew,” since it had not previously been said that anything was absent from the Hebrew. This corrupt passage long troubled learned men: they conjectured either that the edition commonly circulated was not Jerome’s, in which the verse would be found, or that, if it was his, it had been supplied from elsewhere because he lacked a complete Hebrew manuscript].

“And you shall be my people, and I will be your God.”

Their type preceded in Zerubbabel and Ezra, when the people returned, the city began to be rebuilt upon its height, the observance of the Temple’s worship was restored, and the other things contained in Ezra’s book took place.

But this was fulfilled more fully and perfectly in the Lord and Savior and in the Apostles, when the city was built upon its height, of which it is written: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5:14); and the Temple was founded according to its order and ceremonies, so that whatever was done bodily among the former people might be fulfilled spiritually in the Church.

Then praise—or thanksgiving—went forth. For this is what **THODA** (תודה) signifies, so that all the Apostles might say: “Grace to you and peace” (1 Cor. 1:3).

“And the voice of those who play” does not refer to the play in which the people ate, drank, and rose up to play (Exod. 32), but to the play with which David played before the Ark of the Lord (2 Sam. 6).

“And they were multiplied and not diminished,” so that the whole world might believe in the Lord and Savior; “and they were glorified,” so that what is written might be fulfilled: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:2).

And his children—that is, the Apostles—were as they had been at the beginning: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the leaders of the Israelite race.

Then the Lord visited punishment upon all who had afflicted the people of God, namely, the hostile powers. “And his leader was from him”—there is no doubt that this means the Lord and Savior, who according to the flesh came from the race of Israel; and “his prince was brought forth from his midst.”

The Father drew him to himself, and he approached him, so that the Son might say: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:11), because no one can so apply his heart to God or be joined to him as the Son is joined to the Father.

What he says according to the Septuagint—“And you shall be my people, and I will be your God”—we see fulfilled in part in Israel and completely in the multitude of the nations [Note: He should have said “according to the Hebrew,” if what we have just recorded from Victorius is correct. Indeed, he ought not to have cited the Hebrew; but since he expressly says that these words are according to the Septuagint, I have considerable doubt about the correction immediately above, or else the words “according to the Septuagint” should be deleted].

### (Verses 23, 24)

“Behold, the whirlwind of the Lord, his fury going forth, and the rushing storm shall come to rest upon the head of the wicked. The Lord will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he has acted and fulfilled the intention of his heart; in the last days you will understand these things.”

The whirlwind of the Lord’s fury, the rushing storm and tempest, will come to rest upon the head of those men—or of the demons—or of those who blasphemed the Son of God. And he will not turn back the anger of his indignation until he has acted and fulfilled the intention of his heart, and Jerusalem has been surrounded by an army and utterly destroyed. Just as an artisan cannot be understood except after the work has been completed, nor the skill of a physician except after health has been attained, so, when Jerusalem has been overthrown and the former people rejected, believers will then understand that the rejection of the Jews was the occasion of our salvation.

### (Chapter 31, verse 1)

“At that time, says the Lord, I shall be God for all the clans of Israel—or, ‘for the people of Israel’—and they shall be my people.”

Unless the Lord’s intention has been fulfilled and his fury has come to rest upon the head of the wicked, the Lord of the universe cannot be God for the clans of Israel. He says this, however, concerning the remnant that has been saved. If what was said to us is objected: “I shall be God for the people of Israel,” or “for all the clans of Israel,” let us take an example:

“If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of your father” (John 8:39).

And the Apostle writes: “Consider Israel according to the flesh” (1 Corinthians 10:18). By this he teaches that there is another Israel according to the spirit. That Israel, therefore, is the one who perceives God with the mind—or who is most upright before the Lord—and such an Israel will be the people of God.

### (Verse 2)

“Thus says the Lord: The people that remained from the sword found grace in the wilderness; Israel, go to your rest.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: I found warmth in the wilderness among those who had perished by the sword. Go, and do not kill Israel.”

Through ambiguity in the Greek word, the Latin manuscripts have absurdly interpreted it as “lupins” instead of “warmth.” For the Greek θερμόν (*thermon*) signifies both meanings, and this word itself is not found in the Hebrew. What is written is HEN [Hebrew: חן], which Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated as χάριν (*charin*), that is, “grace.” Only the Septuagint rendered it “warmth,” thinking that the final letter was MEM. For if we read HEN with the letter NUN, it means “grace”; if with MEM, it is interpreted as “heat.”

The sense according to the Hebrew is this: The Jewish people, which had remained after the Roman sword—or which certainly had been able to avoid—or, according to the alternative reading, “escape”—the anger of the Lord’s fury—found grace in the wilderness of the nations, so that it might be saved within the multitude of the nations in the Church. Thus Israel will go and find its rest, which it had always hoped for and which the prophecies of the prophets had promised it.
