According to the Septuagint, however, the meaning is this: The Lord found the Apostles and their companions warm and alive in the wilderness of the nations, among those who had been killed by their unbelief and possessed no warmth of life. Therefore the angels and those who are in God’s ministry are commanded not to kill everyone, so that Israel may not be utterly destroyed; and it is said to them: “Go, and do not kill Israel.” Let there be some who live, some who are warmed by the ardor of faith, some who escape the cold of unbelief and death, whom the Lord may find in the wilderness.

### (Verses 3 ff.)

“The Lord appeared to me—or, ‘to him’—from afar; and with everlasting love I have loved you. Therefore I drew you to me, taking pity on you. Again I shall build you, and you shall be built, virgin Israel. Again you shall be adorned—or, ‘crowned’—with your tambourines—or, ‘you shall take up your tambourines’—and you shall go forth in the chorus of those who play. Again you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria; plant the plantations and gather the vintage. For there shall be a day when the watchmen on Mount Ephraim will cry out: ‘Arise, and let us go up to Zion, to the Lord our God.’”

*[Note: In the Vulgate and Jerome’s version: “Those who plant shall plant, and until the time comes they shall not gather the vintage, because there will be a day when,” and so forth. Previously, in place of “for there will be,” the reading “for there was a day” prevailed, contrary to the manuscripts and the Hebrew text.]*

Israel had offended the Lord and had said: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19:15). And: “Come, let us kill him, and the inheritance will be ours” (Mark 12:7). It had withdrawn far from God. Therefore, after a long time, the Lord appeared to it—not in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, after they had again been taken captive, but he loved it with an everlasting love that will be destroyed by no end. And he drew it to himself in pity. It was saved not by merit, but by clemency.

Again he says: “I shall build you, and you shall be built, virgin Israel.” Let us understand this properly of the Church. For those who long for a golden and jeweled Jerusalem, consecrating their greed in the mystery of the Lord’s city, are delirious. “Again you shall be adorned with your tambourines,” so that you may sing to the Lord in the Churches, after all the flesh of evil works has been consumed in you. And you shall go forth “in the chorus of those who play,” with the throngs of the nations. You shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria, not in valleys and low places, but on the mountains of Samaria, which after the captivity of the people of Israel were possessed by foreigners. To them it is said: “Plant the plantations and gather the vintage.”

Then there was the day of the Lord when the watchmen—namely, the Apostles and apostolic men—cried out on Mount Samaria and on Mount Ephraim. One of these names signifies watchfulness, the other fruitfulness. What do the watchmen of Samaria—or rather, what do they cry out on Mount Ephraim?

“Arise, you who lie down; leave the lowly things behind; reject the sacrifices of victims. The sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50).

“Let us go up to Zion,” that is, to the Church, where there is contemplation and the vision of God. And when we have reached Zion—or rather, when we have gone up to it—let us go up together to the Lord our God.

*[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads: “when we have gone up together to it, we shall go up to the Lord,” and so forth.]*

### (Verse 7)

“For thus says the Lord: Rejoice with gladness, O Jacob, and neigh—or, ‘cry out’—against the head of the nations; sound out, sing, and say: ‘Save, O Lord, your people, the remnant of Israel.’”

Significantly, not all Israel is saved, but “the remnant of Israel,” when the Lord commands and says: “Rejoice with gladness, you who are from Jacob, and neigh,” directing everything toward the head of the nations, because once the tail was turned into the head. “Sound out, sing, and say.”

*[Note: The same manuscript reads: “Blow the trumpet, and say.”]*

What are they commanded to say? “Save, O Lord, your people.” Which people? Certainly “the remnant of Israel,” which has been saved according to election. Concerning them Paul also gives Isaiah’s testimony:

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:9; Romans 9:29).

### (Verse 8)

“Behold, I shall bring them from the land of the north, and I shall gather them from the ends of the earth.”

What follows—“at the feast of Passover, and he will beget many children”—is not found in the Hebrew, but is read only in the Septuagint. In its place the following is written among the Hebrews:

“Among them shall be the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and the woman giving birth together: a great Church of those returning here.”

The remnant of the people of Israel is gathered through the Apostles and apostolic men, concerning whom we read above: “The watchmen will cry out on the mountain,” and to whom it is commanded: “Sound out, sing, and say,” so that the remnant of Israel may be saved.

The Lord himself also promises that he will bring them back from the land of the north, which is the most severe of the winds and is called “right”—from unbelief and from the coldness of the Lord’s love—and that he will gather them from the ends of the earth, not at another time but at the feast of Passover, that is, during the days of the Lord’s Passion. When the Lord was crucified, what he himself promised in the Gospel was fulfilled:

“When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw everything to myself” (John 12:32).

Then he begot a great multitude, so that Isaiah’s statement might be fulfilled: “For a nation has been born at once” (Isaiah 66:8, according to the Septuagint). On one day three thousand people believed, and on another five thousand (Acts 2 and 4).

*[Note: In the Vulgate and Hieronymian version, “together” is found instead of “once”; the Hebrew and the Greek εἰς εἴπαξ disagree. See what we have noted above concerning this passage in the Commentary on Isaiah.]*

What is written in the Hebrew—“Among them shall be the blind and the lame, the pregnant woman and the woman giving birth together, a great Church of those returning here”—although it has also been fulfilled according to the literal sense, in that the blind saw and the lame walked, can nevertheless be better understood according to the anagogical sense: those who were previously blind through unbelief afterward believed in the Savior; and those who were lame—those to whom Elijah once said, “How long will you limp on both feet?” (1 Kings 18:21)—afterward walked—or, according to another reading, “saw.” Also: “The people who sat in darkness and the shadow of death saw a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). The lame ran, and the pregnant woman gave birth to children: the great Church of those returning to the faith.

The Jews think that this was fulfilled when, under Ezra, after the day of Passover, they went out from Babylon in order to return to Jerusalem. In this there was a type, not the reality. For they cannot prove—or, according to the alternative reading, were unable to prove—that at that time everything that we have read and shall read was fulfilled.

### (Verse 9)

“They shall come—or, ‘go forth’—with weeping, and I shall bring them back with mercy. I shall lead them through streams of water on a straight road, and they shall not stumble—or, ‘shall not go astray’—on it. For I have become a father to Israel, and Ephraim is my firstborn.”

*[Note: In the Hieronymian version and the Vulgate: “I shall lead them in prayers,” and so forth.]*

If we read according to the Hebrew, “They shall come with weeping”—for this is indicated by JABU [Hebrew: יבאו]—we shall say that sometimes tears are also an indication of excessive joy, according to the saying: “I weep for joy.”

But if, according to the Septuagint, which says, “He shall go forth with weeping, and in mercy—or, ‘for consolation’—I shall bring them back,” we understand it in the sense also expressed in the Psalms:

“Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm 125:7–8).

They wept when they were led into captivity, and they received the greatest consolation when they were brought back by the Lord’s mercy.

The Lord led them through the Apostles and apostolic men, full of waters and of a very abundant river, on a straight road—namely, the road of faith, not of Jewish unbelief. “And they shall not,” he says, “stumble on it,” because they have ceased to be blind. To those who were once blind it had been said:

“If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now, because you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (John 9:41).

We can understand the straight road also as Christ, in whom whoever walks will not stumble (Romans 5).

“I have become,” he says, “a father to Israel,” which has been brought back, “and Ephraim is my firstborn.” For where sin once abounded, grace abounded all the more.

That Ephraim is a type of the people gathered from the nations is attested by Scripture. He was the younger son of Joseph, and he seized the birthright from Manasseh, who by nature was the firstborn (Genesis 48). But in the mystery of the cross, with their hands crossed, the one standing at Jacob’s left received the blessing of his right hand. The one who had stood at the right was blessed with the left and reduced to second rank. And just as Jacob took the birthright from Esau, so Ephraim took it from Manasseh.

The entire people of the ten tribes was called Ephraim, because Jeroboam son of Nebat, from that tribe, was the first to obtain the kingdom in Samaria (ibid., 27).

### (Verses 10 ff.)

“Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and announce it in the distant islands, and say: ‘He who scattered Israel will gather him, and he will guard him as a shepherd guards his flock, because the Lord redeemed Jacob and delivered him from the hand of one more powerful—or, “stronger” [Vulgate: “will redeem and deliver”].’ And they shall come and praise him on Mount Zion, and they shall flow together to the Lord’s good things, to grain, wine, and oil, and to the offspring of sheep and cattle. Their soul shall be like a watered garden—or, ‘like a fruit-bearing tree’—and they shall hunger no more. Then the virgin—or, ‘the virgins’—shall rejoice in the chorus, and the young men and the old men together. I shall turn their mourning into joy, console them, and gladden them after their sorrow. I shall inebriate the soul of the priests with fatness—or, ‘of the sons of Levi’—and my people shall be filled with my good things, says the Lord.”

The calling of the nations is clearly demonstrated, since Scripture says: “Hear the word of the Lord, O nations, and announce it in the distant islands, and say.” What are they to announce to the distant islands? That the Lord who scattered Israel will himself gather him.

Therefore it was not the power of the adversaries that caused Israel to be scattered, but the Lord’s will. “And he will guard him as a shepherd guards his flock.” For the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John 10:11).

“Because the Lord redeemed Jacob” with the price of his blood, “and delivered him from the hand of one more powerful,” or “stronger.” By this it is shown that the opposing powers are stronger by reason of the weakness of human nature. And insofar as strength is concerned in both, they are stronger by nature, but we are stronger through faith—provided that we deserve to be delivered by him who can bind the strong man and plunder his house.

“And they shall come,” he says, certainly those who have been delivered from the hand of the powerful, “and they shall praise their deliverer on Mount Zion,” that is, in the Church. And they shall flow together to the Lord’s good things: the abundance of all things, which is perceived not in the crops and foods of this flesh, but in the variety of virtues.

“To grain,” he says, “and wine, and oil,” from which the Lord’s bread is made, in which the likeness of his blood is fulfilled and the blessing of sanctification is displayed, as Scripture says:

“God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44:8).

“And to the offspring of sheep,” who in the Churches are the simple, “and of cattle,” which have horns and drive away adversaries.

But so that we may know that these blessings refer not to the body but to the soul, it follows:

“Their soul shall be like a watered garden,” or “like a fruit-bearing tree,” which has been planted beside streams of water, “and like the paradise of the Lord in delights” (Psalm 1).

“And they shall hunger no more,” he says—not with that hunger of which it is written, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5:6), but with the hunger that is changed by fullness and excludes the lack of all things.

“Then the virgin shall rejoice in the chorus.” Of her the Apostle writes: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2).

“And the young men,” to whom John says: “I write to you, young men, because you have conquered the evil one”; “and the old men,” to whom the same writer bears witness in mystical language: “I write to you, fathers, because you have known him who is from the beginning” (1 John 2:13–14).

“And I shall turn,” he says, “their mourning into joy,” so that those whom the cross had terrified may be made glad by the resurrection. “And I shall console them and gladden them after their sorrow,” according to the Lord’s saying: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be consoled” (Matthew 5:4).

“And I shall inebriate the soul of the priests,” who possess the knowledge of God, from whose mouth they inquire into the Lord’s law, who believe in him to whom the Prophet sings:

“You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4).

What follows according to the Septuagint—“of the sons of Levi”—is not found in the Hebrew. It is clear that this is not said of those priests who are sons of Levi, but of those for whom Melchizedek went before as a type.

The drunkenness of the priests is also demonstrated in the Apostles, when they were burning with faith and were said to be full of new wine (Acts 2). Hence the place where the Lord was seized is called Gethsemane (Matthew 26:36), which in our language means “valley of fatness.”

And when the priests have been made fat with the Lord’s teaching, and, inebriated at Joseph’s banquet, have said, “Your cup, which inebriates, how excellent it is!” (Genesis 43–44), then this too will take place which the Lord now promises: “My people shall be filled with my good things” (Psalm 22:5).

All these things are now granted in part; then they will be given in full, when we see face to face and the body of our humiliation has been changed into the glory of resurrection.

### (Verse 15)

“Thus says the Lord: A voice has been heard on high, of lamentation, weeping, and mourning: Rachel weeping for her children, and she did not wish to be consoled over her children—or, according to the Vulgate, ‘over them’—because they are not.”

*[Note: Victorius preferred “weeping” in the nominative, or “lamenting,” from the Greek ἀποκλαιομένη, “lamenting.”]*

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord: A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation and weeping and mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and she did not wish to cease, because they are not.”

Neither according to the Hebrew nor according to the Septuagint did Matthew take his testimony. For after describing the slaughter of the infants, we read in him:

“Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet, saying: A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and much wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she did not wish to be consoled, because they are not” (Matthew 2:17–18).

From this it is clear that the Evangelists and Apostles did not follow the interpretation of anyone from the Hebrew, but, as Hebrews from Hebrews, expressed in their own language what they read in Hebrew.

Rachel, the mother of Joseph, when she was coming to Bethlehem, was suddenly seized by the pains of childbirth and gave birth to a son. Since she was dying in childbirth, the midwife called him Benoni, that is, “son of my pain.” But his father Jacob changed the name and called him Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand” (Genesis 35:18).

The question therefore arises: How did Matthew the evangelist transfer the Prophet’s testimony to the slaughter of the little ones, when it is plainly written concerning the ten tribes, whose chief was not Ephratha, and when Ephratha is not in the tribe of Ephraim but in the tribe of Judah? For Bethlehem itself is called by two names, and thus the names of both agree. Bethlehem is called “house of bread”; Ephratha means καρποφορία (*karpophoria*), which we can render “fruitfulness.”

Therefore, because Rachel was buried at Ephratha, that is, at Bethlehem—as both Holy Scripture and the inscription on her tomb still testify—she is said to weep for the children who were killed nearby and in the surrounding regions.

Some Jews interpret this passage as referring to the time when, after Jerusalem was captured under Vespasian, countless thousands of captives from the road to Gaza and Alexandria were sent through that route to Rome. Others refer it to the final captivity under Hadrian, when Jerusalem too was overthrown and an innumerable population of every age and of both sexes was sold in the market at the terebinth.

*[Note: Compare Sozomen, Book II, chapter 4, where he speaks of that market—ἐμπορεία—at the terebinth, and the Paschal Chronicle, p. 253, where it says that those fairs were called Hadrianic down to that time: ἕως τοῦ νῦν ἡ πανήγυρις ἐκείνη λέγεται Ἀδριανή. Also consult our Jerome on chapter 11 of Zechariah.]*

For this reason, they say, it is especially detestable to the Jews to look upon that celebrated market. Let them say what they wish; we shall rightly say that the evangelist Matthew took the testimony with reference to the place where Rachel was buried, so that she might have wept as though they were her own children over the children of the neighboring villages.

*[Note: The particle of negation is absent from the Vatican manuscript.]*

### (Verses 16, 17)

“Thus says the Lord: Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears, because there is a reward for your work, says the Lord. And they shall return from the land of the enemy—or, ‘of enemies’—and there shall be hope for your future, says the Lord; and the children shall return to their own borders.”

This has not yet happened according to the literal sense. For we do not read that the ten tribes, which are exiled in the cities of the Medes and Persians, have returned to the land of Judea. But according to the spirit it was fulfilled, and is still being fulfilled, in the Lord’s Passion, whenever Israel is saved from the whole world and Rachel is told:

“Let your voice cease from weeping and your eyes from tears.”

The sense is this: “Stop weeping, for the Lord has regarded your former works; and your children shall return from the land of the enemy, so that you may not remain bound to your present grief. For there is hope for your future, says the Lord. And your children shall return to their own borders,” which their fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob possessed.

It is better, however, to understand this of the little ones: that they have a reward for the blood poured out on behalf of Christ; that instead of the land of Herod, their enemy, they possess the kingdoms of heaven; and that they will return to their former dwelling when, in place of the body of humiliation, they receive a glorious body.

This is the final hope, when the righteous will shine like the sun (Wisdom 3), and the infants who were once little ones and nursing children, without increase of age and without bodily injury or toil, will rise as a perfect man, to the measure of the fullness of Christ (Ephesians 4:13).

### (Verses 18, 19)

“Hearing, I heard Ephraim migrating—or, ‘lamenting.’ You chastised me, and I was instructed like an untamed young bull—or, ‘like a calf, and I did not learn.’ Convert me, and I shall be converted, because you are the Lord my God. For after you converted me—or, ‘after I was taken captive’—I did penance. And after I knew—or, ‘after you showed me’—I struck my thigh—or, ‘groaned’; I was ashamed and confounded—or, ‘from the day of confusion, and I revealed you’—because I bore the reproach of my youth.”

*[Note: Victorius omits the conjunction “and,” following the Greek: ὥσπερ μόσχος οὐκ ἐδιδάχθην, “like a calf that was not taught.”]*

*[Note: The same editor reverses the order: “after you showed me,” or “after I knew,” “I struck,” and so forth. For “or, ‘I knew,’” the Septuagint has “you showed me,” which is Jerome’s own interpretation. Wherever Jerome’s version is intended, it precedes the Septuagint version.]*

God says that he heard Ephraim speaking and lamenting. There is no doubt that this signifies the ten tribes, whose first ruler was Jeroboam son of Nebat. He also made golden calves at Dan and Bethel, so that the people, deceived by this error, would cease to worship and adore the God of Israel.

“You chastised me,” he says, “and I was chastised.” Every correction contributes to salvation. At present it appears to be a cause of sadness, but afterward it brings peaceful fruits.

What he says—“like an untamed young bull,” or “like a calf, and I did not learn”—means that he was instructed through much labor and blows so that he might be converted to repentance, yet he did not improve.

“Convert me,” he says, “and I shall be converted.” Therefore, even the repentance that we undertake we cannot accomplish unless we strive with God’s help. For after you have converted me, and I have been converted to you, then I shall know that you are the Lord my God, and that my errors and sins will not kill me.

“And after you converted me, I did penance.” See how great is God’s help and how frail the human condition is: even this very repentance that we practice we cannot fulfill unless the Lord first converts us.

“And after,” he says, “you showed me”—either repentance itself or knowledge of you—or “after I knew you, I struck my thigh.” This is an indication of one who is grieving, lamenting, and mourning over his former error: he strikes his thigh with his hand and confesses that previously he was foolish.

“I was confounded,” he says, “and ashamed,” or “from the day of confusion.” What time is not a time of our confusion if we remember our former sins and call to mind everything we have done wrongly?

What the Septuagint says, “and I revealed you,” signifies that after he groaned and recognized his offenses, he progressed so far that he even revealed God to others who were ignorant of him, in accordance with what the repentant David says:

“I shall teach the unjust your ways, and the impious shall be converted to you” (Psalm 50:15).

And when he says, “because I bore the reproach of my youth,” he says that he sinned through the ignorance of age, so that he might more easily obtain pardon, according to what David sings:

“Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24:7).

Hence, in what follows, God also calls him a little one and one abounding in delights. He says this because of the magnitude of his riches and the fertility of the land, in which the tribe of Ephraim luxuriates even to the present day.

### (Verse 20)

“Is Ephraim a son honored—or, ‘beloved’—by me? Is he a delicate child? For from the time I spoke of him—or, ‘my words were in him’—I shall still remember him [the Vulgate omits “remembering”]. Therefore my inward parts are disturbed over him; I shall surely pity him, says the Lord.”

When Ephraim was doing penance and saying, “At the beginning you instructed me, and I was instructed like an untamed young bull,” and finally, “Because I bore the reproach of my youth,” the Lord answered. To one who had turned to him with a complete mind, he gave this consoling oracle:

“Ephraim is a beloved son to me” (Genesis 48), whom I loved from the beginning to such an extent that I preferred him to Manasseh. He is an honored son who, contrary to the order of nature, received the honor of the firstborn by the Lord’s favor.

He is “a delicate child,” concerning whom it is written:

“The sons of Ephraim, bending and shooting the bow, turned back on the day of battle” (Psalm 77:9).

The entire book of the prophet Hosea concerns him and is addressed to him, for Jacob blessed him.

In this passage let us understand “delights” according to what is said in the Psalm:

“Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the requests of your heart” (Psalm 36:4).

For this the Greek and the Hebrew have: “Overflow with delights.” Hence paradise in Eden is called the paradise of delights.

“Because,” he says, “my words were in him, I shall still remember him in remembrance.” Lest the blessing be thought gratuitous, bestowed by the indulgence of the giver rather than according to the merit of the one upon whom it was conferred, he therefore says: “I shall remember him, because my words were in him.” Not in his mouth, not on his lips, but in the innermost affection of his heart.

For this reason also “my inward parts are disturbed over him.” To him he speaks through Hosea:

“What shall I do for you, Ephraim? What shall I do for you, Israel? Shall I make you like Admah? Shall I set you like Zeboiim?” (Hosea 6:4; 11:8).

“My heart is turned within me; my inward parts are disturbed. I shall not act according to the fury of my anger, and I shall not destroy Ephraim. I shall surely pity him,” says the Lord.

Indeed, my words were in him, and he received all my commandments with an eager mind and preserved them in his heart. Yet “I shall surely pity him,” says the Lord, to show that every human righteousness requires the mercy of God.

### (Verses 21, 22)

“Set up watchtowers for yourself; place bitter things before yourself; direct your heart onto the straight road on which you walked. Return, virgin Israel; return to these your cities. How long will you dissolve yourself in delights, wandering daughter? For the Lord has created a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man.”

*[Note: Victorius preferred: “Set yourself up, Zion,” following the Septuagint στῆσον σεαυτὴν Σιών, “establish yourself, Zion,” which he attempts to prove from Jerome’s exposition that follows.]*

The Septuagint: “Set up watchmen for yourself; make punishment; place your heart upon your shoulders; the road on which you walked. Return, virgin Israel; return to your cities, mourning. How long will you turn away, despised daughter? For the Lord has created you as salvation, as a new planting; in your salvation men shall go around you.”

Where we said, “How long will you dissolve yourself in delights,” Symmachus rendered: “How long will you be plunged into the depths?”

I have set out both editions in full so that I might show that this exceedingly obscure passage, containing the mysteries of the Church, was either unknown or omitted by the Septuagint—or by whoever else interpreted this prophet.

The Hebrew word SIONIM [Hebrew: ציונים] can be translated either “watchmen” or “watchtowers,” as Aquila and Symmachus translated it. Hence I am astonished at what the Vulgate edition intended when, instead of SIONIM—that is, instead of “watchmen”—it placed “Zion,” thereby disturbing the reader’s understanding, so that he would think that after Ephraim the word of God had suddenly been addressed to Zion and to the tribe of Judah. The speech, however, continues throughout to concern Ephraim, to whom he said above:

“Hearing, I heard Ephraim,”

and:

“Ephraim is an honored son to me,” or “a delicate child,” to whom he now also speaks:

“Set up watchtowers for yourself,” or “watchmen,” who may announce to you that such great prosperity in all things is coming.

What follows, “bitter things,” which are called THEMRURIM [Hebrew: תמרורים] in Hebrew, for which Symmachus translated “changes,” indicates that he ought to weep either over his former sins or from the greatness of his joy, and turn to the Lord with his whole mind, and place or direct his heart onto the road along which he departed, since from there he will return.

What the Septuagint said instead—“Place your heart upon your shoulders”—signifies that he ought to join thoughts to works, or contemplate the shoulders of those who carry him, bringing him back from captivity. Isaiah explains this more fully when he asserts that they will be brought back on camels, chariots, and pack animals (Isaiah 60).

“Return,” he says, “virgin Israel; return to your cities,” which you abandoned as a captive. “How long will you be dissolved through negligence and wander in profound error?”

Pay close attention to what I am about to say and carefully consider from where such great blessedness is to be expected—or, according to another reading, hoped for. Hear what you had never known before:

“The Lord has created a new thing upon the earth. Without a man’s seed, without intercourse or conception of any kind, a woman shall encompass a man in the womb of her body. According to the stages of age he will appear to advance through crying and infancy in wisdom and age; yet, as a perfect man, he will be contained in a woman’s womb for the customary months.”

Therefore Symmachus and Aquila translated this in agreement with our edition.

What the Vulgate edition intended in this passage I could state, and I could discover some meaning, if it were not sacrilegious to argue about God’s words according to human reasoning. Theodotion, however, also agreeing with the Vulgate edition, translated it:

“The Lord has created a new salvation; in salvation a man shall go around,”

using the singular for the plural.

At the same time, this too should be noted: the birth and conception of the Savior are here called a creation.

### (Verses 23, 24)

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: They shall still speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their captivity: ‘May the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain.’ And Judah and all its cities shall dwell in it together, farmers and those who drive flocks.”

The Septuagint: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: They shall still speak this word in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore its captivity: ‘Blessed is the Lord upon his holy mountain of righteousness,’ and those who dwell in the land of Judea and in all its cities, with the farmer, and he will be raised up in the flock.”

According to the Hebrew, it is clear that when Israel returns and its captivity has been restored to its own land, the cities of Judah will be inhabited, and each of them will be told:

“May the Lord bless you, who is truly the beauty of righteousness and the holy mountain, in which the one who dwells will fear no ambush.”

Judah will dwell without iniquity in its cities, and there will be farmers and a multitude of livestock. This appears to have been fulfilled in part under Zerubbabel and Ezra.

The fullness of the prophecy, however, should be referred to the times of Christ: either to his first coming, when these things took place spiritually, or to his second coming, when everything will be fulfilled—spiritually according to us, but carnally according to the Jews and those among us who Judaize.

According to the Septuagint, the meaning is this:

“This word will still be spoken in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore its captivity.”

What will be said? “Blessed is the Lord upon his holy mountain of righteousness.”

There is no other mountain that can receive the designation of righteousness and holiness except the Savior. Otherwise it is foolish, following Jewish error, to believe that an irrational and insensible mountain is righteous and holy.

He is the one of whom it is also written in what follows:

“And in every city of his”—that is, of the Savior—“with the farmer.”

There is no doubt that this signifies the Lord, concerning whom it is written in the Gospel:

“I am the vine; you are the branches; my Father is the farmer” (John 15:1).

Hence the Apostle says:

“You are God’s cultivation; you are God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What follows—“And he will be raised up in the flock”—shows that in each individual flock the Lord himself, who is righteous, holy, and the farmer, is raised up, and that in his servants and believers he ascends to the heights.

(Verses 25–26.) “For I have intoxicated the weary soul” (or, “for I have intoxicated every thirsty soul”), “and I have satisfied” (or, “filled”) “every hungry soul”; therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me.

[Note: The version of Jerome and the Vulgate reads: “Therefore, as one awakened from sleep, I arose,” etc.]

The change of persons makes the Prophets’ meaning obscure. The Lord had said: “The word shall yet be spoken in the land of Judah and in its cities, when I restore their captivity.” What, then, will they say? Without doubt, what follows: “May the Lord bless you, beauty of righteousness, holy mountain,” and so forth. Again, when they had said these things, the Lord replied to them: “For I have intoxicated the weary,” or thirsty, “soul, and I have satisfied every hungry soul.” When he had said this, the people who had come from captivity replied: “Therefore I awoke and saw, and my sleep was sweet to me.”

For the Lord intoxicates the weary, or thirsty, soul, and says in the Gospel: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7:37). And: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (ibid., 38). He also satisfies every hungry and thirsty soul. Concerning this thirst and hunger the same Gospel testifies: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6).

It must also be noted that drunkenness is used here in a good sense, of which it is said in the Song: “Eat, friends; drink and become drunk, beloved” (Song of Songs 5:1). Joseph too became drunk with his brothers at noon in this kind of drunkenness (Genesis 43). Those who had been weary and hungry, having been intoxicated and satisfied, give thanks, replying: “I awoke and saw”—namely, the Lord awakening and saying: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). “And my sleep,” he says, “was sweet to me,” so that I might imitate the words of my Lord, who says: “I lay down and slept; I awoke, because the Lord received me” [or, “will receive me”] (Psalm 3:6).

[Col. 0882C] (Verses 27 and following.) “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of human beings” [Vulgate: “of a human being”] “and with the seed of animals. And just as I watched over them to uproot, demolish, dissipate, destroy, and afflict them, so I will watch over them to build and plant them, says the Lord. In those days they will no longer say: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’ [Note: Consistently, with the Hieronymian version and the Vulgate editions, here and below the Cistercian manuscript reads “were stupefied”], but each person will die for his own iniquity. Everyone who eats a sour grape—his teeth will be set on edge.”

The words “the house and the house,” that is, “the house of Israel and the house of Judah,” are not found in the Septuagint, but only “Israel and Judah,” so that the text reads: “I will sow Israel and Judah.” What follows—“with the seed of human beings and of animals”—we must refer to rational and simple people.

And just as at the beginning of Jeremiah it was said to him: “Behold, I have appointed you today over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to dissipate and demolish, to build and plant”; and, “I watched over them to do what I had threatened,” so, he says, “I will now watch over them to build and plant.” “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

According to the Jews and our Judaizers, all such promises are thought to be fulfilled in the thousand-year kingdom. But we, following the Apostle’s statement, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (ibid., 6), and the prophet Isaiah’s testimony that the Savior is a builder of walls and houses (Isaiah 58), maintain that these things were fulfilled spiritually at Christ’s first coming—fulfilled in part, not wholly, because “now we see in a mirror and in a riddle, and we do not know as we ought to know” (1 Corinthians 13). But when that which is perfect has come, then that which is partial will be destroyed.

Or certainly we believe that they are to be fulfilled at the second coming, when the Lord will appear in his majesty and “the fullness of the Gentiles will have entered, so that all Israel may be saved,” and no longer in part, through individuals, but so that “God may be all in all” (Romans 11; 1 Corinthians 15).

What follows—“In those days they will no longer say: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge,’” and the rest—we discussed more fully in the explanations of Ezekiel, when we interpreted the passage: “Son of man, what is this proverb among you concerning the children of Israel, who say: ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord, this proverb shall no longer be among you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also is the soul of the son. The soul that sins shall die” (Ezekiel 18:1 and following).

From this we learn that it is not the Lord who causes death, but sin. For “the soul that sins shall die.” The same is said in the present passage: Israel will not be condemned forever for the sins of its fathers, but after a long time it will be saved through its own merits and faith in Christ.

It must also be observed that vices and sins are called “a sour grape,” so that the teeth of those who eat it are set on edge and cannot taste its sweetness, of which it is said: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9). Whoever does not understand the Scriptures according to the truth of the matter eats a sour grape. Hence all heretics, believing perverse things, cannot eat the bread that came down from heaven; rather, their teeth are set on edge—not by the austerity of the food, but by the defect of their teeth.

(Verses 31–32.) “Behold, days are coming” [Vulgate: “will come”], says the Lord, “and I will make” (or, “establish”) “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant” (or, “testament”), “not according to the covenant” (or, “testament”) “which I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. The covenant” (or, “testament”) “which they made void, and I ruled over them” (or, “I disregarded them”), says the Lord.

“And this will be the covenant” (or, “testament”) “that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, says the Lord: I will give my law in their inward parts” (or, “in their mind”), “and I will write it on their heart. I will be their God, and they will be my people. And they will no longer teach one another, each his neighbor and each his brother, saying: ‘Know the Lord,’ for they will all know me, from the least of them to the greatest, says the Lord, because I will be gracious toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.”

The Apostle Paul—or whoever wrote the Epistle—used this testimony in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Thereafter all ecclesiastical writers say that everything was fulfilled at the Savior’s first coming, and that the New Testament, that is, the Gospel, succeeded the Old Testament, with the law of the letter changed into the law of the Spirit, so that all sacrifices, circumcision, and the Sabbath might also be fulfilled spiritually.

Our rendering of *covenant* for *testament* follows the Hebrew truth, although *testament* may rightly be called a covenant, because it contains the will and declaration of those who enter into the covenant.

When Israel was led out of the land of Egypt, God’s intimacy with that people was so great that he is said to have taken them by the hand and given them a covenant, which they made void; and for this reason the Lord disregarded them. Now, in the Gospel, after the cross, resurrection, and ascension, he promises to give a covenant—not on tablets of stone, but on the fleshly tablets of the heart.

When the Lord’s Testament has been written in the minds of believers, he will be their God and they will be his people, so that they will no longer seek Jewish teachers, traditions, and human commandments, but will be taught by the Holy Spirit—if, indeed, they are worthy to hear: “You are God’s temple, and the Spirit of God dwells in you” (1 Corinthians 3:19). “The Spirit blows where it wills,” and possesses various gifts. Knowledge of the one God is possession of all virtues.

“And this,” he says, “will happen because I will be gracious toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more.” From this it is clear, according to the meaning of this *pericope* (περικοπή), that the preceding statements are to be understood as referring to the Savior’s first coming, when he joined both peoples, Israel and Judah, to himself.

If anyone is troubled by why he said, “I will establish with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah a new covenant,” or Testament, “not according to the covenant which I made with their fathers,” let him understand that the Church of Christ was first composed of Jews, and that the Lord the Savior came to them and said: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24). The Apostles themselves confirmed this: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13:46). For it was not right to give the children’s bread to dogs. But because the children did not wish to receive the Father when he came among them, he gave all who received him the power to become children of God (Matthew 15; John 1).

(Verses 35–36.) “Thus says the Lord, who gives the sun for light by day, the order of the moon and stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea and its waves roar”—the Lord of hosts is his name. “If these laws” (or, “these ordinances”) “should cease before me, says the Lord, then the seed of Israel also will cease, so that it will no longer be a nation before me throughout all its days.”

At the beginning of Genesis we read that the sun was placed in the heavens for the light of day, and the moon and stars for the light of night (Genesis 1). And in the Psalm: “Day unto day announces the word, and night unto night reveals knowledge” (Psalm 18:2), showing that night and day succeed one another.

“How,” he says, “the order of things, especially of the heavenly stars, cannot be changed, and the waves of the sounding sea roll toward the shores, while the crash of the waters and the terrible sound of the swelling waves are heard, yet the sea cannot advance farther than God’s command has decreed,” according to the words: “You set a boundary which they shall not pass, nor shall they return to cover the earth” (Psalm 103:9)—“so,” he says, “the seed and race of Israel, by the Lord’s will, will endure forever and will never cease.”

The “laws” here must not be understood as the Mosaic laws, but as the constitution and order of nature. Let us ask the Jews: If the heavens will perish, and all will grow old like a garment, and it is said to the Lord, “But you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 101:28), how can the seed of Israel be perpetual? Either, when the heavens perish, the seed of Israel will also perish; or, if it is perpetual, then the heavens too will not perish.

But if Scripture cannot lie, and the heavens are to perish, then the seed of Israel will also perish—especially since Jacob says to his sons: “Come, and I will announce to you what will happen in the last days” (Genesis 49:1). When it says “in the last days,” therefore the world will cease to exist, and another ordering [or, “dispensation”] of things will take place.

This argument is directed against them. For our part, that this world is not perpetual is also demonstrated by the Gospel, which says: “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24:35). And: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

Let us put it another way: As long as this world exists, the seed of Israel and the Jewish nation will remain—not in those who are now unbelieving, but in those who believed with and through the Apostles, so that the remnant might be saved.

(Verses 37.) “Thus says the Lord: If the heavens above can be measured, and the foundations of the earth below can be investigated, then I too will reject the whole seed of Israel because of all that they have done, says the Lord.”

The Septuagint reads: “Thus says the Lord: If the heaven above has been exalted higher, and if the pavement of the earth below has been humbled lower, then I will not reject the race of Israel, says the Lord, because of all that they have done.”

There is a great difference here between the Hebrew text and the Vulgate edition. Let us first speak according to the Hebrew: “If the heavens above can be measured, and their height known, or if the foundations of the earth can be investigated and their limits comprehended by calculation, then I,” he says, “will reject the whole seed of Israel because of all that they have done, says the Lord.”

Just as it is impossible for us to know the summit of the heavens and the foundations of the earth, so it will be impossible for me to reject the whole seed of Israel. But if I reject the whole seed of Israel, then the summit of the heavens and the limits of the earth will have been measured.

This syllogism is also constructed in the Gospel, when an impossibility is compared with an impossibility:

[Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads: “the impossible is compared with the possible.”]

“It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdoms of heaven” (Matthew 19). For just as the former cannot happen, so neither can the latter. But if the latter happens, then what was thought impossible [or, “impossible”] will also happen.

Therefore those who explain this passage otherwise are mistaken, bringing forward as well the testimony that the Son could have asked the Father and he would have brought twelve legions of angels to his aid.

The Septuagint translated contrary to this meaning, saying: “If the heaven has been exalted higher, and the pavement of the earth humbled lower, then I,” he says, “will not reject the seed of Israel, says the Lord, because of all that they have done.” But if this is so, the race of Israel will be rejected. For just as the heaven cannot be higher than it is, nor the earth lower than it is, so the race of Israel likewise cannot be rejected.

[Note: The same reading is found in the Vatican manuscript: “can be proved.”]

If we see the Jews glorying in this testimony according to the Hebrew, let us agree with them that the whole seed of Israel has not been rejected. For not all have been rejected, but only those who were unbelieving.

(Verses 38.) “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and a city will be built for the Lord, from the tower of Hananel” [or, “Anamehel”] “to the Corner Gate. And the measuring line will go out farther” (or, according to Symmachus, “the measuring cord of it will go out opposite it”) “over the hill of Gareb, and it will surround Goath” (or, according to the Septuagint, “the chosen stones”).

“And the whole valley of ruins”—for which Theodotion placed the Hebrew word itself, *PHAGARIM* ()—“and the ashes, and all Asaremoth”—which we more correctly read as *ASADEMOTH* ():

[Note: In the Book of Names it is also written *Asedemoth*, meaning “fields” or “suburbs.”]

“until the torrent of Kidron, until the corner of the eastern Horse Gate; the holy place of the Lord shall not be uprooted or destroyed forever.”

Those who accept Christ’s thousand-year reign on earth—namely, the Jews and our Judaizers—try to point out the tower of Hananel, the Corner Gate, the hill of Gareb, Goath, the valley of Phagarim, all Asademoth, the torrent of Kidron, and the site of the corner of the eastern Horse Gate. They say that there the sanctuary of the Lord, that is, the temple, will be built and will remain forever.

Because they cannot show that this was fulfilled after the captivity in the time of Zerubbabel and Ezra, they pass on to the times of Christ, whom they say will come at the consummation of the world, so that Jerusalem, golden and adorned with jewels according to John’s Apocalypse, may descend and be built around this area of land—that is, from one place to another (Revelation 21).

They seize upon this little support for their suspicion: that the foundations of the city will be laid from the tower of Anathoth, which today is called Jeremiah’s tower and is three miles distant from Jerusalem, to the torrent of Kidron, which is mentioned in the Gospel (John 18) and lies in the valley of Jehoshaphat, where there was a garden in which Judas the traitor also handed over the Savior.

They say: “We shall read later that Anamehel, the son of Shallum, was Jeremiah’s cousin, from whom he bought the field; and this is the tower of Hananel,” while they are ignorant of the Hebrew truth. Here, according to the Hebrew, it is written “from the tower of *ANANEEL* ()”, with *nun* as the middle letter; but there it says: “Behold, *ANAMEEL* () the son of Shallum, your cousin, will come to you,” with *mem* as the middle letter.

Therefore, invoking the Lord the Savior, who has the key of David, who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens, and who also opened the sealed book of Isaiah and of all the Prophets (Isaiah 22), while the twenty-four elders worshiped holding harps (Revelation 3)—since he alone was able to unlock the divine mysteries—let us approach the building of the city to which the prophetic word is directed:

“Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Psalm 85:2); and: “The force of the river makes glad the city of God” (Psalm 45:4).

The Church, therefore, is built from the tower of obedience, or of the grace and gifts of God—for this is the meaning of *Ananeel*—up to the Corner Gate. Although it may seem to have a lofty beginning, as long as we remain in this flesh we cannot possess the straight line of truth. Rather, we stand at the corner, with the lines broken [or, “having become broken”], and the measuring cord extends beyond, opposite it—that is, opposite the Corner Gate—over the hill of Gareb, which in our language is rendered either “sojourning” or “scabies.”

This teaches us that we are strangers and pilgrims, and that we must not have itching ears or readily give our assent to the novelty of pernicious doctrines.

“And it will surround,” he says, “Goath,” for which the Septuagint translated “around,” with chosen stones that roll across the face of the earth and are bound together by the cornerstone, as the Apostle Peter says:

[Note: Compare the Commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 40, and on Zechariah 9 and Malachi 3. Although Jerome uses this testimony in those passages with the same meaning, he uses different words.]

“And you yourselves, like living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5).

“And the whole valley,” he says, “of Phagarim,” which is interpreted as “ruins”; “and the ashes”—“it will surround” is understood—so that although we may seem to be on the hills, we should nevertheless always fear ruins and consider ashes, and in penitence say with David: “For I ate ashes like bread, and I mingled my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101:10).

Hence also it is said to those who lie fallen: “Will one who falls not rise again?” says the Lord (Jeremiah 8:4).

“And all,” he says, “of Asademoth,” which we render as “the region of death,” dividing one name into two words: *SADE* (), which means “region,” and *MOTH* (), which means “death.” Aquila translated it “suburbs,” or “fields and countryside.”

The region of death is the region of sinners; and the suburbs are the region of pleasures, which extends to the torrent of Kidron, where the Lord was handed over and which means “darkness” (John 18).

See how many places the Church contains, and how the Apostolic statement—“that she might be without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27)—is preserved in the future and in the heavenly realm.

You hear of corners; you hear of scabies; you hear of ruins and ashes; of the region of death and darkness—and yet you glory in your own virtue and sinlessness.

[Note: This was said against the Pelagians, who habitually abused the Apostle’s verse to the Ephesians, in which the Church is called “without spot or wrinkle,” in order to support their heresy of sinlessness.]

Finally, what follows is: “and as far as the corner of the gate.” This corner too shows that no true righteousness and no certain victory is demonstrated in this age.

Although this corner of the gate is eastern, from where the light proceeds, it is nevertheless called the Horse Gate, to teach us that we need running and struggle, so that at last we may deserve to hear with the Lord: “You mounted your horses, and your riding is salvation” (Habakkuk 3:8).

At the Eastern Gate, at the Gate of Chariots, there is the sanctification of the Lord. And [alternative reading: “That”] let us then consider ourselves perfect when we say to the Lord: “The chariot of God is ten thousandfold, thousands rejoicing; the Lord is among them, at Sinai, in the holy place” (Psalm 67:18).

Such a building, founded upon Christ, of which the Apostle also speaks—“As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Corinthians 3:10)—will never be destroyed, but will remain forever.

Obscure and difficult matters must be discussed at greater length, so that we may pass more briefly over what is clear.

1078

(Chapter 32.—Verses 1 and following.) The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah—which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar. At that time the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the Prophet was shut up in the court of the prison, which was in the house of the king of Judah.

For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying: “Why do you prophesy, saying: ‘Thus says the Lord’?”

Not only the words but also the deeds of the Prophets are examples to us of virtue. Jeremiah could have announced favorable things and enjoyed the friendship of King Zedekiah; but he preferred to obey God rather than human beings (Acts 5), and the one who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna rather than the one who has power only over the body (Matthew 10).

It should also be considered that this was the tenth year of Zedekiah’s reign: Jerusalem had already been besieged and consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence, and captivity was near. Yet Zedekiah persisted in his decision. Some evidence of his clemency is shown in the fact that he did not order Jeremiah to be confined in the prison itself, but in the vestibule of the prison—a relatively free custody, so that he could not escape—as though all Jerusalem, enclosed by its fortifications, were not a common prison for its inhabitants.

This was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, who seized power in the fourth year of King Jehoiakim. The entire reason for the king’s anger was that Jeremiah spoke in God’s name the things that had been commanded him.

(Verses 4–5.) “Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it. And Zedekiah king of Judah will not escape from the hand of the Chaldeans, but will be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and his mouth will speak with his mouth, and his eyes will see his eyes. And he will lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there he will remain until I visit him, says the Lord. But if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will have no success.”

This was the reason for the royal anger: Jeremiah preferred truth to falsehood and said that both the city of Jerusalem and King Zedekiah would be captured. More grievously still, he said that Zedekiah would see the face of the Babylonian king and, as a humble captive, speak with a king in the madness of his overwhelming power.

[Note: Perhaps the manuscripts read more correctly *impotentissimi* (“of one most powerless”), namely, of one excessively weak in spirit.]

For it is a more severe terror to see the person whom one fears, and, before enduring the reproach of words, to suffer the anguish of punishments.

“And he will lead Zedekiah to Babylon,” he says, “and there he will remain.” For this the Septuagint translated: “He will enter Babylon.” The one expression signifies being dragged there unwillingly; the other, going there voluntarily.

“And there,” he says, “he will remain.” He uses an ambiguous expression, lest he seem to prophesy torture and misery. What follows—“until I visit him, says the Lord; and if you fight against the Chaldeans, you will have no success”—is not found in the Septuagint.

Wisely, then, he softened the statement, which can be referred either to good or to evil. For visitation, as I have often said, signifies both consolation and punishment.

(Verses 6–7.) And Jeremiah said: “The word of the Lord came to me, saying: Behold, Anameel” [Vulgate: “Anemeel”], “the son of Shallum” (or, “Sallom”), “your cousin”—which in Hebrew is called *DODACH* ()—“has come” [Vulgate: “will come”] “to you, saying: ‘Buy for yourself my field, which is in Anathoth, for the purchase belongs to you by reason of kinship’” [Vulgate: “so that you may buy it”].

No one could have known that God’s word had secretly come to Jeremiah except the one to whom it had come, unless Jeremiah himself disclosed it. He is told beforehand that his cousin Anameel will come to him and offer him the possession of the field that had belonged to him.

The place itself was in Anathoth, among the suburbs that were assigned by the law to the priests in the various tribes and cities. It was not lawful for a possession to pass from one tribe to another, or from one family to another—hence the daughters of Zelophehad also received a portion among their brothers (Numbers 27). In particular, the priests’ suburbs could not be sold to anyone else until the year of release, except to the person whom blood relationship required (Leviticus 25).

Therefore his cousin [alternative reading: “his cousin and uncle”] comes to him and offers him the purchase that belongs to him by reason of kinship.

Hilkiah and Shallum were full brothers. Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah; Anameel was the son of Shallum. *Hilkiah* is interpreted as “the portion of the Lord”; *Jeremiah*, “the sublimity of the Lord.” Rightly, the Lord’s height is born from the Lord’s portion.

*Shallum* is rendered in our language as “peace” or “peaceful.” *Anameel* means “gift” or “grace of God.” Nor should we be surprised that peace is joined to grace, since the beginning of the Apostolic Epistles is also: “Grace to you and peace” (Romans 1:7).

Let us first, then, merit God’s peace; and after peace, grace is born for us—not in the power of the one who possesses it, but in the will of the one who gives it.

The grace of God offers the purchase to the one who has been placed in lofty things, so that although he may seem exalted, he still needs the grace of God.

The expression often sung by the bride in the Song, “My cousin”—that is, *ὅ ἀδελφιδοῦς μου*—is called *DODI* () in Hebrew. Therefore he should not be called *fratruelis*, but *πατράδελφος*, that is, *patruelis* (“a paternal cousin”).

That Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, one of the priests who were in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, is also attested by the opening of this book.

(Verses 8.) And Anameel, the son of my uncle, came to me, according to the word of the Lord, at the vestibule (or, court) of the prison, and said to me: “Take possession of” (or, “buy”) “my field, which is in Anathoth in the land of Benjamin, for the inheritance belongs to you, and you are the relative who should possess it” (or, “buy it”).

What the word of the Lord had announced as future for the Prophet was immediately fulfilled in deed. “Anameel,” he says, “the grace of God, the son of my uncle”—that is, the son of peace—“came to me.”

[Note: Victorius adds “Shallum,” making the interpretation of his name clearer.]

He came to the vestibule of the prison and said to me the things that the Lord had foretold he would say.

This priestly field, whose purchase and possession were being offered to Jeremiah, is in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin. The first name signifies “obedience,” while the second means “son of the right hand.” Accordingly, he seeks to buy it in the place where obedience and the virtue of the Lord were found.

For this the Septuagint translated *πρεσβύτερον*, that is, “elder,” which does not suit this passage.

(Verses 9 and following.) I understood that it was the word of the Lord, and I bought the field from Anameel, the son of my uncle, which is in Anathoth, and I weighed out to him seven *stateres* of silver and ten pieces of silver. I wrote it in a book, sealed it, called in witnesses, and weighed out the silver on the scales. I took the sealed book of possession, the stipulations, and the ratified documents [or, “the ratified stipulation”], and the marks on the outside.

It was certainly difficult and almost incongruous, and worthy of laughter, for the man who was just then prophesying that Jerusalem would be captured, and that all its inhabitants would be led away as captives or perish by sword, famine, and pestilence, to buy a field in Anathoth that he would not possess.

“But I understood,” he says, “that it was the word of the Lord, and that my purchase was to be joined to the Lord’s sign and prophecy. Therefore I obeyed his command to buy; nor had the word concerning this matter come to me from God without purpose.”

He weighed out seventeen *sikla* of silver, which we render as *stateres*. A shekel contains twenty obols, as is written at the end of the book of Ezekiel (Ezekiel 45).

The Prophet bought the field for seventeen shekels. In this number the boy of the Lord, David, sang on the day when the Lord delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and he said: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength. The Lord is my foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer. My God is my helper, and I will hope in him; my protector and the horn of my salvation” (Psalm 17:1).

That ten is a mystical number is shown by the Decalogue, which was written on tablets of stone by the finger of God, and by the day of fasting and propitiation in the seventh month (Exodus 13).

We also prove by many testimonies of Scripture that seven, in which there is true Sabbath-rest and repose, is holy. I would have cited at least a few of them, were it not tedious to teach what is already known.

In this number, therefore, the prophet and priest purchases the possession; it is written in a book and sealed; witnesses are called; and the silver is carefully weighed, so that all the legal requirements of sale and purchase may be observed, and the possession may be secure, strengthened by stipulations and guarantees.

Let those who try to claim false testaments—and sometimes not even testaments—by calling in witnesses hear this.

(Verses 12.) And I gave the book of possession to Baruch, the son of Neriah [Vulgate: “Neri”], the son of Maaseiah, in the sight of Anameel my cousin, and in the sight of the witnesses who were listed in the book of purchase, in the sight of all the Jews who were sitting in the court of the prison.

Although the possession was immediately to be abandoned—indeed, purchased for posterity—and although it was bought from a man who had no children, since he had not taken a wife, nevertheless, obedient to the Lord’s command, Jeremiah carries everything out properly. He gives the sealed book of possession to Baruch, the son of Neri, the son of Maaseiah.

*Baruch* means “blessed” in our language. He was the son of Neri, whose name means “my lamp,” as the Prophet says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a burning light for my paths” (Psalm 118:105).

Neri, the father of Baruch, was the son of Maaseiah, that is, “the work” or “creation of the Lord.”

[Note: In the Book of Names this interpretation of the name Maaseiah was current; there too *Mesaia* is incorrectly written in Latin letters, because it was thought to be called in Hebrew [unreadable in the supplied text], so as to mean “work” or “the creation of God.” But in the Hebrew text it is written not [unreadable in the supplied text] but [unreadable in the supplied text], and this explanation of the name therefore does not fit it.]

Let us therefore observe with how many privileges of virtue Baruch, Jeremiah’s disciple, served, according to David’s words: “Walking in an undefiled way, he served me” (Psalm 108:6).

Hence Elisha, Elijah’s servant, also pleased God so greatly that after his master’s translation he deserved to receive a double spirit (2 Kings 2).

I say this as a warning to those who abuse the services of wicked people and do not dare to cast them off, although they know that they are joined to them by the glue of an evil conscience.

The book is handed over to Baruch in the sight of such a great and distinguished man as Anameel, who had sold the field; of the witnesses who had signed it and whose names were recorded in the book of purchase; and, he says, “in the sight of all the Jews who were sitting in the court of the prison”—those who had either come to console the Prophet or desired, out of reverence for God, to hear the Lord’s words.

(Verses 13 and following.) And I commanded Baruch before them, saying: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Take these books—the sealed book of purchase and this book that is open—and place them in an earthen vessel, so that they may endure for many days. For thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses, fields, and vineyards will yet be possessed in this land.”

With all those whom the preceding account has mentioned present and watching, Baruch, the servant and disciple, is commanded—not by the words of his teacher, but by the authority of God’s command—to take the books: one sealed and the other open.

This custom of purchases is preserved to the present day: what the seals contain when closed within, the open volume displays to those who wish to read it.

[Note: For commentary on this passage, see the very learned work of our compatriot Scipione, Marquis Maffei, entitled *La Diplomatica*.]

Both books are to be placed in an earthen vessel so that they may endure for many days.

The possession, therefore, was secure and destined to remain after a long time, since it was guarded with such care lest the books of purchase, if left outside, be exposed to theft, or, if buried in the ground, be ruined by the earth’s moisture.

All this is done so that those who watched might understand that Jerusalem would again be inhabited and the fields possessed. Although they ought to have understood this by themselves without Jeremiah’s speech, they are nevertheless reminded by the Lord’s words, and it is said to them:

“Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Houses, fields, and vineyards will yet be possessed in this land.”

This is what Jeremiah had said earlier: “I understood that it was the word of the Lord,” and for that reason he bought a field that he himself was not going to possess.

### (Verses 16 ff.)

And I prayed to the Lord after I had delivered the deed of purchase to Baruch son of Neriah, saying:

“Alas, alas, alas, Lord God”—or, “You who are, Lord God.” “Behold, you made heaven and earth by your great strength and by your outstretched”—or “exalted”—arm; nothing”—or “no word”—will be difficult”—or “impossible”—for you; or, according to the Septuagint, “Nothing is hidden from you.” You show mercy to thousands and repay the iniquity of fathers into the bosom of their children after them. Most mighty, great, powerful”—which in Hebrew is called *GIBBOR*—“Lord of hosts”—or “of powers”—is your name. Great in counsel and incomprehensible in thought. Your eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of Adam”—or “of human beings”—to repay each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his devices”—the Vulgate has “his.”

After the purchase of the field had been duly completed, and after the Lord’s sentence in which he promised that houses, fields, and vineyards would henceforth be possessed, the Prophet prays to the Lord and expresses the anguish of his heart with groans, saying: “Alas, alas, alas, Lord God.” For this the Septuagint translated as *ὁ ὢν*, that is, “You who are, Lord God,” in accordance with what is said to Moses: “Go, say to the people of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14). This does not mean that there are no others, but that it is one thing for the creature to exist by the benefit of the Creator, and another for it to exist through the eternity of its nature.

He praises the Lord and proclaims the Creator from his creatures. First he raises his voice in praise of his power, mercy, and justice toward the whole human race; then he turns to Israel and describes in an eloquent—variant: “swift”—discourse how greatly he benefited it. After such great benefits, he says that they were forgetful of his goodness and provoked his clemency into bitterness, so that the city was besieged and, before the enemy made an entry into it, was consumed by famine, sword, and pestilence.

He prefaced all this in order subsequently to introduce what seemed to be spoken in reproach of the divine decree: “And you say to me, Lord God, ‘Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses,’ when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans?” This, for the present, is the entire scope of the passage. Let us now return to its individual parts.

“You made heaven and earth by your great strength.” John says of the Son: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made” (John 1:3). This is the Lord’s strength, as the Apostle confirms: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24).

“And by your outstretched”—or “exalted”—“arm”: both expressions indicate one who strikes. Is this not the arm of which Isaiah speaks: “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53:1)

“Nothing will be difficult for you.” For “the things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God”; or, “nothing is hidden from you” (Matt. 19:26), according to the Psalmist, who says: “For darkness will not be darkened from you, and night will shine as the day” (Ps. 138:12).

“You show mercy to thousands, and repay the iniquity of fathers into the bosom of their children after them.” The Creator’s mercy is great: he extends his mercy through a thousand generations and displays his justice immediately in the succeeding generation—although this too is mingled with mercy. He does not immediately punish the offender, but awaits repentance, so that, if the children imitate their parents’ vices, the punishment, long delayed, may be repaid.

“Most mighty, great, powerful; Lord of hosts”—or “of powers”—“is your name.” These names indicate the Creator’s power. Properly speaking, however, the name of God is “Father,” as it is revealed in the Gospel by the Lord, who says: “Father, I have manifested your name to the human beings” (John 17:6).

“Great in counsel.” Does anyone dare to intrude into the Lord’s secret and pass judgment upon his judgments?

“And incomprehensible in thought.” If thought cannot comprehend him, how can speech comprehend him?

“Your eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of Adam.” Human beings therefore vainly suppose that they can hide themselves from God’s knowledge.

What follows—“to repay each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his devices”—indicates that sometimes, because of his excessive patience, God’s judgments may appear unjust.

[Note: Martianay, following Erasmus, has *sapientia* (“wisdom”) instead of *patientia* (“patience”), which we have retained; the better manuscripts in Victor’s possession also prefer our reading.]

The Apostle explains this passage more fully in the Epistle to the Romans: “Do you not know that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment” (Rom. 2:4–5).

The later the vengeance upon sinners, therefore, the more just it is. So it was with Pharaoh: warned by ten plagues, though not yet punished, he persevered in hardness and was finally overwhelmed by the waves of the Red Sea (Exod. 14).

### (Verses 20 ff.)

“You set signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, even to this day, and in Israel and among human beings”—or “earth-dwellers”—“and made yourself a name, as it is this day. You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror. You gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey. They entered and possessed it, but they did not obey your voice and did not walk in your law; they did not do all that you commanded them to do, and all these evils came upon them.”

He passes from the general to the particular and briefly reviews what he specially bestowed upon Israel. “You set,” he says, “signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,” by which Egypt was afflicted “even to this day,” and in Israel and among human beings—or earth-dwellers.

The expression “even to this day” should be joined to what follows, so that we read: “And in Israel and among all mortals your signs are fulfilled every day.” Or otherwise: you performed signs and wonders not only in Egypt, but even to the present day the same strength of your mercy has saved your people, and by the Creator’s power you assist the whole human race.

It should also be noted that he distinguishes Israel from human beings and earth-dwellers, in accordance with the saying: “Israel is my firstborn son.”

“And you made yourself a name, as it is this day” (Exod. 4:22). “Your praises,” he says, “are celebrated in the speech of the whole world.”

“And you brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt.” He rightly says “your people,” for at the time when they were brought out, they were serving under the Lord’s command.

He brought them out “with signs and wonders,” by which Egypt was struck, “with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, and great terror”: when the Red Sea provided a way for the Israelite people as they crossed and overwhelmed the Egyptian army—variant: “when you provided a way … and overwhelmed.”

“And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them,” namely, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. They therefore received the promised land not through their own merit, but through the virtues of their fathers: “a land flowing with milk and honey.” They were not yet able to take solid food, but were nourished with the milk and honey of infancy. Or certainly, “milk and honey” signifies the fertility and abundance of all things.

“They entered and possessed it.” Immediately there was nothing between possession and disobedience. Abundance produces security, security produces negligence, and negligence produces contempt.

“And they did not obey,” he says, “your voice and did not walk in your law.” In vain, therefore, they promised in the wilderness, saying: “Everything that the Lord has commanded, we will do” (Exod. 19:8). The reward is not in the promise but in the deed. This rebukes the impudence of those who think that a person can accomplish everything he has promised to do.

“They did not do all that you commanded them to do,” although they had promised that they would. “And all these evils came upon them.” They were evils for those who suffered them, but according to the Lord’s judgment they were good, since he repays each according to his ways.

### (Verses 24–25)

“Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city, that it may be captured; and the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans, who fight against it because of the sword, famine, and pestilence. Whatever you have spoken has happened, as you yourself see; and you say to me, Lord God, ‘Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses,’ when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans?”

It was the tenth year of King Zedekiah. For thus it is written: “The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, when the army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem and Jeremiah the prophet was confined in the court of the prison.”

It is rightly said now: “Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city, that it may be captured; and the city has been handed over to the hands of the Chaldeans.” They have no one left whom they might conquer or—variant: “but”—capture, for they have already been consumed by sword, famine, and pestilence. We see that everything you said has been fulfilled. How, then, do you say to me, Lord: “Buy a field with silver and call in witnesses,” when the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans?

He is therefore not reproaching God but asking a question. Nor does he wish so much to learn for himself as for the benefit of the others who were sitting in the court of the prison and perhaps silently reproaching him: how could the same prophet, whom they believed to proclaim the truth, say both that the city would be captured and that he should buy a field as though he were going to possess it?

### (Verses 26 ff.)

And the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, saying:

“Behold, I am the Lord, the God of all flesh. Will anything be difficult”—or “impossible”—“for me? Or will any word be hidden from me?”

[Note: Thus the Vatican manuscript and Rabanus read the passage; Victor formerly restored it in this form, agreeing with the Greek text, *μὴ ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ κρυβήσεταί τι*—“Will anything be hidden from me?” Martianay, following Erasmus, has “that it should be hidden from me.”]

“Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it. And the Chaldeans will come”—or “will enter”—“fighting against it.”

[Note: Following Victor, who brought a torch to this passage, we have restored the reading that Martianay, following Erasmus, left corrupt. The word is genuinely ambiguous and can mean both “to come” and “to enter”; Aquila preferred the latter. This is what Jerome ordinarily notes. Previously, the word “or” was placed before “the Chaldeans will come against this city,” as though it offered a second interpretation of “the Chaldeans will come”: “and they will enter.” That reading was entirely false and confused.]
