“They will come”—or “enter”—“against this city, set it on fire, burn it, and burn the houses on whose rooftops they sacrificed to Baal and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods, provoking me.”

He joins joyful things to sorrowful ones and, after Jerusalem’s destruction, promises the captive people a return. First he explains the causes of the offense and of God’s just anger, so that the greater the sinners’ guilt, the greater the Creator’s clemency toward sinners.

“I,” he says, “am the Lord, the God of all flesh.” He does not say, “the God of all nations,” or “the God of the people of Israel,” or, as he frequently says concerning the saints, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Rather, he says that God is “the God of all flesh,” so that he may be understood to have made both rational and irrational creatures.

There are some who acknowledge the Creator’s providence only as far as rational creatures, but claim that irrational creatures either perish or live by chance. The prophetic word declares, however, that nothing escapes God’s providence and knowledge, because some things were created for their own sake and others for human use.

“Will anything be difficult or impossible for me? Or will any word be hidden from me?” We have already said above: “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God.” Here and in many other passages, “word” should be understood as “thing.” What is meant by the expression, “What has happened is the word”?

“Therefore thus says the Lord.” What had preceded that he should use the causal conjunction “therefore”? “Because,” he says, “it is my concern to govern all things, dispose all things, and repay each according to his ways, therefore I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans and into the hand of the king of Babylon, and they will capture it.”

First the city is surrounded by an army; then, while Nebuchadnezzar is absent, it is captured, and Zedekiah is brought to Riblah and handed over there to the king.

“And the Chaldeans will come,” he says, “fighting against this city.” Aquila translated the written word “will come” more aptly as *εἰσελεύσονται*, that is, “they will enter the city.” They were not absent and thus in need of coming, since they had surrounded Jerusalem, as Scripture testifies: “The army of the king of Babylon was besieging Jerusalem.”

Then: “Behold, siegeworks have been built against the city, that it may be captured, and the city has been given into the hands of the Chaldeans.” How, then, will those who were already present come?

But those who were besieging the city, he says, “will enter, capture it, set it on fire, and burn it to the ground.” For the Hebrew word *BAU* is ambiguous and means both “they will come” and “they will enter.”

[The Hebrew form is printed in the source as an empty parenthesis.]

“And the houses on whose rooftops they sacrificed to Baal, the idol of the Sidonians, and poured out drink offerings to foreign gods, provoking me,” so that they seemed to act not through religious error but through a certain contentiousness and insult against the Creator.

Just as the world is written to perish, in accordance with what is written, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35), because it lies in the Evil One, so the houses themselves and the places in which wicked deeds were committed are subject to God’s anger.

Some, contentiously, refer the statement “the place where the Lord and Savior was crucified is spiritually called Sodom and Egypt” (Rev. 11:8) to those very places. Others think that the whole world is signified under the names Egypt and Sodom. For just as Sodom was destroyed by divine fire, so the world too is to be consumed by God’s judgment.

### (Verse 30)

“For the sons of Judah and the sons of Israel were continually”—or “alone”—“doing evil in my sight from their youth.”

The Hebrew word *ACH* was translated by Aquila as *πλήν*, which signifies “nevertheless” or “however.” The first edition of Symmachus, the Septuagint, and Theodotion translated it as “alone.” The second edition of Symmachus rendered it *διόλον*, which we too have followed here in saying “continually.”

[The Hebrew form is printed in the source as an empty parenthesis.]

Let us therefore begin according to the Hebrew: “The sons of Israel and the sons of Judah continually doing evil.” The ten and the two tribes, he says, committed evil without cessation, and perseverance in wicked deeds was constant among them.

But if “constant” and “always” apply to the whole people, where is everlasting righteousness? According to the Septuagint, which says “alone doing evil,” a question arises: Did the other nations not also do evil at the time when Israel and Judah were sinning?

This is resolved as follows: whoever has knowledge of God and turns away from him sins “alone” in God’s sight; those who remain unbelieving transgress as though he neither saw nor cared. Hence the holy man David, because he had fallen into the sin involving Uriah’s wife, Bathsheba, and later repented (2 Sam. 12), says: “Against you alone have I sinned, and done what is evil in your sight” (Ps. 50:6), that is, in your presence.

Finally, the text continues: “Alone doing evil in my sight”—the variant adds “my”—“in my presence from their youth.”

The following words—“The sons of Israel who even now provoke me by the work of their hands, says the Lord”—are not found in the Septuagint and have been added from the Hebrew.

Since they sinned continually from their youth to the present day, God’s sentence is just, and Scripture rightly continues:

### (Verse 31)

“This city has been for me an object of wrath and indignation from the day when they built it until this day, when it is taken away from my presence.”

If, from the time when the foundations of the city were laid until this day, when it was captured, burned, and removed from the Lord’s presence, it was always in vice and provoked the Lord’s indignation against itself, where is the rest from sinners’ offenses, as we have often already said?

### (Verse 32)

“Because of the wickedness of the sons of Israel and the sons of Judah, which they committed, provoking me to anger—they and their kings, their princes, their priests, their prophets, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

Above he had said: “This city has been for me an object of wrath and indignation from the day when they built it until this day, when it is taken away from my presence,” and had shown that no one in general was without sin. Now he enumerates them individually: their kings, princes, priests, and prophets, gathering them all together in one statement: “the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.”

He aptly does not say, “my kings, my princes, my priests, and my prophets,” but “their kings, their princes, their priests, and their prophets,” because they sinned.

“And they turned their backs to me and not their faces,” in accordance with what is written elsewhere: “They turned their shoulder in rebellion against me” (Zech. 7:11).

One who prays bends his neck, prostrates himself upon the ground, and pours himself out. But one who turns his back indicates by the very gesture of his body that he disregards the one threatening him. “And this,” he says, “they did.”

### (Verse 33)

“When I taught them at dawn and instructed them, they would not listen so as to receive discipline.”

After driving away the darkness of error and refuting every form of idolatrous worship by my judgment, I desired daily to enlighten their hearts and teach them what is right. To preserve free choice, he adds: “And they would not listen so as to receive discipline.”

The text continues:

### (Verse 34)

“And they placed their idols in the house upon which my name was invoked, to defile it.”

It was not only at that time that Judah placed in God’s Temple the statue of an idol that we read about at the beginning of Ezekiel (Ezek. 8). Even today an idol is placed in the house of God—which is interpreted as the Church—or in the heart and soul of believers, whenever a new doctrine is established and, according to Deuteronomy, worshiped in secret (Deut. 4).

“Do you not know,” he says, “that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16)

### (Verse 35)

“And they built the high places”—or “altars”—“of Baal, which are in the valley of the sons of Hinnom, to initiate their sons and daughters to the idol Molech.”

For “to initiate,” the Hebrew has *EBIR*, which Aquila and Symmachus translated as “to lead across”; the Septuagint and Theodotion translated it as “to offer.”

[The Hebrew form is printed in the source as an empty parenthesis.]

We have discussed the valley of the sons of Hinnom, called *GEHENNOM* in Hebrew, more fully above. It lies below the springs of Siloam, and because of its pleasantness and its irrigated location, it enticed the people to luxury, which is followed by the worship of idols.

It should also be noted that “altars” and “high places” are called *BAMOTH* in Hebrew, for the benefit of those who are uncertain what this word means in the books of Samuel and Kings.

[The Hebrew form is printed in the source as an empty parenthesis.]

Molech is the idol of the Ammonites, and the name is translated as “king.” Divine Scripture indicates that in that place the people served not only the idol Baal but also Molech and all the demons.

“What I did not command them, nor did it enter my heart that they should do this abomination and lead Judah into sin.”

The tribes of Judah and Benjamin properly worshiped images of the demons in the sanctuary of Baal and Molech (1 Kings 12). It is clear that the golden calves were in Bethel and Dan, and that the ten tribes called Samaria, Joseph, and Ephraim lived there—or, according to the variant, wished to live there.

The evil committed by the people was so great that God testifies that he had never thought of, nor had it entered his heart, what they would do. All these statements are made *ἀνθρωποπάθως*—“in humanly figurative terms.”

“And now, because of these things, thus says the Lord, the God of Israel, concerning this city of which you say that it is to be given into the hand of the king of Babylon, by sword, famine, and pestilence.”

Just as the prophecy says to those hoping for assistance and trusting in the strength of the walls that Jerusalem is to be overthrown, and that the people are on the point of being captured and will perish before their captivity through sword, famine, and pestilence, so he promises his assistance to those who despair and expect no salvation after the city’s destruction. Thus confidence and pride may receive a just sentence, while despair and humility may receive God’s assistance.

### (Verses 37 ff.)

“Behold, I will gather them from all the lands to which I drove them in my wrath, my anger, and great indignation, and I will bring them back to this place and make them dwell securely. They shall be my people, and I will be their God. I will give them one heart and one way, so that they may fear me all their days, and it may be well with them and with their children after them. I will make with them an everlasting covenant”—or “establish for them an everlasting testament”—“and I will not cease doing good to them. I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they will not depart from me. I will rejoice over them when I do good to them”—or “I will visit them in order to do good to them.” “I will plant them in this land in truth”—or “in faith”—“with all my heart and with all my soul.”

Many think that this was fulfilled in the time of Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and of Jeshua son of Jehozadak the high priest, when Haggai and Zechariah prophesied under Ezra the priest; when the Temple was completed, and under Nehemiah the walls were built all around. Those whom he had previously cast down in wrath, anger, and great indignation from Jerusalem and scattered throughout the whole world, he afterward brought back to dwell securely; they became God’s people, and the Lord became their God, together with the other things that Scripture relates.

But how this can be fitted to that period—“I will make them dwell securely,” and “I will make with them an everlasting covenant,” or “establish for them an everlasting testament”—cannot be accepted at all. For we read in sacred history that they were repeatedly captured not only by neighboring nations but also by the Persians, Macedonians, Egyptians, and Romans, and that they remain servants to this day.

Everything must therefore be referred to the coming of the Savior. We see these things more truly and fully fulfilled in our own age and in the age of faith, and, according to the Apostle, the election of the remnant has been preserved (Rom. 9).

Those who dwell securely in Christ have been given one heart, in accordance with what is written: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32).

“And one way,” he says: the one who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

“And let them fear me all their days.” “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Prov. 9). He says “all their days.” If this does not apply to the Jews, it must be understood of our people, for whom it was, is, and will be well—not only with them but also with their children after them.

With us he made an everlasting covenant, and he will not cease to do us good.

What follows—“I will put my fear in their hearts, so that they will not depart from me”—so grants free choice that even the fear bestowed remains the grace of the giver.

[Note: At this point it is not burdensome to reproduce the gloss that Rabanus adds from his own material and obtrudes under Jerome’s name in the Commentaries:

“Ezekiel also says (chap. 11, verse 19): ‘And I will give them a new heart … and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God.’ By these words we are most clearly taught that the beginning of a good will is granted to us when the Lord inspires it, whether he draws us to the way of salvation and to the perfection of virtues directly, through the exhortation of some person, or through necessity; and that perfection of virtues is likewise bestowed by him. But it is ours to respond to God’s exhortation and assistance, either more sluggishly or more earnestly, and on this account to merit either the reward or the most deserved punishments.”]

“And when I do good to them,” he says, “I will rejoice.” He rejoices because he sees his creature saved. Hence there is also joy among the angels in heaven over one sinner who repents (Luke 15).

“And I will plant them,” he says, “in this land in truth,” or—as the Septuagint translated—“in faith,” so that it properly signifies the Christian people, whose religion is faith.

“With all my heart and with all my soul.” If these are the words of the Lord the Savior, his heart and soul are rightly understood according to the one who says in the Gospel: “I have authority to lay down my soul, and I have authority to take it up again” (John 10:18).

But if we understand the words as spoken by God the Father, they should be interpreted according to the statement: “Your new moons and Sabbaths and feast days my soul hates.”

### (Verses 41 ff.)

“For thus says the Lord: As I have brought upon this people all this great evil, so I will bring upon them all the good that I am speaking to them. Fields shall be bought in this land of which you say, ‘It is desolate, because no human being or animal remains, and it has been given into the hand of the Chaldeans.’ Fields shall be bought with money, deeds shall be written in a book, a seal shall be impressed, and a witness shall be called in the land of Benjamin, in the environs of Jerusalem, in the cities of Judah, in the cities of the hill country, in the cities of the plain”—or *Shephelah*—“and in the cities of the Negeb”—that is, those in the south—“for I will restore their captivity,” says the Lord.

Literally, these things, although they had preceded in type after the return from the Chaldeans, when the people returned to Judea at the command of King Cyrus, are nevertheless fulfilled more truly and fully in Christ and the Apostles in a spiritual sense.

At that time both human beings and animals were brought back into the Church, in accordance with what is written: “You save human beings and animals, Lord”—the rational and the simple alike.

At that time fields were bought with money, so that we might make friends for ourselves from unrighteous mammon, who would receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16).

They were written in a book—without doubt, the book of the living.

The sign of the Lord’s cross, the banner of victory, was impressed; the witnesses were the martyrs and the whole chorus of the saints.

“In the land of Benjamin,” where the Lord’s strength is; “in the environs of Jerusalem,” in which there is the vision of peace and eternal security; “in the cities of Judah,” in which there is the true confession of Christ.

“And in the cities of the hill country,” one of which is the city of which it is said: “A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. 5).

“And in the cities of the plain,” which are called *SEPHELA* in Hebrew, so that from deep and low places we may advance through the levelness of the plains toward the heights.

“And in the cities that are toward the south,” which the Septuagint translated as *Negeb*, where there is midday and the full light of truth.

When all these things have taken place, what is written will be fulfilled: “I will restore their captivity,” says the Lord. Of him it is written: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. 67:19). He received—or, as the Apostle says, “gave”—gifts to human beings (Eph. 4:8).

## HOMILIES ON THE VISIONS OF ISAIAH

### Notice concerning the following homilies

For a long time and with much hesitation we doubted whether the translator into Latin of the following Homilies on the Visions of Isaiah was the great Jerome or some other person of his age. Although many arguments occurred to us on both sides, the arguments formerly seemed stronger in the opposite direction, so that in our earlier recension of Jerome’s works, prepared at Verona more than thirty years ago, we judged that this translation should be denied to the holy Doctor.

At that time, however, we overlooked—or at least did not consider sufficiently important—the irrefutable argument drawn from Rufinus’ most explicit testimony. In the eleventh book of his *Apology*, section 27, he notes certain passages from the works of Origen, “the Adamantine,” in translating which our Jerome had used excessive freedom. He says that, of the errors with which those works teemed, Jerome removed only those that appeared contrary to the Catholic faith concerning the Trinity, while reshaping the others toward a more acceptable meaning by adding some things and removing others.

To prove this by an example, Rufinus cites a passage from the first of these homilies. After Jerome had translated: “Who are these two Seraphim? My Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit,” he added from his own material: “Do not suppose that the nature of the Trinity is divided if the functions of the names are preserved.”

These words are found *κατὰ λέξιν*—“word for word”—in this first homily, shortly after its middle. It is therefore manifest that this work was rendered into Latin by Jerome; and there can be no remaining doubt that the whole of that single volume, which contains the other eight homilies, must likewise be attributed to the same holy Father.

For Rufinus could not have lied with such confidence by thrusting another’s offspring upon Jerome; nor could the holy Father himself, in responding to so great a calumny, have silently endured the hatred it aroused.

The earlier arguments that we had urged against this conclusion therefore prove little, especially Jerome’s silence in his catalogue, where he lists separately other homilies—on Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Luke, for example—but says nothing at all about these on Isaiah. He is also silent in this very Commentary and in the Preface to his Commentary on Isaiah, although there he praises the twenty-five homilies of which these nine are a part, and it would seem that the occasion should have led him to inform his readers of this labor of his.

You could scarcely assign another reason for this than the one that has now occurred to us. He composed this work after compiling the catalogue of his works, but at a time when he had only recently begun to become more hostile toward Origen. Perhaps he did not yet recognize that, becoming more cautious day by day, he had begun to regard Origen’s writings as of little or no value. For in this very work, Book 5 of the Commentaries on Isaiah, he says that Origen “wanders through the fields of allegory” and, interpreting the names of individuals, makes his own ingenuity into the mysteries of the Church.

There was therefore no reason for him to mention and offer for reading works that he himself did not sufficiently approve—not on his own account, but for Origen’s sake.

Moreover, one or another of these homilies—as has been specifically noted concerning the fifth—was seriously corrupt in Greek. It was therefore translated according to its meaning and order, though not according to its words. He may not have judged such an offspring wholly and in every respect worthy of its father.

## Translation by Saint Eusebius Hieronymus, presbyter of Stridon, of nine homilies on the visions of Isaiah by Origen Adamantius

(C, G, S)*

### Homily One

[Note: We have taken this from Genebrard’s most accurate edition, with which we also compared the recent edition of Origen’s works prepared by the Benedictine Fathers in this recension.]

“And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne.” Chapter 6.

1101 I. As long as King Uzziah lived, the prophet Isaiah could not see the vision. For Uzziah was a sinner, doing evil in the sight of the Lord and acting against the will of the divine law. He entered the temple and the Holy of Holies, and for this reason he was covered with leprosy on his forehead, so that, when he went outside the city, he was counted among the unclean. Thus such a ruler of the soul must die if we are to be able to see the vision of God. For it was not written without reason: “And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord” (Isa. VI, 1).

Each of us has a living Uzziah—or Pharaoh—and we do not sigh, because we perform Egyptian works. But if he dies, then we sigh, as it is written in Exodus. If Uzziah lives, we do not see the glory of God; but if he dies, then we see it—immediately after Uzziah dies, we see the glory of God. Let only this one reign in us: the word of him who said, “But I have been appointed king by him” (Ps. II, 6), and let anger not reign.

There is also a king of sin. The Apostle, knowing this, says: “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12). Wretched is the man in whom sin reigns, who submits himself to such a king, despising the kingdom of God and subjecting himself to pleasure. Therefore the lover of pleasure is not a lover of God. And concerning certain people the Apostle says: “Lovers of pleasure more than lovers of God” (2 Tim. III). This, indeed, was not said about those who are altogether unbelievers, but about those who dwell within, loving pleasure more than God—those who have the appearance of piety but deny its power.

These remarks concern the death of King Uzziah, after whose death the Prophet says that he saw the vision. What is the vision? “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne,” and so forth. Not everyone who sees God sees him sitting upon a high and lofty throne. I know that another prophet saw the Lord and saw him sitting upon a throne, but not a high or lofty one. Daniel, expounding Scripture, says: “Thrones were set” (Dan. VII, 9), and that throne was not high. “And I will come, that I may sit to judge the people in the valley of Jehoshaphat.” Therefore he sat in the valley, and in the valley he will judge the one whom he is to condemn.

But it is something else to see him sitting upon a high and lofty throne. And in Micah: “God goes forth and descends” (Mic. I).

[Note: Earlier the text read “Go forth.” We silently correct minor errors.] And in order to see Sodom, he descended. Descending, he says, “I will go down and see whether they have done altogether according to the cry that has come to me” (Gen. XVIII). Thus God is sometimes seen above and sometimes below, according to the dignity of the matters at hand.

“I saw the Lord,” Isaiah says, “sitting upon a high and lofty throne.” If I see God reigning in those who are here below, I do not see him upon a high and lofty throne. If I see him reigning over the heavenly powers, I see him sitting upon a high and lofty throne. What does he mean by “the heavenly powers”? Thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, and virtues are heavenly. And if I see how he reigns over them in the Word: “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne.”

And his house was full of his glory. His throne was also raised above, and his house was full of his glory. I do not think that this earthly house is full of his glory. “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness” (Ps. XXIV). But you will not find the fullness of the glory of God in the present age. Rather, if someone builds a temple for God, the glory of God will be seen; and if he keeps what has been said, the house will appear full of the glory of God. I do not know, however, whether the house is filled with glory in this way.

And in Leviticus, insofar as the present matter is concerned, by God’s generosity it is read in the Collect that follows,

[Note: Previously the word “because” was absent.]

that the Lord commanded certain things to be done so that the glory of the Lord might be seen. Nor will the glory of God ever appear unless these things are done. We shall recognize them when they have been read.

[Col. 0901B]

II. “And the Seraphim stood around him, six wings for one and six wings for the other.” I see two Seraphim, each of them having six wings in itself. Next comes the arrangement of the wings. With two wings they covered the face—not their own, but God’s; with two others they covered the feet—not their own, but God’s; and with two others they flew.

According to what is written, this seems contradictory. If they were standing, they could not fly. Yet it is written: “Two Seraphim stood around him, six wings for one and six wings for the other; with two they covered the face, with two they covered the feet, and with two they flew, and they cried out to one another.”

But these Seraphim who are around God, who alone say by their knowledge, “Holy, holy, holy,” preserve the mysteries [or: mystery] of the Trinity, because they themselves are holy. Among all things that exist, nothing is holier than these. Nor do they lightly say to one another, “Holy, holy, holy”; rather, they proclaim aloud a confession that brings salvation to all.

[Note: These are the words that Rufinus recites in Book II Against Jerome, as though Jerome had added them from his own material. See the preceding Admonition.]

What are these two Seraphim? My Lord Jesus and the Holy Spirit. Do not think that the nature of the Trinity is divided because the functions of the names are preserved.

They covered the face of God. For the beginning of God is unknown. They covered the feet as well. For the final reality that is in our God cannot be comprehended. Only the middle things seem to be seen. I do not know what existed before these; from the things that exist, I understand [Note: The word “God” is absent from the Benedictine edition.] God. What will come after these things, insofar as they are future, I do not know.

Who has declared it to him? Ecclesiastes said: “Declare to me the former things and the last things that shall be, and I shall say that you are gods” (Eccl. XIX). Hence Isaiah also says: “Declare to us the former things, and we shall set our heart upon them and know them; and declare to us the last things that are to come” (Isa. XLI). “Tell us the things that are to come in the future, and we shall say that you are gods.”

If someone declares the past and is also able to declare the last things, he is God. Who, then, can say anything except the Seraphim: “Holy, holy, holy”? The Seraphim unveiled, so to speak, a certain part of God, his middle, and cried out one to another as they stood beside God and said, “Holy, holy, holy.”

They therefore stand and move: they stand with God, and they move while showing God. Understand, then, that they cover the face and cover the feet; the things that are covered do not move, while the things that fly are not covered. And they say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.”

The coming of my Lord Jesus Christ is proclaimed; therefore now the whole earth is full of his glory. Or certainly it is not yet full, but it will be fulfilled when the prayer has been completed that the Lord himself commanded us to pray to the Father: “When you pray, say: Our Father who are in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come. Your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth” (Matt. VI).

At present the Father’s will is in heaven, but on earth his will has not yet been fulfilled, as Jesus himself says according to the dispensation of the flesh that he had assumed: “He gave me all authority, both in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII). Does the one who had authority in heaven not also have authority on earth? And would he who came to what was his own receive something from the world? But so that it might be believed that God is on earth in the same way as he is believed to be in heaven, Christ the man received an authority that he had not previously possessed, and even now he does not yet possess authority over all things on earth.

For he does not yet reign in those who sin. But when authority over them too has been given to him, when all things have been subjected to him, then his authority will be complete, and he will go forth, subjecting all things to himself (1 Cor. XV). Some, however, do not yet wish to be subjected to him, but are still subjected to his enemies. Let us instead say: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” (Ps. LIII); for my salvation is with God.

III. “And with two they flew, and one cried to the other: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the whole earth is full of his glory.’” And the lintel was raised by the voice with which they cried out: by the voice of Jesus Christ and by the voice of the Holy Spirit.

If one of us hears the voice of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit crying out, the lintel is raised and becomes higher than it was at the time when it was raised and it was said: “Lift up your gates, you rulers, and be lifted up, you everlasting gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. XXIV).

IV. “And the house was filled with smoke.” With the outpouring of fire, the entire house was filled. Smoke is the vapor of fire.

“And I said: Woe is me, for I am pierced through, because I am a man and have unclean lips.” I cannot understand why Isaiah humbled himself in this way. Yet he speaks truth: Scripture testifies that his lips were cleansed by one of the Seraphim who was sent to take away his sins.

One of the Seraphim is my Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent by the Father to take away our sins, and he says: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and I have cleansed your sins all around.”

Do not think that the Son’s being sent by the Father is an insult to his nature. Finally, so that you may recognize the unity of the Godhead in the Trinity, in the present reading Christ alone now forgives sins, and yet it is certain that sins are forgiven by the Trinity. Whoever believes in one believes in all.

Let tongs, then, be brought to me from the heavenly altar, that they may touch my lips. If the Lord’s tongs have touched my lips, they cleanse them. Even if they cleanse them and cut them away from vices, as we recently said, I shall open my mouth with the word of God, and no unclean speech shall thereafter come out of my mouth: for, though I am a man and have unclean lips, I dwell in the midst of a people that also has unclean lips.

The Seraphim that was sent cleansed the Prophet’s lips, but it did not cleanse the lips of the people. For he himself confessed that he had unclean lips and dwelt in the midst of a people with unclean lips. But the Seraphim that was sent did not judge the people worthy that their lips too should be cleansed; and for this reason they still act impiously, for this reason they still resist my Lord Jesus Christ, and still curse him with unclean lips.

But I pray that the Seraphim may come and cleanse my lips.

V. “And I saw the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my own eyes.” Why should we not, in the present passage, state a certain Jewish tradition that is plausible, though not true, and explain why we do not accept it?

[Note: Jerome says very elegantly in his commentary on Isaiah, chapter I: “The Hebrews say that Isaiah was put to death for two reasons: because he called them princes of Sodom and people of Gomorrah; and because, when the Lord said to Moses, ‘You cannot see my face,’ he dared to say, ‘I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne’; not considering that the Seraphim covered the face and feet of God—or their own, since the Hebrew is ambiguous—and that Isaiah writes that he saw only his middle parts.”]

They say that Isaiah was therefore cut in pieces by the people, as though he had transgressed the law and proclaimed things outside the Scriptures. For Scripture says: “No one shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII). But he said: “I saw the Lord of Sabaoth.” “Moses,” they say, “did not see him, but you saw him.” For this reason they cut him in pieces and condemned him as an impious man. They did not know that the Seraphim covered the face of God with two wings.

Isaiah saw the Lord, but he did not see his face; nor did Moses see it. Moses saw his back parts, as it is written. Nevertheless, he saw the Lord, even though he did not see his face. This man too saw him, although he did not see his face. Thus they condemned the Prophet unjustly.

“And I saw the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my own eyes, and one of the Seraphim was sent to me.”

There is not only one coming of my Lord Jesus Christ: by it he descended to earth and came to Isaiah, Moses, the people, and each of the prophets. Do not be afraid, even though he has now been received into heaven: he will come again.

But that he also came to human beings before his bodily presence, accept him himself as a witness, announcing and saying: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children” (Matt. XXIII). “How often I wanted to.” He does not say, “I saw you only in this coming,” but says, “How often I wanted to.”

And, turning to each of the prophets, he says: “I was the Christ who spoke through the prophets.” I said this, and now Jesus Christ is being sent. He does not lie. “I am with you,” the Lord says, “all the days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). He does not lie. “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them.”

Since Jesus Christ is therefore present and stands beside us, and since the high priest is ready and girded to offer our intercessions to the Father, let us rise and offer sacrifices to the Father through him. For he himself is the propitiation for our sins. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY TWO

On what is written: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb,” and so forth. Chapter VII.

[Col. 0906C]

1107 I. As far as the wording is concerned, Ahaz acted modestly when he had been commanded to ask for a sign, either in the depths or in the heights, and gave the reason why he did not wish to ask (Isa. VII). For he said: “I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord.”

Yet he is censured for this statement, and it is said to him: “Hear now, house of David: Is it a small thing for you to contend with men, and how do you contend with the Lord?” Then this promise follows: “Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel.”

Let these matters be explained, and we shall consider the rest, needing in those matters also the grace of God so that they may be made clear.

He is commanded to ask for a sign, not simply any sign, but one for himself. For the word says: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depths or in the heights.”

My Lord Jesus Christ is the sign set before us. For this is the sign which he is commanded to ask for himself, in the depths or in the heights. In the depths, because he is the one who descended; in the heights, because he is the one who ascended above all the heavens.

But if my Lord Jesus Christ is set before me as this sign in the depths and in the heights, it does me no good unless the mystery of his depth and height is made a reality for me. When I have received the mystery of Christ Jesus from the depths and the heights, then I shall receive the sign according to the Lord’s command. And it will be said to me, as one who possesses the depths and the heights within himself:

“Do not say in your heart, ‘Who ascended into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down. “Or, ‘Who descended into the abyss?’”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead [variant: “to depart from the dead”]. “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. X).

Therefore we are all commanded to ask for this sign for ourselves, so that the sign which the Lord God gives in the depths and in the heights may become useful to us.

But if someone knows and recognizes through rational contemplation that what was said, “in the depths and in the heights,” was not expressed disjunctively—for it signifies that both are possible—then let him ask for himself a sign from the Lord in the depths and in the heights.

And in the promise the Apostle said: “That we may know what is the depth and the height, the length and the breadth” (Eph. III).

And Ahaz said: “I will not ask.” He was unbelieving. For it had been said: “Ask for yourself.” But even to this day the people do not ask for a sign; therefore they do not have it, and the people who do not receive my Lord Jesus Christ contend with the Lord.

Then another question follows. When Ahaz said, “I will not ask, nor will I tempt the Lord,” and thought that it would be a temptation if he asked for a sign, the response was: “Hear now, house of David: Is it a small thing for you to contend with men, and how do you contend with the Lord?”

But he does not contend with the Lord—and I think he does not contend with men either—who asks for a sign in the depths or in the heights. The contest belongs to God: how he may save a human being. Therefore the one who takes refuge in salvation does not contend with the Lord.

But the one who, while the Lord is contending to save a human being, flees from salvation and withdraws far from the Lord, contends with the Lord.

“Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb [variant: “shall receive”], and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel” (Matt. I, 13).

The true copies of this Prophet say, “You shall call.”

[Note: The Benedictine editors of Origen note that in the Greek copies of Matthew I, 13 one reads either καλέσουσι, “they shall call,” or καλέσεσθε, “you shall call,” or καλέσετε, “you shall call,” but nowhere κληθήσεται, “he shall be called.” Hence they suspect that Jerome translated “you shall call” at this place, and that it was later changed through the carelessness of copyists into “he shall be called,” as the Latin Vulgate has it at Isaiah VII, 14. Moreover, according to the idiom of the Hebrew language, whether καλέσουσι or καλέσεις is read, it amounts to the same as if κληθήσεται were read.]

In Matthew, however, we know that it is commonly read: “And his name shall be called Emmanuel.” We cannot say that something less ought to be made of the Prophet. But how does the Gospel have this reading?

Whether it arose from someone who did not understand and rushed toward easier readings, as has happened in many other places, or whether it was so from the beginning—let whoever wishes decide. The Prophet plainly has: “And you shall call his name Emmanuel.”

I know someone who, at the beginning of his reading of the Gospel Scriptures, read, “And you shall call his name Emmanuel,” and said to himself: “What does ‘you shall call’ mean? Who will call him? Ahaz. And how could Ahaz hear about the Savior, who came many generations later: ‘You shall call his name Emmanuel’? And so, instead of ‘you shall call,’ did he write ‘he shall be called’?”

But observe that it is not said to Ahaz: “And you shall call his name Emmanuel.” Rather, it is plainly said to the house of David: “Hear now, house of David: Is it a small thing for you to contend with men, and how do you contend with the Lord? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb, and shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel.”

But when we do not understand what has been said, let us not therefore make anything less of it, nor run toward easier readings. Let us wait until the grace of God, through the illumination of knowledge, supplies us with the illumination of the question.

[Note: The Benedictine editors here read “explanation” instead of “illumination.”]

Or, in turn, let the grace of God illuminate us through whomever he wishes, so that we no longer need to inquire, but our question may be resolved. If, however, we rashly rush into things not understood, we shall have only ourselves to blame.

What, then, is the house of David? If Christ is David, as I have often proved, the house of David is us, the Church of God. And it is said to us, who are the Church, that we should not contend with God in the manner described above, but should first receive the sign from the Lord.

These things are said to us, not to the house of David. And it is prophesied that if anyone is the house of David, he will call his name Emmanuel. For at the coming of Christ, our Church alone says concerning Christ: “God is with us.”

Having explained these matters, as the grace of God has granted, let us now seek other enigmas.

II. “He shall eat butter and honey.” How is Christ prophesied to eat butter and honey? If this is explained, then, with the Lord granting it, the things that follow will again present another question to us.

Would that we all did what is written: “Search the Scriptures!” Many things named among bodily foods are presented in Scripture as spiritual foods.

“As newborn infants, desire the rational and guileless milk” (1 Pet. II, 2). Therefore there is certainly rational milk, and we ought to seek such milk.

Again, it is written in Proverbs concerning honey: “When you find honey, eat only enough, lest you become full and vomit it up” (Prov. XXV, 16). Did the Holy Spirit concern himself with this honey, the kind that is known, lest we perhaps eat too much?

But since the Holy Spirit perceived spiritual honey, he said: “When you find honey, eat only enough.” What did the Holy Spirit perceive when he commanded us that, if we found honey—which is indeed discoverable—we should eat only enough?

“Go to the bee,” he says, “and learn how she works” (Prov. VI). And the Prophets are found to be bees. For they fashion wax and prepare honey; and, if it is useful for me to say so, their honeycombs are the Scriptures that they left behind.

I came to the Scriptures desiring them, and I found honey. “But eat honey.” And again it is said in Proverbs: “For the honeycomb is good, that your throat may be sweetened” (Prov. XXIV, 13).

Do you think that the Holy Spirit is saying: “Eat honey, the kind that is customary, for it is good”? I do not dare say that the Holy Spirit commands me concerning bodily honey: “Eat honey.”

Suppose I do not have any, or suppose I am of such a nature that I cannot eat honey. How, then, does he say to me, “Eat honey, and do not eat meat, but eat honey, child, for it is good”?

If you see the Prophets as bees and their work as honey or honeycombs, then you will see how, in accordance with the dignity of the Holy Spirit, you should understand: “Eat honey, child, for it is good.”

If someone meditates upon the divine utterances and is nourished by the words of Scripture, let him fulfill the divine command that says: “Eat honey, child.” And by doing what was commanded, he gains the word that follows: “For it is good.”

For this honey found in the Scriptures is good. As for what is said, “Go to the bee,” it is as follows. There is a certain bee, so to speak, above the bees; and just as among the bees there is a certain one who is called their king, so the ruler of the bees is the Lord Jesus Christ. To him the Holy Spirit sends me, so that I may eat honey—for it is good—and his honeycomb, that my throat may be sweetened.

And perhaps the more refined letters will be the honeycombs, while the meaning contained in them will be the honey.

This one who was born from the virgin, Emmanuel, eats butter and honey, and he seeks to eat butter from each one of us. How he seeks butter and honey from each of us, the word will teach.

Our works are sweet, our words most pleasant and useful: these are the honey that Emmanuel eats, which this one who was born of the Virgin eats. But if our words are full of bitterness, anger, hostility, vexation, foul speech, vices, and contention, he has given gall into my mouth, and the Savior does not eat from such words.

The Savior will eat of the words that are among human beings if their words are honey.

Let us confirm this from the Scriptures. “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone opens the door for me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. III, 20).

Therefore he himself promises that he will dine with us on what comes from us. It is certain, however, that we too dine with him if we dine upon him. For, eating from our good words, works, and understanding, he nourishes us with his spiritual, divine, and better foods.

Therefore, because it is blessed to receive the Savior, let us open the doors of our principal heart and prepare honey and his whole banquet for him, so that he himself may lead us to the great banquet of the Father in the kingdom of heaven, which is in Christ Jesus. To him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY THREE

On the seven women. Chapter XI.

1111 I. Seven women suffer reproach and go about seeking to receive one who can take away their reproach. These seven women promise that they will eat their own bread and be clothed with their own garments. They do not need his bread, but the name of the one who can take away their reproach. They do not need the garments of the man whom they take. They have better garments than a human being can provide for them. They have richer foods than the human condition can bestow.

Whose, then, are these seven women, and what is their reproach? This deserves consideration.

The seven women are one, for they are the Spirit of God. And this one is seven. For the Spirit of God is the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord (Isa. XI).

This wisdom suffers reproach from many wisdoms rising up against it. This true understanding bears reproach from false understandings. This great counsel is reproached by many counselings that are not good. This might is cursed by one that, though it is not might, promises that it is might. This knowledge suffers reproach from a certain false-named knowledge that steals its name. This piety is reproached by one that, although it claims to be piety, is impiety and instructs the impious. This fear suffers reproach from one that is thought to be fear.

For many promise divine fear, but they do not fear with knowledge.

Let us consider, then, how these seven suffer reproach. Look at the wisdom of this age, look at the wisdom of the rulers of this world, and see how they reproach the wisdom of my Christ, and how they reproach the wisdom of true Judaism, according to which we are circumcised spiritually, while they are cut off.

Understand, then, how the wisdom of this age and of the rulers of this world curse wisdom. For this reason a human being is sought who may be with these seven spiritual women, so that he may take away their reproach.

There is one particular man who takes away their reproach. Who is this man? Jesus, who came forth according to the flesh from the root of Jesse, made from the seed of David according to the flesh, predestined Son of God in power according to the spirit of justification (Rom. I).

For “a shoot came forth from the root of Jesse.”

[Note: We have supplied the word “Shoot” from the Benedictine edition, with which we also read shortly afterward, “The Shoot is not the firstborn,” where “not” had previously been omitted and only one word had stood.]

“The Shoot is not the firstborn of all creation; the Shoot is not the one who was in the beginning with God, God the Word. Rather, it is the shoot from the root of Jesse to whom he was born according to the flesh. For a shoot came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower rose up from his root.”

What is the flower, and what is the root? Both lie beneath the same reality. The difference concerns their functions.

For if you are a sinner, you do not have the flower, nor will you see the flower that comes from the root of Jesse. For the shoot will come even to you, as the Disciple of the Shoot and the Flower says.

[Note: Previously “Apostle” stood instead of “Disciple.”]

Concerning the shoot he says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod?” Concerning the flower: “Or in the love of God and the spirit of gentleness?”

Therefore a shoot came forth from the root of Jesse: a shoot for the one who is punished with penalties, a shoot for the one who needs rebuke, a shoot for the one who must be reproved.

But the flower is for the one who has already been instructed and does not need harsh correction, or certainly does not need punishments, but has already begun to flourish vigorously and to advance toward perfect fruit. For first the flower appears; then, after the flower, it becomes a shoot and comes forth into fruit.

“A shoot came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up from his root; and the seven women shall rest upon him.” The spirit of the Lord, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, shall rest upon him.

For the spirit of wisdom did not rest upon Moses; the spirit of wisdom did not rest upon Joshua son of Nun; the spirit of wisdom did not rest upon each of the Prophets—upon Isaiah or Jeremiah.

II. Do not stone me as though I were blaspheming when I wish to glorify my Lord Jesus Christ. Rather, bear with what is said and consider it, and you will see that the spirit rested in none of them—not that it came upon none of them, but that it rested in none of them.

It came upon Moses, but Moses did not remain faithful after the spirit of wisdom that came to him. For hear what he says: “Hear, you rebels! Shall we bring water for you out of this rock?”

It came upon all the righteous, and it came upon Isaiah. But what does he say? “I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people with unclean lips” (Isa. VI). The spirit of wisdom came after those tongs and that fire; it came to one who had unclean lips, but it did not rest there. It used him as a minister, but it did not rest there.

The Spirit is troubled whenever it comes to a human being. For every human being sins, and there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin. “No one is clean from defilement, not even if his life is but one day, and his months are numbered” (Job XV).

Therefore it rests upon no one.

We can also prove from the Gospel that the spirit came upon many but did not remain in them. A little earlier we read: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings forever.” He did not say, “It shall not be,” but “It shall not remain.”

John saw one person alone in whom it remained, and this was the sign: “Upon whomever you see the spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the Son of God.”

He did indeed minister to the word of God when the spirit descended; shortly afterward he sins, shortly afterward he speaks an idle word. I do not know whether he remains without sin even then. Do you think that, in the presence of the spirit, permission is given to sin?

Therefore the spirit of God rested upon no one according to what is written: “A shoot came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower rose up from his root, and the spirit of God rests upon him—the spirit of wisdom, the spirit of understanding, the spirit of counsel and might.”

For this reason he is the angel of great counsel; for this reason he grew strong, and, growing strong, he ascended, and the powers marvel at him as he ascends and say of him: “This is the Lord, strong and mighty in battle.”

Therefore I shall still speak of him as ascending into heavenly things, or of his strength: “And the spirit of counsel and strength rested upon him.” “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation.”

Therefore the spirit of God rested upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of wisdom and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him.

III. The women, then, seeking one whom they might take, will seize one man—the seven will seize one man. This depends upon what came before, and we must first understand when the seven women will receive one man.

When the strong men of Jerusalem have been humbled, when the ornaments of the daughters of Zion have mourned, when that woman alone has been abandoned, when she has been struck down to the ground, then the seven women will seize one man, saying:

“We shall eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments; only let your name be invoked over us.”

Then the seven women will seize and truly hold one man, Jesus Christ our Lord, insofar as he is understood as man, insofar as he was born, insofar as he assumed a body.

The seven women will seize one man, saying: “We shall eat our own bread.” Many human beings walk about, and the women seize none of them; no man pleases them. They do not seize one man because men are scarce; rather, they sought the kind of man they wanted and found only one man whom they seized, so that they could say to him: “We shall eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments.”

There is a certain food of wisdom, a certain food of understanding, and likewise of the remaining spirits. What is this food? I am not afraid to say that there is another food outside these: perhaps, just as my food is the word of God, which says, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven, and I give life to the world” (John VI), so the Father himself is the food of wisdom.

For this reason it is said: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to complete his work” (John IV).

Nor should we think that wisdom, understanding, and the other spirits need anything because they have another food, since, by nature, the food of the whole dispensation is the one nature of God.

“We shall eat our own bread and be clothed with our own garments.” There is a certain adornment of wisdom by which it is beautified. Wisdom is adorned with the word. Each of these women has her ornaments.

“Only let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach.”

What is the name of wisdom? Jesus. What does “Let your name be invoked over us” mean? “I am wisdom; I wish to be called by your name, so that I, Wisdom, may be called Jesus; so that understanding, great counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and the fear of God may be named Jesus; so that your name may become all in all.”

“Let your name be invoked over us; take away our reproach.”

[Note: The Benedictine edition does not add “our.”]

Indeed, Jesus has taken away our reproach.

Therefore, rising, let us pray to God, who sent this man so that the seven spirits of the women might rest in him, so that this man might grant us communion with these women. By taking them upon ourselves, may we become wise, understanding in relation to God and human beings, and adorning our soul with virtues in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FOUR

On the vision of God and the Seraphim. Chapter VI.

### I.

It is impossible to discover God’s beginning. You can nowhere comprehend the beginning of God’s origin. I do not mean you, but neither can anyone else, nor anything whatsoever that exists. Only the Savior and the Holy Spirit, who have always been with God, see his face; and perhaps the angels who continually see the face of the Father who is in heaven also see the beginnings of events. Thus, too, the Seraphim conceal their feet before human beings. For the last things, since they are what they are, cannot be narrated. “Who shall announce the last things?” says Scripture (Isa. 41). The things we see—though let it be granted that we see some things—are intermediate. What existed before the world, we do not know. Yet certain things existed before the world. What will follow the world’s end, we do not grasp with certainty. There will, however, be other things after the world.

Thus the things that are written—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss, and the Spirit of God was borne over the waters”—are apprehended (Gen. 1). Those waters over which the Spirit of God brooded were pure. But the darkness that was over the abyss is not uncreated either. Both were created from nothing. Hear the Lord saying through Isaiah: “I am God who formed the light and made the darkness” (Isa. 45). Hear Wisdom proclaiming in Proverbs: “Before all the abysses I was born” (Prov. 8). These things were not uncreated; but when or how they were born, I do not know.

For the Seraphim veil the first things of God’s works, that is, God’s face; and likewise they veil the feet. Who can explain the things that will exist after the end of the age, throughout the ages of ages? It belongs to babbling men to promise knowledge of these things, while they do not know that a human being can grasp only what is intermediate, and what is to occur from the world’s end until the completion in judgment—punishments and recompense. Even many of these matters are hidden from us, so that for this reason it is written: “With two they veiled their face.” They not only veiled it but also covered it—that is, they veiled it in such a way that not even a little of the first things could be seen, by which I mean the face; nor could even a little of the last things be recognized, that is, his feet. “With two they flew.” The intermediate things are open to contemplation.

“And they cried out, one to the other.” Not one to many, but one to the other. No one can hear the holiness of God proclaimed by the Savior according to the dignity of the subject except the Holy Spirit; and, again, no one can dwell in the holiness of God proclaimed by the Holy Spirit except the Savior alone. For this reason they cried out, one to the other, and said: “Holy, holy, holy.” It is not enough for them to cry “holy” once, nor twice; rather, they take up the perfect number of the Trinity (Isa. 6), in order to manifest the abundance of God’s holiness, which is the repeated communion of threefold holiness: the holiness of the Father, the holiness of the Only-Begotten Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, “the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one” (Heb. 2). The one who sanctifies is the Savior, in accordance with the fact that, as man, he receives holiness from God the Father.

Accordingly they say: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth.” Sabaoth is interpreted—as Aquila rendered it—as “Lord of armies.”

### II.

“The whole earth is full of his glory.” Formerly the house was full of glory; now, however, the Seraphim prophesy concerning those who are upon the earth that the time will come when Christ, my God, will fill the whole earth with God’s glory. For in all who glorify God by their way of life there is the glory of God; and thus the whole earth is full of God’s glory.

Formerly the whole earth was not full of God’s glory, but only one corner of the earth, when it was said: “God is known in Judea; his name is great in Israel.” Glory to God, who sent his Son so that the whole earth might become full of his glory.

But what does it profit you if the earth is full because of the churches of the blessed, wherever they are, with the glory of God, while you yourself do not share in the fullness of God’s glory? You, therefore, work and strive in every way to be one who seeks the glory of God, so that it may dwell in you and find a place in you; then you too, together with the whole earth in which God’s glory is found, will become full of his glory.

How does the fullness of God’s glory come about in each one of us? If whatever I do and say is done for the glory of God, my every word and action becomes full of God’s glory. If my going out and my coming in are for the glory of God; if my food, my drink, and everything I do are done for the glory of God, then I too share in the saying: “The earth is full of his glory.”

When I have done all these things, “the lintel was raised” by the voice of the Seraphim with which they cried out. It is blessed, therefore, for each one of us to labor in such a way as to become a participant in the door and the lintel of the door, which in its spiritual meaning is Christ God. For I do not think it improper to call the door flesh and the lintel the Word.

### III.

“The lintel was raised by the voice with which they cried out, and the house was filled with smoke.” This smoke is a gift from the glory of God.

“And I said: ‘O wretched man that I am, for I am pierced with remorse.’” Before seeing the vision, do you not confess that you are wretched, O Isaiah? He does not say: “As long as Uzziah lived, it never entered my mind that I was wretched.” But I begin to know that I am wretched when I see the vision, when King Uzziah, the leper, dies, and I say: “O wretched man that I am” (2 Chron. 26).

Now I too begin to confess to the Lord and to say about myself: “O wretched man that I am!” How does Isaiah say, “O wretched man that I am”? The Apostle too says something very close to this: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). It is blessed, therefore, for me to confess that I am wretched. If I humble myself and, repenting, weep over my sins, God will hear me and give me a deliverer, and I shall say: “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid., 25).

Let us truly say from the heart: “I am wretched.” Let each one recall the causes of his wretchedness and his offenses, and let us rise to prayer and say this, remembering as those who confess, but forgetting as those who no longer commit such things: “O wretched man that I am, for I am pierced with remorse.”

He was not pierced with remorse before he saw the vision, before Uzziah died. When he begins to repent, he immediately says: “For I am pierced with remorse.” If someone lacks understanding with respect to the inner person, though he is a sinner he is not pierced with remorse. Just as, if you apply a spur to the outer limbs of a corpse, the dead body does not feel it, so if you apply divine words to a sinner who has been killed by sin and does not repent, he is neither saddened nor sorry, nor does he possess the grief that produces confession—the grief that is according to God.

But if someone wishes to be saved and hears the words of one who reproves and corrects him, he immediately says: “O wretched man that I am!” Nor is it enough to say, “I am wretched”; one must add: “For I am pierced with remorse.” Would that we might be pierced with remorse more deeply! For the more deeply we are pierced with remorse, the more the bonds of our sins are loosened.

For this reason that Ahab gained little benefit: he was not pierced with remorse very deeply (1 Kings 21), but only once. Hence it was said: “Have you seen how Ahab has been pierced with remorse?” But if someone is such that he does not cease being pierced with remorse, he says, like the Apostle: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Tim. 1). And: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Gal. 1). And: “The saying is trustworthy, that Jesus Christ came into this world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost” (1 Cor. 15).

Do you see how deeply he was pierced with remorse—not once, but always? In writing, speaking, and acting, he was pierced with remorse. So also Isaiah here says: “O wretched man that I am, I am pierced with remorse, for I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people that also has unclean lips.”

Let us note something else: Isaiah’s sins were not in his actions but only in his words. Hence he says: “For I am a man and have unclean lips.” The people too had unclean lips. It was not fitting for him to accuse the people and say that they had more sins than unclean lips.

### IV.

“And I saw the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my eyes.”

Whenever we think about God while we are still sinners, let us also say what the Prophet now says: “And one of the Seraphim was sent to me.” How good God is! “Because,” he says, “I hear Isaiah confessing”—for he said, “O wretched man that I am”; “because I hear him repenting”—for he said, “I am pierced with remorse”; “because he declared his own offenses,” saying, “For I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people that has unclean lips”—I too, while he is still speaking, say: “Here I am.”

“And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and he had a coal in his hand.” The coal is brought to the Prophet so that his lips, which had once sinned, might be cleansed through the burning of fire. Who is this one of the Seraphim? My Lord Jesus Christ. He was sent, according to the dispensation of the flesh, holding a coal in his hand and saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.”

### V.

And would that it were already burning!

“And one of the Seraphim was sent to me, and in his hand he had a coal that he had taken with tongs from the altar.” The Prophet is not cleansed by just any fire, arbitrarily, but by fire that comes from God’s altar.

If you have not been cleansed by the fire of the altar, that other fire remains for you, of which it was said: “Go away from me into the eternal fire that has been prepared for the Devil and his angels.” That fire is not from the altar. All must be handed over to fire, but not all to the same fire. Some are awaited by the fire of the altar; others by the fire that has been prepared for the Devil and his angels.

Therefore let the word of correction touch the lips of our mind and soul, so that we too may say: “And it touched my mouth.” If I cleanse my mouth so that I speak nothing idle, nothing foolish, nothing shameful, nothing buffoonish—to mention everything at once—and none of the things that are forbidden, then we can say: “It touched my mouth.”

But as long as I have unclean lips and perform unclean deeds because of sinful words, the fire from the altar does not touch my mouth, nor is one of the Seraphim sent to me.

### VI.

“And he said: ‘Behold, I have touched your lips, and I have taken away your iniquities, and I have thoroughly cleansed your sins.’”

Let the divine word bite us and burn our souls. Hearing it, let us say: “Was not our heart burning within us?” Thus may our iniquities and sins be taken away, and, having been made clean with a pure mouth, a pure heart, and an entirely pure conscience, let us give thanks to almighty God in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY FIVE

### On what is written, “Who raised up righteousness from the East,” and again, differently, on the vision. Chapter 6.

[Note: These two verses—“This Address,” and so forth, through “translated”—are absent from Benedictus’ edition. This Address was very corrupt in the Greek; therefore it has been translated according to its meaning and sequence, but not according to its wording.]

### I.

The Prophet says that Christ is living righteousness. We had thought that it was said only by the Apostle, because Christ is “righteousness, sanctification, redemption, and wisdom” (1 Cor. 1).

[Note: Earlier, instead of *putabamus nos* (“we had thought”), the text had only *putamus* (“we think”).]

Perhaps, however, the Apostle, instructed by the Prophets, knew that righteousness is animate and living. What is this righteousness? The Only-Begotten of God.

For it did not originate only with the Apostle that Christ is righteousness, living and subsisting righteousness; you will also find this mystery presented to us in the prophetic words. This is certain from the chapter in which the reading has now come to rest: “For who,” he says, “raised up righteousness from the East and called her to his feet?” (Isa. 41).

He called righteousness. It is clear that she is animate, if she walks when called. The Father called Christ so that, for our salvation, he might journey to us and descend from heaven to us. “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.”

He called him from the East—not from this visible east, but from the east of true light. Hence it is written: “Who raised up righteousness from the East and called her to his feet?” The Father called the Son—or, to speak truly, God called the man, righteousness, to his feet; that is, the incarnation of his Son.

Therefore we also adore his footstool, according to what is written: “Adore his footstool, for it is holy.” For the Lord’s flesh assumes the honor of divinity.

Since the beginning of the reading requires a more profound exposition, let us pray to the supreme King that the word which had been called away may return to us again, so that we may explain a few things according to our ability.

### II.

“And it came to pass in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and the house was full of his glory; and Seraphim stood around him, each with six wings. With two they veiled his face, with two they veiled his feet, and with two they flew; and they cried out, one to the other, saying: ‘Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of Sabaoth; the earth is full of his glory,’” and the rest.

But in order that we too may see the vision that Isaiah saw, let us call upon Jesus, who has granted eyes to those who could not see. Even now he can come and enable us, with open eyes, to behold the mysteries spoken in the reading. Let us promise him that we will no longer make Christ’s body the body of a prostitute, nor perform works worthy of mourning.

Let each one of us say these things in his heart to God, and let us pray that his coming may even now take place. For if Jesus has not come, we cannot see these things.

I pray that a Seraphim may also be sent to me and, taking a coal in his tongs, cleanse my lips. And why do I say “my lips”? Holy Isaiah was such that only his lips were cleansed, because he had sinned only with his lips—that is, in speech.

I, however, am not such that I can say that I have only unclean lips. I fear that I may have an unclean heart, unclean eyes, unclean ears, and an unclean mouth. As long as I sin in all these things, I am wholly unclean.

If I look upon a woman in order to lust, I have already committed adultery with her in my heart. Behold, I have unclean eyes. If the worst thoughts—adulteries, fornications, false testimonies—come forth from my breast, behold, I have an unclean heart.

“How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Isa. 52). I, however, fear that, while running toward evil, I may have unclean feet.

I stretch out my hands to the Lord. Perhaps, turning his face away, he says: “When you stretch out your hands, I will turn my face away from you” (Isa. 1:15).

Who, then, cleanses me? Who washes my feet? Jesus, come. I have dirty feet; for my sake become a servant. Pour your water into your basin; come, wash my feet.

I know that what I am saying is audacious. But I fear the warning addressed to the one who says: “If I do not wash your feet, you will have no part with me” (John 13). Therefore wash my feet, so that I may have a part with you.

But why do I say, “Wash my feet”? Peter could say this, for he had no need except that his feet should be washed; he was wholly clean. I, rather, although I have once been washed [reading: “although I am once washed”], need that baptism of which the Lord says: “I have another baptism with which to be baptized.”

Why have we said these things? I am preparing both myself and my hearers for greater mysteries—if only he comes, if the word of God descends to us. For I fear that it may flee from me, and may even disdain my blessing.

Once the word fled from the people because of one sinner, Achar, the son of Zambri, son of Zara, from the tribe of Judah, who disobeyed God and was therefore devoted to destruction (Josh. 7:25).

[Note: The Benedictine editors note that the editions prepared by Genebrard and Erasmus incorrectly have “Achaz”; Merlini’s edition has the somewhat better “Acham”; but the Hebrew manuscript has the best reading, “Achar,” concerning whom Joshua 7:25 speaks.]

And because there is now a multitude of people on account of the Preparation, and especially on the Lord’s Day, which commemorates Christ’s Passion—for the Lord’s Resurrection is not celebrated only once a year, but continually after seven days—

[Note: The same editors say: “The words of the interpretation, fashioned from the corrupt Greek, read as follows: ‘But the matter requires this, because of the preparation day, which commemorates Christ’s Passion, and especially on the Lord’s Day; for neither,’” and so forth.]

pray to almighty God that his word may come to us. Even if you are sinners, pray to the Lord. God hears sinners.

But if you fear what is said in the Gospel—“We know that God does not hear sinners” (John 9:31)—do not fear it, do not believe it. The blind man who said this was speaking blindly. Rather, believe the one who speaks and does not lie: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white like wool” (Isa. 1:18). And: “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land” (ibid., 19).

If you wish even now to hear, let us pray together to the Lord that, when the word arrives, we may at least now be able to understand the prophetic words that have been spoken.

### III.

“It came to pass,” he says, “in the year in which King Uzziah died: I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne.” The vision is assigned to a particular time. Why is the king’s time specified? Pay attention to when the vision arose. When King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne.

If one of us knows who Uzziah was and what he did, he can know what the Prophet taught through the Spirit and what the divine word presents to us.

I shall turn to the life of Uzziah and search the books of Kings and the history of Chronicles concerning Uzziah. There I shall see whether it is necessary that Uzziah the king die if I am to see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne (2 Chron. 26).

This Uzziah, descended from David’s seed and reigning over the people of Judah, did what was right in the sight of the Lord as long as Zechariah, who understood—for so it is written in the Second Book of Chronicles—was alive. Nor was this enough for him: he made great lamps for the Lord, arranged the temple of God, and displayed many virtues in his religious observance.

But when Zechariah, the understanding one, died, he did evil. Who was this one who did evil? He was a king, not a priest. The royal order is one thing, the priestly order another.

He wanted to enter the temple, take the place of a priest, and perform a work that had not been granted to him. He entered ahead of the priests and took up the vessel for the libation. Then the high priest who was in office at that time entered with eighty priests. The high priest said to him: “Are you not Uzziah, and not a priest?”

He persisted violently, and leprosy rose upon his forehead. He was expelled, dead, and left the temple; the Lord brought him out. Thus he became a leper because he had transgressed the law.

Everyone is under a reign, whether of sin or of righteousness. If sin reigns in me, I am one of the kings of Israel who entered the temple violently. If I am righteous according to the measure of my progress, do what is right, and persevere before God’s presence, righteousness reigns over me.

As long as the leper lived, Isaiah had unclean lips. As long as the wicked man lived, Isaiah could not see the Lord of Sabaoth and had unclean lips, for he was under a wicked king. When, then, does he begin to see the vision of God? “In the year in which Uzziah died.”

You will be able to say similar things about many passages of Scripture, with God’s help. In Exodus something of this kind is written: “And it came to pass after some days that the king of Egypt died; and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God” (Exod. 2:23).

As long as Pharaoh lived, the children of Israel did not groan, and, being placed in a worse condition, they did not even have the freedom to sigh. For the king who commanded them to make bricks and gather straw was alive. As long as Pharaoh lived, they did not groan to God; when Pharaoh died, then they were able to raise faces wet with tears.

A wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the Devil lives. Then we make bricks and gather straw; then we swallow our tears in silence and commit works of iniquity first. But when he has died, with the Lord God visiting us, then we groan to the Lord.

Therefore let us pray to the Lord that the reign of sin, which is in our mortal body, may die. For he says: “Sin died, but I came to life” (Rom. 7:9). And again: “Sin revived, but I died” (ibid., 10).

When the one who possesses the reign of sin—Uzziah—dies, Pharaoh also dies. When the most wicked king dies, I raise my eyes to heaven, and God hears my voice, as he heard Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. And I see the Lord of Sabaoth sitting and reigning upon a high throne, whom the people did not see. For Uzziah had not yet died.

I want to insert something similar concerning a good matter that is opposed to this. This same Uzziah, as long as Zechariah, the understanding one, lived, did not commit sin in God’s sight; when Zechariah died, he turned away from the Lord, although he governed the people and ruled the city.

Reading and hearing these things day and night, and hearing the Lord say: “You ought to have put my money with the bankers, and when I came I would have received what was mine with interest” (Matt. 25), let us not hide the mina entrusted to us in a napkin, nor put the money into the ground, but lend it at interest to the peoples.
