And when we have entrusted the Lord’s account to you, you will have to see how you repay what was entrusted to you with interest.

And so forth. Amen.

## HOMILY SIX

### On what is written, “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” and so forth, up to the place where it says, “And they shall turn and I shall heal them.” Chapter 6.

### I.

[Note: The Tours manuscript has “remission”; others have “remissam”; Genebrard had noted that *remissam* for “remission” was a term of the ancient theologians—Tertullian, Cyprian, and others.]

When Isaiah saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, and also saw the Seraphim standing around him, and received remission of sins through the fire that had been brought from the altar and cleansed his lips by its touch, he said that he had heard the voice of the Lord—not commanding but rousing—and saying: “Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?”

Then he says that he answered the Lord: “Here I am; send me.”

When I come to this passage and examine what is written, I find that Moses did one thing and Isaiah another. Moses, chosen to lead the people out of the land of Egypt, said: “Provide another whom you may send” (Exod. 4:13); he even appears to contradict God. Isaiah, however, not chosen but hearing, “Whom shall I send, and who will go?” says: “Here I am; send me.”

It is therefore fitting to compare spiritual things with spiritual things and to ask which of the two acted better: Moses, who, after being chosen, refused; or Isaiah, who, although not even chosen, offered himself to be sent to the people.

I do not know whether anyone, considering the apparent contradiction between the actions of the two, can say that Moses did the same thing as Isaiah. I have boldly compared two holy and blessed men, and have reached a decision, saying that Moses acted more modestly than Isaiah.

Moses was considering the greatness of presiding over the people in order to lead them out of the land of Egypt and to resist the enchantments and sorceries of the Egyptians. For this reason he said: “Provide another whom you may send.”

But Isaiah, without waiting to hear what he would be ordered to say, as though he had already been chosen, said: “Here I am; send me.” Therefore, because he did not know what he would be ordered to say, and as though he had already been chosen said, “Here I am; send me,” he is ordered to say things that were unexpected by the one who spoke.

Was it not unexpected that he should immediately be commanded to prophesy, beginning with curses: “You shall hear with your ears and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive; for the heart of this people has become dull,” and the rest?

Perhaps, then—if it is appropriate to say so boldly—he received the reward of rashness and audacity, being ordered to prophesy the things he did not wish to prophesy.

Since we have compared Isaiah and Moses, let us also set up another closely related comparison, between Isaiah and Jonah. Jonah is sent to preach the overthrow of the Ninevites after three days, and he is reluctant to go because of the city’s evils. Isaiah, however, without waiting to hear what he would be commanded to say, says: “Here I am; send me.”

It is good not to rush toward the dignities, principalities, and mysteries of the Church that come from God, but to imitate Moses and say with him: “Provide another whom you may send.”

For the one who wishes to be saved does not come to the government of the Church—even if he presides—but to the service of the Church, if it is fitting to speak also from the Gospel: “The rulers of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called magistrates. It shall not be so among you; for rulers do not lord it over you, but whoever wishes to be greater among you shall be the least of all” (Mark 9).

“Whoever wishes to be first shall be last of all.”

Whoever, therefore, is called to the episcopate is not called to rule but to serve the whole Church. If you wish to believe from the Scriptures that the one who presides in the Church is the servant of all, let the Savior and Lord himself persuade you—he who became such and so great in the midst of the disciples, not as one reclining at table but as one serving.

For, taking a linen cloth, after removing his garments he girded himself, poured water into a basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet and wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded. And, teaching what those who rule ought to be—namely, servants—he said: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, therefore, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13).

The ruler of the Church is therefore called to service, so that from this service he may be able to proceed to the heavenly throne, as it is written: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 24).

Hear also Paul, so distinguished a man, saying that he was the servant of all believers: “For I am,” he says, “the least of the apostles; I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15).

But lest this seem to approve only his humility and not his service, hear him saying: “We became little ones in the midst of you, as when a nurse cherishes her children, although we could have been burdensome as Christ’s apostles” (1 Thess. 2).

It is therefore fitting for us to be imitators of the humble words and deeds of the Lord himself and of his Apostle, and to do what Moses did, so that even if someone is called to rule, he may say: “Provide another whom you may send” (Exod. 4).

Moses says to God: “I am not worthy, from yesterday and the day before.” “I am weak of voice and slow of tongue.” And because he said humbly to God, “I am weak of voice and slow of tongue,” he hears from God: “Who gave a mouth to man, and who makes him deaf and mute, seeing and blind? Is it not I, the Lord God?”

Believe God; consecrate yourself to him.

[Note: With Benedictus’ edition, we have preferred *consecra* (“consecrate”) instead of *conserva* (“preserve”), which stood in the text.]

Though you have a thin voice and a slow tongue, entrust yourself to the word of God. Later you will say: “I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit” (Ps. 118).

These things have been said because Isaiah said: “Here I am; send me.”

### II.

Let us act in part together with him. For, having already received grace from God, he did not wish to receive it in vain, but to use it for what was necessary.

Seeing the Seraphim, seeing the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a high and exalted throne, he said: “O wretched man that I am, for I am pierced with remorse, because I am a man and have unclean lips, and I dwell among a people that has unclean lips; yet I have seen the King, the Lord of Sabaoth, with my eyes.”

By saying this and making himself wretched, he deserved help, since God received his humility. What was this help? “One of the Seraphim,” he says, “was sent to me, and he had a coal in his tongs, which he had brought from the altar; and he touched my lips and said: ‘Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and I have thoroughly cleansed your sins.’”

He obtained a benefit, was made clean, and received remission of sins.

When he heard: “Whom shall I send to this people, and who will go for us?” he did not dare, because of his former conscience, to say: “Here I am; send me.” But he had heard: “Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.”

Therefore, since holy people are pierced with remorse, and the matter between Moses and Isaiah is under discussion, let us make our case for Moses and also for Isaiah, assigning each of them his portion from the Scriptures.

Moses had not received remission of sins so as to say, as one already conscious of being cleansed, “Send me.” For this reason he said: “Provide another whom you may send.” He had upon his conscience the killing of the Egyptian; and perhaps, as a human being, he knew that he had other sins as well. Therefore he refused.

Isaiah, however, does not request the ministry as one righteous by nature, but as one who has obtained grace. In the same way, if Moses had received a similar grace and had heard, “Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and I have thoroughly cleansed your sins,” perhaps he would by no means have said: “Provide another whom you may send.”

There is therefore some reason both in Moses’ refusal and in Isaiah’s saying: “Here I am; send me.”

### III

But let us also examine what the Lord commanded to be said to the people: “Go and say to the people: With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand; and though you see, you will discern, and you will not see. For the heart of this people has grown fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn back, and I heal them” (Isa. VI, 9–10).

Knowing that the hearing of speech is twofold, and recognizing a twofold constitution in us—that is, one aspect bodily and another spiritual—or else prophesying to the people about what was to happen at Christ’s coming, Isaiah says that there would be a time when they would hear and yet not understand. For when they heard my Lord Jesus Christ, they heard only the sound of what was said, not its meaning. This is clear from the fact that he spoke to the people outside in parables, while in private he explained them to the disciples. He prophesies what came to pass: “With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand” (Matt. XIII).

Moreover, that this prophecy was spoken to the people concerning the Lord’s coming, the Savior himself declares: “Isaiah truly prophesied about you when he said: ‘With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand.’” Let us therefore grant that the people, while listening to the Lord’s words, were unable to understand what was said.

Let us see, however, what follows: “And though you see, you will see, and you will not know.” If someone saw the things the Savior was doing, he could not immediately understand why they were being done. Let us take an example: he washed the disciples’ feet. They certainly saw how the Master washed the disciples’ feet; others who were present saw it as well, but they saw only what was happening, not why it was happening. The washing of the feet was in fact a likeness, because the Word of God washed the disciples’ feet.

For this reason the Savior said to Peter, who resisted and said, “You shall never wash my feet”: What did he say? “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will understand afterward” (John XIII, 7). And what does Peter say that he is doing now? “I see you washing our feet, with the basin set out, yourself girded with a towel, serving us and wiping our feet.” But since this was not a bodily action, but a spiritual one, the Savior, having stripped himself, pours spiritual water into the basin according to the Scriptures and washes the feet of his disciples, so that, once cleansed, they may ascend to the one who says, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6), and may not be full of the dust which he wished to shake off upon those who were unworthy, would not receive peace, and were not worthy of the things that were said.

Because this was what the action signified, he said: “What I am doing you do not know now, but you will understand afterward.” The same thing was also said to the others: “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am. If I, then, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.”

Does he therefore mean that a bishop should pour water into a basin, remove his clothing, gird himself with a towel, and, while I stretch out my feet, wash them? “You ought,” he says, “to wash one another’s feet.” If this is what the saying means, none of you will fulfill the command. No deacon, presbyter, or bishop takes a towel and washes the feet of everyone who comes.

But if you understand what is written, those bishops who are truly blessed, serving the Church, pour the water of the Scriptures into the basin of the soul, according to the Scriptures, and attempt to wash, cleanse, and cast away the dirt from the disciples’ feet. And if the bishops keep the command by imitating Jesus, so also do the presbyters.

Would that I too might now receive water capable of washing the feet of your souls, so that each of you, when he has been washed, may say: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song III, 3). The bride says this in the Song of Songs, not referring to bodily feet that have been washed, but to feet that do not stumble. Concerning these Solomon says: “Let your foot not stumble” (Prov. III, 23). Of these it is also written in the Psalms: “But my feet had almost slipped” (Ps. LXXIII, 2).

And concerning widows who are appointed in the churches, Scripture says: “If she has washed the feet of the saints” (I Tim. V, 10). But if you wish to hear more clearly how a widow washes the feet of the saints, hear Paul elsewhere establishing a rule for widows and saying that they should be good teachers, so as to make the young women chaste, washing the dirt from the feet of young women.

Those widows are worthy of ecclesiastical honor who wash the feet of the saints by the word of spiritual teaching—but of female saints, not male ones. For he does not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man. He wishes women to be good teachers, so that they may exhort not young men but young women to chastity; for it is improper that a woman should become the teacher of a man. Rather, they should exhort young women to chastity and to love their husbands and children.

Let us therefore learn to wash the feet of the disciples. These things have been said because of the words: “Though you see, you will see, and you will not know.” For if anything was done by the Savior, those who did not understand saw it bodily, but did not see it rationally. Those who did understand saw it with their eyes and also with their understanding, so that what was said—“Though you see, you will see, and you will not know”—was not fulfilled in the blessed who see, but in sinners.

Let us also pray that, when we see all the events of the Gospels, we may see them in a twofold way: how they happened bodily when our Savior came to earth, and how each thing that happened in the body was a likeness and type of future things. For example, some man blind from birth recovered his sight (John IX). In reality, this man blind from birth was the Gentile people, to whom the Savior restored sight by anointing his eyes with saliva and sending him to Siloam, which means “sent.”

For he was sending those whom he had anointed with the Spirit to believe to Siloam—that is, to the apostles and teachers. This is why it is written of Siloam that it means “sent.” And whenever we begin to be visited by Jesus, so that we may receive the eyes of the soul, he sends us to Siloam, that is, to the one who has been sent.

Therefore, whenever each of us reads the things done in the Gospels, let him pray that the following saying may not also be fulfilled in him: “Though you see, you will see, and you will not know” (John VII, 7).

### IV

But if, as simpler people suppose, the things that were done were done not for our sake but solely for their own sake, and were not examples of another reality, let them explain what meaning the saying “Though you see, you will see, and you will not know” possesses.

For if the things that were seen did not have some sacred meaning [Note: Others perhaps more correctly read “secret”], so that they could be perceived spiritually as well as with bodily eyes, he would never have said: “Though you see, you will see, and you will not know.”

To confirm this, we shall bring forward another testimony from the Gospel concerning another passage which, according to those who follow only the letter, is false. Our Savior and Lord says to the disciples in the Gospel according to John: “If you believe, you will do not only the works that I do, but you will do greater works than these” (John XIV, 12).

Let us see, then, whether the disciples did any greater works. What is greater than raising the dead? Who—not to speak of one of us, but even of the apostles—raised a dead person? History reports that Paul raised Eutychus from the dead, and Peter raised Tabitha, whose name means Dorcas (Acts IX). These and other similar events can be found. But where are the greater works?

The Savior also made the blind see again, and, what is greater, those who had been born blind. Let those who have witnessed men blind from the womb healed by the hands of the apostles produce them (Matt. IX). One who searches can find countless other examples in the Gospels, because neither the apostles nor their successors have done works greater than these.

Yet the word of Scripture has said something of this kind: “You will do greater works than the bodily works I have done. I caused the dead to rise bodily; you will cause the dead to rise spiritually. I poured this sensible light into the eyes of the blind; you will give spiritual light to those who do not see.”

To this day I see these greater signs, compared with the bodily signs Jesus performed, being accomplished through the most faithful disciples of Jesus. Are there not blind people who now see, and lame people who walk, and lepers who are cleansed? Do not the other things also take place?

If someone who yesterday, blinded by error, approached an idol as though it were God, today calls upon the living God and abandons his former ways, does he not see? If someone who yesterday was lame because of sin now, through the teaching of the disciples, has been taught the true path and walks firmly, was he not lame before, and does he not now walk?

If someone yesterday had a withered hand, useless for doing good, and today receives his hand back alive, is it not restored? If you see someone polluted and bearing leprosy in his soul suddenly repent and be pierced by the word of teaching, do not hesitate to say that it is greater for one who was spiritually leprous to be cleansed than for someone to have been cleansed bodily.

Our discussion has poured forth these observations at greater length because it wished to show what is meant by the saying: “And though you see, you will see, and you will not understand.”

### V

What, then, is the reason that the hearer does not understand and the one who sees does not see? “The heart of this people has grown fat,” he says (Isa. VI).

It is necessary to understand where this comes from. Bodily fatness and spiritual fatness are not the same, nor are bodily thinness and spiritual thinness. What is fat bodily becomes so in the flesh. A fleshy heart does not harm me if it grows fat, nor does it benefit me if it is reduced by illness or by any other cause.

I suppose that the fleshy heart of those who are restrained by fear becomes like this. For just as their whole bodies waste away from illness, so, they say, the thickness and whatever fat surrounds their hearts is reduced.

What harm, then, does it do me if my bodily heart grows fat? And even if my heart becomes thin, what benefit does this bring me?

But by the name “heart,” borrowed from the bodily heart, the governing faculty of our soul is designated, as is clear from the Gospel saying: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. V, 8). Those whose interiors contain no blood or other bodily material are not therefore pure in heart. Rather, “Blessed are the pure in heart” means: “Blessed are those whose governing faculty of the soul is pure.” The governing faculty is designated by the term “heart.”

Since, then, the governing faculty of our soul—which is said to be located in the bodily heart—may be clean or unclean, our heart is unclean when evil thoughts proceed from it: murders, adulteries, thefts, false witness, blasphemies. It is clean when holy thoughts, divine understanding, and a pure mind proceed from it.

For this reason we should understand that the heart is made thin by the Holy Spirit of the one who is being saved, but grows fat and is choked by the wickedness of the one who sins. Concerning the Holy Spirit, who is according to wisdom, it is said that he is “manifold, subtle, mobile” (Wis. VII, 22), and that the righteous receive this subtle spirit.

This spirit differs from all intellectual, pure, subtle spirits. The governing faculty of the heart is therefore thin when it has been compacted through the defect of bodily matter and is filled with bodily thoughts that deserve blame. Thus it is said: “The heart of this people has grown fat.”

Understand the heart to have grown fat because there is nothing in it except human and carnal concerns. Just as bodily matter is fat, so too are bodily understandings and thoughts.

Since, then, two things have been set forth—namely, that the heart grows fat through worldly cares and becomes thin through spiritual concern, when someone thinks about the things of the Lord, casting fatness out of his heart and knowing that if his heart grows fat he will neither receive the words of God nor see the mysteries of salvation—let us also lay aside fatness and take on the thinness that has been described, so that we too may say with the Prophet:

“My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh longs for you. In a desert land, pathless and waterless, so I appeared before you in the sanctuary” (Ps. LXIII, 2–3).

I did not appear before him in the sanctuary as though I had been holy by nature; rather, if the prudence of the flesh wastes away, and if the prudence of the flesh has wasted away, then I shall appear before him in the sanctuary.

These things have been said in explanation of the words: “The heart of this people has grown fat.”

### VI

The passage continues: “And they have heard heavily with their ears.”

It does me no harm if I hear heavily in a bodily sense, nor does this prevent me from hearing the words of God. Just as bodily blindness does not harm me if my soul has not been blinded, so neither the lightness nor the heaviness of bodily hearing hinders me in any way.

There is another kind of heaviness of hearing that harms the human soul. What is this heaviness that affects the soul’s hearing? According to the Scriptures, sin is heavy. Therefore, when someone perceives his sins, he says: “They have weighed heavily upon me like a burden” (Ps. XXXVIII, 5).

And because iniquity is heavy, the woman sits upon a leaden talent, as it is written in Zechariah (Zech. V, 7). The Egyptians were not drowned like lead in the raging water because their bodies were heavy, but because their souls had been weighed down by the leaden talent upon which iniquity sat. For this reason they were drowned like lead in the raging water (Exod. XV, 10).

The heaviness of the ears therefore comes from sin, and lightness from righteousness. What makes hearing hear not heavily but lightly? The wings of the word, the wings of virtue. The wings of the word bring great lightness: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall rest?” (Ps. LIV, 7).

The Prophet says this not while praying to receive bodily wings like a dove’s, but the wings of the dove, the Holy Spirit.

Solomon likewise says of the rich man: “He will fashion wings for himself like an eagle, and he will turn back to the house of the one who rules him” (Prov. XXIII, 5). If, then, we receive wings, we shall hear lightly. But if we sin and are negligent concerning our wings, and our feathers fall away, we shall be weighed down and shall hear heavily.

Therefore sinners heard heavily with their ears. All the Jews who then heard the Savior heard him heavily; for this reason they did not believe. To this day, all who hear the Scriptures but do not hear the spiritual word, which is light, instead hear the letter, which is heavy and kills, and so they hear heavily.

Thus Scripture is heard in two ways. By one who does not understand what is said, it is heard heavily; by one who understands it, it is not only not heard heavily but is heard sharply. Hence the person who becomes understanding becomes a hearer.

### VII

There is also another prophecy concerning the Jewish people and concerning all of us if we sin: “And they have closed their eyes, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart.”

Among those who do not see, some are blind and do not see because of their blindness; some are in darkness and therefore do not see; others are neither in darkness nor blind, but because they close their eyes, they do not see.

The divine Scripture knows these distinctions, which concern the governing faculties of our hearts. The Savior says to those who are in chains, “Come out,” and to those who are in darkness, “Let it be revealed to them.” “Light has risen upon those sitting in the region and shadow of death.”

These people did not see because they were in darkness, until light rose upon them. “Deaf, hear; and blind, look!” These people did not see before because they were blind by nature.

But those who are outside these conditions, and who in comparison with the blind and those in darkness are much worse, are the ones who do not see because they have deliberately closed their eyes.

That this is so, as we have asserted, the Savior will testify to me when he says: “If you were blind, you would not have sin. But now you say, ‘We see’; therefore your sin remains” (John IX, 41).

He rightly says, “You say, ‘We see.’” For they truly say that they see and possess the ability to see, but because they close their eyes, they do not see.

And whenever you see a soul naturally gifted for understanding, quick and alert, yet not meditating on the words of God, recognize that it does not fail to see the things contained in the Scriptures because of blindness, nor because it is in darkness, but because it closes its eyes.

If, therefore, you hear the divine Scripture saying to those who close their eyes, “Open your eyes and see rightly; open your eyes from what you had closed them against,” then you will be able to see rightly and contemplate the light of truth.

It condemns those about whom the question is asked: Why do they close their eyes so that they will not see? But it does not say that it is never beneficial to close the eyes of the soul. For Isaiah makes this clear in what follows: “Who has announced to you the eternal place?” (Isa. XXXIII, 14)—the one “who walks in righteousness and speaks the true way, stopping his ears so that he may not hear the judgment of bloodshed, and closing his eyes so that he may not see iniquity.”

If, when I open the eyes of my soul, I am going to hear and perceive shameful speech, it is better to close my hearing than to hear things that will harm me. When, then, shall I close them? When evil things are being said, so that I may not even understand them.

When should the words of God be seen? When we turn back and God heals us, sending the Word who heals those who wish to be healed in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## SEVENTH HOMILY

On the passage written: “Behold, I and the children,” etc. Chapter VIII.

### I

“Give an opportunity to the wise, and he will become wiser,” says the divine word (Prov. IX, 9). The most sacred apostles received an opportunity for understanding the prophetic words. Let us pray to God that we may receive wisdom and become wiser through the apostles’ opportunity for interpreting the Prophets.

The Apostle, recalling this saying—“Behold, I and the children whom God has given me”—then adds and explains it: “Since, therefore, the children shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise shared in them, so that through death he might destroy the one who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and might deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to slavery for life” (Heb. II, 14–15).

Since, then, the children became participants in blood and flesh, our Savior also shared in flesh and blood. For it was foreign to his nature and divinity to assume blood and flesh; but for our sake he assumed what was foreign to him, so that he might make his own those who had been alienated through sin.

The Apostle explained this by saying: “Since, therefore, the children shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise shared in them.”

I shall add this: just as the children shared in blood and flesh, and he himself likewise shared in them, so also, because children cannot hear stronger words, they ought to hear the words of God as children. For this reason he was made in blood for the sake of the children who shared in flesh and blood. Speaking as to little ones, he speaks not divine and ineffable things, but whatever little ones are able to grasp.

All human beings are little ones when compared with the perfection of the Word—even if you name Moses, even if you mention one of the Prophets, even if you mention John, than whom no one born of women was greater (Matt. XI, 11); even if you come to the apostles—Peter, against whom the gates of Hades shall not prevail, or Paul, who was caught up to the third heaven and heard unspeakable words (II Cor. XII, 2–4).

You do not diminish their glory by saying that even they, in the things they understood, were instructed in the lessons given to human beings as children, when compared with the things they did not understand.

The Savior therefore says—not of those whom Paul calls children in Christ and declares to require milk rather than solid food, but of all human beings together: “Behold, I and my children whom God has given me” (I Cor. III, 1–2).

But just as among children some are more perceptive than others and grasp more quickly what has been taught to them, so, I say, Moses, the Prophets, and the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ were made like gifted children. [Note: In the preceding edition the word “like” (*similem*) was absent through the carelessness of the typesetters.]

Therefore, recognizing that even if they made progress, they made progress with the progress of children, they said: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII, 9). For they did not yet behold the realities of truth, but shadows of realities; not the full light, but an obscure image. Thus they repeated: “Now we see through a mirror and in a riddle, but then face to face” (I Cor. XIII, 12).

Who, then, reading and understanding these things, will become puffed up and exalted over knowledge or over any gift? For all the things that have come to children are far inferior to those reserved for adults. Those who appear to be more perceptive and quicker among children must not therefore become exalted or proud.

By these children he means all human beings, whom the Savior also indicated when he said: “Behold, I and my children whom God has given me.” The Savior too received a gift from God. For no one comes to him unless the one who sent him draws the person who comes to the Savior, as we have learned in the Gospel according to John.

And because he received from the Father as a gift those who believe, the Prophet says concerning them: “Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.” The one who received should not be thought to have lacked them, since the one who gave still possesses them.

### II

Then, in what follows, the Savior prophesies through the Prophet that, when he has received the children, signs and wonders will occur in Israel. The passage reads: “And there will be signs and wonders in Israel from the Lord Sabaoth, who dwells on Mount Zion.”

The one who dwells in the watchtower, and who can contemplate truth in every soul, performs signs and wonders through the Savior, and after the Savior through the apostles. Wherever a soul suited to the ministry of God’s signs and wonders is found—whether for spiritual healing or for visibly encouraging those who come to the faith—God is not idle. The God who then performed signs and wonders still works them now.

“And if they say to you, ‘Seek ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry from the belly; do not the nations seek their god, those who inquire of the dead concerning the living?’” (Isa. VIII, 19).

Pay attention, because these words have been spoken obscurely, and their meaning must be joined to what precedes through God himself giving and revealing it.

He therefore teaches us not to become disciples of other words, but only of heavenly and good ones. There are some who speak and promise true teaching but do not speak heavenly things; they speak earthly things. “The one who is from the earth is earthly and speaks from the earth; the one who comes from heaven is above all, and he testifies to what he has seen and heard” (John III, 31–32).

If someone says to the children who believe in me, “Seek ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry from the belly”—that is, “Seek demons”—he has named all demons metaphorically (*tropikōs*) after one species of demon, the ventriloquist.

If they say to you, “Seek ventriloquists”—that is, “Seek from demons either divination, truth, or sacred contemplation”—answer them as I say: What are they teaching you? The following words tell us.

There are some who send you—or rather, as far as it depends on them, catechumens—to ventriloquists. Those who wish you to go to idols, concerning which it is written, “All the gods of the nations are demons,” wish you to go not only to ventriloquists but to every kind of demon.

Nevertheless, may our God, who does everything in heaven and on earth, tear us away from demons and make us his own through our Savior Jesus Christ.

See, then, that none of your souls is ever deceived, so that it remains uncertain and doubtful when it hears someone say: “In this idol a demon cured that illness; this one and that one foretold the future.” All these things are idols of demons and of human beings who do not know the truth. [Note: Perhaps the holy translator wrote *idolio*, corresponding to Greek εἰδώλιον, “an image or statue of an idol,” or even εἰδωλεῖον, “a temple or shrine of idols,” and similar terms. The reading “All these things” is emended from “Thus all things,” and later “every” from “of all,” etc.]

Lift your mind up to God, who is the creator of all, and compare this piety with every practice that is announced as piety but is not piety. Then see that you are blessed.

“For who is like you, O people saved by the Lord? Blessed is the nation whose Lord is its God, the people whom he chose for his inheritance” (Ps. CXLIV, 15).

The Jewish nation was once blessed, but it lost its blessedness and was driven from its place because, plotting against the one who had been sent and who had the testimony of his Father—not only through the Law and the Prophets, but also through signs and wonders—it killed him.

Blessedness therefore migrated to us, the disciples of Jesus Christ, and we believe in him without wavering and live firmly according to what we have been taught.

### III

And if they say to you, “Seek ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth” (Isa. VIII, 19), because they speak empty things, he called them “empty-speakers.” Every word that is spoken is either empty or full of truth.

Every word that is false is empty. A word is full of truth when it possesses knowledge of God, the ruler of all, and teaches us to believe in God, who promises the kingdoms of heaven to his saints.

See, then, what those say who were not empty-speakers and never appeared empty in the presence of the Lord: “From his fullness we have all received” (John I, 16).

Those who are empty-speakers do not possess this from fullness; rather, they are all empty of truth, empty of virtue, empty of Christ.

If they say to you, “Seek those who cry out from the earth, who speak empty things, who cry from the belly,” I wish also to explain why the discourse has chosen especially this demon, the ventriloquist, when it says: “If they say to you, ‘Seek ventriloquists.’”

You will find that all who make promises but do not possess the truth serve their belly and, in a certain sense, do everything for its pleasure and abundance.

You will find this not only among the Gentiles, but also among those who profess religion in Christ yet are heretics; and not only among them, but also among us who belong to the Church, you will find someone who does everything for the satisfaction of his belly, so that he may be honored and receive the gifts brought into the Church.

Such a person speaks from the belly, and the source of his words is located in the belly. The source of his words does not flow from a good heart, from good thoughts, or from the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, whenever someone promises to teach, observe whether his words have their beginning in the belly or not.

I shall insert an objection that might be made to me, lest one of you, hearing it from someone else, suppose either that Scripture contradicts itself or that I have not examined how one ought to establish an accusatory argument against those who cry out from the belly. [Note: The Benedictine edition incorrectly reads *nos* (“we”) in place of the negative particle.]

What is the objection? “If anyone believes in me, rivers will flow from his belly, a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John VII, 38).

Let someone among those who raise the objection say: If the Savior promises that this fountain of water springing up into eternal life comes from the belly, then it comes from a righteous person, and the righteous person speaks from the belly. For the fountain of water that God promises is in his belly.

But we must say that perhaps we have two bellies: one bodily and another spiritual, just as the other parts that are named in the body may also have corresponding parts in the soul. For example, there are eyes of the body and eyes of the soul.

When it is said concerning the eyes, “The commandment of the Lord is clear, enlightening the eyes” (Ps. CXVIII, 105), I do not think this refers to bodily eyes. And when it is said, “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XIII, 9), we must not think that this refers to the ears of the body, but to those of the soul, possessed by those who are pure in the hearing of the soul.

Even when the promise says, “Your foot shall not stumble” (John XIV, 16), this should not be understood of the bodily foot. There is a foot of the heart that enters toward the one who said, “I am the way.”

Thus, just as there is a bodily belly, so there is a corresponding belly of the soul. The righteous person speaks of it: “Because of your fear, Lord, we conceived and were in labor, and we brought forth the spirit of your salvation, which you have accomplished upon the earth” (Isa. XXVI, 18).

Those who have their belly full of empty words, which are earthly, have a belly whose substance is from the earth. Concerning it, it is written: “But God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI, 13).

The saints therefore have a belly in which, through the fear of the Lord, they have both conceived, and their belly is full of fountains of water springing up into eternal life.

Of this belly that man says: “My ears and my belly are like a wineskin full of new wine and tightly bound” (Job XXXII, 19). He said this not of a bodily belly; for his bodily belly was not full of divine things, nor was it bound like a wineskin with wine near to these things. [Note: On the basis of other books we emend *in ventrem* (“into the belly”), which previously stood here, to *in utrem* (“into a wineskin”).]

This is the resolution of the objection.

### IV

Now let us return to what we began. If, then, they say to you, “Seek ventriloquists and those who cry out from the earth,” answer them as follows:

“Does not a nation inquire of its own god?” The expression is incomplete. It should be understood as: “Answer them: does not a nation inquire of its own god?” Every nation, if it seeks Jupiter, refers what it has sought to its own god.

Answer them: “You Israelites, who possess the true God, who is above all, when you seek, do not seek ventriloquists, nor those who cry out from the earth, nor empty-speakers, but your own God.”

“They inquire of the dead concerning the living.” Demons are dead, deprived of the true life which says, “I am life.” Do not therefore seek the dead concerning the affairs of the living (John XIV, 6).

You have received the Law. O you who could not be persuaded to seek these things from ventriloquists and from those who cry out from the earth, receive the word of truth and the Law as an aid to your Law, and pay attention: in your Law it is written, “You shall not follow idols.” In accordance with the Law, do not pay attention to ventriloquists or to those who cry out from the earth.

For he gave the Law as an aid, so that they might say: “There is no word like this one, for which there is no need to give gifts” (Isa. VI, 5). Whoever has received the Law and knows that the Law is an aid—especially the spiritual Law, which forbids seeking anything from ventriloquists and omens—should, when he understands the Law, admire it and say:

“No word among Greeks or barbarians is as pure as the word of the Law.”

For the Law given to us by God differs from every word and from every teaching that promises truth. He gave the Law as an aid, so that they might say: “There is nothing like this word.”

What does “There is nothing like this word” mean? There are many words, but none like this one. There is no word after the word of Moses, after the word of the Prophets, and much more after the word of Jesus Christ and his apostles.

See whether the meanings of God do not cry out concerning the statement: “He gave the Law as an aid.” Those who received the Law as an aid may say: “There is nothing like this word”—the word Moses spoke in the Law given through angels by the hand of a mediator (Gal. III, 19).

Much more worthily can the Church say this of the Word that became flesh, that dwelt among us, whose glory we have seen—not glory covered by a veil as Moses’ was, but glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth.

“There is nothing like this Word,” which the Church received and in which it believes, through which it will also be saved: the Word who was in the beginning with God, God the Word, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## EIGHTH HOMILY

On the passage written: “Howl, you sculptured images, in Jerusalem and in Samaria,” up to the place where he says, “And I will shake the inhabited cities.” Chapter X.

[Col. 0932D]

### 1139

#### I

Formerly, when the ancient people sinned and fell away from religion, Judah made carved images in Jerusalem, and the people called Israel did so in Samaria. But if even now someone considers the multitude of those who are gathered as sinners, he will not hesitate to say that everyone who makes a god of what he considers good, and serves sin, is accursed—he who makes a carved image, casts a work of the craftsman’s hands, and places it in a hidden place. For in the hiding-place of the heart we make many idols if we sin.

Therefore the word teaches us to do penance and to howl over the carved images and idols that are in Jerusalem and Samaria. If we sin—those of us who desire to belong to the Church—we make carved images in Jerusalem. But if those outside the Church, such as heretics, have sinned, they make idols in Samaria. Nevertheless, almighty God, in accordance with his goodness, calls everyone to repentance, saying: “Howl over the carved images in Jerusalem and in Samaria.” For just as I did to Samaria and its handmade things, so will I do to Jerusalem and its idols.

He threatens to do to those who are of the Church what he did to the Samaritans. But when God has completed everything in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, he will bring against them “the great mind, the prince of the Assyrians, and against the height of the glory of his eyes” (Isaiah 10).

We are taught what will happen to our enemy and to Zabulus (Genesis 3), whom the Prophet now calls a certain great mind. For just as the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that are upon the earth, and the children of this age are wiser than the children of light in their own generation, and the unjust steward acted cleverly according to a bad kind of wisdom, so this one, who is figuratively called the prince of the Assyrians, is a great mind. We should marvel at the greatness of his mind, by which he has misused his powers to instruct the wise of this world, who, with every appearance of truth and every kind of strength, construct and display the falsehood of their sects.

When, therefore, God has done everything in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and has restored the things promised to the righteous, then he will bring against the great mind—the prince of the Assyrians—and against the height of the glory of his eyes. The word recognizes him as lofty in wisdom, and knows that the beginning of his ruin arose from arrogance. Therefore, if we become arrogant, we will fall into the judgment of the devil, into which Zabulus himself fell.

#### II

Let us also consider how great his arrogance is, so that we may avoid it and not allow him to speak truly against us. What, then, does he say? “By strength I will act, and I will take away the wisdom of understanding, the boundaries of the nations” (Isaiah 10).

He thinks that by his own strength he can accomplish in us whatever he wishes. And truly, if we are defeated and afterward sin—if, after the Church, we return again to the circus, to horse-racing, and to the gatherings of the pagans—what else happens except that, having conquered us, he takes possession of us? What did Zabulus say? “By strength I will act.” He achieves in us sinners what he threatened.

And if, after a long period of chastity and after much holiness, we commit fornication, what else happens except that the one who said, “By strength I will act,” is shown to have spoken truly against us?

But let us also observe what else this boaster promises: “And I will take away the wisdom of understanding, the boundaries of the nations.” He promises some kind of wisdom, of which the Prophet also speaks: “There is a foreign wisdom in them” (Jeremiah 8:9). For there is a wisdom alien to the truth, which God will destroy.

Possessing this wisdom, he considers himself wise and says: “I will take away the wisdom of understanding, the boundaries of the nations, and I will consume their strength.” His activity reached all the nations; but the Savior, sending his words to all the nations, rescued those who were held captive by Zabulus among every nation.

“And I will consume their strength.” He threatens that he will plunder our strength and hand us over to those who fight against us. And indeed, one can see him doing this to certain people. When someone is conquered by Zabulus and handed over to demons, to most evil spirits, and to hostile powers, what else has happened than what he said: “And I will consume their strength”? Taking our strength, he consumed us.

“And I will shake the inhabited cities” (Isaiah 10:24). Zabulus also threatens this. He sees the inhabited cities—the Churches of God built in Christ the Lord—and pretends that he will shake them. He has often shaken inhabited cities through persecutions; he has often shaken them through scandals.

But let us try, having our foundation upon the rock, to become such that this one who says, “I will shake the inhabited cities,” cannot shake us through his storms or through hostile spirits. Rather, in everything that happens, let us remain steadfast, since we have our building upon the rock, Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## NINTH HOMILY

On the passage that is written: “And I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?”—and, passing over a short portion, it reaches the place where it is written: “Ask for yourself a sign from the Lord your God, either in the depth or in the height.” Chapters 6 and 7.

### 1141

“And I heard the voice of the Lord saying, ‘Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?’ And I said, ‘Here am I; send me.’ And he said, ‘Go and say to this people: With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand,’” and what follows.

Concerning the passage from the Prophet Isaiah that has now been read, let us pray to God that he may grant us grace, so that we may be able to expound it in a manner worthy of the prophetic Spirit.

“And I heard,” he says (Exodus 4), “the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send?” After the Prophet had been purified in his lips [variant: “lip”], he was ready to accept the Lord’s ministry, and said: “I am here; send me.” But so that he might be more ready for this, he remembered the voice of Moses. For Moses too, using the same expression—“Send me”—became leader of the people, judge, and was called God’s servant.

I heard a certain Hebrew expounding this passage and saying that the Prophet willingly and readily accepted the prophetic office for the people, not knowing what he would have to say to them. But when he heard the grievous things that were to be announced to the people—that is, “With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand,” and so forth (Isaiah 6)—he became more reluctant in what follows. When the voice of God said to him, “Cry out,” he answered and said: “What shall I cry out?”

I think, however, that these things are prophesied concerning the Savior, because it was to happen that those who heard would not hear, and those who saw would not see.

What is being said will become clearer if we consider this passage for a little while: “Seeing, you will look, and you will not see,” means something of this kind. At that time they saw the blind looking; yet they did not understand the reason for the sight. They heard the parables that the Savior explained privately to the disciples. They themselves, however, did not hear, because they did not know what was being said. For this reason he testified against them, saying: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.”

They were not deprived of physical ears, so that they could not hear; rather, their inner ears had become dull for hearing. For this reason he preaches to them and, through the Prophet, foretells what was to come, saying: “With your ears you will hear, and you will not understand; and seeing, you will look, and you will not see. For the heart of this people has become fat.”

Let us examine what is meant by the words: “For the heart of this people has become fat.” The heart of all who are occupied with the cares of the present life has become fat. The heart of those who dwell amid worldly affairs has become fat, as though they were being strangled by thorns. Therefore the heart grows fat and cannot receive the perceptions of a more refined spirit.

Let us flee such cares, then, so that our heart, made thin, may become acceptable to God. Let us flee earthly business. These are the things by which the heart grows fat. For this reason the word was subtle, as it is written in Exodus concerning the statement: “All those who are such because of the thinness of their heart will see God” (Exodus 24). For God is seen with such eyes.

Three things are stated: “For the heart of this people has become fat, and they have heard heavily with their ears, and they have closed their eyes.”

These words spoken in this passage can also be understood in another and clearer way. Many people think that, when they look upon created things and contemplate this world, they see them. And why do I say “people”? Behold, birds and four-footed animals see the sun and moon, and the whole heaven together with its chorus of stars; but they do not understand their rational principles. Only the righteous and holy, comprehending them through the reasoning of God’s wisdom, look upon them rightly.

Therefore David says in the eighth Psalm: “For I shall see your heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars that you established.” For what? Does the Prophet not now see the heaven and the moon? But if we consider what he says, “I shall see,” we shall be able to understand it.

[lacuna]

### 1143

#### [Continuation]

“They turned back to the iniquities.” Whose? He did not say simply “of the fathers,” but with an addition: “of their former fathers.”

We have said that these things are spoken of us and of those sinners who are among us. How, then, have the sinners who are among us turned back to the iniquities of their fathers, and of their former fathers?

We have two kinds of fathers, and one class consists of the worst fathers. Before we believed, the devil was our father, as the Gospel word shows when it says: “You were born from the father, Zabulus.” But when we believed, we became children of God.

If, therefore, after this we sin, we turn back to the iniquities of our fathers—not simply of our fathers, but of our former fathers. To demonstrate this, that we have two kinds of fathers, we also use the testimony of David in the forty-fourth Psalm, where he says: “Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.”

For he begins as though speaking of a father: “Hear, daughter.” Therefore our fathers are of two kinds. But he says: “Forget the house of your former father.” If, then, after forgetting the house of your former father, you turn back again to sins, you have fallen into the sin now described: “They turned back to the iniquities of their former fathers.”

We said earlier that Zabulus was our father before God became our Father—if indeed we do not now also have Zabulus as our father. We establish this from the Epistle of John as well, in which it is written: “Everyone who commits sin has been born from Zabulus.”

As often as we sin, so often are we born from Zabulus. Wretched is the one who is always begotten by Zabulus. Again, greatly blessed is the one who is always born from God. For I will not say merely once that the righteous person has been born from God; rather, through each individual work of virtue, the righteous person is always born from God.

To establish this more fully, let us also speak of the daily birth of our Savior, recognizing clearly in the righteous what has first taken place in the Lord. Our Savior is the radiance of glory. But radiance is not born once and then ceases to be born: whenever the light from which the radiance arises has risen, the radiance of glory also rises.

Our Savior is the Wisdom of God. Wisdom, moreover, is the radiance of eternal light. Thus the Savior is always being born, and for this reason he says: “Before all the hills he begets me”—not, as some read incorrectly, “he begot me.”

If the Lord is always born from the Father, then you also, having only the status of adoption written of you in his likeness, are always begotten by God through each individual understanding and through each individual work, and you become a child of God in Christ Jesus, to whom be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: The rest is lacking. This ninth homily on Isaiah is mutilated in all books, both printed and handwritten. Its final section was once rashly completed by adding the final portion of the likewise ninth homily on Jeremiah, beginning with the words, “They turned back to the iniquities of my fathers,” according to the genuine interpretation of Jerome. Although, as you see, this has no connection either with the subject of the Isaianic text or with the preceding exposition, since the error has persisted for a long time and the proper portion of that homily no longer survives, we append it here, following the copy of Genebrard, leaving only a certain interval for the instruction of the learned reader.]

## APPENDIX: A SHORT SUMMARY ON ISAIAH

[Note: This is the title found in the most ancient codex of the Verona Library, marked number 24 in black ink—there are others marked in red. See what we have said about the author of this little work in the preface to this volume.]

A SUMMARY OF A FEW CHAPTERS, NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME FROM THE VERONA MANUSCRIPT. (C, G, S)*

### 1145

There is one book of the Twelve Prophets. What physicians do in the case of bodily illnesses and wounds, the Prophets, as spiritual physicians, customarily do for wounds of the soul and for various sins.

The Twelve Prophets describe the one who is sick and unwilling to be healed because of his own fault as suffering even unto death; afterward they relate that he is healed after death through Christ, who is the true physician.

What the Twelve Prophets do in parts, and nevertheless briefly indicate themselves, preserving the same order, the Major Prophets customarily do at much greater length.

Ezra, whose name means “helper”; Zerubbabel, whose name means “this prince in Babylon”; and Jesus, whose name in our language means “Savior,” went before the Lord in figure, so that what the other Prophets were unable to cure through their medicinal books, these figures might cure and might lead the people back after the captivity.

### Chapter 1

**“The vision of Isaiah.”** It is called a vision because the Prophets know future things and, with spiritual eyes, behold the coming of the Savior. For this reason the Prophets were formerly called “Seers.”

**“The son of Amos.”** Most people think that Amos, who is the third of the Twelve Prophets, was Isaiah’s father, but they are seriously mistaken. Among the Hebrews the names are written with different letters: one with *sade*, the other with *sin*.

**“Which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.”** Isaiah is sent especially to the two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, and to Jerusalem—that is, to the metropolis, the city of the two tribes.

**“In the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.”** His prophecy extended throughout the reigns of all these kings who ruled in Judah. Even in the book itself we will find which vision was spoken under which king.

This is according to the historical interpretation. According to the tropological interpretation, whatever is said concerning Samaria and the ten tribes is said against the heresies; whatever is said against Jerusalem is said against the Church.

The first understanding of the tropology is this; there is also a second. The soul that has gone astray, fallen away from righteousness, and become subject to vices is called Ephraim and is called Samaria. For it is said to have built golden calves for itself, and it is referred to the ten tribes.

Whoever still perseveres in his purpose and has not broken out into open madness—denying what is said, yet nevertheless remaining subject to vices—is rebuked by the Prophet as Judah, in whom there is a true confession of God, and as Jerusalem, which seems indeed to possess peace, so that it may withdraw from hidden crimes and captivity may not also come upon it.

**“Hear, heavens, and perceive with your ears, earth, for the Lord has spoken.”** In the Song of Deuteronomy it is written that, at the time when Moses, like a cloud of the Lord, was speaking: “Attend, heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my speech be awaited like rain, and let my words descend like dew.” Under these witnesses—heaven and earth, that is, all creatures contained by heaven and earth—he had given the law of God.

For a part indicates the whole (*synecdoche*): what is held in the parts, because everything is included, as we have said.

**“Heaven and earth.”** Because the people transgressed the law of God, he again calls as witnesses the same ones under whom the law was given, so that, since the people scorned hearing, all creatures might hear.

### 1147

**“Hear, heavens, and perceive with your ears, earth.”** According to the historical interpretation, what he says means this: Since the human race has despised me, and among all the creatures and elements that I made this alone is the rebellious race that resists my will, therefore even the creatures thought irrational should hear, so that those considered rational may be more severely condemned.

**“Because the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and exalted children.”** He did not say, “I have begotten children,” as appears in the common interpretation. For it would have been superfluous to say “I have begotten children,” since every child is certainly begotten.

Therefore, by saying “children,” he indicated that they had already been begotten. Now he adds their increase, because everyone who begets also nourishes. Thus he says: I both begot and nourished them. Nor was I content merely to have nourished them, leaving them, as animals and birds do, to their own condition and labor; rather, after nourishing them when they were little, I also made them great and mature, so that, having given them life, I might now give them glory as well.

**“But they despised me.”** For such great benefits, contempt was returned.

**“The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.”** Irrational animals and cattle are compared with rational human beings, so that, when those animals have experienced benefits and even the sense of brutes does not fail to recognize the one whose benefits it experiences, the human race alone may be condemned for having despised God.

**“The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger.”** The ox, which labors, submits its neck to the yoke, and gives its master much more from its labor than it receives from its master, nevertheless understands its owner.

The donkey likewise understands its master’s manger. It recognizes the benefits and gladly sees the place where it is accustomed to receive food.

**“Israel has not known”—** “me” is understood. **“My people has not understood”—** “either owner or master” is understood. At the same time he considers how powerful the examples are.

Although the ox receives food from its master, and although the donkey recognizes its manger, they nevertheless provide their masters with much more by their labor than they receive from them.

[Note: In the manuscript, *accipit* was written incorrectly.]

But I, although I possess no benefits from human beings except that they themselves may be saved—although I have provided so much for them and received nothing—received only contempt in return for all my benefits.

Since, therefore, I have endured so much and have lost the Son whom I nourished and exalted, I do the only thing I can do: I will mourn the one who has been lost and is dead, whom I was unable to heal when he was sick.

**“Woe to the sinful nation, to the people weighed down with iniquity, to the wicked seed, to criminal children.”**

### 1148

They have changed their names:

**“Woe to the sinful nation”**—the nation that was once called my nation.

**“To the people weighed down”**—for they are burdened with heavy sins.

**“To the wicked seed”**—not my seed, according to what is said elsewhere: “And in your seed all the nations shall be blessed.”

**“To criminal children”**—no longer my children. For as soon as we begin to sin, together with the condition of sin we also lose the name of children.

**“They have abandoned the Lord,”** as though he were following them along every path. The several expressions have this meaning: Even though they had done everything and committed every crime, I did not abandon them; rather, I waited for them to return to me at some time. But they, while I stood there and stretched out my hands for their repentance, abandoned me.

And it is not enough for them that they abandoned me—observe the intensification of their sins—but they also blasphemed the Holy One of Israel; they have turned away backward. That is, they began to be what they had been before, before they were called by my name.

**“Over what shall I strike you further, as you add transgression?”** Punishment is inflicted by the Lord, as by a true physician, so that health may follow cauterization and biting powder.

Therefore what he says means this: I applied many plasters; I wanted to heal you with various medicines. I find no kind of remedy, since your illness grows daily. You are not only, he says, failing to be healed of your former vices; while my treatment brings your former sins back to mind, you add new wounds.

**“Over what shall I strike you further?”** These are the words of one who seems to be doubtful; that is: In what way shall I heal you? Since the Lord strikes in order to correct and chastises in order to heal, he says: “Over what shall I strike?”—that is, what plaster shall I apply to you?—“as you add transgression,” joining new sins to old ones every day.

The statement made a little earlier—that the Prophets are spiritual physicians and, as it were, treat the entire class of diseases—can now be demonstrated by a very clear example. See what Scripture says:

**“Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in it; wound, bruise, and swelling sore.”**

[Note: Read *cernatur* (“may be seen”); M. Scipio Maffei had most correctly noted this in the margin of his copy.]

**“Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving.”** I frequently urge us to consider each individual word in the Prophets. For this reason the usefulness of the historical interpretation is not apparent to the unlearned: they do not understand what is said.

**“Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving.”** If someone becomes ill or is oppressed by a very difficult bodily disease, but has a cheerful soul, the illness of the body is sustained by the joy of the spirit.

### 1149

Again, if someone has grief, heartache, and various tribulations, but a strong body, the health of the body supports the weakness of the soul. But when both the body is sick and the soul is in pain, no remedies can provide help.

This, therefore, is what is meant by the medicine: **“Every head is sick, and every heart is grieving.”** At the same time, consider that he compares the ruling part of the soul—that is, the heart [Greek: *hēgemonikon*]—with the ruling part of the body, namely, the head.

All the senses are in the head. Even if the other limbs are cut off, the soul can continue to live; but when the head is cut off, all life is taken away. He did not say “every head is amputated,” for it would have been superfluous, if he had said that, to describe the other limbs and the diseases of the remaining members. Therefore he says “sick,” so that the description of the other members may also have its place.

**“From the sole of the foot to the crown there is no health in it.”** All Israel is sick; not even one holy man can be found, as though in a body some member might appear to be healthy.

For if there were something healthy in the whole body, the other parts too would seem to draw healing from the health of one part.

**“Wound, bruise, and swelling sore.”** The wound is recent sins; the bruise is ancient crimes; the swelling sore is an unhealed and old offense, as though giving birth to pus.

**“It has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.”** This does not mean that God did not do these things. He did everything, and the Prophets would have been sent without purpose if they had not done these things. But because health did not follow, the things that were done appear, in a certain sense, not to have been done.

According to the tropological interpretation:

**“Hear, heavens, and perceive with your ears, earth”**—that is, both you who seem holy and you who are sinners, hear together.

**“I have nourished and exalted children, but they despised me.”** I, God, deigned to have human beings as children. I nourished them and made them great, so that I might call servants friends. But they despised me through their sins, even though they had experienced none of my harshness.

He wisely said “they despised.” No one despises except one whose goodness is excessive. Thus, interpreting my clemency and gentleness as weakness, they despised the one whom they ought to have feared and loved.

He then sets forth the example mentioned above concerning the ox and the donkey. We interpret all this in the Scriptures concerning those who, through their sins, have withdrawn from the Lord: they are much worse than brute animals.

For although animals do not have such great benefits from their masters and owners, they nevertheless do not withdraw from their master. When the ox has been beaten, or the donkey has become angry with its master, it does not dwell on the blows but remembers only the benefits. When it sees its master, it plays with him and expresses the joy of its mind through whatever gestures it can.

Israel, however—that is, the soul that sees God—did not wish to know me, and so forth.

[Note: Let this suffice abundantly to distinguish the compiler’s method. It is not worth the effort to pursue the rest.]
